# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtras)
## Fascicle 1

Translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty by the Tripiṭaka master Gautama Sanghadeva from Kubhā.

---

## First Section: The Chapter on Sevens

---

### 1. Sūtra on Good Dharmas

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu accomplishes seven dharmas, he will obtain joy and delight, and this serves as the basis for the ending of the outflows. What are the seven? It means a bhikṣu knows the Dharma, knows the meaning, knows the time, knows moderation, knows himself, knows the assembly, and knows the superiority or inferiority of persons.

"How does a bhikṣu know the Dharma? A bhikṣu knows the Dharma means he knows the sūtras, the verses, the explanations, the verse narratives, the sūtras spoken in response to questions, that which was spoken, the birth stories, the accounts of unprecedented things, and the expanded discourses. If a bhikṣu does not know the Dharma, that is, does not know the sūtras, the verses, the explanations, the verse narratives, the sūtras spoken in response to questions, that which was spoken, the birth stories, the accounts of unprecedented things, and the expanded discourses, then he is not called one who knows the Dharma. If a bhikṣu indeed knows the Dharma, that is, knows the sūtras, the verses, the explanations, the verse narratives, the sūtras spoken in response to questions, that which was spoken, the birth stories, the accounts of unprecedented things, and the expanded discourses, then he is called one who knows the Dharma. This is how a bhikṣu knows the Dharma.

"How does a bhikṣu know the meaning? A bhikṣu knows the meaning of this statement or that statement, knowing 'this has such and such a meaning' and 'that has such and such a meaning.' If a bhikṣu does not know the meaning, that is, does not know the meaning of this statement or that statement, does not know 'this has such and such a meaning' or 'that has such and such a meaning,' then he is not called one who knows the meaning. If a bhikṣu indeed knows the meaning, that is, knows the meaning of this statement or that statement, knowing 'this has such and such a meaning' and 'that has such and such a meaning,' then he is called one who knows the meaning. This is how a bhikṣu knows the meaning.

"How does a bhikṣu know the time? A bhikṣu knows the time, knowing 'this is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for the practice of yoga, this is the time for sitting in quiet meditation.' If a bhikṣu does not know the time, that is, does not know 'this is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for the practice of yoga, this is the time for sitting in quiet meditation,' then he is not called one who knows the time. If a bhikṣu indeed knows the time, that is, knows 'this is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning, this is the time for the practice of yoga, this is the time for sitting in quiet meditation,' then he is called one who knows the time. This is how a bhikṣu knows the time.

"How does a bhikṣu know moderation? A bhikṣu knows moderation in eating, in drinking, in sleeping and waking, and in sitting and walking. If a bhikṣu does not know moderation, that is, does not know moderation in eating, in drinking, in sleeping and waking, and in sitting and walking, then he is not called one who knows moderation. If a bhikṣu indeed knows moderation, that is, knows moderation in eating, in drinking, in sleeping and waking, and in sitting and walking, then he is called one who knows moderation. This is how a bhikṣu knows moderation.

"How does a bhikṣu know himself? A bhikṣu knows himself, knowing his own degree of faith, of morality, of learning, of generosity, of wisdom, and of eloquence. If a bhikṣu does not know himself, that is, does not know his own degree of faith, of morality, of learning, of generosity, of wisdom, and of eloquence, then he is not called one who knows himself. If a bhikṣu indeed knows himself, that is, knows his own degree of faith, of morality, of learning, of generosity, of wisdom, and of eloquence, then he is called one who knows himself. This is how a bhikṣu knows himself.

"How does a bhikṣu know the assembly? A bhikṣu knows the assembly, knowing 'this is an assembly of kṣatriyas, this is an assembly of brahmins, this is an assembly of householders, this is an assembly of śramaṇas. In that assembly, I should approach in this manner, should stand in this manner, should act in this manner, should sit in this manner, should speak in this manner, and should remain silent in this manner.' If a bhikṣu does not know the assembly, that is, does not know 'this is an assembly of kṣatriyas, this is an assembly of brahmins, this is an assembly of householders, this is an assembly of śramaṇas; in that assembly, I should approach in this manner, should stand in this manner, should act in this manner, should sit in this manner, should speak in this manner, and should remain silent in this manner,' then he is not called one who knows the assembly. If a bhikṣu indeed knows the assembly, that is, knows 'this is an assembly of kṣatriyas, this is an assembly of brahmins, this is an assembly of householders, this is an assembly of śramaṇas; in that assembly, I should approach in this manner, should stand in this manner, should act in this manner, should sit in this manner, should speak in this manner, and should remain silent in this manner,' then he is called one who knows the assembly. This is how a bhikṣu knows the assembly.

"How does a bhikṣu know the superiority or inferiority of persons? A bhikṣu knows that there are two kinds of persons. One kind of person desires to see noble ones, and the other kind of person does not desire to see noble ones. The person who does not desire to see noble ones is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who desires to see noble ones is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who desire to see noble ones, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person desires to hear the True Dharma, and the other kind does not desire to hear the True Dharma. The person who does not desire to hear the True Dharma is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who desires to hear the True Dharma is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who desire to hear the True Dharma, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person listens with attentive ears, and the other kind does not listen with attentive ears. The person who does not listen with attentive ears is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who listens with attentive ears is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who listen with attentive ears, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person, having heard, retains the Dharma, and the other kind, having heard, does not retain the Dharma. The person who, having heard, does not retain the Dharma is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who, having heard, retains the Dharma is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who, having heard, retain the Dharma, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person contemplates the meaning of the retained Dharma, and the other kind does not contemplate the meaning of the retained Dharma. The person who does not contemplate the meaning of the retained Dharma is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who contemplates the meaning of the retained Dharma is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who contemplate the meaning of the retained Dharma, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person, knowing the Dharma and knowing the meaning, practices in accordance with the Dharma, practicing the Dharma in conformity, proceeding in conformity and following along, and acting according to the Dharma. The other kind of person, though knowing the Dharma and knowing the meaning, does not practice in accordance with the Dharma, does not practice the Dharma in conformity, does not proceed in conformity and follow along, and does not act according to the Dharma. The person who does not practice in accordance with the Dharma, does not practice the Dharma in conformity, does not proceed in conformity and follow along, and does not act according to the Dharma is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who practices in accordance with the Dharma, practices the Dharma in conformity, proceeds in conformity and follows along, and acts according to the Dharma is, because of this matter, to be praised. Among those who practice in accordance with the Dharma, practice the Dharma in conformity, proceed in conformity and follow along, and act according to the Dharma, there are again two kinds of persons. One kind of person benefits himself, benefits others, benefits many people, has compassion for the world, and seeks benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans. The other kind of person does not benefit himself, does not benefit others, does not benefit many people, does not have compassion for the world, and does not seek benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans. The person who does not benefit himself, does not benefit others, does not benefit many people, does not have compassion for the world, and does not seek benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans is, because of this matter, to be criticized and reproached. The person who benefits himself, benefits others, benefits many people, has compassion for the world, and seeks benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans is, because of this matter, to be praised.

"In this way, a bhikṣu knows the superiority or inferiority of persons: of these two kinds of persons, the one is to be criticized and reproached, and the other is to be praised. Among those to be criticized and those to be praised, the one to be praised is the foremost, the supreme, the most excellent, the highest. This is how a bhikṣu knows the superiority or inferiority of persons.

"If a bhikṣu accomplishes these seven dharmas, he will obtain joy and delight, and this serves as the basis for the ending of the outflows."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 2. Sūtra on the Chariots

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Friends, King Pasenadi of Kosala, while at Śrāvastī and wishing to go to Sāketa, had seven relay chariots placed between Śrāvastī and Sāketa. He left through the gates of Śrāvastī, mounted the first relay chariot, and driving the first relay chariot, arrived at the second relay chariot. He then abandoned the first relay chariot and mounted the second relay chariot. Driving the second relay chariot, he arrived at the third relay chariot. He then abandoned the second relay chariot and mounted the third relay chariot. Driving the third relay chariot, he arrived at the fourth relay chariot. He then abandoned the third relay chariot and mounted the fourth relay chariot. Driving the fourth relay chariot, he arrived at the fifth relay chariot. He then abandoned the fourth relay chariot and mounted the fifth relay chariot. Driving the fifth relay chariot, he arrived at the sixth relay chariot. He then abandoned the fifth relay chariot and mounted the sixth relay chariot. Driving the sixth relay chariot, he arrived at the seventh relay chariot. He then abandoned the sixth relay chariot and mounted the seventh relay chariot. Driving the seventh relay chariot, he arrived at the gates of Sāketa.

"When he had arrived, his relatives and acquaintances, friends and close ones asked King Pasenadi of Kosala: 'Great King, did you come from Śrāvastī to Sāketa on this chariot?' How should King Pasenadi of Kosala rightly answer? How should he rightly explain?"

The bhikṣus answered: "He should answer thus: 'I was at Śrāvastī and wished to come to Sāketa. I had seven relay chariots placed between Śrāvastī and Sāketa. I left through the gates of Śrāvastī, mounted the first relay chariot, and driving the first relay chariot, arrived at the second relay chariot. I then abandoned the first relay chariot and mounted the second relay chariot. Driving the second relay chariot, I arrived at the third relay chariot. I then abandoned the second relay chariot and mounted the third relay chariot. Driving the third relay chariot, I arrived at the fourth relay chariot. I then abandoned the third relay chariot and mounted the fourth relay chariot. Driving the fourth relay chariot, I arrived at the fifth relay chariot. I then abandoned the fourth relay chariot and mounted the fifth relay chariot. Driving the fifth relay chariot, I arrived at the sixth relay chariot. I then abandoned the fifth relay chariot and mounted the sixth relay chariot. Driving the sixth relay chariot, I arrived at the seventh relay chariot. I then abandoned the sixth relay chariot and mounted the seventh relay chariot. Driving the seventh relay chariot, I arrived at the gates of Sāketa.' Venerable Śāriputra, King Pasenadi of Kosala should rightly answer in this way and rightly explain in this way."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "In the same way, friends, the purification of morality is for the sake of the purification of mind. The purification of mind is for the sake of the purification of view. The purification of view is for the sake of the purification by overcoming doubt. The purification by overcoming doubt is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is and what is not the path. The purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is and what is not the path is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision regarding the practice of the path. The purification of knowledge and vision regarding the practice of the path is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision. The purification of knowledge and vision is for the sake of the attainment of nirvāṇa.

"It is for the sake of the attainment of nirvāṇa that one cultivates the holy life under the World-Honored One."

When the Venerable Śāriputra had finished speaking, one bhikṣu arose from his seat and went to the World-Honored One. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. He then told the World-Honored One all of what the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken. The World-Honored One heard this and praised him: "Good, good! Śāriputra speaks as the meaning truly is. Why? Because the purification of morality is for the sake of the purification of mind. The purification of mind is for the sake of the purification of view. The purification of view is for the sake of the purification by overcoming doubt. The purification by overcoming doubt is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is and what is not the path. The purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is and what is not the path is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision regarding the practice of the path. The purification of knowledge and vision regarding the practice of the path is for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision. The purification of knowledge and vision is for the sake of the attainment of nirvāṇa. It is for the sake of the attainment of nirvāṇa that one cultivates the holy life under me."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 3. Sūtra on the City

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will now speak about the city simile. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "It is like a king's border city, which is well established with seven things and easily obtains the four kinds of food without difficulty or hardship. Therefore, that king's border city cannot be overcome by external enemies and adversaries. What are the seven things with which it is well established? It is like a king's border city with the foundation deeply established, being exceedingly deep and firm, impossible to destroy. This is the first thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city with a moat surrounding it, being exceedingly wide and deep. This is the second thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city with roads encircling it, being exceedingly wide and straight. This is the third thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city in which many soldiers are gathered, that is, elephant soldiers, horse soldiers, chariot soldiers, and foot soldiers. This is the fourth thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city in which weapons are prepared, that is, bows, crossbows, spears, and halberds. This is the fifth thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city which has a general, a brave and wise man of great strategy and resourcefulness, who is clever and prudent, one who shuts out those who should be shut out and admits those who should be admitted. This is the sixth thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city with walls built high and thick, plastered with mud and painted, exceedingly well finished. This is the seventh thing with which the king's border city is well established.

"What are the four kinds of food that it easily obtains without difficulty or hardship? It is like a king's border city in which there is stored much hay, grass, firewood, and timber. This is the first kind of food that it easily obtains.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city in which there is much well-cultivated rice and grain stored in its fields and granaries. This is the second kind of food that it easily obtains.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city in which there are stored many kinds of beans and pulses. This is the third kind of food that it easily obtains.

"Furthermore, it is like a king's border city in which there is stored much ghee, oil, honey, sugarcane juice, fish, salt, dried meat, and similar provisions. This is the fourth kind of food that it easily obtains.

"A king's border city that is well established with these seven things and that easily obtains these four kinds of food without difficulty or hardship cannot be overcome by external enemies and adversaries.

"In the same way, if a noble disciple also accomplishes seven good dharmas and easily obtains the four meditations of the increased mind without difficulty or hardship, then that noble disciple cannot be overcome by the evil demon.

"What are the seven good dharmas that a noble disciple accomplishes? It is like a king's border city with the foundation deeply established, being exceedingly deep and firm, impossible to destroy. In the same way, a noble disciple has faith and deeply plants roots of faith in the Tathāgata, which are firm, impossible to pull out, and cannot be destroyed by any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. This is the first good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city with a moat surrounding it, being exceedingly wide and deep. In the same way, a noble disciple has a sense of shame, feeling shame and disgust at evil, unwholesome actions, feeling shame and disgust at evil, defiled, and unwholesome dharmas. This is the second good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city with roads encircling it, being exceedingly wide and straight. In the same way, a noble disciple has a sense of moral dread, feeling dread and revulsion at evil, unwholesome actions, feeling dread and revulsion at evil, defiled, and unwholesome dharmas. This is the third good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city in which many soldiers are gathered. In the same way, a noble disciple has much learning, retains what he has learned, and accumulates learning. Those dharmas that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, that are complete in meaning and phrasing, that are pure and proclaim the perfectly fulfilled and purified holy life, such dharmas he has abundantly learned, retained in memory, recited and familiarized himself with, mentally contemplated, and penetrated with right view. This is the fourth good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city in which weapons are prepared. In the same way, a noble disciple is constantly diligent in effort, eliminating unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas. He constantly exerts himself with fortitude and firm strength, and does not abandon the task of cultivating wholesome dharmas. This is the fifth good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city which has a general, a brave and wise man. In the same way, a noble disciple possesses mindfulness. The mindfulness he guards is foremost, and he can recall things practiced and spoken long ago. This is the sixth good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"It is like a king's border city with walls built high and thick. In the same way, a noble disciple possesses wisdom. He has the wisdom of arising and ceasing, the noble wisdom that penetrates and correctly leads to the complete ending of suffering. This is the seventh good dharma that a noble disciple accomplishes.

"What are the four meditations of the increased mind that a noble disciple easily obtains without difficulty or hardship? It is like a king's border city in which there is stored much hay, grass, firewood, and timber. In the same way, a noble disciple, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial application and sustained application, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first meditation. This is the first meditation of the increased mind.

"It is like a king's border city in which there is much well-cultivated rice and grain stored. In the same way, a noble disciple, with the stilling of initial application and sustained application, with inner purity and mental unification, without initial application, without sustained application, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and abides in the second meditation. This is the second meditation of the increased mind.

"It is like a king's border city in which there are stored many kinds of beans and pulses. In the same way, a noble disciple, with the fading away of joy, dwelling in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'With equanimity and mindfulness, one dwells in happiness,' enters and abides in the third meditation. This is the third meditation of the increased mind.

"It is like a king's border city in which there is stored much ghee, oil, honey, sugarcane juice, fish, salt, dried meat, and similar provisions. In the same way, a noble disciple, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, enters and abides in the fourth meditation. This is the fourth meditation of the increased mind.

"If a noble disciple accomplishes these seven good dharmas and easily obtains these four meditations of the increased mind without difficulty or hardship, then that noble disciple cannot be overcome by the evil demon."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 4. Sūtra on the Water Simile

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will now speak about the seven kinds of persons who are like those in water. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the seven kinds of persons who are like those in water? There is a person who is always submerged. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, sinks again. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, remains standing. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, remains standing and looks around. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, goes forward. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, reaches a shallow place to stand. There is a person who, having risen to the surface, reaches the far shore, stands on dry ground, is a brahmin, and stands on the bank.

"How is a person always submerged? There is a person who is entirely covered by unwholesome, dark dharmas. This person is called 'always submerged.' It is like a person in the water who is always submerged. I say this person is likewise. This is the first kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, sinks again? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. But his faith does not increase, his morality does not increase, his learning does not increase, his generosity does not increase, and his wisdom does not increase. His faith only decreases, his morality only decreases, his learning only decreases, his generosity only decreases, and his wisdom only decreases. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, sinks again.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, sinks again. I say this person is likewise. This is the second kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, remains standing? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. His faith does not decrease and does not increase, his morality does not decrease and does not increase, his learning does not decrease and does not increase, his generosity does not decrease and does not increase, and his wisdom does not decrease and does not increase. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, remains standing.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, remains standing. I say this person is likewise. This is the third kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, remains standing and looks around? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. With the destruction of the three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into evil states, and is certain to attain complete enlightenment, traversing at most seven existences among gods and humans before making an end of suffering. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, remains standing and looks around.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, remains standing and looks around. I say this person is likewise. This is the fourth kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, goes forward? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. With the destruction of the three fetters, and with the thinning of desire, anger, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner, returning once more to this world before making an end of suffering. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, goes forward.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, goes forward. I say this person is likewise. This is the fifth kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, reaches a shallow place to stand? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. With the destruction of the five lower fetters, he is born in that realm and there attains parinirvāṇa, attaining the dharma of non-return, not returning to this world. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, reaches a shallow place to stand.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, reaches a shallow place to stand. I say this person is likewise. This is the sixth kind of person in the water.

"How is a person one who, having risen to the surface, reaches the far shore, stands on dry ground, is a brahmin, and stands on the bank? There is a person who rises to the surface through faith. He has faith that is good, faith in wholesome dharmas, has a sense of shame, has a sense of moral dread, has energy, and has wisdom. His outflows are ended, his mind is liberated, and his wisdom is liberated. In the present life he himself knows and realizes, abides in and personally witnesses: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this,' and he knows it as it really is. This person is called 'having risen to the surface, reaches the far shore, stands on dry ground, is a brahmin, and stands on the bank.' It is like a person in the water who, having risen to the surface, reaches the far shore, stands on dry ground, is a brahmin, and stands on the bank. I say this person is likewise. This is the seventh kind of person in the water.

"These are the seven kinds of persons who are like those in water."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 5. Sūtra on the Wood Simile

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu, in his mind, always delights in and takes pleasure in crowds, finds enjoyment in crowds, always delights in and takes pleasure in gatherings, finds enjoyment in gatherings, always delights in and takes pleasure in worldly company, finds enjoyment in worldly company, then it is impossible for him to find delight in being alone, in the tranquil liberation of the mind, at the right time and in the right way. Why? Because that bhikṣu's mind always delights in and takes pleasure in crowds, finds enjoyment in crowds, always delights in and takes pleasure in gatherings, finds enjoyment in gatherings, always delights in and takes pleasure in worldly company, and finds enjoyment in worldly company. Therefore, it is impossible for him to find delight in being alone, in the tranquil liberation of the mind, at the right time and in the right way.

"If a bhikṣu, in his mind, does not delight in or take pleasure in crowds, does not find enjoyment in crowds, does not delight in or take pleasure in gatherings, does not find enjoyment in gatherings, does not delight in or take pleasure in worldly company, and does not find enjoyment in worldly company, then it is possible that he will always delight in being alone, in the tranquil liberation of the mind, at the right time and in the right way. Why? Because that bhikṣu's mind does not delight in or take pleasure in crowds, does not find enjoyment in crowds, does not delight in or take pleasure in gatherings, does not find enjoyment in gatherings, does not delight in or take pleasure in worldly company, and does not find enjoyment in worldly company. Therefore, it is possible that he will always delight in being alone, in the tranquil liberation of the mind, at the right time and in the right way.

"Bhikṣus, I do not see even a single form that is as alluring, as intoxicating, as binding, as captivating, as obstructing, and as much an impediment to the attainment of unsurpassed security from bondage as the form of a woman. Sentient beings are infatuated with the form of a woman, bound by it, captivated by it, and blinded by it. For a long time they are subject to birth and death, flowing in the cycle of existence. Bhikṣus, the form of a woman is able to captivate, bind, infatuate, and blind the minds of sentient beings.

"Bhikṣus, I do not see even a single sound, a single smell, a single taste, or a single touch that is as alluring, as intoxicating, as binding, as captivating, as obstructing, and as much an impediment to the attainment of unsurpassed security from bondage as the touch of a woman. Sentient beings are infatuated with the touch of a woman, bound by it, captivated by it, and blinded by it. For a long time they are subject to birth and death, flowing in the cycle of existence. Bhikṣus, the touch of a woman is able to captivate, bind, infatuate, and blind the minds of sentient beings."

The World-Honored One then spoke this verse:

"If one's mind is attracted to form,
Or bound and attached to sound,
Or takes delight in taste and smell,
And is absorbed in the sensation of touch,
This person cannot understand
The dharmas of the upper realm.

"If one's mind is attracted to form,
Or bound and attached to sound,
Or takes delight in taste and smell,
And is absorbed in the sensation of touch,
Such a person is said to be
Flowing in the stream of Māra.

"If one's mind is unattracted to form,
Unbound and unattached to sound,
Without delight in taste and smell,
And unabsorbed in the sensation of touch,
This person can understand
The dharmas of the upper realm.

"If one's mind is unattracted to form,
Unbound and unattached to sound,
Without delight in taste and smell,
And unabsorbed in the sensation of touch,
Such a person is said to be
Having crossed Māra's stream."

The World-Honored One said: "I will now speak a simile for you. The wise understand the meaning through a simile.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a piece of wood that has fallen into a river. If that piece of wood does not stay on this bank, does not stay on the other bank, does not sink in the middle, does not get stranded on high ground, does not get caught by humans, does not get caught by non-humans, does not get caught in a whirlpool, and does not rot internally, then, bhikṣus, that piece of wood will drift, flow, and tend toward the ocean. Why? Because the current of the river drifts, flows, and tends toward the ocean.

"Bhikṣus, you are also like this. If you do not stay on this bank, do not stay on the other bank, do not sink in the middle, do not get stranded on high ground, are not caught by humans, are not caught by non-humans, are not caught in a whirlpool, and do not rot internally, then, bhikṣus, you will drift, flow, and tend toward nirvāṇa. Why? Because right view drifts, flows, and tends toward nirvāṇa."

Then a bhikṣu arose from his seat, arranged his robes to bare one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, clasped his palms toward the Buddha, and asked: "World-Honored One, what is 'this bank'? What is 'the other bank'? What is 'sinking in the middle'? What is 'getting stranded on high ground'? What is 'being caught by humans'? What is 'being caught by non-humans'? What is 'being caught in a whirlpool'? What is 'rotting internally'?"

The World-Honored One said: "'This bank' means the six internal sense bases. 'The other bank' means the six external sense bases. 'Sinking in the middle' means the delight of desire and craving. 'Getting stranded on high ground' means conceit and arrogance. 'Being caught by humans' means when a bhikṣu associates with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows, happy when they are happy, and suffering when they suffer; when tasks arise for them, he personally takes them on and manages them. This is called 'being caught by humans.' 'Being caught by non-humans' means a bhikṣu cultivates the holy life aspiring for a certain heaven, thinking 'By this morality, by this practice, by this austerity, or by this holy life, I shall be reborn as such-and-such a god.' This is called 'being caught by non-humans.' 'Being caught in a whirlpool' means the five desires for sensual pleasure. 'Rotting internally' means a bhikṣu who is immoral, of evil nature, and impure, who engages in filthy actions, not truly being a śramaṇa yet claiming to be a śramaṇa, not truly cultivating the holy life yet claiming to cultivate the holy life, internally rotten, full of defilements and impurities, like a dung heap. This is called 'rotting internally.'

"A bhikṣu Nanda, who is a cowherd from the Kosala region, was present in the assembly and said to the World-Honored One: 'World-Honored One, I do not stay on this bank, do not stay on the other bank, do not sink in the middle, do not get stranded on high ground, am not caught by humans, am not caught by non-humans, am not caught in a whirlpool, and do not rot internally. World-Honored One, I beg to be allowed to receive the going forth under the World-Honored One, to receive the full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣu.'

"The World-Honored One said: 'You, Nanda, go return the cattle to their owner.'

"Nanda the cowherd said: 'World-Honored One, these cattle, being attached to their calves, will return by themselves.'

"The World-Honored One said: 'You, Nanda, go return the cattle to their owner.'

"Then Nanda the cowherd rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and went to return the cattle to their owner. Having returned the cattle, he came back and said to the World-Honored One: 'World-Honored One, the cattle have been returned to their owner. World-Honored One, I now beg to be allowed to receive the going forth under the World-Honored One, to receive the full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣu.'

"Then, in the presence of the World-Honored One, Nanda the cowherd received the going forth, received the full ordination, and attained the status of a bhikṣu.

"The World-Honored One, after ordaining him, then taught him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, benefiting, and delighting him. After the World-Honored One had encouraged, inspired, benefited, and delighted him with the Dharma teaching, the Venerable Nanda arose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.

"The Venerable Nanda, having received the World-Honored One's teaching of the Dharma, went to live alone in seclusion, in a quiet place. He cultivated with diligence and exertion, not being negligent. Living alone in seclusion, in a quiet place, cultivating with diligence and exertion, not being negligent, he accomplished that for the sake of which sons of good family rightly leave the household life for homelessness, wishing to learn the path. In the present life he himself knew and realized, abided in and personally witnessed the unsurpassed completion of the holy life: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this,' and he knew it as it really was.

"The Venerable Nanda thus knew the Dharma, and became one among the arhats."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 6. Sūtra on Good Persons' Going Forth

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "A good person's going forth benefits many people, brings comfort and ease to many people, and is out of compassion for the world, seeking benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans.

"How does a good person's going forth benefit many people, bring comfort and ease to many people, and how is it out of compassion for the world, seeking benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans?

"When the Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arhat, a Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed One, a Trainer of Those Who Are To Be Tamed, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, he teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, displaying the perfectly fulfilled and purified holy life. When a householder or householder's son hears it, he arouses faith. Having aroused faith, he reflects: 'The household life is constricted and dusty; the going forth into homelessness is open and unobstructed. I now live in a household, bound by fetters, unable to purely and fully cultivate the holy life. I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, with sincere faith leave the household life for homelessness, and learn the path.' He later abandons a small or large fortune, leaves a small or large circle of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with sincere faith leaves the household life for homelessness and learns the path.

"Having gone forth, he guards himself with the discipline of the Prātimokṣa, endowed with proper deportment and conduct. He regards minor offenses with fear and dread, upholds and trains in the training rules, and accomplishes pure bodily and verbal actions, with a pure livelihood, perfected in moral conduct, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, constantly mindful and clearly comprehending, content and satisfied.

"How is a bhikṣu perfected in moral conduct? A bhikṣu abandons killing and abstains from killing. He puts aside the knife and the club, has a sense of shame and loving-kindness, is compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings, even insects and worms. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from killing. This is how a bhikṣu is accomplished in moral conduct.

"He abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, delights in what is given. He is always generous and gives without stinginess. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from taking what is not given.

"He abandons unchastity and cultivates chastity. He practices the conduct of purity and celibacy, abandoning the vulgar dharma of sexual intercourse. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from unchastity.

"He abandons false speech and abstains from false speech. He speaks truth and delights in truth. He is steadfast and reliable, not deceiving the world. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from false speech.

"He abandons divisive speech and abstains from divisive speech. He does not carry speech from one side to the other to cause division among them. He reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united. He delights in harmony, loves harmony, and enjoys harmony. He speaks words that create harmony. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from divisive speech.

"He abandons harsh speech and abstains from harsh speech. If words are coarse, harsh, scolding, anger-provoking, displeasing to many, loved by none, causing others suffering, words that create quarrels; he abandons such words. If words are gentle, soft, pleasant to hear, reaching the heart, courteous, loved and delighted in by many, pleasing to many, comforting to many; he speaks such words. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from harsh speech.

"He abandons idle chatter and abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks about the Dharma, speaks about the discipline, speaks words of value. He speaks at the appropriate time, with reason, with measure, and with benefit. He purifies his mind regarding the abstaining from idle chatter.

"He abandons the destruction of seeds and plants. He eats one meal a day, not eating at night, eating at the proper time. He abandons watching dancing, singing, and performances. He abandons adorning himself with garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics. He abandons the use of high and broad beds. He abandons accepting gold, silver, and jewels. He abandons accepting raw grain. He abandons accepting raw meat. He abandons accepting women and girls. He abandons accepting male and female servants. He abandons accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. He abandons accepting chickens and pigs. He abandons accepting fields, houses, and orchards. He abandons acting as a go-between or agent in matters of trade. He abandons buying and selling in the market. He abandons the use of deceptive weights and measures. He abandons the crooked ways of accepting bribes, deception, and fraud. He abandons injuring, killing, binding, ambushing, robbing, and extorting.

"He is content with robes sufficient to cover his body and with food sufficient to sustain himself. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. It is like a bird with wings; wherever it flies, it carries only its wings. A bhikṣu is likewise. He is content with robes sufficient to cover his body and with food sufficient to sustain himself. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him.

"When the bhikṣu has accomplished this noble aggregate of morality, he experiences within himself the happiness of being without fault.

"He guards the doors of the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, he does not grasp at its signs, and does not grasp at its secondary features. If his faculty of sight were left unguarded, covetousness, grief, and evil, unwholesome dharmas would flow into him. Therefore he practices restraint, guarding the faculty of sight and achieving its restraint. When the ear hears a sound, when the nose smells an odor, when the tongue tastes a flavor, when the body contacts a tangible, when the mind cognizes a mental object, he does not grasp at its signs, and does not grasp at its secondary features. If his mental faculty were left unguarded, covetousness, grief, and evil, unwholesome dharmas would flow into him. Therefore he practices restraint, guarding the mental faculty and achieving its restraint. When the bhikṣu has accomplished this noble guarding of the sense faculties, he experiences within himself the happiness of being undefiled.

"He is constantly mindful and clearly comprehending. When going forward, when returning, he acts with good awareness. When looking, when gazing, he acts with good awareness. When bending, when stretching, he acts with good awareness. When donning his saṅghāṭī robe, taking his outer robe, or carrying his bowl, he acts with good awareness. When eating, when drinking, he acts with good awareness. When walking, when standing, when sitting, when sleeping, when waking, when speaking, when being silent, he acts with good awareness.

"When a bhikṣu has accomplished this noble aggregate of morality, has accomplished this noble guarding of the sense faculties, and has accomplished this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he goes to dwell in a secluded place, in a forest, under a tree, in an empty room, by a mountain stream, in a rocky cave, on a bed of grass, in the wilderness, or in the open air, among haystacks. He goes to the forest, sits under a tree, or goes to an empty room. He spreads his sitting mat, crosses his legs, straightens his body, and establishes mindfulness before him.

"He abandons covetousness and dwells with a mind free from covetousness. He purifies his mind of covetousness. He abandons ill will and anger, and dwells with a mind free from ill will. He has compassion and kindness toward all sentient beings and living things, and purifies his mind of ill will and anger. He abandons sloth and torpor, and dwells free from sloth and torpor. He perceives light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. He abandons restlessness and worry, and dwells without restlessness, with an inwardly tranquil mind, and purifies his mind of restlessness and worry. He abandons doubt and crosses beyond doubt. He is not perplexed about wholesome dharmas, and purifies his mind of doubt.

"He abandons these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom. Secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial application and sustained application, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters and abides in the first meditation.

"With the stilling of initial application and sustained application, with inner purity and mental unification, without initial application, without sustained application, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters and abides in the second meditation.

"With the fading away of joy, dwelling in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'With equanimity and mindfulness, one dwells in happiness,' he enters and abides in the third meditation.

"With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he enters and abides in the fourth meditation.

"With his mind concentrated, purified, cleansed, free from defilements, free from secondary defilements, supple, capable of acting, settled, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He recollects the many kinds of past lives: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, the formations of many eons of world-contraction, the formations of many eons of world-expansion, the formations of many eons of both world-contraction and world-expansion. 'There I had such a name, was of such a clan, of such a caste, ate such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, had such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I had such a name, was of such a clan, of such a caste, ate such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, had such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects the many kinds of past lives with their features and details.

"With his mind concentrated, purified, cleansed, free from defilements, free from secondary defilements, supple, capable of acting, settled, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the divine eye. With the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees sentient beings dying and being reborn, of good and bad appearance, in good and bad states, in superior or inferior destinies, according to the actions they have performed. He knows as it really is: 'These sentient beings have accomplished unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, unwholesome mental conduct, have disparaged noble ones, held wrong views, and have accomplished actions based on wrong views. At the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the evil destinies, in hell. And these sentient beings have accomplished wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, wholesome mental conduct, have not disparaged noble ones, have held right views, and have accomplished actions based on right views. At the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in good destinies, in the heavenly realm.' Thus with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees sentient beings dying and being reborn, of good and bad appearance, in good and bad states, in superior or inferior destinies, according to the actions they have performed, and he knows it as it really is.

"With his mind concentrated, purified, cleansed, free from defilements, free from secondary defilements, supple, capable of acting, settled, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'These are the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the origin of the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the outflows.'

"Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, liberated from the outflow of existence, and liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, the knowledge arises: 'I am liberated.' He knows as it really is: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this.'

"When the Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arhat, a Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed One, a Trainer of Those Who Are To Be Tamed, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, he teaches the Dharma to the disciples. The disciples, having received the teaching, practice accordingly, practice to the utmost, and reach the foremost, reaching the ultimate place. Having reached it, they are able to tell others: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this.'

"This is how a good person's going forth benefits many people, brings comfort and ease to many people, and is out of compassion for the world, seeking benefit, welfare, and peace for gods and humans."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 7. Sūtra on the Worldly Merit of the Good Person

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are seven meritorious things of a good person. What are the seven? A good person gives what is difficult to give, does what is difficult to do, and endures what is difficult to endure. He reveals his secrets to others, and keeps others' secrets. When encountering suffering, he does not abandon others. When his wealth is exhausted, he does not look down on others.

"How does a good person give what is difficult to give? A good person is able to give his own provisions and property to others. This is called a good person giving what is difficult to give.

"How does a good person do what is difficult to do? A good person is able to tolerate what others cannot tolerate. This is called a good person doing what is difficult to do.

"How does a good person endure what is difficult to endure? A good person, even when his secret failings are revealed by others, is able to endure it. This is called a good person enduring what is difficult to endure.

"How does a good person reveal his secrets to others? A good person reveals to a close friend his own secrets, telling what is in his heart. This is called a good person revealing his secrets to others.

"How does a good person keep others' secrets? A good person, when a close friend confides in him, does not reveal it. This is called a good person keeping others' secrets.

"How does a good person, when encountering suffering, not abandon others? A good person, when encountering dangers and difficulties, does not abandon his friend. This is called a good person not abandoning others when encountering suffering.

"How does a good person, when his wealth is exhausted, not look down on others? A good person does not look down on or despise another because that person's wealth is exhausted. This is called a good person not looking down on others when their wealth is exhausted.

"A good person gives what is difficult to give, does what is difficult to do, and endures what is difficult to endure. He reveals his secrets to others, and keeps others' secrets. When encountering suffering, he does not abandon others. When wealth is exhausted, he does not look down on others. These are the seven meritorious things of a good person."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"Giving what is difficult to give,
Doing what is difficult to do,
The good person practices this,
While the bad person cannot.

"The dharma of the good person is hard to follow;
The bad person cannot attain it.
Therefore the destinations after death
Of the good and bad are different.

"If one wishes to know a person,
One should observe the company he keeps.
If his companion is not defiled,
Then his companion is truly pure.

"The companion being one's guide,
The one who is kept close being one's intimate,
Associate with a good friend,
And you too will become superior."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 8. Sūtra on the Merits of the Seven Suns

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "All conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation. Why? There will come a time when there will be no rain for a very long period. Because there is no rain for a very long period, all seeds, plants, medicines, herbs, and forests, both the great and the small, will all wither, dry up, and cease to exist. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a second sun will appear. When the second sun appears, all streams, channels, ditches, and rivulets will all dry up and cease to exist. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a third sun will appear. When the third sun appears, all the great rivers, the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Sarabhū, the Ajiravatī, and the Mahī, will all dry up and cease to exist. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a fourth sun will appear. When the fourth sun appears, the great lake from which the five great rivers originate, the lake called Anavatapta, will also dry up and cease to exist. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a fifth sun will appear. When the fifth sun appears, the waters of the great ocean will recede by one hundred yojanas, then recede by two hundred yojanas, then recede by three hundred yojanas, then recede by four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, and even seven hundred yojanas. When the fifth sun appears, the waters of the great ocean will only be seven hundred yojanas deep, then only six hundred yojanas, then only five hundred yojanas, then only four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, one hundred yojanas. When the fifth sun appears, the waters of the great ocean will only be one yojana deep, then only half a yojana, then only as deep as one's waist, then only as deep as one's knees, and finally the waters will only be ankle-deep. Bhikṣus, just as in the autumn, during the great rains, drops of water appear everywhere in the pools and puddles, in the same way, when the fifth sun appears, the waters of the great ocean will be scattered drops here and there. When the fifth sun appears, the waters of the great ocean will not even be enough to fill a finger joint. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a sixth sun will appear. When the sixth sun appears, this entire great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, will emit smoke and steam. Just as when a potter first lights a fire under a kiln and smoke rises in all directions, in the same way, when the sixth sun appears, this entire great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, will emit smoke and steam. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Furthermore, there will come a time when a seventh sun will appear. When the seventh sun appears, this entire great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, will burst into flames, blaze, and become one mass of fire. The winds will carry the flames, reaching even to the Brahmā heavens. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, will burn, crumble, and disintegrate. Pieces one hundred yojanas in size, pieces two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred yojanas in size will crumble and disintegrate, burned up in the fire. When this great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, are burned, not even ashes or soot will remain. Just as when ghee or oil is burned, not even ashes or soot remain, in the same way, when the seventh sun appears, this entire great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, are burned, and not even ashes or soot remain. Therefore, know that all conditioned things are impermanent, they are not eternal, not stable. They are truly sufficient to become wearisome, sufficient to become disenchanting, sufficient to make one seek liberation.

"Who would have believed or heard of this, except those who have seen it and realized it? In the future, this great earth will be burned and destroyed.

"Bhikṣus, although this truth has been spoken, although it has been illuminated and explained, there are still sentient beings who, due to the defilement of ignorance, bound by the fetter of craving, delight in being and take pleasure in being, running and flowing in the stream of being, running and flowing in the stream of being without ceasing, without being able to reach the far shore.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, when you know the meaning of this, you should constantly practice the destruction of the outflows, becoming established in knowledge, making yourself a witness. Why? Because a bhikṣu who has destroyed the outflows can say: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 9. Sūtra on the Seven Chariots

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in the Squirrels' Feeding Ground near Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus: "Once, friends, at a time when the World-Honored One was dwelling at Nādikā in the Brick Hall, I rose early at dawn, went to the World-Honored One, bowed my head at his feet, and stood to one side. I then said to the World-Honored One: 'World-Honored One, what is the meaning of this: one who does not cultivate the body, one who does not cultivate morality, one who does not cultivate the mind, one who does not cultivate wisdom? If such a person, in the present life, says "I know as it really is that birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this," that cannot be the case.'

"'World-Honored One, what is the meaning of this: one who cultivates the body, one who cultivates morality, one who cultivates the mind, one who cultivates wisdom? If such a person, in the present life, says "I know as it really is that birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this," that can be the case?'

"The World-Honored One told me: 'Maudgalyāyana, suppose there are bhikṣus who are hollow, unreal, deceitful, of jealous nature, of excessive pride, unstable, not concentrated, of scattered mind, with their faculties uncontrolled, with the doors of their sense faculties wide open, not guarding the domain of the faculties, not able to protect their moral precepts, not diligently cultivating the increase of mind, not being vigorous and energetic. Maudgalyāyana, regarding such bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate morality, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom, if in the present life they say "I know as it really is that birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what needed to be done has been done, there is no more existence after this," that cannot be the case.

"

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 1

## Chapter One: The Seven Dharmas

Contents: Wholesome Dharmas, The Pāricchattaka Tree, The City Simile, The Water Simile, The Woodpile Simile, The Wholesome Person's Departure, The World's Blessing and the Sun, The Chariot, The Seven of Complete Destruction of the Taints

---

## (1) Sūtra on Wholesome Dharmas, First of the Seven Dharmas Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in seven dharmas, he will attain joy and happiness among the noble ones and proceed directly toward the complete destruction of the taints. What are the seven? That is, a bhikṣu knows the Dharma, knows the meaning, knows the proper time, knows moderation, knows himself, knows assemblies, and knows the superiority and inferiority of persons.

"How does a bhikṣu know the Dharma? That is, a bhikṣu knows the sūtras, verses in song, explanations, stanzas, narratives of conditions, collected accounts, stories of origins, thus-spoken passages, birth stories, extensive expositions, accounts of unprecedented events, and discussions of meaning. This is called a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma. If a bhikṣu does not know the Dharma, it means he does not know the sūtras, verses in song, explanations, stanzas, narratives of conditions, collected accounts, stories of origins, thus-spoken passages, birth stories, extensive expositions, accounts of unprecedented events, and discussions of meaning. Such a bhikṣu does not know the Dharma. If a bhikṣu well knows the Dharma, it means he knows the sūtras, verses in song, explanations, stanzas, narratives of conditions, collected accounts, stories of origins, thus-spoken passages, birth stories, extensive expositions, accounts of unprecedented events, and discussions of meaning. This is called a bhikṣu who well knows the Dharma.

"How does a bhikṣu know the meaning? That is, a bhikṣu knows the meaning of this and that teaching: 'This is the meaning of that; this is the meaning of this.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows the meaning. If a bhikṣu does not know the meaning, it means he does not know the meaning of this and that teaching: 'This is the meaning of that; this is the meaning of this.' Such a bhikṣu does not know the meaning. If a bhikṣu well knows the meaning, it means he knows the meaning of this and that teaching: 'This is the meaning of that; this is the meaning of this.' This is called a bhikṣu who well knows the meaning.

"How does a bhikṣu know the proper time? That is, a bhikṣu knows: 'This is the time to cultivate the sign of lowliness; this is the time to cultivate the sign of elevation; this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows the proper time. If a bhikṣu does not know the proper time, it means he does not know: 'This is the time to cultivate the sign of lowliness; this is the time to cultivate the sign of elevation; this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity.' Such a bhikṣu does not know the proper time. If a bhikṣu well knows the proper time, it means he knows: 'This is the time to cultivate the sign of lowliness; this is the time to cultivate the sign of elevation; this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity.' This is called a bhikṣu who well knows the proper time.

"How does a bhikṣu know moderation? That is, a bhikṣu knows moderation in drinking and eating, in going and staying, in sitting and lying down, in speaking and remaining silent, and in relieving himself; he discards drowsiness and cultivates right awareness. This is called a bhikṣu who knows moderation. If a bhikṣu does not know moderation, it means he does not know moderation in drinking and eating, in going and staying, in sitting and lying down, in speaking and remaining silent, and in relieving himself; he does not discard drowsiness and does not cultivate right awareness. Such a bhikṣu does not know moderation. If a bhikṣu well knows moderation, it means he knows moderation in drinking and eating, in going and staying, in sitting and lying down, in speaking and remaining silent, and in relieving himself; he discards drowsiness and cultivates right awareness. This is called a bhikṣu who well knows moderation.

"How does a bhikṣu know himself? That is, a bhikṣu knows of himself: 'I possess such and such faith, morality, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, knowledge of the scriptures, and attainments.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows himself. If a bhikṣu does not know himself, it means he does not know of himself: 'I possess such and such faith, morality, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, knowledge of the scriptures, and attainments.' Such a bhikṣu does not know himself. If a bhikṣu well knows himself, it means he knows of himself: 'I possess such and such faith, morality, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, knowledge of the scriptures, and attainments.' This is called a bhikṣu who well knows himself.

"How does a bhikṣu know assemblies? That is, a bhikṣu knows: 'This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas. In that assembly I should go in such a way, stand in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and be silent in such a way.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows assemblies. If a bhikṣu does not know assemblies, it means he does not know: 'This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas. In that assembly I should go in such a way, stand in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and be silent in such a way.' Such a bhikṣu does not know assemblies. If a bhikṣu well knows assemblies, it means he knows: 'This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas. In that assembly I should go in such a way, stand in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and be silent in such a way.' This is called a bhikṣu who well knows assemblies.

"How does a bhikṣu know the superiority and inferiority of persons? That is, a bhikṣu knows there are two kinds of people: those with faith and those without faith. Those with faith are superior; those without faith are inferior. Those with faith are again of two kinds: those who frequently visit bhikṣus and those who do not frequently visit bhikṣus. Those who frequently visit bhikṣus are superior; those who do not frequently visit bhikṣus are inferior. Those who frequently visit bhikṣus are again of two kinds: those who pay respect to bhikṣus and those who do not pay respect to bhikṣus. Those who pay respect to bhikṣus are superior; those who do not pay respect to bhikṣus are inferior. Those who pay respect to bhikṣus are again of two kinds: those who inquire about the sūtras and those who do not inquire about the sūtras. Those who inquire about the sūtras are superior; those who do not inquire about the sūtras are inferior. Those who inquire about the sūtras are again of two kinds: those who listen to the sūtras with a unified mind and those who do not listen to the sūtras with a unified mind. Those who listen with a unified mind are superior; those who do not listen with a unified mind are inferior. Those who listen with a unified mind are again of two kinds: those who, having heard, retain the Dharma, and those who, having heard, do not retain the Dharma. Those who, having heard, retain the Dharma are superior; those who, having heard, do not retain the Dharma are inferior. Those who, having heard, retain the Dharma are again of two kinds: those who, having heard the Dharma, contemplate its meaning, and those who, having heard the Dharma, do not contemplate its meaning. Those who, having heard the Dharma, contemplate its meaning are superior; those who, having heard the Dharma, do not contemplate its meaning are inferior. Those who, having heard the Dharma, contemplate its meaning are again of two kinds: those who know the Dharma, know the meaning, proceed toward the Dharma in proper sequence, accord with the Dharma, and practice in accordance with the Dharma; and those who do not know the Dharma, do not know the meaning, do not proceed toward the Dharma in proper sequence, do not accord with the Dharma, and do not practice in accordance with the Dharma. Those who know the Dharma, know the meaning, proceed toward the Dharma in proper sequence, accord with the Dharma, and practice in accordance with the Dharma are superior. Those who do not know the Dharma, do not know the meaning, do not proceed toward the Dharma in proper sequence, do not accord with the Dharma, and do not practice in accordance with the Dharma are inferior. Those who know the Dharma, know the meaning, proceed toward the Dharma in proper sequence, accord with the Dharma, and practice in accordance with the Dharma are again of two kinds: those who benefit themselves and also benefit others, benefit many people, have compassion for the world, and for the sake of devas and humans seek what is meaningful and beneficial, seeking peace, security, and happiness; and those who do not benefit themselves, do not benefit others, do not benefit many people, do not have compassion for the world, and do not for the sake of devas and humans seek what is meaningful and beneficial, seeking peace, security, and happiness. Those who benefit themselves and also benefit others, benefit many people, have compassion for the world, and for the sake of devas and humans seek what is meaningful and beneficial, seeking peace, security, and happiness: these persons, among all those persons, are the very foremost, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most wonderful. Just as from the cow comes milk, from milk comes curds, from curds comes fresh butter, from fresh butter comes clarified butter, and from clarified butter comes the essence of ghee, and the essence of ghee is, among all of these, the very foremost, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most wonderful; so too, if a person benefits himself and also benefits others, benefits many people, has compassion for the world, and for the sake of devas and humans seeks what is meaningful and beneficial, seeking peace, security, and happiness: between these two kinds of persons, as described above, as analyzed above, as set forth above, this one is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most wonderful. This is called a bhikṣu who knows the superiority and inferiority of persons."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on Wholesome Dharmas, the First

---

## (2) Sūtra on the Pāricchattaka Tree, Second of the Seven Dharmas Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "When the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods turn yellow and wither, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree will soon fall. Furthermore, when the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods have already fallen, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree will soon grow back again. Furthermore, when the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods have already grown back, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the Pāricchattaka tree will soon produce a net-like covering. Furthermore, when the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has already produced a net-like covering, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the Pāricchattaka tree will soon produce buds like bird beaks. Furthermore, when the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has already produced buds like bird beaks, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the Pāricchattaka tree will soon open like a bowl. Furthermore, when the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has already opened like a bowl, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods rejoice with delight, knowing that the Pāricchattaka tree will soon be fully in bloom. When the Pāricchattaka tree is fully in bloom, its light illuminates, its color reflects, and its fragrance pervades a circumference of one hundred yojanas. At that time, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, during the four months of midsummer, replete with the five kinds of heavenly sensual pleasures, amuse and delight themselves. This is how the Trāyastriṃśa gods gather and enjoy themselves beneath the Pāricchattaka tree.

"In the same way, when a noble disciple thinks of going forth from the household life, at that time the noble disciple is called 'leaves turning yellow,' just as the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods turn yellow and wither. Furthermore, when a noble disciple shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with complete faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, at that time the noble disciple is called 'leaves fallen,' just as the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods have fallen.
