Furthermore, when a noble disciple, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is called 'leaves grown back,' just as the leaves of the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods have grown back. Furthermore, when a noble disciple, with initial and sustained thought having ceased, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is called 'the net-like covering has formed,' just as the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has produced its net-like covering. Furthermore, when a noble disciple, having departed from the desire for joy, dwells in equanimity without craving, with right mindfulness and right awareness, and experiences happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe it: 'one who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells in happiness and emptiness,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is called 'buds like bird beaks have formed,' just as the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has produced buds like bird beaks. Furthermore, when a noble disciple, with the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, and with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, in a state neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is called 'opened like a bowl,' just as the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has opened like a bowl.

"Furthermore, when a noble disciple has completely destroyed all the taints, and with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life knows and realizes for himself, achieves and dwells in the attainment, knowing as it truly is: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming,' at that time the noble disciple is called 'fully in bloom,' just as the Pāricchattaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is fully in bloom. For that bhikṣu who is an Arhat with taints destroyed, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, gathered in the Hall of the Good Dharma, praise and extol him, saying: 'Such-and-such a venerable disciple, in such-and-such a village or town, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robe, and with complete faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. He has completely destroyed all the taints, and with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life knows and realizes for himself, achieves and dwells in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming. He knows as it truly is.' This is how the Arhat with taints destroyed gathers in assembly, just as the Trāyastriṃśa gods gather in assembly beneath the Pāricchattaka tree."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Pāricchattaka Tree, the Second

---

## (3) Sūtra on the City Simile, Third of the Seven Dharmas Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Just as a king's border city, when equipped with seven things and when four kinds of food are abundant and easy to obtain, cannot be destroyed by external enemies, and can only be ruined from within.

"How is a king's city equipped with seven things? A king's border city has watchtowers constructed, with the ground compacted and made firm, unable to be destroyed, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the first thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city has moats dug and trenches excavated, made extremely deep and wide, well-maintained and dependable, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the second thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city has encircling roads that are cleared, level, and broad, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the third thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city assembles four kinds of military forces: elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the fourth thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city has military weapons prepared in advance: bows, arrows, spears, and halberds, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the fifth thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city appoints a great general to guard the gate, one who is astute, wise, eloquent, courageous, resolute, and of extraordinary strategy, who admits the good and prohibits the bad, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the sixth thing. Furthermore, just as a king's border city has high walls built, made extremely strong and solid, plastered and whitewashed, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city being equipped with the seventh thing.

"How does the king's city have four kinds of food in abundance, easy to obtain? A king's border city has water, grass, and firewood, with provisions prepared in advance, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city having the first kind of food in abundance, easy to obtain. Furthermore, just as a king's border city stores much rice and grain and stockpiles wheat, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city having the second kind of food in abundance, easy to obtain. Furthermore, just as a king's border city accumulates much sticky millet, large beans, and small beans, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city having the third kind of food in abundance, easy to obtain. Furthermore, just as a king's border city stores ghee, oil, honey, as well as sugarcane, sugar, fish, salt, and dried meat, all in complete supply, providing security within and repelling enemies without. This is called the king's city having the fourth kind of food in abundance, easy to obtain. Thus, when a king's city is equipped with seven things and four kinds of food are abundant and easy to obtain, it cannot be destroyed by external enemies; it can only be ruined from within.

"In the same way, if a noble disciple also obtains seven wholesome dharmas and attains four superior states of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult, then the noble disciple cannot be overcome by Māra, does not follow unwholesome dharmas, is not defiled by defilements, and will not undergo further birth.

"How does a noble disciple obtain seven wholesome dharmas? A noble disciple obtains firm faith, is deeply devoted to the Tathāgata, has established the root of faith, and will never follow outside śramaṇas or brahmins, whether devas, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the first wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame, being capable of shame and knowing shame regarding unwholesome dharmas that are defiling afflictions, that produce evil retributions, and that create the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the second wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple constantly practices a sense of moral dread, being capable of moral dread and knowing moral dread regarding unwholesome dharmas that are defiling afflictions, that produce evil retributions, and that create the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the third wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple constantly practices energetic effort, abandoning unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas, always arousing his own resolve, focused, steadfast, and determined, establishing the foundation of all wholesome dharmas, never abandoning skillful means. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the fourth wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple has broad learning and extensive knowledge, retains what he has learned without forgetting, and accumulates vast learning. The Dharma of which I speak is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life. Such dharmas he has broadly learned and extensively studied, practiced and reviewed up to a thousand times, contemplated with his mind, clearly seen, and deeply penetrated. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the fifth wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple constantly practices mindfulness, accomplished in right mindfulness, remembering without forgetting what was long ago practiced and long ago heard. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the sixth wholesome dharma. Furthermore, a noble disciple cultivates wisdom, contemplating the dharmas of arising and passing away, attaining such wisdom, with noble insight that is clear and penetrating, distinguishing and understanding clearly, in order to rightly make a complete end of suffering. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the seventh wholesome dharma.

"How does a noble disciple attain four superior states of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult? A noble disciple, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. This is called the noble disciple attaining the first superior state of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult. Furthermore, a noble disciple, with initial and sustained thought having ceased, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. This is called the noble disciple attaining the second superior state of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult. Furthermore, a noble disciple, having departed from the desire for joy, dwells in equanimity without craving, with right mindfulness and right awareness, and experiences happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe it: 'one who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells in happiness and emptiness,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. This is called the noble disciple attaining the third superior state of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult. Furthermore, a noble disciple, with the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, and with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, in a state neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. This is called the noble disciple attaining the fourth superior state of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult.

"Thus, a noble disciple who has obtained the seven wholesome dharmas and attained four superior states of mind, easy to obtain and not difficult, cannot be overcome by Māra, does not follow unwholesome dharmas, is not defiled by defilements, and will not undergo further birth. Just as a king's border city has watchtowers constructed, with the ground compacted and made firm, unable to be destroyed, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple obtains firm faith, is deeply devoted to the Tathāgata, has established the root of faith, and will never follow outside śramaṇas or brahmins, whether devas, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the watchtower of faith, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city has moats and trenches dug and excavated, made extremely deep and wide, well-maintained and dependable, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame, being capable of shame and knowing shame regarding unwholesome dharmas that are defiling afflictions, that produce evil retributions, and that create the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the moat and trench of shame, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city has encircling roads that are cleared, level, and broad, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple constantly practices a sense of moral dread, being capable of moral dread and knowing moral dread regarding unwholesome dharmas that are defiling afflictions, that produce evil retributions, and that create the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the level road of moral dread, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city assembles four kinds of military forces: elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple constantly practices energetic effort, abandoning unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas, always arousing his own resolve, focused, steadfast, and determined, establishing the foundation of all wholesome dharmas, never abandoning skillful means. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the military force of energetic effort, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city has military weapons prepared in advance: bows, arrows, spears, and halberds, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple has broad learning and extensive knowledge, retains what he has learned without forgetting, and accumulates vast learning. The Dharma of which I speak is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life. Such dharmas he has broadly learned and extensively studied, practiced and reviewed up to a thousand times, contemplated with his mind, clearly seen, and deeply penetrated. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the military weapons of extensive learning, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city appoints a great general to guard the gate, one who is astute, wise, eloquent, courageous, resolute, and of extraordinary strategy, who admits the good and prohibits the bad, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple constantly practices mindfulness, accomplished in right mindfulness, remembering without forgetting what was long ago practiced and long ago heard. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the great gate-guarding general of mindfulness, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city has high walls built, made extremely strong and solid, plastered and whitewashed, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple cultivates wisdom, contemplating the dharmas of arising and passing away, attaining such wisdom, with noble insight that is clear and penetrating, distinguishing and understanding clearly, in order to rightly make a complete end of suffering. This is called the noble disciple obtaining the wall of wisdom, abandoning what is unwholesome and cultivating wholesome dharmas.

"Just as a king's border city has water, grass, and firewood, with provisions prepared in advance, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, dwelling in happiness without lack, in peace, security, and happiness, leading himself to nirvāṇa.

"Just as a king's border city stores much rice and grain and stockpiles wheat, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple, with initial and sustained thought having ceased, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, dwelling in happiness without lack, in peace, security, and happiness, leading himself to nirvāṇa.

"Just as a king's border city accumulates much sticky millet, large beans, and small beans, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple, having departed from the desire for joy, dwells in equanimity without craving, with right mindfulness and right awareness, and experiences happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe it: 'one who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells in happiness and emptiness,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna, dwelling in happiness without lack, in peace, security, and happiness, leading himself to nirvāṇa.

"Just as a king's border city stores ghee, oil, honey, as well as sugarcane, sugar, fish, salt, and dried meat, all in complete supply, providing security within and repelling enemies without; so too, a noble disciple, with the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, and with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, in a state neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, dwelling in happiness without lack, in peace, security, and happiness, leading himself to nirvāṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the City Simile, the Third

---

## (4) Sūtra on the Water Simile, Fourth of the Seven Dharmas Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain to you the seven kinds of persons compared to those in water. Listen carefully, listen carefully! Consider it well and remember it." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? There is one person who always lies submerged in water. There is another person who emerges from the water but sinks back in. There is another person who emerges from the water and remains standing. There is another person who emerges from the water and remains standing, and having stood, looks around. There is another person who emerges from the water and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over. There is another person who emerges from the water and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore. There is another person who emerges from the water and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, is called a person who stands on the shore. In this way, I shall further explain to you the seven kinds of persons using the water simile. Listen carefully, listen carefully! Consider it well and remember it." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? There is a person who always lies submerged. There is another person who, having emerged, sinks back in. There is another person who, having emerged, remains standing. There is another person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around. There is another person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over. There is another person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore. There is another person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, is called a brahmin who stands on the shore. These are the seven kinds of persons illustrated by the water simile, which I have briefly stated. As described above, as set forth above, do you understand the meaning? What distinctions are there? What are the reasons?"

At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. We wish that you would explain it, and having heard, we shall come to know the meaning in full."

The Buddha then told them: "Listen carefully! Consider it well and remember it. I shall distinguish the meaning for you." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "How is there a person who always lies submerged? There is a person who is covered over by unwholesome dharmas, defiled by defilements, receiving the retribution of evil dharmas, creating the root of birth and death. This is called a person who always lies submerged. It is like a person who has drowned and lies submerged in water. I say that person is likewise. This is the first person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, sinks back in? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. But later he loses his faith, which becomes unsteady; he loses his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom, which become unsteady. This is called a person who, having emerged, sinks back in. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges but sinks back in. I say that person is likewise. This is the second person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, remains standing? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. Later his faith remains firm and is not lost; his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom remain firm and are not lost. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains standing. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges and remains standing. I say that person is likewise. This is the third person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. Later his faith remains firm and is not lost; his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom remain firm and are not lost. Abiding in wholesome dharmas, he knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. When he knows and sees thus, three fetters are completely destroyed, namely: the view of a self in the body, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt. With these three fetters destroyed, he attains the fruit of stream-entry. He will not fall into evil states and is certain to proceed toward right awakening. He will undergo at most seven more existences; after seven passages between the heavenly and human realms, he will reach the end of suffering. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges and remains standing, and having stood, looks around. I say that person is likewise. This is the fourth person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. Later his faith remains firm and is not lost; his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom remain firm and are not lost. Abiding in wholesome dharmas, he knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. When he knows and sees thus, three fetters are completely destroyed, namely: the view of a self in the body, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt. With these three fetters destroyed, and with lust, anger, and delusion attenuated, he attains once-returning. After one more passage between the heavenly and human realms, he will reach the end of suffering. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over. I say that person is likewise. This is the fifth person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. Later his faith remains firm and is not lost; his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom remain firm and are not lost. Abiding in wholesome dharmas, he knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. When he knows and sees thus, the five lower fetters are completely destroyed, namely: sensual desire, ill-will, the view of a self in the body, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt. With the five lower fetters destroyed, he is born in that realm and there attains nirvāṇa, having obtained the dharma of non-returning, never to return to this world. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore. I say that person is likewise. This is the sixth person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world.

"How is there a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, is called a brahmin who stands on the shore? There is a person who has emerged and obtained faith in wholesome dharmas: morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom; he cultivates wholesome dharmas. Later his faith remains firm and is not lost; his morality, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom remain firm and are not lost. Abiding in wholesome dharmas, he knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming.' He knows as it truly is. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, is called a brahmin who stands on the shore. It is like a person drowning in water who emerges and remains standing, and having stood, looks around, and having looked around, crosses over, and having crossed over, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, is called a person who stands on the shore. I say that person is likewise. This is the seventh person illustrated by the water simile. Such a person truly exists in the world. What I previously said, that I would explain to you the seven kinds of persons in water, was said for this reason."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Water Simile, the Fourth

---

## (5) Sūtra on the Woodpile Simile, Fifth of the Seven Dharmas Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Kosala, among the people, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One, while on the road, suddenly saw in a certain place a great woodpile, completely ablaze and burning fiercely. Having seen this, the World-Honored One descended from the road to the side, went to another tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat down cross-legged.

After the World-Honored One had sat down, he addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you see that great woodpile, completely ablaze and burning fiercely?"

The bhikṣus replied: "We see it, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? Regarding that great woodpile, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, if one were to embrace it, sit on it, or lie on it; or regarding a kṣatriya woman, a brahmin, householder, or artisan woman, in the bloom of youth, bathed and anointed with fragrance, wearing clean and bright clothing, adorned with flower garlands and jeweled necklaces decorating her body, if one were to embrace her, sit with her, or lie with her: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! To embrace, sit on, or lie on a great woodpile, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! To embrace, sit with, or lie with a kṣatriya woman, a brahmin, householder, or artisan woman, in the bloom of youth, bathed and anointed with fragrance, wearing clean and bright clothing, adorned with flower garlands and jeweled necklaces decorating her body, would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to embrace a woodpile completely ablaze and burning fiercely, to sit on it or lie on it. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and embraces a kṣatriya woman, a brahmin, householder, or artisan woman, in the bloom of youth, bathed and anointed with fragrance, wearing clean and bright clothing, adorned with flower garlands and jeweled necklaces decorating her body, or sits with her or lies with her, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take a tightly wound rope of hair and twist it around one's shins until it cut through the skin, and having cut through the skin, cut through the flesh, and having cut through the flesh, cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews, cut through the bone, and having cut through the bone, reached the marrow and remained there; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, having them massage one's body, limbs, hands, and feet: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take a tightly wound rope of hair and twist it around one's shins until it cut through the skin, and having cut through the skin, cut through the flesh, and having cut through the flesh, cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews, cut through the bone, and having cut through the bone, reached the marrow and remained there, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, having them massage one's body, limbs, hands, and feet, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take a tightly wound rope of hair and twist it around one's shins until it cut through the skin, and having cut through the skin, cut through the flesh, and having cut through the flesh, cut through the sinews, and having cut through the sinews, cut through the bone, and having cut through the bone, reach the marrow and remain there. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, having them massage his body, limbs, hands, and feet, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take a polished and sharpened knife and sever one's thigh; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, prostrations, respectful greetings, and welcoming attendance: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take a polished and sharpened knife and sever one's thigh, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, prostrations, respectful greetings, and welcoming attendance, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take a polished and sharpened knife and sever one's thigh. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings, prostrations, respectful greetings, and welcoming attendance, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take iron and copper plates, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and wrap them around one's body; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of clothing: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take iron and copper plates, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and wrap them around one's body, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of clothing, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take iron and copper plates, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and wrap them around one's body. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of clothing, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take hot iron tongs and pry open one's mouth, then place an iron ball, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, into one's mouth, and that hot iron ball burned the lips, and having burned the lips, burned the tongue, and having burned the tongue, burned the gums, and having burned the gums, burned the throat, and having burned the throat, burned the heart, and having burned the heart, burned the stomach and intestines, and having burned the stomach and intestines, passed through below; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of food with innumerable flavors: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take hot iron tongs and pry open one's mouth, then place an iron ball, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, into one's mouth, and that hot iron ball burned the lips, and having burned the lips, burned the tongue, and having burned the tongue, burned the gums, and having burned the gums, burned the throat, and having burned the throat, burned the heart, and having burned the heart, burned the stomach and intestines, and having burned the stomach and intestines, passed through below, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of food with innumerable flavors, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take hot iron tongs and pry open one's mouth, then place an iron ball, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, into one's mouth, and that hot iron ball burn the lips, and having burned the lips, burn the tongue, and having burned the tongue, burn the gums, and having burned the gums, burn the throat, and having burned the throat, burn the heart, and having burned the heart, burn the stomach and intestines, and having burned the stomach and intestines, pass through below. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of food with innumerable flavors, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take an iron and copper bed, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and force a person to sit or lie upon it; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of beds, chairs, and bedding: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take an iron and copper bed, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and force a person to sit or lie upon it, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of beds, chairs, and bedding, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take an iron and copper bed, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, and force one to sit or lie upon it. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of beds, chairs, and bedding, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? If a strong man were to take a great iron and copper cauldron, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, seize a person, lift him up, and throw him upside down into the cauldron; or if one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of dwellings, plastered and whitewashed, with windows and doors securely sealed, and warmed by a stove fire: which of these would be pleasant?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! If a strong man were to take a great iron and copper cauldron, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, seize a person, lift him up, and throw him upside down into the cauldron, that would be extremely painful, World-Honored One! If one were to receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of dwellings, plastered and whitewashed, with windows and doors securely sealed, and warmed by a stove fire, that would be extremely pleasant, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One said: "I tell you this so that you who study the way of a śramaṇa will not lose the way of a śramaṇa. If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better to let a strong man take a great iron and copper cauldron, completely ablaze and burning fiercely, seize one, lift one up, and throw one upside down into the cauldron. Although one might suffer or die because of this, one would not, at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, fall into an evil destination and be reborn in hell. But if a foolish person violates the precepts, is not diligent, gives rise to evil and unwholesome dharmas, is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, and receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans their faithful offerings of dwellings, plastered and whitewashed, with windows and doors securely sealed, and warmed by a stove fire, that foolish person, because of this, through the long night of unwholesomeness and unrighteousness, receives the retribution of evil dharmas, and at the breaking up of the body at the end of life, falls into an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Therefore, you should contemplate your own benefit, contemplate the benefit of others, and contemplate the benefit of both. You should think thus: 'My going forth to study the Way shall not be in vain, not empty, but with fruit and reward, with supreme peace and happiness, born in good realms and attaining long life. In receiving the faithful offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine from others, I shall cause those donors to obtain great merit, great reward, and great radiance.' You should train in this way."

When this Dharma was taught, sixty bhikṣus completely destroyed the taints and were freed from all bonds, and sixty bhikṣus abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life. Why was this? The World-Honored One's admonishment was extremely profound and extremely difficult, and the study of the Way is also extremely profound and extremely difficult.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Woodpile Simile, the Fifth

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama)

## Fascicle Three

---

### (10) Sūtra on Salt

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If someone says, 'Whatever actions a person performs, that person must experience the results accordingly,' then there would be no cultivation of the holy life, and there would be no opportunity for the complete ending of suffering. If someone says, 'Whatever actions a person performs, that person experiences results corresponding to those actions,' then there is cultivation of the holy life, and there is the opportunity for the complete ending of suffering.

"Bhikṣus, if a person has not cultivated the body, has not cultivated morality, has not cultivated the mind, and has not cultivated wisdom, their life is limited, and such a person is called insignificant and lowly. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will be led to hell. Bhikṣus, it is like someone placing a lump of salt into a small amount of water in a cup. What do you think? Would that small amount of water in the cup become salty and undrinkable because of the salt?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, World-Honored One. Why is that? Because the salt is substantial, while the water in the cup is minimal, so the salt would make the water salty and undrinkable."

"Bhikṣus, if a person has cultivated the body, has cultivated morality, has cultivated the mind, and has cultivated wisdom, their life is vast, and such a person is called a great person. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will experience the result in the present life. Perhaps it will manifest only slightly, and it will certainly not come to extensive fruition. Bhikṣus, it is like someone throwing a lump of salt into the Ganges River. What do you think? Would the Ganges River become salty and undrinkable because of that lump of salt?"

The bhikṣus replied: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? Because the Ganges River is vast, that lump of salt would not be able to make it salty and undrinkable."

"Bhikṣus, it is like someone who, on account of stealing half a coin, is bound and imprisoned, flogged and tortured. Another person who steals half a coin is not bound and imprisoned, not flogged and tortured. What sort of person, on account of stealing half a coin, is bound and imprisoned, flogged and tortured? It is someone who is poor, impoverished, and destitute. Such a person, on account of stealing half a coin, is bound and imprisoned, flogged and tortured. What sort of person, having stolen half a coin, is not bound and imprisoned, not flogged and tortured? It is someone who is wealthy, with abundant treasures and possessions. Such a person, having stolen half a coin, is not bound and imprisoned, not flogged and tortured. Bhikṣus, the poor and impoverished person who, on account of stealing half a coin, is bound and imprisoned, flogged and tortured, is just like the person who has not cultivated the body, not cultivated morality, not cultivated the mind, and not cultivated wisdom, whose life is limited, who is called insignificant and lowly. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will be led to hell. Bhikṣus, the wealthy person with abundant treasures and possessions who, having stolen half a coin, is not bound and imprisoned, not flogged and tortured, is just like the person who has cultivated the body, cultivated morality, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom, whose life is vast, who is called a great person. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will experience the result in the present life. Perhaps it will manifest only slightly, and it will certainly not come to extensive fruition.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a butcher or shepherd of goats who, seeing someone stealing goats, is able to seize, beat, or restrain that person at will. But seeing another person stealing goats, he cannot seize, beat, or restrain that person, and instead rises from his seat to greet him, saying, 'Welcome, friend!' What sort of person who steals goats can be seized, beaten, or restrained at will? It is a poor, impoverished, and destitute person. What sort of person who steals goats cannot be seized, beaten, or restrained? It is a powerful king, or a king's minister, who is mighty and influential. When such a person takes goats, that butcher or shepherd cannot seize, beat, or restrain him. Instead he merely rises from his seat to greet him, saying, 'Welcome, friend! Take whatever goats or sheep you wish.' Bhikṣus, the poor and destitute person who, having stolen goats, can be seized, beaten, or restrained, is just like the person who has not cultivated the body, not cultivated morality, not cultivated the mind, and not cultivated wisdom, whose life is limited, who is called insignificant and lowly. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will be led to hell. The powerful king or king's minister who steals goats and whom the butcher cannot seize, beat, or restrain, instead greeting him, 'Welcome, friend! Take whatever goats or sheep you wish,' is just like the person who has cultivated the body, cultivated morality, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom, whose life is vast, who is called a great person. Such a person, even through a minor unwholesome action, will experience the result in the present life. Perhaps it will manifest only slightly, and it will certainly not come to extensive fruition.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, if someone says, 'Whatever actions a person performs, that person must experience the results accordingly,' then there would be no cultivation of the holy life, and there would be no opportunity for the complete ending of suffering. If someone says, 'Whatever actions a person performs, that person experiences results corresponding to those actions,' then there is cultivation of the holy life, and there is the opportunity for the complete ending of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (11) Sūtra on Salt (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three characteristics by which an unwise, ignorant fool can be recognized and distinguished. What are the three? Here, an unwise, ignorant fool conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action. If this unwise, ignorant fool did not conceive evil in thought, speak evil in speech, or perform evil in action, how would the wise know: 'This is an unwise, ignorant fool'? Because the unwise, ignorant fool conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action, therefore the wise know: 'This is an unwise, ignorant fool.'

"That unwise, ignorant fool experiences suffering in three ways in this present life. If the unwise, ignorant fool sits in an assembly, or on the roadside, or at a crossroads, and the people in that place discuss relevant matters, and if this unwise, ignorant fool has committed acts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol, then the unwise, ignorant fool thinks: 'I have committed those evil actions: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol. The people in this place are discussing such matters. I have committed such actions.' This is the first suffering and distress that the unwise, ignorant fool experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, the unwise, ignorant fool sees a king seize a criminal, inflicting various punishments: whipping, flogging, cutting off hands, cutting off feet, or cutting off hands and feet, cutting off ears, cutting off the nose, or cutting off ears and nose, or the punishment of boiling gruel, or the crown of thorns, or the flaying of skin, or the rinsing of the mouth, or the torch of fire, or the flaming hands, or the grass clothing, or the bark garment, or the antelope punishment, or the meat hook, or the coin punishment, or the lye washing, or the turning stake, or the straw mat, or pouring boiling oil, or being devoured by dogs, or being impaled alive, or being beheaded by sword. The unwise, ignorant fool sees these punishments and thinks: 'I too have committed such evil deeds. If the king were to seize me, he would also inflict these various punishments upon me.' This is the second suffering and distress that the unwise, ignorant fool experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, when the unwise, ignorant fool lies on his bed, whether at the end of life or at another time, the evil, unwholesome actions he previously committed by body, speech, and mind all come to overshadow him, cover him, and engulf him. It is like the shadow of a great mountain peak, as the sun sets in the evening, covering the ground, overshadowing and engulfing the earth. In the same way, when the unwise, ignorant fool lies on his bed, whether at the end of life or at another time, all the evil, unwholesome actions he previously committed by body, speech, and mind come to overshadow him, cover him, and engulf him. At that time, the unwise, ignorant fool thinks: 'I did not do good, I did not make merit, I did not establish a refuge against fear. I only committed evil, cruelty, and wrong deeds. If there is a destination for those who did no good, made no merit, and established no refuge against fear, who only committed evil, cruelty, and wrong deeds, then I shall go there.' Because of this, he feels regret, and feeling regret, he dies in confusion. This is the third suffering and distress that the unwise, ignorant fool experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, the unwise, ignorant fool, having conceived evil in thought, experiences suffering and grief upon the disintegration of the body after death, and goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, falling into hell.

"Bhikṣus, there are three characteristics by which a wise person can be recognized and distinguished. What are the three? Here, a wise person conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action. If the wise person did not conceive good in thought, speak good in speech, or perform good in action, how would the wise know: 'This is a wise person'? Because the wise person conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action, therefore the wise know: 'This is a wise person.'

"That wise person experiences joy in three ways in this present life. If the wise person sits in an assembly, or on the roadside, or at a crossroads, and the people in that place discuss relevant matters, and if this wise person has refrained from killing, refrained from stealing, refrained from sexual misconduct, refrained from lying, and refrained from drinking alcohol, then the wise person thinks: 'I have not committed those evil actions: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol. The people in this place are discussing such matters. I have not committed such actions.' This is the first joy and happiness that the wise person experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, the wise person sees a king seize a criminal, inflicting various punishments: whipping, flogging, cutting off hands, cutting off feet, or cutting off hands and feet, cutting off ears, cutting off the nose, or cutting off ears and nose, or the punishment of boiling gruel, or the crown of thorns, or the flaying of skin, or the rinsing of the mouth, or the torch of fire, or the flaming hands, or the grass clothing, or the bark garment, or the antelope punishment, or the meat hook, or the coin punishment, or the lye washing, or the turning stake, or the straw mat, or pouring boiling oil, or being devoured by dogs, or being impaled alive, or being beheaded by sword. The wise person sees these punishments and thinks: 'I have not committed such evil deeds. If the king were to seize me, he would not inflict these various punishments upon me.' This is the second joy and happiness that the wise person experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, when the wise person lies on his bed, whether at the end of life or at another time, the wholesome actions he previously committed by body, speech, and mind come to overshadow him, cover him, and surround him. It is like the shadow of a great mountain peak, as the sun sets in the evening, covering the ground, overshadowing and engulfing the earth. In the same way, when the wise person lies on his bed, whether at the end of life or at another time, the wholesome actions he previously committed by body, speech, and mind all come to overshadow him, cover him, and surround him. At that time, the wise person thinks: 'I did not do evil, I did not commit cruelty, I did not commit wrong deeds. I only did good, made merit, and established a refuge against fear. If there is a destination for those who did good, made merit, and established a refuge against fear, who did not commit evil, cruelty, or wrong deeds, then I shall go there.' Because of this, he feels no regret, and feeling no regret, he dies peacefully. This is the third joy and happiness that the wise person experiences in this present life.

"Furthermore, the wise person, having conceived good in thought, upon the disintegration of the body after death, surely goes to a good destination and is reborn in heaven.

"I have now spoken of the three characteristics of the unwise fool, and I have spoken of the three sufferings of the unwise fool. I have spoken of the three characteristics of the wise person, and I have spoken of the three joys of the wise person. Whatever should be done by a compassionate teacher who, out of great compassion, seeks the benefit and welfare of his disciples, I have already done for you. Bhikṣus, you should sit in meditation under trees, in empty, quiet places. Practice diligently and do not be negligent, lest you have regret later. This is my teaching to you."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (12) Sūtra on Harmony

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the dharma for harmony and the dharma for dispute. Listen well, listen well, and reflect carefully on it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the dharma for dispute? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu generates desire and is defiled by unwholesome dharmas, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, and abides having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, he might think: 'I abide having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation.' But another bhikṣu has not generated desire, has not been defiled by unwholesome dharmas, has not attained the first jhāna accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, approaches the bhikṣu who has not attained it and says: 'Venerable one, you have not generated desire, you are not defiled by unwholesome dharmas, you have not attained the first jhāna accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not generated desire either, you are not defiled by unwholesome dharmas either, you have not attained the first jhāna accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu generates desire and is defiled by unwholesome dharmas, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, and abides having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, he might think: 'I abide having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation.' Another bhikṣu has also generated desire, is also defiled by unwholesome dharmas, also accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, and also abides having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness. That bhikṣu who abides having attained the first jhāna, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have generated desire, you too are defiled by unwholesome dharmas, you too have attained the first jhāna accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have generated desire, you too are defiled by unwholesome dharmas, you too have attained the first jhāna accompanied by reasoning and deliberation, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having stilled reasoning and deliberation, with inner purity, with unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, abides having attained the second jhāna, born of concentration, with joy and happiness, he might think: 'I abide having attained the second jhāna, born of concentration, with joy and happiness, without reasoning and without deliberation, with inner purity and unified mind.' But another bhikṣu has not stilled reasoning and deliberation, has not attained inner purity, unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, the second jhāna born of concentration, with joy and happiness, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the second jhāna approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not stilled reasoning and deliberation, you have not attained inner purity, unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, the second jhāna born of concentration, with joy and happiness, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not stilled reasoning and deliberation either, you have not attained inner purity, unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, the second jhāna born of concentration, with joy and happiness either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having stilled reasoning and deliberation, with inner purity, with unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, abides having attained the second jhāna, born of concentration, with joy and happiness. Another bhikṣu has also stilled reasoning and deliberation, also with inner purity, also with unified mind, also without reasoning and without deliberation, and also abides having attained the second jhāna, born of concentration, with joy and happiness. That bhikṣu who abides in the second jhāna approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have stilled reasoning and deliberation, you too have attained inner purity, unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, the second jhāna born of concentration, with joy and happiness, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have stilled reasoning and deliberation, you too have attained inner purity, unified mind, without reasoning and without deliberation, the second jhāna born of concentration, with joy and happiness, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having departed from joy and with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'With equanimity, mindfulness, and abiding in happiness,' abides having attained the third jhāna, he might think: 'I abide having attained the third jhāna, having departed from joy and with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body.' But another bhikṣu has not departed from joy, has not attained equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, has not experienced happiness with the body, has not attained the third jhāna, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the third jhāna approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not departed from joy, you have not attained equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, you have not experienced happiness with the body, you have not attained the third jhāna, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not departed from joy either, you have not attained equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension either, you have not experienced happiness with the body either, you have not attained the third jhāna either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having departed from joy and with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, abides having attained the third jhāna. Another bhikṣu has also departed from joy, also with equanimity, also mindful and clearly comprehending, also experiencing happiness with the body, and also abides having attained the third jhāna. That bhikṣu who abides in the third jhāna approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have departed from joy, you too have attained equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, you too have experienced happiness with the body, you too have attained the third jhāna, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have departed from joy, you too have attained equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, you too have experienced happiness with the body, you too have attained the third jhāna, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness and the earlier cessation of suffering, and with the disappearance of former joy and grief, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindful purification, abides having attained the fourth jhāna, he might think: 'I abide having attained the fourth jhāna, with the cessation of happiness, the earlier cessation of suffering, the disappearance of former joy and grief, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindful purification.' But another bhikṣu has not attained the cessation of happiness, has not had the earlier cessation of suffering, has not had the disappearance of former joy and grief, has not attained neither suffering nor happiness, equanimity, and mindful purification, has not attained the fourth jhāna, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the fourth jhāna approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not attained the cessation of happiness, you have not had the earlier cessation of suffering, you have not had the disappearance of former joy and grief, you have not attained neither suffering nor happiness, equanimity, and mindful purification, you have not attained the fourth jhāna, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not attained the cessation of happiness either,' up to 'you have not attained the fourth jhāna either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness and the earlier cessation of suffering, the disappearance of former joy and grief, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindful purification, abides having attained the fourth jhāna. Another bhikṣu has also attained the cessation of happiness, also the earlier cessation of suffering, also the disappearance of former joy and grief, also neither suffering nor happiness, also equanimity and mindful purification, and also abides having attained the fourth jhāna. That bhikṣu who abides in the fourth jhāna approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have attained the cessation of happiness, you too have had the earlier cessation of suffering, you too have had the disappearance of former joy and grief, you too have attained neither suffering nor happiness, equanimity, and mindful purification, you too have attained the fourth jhāna, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have attained the cessation of happiness,' up to 'you too have attained the fourth jhāna, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters and abides in the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'Space is infinite.' He might think: 'I abide having attained the sphere of infinite space.' But another bhikṣu has not completely transcended perceptions of form, has not had the cessation of perceptions of resistance, has not ceased attending to perceptions of diversity, has not entered the sphere of infinite space, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of infinite space approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended perceptions of form, you have not had the cessation of perceptions of resistance, you have not ceased attending to perceptions of diversity, you have not entered the sphere of infinite space, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended perceptions of form either, you have not had the cessation of perceptions of resistance either, you have not ceased attending to perceptions of diversity either, you have not entered the sphere of infinite space either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters and abides in the sphere of infinite space. Another bhikṣu has also completely transcended perceptions of form, also with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, also not attending to perceptions of diversity, and also enters and abides in the sphere of infinite space. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of infinite space approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended perceptions of form, you too have had the cessation of perceptions of resistance, you too have ceased attending to perceptions of diversity, you too have entered the sphere of infinite space, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended perceptions of form, you too have had the cessation of perceptions of resistance, you too have ceased attending to perceptions of diversity, you too have entered the sphere of infinite space, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, enters and abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking 'Consciousness is infinite.' He might think: 'I abide having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness.' But another bhikṣu has not completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, has not entered the sphere of infinite consciousness, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, you have not entered the sphere of infinite consciousness, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of infinite space either, you have not entered the sphere of infinite consciousness either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, enters and abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Another bhikṣu has also completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, and also enters and abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, you too have entered the sphere of infinite consciousness, and you too abide therein.'
