Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, you too have entered the sphere of infinite consciousness, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, enters and abides in the sphere of nothingness, thinking 'There is nothing whatsoever.' He might think: 'I abide having attained the sphere of nothingness.' But another bhikṣu has not completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, has not entered the sphere of nothingness, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of nothingness approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, you have not entered the sphere of nothingness, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness either, you have not entered the sphere of nothingness either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, enters and abides in the sphere of nothingness. Another bhikṣu has also completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, and also enters and abides in the sphere of nothingness. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of nothingness approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, you too have entered the sphere of nothingness, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, you too have entered the sphere of nothingness, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and abides in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. He might think: 'I abide having attained the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.' But another bhikṣu has not completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, has not entered the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and does not abide therein. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception approaches that other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, you have not entered the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and you do not abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you have not completely transcended the sphere of nothingness either, you have not entered the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception either, and you do not abide therein either.' Thus they dispute with each other. This is called the dharma for dispute.

"What is the dharma for harmony? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and abides in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Another bhikṣu has also completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, and also enters and abides in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. That bhikṣu who abides in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception approaches the other bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, you too have entered the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and you too abide therein.' Then that other bhikṣu approaches the first bhikṣu and says: 'Venerable one, you too have completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, you too have entered the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and you too abide therein.' Thus they are in harmony with each other. This is called the dharma for harmony.

"This is what I call the dharma for harmony and the dharma for dispute."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (13) Sūtra on Explaining the Foundations

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the dharma of explaining the foundations. Listen well, listen well, and reflect carefully on it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the dharma of explaining the foundations? A person might conceive evil in thought, speak evil in speech, and perform evil in action. Having conceived evil in thought, spoken evil in speech, and performed evil in action, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell. Another person might also conceive evil in thought, speak evil in speech, and perform evil in action. Having conceived evil in thought, spoken evil in speech, and performed evil in action, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person is reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world.

"If someone says: 'Whoever conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action will, upon the disintegration of the body after death, definitely go to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and fall into hell,' I do not grant this. If someone says: 'Whoever conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action will, upon the disintegration of the body after death, definitely be reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world,' I do not grant this either. Why is that? Because karmic actions are not fixed in their results. There are evil actions that are experienced as leading to a lower realm, and there are evil actions that are experienced as not leading to a lower realm.

"Furthermore, a person might conceive good in thought, speak good in speech, and perform good in action. Having conceived good in thought, spoken good in speech, and performed good in action, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a good destiny and is reborn in a heavenly world. Another person might also conceive good in thought, speak good in speech, and perform good in action. Having conceived good in thought, spoken good in speech, and performed good in action, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell.

"If someone says: 'Whoever conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action will, upon the disintegration of the body after death, definitely go to a good destiny and be reborn in a heavenly world,' I do not grant this. If someone says: 'Whoever conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action will, upon the disintegration of the body after death, definitely go to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and fall into hell,' I do not grant this either. Why is that? Because karmic actions are not fixed in their results. There are good actions that are experienced as leading to a good destiny, and there are good actions that are experienced as not leading to a good destiny.

"Bhikṣus, that person who conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action, and who upon the disintegration of the body after death, goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell: either previously, that person created unwholesome karmic actions that are to bear results and lead to feeling; or at the time of dying, evil wrong views arose; or at the end of life, evil wrong views arose. Because of this, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell.

"Bhikṣus, if a person conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action, that person must experience the results of those actions, either in this present life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life.

"Bhikṣus, that person who conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action, and who upon the disintegration of the body after death, is reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world: either previously, that person created wholesome karmic actions that are to bear results and lead to feeling; or at the time of dying, right views arose; or at the end of life, right views arose. Because of this, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person is reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world.

"Bhikṣus, if a person conceives evil in thought, speaks evil in speech, and performs evil in action, that person must experience the results of those actions, either in this present life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life.

"Bhikṣus, that person who conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action, and who upon the disintegration of the body after death, goes to a good destiny and is reborn in a heavenly world: either previously, that person created wholesome karmic actions that are to bear results and lead to feeling; or at the time of dying, right views arose; or at the end of life, right views arose. Because of this, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a good destiny and is reborn in a heavenly world.

"Bhikṣus, if a person conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action, that person must experience the results of those actions, either in this present life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life.

"Bhikṣus, that person who conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action, and who upon the disintegration of the body after death, goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell: either previously, that person created unwholesome karmic actions that are to bear results and lead to feeling; or at the time of dying, evil wrong views arose; or at the end of life, evil wrong views arose. Because of this, upon the disintegration of the body after death, that person goes to a lower realm, an evil destiny, and falls into hell.

"Bhikṣus, if a person conceives good in thought, speaks good in speech, and performs good in action, that person must experience the results of those actions, either in this present life, or in the next life, or in a subsequent life."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (14) Sūtra on Rāhula

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula went to the World-Honored One, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One addressed Rāhula: "Do you know how to contemplate the internal bases, the external bases, and the internal and external bases?"

Rāhula said: "I do not yet know, World-Honored One. I do not yet know, Well-Gone One."

The World-Honored One admonished Rāhula: "You should learn how to contemplate the internal bases, the external bases, and the internal and external bases."

Having received the teaching, Rāhula paid homage at the Buddha's feet, rose from his seat, and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula, in a secluded and quiet place, reflected on the teaching and thought: "The World-Honored One admonished me, saying: 'Learn how to contemplate the internal bases, the external bases, and the internal and external bases.' I should now go to the Venerable Śāriputra."

The Venerable Rāhula then went to the Venerable Śāriputra, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. He said to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable one, how does one contemplate the internal bases, the external bases, and the internal and external bases?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said to Rāhula: "Rāhula, do you know the five aggregates of clinging?"

Rāhula said: "I do not yet know, Venerable one."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Rāhula, there are five aggregates of clinging. The first is the aggregate of form, the second is the aggregate of feeling, the third is the aggregate of perception, the fourth is the aggregate of mental formations, and the fifth is the aggregate of consciousness. Rāhula, you should contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self."

Rāhula, having received this instruction from the Venerable Śāriputra, paid homage at his feet, rose from his seat, and returned to the World-Honored One, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. He said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I went to the Venerable Śāriputra and asked about the contemplation of the internal bases, the external bases, and the internal and external bases. The Venerable Śāriputra asked me: 'Rāhula, do you know the five aggregates of clinging?' I said: 'I do not yet know.' The Venerable Śāriputra said to me: 'Rāhula, there are five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Rāhula, you should contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self.'"

The World-Honored One asked Rāhula: "You heard what Śāriputra taught. What benefit did you obtain? What did you realize?"

Rāhula said to the World-Honored One: "I contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent, I understood that the aggregate of form is also suffering. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent and suffering, I contemplated the aggregate of form as non-self. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, no longer did I perceive the aggregate of form as self, as belonging to self, or as within self, or self as within the aggregate of form. I truly contemplated it with right wisdom as it really is. Regarding the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, the contemplation is likewise."

The World-Honored One praised Rāhula: "Good, good! Rāhula, you should further cultivate this contemplation of the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self, and thereby you will destroy the arising of conceit."

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula, having heard the Buddha's teaching, went to a secluded and quiet place, a forest, or under a tree, or in an empty room, sat cross-legged with body upright, established mindfulness before him, and contemplated the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, as non-self. He contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent, he understood that the aggregate of form is also suffering. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent and suffering, he contemplated the aggregate of form as non-self. Having contemplated the aggregate of form as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, no longer did he perceive the aggregate of form as self, as belonging to self, or as within self, or self as within the aggregate of form. He truly contemplated it with right wisdom as it really is. Regarding the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, the contemplation was likewise.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula, contemplating in this way, his mind was liberated from the outflows, without further clinging. With liberation from the outflows of sensual desire, liberation from the outflows of becoming, and liberation from the outflows of ignorance, in liberation he knew: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being."

The Venerable Rāhula became an arhat.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Rāhula and the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (15) Sūtra on Contemplation

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is unable to skillfully contemplate the mind of another, he should skillfully contemplate his own mind. How does a bhikṣu skillfully contemplate his own mind? Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu should contemplate thus: 'Do I often generate and practice covetousness or not? Do I often generate and practice ill-will or not? Do I often generate and practice sloth and torpor or not? Do I often generate and practice restlessness and remorse or not? Do I often generate and practice doubt or not? Do I often generate and practice anger or not? Do I often generate and practice defiled thoughts or not? Do I often generate and practice bodily defilement or not? Do I often generate and practice laziness or not? Do I often generate and practice lack of concentration or not?'

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, upon self-examination, finds that he often generates and practices these evil, unwholesome dharmas, then that bhikṣu, for the sake of abandoning these evil, unwholesome dharmas, should swiftly apply effort with increased desire, vigor, and diligence. It is like a person whose clothes or hair have caught fire; for the sake of extinguishing the fire, he would swiftly apply increased effort, desire, vigor, and diligence. In the same way, that bhikṣu, for the sake of abandoning those evil, unwholesome dharmas, should swiftly apply effort with increased desire, vigor, and diligence.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, upon self-examination, finds that he does not often generate and practice these evil, unwholesome dharmas, then that bhikṣu should abide in joyful effort and should, day and night, cultivate and practice wholesome dharmas.

"It is like a person who, upon examining himself, sees only a pure reflection. That person is greatly delighted. In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, upon self-examination, finds that he does not often generate and practice these evil, unwholesome dharmas, then that bhikṣu should abide in joyful effort and should, day and night, cultivate and practice wholesome dharmas."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (16) Sūtra on Kālāma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and he arrived at a village of the Kālāmas called Kesamutti.

At that time, the Kālāma people of Kesamutti heard: "The śramaṇa Gautama, son of the Śākya clan, having left the household of the Śākyas, shaved his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, and, out of faith, left home to practice the path. He is now traveling in the country of Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus and has arrived at our Kesamutti village. This Venerable Gautama has a great reputation. It is said of him: 'This is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Awakened One, the World-Honored One. Among the various gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, from gods to humans, he has by himself realized with direct knowledge and declared it for others. The dharma he teaches is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life.' It would be good for us to go and see such a venerable one."

Then the Kālāma people of Kesamutti, each together with their entourage, went toward where the Buddha was. Some of them, upon arriving, paid homage at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat to one side. Some joined their palms and paid respect to the Buddha, and sat to one side. Some announced their name and clan from a distance, and sat to one side. Some silently sat to one side.

Having sat to one side, the Kālāma people of Kesamutti said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who come to our Kesamutti. They expound and illuminate only their own doctrines, but disparage, attack, belittle, and dismiss the doctrines of others. World-Honored One, then there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who also come to our Kesamutti. They too expound and illuminate only their own doctrines, but disparage, attack, belittle, and dismiss the doctrines of others. World-Honored One, we have doubts and perplexity about all of them. Among these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who speaks truth and who speaks falsehood?"

The World-Honored One said: "Kālāmas, you should indeed be doubtful, you should indeed be perplexed. When there is a matter for doubt, perplexity naturally arises. Kālāmas, do not accept something merely because of oral tradition. Do not accept something merely because of lineage of teaching. Do not accept something merely because of hearsay. Do not accept something merely because it is in a collection of scriptures. Do not accept something merely because of logical reasoning. Do not accept something merely because of inferential reasoning. Do not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons. Do not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view. Do not accept something merely because the speaker appears competent. Do not accept something merely because you think, 'This śramaṇa is our teacher.'

"Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are unwholesome, these dharmas are blameworthy, these dharmas are censured by the wise, and if undertaken and practiced, these dharmas lead to harm and suffering.' If so, then you should abandon them.

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person generates greed, is it for benefit or for harm?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For harm, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this greedy person, being overcome by greed, with mind ensnared, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery with others' spouses, speaks falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term harm and suffering?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person generates anger, is it for benefit or for harm?"

"For harm, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this angry person, being overcome by anger, with mind ensnared, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery with others' spouses, speaks falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term harm and suffering?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person generates delusion, is it for benefit or for harm?"

"For harm, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this deluded person, being overcome by delusion, with mind ensnared, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery with others' spouses, speaks falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term harm and suffering?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these dharmas wholesome or unwholesome?"

"Unwholesome, World-Honored One."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameworthy, World-Honored One."

"Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"

"Censured by the wise, World-Honored One."

"If undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What do you think?"

"World-Honored One, if undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering. This is what we think."

"Therefore, Kālāmas, I said earlier: 'Do not accept something merely because of oral tradition, do not accept something merely because of lineage of teaching, do not accept something merely because of hearsay, do not accept something merely because it is in a collection of scriptures, do not accept something merely because of logical reasoning, do not accept something merely because of inferential reasoning, do not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons, do not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view, do not accept something merely because the speaker appears competent, do not accept something merely because you think this śramaṇa is our teacher. You should know for yourselves: these dharmas are unwholesome, these dharmas are blameworthy, these dharmas are censured by the wise, and if undertaken and practiced, these dharmas lead to harm and suffering. If so, then you should abandon them.'

"Kālāmas, do not accept something merely because of oral tradition. Do not accept something merely because of lineage of teaching. Do not accept something merely because of hearsay. Do not accept something merely because it is in a collection of scriptures. Do not accept something merely because of logical reasoning. Do not accept something merely because of inferential reasoning. Do not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons. Do not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view. Do not accept something merely because the speaker appears competent. Do not accept something merely because you think, 'This śramaṇa is our teacher.'

"Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are wholesome, these dharmas are blameless, these dharmas are praised by the wise, and if undertaken and practiced, these dharmas lead to benefit and happiness.' If so, then you should accept them and abide in them.

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person is without greed, is it for benefit or for harm?"

"For benefit, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this person without greed, not being overcome by greed, with mind not ensnared, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery with others' spouses, does not speak falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person is without anger, is it for benefit or for harm?"

"For benefit, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this person without anger, not being overcome by anger, with mind not ensnared, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery with others' spouses, does not speak falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When a person is without delusion, is it for benefit or for harm?"

"For benefit, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, this person without delusion, not being overcome by delusion, with mind not ensnared, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery with others' spouses, does not speak falsehood, and instigates others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these dharmas wholesome or unwholesome?"

"Wholesome, World-Honored One."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameless, World-Honored One."

"Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"

"Praised by the wise, World-Honored One."

"If undertaken and practiced, do they lead to benefit and happiness, or not? What do you think?"

"World-Honored One, if undertaken and practiced, they lead to benefit and happiness. This is what we think."

"Therefore, Kālāmas, I said earlier: 'Do not accept something merely because of oral tradition, do not accept something merely because of lineage of teaching, do not accept something merely because of hearsay, do not accept something merely because it is in a collection of scriptures, do not accept something merely because of logical reasoning, do not accept something merely because of inferential reasoning, do not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons, do not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view, do not accept something merely because the speaker appears competent, do not accept something merely because you think this śramaṇa is our teacher. You should know for yourselves: these dharmas are wholesome, these dharmas are blameless, these dharmas are praised by the wise, and if undertaken and practiced, these dharmas lead to benefit and happiness. If so, then you should accept them and abide in them.'

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple who is free from covetousness, free from ill-will, not deluded, with right mindfulness and right awareness, pervades one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and all around. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, great, boundless, free from hatred, and free from enmity, he pervades everywhere and abides therein. In the same way, he pervades with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and with equanimity, pervading one direction and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, above, below, and all around. With a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, great, boundless, free from hatred, and free from enmity, he pervades everywhere and abides therein.

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple who has a mind free from enmity and free from ill-will, a mind undefiled and a mind purified, obtains four assurances in this present life. The first assurance: 'If there is an afterlife, and if there is fruit and retribution for good and evil actions, then upon the disintegration of the body after death, I shall be reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world.' He obtains this first assurance. The second assurance: 'If there is no afterlife, and if there is no fruit and retribution for good and evil actions, then in this present life I abide without enmity, without ill-will, without trouble, and in happiness.' He obtains this second assurance. The third assurance: 'If one who does evil receives evil results, and I have no evil intention toward anyone, then how could suffering come to me, one who has done no evil?' He obtains this third assurance. The fourth assurance: 'If one who does evil does not receive evil results, then I see myself purified in both ways.' He obtains this fourth assurance.

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple who has a mind free from enmity and free from ill-will, a mind undefiled and a mind purified, obtains these four assurances in this present life."

The Kālāmas said to the World-Honored One: "So it is, World-Honored One. The noble disciple who has a mind free from enmity and free from ill-will, a mind undefiled and a mind purified, obtains these four assurances in this present life. The first assurance: 'If there is an afterlife, and if there is fruit and retribution for good and evil actions, then upon the disintegration of the body after death, I shall be reborn in a good destiny, in a heavenly world.' He obtains this first assurance. The second assurance: 'If there is no afterlife, and if there is no fruit and retribution for good and evil actions, then in this present life I abide without enmity, without ill-will, without trouble, and in happiness.' He obtains this second assurance. The third assurance: 'If one who does evil receives evil results, and I have no evil intention toward anyone, then how could suffering come to me, one who has done no evil?' He obtains this third assurance. The fourth assurance: 'If one who does evil does not receive evil results, then I see myself purified in both ways.' He obtains this fourth assurance.

"World-Honored One, it is excellent, it is excellent! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. In the same way, the World-Honored One has, through various methods, expounded the Dharma and illuminated its meaning. We now take refuge in the Buddha, in the Dharma, and in the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept us as lay followers who, from this day forward and for the rest of our lives, take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Kālāma people of Kesamutti and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (17) Sūtra on Mahākātyāyana

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, rising from his afternoon meditation, went to the World-Honored One, paid homage at his feet, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One said to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana: "Kātyāyana, I admonish you: Kātyāyana, I instruct you. Kātyāyana, will you accept from me the brief teaching?"

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One admonish me, may the Well-Gone One instruct me. Having heard the teaching, I shall accept it and practice it in a secluded place."

The World-Honored One said: "Kātyāyana, a bhikṣu should not be distracted and confused by the eye when seeing a form, should not get a distracted mind, and should not let the mind be scattered. He should guard the faculty of the eye. For one who does not guard the faculty of the eye, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome dharmas will flow in. He should practice restraint. He should guard the faculty of the eye. In the same way, regarding the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental objects, a bhikṣu should not be distracted and confused, should not get a distracted mind, and should not let the mind be scattered. He should guard the faculty of the mind. For one who does not guard the faculty of the mind, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome dharmas will flow in. He should practice restraint. He should guard the faculty of the mind.

"Kātyāyana, you should train in this way. Kātyāyana, when you have trained in this way, Kātyāyana, when walking, you should simply walk. When standing, you should simply stand. When sitting, you should simply sit. When lying down, you should simply lie down. Kātyāyana, you should train in this way."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having received the Buddha's brief teaching, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, rose from his seat, departed, and went to a secluded and quiet place, a forest, or under a tree, or in an empty room. He diligently cultivated this practice, living in seclusion, without negligence, and applied himself to the practice. He shaved his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, and out of faith left home to practice the path, solely for the purpose of which sons of good families rightly leave home to practice the path. In this very life, with his own direct knowledge, he realized, verified, and accomplished it, and he knew: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana became an arhat, and having attained arhatship, his mind was liberated.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Ven

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 2

---

## (6) Sūtra on the Destinations of Good Persons, Sixth of the Seven Dharmas Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the seven destinations to which good persons proceed and the nirvāṇa without remainder. Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect well upon this." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? A bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like burning chaff: as soon as it catches fire, it is immediately extinguished. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. This is called the first destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and are immediately extinguished upon rising. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. This is called the second destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air, and returning downward from above, are extinguished before reaching the ground. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. This is called the third destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall to the ground, where they are extinguished. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa upon taking birth. This is called the fourth destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a small pile of kindling and grass, where they smoke and flame, and having flamed, are extinguished. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa with exertion. This is called the fifth destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a large pile of kindling and grass, where they smoke and flame, and having consumed all the fuel, are extinguished. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa without exertion. This is called the sixth destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, yet has not yet realized it. A bhikṣu who practices thus, to what destination does he proceed? It is like a piece of iron, heated through and thoroughly glowing: if struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a large pile of kindling and grass, where they smoke and flame, and having flamed, burn villages and towns, cities and fortresses, mountains and forests, and open wilderness. Having burned villages and towns, cities and fortresses, mountains and forests, and open wilderness, the fire either reaches a road, or reaches water, or reaches flat ground, and is extinguished. Know that, bhikṣus, it is likewise so. With a slight conceit not yet exhausted, having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa by ascending to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. This is called the seventh destination to which good persons proceed, which truly exists in the world.

"What is nirvāṇa without remainder? A bhikṣu should practice as follows: 'The self has no self, nor is there anything belonging to a self. In the future there will be no self, nor anything belonging to a self.' What already exists one cuts off; having cut it off, one attains relinquishment. Having pleasure, one is not defiled by it; encountering combination, one is not attached. One who practices thus has seen the unsurpassed cessation through wisdom, and has already realized it. I say that bhikṣu does not go to the east, does not go to the west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below, but right in the present life attains the cessation and final extinction.

"What I have previously spoken of as the seven destinations to which good persons proceed and nirvāṇa without remainder has been explained on account of this."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Destinations of Good Persons, Sixth.

---

## (7) Madhyamāgama, Seven Dharmas Chapter: Sūtra on Worldly Merit, Seventh

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kauśāmbī, staying in the Ghoṣila Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahācunda, in the late afternoon, rose from meditation and went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, he paid respects and sat down to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is it possible to set forth worldly merit?"

The World-Honored One said: "It is possible. Cunda, there are seven worldly merits that bring great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue. What are the seven? Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family donate to the bhikṣu Sangha dwelling places, halls, and pavilions, this, Cunda, is called the first worldly merit, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Furthermore, Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family furnish dwelling places with beds and seats, carpets, rugs, felt mats, bedding, and sleeping materials, this, Cunda, is called the second worldly merit, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Furthermore, Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family furnish dwelling places with all manner of new, clean, and fine robes, this, Cunda, is called the third worldly merit, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Furthermore, Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family furnish dwelling places and constantly provide the community with morning gruel and midday meals, and also supply park attendants and servants, and when there is wind, rain, cold, or snow, they personally go to the park to increase their offerings, so that the bhikṣu Sangha, having eaten, is not troubled by wind, rain, cold, or snow soaking their robes, and day and night they dwell in peace and happiness, in meditative calm and contemplation, this, Cunda, is called the seventh worldly merit, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family have obtained these seven worldly merits, whether going or coming, whether standing or sitting, whether sleeping or waking, whether by day or by night, their merit is constantly generated, ever increasing and ever expanding. Cunda, it is like the waters of the Ganges River, flowing from their source into the great ocean, and in between, growing ever deeper and ever broader. Cunda, in the same way, when faithful sons or daughters of good family have obtained these seven worldly merits, whether going or coming, whether standing or sitting, whether sleeping or waking, whether by day or by night, their merit is constantly generated, ever increasing and ever expanding."

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahācunda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, knelt upright with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is it possible to set forth merit that transcends the world?"

The World-Honored One said: "It is possible. Cunda, there are seven further merits that transcend the world, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue. What are the seven? Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family hear that the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples are residing in a certain place, and upon hearing this they rejoice and are filled with the utmost delight, this, Cunda, is called the first merit transcending the world, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Furthermore, Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family hear that the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples intend to come from that place to this place, and upon hearing this they rejoice and are filled with the utmost delight, this, Cunda, is called the second merit transcending the world, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Furthermore, Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family hear that the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples have already come from that place to this place, and upon hearing this they rejoice and are filled with the utmost delight, and with a pure mind they personally go to pay their respects, venerate and make offerings, and having made offerings, take the threefold refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Bhikṣu Sangha, and undertake the precepts, this, Cunda, is called the seventh merit transcending the world, bringing great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Cunda, when faithful sons or daughters of good family have obtained these seven worldly merits and also the seven further merits transcending the world, their merit cannot be counted. One cannot say 'there is this much merit, this much fruit of merit, this much reward of merit.' It is simply unlimited, immeasurable, and one cannot reckon the quantity of this great merit. Cunda, it is like the five rivers that flow from the Jambudvīpa continent: the first is called the Ganges, the second the Yamunā, the third the Sarabhū, the fourth the Aciravatī, and the fifth the Mahī. They flow into the great ocean, and in between, the water cannot be counted. One cannot say 'there are this many liters and bushels.' It is simply unlimited, immeasurable, and one cannot reckon the quantity of that great water. Cunda, in the same way, when faithful sons or daughters of good family have obtained these seven worldly merits and also the seven further merits transcending the world, their merit cannot be counted. One cannot say 'there is this much merit, this much fruit of merit, this much reward of merit.' It is simply unlimited, immeasurable, and one cannot reckon the quantity of this great merit."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"The river Ganges, pure and easy to ford;
The ocean, rich in treasures, king of all waters.
Just as the river waters are honored by people of the world,
And all streams flow and are drawn into the great ocean;
So too does a person who gives robes, food, and drink,
Beds, cushions, mats, and various seats,
Gain immeasurable merit, leading to a wondrous destination,
Just as the river waters are drawn into the great ocean."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Mahācunda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Worldly Merit, Seventh.

---

## (8) Madhyamāgama, Seven Dharmas Chapter: Sūtra on the Seven Suns, Eighth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Vaiśālī, staying in the grove of the Nāya clan.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "All conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them. Why is this so? There are times when it does not rain, and when it does not rain, all trees, the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and plants all wither, crumble, and perish completely, unable to endure. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when two suns appear in the world. When two suns appear, all ditches, channels, streams, and rivers all dry up completely, unable to endure. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when three suns appear in the world. When three suns appear, all the great rivers dry up completely, unable to endure. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when four suns appear in the world. When four suns appear, the great springs from which flow the five rivers of Jambudvīpa, the first called the Ganges, the second the Yamunā, the third the Sarabhū, the fourth the Aciravatī, and the fifth the Mahī, those great springs all dry up completely, unable to endure. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when five suns appear in the world. When five suns appear, the water of the great ocean recedes by one hundred yojanas, and continues to recede down to seven hundred yojanas. When five suns appear, the remaining ocean water is seven hundred yojanas deep, and continues to recede down to one hundred yojanas. When five suns appear, the ocean water recedes by the height of one tāla tree, and continues to recede down to seven tāla trees. When five suns appear, the remaining ocean water is the depth of seven tāla trees, and continues to recede down to one tāla tree. When five suns appear, the ocean water recedes to the depth of one person, and continues to recede down to seven persons. When five suns appear, the remaining ocean water is the depth of seven persons, and continues to recede down to one person. When five suns appear, the ocean water recedes to neck level, to shoulder level, to waist level, to hip level, to knee level, to ankle level. There are times when the ocean water is entirely consumed, not even enough to submerge a finger. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when six suns appear in the world. When six suns appear, the entire great earth and Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, all begin to smoke, the smoke merging into one mass. It is like when a potter first fires his kiln and smoke rises up, merging into one mass. In the same way, when six suns appear, the entire great earth and Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, all begin to smoke, the smoke merging into one mass. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there are times when seven suns appear in the world. When seven suns appear, the entire great earth and Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, blaze and burn thoroughly, merging into one conflagration. When seven suns appear, the entire great earth and Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, blaze and burn thoroughly, merging into one conflagration; the wind carries the flames upward, reaching even to the Brahmā heavens. At that time, the radiant gods who have recently been born in those heavens, who are unfamiliar with the formation and destruction of the world, who have never seen the formation and destruction of the world, who do not know the formation and destruction of the world, upon seeing the great fire, are all terrified with their hair standing on end, and they think: 'Will the fire not reach here? Will the fire not reach here?' The gods who were born earlier, who are familiar with the formation and destruction of the world, who have seen the formation and destruction of the world, who know the formation and destruction of the world, upon seeing the great fire, console the other gods, saying: 'Do not be afraid. The fire by its nature reaches only so far and will never come here.' When seven suns appear, Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, collapses, scatters, disintegrates, and is destroyed for a hundred yojanas, for two hundred yojanas, for three hundred yojanas, up to seven hundred yojanas, collapsing, scattering, disintegrating, and being completely destroyed. When seven suns appear, Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, and this great earth are burned, consumed, and vanish, leaving neither embers nor ashes. It is like burning ghee, which when heated is entirely consumed, leaving neither smoke nor residue. In the same way, when seven suns appear, Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, and this great earth leave neither embers nor ashes. Therefore, all conditioned things are impermanent, are phenomena that do not endure, are phenomena that quickly change, and are phenomena that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not take delight in conditioned things; one should be wearied of and disgusted with them, and should seek to relinquish them, should seek liberation from them.

"I now tell you that Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, shall collapse and be completely destroyed. Who could believe this? Only those who have seen the truth. I now tell you that the water of the great ocean shall dry up and be completely exhausted. Who could believe this? Only those who have seen the truth. I now tell you that the entire great earth shall burn and be completely consumed. Who could believe this? Only those who have seen the truth. Why is this so? Bhikṣus, in the past there was a great teacher named Sunetra, who was revered as master by the ascetics of other paths. He had abandoned sensual desire and attained supernormal powers. The great teacher Sunetra had countless hundreds of thousands of disciples. The great teacher Sunetra taught his disciples the way to the Brahmā world. When the great teacher Sunetra taught the way to the Brahmā world, those of his disciples who did not fully practice the Dharma, upon their death, were reborn among the Four Great Kings, or among the Thirty-Three Gods, or among the Yāma Gods, or among the Tuṣita Gods, or among the Nirmāṇarati Gods, or among the Paranirmitavaśavartin Gods. When the great teacher Sunetra taught the way to the Brahmā world, those of his disciples who did fully practice the Dharma cultivated the four Brahmā-abodes, abandoned desire, and upon their death were reborn in the Brahmā heaven. At that time, the great teacher Sunetra thought: 'I should not arrive together with my disciples in the same place in the next life. I should now further cultivate the higher practice of loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness, upon my death I shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven.' At a later time, the great teacher Sunetra further cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness, upon his death he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven. The great teacher Sunetra and his disciples did not practice the path in vain; they obtained great rewards.

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? The great teacher Sunetra of the past, who was revered as master by the ascetics of other paths, who had abandoned sensual desire and attained supernormal powers: do you suppose he was someone else? Do not think so. Know that he was none other than myself. At that time I was named the great teacher Sunetra, revered as master by the ascetics of other paths, having abandoned sensual desire and attained supernormal powers. At that time I had countless hundreds of thousands of disciples. At that time I taught my disciples the way to the Brahmā world. When I taught the way to the Brahmā world, those of my disciples who did not fully practice the Dharma, upon their death, were reborn among the Four Great Kings, or among the Thirty-Three Gods, or among the Yāma Gods, or among the Tuṣita Gods, or among the Nirmāṇarati Gods, or among the Paranirmitavaśavartin Gods. When I taught the way to the Brahmā world, those of my disciples who did fully practice the Dharma cultivated the four Brahmā-abodes, abandoned desire, and upon their death were reborn in the Brahmā heaven. At that time I thought: 'I should not arrive together with my disciples in the same place in the next life. I should now further cultivate the higher practice of loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness, upon my death I shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven.' At a later time, I further cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher practice of loving-kindness, upon my death I was reborn in the Ābhāsvara heaven. At that time, I and my disciples did not practice the path in vain; we obtained great rewards. At that time, I personally walked that path, for my own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking benefit and welfare for gods and humans, seeking peace and happiness. But the Dharma I taught at that time did not reach the ultimate, was not ultimately pure, was not the ultimate holy life, was not the ultimate completion of the holy life. At that time, I was not free from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow, nor had I been able to attain liberation from all suffering.

"Bhikṣus, I have now appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, Trainer of Persons to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One. I now benefit myself and also benefit others, benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking benefit and welfare for gods and humans, seeking peace and happiness. The Dharma I now teach has reached the ultimate, is ultimately pure, is the ultimate holy life, is the ultimate completion of the holy life. I have now been freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow. I have now attained liberation from all suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Seven Suns, Eighth.

---

## (9) Madhyamāgama, Seven Dharmas Chapter: Sūtra on the Seven Chariots, Ninth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove Monastery, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus for the rains retreat. The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was also undertaking the rains retreat in his native land. At that time, the bhikṣus of that native land, having completed the rains retreat, after the three months had passed, having mended their robes, gathered their robes and took up their bowls, departed from the native land toward Rājagṛha. Traveling onward, they arrived in Rājagṛha and stayed at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣus from the native land went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated in reverence, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Bhikṣus, from where have you come? Where did you undertake the rains retreat?"

The bhikṣus from the native land replied: "World-Honored One, we have come from the native land. We undertook the rains retreat in the native land."

The World-Honored One asked: "Among the bhikṣus of that native land, which bhikṣu is praised by the other bhikṣus as one who himself is of few desires and content, and who praises few desires and contentment; who himself dwells in seclusion, and who praises seclusion; who himself is diligent, and who praises diligence; who himself has right mindfulness, and who praises right mindfulness; who himself has concentration, and who praises concentration; who himself has wisdom, and who praises wisdom; who himself has exhausted the outflows, and who praises the exhaustion of the outflows; who himself encourages, inspires, and accomplishes joy in others, and who praises encouraging, inspiring, and accomplishing joy?"

The bhikṣus from the native land replied: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta is the one praised by the bhikṣus in that native land as one who himself is of few desires and content, and who praises few desires and contentment; who himself dwells in seclusion, and who praises seclusion; who himself is diligent, and who praises diligence; who himself has right mindfulness, and who praises right mindfulness; who himself has concentration, and who praises concentration; who himself has wisdom, and who praises wisdom; who himself has exhausted the outflows, and who praises the exhaustion of the outflows; who himself encourages, inspires, and accomplishes joy in others, and who praises encouraging, inspiring, and accomplishing joy."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting in the assembly. The Venerable Śāriputra thought: "The World-Honored One has questioned the bhikṣus of the native land just as one would inquire about such matters, and the bhikṣus of the native land have greatly praised the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta as one who himself is of few desires and content, and who praises few desires and contentment; who himself dwells in seclusion, and who praises seclusion; who himself is diligent, and who praises diligence; who himself has right mindfulness, and who praises right mindfulness; who himself has concentration, and who praises concentration; who himself has wisdom, and who praises wisdom; who himself has exhausted the outflows, and who praises the exhaustion of the outflows; who himself encourages, inspires, and accomplishes joy in others, and who praises encouraging, inspiring, and accomplishing joy."

The Venerable Śāriputra further thought: "When will I be able to meet with the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and discuss some points of the Dharma with him? Perhaps he will be willing to answer my questions."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having completed the rains retreat in Rājagṛha, after the three months had passed, having mended his robes, gathered his robes and took up his bowl, departed from Rājagṛha toward Śrāvastī. Traveling onward, he arrived in Śrāvastī and stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus from the native land stayed together in Rājagṛha for a few days, then gathered their robes and took up their bowls, headed toward Śrāvastī. Traveling onward, they arrived in Śrāvastī and together stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, having completed the rains retreat in the native land, after the three months had passed, having mended his robes, gathered his robes and took up his bowl, departed from the native land toward Śrāvastī. Traveling onward, he arrived in Śrāvastī and also stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated in reverence, and before the Tathāgata spread out his sitting cloth and sat cross-legged.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked another bhikṣu: "Friend, which one is the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta?"

The bhikṣus told the Venerable Śāriputra: "Indeed, Venerable One, the one sitting before the Tathāgata, fair-skinned with a prominent nose, like a parrot's beak, that is he."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having noted Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta's appearance, well committed it to memory.

The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, the next morning at dawn, put on his robes and took up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms. Having eaten, after midday, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth on his shoulder, and went to the Andhavana grove, to a place for walking meditation. The Venerable Śāriputra likewise, the next morning at dawn, put on his robes and took up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms. Having eaten, after midday, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth on his shoulder, and went to the Andhavana grove, to a place for walking meditation.

At that time, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta arrived at the Andhavana grove and, under a certain tree, spread out his sitting cloth and sat cross-legged. The Venerable Śāriputra also arrived at the Andhavana grove and, not far from Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, under a certain tree, spread out his sitting cloth and sat cross-legged.

The Venerable Śāriputra, in the late afternoon, rose from meditation and went to where the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta was. They exchanged greetings, and he sat to one side. He then asked the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta: "Friend, do you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama?"

He answered: "Yes, that is so."

"How is it, friend? Is it for the sake of purity of moral conduct that you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama?"

He answered: "No."

"Is it for the sake of purity of mind, or purity of view, or purity from doubt and uncertainty, or purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, or purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path, or purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, that you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama?"

He answered: "No."

He further asked: "Earlier I asked you whether you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama, and you said yes. Now I ask whether it is for the sake of purity of moral conduct that you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama, and you say no. Whether for the sake of purity of mind, or purity of view, or purity from doubt and uncertainty, or purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, or purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path, or purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, that you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama, and you say no. Then for what purpose do you practice the holy life under the Śramaṇa Gautama?"

He answered: "Friend, for the sake of nirvāṇa without remainder."

He further asked: "How is it, friend? Is it because of purity of moral conduct that the Śramaṇa Gautama sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder?"

He answered: "No."

"Is it because of purity of mind, or purity of view, or purity from doubt and uncertainty, or purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, or purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path, or purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, that the Śramaṇa Gautama sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder?"

He answered: "No."

He further asked: "Earlier I asked you whether it is because of purity of moral conduct that the Śramaṇa Gautama sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder, and you said no. Whether because of purity of mind, or purity of view, or purity from doubt and uncertainty, or purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, or purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path, or purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, that the Śramaṇa Gautama sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder, and you said no. What then is the meaning of what you say? How should it be understood?"

He answered: "Friend, if it were because of purity of moral conduct that the World-Honored One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, set forth nirvāṇa without remainder, then he would be designating as 'without remainder' something that still has remainder. If because of purity of mind, or purity of view, or purity from doubt and uncertainty, or purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, or purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path, or purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, the World-Honored One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, set forth nirvāṇa without remainder, then he would be designating as 'without remainder' something that still has remainder. Friend, if, apart from these dharmas, the World-Honored One set forth nirvāṇa without remainder, then ordinary worldlings would also attain parinirvāṇa, since ordinary worldlings are also apart from these dharmas. Friend, rather, it is because of purity of moral conduct that one attains purity of mind; because of purity of mind that one attains purity of view; because of purity of view that one attains purity from doubt and uncertainty; because of purity from doubt and uncertainty that one attains purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path; because of purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path that one attains purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path; because of purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path that one attains purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path; and because of purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, the World-Honored One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder.

"Friend, listen further. In the past, King Prasenajit of Kosala was in Śrāvastī and had some business in Sāketa. He thought: 'By what means can I travel in a single day from Śrāvastī to Sāketa?' He further thought: 'I should now arrange seven chariots between Śrāvastī and Sāketa.' At that time, he arranged seven chariots between Śrāvastī and Sāketa. Having arranged the seven chariots, he departed from Śrāvastī, reached the first chariot, mounted the first chariot, and rode to the second chariot. He left the first chariot and mounted the second chariot, riding to the third chariot. He left the second chariot and mounted the third chariot, riding to the fourth chariot. He left the third chariot and mounted the fourth chariot, riding to the fifth chariot. He left the fourth chariot and mounted the fifth chariot, riding to the sixth chariot. He left the fifth chariot and mounted the sixth chariot, riding to the seventh chariot. Mounting the seventh chariot, in a single day he arrived in Sāketa.

"Having completed his business in Sāketa, surrounded by his great ministers, seated in the royal court, the ministers asked: 'How is it, Your Majesty? Did you travel in a single day from Śrāvastī to Sāketa?' The king said: 'Yes, that is so.' 'How is it, Your Majesty? Did you ride the first chariot all the way from Śrāvastī to Sāketa in a single day?' The king said: 'No.' 'Did you ride the second chariot, or the third, up to the seventh chariot, from Śrāvastī to Sāketa?' The king said: 'No.' How then, friend, should King Prasenajit of Kosala answer the further questions of his ministers?

"The king answered the ministers: 'I was in Śrāvastī and had business in Sāketa. I thought: "By what means can I travel in a single day from Śrāvastī to Sāketa?" I further thought: "I should now arrange seven chariots between Śrāvastī and Sāketa." At that time, I arranged seven chariots between Śrāvastī and Sāketa. Having arranged the seven chariots, I departed from Śrāvastī, reached the first chariot, mounted the first chariot, and rode to the second chariot. I left the first chariot and mounted the second chariot, riding to the third chariot. I left the second chariot and mounted the third chariot, riding to the fourth chariot. I left the third chariot and mounted the fourth chariot, riding to the fifth chariot. I left the fourth chariot and mounted the fifth chariot, riding to the sixth chariot. I left the fifth chariot and mounted the sixth chariot, riding to the seventh chariot. Mounting the seventh chariot, in a single day I arrived in Sāketa.'

"In this way, friend, King Prasenajit of Kosala answered the questions of his ministers in this manner. In the same way, friend, it is because of purity of moral conduct that one attains purity of mind; because of purity of mind that one attains purity of view; because of purity of view that one attains purity from doubt and uncertainty; because of purity from doubt and uncertainty that one attains purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path; because of purity of knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path that one attains purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path; because of purity of knowledge and vision of the course of the path that one attains purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path; and because of purity of knowledge through the cutting off along the course of the path, the World-Honored One sets forth nirvāṇa without remainder."

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta: "Friend, what is your name? How do your fellow practitioners of the holy life address you?"

The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta answered: "Friend, my given name is Puṇṇa. My mother's name is Mantāṇī, and so my fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta."

The Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent, excellent! The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, as a disciple of the Tathāgata, possesses wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness; is secure and fearless; has accomplished mastery; has attained great eloquence; has obtained the banner of the deathless; and in the realm of the deathless, has personally realized and accomplished the abiding. Because when I questioned you on the most profound meanings, you were able to answer them all. Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, your fellow practitioners of the holy life have gained great benefit by encountering you. They may visit you at any time and pay respects to you at any time. I too have gained great benefit, and may visit you and pay respects to you at any time. Your fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes and carry the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta on the crown of their heads, for they have gained great benefit. I too have gained great benefit, and may visit you and pay respects to you at any time."

The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta asked the Venerable Śāriputra: "Friend, what is your name? How do your fellow practitioners of the holy life address you?"

The Venerable Śāriputra answered: "Friend, my given name is Upatissa. My mother's name is Śārī, and so my fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Śāriputra."

The Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta exclaimed: "I have been conversing with a disciple of the World-Honored One without knowing it! I have been conversing with the second most honored without knowing it! I have been conversing with the General of the Dharma without knowing it! I have been conversing with one who turns the wheel of Dharma after it has been turned, the disciple, without knowing it! Had I known that you were the Venerable Śāriputra, I would not have been able to answer even a single sentence, let alone discourse at such depth! Excellent, excellent!
