The Venerable Śāriputra, as a disciple of the Tathāgata, possesses wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness; is secure and fearless; has accomplished mastery; has attained great eloquence; has obtained the banner of the deathless; and in the realm of the deathless, has personally realized and accomplished the abiding, because of the Venerable's profoundly deep questions. Venerable Śāriputra, your fellow practitioners of the holy life have gained great benefit by encountering you. They may visit you at any time and pay respects to you at any time. I too have gained great benefit, and may visit you and pay respects to you at any time. Your fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes and carry the Venerable Śāriputra on the crown of their heads, for they have gained great benefit. I too have gained great benefit, and may visit you and pay respects to you at any time."

Thus these two worthies praised and extolled each other. Having praised and commended each other with joy, they practiced accordingly, rose from their seats, and each returned to his own dwelling.

End of the Sūtra on the Seven Chariots, Ninth.

---

## (10) Madhyamāgama, Seven Dharmas Chapter: Sūtra on the Exhaustion of the Outflows, Tenth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kuru, in the Kuru town of Kammāssadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "It is through knowing and seeing that all outflows are exhausted, not through not knowing and not seeing. How is it through knowing and seeing that all outflows are exhausted? There is proper attention and improper attention. If one gives improper attention, then outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase. If one gives proper attention, then outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease.

"However, the unlearned ordinary person who has not heard the true Dharma, who has not encountered a genuine spiritual friend, who does not know the noble Dharma, who has not trained in the noble Dharma, who does not know the Dharma as it truly is: through improper attention, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase. Through proper attention, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease. Because he does not know the Dharma as it truly is, he attends to what should not be attended to, and does not attend to what should be attended to. Because he attends to what should not be attended to and does not attend to what should be attended to, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase.

"The well-learned noble disciple who has heard the true Dharma, who has encountered a genuine spiritual friend, who has trained in the noble Dharma, who knows the Dharma as it truly is: through improper attention, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase. Through proper attention, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will cease. Having known the Dharma as it truly is, what should not be attended to he does not attend to, and what should be attended to he does attend to. Because what should not be attended to he does not attend to, and what should be attended to he does attend to, outflows of desire that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those that have already arisen cease; outflows of existence and outflows of ignorance that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those that have already arisen cease.

"There are seven methods for cutting off outflows, afflictions, and grief. What are the seven? There are outflows to be cut off by seeing. There are outflows to be cut off by guarding. There are outflows to be cut off by avoiding. There are outflows to be cut off by using. There are outflows to be cut off by enduring. There are outflows to be cut off by removing. There are outflows to be cut off by cultivation.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by seeing? The unlearned ordinary person who has not heard the true Dharma, who has not encountered a genuine spiritual friend, who does not know the noble Dharma, who has not trained in the noble Dharma, who does not know the Dharma as it truly is, through improper attention thinks: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was the cause of my past existence? How was my past existence? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will be the cause of my future existence? How will my future existence be?' He doubts about himself: 'What is this? How is this? Where did this being come from? Where will it go? What was its former cause of existence? What will be its future cause of existence?' Through such improper attention, among six views, whichever view arises in him, it arises. The view arises: 'There truly is a self.' This view arises. The view arises: 'There truly is no self.' This view arises. The view arises: 'The self perceives the self.' This view arises. The view arises: 'The self perceives what is not self.' This view arises. The view arises: 'What is not self perceives the self.' This view arises. The view arises: 'This is my self, which speaks, knows, acts, directs action, initiates, directs initiation, is born in various places, receives the rewards of good and evil; it definitely does not come from anywhere; it definitely does not exist; it definitely will not exist.' These are the defects of views. One is disturbed by views and bound by the fetter of views. The unlearned ordinary person, because of this, undergoes the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

"The well-learned noble disciple who has heard the true Dharma, who has encountered a genuine spiritual friend, who has trained in the noble Dharma, who knows the Dharma as it truly is, knows suffering as it truly is, knows the arising of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. Having thus known as it truly is, the three fetters are exhausted. The three fetters of identity-view, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt being exhausted, one attains the fruit of stream-entry. One does not fall into evil destinies and is certain to proceed toward right enlightenment. One will undergo at most seven more existences; after seven passages between the heavens and the human world, one will reach the end of suffering. If one does not know and see, then afflictions and grief arise; knowing and seeing, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by seeing.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by guarding? A bhikṣu who guards the eye-faculty upon seeing forms does so through proper attention with contemplation of impurity. One who does not guard the eye-faculty does so through improper attention with contemplation of purity. If one does not guard, then afflictions and grief arise; guarding, afflictions and grief do not arise. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind knowing dharmas: guarding the mind-faculty is through proper attention with contemplation of impurity; not guarding the mind-faculty is through improper attention with contemplation of purity. If one does not guard, then afflictions and grief arise; guarding, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by guarding.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by avoiding? A bhikṣu who sees a dangerous elephant should keep away from it; likewise dangerous horses, dangerous cattle, dangerous dogs, poisonous snakes, perilous roads, ditches, pits, latrines, rivers, deep springs, and mountain cliffs. Evil friends, evil companions, evil heterodox paths, evil neighborhoods, evil dwelling places: wherever fellow practitioners of the holy life, if living together with such, would cause people who were without suspicion to become suspicious, a bhikṣu should keep away. Evil friends, evil companions, evil heterodox paths, evil neighborhoods, evil dwelling places: wherever fellow practitioners of the holy life, if living together with such, would cause people who were without suspicion to become suspicious, all should be kept far away from. If one does not avoid, then afflictions and grief arise; avoiding, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by avoiding.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by using? A bhikṣu, when using robes, does so not for profit, not out of pride, not for adornment, but only because of mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, cold, and heat, and because of a sense of shame and modesty. When using food and drink, it is not for profit, not out of pride, not to fatten or beautify the body, but only to sustain the body for a long time, to remove afflictions and grief, to practice the holy life, so that old ailments may be cut off and new ailments may not arise, and so that one may live long in good health without illness. When using dwelling places, buildings, beds, and bedding, it is not for profit, not out of pride, not for adornment, but only so that fatigue and weariness may find rest, and so that one may sit in quiet meditation. When using medicines, it is not for profit, not out of pride, not to fatten or beautify the body, but only to remove illness and affliction, to preserve the life-faculty, and to dwell in good health without illness. If one does not use properly, then afflictions and grief arise; using properly, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by using.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by enduring? A bhikṣu, striving diligently to cut off evil and unwholesome states and to cultivate wholesome states, constantly maintains the thought of effort, is single-minded and diligent, even if the body, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, blood, and marrow were all to dry up. One does not abandon effort, and only when one has attained what is sought does one relinquish effort. Furthermore, a bhikṣu should endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and lice, the affliction of wind and sun, harsh words and blows. One should also endure bodily illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point of life threatening, and all manner of unpleasant things. If one does not endure, then afflictions and grief arise; enduring, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by enduring.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by removing? A bhikṣu in whom thoughts of desire have arisen does not remove, cut off, relinquish, or abandon them; in whom thoughts of ill-will or thoughts of harming have arisen does not remove, cut off, relinquish, or abandon them. If one does not remove, then afflictions and grief arise; removing, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by removing.

"How are there outflows to be cut off by cultivation? A bhikṣu cultivates the first awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, progressing toward relinquishment. Likewise with the Dharma, with effort, with joy, with tranquility, with concentration. One cultivates the seventh awakening factor of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, progressing toward relinquishment. If one does not cultivate, then afflictions and grief arise; cultivating, afflictions and grief do not arise. This is how outflows are cut off by cultivation.

"If a bhikṣu has outflows to be cut off by seeing, he cuts them off through seeing. If he has outflows to be cut off by guarding, he cuts them off through guarding. If he has outflows to be cut off by avoiding, he cuts them off through avoiding. If he has outflows to be cut off by using, he cuts them off through using. If he has outflows to be cut off by enduring, he cuts them off through enduring. If he has outflows to be cut off by removing, he cuts them off through removing. If he has outflows to be cut off by cultivation, he cuts them off through cultivation. This is called a bhikṣu who has exhausted all outflows, who has resolved all fetters, and who through right knowledge has reached the end of suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Exhaustion of the Outflows, Tenth.

## (11) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra of the Salt Simile, First

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If one were to say, 'Whatever action a person performs, that person receives its retribution accordingly; thus, without practicing the holy life, one cannot make an end of suffering,' then if one were to say, 'Whatever action a person performs, that person receives its retribution accordingly; thus, by practicing the holy life, one can make an end of suffering.' Why is this? If there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell, how is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. It is like someone who casts one liang of salt into a small amount of water, wishing to make the water salty and undrinkable. What do you think? Can this one liang of salt make the small amount of water salty and undrinkable?"

They answered: "So it is, World-Honored One. Why is that? The salt is much and the water is little; therefore it can make it salty and undrinkable."

"Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell."

"Furthermore, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. It is like someone who casts one liang of salt into the waters of the Ganges, wishing to make the water salty and undrinkable. What do you think? Can this one liang of salt make the Ganges water salty and undrinkable?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? The Ganges water is very great, and one liang of salt is little; therefore it cannot make it salty and undrinkable."

"Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life.

"Furthermore, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. It is like a person who seizes another's sheep. How is it that a person seizes another's sheep? The one who seizes the sheep is either a king or a king's minister, someone with great power and authority, while the owner of the sheep is poor, lowly, and powerless. Because he is powerless, he approaches in various ways, joins his palms, and begs, saying: 'Venerable sir, please return my sheep, or else give me its price.' This is what is meant by a person who seizes another's sheep. Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell.

"Furthermore, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. It is like a person who, although he steals another's sheep, the owner takes it back. How is it that a person, although he steals another's sheep, the owner takes it back? The one who steals the sheep is poor, lowly, and without power, while the sheep's owner is either a king or a king's minister, someone with great power and authority. Because he has power, he seizes and binds the thief and takes back the sheep. This is what is meant by a person who, although he steals another's sheep, the owner takes it back. Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life.

"Furthermore, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. It is like a person who, owing another five coins, is bound by the creditor; even owing one coin, he is bound by the creditor. How is it that a person, owing another five coins, is bound by the creditor, and even owing one coin is bound by the creditor? The debtor is poor, without power or influence. Because he is poor and without power, owing another five coins, he is bound by the creditor, and even owing one coin he is bound by the creditor. This is what is meant by a person who, owing another five coins, is bound by the creditor, and even owing one coin is bound by the creditor. Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell? It is that there is a certain person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate precepts, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is very short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in hell.

"Furthermore, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. It is like a person who, although owing a hundred coins, is not bound by the creditor; even owing ten million, he is not bound by the creditor. How is it that a person, although owing a hundred coins, is not bound by the creditor, and even owing ten million is not bound by the creditor? The debtor has immeasurable wealth and great power and influence. Because of this, although he owes a hundred coins, he is not bound by the creditor, and even owing ten million he is not bound by the creditor. This is what is meant by a person who, although owing a hundred coins, is not bound by the creditor, and even owing ten million is not bound by the creditor. Just so, there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. How is it that there is a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life? It is that there is a certain person who cultivates the body, cultivates precepts, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is very long. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome actions and must receive the bitter fruit of retribution in this present life. That person, in this present life, even if he receives the retribution of good and bad actions, it is light and minor."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Salt Simile Sūtra, the First.

---

## (12) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra of Happavāda, Second

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the Śākyan land of Kapilavatthu, staying in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a group of bhikṣus, after the midday meal, having some matter to attend to, gathered and sat in the lecture hall. At that time, there was a disciple of the Nirgranthas, a Śākyan named Happavāda, who in the afternoon was wandering about and came to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked him about this matter: "What do you think, Happavāda? If there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, do you see any ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life?"

Happavāda answered: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, I do see a ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if there were unwholesome actions performed in past lives, because of these, unwholesome taints arise, leading to a future life."

Later, the World-Honored One, sitting in a quiet place in meditative calm, with his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda, discussing in this way. Having heard this, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, arose from his meditative calm and went to the lecture hall. Before the assembly of bhikṣus, he had a seat arranged and sat down. Having sat down, the World-Honored One asked: "Maudgalyāyana, what were you just discussing with the Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda? And for what reason did you gather and sit in the lecture hall?"

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "World-Honored One, today I and the assembly of bhikṣus, after the midday meal, having some matter to attend to, gathered and sat in the lecture hall. This Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda, in the afternoon was wandering about and came to where I was. We exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. I asked him thus: 'What do you think, Happavāda? If there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, do you see any ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life?' The Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda, answered me thus: 'If there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, I do see a ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if there were unwholesome actions performed in past lives, because of these, unwholesome taints arise, leading to a future life.' World-Honored One, we were just discussing this with the Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda, and it was for this matter that we gathered and sat in the lecture hall."

Then the World-Honored One addressed the Nirgrantha disciple, the Śākyan Happavāda, saying: "If what I say is correct, you should say it is correct. If it is not correct, you should say it is not correct. If you have any doubt, you may ask me: 'Śramaṇa Gautama, what is the meaning of this? What is the purpose of this?' According to what I say, if you are able to accept it, I will discuss this matter with you."

Happavāda answered: "Śramaṇa Gautama, if what you say is correct, I will say it is correct. If it is not correct, I will say it is not correct. If I have any doubt, I will ask Gautama: 'Gautama, what is the meaning of this? What is the purpose of this?' According to what Śramaṇa Gautama says, I will accept and uphold it. Let Śramaṇa Gautama discuss this matter with me."

The World-Honored One asked: "What do you think, Happavāda? If there is a bhikṣu who has given rise to unwholesome bodily actions, with taints, afflictive heat, and grief, and that person afterwards abandons unwholesome bodily actions, does not create new karma, discards old karma, and right in this present life attains completeness, free from afflictive heat, abiding permanently without change, as seen by noble wisdom, as known by noble wisdom. If unwholesome bodily actions, unwholesome verbal actions, unwholesome mental actions, and unwholesome ignorance-actions arise, with taints, afflictive heat, and grief, and that person afterwards abandons unwholesome ignorance-actions, does not create new karma, discards old karma, and right in this present life attains completeness, free from afflictive heat, abiding permanently without change, as seen by noble wisdom, as known by noble wisdom. How is it, Happavāda? For such a bhikṣu who guards body, speech, and mind, do you see any ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life?"

Happavāda answered: "Gautama, if there is a bhikṣu who guards body, speech, and mind in this way, I do not see any ground by which unwholesome taints might arise from this, leading to a future life."

The World-Honored One praised him: "Excellent, Happavāda! How is it, Happavāda? If there is a bhikṣu whose ignorance is already exhausted and whose clear knowledge has arisen, that bhikṣu whose ignorance is already exhausted and whose clear knowledge has arisen, when the feeling of a final body arises, knows it as the feeling of a final body; when the feeling of a final life arises, knows it as the feeling of a final life. When the body breaks apart and life ends, and the lifespan is fully exhausted, right in this present life all feelings come to complete cessation and rest. Know that this is ultimate cooling. Happavāda, it is like a tree that casts a shadow. If someone were to come with a sharp axe and chop the tree at its root, cut it into segments, break it into ten parts or a hundred parts, burn it to ashes with fire, or scatter it with a great wind, or cast it into water. What do you think, Happavāda? The shadow depended on the tree; has that shadow, from this point on, had its cause cut off and ceased to arise?"

Happavāda answered: "So it is, Gautama."

"Happavāda, you should know that the bhikṣu is also like this. When ignorance is already exhausted and clear knowledge has arisen, that bhikṣu whose ignorance is already exhausted and whose clear knowledge has arisen, when the feeling of a final body arises, knows it as the feeling of a final body; when the feeling of a final life arises, knows it as the feeling of a final life. When the body breaks apart and life ends, and the lifespan is fully exhausted, right in this present life all feelings come to complete cessation and rest. Know that this is ultimate cooling. Happavāda, when a bhikṣu has thus rightly liberated his mind, he attains six good abiding places. What are the six? Happavāda, when a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he is neither pleased nor grieved; abandoning seeking, he abides in non-doing, with right mindfulness and right knowledge. Happavāda, when a bhikṣu has thus rightly liberated his mind, this is called attaining the first good abiding place. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind knowing dharmas, he is neither pleased nor grieved; abandoning seeking, he abides in non-doing, with right mindfulness and right knowledge. Happavāda, when a bhikṣu has thus rightly liberated his mind, this is called attaining the sixth good abiding place. Happavāda, when a bhikṣu has thus rightly liberated his mind, he attains these six good abiding places."

Happavāda said: "So it is, Gautama. When a well-learned noble disciple has thus rightly liberated his mind, he attains six good abiding places. What are the six? Gautama, when a well-learned noble disciple sees forms with the eye, he is neither pleased nor grieved; abandoning seeking, he abides in non-doing, with right mindfulness and right knowledge. Gautama, when a well-learned noble disciple has thus rightly liberated his mind, this is called attaining the first good abiding place. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind knowing dharmas, he is neither pleased nor grieved; abandoning seeking, he abides in non-doing, with right mindfulness and right knowledge. Thus, Gautama, when a well-learned noble disciple has thus rightly liberated his mind, this is called attaining the sixth good abiding place. Thus, Gautama, when a well-learned noble disciple has thus rightly liberated his mind, he attains these six good abiding places."

Then Happavāda addressed the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. Gautama, it is like a person with clear eyes who turns the overturned upright, reveals what is concealed, shows the way to one who is lost, and holds up a light in the darkness so that those with eyes can see forms. Just so, Śramaṇa Gautama has likewise, with immeasurable skillful means, expounded the Dharma and revealed its meaning, following all the various paths. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge, even until the end of my life.

"World-Honored One, it is like a person who raises an unworthy horse, hoping to profit from it, but toils in vain without gaining any benefit. World-Honored One, I am just like this. That foolish Nirgrantha is not well-versed, unable to comprehend, does not recognize good fields, and does not examine himself. For a long night I have revered, served, and paid homage to him, hoping for benefit, but it has been vain suffering without gain. World-Honored One, I now for a second time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge, even until the end of my life.

"World-Honored One, formerly I was ignorant and had faith in and reverence for the foolish Nirgrantha. From this day I sever that. Why? Because he deceived me. World-Honored One, I now for a third time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge, even until the end of my life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Śākyan Happavāda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Happavāda Sūtra, the Second.

---

## (13) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra on Crossing Over, Third

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three doctrinal positions, of different lineages, different names, different schools, and different teachings. Even if a wise person well receives and firmly grasps them and expounds them for others, still no benefit is gained. What are the three? There are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim: 'Whatever a person does is all caused by past-life destiny.' Again, there are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim: 'Whatever a person does is all caused by the creation of a supreme lord.' Again, there are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim: 'Whatever a person does is all without cause and without condition.'

"Among these, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim, 'Whatever a person does is all caused by past-life destiny,' I go to them. Having arrived, I ask them: 'Venerables, is it true that you hold this view and make this claim, that whatever a person does is all caused by past-life destiny?' They answer: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'If that is so, then all of you, venerables, are killers of living beings. Why? Because everything is caused by past-life destiny. Likewise, all of you, venerables, take what is not given, commit sexual misconduct, speak falsehood, and so forth up to holding wrong views. Why? Because everything is caused by past-life destiny. Venerables, if everything is caused by past-life destiny, and if one sees it as truly so, then regarding internal causes, whether one acts or does not act, there is altogether no desire and no method. Venerables, if regarding action and non-action one does not know it as it truly is, then one loses right mindfulness, lacks right knowledge, and there is nothing with which to instruct, as befits the way of a śramaṇa. If one speaks thus, one can thereby, by reason, refute those śramaṇas and brahmins.'

"Among these, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim, 'Whatever a person does is all caused by the creation of a supreme lord,' I go to them. Having arrived, I ask them: 'Venerables, is it true that you hold this view and make this claim, that whatever a person does is all caused by the creation of a supreme lord?' They answer: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'If that is so, then all of you, venerables, are killers of living beings. Why? Because everything is caused by the creation of a supreme lord. Likewise, all of you, venerables, take what is not given, commit sexual misconduct, speak falsehood, and so forth up to holding wrong views. Why? Because everything is caused by the creation of a supreme lord. Venerables, if everything is caused by the creation of a supreme lord, and if one sees it as truly so, then regarding internal causes, whether one acts or does not act, there is altogether no desire and no method. Venerables, if regarding action and non-action one does not know it as it truly is, then one loses right mindfulness, lacks right knowledge, and there is nothing with which to instruct, as befits the way of a śramaṇa. If one speaks thus, one can thereby, by reason, refute those śramaṇas and brahmins.'

"Among these, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this claim, 'Whatever a person does is all without cause and without condition,' I go to them. Having arrived, I ask them: 'Venerables, is it true that you hold this view and make this claim, that whatever a person does is all without cause and without condition?' They answer: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'If that is so, then all of you, venerables, are killers of living beings. Why? Because everything is without cause and without condition. Likewise, all of you, venerables, take what is not given, commit sexual misconduct, speak falsehood, and so forth up to holding wrong views. Why? Because everything is without cause and without condition. Venerables, if everything is without cause and without condition, and if one sees it as truly so, then regarding internal causes, whether one acts or does not act, there is altogether no desire and no method. Venerables, if regarding action and non-action one does not know it as it truly is, then one loses right mindfulness, lacks right knowledge, and there is nothing with which to instruct, as befits the way of a śramaṇa. If one speaks thus, one can thereby, by reason, refute those śramaṇas and brahmins.'

"The Dharma that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself, which I teach to you, cannot be refuted by any śramaṇas or brahmins, nor by gods, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world; cannot be defiled; cannot be overcome. What is this Dharma that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself, which I teach to you, that cannot be refuted, defiled, or overcome by śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world? It is the teaching of the six sense bases, which I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you, that cannot be refuted, defiled, or overcome by śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. Furthermore, it is the teaching of the six elements, which I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you, that cannot be refuted, defiled, or overcome by śramaṇas or brahmins, gods, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.

"What is the teaching of the six sense bases that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you? They are the eye-base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases. This is called the teaching of the six sense bases that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you. What is the teaching of the six elements that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you? They are the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. This is called the teaching of the six elements that I have known by myself and awakened to by myself and teach to you.

"Through the combination of the six elements, there is conception in the mother's womb. Based on the six elements, there are the six sense bases. Based on the six sense bases, there is contact. Based on contact, there is feeling. Bhikṣus, one who has feeling can know suffering as it truly is, can know the arising of suffering, can know the cessation of suffering, and can know the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. How does one know suffering as it truly is? That is: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with what one resents, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and in brief, the suffering of the five grasping aggregates. This is called knowing suffering as it truly is. How does one know the arising of suffering as it truly is? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking pleasure here and there. This is called knowing the arising of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of suffering as it truly is? It is the complete cessation of this very craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking pleasure here and there; its abandonment without remainder, its relinquishment, its release, its exhaustion, its fading away, its cessation, its stilling, its disappearance. This is called knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, and so forth up to right samādhi, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. Bhikṣus, you should know suffering as it truly is, you should abandon the arising of suffering, you should realize the cessation of suffering, and you should cultivate the path to the cessation of suffering. If a bhikṣu knows suffering as it truly is, abandons the arising of suffering, realizes the cessation of suffering, and cultivates the path to the cessation of suffering, this is called a bhikṣu who has exhausted all taints, who has resolved all fetters, and who, through right knowledge, has reached the end of suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Crossing Over, the Third.

---

## (14) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra of Rāhula, Fourth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, Kalandaka's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was also dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Hot Springs Grove. Then the World-Honored One, at dawn the next morning, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. After he had finished begging for food, he went to the Hot Springs Grove where Rāhula was staying. The Venerable Rāhula, seeing the Buddha coming from afar, went forward to meet him, took the Buddha's robes and bowl, spread out a seat, and drew water to wash his feet. When the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat down on Rāhula's seat.

Then the World-Honored One took a water vessel and poured out the water, leaving only a little, and asked: "Rāhula, do you now see that I took this water vessel and poured out the water, leaving only a little?"

Rāhula answered: "I see it, World-Honored One."

The Buddha told Rāhula: "I say that the path of that person is also just as little as this, for one who, knowing it to be false, speaks falsehood, is neither ashamed nor remorseful, and is without conscience and without shame. Rāhula, for such a person there is no evil he will not do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: you must not speak falsehood even in jest."

The World-Honored One then took the vessel with the remaining little water and poured it all out. He then asked: "Rāhula, do you also see that I took the vessel with the little water and poured it all out?"

Rāhula answered: "I see it, World-Honored One."

The Buddha told Rāhula: "I say that the path of that person is also cast away entirely like this, for one who, knowing it to be false, speaks falsehood, is neither ashamed nor remorseful, and is without conscience and without shame. Rāhula, for such a person there is no evil he will not do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: you must not speak falsehood even in jest."

The World-Honored One then took the empty water vessel and turned it upside down on the ground. He then asked: "Rāhula, do you also see that I took the empty water vessel and turned it upside down on the ground?"

Rāhula answered: "I see it, World-Honored One."

The Buddha told Rāhula: "I say that the path of that person is also overturned like this, for one who, knowing it to be false, speaks falsehood, is neither ashamed nor remorseful, and is without conscience and without shame. Rāhula, for such a person there is no evil he will not do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: you must not speak falsehood even in jest."

The World-Honored One then took the overturned water vessel and turned it upright again. He then asked: "Rāhula, do you also see that I took the overturned water vessel and turned it upright?"

Rāhula answered: "I see it, World-Honored One."

The Buddha told Rāhula: "I say that the path of that person is also just as empty as this, for one who, knowing it to be false, speaks falsehood, is neither ashamed nor remorseful, and is without conscience and without shame. Rāhula, for such a person there is no evil he will not do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: you must not speak falsehood even in jest.

"Rāhula, it is like a king's great elephant entering into battle. In battle, he uses his front legs, his hind legs, his tail, his haunches, his back, his flanks, his neck, his forehead, his ears, and his tusks; he uses everything, but he protects his trunk alone. When the elephant trainer sees this, he thinks: 'This king's great elephant still cherishes his life. Why is that? Because when this king's great elephant enters battle, he uses his front legs, his hind legs, his tail, his haunches, his back, his flanks, his neck, his forehead, his ears, and his tusks; he uses everything, but he protects his trunk alone.' Rāhula, if the king's great elephant enters battle and uses his front legs, his hind legs, his tail, his haunches, his back, his flanks, his neck, his forehead, his ears, his tusks, and his trunk, using everything completely, the elephant trainer, seeing this, thinks: 'This king's great elephant no longer cherishes his life. Why is that? Because this king's great elephant enters battle and uses his front legs, his hind legs, his tail, his haunches, his back, his flanks, his neck, his forehead, his ears, his tusks, and his trunk; he uses everything completely.' Rāhula, if the king's great elephant enters battle and uses his front legs, his hind legs, his tail, his haunches, his back, his flanks, his neck, his forehead, his ears, his tusks, and his trunk, using everything completely, Rāhula, I say that this king's great elephant entering battle will do no evil deed that he will not commit. Just so, Rāhula, one who, knowing it to be false, speaks falsehood, is neither ashamed nor remorseful, and is without conscience and without shame, Rāhula, I say that for such a person there is no evil he will not do. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: you must not speak falsehood even in jest."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"A person who transgresses one thing, namely speaking falsehood,
Not fearing the next world, there is no evil he will not do.
Better to swallow iron balls, as hot as fire,
Than to break the precepts and accept the faithful offerings of the world.
If one fears suffering and does not love it,
In hidden and open places, do not commit evil deeds.
If unwholesome deeds have already been done or are being done now,
One can never escape; there is no place to hide."

After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he further asked Rāhula: "What do you think? What does a person use a mirror for?"

The Venerable Rāhula answered: "World-Honored One, one wishes to observe one's face to see whether it is clean or not clean."

"Just so, Rāhula. If you are about to perform a bodily action, you should examine that bodily action: 'The bodily action I am about to perform, is it pure or impure? Is it for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I am about to perform is impure, whether for myself or for others, it is unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should abandon that bodily action you are about to perform. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I am about to perform is pure, whether for myself or for others, it is wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should undertake that bodily action you are about to perform.

"Rāhula, if you are presently performing a bodily action, you should examine this bodily action: 'The bodily action I am presently performing, is it pure or impure? Is it for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I am presently performing is impure, whether for myself or for others, it is unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should abandon this bodily action you are presently performing. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I am presently performing is pure, whether for myself or for others, it is wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should continue this bodily action you are presently performing.

"Rāhula, if you have already performed a bodily action, you should examine that bodily action: 'The bodily action I have already performed, that bodily action that is already past, extinguished, and changed, is it pure or impure? Is it for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I have already performed, that bodily action that is already past, extinguished, and changed, is impure, whether for myself or for others, it is unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should go to a good friend, a person of the holy life, and regarding that bodily action already performed, with a sincere mind confess it, repent and declare it. Be careful not to conceal it, and further guard yourself well. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'The bodily action I have already performed, that bodily action that is already past, extinguished, and changed, is pure, whether for myself or for others, it is wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should dwell day and night in joy, with right mindfulness and right knowledge. The same applies to verbal actions.

"Rāhula, regarding mental actions that have arisen due to past conduct, you should examine those mental actions: 'If, due to past conduct, mental actions have already arisen, are those mental actions pure or impure? Are they for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to past conduct, mental actions have already arisen; those mental actions that are already past, extinguished, and changed are impure, whether for myself or for others, they are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should abandon those past mental actions. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to past conduct, mental actions have already arisen; those mental actions that are already past, extinguished, and changed are pure, whether for myself or for others, they are wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should accept those past mental actions.

"Rāhula, regarding mental actions that will arise due to future conduct, you should examine those mental actions: 'If, due to future conduct, mental actions will arise, are those mental actions pure or impure? Are they for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to future conduct, mental actions will arise; those mental actions are impure, whether for myself or for others, they are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should abandon those future mental actions. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to future conduct, mental actions will arise; those mental actions are pure, whether for myself or for others, they are wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should accept those future mental actions.

"Rāhula, regarding mental actions that are presently arising due to present conduct, you should examine these mental actions: 'If, due to present conduct, mental actions are presently arising, are these mental actions pure or impure? Are they for myself or for others?' Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to present conduct, mental actions are presently arising; these mental actions are impure, whether for myself or for others, they are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should abandon these present mental actions. Rāhula, if upon examination you know: 'Due to present conduct, mental actions are presently arising; these mental actions are pure, whether for myself or for others, they are wholesome, yielding pleasant fruit and receiving pleasant retribution,' then, Rāhula, you should accept these present mental actions.

"Rāhula, whatever śramaṇas and brahmins of the past have examined and purified their bodily, verbal, and mental actions, all of them did so in just this way: examining by examination, purifying by purification of these very bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Rāhula, whatever śramaṇas and brahmins of the future will examine and purify their bodily, verbal, and mental actions, all of them will do so in just this way: examining by examination, purifying by purification of these very bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Rāhula, whatever śramaṇas and brahmins of the present are examining and purifying their bodily, verbal, and mental actions, all of them do so in just this way: examining by examination, purifying by purification of these very bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: 'I too will examine by examination and purify by purification these very bodily, verbal, and mental actions in the present.'"

Then the World-Honored One further spoke these verses:

"Bodily action, verbal action, mental action, Rāhula,
Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas: you should constantly examine them.
Knowing it to be false, Rāhula, do not speak it.
A shaven-head who lives dependent on others, how can he speak falsehood?
Concealing the way of the śramaṇa, empty and without truth,
That is what speaking falsehood means: not guarding one's mouth.
Therefore do not speak falsely. The children of the Perfectly Awakened One,
This is the śramaṇa's way. Rāhula, you should learn it.
In every direction, prosperity and joy, peace and security without fear.
Rāhula, going there, do not cause harm to others."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Rāhula and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Rāhula Sūtra, the Fourth.

---

## (15) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra on Intention, Fifth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there is intentional action, I say that one must receive its retribution, either in this present life or in a future life. If there is unintentional action, I say that one does not necessarily receive its retribution. Among these, there are three intentional bodily actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution. There are four verbal actions and three mental actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution.

"What are the three intentional bodily actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution? The first is killing living beings: being extremely cruel and bloodthirsty, desiring to harm, lacking compassion toward sentient beings, including even insects. The second is taking what is not given: coveting others' possessions and taking them with a thieving mind. The third is sexual misconduct. If there is a woman protected by her father, or protected by her mother, or protected by both father and mother, or protected by a sister, or protected by a brother, or protected by her parents-in-law, or protected by relatives, or protected by clansmen, or if she is another's wife, or a woman subject to punishment or intimidation, or even one given as a betrothed bride marked with a garland, one who violates such a woman. These are called the three intentional bodily actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution.

"What are the four intentional verbal actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution? The first is false speech. If one is among an assembly, or among relatives, or in the king's court, and is called and questioned, saying 'Speak what you know,' then not knowing, one says one knows; knowing, one says one does not know; not seeing, one says one sees; seeing, one says one does not see. For oneself, for others, or for the sake of material gain, knowing it to be so, one speaks falsely. The second is divisive speech. Desiring to separate others, one hears speech here and repeats it there, wishing to break apart these people; one hears speech there and repeats it here, wishing to break apart those people. Those who are united, one wishes to divide; those already divided, one further divides. One forms factions, delights in factions, and praises factions. The third is harsh speech. If one's words are rough and fierce in tone, with an ugly sound offensive to the ear, displeasing to many, unloved by many, causing others suffering and preventing them from attaining concentration, one speaks such words. The fourth is frivolous speech. One speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is meaningless, speaks what is contrary to the Dharma, speaks what is not conducive to cessation; furthermore, one praises things that are not conducive to cessation, going against the proper time and neither teaching well nor admonishing well. These are called the four intentional verbal actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution.

"What are the three intentional mental actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution? The first is covetousness. Seeing others' possessions and means of livelihood, one constantly watches and hopes, desiring that one may obtain them. The second is ill will and anger. One harbors resentment and hatred in the mind and thinks: 'Those beings should be killed, should be bound, should be seized, should be fined, should be banished and expelled.' One desires that they suffer immeasurable misery. The third is wrong views. One's views are inverted. One holds this view and makes this claim: 'There is no giving, no offering, no incantation. There are no wholesome or unwholesome actions, no retribution of wholesome or unwholesome actions. There is no this world or next world, no father, no mother. In the world there are no true persons who go to the good place, going well and heading well, who in this world and the next world, by their own knowledge, their own awakening, and their own realization, dwell having accomplished it.' These are called the three intentional mental actions that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruit and receiving bitter retribution.

"The well-learned noble disciple abandons unwholesome bodily actions and cultivates wholesome bodily actions; abandons unwholesome verbal and mental actions and cultivates wholesome verbal and mental actions. That well-learned noble disciple, being thus endowed with diligent effort and virtuous conduct, accomplishes pure bodily action, accomplishes pure verbal and mental action. Free from anger and free from contention, having removed drowsiness, without restlessness or arrogance, having cut off doubt and crossed over conceit, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, without delusion, that person, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction, dwells having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally pervading all, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well-cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwelling having accomplished it. That person then thinks: 'Formerly this mind of mine was little, not well cultivated. Now this mind of mine is immeasurably well cultivated.' The well-learned noble disciple whose mind is thus immeasurably well cultivated, if formerly, due to bad companions, one engaged in heedless conduct and performed unwholesome actions, those unwholesome actions cannot lead one away, cannot defile one, and no longer follow one. If there were a young boy or girl who, from the moment of birth, were able to practice the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, would their body, speech, or mind afterward be able to perform unwholesome actions?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? If one does not personally create unwholesome actions, from where would unwholesome actions arise?"

"Therefore, men and women, whether householders or those who have gone forth, should always diligently cultivate the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. If a man or woman, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, cultivates the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, one does not carry this body to the next world; rather, one goes according to the mind. A bhikṣu should think thus: 'Formerly I was heedless and performed unwholesome actions. All of that can now receive its retribution in this life, and will not extend to future lives.' If one practices the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, immeasurably well cultivated in this way, one will certainly attain the stage of non-returner, or even something higher. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwelling having accomplished it. That person then thinks: 'Formerly this mind of mine was little, not well cultivated. Now this mind of mine is immeasurably well cultivated.' The well-learned noble disciple whose mind is thus immeasurably well cultivated, if formerly, due to bad companions, one engaged in heedless conduct and performed unwholesome actions, those unwholesome actions cannot lead one away, cannot defile one, and no longer follow one. If there were a young boy or girl who, from the moment of birth, were able to practice the liberation of mind through equanimity, would their body, speech, or mind afterward be able to perform unwholesome actions?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? If one does not personally create unwholesome actions, from where would unwholesome actions arise?"

"Therefore, men and women, whether householders or those who have gone forth, should always diligently cultivate the liberation of mind through equanimity. If a man or woman, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, cultivates the liberation of mind through equanimity, one does not carry this body to the next world; rather, one goes according to the mind. A bhikṣu should think thus: 'Formerly I was heedless and performed unwholesome actions. All of that can now receive its retribution in this life, and will not extend to future lives.' If one practices the liberation of mind through equanimity, immeasurably well cultivated in this way, one will certainly attain the stage of non-returner, or even something higher."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Intention, the Fifth.

---

## (16) Madhyamāgama, Section on Kamma: The Sūtra of the Kālāmas, Sixth

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the Kālāma Garden with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and came to Kesamutti, staying in the Śiśapā Grove north of Kesamutti village.

At that time, the Kālāma people of Kesamutti heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who had left the Śākyan clan to go forth and study the Way, was travelling in the Kālāma Garden with a great assembly of bhikṣus and had come to Kesamutti, staying in the Śiśapā Grove north of Kesamutti village. That śramaṇa Gautama has great fame and renown, heard of in all ten directions. The śramaṇa Gautama is a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One. In this world, among gods and Māra and Brahmā, among śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans to gods, by his own knowledge and his own awakening, he has realized and dwells having accomplished it. When he teaches the Dharma, it is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life. If one can see the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, revere him, pay homage, make offerings, and attend upon him, one gains excellent benefit. We should go together to see the śramaṇa Gautama, pay homage, and make offerings.

Having heard this, the Kālāma people, each with their companions and relatives, departed from Kesamutti, heading north to the Śiśapā Grove, wishing to see the World-Honored One, pay homage, and make offerings. Having come to the Buddha, some of the Kālāma people bowed at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down silently. At that time, when the Kālāma people had all settled in their seats, the Buddha taught them the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them. With immeasurable skillful means he taught them the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them, and then sat in silence.

At that time, the Kālāma people, after the Buddha had taught them the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them, each rose from their seats, bared one shoulder, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One: "Gautama, there are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who come to visit Kālāma. They only praise and extol their own knowledge and views, while disparaging and denigrating the knowledge and views of others. Gautama, again there are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who come to visit Kālāma, and they likewise praise and extol their own knowledge and views, while disparaging and denigrating the knowledge and views of others. Gautama, when we hear this, we develop doubt and confusion: 'Among these śramaṇas and brahmins, which ones speak truth and which ones speak falsely?'"

The World-Honored One said: "Kālāmas, do not give rise to doubt and confusion. Why is that? Because when there is doubt and confusion, uncertainty arises. Kālāmas, you yourselves have no pure knowledge as to whether there is a next world or no next world. Kālāmas, you likewise have no pure knowledge as to whether actions are sinful or actions are not sinful. Kālāmas, you should know that there are three kinds of actions, with their habitual origins and root sources. What are the three? Kālāmas, greed is actions' habitual origin and root source. Kālāmas, aversion and delusion are actions' habitual origin and root source. Kālāmas, the greedy person, covered by greed, with an insatiable mind, may kill living beings, may take what is not given, may commit sexual misconduct, may knowingly speak falsehood, or may drink intoxicants. Kālāmas, the aversive person, covered by aversion, with an insatiable mind, may kill living beings, may take what is not given, may commit sexual misconduct, may knowingly speak falsehood, or may drink intoxicants. Kālāmas, the deluded person, covered by delusion, with an insatiable mind, may kill living beings, may take what is not given, may commit sexual misconduct, may knowingly speak falsehood, or may drink intoxicants.

"Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons killing and refrains from killing. Having put aside the knife and the cudgel, with conscience and shame, with a compassionate and merciful mind, benefiting all beings including even insects, that person purifies the mind from killing. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons taking what is not given and refrains from taking what is not given. Only when something is given does one take it; one delights in giving, constantly enjoys generosity, is joyful and unstinting, does not hope for recompense. That person purifies the mind from taking what is not given. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons unchaste conduct and refrains from unchaste conduct. One diligently cultivates the holy life, with assiduous and excellent practice, pure and undefiled, free from desire and cutting off lust. That person purifies the mind from unchaste conduct. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons false speech and refrains from false speech. One speaks truth, delights in truth, abides in truth without wavering, trustworthy in all things, not deceiving the world. That person purifies the mind from false speech.

"Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons divisive speech and refrains from divisive speech. One practices non-divisive speech, not breaking apart others. One does not hear speech here and repeat it there wishing to break apart these people, nor hear speech there and repeat it here wishing to break apart those people. Those who are separated, one wishes to unite; those united, one causes to rejoice. One does not form factions, does not delight in factions, does not praise factions. That person purifies the mind from divisive speech. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons harsh speech and refrains from harsh speech. If there are words that are rough and fierce in tone, with ugly sounds offensive to the ear, displeasing to many, unloved by many, causing others suffering and preventing them from attaining concentration, one refrains from such words. If one has something to say, it is gentle and harmonious, soft and smooth, agreeable to the ear, entering into the heart, pleasing and lovable, bringing others ease and comfort. One's verbal expression is clear and complete, not frightening to people, enabling others to attain concentration. One speaks such words. That person purifies the mind from harsh speech. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons frivolous speech and refrains from frivolous speech. One speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks of the Dharma, speaks of meaning, speaks of cessation, delights in speaking of cessation. Following the matter, at the appropriate time, one teaches well and admonishes well. That person purifies the mind from frivolous speech. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons covetousness and refrains from covetousness. One's mind does not harbor contention. Seeing others' possessions and means of livelihood, one does not give rise to covetousness, desiring to obtain them. That person purifies the mind from covetousness.

"Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons ill will and refrains from ill will. With conscience and shame, with a compassionate and merciful mind, one benefits all beings including even insects. That person purifies the mind from resentment and ill will. Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple abandons wrong views and refrains from wrong views. One practices right views without inversion, holding this view and making this claim: 'There is giving, there is offering, there are also incantations. There are retributions of wholesome and unwholesome actions. There is this world and the next world. There is father and mother. In the world there are true persons who go to the good place, going well and heading well, who in this world and the next world, by their own knowledge, their own awakening, and their own realization, dwell having accomplished it.' That person purifies the mind from wrong views.

"In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple accomplishes pure bodily action, accomplishes pure verbal and mental action. Free from anger and free from contention, having removed drowsiness, without restlessness or arrogance, having cut off doubt and crossed over conceit, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, without delusion. That person, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction, dwells having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally pervading all, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwelling having accomplished it. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwelling having accomplished it.

"In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, thereby obtains four secure abiding places. What are the four? 'There is this world and the next world; there are retributions of wholesome and unwholesome actions. I have obtained actions in accordance with right view; I accept and uphold them completely. When my body breaks apart and life ends, I will certainly go to a good place, and will be born in the heavens.' In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, this is called obtaining the first secure abiding place. Furthermore, Kālāmas, 'If there is no this world or next world, no retribution of wholesome and unwholesome actions, then in this present life I am not thereby censured by others, but am praised by those with right knowledge. Persons of diligent effort and right view declare that such a one exists.' In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, this is called obtaining the second secure abiding place. Furthermore, Kālāmas, 'If there are actions to be done, I certainly do not do evil. I do not think of evil. Why? Since I myself do not do evil, from where would suffering arise?' In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, this is called obtaining the third secure abiding place. Furthermore, Kālāmas, 'If there are actions to be done, I certainly do not do evil. I do not transgress against the world, whether in frightful or non-frightful situations. I constantly have compassion for all the world. My mind does not contend with sentient beings, and I dwell in joy without defilement.' In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, this is called obtaining the fourth secure abiding place. In this way, Kālāmas, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, is said to obtain the four secure abiding places."

The Kālāmas addressed the World-Honored One: "So it is, Gautama. The well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, obtains four secure abiding places. What are the four? 'There is this world and the next world; there are retributions of wholesome and unwholesome actions. I have obtained actions in accordance with right view; I accept and uphold them completely. When my body breaks apart and life ends, I will certainly go to a good place, even up to the heavens.' Thus, Gautama, the well-learned noble disciple, whose mind is without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, this is called obtaining the first secure abiding place. Furthermore, Gautama, 'If there is no this world or next world, no retribution of wholesome and unwholesome actions, in this present life I am not thereby censured by others, but am

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgama)
## Fascicle 4

## Chapter on Causation (業相應品), Second

---

### **(15) Sūtra on Thought**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person has thought and acts, and makes merit, then that person's mind attains merit. If a person has thought and acts, and makes demerit, then that person's mind attains demerit. If a person has thought and acts, and neither makes merit nor demerit, then that person's mind attains neither merit nor demerit.

"Bhikṣus, I say that actions are of three kinds. What three? They are bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.

"Among these actions, which action do I explain as the most grave, giving rise to the most severe wrongdoing, giving rise to the most severe evil? That is, mental action is the most grave, giving rise to the most severe wrongdoing, giving rise to the most severe evil. It is not bodily action and not verbal action.

"Bhikṣus, I declare that there is a cause and condition for mental action: because of that cause and condition, mental action arises. Bhikṣus, I also declare there is a cause and condition for bodily action: because of that cause and condition, bodily action arises. Bhikṣus, I also declare there is a cause and condition for verbal action: because of that cause and condition, verbal action arises.

"Bhikṣus, what is the cause and condition by which mental action arises? Bhikṣus, it is contact as cause and condition; because of contact as cause and condition, mental action arises.
