Bhikṣus, what is the cause and condition by which bodily action arises? Bhikṣus, it is contact as cause and condition; because of contact as cause and condition, bodily action arises. Bhikṣus, what is the cause and condition by which verbal action arises? Bhikṣus, it is contact as cause and condition; because of contact as cause and condition, verbal action arises.

"Bhikṣus, because of the arising of contact, there is the arising of action. Because of the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of action. This eightfold noble path is the path leading to the cessation of action, namely: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. When the noble disciple's mind is thus liberated, that is called the noble disciple, who has removed the root, destroyed the heap, so that in the future there is no further arising."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(16) Sūtra on Kalāma**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kosala, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, gradually approaching a town of the Kalāmas called Kesamutta.

The Kalāmas of Kesamutta heard: "The ascetic Gautama, son of the Śākya clan, who left the Śākya household to go forth, is now traveling in Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus and has arrived at Kesamutta. Now regarding the ascetic Gautama, a fine reputation has spread thus: 'He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from gods to humans, he has himself realized through direct knowledge and declares it. His Dharma is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. It is complete in meaning and phrasing, perfectly pure, and he proclaims the holy life.' It would be good to visit such an arhat and pay respects to him."

Then the Kalāmas of Kesamutta, each with their retinues, proceeded to where the Buddha was. Some bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, then sat to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Buddha, then sat to one side. Some joined their palms toward the Buddha, then sat to one side. Some stated their names, then sat to one side. Some remained silent, then sat to one side.

After the Kalāmas of Kesamutta had sat down, they addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, there are some ascetics and brahmins who come to Kesamutta. They explain and illuminate their own doctrines, but they disparage, denigrate, scorn, and dismiss the doctrines of others. World-Honored One, then other ascetics and brahmins also come to Kesamutta. They too explain and illuminate their own doctrines, but they disparage, denigrate, scorn, and dismiss the doctrines of others. World-Honored One, regarding these, we have doubt and perplexity: 'Among these ascetics and brahmins, who speaks truth and who speaks falsehood?'"

The Buddha addressed the Kalāmas: "Do not be led by oral tradition, do not be led by lineage of teaching, do not be led by hearsay, do not be led by a collection of scriptures, do not be led by logical reasoning, do not be led by inferential reasoning, do not be led by reflection on appearances, do not be led by agreement through pondering views, do not be led by the seeming competence of a speaker, and do not be led by thinking 'this ascetic is our teacher.'

"Kalāmas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,' then you should abandon them.

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When greed arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's harm."

"Kalāmas, this greedy person, being overcome by greed, with mind consumed by it, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, and speaks falsely. He also induces others to do such things. Will this lead to his long-lasting harm and suffering?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When hatred arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's harm."

"Kalāmas, this hateful person, being overcome by hatred, with mind consumed by it, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, and speaks falsely. He also induces others to do such things. Will this lead to his long-lasting harm and suffering?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When delusion arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's harm."

"Kalāmas, this deluded person, being overcome by delusion, with mind consumed by it, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, and speaks falsely. He also induces others to do such things. Will this lead to his long-lasting harm and suffering?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Unwholesome, World-Honored One."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameworthy, World-Honored One."

"Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"

"Censured by the wise, World-Honored One."

"If undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What do you think?"

"If undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering. This is what we think, World-Honored One."

"Therefore, Kalāmas, I said: Do not be led by oral tradition, do not be led by lineage of teaching, do not be led by hearsay, do not be led by a collection of scriptures, do not be led by logical reasoning, do not be led by inferential reasoning, do not be led by reflection on appearances, do not be led by agreement through pondering views, do not be led by the seeming competence of a speaker, and do not be led by thinking 'this ascetic is our teacher.' Kalāmas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are unwholesome; these things are blameworthy; these things are censured by the wise; these things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,' then you should abandon them. This is why I spoke thus.

"Kalāmas, do not be led by oral tradition, do not be led by lineage of teaching, do not be led by hearsay, do not be led by a collection of scriptures, do not be led by logical reasoning, do not be led by inferential reasoning, do not be led by reflection on appearances, do not be led by agreement through pondering views, do not be led by the seeming competence of a speaker, and do not be led by thinking 'this ascetic is our teacher.'

"Kalāmas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to benefit and happiness,' then you should accept and practice them.

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When non-greed arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's benefit."

"Kalāmas, this non-greedy person, not being overcome by greed, with mind not consumed by it, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit sexual misconduct, and does not speak falsely. He also induces others to do likewise. Will this lead to his long-lasting benefit and happiness?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When non-hatred arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's benefit."

"Kalāmas, this non-hateful person, not being overcome by hatred, with mind not consumed by it, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit sexual misconduct, and does not speak falsely. He also induces others to do likewise. Will this lead to his long-lasting benefit and happiness?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? When non-delusion arises in a person, is it for that person's benefit or for that person's harm?"

The Kalāmas answered: "For that person's benefit."

"Kalāmas, this non-deluded person, not being overcome by delusion, with mind not consumed by it, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit sexual misconduct, and does not speak falsely. He also induces others to do likewise. Will this lead to his long-lasting benefit and happiness?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Kalāmas, what do you think? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?"

The Kalāmas answered: "Wholesome, World-Honored One."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

"Blameless, World-Honored One."

"Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"

"Praised by the wise, World-Honored One."

"If undertaken and practiced, do they lead to benefit and happiness, or not? What do you think?"

"If undertaken and practiced, they lead to benefit and happiness. This is what we think, World-Honored One."

"Therefore, Kalāmas, I said: Do not be led by oral tradition, do not be led by lineage of teaching, do not be led by hearsay, do not be led by a collection of scriptures, do not be led by logical reasoning, do not be led by inferential reasoning, do not be led by reflection on appearances, do not be led by agreement through pondering views, do not be led by the seeming competence of a speaker, and do not be led by thinking 'this ascetic is our teacher.' Kalāmas, when you know for yourselves: 'These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to benefit and happiness,' then you should accept and practice them. This is why I spoke thus.

"Kalāmas, the noble disciple who is thus free from covetousness and free from ill will, who is unconfused, with right mindfulness and right knowing, pervades one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will.

"He pervades one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will.

"He pervades one direction with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will.

"He pervades one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will.

"Kalāmas, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from ill will, undefiled, and pure, gains four comforts in this present life.

"The first comfort: 'If there is an afterlife, if there is karmic fruit of good and bad actions, then at the dissolution of the body after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He gains this first comfort.

"The second comfort: 'If there is no afterlife, if there is no karmic fruit of good and bad actions, then in this present life I live happily, free from enmity, free from ill will.' He gains this second comfort.

"The third comfort: 'If evil befalls an evildoer, then I, who intends no evil toward anyone, how shall evil befall me, since I have done no evil deed?' He gains this third comfort.

"The fourth comfort: 'If evil does not befall an evildoer, then in either case, I see myself as pure.' He gains this fourth comfort.

"Kalāmas, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from ill will, undefiled, and pure, gains these four comforts in this present life."

The Kalāmas addressed the Buddha: "So it is, World-Honored One! The noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from ill will, undefiled, and pure, gains four comforts in this present life.

"The first comfort: 'If there is an afterlife, if there is karmic fruit of good and bad actions, then at the dissolution of the body after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He gains this first comfort.

"The second comfort: 'If there is no afterlife, if there is no karmic fruit of good and bad actions, then in this present life I live happily, free from enmity, free from ill will.' He gains this second comfort.

"The third comfort: 'If evil befalls an evildoer, then I, who intends no evil toward anyone, how shall evil befall me, since I have done no evil deed?' He gains this third comfort.

"The fourth comfort: 'If evil does not befall an evildoer, then in either case, I see myself as pure.' He gains this fourth comfort.

"World-Honored One, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from ill will, undefiled, and pure, gains these four comforts in this present life.

"World-Honored One, how excellent! How excellent! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what had been hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. Likewise, the World-Honored One has explained the Dharma in various ways. We now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept us as lay disciples. From today until the end of our lives, we take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Kalāmas of Kesamutta, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(17) Sūtra on Kamma (Iti)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three causes and conditions for the arising of actions. What are the three? Greed is a cause and condition for the arising of actions. Hatred is a cause and condition for the arising of actions. Delusion is a cause and condition for the arising of actions.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from greed, born from greed, caused by greed, conditioned by greed: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from hatred, born from hatred, caused by hatred, conditioned by hatred: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from delusion, born from delusion, caused by delusion, conditioned by delusion: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that.

"Bhikṣus, it is like seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, fresh and intact, well preserved, planted in good soil, sown in fertile ground. Would these seeds thereby grow?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, actions arising from greed, born from greed, caused by greed, conditioned by greed: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that. Actions arising from hatred, born from hatred, caused by hatred, conditioned by hatred: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that. Actions arising from delusion, born from delusion, caused by delusion, conditioned by delusion: wherever that person is reborn, the karmic results ripen there. Where the karmic results ripen, there that person experiences the fruits of those actions, whether in this present life, or in a subsequent life, or in a life after that.

"Bhikṣus, there are three causes and conditions for the arising of actions. What are the three? Non-greed is a cause and condition for the arising of actions. Non-hatred is a cause and condition for the arising of actions. Non-delusion is a cause and condition for the arising of actions.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from non-greed, born from non-greed, caused by non-greed, conditioned by non-greed: when greed is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from non-hatred, born from non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, conditioned by non-hatred: when hatred is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise.

"Bhikṣus, actions arising from non-delusion, born from non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, conditioned by non-delusion: when delusion is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise.

"Bhikṣus, it is like seeds that are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, fresh and intact, well preserved; but if one burns them with fire and reduces them to ashes, and then scatters them in strong wind or casts them into a swift river. Bhikṣus, would these seeds thereby grow?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, actions arising from non-greed, born from non-greed, caused by non-greed, conditioned by non-greed: when greed is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise. Actions arising from non-hatred, born from non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, conditioned by non-hatred: when hatred is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise. Actions arising from non-delusion, born from non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, conditioned by non-delusion: when delusion is already ended, those actions are thereby abandoned, cut off at the root, like a palmyra stump that can never grow again, and in the future will not arise."

Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"Greed, hatred, and delusion:
From oneself arise evil thoughts.
They bring harm to oneself,
As a seed produces its own fruit.

Without greed, without hatred,
And without delusion:
The wise one discards evil thoughts,
As a seed once burned does not grow."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(18) Sūtra on the Brahmin Dhānañjāni (First)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the brahmin Dhānañjāni, by various means, lived unrighteously through wrong livelihood, making his living by deceiving and defrauding. Relying on the king, he cheated the brahmins and householders. Relying on the brahmins and householders, he cheated the king.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra heard that the brahmin Dhānañjāni, by various means, lived unrighteously through wrong livelihood, making his living by deceiving and defrauding. Relying on the king, he cheated the brahmins and householders. Relying on the brahmins and householders, he cheated the king.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the brahmin Dhānañjāni was. Having arrived, he sat down on a prepared seat. The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the brahmin Dhānañjāni: "What are you doing? I have heard that you, by various means, live unrighteously through wrong livelihood, making your living by deceiving and defrauding. Relying on the king, you cheat the brahmins and householders. Relying on the brahmins and householders, you cheat the king. Is this true?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, what can I do? I must support my father and mother. I must support my wife and children. I must support my servants and workers. I must make offerings to friends and acquaintances. I must make offerings to relatives and kin. I must make offerings to guests. I must make offerings for deceased ancestors. I must make offerings to the gods. I must pay tribute to the king. Furthermore, this body must be nourished to sustain its life. Therefore, Venerable Śāriputra, I must by various means live through wrong livelihood."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of his father and mother, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of my father and mother. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could his father and mother say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of his wife and children, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of my wife and children. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could his wife and children say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of his servants and workers, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of my servants and workers. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could his servants and workers say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of friends and acquaintances, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of my friends and acquaintances. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could his friends and acquaintances say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of relatives and kin, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of my relatives and kin. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could his relatives and kin say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of guests, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of guests. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could the guests say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of deceased ancestors, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of deceased ancestors. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could the deceased ancestors say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of the gods, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of the gods. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could the gods say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of the king, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of the king. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could the king say: 'He lived unrighteously for our sake. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of nourishing this body, by various means lives unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Because of this unrighteous action, the hell-keepers seize him and drag him to hell. Could he then say: 'I lived unrighteously for the sake of nourishing this body. Hell-keepers, do not drag me to hell!'? Or could anyone else say: 'He lived unrighteously for the sake of nourishing the body. Hell-keepers, do not drag him to hell! We will suffer in his place!'?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "No, Venerable Śāriputra. Even as he cries out, the hell-keepers would cast him into hell."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Which is better: to live unrighteously through wrong livelihood for the sake of father and mother, or to live righteously through right livelihood?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, to live righteously through right livelihood is better, not to live unrighteously through wrong livelihood. Venerable Śāriputra, one who lives righteously through right livelihood can, at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Which is better: to live unrighteously through wrong livelihood for the sake of wife and children, or to live righteously through right livelihood?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, to live righteously through right livelihood is better. One who lives righteously through right livelihood can, at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Which is better: to live unrighteously through wrong livelihood for the sake of servants and workers, friends and acquaintances, relatives and kin, guests, deceased ancestors, the gods, the king, or for nourishing this body, or to live righteously through right livelihood?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, to live righteously through right livelihood is better. One who lives righteously through right livelihood can, at the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, a person can, through righteous means, support his father and mother, and also support his wife and children, servants and workers, friends and acquaintances, relatives and kin, guests, make offerings for deceased ancestors, make offerings to the gods, pay tribute to the king, and also nourish this body. One does not need to live unrighteously through wrong livelihood."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra said, was delighted and pleased. He rose from his seat and departed.

At a later time, the brahmin Dhānañjāni fell ill with a painful ailment. He said to someone: "Go to the World-Honored One, bow your head at the Buddha's feet on my behalf, and ask after his health, saying: 'May the World-Honored One be free from illness and distress, with ease of body, strength, and comfort.' Also go to the Venerable Śāriputra, bow your head at his feet on my behalf, and ask after his health, saying: 'May the Venerable Śāriputra be free from illness and distress, with ease of body, strength, and comfort.' Then say: 'May the Venerable Śāriputra have compassion and come to the brahmin Dhānañjāni's home.'"

That person received the instruction and went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. He addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the brahmin Dhānañjāni bows his head at the World-Honored One's feet and asks after your health: 'May the World-Honored One be free from illness and distress, with ease of body, strength, and comfort.'"

Then he went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side. He addressed the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni bows his head at the Venerable's feet and asks after your health: 'May the Venerable Śāriputra be free from illness and distress, with ease of body, strength, and comfort. May the Venerable Śāriputra have compassion and come to the brahmin Dhānañjāni's home.'"

The Venerable Śāriputra, having received the request, silently consented. He put on his robe, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. After his meal, he went to the brahmin Dhānañjāni's home. Having arrived, he sat on a prepared seat.

The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the brahmin Dhānañjāni: "How are you feeling? Is your illness getting better or worse? Is the pain increasing or decreasing?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I am not at ease. The illness is getting worse, not better. The pain is increasing, not decreasing. It is as if a strong man were boring into my head with a sharp awl; so is the severe pain in my head. Venerable Śāriputra, I am not at ease. The illness is getting worse, not better. The pain is increasing, not decreasing. It is as if a strong man were tying a leather strap around my head and tightening it; so is the severe pain in my head. Venerable Śāriputra, I am not at ease. It is as if a skilled butcher were cutting open a living ox's belly with a sharp knife; so is the severe pain in my belly. Venerable Śāriputra, I am not at ease. It is as if two strong men were to seize a weaker man and roast him over a fire pit; so does my entire body burn with heat."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, I will now ask you. Answer as you see fit. Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Which is better, hell or the animal realm?"

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "The animal realm is better than hell."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the animal realm or the realm of hungry ghosts?"

"The realm of hungry ghosts is better than the animal realm."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the realm of hungry ghosts or the human realm?"

"The human realm is better than the realm of hungry ghosts."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the human realm or the heaven of the Four Great Kings?"

"The heaven of the Four Great Kings is better than the human realm."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the heaven of the Four Great Kings or the heaven of the Thirty-Three?"

"The heaven of the Thirty-Three is better than the heaven of the Four Great Kings."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the heaven of the Thirty-Three or the Yāma heaven?"

"The Yāma heaven is better than the heaven of the Thirty-Three."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the Yāma heaven or the Tuṣita heaven?"

"The Tuṣita heaven is better than the Yāma heaven."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the Tuṣita heaven or the Nirmāṇarati heaven?"

"The Nirmāṇarati heaven is better than the Tuṣita heaven."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the Nirmāṇarati heaven or the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven?"

"The Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven is better than the Nirmāṇarati heaven."

"Dhānañjāni, which is better, the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven or the Brahma heavenly world?"

"The Venerable Śāriputra mentions the Brahma world! The Venerable Śāriputra mentions the Brahma world!"

Then the Venerable Śāriputra thought: "This brahmin Dhānañjāni has long had faith in and reverence for Brahmā. Let me teach him the path to rebirth in the Brahma world."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, I will now teach you the path leading to union with the Brahma world. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

"Dhānañjāni, what is the path leading to union with the Brahma world? A bhikṣu pervades one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will. In the same way with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he pervades one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, and above, below, and all around, pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without ill will. Dhānañjāni, this is the path leading to union with the Brahma world."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, please bow to the Buddha's feet on my behalf and say: 'The brahmin Dhānañjāni is ill and in suffering. He is unable to come and wishes to bow at the World-Honored One's feet.'"

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having taught the brahmin Dhānañjāni the path of the four immeasurables leading to the Brahma world, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after the Venerable Śāriputra had left, the brahmin Dhānañjāni passed away. His mind at the time of death was established in the Brahma world, and he was reborn in that Brahma world.

The Venerable Śāriputra, having left the brahmin Dhānañjāni's home, returned to the Buddha. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. He addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the brahmin Dhānañjāni bows his head at the World-Honored One's feet and says: 'I am ill and in suffering. I am unable to come and wish to bow at the World-Honored One's feet.' World-Honored One, I went to the brahmin Dhānañjāni's home and taught him the path of the four immeasurables leading to the Brahma world."

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, why did you teach the brahmin Dhānañjāni only the path of the four immeasurables leading to the Brahma world? Śāriputra, there is a higher teaching. Śāriputra, you should have gone further and taught the brahmin Dhānañjāni the path beyond, so that he could have attained something higher. Having listened, he would have been able to attain liberation from the fetters of this world. Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni has now passed away and been reborn in the Brahma world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(19) Sūtra on the Brahmin Dhānañjāni (Second)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, a brahmin named Dhānañjāni went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, then sat to one side.

The brahmin Dhānañjāni addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, I now declare: 'I speak truth, not falsehood.' This is my assertion."

The Buddha said: "Dhānañjāni, if you declare: 'I speak truth, not falsehood,' then regarding this assertion, you should examine: 'Does this bring benefit to myself? Does this bring benefit to others? Does this bring benefit to both?' If it brings benefit to myself, benefit to others, and benefit to both, then such speech should be spoken, should be widely proclaimed; it is not evil, it produces no suffering, and its fruit brings happiness. For this reason, you should speak it extensively.

"Dhānañjāni, if you declare: 'I speak truth, not falsehood,' but upon examining, you find: 'This brings no benefit to myself, no benefit to others, and no benefit to both,' then such speech should not be spoken. It produces evil, it produces suffering, and its fruit brings suffering.

"Dhānañjāni, a foolish, ignorant person does not examine beforehand whether speech brings benefit to oneself, benefit to others, and benefit to both. He simply speaks it. After speaking, he regrets it.

"Dhānañjāni, a wise, learned person first examines whether speech brings benefit to oneself, benefit to others, and benefit to both. If it brings benefit to all, he speaks it. After speaking, he does not regret it."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how excellent! How excellent! The World-Honored One has expounded the Dharma in various ways. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Dhānañjāni, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(20) Sūtra on Pāṭaliya**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Aṅga, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, and arrived at a town of Aṅga called Āpaṇa.

At that time, the householder Pāṭaliya heard: "The ascetic Gautama, son of the Śākya clan, who left the Śākya household to go forth, is now traveling in Aṅga with a great assembly of bhikṣus and has arrived at Āpaṇa. Now regarding the ascetic Gautama, a fine reputation has spread thus: 'He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from gods to humans, he has himself realized through direct knowledge and declares it. His Dharma is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. It is complete in meaning and phrasing, perfectly pure, and he proclaims the holy life.' It would be good to visit such an arhat and pay respects to him."

Then the householder Pāṭaliya prepared a chariot and, accompanied by a retinue, departed from Āpaṇa, proceeding to where the Buddha was. He dismounted from the chariot, approached on foot, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One gradually taught the Dharma to the householder Pāṭaliya, instructing, benefiting, and delighting him, teaching about generosity, about morality, about rebirth in heaven, about the perils, defilement, and impurity of desires, and about the benefit of renunciation. When the World-Honored One knew that the householder Pāṭaliya's mind was ready, soft, free of hindrances, uplifted, and joyful, as all Buddhas customarily teach the Dharma, he explained suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean, unstained white cloth can easily absorb dye, so too did the householder Pāṭaliya, right there on his seat, gain the pure Dharma-eye with regard to all phenomena: all that is subject to arising is subject to cessation.

Then the householder Pāṭaliya, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, penetrated the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, removed perplexity, was self-assured, and did not depend on another for the Teacher's teaching. He addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts. I shall not kill living beings, not take what is not given, not commit sexual misconduct, not speak falsely, and not drink alcohol."

The householder Pāṭaliya, having heard what the Buddha taught, was delighted and pleased. He rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

The householder Pāṭaliya then went to where the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra was. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings and sat to one side.

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Householder, did you go to see the ascetic Gautama?"

"Yes, I went to see him."

"Householder, did the ascetic Gautama speak of actions? Does the ascetic Gautama teach about actions?"

The householder Pāṭaliya answered: "The ascetic Gautama certainly speaks of actions, certainly teaches about actions."

Then the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra looked around at his assembly and said: "All of you, listen. This householder Pāṭaliya speaks truly, does not speak falsely. The ascetic Gautama teaches actions. If the ascetic Gautama teaches actions, then the ascetic Gautama is no different from me. Why? Because I too teach actions."

Then the householder Pāṭaliya addressed the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra: "Venerable sir, please do not say that. Why? Because the World-Honored One teaches three kinds of actions, establishing three kinds of actions. He teaches bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. Among these, bodily action is one thing, verbal action is another, and mental action is yet another. Among these three actions, the World-Honored One says mental action is the most grave, giving rise to the most severe evil. He does not say bodily action or verbal action is most grave."

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Householder, among these three actions, I say bodily action is the most grave, giving rise to the most severe evil. I do not say verbal action or mental action is most grave. Householder, bodily action is the most grave."

The householder Pāṭaliya, wishing to dissuade the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra three times, but being unable to change his view, rose from his seat and departed.

At another time, a Nigaṇṭha disciple named Upāli, who was a prominent householder, addressed the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra: "Venerable sir, this householder Pāṭaliya went to see the ascetic Gautama and was unable to refute his views. He instead accepted the ascetic Gautama's views. Venerable sir, I wish to go to the ascetic Gautama and refute his views."

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Upāli, you may go to refute the ascetic Gautama's views. Either I can refute the ascetic Gautama's views, or the householder Upāli can refute them."

Then the Nigaṇṭha disciple Tapassī addressed the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra: "Venerable sir, I fear that the householder Upāli may be unable to refute the ascetic Gautama's views. I fear the ascetic Gautama may instead convert Upāli to accept his own views."

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Tapassī, there is no possibility that the householder Upāli could accept the ascetic Gautama's views. It is only possible that the ascetic Gautama would accept Upāli's views."

He said this a second and a third time: "Tapassī, there is no possibility that the householder Upāli could accept the ascetic Gautama's views. It is only possible that the ascetic Gautama would accept Upāli's views. Upāli, go now."

Then the householder Upāli bowed at the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra's feet and went to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side.

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, did the householder Pāṭaliya come here?"

The Buddha said: "Yes, the householder Pāṭaliya came here."

"Gautama, did you teach the householder Pāṭaliya about three kinds of actions, establishing three kinds of actions?"

The Buddha said: "Yes, I taught the householder Pāṭaliya about three kinds of actions, establishing three kinds of actions. I taught bodily action, verbal action, and mental action."

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, regarding these three actions, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, are these three actions different, or are they the same?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, regarding these three actions, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, these three actions are each different. Bodily action is one thing, verbal action is another, and mental action is yet another."

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, among these three actions, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, which does Gautama say is the most grave, giving rise to the most severe evil?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, among these three actions, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, mental action is the most grave, giving rise to the most severe evil. I do not say bodily action or verbal action is most grave."

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, did you say mental action is the most grave?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, I said mental action is the most grave."

"Gautama, did you truly say mental action is the most grave?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, I truly said mental action is the most grave."

"Gautama, did you truly say mental action is the most grave?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, I truly said mental action is the most grave."

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, I now base my argument on this: I will ask Gautama questions, and I request Gautama to answer me."

The Buddha said: "Upāli, ask as you wish. I will consider and answer."

The householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, suppose there were a Nigaṇṭha who was ill, in pain, and suffering, and he refused cold water, accepting only warm water. Being unable to obtain warm water, he died. Gautama, where does the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra say such a person is reborn?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, there are gods called Mind-Bound. That Nigaṇṭha is reborn among those gods. Why? Because when that person died, his mind was bound. Upāli, a person's rebirth accords with whatever their mind is bound to at the time of death."

The householder Upāli, having heard this, thought: "How excellent, what the ascetic Gautama has said is well spoken." And he thought: "There is only one action that is the most grave, that is mental action, not bodily action and not verbal action."

Though Upāli thought this, he still wished to argue with the Buddha and addressed him: "Gautama, I now ask Gautama a question. I request Gautama to answer. Suppose someone, without thought, without deliberation, neither by bodily action nor verbal action, but by mental action alone, were to cause the destruction of a village or town or city, causing many living beings to die. This would be a grave mental action, would it not?"

The Buddha said: "Upāli, so it is. One person, by mental action, could destroy an entire village or town or city."

Upāli said: "Gautama speaks well!"

In this way, the householder Upāli, point by point, was unable to refute the Buddha's teaching. Then the householder Upāli addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how excellent! How excellent! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what had been hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. Likewise, the World-Honored One has explained the Dharma in various ways. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha said: "Upāli, you should consider carefully. It is not fitting for a well-known person like you to act hastily."

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, how excellent! If other ascetics and brahmins were to gain me as a disciple, they would parade it throughout the town with banners, saying: 'The householder Upāli has become my disciple.' But the World-Honored One tells me: 'Upāli, you should consider carefully. It is not fitting for a well-known person like you to act hastily.' World-Honored One, I now a second time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha said: "Upāli, you have long supported the Nigaṇṭha community. You should consider continuing to provide offerings to them as before."

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, how excellent! This is even more exceptional. World-Honored One, I now a third time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

Then the World-Honored One gradually taught the Dharma to the householder Upāli, instructing, benefiting, and delighting him, teaching about generosity, about morality, about rebirth in heaven, about the perils, defilement, and impurity of desires, and about the benefit of renunciation. When the World-Honored One knew that the householder Upāli's mind was ready, soft, free of hindrances, uplifted, and joyful, as all Buddhas customarily teach the Dharma, he explained suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as a clean, unstained white cloth can easily absorb dye, so too did the householder Upāli, right there on his seat, gain the pure Dharma-eye with regard to all phenomena: all that is subject to arising is subject to cessation.

Then the householder Upāli, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the Dharma, penetrated the Dharma, crossed beyond doubt, removed perplexity, was self-assured, and did not depend on another for the Teacher's teaching. He addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I now must take my leave."

The Buddha said: "Upāli, you may go as you see fit."

The householder Upāli rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He returned home and instructed his gatekeeper: "From today onward, I close my gate to Nigaṇṭha men and women. The gate is open to the Buddha's bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, lay men, and lay women. If any Nigaṇṭha comes, tell them: 'The householder Upāli has now become a disciple of the Buddha. The gate is closed to Nigaṇṭha men and women. The gate is open to the Buddha's bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, lay men, and lay women. If you need food, please wait here and it will be brought out to you.'"

The gatekeeper received the instruction: "Yes, sir."

Then a Nigaṇṭha disciple named Tapassī heard that the householder Upāli had become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama. He went to the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra and said: "Venerable sir, I have heard that the householder Upāli has become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama."

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Tapassī, there is no possibility that the householder Upāli could become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama. It is only possible that the ascetic Gautama could become a disciple of Upāli."

He said this a second and a third time: "Tapassī, there is no possibility that the householder Upāli could become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama. It is only possible that the ascetic Gautama could become a disciple of Upāli."

Tapassī said a second and a third time: "Venerable sir, if someone agrees to wager on this matter, I dare say: the householder Upāli has certainly become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama; the ascetic Gautama has not become a disciple of Upāli. Venerable sir, if you do not believe me, you may go yourself and investigate."

Then the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra, accompanied by a large retinue, went to the householder Upāli's home. The gatekeeper saw the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra coming from afar and said: "Venerable sir, please stop. The householder Upāli has now become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama. The gate is closed to Nigaṇṭha men and women. The gate is open to the Buddha's bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, lay men, and lay women. If you need food, please wait here and it will be brought out to you."

The Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Good gatekeeper, I do not need food. I only need to see the householder Upāli."

The gatekeeper said: "Venerable sir, please wait. I will go and announce you."

The gatekeeper went in and announced: "Sir, the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra is outside at the gate with a large retinue, and he wishes to see you."

The householder Upāli said: "Let the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra into the middle hall."

The gatekeeper received the instruction and went to the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra: "Sir, the householder Upāli invites you to the middle hall."

Then the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra went to the middle hall. There the householder Upāli had formerly placed a high, broad seat with a magnificent canopy for the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra, but now he himself sat upon it. When the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra entered and saw this, he said: "Upāli, is it true that you have now become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama?"

The householder Upāli said: "Venerable sir, you should know: the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, is my true Teacher. I am the Buddha's disciple."

Then the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra said: "Upāli, you have been deceived by the ascetic Gautama's illusory transformation!"

The householder Upāli said: "Venerable sir, the ascetic Gautama's illusory transformation is most excellent. If my dear relatives, my father and mother, wife and children, and all the brahmins and householders, were to be transformed by such an illusory transformation, it would bring them long-lasting benefit and happiness."

Then the Nigaṇṭha Jñātiputra, unable to convert the householder Upāli, hot blood gushed from his mouth. He departed from the householder Upāli's home and returned to his own place.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### **(21) Sūtra on Equanimity (First)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing, perfectly pure, proclaiming the holy life, namely the Sūtra on Equanimity. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we will listen."

The Buddha said: "

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 4

---

## (18) Sūtra on Sīha, Eighth of the Chapter on Deeds

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Vaiśālī, staying at the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pond.

At that time, many Licchavi nobles of Vaiśālī had gathered in the assembly hall and repeatedly praised the Buddha, repeatedly praised the Dharma, and praised the community of bhikṣus. At that time, the general Sīha, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, was also in the assembly.

At that time, General Sīha wished to go and see the Buddha, to make offerings and pay respects. General Sīha first went to the Nirgranthas and addressed them, saying: "Venerable ones, I wish to go and see the śramaṇa Gautama."

At that time, the Nirgranthas rebuked Sīha, saying: "You should not wish to see the śramaṇa Gautama. Why is that? The śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action. Sīha, if you see one who fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action, it will be inauspicious; to make offerings and pay respects to him will also be inauspicious."

Those many Licchavi nobles of Vaiśālī gathered a second and a third time in the assembly hall, repeatedly praising the Buddha, repeatedly praising the Dharma, and praising the community of bhikṣus. At that time, the general Sīha, disciple of the Nirgranthas, was also a second and a third time present in that assembly. At that time, General Sīha also wished a second and a third time to go and see the Buddha, to make offerings and pay respects.

General Sīha then, without taking leave of the Nirgranthas, went to visit the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side and spoke these words: "I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action. Gautama, if it is said thus, that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action, do those who say this not slander the śramaṇa Gautama? Do they speak the truth? Do they speak what is Dharma? Do they speak Dharma in accordance with Dharma? Is there in accordance with Dharma no fault, no grounds for reproach?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Sīha, if it is said thus, that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action, those who say this do not slander the śramaṇa Gautama. They speak the truth, they speak what is Dharma, they speak Dharma in accordance with Dharma; in the Dharma there is no fault, nor any grounds for reproach. Why is that? Sīha, there is a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of action and also teaches others the doctrine of action. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of annihilation and also teaches others the doctrine of annihilation. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of abhorrence and also teaches others the doctrine of what is abhorrent. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the Dharma and Vinaya and also teaches others the doctrine of Dharma and Vinaya. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of austerity and also teaches others the doctrine of austerity. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-entry into the womb and also teaches others the doctrine of non-entry into the womb. Sīha, there is again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of security and also teaches others the doctrine of security.

"Sīha, how is there a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action? Sīha, I teach that evil conduct of body should not be done, and that evil conduct of speech and mind should also not be done. Sīha, all such innumerable unwholesome, defiled dharmas that are the basis for future existence, that bring the affliction of painful retribution, and that are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death: I teach that all these should not be done. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-action and also teaches others the doctrine of non-action.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of action and also teaches others the doctrine of action? Sīha, I teach that wholesome conduct of body should be done, and that wholesome conduct of speech and mind should also be done. Sīha, all such innumerable wholesome dharmas that bear pleasant fruit, that receive pleasant retribution, that lead to birth in good realms and the attainment of long life: I teach that all these should be done. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of action and also teaches others the doctrine of action.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of annihilation and also teaches others the doctrine of annihilation? Sīha, I teach that evil conduct of body should be annihilated, and that evil conduct of speech and mind should also be annihilated. Sīha, all such innumerable unwholesome, defiled dharmas that are the basis for future existence, that bring the affliction of painful retribution, and that are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death: I teach that all these should be annihilated. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of annihilation and also teaches others the doctrine of annihilation.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of abhorrence and also teaches others the doctrine of what is abhorrent? Sīha, I teach that evil conduct of body is to be abhorred, and that evil conduct of speech and mind is also to be abhorred. Sīha, all such innumerable unwholesome, defiled dharmas that are the basis for future existence, that bring the affliction of painful retribution, and that are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death: I teach that all these are to be abhorred. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of abhorrence and also teaches others the doctrine of what is abhorrent.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the Dharma and Vinaya and also teaches others the doctrine of Dharma and Vinaya? Sīha, I teach the Dharma and Vinaya for the purpose of cutting off sensual desire, I teach the Dharma and Vinaya for the purpose of cutting off anger and delusion. Sīha, all such innumerable unwholesome, defiled dharmas that are the basis for future existence, that bring the affliction of painful retribution, and that are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death: I teach the Dharma and Vinaya for the purpose of cutting them off. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the Dharma and Vinaya and also teaches others the doctrine of Dharma and Vinaya.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of austerity and also teaches others the doctrine of austerity? Sīha, there are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who go naked and without clothing, or use their hands as clothing, or use leaves as clothing, or use beads as clothing; who do not take water with a vessel, who do not take water with a ladle; who do not eat food obtained by the sword, staff, or plunder; who do not eat food obtained by deceit; who do not go themselves to receive food, who do not send a messenger, who do not come when honored, who do not accept with delight what is honored, who do not accept what is offered while standing. If two persons are eating, they do not eat among them. They do not eat at the home of a pregnant woman, they do not eat at a home that keeps dogs. If flies come to the home because of refuse, they do not eat there. They do not eat fish, they do not eat meat, they do not drink liquor, they do not drink foul water; or they drink nothing at all and practice the conduct of non-drinking. Or they eat one mouthful and are satisfied with one mouthful; or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, and are satisfied with seven mouthfuls. Or they eat from one alms-receiving and are satisfied with one receiving; or two, three, four, up to seven receivings, and are satisfied with seven receivings. Or they eat once a day and are satisfied with one meal; or once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once a half-month, or once a month, and are satisfied with one meal. Or they eat herbs and greens, or eat millet, or eat unhusked rice, or eat mixed coarse grains, or eat rice chaff, or eat coarse food. Or they go to a deserted place and rely on seclusion. Or they eat roots, or eat fruits, or eat naturally fallen fruits. Or they wear garments of joined pieces, or wear wool garments, or wear garments of head-hair, or wear garments of mixed wool and head-hair, or wear whole hides, or wear perforated hides, or wear both whole and perforated hides. Or they let their hair hang loose, or they braid their hair, or they have both loose and braided hair. Or they shave their head, or they shave their beard, or they shave both beard and head-hair. Or they pull out their head-hair, or they pull out their beard, or they pull out both beard and head-hair. Or they stand continuously and refuse to sit, or they practice squatting, or they lie on thorns and use thorns as their bed, or they lie on fruits and use fruits as their bed. Or they worship water and scoop it with their hands day and night, or they worship fire and keep it burning all night long, or they worship the sun and moon, honoring great spirits, pressing their palms together toward them. In such ways as these, they undergo immeasurable suffering and practice the conduct of affliction and austerity. Sīha, such austerities exist; I do not say they do not. Sīha, however, such austerities are base practices, leading to utmost suffering and hardship, practiced by ordinary people, and are not the noble path. Sīha, if there are śramaṇas or brahmins who know those austere dharmas to be completely annihilated and extinguished, their roots entirely uprooted, ultimately never to arise again, then I call them practitioners of austerity. Sīha, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, knows those austere dharmas to be completely annihilated and extinguished, their roots entirely uprooted, ultimately never to arise again; therefore I am an ascetic. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of austerity and also teaches others the doctrine of austerity.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-entry into the womb and also teaches others the doctrine of non-entry into the womb? Sīha, if there are śramaṇas or brahmins for whom the future womb-birth is known to be completely annihilated and extinguished, its roots entirely uprooted, ultimately never to arise again, then I call them ones who do not enter the womb. Sīha, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, knows the future womb-birth to be completely annihilated and extinguished, its roots entirely uprooted, ultimately never to arise again; therefore I do not enter the womb. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of non-entry into the womb and also teaches others the doctrine of non-entry into the womb.

"Sīha, how is there again a matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of security and also teaches others the doctrine of security? Sīha, when sons of good family shave off their beards and hair, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household life to become homeless and study the path, they do so solely to bring the unsurpassed holy life to its fulfillment. In the present Dharma, I know for myself, realize for myself, and personally attain and abide in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, I will not receive further existence.' I know this as it truly is. I myself am secure, and I also bring security to other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. I have already secured them; for beings subject to birth, I liberate them from birth. For beings subject to old age, sickness, death, and the defilements of grief and sorrow, I liberate them from the defilements of grief and sorrow. Sīha, this is what is meant by the matter on account of which, in accordance with true Dharma, one cannot be reproached for saying that the śramaṇa Gautama fundamentally holds the doctrine of security and also teaches others the doctrine of security."

General Sīha addressed the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. Gautama, it is as if a person with clear sight were to turn up what was overturned, uncover what was concealed, show the way to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes may see forms. The śramaṇa Gautama has likewise, through innumerable skillful means, expounded the Dharma, revealed its meaning, and shown its various paths. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days. World-Honored One, just as a person who feeds unworthy horses hoping to gain profit toils in vain and gains nothing, so too, World-Honored One, have I been. Those foolish Nirgranthas, lacking understanding, unable to know themselves, not recognizing the good field, and not examining themselves, I have for a long night revered, made offerings, and paid respects to them, hoping to gain profit, but have suffered in vain without benefit. World-Honored One, I now a second time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days. World-Honored One, formerly, in my ignorance, I had faith in and reverence for the foolish Nirgranthas. From this day I sever that. Why? Because they deceived me. World-Honored One, I now a third time take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days."

Thus spoke the Buddha. General Sīha and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

---

## (19) Sūtra on the Nirgranthas, Ninth of the Chapter on Deeds in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Śākyan country, in the town of Devadaha.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The Nirgranthas hold this view and make this statement: 'Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions. If past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted. When all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted. When suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.'

"I then went to them and, upon arriving, asked: 'Nirgranthas, do you truly hold this view and make this statement: Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions; if past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted; when all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering?'

"They answered me: 'It is so, Gautama.'

"I then asked the Nirgranthas again: 'Do you yourselves have the pure knowledge to know whether in the past you existed or did not exist, whether in the past you did evil or did not do evil, whether such-and-such suffering has been exhausted or such-and-such suffering has not been exhausted, and that when it is exhausted one attains exhaustion, so that in the present life one cuts off all unwholesome dharmas, attains all wholesome dharmas, and cultivates and realizes them?'

"They answered me: 'No, Gautama.'

"I then said to the Nirgranthas: 'You yourselves lack the pure knowledge to know whether in the past you existed or did not exist, whether in the past you did evil or did not do evil, whether such-and-such suffering has been exhausted or such-and-such suffering has not been exhausted, and that when it is exhausted one attains exhaustion, so that in the present life one cuts off all unwholesome dharmas, attains all wholesome dharmas, and cultivates and realizes them. Yet you make this statement: Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions; if past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted; when all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.

"'Nirgranthas, if you yourselves had the pure knowledge to know whether in the past you existed or did not exist, whether in the past you did evil or did not do evil, whether such-and-such suffering has been exhausted or such-and-such suffering has not been exhausted, and that when it is exhausted one attains exhaustion, so that in the present life one cuts off all unwholesome dharmas, attains all wholesome dharmas, and cultivates and realizes them, then, Nirgranthas, you could indeed make this statement: Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions; if past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted; when all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.'

"Nirgranthas, it is like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow. Because of being struck by the poisoned arrow, he experiences extreme suffering. His relatives, out of compassion and pity, wishing to benefit him and bring him security, immediately call an arrow-removing physician. The arrow-removing physician comes and uses a sharp knife to open the wound. During the opening of the wound, there is again extreme suffering. Having opened the wound, he searches for the arrowhead. During the search for the arrowhead, there is again extreme suffering. Having found the arrowhead, he then pulls it out. During the pulling out, there is again extreme suffering. After the arrowhead has been pulled out, a thin poultice is wrapped around the wound. During the wrapping of the wound, there is again extreme suffering. After the arrowhead has been removed, the man regains his strength and is free from illness; his faculties are unimpaired and he recovers as before.

"Nirgranthas, that person himself possesses the pure knowledge and thinks thus: 'Formerly I was struck by a poisoned arrow. Because of being struck by the poisoned arrow, I experienced extreme suffering. My relatives, seeing me, out of compassion and pity, wishing to benefit me and bring me security, immediately called an arrow-removing physician. The arrow-removing physician came and used a sharp knife to open my wound. During the opening of the wound, I again experienced extreme suffering. Having opened the wound, he searched for the arrowhead. During the search for the arrowhead, I again experienced extreme suffering. Having found the arrowhead, he then pulled it out. During the pulling out, I again experienced extreme suffering. After the arrowhead was pulled out, a thin poultice was wrapped around the wound. During the wrapping of the wound, I again experienced extreme suffering. After the arrowhead was removed, I regained my strength and am free from illness; my faculties are unimpaired and I have recovered as before.'

"Likewise, Nirgranthas, if you yourselves had the pure knowledge to know whether in the past you existed or did not exist, whether in the past you did evil or did not do evil, whether such-and-such suffering has been exhausted or such-and-such suffering has not been exhausted, and that when it is exhausted one attains exhaustion, so that in the present life one cuts off all unwholesome dharmas, attains all wholesome dharmas, and cultivates and realizes them, then, Nirgranthas, you could indeed make this statement: Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions; if past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted; when all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering. When I questioned them thus, I did not see that the Nirgranthas could answer me: "It is so, Gautama," or "It is not so."
