"Furthermore, I asked the Nirgranthas: 'If the Nirgranthas undertake supreme cutting-off and supreme austerity, do the Nirgranthas at that time experience supreme suffering?' They answered me: 'It is so, Gautama.' 'If there is middling cutting-off and middling austerity, do the Nirgranthas at that time experience middling suffering?' They answered me: 'It is so, Gautama.' 'If there is lesser cutting-off and lesser austerity, do the Nirgranthas at that time experience lesser suffering?' They answered me: 'It is so, Gautama.'

"Thus, when the Nirgranthas undertake supreme cutting-off and supreme austerity, then the Nirgranthas experience supreme suffering. When there is middling cutting-off and middling austerity, then the Nirgranthas experience middling suffering. When there is lesser cutting-off and lesser austerity, then the Nirgranthas experience lesser suffering. If when the Nirgranthas undertake supreme cutting-off and supreme austerity, then the Nirgranthas' supreme suffering ceased; if when there is middling cutting-off and middling austerity, then the Nirgranthas' middling suffering ceased; if when there is lesser cutting-off and lesser austerity, then the Nirgranthas' lesser suffering ceased; if whether acting thus or not acting thus, the most extreme and gravest suffering ceased, then one should know that the Nirgranthas create suffering in the present life itself. But the Nirgranthas, covered by delusion, bound by delusion, make this statement: 'Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions; if past deeds are extinguished through austerity and no new deeds are created, then all deeds will be exhausted; when all deeds are exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.' When I questioned them thus, I did not see that the Nirgranthas could answer me: 'It is so, Gautama,' or 'It is not so.'

"Furthermore, I asked the Nirgranthas: 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed that is to be retributed with pleasure, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed with suffering?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.' 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed that is to be retributed with suffering, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed with pleasure?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.' 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed to be retributed in the present life, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed in a future life?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.' 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed to be retributed in a future life, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed in the present life?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.' 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed whose retribution has not yet matured, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one whose retribution has matured?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.' 'Nirgranthas, if there is a deed whose retribution has matured, can that deed, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into something different?' They answered me: 'No, Gautama.'

"'Nirgranthas, thus a deed that is to be retributed with pleasure cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed with suffering. Nirgranthas, a deed that is to be retributed with suffering cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed with pleasure. Nirgranthas, a deed to be retributed in the present life cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed in a future life. Nirgranthas, a deed to be retributed in a future life cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one retributed in the present life. Nirgranthas, a deed whose retribution has not yet matured cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into one whose retribution has matured. Nirgranthas, a deed whose retribution has matured cannot, through cutting-off and austerity, be transformed into something different. Therefore, Nirgranthas, your efforts are vain, your cutting-off is empty and yields nothing.'

"Those Nirgranthas then replied to me: 'Gautama, we have a venerable teacher named Nirgrantha Jñātaputra, who makes this statement: "Nirgranthas, whatever evil deeds you committed in the past, all those deeds can be extinguished through this austerity. If now you guard your body, speech, and mind, then by this you will create no further evil deeds."'

"I then asked those Nirgranthas again: 'Do you believe your venerable teacher Nirgrantha Jñātaputra without doubt or hesitation?' They answered me: 'Gautama, we believe our venerable teacher Nirgrantha Jñātaputra without any doubt or hesitation.'

"I then said to the Nirgranthas: 'There are five kinds of dharmas that in the present life produce two kinds of results: faith, inclination, what is heard, recollection, and what is seen through careful examination. Nirgranthas, can a person's own false words be considered trustworthy, agreeable, worthy of being heard, memorable, and well-examined?' They answered me: 'It is so, Gautama.'

"I then said to the Nirgranthas: 'These false words, what is there to trust, what is there to find agreeable, what is there to hear, what is there to recollect, what is there to carefully examine? Regarding a person's own false words, there may be faith, there may be inclination, there may be hearing, there may be recollection, there may be careful examination.'

"If the Nirgranthas make such statements, they are subject to five reproaches in accordance with Dharma, which are detestable. What are the five? As for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by past actions: if that is so, the Nirgranthas must have done evil deeds in the past. Why? Because of those past deeds, the Nirgranthas now experience extremely heavy suffering. This is the first detestable reproach of the Nirgranthas.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by combinations of elements: if that is so, the Nirgranthas must have had evil combinations in the past. Why? Because of those combinations, the Nirgranthas now experience extremely heavy suffering. This is the second detestable reproach of the Nirgranthas.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by one's life-destiny: if that is so, the Nirgranthas must have had an evil life-destiny in the past. Why? Because of that, the Nirgranthas now experience extremely heavy suffering. This is the third detestable reproach of the Nirgranthas.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by views: if that is so, the Nirgranthas must have had evil views in the past. Why? Because of those views, the Nirgranthas now experience extremely heavy suffering. This is the fourth detestable reproach of the Nirgranthas.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by a supreme creator: if that is so, the Nirgranthas must have had an evil supreme creator in the past. Why? Because of that, the Nirgranthas now experience extremely heavy suffering. This is the fifth detestable reproach of the Nirgranthas.

"If the Nirgranthas' past evil deeds, evil combinations, evil life-destiny, evil views, and evil supreme creator, created by an evil supreme creator, are the cause of the Nirgranthas now experiencing extremely heavy suffering, then on account of these matters, the Nirgranthas are detestable.

"The Dharma that I myself have known and realized and teach for you: neither śramaṇas nor brahmins, neither devas, Māra, Brahmā, nor any others in the world can refute it, defile it, or overcome it. How is it that the Dharma I myself have known and realized and teach for you cannot be refuted, defiled, or overcome by śramaṇas or brahmins, devas, Māra, Brahmā, or any others in the world?

"If a bhikṣu abandons unwholesome conduct of body and cultivates wholesome conduct of body, abandons unwholesome conduct of speech and mind and cultivates wholesome conduct of speech and mind, then regarding future suffering, he himself knows: 'I have no future suffering.' He thus obtains happiness in accordance with the Dharma without abandoning it. If he wishes to cut off the cause of suffering through exertion, he cultivates exertion; if he wishes to cut off the cause of suffering through equanimity, he cultivates equanimity. If he wishes to cut off the cause of suffering through exertion, he cultivates that exertion, and what has been cut off, suffering is thereby exhausted. If he wishes to cut off the cause of suffering through equanimity, he cultivates that equanimity, and what has been cut off, suffering is thereby exhausted.

"If that bhikṣu then thinks thus: 'Whenever I engage in certain actions and certain conduct, unwholesome dharmas arise and wholesome dharmas decline. If I cut off suffering by myself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise. I should now cut off suffering by myself.' He then cuts off suffering by himself. Having cut off suffering by himself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise, and he no longer cuts off suffering. Why? Bhikṣus, what he originally intended has already been accomplished. If he were to continue cutting off suffering, that would not be appropriate.

"Bhikṣus, it is like an arrow-maker who uses a straightening device to straighten an arrow. Once the arrow is straight, the straightening device is no longer used. Why? What the person originally intended has already been accomplished. If the straightening device were used again, that would not be appropriate.

"Likewise, the bhikṣu then thinks: 'Whenever I engage in certain actions and certain conduct, unwholesome dharmas arise and wholesome dharmas decline. If I cut off suffering by myself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise. I should now cut off suffering by myself.' He then cuts off suffering by himself. Having cut off suffering by himself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise, and he no longer cuts off suffering. Why? What he originally intended has already been accomplished. If he were to continue cutting off suffering, that would not be appropriate.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a man who loves, is attached to, and cherishes a certain woman. Yet that woman speaks with another man, exchanges greetings, comes and goes, and stays overnight with him. Would that man, on account of this, experience physical and mental suffering, anguish, and deep distress?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One. Why? Because that man loves, is attached to, and deeply cherishes that woman. Yet that woman speaks with another man, exchanges greetings, comes and goes, and stays overnight with him. How could that man's body and mind not experience suffering, anguish, and distress?"

"Bhikṣus, suppose that man then thinks: 'In vain do I love and cherish that woman, yet that woman speaks with another man, exchanges greetings, comes and goes, and stays overnight with him. Should I not, because of my own suffering and distress, cut off my love and attachment for that woman?' Thereafter, because of his own suffering and distress, he cuts off his love and attachment for that woman. If that woman still speaks with another man, exchanges greetings, comes and goes, and stays overnight with him, would that man afterward still experience physical and mental suffering, anguish, and deep distress?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why? That man no longer has any love or attachment for that woman. If that woman still speaks with another man, exchanges greetings, comes and goes, and stays overnight with him, and if that man were to experience physical and mental suffering, anguish, and deep distress because of this, that would not be possible."

"Likewise, when the bhikṣu thinks: 'Whenever I engage in certain actions and certain conduct, unwholesome dharmas arise and wholesome dharmas decline. If I cut off suffering by myself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise. I should now cut off suffering by myself.' He then cuts off suffering by himself. Having cut off suffering by himself, unwholesome dharmas decline and wholesome dharmas arise, and he no longer cuts off suffering. Why? What he originally intended has already been accomplished. If he were to continue cutting off suffering, that would not be appropriate.

"He then further thinks: 'If what I needed to cut off for the sake of cutting off suffering has already been cut off, yet my desire has still not been cut off, I should now seek to cut off desire.' He then seeks to cut off desire. In order to cut off desire, he dwells alone in seclusion, in a deserted place, or at the foot of a tree in a quiet place, in a mountain cave or rocky chamber, on open ground amid haystacks, in a forest, or among burial mounds. Having gone to the deserted place, or at the foot of a tree in a quiet place, he spreads out his sitting mat, sits cross-legged, straightens his body, sets his resolve upright, turns his mindfulness inward, and cuts off covetousness. His mind is free of contention. Seeing the possessions and living goods of others, he does not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for himself. He purifies his mind of covetousness. Likewise, he cuts off anger, drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. He crosses beyond perplexity and has no hesitation regarding wholesome dharmas. He purifies his mind of doubt and perplexity.

"Having cut off these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom, he separates from desires, separates from evil unwholesome dharmas, and attains up to the fourth dhyāna, abiding in its attainment. Having attained such concentration, with a mind that is pure, unblemished, free from affliction, pliable, well-settled, having attained an imperturbable mind, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows and the realization through direct witness. He then knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. He also knows the outflows as they truly are, knows the origin of the outflows, knows the cessation of the outflows, and knows the path to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire, liberated from the outflow of existence, and liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, I will not receive further existence.' He knows this as it truly is.

"When the Tathāgata's mind is thus rightly liberated, he obtains five praises, in accordance with the Dharma, without contention, lovable and worthy of respect. What are the five?

"As for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by past actions: if that is so, the Tathāgata must have had wonderful deeds in the past. Because of those deeds, the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. This is the first praise that the Tathāgata obtains.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by combinations: if that is so, the Tathāgata must have had wonderful combinations in the past. Because of those combinations, the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. This is the second praise that the Tathāgata obtains.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by life-destiny: if that is so, the Tathāgata must have had a wonderful life-destiny in the past. Because of that, the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. This is the third praise that the Tathāgata obtains.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by views: if that is so, the Tathāgata must have had wonderful views in the past. Because of those views, the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. This is the fourth praise that the Tathāgata obtains.

"Furthermore, as for the claim that all the suffering and happiness that beings experience is caused by a supreme creator: if that is so, the Tathāgata must have had a wonderful supreme creator in the past. Because of that, the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. This is the fifth praise that the Tathāgata obtains.

"Thus, the Tathāgata's past wonderful deeds, wonderful combinations, wonderful life-destiny, wonderful views, and wonderful supreme creator, created by a wonderful supreme creator, are why the Tathāgata now experiences holy, outflow-free happiness, the tranquil cessation, and the feeling of bliss. On this account, the Tathāgata now obtains five praises.

"There are five causes and conditions by which sorrow and suffering arise in the mind. What are the five? When one is bound by the fetter of sensual desire, because of the fetter of sensual desire, sorrow and suffering arise in the mind. Likewise with the fetters of anger, drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt: when one is bound by the fetter of doubt, because of the fetter of doubt, sorrow and suffering arise in the mind. These are the five causes and conditions by which sorrow and suffering arise in the mind.

"There are five causes and conditions by which sorrow and suffering in the mind are extinguished. What are the five? When one is bound by the fetter of sensual desire, because of the fetter of sensual desire, sorrow and suffering arise in the mind. When the fetter of sensual desire is removed, sorrow and suffering are extinguished. The sorrow and suffering that arose due to the fetter of sensual desire, in the present Dharma, reach complete fulfillment: free from affliction, free from torment, permanent and unchanging. This is known by the noble ones and seen by the noble ones. Likewise with the fetters of anger, drowsiness, and restlessness and remorse. When one is bound by the fetter of doubt, because of the fetter of doubt, sorrow and suffering arise in the mind. When the fetter of doubt is removed, sorrow and suffering are extinguished. The sorrow and suffering that arose due to the fetter of doubt, in the present Dharma, reach complete fulfillment: free from affliction, free from torment, permanent and unchanging. This is known by the noble ones and seen by the noble ones. These are the five causes and conditions by which sorrow and suffering in the mind are extinguished.

"Furthermore, there is yet another present Dharma that reaches complete fulfillment: free from affliction, free from torment, permanent and unchanging, known by the noble ones and seen by the noble ones. What is this further present Dharma that reaches complete fulfillment: free from affliction, free from torment, permanent and unchanging, known by the noble ones and seen by the noble ones? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration; these are the eight. This is the further present Dharma that reaches complete fulfillment: free from affliction, free from torment, permanent and unchanging, known by the noble ones and seen by the noble ones."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Nirgrantha Sūtra, the Ninth.

## (20) Sūtra on Pāṭaliya, Tenth of the Chapter on Deeds in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Koliya country with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He went to the northern village and stayed in the Śiṃśapā grove to the north of the northern village.

At that time, Pāṭaliya the headman heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyan clan, who had left the Śākyan lineage to leave home and study the path, was traveling in the Koliya country with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He had come to this northern village and was staying in the Śiṃśapā grove to the north of the northern village. The śramaṇa Gautama has great renown, proclaimed throughout the ten directions. The śramaṇa Gautama is a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer and Guide, Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. In this world, among devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to devas, he knows for himself, realizes for himself, and personally attains and abides in the attainment. When he teaches the Dharma, it is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it has meaning and eloquence, is complete in purity, and reveals the holy life. If one sees the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, and reverently bows, makes offerings, and attends upon him, one gains excellent benefit.

He then thought: "I should go and see the śramaṇa Gautama, to pay respects and make offerings."

Having heard this, Pāṭaliya the headman departed from the northern village and went northward to the Śiṃśapā grove, wishing to see the World-Honored One and pay respects and make offerings. Pāṭaliya the headman saw the World-Honored One from afar, among the forest trees, handsome and beautiful, like the moon among the stars, radiant and brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, endowed with all excellent marks, majestic in spiritual power, his faculties tranquil and unobstructed, having accomplished the taming and guiding of himself, his mind calm and still. Pāṭaliya the headman, having seen the Buddha from afar, approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One: "I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama knows illusion to be illusion. Gautama, if it is said thus, that the śramaṇa Gautama knows illusion to be illusion, do those who say this not slander the śramaṇa Gautama? Do they speak the truth? Do they speak what is Dharma? Do they speak Dharma in accordance with Dharma? Is there in accordance with Dharma no fault, no grounds for reproach?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Headman, if it is said thus, that the śramaṇa Gautama knows illusion to be illusion, those who say this do not slander the śramaṇa Gautama. They speak the truth, they speak what is Dharma, they speak Dharma in accordance with Dharma; in the Dharma there is no fault, nor any grounds for reproach. Why? Headman, I know that illusion, but I myself am not an illusionist."

Pāṭaliya said: "Those śramaṇas and brahmins speak the truth, yet I do not believe their statement that the śramaṇa Gautama knows illusion and is therefore an illusionist."

The World-Honored One said: "Headman, does knowing illusion make one an illusionist?"

Pāṭaliya replied: "It is so, World-Honored One. It is so, Well-Gone One."

The World-Honored One said: "Headman, do not bring harm upon yourself by slandering me. If you slander me, you will harm yourself. There will be contention and offense, which the noble and wise abhor, and you will incur great transgression. Why? This is truly not as you have stated. Headman, have you heard that the Koliyas have soldiers?"

He answered: "I have heard so."

"Headman, what do you think? For what purpose do the Koliyas maintain those soldiers?"

He answered: "Gautama, they serve as messengers, slay bandits; for these purposes the Koliyas maintain those soldiers."

"Headman, what do you think? Do the Koliya soldiers observe precepts or not?"

He answered: "Gautama, if there are people in the world without moral virtue, none surpass the Koliya soldiers. Why? The Koliya soldiers grievously violate the precepts and practice only evil deeds."

The Buddha further asked: "Headman, you see it thus and know it thus. Now, I am not asking you this, but if someone else were to ask you: 'Pāṭaliya the headman knows that the Koliya soldiers grievously violate the precepts and practice only evil deeds; on this account, Pāṭaliya the headman grievously violates the precepts and practices only evil deeds.' If someone spoke thus, would that be a true statement?"

He answered: "No, Gautama. Why? The Koliya soldiers have different views, different desires, and different aspirations from mine. The Koliya soldiers grievously violate the precepts and practice only evil deeds; I strictly observe the precepts and do not practice evil deeds."

The Buddha further asked: "Headman, you know that the Koliya soldiers grievously violate the precepts and practice only evil deeds, yet you are not thereby considered one who violates the precepts and practices evil deeds. How then can the Tathāgata not know illusion without himself being an illusionist? Why? I know illusion, I know the person who practices illusion, I know the retribution for illusion, and I know the cutting off of illusion. Headman, I also know killing, I know the person who kills, I know the retribution for killing, and I know the cutting off of killing. Headman, I know taking what is not given, I know the person who takes what is not given, I know the retribution for taking what is not given, and I know the cutting off of taking what is not given. Headman, I know false speech, I know the person who speaks falsely, I know the retribution for false speech, and I know the cutting off of false speech. Headman, knowing thus and seeing thus, if someone were to say that the śramaṇa Gautama knows illusion and is therefore an illusionist, if that person has not abandoned such speech, has not abandoned that thought, desire, wish, perception, recollection, and examination, then in the bending of an arm, upon death he would be reborn in hell."

Pāṭaliya the headman, having heard this, was terrified and trembling, with his hair standing on end. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One: "I repent, Gautama! I confess, Well-Gone One! Like a fool, like one deluded, like one unsteady, like one lacking in goodness. Why? Because I falsely stated that the śramaṇa Gautama is an illusionist. I only pray that Gautama will accept my repentance. Having seen my transgression, I disclose it openly. Having repented, I will guard against repeating it."

The World-Honored One said: "Indeed so, headman. You truly were like a fool, like one deluded, like one unsteady, like one lacking in goodness. Why? Because you falsely spoke of the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, as an illusionist. However, since you are able to repent, to see your transgression and disclose it openly, and to guard against repeating it, then, headman, if one repents, sees one's transgression and discloses it openly, and guards against repeating it, this nurtures the noble Dharma without loss."

Thereupon Pāṭaliya the headman, with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One: "Gautama, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and make this statement: 'Whoever commits killing, all of them will immediately receive retribution in the present life, and because of it they will experience sorrow and suffering. Whoever commits taking what is not given or false speech, all of them will immediately receive retribution in the present life, and because of it they will experience sorrow and suffering.' What does the śramaṇa Gautama think of this?"

The World-Honored One said: "Headman, I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Headman, what do you think? If in a village or town there were a person wearing garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king. If someone asked: 'What did this person formerly do, that he now wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king?' And someone answered: 'This person killed the king's enemy for him. The king was pleased and bestowed a reward upon him. That is why this person wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, again, have you seen a king arrest a criminal, bind his hands behind his back, beat drums and announce his crime, lead him out through the south gate of the city, seat him beneath a high stake, and behead him? If someone asked: 'What crime did this person commit to be executed by the king?' And someone answered: 'This person wrongfully killed an innocent person of the king's household. That is why the king ordered such punishment.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, if certain śramaṇas and brahmins hold this view and make this statement: 'Whoever commits killing, all of them will immediately receive retribution in the present life, and because of it they will experience sorrow and suffering.' Do they speak the truth, or do they speak falsely?"

He answered: "They speak falsely, Gautama."

"If they speak falsely, do you believe them?"

He answered: "I do not believe them, Gautama."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, headman!"

He then further asked: "Headman, what do you think? If in a village or town there were a person wearing garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king. If someone asked: 'What did this person formerly do, that he now wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king?' And someone answered: 'This person committed theft in another country. That is why this person wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, again, have you seen a king arrest a criminal, bind his hands behind his back, beat drums and announce his crime, lead him out through the south gate of the city, seat him beneath a high stake, and behead him? If someone asked: 'What crime did this person commit to be executed by the king?' And someone answered: 'This person committed theft in the king's domain. That is why the king ordered such punishment.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, if certain śramaṇas and brahmins hold this view and make this statement: 'Whoever commits taking what is not given, all of them will immediately receive retribution in the present life, and because of it they will experience sorrow and suffering.' Do they speak the truth, or do they speak falsely?"

He answered: "They speak falsely, Gautama."

"If they speak falsely, do you believe them?"

He answered: "I do not believe them, Gautama."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, headman!"

He then further asked: "Headman, what do you think? If in a village or town there were a person wearing garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king. If someone asked: 'What did this person formerly do, that he now wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king?' And someone answered: 'This person is an entertainer who can jest and make witty jokes. By his false words he pleased the king. The king, being pleased, bestowed a reward upon him. That is why this person wears garlands of flowers on his head, his body anointed with various fragrances, making music, singing and dancing for his own amusement, performing in the manner of female entertainers, delighting like a king.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, again, have you seen a king arrest a criminal, beat him to death with a staff, confine him in a wooden cage, carry him on an open cart, lead him out through the north gate of the city, and cast him into a ditch? If someone asked: 'What crime did this person commit to be killed by the king?' And someone answered: 'This person bore false witness before the king, deceiving the king with false words. That is why the king ordered him to be treated thus.' Headman, have you ever seen or heard of such a thing?"

He answered: "I have seen it, Gautama. I have heard of it, and will hear of it again."

"Headman, what do you think? If certain śramaṇas and brahmins hold this view and make this statement: 'Whoever speaks falsely, all of them will immediately receive retribution in the present life, and because of it they will experience sorrow and suffering.' Do they speak the truth, or do they speak falsely?"

He answered: "They speak falsely, Gautama."

"If they speak falsely, do you believe them?"

He answered: "I do not believe them, Gautama."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, headman!"

Thereupon Pāṭaliya the headman rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One: "How extraordinary! What Gautama has said is supremely wonderful, with excellent similes and excellent proofs. Gautama, in the northern village I have built a tall hall, furnished with beds and cushions, provided with water vessels, and lit with a great bright lamp. Whenever diligent śramaṇas and brahmins come to stay in the tall hall, I supply them with whatever they need according to my ability. There are four debaters, each holding different views, contradicting one another, who came and gathered in the tall hall.

"Among them, one debater holds this view and makes this statement: 'There is no giving, no sacrifice, no incantation, no good or evil deeds, no retribution of good or evil deeds, no this world or other world, no father or mother. In the world there is no true person who goes to a good destination, who goes well and proceeds well, who in this world and the other world knows for himself, realizes for himself, and personally attains and abides in the attainment.'

"The second debater holds right views, opposing the first debater's views and knowledge, and holds this view and makes this statement: 'There is giving, there is sacrifice, there are incantations. There are good and evil deeds, and retribution of good and evil deeds. There is this world and the other world, there is father and mother. In the world there is a true person who goes to a good destination, who goes well and proceeds well, who in this world and the other world knows for himself, realizes for himself, and personally attains and abides in the attainment.'

"The third debater holds this view and makes this statement: 'Whether one acts oneself or teaches others to act, whether one cuts down or teaches others to cut down, whether one burns or teaches others to burn, whether one grieves, is afflicted, beats one's breast in anguish, wails in delusion; whether one kills, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, drinks liquor, breaks through walls, opens treasuries, robs in alleyways, devastates villages, destroys towns, and overthrows kingdoms: one who does all this does no evil. Furthermore, if with an iron wheel sharp as a razor, one were to reduce all living beings on this earth in a single day to a heap of flesh by chopping, cutting, slicing, peeling, tearing, and hacking, making them into a single mass, a single pile, because of this there would be no evil deed, and because of this there would be no retribution for evil deeds. If on the south bank of the Ganges one kills, cuts, and burns, and on the north bank of the Ganges one gives, makes sacrifice, and performs incantations, because of this there would be no transgression and no merit, and because of this there would be no retribution for transgression and merit. Giving, taming, guarding, restraining, praising, benefiting, generosity, kind speech, beneficial acts, and equitable treatment: because of these there would be no merit, and because of these there would be no retribution for merit.'

"The fourth debater holds right views, opposing the third debater's knowledge and views, and holds this view and makes this statement: 'Whether one acts oneself or teaches others to act, whether one cuts down or teaches others to cut down, whether one burns or teaches others to burn, whether one grieves, is afflicted, beats one's breast in anguish, wails in delusion; whether one kills, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, drinks liquor, breaks through walls, opens treasuries, robs in alleyways, devastates villages, destroys towns, and overthrows kingdoms: one who does all this truly does evil. Furthermore, if with an iron wheel sharp as a razor, one were to reduce all living beings on this earth in a single day to a heap of flesh by chopping, cutting, slicing, peeling, tearing, and hacking, making them into a single mass, a single pile, because of this there would be evil deeds, and because of this there would be retribution for evil deeds. If on the south bank of the Ganges one kills, cuts, and burns, and on the north bank of the Ganges one gives, makes sacrifice, and performs incantations, because of this there would be transgression and merit, and because of this there would be retribution for transgression and merit. Giving, taming, guarding, restraining, praising, benefiting, generosity, kind speech, beneficial acts, and equitable treatment: because of these there would be merit, and because of these there would be retribution for merit.'

"Gautama, when I heard this, doubt and perplexity arose in me: which of these śramaṇas and brahmins speaks the truth, and which speaks falsely?"

The World-Honored One said: "Headman, do not give rise to doubt and perplexity. Why? Because doubt and perplexity give rise to hesitation. Headman, you yourself lack the pure knowledge to determine whether there is an afterlife or there is no afterlife. Headman, you also lack the pure knowledge to determine whether one's actions are evil or one's actions are good. Headman, there is a meditation practice called 'seclusion.' Through this meditation, you can attain right mindfulness and attain one-pointedness of mind. Thus, in the present Dharma, you can cut off doubt and perplexity and progress upward."

Thereupon Pāṭaliya the headman again rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One: "Gautama, what is this meditation practice called 'seclusion,' through which I can attain right mindfulness and attain one-pointedness of mind, and thus in the present Dharma cut off doubt and perplexity and progress upward?"

The World-Honored One said: "Headman, a well-learned noble disciple separates from killing and cuts off killing, cuts off taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, until he cuts off wrong views and attains right views. During the daytime he directs his farming and plowing. At evening he rests and retires, enters his room and sits in meditation. After the night passes and dawn comes, he thinks thus: 'I have separated from killing and cut off killing, cut off taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, until I cut off wrong views and attained right views.' He then sees for himself: 'I have cut off the ten unwholesome courses of action and am mindful of the ten wholesome courses of action.' Having seen for himself that he has cut off the ten unwholesome courses of action and is mindful of the ten wholesome courses of action, joy arises. From the arising of joy, delight arises. ## The Chapter on Deeds, Fourth

### 36. Sūtra on the Bhūmija (The Venerable Bhūmija)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Bhūmija, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation, went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmija said to the Venerable Śāriputra:

"Venerable Śāriputra, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold this view and speak this doctrine: 'If a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life, that person cannot attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations and practices the holy life, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations and practices the holy life, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life, that person also cannot attain the fruit.' What does the Venerable Śāriputra say about this?"

The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Bhūmija, I do not say this based on hearing it from others. I will now state my own understanding. If a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person cannot attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person also cannot attain the fruit.

"Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person can attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person also can attain the fruit. If a person both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person also can attain the fruit. If a person neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person also can attain the fruit."

At that time, the Venerable Bhūmija heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, well received and well retained it, then rose from his seat, bowed at the Venerable Śāriputra's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

The Venerable Bhūmija then went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmija recounted to the World-Honored One all that had been discussed with the Venerable Śāriputra.

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Bhūmija, as Śāriputra has explained, so should it be understood. Why? Because I also speak in this way.

"Bhūmija, suppose a person seeks oil and takes sesame seeds, places them in a vessel, adds water, and presses them. That person seeking oil, taking sesame seeds, placing them in a vessel, adding water, and pressing them, can indeed obtain oil. If a person seeks oil and takes sand, places it in a vessel, adds water, and presses it, that person seeking oil, taking sand, placing it in a vessel, adding water, and pressing it, cannot obtain oil no matter how much effort is applied.

"Why is this? Because sand is not the cause, not the condition for obtaining oil. In the same way, Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person cannot attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations... both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations... neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person cannot attain the fruit. Why is this? Because wrong methods are not the cause, not the condition for attaining the fruit.

"Bhūmija, suppose a person seeks milk and milks a cow. That person seeking milk and milking a cow can indeed obtain milk. If a person seeks milk and pulls the horn of a cow, that person seeking milk and pulling the horn of a cow cannot obtain milk no matter how much effort is applied. Why is this? Because pulling the horn is not the cause, not the condition for obtaining milk.

"In the same way, Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person can attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations... both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations... neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person can attain the fruit. Why is this? Because right methods are the cause, are the condition for attaining the fruit.

"Bhūmija, suppose a person seeks butter and takes milk, adds curds and churns it. That person seeking butter, taking milk, adding curds and churning it, can indeed obtain butter. If a person seeks butter and takes water, adds curds and churns it, that person seeking butter, taking water, adding curds and churning it, cannot obtain butter no matter how much effort is applied. Why is this? Because water is not the cause, not the condition for obtaining butter.

"In the same way, Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person cannot attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations... both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations... neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person cannot attain the fruit. Why is this? Because wrong methods are not the cause, not the condition for attaining the fruit.

"Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person can attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations... both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations... neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person can attain the fruit. Why is this? Because right methods are the cause, are the condition for attaining the fruit.

"Bhūmija, suppose a person seeks fire and takes a fire-drill, using dry wood, and drills it. That person seeking fire, taking a fire-drill, using dry wood, and drilling it, can indeed obtain fire. If a person seeks fire and takes a fire-drill, using wet wood, and drills it, that person seeking fire, taking a fire-drill, using wet wood, and drilling it, cannot obtain fire no matter how much effort is applied. Why is this? Because wet wood is not the cause, not the condition for obtaining fire.

"In the same way, Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong samādhi, that person cannot attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person also cannot attain the fruit. If a person neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with wrong view and the wrong eightfold path, that person also cannot attain the fruit. Why is this? Because wrong methods are not the cause, not the condition for attaining the fruit.

"Bhūmija, if a person makes aspirations and practices the holy life with right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi, that person can attain the fruit. If a person makes no aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person also can attain the fruit. If a person both makes aspirations and does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person also can attain the fruit. If a person neither makes aspirations nor does not make aspirations and practices the holy life with right view and the right eightfold path, that person also can attain the fruit. Why is this? Because right methods are the cause, are the condition for attaining the fruit."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Bhūmija and the monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 37. Sūtra on the Camphor Tree (瞻波經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Campā, beside the Gaggarā lotus pond.

At that time, the World-Honored One, on the fifteenth day, the poṣadha day, sat in the open among the assembly of monks. The World-Honored One sat silently, surveying the assembly of monks. The first watch of the night passed, and a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt with joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:

"World-Honored One, the first watch of the night has already passed. The assembly of monks has been sitting for a long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa for the bhikṣus."

The World-Honored One remained silent and did not respond. When the middle watch of the night passed, that bhikṣu again rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt with joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:

"World-Honored One, the first watch of the night has already passed, and the middle watch of the night has also passed. The assembly of monks has been sitting for a very long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa for the bhikṣus."

The World-Honored One again remained silent and did not respond. When the last watch of the night passed, dawn appeared and the sky began to brighten. That bhikṣu again rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt with joined palms toward the Buddha, and said:

"World-Honored One, the first watch of the night has already passed, the middle watch of the night has passed, and the last watch of the night has also passed. Dawn has appeared and the sky is brightening. The assembly of monks has been sitting for a very long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa for the bhikṣus."

The World-Honored One said: "This assembly is not pure."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was sitting in this assembly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then thought: "Which person in this assembly is the one that the World-Honored One says makes it not pure?" The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then entered samādhi with his mind, and with his mental power surveyed the minds of all in the assembly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then saw that person who was impure in conduct, impure in deeds, unclean, of suspicious behavior, covered in their actions, not a śramaṇa yet claiming to be a śramaṇa, not practicing the holy life yet claiming to practice the holy life, inwardly rotten and leaking, full of defilements, sitting in this assembly.

Having seen this, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, went to that person, and said: "Rise! Rise! The World-Honored One already knows you. You should not sit together with the bhikṣus in this assembly."

That person remained silent. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana repeated this a second time, saying: "Rise! Rise! The World-Honored One already knows you. You should not sit together with the bhikṣus in this assembly."

That person again remained silent. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said a third time: "Rise! Rise! The World-Honored One already knows you. You should not sit together with the bhikṣus in this assembly."

That person remained silent a third time. Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana grasped that person's arm, led him outside the door, closed and bolted the door, and then went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One, that person has been expelled from the assembly. The assembly is now pure and settled. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa for the bhikṣus."

The World-Honored One said: "Wonderful, wonderful! Maudgalyāyana, that foolish person was made to rise only when he was about to be seized and dragged."

Then the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "From now on, I will no longer perform the poṣadha or recite the Prātimokṣa. From now on, you bhikṣus shall yourselves perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa. Why is this? If the Tathāgata were to recite the Prātimokṣa when the assembly is not pure, that would be impossible. Monks, it is like the great ocean, which has no corpses in it. If there is a corpse, the waves immediately cast it ashore. In the same way, that person was impure in conduct, impure in deeds, unclean, of suspicious behavior, covered in his actions, not a śramaṇa yet claiming to be a śramaṇa, not practicing the holy life yet claiming to practice the holy life, inwardly rotten and leaking, full of defilements. The assembly expelled him.

"Monks, the great ocean has eight extraordinary and marvelous qualities, which the asuras delight in seeing. What are the eight?

"Monks, the great ocean gradually slopes, gradually descends, and gradually deepens; it does not suddenly become steep. Monks, the great ocean gradually sloping, gradually descending, and gradually deepening, not suddenly becoming steep, this is the first extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, in my Dharma and Vinaya, learning is gradual, practice is gradual, the path is gradual; it does not suddenly arrive at the knowledge of all. In my Dharma and Vinaya, learning being gradual, practice being gradual, the path being gradual, not suddenly arriving at the knowledge of all, this is the first extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, the great ocean is full and does not overflow its banks. Monks, the great ocean being full and not overflowing its banks, this is the second extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, I have established precepts for my disciples, and my disciples, even at the cost of their lives, would not transgress them. That I have established precepts for my disciples, and my disciples, even at the cost of their lives, would not transgress them, this is the second extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, the great ocean does not retain corpses. If there is a corpse, the waves immediately cast it ashore. Monks, the great ocean not retaining corpses, this is the third extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, if a person is impure in conduct, impure in deeds, unclean, of suspicious behavior, covered in their actions, not a śramaṇa yet claiming to be a śramaṇa, not practicing the holy life yet claiming to practice the holy life, inwardly rotten and leaking, full of defilements, the Sangha does not live together with that person. The Sangha quickly assembles, assembles together and expels that person. Even though that person sits in the midst of the bhikṣu Sangha, that person is still far from the Sangha, and the Sangha is far from that person. The Sangha not living together with such a person, this is the third extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, all great rivers, such as the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Sarabhū, the Airāvatī, and the Mahī, when these rivers enter the great ocean, they all abandon their former names and are collectively called the great ocean. Monks, all great rivers entering the great ocean and all abandoning their former names to be collectively called the great ocean, this is the fourth extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, there are four castes: kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. They leave home, shave their heads, don the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith go forth from household life to homelessness, learning the path. They all abandon their former names and clans and are collectively called śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya son. Monks, the four castes all abandoning their former names and clans to be collectively called śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākya son, this is the fourth extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, all the waters in the world flow into the great ocean, and the rains from the sky fall into it, yet the great ocean neither increases nor decreases. Monks, all the waters in the world flowing into the great ocean and the rains from the sky falling into it, yet the great ocean neither increasing nor decreasing, this is the fifth extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, the bhikṣus enter the remainderless nirvāṇa realm, yet the nirvāṇa realm neither increases nor decreases. Monks, the bhikṣus entering the remainderless nirvāṇa realm yet the nirvāṇa realm neither increasing nor decreasing, this is the fifth extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, the great ocean has only one taste, the taste of salt. Monks, the great ocean having only one taste, the taste of salt, this is the sixth extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, my Dharma also has only one taste, the taste of liberation, the taste of desirelessness, the taste of cessation, the taste of the path. My Dharma having only one taste, the taste of liberation, the taste of desirelessness, the taste of cessation, the taste of the path, this is the sixth extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, the great ocean contains many treasures, various kinds of precious things. Within the great ocean there is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, mother-of-pearl, agate, and many other treasures, various kinds of precious things. Monks, the great ocean containing many treasures, various kinds of precious things, this is the seventh extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, my Dharma and Vinaya also contains many treasures, various kinds of precious things. Within my Dharma and Vinaya there are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of supernatural power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the Noble Eightfold Path. My Dharma and Vinaya containing many treasures, various kinds of precious things, this is the seventh extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"Furthermore, monks, the great ocean contains many great beings dwelling in it. Within the great ocean there are creatures whose bodies measure one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, five hundred yojanas, six hundred yojanas, and even up to seven hundred yojanas. Monks, the great ocean containing many great beings dwelling in it, this is the eighth extraordinary and marvelous quality of the great ocean, which the asuras delight in seeing.

"In the same way, monks, my Dharma and Vinaya also contains many great beings dwelling in it. Within my Dharma and Vinaya there are those who are stream-enterers who practice to realize the fruit of stream-entry, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, those who are once-returners who practice to realize the fruit of once-returning, those who have attained the fruit of once-returning, those who are non-returners who practice to realize the fruit of non-returning, those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, those who are arhats who practice to realize the fruit of arhatship, and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship. My Dharma and Vinaya containing many great beings dwelling in it, this is the eighth extraordinary and marvelous quality of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus delight in seeing.

"These are the eight extraordinary and marvelous qualities of my Dharma and Vinaya, which the bhikṣus constantly delight in seeing."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 38. Sūtra on Potalaka (郁伽長者經, Upper Part)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Great Forest, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

At that time, the householder Ugra of Vaiśālī heard that the World-Honored One had come to Vaiśālī and was dwelling in the Great Forest, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. The householder Ugra, together with a large retinue from Vaiśālī, with carriages following upon carriages, with great majesty and great power, departed from Vaiśālī and went to the Great Forest to visit the World-Honored One. Going a certain distance, the householder Ugra descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Ugra, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him. Having taught the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him with various methods, the World-Honored One then sat silently.

The householder Ugra, having been taught the Dharma by the World-Honored One, encouraged, inspired, and delighted, then said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One together with the bhikṣu Sangha accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal."

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted. The householder Ugra, knowing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Having returned home, the householder Ugra immediately that night prepared all kinds of exquisite foods and drinks, and when dawn came, he spread out seats and arranged clean water. When the time had come, he sent a messenger to announce: "World-Honored One, the food is ready. May the World-Honored One know that the time has come."

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the early morning, put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the householder Ugra's home. Having arrived, he sat on the seat that had been prepared. The bhikṣu Sangha, preceded by the Buddha, all sat in order.

The householder Ugra then with his own hands served and offered all kinds of exquisite foods and drinks to the Buddha and the bhikṣu Sangha. After the World-Honored One had finished eating, had washed his bowl and hands, the householder Ugra took a low seat and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.

The householder Ugra said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we wish to always offer to the bhikṣu Sangha: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for illness, all the requisites of life."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder, you should do as you have said."

The householder Ugra further said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, if any bhikṣu comes to Vaiśālī, whether coming or going, we wish to always offer food and drink to them."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder."

The householder Ugra further said: "World-Honored One, if the Sangha constructs a building or a hall, we wish to contribute and provide assistance until it is completed."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder."

The householder Ugra further said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, from today onward, I open my doors to the Sangha, especially to bhikṣus who come from the four directions. May the World-Honored One accept this."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder, your vows are great and broad. You have established the root of great merit. Whoever makes such vows of great and broad giving is a person who abides in the nectar of immortality, who shares the nectar of immortality."

Then the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Ugra, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him, and rose from his seat and departed.

At a later time, the householder Ugra was drinking liquor with his companions and relatives. At that time, he saw from afar the Venerable Ānanda coming to beg for alms, entering Vaiśālī. Having seen him, the householder Ugra immediately rose and went to the Venerable Ānanda, bowed his head at his feet, joined his palms, and said: "Venerable Ānanda, it has been a long time since you last came to our home. Please, Venerable, come sit and rest for a while."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Enough, householder. I have heard that today you are drinking liquor."

The householder Ugra said: "Venerable Ānanda, we are not only drinking liquor; we also have all kinds of exquisite foods. Venerable Ānanda, please come sit and eat."

The Venerable Ānanda again said: "Enough, householder. I have already finished my meal for today."

The Venerable Ānanda then departed, and later went to the World-Honored One and reported this matter.

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, the householder Ugra, even though he still drinks liquor, has great benefit, great merit. Why is this? Because the householder Ugra has faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. He has undertaken the eight qualities of a lay disciple."

The World-Honored One then said: "Ānanda, there are eight qualities of a lay disciple. What are the eight?

"Ānanda, a lay disciple takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, takes refuge in the Sangha. This is the first quality.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a lay disciple does not take life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not drink liquor. This is the second through the sixth qualities.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a lay disciple has faith, and the wealth obtained through his own effort by the strength of his arms, by the sweat of his brow, through righteous and lawful means, he is able to give and share broadly with śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the destitute, the homeless, beggars, and those in need. This is the seventh quality.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a lay disciple has no jealousy. Toward others' gains, honors, respect, reverence, worship, and offerings, he does not become jealous or angry. This is the eighth quality.

"Ānanda, if a lay disciple possesses these eight qualities, then wherever he is reborn, he will obtain wealth and great gain."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 39. Sūtra on the Householder Ugra (郁伽長者經, Lower Part)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the country of the Aṅgas, in the town called Āpaṇa.

At that time, the householder Ugra of Āpaṇa heard that the World-Honored One had come to the Aṅga country and was dwelling in the town called Āpaṇa. The householder Ugra then went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Ugra, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him. Having taught the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him with various methods, the World-Honored One then sat silently.

The householder Ugra, having been taught the Dharma by the World-Honored One, encouraged, inspired, and delighted, said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One together with the bhikṣu Sangha accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal."

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted. The householder Ugra, knowing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Having returned home, the householder Ugra immediately that night prepared all kinds of exquisite foods and drinks. When dawn came, he spread out seats and arranged clean water. When the time had come, he sent a messenger to announce: "World-Honored One, the food is ready. May the World-Honored One know that the time has come."

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the early morning, put on his robes, took his bowl, and together with the bhikṣu Sangha went to the householder Ugra's home. Having arrived, he sat on the seat that had been prepared. The householder Ugra then with his own hands served and offered all kinds of exquisite foods and drinks to the Buddha and the bhikṣu Sangha. After the World-Honored One had finished eating, had washed his bowl and hands, the householder Ugra took a low seat and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the householder Ugra said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I now wish to open my home as an offering to the bhikṣus coming from the four directions."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good!"

The householder Ugra further said: "World-Honored One, from today onward, I wish to always provide food and drink for the Sangha."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good!"

The householder Ugra further said: "World-Honored One, from today onward, I wish that if any bhikṣu comes to Āpaṇa, whether coming or going, I will provide food and drink."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good!"

The householder Ugra further said: "World-Honored One, from today onward, I wish to always provide for the Sangha: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for illness."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good!"

The householder Ugra further said: "World-Honored One, from today onward, I wish that if the Sangha constructs any building, I will contribute and help until it is completed."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder, your vows are great and broad. You have established the root of great merit. Whoever makes such vows of great and broad giving is a person who abides in the nectar of immortality, who shares the nectar of immortality."

Then the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Ugra, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him, and rose from his seat and departed.

At a later time, the householder Ugra fell seriously ill, suffering greatly, and his life was in danger. At that time, the World-Honored One heard that the householder Ugra was seriously ill. In the late afternoon, the World-Honored One rose from his meditation and went to the householder Ugra's home. The householder Ugra saw from afar the World-Honored One coming. Having seen him, he struggled to rise from his bed.

The World-Honored One saw the householder Ugra struggling to rise and said: "Enough, householder. Do not rise. Are there other seats here?"

The householder Ugra replied: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One then sat on another seat and asked: "Householder, can you bear your pain? Is your illness improving or growing worse? Is it diminishing or increasing?"

The householder Ugra said: "World-Honored One, I cannot bear my pain. The illness is growing worse and not diminishing; it only increases and does not subside."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, you should train yourself thus. Take refuge in the Buddha with unwavering faith, take refuge in the Dharma with unwavering faith, take refuge in the Sangha with unwavering faith. And keep the precepts completely, unbroken, unfragmented, unstained, and liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, conducive to samādhi.

"Householder, you should train yourself thus. With right faith, you have rightly abandoned the five fears and five hatreds. You are endowed with the four limbs of stream-entry, and with wisdom you have well seen, well penetrated the noble method.

"Householder, what are the five fears and five hatreds that have been abandoned? Householder, one who takes life, because of taking life, creates fear and hatred in the present life and creates fear and hatred in the future life, and also experiences mental suffering and anxiety. If one abstains from taking life, one does not create fear and hatred in the present life and does not create fear and hatred in the future life, and also does not experience mental suffering and anxiety. For one who abstains from taking life, this fear and hatred is well extinguished.

"Furthermore, householder, one who takes what is not given, because of taking what is not given, creates fear and hatred in the present life and creates fear and hatred in the future life, and also experiences mental suffering and anxiety. If one abstains from taking what is not given, one does not create fear and hatred in the present life and does not create fear and hatred in the future life, and also does not experience mental suffering and anxiety. For one who abstains from taking what is not given, this fear and hatred is well extinguished.

"Furthermore, householder, one who engages in sexual misconduct, because of sexual misconduct, creates fear and hatred in the present life and creates fear and hatred in the future life, and also experiences mental suffering and anxiety. If one abstains from sexual misconduct, one does not create fear and hatred in the present life and does not create fear and hatred in the future life, and also does not experience mental suffering and anxiety. For one who abstains from sexual misconduct, this fear and hatred is well extinguished.

"Furthermore, householder, one who speaks falsely, because of speaking falsely, creates fear and hatred in the present life and creates fear and hatred in the future life, and also experiences mental suffering and anxiety. If one abstains from speaking falsely, one does not create fear and hatred in the present life and does not create fear and hatred in the future life, and also does not experience mental suffering and anxiety. For one who abstains from speaking falsely, this fear and hatred is well extinguished.

"Furthermore, householder, one who drinks liquor, because of drinking liquor, creates fear and hatred in the present life and creates fear and hatred in the future life, and also experiences mental suffering and anxiety. If one abstains from drinking liquor, one does not create fear and hatred in the present life and does not create fear and hatred in the future life, and also does not experience mental suffering and anxiety. For one who abstains from drinking liquor, this fear and hatred is well extinguished.

"These are the five fears and five hatreds that have been extinguished.

"Householder, what are the four limbs of stream-entry that one is endowed with? The noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Buddha: 'The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Persons, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' This is the first limb of stream-entry.

"Furthermore, householder, the noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Dharma: 'The Dharma of the World-Honored One is well proclaimed, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be individually known by the wise.' This is the second limb of stream-entry.

"Furthermore, householder, the noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples practices well, practices directly, practices in accordance with the Dharma, practices properly. In this Sangha there are the four pairs and eight types of persons. This Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverence, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' This is the third limb of stream-entry.

"Furthermore, householder, the noble disciple is endowed with the precepts loved by the noble ones, unbroken, unfragmented, unstained, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, conducive to samādhi. This is the fourth limb of stream-entry.

"Householder, what is the noble method that is well seen and well penetrated with wisdom? The noble disciple contemplates dependent origination well, with right wisdom: 'When this exists, that exists; when this arises, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not exist; when this ceases, that ceases. That is: conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging; conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus the entire great mass of suffering arises.
