"'When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; when consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases; when name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease; when the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; when contact ceases, feeling ceases; when feeling ceases, craving ceases; when craving ceases, clinging ceases; when clinging ceases, becoming ceases; when becoming ceases, birth ceases; when birth ceases, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus the entire great mass of suffering ceases.'

"Householder, this is the noble method that is well seen and well penetrated with wisdom."

At that time, the householder Ugra said: "World-Honored One, concerning these five fears, five hatreds to be extinguished, the four limbs of stream-entry, and the noble method to be well seen and well penetrated with wisdom, all of these I possess. I am in accord with the Dharma, and the Dharma is in accord with me.

"World-Honored One, I have unwavering faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. I keep the precepts unbroken, unfragmented, unstained, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, conducive to samādhi. World-Honored One, whatever a lay disciple should accomplish, I have accomplished all of it."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householder, you have now declared for yourself the fruit of once-returning."

The householder Ugra said: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One and the bhikṣu Sangha accept my invitation to stay in Āpaṇa for the rains retreat."

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted. Then the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Ugra, encouraging, inspiring, and delighting him, and rose from his seat and departed.

Then the World-Honored One, for the sake of the householder Ugra, stayed in Āpaṇa for the rains retreat. The householder Ugra constantly made offerings to the World-Honored One and the bhikṣu Sangha throughout the rains retreat.

At the end of the rains retreat, the World-Honored One made robes, and taking his bowl and robes, traveled through the land. After the World-Honored One had departed, the householder Ugra passed away shortly thereafter.

Then many bhikṣus, having heard that the householder Ugra had passed away, went to the World-Honored One, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the householder Ugra of Āpaṇa, whom the World-Honored One taught the Dharma, has passed away. Where has he been reborn? What is his destination?"

The World-Honored One said: "The householder Ugra of Āpaṇa was wise, practiced in accordance with the Dharma, and did not trouble me with questions about the Dharma. The householder Ugra of Āpaṇa has severed the five lower fetters, has been spontaneously reborn in a higher realm, and will attain final nirvāṇa there, never to return to this world. The householder Ugra has attained the fruit of non-returning."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 40. Sūtra on Hand (手長者經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the country of Nādika, at the Brick Hall.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also dwelling in Nādika, at the Brick Hall.

Then the householder named Hand of Nādika had passed away. Another householder named Hand had also passed away. And there was a householder named Unhand, who had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Kakuda had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Kāḷinga had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Nikaṭa had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Kaṭissaha had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Tuṭṭha had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Santuṭṭha had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Bhadda had also passed away. And a lay disciple named Subhadda had also passed away.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda heard that these householders and lay disciples of Nādika had all passed away. Having heard this, the Venerable Ānanda then went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the householder named Hand of Nādika has passed away. Where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the other householder named Hand, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the householder named Unhand, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Kakuda, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Kāḷinga, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Nikaṭa, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Kaṭissaha, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Tuṭṭha, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Santuṭṭha, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Bhadda, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?

"And the lay disciple Subhadda, who has also passed away, where has he been reborn? What is his destination?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, the householder Hand, who had faith, kept the precepts, had learned much, was generous, and possessed wisdom, has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn in a higher realm and will attain final nirvāṇa there, never to return to this world. The householder Hand has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the other householder Hand, who also had faith, kept the precepts, had learned much, was generous, and possessed wisdom, has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he too has been spontaneously reborn in a higher realm and will attain final nirvāṇa there, never to return to this world. He has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the householder Unhand, who had faith, kept the precepts, had learned much, was generous, and possessed wisdom, has passed away. Having severed the three fetters, with the attenuation of desire, anger, and delusion, he has become a once-returner, who will return once more to this world and then make an end of suffering.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Kakuda has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn in a higher realm and will attain final nirvāṇa there, never to return to this world. He has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Kāḷinga has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn and has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Nikaṭa has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn and has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Kaṭissaha has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn and has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Tuṭṭha has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn and has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Santuṭṭha has passed away. Having severed the five lower fetters, he has been spontaneously reborn and has attained the fruit of non-returning.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Bhadda has passed away. Having severed the three fetters, with the attenuation of desire, anger, and delusion, he has become a once-returner.

"Ānanda, the lay disciple Subhadda has passed away. Having severed the three fetters, he has become a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into evil destinies, certain of attaining perfect enlightenment, passing through at most seven more existences among gods and humans, and then making an end of suffering.

"Ānanda, more than fifty lay disciples of Nādika have passed away, having severed the five lower fetters and been spontaneously reborn, attaining the fruit of non-returning. More than ninety lay disciples of Nādika have passed away, having severed the three fetters, with the attenuation of desire, anger, and delusion, becoming once-returners. More than five hundred lay disciples of Nādika have passed away, having severed the three fetters, becoming stream-enterers.

"Ānanda, it is not strange that a human being should die. But if each time one dies, you come and ask the Tathāgata about it, this would be troublesome for the Tathāgata. Therefore, Ānanda, I will now teach you the mirror of the Dharma, by which a noble disciple, if they wish, may declare of themselves: 'I have ended the hells, I have ended the animal realm, I have ended the hungry ghost realm, I have ended all evil destinies and bad rebirths. I am a stream-enterer, not subject to falling, certain of attaining perfect enlightenment.'

"Ānanda, what is this mirror of the Dharma, by which a noble disciple may declare of themselves such things?

"Ānanda, a noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Buddha: 'The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Persons, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.'

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Dharma: 'The Dharma of the World-Honored One is well proclaimed, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be individually known by the wise.'

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a noble disciple has unwavering faith in the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples practices well, practices directly, practices in accordance with the Dharma, practices properly. In this Sangha there are the four pairs and eight types of persons. This Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverence, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a noble disciple is endowed with the precepts loved by the noble ones, unbroken, unfragmented, unstained, untarnished, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, conducive to samādhi.

"Ānanda, this is the mirror of the Dharma, by which a noble disciple, if they wish, may declare of themselves: 'I have ended the hells, I have ended the animal realm, I have ended the hungry ghost realm, I have ended all evil destinies and bad rebirths. I am a stream-enterer, not subject to falling, certain of attaining perfect enlightenment.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 41. Sūtra on the Householder of Sālā (手長者經, Part 2)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling among the Kosalans, traveling through the country, and arrived at a brāhmaṇa village called Sālā.

The brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, who had gone forth from the Śākya household, was traveling among the Kosalans and had arrived at Sālā. This śramaṇa Gautama had a great reputation and great fame, and was known as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed One, a Tamer of Persons, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One. Among devas, māras, brahmās, among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans, he had realized by his own direct knowledge and declared it. He taught the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, displaying the holy life. It would be good to see such an arhat. Having heard this, the brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā went together to the World-Honored One.

Some bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Some joined their palms toward the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Some stated their names and clans to the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Some remained silent and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One addressed the brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā: "Householders, if wandering ascetics of other traditions should ask you: 'Householders, what kinds of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not be revered, honored, respected, and served?' Then you should answer those wandering ascetics thus: 'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose eyes, upon seeing forms, still have desire and passion, whose minds are not inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct is not at peace, whose verbal conduct is not at peace, whose mental conduct is not at peace, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not be revered, honored, respected, and served.' Why? Because we ourselves, regarding eyes seeing forms, still have desire and passion, our minds are not inwardly purified, our bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are not at peace. Since they are no different from us, we do not revere, honor, respect, and serve such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

"'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose ears, upon hearing sounds... whose nose, upon smelling scents... whose tongue, upon tasting flavors... whose body, upon experiencing tangibles... whose mind, upon cognizing dharmas, still have desire and passion, whose minds are not inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are not at peace, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should not be revered, honored, respected, and served.' Why? Because we ourselves are the same.

"Householders, if wandering ascetics of other traditions should ask you: 'Householders, what kinds of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should be revered, honored, respected, and served?' Then you should answer those wandering ascetics thus: 'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose eyes, upon seeing forms, no longer have desire and passion, whose minds are inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct is at peace, whose verbal conduct is at peace, whose mental conduct is at peace, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should be revered, honored, respected, and served.' Why? Because we ourselves, regarding eyes seeing forms, still have desire and passion, our minds are not inwardly purified, our bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are not at peace. Since they are different from and surpass us, therefore we revere, honor, respect, and serve such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

"'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose ears, upon hearing sounds... whose nose, upon smelling scents... whose tongue, upon tasting flavors... whose body, upon experiencing tangibles... whose mind, upon cognizing dharmas, no longer have desire and passion, whose minds are inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are at peace, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should be revered, honored, respected, and served.'

"Householders, what do you think? If those wandering ascetics of other traditions asked you thus, and you answered them thus, would those wandering ascetics have anything further to say?"

The brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā said: "World-Honored One, if those wandering ascetics of other traditions asked us thus, and we answered them thus, they would have nothing further to say. Why? Because our answer would be in accordance with the principle and appropriate."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householders, it is so.

"Householders, you should further examine this: Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose eyes, upon seeing forms, still have desire and passion, whose minds are not inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are not at peace, do those persons have or not have the knowledge and vision of a sage worthy of noble knowledge? Do those persons have or not have the attainment of realization?"

The householders said: "No, World-Honored One."

"Good, good! Householders, I also say this is so. Those persons who still have desire and passion, whose bodily, verbal, and mental conduct are not at peace, they do not possess the knowledge and vision of a sage worthy of noble knowledge. They do not possess the attainment of realization.

"Householders, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose eyes, upon seeing forms, no longer have desire and passion, whose minds are inwardly purified, whose bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct are at peace, do those persons have the knowledge and vision of a sage worthy of noble knowledge? Do those persons have the attainment of realization?"

The householders said: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Good, good! Householders, I also say this is so. Those persons who no longer have desire and passion, whose bodily, verbal, and mental conduct are at peace, they possess the knowledge and vision of a sage worthy of noble knowledge. They possess the attainment of realization.

"Householders, what do you think about me? Do my eyes, upon seeing forms, still have desire and passion? Is my mind not inwardly purified? Is my bodily, verbal, and mental conduct not at peace? Or do my eyes, upon seeing forms, no longer have desire and passion? Is my mind inwardly purified? Is my bodily, verbal, and mental conduct at peace?"

The householders said: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One's eyes, upon seeing forms, no longer have desire and passion. The World-Honored One's mind is inwardly purified. The World-Honored One's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct are at peace. The same applies to the ears hearing sounds, the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, the body experiencing tangibles, and the mind cognizing dharmas. The World-Honored One no longer has desire and passion. The World-Honored One's mind is inwardly purified. The World-Honored One's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct are at peace."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Householders, you have well explained this. What I have thoroughly known and thoroughly seen, you too explain accordingly, saying: 'The World-Honored One's eyes, upon seeing forms, no longer have desire and passion. The World-Honored One's mind is inwardly purified, and the World-Honored One's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct are at peace.' And regarding the other five sense bases, it is likewise."

At that time, the brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā said to the World-Honored One: "Excellent! Excellent! World-Honored One, it is like straightening what was bent, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes can see forms. The World-Honored One, with countless methods, has proclaimed and illuminated the Dharma. We now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Sangha. May the World-Honored One accept us as lay disciples. From today until the end of our lives, we take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brāhmaṇa householders of Sālā, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 9 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 5

## Chapter 3: Connected with Śāriputra

Equal-Mind, Accomplishment of Virtue, Knowledge, Lion's Roar, Water Simile, Kuṇḍaliya, Dhānañjāni, Brahma's Teaching on Illness, Kokālika, Elephant-Footprint Simile, Analysis of the Four Truths is last.

---

## Sūtra 21: The Equal-Mind Sūtra, First of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, together with an assembly of bhikṣus, gathered at night in the lecture hall. On account of inner fetters and outer fetters, he explained the meaning to the bhikṣus: "Venerables, in the world there truly exist two kinds of people. What are the two? There is the person with inner fetters who is an anāgāmin, one who does not return to this world. And there is the person with outer fetters who is not an anāgāmin, one who returns to this world.

"Venerables, how is the person with inner fetters an anāgāmin who does not return to this world? Suppose there is a person who cultivates the precepts, without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished. Because he cultivates the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished, he further trains in revulsion toward desire, dispassion toward desire, and the cutting off of desire. Because he trains in revulsion toward desire, dispassion toward desire, and the cutting off of desire, he attains tranquility and liberation of mind. Having attained it, he cherishes and clings to its bliss without letting go, and in this present life he does not attain final knowledge. When his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. Having been reborn there, he thinks: 'When I was formerly a human, I cultivated the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished. Because I cultivated the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished, I further trained in revulsion toward desire, dispassion toward desire, and the cutting off of desire. Because I trained in revulsion toward desire, dispassion toward desire, and the cutting off of desire, I attained tranquility and liberation of mind. Having attained it, I cherished and clung to its bliss without letting go, and in that present life I did not attain final knowledge. When my body broke up and life ended, I passed beyond the gods who feed on material food and was reborn among the other mind-born gods, here in this place.'

"Venerables, there is also a person who cultivates the precepts, without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished. Because he cultivates the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished, he further trains in the cutting off of existence in the form realm, the work of cutting off craving, and trains in the relinquishment of desire. Because he trains in the cutting off of existence in the form realm, the work of cutting off craving, and trains in the relinquishment of desire, he attains tranquility and liberation of mind. Having attained it, he cherishes and clings to its bliss without letting go, and in this present life he does not attain final knowledge. When his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. Having been reborn there, he thinks: 'When I was formerly a human, I cultivated the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished. Because I cultivated the precepts without breach, without gap, without stain, without impurity, abundantly and without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well cultivated and well accomplished, I further trained in the cutting off of existence in the form realm, the work of cutting off craving, and trained in the relinquishment of desire. Because I trained in the cutting off of existence in the form realm, the work of cutting off craving, and trained in the relinquishment of desire, I attained tranquility and liberation of mind. Having attained it, I cherished and clung to its bliss without letting go, and in that present life I did not attain final knowledge. When my body broke up and life ended, I passed beyond the gods who feed on material food and was reborn among the other mind-born gods, here in this place.' Venerables, this is called the person with inner fetters who is an anāgāmin and does not return to this world.

"Venerables, how is the person with outer fetters not an anāgāmin, one who returns to this world? Suppose there is a person who cultivates the precepts, guards and follows the code of liberation, and moreover well governs his deportment and etiquette, seeing danger in the slightest faults, ever harboring fearful caution, and upholds the training rules. Venerables, this is called the person with outer fetters who is not an anāgāmin and returns to this world."

Then a great number of Equal-Mind gods, their forms majestic, their radiance brilliant, as the night was turning toward dawn, came to the place of the Buddha, bowed their heads in homage, withdrew and stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Śāriputra last night, together with the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall, on account of inner fetters and outer fetters, explained the meaning to the bhikṣus: 'Venerables, in the world there truly exist two kinds of people: the person with inner fetters and the person with outer fetters.' World-Honored One, the assembly was delighted. We humbly wish that the World-Honored One, with compassion and kindness, would go to the lecture hall." At that time, the World-Honored One silently consented for the Equal-Mind gods. The Equal-Mind gods, knowing the World-Honored One had silently consented, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and vanished from that place.

Not long after the Equal-Mind gods had departed, the World-Honored One went to the lecture hall, and a seat was spread for him before the assembly of bhikṣus, and he sat down. After the World-Honored One had sat down, he praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! You have done exceedingly well. Why is that? Last night you, together with the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall, on account of inner fetters and outer fetters, explained the meaning to the bhikṣus: 'Venerables, in the world there truly exist two kinds of people: the person with inner fetters and the person with outer fetters.' Śāriputra, last night toward dawn, the Equal-Mind gods came to my place, bowed their heads in homage, withdrew and stood to one side, and said to me: 'World-Honored One, the Venerable Śāriputra last night, together with the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall, on account of inner fetters and outer fetters, explained the meaning to the bhikṣus: "Venerables, in the world there truly exist two kinds of people: the person with inner fetters and the person with outer fetters." World-Honored One, the assembly was delighted. We humbly wish that the World-Honored One, with compassion and kindness, would go to the lecture hall.' Śāriputra, I then silently consented for the Equal-Mind gods. The Equal-Mind gods, knowing I had silently consented, bowed at my feet, circumambulated three times, and vanished from that place.

"Śāriputra, the Equal-Mind gods, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty, dwell together on the point of a needle-tip, without hindering one another. Śāriputra, it is not the case that the Equal-Mind gods, having been born there, only then cultivate their wholesome minds to be extremely broad and great, enabling the Equal-Mind gods, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty, to dwell together on the point of a needle-tip without hindering one another. Rather, Śāriputra, the Equal-Mind gods, when they were formerly humans, had already cultivated their wholesome minds to be extremely broad and great. Because of this, the Equal-Mind gods, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty, dwell together on the point of a needle-tip without hindering one another. Therefore, Śāriputra, you should train in tranquility: the faculties tranquil, the mind and intention tranquil, deeds of body, speech, and mind tranquil, directed toward the World-Honored One and the wise companions in the holy life. Śāriputra, the false heterodox practitioners suffer long decline and eternal loss. Why is that? Because they do not get to hear such a wondrous Dharma."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Equal-Mind Sūtra, the First.

---

## Sūtra 22: The Accomplishment of Virtue Sūtra, Second of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, then he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling in this present life. There assuredly is this possibility. If in this present life he does not attain final knowledge, when his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. There too he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling. There assuredly is this possibility."

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was also in the assembly. The Venerable Udāyin said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu is reborn among the other mind-born gods and enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, this is certainly not possible."

The Venerable Śāriputra again, a second and third time, addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, then he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling in this present life. There assuredly is this possibility. If in this present life he does not attain final knowledge, when his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. There too he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling. There assuredly is this possibility."

The Venerable Udāyin also again, a second and third time, said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu is reborn among the other mind-born gods and enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, this is certainly not possible."

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought: "This bhikṣu has three times objected to what I said, and not a single bhikṣu has praised what I said. I should go to the World-Honored One." So the Venerable Śāriputra went to the Buddha, bowed his head in homage, and sat down to one side.

Not long after the Venerable Śāriputra had departed, the Venerable Udāyin and the other bhikṣus also went to the Buddha, bowed their heads in homage, and sat down to one side. There, the Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, then he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling in this present life. There assuredly is this possibility. If in this present life he does not attain final knowledge, when his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. There too he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling. There assuredly is this possibility."

The Venerable Udāyin again said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu is reborn among the other mind-born gods and enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, this is certainly not possible."

The Venerable Śāriputra again, a second and third time, addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, then he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling in this present life. There assuredly is this possibility. If in this present life he does not attain final knowledge, when his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. There too he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling. There assuredly is this possibility."

The Venerable Udāyin also again, a second and third time, said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu is reborn among the other mind-born gods and enters and emerges from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, this is certainly not possible."

The Venerable Śāriputra then had this thought: "This bhikṣu, even in the presence of the World-Honored One, has three times objected to what I said, and not a single bhikṣu has praised what I said. I should remain silent."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, do you say the mind-born gods are of form?"

The Venerable Udāyin said to the World-Honored One: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One rebuked the Venerable Udāyin to his face: "You foolish person! Blind and without eyes, on what basis do you discuss the profound Abhidharma?" Thereupon, the Venerable Udāyin, having been rebuked to his face by the Buddha, felt inwardly distressed and sorrowful, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence and had no words, as if absorbed in thought.

After the World-Honored One had rebuked the Venerable Udāyin to his face, he spoke to the Venerable Ānanda: "When an eminent and revered senior bhikṣu is challenged by another, why do you let it pass without correction? You foolish person! Without a compassionate mind, you turned your back on the eminent and revered senior."

Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyin and the Venerable Ānanda to their faces, told the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, then he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling in this present life. There assuredly is this possibility. If in this present life he does not attain final knowledge, when his body breaks up and life ends, he passes beyond the gods who feed on material food and is reborn among the other mind-born gods. There too he can enter and emerge from the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling. There assuredly is this possibility." Having spoken thus, the Buddha entered his meditation chamber and sat in silent meditation.

At that time, the Venerable Bai Jing was in the assembly. The Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Bai Jing: "This was another's doing, yet I received the blame. Venerable Bai Jing, in the afternoon the World-Honored One will certainly emerge from his meditation chamber, come before the assembly of bhikṣus, spread his seat and sit down, and discuss this matter further. Venerable Bai Jing should answer this matter, for I am extremely ashamed before the World-Honored One and the companions in the holy life."

Then the World-Honored One, in the afternoon, emerged from his meditation chamber, came before the assembly of bhikṣus, spread his seat and sat down, and asked: "Bai Jing, how many qualities does a senior bhikṣu have that make the companions in the holy life love, respect, and revere him?"

The Venerable Bai Jing said: "World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu who has five qualities is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life. What are the five? World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu cultivates the precepts, guards and follows the code of liberation, and moreover well governs his deportment and etiquette, seeing danger in the slightest faults, ever harboring fearful caution, and upholds the training rules. World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu eminent in precepts is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu is broadly learned and widely heard, remembers and does not forget, accumulates extensive learning. The so-called Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and also good at the end, with meaning and with expression, complete and pure, revealing the holy life; such teachings he has broadly learned and widely heard, studied and practiced up to a thousand times, contemplated in his mind, clearly seen and deeply penetrated. World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu eminent in learning is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu attains the four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty. World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu eminent in meditation is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu cultivates wisdom, contemplating the law of arising and passing away, attaining such knowledge, noble wisdom, clear understanding, distinguishing and comprehending, rightly making an end of suffering. World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu eminent in wisdom is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu whose outflows are entirely exhausted, who has no more fetters, liberated in mind and liberated in wisdom, who in this present life knows for himself, realizes for himself, personally witnesses and dwells in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' knowing it as it truly is. World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu eminent in the exhaustion of outflows is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life.

"World-Honored One, a senior bhikṣu who is accomplished in these five qualities is loved, respected, and revered by the companions in the holy life."

The World-Honored One asked: "Bai Jing, if a senior bhikṣu lacks these five qualities, for what reason would the companions in the holy life love, respect, and revere him?"

The Venerable Bai Jing said: "World-Honored One, if a senior bhikṣu lacks these five qualities, there is no other reason for the companions in the holy life to love, respect, and revere him, except that he is old and aged, white-haired and with fallen teeth, his youthful vigor daily declining, his body bent and legs crooked, heavy of body with labored breath, walking with a staff, his flesh shrunken and skin slack, wrinkled like sesame seeds, his faculties deteriorated, his appearance ugly. It is because of this that the companions in the holy life love, respect, and revere him."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is. If a senior bhikṣu lacks these five qualities, there is no other reason for the companions in the holy life to love, respect, and revere him, except that he is old and aged, white-haired and with fallen teeth, his youthful vigor daily declining, his body bent and legs crooked, heavy of body with labored breath, walking with a staff, his flesh shrunken and skin slack, wrinkled like sesame seeds, his faculties deteriorated, his appearance ugly. It is because of this that the companions in the holy life love, respect, and revere him.

"Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses these five qualities; you all should love, respect, and revere him. Why is that? Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra cultivates the precepts, guards and follows the code of liberation, and moreover well governs his deportment and etiquette, seeing danger in the slightest faults, ever harboring fearful caution, and upholds the training rules.

"Furthermore, Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is broadly learned and widely heard, remembers and does not forget, accumulates extensive learning. The so-called Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and also good at the end, with meaning and with expression, complete and pure, revealing the holy life; such teachings he has broadly learned and widely heard, studied and practiced up to a thousand times, contemplated in his mind, clearly seen and deeply penetrated.

"Furthermore, Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra attains the four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty.

"Furthermore, Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra cultivates wisdom, contemplating the law of arising and passing away, attaining such knowledge, noble wisdom, clear understanding, distinguishing and comprehending, rightly making an end of suffering.

"Furthermore, Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra, whose outflows are entirely exhausted, who has no more fetters, liberated in mind and liberated in wisdom, who in this present life knows for himself, realizes for himself, personally witnesses and dwells in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' knowing it as it truly is.

"Bai Jing, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is accomplished in these five qualities; you all should love, respect, and revere him."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Bai Jing and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Accomplishment of Virtue Sūtra, the Second.

---

## Sūtra 23: The Knowledge Sūtra, Third of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Mūḷhapaguṇa had abandoned the precepts and left the path. The bhikṣu Kāḷadanta heard that the bhikṣu Mūḷhapaguṇa had abandoned the precepts and left the path, and immediately went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed at his feet, withdrew and sat to one side. Having sat down, he said: "Venerable Śāriputra, you should know that the bhikṣu Mūḷhapaguṇa has abandoned the precepts and left the path."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Did the bhikṣu Mūḷhapaguṇa ever take delight in this Dharma?"

The bhikṣu Kāḷadanta asked: "Venerable Śāriputra, do you take delight in this Dharma?"

The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Kāḷadanta, regarding this Dharma I have no doubt whatsoever."

The bhikṣu Kāḷadanta then asked further: "Venerable Śāriputra, regarding future matters, what do you say?"

The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Kāḷadanta, regarding future matters too I have no hesitation."

The bhikṣu Kāḷadanta, having heard this, immediately rose from his seat and went to the Buddha, bowed his head in homage, withdrew and sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Śāriputra now declares of himself that he has attained knowledge: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' knowing it as it truly is."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, told a bhikṣu: "Go to where Śāriputra is and say: 'Śāriputra, the World-Honored One summons you.'"

The bhikṣu, having received the instruction, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. He went to the Venerable Śāriputra and said: "The World-Honored One summons the Venerable Śāriputra." The Venerable Śāriputra, having heard this, immediately went to the Buddha, bowed his head in homage, and sat down to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, have you truly declared of yourself that you have attained knowledge: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' knowing it as it truly is?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, I did not use those words or those phrases; I merely spoke of the meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, when a son of good family, by whatever manner of expression, declares that he has attained knowledge, that constitutes declaring that he has attained knowledge."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, I have already said that I did not use those words or those phrases; I merely spoke of the meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how do you know and how do you see, that you declare of yourself that you have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming," knowing it as it truly is?' Śāriputra, having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how do you know and how do you see, that you declare of yourself that you have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming," knowing it as it truly is?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, birth has a cause. When this cause of birth is exhausted, knowing that the cause of birth is exhausted, I declare of myself that I have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming," knowing it as it truly is.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of birth? From what does birth arise? What is its root?' Having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of birth? From what does birth arise? What is its root?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, birth is caused by existence and conditioned by existence; from existence birth arises, and existence is its root.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of existence? From what does existence arise? What is its root?' Having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of existence? From what does existence arise? What is its root?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, existence is caused by clinging and conditioned by clinging; from clinging existence arises, and clinging is its root.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of clinging? From what does clinging arise? What is its root?' Having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is the cause and condition of clinging? From what does clinging arise? What is its root?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, clinging is caused by craving and conditioned by craving; from craving clinging arises, and craving is its root.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is craving?' Having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, what is craving?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, there are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Among these, the desire for and attachment to pleasure is what is called craving.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how do you know and how do you see so that among the three feelings you are without desire or attachment to pleasure?' Having heard this, how would you answer?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how do you know and how do you see so that among the three feelings you are without desire or attachment to pleasure?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, these three feelings are of the nature of impermanence, of the nature of suffering, of the nature of cessation. What is impermanent is suffering. Having seen suffering, one is without desire or attachment to pleasure among the three feelings.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, this teaching has a further meaning that can be answered in brief. Śāriputra, what further meaning does this teaching have that can be answered in brief? Whatever is felt, whatever is experienced, all of it is suffering. Śāriputra, this is the further meaning that can be answered in brief."

The World-Honored One asked: "Śāriputra, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask you: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how have you turned away and not turned toward, that you declare of yourself that you have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming," knowing it as it truly is?'"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to come and ask me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, how have you turned away and not turned toward, that you declare of yourself that you have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming," knowing it as it truly is?' World-Honored One, having heard this, I would answer thus: 'Venerables, inwardly I have turned away and do not turn toward: all cravings are exhausted, without alarm, without fear, without doubt, without confusion. Practicing such guarding, and having so guarded, unwholesome outflows do not arise.' World-Honored One, if companions in the holy life were to ask me thus, I would answer in this way."

The World-Honored One praised: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! If companions in the holy life were to ask you thus, you should answer in this way. Why is that? One who speaks thus should be known to speak of the true meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, furthermore there is a meaning that can be answered in brief regarding this teaching. Whatever fetters śramaṇas speak of, those fetters are not in me. Practicing such guarding, and having so guarded, unwholesome outflows do not arise. Śāriputra, this is the further meaning that can be answered in brief regarding this teaching." Having spoken thus, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and entered his chamber to sit in meditation.

Not long after the World-Honored One had entered his chamber, the Venerable Śāriputra told the bhikṣus: "Venerables, at first I had not prepared my mind for it, and the World-Honored One suddenly asked me about this meaning. I had the thought: 'I fear I may not be able to answer.' Venerables, when I first stated one meaning and was thereupon praised and approved by the World-Honored One, I then had the thought: 'If the World-Honored One were to question me about this meaning for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases, I would be able to answer the World-Honored One for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases. If the World-Honored One were to question me for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases, I would likewise be able to answer the World-Honored One for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases.'"

The bhikṣu Kāḷadanta, having heard the Venerable Śāriputra speak thus, immediately rose from his seat, quickly went to the Buddha, and said to the World-Honored One: "Not long after the World-Honored One entered his chamber, the Venerable Śāriputra made the supreme declaration, a one-pointed lion's roar: 'Venerables, at first I had not prepared my mind for it, and the World-Honored One suddenly asked me about this meaning. I had the thought: "I fear I may not be able to answer." Venerables, when I first stated one meaning and was thereupon praised and approved by the World-Honored One, I then had the thought: "If the World-Honored One were to question me about this meaning for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases, I would be able to answer the World-Honored One for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases. Venerables, if the World-Honored One were to question me for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases, I would likewise be able to answer the World-Honored One for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases."'"

The World-Honored One said: "Kāḷadanta, so it is, so it is. If I were to question the bhikṣu Śāriputra about this meaning for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases, the bhikṣu Śāriputra would certainly be able to answer me for one day and one night, with different words and different phrases. Kāḷadanta, if I were to question the bhikṣu Śāriputra for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases, the bhikṣu Śāriputra would likewise be able to answer me for two, three, four, up to seven days and seven nights, with different words and different phrases. Why is that? Kāḷadanta, because the bhikṣu Śāriputra has deeply penetrated the Dharma-realm."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Knowledge Sūtra, the Third.

---

## Sūtra 24: The Lion's Roar Sūtra, Fourth of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, received the rains retreat in Śrāvastī. The Venerable Śāriputra was also traveling in Śrāvastī and received the rains retreat. Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having completed the rains retreat in Śrāvastī, after three months had passed, having finished mending his robes, took up his robes and bowl and went to the Buddha, bowed at his feet, withdrew and sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, I have completed the rains retreat in Śrāvastī. World-Honored One, I wish to travel about among the people."

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, go wherever you wish. Those who have not yet crossed over, cause them to cross over. Those who have not yet been liberated, cause them to be liberated. Those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa, cause them to attain parinirvāṇa. Śāriputra, go wherever you wish."

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha said, received it well and retained it well, then rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He returned to his own room, put away his bed and seat, took up his robes and bowl, and set out to travel among the people.

Not long after the Venerable Śāriputra had departed, a certain practitioner of the holy life, in the presence of the Buddha, committed an offense of contrariness and said to the World-Honored One: "Today the Venerable Śāriputra has treated me with contempt and has gone off traveling among the people."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, told a bhikṣu: "Go to where Śāriputra is and say to him: 'The World-Honored One summons you. Not long after you departed, a certain practitioner of the holy life, in my presence, committed an offense of contrariness and said: "World-Honored One, today the Venerable Śāriputra has treated me with contempt and has gone off traveling among the people."'"

The bhikṣu, having received the instruction, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding the fan to attend the Buddha.

Not long after the bhikṣu had departed, the Venerable Ānanda took the door key and went to every room. Seeing the bhikṣus, he said: "Excellent, Venerables! Quickly go to the lecture hall. Now the Venerable Śāriputra will make a lion's roar in the presence of the Buddha. Whatever the Venerable Śāriputra says will be extremely profound, the most tranquil of the tranquil, the most wondrous of the wondrous. If he speaks in this way, you Venerables and I, having heard it, should well recite it and well retain it." At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard the Venerable Ānanda's words, all went to the lecture hall.

Then the bhikṣu went to the Venerable Śāriputra and said: "The World-Honored One summons you. Not long after you departed, a certain practitioner of the holy life, in my presence, committed an offense of contrariness and said: 'World-Honored One, today the Venerable Śāriputra has treated me with contempt and has gone off traveling among the people.'"

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard this, immediately rose from his seat and returned to the Buddha, bowed at his feet, withdrew and sat to one side. The Buddha then said: "Śāriputra, not long after you departed, a certain practitioner of the holy life, in my presence, committed an offense of contrariness and said: 'World-Honored One, today the Venerable Śāriputra has treated me with contempt and has gone off traveling among the people.' Śāriputra, did you truly treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and then travel among the people?"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as a bull with sawn-off horns, supremely patient, gentle, well trained and well tamed, going from village to village, from lane to lane, wherever it travels, it harms nothing. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like a bull with sawn-off horns: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as a caṇḍāla youth whose two hands have been cut off, whose attitude is utterly humble, going from village to village, from town to town, wherever he travels, he harms nothing. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like a caṇḍāla youth whose hands have been cut off: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as the earth receives both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it accepts everything. The earth does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like that earth: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as water washes both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it washes everything. Water does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like that water: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as fire burns both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it burns everything. Fire does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like that fire: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as the wind blows on both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it blows on everything. The wind does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like that wind: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as a broom sweeps both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it sweeps everything. The broom does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like a broom: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as a cleaning rag wipes both clean and unclean things: feces, urine, mucus, spittle, it wipes everything. The cleaning rag does not on account of this have aversion or fondness, is not ashamed, not embarrassed, not humiliated. World-Honored One, I am likewise. My mind is like a cleaning rag: without fetters, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all the world, dwelling in accomplishment. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as an oil pot cracked everywhere, filled with oil and placed in the sun, leaking everywhere, oozing everywhere, seeping everywhere. If a person with eyes were to come and stand to one side, he would see this oil pot cracked everywhere, filled with oil and placed in the sun, leaking everywhere, oozing everywhere, seeping everywhere. World-Honored One, I am likewise. I constantly observe this body with its nine openings of impurity, leaking everywhere, oozing everywhere, seeping everywhere. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?

"World-Honored One, just as there were a young person who delights in adornment, having bathed and washed clean, perfumed with fragrant ointments, wearing white clean garments, adorned with jewels, with beard trimmed and hair groomed, wearing a garland of flowers on the head, and if three corpses were tied around his neck: a dead snake, a dead dog, and a dead person, blue-black, bloated, swollen, extremely foul, rotten and decayed, with impure fluids flowing out, that person would feel ashamed and humiliated, utterly loathing the filth. World-Honored One, I am likewise. I constantly observe this body as a foul and impure thing, and my mind feels ashamed and humiliated, utterly loathing the filth. World-Honored One, if one is without mindfulness of the body directed at the body, that person would treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people. World-Honored One, I am well established in mindfulness of the body directed at the body. How could I treat a companion in the holy life with contempt and travel among the people?"

Thereupon, that bhikṣu immediately rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and said to the World-Honored One: "I repent, World-Honored One! I confess, Sugata! I was like a fool, like one deluded, like one unsettled, like one unskillful. Why is that? I falsely and wrongly slandered the pure practitioner of the holy life, the bhikṣu Śāriputra. World-Honored One, I now repent. May you accept my confession. Having seen my fault, I lay it open, and henceforth I shall not repeat it."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, bhikṣu. You were truly like a fool, like one deluded, like one unsettled, like one unskillful. Why is that? You falsely, wrongly, and without truth slandered the pure practitioner of the holy life, the bhikṣu Śāriputra. You are able to repent. Having seen your fault, you lay it open, and henceforth you shall not repeat it. If one repents, having seen one's fault, lays it open, and does not repeat it, then one grows and develops in the noble Dharma and Vinaya without decline."

Then the Buddha told the Venerable Śāriputra: "Quickly accept this foolish person's repentance, lest this bhikṣu's head split into seven pieces right before you."

The Venerable Śāriputra, out of compassion for that bhikṣu, then accepted his repentance.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Lion's Roar Sūtra, the Fourth.

---

## Sūtra 25: The Water Simile Sūtra, Fifth of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, I will now explain to you the five methods for removing vexation. Listen attentively, listen attentively! Reflect well upon it." The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "What are the five? Venerables, there may be a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed. Furthermore, Venerables, there may be a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed. Furthermore, Venerables, there may be a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, but whose mind has a little purity. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed. Furthermore, Venerables, there may be a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal and mental conduct are impure. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed. Furthermore, Venerables, there may be a person whose bodily conduct is pure and whose verbal and mental conduct are pure. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed.

"Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, how should it be removed? Venerables, just as a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who wears rag-robes sees in a refuse heap a discarded tattered garment, soiled with feces, or urine, mucus, spittle, and other impurities. Seeing it, he takes it up with his left hand and stretches it out with his right hand. Wherever it is not soiled by feces, urine, mucus, spittle, or other impurities, and is not torn, he tears off that piece and takes it. In the same way, Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure, do not think of his impure bodily conduct; rather, think only of his pure verbal conduct. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed in this way.

"Venerables, when there is a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, how should it be removed? Venerables, just as not far from a village there is a deep pool of water covered over with straw and grass. If a person were to come, extremely hot and afflicted, hungry and thirsty, weary and exhausted, oppressed by wind and heat, having arrived at the pool, he would take off his clothes and place them on the bank, then enter the pool, parting the straw with both hands, and bathe to his satisfaction, removing the heat, affliction, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. In the same way, Venerables, when there is a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure, do not think of his impure verbal conduct; rather, think only of his pure bodily conduct. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed in this way.

"Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, but whose mind has a little purity, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, how should it be removed? Venerables, just as at a crossroads there is a puddle of water in a cow's hoof-print. If a person were to come, extremely hot and afflicted, hungry and thirsty, weary and exhausted, oppressed by wind and heat, he would think: 'At this crossroads there is but a little water in a cow's hoof-print. If I try to take it with my hand or a leaf, I would stir it up and make it muddy, and it would not relieve my extreme heat, affliction, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. I should rather kneel down, put my hands and knees on the ground, and drink the water with my mouth.' He would then kneel, place his hands and knees on the ground, and drink the water with his mouth, and thereby he would relieve the extreme heat, affliction, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. In the same way, Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, but whose mind has a little purity, do not think of his impure bodily conduct or impure verbal conduct; rather, think only of the little purity of his mind. Venerables, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed in this way.

"Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal and mental conduct are impure, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, how should it be removed? Venerables, just as there were a person traveling a long road who fell ill along the way, extremely weak and exhausted, alone without companions, the village behind far away, and the village ahead not yet reached. If another person were to come and stand to one side, seeing this traveler on the long road who fell ill along the way, extremely weak and exhausted, alone without companions, the village behind far away, and the village ahead not yet reached, and if that person could obtain an attendant to bring the traveler from the wilderness to a village or town, provide excellent medicine, nourish him with fine food, and care for him well, then this person's illness would certainly be cured. This shows that the person has the utmost compassion and kindly thought toward the sick person. In the same way, Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal and mental conduct are impure, if a wise person sees this, he should think: 'This good person's bodily conduct is impure, and his verbal and mental conduct are impure. May this good person not, because of impure bodily conduct and impure verbal and mental conduct, when his body breaks up and life ends, fall into an evil state and be reborn in hell. If this good person were to gain a good spiritual friend, he would abandon impure bodily conduct and cultivate pure bodily conduct, abandon impure verbal and mental conduct and cultivate pure verbal and mental conduct. In this way, this good person, because of pure bodily conduct and pure verbal and mental conduct, when his body breaks up and life ends, would surely reach a good destination and be reborn in heaven.' This shows that the wise person has the utmost compassion and kindly thought for this good person. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed in this way.

"Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is pure and whose verbal and mental conduct are pure, if a wise person sees this and vexation arises, how should it be removed? Venerables, just as not far from a village there is a fine pool of water, both clear and lovely, its depths even and full, green grass covering the banks, flowering trees on all four sides. If a person were to come, extremely hot and afflicted, hungry and thirsty, weary and exhausted, oppressed by wind and heat, having arrived at the pool, he would take off his clothes and place them on the bank, then enter the pool and bathe to his satisfaction, removing the heat, affliction, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. In the same way, Venerables, when there is a person whose bodily conduct is pure and whose verbal and mental conduct are pure, one should always think of his pure bodily conduct and his pure verbal and mental conduct. If a wise person sees this and vexation arises, it should be removed in this way. Venerables, what I have previously explained as the five methods for removing vexation was taught for this reason."

The Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard it, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Water Simile Sūtra, the Fifth.

---

End of Fascicle 5 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtra)
## Fascicle 6

*Translated from Chinese by Gautama Sanghadeva of the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

## Chapter on Related Topics, Third (continued)

### (24) Sūtra on the Lion's Roar

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Great Forest, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra came to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew and sat to one side. He then said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have such confidence in the World-Honored One that among those of the past, future, or present, there is no śramaṇa or brahmin who is superior to the World-Honored One in terms of awakening, that is, with respect to the supreme, right, and complete enlightenment."

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, you have uttered this bold, extraordinary declaration, this one-pointed statement, this lion's roar, saying: 'I have such confidence in the World-Honored One that among those of the past, future, or present, there is no śramaṇa or brahmin who is superior to the World-Honored One in terms of awakening, that is, with respect to the supreme, right, and complete enlightenment.'
