"Śāriputra, have you then, with your mind, comprehended and fully known the minds of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, knowing their morality was thus, their dharmas were thus, their wisdom was thus, their abiding was thus, their liberation was thus?"

Śāriputra replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, have you then, with your mind, comprehended and fully known the minds of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the future, knowing their morality was thus, their dharmas were thus, their wisdom was thus, their abiding was thus, their liberation was thus?"

Śāriputra replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, have you then, with your mind, comprehended and fully known the mind of myself, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Fully Awakened One, knowing my morality is thus, my dharmas are thus, my wisdom is thus, my abiding is thus, my liberation is thus?"

Śāriputra replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, since you do not know the minds of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, why then do you make this bold, extraordinary declaration, this one-pointed statement, this lion's roar?"

Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, although I do not, with my mind, comprehend and fully know the minds of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, still I understand the general principle of the Dharma. World-Honored One, it is as if at the border of a kingdom there were a fortress, with walls solid and strong, without any gaps, with only a single gate. A gatekeeper there, wise and intelligent, with fine discernment, would keep out those not known and admit those who are known. He might make a circuit around the perimeter of the entire fortress and not see any gap in the walls, not even one through which a cat could exit. He might then think: 'Whatever large creatures enter or leave this fortress must all go through this gate.'

"World-Honored One, in the same way I understand the general principle of the Dharma. World-Honored One, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Fully Awakened Ones of the past, all those World-Honored Ones, abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, established their minds in the four foundations of mindfulness, cultivated the seven factors of awakening as they truly are, and attained the supreme, right, and complete enlightenment.

"World-Honored One, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Fully Awakened Ones of the future, all those World-Honored Ones, will abandon the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, will establish their minds in the four foundations of mindfulness, will cultivate the seven factors of awakening as they truly are, and will attain the supreme, right, and complete enlightenment.

"World-Honored One, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Fully Awakened One, has also abandoned the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, has established the mind in the four foundations of mindfulness, has cultivated the seven factors of awakening as they truly are, and has attained the supreme, right, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "What do you think? For what reason should you from time to time go visit the bhikṣu Śāriputra? Bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is indeed wise, of great wisdom, of vast wisdom, of joyful wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of penetrating wisdom. Bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Śāriputra, for half a month, comprehends in its entirety the essential meaning of the Dharma. With regard to this, the bhikṣu Śāriputra makes a lion's roar, meaning what he has spoken."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (25) Sūtra on the Water Simile

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain for you the simile of the water. Listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the simile of the water? It is like a person who sinks and stays submerged in the water; like a person who, having emerged from the water, then sinks again; like a person who, having emerged from the water, stays emerged; like a person who, having emerged from the water, looks around in all directions; like a person who, having emerged from the water, goes forward and crosses to the other shore; like a person who, having emerged from the water, reaches the other shore, and having reached the other shore, stands on dry ground. This is called the simile of the water.

"What is meant by a person who sinks and stays submerged in the water? There is a person who is completely enveloped by unwholesome, dark dharmas. This is called a person who sinks and stays submerged in the water. It is like a person who sinks and stays submerged in the water; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having emerged from the water, then sinks again? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. But this faith of his does not abide long; it diminishes, recedes, and changes, and does not exist for long. This is called a person who, having emerged from the water, then sinks again. It is like a person who, having emerged from the water, then sinks again; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having emerged from the water, stays emerged? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. And this faith of his abides, does not diminish, does not recede, does not change, and exists for a long time. This is called a person who, having emerged from the water, stays emerged. It is like a person who, having emerged from the water, stays emerged; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having emerged from the water, looks around in all directions? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. And he, with the complete exhaustion of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into evil destinies, definitely destined for complete enlightenment, passing through at most seven existences among devas and humans before making an end of suffering. This is called a person who, having emerged from the water, looks around in all directions. It is like a person who, having emerged from the water, looks around in all directions; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having emerged from the water, goes forward? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. And he, with the complete exhaustion of the three fetters and with desire, hatred, and delusion diminished, becomes a once-returner, returning to this world only one more time before making an end of suffering. This is called a person who, having emerged from the water, goes forward. It is like a person who, having emerged from the water, goes forward; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having emerged from the water, crosses to the other shore? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. And he, with the complete exhaustion of the five lower fetters, is reborn by transformation, attains parinirvāṇa there, and does not return from that world. This is called a person who, having emerged from the water, crosses to the other shore. It is like a person who, having emerged from the water, crosses to the other shore; I say this person is also like that.

"What is meant by a person who, having reached the other shore, stands on dry ground? There is a person who, having emerged, possesses faith in wholesome dharmas: faith in morality, faith in learning, faith in generosity, and faith in wisdom. And he, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life, through his own higher knowledge, realizes and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. This is called a person who, having reached the other shore, stands on dry ground. It is like a person who, having reached the other shore, stands on dry ground; I say this person is also like that.

"This is what I call the simile of the water."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (26) Sūtra on the Simile of the Valūka River

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain for you the simile of the Valūka River. Listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the simile of the Valūka River? It is as if the Valūka River were full and overflowing with water, and a person with tasks to accomplish came, wanting to cross to the other shore for some purpose, seeking a crossing, seeking a ford. He would stand on this shore and look across. What he would see with his eyes, what he would hear with his ears, he would know, he would discern. Bhikṣus, what do you think? Could this person cross the Valūka River to reach the other shore, or not?"

The bhikṣus replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "In the same way, bhikṣus, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who do not know as it really is that 'this is suffering,' do not know as it really is that 'this is the arising of suffering,' do not know as it really is that 'this is the cessation of suffering,' and do not know as it really is that 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' They take delight in formations that produce rebirth, delight in and cling to formations that produce rebirth. Because they take delight in and cling to formations that produce rebirth, they delight in formations that produce aging, delight in and cling to formations that produce aging. Because they take delight in and cling to formations that produce aging, they delight in formations that produce illness, delight in and cling to formations that produce illness. Because they take delight in and cling to formations that produce illness, they delight in formations that produce death, delight in and cling to formations that produce death. Because they take delight in and cling to formations that produce death, they delight in formations that produce suffering, delight in and cling to formations that produce suffering. Because they take delight in and cling to formations that produce suffering, they cannot be liberated from birth, cannot be liberated from aging, cannot be liberated from illness, cannot be liberated from death, cannot be liberated from suffering and sorrow. I say these people cannot escape from suffering.

"It is as if the Valūka River were full and overflowing with water, and a person with tasks to accomplish came, wanting to cross to the other shore for some purpose, seeking a crossing, seeking a ford. This person, being strong and capable, standing on this shore and looking across, what he sees with his eyes, what he hears with his ears, he knows and discerns. Bhikṣus, what do you think? Could this person cross the Valūka River to reach the other shore, or not?"

The bhikṣus replied: "He could, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "In the same way, bhikṣus, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who know as it really is that 'this is suffering,' know as it really is that 'this is the arising of suffering,' know as it really is that 'this is the cessation of suffering,' and know as it really is that 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' They do not take delight in formations that produce rebirth, do not delight in or cling to formations that produce rebirth. Because they do not take delight in or cling to formations that produce rebirth, they do not delight in formations that produce aging, do not delight in or cling to formations that produce aging. Because they do not take delight in or cling to formations that produce aging, they do not delight in formations that produce illness, do not delight in or cling to formations that produce illness. Because they do not take delight in or cling to formations that produce illness, they do not delight in formations that produce death, do not delight in or cling to formations that produce death. Because they do not take delight in or cling to formations that produce death, they do not delight in formations that produce suffering, do not delight in or cling to formations that produce suffering. Because they do not take delight in or cling to formations that produce suffering, they are liberated from birth, liberated from aging, liberated from illness, liberated from death, liberated from suffering and sorrow. I say these people can escape from suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (27) Sūtra on the Simile of the Brahmin, Established by Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain for you the simile of the brahmin established by Dharma. Listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the simile of the brahmin established by Dharma? It is as if a brahmin had a ripe, mature grain field and the guardian of the field was not negligent. Bhikṣus, even though the grain in the brahmin's field is ripe, yet if someone comes and steals it or if cattle damage it, or it is destroyed by fire or by water, or if the seeds themselves are spoiled, that field will come to decline and ruin. But if no one comes to steal it, no cattle damage it, no fire destroys it, no water destroys it, and the seeds themselves are not spoiled, then the grain in this brahmin's field, being already ripe and mature, and the guardian of the field not being negligent, this brahmin will reap much grain.

"Bhikṣus, I likewise say the same. In my teaching, the essential point, the core intent, concerns the end of taints, the destruction of taints. If among my disciples there are those who, following my teaching of the taintless end of taints and destruction of taints, practice rightly, practice according to Dharma, follow the proper path, and practice the Dharma accordingly, they can attain the knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.

"Just as those who have already crossed come first, those who are now crossing come next, and those who will cross come after. Bhikṣus, in the same way, among my disciples, those who, following my teaching of the taintless end of taints and destruction of taints, practice rightly, practice according to Dharma, follow the proper path, and practice the Dharma accordingly, can attain the knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.

"Bhikṣus, I have accomplished what a teacher should accomplish, out of compassion, seeking benefit, seeking peace, seeking safety, speaking out of compassion and sympathy. You too should accomplish what you should accomplish. You should go to the shade of trees or to empty, quiet places, sit in meditation and contemplate. Do not be negligent. Practice diligently. Do not let there be later regret. This is my teaching and instruction for you."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (28) Sūtra on the Simile of the Honey Ball

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyans, in the city of Kapilavastu, at Nigrodha Park.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One put on his robe, took his bowl, and entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. After his meal, he stored away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, and with his sitting cloth over his shoulder, went to a certain grove of trees. Having entered the grove, he sat down at the root of a tree to spend the midday.

At that time, a Śākyan named Daṇḍapāṇi was walking about and came to that grove. He went to the World-Honored One, exchanged greetings with him, and then leaning on his staff, stood to one side and asked: "Śramaṇa, what do you teach? What do you proclaim?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Daṇḍapāṇi, my teaching is such that one does not dispute with anyone in the world, with māras, with Brahmā devas, with śramaṇas and brahmins, from kings down to the common people. My proclamation is such that perceptions do not follow and abide in the brahmin who dwells detached from sensual desires, without perplexity, with remorse eliminated, free from craving for any existence or non-existence. This is what I teach, this is what I proclaim."

Then the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, hearing what the Buddha said, shook his head and wagged his tongue, showing a furrowed brow with three wrinkles on his forehead. Leaning on his staff, he departed.

Then in the evening, the World-Honored One arose from sitting meditation and went to Nigrodha Park. He spread his sitting cloth, sat down cross-legged, and addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, today in the early morning I put on my robe, took my bowl, and entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. After my meal, I stored away my robe and bowl, washed my hands and feet, and with my sitting cloth over my shoulder, went to a certain grove of trees. Having entered the grove, I sat down at the root of a tree to spend the midday.

"At that time, a Śākyan named Daṇḍapāṇi came to me, exchanged greetings, and then leaning on his staff, stood to one side and asked me: 'Śramaṇa, what do you teach? What do you proclaim?'

"I replied: 'Daṇḍapāṇi, my teaching is such that one does not dispute with anyone in the world, with māras, with Brahmā devas, with śramaṇas and brahmins, from kings down to the common people. My proclamation is such that perceptions do not follow and abide in the brahmin who dwells detached from sensual desires, without perplexity, with remorse eliminated, free from craving for any existence or non-existence. This is what I teach, this is what I proclaim.'

"Then the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, hearing what I said, shook his head and wagged his tongue, showing a furrowed brow with three wrinkles on his forehead. Leaning on his staff, he departed."

When this was said, a certain bhikṣu asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is the teaching such that one does not dispute with anyone in the world, with māras, with Brahmā devas, with śramaṇas and brahmins, from kings down to the common people? What is the proclamation such that perceptions do not follow and abide in the brahmin who dwells detached from sensual desires, without perplexity, with remorse eliminated, free from craving for any existence or non-existence?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhikṣu, whatever is the source from which a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving, if there is nothing there to delight in, to welcome, or to cling to, then this is the end of the underlying tendencies of desire, the end of the underlying tendencies of aversion, the end of the underlying tendencies of views, the end of the underlying tendencies of doubt, the end of the underlying tendencies of conceit, the end of the underlying tendencies of craving for existence, and the end of the underlying tendencies of ignorance. This is the end of taking up swords and clubs, quarrels, disputes, arguments, accusations, slander, and false speech. These evil, unwholesome dharmas are extinguished without remainder. This is the teaching such that one does not dispute with anyone in the world, with māras, with Brahmā devas, with śramaṇas and brahmins, from kings down to the common people. This is the proclamation such that perceptions do not follow and abide in the brahmin who dwells detached from sensual desires, without perplexity, with remorse eliminated, free from craving for any existence or non-existence."

Having said this, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.

After the World-Honored One had left, the bhikṣus thought: "The World-Honored One has given us this brief teaching without a detailed explanation, and has entered his dwelling. Who can now explain the meaning in detail?" The bhikṣus then thought: "The Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the Buddha and esteemed by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana can explain the meaning in detail. Let us now go to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana and ask him about this meaning."

Then the bhikṣus went to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and recounted the whole matter, saying: "Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the World-Honored One gave us this brief teaching without a detailed explanation, and entered his dwelling. We thought: 'Who can explain the meaning in detail?' We then thought: 'The Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the Buddha and esteemed by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana can explain the meaning in detail.' Please, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, explain it for us."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the bhikṣus: "Listen, and I will analyze and explain it for you. Bhikṣus, it is as if a person were seeking the heartwood of a tree. Having found a great tree with heartwood standing there, he bypasses the root and the trunk and thinks to seek the heartwood in the branches and leaves. It is like this for you venerable ones: having the Teacher face to face, you bypass him and think to ask me about this meaning. Why is that? The World-Honored One is the one who knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen. He is the eye, he is the knowledge, he is the Dharma, he is the lord of Dharma, he is the proclaimer, he is the judge, he is the one who reveals the meaning, he is the one who bestows the deathless, he is the lord of the Dharma, he is the Tathāgata. You should have asked the World-Honored One at the appropriate time, and whatever the World-Honored One explained, you should have received and upheld it accordingly."

The bhikṣus said: "Indeed, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the World-Honored One is the one who knows, the one who sees. He is the eye, he is the knowledge, he is the Dharma, he is the lord of Dharma, he is the proclaimer, he is the judge, he is the one who reveals the meaning, he is the one who bestows the deathless, he is the lord of the Dharma, he is the Tathāgata. We should indeed have asked the World-Honored One at the appropriate time, and whatever the World-Honored One explained, we should have received and upheld it accordingly. However, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the Buddha and esteemed by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana is able to explain the meaning of this brief teaching in detail. Please, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion, explain it for us."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said to the bhikṣus: "Then listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana said: "Bhikṣus, regarding what the World-Honored One gave as a brief teaching without a detailed explanation, and then entered his dwelling, saying: 'Whatever is the source from which a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving, if there is nothing there to delight in, to welcome, or to cling to, then this is the end of the underlying tendencies of desire, the end of the underlying tendencies of aversion, the end of the underlying tendencies of views, the end of the underlying tendencies of doubt, the end of the underlying tendencies of conceit, the end of the underlying tendencies of craving for existence, and the end of the underlying tendencies of ignorance. This is the end of taking up swords and clubs, quarrels, disputes, arguments, accusations, slander, and false speech. These evil, unwholesome dharmas are extinguished without remainder.' I understand the meaning of this brief teaching in full as follows:

"Bhikṣus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present forms cognizable by the eye.

"Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present sounds cognizable by the ear.

"Dependent on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present odors cognizable by the nose.

"Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present tastes cognizable by the tongue.

"Dependent on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present tangibles cognizable by the body.

"Dependent on the mind and dharmas, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. What one feels, one perceives. What one perceives, one thinks about. What one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present dharmas cognizable by the mind.

"Bhikṣus, when there is the eye, when there are forms, when there is eye-consciousness, one knows contact due to the coming together of conditions. When there is contact due to the coming together of conditions, one knows feeling. When one feels, one perceives. When one perceives, one thinks about. When one thinks about, one proliferates. Due to proliferation, a person is assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present forms cognizable by the eye.

"Similarly for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and dharmas, the same applies.

"Bhikṣus, when there is no eye, when there are no forms, when there is no eye-consciousness, then there is no contact due to the coming together of conditions. When there is no contact due to the coming together of conditions, there is no feeling. When there is no feeling, there is no perception. When there is no perception, there is no thinking. When there is no thinking, there is no proliferation. When there is no proliferation, a person is not assailed by the proliferations and perceptions of craving with respect to past, future, and present forms cognizable by the eye.

"Similarly for the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and dharmas, the same applies.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the World-Honored One's brief teaching given without a detailed explanation, in which he then entered his dwelling, I understand the meaning in full in this way. You venerable ones, if you wish, you may go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning. As the World-Honored One explains it, so should you receive and uphold it."

Then the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said, were well pleased and delighted. They rose from their seats, went to the World-Honored One, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, withdrew and sat to one side. They recounted the entire matter from beginning to end and then said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana explained the meaning to us using these words, these phrases, these expressions."

The World-Honored One said: "Excellent, excellent! Mahākātyāyana is endowed with great wisdom. Why is that? Because if you had asked me about this meaning, I would have explained it in exactly the same way as Mahākātyāyana did. This is precisely the meaning, and you should receive and uphold it accordingly."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (29) Sūtra on the Great Simile of Heartwood

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain for you the simile of the heartwood of a tree. Listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "It is like a person seeking heartwood. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he enters the mountains and forests. He sees a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He bypasses the heartwood, bypasses the sapwood, bypasses the bark, bypasses the outer bark, and instead cuts away the branches and leaves, thinking he has obtained the heartwood.

"A person of clear vision seeing this would say: 'This person does not know the heartwood, does not know the sapwood, does not know the bark, does not know the outer bark, does not know the branches and leaves. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. But he bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, bypassed the bark, bypassed the outer bark, and instead cut away the branches and leaves, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served.'

"It is like a person seeking heartwood. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he enters the mountains and forests. He sees a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He bypasses the heartwood, bypasses the sapwood, bypasses the bark, and instead cuts away the outer bark, thinking he has obtained the heartwood.

"A person of clear vision seeing this would say: 'This person does not know the heartwood, does not know the sapwood, does not know the bark, does not know the outer bark, does not know the branches and leaves. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. But he bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, bypassed the bark, and instead cut away the outer bark, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served.'

"It is like a person seeking heartwood. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he enters the mountains and forests. He sees a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He bypasses the heartwood, bypasses the sapwood, and instead strips away the bark, thinking he has obtained the heartwood.

"A person of clear vision seeing this would say: 'This person does not know the heartwood, does not know the sapwood, does not know the bark, does not know the outer bark, does not know the branches and leaves. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. But he bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, and instead stripped away the bark, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served.'

"It is like a person seeking heartwood. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he enters the mountains and forests. He sees a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He bypasses the heartwood and instead cuts away the sapwood, thinking he has obtained the heartwood.

"A person of clear vision seeing this would say: 'This person does not know the heartwood, does not know the sapwood, does not know the bark, does not know the outer bark, does not know the branches and leaves. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. But he bypassed the heartwood and instead cut away the sapwood, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served.'

"It is like a person seeking heartwood. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he enters the mountains and forests. He sees a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He cuts away the heartwood itself, knowing it is the heartwood and taking only the heartwood.

"A person of clear vision seeing this would say: 'This person knows the heartwood, knows the sapwood, knows the bark, knows the outer bark, knows the branches and leaves. For the sake of seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, he entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He cut away the heartwood itself, knowing it is the heartwood and taking only the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will be served.'

"In the same way, bhikṣus, there are certain clansmen who, with faith, leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless. They think: 'I am drowning in birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. I am drowning in suffering, submerged in suffering. Perhaps I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.' After this clansman has left the household life, he obtains offerings of gain, fame, and honor. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he is pleased and his wishes are fulfilled. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he praises himself and denigrates others, saying: 'I have gain, fame, and honor, but those other bhikṣus do not have gain, fame, and honor.' He does not, on account of that gain, fame, and honor, generate aspiration for further attainment, does not practice diligently, but instead dwells in negligence. Because of negligence, he falls. This is like a person who, seeking heartwood, came upon a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight, but bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, bypassed the bark, bypassed the outer bark, and instead cut away the branches and leaves, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served. I say this person is also like that.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are certain clansmen who, with faith, leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless. They think: 'I am drowning in birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. I am drowning in suffering, submerged in suffering. Perhaps I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.' After this clansman has left the household life, he obtains offerings of gain, fame, and honor. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that gain, fame, and honor, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of morality. Because of that morality, he is pleased and his wishes are fulfilled. Because of that morality, he praises himself and denigrates others, saying: 'I have morality and am pure, but those other bhikṣus have no morality and are impure.' He does not, on account of that morality, generate aspiration for further attainment, does not practice diligently, but instead dwells in negligence. Because of negligence, he falls. This is like a person who, seeking heartwood, came upon a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight, but bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, bypassed the bark, and instead cut away the outer bark, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served. I say this person is also like that.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are certain clansmen who, with faith, leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless. They think: 'I am drowning in birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. I am drowning in suffering, submerged in suffering. Perhaps I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.' After this clansman has left the household life, he obtains offerings of gain, fame, and honor. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that gain, fame, and honor, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of morality. Because of that morality, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that morality, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of samādhi. Because of that samādhi, he is pleased and his wishes are fulfilled. Because of that samādhi, he praises himself and denigrates others, saying: 'I have samādhi and am focused, but those other bhikṣus have no samādhi and are unfocused.' He does not, on account of that samādhi, generate aspiration for further attainment, does not practice diligently, but instead dwells in negligence. Because of negligence, he falls. This is like a person who, seeking heartwood, came upon a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight, but bypassed the heartwood, bypassed the sapwood, and instead stripped away the bark, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served. I say this person is also like that.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are certain clansmen who, with faith, leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless. They think: 'I am drowning in birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. I am drowning in suffering, submerged in suffering. Perhaps I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.' After this clansman has left the household life, he obtains offerings of gain, fame, and honor. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that gain, fame, and honor, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of morality. Because of that morality, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that morality, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of samādhi. Because of that samādhi, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that samādhi, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He attains knowledge and vision. Because of that knowledge and vision, he is pleased and his wishes are fulfilled. Because of that knowledge and vision, he praises himself and denigrates others, saying: 'I have knowledge and vision and can see, but those other bhikṣus have no knowledge and vision and cannot see.' He does not, on account of that knowledge and vision, generate aspiration for further attainment, does not practice diligently, but instead dwells in negligence. Because of negligence, he falls. This is like a person who, seeking heartwood, came upon a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight, but bypassed the heartwood and instead cut away the sapwood, thinking he had obtained the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will not be served. I say this person is also like that.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are certain clansmen who, with faith, leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless. They think: 'I am drowning in birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. I am drowning in suffering, submerged in suffering. Perhaps I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.' After this clansman has left the household life, he obtains offerings of gain, fame, and honor. Because of this gain, fame, and honor, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that gain, fame, and honor, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of morality. Because of that morality, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that morality, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He achieves the accomplishment of samādhi. Because of that samādhi, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that samādhi, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He attains knowledge and vision. Because of that knowledge and vision, he is not pleased nor are his wishes fulfilled. He does not praise himself and denigrate others. He, on account of that knowledge and vision, generates aspiration for further attainment and practices diligently, not dwelling in negligence. He attains the ultimate, unsurpassed liberation. This liberation cannot decline or change.

"Bhikṣus, this is like a person who, seeking heartwood, carrying an axe, entered the mountains and forests. He saw a great tree with heartwood standing there, tall and straight. He neither bypassed the heartwood, nor the sapwood, nor the bark, nor the outer bark, nor the branches and leaves. He cut away the heartwood itself, knowing it is the heartwood and taking only the heartwood. Whatever this person wants to use the heartwood for, his purpose will be served. I say this person is also like that.

"Bhikṣus, this holy life is not practiced for the sake of gain, fame, and honor, nor for the sake of morality, nor for the sake of samādhi, nor for the sake of knowledge and vision. Bhikṣus, this unwavering, unsurpassed liberation of mind is the goal of this holy life, this is its heartwood, this is its final conclusion."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

### (30) Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain for you the simile of the elephant's footprint. Listen well and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "It is as if an elephant tracker enters a forest and sees a large elephant footprint in the forest, long and broad. A skilled elephant tracker would not immediately conclude: 'This is the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why not? Because in the forest there are female elephants that are stunted and small. These might have large feet that leave large footprints, long and broad. He would follow it further and see a large elephant footprint that is long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up. A skilled elephant tracker would still not immediately conclude: 'This is the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why not? Because in the forest there are female elephants that are half-stunted. These might have large feet that leave large footprints, long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up. He would follow it further and see a large elephant footprint that is long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up and marks of tearing and breaking on trees high up. A skilled elephant tracker would still not immediately conclude: 'This is the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why not? Because in the forest there are female elephants with long teeth. These might have large feet that leave large footprints, long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up and marks of tearing and breaking on trees high up. He would follow it further and see a large elephant footprint that is long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up, marks of tearing and breaking on trees high up, and then he sees a great bull elephant standing under or near a tree, walking about, sitting or lying down. The skilled elephant tracker then sees and knows: 'This is indeed a great bull elephant.'

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, the Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, then at the beginning it is good, in the middle it is good, and at the end it is good; its meaning is good, its phrasing is good. It reveals the complete, pure, and fulfilled holy life.

"If a householder or the son of a householder hears this Dharma, he gains faith. With this faith, he thinks: 'The household life is constricting and dusty. Leaving the household life leads to the open air. But now, living in a household, I cannot practice the completely pure, completely fulfilled holy life. Let me now shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless.' He then, at some later time, abandoning a small amount of wealth or a great amount of wealth, abandoning a small circle of relatives or a great circle of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life to practice the Way, becoming homeless.

"Having left the household life and obtained the precepts of a bhikṣu, he abandons killing and abstains from killing. He abandons the sword and the club. He is conscientious and modest, has kindness and compassion, and benefits all living beings, even insects and small creatures. He purifies his mind of killing living beings.

"He abandons taking what is not given and abstains from taking what is not given. He accepts what is given and awaits what is given. He is himself without theft, and purifies his mind of taking what is not given.

"He abandons unchastity and practices the holy life of celibacy, being pure and detached, abstaining from sexual conduct, from the dharma of the common person. He purifies his mind of unchastity.

"He abandons false speech and abstains from false speech. He speaks the truth, he delights in truth, he abides in truth, his words are trustworthy, he does not deceive the world. He purifies his mind of false speech.

"He abandons divisive speech and abstains from divisive speech. He does not carry speech from here to cause discord there, nor carry speech from there to cause discord here. He wishes to reconcile those who are divided and to encourage those who are united. He does not create factions. He does not take pleasure in factions. He does not praise faction-making. He purifies his mind of divisive speech.

"He abandons harsh speech and abstains from harsh speech. Whatever speech is gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, going to the heart, urbane, agreeable to many, pleasing to many, he speaks such speech. He purifies his mind of harsh speech.

"He abandons idle chatter and abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks of the Dharma, speaks of the discipline. His speech is to be treasured, timely, reasoned, measured, and beneficial. He purifies his mind of idle chatter.

"He abandons harming seeds and plant life.

"He eats one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times.

"He abandons watching and listening to dancing, singing, and musical performances.

"He abandons wearing flower garlands, applying perfumes and ointments, and adorning himself.

"He abandons high and broad beds.

"He abandons accepting gold and silver.

"He abandons accepting raw grain.

"He abandons accepting raw meat.

"He abandons accepting women and girls.

"He abandons accepting male and female servants.

"He abandons accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep.

"He abandons accepting chickens and pigs.

"He abandons accepting fields and properties.

"He abandons accepting messages and serving as a go-between.

"He abandons buying and selling.

"He abandons scales and measures, deceiving and defrauding.

"He abandons bribery, deception, trickery, and dishonesty.

"He abandons cutting, beating, binding, ambushing, robbing, and plundering.

"He is content with robes to cover his body and with almsfood to sustain himself. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. It is like a bird that wherever it flies takes only its two wings. In the same way, a bhikṣu is content with robes to cover his body and with almsfood to sustain himself. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him.

"He, possessing this noble aggregate of morality, experiences the blameless bliss within.

"He, when he sees a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs, does not grasp at its details. Because if he left the faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and sorrow, evil, unwholesome dharmas would assail him. He therefore guards the faculty of the eye, he achieves the guarding of the faculty of the eye.

"When he hears a sound with the ear, smells an odor with the nose, tastes a flavor with the tongue, touches a tangible with the body, or cognizes a dharma with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs, does not grasp at its details. Because if he left the faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and sorrow, evil, unwholesome dharmas would assail him. He therefore guards the faculty of the mind, he achieves the guarding of the faculty of the mind.

"He, possessing this noble guarding of the sense faculties, experiences the unsullied bliss within.

"He, in going forward and returning, acts with clear comprehension. In looking forward and looking around, he acts with clear comprehension. In bending and stretching, he acts with clear comprehension. In wearing his saṅghāṭī robe and holding his bowl, he acts with clear comprehension. In eating and drinking, he acts with clear comprehension. In walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and being silent, he acts with clear comprehension.

"He, possessing this noble aggregate of morality, possessing this noble guarding of the sense faculties, and possessing this noble clear comprehension, resorts to a secluded place: the wilderness, under trees, in mountain caves, in rocky crevices, in open ground, or in haystacks. After the midday meal, returning from alms-round, he sits cross-legged with body upright, establishing mindfulness before him.

"He abandons covetousness, dwells with a mind free from covetousness, and purifies his mind of covetousness.

"He abandons ill-will and hatred, dwells with a mind free from ill-will, with compassion and kindness toward all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred.

"He abandons sloth and torpor, dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.

"He abandons restlessness and remorse, dwells without restlessness, with inner peace of mind, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.

"He abandons doubt, dwells having crossed over doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome dharmas, and purifies his mind of doubt.

"He abandons these five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom. Detached from sensual desires, detached from evil, unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of detachment, he enters and abides in the first dhyāna.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the first dhyāna, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the stilling of initial thought and sustained thought, with inner clarity and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of samādhi, he enters and abides in the second dhyāna.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the second dhyāna, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the fading away of joy, dwelling in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe it: 'One who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness,' he enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the third dhyāna, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, with neither-pain-nor-pleasure and the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the fourth dhyāna, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"With the mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, without blemish, free from defilements, supple, workable, established, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births, and the forming and dissolving of many world-ages: 'There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn here. Here I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Dying from here, I was reborn there.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their characteristics and details.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"With the mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, without blemish, free from defilements, supple, workable, established, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the divine eye. With the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies, superior and inferior. He knows beings according to their actions: 'These beings, endowed with bad conduct of body, endowed with bad conduct of speech, endowed with bad conduct of mind, who revile the noble ones, who hold wrong views, who undertake actions under the influence of wrong views, when their bodies break up after death, they are reborn in the lower realms, in bad destinies, in ruin, in hell. But these beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind, who do not revile the noble ones, who hold right views, who undertake actions under the influence of right views, when their bodies break up after death, they are reborn in good destinies, in the heavenly realms.' Thus with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies, superior and inferior. He knows beings according to their actions.

"Bhikṣus, a skilled elephant tracker, not yet having seen the great elephant itself but only having seen its footprint, would not immediately conclude this is a great bull elephant. In the same way, when a disciple of mine has not yet attained the knowledge of the divine eye, he should not yet conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'

"With the mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, without blemish, free from defilements, supple, workable, established, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the arising of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'These are the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the arising of the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.' When he knows and sees in this way, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been fulfilled, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more coming to any state of being.'

"Bhikṣus, it is as if a skilled elephant tracker enters the forest and sees a large elephant footprint, long and broad, with marks of tusk rubbings high up, with marks of tearing and breaking on trees high up, and then sees a great bull elephant standing under or near a tree, walking about, sitting or lying down. The skilled elephant tracker then knows: 'This is indeed a great bull elephant.'

"In the same way, bhikṣus, when a disciple of mine attains the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he should then conclude: 'The World-Honored One is a Fully Awakened One. The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One. The Sangha practices well.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced it respectfully.

---

*End of Fascicle 6 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 6

---

## (26) Sūtra on Guṇika, Sixth in the Section Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the bhikṣu Guṇika was also traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in a secluded dwelling. He was jesting and arrogant, restless and forgetful, his mind like a monkey. The bhikṣu Guṇika had gone to Rājagṛha on some minor business. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, together with a company of bhikṣus, after the midday meal, had gathered in the lecture hall on account of a small matter. The bhikṣu Guṇika, having completed his business in Rājagṛha, went to the lecture hall.

The Venerable Śāriputra saw Guṇika coming from afar, and on account of Guṇika, he addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in being respectful and in observing with compliance. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion is mostly disrespectful and does not observe with compliance, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet is mostly disrespectful and does not observe with compliance.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in being respectful, so as to observe with compliance.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not jesting and not being restless. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion engages much in jesting and restlessness, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet engages much in jesting and restlessness.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not jesting and not being restless.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not engaging in animal talk. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion engages much in animal talk, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet engages much in animal talk.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not engaging in animal talk.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not being arrogant and in speaking little. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion is much given to arrogance and much given to talk, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet is much given to arrogance and much given to talk.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in not being arrogant and in speaking little.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in guarding the sense faculties. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion mostly does not guard the sense faculties, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet mostly does not guard the sense faculties.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in guarding the sense faculties.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing moderation in eating. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion is greedy for extra food, eats excessively, and does not know moderation, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet is greedy for extra food, eats excessively, and does not know moderation.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing moderation in eating.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in being energetic and not negligent. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion is mostly lacking in energy and is negligent, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet is mostly lacking in energy and is instead negligent.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in being energetic and not negligent.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in right mindfulness and right awareness. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion is mostly without right mindfulness and without right awareness, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet is mostly without right mindfulness and without right awareness.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in right mindfulness and right awareness.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing proper timing and good timing. He should not enter the village too early to beg for food, nor leave too late. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion enters the village too early to beg for food and also leaves too late, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet enters the village too early to beg for food and also leaves too late.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing proper timing and good timing.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing proper seating and good seating. He should not press close to the elders when sitting, for which junior bhikṣus would reproach him. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion presses close to the elders when sitting and is reproached by junior bhikṣus, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet presses close to the elders when sitting and is reproached by junior bhikṣus.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in knowing proper seating and good seating.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the Vinaya and Abhidharma. Why is this? Venerables, when a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices in seclusion, someone may come and ask about the Vinaya and Abhidharma. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion does not know how to answer questions about the Vinaya and Abhidharma, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet does not know how to answer questions about the Vinaya and Abhidharma.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the Vinaya and Abhidharma.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the peaceful liberations, from the form realm to the formless attainments. Why is this? Venerables, when a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices in seclusion, someone may come and ask about the peaceful liberations, from the form realm to the formless attainments. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion does not know how to answer questions about the peaceful liberations, from the form realm to the formless attainments, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet does not know how to answer questions about the peaceful liberations, from the form realm to the formless attainments.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the peaceful liberations, from the form realm to the formless attainments.

"Venerables! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the superknowledge of the destruction of the defilements. Why is this? Venerables, when a forest-dwelling bhikṣu practices in seclusion, someone may come and ask about the superknowledge of the destruction of the defilements. Venerables, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion does not know how to answer questions about the superknowledge of the destruction of the defilements, then bhikṣus will reproach, censure, and interrogate him, saying: 'This venerable one dwells in seclusion; why does he practice in seclusion? Why is this? This venerable one dwells in seclusion and practices in seclusion, yet does not know how to answer questions about the superknowledge of the destruction of the defilements.' If he comes into the assembly, bhikṣus will likewise reproach, censure, and interrogate him. Therefore, venerables, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices in seclusion should train in discussing the superknowledge of the destruction of the defilements."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also in the assembly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Venerable Śāriputra! Is it only forest-dwelling bhikṣus practicing in seclusion who should train in such qualities, and not bhikṣus living among people?"

The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If even forest-dwelling bhikṣus practicing in seclusion should train in such qualities, how much more so bhikṣus living among people!"

Thus the two venerable ones mutually praised each other and commended it as excellent. Having heard what was said, they rose from their seats and departed.

Respectfulness, not jesting,
Not engaging in animal talk, not being arrogant,
Guarding the faculties, knowing moderation in eating,
Energy, right mindfulness and awareness,
Knowing proper timing, and good seating,
Discussing the Vinaya and Abhidharma,
And discussing the peaceful liberations,
And likewise the superknowledge of the destruction of defilements.

End of the Guṇika Sūtra, the Sixth.

---

## (27) Sūtra on the Brahmin Dhānañjāni, Seventh in the Section Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great company of bhikṣus, and they were together undertaking the summer retreat. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was in Śrāvastī, also undertaking the summer retreat.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who had undertaken the summer retreat in Rājagṛha. After the three months had passed, having mended his robes, he gathered his robes and took his bowl, and traveled from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. That bhikṣu went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side.

The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Venerable one, where have you come from, and where did you undertake the summer retreat?"

That bhikṣu answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, I have come from Rājagṛha and undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the World-Honored One undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha. Is his holy body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength as usual?"

He answered: "It is so. Venerable Śāriputra, the World-Honored One undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha. His holy body is well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength is as usual."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs who undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha, are their holy bodies well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength as usual? Do they wish to see the Buddha frequently and delight in hearing the Dharma?"

He answered: "It is so. Venerable Śāriputra, the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs who undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha, their holy bodies are well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength is as usual. They wish to see the Buddha frequently and all delight in hearing the Dharma."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās dwelling in Rājagṛha, are their bodies well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength as usual? Do they wish to see the Buddha frequently and delight in hearing the Dharma?"

He answered: "It is so. Venerable Śāriputra, the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās dwelling in Rājagṛha, their bodies are well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength is as usual. They wish to see the Buddha frequently and all delight in hearing the Dharma."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the various heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins who undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha, are their bodies well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength as usual? Do they wish to see the Buddha frequently and delight in hearing the Dharma?"

He answered: "It is so. Venerable Śāriputra, the various heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins who undertook the summer retreat in Rājagṛha, their bodies are well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and their strength is as usual. They wish to see the Buddha frequently and all delight in hearing the Dharma."

He further asked: "Venerable one, dwelling in Rājagṛha there is a certain brahmin named Dhānañjāni, who was my friend before I left the household life. Do you know him?"

He answered: "I know him."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the brahmin Dhānañjāni dwelling in Rājagṛha, is his body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength as usual? Does he wish to see the Buddha frequently and delight in hearing the Dharma?"

He answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni dwelling in Rājagṛha, his body is well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength is as usual. However, he does not wish to see the Buddha and does not delight in hearing the Dharma. Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni is not diligent and transgresses the precepts. He relies upon the king to deceive the brahmins and householders, and relies upon the brahmins and householders to deceive the king."

The Venerable Śāriputra, having heard this, when the summer retreat in Śrāvastī was completed and the three months had passed, having mended his robes, he gathered his robes and took his bowl, and traveled from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden.

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, after the night had passed, at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha, going from house to house begging for food. After begging for food, he went to the home of the brahmin Dhānañjāni. At that time, the brahmin Dhānañjāni had gone out from his house to a spring, where he was harshly overseeing the common people. The brahmin Dhānañjāni saw the Venerable Śāriputra coming from afar, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Śāriputra, and praised him saying: "Welcome, Śāriputra! It has been long since Śāriputra came here." Then the brahmin Dhānañjāni, with a respectful heart, embraced the Venerable Śāriputra and led him into his house, where he spread a fine seat and invited him to sit.
