The Venerable Śāriputra sat on that seat. The brahmin Dhānañjāni, seeing the Venerable Śāriputra seated, took a golden water vessel and invited the Venerable Śāriputra to eat.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Enough, enough, Dhānañjāni! Just let the thought of joy suffice."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni again invited him to eat a second and third time. The Venerable Śāriputra likewise said a second and third time: "Enough, enough, Dhānañjāni. Just let the thought of joy suffice."

At that time, the brahmin Dhānañjāni asked: "Śāriputra, why have you come to such a house and yet refuse to eat?"

He answered: "Dhānañjāni, you are not diligent and transgress the precepts. You rely upon the king to deceive the brahmins and householders, and you rely upon the brahmins and householders to deceive the king."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni answered: "Śāriputra, you should know that I am now a householder, and household affairs are my concern. I should provide comfort for myself, support and serve my parents, look after my wife and children, supply my servants, pay taxes to the king, make offerings to the gods, perform rites for my ancestors, and also give to śramaṇas and brahmins, so that afterward I may be born in heaven, attain long life, and obtain pleasant fruits of reward. Śāriputra, in all these matters there should be no doubt; they should single-mindedly accord with the Dharma."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, I will now question you; answer as you understand. Brahmin Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose a person, for the sake of his parents, commits evil deeds. Because of committing evil deeds, when his body perishes and his life ends, he goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. Having been born in hell, when the hell wardens seize him and inflict extreme painful treatment upon him, suppose he says to the hell wardens: 'Hell wardens, you should know, do not inflict painful treatment upon me. Why is this? I committed evil deeds for the sake of my parents.' What do you think, Dhānañjāni? Can that person be freed from this suffering by the hell wardens?"

He answered: "No."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose there is another person who, for the sake of his wife and children, commits evil deeds. Because of committing evil deeds, when his body perishes and his life ends, he goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. Having been born in hell, when the hell wardens seize him and inflict extreme painful treatment upon him, suppose he says to the hell wardens: 'Hell wardens, you should know, do not inflict painful treatment upon me. Why is this? I committed evil deeds for the sake of my wife and children.' What do you think, Dhānañjāni? Can that person be freed from this suffering by the hell wardens?"

He answered: "No."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose there is another person who, for the sake of his servants, commits evil deeds. Because of committing evil deeds, when his body perishes and his life ends, he goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. Having been born in hell, when the hell wardens seize him and inflict extreme painful treatment upon him, suppose he says to the hell wardens: 'Hell wardens, you should know, do not inflict painful treatment upon me. Why is this? I committed evil deeds for the sake of my servants.' What do you think, Dhānañjāni? Can that person be freed from this suffering by the hell wardens?"

He answered: "No."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Suppose there is another person who, for the sake of the king, for the sake of the gods, for the sake of his ancestors, and for the sake of śramaṇas and brahmins, commits evil deeds. Because of committing evil deeds, when his body perishes and his life ends, he goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. Having been born in hell, when the hell wardens seize him and inflict extreme painful treatment upon him, suppose he says to the hell wardens: 'Hell wardens, you should know, do not inflict painful treatment upon me. Why is this? I committed evil deeds for the sake of the king, for the sake of the gods, for the sake of my ancestors, and for the sake of śramaṇas and brahmins.' What do you think, Dhānañjāni? Can that person be freed from this suffering by the hell wardens?"

He answered: "No."

"Dhānañjāni, a clansman can obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and then respectfully, reverently, and filially support his parents, perform meritorious deeds, and not commit evil deeds. Dhānañjāni, if a clansman obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and respectfully, reverently, and filially supports his parents, performs meritorious deeds, and does not commit evil deeds, then his parents will cherish and love him, and they will say: 'May you be strong and healthy, and may your life be boundless. Why is this? Because of you, we live in comfort and happiness.' Dhānañjāni, if a person is greatly cherished and loved by his parents, his virtue will increase daily and never decline.

"Dhānañjāni, a clansman can obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and then lovingly care for his wife and children, provide for and look after them, perform meritorious deeds, and not commit evil deeds. Dhānañjāni, if a clansman obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and lovingly cares for his wife and children, provides for and looks after them, performs meritorious deeds, and does not commit evil deeds, then his wife and children will revere him and say: 'May our lord be strong and healthy, and may his life be boundless. Why is this? Because of our lord, we live in comfort and happiness.' Dhānañjāni, if a person is greatly revered by his wife and children, his virtue will increase daily and never decline.

"Dhānañjāni, a clansman can obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and then compassionately care for his servants, provide aid and look after them, perform meritorious deeds, and not commit evil deeds. Dhānañjāni, if a clansman obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and compassionately cares for his servants, provides aid and looks after them, performs meritorious deeds, and does not commit evil deeds, then his servants will revere him and say: 'May our master be strong and healthy, and may his life be boundless. Why is this? Because of our master, we obtain comfort.' Dhānañjāni, if a person is greatly revered by his servants, his virtue will increase daily and never decline.

"Dhānañjāni, a clansman can obtain wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and then respectfully make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, perform meritorious deeds, and not commit evil deeds. Dhānañjāni, if a clansman obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with proper livelihood, and in accordance with merit, and respectfully makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, performs meritorious deeds, and does not commit evil deeds, then the śramaṇas and brahmins will greatly cherish and love him, and they will say: 'May the benefactor be strong and healthy, and may his life be boundless. Why is this? Because of the benefactor, we obtain comfort and happiness.' Dhānañjāni, if a person is greatly cherished and loved by śramaṇas and brahmins, his virtue will increase daily and never decline."

Then the brahmin Dhānañjāni rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Śāriputra, and said: "Śāriputra, I have a beloved wife named Beautiful. Because I am infatuated with her, I have become heedless and committed great evil deeds. Śāriputra, from this day forward, I renounce the wife Beautiful and take refuge in the Venerable Śāriputra."

The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "Dhānañjāni, do not take refuge in me. The one in whom I take refuge, the Buddha, you should take refuge in him."

The brahmin Dhānañjāni said: "Venerable Śāriputra, from this day forward I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. I pray that the Venerable Śāriputra will accept me as a Buddhist upāsaka, taking refuge for the rest of my life, until the end of my days."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra taught the Dharma to the brahmin Dhānañjāni, exhorting and inspiring him, producing joy, and by countless skillful means taught the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him, producing joy. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed. He traveled in Rājagṛha, and after staying for several days, he gathered his robes and took his bowl, departed from Rājagṛha, and went to the Southern Mountains, staying in the Śiśapā Forest north of a village in the Southern Mountains.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu traveling in Rājagṛha who, after staying for several days, gathered his robes and took his bowl, departed from Rājagṛha, and also went to the Southern Mountains, staying in the Śiśapā Forest north of a village in the Southern Mountains.

Then that bhikṣu went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side.

The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Venerable one, where have you come from? Where have you been traveling?"

The bhikṣu answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, I have come from Rājagṛha, traveling in Rājagṛha."

He further asked: "Venerable one, do you know that in Rājagṛha there is a brahmin named Dhānañjāni, who was my friend before I left the household life?"

He answered: "I know him."

He further asked: "Venerable one, the brahmin Dhānañjāni dwelling in Rājagṛha, is his body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength as usual? Does he wish to see the Buddha frequently and delight in hearing the Dharma?"

He answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni wishes to see the Buddha frequently and wishes to hear the Dharma frequently, but he is not well, and his strength is declining. Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra, the brahmin Dhānañjāni is now seriously ill, extremely critical and in grave danger. He may die from this."

The Venerable Śāriputra, having heard these words, immediately gathered his robes and took his bowl, departed from the Southern Mountains, and went to Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden. Then the Venerable Śāriputra, after the night had passed, at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the home of the brahmin Dhānañjāni. The brahmin Dhānañjāni saw the Venerable Śāriputra coming from afar, and upon seeing him, he tried to rise from his bed. The Venerable Śāriputra, seeing the brahmin Dhānañjāni trying to rise from his bed, stopped him saying: "Brahmin Dhānañjāni, lie still and do not rise. There are other seats; I will sit separately."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra sat on a seat. Having sat, he asked: "Dhānañjāni, how is your illness now? Are you taking food? Is the pain of your illness diminishing and not increasing?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "My illness has reached an extreme. I cannot take food. The pain only increases and does not diminish at all. Venerable Śāriputra, just as if a strong man were to stab my head with a sharp knife, producing only extreme pain, so too is my headache. Venerable Śāriputra, just as if a strong man were to bind and wrap my head with a tight rope, producing only extreme pain, so too is my headache. Venerable Śāriputra, just as if a butcher's apprentice were to cut open a cow's belly with a sharp knife, producing only extreme pain, so too is my belly pain. Venerable Śāriputra, just as if two strong men were to seize a weak person and roast him over a fire, producing only extreme pain, so too is my bodily pain; my entire body produces suffering, which only increases and does not diminish."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, I will now question you; answer as you understand. Brahmin Dhānañjāni, what do you think? Between hell and the animal realm, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The animal realm is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the animal realm and the hungry ghost realm, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The hungry ghost realm is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, compared to humans, which is superior, hungry ghosts or humans?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "Humans are superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between humans and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Heaven of the Four Great Kings is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Heaven of the Thirty-Three is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and the Yāma Heaven, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Yāma Heaven is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Yāma Heaven and the Tuṣita Heaven, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Tuṣita Heaven is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Tuṣita Heaven and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Nirmāṇarati Heaven is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven is superior."

He further asked: "Dhānañjāni, between the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven and the Brahmā Heaven, which is superior?"

Dhānañjāni answered: "The Brahmā Heaven is the most superior! The Brahmā Heaven is the most superior!"

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Dhānañjāni, the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught four Brahmā dwellings. Clansmen and clanswomen who cultivate and frequently cultivate them, abandoning desire and relinquishing the thought of desire, when the body perishes and life ends, are born in the Brahmā Heaven. What are the four? Dhānañjāni, a well-learned noble disciple, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and dwelling in its accomplishment; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells in its accomplishment. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells in its accomplishment. These, Dhānañjāni, are what the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught as the four Brahmā dwellings. Clansmen and clanswomen who cultivate and frequently cultivate them, abandoning desire and relinquishing the thought of desire, when the body perishes and life ends, are born in the Brahmā Heaven."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having taught Dhānañjāni and expounded to him the teaching of the Brahmā Heaven, rose from his seat and departed. After the Venerable Śāriputra had left Rājagṛha, before he reached the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden, in that interval, the brahmin Dhānañjāni cultivated the four Brahmā dwellings, abandoned desire and relinquished the thought of desire, and when his body perished and his life ended, he was born in the Brahmā Heaven.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a countless great assembly, was teaching the Dharma. The World-Honored One saw the Venerable Śāriputra coming from afar and addressed the bhikṣus: "The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses keen wisdom, swift wisdom, quick wisdom, sharp wisdom, broad wisdom, deep wisdom, wisdom of the way of liberation, wisdom of clear understanding, and wisdom of eloquence. The bhikṣu Śāriputra has accomplished true wisdom. Yet this bhikṣu Śāriputra taught the brahmin Dhānañjāni only the Brahmā Heaven teaching. If he had taught him something higher, Dhānañjāni would have swiftly known the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra went to the Buddha, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, why did you not teach the brahmin Dhānañjāni beyond the Brahmā Heaven teaching? If you had taught him something higher, he would have swiftly known the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, those brahmins have for a long time loved and been attached to the Brahmā Heaven, delighted in the Brahmā Heaven, regarded the Brahmā Heaven as the ultimate, honored the Brahmā Heaven, affirmed the reality of the Brahmā Heaven, and considered the Brahmā Heaven as their own. Therefore, World-Honored One, I responded accordingly."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Śāriputra and the countless hundreds of thousands in the assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Brahmin Dhānañjāni Sūtra, the Seventh.

---

## (28) Sūtra on Teaching the Sick, Eighth in the Section Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was gravely and critically ill. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada told a messenger: "Go to the Buddha, and on my behalf bow your head in homage at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire after the World-Honored One, saying: 'Is the holy body of the World-Honored One well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength as usual?' Speak thus: 'The householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows at the Buddha's feet and inquires of the World-Honored One: "Is the holy body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and strength as usual?"' After you have inquired of the Buddha on my behalf, go to the Venerable Śāriputra, and on my behalf bow your head in homage at his feet, and inquire after the Venerable One, saying: 'Is the holy body of the Venerable One well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and his strength as usual?' Speak thus: 'The householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows at the Venerable Śāriputra's feet and inquires of the Venerable One: "Is the holy body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and strength as usual?" Venerable Śāriputra, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is extremely ill and in grave danger, critically so. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada wholeheartedly wishes to see the Venerable Śāriputra, but his body is extremely weak and frail, and he lacks the strength to come to the Venerable Śāriputra's presence. It would be excellent, Venerable Śāriputra, out of compassion, if you would come to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.'"

Then the messenger, having received the instructions of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at his feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows at the Buddha's feet and inquires of the World-Honored One: 'Is the holy body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and strength as usual?'"

At that time, the World-Honored One told the messenger: "May the householder Anāthapiṇḍada be at ease and happy. May the gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all various kinds of beings be at ease and happy."

Then the messenger, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed his head at his feet, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows at the Venerable Śāriputra's feet and inquires of the Venerable One: 'Is the holy body well and strong, comfortable and free from illness, rising and moving with ease, and strength as usual?' Venerable Śāriputra, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada is extremely ill and in grave danger, critically so. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada wholeheartedly wishes to see the Venerable Śāriputra, but his body is extremely weak and frail, and he lacks the strength to come to the Venerable Śāriputra's presence. It would be excellent, Venerable Śāriputra, out of compassion, if you would go to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada."

The Venerable Śāriputra, for his sake, silently consented. The messenger, knowing the Venerable Śāriputra had silently consented, immediately rose from his seat, bowed in homage, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

The Venerable Śāriputra, after the night had passed, at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the Venerable Śāriputra coming from afar, and upon seeing him, he tried to rise from his bed.

The Venerable Śāriputra, seeing the householder trying to rise from his bed, stopped him saying: "Householder, do not rise! Householder, do not rise! There are other seats; I will sit separately."

The Venerable Śāriputra sat on a seat. Having sat, he asked: "Householder, how is your illness now? Are you taking food? Is the pain of your illness diminishing and not increasing?"

The householder answered: "My illness has reached an extreme. I cannot take food. The pain only increases and does not diminish at all."

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, endowed with lack of faith, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder today has no lack of faith; he has only supreme faith. Because of the householder's supreme faith, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of supreme faith, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of evil conduct, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no evil conduct; he has only good conduct. Because of the householder's good conduct, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of good conduct, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of not having learned much, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder is not one who has not learned much; he has only much learning. Because of the householder's much learning, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of much learning, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of miserliness and greed, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no miserliness or greed; he has only generosity. Because of the householder's generosity, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of generosity, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of bad wisdom, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no bad wisdom; he has only good wisdom. Because of the householder's good wisdom, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of good wisdom, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of wrong view, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no wrong view; he has only right view. Because of the householder's right view, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of right view, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of wrong intention, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no wrong intention; he has only right intention. Because of the householder's right intention, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of right intention, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of wrong liberation, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no wrong liberation; he has only right liberation. Because of the householder's right liberation, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of right liberation, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of wrong deliverance, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no wrong deliverance; he has only right deliverance. Because of the householder's right deliverance, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of right deliverance, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry.

"Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? If a foolish ordinary person, because of wrong knowledge, when his body perishes and his life ends, goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. But the householder has no wrong knowledge; he has only right knowledge. Because of the householder's right knowledge, either the painful suffering will be extinguished and extreme happiness will arise, or because of right knowledge, the fruit of a once-returner may be attained, or the fruit of a non-returner. The householder has already attained the fruit of stream-entry."

Then the householder's illness was immediately healed and he recovered as before. He sat up from lying down and praised the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Teaching the Dharma for the sick! How wonderful! How remarkable! Venerable Śāriputra, upon hearing this teaching of the Dharma for the sick, my painful suffering was immediately extinguished and extreme happiness arose. Venerable Śāriputra, my illness is now healed and I have recovered as before. Venerable Śāriputra, once in the past, I had some business that took me to Rājagṛha, and I lodged at a householder's home. At that time, that householder was to feed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus the next morning. That householder, as the night was turning toward dawn, instructed his sons, grandsons, servants, and family members: 'All of you, rise early and together prepare everything.' Each of them received the instructions and together set up the kitchen, preparing various fine and delicious foods, and the householder personally arranged a lofty seat with immeasurable adornments.

"Venerable Śāriputra, when I saw this, I thought: 'Is this householder preparing for a wedding, a bride's reception, a festival gathering, inviting the king, summoning great ministers, or holding a vegetarian feast and making a great offering?' Venerable Śāriputra, having thought this, I asked the householder: 'Are you preparing for a wedding, a bride's reception, a festival gathering, inviting the king, summoning great ministers, or holding a vegetarian feast and making a great offering?' At that time, the householder answered me, saying: 'I have no wedding, nor am I receiving a bride, nor is this a festival gathering. I am not inviting the king or summoning great ministers. It is a vegetarian feast with a great offering; tomorrow I shall feed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.'

"Venerable Śāriputra, I had never heard the name 'Buddha' before. Upon hearing it, the hair on my entire body stood on end. I then asked: 'Householder, you speak of the Buddha; what is meant by "Buddha"?' At that time, the householder answered me, saying: 'Sir, have you not heard? There is a son of the Śākya clan who left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith left the household life to be homeless and train in the Way. He attained unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. He is called "Buddha."' I then asked: 'Householder, you speak of the Sangha; what is meant by "Sangha"?' At that time, the householder answered me again, saying: 'There are those of various surnames, various names, and various clans who have shaved off their hair and beards, put on the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith left the household life to be homeless, studying the Way under the Buddha. This is called the "Sangha." It is this Buddha and this Sangha whom I have invited.' Venerable Śāriputra, I then asked that householder: 'Where is the World-Honored One now? I wish to go and see him.' At that time, the householder answered me again, saying: 'The World-Honored One is now in this city of Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden. If you wish to go, you may do so as you please.'

"Venerable Śāriputra, I then thought: 'If only dawn would come quickly, so I could hasten to see the Buddha.' Venerable Śāriputra, at that time, with my mind intent on going to see the Buddha, during that very night a perception of daylight arose. I then left the householder's home and went toward the city's resting gate. At that time, there were two watchmen at the city's resting gate: one guarded the first watch of the night, allowing visiting travelers and messengers to enter without obstruction; the other guarded the last watch of the night, and if travelers or messengers wished to leave, they likewise were not obstructed. Venerable Śāriputra, I then thought: 'It is not yet dawn.' Why is this? Because at the city's resting gate there were two watchmen: one guarded the first watch, allowing visiting travelers and messengers to enter without obstruction; the other guarded the last watch, and travelers or messengers leaving were likewise not obstructed. Venerable Śāriputra, after passing through the city's resting gate, not long after going outside, the light vanished and it became dark again. Venerable Śāriputra, I became frightened, and the hair on my entire body stood on end. I feared that some human or non-human might come to trouble and harm me.

"At that time, a deva at the city's resting gate, from Rājagṛha all the way to the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden, radiated light everywhere and came and spoke to me, saying: 'Householder, do not be afraid! Householder, do not be afraid! Why is this? In a previous life I was your friend, named Mitsuki, and as a young man I was extremely fond of you. Householder, once in the past, I went to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, bowed my head at his feet, and sat to one side. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana taught me the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring me, producing joy, and by countless skillful means taught me the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring me, producing joy, and then bestowed upon me the three refuges and conferred the five precepts. Householder, because of the three refuges and upholding the five precepts, when my body perished and my life ended, I was born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and now dwell at this city's resting gate. Householder, go quickly! Householder, go quickly! Going is truly better than staying.' That deva encouraged me and spoke this verse:

"'A hundred horses, a hundred ministers' daughters,
A hundred chariots filled with treasures:
Going one step toward the Buddha
Is not worth a sixteenth part thereof.
A hundred white elephants, the finest,
With saddles and bridles of gold and silver:
Going one step toward the Buddha
Is not worth a sixteenth part thereof.
A hundred women of beautiful appearance,
Adorned with garlands and ornaments:
Going one step toward the Buddha
Is not worth a sixteenth part thereof.
Revered by a wheel-turning king,
The jewel-woman foremost:
Going one step toward the Buddha
Is not worth a sixteenth part thereof.'

"After the deva spoke this verse, he further encouraged me: 'Householder, go quickly! Householder, go quickly! Going is truly better than staying.' Venerable Śāriputra, I then thought: 'The Buddha is honored and blessed with virtue, and the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus are also honored and blessed with virtue. Why is this? Even the devas wish to cause beings to see him.'

"Venerable Śāriputra, relying on this light, I went to the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden. At that time, the World-Honored One, as the night was turning toward dawn, had come out of his meditation chamber and was walking in the open air, waiting for me. Venerable Śāriputra, from afar I saw the Buddha, upright and beautiful, like the moon among the stars, radiant and brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, replete with the marks, of majestic and imposing spiritual power, with sense faculties calm and settled, without any obstruction, accomplished in self-mastery, with a mind stilled and serene. Having seen him, I was overjoyed. I went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and walking alongside the Buddha, spoke a verse of greeting in the manner of a householder:

"'Did the World-Honored One sleep in peace?
Was the sleep throughout the night pleasant?
Like a brahmin who has attained cessation,
Having no attachment to desires,
Having abandoned all aspirations,
Having reached ultimate peace,
With a mind free of fever and torment,
Joyful at heart, sleeping in happiness.'

"Then the World-Honored One went to the end of the walking path, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat in the cross-legged posture. Venerable Śāriputra, I bowed at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The World-Honored One taught me the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring me, producing joy, and by countless skillful means taught me the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring me, producing joy. As is the way of all Buddhas, he first taught the upright Dharma that delights those who hear it, namely: teaching about generosity, teaching about morality, teaching about being born in heaven, deprecating desires as calamitous, declaring the cycle of birth and death to be defilement, and praising desirelessness as the wondrous Way and the pure and white factors of the path. After the World-Honored One had taught me such Dharma, the Buddha knew that my mind was joyful, ready, soft, capable, elevated, one-pointed, free of doubt, free of hindrances, and possessed of the capacity and power to receive the true Dharma. Then, as all Buddhas teach the essential and true teaching, the World-Honored One immediately taught me suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Venerable Śāriputra, right there on my seat I saw the four noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, just as a white cloth is easily dyed with color; so too did I, right there on my seat, see the four noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

"Venerable Śāriputra, having seen the Dharma, obtained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, cut off doubt and crossed over perplexity, with no other teacher to follow, no longer dependent on another, without any hesitation, having established myself in the fruit and its realization, having attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma, I immediately rose from my seat, bowed to the Buddha, and said: 'World-Honored One, from this day I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. I pray that the World-Honored One will accept me as an upāsaka, taking refuge from this day forward for the rest of my life, until the end of my days.' Venerable Śāriputra, I then joined my palms and said: 'World-Honored One, please accept my invitation to undertake the summer retreat in the country of Śrāvastī, together with the community of bhikṣus.' At that time, the Buddha asked me: 'What is your name? What do the people of the country of Śrāvastī call you?' I answered: 'My name is Sudatta. Because I provide for all those who are destitute, the people of the country of Śrāvastī call me Anāthapiṇḍada.' At that time, the World-Honored One further asked me: 'Are there dwellings in the country of Śrāvastī?' I again answered: 'There are no dwellings in the country of Śrāvastī.' At that time, the World-Honored One told me: 'Householder, you should know that if there are dwellings, the bhikṣus can come and go, and can stay and abide.' I again said: 'Just so, World-Honored One. I shall accordingly build dwellings, so that the bhikṣus can come and go, and can stay and abide in the country of Śrāvastī. I pray that the World-Honored One will assign someone to assist me.' At that time, the World-Honored One immediately assigned the Venerable Śāriputra, dispatching the Venerable Śāriputra to provide assistance.

"At that time, having heard what the Buddha said and received and retained it well, I immediately rose from my seat, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed. After completing my affairs in Rājagṛha, I traveled together with the Venerable Śāriputra to the country of Śrāvastī. Without entering the city of Śrāvastī or going home, right outside the city I walked around examining the land, looking for a place that was most suitable for coming and going, quiet during the day and peaceful at night, without mosquitoes or gnats, without flies or fleas, neither too cold nor too hot, where dwellings could be built as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha. Venerable Śāriputra, at that time I saw only the grove of Prince Jeta as most suitable for coming and going, quiet during the day and peaceful at night, without mosquitoes or gnats, without flies or fleas, neither too cold nor too hot. Having seen this, I thought: 'Only this place is suitable; here dwellings can be built as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha.'

"Venerable Śāriputra, at that time I entered the city of Śrāvastī but did not return home. Instead, I first went to Prince Jeta and said: 'Prince, will you sell this grove to me?' At that time, the prince said to me: 'Householder, you should know, I will not sell the grove.' Thus I asked three times: 'Prince, will you sell this grove to me?' At that time, the prince also replied three times: 'I will not sell the grove; not unless hundreds of millions of gold coins are spread to cover it entirely.' I then said: 'Prince, you have now fixed the price; you need only accept the payment.' Venerable Śāriputra, the prince and I disputed, one saying the price was fixed, the other saying it was not. We argued greatly and then went together to the great adjudicator of the country of Śrāvastī to have the matter decided. At that time, the great adjudicator of the country of Śrāvastī told Prince Jeta: 'Prince, you yourself fixed the price; you need only accept the payment.'

"Venerable Śāriputra, I then entered the city of Śrāvastī, returned home, and brought out money. By elephants, horses, and carts, carrying and transporting it, I brought out hundreds of millions and spread them on the ground. A small area was not yet covered. Venerable Śāriputra, I thought: 'From which treasury, neither too large nor too small, shall I bring more to cover this remaining area?' At that time, Prince Jeta said to me: 'Householder, if you regret it, take back your money and return the grove land to me.' I said to the prince: 'I truly have no regret. I am only pondering: from which treasury, neither too large nor too small, shall I bring more to fill this remaining area?' At that time, Prince Jeta thought: 'The Buddha must be greatly honored and possessed of great virtue and blessings, and the Dharma and the community of bh

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Discourses)
## Fascicle 7

---

### (30) Sūtra on the Elephant's Footprint Simile

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will now teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, the purified holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Just as among all the footprints of living beings, the elephant's footprint is the greatest, able to contain all of them; in the same way, among all good dharmas, the Four Noble Truths encompass and contain all good dharmas. What are the four? The Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? It is: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with those one dislikes is suffering, separation from those one loves is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

"What is 'birth is suffering'? For each class of beings, in their respective category, being born, coming into existence, entering a womb, being generated, the arising of the aggregates, obtaining the sense-bases: this is called birth. The suffering and distress associated with such birth, this is called 'birth is suffering.'

"What is 'aging is suffering'? For each class of beings, in their respective category, aging, the teeth falling out, the hair turning white, the skin becoming wrinkled, the decline of the life span, the decay of the faculties: this is called aging. The suffering and distress associated with such aging, this is called 'aging is suffering.'

"What is 'illness is suffering'? Headache, eye pain, ear pain, nose pain, face pain, lip pain, tooth pain, tongue pain, throat pain, wind conditions, disorders of the bile, phlegm conditions, joint pains, and the assemblage of many illnesses: this is called illness. The suffering and distress associated with such illness, this is called 'illness is suffering.'

"What is 'death is suffering'? For each class of beings, in their respective category, perishing, passing away, dissolution, the dispersal of the aggregates, the end of life, the cessation of life, the expiration of the life span: this is called death. The suffering and distress associated with such death, this is called 'death is suffering.'

"What is 'association with those one dislikes is suffering'? There are unpleasant forms, unpleasant sounds, unpleasant smells, unpleasant tastes, unpleasant tangible objects, and unpleasant mind-objects. Or there are those who desire one's misfortune, desire one's loss, desire one's discomfort, desire one's non-peace, and one encounters, meets, gathers with, and associates with them. This is called 'association with those one dislikes is suffering.'

"What is 'separation from those one loves is suffering'? There are pleasant forms, pleasant sounds, pleasant smells, pleasant tastes, pleasant tangible objects, and pleasant mind-objects. Or there are those who desire one's fortune, desire one's benefit, desire one's comfort, desire one's peace, such as father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, relatives, and friends, and one becomes separated from them, unable to meet, unable to gather with, unable to associate with. This is called 'separation from those one loves is suffering.'

"What is 'not obtaining what one seeks is suffering'? Beings subject to the nature of birth wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to birth!' But this cannot be obtained by wishing. Beings subject to the nature of aging wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to aging!' Beings subject to the nature of illness wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to illness!' Beings subject to the nature of death wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to death!' Beings subject to suffering and distress wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to suffering and distress!' But this cannot be obtained by wishing. This is called 'not obtaining what one seeks is suffering.'

"What are 'the five aggregates of clinging are suffering'? The aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. This is called 'the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.'

"What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This craving, when it arises, where does it arise? When it settles, where does it settle? In the world, whatever is lovely and pleasing, there this craving arises and there it settles. What in the world is lovely and pleasing? The eye in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, perception of tangible objects, and perception of mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Intention regarding forms, intention regarding sounds, intention regarding smells, intention regarding tastes, intention regarding tangible objects, and intention regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Directed thought regarding forms, directed thought regarding sounds, directed thought regarding smells, directed thought regarding tastes, directed thought regarding tangible objects, and directed thought regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles.

"Sustained thought regarding forms, sustained thought regarding sounds, sustained thought regarding smells, sustained thought regarding tastes, sustained thought regarding tangible objects, and sustained thought regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. This is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of this very craving, its abandonment, its relinquishment, liberation from it, and detachment from it. This craving, when it ceases, where does it cease? When it is abandoned, where is it abandoned? In the world, whatever is lovely and pleasing, there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. What in the world is lovely and pleasing? The eye in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, perception of tangible objects, and perception of mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Intention regarding forms, intention regarding sounds, intention regarding smells, intention regarding tastes, intention regarding tangible objects, and intention regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Directed thought regarding forms, directed thought regarding sounds, directed thought regarding smells, directed thought regarding tastes, directed thought regarding tangible objects, and directed thought regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned.

"Sustained thought regarding forms, sustained thought regarding sounds, sustained thought regarding smells, sustained thought regarding tastes, sustained thought regarding tangible objects, and sustained thought regarding mind-objects in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"What is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called right view.

"What is right intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill-will, and intention of non-cruelty. This is called right intention.

"What is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. This is called right speech.

"What is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. This is called right action.

"What is right livelihood? A noble disciple abandons wrong livelihood and sustains life by right livelihood. This is called right livelihood.

"What is right effort? A bhikṣu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, fullness, development, and completion of arisen wholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. This is called right effort.

"What is right mindfulness? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. Contemplates the body as body externally. Contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. In the same way, contemplates feelings as feelings, contemplates mind as mind, and contemplates dharmas as dharmas internally, externally, and both internally and externally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. This is called right mindfulness.

"What is right concentration? A bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with directed thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of directed thought and sustained thought, with internal confidence and unification of mind, without directed thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and abides in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, abiding in equanimity, with mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, abiding in happiness,' enters and abides in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the earlier disappearance of joy and sorrow, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna. This is called right concentration.

"This is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (31) Sūtra on Discrimination of the Noble Truths

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are Four Noble Truths. What are the four? The first is the Noble Truth of Suffering, the second is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the third is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the fourth is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

"These Four Noble Truths are real, not false, not different from what they are. They are truly discovered by the Tathāgata, and therefore they are called Noble Truths. Throughout the world, with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, among beings including ascetics, brahmins, gods, and humans, the Tathāgata is the supreme one, and therefore they are called Noble Truths.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that these Four Noble Truths encompass all good dharmas. Just as among all the footprints of living beings, the elephant's footprint is the greatest, able to contain all of them; in the same way, these Four Noble Truths encompass and contain all good dharmas.

"What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?

"Birth is suffering. What is birth? For each class of beings, in their respective category, being born, coming into existence, entering a womb, being generated, the arising of the aggregates, obtaining the sense-bases: this is called birth. This birth, when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Aging is suffering. What is aging? For each class of beings, in their respective category, aging, the teeth falling out, the hair turning white, the skin becoming wrinkled, the decline of the life span, the decay of the faculties: this is called aging. This aging, when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Illness is suffering. What is illness? Headache, eye pain, ear pain, nose pain, face pain, lip pain, tooth pain, tongue pain, throat pain, wind conditions, bile disorders, phlegm conditions, joint pains, and the assemblage of many illnesses: this is called illness. This illness, when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Death is suffering. What is death? For each class of beings, in their respective category, perishing, passing away, dissolution, the dispersal of the aggregates, the end of life, the cessation of life, the expiration of the life span: this is called death. This death, when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Association with those one dislikes is suffering. What is 'association with those one dislikes'? There are unpleasant forms, unpleasant sounds, unpleasant smells, unpleasant tastes, unpleasant tangible objects, and unpleasant mind-objects. Or there are those who desire one's misfortune, desire one's loss, desire one's discomfort, desire one's non-peace, and one encounters, meets, gathers with, and associates with them. This is called 'association with those one dislikes.' This 'association with those one dislikes,' when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Separation from those one loves is suffering. What is 'separation from those one loves'? There are pleasant forms, pleasant sounds, pleasant smells, pleasant tastes, pleasant tangible objects, and pleasant mind-objects. Or there are those who desire one's fortune, desire one's benefit, desire one's comfort, desire one's peace, such as father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, relatives, and friends, and one becomes separated from them, unable to meet, unable to gather with, unable to associate with. This is called 'separation from those one loves.' This 'separation from those one loves,' when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"Not obtaining what one seeks is suffering. What is 'not obtaining what one seeks'? Beings subject to the nature of birth wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to birth!' But this cannot be obtained by wishing. Beings subject to the nature of aging wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to aging!' Beings subject to the nature of illness wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to illness!' Beings subject to the nature of death wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to death!' Beings subject to suffering and distress wish: 'Oh, may I not be subject to suffering and distress!' But this cannot be obtained by wishing. This is called 'not obtaining what one seeks.' This 'not obtaining what one seeks,' when it arises, suffering arises; when it is generated, suffering is generated; when it appears, suffering appears; when it occurs, suffering occurs.

"In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. What are the five aggregates of clinging? The aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. These are called the five aggregates of clinging. These five aggregates of clinging, when they arise, suffering arises; when they are generated, suffering is generated; when they appear, suffering appears; when they occur, suffering occur. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is this craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there. That is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

"This craving, when it arises, where does it arise? When it settles, where does it settle? In the world, whatever is lovely and pleasing, there this craving arises and there it settles. What in the world is lovely and pleasing?

"The eye in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise.

"Forms in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mind-objects are likewise.

"Eye-consciousness in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are likewise.

"Eye-contact in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are likewise.

"Feeling born of eye-contact in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact are likewise.

"Perception of forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, perception of tangible objects, and perception of mind-objects are likewise.

"Intention regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Intention regarding sounds, intention regarding smells, intention regarding tastes, intention regarding tangible objects, and intention regarding mind-objects are likewise.

"Craving for forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mind-objects are likewise.

"Directed thought regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Directed thought regarding sounds, directed thought regarding smells, directed thought regarding tastes, directed thought regarding tangible objects, and directed thought regarding mind-objects are likewise.

"Sustained thought regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving arises and there it settles. Sustained thought regarding sounds, sustained thought regarding smells, sustained thought regarding tastes, sustained thought regarding tangible objects, and sustained thought regarding mind-objects are likewise. This is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of this very craving, its abandonment, its relinquishment, liberation from it, and detachment from it.

"This craving, when it ceases, where does it cease? When it is abandoned, where is it abandoned? In the world, whatever is lovely and pleasing, there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. What in the world is lovely and pleasing?

"The eye in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise.

"Forms in the world are lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mind-objects are likewise.

"Eye-consciousness in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are likewise.

"Eye-contact in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are likewise.

"Feeling born of eye-contact in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact are likewise.

"Perception of forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, perception of tangible objects, and perception of mind-objects are likewise.

"Intention regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Intention regarding sounds, intention regarding smells, intention regarding tastes, intention regarding tangible objects, and intention regarding mind-objects are likewise.

"Craving for forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mind-objects are likewise.

"Directed thought regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Directed thought regarding sounds, directed thought regarding smells, directed thought regarding tastes, directed thought regarding tangible objects, and directed thought regarding mind-objects are likewise.

"Sustained thought regarding forms in the world is lovely and pleasing; there this craving ceases and there it is abandoned. Sustained thought regarding sounds, sustained thought regarding smells, sustained thought regarding tastes, sustained thought regarding tangible objects, and sustained thought regarding mind-objects are likewise. This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.

"What is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"What is right view? Right view is of two kinds. There is right view that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging. There is right view that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right view that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging? It is the view: 'There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there are the fruits and results of good and evil actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously born beings; there are in this world ascetics and brahmins who have rightly gone, rightly practiced, who having realized this world and the other world through their own direct knowledge, make it known to others.' This is called right view that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging.

"What is right view that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path? It is the noble disciple who, with the noble mind, the mind without outflows, the noble path-mind, cultivates the noble path. The wisdom, faculty of wisdom, power of wisdom, investigation of dharmas, right view that is the factor of the path of the awakening factor of investigation of dharmas, this is called right view that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right intention? Right intention is also of two kinds. There is right intention that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging. There is right intention that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right intention that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging? It is the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill-will, and the intention of non-cruelty. This is called right intention that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging.

"What is right intention that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path? It is the noble disciple who, with the noble mind, the mind without outflows, the noble path-mind, cultivates the noble path. The thinking, the examining, the directing, the intention, the complete intention, the aim of the mind, the verbal formation, this is called right intention that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right speech? Right speech is also of two kinds. There is right speech that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging. There is right speech that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right speech that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging? It is abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. This is called right speech that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging.

"What is right speech that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path? It is the noble disciple who, with the noble mind, the mind without outflows, the noble path-mind, cultivates the noble path, and with regard to the four kinds of verbal misconduct, the abstaining, refraining, not doing, not creating, guarding against transgression, not violating: this is called right speech that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right action? Right action is also of two kinds. There is right action that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging. There is right action that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right action that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging? It is abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, and abstaining from sexual misconduct. This is called right action that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging.

"What is right action that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path? It is the noble disciple who, with the noble mind, the mind without outflows, the noble path-mind, cultivates the noble path, and with regard to the three kinds of bodily misconduct, the abstaining, refraining, not doing, not creating, guarding against transgression, not violating: this is called right action that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right livelihood? Right livelihood is also of two kinds. There is right livelihood that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging. There is right livelihood that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right livelihood that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging? A noble disciple abandons wrong livelihood and sustains life by right livelihood. This is called right livelihood that has outflows, has merit, and results in the fruition of clinging.

"What is right livelihood that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path? It is the noble disciple who, with the noble mind, the mind without outflows, the noble path-mind, cultivates the noble path, and with regard to the wrongness of livelihood, the abstaining, refraining, not doing, not creating, guarding against transgression, not violating: this is called right livelihood that is noble, without outflows, supramundane, and a factor of the path.

"What is right effort? A bhikṣu generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. Generates desire for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, fullness, development, and completion of arisen wholesome dharmas, makes effort, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives. This is called right effort.

"What is right mindfulness? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. Contemplates the body as body externally. Contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. In the same way, contemplates feelings as feelings, contemplates mind as mind, and contemplates dharmas as dharmas internally, externally, and both internally and externally, with diligence, right knowledge, and right mindfulness, overcoming desire and sorrow with regard to the world. This is called right mindfulness.

"What is right concentration? A bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with directed thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of directed thought and sustained thought, with internal confidence and unification of mind, without directed thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and abides in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, abiding in equanimity, with mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, abiding in happiness,' enters and abides in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the earlier disappearance of joy and sorrow, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna. This is called right concentration.

"This is called the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (32) Sūtra on the Parable of the Uninstructed

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The uninstructed ordinary person might become disenchanted with this body composed of the four great elements, might become dispassionate toward it, and might be liberated from it. Why is this? The growth and decline of this body composed of the four great elements can be seen: it is taken up and set aside. Therefore, the uninstructed ordinary person might become disenchanted with it, might become dispassionate toward it, and might be liberated from it.

"However, that which is called 'mind,' or 'intention,' or 'consciousness,' the uninstructed ordinary person is unable to become disenchanted with it, unable to become dispassionate toward it, unable to be liberated from it. Why is this? For a long time, the uninstructed ordinary person has embraced it, clung to it, and held it firmly, thinking: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.' Therefore, the uninstructed ordinary person is unable to become disenchanted with it, unable to become dispassionate toward it, unable to be liberated from it.

"Bhikṣus, it would be better for the uninstructed ordinary person to regard this body composed of the four great elements as self, rather than the mind. Why is this? This body composed of the four great elements may last for one year, may last for two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred years, or longer. But that which is called 'mind,' or 'intention,' or 'consciousness,' arises as one thing and ceases as another, day and night, without ceasing. Just as a monkey roaming through a forest grabs one branch, then releases it and grabs another, then releases that and grabs another, so too that which is called 'mind,' or 'intention,' or 'consciousness,' arises as one thing and ceases as another, day and night, without ceasing.

"In this regard, the instructed noble disciple well and carefully reflects on dependent origination: 'When this exists, that comes to be. With the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be. With the cessation of this, that ceases.' That is: conditioned by ignorance, there are formations. Conditioned by formations, there is consciousness. Conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form. Conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense-bases. Conditioned by the six sense-bases, there is contact. Conditioned by contact, there is feeling. Conditioned by feeling, there is craving. Conditioned by craving, there is clinging. Conditioned by clinging, there is existence. Conditioned by existence, there is birth. Conditioned by birth, there are aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. Thus, there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"If ignorance ceases without remainder, then formations cease. If formations cease, then consciousness ceases. If consciousness ceases, then name-and-form ceases. If name-and-form ceases, then the six sense-bases cease. If the six sense-bases cease, then contact ceases. If contact ceases, then feeling ceases. If feeling ceases, then craving ceases. If craving ceases, then clinging ceases. If clinging ceases, then existence ceases. If existence ceases, then birth ceases. If birth ceases, then aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease. Thus, there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
