"Bhikṣus, having seen this, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with perception, becomes disenchanted with formations, becomes disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Being liberated, there is knowledge: 'Liberation is achieved.' One knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (33) Sūtra on the Parable of the Foam

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Ayodhyā, on the bank of the Ganges River.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "It is just as if, on this Ganges River, a great mass of foam were floating along. A person with clear eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one would find it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in a mass of foam? In the same way, bhikṣus, whatever forms there are, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikṣu observes them, examines them, and analyzes them carefully. Observing them, examining them, and analyzing them carefully, one finds them to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in form?

"Bhikṣus, it is just as when rain is falling and a water bubble appears on the water, arising and quickly bursting. A person with clear eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one would find it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in a water bubble? In the same way, bhikṣus, whatever feelings there are, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikṣu observes them, examines them, and analyzes them carefully. Observing them, examining them, and analyzing them carefully, one finds them to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in feeling?

"Bhikṣus, it is just as in the last month of spring, in the middle of the day when it is hot, a shimmering mirage appears. A person with clear eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one would find it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in a mirage? In the same way, bhikṣus, whatever perceptions there are, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikṣu observes them, examines them, and analyzes them carefully. Observing them, examining them, and analyzing them carefully, one finds them to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in perception?

"Bhikṣus, it is just as if a person needing heartwood were to take a sharp axe and go into the forest. There one sees a great plantain tree, tall and straight, young and without a knot. One cuts it down at the root, chops off the top, and peels away the outer layers. Peeling away the outer layers, one would not even find sapwood, let alone heartwood. A person with clear eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one would find it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in a plantain tree? In the same way, bhikṣus, whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikṣu observes them, examines them, and analyzes them carefully. Observing them, examining them, and analyzing them carefully, one finds them to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in formations?

"Bhikṣus, it is just as if a magician or a magician's apprentice were to display a magical illusion at a crossroads. A person with clear eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one would find it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in a magical illusion? In the same way, bhikṣus, whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, a bhikṣu observes it, examines it, and analyzes it carefully. Observing it, examining it, and analyzing it carefully, one finds it to be empty, to be hollow, to be without substance. How could there be any substance in consciousness?

"Bhikṣus, having seen this, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with perception, becomes disenchanted with formations, becomes disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Being liberated, there is knowledge: 'Liberation is achieved.' One knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"Form is like a mass of foam,
Feeling like a water bubble,
Perception like a mirage,
Formations like a plantain tree,
Consciousness like a magical illusion:
So taught the Kinsman of the Sun.

"However one observes them,
However one carefully examines them,
They are empty, they are hollow,
When one sees them with right wisdom.

"Regarding this body as taught
By the One of Broad Wisdom:
When three things are abandoned,
One sees that form is cast off.

"Life-warmth and consciousness:
When these three dharmas leave the body,
Then the body lies discarded,
Cast aside, without feeling, like a log."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (34) Sūtra on Bhadra

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Bhadra went to where the Buddha was, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhadra said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, they speak of 'an evil person, an evil person.' World-Honored One, what is an evil person?"

The Buddha addressed Bhadra: "Good, good! Bhadra, it is good that you can ask the Tathāgata about this meaning. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The Venerable Bhadra received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Bhadra, if a person has wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration, this is called an evil person.

"Bhadra, they speak of 'a very evil person, a very evil person.' What is a very evil person? If a person himself has wrong view and also encourages others to have wrong view, himself has wrong intention and also encourages others to have wrong intention, himself has wrong speech and also encourages others to have wrong speech, himself has wrong action and also encourages others to have wrong action, himself has wrong livelihood and also encourages others to have wrong livelihood, himself has wrong effort and also encourages others to have wrong effort, himself has wrong mindfulness and also encourages others to have wrong mindfulness, himself has wrong concentration and also encourages others to have wrong concentration, this is called a very evil person.

"Bhadra, they speak of 'a good person, a good person.' What is a good person? If a person has right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, this is called a good person.

"Bhadra, they speak of 'a very good person, a very good person.' What is a very good person? If a person himself has right view and also encourages others to have right view, himself has right intention and also encourages others to have right intention, himself has right speech and also encourages others to have right speech, himself has right action and also encourages others to have right action, himself has right livelihood and also encourages others to have right livelihood, himself has right effort and also encourages others to have right effort, himself has right mindfulness and also encourages others to have right mindfulness, himself has right concentration and also encourages others to have right concentration, this is called a very good person."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Bhadra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (35) Sūtra on Asura

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at Kalandaka's Park.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, in the morning, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. At that time, he thought: "It is still too early to enter Rājagṛha to beg for food. Let me go to the park of the non-Buddhist wanderers."

Then that bhikṣu went to the park of the non-Buddhist wanderers. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the non-Buddhist wanderers, and after exchanging greetings and courteous words, he sat to one side. At that time, the non-Buddhist wanderers said to this bhikṣu: "Friend, the ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma to his disciples thus: 'Bhikṣus, you should abandon all dharmas, you should thoroughly understand all dharmas.' Friend, we also teach the Dharma to our disciples thus: 'You should abandon all dharmas, you should thoroughly understand all dharmas.' Friend, in what way are there any differences between the ascetic Gautama and us? What difference in Dharma teaching, what difference in instruction? Both teach the same Dharma."

At that time, that bhikṣu, hearing the words of the non-Buddhist wanderers, neither approved nor reproached them. Neither approving nor reproaching them, he rose from his seat and left, thinking: "I should understand the meaning of these words in the presence of the World-Honored One."

Then that bhikṣu, having begged for food in Rājagṛha, after his meal, put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and went to where the Buddha was. He paid homage at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikṣu told the Buddha everything that had happened, and said: "World-Honored One, when the non-Buddhist wanderers spoke thus, how should one answer them? How should one explain the Dharma? How can I not misrepresent the World-Honored One? How can I explain in accord with the Dharma, so that fellow practitioners of the Dharma will not criticize me?"

The Buddha addressed that bhikṣu: "If the non-Buddhist wanderers speak thus, you should ask them: 'Friends, what is the root of all dharmas? What is the origin of all dharmas? What is the arising of all dharmas? What is the convergence of all dharmas? What is the forerunner of all dharmas? What is the master of all dharmas? What is the supreme of all dharmas? What is the essential meaning of all dharmas? What is the culmination of all dharmas? What is the final conclusion of all dharmas?'

"When the non-Buddhist wanderers are asked this, they will not be able to answer; moreover, they will be perplexed. Why is this? Because it is outside their domain.

"Bhikṣus, I do not see anyone in this world, with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, among beings including ascetics, brahmins, gods, and humans, who could answer these questions to satisfy the mind, except for the Tathāgata, a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.

"Bhikṣus, 'What is the root of all dharmas?' If one is asked thus, one should answer: 'Desire is the root of all dharmas.'

"'What is the origin of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Contact is the origin of all dharmas.'

"'What is the arising of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Feeling is the arising of all dharmas.'

"'What is the convergence of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Concentration is the convergence of all dharmas.'

"'What is the forerunner of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Mindfulness is the forerunner of all dharmas.'

"'What is the master of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Wisdom is the master of all dharmas.'

"'What is the supreme of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Liberation is the supreme of all dharmas.'

"'What is the essential meaning of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'Nirvāṇa is the essential meaning of all dharmas.'

"'What is the culmination of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'The deathless is the culmination of all dharmas.'

"'What is the final conclusion of all dharmas?' One should answer: 'The deathless is the final conclusion of all dharmas.'

"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train thus: We will understand desire, contact, feeling, concentration, mindfulness, wisdom, liberation, nirvāṇa, and the deathless."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (36) Sūtra on the Earth

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, the purified holy life, that is, the sūtra on the Parable of the Earth. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "In the distant past, a certain person went eastward. Taking a brush, he dipped it in red paint. As he traveled east, he thought: 'I will paint the earth completely red, without leaving any unpainted.' What do you think, bhikṣus? Could this person paint the earth completely red?"

"No, World-Honored One. Why not? Because the earth is vast and boundless. It is not possible to paint it all, and this person, before finishing, would have his life span exhausted, his energy depleted."

"Bhikṣus, just as this person cannot paint all the earth, in the same way, if I were to explain in detail the nature of being born as a mother, the suffering endured could not be fully described. Also, if I were to explain in detail the nature of being born as a father, the suffering endured could not be fully described.

"Bhikṣus, it is just as a person going south, west, or north, taking a brush, dipping it in red paint, wishing to paint the earth completely red. Bhikṣus, could this person paint the earth completely red?"

"No, World-Honored One. Why not? Because the earth is vast and boundless. It is not possible to paint it all, and this person, before finishing, would have his life span exhausted, his energy depleted."

"Bhikṣus, just as this person cannot paint all the earth, in the same way, in this long course of transmigration, being born, dying, passing from one existence to another, if I were to explain in detail all the suffering endured in that transmigration, it could not be fully described. Why is this? Because this transmigration has no conceivable beginning. No beginning can be found for beings who, obstructed by ignorance and bound by craving, transmigrate and wander in the cycle of birth and death. Thus, bhikṣus, you have long experienced suffering, long experienced distress, long experienced calamity, and the charnel grounds have long been filled. You should be enough to become disenchanted with all conditioned dharmas, enough to become dispassionate toward them, and enough to seek liberation."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 7 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 7

## Sūtra 29: The Sūtra on Mahākoṣṭhila, Ninth of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, in the afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila. They exchanged greetings with each other, and he sat down to one side.

The Venerable Śāriputra said to the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila: "I wish to ask you something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, if you wish to ask, please ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there some matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows the unwholesome and knows the roots of the unwholesome. How does one know the unwholesome? Bodily misconduct is unwholesome; verbal and mental misconduct are unwholesome. This is called knowing the unwholesome. How does one know the roots of the unwholesome? Greed is an unwholesome root; aversion and delusion are unwholesome roots. This is called knowing the roots of the unwholesome. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows the unwholesome and the roots of the unwholesome, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows the wholesome and knows the roots of the wholesome. How does one know the wholesome? Bodily good conduct is wholesome; verbal and mental good conduct are wholesome. This is called knowing the wholesome. How does one know the roots of the wholesome? Non-greed is a wholesome root; non-aversion and non-delusion are wholesome roots. This is called knowing the roots of the wholesome. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows the wholesome and knows the roots of the wholesome, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows nutriment as it truly is, knows the arising of nutriment, knows the cessation of nutriment, and knows the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is. How does one know nutriment as it truly is? There are four kinds of nutriment: first, physical food, coarse and fine; second, the nutriment of contact; third, the nutriment of mental volition; fourth, the nutriment of consciousness. This is called knowing nutriment as it truly is. How does one know the arising of nutriment as it truly is? It is because of craving that there is nutriment. This is called knowing the arising of nutriment as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of nutriment as it truly is? When craving ceases, nutriment ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of nutriment as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows nutriment as it truly is, knows the arising of nutriment, knows the cessation of nutriment, and knows the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows the taints as they truly are, knows the arising of the taints, knows the cessation of the taints, and knows the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is. How does one know the taints as they truly are? There are three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. This is called knowing the taints as they truly are. How does one know the arising of the taints as it truly is? It is because of ignorance that there are taints. This is called knowing the arising of the taints as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of the taints as it truly is? When ignorance ceases, the taints cease. This is called knowing the cessation of the taints as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows the taints as they truly are, knows the arising of the taints, knows the cessation of the taints, and knows the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows suffering as it truly is, knows the arising of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. How does one know suffering as it truly is? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is hated is suffering, separation from what is loved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering, and in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This is called knowing suffering as it truly is. How does one know the arising of suffering as it truly is? It is because of old age and death that there is suffering. This is called knowing the arising of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of suffering as it truly is? When old age and death cease, suffering ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows suffering as it truly is, knows the arising of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows old age and death as they truly are, knows the arising of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is. How does one know old age? It is when one is aged and decrepit, with white hair and fallen teeth, with vigor declining day by day, the body bent and the feet crooked, the body heavy and breathing labored, walking supported by a staff, with flesh shrunken and skin loose, wrinkled like a sesame seed, the faculties deteriorated and decayed, and the complexion ugly. This is called old age. How does one know death? It is when those beings, of whatever class of beings, come to the end of life, are impermanent, die and perish, are destroyed and scattered, when their lifespan is exhausted and they are broken apart, when the life-faculty is cut off. This is called death. This is what is called death; what was previously described is called old age. Together they are called old age and death. This is called knowing old age and death as they truly are. How does one know the arising of old age and death as it truly is? It is because of birth that there is old age and death. This is called knowing the arising of old age and death as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of old age and death as it truly is? When birth ceases, old age and death cease. This is called knowing the cessation of old age and death as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows old age and death as they truly are, knows the arising of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows birth as it truly is, knows the arising of birth, knows the cessation of birth, and knows the path leading to the cessation of birth as it truly is. How does one know birth as it truly is? It is when those beings, of whatever class of beings, are born, then they are born; come forth, then they come forth; are produced, then they are produced; the five aggregates arise, and the life-faculty is obtained. This is called knowing birth as it truly is. How does one know the arising of birth as it truly is? It is because of existence that there is birth. This is called knowing the arising of birth as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of birth as it truly is? When existence ceases, birth ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of birth as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of birth as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of birth as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows birth as it truly is, knows the arising of birth, knows the cessation of birth, and knows the path leading to the cessation of birth as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows existence as it truly is, knows the arising of existence, knows the cessation of existence, and knows the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is. How does one know existence as it truly is? There are three kinds of existence: existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm. This is called knowing existence as it truly is. How does one know the arising of existence as it truly is? It is because of clinging that there is existence. This is called knowing the arising of existence as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of existence as it truly is? When clinging ceases, existence ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of existence as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows existence as it truly is, knows the arising of existence, knows the cessation of existence, and knows the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows clinging as it truly is, knows the arising of clinging, knows the cessation of clinging, and knows the path leading to the cessation of clinging as it truly is. How does one know clinging as it truly is? There are four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual desires, clinging to precepts and vows, clinging to views, and clinging to a doctrine of self. This is called knowing clinging as it truly is. How does one know the arising of clinging as it truly is? It is because of craving that there is clinging. This is called knowing the arising of clinging as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of clinging as it truly is? When craving ceases, clinging ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of clinging as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of clinging as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of clinging as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows clinging as it truly is, knows the arising of clinging, knows the cessation of clinging, and knows the path leading to the cessation of clinging as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila." Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows craving as it truly is, knows the arising of craving, knows the cessation of craving, and knows the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is. How does one know craving as it truly is? There are three kinds of craving: craving for sensual desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless. This is called knowing craving as it truly is. How does one know the arising of craving as it truly is? It is because of feeling that there is craving. This is called knowing the arising of craving as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of craving as it truly is? When feeling ceases, craving ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of craving as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows craving as it truly is, knows the arising of craving, knows the cessation of craving, and knows the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows feeling as it truly is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, and knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is. How does one know feeling as it truly is? There are three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. This is called knowing feeling as it truly is. How does one know the arising of feeling as it truly is? It is because of contact that there is feeling. This is called knowing the arising of feeling as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of feeling as it truly is? When contact ceases, feeling ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of feeling as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows feeling as it truly is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, and knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows contact as it truly is, knows the arising of contact, knows the cessation of contact, and knows the path leading to the cessation of contact as it truly is. How does one know contact as it truly is? There are three kinds of contact: pleasant contact, painful contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact. This is called knowing contact as it truly is. How does one know the arising of contact as it truly is? It is because of the six sense bases that there is contact. This is called knowing the arising of contact as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of contact as it truly is? When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of contact as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of contact as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of contact as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows contact as it truly is, knows the arising of contact, knows the cessation of contact, and knows the path leading to the cessation of contact as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows the six sense bases as they truly are, knows the arising of the six sense bases, knows the cessation of the six sense bases, and knows the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is. How does one know the six sense bases as they truly are? They are the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. This is called knowing the six sense bases as they truly are. How does one know the arising of the six sense bases as it truly is? It is because of name-and-form that there are the six sense bases. This is called knowing the arising of the six sense bases as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is? When name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease. This is called knowing the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows the six sense bases as they truly are, knows the arising of the six sense bases, knows the cessation of the six sense bases, and knows the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows name-and-form as it truly is, knows the arising of name-and-form, knows the cessation of name-and-form, and knows the path leading to the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is. How does one know name? The four immaterial aggregates constitute name. How does one know form? The four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements constitute form. This is what is called form; what was previously described is called name. Together they are called name-and-form. This is called knowing name-and-form as it truly is. How does one know the arising of name-and-form as it truly is? It is because of consciousness that there is name-and-form. This is called knowing the arising of name-and-form as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is? When consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows name-and-form as it truly is, knows the arising of name-and-form, knows the cessation of name-and-form, and knows the path leading to the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows consciousness as it truly is, knows the arising of consciousness, knows the cessation of consciousness, and knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is. How does one know consciousness as it truly is? There are six kinds of consciousness: eye consciousness, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness. This is called knowing consciousness as it truly is. How does one know the arising of consciousness as it truly is? It is because of volitional formations that there is consciousness. This is called knowing the arising of consciousness as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of consciousness as it truly is? When volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases. This is called knowing the cessation of consciousness as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows consciousness as it truly is, knows the arising of consciousness, knows the cessation of consciousness, and knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikṣu achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?"

He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra. If a bhikṣu knows volitional formations as they truly are, knows the arising of volitional formations, knows the cessation of volitional formations, and knows the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is. How does one know volitional formations as they truly are? There are three kinds of volitional formations: bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations. This is called knowing volitional formations as they truly are. How does one know the arising of volitional formations as it truly is? It is because of ignorance that there are volitional formations. This is called knowing the arising of volitional formations as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is? When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease. This is called knowing the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu thus knows volitional formations as they truly are, knows the arising of volitional formations, knows the cessation of volitional formations, and knows the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations as it truly is, this is called a bhikṣu who achieves right view, attains right view, gains unshakable confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

The Venerable Śāriputra further asked: "Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila, if a bhikṣu has already ended ignorance and given rise to clear knowledge, what more is there for him to do?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu has already ended ignorance and given rise to clear knowledge, there is nothing more for him to do."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra praised him: "Excellent! Excellent, Worthy Mahākoṣṭhila!"

Thus the two venerable ones mutually discussed the meaning, and each rejoicing and accepting the teaching, rose from their seats and departed.

End of the Sūtra on Mahākoṣṭhila, Ninth.

## Sūtra 30: The Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint, Tenth of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Worthy ones, whatever immeasurable wholesome dharmas there may be, all of them are included within the Four Noble Truths, subsumed under the Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths are the foremost among all dharmas. Why is this? Because they encompass all wholesome dharmas. Worthy ones, just as among all the footprints of animals, the elephant's footprint is the foremost. Why is this? Because the elephant's footprint is the largest. In the same way, worthy ones, whatever immeasurable wholesome dharmas there may be, all of them are included within the Four Noble Truths, subsumed under the Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths are the foremost among all dharmas. What are the four? They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the arising of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Worthy ones, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is hated is suffering, separation from what is loved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering, and in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

"Worthy ones, what are the five aggregates of clinging? They are the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Worthy ones, what is the aggregate of clinging to form? Whatever form there is, all of it is the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements. Worthy ones, what are the four great elements? They are the earth element, the water, fire, and wind elements. Worthy ones, what is the earth element? The earth element is of two kinds: there is the internal earth element and the external earth element. Worthy ones, what is the internal earth element? That which is within the body, internal, belonging to oneself, that which is solid, of a solid nature, and internally appropriated. What does this refer to? It refers to hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, spleen, intestines, stomach, feces, and whatever else of this kind remains within the body, internal, belonging to oneself, that is solid, of a solid nature, and internally appropriated. Worthy ones, this is called the internal earth element. Worthy ones, as for the external earth element, it is vast, it is pure, it is not repulsive. Worthy ones, there are times when a water disaster occurs, and at that time the external earth element is destroyed.

"Worthy ones, this external earth element is extremely vast, extremely pure, and extremely not repulsive, yet it is subject to the law of impermanence, subject to exhaustion, subject to decline, and subject to change. How much more so this body, which endures but briefly and is sustained by craving? The unlearned, ignorant ordinary person thinks: 'This is mine, this is my self, I belong to this.' The learned noble disciple does not think: 'This is mine, this is my self, I belong to this.' How should he think? If other people come to abuse, beat, scold, and reproach him with anger, he should think: 'This suffering that has arisen in me has arisen from conditions, not without conditions. What is the condition? The condition is painful contact.' He contemplates this contact as impermanent, contemplates feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as impermanent. His mind, abiding with the element as its object, is stilled, unified in one-pointedness, concentrated and unshaken. If at a later time other people come and speak to him with gentle and soft words, he should think: 'This pleasure that has arisen in me has arisen from conditions, not without conditions. What is the condition? The condition is pleasant contact.' He contemplates this contact as impermanent, contemplates feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness as impermanent. His mind, abiding with the element as its object, is stilled, unified in one-pointedness, concentrated and unshaken. If at a later time, whether young, middle-aged, or elderly people come and commit offensive acts against him, striking him with fists, throwing stones at him, or attacking him with knives and clubs, he should think: 'I have received this body, which is material, coarse in substance, composed of the four great elements, born from father and mother, nourished by food and drink, constantly covered with clothing, supported by sitting, lying, massage, bathing, and endurance. It is subject to destruction, subject to complete annihilation, subject to dispersal and disintegration. It is because of this body that I receive blows from fists, stones thrown at me, and attacks with knives and clubs.' Therefore, he strives with utmost diligence without slackening, with body upright and mind attentive, not forgetful, not deluded, calm and one-pointed. He should think: 'I strive with utmost diligence without slackening, with body upright and mind attentive, not forgetful, not deluded, calm and one-pointed. Having received this body, it is natural that I should receive blows from fists, stones, and attacks with knives and clubs. I should simply strive diligently to practice the Dharma of the World-Honored One.'

"Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has also said thus: 'If bandits should come and saw your body apart limb by limb with a sharp saw, and if at the time when bandits are sawing your body apart limb by limb with a sharp saw, your mind should change or you should speak evil words, then you have fallen into decline. You should think thus: "If bandits should come and saw my body apart limb by limb with a sharp saw, because of this I should not let my mind change or speak evil words. I should give rise to a mind of compassion toward those who are sawing my body apart limb by limb. For the sake of those people, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, I should pervade one direction and dwell having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing everything, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, I should dwell having accomplished it."'

"Worthy ones, if that bhikṣu, on account of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, cannot abide in equanimity associated with what is wholesome, then, worthy ones, that bhikṣu should feel shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach: 'I have gained no benefit in what is beneficial, I have gained no virtue in what is virtuous, in that on account of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, I cannot abide in equanimity associated with what is wholesome.' Worthy ones, just as a newly wed bride, when she sees her parents-in-law or sees her husband, feels shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach. Worthy ones, you should know that a bhikṣu is likewise. He should feel shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach: 'I have gained no benefit in what is beneficial, I have gained no virtue in what is virtuous, in that on account of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, I cannot abide in equanimity associated with what is wholesome.' Because of that shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach, he then abides in equanimity associated with what is wholesome. This is the sublime peace and stillness: the relinquishment of all existence, the abandonment of craving, desirelessness, cessation without remainder. Worthy ones, this is called a bhikṣu's complete great training.

"Worthy ones, what is the water element? The water element is of two kinds: there is the internal water element and the external water element. Worthy ones, what is the internal water element? That which is within the body, internal, belonging to oneself, that which is water, of a liquid nature, and internally appropriated. What does this refer to? It refers to the brain, the brain membrane, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, phlegm, bile, and urine, and whatever else of this kind remains within the body, internal, belonging to oneself, that is water, of a liquid nature, and internally appropriated. Worthy ones, this is called the internal water element. Worthy ones, as for the external water element, it is vast, it is pure, it is not repulsive. Worthy ones, there are times when a fire disaster occurs, and at that time the external water element is destroyed.

It is because of this body that I receive blows from fists, stones thrown at me, and attacks with knives and clubs.' Therefore, he strives with utmost diligence without slackening, with body upright and mind attentive, not forgetful, not deluded, calm and one-pointed. Having burned them, it either reaches a road or reaches water, and having no fuel, it is extinguished. Worthy ones, just as a newly wed bride, when she sees her parents-in-law or sees her husband, feels shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach. Worthy ones, you should know that a bhikṣu is likewise. He should feel shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach: 'I have gained no benefit in what is beneficial, I have gained no virtue in what is virtuous, in that on account of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, I cannot abide in equanimity associated with what is wholesome.' Because of that shame, embarrassment, and self-reproach, he then abides in equanimity associated with what is wholesome. This is the sublime peace and stillness: the relinquishment of all existence, the abandonment of craving, desirelessness, cessation without remainder. Worthy ones, this is called a bhikṣu's complete great training.

"Worthy ones, just as when, depending on timber and wood, depending on clay and earth, depending on water and grass, one encloses an empty space, and the designation 'house' arises; worthy ones, you should know that this body is likewise. Depending on sinews and bones, depending on skin, depending on flesh and blood, one wraps around an empty space, and the designation 'body' arises. Worthy ones, if the internal eye base is impaired, external forms are not illuminated by light, and there is no attention, then eye consciousness cannot arise. Worthy ones, if the internal eye base is not impaired, external forms are illuminated by light, and there is attention, then eye consciousness arises. Worthy ones, the internal eye base together with form, and eye consciousness knowing external form, belong to the aggregate of form. If there is feeling, it belongs to the aggregate of feeling. If there is perception, it belongs to the aggregate of perception. If there is volition, it belongs to the aggregate of volitional formations. If there is consciousness, it belongs to the aggregate of consciousness. Thus one contemplates the combination and meeting of the aggregates.

"Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has also said thus: 'If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma. If one sees the Dharma, one sees dependent origination.' Why is this? Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has said that the five aggregates of clinging arise from conditions: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Worthy ones, if the internal ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases are impaired, external dharmas are not illuminated by light, and there is no attention, then mind consciousness cannot arise. Worthy ones, if the internal mind base is not impaired, external dharmas are illuminated by light, and there is attention, then mind consciousness arises. Worthy ones, the internal mind base together with dharmas, and mind consciousness knowing external form-dharmas, belong to the aggregate of form. If there is feeling, it belongs to the aggregate of feeling. If there is perception, it belongs to the aggregate of perception. If there is volition, it belongs to the aggregate of volitional formations. If there is consciousness, it belongs to the aggregate of consciousness. Thus one contemplates the combination and meeting of the aggregates. Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has also said thus: 'If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma. If one sees the Dharma, one sees dependent origination.' Why is this? Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has said that the five aggregates of clinging arise from conditions: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. One becomes disenchanted with these past, future, and present five aggregates of clinging. Being disenchanted, one becomes free from desire. Being free from desire, one is liberated. Being liberated, one knows that one is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further existence to be received.' One knows this as it truly is. Worthy ones, this is called a bhikṣu's complete great training."

What the Venerable Śāriputra said was thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra said, rejoiced and accepted the teaching.

End of the Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint, Tenth.

## Sūtra 31: The Sūtra on the Analysis of the Noble Truths, Eleventh of the Chapter Connected with Śāriputra in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "This is the correct way of teaching the Dharma: the Four Noble Truths, broadly encompassed, broadly contemplated, analyzed, revealed, disclosed, established, displayed, and directed toward. All past Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones also had this correct way of teaching the Dharma: the Four Noble Truths, broadly encompassed, broadly contemplated, analyzed, revealed, disclosed, established, displayed, and directed toward. All future Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones will also have this correct way of teaching the Dharma: the Four Noble Truths, broadly encompassed, broadly contemplated, analyzed, revealed, disclosed, established, displayed, and directed toward. I, the present Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, also have this correct way of teaching the Dharma: the Four Noble Truths, broadly encompassed, broadly contemplated, analyzed, revealed, disclosed, established, displayed, and directed toward.

"The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses keen wisdom, swift wisdom, quick wisdom, sharp wisdom, broad wisdom, deep wisdom, wisdom of renunciation, clear and penetrating wisdom, and the wisdom of eloquent discourse. The bhikṣu Śāriputra is accomplished in true wisdom. Why is this? When I briefly teach these Four Noble Truths, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is able to broadly teach and broadly contemplate them for others, to analyze, reveal, disclose, establish, display, and direct toward them. When the bhikṣu Śāriputra broadly teaches and broadly shows these Four Noble Truths, analyzing, revealing, disclosing, establishing, displaying, and directing toward them, he causes countless people to gain insight. The bhikṣu Śāriputra is able to guide with right view. The bhikṣu Mahāmaudgalyāyana is able to establish people in the highest true reality, namely, the ultimate exhaustion of the taints. The bhikṣu Śāriputra gives birth to those practicing the holy life, just as a birth mother does. The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana nurtures those practicing the holy life, just as a nurturing mother does. Therefore, those practicing the holy life should attend upon, make offerings to, respect, and pay homage to the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Why is this? Because the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana seek benefit and welfare for those practicing the holy life, seeking their safety, happiness, and joy." At that time, the World-Honored One, having said this, rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation.

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Worthy ones, the World-Honored One has appeared in the world for our sake, namely, to broadly teach and broadly show these Four Noble Truths to others, to analyze, reveal, disclose, establish, display, and direct toward them. What are the four? They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the arising of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Worthy ones, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is hated is suffering, separation from what is loved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering, and in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. Worthy ones

## The Chapter on Kings, Third
