### (68) Sūtra on the Great Good-Seeing King (大善見王經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling between the twin śāla trees in the śāla grove of the Mallas at Kuśinagara, about to enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda arose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, please do not enter parinirvāṇa in this small town, this town of brambles, this remote border town. Why? Because there are other great cities, such as Campā, Rājagṛha, Śrāvastī, Sāketa, Kauśāmbī, and Vārāṇasī. In those places there are many wealthy kṣatriyas, wealthy brahmins, and wealthy householders who have deep faith in the Tathāgata. They would make offerings for the Tathāgata's final rites. I wish the World-Honored One would go to those places and enter parinirvāṇa there. Please do not enter parinirvāṇa in this small town, this town of brambles, this remote border town."

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, do not say such things. Do not say, 'This is a small town, a town of brambles, a remote border town.' Why? Ānanda, in the distant past there was a king named Great Good-Seeing. He was a wheel-turning sage king who ruled with the Dharma, a king of the Dharma. He possessed the seven treasures, and the four regions were under his domain. His life was exceedingly long, and he lived in comfort.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing made his capital here at Kuśinagara. At that time, the city was named Kuśāvatī. From east to west, the city extended twelve yojanas, and from north to south, seven yojanas. Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī was prosperous, abundant, peaceful, and well-populated, just as the celestial city of Ālakamandā, the capital of the king of the gods, is prosperous, abundant, peaceful, and well-populated. Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī was also like this.

"Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī had no time, whether day or night, when it was free from the ten kinds of sounds. What are the ten? The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of drums, the sound of small drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of singing, the sound of cymbals, the sound of conches, and the sound of calling out, 'Eat, drink, and be merry!' Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī had no time, whether day or night, when it was free from these ten kinds of sounds.

"Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī was surrounded on all four sides by seven rows of tāla trees. The tāla trees were of various colors: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. The golden trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits. The silver trees had golden leaves, flowers, and fruits. The beryl trees had crystal leaves, flowers, and fruits. The crystal trees had beryl leaves, flowers, and fruits. Ānanda, when a breeze moved those rows of tāla trees, they produced wonderful and pleasant sounds, just as the five kinds of musical instruments, when played by skilled musicians, produce wonderful and pleasant sounds. Ānanda, when a breeze moved those rows of tāla trees, the sounds they produced were also like this.

"Ānanda, at that time in the city of Kuśāvatī, those who were gamblers, drunkards, and dissolute persons all enjoyed themselves listening to the sounds of those rows of tāla trees.

"Ānanda, the city of Kuśāvatī was surrounded by seven rows of tāla trees on all four sides, and it also had seven rows of moats. The moats were of various kinds: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. The golden moats had silver bases, with golden stairs and silver railings. The silver moats had golden bases, with silver stairs and golden railings. The beryl moats had crystal bases, with beryl stairs and crystal railings. The crystal moats had beryl bases, with crystal stairs and beryl railings. Ānanda, each moat was filled with water possessing eight qualities. What are the eight? It was clear, pure, cool, soft, light, sweet in taste, free from impurities when drunk, and soothing to the throat. On the surface of the water, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and pink lotuses grew everywhere. The banks on both sides were covered with various flowers and various trees bearing fruits of all kinds, lined up in beautiful array.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing had a Dharma hall named Dharma Assembly. From east to west it extended one yojana, and from north to south half a yojana. Ānanda, the Dharma Assembly hall was made with seven kinds of treasures: gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, diamond, and all manner of precious substances. The golden pillars had silver capitals. The silver pillars had golden capitals. The beryl pillars had crystal capitals. The crystal pillars had beryl capitals. The red pearl pillars had diamond capitals. The diamond pillars had various precious capitals. The Dharma Assembly hall was covered with a golden net, and on the golden net were hung silver bells. There was a silver net, and on the silver net were hung golden bells. The Dharma Assembly hall had various draperies and was adorned with celestial flower garlands and celestial perfumes.

"Ānanda, in the Dharma Assembly hall, on all four sides were placed seats and cushions of various kinds. On the eastern wall, silver seats were placed with golden cushions. On the southern wall, golden seats were placed with silver cushions. On the western wall, beryl seats were placed with crystal cushions. On the northern wall, crystal seats were placed with beryl cushions.

"Ānanda, beside the Dharma Assembly hall, to the east, there was a tāla tree garden named Dharma Garden. From east to west it extended one yojana, and from north to south half a yojana. The tāla trees were of various colors: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. The golden trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits. The silver trees had golden leaves, flowers, and fruits. The beryl trees had crystal leaves, flowers, and fruits. The crystal trees had beryl leaves, flowers, and fruits.

"Ānanda, beside the Dharma Assembly hall, to the south, there was a lotus pond named Dharma Pond. From east to west it extended one yojana, and from north to south half a yojana. The Dharma Pond was filled with water possessing eight qualities. What are the eight? It was clear, pure, cool, soft, light, sweet in taste, free from impurities when drunk, and soothing to the throat. The pond was built with four kinds of treasures: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. With golden stairs and silver railings, silver stairs and golden railings, beryl stairs and crystal railings, crystal stairs and beryl railings. The banks on both sides were covered with various flowers, various trees bearing fruits of all kinds, lined up in beautiful array. On the surface of the water, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and pink lotuses grew everywhere.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing thought: 'I should place caretakers at this lotus pond, so that those who wish to pick flowers may pick them freely.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then placed caretakers at the lotus pond, and those who wished to pick flowers could pick them freely.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then thought: 'I should place givers of food along all the roads on both sides, so that travelers who are hungry can be given food, those who are thirsty can be given drink, and those who need provisions can be given provisions.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then placed givers of food along all the roads on both sides. Travelers who were hungry were given food, those who were thirsty were given drink, and those who needed provisions were given provisions.

"Ānanda, then the eighty-four thousand minor kings among the subjects came to King Great Good-Seeing and said: 'Your Majesty, we wish to build for you. May Your Majesty accept our offering.'

"King Great Good-Seeing remained silent and did not accept.

"A second time, those eighty-four thousand minor kings addressed King Great Good-Seeing: 'Your Majesty, we wish to build for you. May Your Majesty accept our offering.'

"King Great Good-Seeing again remained silent and did not accept.

"A third time, those eighty-four thousand minor kings addressed King Great Good-Seeing: 'Your Majesty, we wish to build for you. May Your Majesty accept our offering. Each of us has gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, diamond, and all manner of precious substances in great abundance. May Your Majesty please accept.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing thought: 'These minor kings wish a third time to offer me building materials. I should now accept them.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then accepted their offering. Those eighty-four thousand minor kings then built for King Great Good-Seeing eighty-four thousand cities. Among those eighty-four thousand cities, the foremost was the city of Kuśāvatī.

"They built eighty-four thousand palaces. Among those eighty-four thousand palaces, the foremost was the Dharma Assembly palace.

"They built eighty-four thousand halls. Among those eighty-four thousand halls, the foremost was the Great Correct Hall.

"They built eighty-four thousand couches. Those eighty-four thousand couches were made of gold, silver, beryl, and crystal, covered with fine spreads, laid with woolen blankets, silk blankets, brocade spreads, and the finest antelope-skin covers.

"They built eighty-four thousand garment storehouses, filled with garments of the finest kind.

"They raised eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold and silver ornaments, draped with golden nets, with golden banners on top. Among those eighty-four thousand elephants, the foremost was the king's elephant named Upoṣadha.

"They raised eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold and silver ornaments, draped with golden nets, with golden banners on top. Among those eighty-four thousand horses, the foremost was the king's horse named Valāhaka.

"They prepared eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins, draped with various colored fabrics, adorned with gold and silver ornaments, with golden banners on top. Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, the foremost was the king's chariot named Vejayanta.

"They prepared eighty-four thousand jewels. Among those eighty-four thousand jewels, the foremost was the maṇi jewel.

"They had eighty-four thousand consorts. Among those eighty-four thousand consorts, the foremost was the queen, a kṣatriya woman or a vaiśya woman.

"They prepared eighty-four thousand seats and cushions, decorated with fine spreads and brocades.

"They prepared eighty-four thousand koṭis of food, morning and evening providing sustenance.

"Ānanda, at that time, among those eighty-four thousand elephants, King Great Good-Seeing rode only one elephant. Among those eighty-four thousand horses, he rode only one horse. Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, he rode only one chariot. Among those eighty-four thousand cities, he dwelt in only one city, the city of Kuśāvatī. Among those eighty-four thousand palaces, he used only one palace, the Dharma Assembly palace. Among those eighty-four thousand halls, he used only one hall, the Great Correct Hall. Among those eighty-four thousand couches, he used only one couch. Among those eighty-four thousand garment storehouses, he used garments from only one storehouse. Among those eighty-four thousand consorts, only one consort attended to him. Among those eighty-four thousand koṭis of food, he ate only the amount from one golden vessel.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing, endowed with those eighty-four thousand palaces and all those various possessions, thought: 'What previous deeds of mine have produced this fruit and this reward, so that I have such great supernatural power and such great majesty?'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then further thought: 'It is from three causes that I have obtained this fruit and this reward, giving me such great supernatural power and such great majesty. What are the three? They are giving, self-control, and restraint.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then thought: 'I have already enjoyed the pleasures of human desires. I should now seek divine pleasures. I should now cultivate the four immeasurables.'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing then ascended to the Dharma Assembly hall and stood at the silver door on the eastern side. He joined his palms and said: 'Let thoughts of desire cease! Let thoughts of ill will cease! Let thoughts of harming cease! Thoughts of desire, do not arise again! Thoughts of ill will, do not arise again! Thoughts of harming, do not arise again!'

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing, having ascended to the Dharma Assembly hall and stood at the silver door on the eastern side, having joined his palms, having caused thoughts of desire, ill will, and harming to cease, then pervaded one direction with a mind of loving-kindness and dwelt therein. Likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere, in all places, for the sake of all beings, with a mind of loving-kindness that was free from enmity, free from ill will, free from anger, free from rivalry, extremely vast, extremely great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, he pervaded the entire world and dwelt therein.

"In the same way, with compassion, with sympathetic joy, with equanimity, he pervaded one direction and dwelt therein. Likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere, in all places, for the sake of all beings, with a mind of equanimity that was free from enmity, free from ill will, free from anger, free from rivalry, extremely vast, extremely great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, he pervaded the entire world and dwelt therein.

"Ānanda, at that time Queen Subhadrā thought: 'It has been a long time since I have seen King Great Good-Seeing. I should go and visit the king.'

"Queen Subhadrā then told the women: 'Each of you quickly bathe and adorn yourselves with garlands. We shall go to visit King Great Good-Seeing.'

"The women answered: 'Yes, Your Majesty,' and quickly bathed and adorned themselves with garlands.

"Queen Subhadrā then told the officer of the women's quarters: 'Prepare the eighty-four thousand chariots. We wish to go and visit King Great Good-Seeing.'

"The officer answered: 'Yes, Your Majesty,' and at once prepared the eighty-four thousand chariots, then reported: 'The chariots are ready. May it please Your Majesty.'

"Queen Subhadrā then led the eighty-four thousand women and, together with the eighty-four thousand chariots, went to the Dharma Assembly hall where King Great Good-Seeing was. Arriving there, she descended from her chariot, walked to the silver door on the eastern side, opened the door, entered, and came before the king. She bowed her head at his feet and stood to one side.

"Ānanda, Queen Subhadrā then addressed King Great Good-Seeing: 'Great King, you should know that the eighty-four thousand minor kings wish to attend upon you. May the Great King accept and allow them to come.'

"King Great Good-Seeing said: 'Subhadrā, do not speak thus. Why? They have come from afar. You should provide food and drink for them, and attend to their needs.'

"Queen Subhadrā then knelt, joined her palms, and addressed King Great Good-Seeing: 'Great King, the eighty-four thousand cities, among which the foremost is the city of Kuśāvatī; the eighty-four thousand palaces, among which the foremost is the Dharma Assembly palace; the eighty-four thousand halls, among which the foremost is the Great Correct Hall; the eighty-four thousand couches; the eighty-four thousand garment storehouses; the eighty-four thousand elephants, among which the foremost is the king's elephant Upoṣadha; the eighty-four thousand horses, among which the foremost is the king's horse Valāhaka; the eighty-four thousand chariots, among which the foremost is the king's chariot Vejayanta; the eighty-four thousand consorts, of whom I, Subhadrā, am the foremost: all these the Great King should enjoy. May the Great King put aside this meditation. May the Great King enjoy these pleasures.'

"King Great Good-Seeing said: 'Subhadrā, do not speak thus. Why? You should rather encourage me, saying, "May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand cities, among which the foremost is the city of Kuśāvatī. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand palaces, among which the foremost is the Dharma Assembly palace. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand halls, among which the foremost is the Great Correct Hall. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand couches. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand garment storehouses. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand elephants, among which the foremost is the king's elephant Upoṣadha. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand horses, among which the foremost is the king's horse Valāhaka. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand chariots, among which the foremost is the king's chariot Vejayanta. May the Great King put aside these eighty-four thousand consorts, of whom I, Subhadrā, am the foremost. May the Great King not cling to any of these."'

"Queen Subhadrā, weeping with tears flowing, wiped her face and addressed King Great Good-Seeing: 'Yes, Great King. The eighty-four thousand cities, among which the foremost is the city of Kuśāvatī: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand palaces, among which the foremost is the Dharma Assembly palace: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand halls, among which the foremost is the Great Correct Hall: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand couches: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand garment storehouses: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand elephants, among which the foremost is the king's elephant Upoṣadha: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand horses, among which the foremost is the king's horse Valāhaka: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand chariots, among which the foremost is the king's chariot Vejayanta: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them. The eighty-four thousand consorts, of whom I, Subhadrā, am the foremost: may the Great King put them aside, not clinging to them.'

"Ānanda, not long after this, King Great Good-Seeing passed away. Ānanda, just as a householder or a householder's son, having eaten a fine meal, feels satisfaction and pleasure, so King Great Good-Seeing, when he passed away, experienced the feeling of death as pleasant, and he was reborn in the Brahma realm.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing had a lifespan of eighty-four thousand years. He played as a crown prince for eighty-four thousand years. He ruled as a minor king for eighty-four thousand years. He ruled as a wheel-turning king for eighty-four thousand years. He practiced the holy life as a householder in the Dharma Assembly hall for eighty-four thousand years.

"Ānanda, King Great Good-Seeing cultivated the four immeasurables and, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

"Ānanda, do you think that King Great Good-Seeing at that time was someone else? You should not think so. Why? I was King Great Good-Seeing at that time.

"At that time I had eighty-four thousand cities, among which the foremost was the city of Kuśāvatī. At that time I had eighty-four thousand palaces, among which the foremost was the Dharma Assembly palace. At that time I had eighty-four thousand halls, among which the foremost was the Great Correct Hall. At that time I had eighty-four thousand couches. At that time I had eighty-four thousand garment storehouses. At that time I had eighty-four thousand elephants, among which the foremost was the king's elephant Upoṣadha. At that time I had eighty-four thousand horses, among which the foremost was the king's horse Valāhaka. At that time I had eighty-four thousand chariots, among which the foremost was the king's chariot Vejayanta. At that time I had eighty-four thousand consorts, among whom the foremost was Queen Subhadrā. At that time I had eighty-four thousand koṭis of food.

"Ānanda, among those eighty-four thousand cities, I dwelt in only one city, the city of Kuśāvatī. Among those eighty-four thousand palaces, I used only one palace, the Dharma Assembly palace. Among those eighty-four thousand halls, I used only one hall, the Great Correct Hall. Among those eighty-four thousand couches, I used only one couch. Among those eighty-four thousand garment storehouses, I used garments from only one storehouse. Among those eighty-four thousand elephants, I rode only one elephant. Among those eighty-four thousand horses, I rode only one horse. Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, I rode only one chariot. Among those eighty-four thousand consorts, only one consort attended to me. Among those eighty-four thousand koṭis of food, I ate only the amount from one golden vessel.

"Ānanda, see how all those conditioned things have passed away, ceased, and changed. Ānanda, conditioned things are indeed impermanent. They are things that will be exhausted, things that will decay, things that will fade away. Therefore one should be thoroughly disgusted with all conditioned things, one should be free from desire for them, and one should seek liberation.

"Ānanda, in this place I have previously discarded my body six times, being reborn as a wheel-turning sage king who ruled with the Dharma. Now again, for the seventh time, I discard my body here, as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Ānanda, I do not see any place in the world, whether among gods, Māra, Brahmā, among ascetics, brahmins, from gods to humans, where I would again discard my body an eighth time. There is no such possibility."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

### (69) Sūtra on the Three Examinations (三十喻經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there were no pleasure in desires, beings would not become attached to desires. Because there is pleasure in desires, beings become attached to desires. If there were no suffering in desires, beings would not become disgusted with desires. Because there is suffering in desires, beings become disgusted with desires. If there were no escape from desires, beings could not escape from desires. Because there is escape from desires, beings can escape from desires.

"If there were no pleasure in forms, beings would not become attached to forms. Because there is pleasure in forms, beings become attached to forms. If there were no suffering in forms, beings would not become disgusted with forms. Because there is suffering in forms, beings become disgusted with forms. If there were no escape from forms, beings could not escape from forms. Because there is escape from forms, beings can escape from forms.

"If there were no pleasure in feelings, beings would not become attached to feelings. Because there is pleasure in feelings, beings become attached to feelings. If there were no suffering in feelings, beings would not become disgusted with feelings. Because there is suffering in feelings, beings become disgusted with feelings. If there were no escape from feelings, beings could not escape from feelings. Because there is escape from feelings, beings can escape from feelings.

"Bhikṣus, so long as I did not know, as they truly are, the pleasure of desires as pleasure, the suffering of desires as suffering, and the escape from desires as escape; the pleasure of forms as pleasure, the suffering of forms as suffering, and the escape from forms as escape; the pleasure of feelings as pleasure, the suffering of feelings as suffering, and the escape from feelings as escape, then I did not attain unsurpassed, right and perfect enlightenment among the devas, Māra, Brahmā, among ascetics and brahmins, from devas to humans.

"Bhikṣus, since I came to know, as they truly are, the pleasure of desires as pleasure, the suffering of desires as suffering, and the escape from desires as escape; the pleasure of forms as pleasure, the suffering of forms as suffering, and the escape from forms as escape; the pleasure of feelings as pleasure, the suffering of feelings as suffering, and the escape from feelings as escape, I then attained unsurpassed, right and perfect enlightenment among the devas, Māra, Brahmā, among ascetics and brahmins, from devas to humans. Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My liberation is unshakable. This is my final birth. There will be no further becoming.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (70) Sūtra on Transference of Merit (轉輪王經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Mātulā, at the Mango Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the wheel-turning sage king. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, in the distant past there was a wheel-turning king named Daḷhanemi. He was a king who ruled with the Dharma, a Dharma king. He possessed the seven treasures: the golden wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure. He had a full thousand sons, all brave and heroic in appearance, able to conquer enemies. He ruled over this entire earth, bounded by the four seas, and governed it without using punishment or weapons, but with the Dharma, enabling the people to live in peace.

"Bhikṣus, after a very long time, King Daḷhanemi's golden wheel treasure slightly shifted from its position. A minister saw this and went to report to King Daḷhanemi: 'Great King, you should know that your golden wheel treasure has slightly shifted from its position.'

"King Daḷhanemi, hearing this, thought: 'I have heard from the ancients that when a wheel-turning king's golden wheel treasure shifts from its position, the king's remaining life will not be long. I have already enjoyed human pleasures. I should now seek celestial pleasures. I shall hand over the kingdom to my eldest son, the crown prince, shave my head, put on the kāṣāya robes, leave the household life, and become a renunciant.'

"Bhikṣus, King Daḷhanemi then summoned his eldest son, the crown prince, and told him: 'My golden wheel treasure has shifted from its position. I have heard from the ancients that when a wheel-turning king's golden wheel treasure shifts from its position, the king's remaining life will not be long. I have already enjoyed human pleasures. I now wish to seek celestial pleasures. Prince, I hand over the great kingdom to you. I shall shave my head, put on the kāṣāya robes, leave the household life, and become a renunciant. You should now appoint a crown prince of your own, and after entrusting the kingdom to him, you too should shave your head, put on the kāṣāya robes, leave the household life, and become a renunciant.'

"Bhikṣus, King Daḷhanemi, having instructed his eldest son the crown prince in detail, shaved his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, left the household life, and became a renunciant. After the king had gone forth for seven days, the golden wheel treasure disappeared.

"A minister went to report to the new king: 'Great King, you should know that the golden wheel treasure has disappeared.'

"The new king, hearing that the golden wheel treasure had disappeared, was troubled and displeased. He went to where the royal sage had retired and addressed him: 'Great King, you should know that the golden wheel treasure has disappeared.'

"The royal sage told the new king: 'My son, do not be troubled or displeased that the golden wheel treasure has disappeared. Why? The golden wheel treasure is not something inherited from your father. My son, you should practice the noble wheel-turning duty. If you practice the noble wheel-turning duty, then on the fifteenth day of the month, the day of the upoṣadha, when you have bathed your head, gone up to the upper terrace of the palace, and are surrounded by your attendants, the golden wheel treasure will naturally appear before you, complete with a thousand spokes, with hub, rim, and all its parts, not made by an artisan, but composed of pure gold.'

"The new king asked the royal sage: 'What is the noble wheel-turning duty?'

"The royal sage replied: 'My son, you should rely on the Dharma, honor the Dharma, revere the Dharma, esteem the Dharma, worship the Dharma, and take the Dharma as your banner and standard. With the Dharma you should provide just protection and security for your inner court, your kṣatriya nobles, your army, your brahmins and householders, your townspeople and country folk, your ascetics and brahmins, and the beasts and birds. Do not allow any wrongdoing in your kingdom. If there are poor people in your kingdom, give them wealth.

"'And if there are ascetics and brahmins in your kingdom who have refrained from negligence and arrogance, who are established in patience and gentleness, who tame themselves, calm themselves, and lead themselves to nirvāṇa, you should go to them from time to time and ask questions: "Venerable ones, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be practiced? What should not be practiced? What actions will bring me long-lasting suffering and harm? What actions will bring me long-lasting welfare and happiness?" Having heard them, you should abandon what is unwholesome and practice what is wholesome. My son, this is the noble wheel-turning duty.'

"The new king replied: 'Yes, sir,' and he practiced the noble wheel-turning duty. Having practiced it, on the fifteenth day of the month, the day of the upoṣadha, when he had bathed his head, gone up to the upper terrace of the palace, and was surrounded by his attendants, the golden wheel treasure naturally appeared before him, complete with a thousand spokes, with hub, rim, and all its parts, not made by an artisan, but composed of pure gold.

"The new king saw this and thought: 'I have heard that when a kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day of the month, the upoṣadha day, after bathing his head, going up to the upper terrace, surrounded by attendants, has the golden wheel treasure appear before him, he becomes a wheel-turning king. Am I then a wheel-turning king?'

"Bhikṣus, that king then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, took the golden wheel treasure in his left hand, sprinkled it with his right hand, and rolled it forward, saying: 'May this wheel treasure roll to the east and conquer.'

"The golden wheel treasure then rolled to the east, and the king followed it with his fourfold army. Wherever the golden wheel treasure stopped, the king encamped with his fourfold army. The eastern kings, seeing this, came to the king and said: 'Welcome, Great King! These lands all belong to the Great King. The Great King may instruct us.'

"The king said to them: 'You should not kill living beings. You should not steal. You should not commit sexual misconduct. You should not speak falsely. You should not drink intoxicants. You should eat in moderation.'

"Those eastern kings all submitted and followed him.

"The golden wheel treasure then rolled into the eastern sea, then turned south. The golden wheel treasure rolled to the south, and the king followed it with his fourfold army. Wherever the golden wheel treasure stopped, the king encamped with his fourfold army. The southern kings, seeing this, came to the king and said: 'Welcome, Great King! These lands all belong to the Great King. The Great King may instruct us.'

"The king also told them: 'You should not kill living beings. You should not steal. You should not commit sexual misconduct. You should not speak falsely. You should not drink intoxicants. You should eat in moderation.'

"Those southern kings all submitted and followed him.

"The golden wheel treasure then rolled into the southern sea, then turned west. The golden wheel treasure rolled to the west, and the king followed it with his fourfold army. Wherever the golden wheel treasure stopped, the king encamped with his fourfold army. The western kings, seeing this, came to the king and said: 'Welcome, Great King! These lands all belong to the Great King. The Great King may instruct us.'

"The king also told them: 'You should not kill living beings. You should not steal. You should not commit sexual misconduct. You should not speak falsely. You should not drink intoxicants. You should eat in moderation.'

"Those western kings all submitted and followed him.

"The golden wheel treasure then rolled into the western sea, then turned north. The golden wheel treasure rolled to the north, and the king followed it with his fourfold army. Wherever the golden wheel treasure stopped, the king encamped with his fourfold army. The northern kings, seeing this, came to the king and said: 'Welcome, Great King! These lands all belong to the Great King. The Great King may instruct us.'

"The king also told them: 'You should not kill living beings. You should not steal. You should not commit sexual misconduct. You should not speak falsely. You should not drink intoxicants. You should eat in moderation.'

"Those northern kings all submitted and followed him.

"Bhikṣus, the golden wheel treasure, having conquered all the lands within the four seas, returned to the capital and stopped before the gate of the king's palace, illuminating it brilliantly.

"Bhikṣus, the second wheel-turning king, after a very long time, also saw his golden wheel treasure shift slightly from its position. Seeing this, he also thought: 'I have heard from the ancients that when a wheel-turning king's golden wheel treasure shifts from its position, the king's remaining life will not be long. I have already enjoyed human pleasures. I should now seek celestial pleasures. I shall hand over the kingdom to my eldest son, the crown prince, shave my head, put on the kāṣāya robes, leave the household life, and become a renunciant.'

"He then summoned his eldest son, the crown prince, entrusted the great kingdom to him, shaved his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, left the household life, and became a renunciant. After the king had gone forth for seven days, the golden wheel treasure disappeared.

"A minister went to report to the new king: 'Great King, you should know that the golden wheel treasure has disappeared.'

"Hearing this, the new king was troubled and displeased. He went to the royal sage and said: 'Great King, the golden wheel treasure has disappeared.'

"The royal sage told the new king: 'My son, do not be troubled or displeased. The golden wheel treasure is not something inherited from your father. My son, you should practice the noble wheel-turning duty. If you practice the noble wheel-turning duty, then on the fifteenth day, the upoṣadha day, when you have bathed your head, gone up to the upper terrace of the palace, surrounded by attendants, the golden wheel treasure will naturally appear before you.'

"The new king asked: 'What is the noble wheel-turning duty?'

"The royal sage explained to him in detail, just as before. The new king then practiced the noble wheel-turning duty, and the golden wheel treasure appeared, and he conquered all the four directions, just as before.

"Bhikṣus, in this manner, generation after generation, the kings practiced the noble wheel-turning duty, and the golden wheel treasure appeared for them. Up to the seventh king, after a very long time, that seventh king also saw his golden wheel treasure shift from its position. He too entrusted the kingdom to his eldest son, shaved his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, and went forth.

"After seven days, the golden wheel treasure disappeared. A minister reported this to the new king. The new king was troubled and displeased, but he did not go to the royal sage to ask about the noble wheel-turning duty. Instead, he governed the realm according to his own ideas.

"Because he governed according to his own ideas and did not practice the noble wheel-turning duty, the country gradually declined. The people became poor, and because of poverty, there arose stealing. Because of stealing, there arose the use of weapons. Because of weapons, there arose killing. Because of killing, there arose lying. Because of lying, there arose slander. Because of slander, there arose sexual misconduct. Because of these unwholesome actions, beings' lifespans decreased, and their beauty decreased.

"In the time when beings had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, their children had a lifespan of forty thousand years. In the time when beings had a lifespan of forty thousand years, among those people some were beautiful and some were ugly. The ugly ones, envying the beautiful ones, committed adultery with others' wives.

"Bhikṣus, because beings did not give wealth to the poor, poverty increased greatly. Because poverty increased greatly, stealing increased greatly. Because stealing increased greatly, the use of weapons increased greatly. Because the use of weapons increased greatly, killing increased greatly. Because killing increased greatly, lying increased greatly. Because lying increased greatly, slander increased greatly. Because slander increased greatly, sexual misconduct increased greatly. Because of these three unwholesome actions, beings' lifespans decreased and their beauty decreased. When beings had a lifespan of forty thousand years, their children had a lifespan of twenty thousand years.

"In the time when beings had a lifespan of twenty thousand years, among those people some were beautiful and some were ugly. The ugly ones, envying the beautiful ones, committed adultery with others' wives. Thus further, harsh speech increased. Because of harsh speech, lifespans decreased, and beings with a lifespan of twenty thousand years had children with a lifespan of ten thousand years.

"In the time when beings had a lifespan of ten thousand years, among those people some were beautiful and some were ugly. The ugly ones, envying the beautiful ones, committed adultery with others' wives. Thus further, frivolous speech increased. Because of frivolous speech, lifespans decreased, and beings with a lifespan of ten thousand years had children with a lifespan of five thousand years.

"In the time when beings had a lifespan of five thousand years, three unwholesome things flourished: covetousness, ill will, and wrong views. Because these three unwholesome things flourished, lifespans decreased, and beings with a lifespan of five thousand years had children with a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years. Further, lifespans continued to decrease: from two thousand five hundred years to one thousand years, from one thousand years to five hundred years, from five hundred years to two hundred fifty years, from two hundred fifty years to one hundred years.

"Bhikṣus, in the present age, the human lifespan is one hundred years. Among those living one hundred years, few cross beyond.

"Bhikṣus, the time will come when human beings will have a lifespan of only ten years. When the lifespan is ten years, girls at five years of age will be marriageable. When the lifespan is ten years, such tastes as ghee, butter, oil, honey, sugar, and salt will all disappear. When the lifespan is ten years, the finest food will be millet grain, just as today the finest food is rice and white flour.

"When the lifespan is ten years, the ten wholesome courses of action will completely disappear, and the ten unwholesome courses of action will greatly flourish. When the lifespan is ten years, the very word 'wholesome' will not exist, much less anyone who does good deeds. When the lifespan is ten years, those who do not honor father or mother, who do not honor ascetics and brahmins, who do not respect elders in the family, will be praised and exalted, just as today those who honor father and mother, who honor ascetics and brahmins, who respect family elders, are praised and exalted.

"Bhikṣus, when the lifespan is ten years, there will be no distinctions of mother, aunt, mother-in-law, teacher's wife, or uncle's wife. The world will be mixed together, like goats, chickens, pigs, dogs, and jackals.

"When the lifespan is ten years, beings will bear great enmity and hatred toward each other, great ill will, great malice, and great desire to kill. Mother toward child, child toward mother, father toward child, child toward father, brother toward brother, brother toward sister, sister toward brother, all will bear great enmity, hatred, ill will, malice, and desire to kill. Just as a hunter seeing a deer bears great enmity and desire to kill, so will it be among those beings.

"Bhikṣus, when the lifespan is ten years, there will be a period of seven days called the 'sword-interval.' During those seven days, beings will take up grasses, sticks, and any objects as weapons, each killing the other. After seven days, some beings will think: 'We do not want to be killed by others, and we do not want to kill others. Let us hide in the thickets of grass and trees, in the mountain valleys and ravines, and sustain ourselves on roots and fruits.'

"They will hide in the thickets for seven days. After seven days, they will emerge from the thickets, and seeing each other, they will embrace and weep, saying: 'How wonderful that you are alive! How wonderful that you are alive!'

"At that time those beings will think: 'We have suffered the loss of many relatives because of unwholesome actions. Let us now do good. What good can we do? Let us refrain from killing. Let us take up and practice this wholesome course of action.'

"Because they refrain from killing, their lifespans will increase and their beauty will increase. With a lifespan of ten years, their children will have a lifespan of twenty years. Then they will think: 'Because we practiced wholesome actions, our lifespans increased and our beauty increased. Let us do more good. Let us refrain from stealing, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, from frivolous speech. Let us abandon covetousness, ill will, and wrong views.'

"Because they practice these ten wholesome courses of action, their lifespans will increase and their beauty will increase. With a lifespan of twenty years, their children will have a lifespan of forty years. With forty years, eighty years. With eighty years, one hundred sixty years. With one hundred sixty years, three hundred twenty years. With three hundred twenty years, six hundred forty years. With six hundred forty years, two thousand years. With two thousand years, five thousand years. With five thousand years, ten thousand years. With ten thousand years, twenty thousand years. With twenty thousand years, forty thousand years. With forty thousand years, eighty thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, Jambudvīpa will be prosperous and abundant. Villages and cities will be so close that a rooster can fly from one to the next. When human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, girls will be marriageable at five hundred years. When human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, they will have only such illnesses as needing to defecate, needing to urinate, desire, eating, and aging. There will be no other illnesses.

"Bhikṣus, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will arise in this world a king named Śaṅkha. He will be a wheel-turning king who rules with the Dharma, possessing the seven treasures: the golden wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure. He will have a full thousand sons, all brave and heroic, able to conquer enemies. He will rule over this entire earth up to the ocean, not with punishment or weapons, but with the Dharma, enabling the people to live in peace.

"Bhikṣus, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will arise in this world a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Devas and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, just as I have now arisen in the world. He will, by his own direct knowledge, realize and teach the Dharma to this world with its devas, Māra, Brahmā, its ascetics and brahmins, from devas to humans, just as I now do. He will teach the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right words, complete and pure, and he will proclaim the holy life, just as I now do. He will have a Sangha of thousands of bhikṣus, just as I now have a Sangha of hundreds of bhikṣus.

"Bhikṣus, at that time King Śaṅkha will raise up the Dharma Assembly hall that was built by King Great Good-Seeing, and he will live in it. After having given gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, and wayfarers, he will shave his head, put on the kāṣāya robes, leave the household life, and become a renunciant under the World-Honored One Maitreya. Having gone forth, he will dwell alone in a quiet place, diligent, zealous, and resolute. Before long, he will realize by his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme goal of the holy life for which sons of good family rightly leave the household life for homelessness. He will know: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming.'

"Bhikṣus, King Śaṅkha will become an arhat under the World-Honored One Maitreya.

"Bhikṣus, therefore you should practice wholesome actions. By practicing wholesome actions, your lifespans will increase, your beauty will increase, your comfort will increase, your wealth will increase, and your strength will increase.

"Bhikṣus, what does it mean to 'increase one's lifespan'? A bhikṣu cultivates the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of intention together with the formations of striving. He cultivates the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of energy together with the formations of striving. He cultivates the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of mind together with the formations of striving. He cultivates the base of spiritual power endowed with the concentration of investigation together with the formations of striving. Because he repeatedly cultivates these four bases of spiritual power, he can, if he wishes, remain for a kalpa or more. This is called 'increasing one's lifespan.'

"What does it mean to 'increase beauty'? A bhikṣu practices the moral precepts, guarding the Prātimokṣa with right conduct and right domain, seeing danger in the slightest fault, undertaking and training in the rules of training. This is called 'increasing beauty.'

"What does it mean to 'increase comfort'? A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial and sustained application of mind, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of initial and sustained application of mind, with inner tranquility, with unification of mind, without initial or sustained application, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna. With the fading of joy, he dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, which the noble ones describe as 'dwelling with equanimity, mindful, in happiness,' he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the earlier disappearance of gladness and sadness, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. This is called 'increasing comfort.'

"What does it mean to 'increase wealth'? A bhikṣu abides pervading one direction with a mind of loving-kindness. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere, for all beings, with a mind of loving-kindness free from enmity, free from ill will, free from anger, free from rivalry, extremely vast, extremely great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, he pervades the entire world and dwells therein. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, with equanimity. This is called 'increasing wealth.'

"What does it mean to 'increase strength'? A bhikṣu, with the destruction of the taints, in this very life by his own direct knowledge realizes the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and enters and dwells therein. This is called 'increasing strength.'

"Bhikṣus, I do not see any other strength that is so hard to conquer as the strength of Māra. It is by adopting wholesome states that this merit is obtained."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

*End of Fascicle Fifteen of the Madhyamāgama*

# Fascicle Eight

# Chapter Four: Unprecedented Dharmas

Unprecedented, Attendant, Bakkula, Asura,
Earthquake, and Campā, Uggaha, Hands, each two.

---

## (32) Sūtra on Unprecedented Dharmas, First of the Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I have heard that the World-Honored One first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. If it is true that the World-Honored One first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. If it is true that the World-Honored One, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. The World-Honored One, upon his later birth, surpassed the previous inhabitants of the Tuṣita heaven in three ways: in heavenly lifespan, heavenly beauty, and heavenly renown. For this reason, the gods of Tuṣita rejoiced and were elated, praising this celestial being: 'How extraordinary! How remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might. Why is this? Because this one who has come to be born later surpasses the previous inhabitants of the Tuṣita heaven in three ways: in heavenly lifespan, heavenly beauty, and heavenly renown.' If it is true that the World-Honored One, at the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, first aspired to the path of Buddhahood and practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven, and the World-Honored One, upon his later birth, surpassed the previous inhabitants of the Tuṣita heaven in three ways: in heavenly lifespan, heavenly beauty, and heavenly renown, and for this reason the gods of Tuṣita rejoiced and were elated, praising this celestial being: 'How extraordinary! How remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might. Why is this? Because this one who has come to be born later surpasses the previous inhabitants of the Tuṣita heaven in three ways: in heavenly lifespan, heavenly beauty, and heavenly renown,' I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was in the Tuṣita heaven, upon passing away from that life, he knowingly entered his mother's womb. At that time, all heaven and earth trembled and shook, and a great wondrous radiance universally illuminated the world, reaching even the hidden, dark, and obscure places without obstruction. Even those places where this sun and moon, which possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might, and whose light does not reach, were all bathed in that brilliance. The beings there, because of this wondrous light, each came to know: 'An extraordinary being has been born! An extraordinary being has been born!' If it is true that when the World-Honored One was in the Tuṣita heaven, upon passing away from that life, he knowingly entered his mother's womb, and at that time all heaven and earth trembled and shook, and a great wondrous radiance universally illuminated the world, reaching even the hidden, dark, and obscure places without obstruction, and even those places where this sun and moon, which possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might, and whose light does not reach, were all bathed in that brilliance, and the beings there, because of this wondrous light, each came to know: 'An extraordinary being has been born! An extraordinary being has been born!' I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One knowingly dwelt in his mother's womb, resting upon the right side. If it is true that the World-Honored One knowingly dwelt in his mother's womb, resting upon the right side, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One. I have heard that the World-Honored One dwelt in his mother's womb with body outstretched. If it is true that the World-Honored One dwelt in his mother's womb with body outstretched, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One. I have heard that the World-Honored One dwelt in his mother's womb protected and enclosed, not stained by blood, nor stained by semen or any impurities. If it is true that the World-Honored One dwelt in his mother's womb protected and enclosed, not stained by blood, nor stained by semen or any impurities, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One knowingly emerged from his mother's womb, at that time all heaven and earth trembled and shook, and a great wondrous radiance universally illuminated the world, reaching even the hidden, dark, and obscure places without obstruction. Even those places where this sun and moon, which possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might, and whose light does not reach, were all bathed in that brilliance. The beings there, because of this wondrous light, each came to know: 'An extraordinary being has been born! An extraordinary being has been born!' If it is true that when the World-Honored One knowingly emerged from his mother's womb, at that time all heaven and earth trembled and shook, and a great wondrous radiance universally illuminated the world, reaching even the hidden, dark, and obscure places without obstruction, and even those places where this sun and moon, which possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might, and whose light does not reach, were all bathed in that brilliance, and the beings there, because of this wondrous light, each came to know: 'An extraordinary being has been born! An extraordinary being has been born!' I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother's womb with body outstretched. If it is true that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother's womb with body outstretched, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One. I have heard that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother's womb protected and enclosed, not stained by blood, nor stained by semen or any impurities. If it is true that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother's womb protected and enclosed, not stained by blood, nor stained by semen or any impurities, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, four heavenly sons holding extremely fine garments stood before his mother, causing her to rejoice, and praised this child: 'How extraordinary! How remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might.' If it is true that when the World-Honored One was first born, four heavenly sons holding fine garments stood before his mother, causing her to rejoice, and praised this child: 'How extraordinary! How remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might,' I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, he immediately took seven steps, without alarm, without fear, without dread, and surveyed all directions. If it is true that when the World-Honored One was first born, he immediately took seven steps, without alarm, without fear, without dread, and surveyed all directions, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, a great pool appeared before his mother, its water filled to the brim, so that his mother could use it for cleansing. If it is true that when the World-Honored One was first born, a great pool appeared before his mother, its water filled to the brim, so that his mother could use it for cleansing, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, from the sky above, streams of water rained down, one cold and one warm, bathing the body of the World-Honored One. If it is true that when the World-Honored One was first born, from the sky above, streams of water rained down, one cold and one warm, bathing the body of the World-Honored One, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, the devas above played celestial music, and heavenly blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, white lotuses, heavenly mandārava flowers, and finely powdered sandalwood incense were scattered upon the World-Honored One. If it is true that when the World-Honored One was first born, the devas above played celestial music, and heavenly blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, white lotuses, heavenly mandārava flowers, and finely powdered sandalwood incense were scattered upon the World-Honored One, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once at his father King Śuddhodana's estate, during the day overseeing the farming work, seated beneath a jambu tree. Separated from desires and separated from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of separation, he attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna. At that time, past midday, the shadows of all other trees had shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the jambu tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. Then the Śākyan Śuddhodana went to observe the farming work, and upon reaching the workers, he asked: 'Workers! Where is the boy?' The workers answered: 'The divine boy is now under the jambu tree.' Then the Śākyan Śuddhodana went to the jambu tree. At that time, past midday, the Śākyan Śuddhodana saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the jambu tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. He then thought: 'This boy is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might. Why is this? Because past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the jambu tree did not move, sheltering the boy's body.' If it is true that past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the jambu tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once traveling in Vaiśālī, in the Great Forest. At that time, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for food. After begging for food was finished, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, went into the forest, arrived at a tāla tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat in full cross-legged posture. Past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the tāla tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. At that time, the Śākyan Mahānāma, past midday, was strolling about and came to the Great Forest. Past midday, the Śākyan Mahānāma saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the tāla tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. He then thought: 'The ascetic Gautama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might. Why is this? Because past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the tāla tree did not move, sheltering the body of the ascetic Gautama.' If it is true that past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the tāla tree did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once traveling in Vaiśālī, in the Great Forest. At that time, the bhikṣus had placed their bowls out in the open. The World-Honored One's bowl was also among them. A monkey took the Buddha's bowl and departed. The bhikṣus scolded it, fearing it would break the Buddha's bowl. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'Stop! Stop! Do not scold it. It will not break the bowl.' At that time, the monkey took the Buddha's bowl and went to a śāla tree. It slowly climbed the tree, and from atop the śāla tree took honey until the bowl was full, then slowly descended the tree, returned to where the Buddha was, and offered the bowl of honey up to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One did not accept it. Then the monkey went aside, removed the twigs and insects. Having removed the insects, it brought it back to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha again did not accept it. The monkey again went aside, took water and mixed it into the honey, then brought it back to offer to the Buddha. The World-Honored One then accepted it. When the monkey saw the Buddha take the honey bowl, it rejoiced and was elated, danced about playfully stepping backward, whirled around, and departed. If it is true that the World-Honored One caused that monkey, upon seeing the World-Honored One take the honey bowl, to rejoice and be elated, to dance about playfully stepping backward, whirl around, and depart, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once traveling in Vaiśālī at the Monkey Pond Pavilion. At that time, the World-Honored One was airing his bedding in the sun, shaking and dusting it. At that time, a great unseasonable cloud came and covered the entire sky, about to rain, yet it waited for the World-Honored One. After the World-Honored One had aired his bedding in the sun, shaken and dusted it, and put it away in one place, he took a broom and stood on the platform of the building. Then the great cloud, having seen the World-Honored One put away his bedding, poured down a heavy rain, flooding the low and high ground until it was level and full. If it is true that the World-Honored One caused that great cloud, having seen the World-Honored One put away his bedding, to pour down a heavy rain, flooding the low and high ground until it was level and full, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once traveling among the Vajjians, seated under the king of śāla trees in the Hot Springs Grove. Past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the king of śāla trees did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. At that time, the caretaker of Rāma's park, while making his rounds, past midday, saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the king of śāla trees did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One. He then thought: 'The ascetic Gautama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual might. Why is this? Because past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the king of śāla trees did not move, sheltering the body of the ascetic Gautama.' If it is true that past midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted and moved, but only the shadow of the king of śāla trees did not move, sheltering the body of the World-Honored One, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once in the Āpana spirit hall. At that time, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village of Āpana to beg for food. After begging for food was finished, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, entered the spirit hall and sat in meditation. At that time, there was a great thunderstorm with hail that killed four oxen and two plowmen. When they were carrying out the funeral, a great crowd was in an uproar, with loud voices and sounds that shook the air. Then the World-Honored One, in the afternoon, rose from meditation, came out of the spirit hall, and walked in the open air. At that time, one person in that great crowd saw the World-Honored One in the afternoon rise from meditation, come out of the spirit hall, and walk in the open air. He then went to the Buddha, bowed his head in salutation, and followed the Buddha in walking meditation. The Buddha saw him behind and asked that person: 'For what reason was the great crowd in an uproar, with loud voices and sounds that shook the air?' The person said: 'World-Honored One! Today there was a great thunderstorm with hail that killed four oxen and two plowmen. When they were carrying out the funeral, the great crowd was in an uproar, with loud voices and sounds that shook the air. World-Honored One! Did you not hear the sound just now?' The World-Honored One replied: 'I did not hear the sound.' He further asked: 'World-Honored One! Were you asleep just now?' He answered: 'No.' He further asked: 'World-Honored One! Were you awake but did not hear this great sound?' He answered: 'That is so.' At that time, the person thought: 'How extraordinary! How remarkable! How extremely calm and peaceful are the practices of the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One! Why is this? Because while awake, he did not hear this great sound.' If it is true that the World-Honored One, while awake, did not hear this great sound, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One was once at Uruvelā, by the Nairañjanā River, under the Ajapāla banyan tree, having first attained the way of Buddhahood. At that time, a great rain fell for seven days, and both high and low ground were completely flooded, with floodwaters flowing everywhere. Yet the World-Honored One walked in meditation in the open air amidst this, and where he walked, dust arose. If it is true that while floodwaters flowed everywhere, the World-Honored One walked in meditation in the open air amidst this, and where he walked, dust arose, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that Māra, the Evil One, pursued the Buddha for six years, seeking his faults and weaknesses, but could find no opportunity. Wearied, he departed. If it is true that Māra, the Evil One, pursued the World-Honored One for six years, seeking his faults and weaknesses, but could find no opportunity, and wearied, departed, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One practiced mindfulness of the body for seven years, with constant mindfulness unbroken. If it is true that the World-Honored One practiced mindfulness of the body for seven years, with constant mindfulness unbroken, I accept and uphold this as an unprecedented dharma of the World-Honored One."

Then the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! You should further accept and uphold from the Tathāgata this unprecedented dharma. Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows when feelings arise, knows when they persist, knows when they cease; he always knows, and there is no time when he does not know. Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows when thoughts arise, knows when they persist, knows when they cease; he always knows, and there is no time when he does not know. Therefore, Ānanda, you should further accept and uphold from the Tathāgata this unprecedented dharma."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Unprecedented Dharmas, the First.

---

## (33) Sūtra on the Attendant, Second of the Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha.

At that time, many well-known, virtuous, senior elder bhikṣus and great disciples were present: the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika the Śākyan prince, the Venerable Mahānāma Kaulya, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāṃpati, the Venerable Sudāya, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandika, the Venerable Kimbila, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra the Elder, the Venerable Yaśas the tally-keeper Elder, and many other such well-known, virtuous, senior elder bhikṣus and great disciples, who were also traveling in Rājagṛha, all staying near the Buddha's leaf hut.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I am now old. My body grows increasingly decrepit, and my lifespan is nearly at its end. I should have an attendant. You should nominate an attendant for me, one who can attend to me, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and who can receive what I teach without losing its meaning."

Then the Venerable Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, put his palms together toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! I am willing to serve and attend, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what you teach without losing its meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Kauṇḍinya! You yourself are old. Your body grows increasingly decrepit, and your lifespan is nearly at its end. You yourself should have someone to attend to you. Kauṇḍinya! Return to your seat." Then the Venerable Kauṇḍinya bowed at the Buddha's feet and returned to his seat.

Likewise, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika the Śākyan prince, the Venerable Mahānāma Kaulya, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāṃpati, the Venerable Sudāya, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandika, the Venerable Kimbila, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra the Elder.

The Venerable Yaśas the tally-keeper Elder rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, put his palms together toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! I am willing to serve and attend, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what you teach without losing its meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Yaśas! You yourself are old. Your body grows increasingly decrepit, and your lifespan is nearly at its end. You yourself should have someone to attend to you. Yaśas! Return to your seat." Then the Venerable Yaśas bowed at the Buddha's feet and returned to his seat.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who was in that assembly, thought: "Whom does the World-Honored One wish to have as his attendant? Which bhikṣu does he have in mind, to attend to him, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what he teaches without losing its meaning? I should enter a samādhi of corresponding form and observe the minds of the assembled bhikṣus." Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered a samādhi of corresponding form and observed the minds of the assembled bhikṣus. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew that the World-Honored One wished the Venerable Ānanda to be his attendant, that his mind was set on Ānanda, to attend to him, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what he teaches without losing its meaning. Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from samādhi and addressed the assembled bhikṣus: "Venerables, did you know? The World-Honored One wishes the Venerable Ānanda to be his attendant. His mind is set on Ānanda, to attend to him, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what he teaches without losing its meaning. Venerables, we should all go together to the Venerable Ānanda's place and encourage him to become the World-Honored One's attendant."

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the bhikṣus all went to the Venerable Ānanda's place, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having sat down, said: "Venerable Ānanda! Do you know? The Buddha wishes you to be his attendant. 'His mind is set on Ānanda, to attend to me, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what I teach without losing its meaning.' Ānanda, it is like a pavilion outside a village, not far away, with windows opening to the east; when the sun rises, its light falls upon the western wall. Venerable Ānanda! The World-Honored One is likewise. He wishes the Venerable Ānanda to be his attendant. 'His mind is set on Ānanda, to attend to me, approving what is right and disapproving what is not, and to receive what I teach without losing its meaning.' Venerable Ānanda! You should now become the World-Honored One's attendant."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana! I am not capable of serving the World-Honored One. Why is this? All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, are difficult to serve and difficult to attend to as attendants. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, it is like a king's great bull elephant, full sixty years old, proud and vigorous, with powerful tusks, feet, and body complete, difficult to approach and difficult to attend to as a caretaker. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One is likewise; he is difficult to approach and difficult to serve as an attendant. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, for this reason, I am not fit to be his attendant."

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana further said: "Venerable Ānanda! Hear my simile. The wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Venerable Ānanda, it is like the udumbara flower, which appears in the world only from time to time. Venerable Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One likewise appears in the world only from time to time. Venerable Ānanda! You should quickly become the World-Honored One's attendant. Gautama will obtain great fruit."

The Venerable Ānanda further replied: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If the World-Honored One grants me three wishes, I will then agree to become the Buddha's attendant. What are the three? I wish not to wear the Buddha's new or old robes. I wish not to eat food from special invitations meant for the Buddha. I wish not to see the Buddha at improper times. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the World-Honored One grants me these three wishes, then I will become the Buddha's attendant."

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having encouraged the Venerable Ānanda to become the attendant, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda, and then departed. He went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I have encouraged the Venerable Ānanda to become the Buddha's attendant. World-Honored One, the Venerable Ānanda requests three wishes from the Buddha. 'What are the three? I wish not to wear the Buddha's new or old robes. I wish not to eat food from special invitations meant for the Buddha. I wish not to see the Buddha at improper times. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the World-Honored One grants me these three wishes, then I will become the Buddha's attendant.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana! The bhikṣu Ānanda is wise and intelligent; he foresaw that there might be criticism, with fellow practitioners of the holy life saying: 'The bhikṣu Ānanda serves the World-Honored One for the sake of robes.' Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the bhikṣu Ānanda, being wise and intelligent, foresaw that there might be criticism, with fellow practitioners of the holy life saying: 'The bhikṣu Ānanda serves the World-Honored One for the sake of robes,' this is an unprecedented dharma of the bhikṣu Ānanda. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Ānanda is wise and intelligent; he foresaw that there might be criticism, with fellow practitioners of the holy life saying: 'The bhikṣu Ānanda serves the World-Honored One for the sake of food.' Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the bhikṣu Ānanda, being wise and intelligent, foresaw that there might be criticism, with fellow practitioners of the holy life saying: 'The bhikṣu Ānanda serves the World-Honored One for the sake of food,' this is an unprecedented dharma of the bhikṣu Ānanda.
