Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu Ānanda knows the proper time well and distinguishes the time well. He knows when it is the proper time for him to go and see the Tathāgata. He knows when it is not the proper time for him to go and see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows which of those many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are able to debate with the Tathāgata. He knows which of those many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are not able to debate with the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, brings ease and benefit to the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, does not bring ease and benefit to the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, allows the Tathāgata to attain eloquence in teaching the Dharma. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, does not allow the Tathāgata to attain eloquence in teaching the Dharma. This is an unprecedented dharma of the bhikṣu Ānanda.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, although the bhikṣu Ānanda does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, he nevertheless knows well when the Tathāgata rises from meditation in the afternoon, and announces in advance to people: 'Today the Tathāgata practices in such and such a way, abiding in the bliss of the present dharma.' What he says is truly accurate, without any discrepancy. This is an unprecedented dharma of the bhikṣu Ānanda."

The Venerable Ānanda made this statement: "Venerables, I have attended the Buddha for twenty-five years. If, because of this, I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is no such occurrence." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I have attended the Buddha for twenty-five years, and I have never once gone to see the Buddha at an improper time." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I have attended the Buddha for twenty-five years, and I have never been rebuked by the Buddha, except for one occasion, and that too was on account of another person." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I received eighty thousand collections of Dharma from the Tathāgata, received and upheld them without forgetting. If, because of this, I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is no such occurrence." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I received eighty thousand collections of Dharma from the Tathāgata. I never once had to ask again, except for one passage, and that one also remained unchanged." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I received and upheld eighty thousand collections of Dharma from the Tathāgata. I never once recalled receiving Dharma from any other person." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I received and upheld eighty thousand collections of Dharma from the Tathāgata. I never once had the thought: 'I receive this Dharma in order to teach and tell others.' Venerables, it was only for the sake of self-mastery, self-calming, and self-attainment of nirvāṇa." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, this is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! That the fourfold assembly comes to my place to hear the Dharma. If, because of this, I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is absolutely no such occurrence. Nor did I ever plan in advance, thinking: 'If someone comes to ask, I shall answer in such and such a way.' Venerables, it is only at the time of being seated that I respond according to the meaning as appropriate." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, this is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! That many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins come to question me. If, because of this, I had any fear, any dread, or my hair stood on end, there is absolutely no such occurrence. Nor did I ever plan in advance, thinking: 'If someone comes to ask, I shall answer in such and such a way.' Venerables, it is only at the time of being seated that I respond according to the meaning as appropriate." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

Furthermore, at one time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Ānanda were in the state of Śrāvastī, on Mount Bāralā. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Venerable Ānanda! You have attended the Buddha for twenty-five years. Do you recall ever having given rise to desire?" The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Śāriputra! I am a learner and have not yet eliminated desire." The Venerable Śāriputra further said: "Venerable Ānanda! I am not asking whether you are a learner or beyond learning. I am only asking whether, in the twenty-five years you have attended the Buddha, you recall ever having given rise to desire." The Venerable Śāriputra asked a second and a third time: "Venerable Ānanda! In the twenty-five years you have attended the Buddha, do you recall ever having given rise to desire?" The Venerable Ānanda also replied a second and a third time: "Venerable Śāriputra! I am a learner and have not yet eliminated desire." The Venerable Śāriputra further said: "Venerable Ānanda! I am not asking whether you are a learner or beyond learning. I am only asking whether, in the twenty-five years you have attended the Buddha, you recall ever having given rise to desire." Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Venerable Ānanda! Answer quickly, answer quickly. Ānanda, do not cause trouble for the senior elder." Then the Venerable Ānanda replied: "Venerable Śāriputra! In the twenty-five years I have attended the Buddha, I do not recall ever having given rise to desire. Why is this? Because I always had a sense of shame and conscience toward the Buddha and toward the wise practitioners of the holy life." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

Furthermore, at one time, the World-Honored One was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying at the Vulture Peak. At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! When you lie down, you should follow the lion's method of lying." The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! What is the lion king's method of lying?" The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, during the day, the lion king goes out seeking food. When done, he enters his cave. When he wishes to sleep, he places one paw upon the other, extends his tail behind him, and lies on his right side. After the night has passed at dawn, he turns his head and looks at his body. If the lion king's body is not properly arranged, seeing this, he is displeased. If the lion king's body is properly arranged, seeing this, he is pleased. After rising from lying, he comes out from his cave. Having come out, he stretches. Having stretched, he examines his own body. Having examined his own body, he looks in all four directions. Having looked in all four directions, he roars three times. Having roared three times, he goes out seeking food. Such is the lion king's method of lying."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! Such is the lion king's method of lying. How then should a bhikṣu lie?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, when a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village, after the night has passed at dawn, he puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village to beg for food, properly guarding his body, restraining his faculties, and establishing right mindfulness. When begging for food in the village is finished, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and goes to a secluded place, or to the base of a tree, or to an empty room. He either walks in meditation or sits in meditation, purifying his mind of obstructive dharmas. During the day, either walking in meditation or sitting in meditation, having purified his mind of obstructive dharmas, then in the first watch of the night, he either walks in meditation or sits in meditation, purifying his mind of obstructive dharmas. In the first watch of the night, either walking in meditation or sitting in meditation, having purified his mind of obstructive dharmas, in the middle watch of the night, he enters his room wishing to lie down. He folds his outer robe four times and spreads it on the bed, folds his saṅghāṭī to make a pillow, lies on his right side, places one foot upon the other, fixes his attention on the perception of light, with right mindfulness and clear awareness, and constantly contemplates the thought of arising. In the last watch of the night, he quickly rises from lying and either walks in meditation or sits in meditation, purifying his mind of obstructive dharmas. Such is the bhikṣu's lion method of lying." The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! Such is the bhikṣu's lion method of lying."

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, since the World-Honored One taught me the simile of the lion's method of lying, from that time on, I have never once lain on my left side." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

Furthermore, at one time, the World-Honored One was traveling in Kuśinagara, staying in the Mallas' śāla grove at Upavattana. At that time, the World-Honored One, about to take final nirvāṇa for the last time, said: "Ānanda! Go to the space between the twin śāla trees and prepare a bed for the Tathāgata with the head pointing north. The Tathāgata will attain final nirvāṇa in the middle of the night."

The Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Tathāgata's instruction, went to the twin trees and prepared a bed for the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees with the head pointing north. When the bed was prepared, he returned to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! The bed has been prepared for the Tathāgata between the twin trees with the head pointing north. May the World-Honored One know the proper time."

Then the World-Honored One, accompanied by the Venerable Ānanda, went to the space between the twin trees. He folded his outer robe four times and spread it on the bed, folded his saṅghāṭī to make a pillow, and lay on his right side with one foot upon the other. At the time of his final nirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda held a fan and attended the Buddha, wiping away tears with his hand, and thought: "Previously, bhikṣus from various regions would come wishing to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings and pay respects, and all could see the World-Honored One in due time, making offerings and paying respects. If they hear that the World-Honored One has attained final nirvāṇa, they will no longer come to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings and pay respects. I too will no longer be able to see the Buddha in due time, to make offerings and pay respects."

Then the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?" At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One! The Venerable Ānanda is holding a fan and attending the Buddha, wiping away tears with his hand, and thinking: 'Previously, bhikṣus from various regions would come wishing to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings and pay respects, and all could see the World-Honored One in due time, making offerings and paying respects. If they hear that the World-Honored One has attained final nirvāṇa, they will no longer come to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings and pay respects. I too will no longer be able to see the Buddha in due time, to make offerings and pay respects.'"

Then the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! Do not weep, and do not be sorrowful. Why is this? Ānanda, you have attended me with bodily acts of lovingkindness, verbal and mental acts of lovingkindness, with never a duplicitous heart, immeasurable, boundless, and limitless in comfort and well-being. Ānanda, if in the past there were Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones who had attendants, none surpassed you. Ānanda, if in the future there will be Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have attendants, none will surpass you. Ānanda, for me, the present Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, if there is an attendant, none surpasses you. Why is this? Ānanda knows the proper time well and distinguishes the time well. He knows when it is the proper time for him to go and see the Tathāgata. He knows when it is not the proper time for him to go and see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the community of upāsakas and the community of upāsikās should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins should go to see the Tathāgata. He knows when the many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins should not go to see the Tathāgata. He knows which of those many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are able to debate with the Tathāgata. He knows which of those many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are not able to debate with the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, brings ease and benefit to the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, does not bring ease and benefit to the Tathāgata. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, allows the Tathāgata to attain eloquence in teaching the Dharma. He knows which food, when eaten and digested, does not allow the Tathāgata to attain eloquence in teaching the Dharma. Furthermore, Ānanda, although you do not possess the knowledge of others' minds, you nevertheless anticipate that when the Tathāgata rises from meditation in the afternoon, you announce in advance to people: 'Today the Tathāgata practices in such and such a way, abiding in the bliss of the present dharma.' What you say is truly accurate, without any discrepancy."

Then the World-Honored One, wishing to bring joy to the Venerable Ānanda, addressed the bhikṣus: "A wheel-turning holy king obtains four unprecedented dharmas. What are the four? When the kṣatriya assembly goes to see the wheel-turning king, if he is silent, they are pleased upon seeing him; if he speaks, they are pleased upon hearing him. When the brahmin assembly, the householder assembly, and the śramaṇa assembly go to see the wheel-turning king, if he is silent, they are pleased upon seeing him; if he speaks, they are pleased upon hearing him. The bhikṣu Ānanda likewise obtains four unprecedented dharmas. What are the four? When the community of bhikṣus goes to see Ānanda, if he is silent, they are pleased upon seeing him; if he speaks, they are pleased upon hearing him. When the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the community of upāsakas, and the community of upāsikās go to see Ānanda, if he is silent, they are pleased upon seeing him; if he speaks, they are pleased upon hearing him.

"Furthermore, when Ānanda teaches the Dharma to the assembly, there are four unprecedented dharmas. What are the four? When the bhikṣu Ānanda teaches the Dharma to the community of bhikṣus, he teaches wholeheartedly, not insincerely. That community of bhikṣus also thinks: 'May the Venerable Ānanda always teach the Dharma and never stop midway.' That community of bhikṣus, hearing the Venerable Ānanda teach the Dharma, is never satiated; yet the bhikṣu Ānanda stops on his own and abides in silence. When he teaches the Dharma to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the community of upāsakas, and the community of upāsikās, he teaches wholeheartedly, not insincerely. The community of upāsikās also thinks: 'May the Venerable Ānanda always teach the Dharma and never stop midway.' The community of upāsikās, hearing the Venerable Ānanda teach the Dharma, is never satiated; yet the bhikṣu Ānanda stops on his own and abides in silence."

Furthermore, at one time, not long after the Buddha's final nirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling in Vajra, staying in the village of Vajra. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, with countless hundreds of thousands surrounding him in front and behind, was teaching the Dharma. At that time, the Venerable Vajrapuṭa was also in the assembly. The Venerable Vajrapuṭa thought: "This Venerable Ānanda, is he still a learner who has not yet eliminated desire? I should enter a samādhi of corresponding form, and with the samādhi of corresponding form, observe the mind of the Venerable Ānanda." Then the Venerable Vajrapuṭa entered a samādhi of corresponding form, and with the samādhi of corresponding form, observed the mind of the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Vajrapuṭa then knew that the Venerable Ānanda was still a learner who had not yet eliminated desire.

Then the Venerable Vajrapuṭa rose from samādhi and, facing the Venerable Ānanda, spoke this verse:

"In mountain forests, quietly contemplate;
Let nirvāṇa enter your heart.
Gautama, meditate without distraction;
Before long, you will realize and attain cessation of the path."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, receiving the instruction of the Venerable Vajrapuṭa, left the assembly and went alone, practicing with diligence and without distraction. Leaving the assembly and going alone, practicing with diligence and without distraction, as a son of good family who, having shaved off his beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household for homelessness to train in the path, seeks only the completion of the supreme holy life. He then, in the present life, knew for himself, realized for himself, and abiding in self-realization, attained the accomplishment: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence." He knew it as it truly is. The Venerable Ānanda, having known the Dharma, ultimately attained arhatship. The Venerable Ānanda made this statement: "Venerables, while I was on my bed, before my head had even reached the pillow, I cut off all the outflows and attained liberation of mind." If the Venerable Ānanda made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

The Venerable Ānanda further made this statement: "Venerables, I shall sit in full cross-legged posture and attain final nirvāṇa." The Venerable Ānanda then sat in full cross-legged posture and attained final nirvāṇa. If the Venerable Ānanda sat in full cross-legged posture and attained final nirvāṇa, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Ānanda.

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Attendant, the Second.

---

## (34) Sūtra on Bakkula, Third of the Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, not long after the Buddha's final nirvāṇa, the Venerable Bakkula was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, Kalandaka Park.

At that time, a certain non-Buddhist wanderer, who had been a close friend of the Venerable Bakkula before he left the household life, in the afternoon came strolling to the place of the Venerable Bakkula. They exchanged greetings, and the wanderer sat to one side. The wanderer said: "Venerable Bakkula! I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to be heard?"

The Venerable Bakkula answered: "Wanderer! Ask as you wish. Having heard, I shall consider."

The wanderer asked: "Venerable Bakkula! How long have you been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya?"

The Venerable Bakkula answered: "Wanderer! I have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya for eighty years."

The wanderer further asked: "Venerable Bakkula! In the eighty years since you have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, do you recall ever having engaged in sexual intercourse?"

The Venerable Bakkula said to the wanderer: "You should not ask such a question. Ask something else instead. You should ask: 'Venerable Bakkula, in the eighty years since you have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, do you recall ever having given rise to thoughts of desire?' Wanderer, you should ask it in this way."

Then the wanderer said: "I will now ask the Venerable Bakkula again. In the eighty years since you have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, do you recall ever having given rise to thoughts of desire?"

Then the Venerable Bakkula, on account of the wanderer's question, addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, in the eighty years since I have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, if because of this I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is absolutely no such thought." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, in the eighty years since I have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, I have never had a thought of desire." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, I have worn rag-robes for eighty years. If because of this I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is absolutely no such occurrence." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, I have worn rag-robes for eighty years. I have never recalled accepting robes from householders, never cut and sewn robes, never asked another bhikṣu to make robes for me, never used a needle to sew robes, never held a needle and sewing pouch, not even for a single thread." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, I have begged for food for eighty years. If because of this I had ever given rise to arrogance, there is absolutely no such occurrence." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, I have begged for food for eighty years. I have never recalled accepting a householder's invitation to a meal, never skipped houses while begging for food, never begged from a wealthy family thinking that I would receive pure, excellent, supremely fine, abundant food to eat and consume. I have never looked at a woman's face, never recalled entering a bhikṣuṇī's quarters, never recalled exchanging greetings with a bhikṣuṇī, and not even on the road have I spoken with one." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, in the eighty years since I have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, I have never recalled having a novice attendant, and I have never recalled teaching the Dharma to a layperson, not even a four-line verse." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, in the eighty years since I have been training in the path in this True Dharma and Vinaya, I have never been ill, not even for a moment as brief as a finger-snap have I had a headache, and I have never recalled taking medicine, not even a single piece of myrobalan." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, in eighty years of sitting cross-legged, I have never leaned against a wall or leaned against a tree." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, within three days and nights, I attained the three knowledges and realized them." If the Venerable Bakkula made this statement, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: "Venerables, I shall sit in full cross-legged posture and attain final nirvāṇa." The Venerable Bakkula then sat in full cross-legged posture and attained final nirvāṇa. If the Venerable Bakkula sat in full cross-legged posture and attained final nirvāṇa, this is an unprecedented dharma of the Venerable Bakkula.

Thus spoke the Venerable Bakkula. At that time, the wanderer and the bhikṣus, having heard what was said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Bakkula, the Third.

---

## (35) Sūtra on the Asura, Fourth of the Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Verañjā, in the Reed Park.

At that time, Pāhārāda, king of the asuras, son of Mauliśīrṣa the asura, splendid in appearance and shining with radiance, as night was drawing toward dawn, went to where the Buddha was. He bowed at the World-Honored One's feet and stood to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Pāhārāda! In the great ocean among the asuras, is there no decline in the asuras' lifespan, the asuras' beauty, the asuras' happiness, or the asuras' power? Do the asuras take delight in the great ocean?"

Pāhārāda, king of the asuras, son of Mauliśīrṣa the asura, answered: "World-Honored One! In my great ocean, among the asuras, there is no decline in the asuras' lifespan, the asuras' beauty, the asuras' happiness, or the asuras' power. The asuras take delight in the great ocean."

The World-Honored One further asked: "Pāhārāda! How many unprecedented dharmas does the great ocean possess, that cause the asuras, upon seeing them, to take delight therein?"

Pāhārāda answered: "World-Honored One! My great ocean possesses eight unprecedented dharmas that cause the asuras, upon seeing them, to take delight therein. What are the eight? World-Honored One, my great ocean, from bottom to top, widens gradually all around, slopes upward evenly, and thus forms its shores. Its water is always full and has never overflowed. World-Honored One, if my great ocean, from bottom to top, widens gradually all around, slopes upward evenly, and thus forms its shores, and its water is always full and has never overflowed, this is the first unprecedented dharma of my great ocean, which the asuras, upon seeing, take delight in.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, my great ocean's tides never miss their time. World-Honored One, if my great ocean's tides never miss their time, this is the second unprecedented dharma of my great ocean, which the asuras, upon seeing, take delight in.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, my great ocean's water is extremely deep and bottomless, vastly broad and boundless. World-Honored One, if my great ocean is extremely deep and bottomless, vastly broad and boundless, this is the third unprecedented dharma of my great ocean, which the asuras, upon seeing, take delight in.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, my great ocean's water is salty, all of one single flavor. World-Honored One, if my great ocean's water is salty, all of one single flavor, this is the fourth unprecedented dharma of my great ocean, which the asuras, upon seeing, take delight in.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, my great ocean contains many precious treasures, immeasurably varied and rare, of all kinds and types, filling it throughout. The names of these treasures are: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi gems, pearls, jade, white shells, conch shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, carnelian, and rosary beads. World-Honored One, if my great ocean contains many precious treasures, immeasurably varied and rare, of all kinds and types, filling it throughout, and the names of these treasures are: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi gems, pearls, jade, white shells, conch shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, carnelian, and rosary beads, this is the fifth unprecedented dharma

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 17

## (72) Sūtra on the Simile of the Long-Lived King (長壽王本起經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Long ago, in the distant past, there was a king named Long-Lived (Dīrghāyus). King Long-Lived was endowed with the Dharma, a Dharma-king who ruled by the Dharma. He governed the four kinds of people: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and workers. Each of these was governed according to the Dharma, and he did not rule unjustly. He practiced the ten wholesome courses of action and also taught the people to practice the ten wholesome courses of action. He abstained from killing living beings and abandoned killing living beings. He abandoned what is not given and abstained from taking what is not given. He abandoned sexual misconduct and abstained from sexual misconduct. He abandoned false speech and abstained from false speech. He abandoned divisive speech and abstained from divisive speech. He abandoned harsh speech and abstained from harsh speech. He abandoned idle chatter and abstained from idle chatter. He was without covetousness. He was without ill will. He held right views. He practiced these ten wholesome courses of action and also taught the people to practice these ten wholesome courses of action.

"At that time, King Long-Lived had a neighboring king named Brahmadatta, the king of Kāśī. King Brahmadatta was also endowed with power, but he was not a Dharma-king. He assembled his four armies: the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariots, and the infantry, and he marched against King Long-Lived's domain, wishing to attack it.

"King Long-Lived heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī had assembled his four armies and was marching to attack his domain. Having heard this, he reflected thus: 'King Brahmadatta of Kāśī has assembled his four armies and is coming to attack my domain. Even if I were to fight with him, on both sides many people would be killed and injured. I do not wish for the sake of a kingdom to cause the suffering and distress of sentient beings. Let me now abandon this kingdom and depart.'

"At that time, King Long-Lived, together with his chief queen and his crown prince named Long (Dīrgha), left his kingdom, taking only a single chariot, and departed. King Brahmadatta of Kāśī then took over King Long-Lived's kingdom entirely.

"King Long-Lived, having left his kingdom, traveled from place to place and eventually reached the city of Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśī. He stayed outside the city, in a certain place, disguised as a wanderer, and dwelt there with his queen. Before long, the queen became pregnant. At the time of her pregnancy, she developed an unusual craving: she wished to see an army arrayed in formation at sunrise, and to drink the water used for washing swords. She said to King Long-Lived: 'I now have a pregnancy craving. I wish to see, at the time of the rising sun, an army arrayed in four divisions, and I wish to drink the water used for washing swords. If I cannot obtain this, I may surely die.'

"King Long-Lived said: 'This is most difficult! We are in distressed circumstances. Where can we find such things?' He then went to a brahmin who served as the royal chaplain of King Brahmadatta, one with whom he had formerly been on good terms. He went to him and said: 'My friend, you should know that my wife is pregnant and has developed a craving. She wishes to see, at sunrise, the four armies arrayed, and to drink the water used for washing swords. My friend, please assist me.'

"The brahmin chaplain said: 'Do not worry. I will manage this for you.' He then went to King Brahmadatta and said: 'Your Majesty should know that the signs of the stars indicate that there will be a calamity. You should array the four armies at the time of sunrise to ward off the disaster, and the swords should be washed with water.' King Brahmadatta accepted the chaplain's words and ordered the four armies to be arrayed at the time of sunrise, and the swords to be washed with water.

"Then King Long-Lived led his queen to a place where they could observe. At sunrise, she saw the four armies arrayed and drank the water used for washing swords. Her craving was fulfilled.

"Before long, the queen gave birth to a son. His features were upright and handsome, and they named him Prince Long (Dīrgha). Prince Long gradually grew up and became intelligent and wise, accomplished in all arts. He could learn anything after hearing it only once.

"At that time, King Long-Lived thought: 'King Brahmadatta of Kāśī has taken my kingdom and has been my enemy. If someone should recognize me, he would surely kill all three of us: myself, my queen, and my son. Let me now send the prince away so that he may live elsewhere.' He then sent Prince Long away.

"Prince Long departed and went to a distant place, where he learned all the arts and became accomplished in every skill.

"After Prince Long had departed, before long, a certain person who had formerly been a subject of King Long-Lived recognized him and went to report to King Brahmadatta: 'Your Majesty should know that King Long-Lived, the former ruler, is now residing in the city of Vārāṇasī, disguised as a wanderer, together with his queen.'

"King Brahmadatta immediately ordered his men to seize King Long-Lived and his queen and bind them. He then ordered them to be paraded through the streets of Vārāṇasī, taken out through the southern gate, and executed at the southern charnel ground by cutting them into pieces.

"At that time, King Long-Lived and his queen were bound and paraded through the streets and marketplaces. At that time, Prince Long had returned and was in the city of Vārāṇasī. He was in the crowd and saw his father, King Long-Lived, bound and being paraded through the streets.

"King Long-Lived saw Prince Long in the crowd from afar. He then called out in a loud voice: 'Dear Long, do not look far, do not look near! For hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred. Dear Long, do not look far, do not look near! For hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred.'

"The people in the crowd all said: 'This King Long-Lived has gone mad! Who is this "Long" he is calling to? There is no one named Long here.' But King Long-Lived was in fact instructing his son Prince Long, and Prince Long understood his father's meaning.

"Then King Long-Lived and his queen were taken out through the southern gate and executed at the charnel ground, their bodies cut into pieces.

"Prince Long then went, procured wine, and gave it to the charnel ground guards to drink until they were drunk and fell asleep. He then gathered the remains of his father and mother, piled up wood, and cremated them. He joined his palms, circumambulated the pyre three times, and departed.

"Prince Long then went to the forest and wept bitterly, shedding tears until he was exhausted. He then wiped his tears and entered the city of Vārāṇasī. He went to the royal elephant stables and became an attendant, serving in the elephant stables. He would rise early in the morning and play music and sing songs. His voice was exceedingly beautiful.

"King Brahmadatta heard this voice from his palace and asked his attendants: 'Who is it that rises so early and plays music and sings? The voice is exceedingly beautiful.' The attendants replied: 'Your Majesty, it is a young man who recently came to serve in the elephant stables.'

"King Brahmadatta then summoned him and had him attend upon himself personally. Before long, Prince Long gained the king's deep trust and affection. The king appointed him to attend closely upon him in all matters, both inside and outside the palace. Whatever the king entrusted to him, he managed everything well.

"On one occasion, King Brahmadatta went hunting in the forest. Prince Long drove the chariot. He deliberately drove the chariot far from the rest of the hunting party until they were completely separated from the retinue and army. King Brahmadatta, being weary from the hunt, said to Prince Long: 'Dear young man, I am weary. I wish to rest and sleep for a while. Please watch over me.' Prince Long replied: 'Yes, Your Majesty, rest well. I will watch over you.' Then King Brahmadatta laid his head upon Prince Long's lap and fell asleep.

"Prince Long then thought: 'This King Brahmadatta has been the enemy of our family. He killed my father and mother and took our kingdom. Now he is my great enemy, and today the enemy is in my hands!' He then drew the king's sword and was about to strike, intending to cut off the king's head.

"But then he recalled his father's words: 'Dear Long, do not look far, do not look near! For hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred.' He then returned the sword to its sheath.

"He reflected again: 'My father and mother were killed by this man. He took our kingdom. He is truly my great enemy.' He drew the sword again.

"Again he recalled his father's words: 'Dear Long, do not look far, do not look near! For hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred.' He returned the sword to its sheath again.

"A third time the same thing happened. Three times he drew the sword and three times he returned it, each time recalling his father's admonition.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta had a nightmare in which he saw Prince Long, the son of King Long-Lived, drawing a sword to kill him. He awoke in terror and sat up abruptly. Prince Long said: 'Your Majesty, why are you so frightened?'

"King Brahmadatta said: 'Just now in a dream I saw Prince Long, the son of King Long-Lived, drawing a sword to kill me. That is why I am frightened.'

"Then Prince Long grasped King Brahmadatta's head with his left hand and drew the sword with his right hand, and said: 'I am Prince Long, the son of King Long-Lived! You killed my father and mother and took our kingdom. You are my great enemy. Now the time for revenge has come!'

"King Brahmadatta immediately bowed his head at Prince Long's feet and said: 'Dear Prince Long, please spare my life! Please spare my life!'

"Prince Long said: 'I can spare Your Majesty's life, but can Your Majesty spare my life? For I have plotted against the king, and the king may later wish to kill me.'

"King Brahmadatta said: 'Dear Prince Long, I grant you your life. Please grant me mine.'

"Then they each swore oaths to spare one another's lives. King Brahmadatta then said to Prince Long: 'What did your father mean when, as he was being led through the streets, he cried out: "Dear Long, do not look far, do not look near! For hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred"? What is the meaning of these words?'

"Prince Long replied: 'Your Majesty, my father's words, "do not look far," meant: do not let hatred last long. "Do not look near" meant: do not be quick to fall out with friends. "Hatred is not appeased by hatred; hatred is appeased only by non-hatred" meant: Your Majesty killed my father and mother. If I were to take revenge on Your Majesty, then Your Majesty's supporters would seek to kill me, and my supporters would seek to kill them. Thus, hatred would never cease. But now Your Majesty has granted me my life, and I have granted Your Majesty yours. Hatred is thus appeased by non-hatred. This is the meaning of my father's words.'

"King Brahmadatta was deeply moved and reflected: 'How wonderfully wise and accomplished this Prince Long is! He was able to understand such profound meaning from his father's brief words.' He then restored to Prince Long his father's kingdom, returned the queen's treasures, and gave his own daughter to Prince Long in marriage. The two kingdoms henceforth were at peace.

"Bhikṣus, King Long-Lived and Prince Long were both laypeople who were able to practice patient endurance with each other. How much more should you, who have shaved your heads and donned the kāṣāya robes, left home to practice the Way, practice patient endurance and gentleness, and be able to forgive one another!

"Bhikṣus, if you do not practice patient endurance and gentleness, and do not forgive one another, then this is not the practice of a renunciant. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall practice patient endurance and gentleness, and we shall be able to forgive one another.'

"Bhikṣus, you should train in this way."

When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, they were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (73) Sūtra on the Heavenly Palace (天經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are four kinds of persons found in the world. What are the four? The first is a person who practices that which is disadvantageous to himself and not beneficial to others. The second is a person who practices that which is beneficial to others but not to himself. The third is a person who practices that which is neither beneficial to himself nor to others. The fourth is a person who practices that which is beneficial both to himself and to others.

"What is the person who practices that which is disadvantageous to himself and not beneficial to others? Here, a certain person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, drinks alcohol, and brings harm upon himself through such practices. Furthermore, he does not encourage others to give, does not encourage others to keep the precepts, and does not benefit others. This is called a person who practices that which is disadvantageous to himself and not beneficial to others.

"What is a person who practices that which is beneficial to others but not to himself? Here, a certain person himself kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and drinks alcohol. Yet he encourages others to give, encourages others to keep the precepts, and benefits others. This is called a person who practices that which is beneficial to others but not to himself.

"What is a person who practices that which is neither beneficial to himself nor to others? Here, a certain person himself kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and drinks alcohol. He also does not encourage others to give, does not encourage others to keep the precepts, and does not benefit others. This is called a person who practices that which is neither beneficial to himself nor to others.

"What is a person who practices that which is beneficial both to himself and to others? Here, a certain person himself does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not drink alcohol. He also encourages others to give, encourages others to keep the precepts, and benefits others. This is called a person who practices that which is beneficial both to himself and to others.

"Among these four kinds of persons, the one who practices that which is neither beneficial to himself nor to others is the lowest and most inferior. The one who practices that which is disadvantageous to himself but beneficial to others is superior to the previous one. The one who practices that which is beneficial to himself but not to others is superior to the previous two. The one who practices that which is beneficial both to himself and to others is the foremost, the highest, the best, the most supreme among the four.

"Just as from the cow comes milk, from milk comes cream, from cream comes butter, from butter comes clarified butter, and clarified butter is the foremost and most supreme, so too, among these four kinds of persons, the one who practices that which is beneficial both to himself and to others is the foremost, the highest, the best, and the most supreme."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and practiced accordingly.

---

## (74) Sūtra on the Eight Thoughts (八念經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Bhagga country, in the Deer Park at Suṃsumāragiri, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying in the country of Cedi, in a certain forest grove. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was sitting in quiet contemplation, and this thought arose in his mind: "This Dharma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires. This Dharma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This Dharma is for one who delights in seclusion, not for one who delights in company. This Dharma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy. This Dharma is for one who is mindful, not for one who is forgetful. This Dharma is for one whose mind is concentrated, not for one whose mind is scattered. This Dharma is for one who has wisdom, not for one who lacks wisdom."

At that time, the World-Honored One, through supernatural power, knew what the Venerable Anuruddha was thinking. Just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, in that instant, the World-Honored One vanished from the Deer Park at Suṃsumāragiri in Bhagga country and appeared before the Venerable Anuruddha in the country of Cedi.

The World-Honored One sat down on a prepared seat, and the Venerable Anuruddha paid homage to the World-Honored One, then sat to one side. The World-Honored One said to the Venerable Anuruddha: "Excellent, excellent! Anuruddha, you have rightly contemplated the thoughts of a great person. You have thought: 'This Dharma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires. This Dharma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This Dharma is for one who delights in seclusion, not for one who delights in company. This Dharma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy. This Dharma is for one who is mindful, not for one who is forgetful. This Dharma is for one whose mind is concentrated, not for one whose mind is scattered. This Dharma is for one who has wisdom, not for one who lacks wisdom.'

"Anuruddha, you should now contemplate the eighth thought of a great person: 'This Dharma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who practices non-proliferation, and who takes pleasure in non-proliferation. It is not for one who delights in conceptual proliferation, who practices conceptual proliferation.'

"Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person, then whenever you wish, separated from sensual desires, separated from unwholesome dharmas, with initial application and sustained application, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, you will attain and dwell in the first dhyāna.

"Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person, then whenever you wish, with the stilling of initial application and sustained application, with inner tranquility and mental unification, without initial application and without sustained application, with joy and happiness born of concentration, you will attain and dwell in the second dhyāna.

"Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person, then whenever you wish, with the fading away of joy, you will abide in equanimity, mindful and clearly knowing, and experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous, mindful, and happily abiding,' you will attain and dwell in the third dhyāna.

"Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person, then whenever you wish, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the prior cessation of gladness and sadness, with neither-suffering-nor-happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, you will attain and dwell in the fourth dhyāna.

"Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person and also attain these four dhyānas, the happiness of the mind being attained at will, without difficulty and without trouble, then Anuruddha, just as a person who has many garments, whatever garment he wishes to wear in the morning, he wears it; whatever garment he wishes to wear at midday, he wears it; whatever garment he wishes to wear in the evening, he wears it. In the same way, Anuruddha, if you contemplate these eight thoughts of a great person and also attain these four dhyānas, obtaining the happiness of the mind at will, without difficulty and without trouble, you will then dwell in ease.

"Anuruddha, I now say to you: you should remain in this state and not be negligent. You should dwell in a secluded place, a forest, under a tree, in an empty and quiet place, in a mountain cave, or in the open wilderness. You should sit in meditation, mindfully contemplating, and not be negligent. Do not let there later be regret. This is my instruction to you."

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha, having heard the Buddha's teaching, was delighted and practiced accordingly. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, contemplating these eight thoughts of a great person, dwelling in a secluded place, practicing with diligence and without negligence, before long achieved the goal for which a son of good family rightly leaves the household life to practice the homeless life. In this present life, he himself realized through direct knowledge, attained, and dwelt in the state of the destruction of the outflows, the unsurpassed completion of the holy life. He knew: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being." The Venerable Anuruddha attained arhatship and became one of the arhats.

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha attained arhatship and spoke these verses:

"Knowing my thoughts from afar,
The Teacher of the world, the unsurpassed one,
Came to me by supernatural power,
And taught me more than I had thought.

The Buddha taught non-proliferation,
Delighting in the practice of non-proliferation.
I understood the Buddha's teaching,
And dwelt in accordance with the true Dharma.

Having mastered the three knowledges,
I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching.

In the last five hundred years,
A final bhikṣu am I.
All fetters are completely cut;
There is no more becoming.

Just as the Buddha, the Sun of Dharma,
Illuminates the teaching,
I too now pay homage
To the Supreme One, the Foremost."

When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, they were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (75) Sūtra on the Pure Way (淨不動道經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kuru, in the town of the Kurus called Kammāsadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The sensual pleasures of the world are impermanent, empty, false, deceptive, and of the nature of delusion. They are the talk of fools. The sensual pleasures of the present and the sensual pleasures of the future, the sensual perceptions of the present and the sensual perceptions of the future, are all the domain of Māra, the food of Māra, the lure of Māra. Because of them, unwholesome mental states arise: covetousness, ill will, and hostility. They become obstructions for a noble disciple who is training here.

"A noble disciple reflects thus: 'The sensual pleasures of the world in the present and in the future, the sensual perceptions of the present and in the future, are all the domain of Māra. Because of them, various unwholesome mental states arise in me. Let me now arouse a mind that is vast and boundless, and cultivate it. When I have cultivated a vast and boundless mind, then those unwholesome mental states of covetousness, ill will, and hostility that have arisen because of sensual pleasures will no longer exist, and they will no longer persist.'

"Having practiced this, having cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one attains the imperturbable, or one places confidence in wisdom. After the breakup of the body and the end of life, it is possible that the consciousness that has passed on and been reborn will attain the imperturbable. This is called the first path to the purification of the imperturbable.

"Furthermore, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Whatever there is of form, all form is the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.' When he thus contemplates form, he becomes disenchanted with form, his mind is freed from form, and his mind is liberated. Having practiced this, having cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one attains the imperturbable, or one places confidence in wisdom. After the breakup of the body and the end of life, it is possible that the consciousness that has passed on and been reborn will attain the imperturbable. This is called the second path to the purification of the imperturbable.

"Furthermore, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Whatever there is of sensual pleasures of the present or the future, sensual perceptions of the present or the future, whatever there is of form of the present or the future, form-perceptions of the present or the future, and whatever are the imperturbable perceptions: all these perceptions are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Having thus known and seen, one attains the base of nothingness.' Having practiced this, having cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one attains the base of nothingness, or one places confidence in wisdom. After the breakup of the body and the end of life, it is possible that the consciousness that has passed on and been reborn will attain the base of nothingness. This is called the first path to the purification of the base of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a noble disciple dwelling in a forest or at the root of a tree, in an empty and quiet place, reflects thus: 'This is empty of self or of what belongs to self.' Having practiced this, having cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one attains the base of nothingness, or one places confidence in wisdom. After the breakup of the body and the end of life, it is possible that the consciousness that has passed on and been reborn will attain the base of nothingness. This is called the second path to the purification of the base of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'I am not anything belonging to anyone anywhere, and there is nothing belonging to me in anyone anywhere.' Having practiced this, having cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one attains the base of nothingness, or one places confidence in wisdom. After the breakup of the body and the end of life, it is possible that the consciousness that has passed on and been reborn will attain the base of nothingness. This is called the third path to the purification of the base of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Whatever there is of sensual pleasures of the present or the future, sensual perceptions of the present or the future, whatever there is of form of the present or the future, form-perceptions of the present or the future, whatever are the imperturbable perceptions, whatever are the perceptions of the base of nothingness: all these perceptions are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' When he has thus known and seen, the mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the outflow of becoming, and the mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, one knows: 'I am liberated.' One knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'

"Furthermore, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'Whatever there is of sensual pleasures of the present or the future, sensual perceptions of the present or the future, whatever there is of form of the present or the future, form-perceptions of the present or the future, whatever are the imperturbable perceptions, whatever are the perceptions of the base of nothingness, whatever are the perceptions of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: all these are this identity, this identity is a disease, this identity is an abscess, this identity is a dart. That which is the cessation of this identity, that is the peaceful, that is the sublime, namely: the cessation of all formations, the relinquishing of all substrates of rebirth, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.'

"Having thus practiced, having thus cultivated this often, the mind finds joy in it. Having found joy, either in this present life one obtains the destruction of the outflows, or if there is any residual attachment, due to the delight in the Dharma and the delight in it, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, one is reborn spontaneously, attains parinirvāṇa there, and does not return from that world. This is called the path to the purification of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? If a bhikṣu practices in this way, is it possible that his practice will be detachment?"

The bhikṣus replied: "It can be so, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu practices in this way, this practice can indeed be called detachment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and practiced accordingly.

---

## (76) Sūtra on the郁伽支羅 (Ukkacela)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Vaiśālī, at Ukkacela, on the bank of the River Ganges.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Formerly, before the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa had appeared in the world, solitary pratyekabuddhas, numbering five hundred, dwelt together on Mount Isigili. They were seen entering the mountain but not seen coming out. The people therefore named that mountain Isigili, meaning 'the mountain that swallowed the sages.'

"I now shall recite the names of those pratyekabuddhas. If there is anyone who hears the names of these pratyekabuddhas and keeps them in mind, it will bring them benefit and happiness for a long time.

"Bhikṣus, there was a pratyekabuddha named Ariṭṭha. There was a pratyekabuddha named Upariṭṭha. There was a pratyekabuddha named Tagaraśikhin. There was a pratyekabuddha named Yasassin. There was a pratyekabuddha named Sudassana. There were pratyekabuddhas named Piyadassin, Gandhāra, Piṇḍola, Upāsabha, Nītha, Tatha, Sutavā, Bhāvitatta, and others."

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"I now bow my head in homage
To the five hundred pratyekabuddhas
Of Isigili Mountain,
All those who have passed beyond suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and practiced accordingly.

---

*End of Fascicle 17 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 9

## (36) Sūtra on the Earthquake, Fifth of the Chapter on Unprecedented Qualities

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Vajjian country, in a city called Bhūmi.

At that time, there was a great earthquake in that land. When the great earthquake occurred, great winds arose from all four sides, comets appeared in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapsed and were completely destroyed. Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda saw the great earthquake. When the great earthquake occurred, great winds arose from all four sides, comets appeared in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapsed and were completely destroyed.

Having seen this, the Venerable Ānanda was frightened, with hair standing on end all over his body. He went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! There has now been a great earthquake. When the great earthquake occurred, great winds arose from all four sides, comets appeared in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapsed and were completely destroyed."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "So it is, Ānanda! There has now been a great earthquake. So it is, Ānanda! When the great earthquake occurred, great winds arose from all four sides, comets appeared in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapsed and were completely destroyed."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! How many causes and conditions are there that produce a great earthquake, such that when the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! There are three causes and conditions that produce a great earthquake, such that when the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed. What are the three? Ānanda! This earth rests upon water, the water rests upon wind, and the wind depends upon space. Ānanda! At times a great wind arises in space; when the wind arises, the water is agitated; when the water is agitated, the earth quakes. This is called the first cause and condition that produces a great earthquake, such that when the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who possesses great psychic power, great authority, great merit, and great supernatural might, whose mind has mastery over psychic power: he forms a perception of the earth as small, and a perception of water as boundless. Because of this, the earth, according to his wish and according to his intention, is agitated again and again, shaken again and again. The guardian deva of the bhikṣu is likewise: possessing great psychic power, great authority, great merit, and great supernatural might, his mind having mastery over psychic power. He forms a perception of the earth as small, and a perception of water as boundless. Because of this, the earth, according to his wish and according to his intention, is agitated again and again, shaken again and again. This is called the second cause and condition that produces a great earthquake, such that when the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata will, in not long, after three months have passed, enter parinirvāṇa, because of this the earth quakes greatly. When the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed. This is called the third cause and condition that produces a great earthquake, such that when the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these words, wept with tears streaming, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! How extraordinary! How remarkable! The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has accomplished such merit and attained unprecedented qualities. Why is this? It is that when the Tathāgata will, in not long, after three months have passed, enter parinirvāṇa, at that time the earth quakes greatly. When the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed."

The World-Honored One said to the Venerable Ānanda: "So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda! How extraordinary! How remarkable! The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has accomplished such merit and attained unprecedented qualities. Why is this? It is that when the Tathāgata will, in not long, after three months have passed, enter parinirvāṇa, at that time the earth quakes greatly. When the great earthquake occurs, great winds arise from all four sides, comets appear in all four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are completely destroyed.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, I have gone to visit countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies of kṣatriyas, sat together with them in conversation, and made them pleased. After sitting together and settling in, my appearance became like their appearance; my voice became like their voice; my deportment and etiquette became like their deportment and etiquette. When they asked about the meaning, I answered their questions about the meaning. Furthermore, I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. With immeasurable skillful means I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. Having done so, I disappeared from that very place. After I had disappeared, they did not know who it was, whether a human or a non-human. Ānanda! This is how extraordinary, how remarkable it is! The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has accomplished such merit and attained unprecedented qualities. It is the same with assemblies of brahmins, assemblies of householders, and assemblies of śramaṇas.

"Ānanda! I have gone to visit countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies of the Four Great Kings' devas, sat together with them in conversation, and made them pleased. After sitting together and settling in, my appearance became like their appearance; my voice became like their voice; my deportment and etiquette became like their deportment and etiquette. When they asked about the meaning, I answered their questions about the meaning. Furthermore, I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. With immeasurable skillful means I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. Having done so, I disappeared from that very place. After I had disappeared, they did not know who it was, whether a deva or some other deva. Ānanda! This is how extraordinary, how remarkable it is! The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has accomplished such merit and attained unprecedented qualities. It is the same with the Thirty-Three devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, the Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Parīttābha devas, the Apramāṇābha devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Parīttaśubha devas, the Apramāṇaśubha devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Anābhraka devas, the Puṇyaprasava devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, the Avṛha devas, the Atapa devas, the Sudṛśa devas, and the Sudarśana devas.

"Ānanda! I have gone to visit countless hundreds of thousands of assemblies of the Akaniṣṭha devas, sat together with them in conversation, and made them pleased. After sitting together and settling in, my appearance became like their appearance; my voice became like their voice; my deportment and etiquette became like their deportment and etiquette. When they asked about the meaning, I answered their questions about the meaning. Furthermore, I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. With immeasurable skillful means I taught them the Dharma, arousing their aspiration and thirst, bringing them to accomplishment in joy. Having done so, I disappeared from that very place. After I had disappeared, they did not know who it was, whether a deva or some other deva. Ānanda! This is how extraordinary, how remarkable it is! The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has accomplished such merit and attained unprecedented qualities."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Fifth Sūtra, the Earthquake Sūtra.

---

## (37) Campā Sūtra, Sixth of the Chapter on Unprecedented Qualities in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Campā, staying beside the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.

At that time, the World-Honored One, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of reciting the Prātimokṣa, had a seat spread before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. After the World-Honored One sat down, he entered concentration, and with the knowledge of others' minds surveyed the minds of the assembly. Having surveyed the minds of the assembly, he sat in silence until the end of the first watch of the night.

Thereupon, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! The first watch of the night has ended. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been gathered sitting here for a long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa." At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.

Then the World-Honored One again sat in silence until the middle watch of the night. That bhikṣu rose from his seat a second time, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! The first watch has already passed and the middle watch is about to end. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been gathered sitting here for a long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa." The World-Honored One again remained silent and did not reply.

Then the World-Honored One again sat in silence until the last watch of the night. That bhikṣu rose from his seat a third time, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! The first watch has already passed, the middle watch is also ended, the last watch is nearly finished, dawn is approaching, and sunrise will not be long. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been gathered sitting here for an extremely long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa."

At that time, the World-Honored One told that bhikṣu: "In this assembly, there is one bhikṣu who has become impure." At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had this thought: "For which bhikṣu did the World-Honored One say that in this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure? I should enter the corresponding concentration and, with the knowledge of others' minds in that corresponding concentration, survey the minds of the assembly." The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then entered the corresponding concentration and, with the knowledge of others' minds in that corresponding concentration, surveyed the minds of the assembly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew the bhikṣu for whom the World-Honored One had said that in this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure.

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana emerged from concentration, went before that bhikṣu, grasped his arm and led him out, opened the door and put him outside, saying: "Foolish one, go far away! Do not remain here. You shall no longer be allowed to assemble with the community of bhikṣus. From now on, you are no longer a bhikṣu." He closed the door and locked it, then returned to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! The bhikṣu for whom the World-Honored One said that in this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure, I have already expelled him. World-Honored One! The first watch has already passed, the middle watch is also ended, the last watch is nearly finished, dawn is approaching, and sunrise will not be long. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been gathered sitting here for an extremely long time. May the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa."

The World-Honored One said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana! That foolish person will incur great wrongdoing for having disturbed and annoyed the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the Tathāgata were to recite the Prātimokṣa in an impure assembly, that person's head would split into seven pieces. Therefore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, from now on you all shall recite the Prātimokṣa; the Tathāgata will no longer recite the Prātimokṣa. Why is this? Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as the great ocean, from the bottom upward, gradually widens all around, uniformly slopes upward, forming its shore, and its water is always full, never overflowing, so too, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: there is gradual practice, gradual learning, gradual completion, and gradual instruction. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if my True Dharma and Vinaya have gradual practice, gradual learning, gradual completion, and gradual instruction, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as the great ocean's tides never miss their time, so too, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: the precepts established for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, the sons and daughters of good family will never, even unto the end of their lives, transgress the precepts. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if in my True Dharma and Vinaya the precepts established for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, the sons and daughters of good family will never, even unto the end of their lives, transgress the precepts, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as the waters of the great ocean are exceedingly deep and bottomless, extremely vast and boundless, so too, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: the dharmas are exceedingly profound, profoundly bottomless, extremely vast and boundless. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if in my True Dharma and Vinaya the dharmas are exceedingly profound, profoundly bottomless, extremely vast and boundless, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as the ocean water is salty, all of one taste, so too, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: the taste of desirelessness, the taste of awakening, the taste of cessation, and the taste of the path. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if my True Dharma and Vinaya have the taste of desirelessness, the taste of awakening, the taste of cessation, and the taste of the path, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as in the great ocean there are many precious treasures, countless marvels, all manner of rare wonders filling it. The names of these treasures are: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi gems, pearls, jade, white conch, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and bright jewels. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: there are many precious treasures, countless marvels, all manner of rare wonders filling it. The names of these treasures are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if my True Dharma and Vinaya have many precious treasures, countless marvels, all manner of rare wonders filling it, and the names of these treasures are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the Noble Eightfold Path, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as in the great ocean dwell great spirits. The names of these great spirits are: asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, fish, makara, turtles, crocodiles, pāluṇi, timiṅgila, timiṅgilagala, and titimiṅgilagala. Furthermore, in the great ocean, most extraordinary and remarkable, there are beings whose bodies are one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, up to seven hundred yojanas in length, and all dwell in the ocean. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: the noble assembly of great spirits all dwell therein. The names of these great spirits are: arhats, those on the path toward arhatship, non-returners, those on the path toward non-returning, once-returners, those on the path toward once-returning, stream-enterers, and those on the path toward stream-entry. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if in my True Dharma and Vinaya the noble assembly of great spirits all dwell therein, and the names of these great spirits are: arhats, those on the path toward arhatship, non-returners, those on the path toward non-returning, once-returners, those on the path toward once-returning, stream-enterers, and those on the path toward stream-entry, this is called an unprecedented quality in my True Dharma and Vinaya.

"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, just as the great ocean is pure and does not accept corpses. If someone dies therein, during the night the wind blows the body to the shore. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, my True Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: the noble assembly is pure and does not accept corpses. If there is someone who is not diligent, who is of evil birth, who is not living the holy life yet claims to live the holy life, who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, although he may remain among the noble assembly, he is far from the noble assembly, and the noble assembly is also far removed from him.
