## (78) Sūtra on Brahmā's Request

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Uruvelā, by the bank of the Nerañjarā River, beneath the Bodhi tree, having just attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having been in samādhi for seven days, at the end of seven days emerged from samādhi and, during the last watch of the night, with respect to dependent origination, contemplated it in forward and reverse order:

"This exists, therefore that exists; this arises, therefore that arises. Conditioned by ignorance, there are formations; conditioned by formations, there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging; conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there are old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire mass of suffering.

"This does not exist, therefore that does not exist; this ceases, therefore that ceases. Ignorance ceases, therefore formations cease; formations cease, therefore consciousness ceases; consciousness ceases, therefore name-and-form ceases; name-and-form ceases, therefore the six sense bases cease; the six sense bases cease, therefore contact ceases; contact ceases, therefore feeling ceases; feeling ceases, therefore craving ceases; craving ceases, therefore clinging ceases; clipping ceases, therefore becoming ceases; becoming ceases, therefore birth ceases; birth ceases, therefore old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair all cease. Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this meaning, then spoke these verses:

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
Then all his doubts and perplexities
Are entirely eliminated,
Because he has understood the dharmas,
Together with their causes and conditions."

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
He can dispel Māra's army,
Like the sun illuminating the sky."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having been in samādhi for seven days, at the end of seven days emerged from samādhi and, during the last watch of the night, with respect to dependent origination, contemplated it in forward and reverse order:

"This exists, therefore that exists; this arises, therefore that arises. Conditioned by ignorance, there are formations; conditioned by formations, there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging; conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there are old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire mass of suffering.

"This does not exist, therefore that does not exist; this ceases, therefore that ceases. Ignorance ceases, therefore formations cease; formations cease, therefore consciousness ceases; consciousness ceases, therefore name-and-form ceases; name-and-form ceases, therefore the six sense bases cease; the six sense bases cease, therefore contact ceases; contact ceases, therefore feeling ceases; feeling ceases, therefore craving ceases; craving ceases, therefore clinging ceases; clinging ceases, therefore becoming ceases; becoming ceases, therefore birth ceases; birth ceases, therefore old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair all cease. Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this meaning, then spoke these verses:

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
Then all his doubts and perplexities
Are entirely eliminated,
Because he has understood that suffering
Arises from causes and conditions."

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
He can dispel Māra's army,
Like the sun illuminating the sky."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having been in samādhi for seven days, at the end of seven days emerged from samādhi and, during the last watch of the night, with respect to dependent origination, contemplated it in forward and reverse order:

"This exists, therefore that exists; this arises, therefore that arises. Conditioned by ignorance, there are formations; conditioned by formations, there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact; conditioned by contact, there is feeling; conditioned by feeling, there is craving; conditioned by craving, there is clinging; conditioned by clinging, there is becoming; conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there are old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire mass of suffering.

"This does not exist, therefore that does not exist; this ceases, therefore that ceases. Ignorance ceases, therefore formations cease; formations cease, therefore consciousness ceases; consciousness ceases, therefore name-and-form ceases; name-and-form ceases, therefore the six sense bases cease; the six sense bases cease, therefore contact ceases; contact ceases, therefore feeling ceases; feeling ceases, therefore craving ceases; craving ceases, therefore clinging ceases; clinging ceases, therefore becoming ceases; becoming ceases, therefore birth ceases; birth ceases, therefore old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair all cease. Thus ceases this entire mass of suffering."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this meaning, then spoke these verses:

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
He stands firm and dispels all doubts,
Because he has understood
The cessation of causes and conditions."

"When a brāhmaṇa, through diligent practice,
Realizes all dharmas,
He can dispel Māra's army,
Like the sun illuminating the sky."

At that time, the World-Honored One thought: "The Dharma that I have attained is extremely profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand. It is quiescent, subtle, and wondrous; it is not something that can be reached through intellectual discrimination, and only the wise can know it. But the beings in this world take delight in attachment, rejoice in attachment, and are fond of attachment. For beings who take delight in attachment, rejoice in attachment, and are fond of attachment, this matter is extremely difficult to see, namely: the conditionality of this and that, dependent origination. This matter is also extremely difficult to see, namely: the stilling of all formations, the abandonment of all defilements, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa. If I were to teach the Dharma, others would not understand it. This would only bring me weariness and trouble."

At that time, the World-Honored One then quickly spoke these verses that had not been heard before:

"I have with great effort attained this Dharma;
I should not now quickly teach it.
This Dharma is hard for those with desire and anger to attain;
Going against the worldly current, it is extremely subtle and profound,
Delicate and wondrous, not discernible by those with great desire."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having had this thought, inclined toward inaction and did not wish to teach the Dharma. At that time, Brahmā, knowing in his mind the thoughts in the World-Honored One's mind, thought: "Now this world will surely be lost! This world will surely be ruined! For the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines toward inaction and does not wish to teach the Dharma."

At that time, Brahmā, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, in the same way, disappeared from the Brahmā heaven and appeared before the Buddha. He bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, placed his palms together facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, please teach the Dharma! Please teach the Dharma! There are beings with little dust in their eyes. If they do not hear the Dharma, they will decline and fall. Yet there are those who can understand the Dharma."

At that time, Brahmā spoke further in verse:

"In Magadha, in the past,
Impure dharmas were proclaimed.
Open now the gate of the deathless;
Let them hear the Dharma that the Purified One has realized.
Just as one standing atop a mountain peak
Can see people all around below,
So too, O all-wise sage,
Please ascend the palace of the Dharma.
The one free from sorrow surveys the sorrowing multitudes,
Those oppressed by birth, old age, and death.
Arise, O hero who has won the battle!
O caravan leader, free from debt,
Please walk through the world!
May the World-Honored One teach the Dharma;
There are surely those who can understand it."

At that time, the World-Honored One heard Brahmā's request and, out of compassion for all beings, observed the world with his Buddha-eye. The World-Honored One, observing the world with his Buddha-eye, saw that among beings there were some with little dust in their eyes and some with much dust in their eyes, some with sharp faculties and some with dull faculties, some with good dispositions and some with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach. Among those easy to teach, some could see the fear in the faults of the other world. It was like a pond with blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses. Some blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged beneath the water. Some blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and are level with the water's surface. Some blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, undefiled by the water.

In the same way, the World-Honored One observed the world with his Buddha-eye and saw that among beings there were some with little dust in their eyes and some with much dust in their eyes, some with sharp faculties and some with dull faculties, some with good dispositions and some with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach. Among those easy to teach, some could see the fear in the faults of the other world.

Having seen this, he said to Brahmā: "I now open wide the gate of the deathless for them. Let those with ears release their faith. Brahmā, it was because I perceived trouble that I did not wish to teach the Dharma to people; it was not out of spite or stinginess."

At that time, Brahmā knew that the World-Honored One had accepted his request and would teach the Dharma. He rejoiced, made obeisance at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and then disappeared.

Not long after Brahmā had departed, the World-Honored One thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" He then further thought: "Ārāḍa Kālāma is bright, intelligent, and wise. He has long had little dust in his eyes. I should first teach the Dharma to Ārāḍa Kālāma. He will be able to quickly understand this Dharma." Then a deva came through the air and said to the World-Honored One: "Ārāḍa Kālāma died seven days ago."

The World-Honored One also by himself knew: "Ārāḍa Kālāma died seven days ago." The World-Honored One then thought: "Ārāḍa Kālāma has suffered a great loss. If he had heard this Dharma, he would have been able to quickly understand it."

The World-Honored One again thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" He then further thought: "Udraka Rāmaputra is bright, intelligent, and wise. He has long had little dust in his eyes. I should first teach the Dharma to Udraka Rāmaputra. He will be able to quickly understand this Dharma." Then a deva came through the air and said to the World-Honored One: "Udraka Rāmaputra died last night."

The World-Honored One also by himself knew: "Udraka Rāmaputra died last night." The World-Honored One then thought: "Udraka Rāmaputra has suffered a great loss. If he had heard this Dharma, he would have been able to quickly understand it."

The World-Honored One again thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" He then further thought: "The group of five bhikṣus served me and attended to me for a long time during my practice of austerities. I should first teach the Dharma to the group of five bhikṣus." He further thought: "Where is the group of five bhikṣus now staying?" The World-Honored One then knew: "The group of five bhikṣus is now in Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana."

At that time, the World-Honored One, after staying at Uruvelā as long as he wished, set out on the road toward Vārāṇasī. Along the way, an Ājīvika named Upaka saw the World-Honored One coming from afar. Having seen him, he said: "Venerable Gautama, your faculties are serene, your complexion is pure and radiant. Venerable Gautama, under whom did you leave the household life? Who is your teacher? Whose Dharma do you delight in?"

At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Ājīvika Upaka in verse:

"I am the one who has overcome all,
The one who knows all dharmas.
Among all dharmas, I am undefiled;
I have abandoned everything and am liberated through the destruction of craving.
Having understood by myself, whom should I call my teacher?
I have no teacher;
No one is equal to me.
In this world with its devas,
None can match me.
I am the Arhat in this world;
I am the unsurpassed teacher.
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One;
My passions are cooled, and I have attained nirvāṇa.
I now go to the city of Kāśī
To beat the drum of the deathless.
In this world of darkness,
I will turn the unsurpassed Dharma wheel."

Upaka said: "Venerable Gautama, as you yourself claim, you should be the Victor of the Infinite." The World-Honored One replied: "Those who have attained the destruction of the outflows are indeed like me, the Victor. I have conquered all evil dharmas; therefore, Upaka, I am the Victor."

When the Ājīvika Upaka heard these words, he shook his head and departed, taking a different road. The World-Honored One, journeying gradually, arrived at Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, and approached the group of five bhikṣus.

The group of five bhikṣus saw the World-Honored One coming from afar. They saw him and agreed among themselves: "Here comes the ascetic Gautama. He is undisciplined and has abandoned his efforts, returning to a life of abundance. We should not rise to greet him, should not pay respect to him, should not receive his robe and bowl, but we should merely set out a seat. If he wishes to sit, let him sit."

When the World-Honored One approached, the group of five bhikṣus, unable to maintain their agreement, all rose from their seats and went out to greet him. One took his robe and bowl, one prepared a seat, one brought water for washing his feet. They addressed the World-Honored One by his given name and called him "friend."

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the group of five bhikṣus: "You should not address the Tathāgata by his given name or call him 'friend.' Why? Because the Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus: I have attained the deathless. I will instruct you and teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach, before long, sons of good families who leave the household life and shave their heads, donning the kāṣāya robes, faithfully leaving home for homelessness, will, in this very life, with their own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme end of the holy life, knowing: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more returning to any state of being.'"

The group of five bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, in the past, with your practices and austere ways, you were still unable to attain the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision. How can you now, living in abundance and having abandoned your efforts, returning to a life of luxury, have attained the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One said to the group of five bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata does not live in abundance and has not abandoned his efforts, returning to a life of luxury. The Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus: I have attained the deathless. I will instruct you and teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach, before long you will, in this very life, with your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme end of the holy life."

A second time, the group of five bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, in the past, with your practices and austere ways, you were still unable to attain the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision. How can you now, living in abundance and having abandoned your efforts, have attained the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One again said to the group of five bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata does not live in abundance and has not abandoned his efforts. The Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus: I have attained the deathless. I will instruct you and teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach, before long you will, in this very life, with your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme end of the holy life."

A third time, the group of five bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, in the past, with your practices and austere ways, you were still unable to attain the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision. How can you now, living in abundance and having abandoned your efforts, have attained the superior dharma of the truly noble knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One said to the group of five bhikṣus: "Have you ever heard me speak in this way before?"

The group of five bhikṣus replied: "No, we have not, World-Honored One."

"The Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus: I have attained the deathless. I will instruct you and teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach, before long you will, in this very life, with your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme end of the holy life, knowing: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more returning to any state of being.'"

At that time, the World-Honored One was able to persuade the group of five bhikṣus. From the group of five bhikṣus, sometimes two or three would attend upon the World-Honored One while the others went for alms. When those who went for alms returned, they would share with the entire group of six. Sometimes three or four would attend upon the World-Honored One while the others went for alms. When those who went for alms returned, they would share with the entire group of six.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the group of five bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, there are two extremes that one who has gone forth should not pursue. What are the two? One is attachment to sense pleasures, which is base, vulgar, the way of ordinary people, ignoble and unbeneficial. The other is attachment to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata, having abandoned these two extremes, has realized the Middle Way, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to nirvāṇa.

"What is the Middle Way that produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to nirvāṇa? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"Bhikṣus, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering: birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

"Bhikṣus, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering: it is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, seeking delight here and there, namely: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

"Bhikṣus, this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering: it is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandonment, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.

"Bhikṣus, this is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering: it is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"This is suffering: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This suffering should be fully known: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This suffering has been fully known: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the origin of suffering: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This origin should be abandoned: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This origin has been abandoned: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the cessation of suffering: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This cessation should be realized: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This cessation has been realized: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This path should be cultivated: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose. This path has been cultivated: with regard to dharmas not previously heard, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"Bhikṣus, as long as my knowledge and vision of these Four Noble Truths with their three turnings and twelve aspects was not thoroughly purified, I did not claim to have attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, ascetics, brāhmaṇas, and the multitude of devas and humans.

"But when my knowledge and vision of these Four Noble Truths with their three turnings and twelve aspects was thoroughly purified, then I claimed to have attained the supreme, perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, ascetics, brāhmaṇas, and the multitude of devas and humans.

"Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Unshakable is my liberation. This is my last birth. There will be no more renewed existence.'"

This is what the World-Honored One taught. The group of five bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, delighted in it and received it with joy.

When this teaching was being expounded, the Venerable Koṇḍañña had the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arise: "All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation."

When the World-Honored One turned the Dharma wheel, the earth-dwelling devas raised a cry: "The World-Honored One, at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, has turned the unsurpassed Dharma wheel that no ascetic, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world can turn."

When the earth-dwelling devas raised this cry, the devas of the Four Great Kings, hearing the cry of the earth-dwelling devas, also raised a cry: "The World-Honored One, at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, has turned the unsurpassed Dharma wheel that no ascetic, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world can turn."

Thus, in an instant, the cry spread upward, reaching the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, and the Brahmā heaven. The Brahmā-world devas also raised a cry: "The World-Honored One, at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, has turned the unsurpassed Dharma wheel that no ascetic, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world can turn."

At the moment the World-Honored One turned the Dharma wheel, the great earth trembled and shook. A great, measureless, brilliant, surpassing light appeared in the world, surpassing the radiance of the devas.

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Koṇḍañña has understood! Koṇḍañña has understood!" Therefore the Venerable Koṇḍañña was named Ājñāta Koṇḍañña ("Koṇḍañña Who Has Understood").

The Venerable Ājñāta Koṇḍañña, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having understood the Dharma, having penetrated the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, without any further uncertainty, not relying on others, dwelling in the Teacher's teaching with confidence, said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I wish to go forth under the World-Honored One and receive the full ordination."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣu! The Dharma has been well proclaimed. Practice the holy life to make a complete end of suffering." This was the Venerable Ājñāta Koṇḍañña's ordination.

Then the World-Honored One taught and instructed the remaining bhikṣus. When the World-Honored One taught and instructed them, the Venerable Assaji and the Venerable Mahānāma had the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arise: "All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation."

They, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having understood the Dharma, having penetrated the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, without any further uncertainty, not relying on others, dwelling in the Teacher's teaching with confidence, said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we wish to go forth under the World-Honored One and receive the full ordination."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣus! The Dharma has been well proclaimed. Practice the holy life to make a complete end of suffering." This was the Venerables Assaji's and Mahānāma's ordination.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with these three bhikṣus, taught and instructed the others. When the World-Honored One taught and instructed them, the Venerable Vappa and the Venerable Bhadrika had the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arise: "All that is subject to arising is subject to cessation."

They, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having understood the Dharma, having penetrated the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, without any further uncertainty, not relying on others, dwelling in the Teacher's teaching with confidence, said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we wish to go forth under the World-Honored One and receive the full ordination."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣus! The Dharma has been well proclaimed. Practice the holy life to make a complete end of suffering." This was the Venerables Vappa's and Bhadrika's ordination.

The World-Honored One then further taught and instructed the group of five bhikṣus: "Form is not the self. If form were the self, then form would not lead to affliction, and one could direct form thus: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.' But because form is not the self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot direct form thus: 'Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.'

"Feeling is not the self. If feeling were the self, then feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could direct feeling thus: 'Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be thus.' But because feeling is not the self, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and one cannot direct feeling thus.

"Perception is not the self. If perception were the self, then perception would not lead to affliction, and one could direct perception thus: 'Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be thus.' But because perception is not the self, therefore perception leads to affliction, and one cannot direct perception thus.

"Formations are not the self. If formations were the self, then formations would not lead to affliction, and one could direct formations thus: 'Let my formations be thus; let my formations not be thus.' But because formations are not the self, therefore formations lead to affliction, and one cannot direct formations thus.

"Consciousness is not the self. If consciousness were the self, then consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could direct consciousness thus: 'Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.' But because consciousness is not the self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot direct consciousness thus: 'Let my consciousness be thus; let my consciousness not be thus.'

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

They answered: "It is impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

They answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can a learned noble disciple see therein: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, whatever form, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever feeling, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all feeling should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever perception, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all perception should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever formations, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all formations should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Bhikṣus, a learned noble disciple who contemplates thus becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more returning to any state of being.'"

When the World-Honored One taught this discourse, the group of five bhikṣus, their minds being freed from the outflows without clinging, were delighted and received it with joy.

At that time, there were six Arhats in the world.

Thus the Buddha has spoken. The group of five bhikṣus and all the devas heard what the Buddha said, delighted in it, and received it with joy.

---

## (79) Sūtra on the Greatly Adorned King with Regard to Having Conviction

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus: "In the past, long ago, there was a king named Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, who was a wheel-turning king, a virtuous Dharma king who ruled the four continents. He had conquered this land and possessed the seven treasures, namely: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-general treasure. He had a full thousand sons, all brave and heroic, with handsome features, able to vanquish hostile forces. He ruled over this entire earth, bounded by the ocean, without clubs or swords, through the Dharma alone, making it peaceful and secure.

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ had this thought: 'I now possess great merit and great power. I have this entire earth, bounded by the four oceans. I have also conquered the land and possess the seven treasures. I have ruled over this land. I wish now to ascend to the heaven of the Four Great Kings.' 

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, together with his fourfold army and the people of the land, ascended to the heaven of the Four Great Kings. The four deva kings, seeing King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ coming from afar, went out to welcome him and said: 'Welcome, great king! Great king, please come. Here in the heaven of the Four Great Kings, you may enjoy and amuse yourself according to your wish.'

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, together with his fourfold army and the people of the land, ruled over the heaven of the Four Great Kings. He enjoyed pleasures there for an exceedingly long time.

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ then had this thought: 'I now possess great merit and great power. I have this entire earth, bounded by the four oceans. I have also conquered the land and possess the seven treasures. I rule over this land and also over the heaven of the Four Great Kings. I wish now to ascend to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.'

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, together with his fourfold army and the people of the land, ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Śakra, lord of the devas, seeing King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ coming from afar, went out to welcome him and said: 'Welcome, great king! Great king, please come. Here in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, you may enjoy and amuse yourself according to your wish.'

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, together with his fourfold army and the people of the land, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, Śakra, lord of the devas, shared half his seat with King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ. Then King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ sat together with Śakra, lord of the devas. The two were alike in appearance, equally handsome, with no difference except that their eye-blinking was different. King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ, together with his fourfold army and the people of the land, ruled over the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. He enjoyed pleasures there for an exceedingly long time.

"Bhikṣus, at that time, Śakra, lord of the devas, had this thought: 'This King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ now possesses great merit and great power. He has the entire earth, bounded by the four oceans. He has conquered the land and possesses the seven treasures. He rules over this land and also over the heaven of the Four Great Kings. Now he has come here and shares half my seat, ruling over the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Moreover, the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa devas is exceedingly long. What if this King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ were to drive me away and seize my throne?'

"Bhikṣus, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ's faculties then gradually declined. When his faculties declined, he lost his supernatural power and fell from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to Jambudvīpa. Upon falling to Jambudvīpa, he became gravely ill. When he was about to die, his ministers asked: 'If anyone asks, "What did King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ say before his death?", how shall we answer?'

"King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ answered his ministers: 'If anyone asks you, "What did King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ say before his death?", you should answer thus: "King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ was a wheel-turning king who ruled over the four continents. He conquered this land and possessed the seven treasures. He also ascended to the heaven of the Four Great Kings and ruled there. He then ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and shared half the seat with Śakra, lord of the devas, ruling over the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Even with such merit and power, King Mahāmaṇḍhātṛ was still not satisfied in his desires when he died."'"

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"Even if it rained gold coins,
One's desires would still not be satisfied.
The wise know that desires bring little pleasure and much suffering;
Even heavenly desires cannot bring contentment.
One who has understood this turns away from desire;
Such a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha
Delights in the destruction of craving,
Taking refuge in the true Dharma."

This is what the Buddha said. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, delighted in it and received it with joy.

---

## (80) Sūtra on King迦絺那

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus: "I shall now tell you a parable. A wise person, by means of a parable, can understand the meaning.

"Bhikṣus, suppose there is a dog that is weak from hunger and starvation. It comes upon a butcher's pile of bleached bones, bones with no flesh and no blood, only sinews binding them together. What do you think, bhikṣus? Could that dog, gnawing on those bleached bones with no flesh and no blood, only sinews binding them, satisfy its hunger?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because those are merely bleached bones with no flesh and no blood. Even if the dog were to gnaw on them for a long time, it would only wear itself out and gain nothing."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like bones, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose there is a vulture, a hawk, or an eagle that has seized a piece of meat. Other vultures, hawks, and eagles chase after it and try to snatch the meat. What do you think, bhikṣus? If that vulture, hawk, or eagle does not quickly let go of the meat, would it not thereby meet with death or mortal suffering?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose there is a man carrying a grass torch, walking against the wind. What do you think, bhikṣus? If that man does not quickly let go of the torch, would not the fire burn his hand, his arm, or other parts of his body, and thereby cause him to meet with death or mortal suffering?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose there is a great pit of glowing charcoal, deeper than a man's height, completely filled with burning charcoal, without smoke and without flame. Then a man comes along who loves life and does not wish to die, who seeks happiness and abhors suffering. Two strong men seize him by both arms and drag him toward the pit of glowing charcoal. What do you think, bhikṣus? Would that man not struggle with all his might, twisting his body this way and that? Why? Because that man knows: 'If I fall into this pit of glowing charcoal, I will surely die or suffer mortal agony.'"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like a pit of charcoal, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose a man dreams of beautiful gardens, beautiful ponds, beautiful lands, beautiful mountains, and beautiful rivers. When he awakens, he sees nothing at all. Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like a dream, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose a man borrows treasures, precious carriages, splendid garlands, and fine clothing, and he goes parading through the marketplace. People see him and say: 'What a wealthy man! The wealthy enjoy such pleasures as these!' Then the owner sees him and takes back the possessions. What do you think, bhikṣus? Would that man not become distressed?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One. Why? Because the owner has taken back the possessions."

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a learned noble disciple reflects: 'The World-Honored One has said that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods, bringing much suffering and much affliction, and that in them the danger is even greater.' Having truly seen this with right wisdom, he abandons the equanimity connected with diversity and cultivates the equanimity connected with unity, in which clinging to the material things of the world is entirely abandoned without remainder.

"Bhikṣus, suppose near a village there is a dense forest. Then a man comes along and sees the forest. In that forest there is a large area of flat, open ground. He sees it and thinks: 'This is flat, open ground.' Further on, there is a stretch of dangerous terrain. He sees it and thinks: 'This is dangerous terrain.' Further on, there is an area of delightful, pleasant ground with flowing streams and ponds. He sees it and thinks: 'This is delightful ground.' But there is no bridge, no boat, and no way across.

"That man then thinks: 'On this side is the delightful, pleasant ground, but on the far side there is also such terrain. Yet there is no bridge, no boat, and no way across. I should gather grass and branches, bind them into a raft, and by means of this raft, exerting myself with my hands and feet, safely cross to the other shore.'

"Bhikṣus, that man then gathers grass and branches, binds them into a raft, and by means of this raft, exerting himself with his hands and feet, safely crosses to the other shore. Having crossed to the other shore, the man thinks: 'This raft has been of great benefit to me. By means of this raft, exerting myself with my hands and feet, I safely crossed from the dangerous side to the safe shore. I should now carry this raft on my head or on my shoulder wherever I go.'

"What do you think, bhikṣus? Would that man, by doing thus with the raft, be doing what should be done with it?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Then what should that man do to properly deal with the raft? After having crossed to the other shore, the man should think: 'This raft has been of great benefit to me. By means of this raft, exerting myself with my hands and feet, I safely crossed from the dangerous side to the safe shore. I should now beach this raft on the shore, or submerge it in the water, and then go wherever I wish.' Bhikṣus, that man, by doing thus with the raft, would be doing what should be done with it.

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, I have taught the Dharma like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding on to. Bhikṣus, you who understand the Dharma as being like a raft should abandon even the Dharma, how much more so what is not the Dharma.

"Bhikṣus, there are six bases of views. What are the six? Bhikṣus, an unlearned ordinary person, who does not see the noble ones and is unskilled in their Dharma, who does not see good people and is unskilled in their Dharma, regards form as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.' He regards feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.' He regards what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, what is attained, sought, and mentally considered, as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.'

"And this view-basis, namely, 'There is a self and there is a world; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change,' this too he regards as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.'

"Bhikṣus, a learned noble disciple, who sees the noble ones and is skilled in their Dharma, who sees good people and is skilled in their Dharma, does not regard form as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.' He does not regard feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.' He does not regard what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, what is attained, sought, and mentally considered, as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.'

"And this view-basis, namely, 'There is a self and there is a world; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change,' this too he does not regard as: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self.'

"Viewing thus, he is not disturbed by what does not exist."

When this was said, a certain bhikṣu asked the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, can one be disturbed by what does not exist externally?"

The World-Honored One said: "There can be such a case. Here, someone thinks: 'Alas, I had it, and now I have it no more! Alas, if only I could have it, but I cannot obtain it!' He then sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into bewilderment. Bhikṣu, this is how one is disturbed by what does not exist externally."

"World-Honored One, can one not be disturbed by what does not exist externally?"

The World-Honored One said: "There can be such a case. Here, someone does not think: 'Alas, I had it, and now I have it no more! Alas, if only I could have it, but I cannot obtain it!' He does not sorrow, does not grieve, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into bewilderment. Bhikṣu, this is how one is not disturbed by what does not exist externally."

"World-Honored One, can one be disturbed by what does not exist internally?"

The World-Honored One said: "There can be such a case. Here, someone has the view: 'There is a self and there is a world; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change.' He then hears the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples teaching the Dharma for the removal of all view-standpoints, all attachment-grounds, all self-determinations, for the abandonment of all possessiveness, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa. He then thinks: 'I will be annihilated! I will be destroyed! I will no longer exist!' He then sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and falls into bewilderment. Bhikṣu, this is how one is disturbed by what does not exist internally."

"World-Honored One, can one not be disturbed by what does not exist internally?"

The World-Honored One said: "There can be such a case. Here, someone does not have the view: 'There is a self and there is a world; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change.' He then hears the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples teaching the Dharma for the removal of all view-standpoints, all attachment-grounds, all self-determinations, for the abandonment of all possessiveness, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, cessation, and nirvāṇa. He does not think: 'I will be annihilated! I will be destroyed! I will no longer exist!' He does not sorrow, does not grieve, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into bewilderment. Bhikṣu, this is how one is not disturbed by what does not exist internally.

"Bhikṣus, you may take hold of a possession that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change. Do you see any such possession that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Good, bhikṣus! I also do not see any possession that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change.

"Bhikṣus, you may rely on a self-doctrine that, when relied upon, does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Do you see any such self-doctrine?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Good, bhikṣus! I also do not see any self-doctrine that, when relied upon, does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

"Bhikṣus, you may rely on a view that, when relied upon, does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Do you see any such view?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Good, bhikṣus! I also do not see any view that, when relied upon, does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

"Bhikṣus, if there were a self, would there be what belongs to a self?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, if there were what belongs to a self, would there be a self?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, since self and what belongs to a self cannot truly and certainly be found, then this view-basis, namely, 'There is a self and there is a world; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, and not subject to change,' is this not an entirely and completely foolish teaching?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One. This is an entirely and completely foolish teaching."

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

They answered: "It is impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

They answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can a learned noble disciple see therein: 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, whatever form, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form is not the self. This should be seen with right wisdom as it really is.

"Whatever feeling, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all feeling is not the self. This should be seen with right wisdom as it really is.

"Whatever perception, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all perception is not the self. This should be seen with right wisdom as it really is.

"Whatever formations, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all formations are not the self. This should be seen with right wisdom as it really is.

"Whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness is not the self. This should be seen with right wisdom as it really is.

"Bhikṣus, a learned noble disciple who contemplates thus becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more returning to any state of being.'"

This is what the Buddha said. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, delighted in it and received it with joy.

---

## (81) Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Body

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after the midday meal, had gathered in the assembly hall and were sitting together, discussing this question: "How marvelous, how extraordinary! Mindfulness of the body, if cultivated and practiced frequently, has great fruit and great benefit."

Their discussion had not yet concluded when the World-Honored One arose from meditation in the late afternoon and went to the assembly hall. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat and asked the bhikṣus: "What were you discussing just now as you sat here together?"

The bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, after the midday meal, we gathered in the assembly hall and were sitting together, discussing this question: 'How marvelous, how extraordinary! Mindfulness of the body, if cultivated and practiced frequently, has great fruit and great benefit.' World-Honored One, this was the discussion we were having when you arrived."

The World-Honored One asked: "Bhikṣus, how is mindfulness of the body cultivated and practiced frequently so that it has great fruit and great benefit?"

The bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One is the Dharma-root, the Dharma-lord, the Dharma-support. May the World-Honored One please teach us. After hearing it, the bhikṣus will receive and practice it."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, listen well and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "We will listen, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body goes to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet place, sits cross-legged with body upright, establishes mindfulness before him, and, without any other thoughts, with focused mind practices mindfulness of the body.

"He breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully. When breathing in long, he knows: 'I breathe in long.' When breathing out long, he knows: 'I breathe out long.' When breathing in short, he knows: 'I breathe in short.' When breathing out short, he knows: 'I breathe out short.' He trains: 'Experiencing the whole body, I breathe in.' He trains: 'Experiencing the whole body, I breathe out.' He trains: 'Calming bodily formations, I breathe in.' He trains: 'Calming bodily formations, I breathe out.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body. He abides contemplating internally, he abides contemplating externally, he abides contemplating both internally and externally. He contemplates arising phenomena, he contemplates passing phenomena, he contemplates both arising and passing phenomena. His mindfulness is established to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and continuous mindfulness, and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Bhikṣus, this is how a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body knows, when walking: 'I am walking.' He knows, when standing: 'I am standing.' He knows, when sitting: 'I am sitting.' He knows, when lying down: 'I am lying down.' Whatever posture his body is in, he knows it accordingly.

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, in going forward and returning, applies full awareness. In looking and gazing, he applies full awareness. In bending and stretching, he applies full awareness. In holding his saṃghāṭī robe and bowl, he applies full awareness. In eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, he applies full awareness. In walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, he applies full awareness.

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward, enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, fat, grease, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fluid of the joints, and urine.'

"Bhikṣus, it is like a sack with two openings, filled with various kinds of grain, such as rice, millet, sesame, and beans. A person with good eyesight opens it and examines: 'This is rice, this is millet, this is sesame, this is beans.' In the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward, enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities.

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body contemplates the elements of this body: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.' Just as a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice slaughters a cow, places it at a crossroads, and divides it into parts, in the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates the elements of this body: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, as though he were to see a corpse abandoned in a charnel ground, dead for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days, bloated, discolored, and oozing, he compares it with his own body: 'My body is also of such a nature, will become like this, and has not gone beyond this.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, as though he were to see a corpse abandoned in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various kinds of worms, he compares it with his own body: 'My body is also of such a nature, will become like this, and has not gone beyond this.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, as though he were to see a corpse abandoned in a charnel ground, with bones connected by sinews, with some flesh and blood remaining; or bones connected by sinews, stripped of flesh and smeared with blood; or bones connected by sinews, without flesh and blood; or bones disconnected and scattered in all directions, here a hand bone, there a foot bone, a shin bone, a thigh bone, a hip bone, a spine bone, a rib bone, a shoulder bone, a neck bone, a jaw bone, a skull, he compares it with his own body: 'My body is also of such a nature, will become like this, and has not gone beyond this.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, as though he were to see a corpse abandoned in a charnel ground, the bones white like shells, or blue like pigeons, or red like they were smeared with blood, or decomposed and crumbling, or reduced to dust, he compares it with his own body: 'My body is also of such a nature, will become like this, and has not gone beyond this.'

"In this way he practices mindfulness of the body regarding the body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who practices mindfulness of the body, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with

## (42) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on What Purpose, Number One

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, then stood to one side and said: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of keeping the precepts?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, keeping the precepts has the purpose of non-regret. Ānanda, if one keeps the precepts, one attains non-regret."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of non-regret?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, non-regret has the purpose of gladness. Ānanda, if one has non-regret, one attains gladness."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of gladness?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, gladness has the purpose of joy. Ānanda, if one has gladness, one attains joy."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of joy?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, joy has the purpose of tranquility. Ānanda, if one has joy, one attains bodily tranquility."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of tranquility?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, tranquility has the purpose of happiness. Ānanda, if one has tranquility, one experiences happiness."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of happiness?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, happiness has the purpose of concentration. Ānanda, if one has happiness, one attains a concentrated mind."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of concentration?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, concentration has the purpose of seeing as it really is and knowing as it truly is. Ānanda, if one has concentration, one sees as it really is and knows as it truly is."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of seeing as it really is and knowing as it truly is?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, seeing as it really is and knowing as it truly is has the purpose of disenchantment. Ānanda, if one sees as it really is and knows as it truly is, one attains disenchantment."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of disenchantment?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, disenchantment has the purpose of dispassion. Ānanda, if one has disenchantment, one attains dispassion."

He further asked: "World-Honored One, what is the purpose of dispassion?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Ānanda, dispassion has the purpose of liberation. Ānanda, if one has dispassion, one attains liberation from all lust, anger, and delusion. Thus, Ānanda, because of keeping the precepts one attains non-regret; because of non-regret one attains gladness; because of gladness one attains joy; because of joy one attains tranquility; because of tranquility one attains happiness; because of happiness one attains concentration. Ānanda, the learned noble disciple, because of concentration, sees as it really is and knows as it truly is; because of seeing as it really is and knowing as it truly is, one attains disenchantment; because of disenchantment one attains dispassion; because of dispassion one attains liberation; because of liberation one knows of liberation: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of any state of being.' One knows as it truly is. Ānanda, this is how one dharma benefits another dharma, one dharma conditions another dharma. In this way, these precepts lead to the highest, that is, crossing from this shore to reach the other shore."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

End of Sūtra on What Purpose, Number One.

---

## (43) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on Not Thinking, Number Two

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, one who keeps the precepts should not think, 'May I attain non-regret.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who keeps the precepts attains non-regret. Ānanda, one who has non-regret should not think, 'May I attain gladness.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has non-regret attains gladness. Ānanda, one who has gladness should not think, 'May I attain joy.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has gladness attains joy. Ānanda, one who has joy should not think, 'May I attain tranquility.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has joy attains bodily tranquility. Ānanda, one who has tranquility should not think, 'May I attain happiness.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has tranquility experiences happiness. Ānanda, one who has happiness should not think, 'May I attain concentration.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has happiness attains a concentrated mind. Ānanda, one who has concentration should not think, 'May I see as it really is and know as it truly is.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has concentration sees as it really is and knows as it truly is. Ānanda, one who sees as it really is and knows as it truly is should not think, 'May I attain disenchantment.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who sees as it really is and knows as it truly is attains disenchantment. Ānanda, one who has disenchantment should not think, 'May I attain dispassion.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has disenchantment attains dispassion. Ānanda, one who has dispassion should not think, 'May I attain liberation.' Ānanda, it is simply the natural way of things that one who has dispassion attains liberation from all lust, anger, and delusion.

"Ānanda, thus because of keeping the precepts one attains non-regret; because of non-regret one attains gladness; because of gladness one attains joy; because of joy one attains tranquility; because of tranquility one attains happiness; because of happiness one attains a concentrated mind. Ānanda, the learned noble disciple, having a concentrated mind, sees as it really is and knows as it truly is; because of seeing as it really is and knowing as it truly is, one attains disenchantment; because of disenchantment one attains dispassion; because of dispassion one attains liberation; because of liberation one knows of liberation: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of any state of being.' One knows as it truly is. Ānanda, this is how one dharma benefits another dharma, one dharma conditions another dharma. In this way, these precepts lead to the highest, that is, crossing from this shore to reach the other shore."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

End of Sūtra on Not Thinking, Number Two.

## (44) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on Mindfulness, Number Three

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is often forgetful and lacks right awareness, this harms right mindfulness and right awareness. If there is no right mindfulness and right awareness, this harms guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, non-regret, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing as it really is, knowing as it truly is, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation. If there is no liberation, this harms nirvāṇa. If a bhikṣu is not often forgetful and has right awareness, this cultivates right mindfulness and right awareness. If there is right mindfulness and right awareness, this cultivates guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, non-regret, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing as it really is, knowing as it truly is, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation. If there is liberation, this cultivates nirvāṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

End of Sūtra on Mindfulness, Number Three.

## (46) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on Shame and Conscience, Number Five

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, if a bhikṣu has no shame and no conscience, this harms love and respect. If there is no love and respect, this harms faith. If there is no faith, this harms right thinking. If there is no right thinking, this harms right mindfulness and right awareness. If there is no liberation, this harms nirvāṇa. Venerables, you should know that it is just the same for a bhikṣu. If he has no shame and no conscience, this harms love and respect. If there is no love and respect, this harms faith. If there is no faith, this harms right thinking. If there is no right thinking, this harms right mindfulness and right awareness. If there is liberation, this cultivates nirvāṇa."

## (49) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on Reverence, Number Eight

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus should practice reverence, careful observation, and respect toward fellow practitioners of the holy life. If a bhikṣu does not practice reverence, does not carefully observe, and does not respect fellow practitioners of the holy life, then for him to fulfill the code of proper conduct is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the code of proper conduct, for him to fulfill the rules of training is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the rules of training, for him to fulfill the aggregate of morality is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the aggregate of morality, for him to fulfill the aggregate of concentration is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the aggregate of concentration, for him to fulfill the aggregate of wisdom is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the aggregate of wisdom, for him to fulfill the aggregate of liberation is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the aggregate of liberation, for him to fulfill the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation is certainly impossible. Without fulfilling the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, for him to fulfill nirvāṇa is certainly impossible.

"If a bhikṣu practices reverence, careful observation, and respect toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, then for him to fulfill the code of proper conduct is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the code of proper conduct, for him to fulfill the rules of training is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the aggregate of morality, for him to fulfill the aggregate of concentration is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the aggregate of concentration, for him to fulfill the aggregate of wisdom is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the aggregate of wisdom, for him to fulfill the aggregate of liberation is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the aggregate of liberation, for him to fulfill the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation is certainly possible. Having fulfilled the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, for him to fulfill nirvāṇa is certainly possible."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

End of Sūtra on Reverence, Number Eight.
