## (51) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on the Primordial Beginning, Number Ten

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The primordial beginning of craving for existence cannot be known. Originally there was no craving for existence, yet now craving for existence has arisen, and the conditions for the arising of craving for existence can be known. Craving for existence has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of craving for existence? The answer is: ignorance is its correlate. Ignorance also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of ignorance? The answer is: the five hindrances are its correlate. The five hindrances also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of the five hindrances? The answer is: the three evil conducts are their correlate. The three evil conducts also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of the three evil conducts? The answer is: not guarding the sense faculties is their correlate. Not guarding the sense faculties also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of not guarding the sense faculties? The answer is: lack of right mindfulness and right awareness is its correlate. Lack of right mindfulness and right awareness also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of lack of right mindfulness and right awareness? The answer is: wrong thinking is its correlate. Wrong thinking also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of wrong thinking? The answer is: lack of faith is its correlate. Lack of faith also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of lack of faith? The answer is: hearing unwholesome teachings is its correlate. Hearing unwholesome teachings also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of hearing unwholesome teachings? The answer is: associating with bad companions is its correlate. Associating with bad companions also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of associating with bad companions? The answer is: bad people are its correlate.

"Thus, when one is equipped with bad people, one becomes equipped with associating with bad companions. When equipped with associating with bad companions, one becomes equipped with hearing unwholesome teachings. When equipped with hearing unwholesome teachings, one becomes equipped with giving rise to lack of faith. When equipped with giving rise to lack of faith, one becomes equipped with wrong thinking. When equipped with wrong thinking, one becomes equipped with lack of right mindfulness and right awareness. When equipped with lack of right mindfulness and right awareness, one becomes equipped with not guarding the sense faculties. When equipped with not guarding the sense faculties, one becomes equipped with the three evil conducts. When equipped with the three evil conducts, one becomes equipped with the five hindrances. When equipped with the five hindrances, one becomes equipped with ignorance. When equipped with ignorance, one becomes equipped with craving for existence. In this way, this craving for existence is progressively brought to completion.

"Knowledge and liberation also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of knowledge and liberation? The answer is: the seven factors of awakening are their correlate. The seven factors of awakening also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of the seven factors of awakening? The answer is: the four establishments of mindfulness are their correlate. The four establishments of mindfulness also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of the four establishments of mindfulness? The answer is: the three excellent conducts are their correlate. The three excellent conducts also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of the three excellent conducts? The answer is: guarding the sense faculties is their correlate. Guarding the sense faculties also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of guarding the sense faculties? The answer is: right mindfulness and right awareness are its correlate. Right mindfulness and right awareness also have a correlate; they are not without a correlate. What is the correlate of right mindfulness and right awareness? The answer is: right thinking is their correlate. Right thinking also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of right thinking? The answer is: faith is its correlate. Faith also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of faith? The answer is: hearing the good Dharma is its correlate. Hearing the good Dharma also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of hearing the good Dharma? The answer is: associating with good companions is its correlate. Associating with good companions also has a correlate; it is not without a correlate. What is the correlate of associating with good companions? The answer is: good people are its correlate.

"Thus, when one is equipped with good people, one becomes equipped with associating with good companions. When equipped with associating with good companions, one becomes equipped with hearing the good Dharma. When equipped with hearing the good Dharma, one becomes equipped with giving rise to faith. When equipped with giving rise to faith, one becomes equipped with right thinking. When equipped with right thinking, one becomes equipped with right mindfulness and right awareness. When equipped with right mindfulness and right awareness, one becomes equipped with guarding the sense faculties. When equipped with guarding the sense faculties, one becomes equipped with the three excellent conducts. When equipped with the three excellent conducts, one becomes equipped with the four establishments of mindfulness. When equipped with the four establishments of mindfulness, one becomes equipped with the seven factors of awakening. When equipped with the seven factors of awakening, one becomes equipped with knowledge and liberation. In this way, this knowledge and liberation are progressively brought to completion."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

End of Sūtra on the Primordial Beginning, Number Ten.

Craving for existence has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of craving for existence? The answer is: ignorance is its nutriment. Ignorance also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of ignorance? The answer is: the five hindrances are its nutriment. The five hindrances also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the five hindrances? The answer is: the three evil conducts are their nutriment. The three evil conducts also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the three evil conducts? The answer is: not guarding the sense faculties is their nutriment. Not guarding the sense faculties also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of not guarding the sense faculties? What is the nutriment of lack of right mindfulness and right awareness? The answer is: wrong thinking is its nutriment. Wrong thinking also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of wrong thinking? The answer is: lack of faith is its nutriment. Lack of faith also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of lack of faith? The small rivers also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the small rivers? The answer is: the large streams are their nutriment. The small streams also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the small streams? The answer is: the mountain cliffs, ravines, gorges, and marshlands are their nutriment. The mountain cliffs, ravines, gorges, and marshlands also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the mountain cliffs, ravines, gorges, and marshlands? The answer is: rain is their nutriment. When at times there is heavy rain, after the heavy rain, the mountain cliffs, ravines, gorges, and marshlands become full of water. When the mountain cliffs, ravines, gorges, and marshlands are full of water, then the small streams become full. When the small streams are full, then the large streams become full. When the large streams are full, then the small rivers become full. When the small rivers are full, then the great rivers become full. When the great rivers are full, then the great ocean becomes full. In this way, the great ocean is progressively filled to completion.

"In this way, craving for existence also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of craving for existence? The answer is: ignorance is its nutriment. Ignorance also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of ignorance? The answer is: the five hindrances are its nutriment. The five hindrances also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the five hindrances? The answer is: the three evil conducts are their nutriment. The three evil conducts also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of the three evil conducts? The answer is: not guarding the sense faculties is their nutriment. Not guarding the sense faculties also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of not guarding the sense faculties? The answer is: lack of right mindfulness and right awareness is its nutriment. Lack of right mindfulness and right awareness also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of lack of right mindfulness and right awareness? The answer is: wrong thinking is its nutriment. Wrong thinking also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of wrong thinking? The answer is: lack of faith is its nutriment. Lack of faith also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of lack of faith? The answer is: hearing unwholesome teachings is its nutriment. Hearing unwholesome teachings also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of hearing unwholesome teachings? "Knowledge and liberation also have nutriment; they are not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of knowledge and liberation? The answer is: the seven factors of awakening are their nutriment. The answer is: associating with good companions is its nutriment. Associating with good companions also has nutriment; it is not without nutriment. ## (56) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Correlates of Practice: Sūtra on Meghiya, Number Fifteen

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the land of Magadha, at the Mango Grove Cave near the village of Jantuka.

At that time, the Venerable Meghiya was his attendant. Then the Venerable Meghiya, after the night had passed, at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village of Jantuka to go on his alms round. When he had finished his alms round, he went to the bank of the Kimikālā River, where he saw level ground with a fine mango grove. The water of the Kimikālā River was exceedingly beautiful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, neither too cold nor too warm. Seeing this, he was delighted and thought: "This ground is level, and the mango grove is fine. The water of the Kimikālā River is exceedingly beautiful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, neither too cold nor too warm. If a son of good family wishes to practice and abandon defilements, he should do so in this place. I too have things to abandon. Would it not be good for me to practice and abandon defilements in this quiet place?"

## The Chapter on Long Life, Second Section

### 85. Sūtra on the True Person

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvatī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the Dharma of a true person and the Dharma of one who is not a true person. Listen well, listen well, and reflect upon it carefully. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we will listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the Dharma of one who is not a true person? Here, a person who is not a true person, if he comes from a noble family, because of coming from a noble family, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of coming from a noble family that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not come from a noble family, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of birth, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he has a fine appearance, because of his fine appearance, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of a fine appearance that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not have a fine appearance, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of appearance, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he possesses great wealth, because of possessing great wealth, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of possessing great wealth that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not possess great wealth, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of wealth, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he possesses extensive learning, because of possessing extensive learning, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of possessing extensive learning that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not possess extensive learning, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of learning, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he recites the sūtras, because of reciting the sūtras, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of reciting the sūtras that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not recite the sūtras, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of recitation, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he expounds the Dharma, because of expounding the Dharma, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of expounding the Dharma that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not expound the Dharma, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside the matter of expounding the Dharma, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he dwells in a secluded place, wears robes of rags, because of dwelling in a secluded place and wearing robes of rags, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of dwelling in a secluded place or wearing robes of rags that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not dwell in a secluded place or wear robes of rags, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he eats only one meal a day, because of eating only one meal a day, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of eating only one meal a day that one can extinguish greed, extinguish hatred, extinguish delusion. Even if a person does not eat only one meal a day, yet if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, conducts himself in accord with the Dharma, then he is respected and praised for this.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the first dhyāna, because of attaining the first dhyāna, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the first dhyāna as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, because of attaining the fourth dhyāna, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the fourth dhyāna as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the sphere of infinite space, because of attaining the sphere of infinite space, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the sphere of infinite space as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the sphere of infinite consciousness, because of attaining the sphere of infinite consciousness, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the sphere of infinite consciousness as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the sphere of nothingness, because of attaining the sphere of nothingness, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the sphere of nothingness as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, if he attains the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, because of attaining the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, he exalts himself and denigrates others. This is the Dharma of one who is not a true person. A true person reflects thus: 'The World-Honored One has spoken of the nature of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception as being a mental fabrication. Whatever is fabricated, the Tathāgata has said is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Thus, having set aside such matters, he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, practices according to what is appropriate, and conducts himself in accord with the Dharma. This is the Dharma of a true person.

"A true person then further completely transcends the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and attains the cessation of perception and feeling, and abides therein. Having seen with wisdom, his outflows are completely exhausted. This bhikṣu does not conceive any conception whatsoever: he does not conceive of himself as being in the sphere of infinite space, does not conceive of himself as being in the sphere of infinite consciousness, does not conceive of himself as being in the sphere of nothingness, does not conceive of himself as being in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, does not conceive of himself as being in the cessation of perception and feeling. Yet he has perception. What does he perceive? He perceives that this is the ending of suffering, the exhaustion of suffering. He perceives that this is the Dharma free from outflows, that which is unconditioned."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 86. Sūtra on Explaining

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvatī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the Dharma. It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. It has good meaning and good phrasing, and is complete, pure, and displays the pure practice. That is, the Sūtra on Explaining. Listen well, listen well, and reflect upon it carefully. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we will listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the Sūtra on Explaining? It means: do not practice lowly dharmas, do not practice self-mortification, and abide in the middle path. Do not seek pleasure through desire, which is a lowly dharma of common worldlings. Do not seek to practice self-mortification, which is a painful, ignoble dharma that brings no benefit. Having abandoned both of these extremes, there is the middle path. The Tathāgata's realization of this middle path gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, is conducive to samādhi, is conducive to wisdom, is conducive to awakening, and is conducive to nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, there are five aggregates of clinging. What are the five? They are: the aggregate of form and clinging, the aggregate of feeling and clinging, the aggregate of perception and clinging, the aggregate of formations and clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness and clinging.

"What is the aggregate of form and clinging? It refers to the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements. This is called the aggregate of form and clinging. What is the cause and condition giving rise to form? With desire as its cause and condition, the aggregate of form and clinging arises.

"What is the aggregate of feeling and clinging? There are three types of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. What is the cause and condition giving rise to feeling? With contact as its cause and condition, the aggregate of feeling and clinging arises.

"What is the aggregate of perception and clinging? There are six types of perception: perception of form, perception of sound, perception of smell, perception of taste, perception of touch, and perception of dharmas. What is the cause and condition giving rise to perception? With contact as its cause and condition, the aggregate of perception and clinging arises.

"What is the aggregate of formations and clinging? There are six types of volition: volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, volition regarding smells, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding touches, and volition regarding dharmas. What is the cause and condition giving rise to formations? With contact as its cause and condition, the aggregate of formations and clinging arises.

"What is the aggregate of consciousness and clinging? There are six types of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. What is the cause and condition giving rise to consciousness? With name-and-form as its cause and condition, the aggregate of consciousness and clinging arises.

"If a bhikṣu knows form in this way, knows the arising of form, and knows the cessation of form; knows feeling in this way, knows the arising of feeling, and knows the cessation of feeling; knows perception in this way, knows the arising of perception, and knows the cessation of perception; knows formations in this way, knows the arising of formations, and knows the cessation of formations; knows consciousness in this way, knows the arising of consciousness, and knows the cessation of consciousness; this is called a bhikṣu who is skilled in the aggregates and in the bases of the aggregates.

"Furthermore, there are six internal sense bases and six external sense bases. The six internal sense bases are: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base. The six external sense bases are: the form base, the sound base, the smell base, the taste base, the touch base, and the dharma base.

"Because of the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality. Because of the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality. Because of the nose and smells, nose-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality. Because of the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality. Because of the body and touches, body-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality. Because of the mind and dharmas, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. From feeling, craving arises. This is truly knowing the arising of suffering according to reality.

"Because of the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality. Because of the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality. Because of the nose and smells, nose-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality. Because of the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality. Because of the body and touches, body-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality. Because of the mind and dharmas, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is contact. From contact, feeling arises. If craving is completely exhausted, without remainder, then there is abandonment, vomiting out, cessation, non-attachment, and release. This is truly knowing the cessation of suffering according to reality.

"Furthermore, there is dependent arising. With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With formations as condition, there is consciousness. With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases. With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. With contact as condition, there is feeling. With feeling as condition, there is craving. With craving as condition, there is clinging. With clinging as condition, there is becoming. With becoming as condition, there is birth. With birth as condition, there arise aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. In this way the entire great mass of suffering arises.

"If ignorance ceases without remainder, then formations cease. If formations cease, then consciousness ceases. If consciousness ceases, then name-and-form ceases. If name-and-form ceases, then the six sense bases cease. If the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases. If contact ceases, then feeling ceases. If feeling ceases, then craving ceases. If craving ceases, then clinging ceases. If clinging ceases, then becoming ceases. If becoming ceases, then birth ceases. If birth ceases, then aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair all cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases.

"Furthermore, there are four noble truths. The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the arising of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

"What is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is disliked is suffering, separation from what is liked is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

"What is the noble truth of the arising of suffering? It is that craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and attachment, seeking delight here and there: that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

"What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandonment, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment.

"What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi.

"If a bhikṣu, with regard to these four noble truths, truly knows and truly sees them according to reality, with correct wisdom, then he is called a bhikṣu who has arrived at the right Dharma, who has arrived at the ultimate, who has realized the true Dharma, and who stands upon the ground of the true Dharma.

"Furthermore, when a noble disciple has obtained these four fruits, he does not deceive himself, does not deceive the World-Honored One, and does not deceive the wise ones. What are the four? When a noble disciple has realized the fruit of stream-entry, he truly knows: 'My births are exhausted at this point, the three lower fetters are exhausted, and I certainly will not fall into evil destinies. I am destined for correct enlightenment, and will be reborn at most seven more times, wandering among gods and humans seven times at most, before making an end of suffering.'

"When a noble disciple has realized the fruit of once-returning, he truly knows: 'I have exhausted the three lower fetters, and with greed, hatred, and delusion greatly diminished, I will return to this world once more before making an end of suffering.'

"When a noble disciple has realized the fruit of non-returning, he truly knows: 'The five lower fetters have been exhausted. I will attain parinirvāṇa in that realm and will not return to this world.'

"When a noble disciple has realized the fruit of arhatship, he truly knows: 'Birth is exhausted, the pure practice has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there will be no more existence hereafter.' This is truly knowing according to reality."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 87. Sūtra on the Thoroughbred

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvatī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In the world there exist good thoroughbred horses possessing eight qualities which are highly valued by people and are worthy of a king. What are the eight?

"Here, a good thoroughbred horse is born of a noble breed on both its father's and mother's side. It is raised in a land where good horses dwell. This is the first quality of a good thoroughbred horse possessing which it is highly valued by people and is worthy of a king.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse eats fine grass and good grain, and is selective about its food, not eating just anything. This is the second quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse, seeing dead carcasses, is disgusted and repelled, and does not wish to approach them. This is the third quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse is of fine appearance, clean and beautiful, and pleasing to see. This is the fourth quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse has great strength, capable of overcoming other horses that are weak. This is the fifth quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse runs swiftly, galloping with great speed. This is the sixth quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse, when whipped by the rider, can endure it and bears it patiently. This is the seventh quality.

"Furthermore, a good thoroughbred horse, when it runs along a road, always follows the correct path and does not deviate. This is the eighth quality.

"In this way, a good thoroughbred horse possessing these eight qualities is highly valued by people and is worthy of a king.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu possessing eight qualities is worthy of receiving offerings, worthy of receiving hospitality, worthy of receiving gifts, worthy of being reverenced with joined palms, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the eight?

"Here, a bhikṣu is endowed with morality, he guards the Prātimokṣa discipline, is perfect in deportment and conduct, sees danger in the slightest faults, receives and trains in the training rules. Just as a good thoroughbred horse is born of a noble breed on both its father's and mother's side and is raised in a land where good horses dwell, in the same way, a bhikṣu is endowed with morality, guards the Prātimokṣa discipline, is perfect in deportment and conduct, sees danger in the slightest faults, and receives and trains in the training rules. This is the first quality of a bhikṣu possessing which he is worthy of receiving offerings, worthy of receiving hospitality, worthy of receiving gifts, worthy of being reverenced with joined palms, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu eats fine food and is selective, taking what is fitting and not eating excessively. He reflects wisely on the purpose of food: not for enjoyment, not for intoxication, not for beauty, not for attractiveness, but merely for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, to put an end to old suffering and not give rise to new suffering, so that he may continue practicing the pure life. Just as a good thoroughbred horse eats fine grass and good grain and is selective about its food, in the same way, a bhikṣu eats food with wise reflection. This is the second quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, seeing birth, aging, illness, and death, is disgusted and repelled, and does not delight in them. Just as a good thoroughbred horse, seeing dead carcasses, is disgusted and repelled, in the same way, a bhikṣu is disgusted and repelled by birth, aging, illness, and death. This is the third quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu possesses fine deportment, is well restrained, and his conduct is worthy and dignified. He is pleasing to see and brings faith to those who behold him. Just as a good thoroughbred horse is of fine appearance, clean and beautiful, in the same way, a bhikṣu possesses fine deportment and brings faith to those who see him. This is the fourth quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu possesses great wisdom. He has the wisdom of arising and passing away, the noble wisdom of penetration that leads to the complete ending of suffering. Just as a good thoroughbred horse has great strength, in the same way, a bhikṣu possesses great wisdom. This is the fifth quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when asked about the Dharma, can explain the Dharma of the Tathāgata extensively, bringing joy to those who hear it. Just as a good thoroughbred horse runs swiftly with great speed, in the same way, a bhikṣu can explain the Dharma extensively. This is the sixth quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu has obtained the four dhyānas, the increase of mind, and the present happiness of dwelling. He attains them at will, without difficulty and without hardship. Just as a good thoroughbred horse, when whipped by the rider, can endure it and bears it patiently, in the same way, a bhikṣu has obtained the four dhyānas at will. This is the seventh quality.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the exhaustion of the outflows, realizes the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are without outflows, and in this very life, having personally realized it with direct knowledge, he abides therein. He knows: 'Birth is exhausted, the pure practice has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there will be no more existence hereafter.' Just as a good thoroughbred horse always follows the correct path and does not deviate, in the same way, a bhikṣu has exhausted the outflows. This is the eighth quality.

"In this way, a bhikṣu possessing these eight qualities is worthy of receiving offerings, worthy of receiving hospitality, worthy of receiving gifts, worthy of being reverenced with joined palms, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### 88. Sūtra on Seeking the Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvatī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are two kinds of seeking. What are the two? There is the noble seeking and there is the ignoble seeking. What is the ignoble seeking? Here, a person is himself subject to birth, yet seeks what is subject to birth. He is himself subject to aging, yet seeks what is subject to aging. He is himself subject to illness, yet seeks what is subject to illness. He is himself subject to death, yet seeks what is subject to death. He is himself subject to sorrow, yet seeks what is subject to sorrow. He is himself subject to defilement, yet seeks what is subject to defilement.

"And what is it that is subject to birth? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to birth. A person who is himself subject to birth, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to birth.

"And what is it that is subject to aging? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to aging. A person who is himself subject to aging, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to aging.

"And what is it that is subject to illness? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to illness. A person who is himself subject to illness, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to illness.

"And what is it that is subject to death? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to death. A person who is himself subject to death, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to death.

"And what is it that is subject to sorrow? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to sorrow. A person who is himself subject to sorrow, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to sorrow.

"And what is it that is subject to defilement? Wife and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, gold, silver, jewels, and various kinds of property. These are subject to defilement. A person who is himself subject to defilement, being deeply attached and submerged, seeks these things that are subject to defilement. This is called the ignoble seeking.

"What is the noble seeking? Here, a person is himself subject to birth, and knowing the danger of what is subject to birth, he seeks the unborn, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. He is himself subject to aging, and knowing the danger of what is subject to aging, he seeks the unaging, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. He is himself subject to illness, and knowing the danger of what is subject to illness, he seeks the freedom from illness, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. He is himself subject to death, and knowing the danger of what is subject to death, he seeks the deathless, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. He is himself subject to sorrow, and knowing the danger of what is subject to sorrow, he seeks the freedom from sorrow, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. He is himself subject to defilement, and knowing the danger of what is subject to defilement, he seeks the freedom from defilement, the unsurpassed peace and security, nirvāṇa. This is called the noble seeking."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 21 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 11

## Chapter Six: The King Correlates

Seven Treasures; Marks; Four Continents; Cow Dung; King Magadha;
Bimbisāra; Liṅgī; Messengers of Death, last of all.

## (58) Sūtra on the Seven Treasures, First of the King Correlates Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "When a wheel-turning king appears in the world, you should know that seven treasures appear in the world. What are the seven? The wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure. These are the seven. When a wheel-turning king appears in the world, you should know that these seven treasures appear in the world. In the same way, when a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One appears in the world, you should know that seven awakening-factor treasures also appear in the world. What are the seven? The mindfulness awakening-factor treasure, the investigation-of-dharmas awakening factor, the energy awakening factor, the joy awakening factor, the tranquility awakening factor, the concentration awakening factor, and the equanimity awakening-factor treasure. These are the seven. When a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One appears in the world, you should know that these seven awakening-factor treasures appear in the world."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Seven Treasures, the First.

---

## (59) Sūtra on the Thirty-Two Marks, Second of the King Correlates Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, after the midday meal, the bhikṣus gathered and sat in the lecture hall, discussing this matter together: "Venerables! How wonderful! How extraordinary! A great person endowed with the thirty-two marks must certainly have one of two destinies, truly and without falsehood. If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He will certainly rule over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. If he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, his fame spreading and being heard throughout the ten directions."

At that time, the World-Honored One was in quiet meditation, and with the pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, he heard the bhikṣus, after the midday meal, gathered and sitting in the lecture hall, discussing this matter together: "Venerables! How wonderful! How extraordinary! A great person endowed with the thirty-two marks must certainly have one of two destinies, truly and without falsehood. If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He will certainly rule over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. If he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, his fame spreading and being heard throughout the ten directions."

Having heard this, the World-Honored One rose from his quiet meditation in the late afternoon, went to the lecture hall, spread his seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down, and asked the bhikṣus: "What matter have you been discussing today, gathered together in the lecture hall?"

Then the bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One! Today we gathered and sat in the lecture hall discussing this matter: 'Venerables! How wonderful! How extraordinary! A great person endowed with the thirty-two marks must certainly have one of two destinies, truly and without falsehood. If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He will certainly rule over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. If he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, his fame spreading and being heard throughout the ten directions.' World-Honored One! We were discussing this matter, and therefore we gathered and sat in the lecture hall."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus! Would you like to hear from the Tathāgata about the thirty-two marks? That is, those which a great person possesses, who must certainly have one of two destinies, truly and without falsehood. If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He will certainly rule over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. If he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, his fame spreading and being heard throughout the ten directions."

Then the bhikṣus, having heard this, said: "World-Honored One! Now is the proper time. Sugata! Now is the proper time. If the World-Honored One will explain the thirty-two marks for the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus, having heard, will well receive and retain them."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus! Listen carefully, listen carefully! Reflect well upon it. I shall explain it to you in detail." The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "The great person's feet stand evenly and flat. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has wheels on the soles of his feet, with a thousand spokes, all complete. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has long, slender fingers and toes. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's feet are broad and straight. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's heels and ankles are even and full on both sides. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's two ankles are well-proportioned. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's body hair curls upward. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has webbed hands and feet, like a royal goose. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's hands and feet are supremely soft, tender, and delicate, like tūla cotton. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's skin is smooth and fine, so that dust and water do not cling to it. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person.

"Furthermore, the great person has one hair per pore; each hair per pore means one hair grows from each pore of the body, its color like dark blue, spiraling to the right like a conch shell. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has calves like those of a deer, like a deer king. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's male organ is sheathed, like that of a fine stallion king. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's body is round and well-proportioned, like a nyagrodha tree, symmetrically proportioned above and below. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's body does not bend forward; his body not bending means that standing upright, he can extend his hands and touch his knees. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's body is golden in color, like refined purple gold. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has seven places that are full; the seven full places are the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the neck. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's upper body is large, like that of a lion. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has jaws like those of a lion. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person.

"Furthermore, the great person's spine and back are level and straight. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's two shoulders are connected, linking to the neck, even and full. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has forty teeth; even teeth, teeth without gaps, white teeth, and teeth that discern the foremost flavor. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has a Brahma voice that is pleasing; his voice is like that of a kalaviṅka bird. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has a broad, long tongue; a broad, long tongue means the tongue extends from the mouth and covers his entire face. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's tear ducts are full, like those of a bull king. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person's eyes are deep blue in color. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has a fleshy protuberance on the crown of his head, round and symmetrically proportioned, with hair spiraling to the right. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person. Furthermore, the great person has a hair growing between his eyebrows, pure white and curling to the right. This is a mark of a great person, a mark of a great person.

"Bhikṣus! A great person endowed with these thirty-two marks must certainly have one of two destinies, truly and without falsehood. If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He will certainly rule over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. If he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, his fame spreading and being heard throughout the ten directions."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Thirty-Two Marks, the Second.

---

## (60) Sūtra on the Four Continents, Third of the King Correlates Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and he had this thought: "Very few people in the world can have a mind satisfied with desires, and very few die having become weary of desires. That people should have a mind satisfied with desires and die having become weary of desires is exceedingly rare."

In the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, arrived and paid his respects, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Today I was in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and I had this thought: 'Very few people in the world can have a mind satisfied with desires, and very few die having become weary of desires. That people should have a mind satisfied with desires and die having become weary of desires is exceedingly rare.'"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is. Very few people in the world can have a mind satisfied with desires, and very few die having become weary of desires. Ānanda! That people should have a mind satisfied with desires and die having become weary of desires is exceedingly rare. Ānanda! It is extremely rare, extremely rare for people to have a mind satisfied with desires and die having become weary of desires. Ānanda! Rather, people in the world are very many, very many who have no satisfaction with desires, who do not become weary of desires, and who die thus. Why is this? Ānanda! In the distant past there was a king named Mūrdhagata, who was a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority; a righteous Dharma King endowed with seven treasures. Those seven treasures were: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure; these were the seven. He had a thousand sons, complete, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to vanquish rival forces. He certainly ruled over all this land extending to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by Dharma instruction, causing beings to attain peace and happiness. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time, had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete. I wish to have treasures rain in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata had great supernormal power, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. No sooner had he given rise to this thought than treasures rained in his palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time thereafter, again had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete, and treasures have rained in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees. I recall having heard from the ancients that in the west there is a continent called Godānīya, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I now wish to go and see the continent of Godānīya, and upon arriving, to rule it.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata had great supernormal power, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. No sooner had he given rise to this thought than he traveled through the sky by his supernormal power, together with his four kinds of armies. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata immediately arrived and took up residence on the continent of Godānīya. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, having taken up residence, ruled the continent of Godānīya for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of years.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time thereafter, again had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete, and treasures have rained in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees. I also possess the continent of Godānīya. I have further heard from the ancients that in the east there is a continent called Pūrvavideha, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I now wish to go and see the continent of Pūrvavideha, and upon arriving, to rule it.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata had great supernormal power, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. No sooner had he given rise to this thought than he traveled through the sky by his supernormal power, together with his four kinds of armies. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata immediately arrived and took up residence on the continent of Pūrvavideha. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, having taken up residence, ruled the continent of Pūrvavideha for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of years.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time thereafter, again had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete, and treasures have rained in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees. I also possess the continent of Godānīya, and also the continent of Pūrvavideha. I have further heard from the ancients that in the north there is a continent called Uttarakuru, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people, though there is no notion of self nor any possessions. I now wish to go and see the continent of Uttarakuru, and upon arriving, to rule it, together with my retinue.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata had great supernormal power, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. No sooner had he given rise to this thought than he traveled through the sky by his supernormal power, together with his four kinds of armies.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata saw from afar the flat white land and addressed his ministers, saying: 'Do you see the flat white land of Uttarakuru?' The ministers replied: 'We see it, Divine King!' The king further said: 'Do you know what that is? That is the naturally growing rice of the people of Uttarakuru, what the people of Uttarakuru always eat. You also should eat this food together.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata again saw from afar, within the continent of Uttarakuru, various kinds of trees, pure and beautifully adorned, of various colors, within railings, and addressed his ministers, saying: 'Do you see, within the continent of Uttarakuru, the various kinds of trees, pure and beautifully adorned, of various colors, within railings?' The ministers replied: 'We see them, Divine King!' The king further said: 'Do you know what those are? Those are the clothing trees of the people of Uttarakuru. The people of Uttarakuru take clothes from these trees and wear them. You also should take these clothes and wear them.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata immediately arrived and took up residence on the continent of Uttarakuru. Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, having taken up residence, ruled the continent of Uttarakuru for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ten-thousands of years, together with his retinue.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time thereafter, again had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete, and treasures have rained in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees. I also possess the continent of Godānīya, also the continent of Pūrvavideha, and also the continent of Uttarakuru. I have further heard from the ancients that there is a heaven called the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. I now wish to go and see the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata had great supernormal power, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. No sooner had he given rise to this thought than he traveled through the sky by his supernormal power, together with his four kinds of armies, going toward the sunlight.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata saw from afar, in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, upon Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, something that appeared like a great cloud, and addressed his ministers, saying: 'Do you see, in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, upon Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, something that appears like a great cloud?' The ministers replied: 'We see it, Divine King!' The king further said: 'Do you know what that is? That is the Pārijāta tree of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. The gods of the Thirty-Three sit beneath this tree during the four months of summer, fully endowed with the five desires, and enjoy themselves.' Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata again saw from afar, in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, upon Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, near the southern side, something that appeared like a great cloud, and addressed his ministers, saying: 'Do you see, in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, upon Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, near the southern side, something that appears like a great cloud?' The ministers replied: 'We see it, Divine King!' The king further said: 'Do you know what that is? That is the Hall of Right Dharma of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. The gods of the Thirty-Three, in this hall, on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day, for the sake of gods and humans, contemplate the Dharma and contemplate its meaning.'

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata then arrived at the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. That King Mūrdhagata, having arrived at the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, then entered the Dharma hall. Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, offered King Mūrdhagata half of his seat and invited him to sit. That King Mūrdhagata then sat on Śakra's half-seat. Then, between King Mūrdhagata and Śakra, Lord of the Gods, there was no difference whatsoever: their radiance was the same, their complexion was the same, their form was the same, their deportment and etiquette and their garments were also the same. Only in the blinking of the eyes was there a difference.

"Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata, after a very long time thereafter, again had this thought: 'I possess Jambudvīpa, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people. I have the seven treasures, and a thousand sons complete, and treasures have rained in my palace for seven days, accumulating up to the knees. I also possess the continent of Godānīya, also the continent of Pūrvavideha, and also the continent of Uttarakuru. I have also seen the great assembly of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three gathered together. I have already entered the Dharma hall of the gods. Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, has given me half his seat, and I have already sat on Śakra's half-seat. Between myself and Śakra there is no difference whatsoever: our radiance is the same, our complexion is the same, our form is the same, our deportment and etiquette and our garments are also the same. Only in the blinking of the eyes is there a difference. Why should I not drive Śakra away, seize the other half of the seat, and become king of gods and humans, sovereign by my own authority?'

"Ānanda! No sooner had that King Mūrdhagata given rise to this thought than, without realizing it, he had already descended back to Jambudvīpa. He then lost his supernormal power and fell gravely ill. When he was about to die, his ministers came to King Mūrdhagata and said: 'Divine King! If brahmins, householders, ministers, or common people come and ask us: "What did King Mūrdhagata say when he was at the point of death?" Divine King! How should we answer the brahmins, householders, ministers, and common people?'

"Then King Mūrdhagata addressed his ministers: 'If brahmins, householders, ministers, or common people come and ask you: "What did King Mūrdhagata say when he was at the point of death?" you should answer them thus: "King Mūrdhagata obtained Jambudvīpa, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata obtained the seven treasures, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. He had a thousand sons complete, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata had treasures rain for seven days, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata obtained the continent of Godānīya, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata obtained the continent of Pūrvavideha, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata obtained the continent of Uttarakuru, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata saw the assembly of the gods gathered together, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died. King Mūrdhagata was fully endowed with the merit of the five desires: form, sound, scent, taste, and touch, yet his mind was unsatisfied, and he died." If brahmins, householders, ministers, or common people come and ask you: "What did King Mūrdhagata say when he was at the point of death?" you should answer them thus.'"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"Though the heavens rain wondrous treasures,
The desirous are never satisfied.
Desires bring suffering, not happiness;
The wise should understand this.

Even if one gained a heap of gold
As great as a snowy mountain,
One after another there would be no sufficiency;
The wise person thinks thus.

Even gaining the wondrous five desires of heaven,
One is not made happy by these five pleasures.
Cutting off craving, unattached to desires:
Such is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! That King Mūrdhagata of old, do you think he was someone else? Do not think so. You should know that he was none other than myself. Ānanda! At that time I acted for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking meaning, benefit, peace, and happiness for gods and humans. At that time my teaching of the Dharma did not reach the ultimate; it was not the ultimate purity; it was not the ultimate holy life; the ultimate holy life was not completed. At that time I had not left behind birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, sorrow, and grief, nor was I able to attain liberation from all suffering. Ānanda! Now I have appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Trainer in the Way of Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Now I act for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking meaning, benefit, peace, and happiness for gods and humans. Now my teaching of the Dharma has reached the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate holy life is completed. Now I have left behind birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, sorrow, and grief. Now I have attained liberation from all suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Four Continents, the Third.

---

## (61) Sūtra of the Simile of Cow Dung, Fourth of the King Correlates Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu was in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and he had this thought: "Could there possibly be form that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring? Could there possibly be feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring?"

That bhikṣu, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head in respect, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Today I was in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and I had this thought: 'Could there possibly be form that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring? Could there possibly be feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring?'"

The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "There is no form whatsoever that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring. There is no feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, with his fingernail, scooped up a small amount of cow dung, and said: "Bhikṣu! Do you now see me scoop up a small amount of cow dung with my fingernail?"

The bhikṣu said: "I see it, World-Honored One!"

The Buddha further said: "Bhikṣu! Just so, there is not even this small amount of form that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring. Just so, there is not even this small amount of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that is permanent, unchanging, entirely pleasant, and eternally enduring. Why is this? Bhikṣu! I recall that in the past, through a long night I created merit, and having long created merit, I long received pleasant rewards. Bhikṣu! In the past I practiced loving-kindness for seven years. Through seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction, I did not return to this world. When the world was being destroyed, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. When the world was being established, I descended and was born in an empty Brahmā Palace. In that Brahmā realm I became a Great Brahmā. A thousand times elsewhere I became a Sovereign Lord, and thirty-six times I became Śakra, Lord of the Gods. Again, innumerable times I became a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata.

"Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand great elephants, outfitted with fine trappings and adorned with manifold jewels, covered with white pearl necklaces, with the elephant king Uposatha at their head. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand horses, outfitted with fine trappings and adorned with manifold jewels, with necklaces of gold and silver, with the horse king Valāhaka at their head. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with four kinds of ornaments, decorated with manifold fine coverings of lion, tiger, and leopard skins with spotted patterns, woven in various colors, with all manner of adornments, the foremost being an extremely swift chariot called Joyful Sound. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand great cities, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people, with the royal city of Kuśāvatī at their head. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand towers, made of four kinds of jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, with the Hall of Right Dharma at their head.

"Bhikṣu!
