When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand thrones, made of four kinds of jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, spread with woolen rugs and fine carpets, covered with brocade, gauze, and silk, with body-fitting quilts and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga and pavarapaccattharaṇa fabric. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand pairs of garments: fine linen garments, brocade garments, silk garments, cotton garments, and kaliṅga and pavarapaccattharaṇa garments. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand women, their bodies radiant, brilliantly pure, of beauty surpassing humans, only slightly less than celestials, with elegant and proper features, delightful to behold, fully adorned with jeweled ornaments, all of the Kṣatriya caste, with innumerable others from other clans. Bhikṣu! When I was a Kṣatriya King Mūrdhagata, I had eighty-four thousand kinds of food, constantly prepared day and night, set out for my sake, for me to eat.

"Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand kinds of food, there was one kind of food, supremely delicious, pure and clean, of innumerable flavors, that I always ate. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand women, there was one Kṣatriya woman, the most beautiful and lovely, who always attended upon me. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand pairs of garments, there was one pair of garments, either fine linen, or brocade, or silk, or cotton, or kaliṅga and pavarapaccattharaṇa fabric, that I always wore. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand thrones, there was one throne, either of gold, or silver, or lapis lazuli, or crystal, spread with woolen rugs and fine carpets, covered with brocade, gauze, and silk, with body-fitting quilts and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga and pavarapaccattharaṇa fabric, where I always reclined. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand towers, there was one tower, either of gold, or silver, or lapis lazuli, or crystal, named the Hall of Right Dharma, where I always resided.

"Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand great cities, there was one city, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with many people, named Kuśāvatī, where I always dwelt. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was one chariot, decorated with manifold fine coverings of lion, tiger, and leopard skins with spotted patterns, woven in various colors, with all manner of adornments, an extremely swift chariot called Joyful Sound, that I always rode when going out to view gardens and parks. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was one horse, its body dark blue in color, with a head shaped like a crow's, named the horse king Valāhaka, that I always rode when going out to view gardens and parks. Bhikṣu! Among those eighty-four thousand great elephants, there was one elephant, its entire body extremely white, with all seven limbs perfectly formed, named the elephant king Uposatha, that I always rode when going out to view gardens and parks.

"Bhikṣu! I had this thought: 'What karmic fruit, what karmic reward is it that gives me today such great supernormal power, such great majestic virtue, such great blessings, and such great spiritual authority?' Bhikṣu! I further had this thought: 'It is the fruit of three kinds of karma, the reward of three kinds of karma, that gives me today such great supernormal power, such great majestic virtue, such great blessings, and such great spiritual authority. The first is generosity, the second is self-discipline, and the third is restraint.' Bhikṣu! Observe that all of those possessions have completely perished, and the supernormal power was also lost. Bhikṣu! What do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

He replied: "Impermanent, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?"

He replied: "It is suffering and subject to change, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-learned noble disciple accept it as 'This is myself,' 'This belongs to me,' or 'I belong to it'?"

He replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "Bhikṣu! What do you think? Are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"

He replied: "Impermanent, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If they are impermanent, are they suffering or not suffering?"

He replied: "They are suffering and subject to change, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If they are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-learned noble disciple accept them as 'This is myself,' 'This belongs to me,' or 'I belong to them'?"

He replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Therefore, bhikṣu, you should train thus. Whatever form, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether good or bad, whether near or far, all of it is not myself, not belonging to me, and I do not belong to it. One should observe and know this as it truly is with wisdom. Whatever feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether good or bad, whether near or far, all of it is not myself, not belonging to me, and I do not belong to it. One should observe and know this as it truly is with wisdom. Bhikṣu! If a well-learned noble disciple observes in this way, he becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Being dispassionate, he becomes liberated. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more becoming.' He knows this as it truly is."

Thereupon, that bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, well received and well retained it, then rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

That bhikṣu, having received the Buddha's instruction, dwelt alone and secluded, his mind without negligence, diligently practicing. Dwelling alone and secluded, his mind without negligence, diligently practicing, that son of good family, for whose sake he had shaved off his beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya robe, and with perfect faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, realized the unsurpassed completion of the holy life, and in this present life, by his own knowledge, his own realization, and his own direct witness, he achieved and abided in the attainment: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more becoming." He knew this as it truly is. Thus that bhikṣu, having understood the Dharma, attained the state of an Arhat.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra of the Simile of Cow Dung, the Fourth.

---

## (62) Sūtra of King Bimbisāra Going to Welcome the Buddha, Fifth of the King Correlates Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Magadha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, one thousand bhikṣus, all of them Worthy Ones who had realized the truth, all formerly matted-hair ascetics, going to the city of Rājagṛha in the Magadha domain. Thereupon, King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the World-Honored One was traveling in the country of Magadha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, one thousand bhikṣus, all of them Worthy Ones who had realized the truth, all formerly matted-hair ascetics, and that he was coming to the city of Rājagṛha in the Magadha domain. King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard this, assembled his four kinds of armies: elephant army, horse army, chariot army, and infantry. Having assembled the four kinds of armies, together with a countless multitude, he went the distance of one yojana to where the Buddha was. At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar King Bimbisāra of Magadha approaching, and so he left the road and went to a splendid nyagrodha tree king, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged, together with the assembly of bhikṣus.

King Bimbisāra of Magadha saw from afar the World-Honored One among the forest trees, of proper and beautiful appearance, like the moon among the stars, radiantly brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, fully endowed with marks of excellence, of awesome spiritual majesty, with faculties calm and settled, without obstruction, having accomplished self-mastery, his mind stilled in silent tranquility. Having seen this, he descended from his chariot. As for all kings of the Kṣatriya class who have been consecrated with water and become rulers of men, governing the great earth, they have five ceremonial articles: first, a sword; second, a canopy; third, a heavenly crown; fourth, a jewel-handled whisk; fifth, ornamental sandals. He set all of these aside, together with his four kinds of armies, and proceeded on foot to the Buddha. Having arrived, he paid his respects, and three times he announced his own name and clan: "World-Honored One! I am Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha." He did this three times.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Great King! So it is, so it is. You are Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha."

Thereupon, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha, having three times announced his own name and clan, paid his respects to the Buddha and sat to one side. Among the people of Magadha, some bowed at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side; some greeted the Buddha and sat to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; some, upon seeing the Buddha from afar, silently sat down.

At that time, the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was also sitting in the assembly. The Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was the one upon whom the minds of the people of Magadha were fixed, regarding him as a great venerable teacher, a Worthy One who had realized the truth. Thereupon, the people of Magadha all had this thought: "Does the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under Uruvilvā Kāśyapa? Or does Uruvilvā Kāśyapa practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, addressed the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and spoke these verses:

"Uruvilvā, what did you see,
That you abandoned the fire worship and came here?
Kāśyapa, tell me
The reason you ceased worshipping fire."

"Various flavors of food and drink;
For the sake of desire I worshipped fire.
Seeing the reality within birth,
Therefore I took no pleasure in the worship."

"Kāśyapa, your mind took no pleasure
In the various flavors of food and drink.
Why not delight in gods and humans?
Kāśyapa, tell me."

"Seeing the peace of quiescence and extinction,
The unconditioned, without desire for existence,
And that there is no higher deity,
Therefore I do not worship fire.
The World-Honored One is the most supreme;
The World-Honored One is free from wrong thought.
Having fully understood and awakened to all dharmas,
I received the most supreme Dharma."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa! You should now display your supernormal powers for this assembly, so that all may come to believe with joy."

Thereupon, the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, in accordance with his ability, performed supernormal feats. He vanished from his seat, emerged from the east, flew up into the sky, and displayed the four kinds of deportment: first, walking; second, standing; third, sitting; fourth, lying down. Furthermore, he entered the fire samādhi. The Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having entered the fire samādhi, from his body there issued forth various kinds of flames: blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal. From the lower body fire issued forth, from the upper body water issued forth; from the upper body fire issued forth, from the lower body water issued forth. In the same way from the south, west, and north, he flew up into the sky and displayed the four kinds of deportment: first, walking; second, standing; third, sitting; fourth, lying down. Furthermore, he entered the fire samādhi. The Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having entered the fire samādhi, from his body there issued forth various kinds of flames: blue, yellow, red, white, and the color of crystal. From the lower body fire issued forth, from the upper body water issued forth; from the upper body fire issued forth, from the lower body water issued forth.

Thereupon, the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, having concluded his display of supernormal powers, paid his respects to the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! The Buddha is my teacher, and I am the Buddha's disciple. The Buddha possesses all-knowledge; I do not possess all-knowledge."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Kāśyapa! So it is, Kāśyapa! I possess all-knowledge; you do not possess all-knowledge."

At that time, the Venerable Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, on account of his own experience, spoke these verses:

"In former times, when I was without knowledge,
For the sake of liberation I worshipped the fire.
Though old, I was still like one born blind,
Wrongly failing to see the true limit.

Now I have seen the supreme path,
Spoken by the Unsurpassed Dragon.
In the unconditioned, suffering is exhaustively liberated;
Having seen this, birth and death are ended."

The people of Magadha, having seen all this, then had this thought: "The ascetic Gautama does not practice the holy life under Uruvilvā Kāśyapa. Rather, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa practices the holy life under the ascetic Gautama."

The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, then taught the Dharma for Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha, encouraging him, inspiring his aspiration, and bringing about his joy. By immeasurable skillful means he taught the Dharma for him, encouraging him, inspiring his aspiration, and bringing about his joy. As is the method of all Buddhas, he first spoke of the proper and beautiful Dharma, which delights those who hear it: that is, he spoke of giving, spoke of moral conduct, spoke of the Dharma of rebirth in heaven; he denounced desires as calamitous, and birth-and-death as defilement; he praised the absence of desire as the wondrous Way, the pure and white path of the factors of awakening. The World-Honored One taught this for that great king. When the Buddha knew that the king's mind was joyful, complete, soft, receptive, elevated, one-pointed, without doubt, and inexhaustible, that he had the capacity and strength to receive the true Dharma, then, as all Buddhas teach what is essential, the World-Honored One taught him about suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. "Great King! Form arises and perishes; you should understand that form arises and perishes. Great King! Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arise and perish; you should understand that consciousness arises and perishes. Great King! Just as when there is a great rain, bubbles on the water either arise or perish, Great King, so too does form arise and perish; you should understand that form arises and perishes. Great King! Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arise and perish; you should understand that consciousness arises and perishes.

"Great King! If a son of good family knows that form arises and perishes, he then knows that future form will not arise again. Great King! If a son of good family knows that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arise and perish, he then knows that future consciousness will not arise again. Great King! If a son of good family knows form as it truly is, he does not cling to form, does not conceptualize form, is not defiled by form, does not abide in form, and does not delight in 'form is my self.' Great King! If a son of good family knows feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are, he does not cling to consciousness, does not conceptualize consciousness, is not defiled by consciousness, does not abide in consciousness, and does not delight in 'consciousness is my self.' Great King! If a son of good family does not cling to form, does not conceptualize form, is not defiled by form, does not abide in form, and does not delight in 'form is my self,' then he will not again receive future form. Great King! If a son of good family does not cling to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, does not conceptualize consciousness, is not defiled by consciousness, does not abide in consciousness, and does not delight in 'consciousness is my self,' then he will not again receive future consciousness. Great King! Such a son of good family is immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, and attains peaceful cessation. Having relinquished these five aggregates, he does not again receive aggregates."

Thereupon, the people of Magadha had this thought: "If form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent, then who lives? Who experiences suffering and happiness?"

The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, then addressed the bhikṣus: "Foolish, unlearned ordinary people, not having heard the teaching, see the self as the self and cling to the self. But there is no self, no self's possessions; empty of self, empty of self's possessions. Dharmas arise when they arise, and dharmas perish when they perish. All arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, producing suffering. If there are no causes and conditions, all sufferings cease. Beings, through the continuous conjunction of causes and conditions, give rise to all dharmas. The Tathāgata, having seen the continuous arising of beings, then makes this statement: 'There is birth and there is death. With my pure divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see beings at the time of death, at the time of birth, whether of good appearance or bad appearance, whether excellent or not excellent, going to good destinies or bad destinies, according to the karma that these beings have performed. I see it as it truly is. If beings have accomplished bodily misconduct, verbal and mental misconduct, who slander noble ones, who have accomplished wrong views and the karma of wrong views, then due to these causes and conditions, when the body breaks apart and life ends, they will certainly go to a bad destiny and be born in hell. If beings have accomplished good bodily conduct, good verbal and mental conduct, who do not slander noble ones, who have accomplished right views and the karma of right views, then due to these causes and conditions, when the body breaks apart and life ends, they will certainly ascend to a good destiny, up to the heavens.' I know this to be so, yet I do not say to them: 'This is my self that can perceive, can speak, that acts, initiates, teaches, and causes to initiate, that in such-and-such a place receives the reward of good and evil karma.' Among them, some have this thought: 'This is not fitting, this cannot stand. Its process follows the Dharma: because of this, that arises; if this were absent, that would not arise. Because of this, there is that; if this ceases, then that ceases.' That is, conditioned by ignorance there are formations, and so on up to conditioned by birth there are old age and death. If ignorance ceases, then formations cease, and so on up to if birth ceases, then old age and death cease. Great King! What do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

He answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering?"

He answered: "It is suffering and subject to change, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-learned noble disciple accept it as 'This is myself,' 'This belongs to me,' or 'I belong to it'?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Great King! What do you think? Are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?"

He answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If they are impermanent, are they suffering or not suffering?"

He answered: "They are suffering and subject to change, World-Honored One!"

He further asked: "If they are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a well-learned noble disciple accept them as 'This is myself,' 'This belongs to me,' or 'I belong to them'?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Great King! Therefore you should train thus. Whatever form, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether good or bad, whether near or far, all of it is not myself, not belonging to me, and I do not belong to it. One should observe and know this as it truly is with wisdom. Great King! Whatever feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether good or bad, whether near or far, all of it is not myself, not belonging to me, and I do not belong to it. One should observe and know this as it truly is with wisdom. Great King! If a well-learned noble disciple observes in this way, he becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Being dispassionate, he attains liberation. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more becoming.' He knows this as it truly is."

When the Buddha taught this Dharma, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha, became free from dust, free from defilement, and the Dharma Eye arose regarding all dharmas. And eighty thousand devas, together with twelve thousand people of Magadha, became free from dust, free from defilement, and the Dharma Eye arose regarding all dharmas. Thereupon, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha, having seen the Dharma, obtained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, cut off doubt, crossed beyond perplexity, had no other teacher, no longer followed others, was without hesitation, had already abided in the fruit of realization, and in the Dharma of the World-Honored One attained fearlessness. He then rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One! Today I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. I only ask that the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for my entire life I take refuge, even until the end of my life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Śreṇya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha, and eighty thousand devas, twelve thousand people of Magadha, and the thousand bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra of King Bimbisāra Going to Welcome the Buddha, the Fifth.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtra)
## Fascicle 23

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva during the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

---

### (88) The Sūtra on Seeking the Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are two kinds of seeking. What are the two? There is noble seeking and there is ignoble seeking. What is ignoble seeking? Here, someone who is himself subject to birth seeks what is also subject to birth; himself subject to aging, seeks what is also subject to aging; himself subject to illness, seeks what is also subject to illness; himself subject to death, seeks what is also subject to death; himself subject to sorrow, seeks what is also subject to sorrow; himself subject to defilement, seeks what is also subject to defilement.

"What things are subject to birth? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to birth. A person who is himself subject to birth deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to birth.

"What things are subject to aging? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to aging. A person who is himself subject to aging deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to aging.

"What things are subject to illness? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to illness. A person who is himself subject to illness deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to illness.

"What things are subject to death? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to death. A person who is himself subject to death deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to death.

"What things are subject to sorrow? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to sorrow. A person who is himself subject to sorrow deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to sorrow.

"What things are subject to defilement? Wives and children, male and female servants, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, pigs, fields, houses, money, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, amber, agates, carnelians, crystal, cowries, and various kinds of treasures are subject to defilement. A person who is himself subject to defilement deeply craves, seeks, and pursues such things that are subject to defilement. This is called ignoble seeking.

"What is noble seeking? Here, someone who is himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Himself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seeks the unaging, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Himself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, seeks the illness-free, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Himself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, seeks the deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Himself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, seeks the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Himself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeks the undefiled, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. This is called noble seeking.

"I too, before attaining awakening, when I was still an unawakened bodhisattva, being myself subject to birth, sought what was also subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, sought what was also subject to aging; being myself subject to illness, sought what was also subject to illness; being myself subject to death, sought what was also subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, sought what was also subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, sought what was also subject to defilement.

"At that time I thought: 'Why do I, being myself subject to birth, seek what is also subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging, illness, death, sorrow, and defilement, why do I seek what is also subject to aging, illness, death, sorrow, and defilement? What if I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, were to seek the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa? What if I, being myself subject to aging, illness, death, sorrow, and defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, illness, death, sorrow, and defilement, were to seek the unaging, illness-free, deathless, sorrowless, undefiled, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa?'

"At that time I was a young man, with black hair, in the prime of youth, enjoying the blessings of my youth. My mother and father did not consent, and tears streamed down their faces. Yet I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, left the household life in faith, and went forth into homelessness.

"Having gone forth, I upheld the training and the way of life, guarding my body's actions and perfecting them, guarding my speech's actions and perfecting them. I protected my livelihood and purified it, I fulfilled moral conduct, I guarded the sense faculties, I was endowed with right mindfulness and right knowing, and I was contented.

"How does a bhikṣu guard his body's actions and perfect them? Here, a bhikṣu abandons the taking of life, refrains from the taking of life. He puts down the rod, puts down the knife, is modest and full of kindness, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, including insects. He purifies his mind with regard to the taking of life. He abandons the taking of what is not given, refrains from the taking of what is not given. He takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and his own self abides in purity without theft. He purifies his mind with regard to the taking of what is not given. He abandons unchastity and practices celibacy, diligently practicing the way of purity. He is entirely pure and clean, parting from sensual desire, refraining from unchaste conduct. He purifies his mind with regard to unchaste conduct. Thus does a bhikṣu guard his body's actions and perfect them.

"How does a bhikṣu guard his speech's actions and perfect them? Here, a bhikṣu abandons false speech, refrains from false speech. He speaks truth, he delights in truth, he abides in truth without wavering. He is trustworthy and does not deceive the world. He purifies his mind with regard to false speech. He abandons divisive speech, refrains from divisive speech. He does not carry reports from here to there in order to cause division there, nor does he carry reports from there to here in order to cause division here. He reconciles the divided and encourages the united. He delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, enjoys harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. He purifies his mind with regard to divisive speech. He abandons harsh speech, refrains from harsh speech. Whatever speech is gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, going to the heart, courteous, desired and agreeable to the many, he speaks such words. He purifies his mind with regard to harsh speech. He abandons idle chatter, refrains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks about the meaning, speaks about the Dharma, speaks about the Vinaya. His speech is timely, well-reasoned, well-defined, and connected with the goal. He purifies his mind with regard to idle chatter. Thus does a bhikṣu guard his speech's actions and perfect them.

"How does a bhikṣu protect his livelihood and purify it? Here, a bhikṣu does not engage in wrong means of livelihood: reading signs of the limbs, reading signs of omens, interpreting dreams, reading signs of physiognomy, or reading signs of whether a woman will bear many or few children. He makes his livelihood pure. He purifies his mind with regard to wrong livelihood. Thus does a bhikṣu protect his livelihood and purify it.

"How does a bhikṣu fulfill moral conduct? Here, a bhikṣu abandons and refrains from killing living beings. He puts down the rod, puts down the knife, is modest and full of kindness, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, including insects. He purifies his mind with regard to killing living beings. He abandons and refrains from the taking of what is not given. He takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and his own self abides in purity without theft. He purifies his mind with regard to the taking of what is not given. He abandons unchastity and practices celibacy, diligently practicing the way of purity. He is entirely pure and clean, parting from sensual desire, refraining from unchaste conduct. He purifies his mind with regard to unchaste conduct.

"He abandons and refrains from false speech. He speaks truth, he delights in truth, he abides in truth without wavering. He is trustworthy and does not deceive the world. He purifies his mind with regard to false speech. He abandons and refrains from divisive speech. He does not carry reports from here to there in order to cause division there, nor does he carry reports from there to here in order to cause division here. He reconciles the divided and encourages the united. He delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, enjoys harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. He purifies his mind with regard to divisive speech. He abandons and refrains from harsh speech. Whatever speech is gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, going to the heart, courteous, desired and agreeable to the many, he speaks such words. He purifies his mind with regard to harsh speech. He abandons and refrains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks about the meaning, speaks about the Dharma, speaks about the Vinaya. His speech is timely, well-reasoned, well-defined, and connected with the goal. He purifies his mind with regard to idle chatter.

"He abandons and refrains from damaging seeds and plants. He eats one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times. He abandons and refrains from watching dancing, singing, and musical performances. He abandons and refrains from wearing garlands and perfuming and adorning the body. He abandons and refrains from high and broad beds. He abandons and refrains from accepting gold, silver, and treasures. He abandons and refrains from accepting raw grain. He abandons and refrains from accepting raw meat. He abandons and refrains from accepting women and girls. He abandons and refrains from accepting male and female servants. He abandons and refrains from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. He abandons and refrains from accepting chickens and pigs. He abandons and refrains from accepting fields, houses, and gardens. He abandons and refrains from acting as a messenger or go-between. He abandons and refrains from buying and selling. He abandons and refrains from using fraudulent weights, measures, and scales. He abandons and refrains from the crookedness of bribery, deception, and fraud. He abandons and refrains from cutting, striking, binding, ambushing, plundering, and extorting. He purifies his mind with regard to these matters. Thus does a bhikṣu fulfill moral conduct.

"How does a bhikṣu guard the sense faculties? Here, when a bhikṣu sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its sign and does not grasp at its features. If he were to leave the eye faculty unguarded, covetousness and grief, evil unwholesome states, would flow into him. Therefore he practices restraint, he guards the eye faculty and achieves restraint of the eye faculty. When he hears a sound with the ear, smells an odor with the nose, tastes a flavor with the tongue, feels a tangible with the body, or cognizes a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its sign and does not grasp at its features. If he were to leave the mind faculty unguarded, covetousness and grief, evil unwholesome states, would flow into him. Therefore he practices restraint, he guards the mind faculty and achieves restraint of the mind faculty. Thus does a bhikṣu guard the sense faculties.

"How is a bhikṣu endowed with right mindfulness and right knowing? Here, when a bhikṣu goes forward and returns, he acts with right knowing. When he looks ahead and looks aside, he acts with right knowing. When he bends and extends his limbs, he acts with right knowing. When he holds his saṅghāṭī robe, bowl, and robes, he acts with right knowing. When he walks, stands, sits, lies down, sleeps, wakes, speaks, and is silent, he acts with right knowing. Thus is a bhikṣu endowed with right mindfulness and right knowing.

"How is a bhikṣu contented? Here, a bhikṣu is contented with robes to cover his body and with almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he takes along only these things. Just as a bird flies here and there with only the burden of its two wings, in the same way a bhikṣu is contented with robes to cover his body and almsfood to sustain his belly, and wherever he goes he takes along only these things. Thus is a bhikṣu contented.

"He, endowed with this aggregate of noble moral conduct, endowed with this noble guarding of the sense faculties, endowed with this noble right mindfulness and right knowing, endowed with this noble contentment, dwells in a secluded place: in a forest, under a tree, in an empty cave, on a mountain, in a gorge, in a rocky shelter, in a charnel ground, in a remote grove, in the open, or on a straw mat.

"After his meal, when he returns from his almsround, he sits cross-legged, holds his body upright, establishes mindfulness before him, and abandons covetousness for the world. With a mind free from covetousness he dwells, purifying his mind of covetousness. In the same way, he abandons ill will, anger, and resentment. He has compassion for the benefit of all living beings. He purifies his mind of ill will and anger. He abandons sloth and torpor and dwells perceiving light, mindful and clearly knowing. He purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. He abandons restlessness and remorse and dwells without agitation, with an inwardly peaceful mind. He purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. He abandons doubt and has crossed beyond doubt. He has no doubt regarding wholesome states. He purifies his mind of doubt.

"He, having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, with examination, with sustained thought, with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna.

"When his examination and sustained thought cease, with internal confidence, with unification of mind, without examination, without sustained thought, with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna.

"With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly knowing, and he experiences happiness with the body. What the noble ones describe as 'dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness,' he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.

"With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, with neither suffering nor happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"Having attained concentration of mind in this way, with a pure mind, a mind free from defilement, a mind that is pliant and supple, a mind that is stable, a mind that has attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, one hundred births, one thousand births, one hundred thousand births, the formations and destructions of countless eons of world systems, the formations and destructions of countless eons of world systems. 'At that place I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food, I experienced such happiness and suffering, I had such a lifespan. Passing away from that place, I was reborn in another place. At that other place I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food, I experienced such happiness and suffering, I had such a lifespan. Passing away from that place, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with all their details and features. This was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose. Darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens for one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute.

"Having attained concentration of mind in this way, with a pure mind, a mind free from defilement, a mind that is pliant and supple, a mind that is stable, a mind that has attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies. He understands how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings who were endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind, who reviled the noble ones, who held wrong views and undertook actions based on wrong views, after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. But these beings who were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views and undertook actions based on right views, after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies, and understands how beings fare according to their actions. This was the second knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose. Darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens for one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute.

"Having attained concentration of mind in this way, with a pure mind, a mind free from defilement, a mind that is pliant and supple, a mind that is stable, a mind that has attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'These are the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.'

"Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of existence, and liberated from the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, there is the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' This was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose. Darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens for one who is diligent, ardent, and resolute.

"Having thus realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening, I then thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I further thought: 'This Dharma that I have attained is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, quiescent, sublime, beyond the realm of logic, subtle, to be understood by the wise. But these beings delight in attachment, take pleasure in attachment, and rejoice in attachment. For beings who delight in attachment, take pleasure in attachment, and rejoice in attachment, this matter is difficult to see: that is to say, conditioned arising. This matter is also difficult to see: the calming of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa. If I were to teach the Dharma and others could not understand me, that would be wearying and troublesome for me.'

"At that time there arose in my mind, spontaneously, these verses never heard before:

'I have realized this Dharma so profound,
Hard to see and hard to understand.
Now to explain it to others would be futile toil,
For I alone would bear this burden in vain.

This Dharma cannot be conveyed by words;
It goes against the worldly stream.
Subtle, profound, difficult to perceive,
Those shrouded in the darkness of desire cannot see it.'

"After contemplating in this way, my mind inclined toward resting at ease and not teaching the Dharma.

"At that time, the Brahmā King knew with his own mind the thoughts in my mind. He thought: 'Alas, the world will be ruined! Alas, the world will perish! Now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, has realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening, yet inclines toward resting at ease and not teaching the Dharma.'

"Then the Brahmā King, as quickly as a strong man extends his bent arm or bends his extended arm, vanished from the Brahmā world and appeared before me. He arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms toward me, and said: 'World-Honored One, please teach the Dharma! Please teach the Dharma! There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are declining because they do not hear the Dharma. There will be those who can understand the Dharma.'

"The Brahmā King further said in verse:

'In the land of Magadha there appeared previously
An impure Dharma, conceived by the defiled.
Open now the gate of the deathless!
Let them hear the Dharma realized by the Stainless One.

As one standing atop a mountain peak
Looks down upon the people all around,
So too, O Wise One, with the Dharma-eye complete,
Ascend the palace of the Dharma
And look upon the sorrowing multitudes,
Oppressed by birth, old age, and death.

Rise up, O Hero who has conquered in battle!
O leader of caravans, free from debt in the world!
I pray the World-Honored One will teach the Dharma;
There will surely be those who can understand it.'

"At that time, I knew the entreaty of the Brahmā King, and out of compassion for living beings, with the Buddha-eye I surveyed the world. With the Buddha-eye I surveyed the world and saw beings with much dust in their eyes and beings with little dust in their eyes, beings with sharp faculties and beings with dull faculties, beings with good qualities and beings with bad qualities, beings easy to teach and beings difficult to teach. Among them, some feared the blame of the other world and of wrongdoing; some did not fear such blame.

"Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, remain under the water and flourish below the surface; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and are level with the water's surface; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, but rise above the water and are not wetted by it. In the same way, with the Buddha-eye I surveyed the world and saw beings with much dust in their eyes and beings with little dust in their eyes, beings with sharp faculties and beings with dull faculties, beings with good qualities and beings with bad qualities, beings easy to teach and beings difficult to teach. Among them, some feared the blame of the other world and of wrongdoing; some did not fear such blame.

"At that time, I spoke to the Brahmā King in verse:

'I now open for them
The gate of the deathless.
Those who have ears, let them release their faith.
O Brahmā, I did not speak the Dharma among people
Out of the thought that it would be troublesome,
Not out of ill will or jealousy.'

"Then the Brahmā King knew that the Buddha had consented to teach the Dharma. He bowed his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times, and suddenly vanished.

"I then thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I further thought: 'I should first teach it to Ārāḍa Kālāma, for he would be able to quickly understand this Dharma.'

"Then a deity came to me and said: 'World-Honored One, Ārāḍa Kālāma passed away seven days ago.'

"I also had the knowledge and vision that Ārāḍa Kālāma had passed away seven days ago. I then thought: 'It is a great loss for Ārāḍa Kālāma. If he had heard this Dharma, he would have quickly understood it.'

"I further thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I again thought: 'I should first teach it to Udraka Rāmaputra, for he would be able to quickly understand this Dharma.'

"Then a deity came to me and said: 'World-Honored One, Udraka Rāmaputra passed away last night.'

"I also had the knowledge and vision that Udraka Rāmaputra had passed away last night. I then thought: 'It is a great loss for Udraka Rāmaputra. If he had heard this Dharma, he would have quickly understood it.'

"I further thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I again thought: 'The group of five bhikṣus attended to me and served me for a long time. When I was practicing austerities, they provided me with various services. I should now first teach the Dharma to the group of five bhikṣus.'

"I further thought: 'Where are the group of five bhikṣus dwelling now?' With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw that the group of five bhikṣus were dwelling in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī. Having stayed under the bodhi tree as long as I wished, I then set out toward Vārāṇasī.

"On the way, between Gayā and the place of awakening, the Ājīvika Upaka saw me from afar. Having seen me, he said: 'Venerable Gautama, your faculties are serene and your complexion is bright and pure. Venerable Gautama, under whom did you go forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dharma do you profess?'

"At that time I answered Upaka the Ājīvika in verse:

'I am the All-Transcending One, the All-Knowing One,
Unstained by all phenomena.
I have abandoned everything, liberated through the ending of craving.
Having realized by myself, whom would I point to as my teacher?

I have no teacher;
No one is my equal.
In the world with its gods,
There is no one comparable to me.

I am the Arhat in the world,
The unsurpassed Teacher.
I alone am the Fully Awakened One,
Having become cool, having attained nirvāṇa.

I go to the city of Kāśī
To turn the Wheel of the Dharma.
In this blinded world,
I shall beat the drum of the deathless.'

"Upaka the Ājīvika said: 'Venerable Gautama, based on what you are saying, you should be the Boundless Victor.'

"I answered Upaka: 'Those who are like me are indeed victors. Those who have attained the destruction of the taints are victors. I have conquered all evil states; therefore, Upaka, I am the Victor.'

"After I said this, Upaka the Ājīvika shook his head and departed by a side path.

"I then traveled to Vārāṇasī, to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, and went to where the group of five bhikṣus were staying. The group of five bhikṣus saw me coming from afar, and seeing me, they agreed among themselves: 'This ascetic Gautama is coming. He is extravagant and has abandoned his efforts. He has returned to a life of abundance. We should not pay homage to him, should not rise to greet him, should not receive his robe and bowl, but we may set out a seat for him. If he wishes to sit, let him sit.'

"As I drew nearer, the group of five bhikṣus could not keep to their agreement. They all rose to greet me. Some took my robe and bowl, some prepared a seat, and some brought water for washing my feet. However, they addressed me by name and called me 'friend.'

"I said to the group of five bhikṣus: 'Do not address the Tathāgata by name, and do not call him "friend." Why? The Tathāgata is an Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, who has realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus! I have attained the deathless. I shall instruct you, I shall teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach you, before long, within this very life, you will realize for yourselves through direct knowledge that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered it, you will dwell in it.'

"The group of five bhikṣus said to me: 'Friend Gautama, even with the conduct, practice, and austerities you formerly maintained, you were not able to attain any superhuman distinction of knowledge or vision worthy of the noble ones. Now that you are extravagant and have abandoned your efforts and returned to a life of abundance, how can you have attained any superhuman distinction of knowledge or vision worthy of the noble ones?'

"I said to the group of five bhikṣus: 'Do not speak in that way. Do not speak in that way. The Tathāgata is not extravagant, has not abandoned his efforts, and has not returned to a life of abundance. The Tathāgata is an Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, who has realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus! I have attained the deathless. I shall instruct you, I shall teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach you, before long, within this very life, you will realize for yourselves through direct knowledge that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered it, you will dwell in it.'

"The group of five bhikṣus addressed me a second time: 'Friend Gautama, even with the conduct, practice, and austerities you formerly maintained, you were not able to attain any superhuman distinction. Now that you are extravagant and have abandoned your efforts and returned to a life of abundance, how can you have attained any superhuman distinction of knowledge or vision worthy of the noble ones?'

"I said to the group of five bhikṣus a second time: 'Do not speak in that way. Do not speak in that way. The Tathāgata is not extravagant, has not abandoned his efforts, and has not returned to a life of abundance. The Tathāgata is an Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, who has realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus! I have attained the deathless. I shall instruct you, I shall teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach you, before long, within this very life, you will realize for yourselves through direct knowledge that unsurpassed goal of the holy life, and having entered it, you will dwell in it.'

"The group of five bhikṣus addressed me a third time: 'Friend Gautama, even with the conduct, practice, and austerities you formerly maintained, you were not able to attain any superhuman distinction. Now that you are extravagant and have abandoned your efforts and returned to a life of abundance, how can you have attained any superhuman distinction of knowledge or vision worthy of the noble ones?'

"I said to the group of five bhikṣus: 'Have you ever heard me speak like this before?'

"The group of five bhikṣus answered me: 'No, we have not, World-Honored One.'

"'Group of five bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is an Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, who has realized the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening. Listen well, group of five bhikṣus! I have attained the deathless. I shall instruct you, I shall teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I teach you, before long, within this very life, you will realize for yourselves through direct knowledge that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered it, you will dwell in it.'

"I was then able to persuade the group of five bhikṣus. At times I would teach two bhikṣus, and three bhikṣus would go on almsround. What the three bhikṣus obtained on almsround, the six of us would share and eat. At times I would teach three bhikṣus, and two bhikṣus would go on almsround. What the two bhikṣus obtained on almsround, the six of us would share and eat.

"When I taught the group of five bhikṣus in this way, they being themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, sought the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Being themselves subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, they sought the unaging, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the unaging, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Being themselves subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, they sought the illness-free, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the illness-free, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Being themselves subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, they sought the deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Being themselves subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, they sought the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Being themselves subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, they sought the undefiled, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa, and they attained the undefiled, the unsurpassed security from bondage, nirvāṇa. Knowledge and vision arose in them: 'Our liberation is unshakable. This is our last birth. There is no more renewal of being.'

"Bhikṣus, there are five kinds of sensual pleasures. What are the five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear, odors cognizable by the nose, flavors cognizable by the tongue, and tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These are the five kinds of sensual pleasures.

"Those ascetics and brahmins who are bound, infatuated, attached, and do not see the danger, and use these five kinds of sensual pleasures without the wisdom to escape from them, should be understood to have met with misfortune, to have met with calamity, to have been dealt with by the Evil One as he wishes. Just as a wild deer that is caught in a trap should be understood to have met with misfortune, to have met with calamity, to have been dealt with by the hunter as he wishes, unable to go wherever the hunter goes; in the same way, those ascetics and brahmins who are bound, infatuated, attached, and do not see the danger, and use these five kinds of sensual pleasures without the wisdom to escape from them, should be understood to have met with misfortune, to have met with calamity, to have been dealt with by the Evil One as he wishes, unable to go wherever the Evil One goes.

"Those ascetics and brahmins who are not bound, not infatuated, not attached, who see the danger, and who use these five kinds of sensual pleasures with the wisdom to escape from them, should be understood to have met with good fortune, not to have met with calamity, and not to have been dealt with by the Evil One as he wishes. Just as a wild deer that is not caught in a trap should be understood to have met with good fortune, not to have met with calamity, not to have been dealt with by the hunter as he wishes, and the hunter cannot go wherever the deer goes; in the same way, those ascetics and brahmins who are not bound, not infatuated, not attached, who see the danger, and who use these five kinds of sensual pleasures with the wisdom to escape from them, should be understood to have met with good fortune, not to have met with calamity, and not to have been dealt with by the Evil One as he wishes. The Evil One cannot go wherever they go.

"Just as a wild deer roaming in the wilderness, walking on a hillside, may go with confidence, may stand with confidence, may sit with confidence, and may lie down with confidence. Why? Because it is beyond the reach of the hunter. In the same way, a bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, with examination, with sustained thought, with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when examination and sustained thought cease, with internal confidence, with unification of mind, without examination, without sustained thought, with the rapture and happiness born of concentration, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly knowing, and experiences happiness with the body. What the noble ones describe as 'dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness,' he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, with neither suffering nor happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impingement, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving 'Space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving 'Consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving 'There is nothing,' enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are completely destroyed. This bhikṣu is said to have bound Māra, to have blinded Māra's eye, made it invisible, and to have gone where the Evil One cannot see him. He has crossed beyond attachment to the world."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (89) The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu's Request

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the night had passed, at dawn, arose, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, may it please the World-Honored One to briefly teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, I will dwell alone, in seclusion, diligent, not negligent. Having dwelt alone, in seclusion, diligent, not negligent, I will then realize the purpose for which a son of good family rightly goes forth from the household life into homelessness, and I will realize in this very life, through direct knowledge, the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, and having entered it, I will dwell in it, knowing: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'"

The World-Honored One told him: "Bhikṣu, what do you think? Is the eye permanent or impermanent?"

He answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

He answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, being subject to change, would a learned noble disciple perceive in it a self, or what belongs to a self, or a self within it, or it within a self?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: are they permanent or impermanent?"

He answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent, are they suffering?"

He answered: "They are suffering, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent and suffering, being subject to change, would a learned noble disciple perceive in them a self, or what belongs to a self, or a self within them, or them within a self?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Therefore, bhikṣu, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Whatever perception there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all perception should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all formations should be seen as they really are with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Bhikṣu, a learned noble disciple who sees thus becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, and disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, there is the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'"

At that time, when that bhikṣu heard what the Buddha taught, he was delighted and joyful. He rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, and departed. Having dwelt alone, in seclusion, diligent, not negligent, he practiced as taught. Having dwelt alone, in seclusion, diligent, not negligent, practicing as taught, the purpose for which a son of good family rightly goes forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, he realized in this very life, through direct knowledge, and having entered it, he dwelt in it, knowing: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being."

That venerable one, having heard the Buddha's teaching, through diligent practice, attained arhatship.

Thus spoke the Buddha. That bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (90) The Sūtra on Knowing the Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the method for knowing the Dharma. Listen well and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, World-Honored One, we wish to hear."

The Buddha said: "What is the method for knowing the Dharma? A bhikṣu should know the Dharma thus: 'Do I or do I not have internal covetousness?' If a bhikṣu has internal covetousness, he knows as it really is: 'I have internal covetousness.' If a bhikṣu does not have internal covetousness, he knows as it really is: 'I do not have internal covetousness.' If a bhikṣu formerly had internal covetousness and now is rid of it, he knows this as it really is. If a bhikṣu has rid himself of internal covetousness and in the future it will not arise again, he knows this as it really is.

"In the same way, regarding ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt: a bhikṣu should know the Dharma thus: 'Do I or do I not have internal doubt?' If a bhikṣu has internal doubt, he knows as it really is: 'I have internal doubt.' If a bhikṣu does not have internal doubt, he knows as it really is: 'I do not have internal doubt.' If a bhikṣu formerly had internal doubt and now is rid of it, he knows this as it really is. If a bhikṣu has rid himself of internal doubt and in the future it will not arise again, he knows this as it really is.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu should know the Dharma thus: regarding the mindfulness awakening factor, 'Do I or do I not have the internal mindfulness awakening factor?' If a bhikṣu has the internal mindfulness awakening factor, he knows as it really is: 'I have the internal mindfulness awakening factor.' If a bhikṣu does not have the internal mindfulness awakening factor, he knows as it really is: 'I do not have the internal mindfulness awakening factor.' If the mindfulness awakening factor has not yet arisen, he knows how it comes to arise. If it has arisen, he knows how it reaches fulfillment through development.

"In the same way, regarding the investigation of phenomena awakening factor, the effort awakening factor, the rapture awakening factor, the tranquility awakening factor, the concentration awakening factor, and the equanimity awakening factor: a bhikṣu should know the Dharma thus: regarding the equanimity awakening factor, 'Do I or do I not have the internal equanimity awakening factor?' If a bhikṣu has the internal equanimity awakening factor, he knows as it really is: 'I have the internal equanimity awakening factor.' If a bhikṣu does not have the internal equanimity awakening factor, he knows as it really is: 'I do not have the internal equanimity awakening factor.' If the equanimity awakening factor has not yet arisen, he knows how it comes to arise. If it has arisen, he knows how it reaches fulfillment through development. This is called a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma.

"What is the method for knowing meaning? A bhikṣu knows the meaning of this or that statement, knowing: 'This is the meaning of this statement, and that is the meaning of that statement.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows meaning.

"What is the method for knowing time? A bhikṣu knows: 'This is the time to cultivate the samādhi of examination; this is the time to cultivate the samādhi of non-examination; this is the time for instruction; this is the time for silence.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows time.

"What is the method for knowing moderation? A bhikṣu knows moderation in eating, drinking, going, sitting, lying down, speaking, being silent, practicing walking meditation, and so forth. This is called a bhikṣu who knows moderation.

"What is the method for knowing oneself? A bhikṣu knows himself: 'I have this much faith, this much moral conduct, this much learning, this much generosity, this much wisdom, this much ready wit, this much attainment in various doctrines.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows himself.

"What is the method for knowing assemblies? A bhikṣu knows assemblies: 'This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of ascetics. In such an assembly, I should approach thus, I should stand thus, I should act thus, I should sit thus, I should speak thus, I should be silent thus.' This is called a bhikṣu who knows assemblies.

"What is the method for knowing persons? A bhikṣu evaluates persons by comparing them with others. If there is a person who has faith, who does not seek association with and attendance on good friends, who does not often go to hear the good Dharma, who does not concentrate his mind on retaining what he has heard, who does not contemplate the meaning and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, then because he does not seek association with and attendance on good friends, because he does not often go to hear the good Dharma, because he does not concentrate his mind on retaining what he has heard, because he does not contemplate the meaning and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, this person declines, regresses, and does not grow in the good Dharma. One should know this about this person.

"Just as the moon in the dark half of the month, night by night its brilliance decreases, its form decreases, its light decreases, its circumference decreases; in the same way, this person, though he has faith, does not seek association with and attendance on good friends, does not often go to hear the good Dharma, does not concentrate his mind on retaining what he has heard, does not contemplate the meaning and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Because he does not seek association with and attendance on good friends, because he does not often go to hear the good Dharma, because he does not concentrate his mind on retaining what he has heard, because he does not contemplate the meaning and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, this person declines, regresses, and does not grow in the good Dharma. One should know this about this person.

"Furthermore, there is a person who has faith, who seeks association with and attendance on good friends, who often goes to hear the good Dharma, who concentrates his mind on retaining what he has heard, who contemplates the meaning and practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Because he seeks association with and attendance on good friends, because he often goes to hear the good Dharma, because he concentrates his mind on retaining what he has heard, because he contemplates the meaning and practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, this person does not decline, does not regress, and grows in the good Dharma. One should know this about this person.

"Just as the moon in the bright half of the month, night by night its brilliance increases, its form increases, its light increases, its circumference increases; in the same way, this person has faith, seeks association with and attendance on good friends, often goes to hear the good Dharma, concentrates his mind on retaining what he has heard, contemplates the meaning and practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Because he seeks association with and attendance on good friends, because he often goes to hear the good Dharma, because he concentrates his mind on retaining what he has heard, because he contemplates the meaning and practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, this person does not decline, does not regress, and grows in the good Dharma. One should know this about this person. This is called a bhikṣu who knows persons.

"If a bhikṣu does not know the Dharma, does not know meaning, does not know time, does not know moderation, does not know himself, does not know assemblies, and does not know persons, whether superior or inferior, then that bhikṣu is not called one who knows the Dharma and knows meaning.

"If a bhikṣu knows the Dharma, knows meaning, knows time, knows moderation, knows himself, knows assemblies, and knows persons, whether superior or inferior, then that bhikṣu is called one who knows the Dharma and knows meaning.

"Bhikṣus, I have now explained to you the method for knowing the Dharma, the method for knowing meaning, the method for knowing time, the method for knowing moderation, the method for knowing oneself, the method for knowing assemblies, and the method for knowing persons. What a teacher should do for his disciples, out of compassion and seeking their welfare, I have already done for you. You should further practice among the trees, in empty and quiet places, practice sitting meditation, and do not be negligent. Do not let there be cause for later regret. This is my teaching to you."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (91) The Sūtra on Cunda the Silversmith

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Malla country together with a large community of bhikṣus, and arrived at Pāvā. The World-Honored One stayed in the mango grove of Cunda the silversmith.

At that time, Cunda the silversmith heard that the Buddha was traveling in Malla country together with a large community of bhikṣus, had arrived at Pāvā, and was staying in his mango grove. Cunda the silversmith then prepared various kinds of food and drink: the most refined and choicest delicacies, and also sandalwood mushrooms. When all was prepared, he went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, I have prepared a meal. May the World-Honored One consent to accept it."

At that time, the World-Honored One consented by remaining silent. Cunda the silversmith, knowing that the Buddha had consented, rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him, and departed.

When the night had passed and dawn arrived, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and together with the community of bhikṣus went to the home of Cunda the silversmith. Having arrived, they sat down on the seats prepared for them. Cunda the silversmith then personally served various kinds of food and drink, and also sandalwood mushrooms. The World-Honored One then told Cunda: "Do not serve the sandalwood mushrooms to the bhikṣus. Serve them only to me. Why? Cunda, there is someone in the world who alone can digest these sandalwood mushrooms. Cunda, there is no other ascetic or brahmin, no Māra, no Brahmā, nor anyone else in the world who can properly digest these sandalwood mushrooms, except the Tathāgata alone."
