Cunda the silversmith, having been so instructed by the World-Honored One, served the sandalwood mushrooms only to the Buddha, and served the other food and drink to the bhikṣu Sangha.

At that time, the World-Honored One told Cunda: "The remaining sandalwood mushrooms, bury them in a pit. Why? I see no one in the world, neither among gods, Māras, Brahmās, ascetics, brahmins, nor any other being, except the Tathāgata, who could properly digest these mushrooms."

Cunda the silversmith received this instruction and took the remaining sandalwood mushrooms and buried them in a pit.

He then returned, sat down before the Buddha, and the World-Honored One taught him the Dharma, instructed, benefited, and delighted him, and then rose from his seat and departed.

After the World-Honored One had eaten Cunda's sandalwood mushrooms, a severe illness arose, with intense pain and bloody dysentery, close to death. The World-Honored One was mindful and clearly knowing, and endured it without complaint.

The World-Honored One then told the Venerable Ānanda: "Let us go to Kuśinagara."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One then set out on the road together with a large community of bhikṣus, heading for Kuśinagara. Along the way, the World-Honored One left the road and went to the foot of a tree. He told the Venerable Ānanda: "Please fold a robe in four for me. I am weary and wish to rest."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, World-Honored One," and immediately folded a robe in four.

The World-Honored One sat down and told the Venerable Ānanda: "Please fetch me some water. I am thirsty and wish to drink."

The Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, just now five hundred carts have crossed through this stream, and the water has been stirred up and is muddy and not clean. Please, World-Honored One, the Kukusthā River is not far from here. Its water is clear, cool, and pleasant. The World-Honored One can drink there and also bathe his body."

A second time the World-Honored One told the Venerable Ānanda: "Please fetch me some water. I am thirsty and wish to drink."

A second time the Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, just now five hundred carts have crossed through this stream, and the water has been stirred up and is muddy and not clean. Please, World-Honored One, the Kukusthā River is not far from here. Its water is clear, cool, and pleasant. The World-Honored One can drink there and also bathe his body."

A third time the World-Honored One told the Venerable Ānanda: "Please fetch me some water. I am thirsty and wish to drink."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, World-Honored One." He immediately took a bowl and went to fetch water from the stream. That stream, which had been churned by the five hundred carts and was muddy, when the Venerable Ānanda arrived, spontaneously became clear, pure, and without sediment.

The Venerable Ānanda thought: "The Tathāgata's great supernatural powers are truly remarkable and extraordinary! This stream that had been churned by the five hundred carts and was muddy, when I arrived, spontaneously became clear, pure, and without sediment."

He then took the water and brought it back, saying to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata's great supernatural powers are truly remarkable and extraordinary! That stream that had been churned by the five hundred carts and was muddy, when I arrived, spontaneously became clear, pure, and without sediment. I now offer the water. May the World-Honored One know the proper time to drink."

The World-Honored One then drank the water. Having finished, he rose and went on to the Kukusthā River with the community of bhikṣus. There at the river, the World-Honored One bathed and drank.

After coming out of the water, he went to one side and sat beneath a tree. He told the Venerable Ānanda: "Please fold a robe in four for me. I am weary and my back is aching. I wish to rest."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, World-Honored One," and folded a robe in four. The World-Honored One lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one foot placed on the other, mindful and clearly knowing.

At that time, the World-Honored One told the Venerable Ānanda: "If anyone were to make Cunda the silversmith feel remorseful by saying, 'It is not profitable for you, Cunda. You have gained no good fortune. The Tathāgata ate his last meal at your home and then passed into final nirvāṇa,' then Cunda's remorse should be removed by saying: 'It is profitable for you, Cunda. You have gained great good fortune. The Tathāgata ate his last meal at your home and then passed into final nirvāṇa.' Why? I have heard it from the Buddha himself, have received it from the Buddha face to face: There are two offerings of food that are equal in merit, equal in result, vastly surpassing other offerings, and yielding the greatest fruit and greatest benefit. What are the two? The meal eaten before the Tathāgata attains the unsurpassed, true, and right awakening, and the meal eaten before the Tathāgata passes into the nirvāṇa without remainder. These two offerings of food are equal in merit, equal in result, vastly surpassing other offerings, and yielding the greatest fruit and greatest benefit.

"Ānanda, you should speak thus to Cunda the silversmith: 'It is profitable for you, Cunda. You have gained great good fortune, because the Tathāgata ate his last meal at your home and then passed into final nirvāṇa. I have heard from the Buddha himself, have received it from the Buddha face to face, that these two offerings of food are equal in merit, equal in result, vastly surpassing other offerings, and yielding the greatest fruit and greatest benefit. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to long life. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to beautiful appearance. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to happiness. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to fame and reputation. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to rebirth in heaven. Cunda has accumulated meritorious deeds that lead to sovereignty.'"

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"For one who gives, merit increases;
Through self-restraint, enmity does not arise.
One who is skilled abandons evil;
Through the destruction of desire, anger, and delusion, one att

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 12

## (63) The Sūtra on Vebhaliṅga, Sixth in the Section on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Kosala.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking along the road together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and on the way he joyfully smiled. Venerable Ānanda, seeing the World-Honored One smile, joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One, what is the cause and condition for this smile? Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones never smile without cause. I wish to hear the meaning of this."

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, in this very place, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sat in this spot and taught the Dharma to his disciples."

Thereupon Venerable Ānanda, at that very place, quickly spread out a seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, I wish that the World-Honored One would also sit in this place and teach the Dharma to his disciples, so that this place will have been used by two Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones."

At that time, the World-Honored One sat down on the seat that Venerable Ānanda had prepared for him, and having sat down, he said: "Ānanda, in this very place, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a lecture hall. The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sat within it and taught the Dharma to his disciples. Ānanda, in this very place there was formerly a village called Vebhaliṅga, which was extremely prosperous and pleasant, with many people.

"Ānanda, in the village of Vebhaliṅga there was a brahmin great householder named Akrodhana, who was extremely wealthy and happy, with immeasurable riches and possessions, with livestock and property beyond reckoning, with fiefs and food-villages all fully equipped. Ānanda, the brahmin great householder Akrodhana had a son named Uttara the young brahmin, who was acknowledged by his father and mother, of pure birth, with an unbroken lineage of parents for seven generations, born without blemish in each generation, broadly learned and retentive, having mastered the four Vedic scriptures, and deeply versed in the five types of exposition: causation, correlation, proper form, grammar, and exegesis. Ānanda, the young man Uttara had a good friend named Nandipāla the potter, who was always beloved and cherished by the young man Uttara, who delighted in seeing him and never grew weary of it.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter had taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus. He did not doubt the Three Honored Ones, was not confused about suffering, its origination, its cessation, and the path. He had attained faith, upheld the precepts, was broadly learned, generous in giving, and accomplished in wisdom. He abstained from killing and had abandoned killing, cast aside knives and weapons, had shame and conscience, had a compassionate heart, and benefited all beings even down to insects. His mind was purified and freed from killing.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from taking what was not given and had abandoned taking what was not given. He took only what was given, delighted in taking what was given, always loved to give, was joyful and without stinginess, and did not hope for any return. His mind was purified and freed from taking what was not given.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from unchaste conduct and had abandoned unchaste conduct. He diligently cultivated the holy life, was energetic in excellent practice, pure and undefiled, free from desire and having abandoned sexual conduct. His mind was purified and freed from unchaste conduct.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from false speech and had abandoned false speech. He spoke truthfully, delighted in truth, abided in truth without wavering, was entirely trustworthy, and did not deceive the world. His mind was purified and freed from false speech.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from divisive speech and had abandoned divisive speech. He practiced non-divisive speech and did not cause the ruin of others. He did not hear something here and tell it there to cause ruin here, nor hear something there and tell it here to cause ruin there. He wished to unite those who were separated, and those who were united he made joyful. He did not form factions, did not delight in factions, and did not praise factions. His mind was purified and freed from divisive speech.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from harsh speech and had abandoned harsh speech. Whatever words were rough and coarse in manner, harsh-sounding and offensive to the ear, displeasing and unlovable to all, causing others suffering and distress, preventing concentration, such speech he abandoned. Whatever he said was clear, gentle, and smooth, pleasing to the ear and entering the heart, agreeable and lovable, bringing others ease and comfort, his words being distinct and clear, not causing fear in others, enabling others to attain concentration; such was the speech he spoke. His mind was purified and freed from harsh speech.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from frivolous speech and had abandoned frivolous speech. He spoke at the right time, spoke truthfully, spoke of the Dharma, spoke of meaning, spoke of cessation, and delighted in speaking of cessation. His words were appropriate to the occasion, well-instructing and well-admonishing. His mind was purified and freed from frivolous speech.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from trading and had abandoned trading. He had cast aside scales and measuring vessels, did not accept goods in trade, did not bind or restrain people, did not hope to cheat with false measures, and did not use small gains to encroach upon or deceive others. His mind was purified and freed from trading.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting widows and young girls, and had abandoned accepting widows and young girls. His mind was purified and freed from accepting widows and young girls.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting male and female slaves, and had abandoned accepting male and female slaves. His mind was purified and freed from accepting male and female slaves.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and had abandoned accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. His mind was purified and freed from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting chickens and pigs, and had abandoned accepting chickens and pigs. His mind was purified and freed from accepting chickens and pigs.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting farmlands and shops, and had abandoned accepting farmlands and shops. His mind was purified and freed from accepting farmlands and shops.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans, and had abandoned accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans. His mind was purified and freed from accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from alcohol and had abandoned alcohol. His mind was purified and freed from drinking alcohol.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from high and broad great beds and had abandoned high and broad great beds. His mind was purified and freed from high and broad great beds.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders, and had abandoned flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders. His mind was purified and freed from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them, and had abandoned singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them. His mind was purified and freed from singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from accepting raw gold, silver, and precious jewels, and had abandoned accepting raw gold, silver, and precious jewels. His mind was purified and freed from raw gold, silver, and precious jewels.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter abstained from eating after midday and had abandoned eating after midday. He always ate one meal, did not eat at night, and trained in eating at the proper time. His mind was purified and freed from eating after midday.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter, for his entire life, kept his hands away from plowshares and spades. He did not dig the ground himself, nor did he instruct others to do so. If riverbanks collapsed or rats disturbed the soil, he would take that earth and use it to make vessels. He would place them to one side and say to buyers: 'If you have peas, rice, wheat, large or small hemp beans, cowpeas, or mustard seeds, pour them out and take the vessels away, as you wish.'

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter, for his entire life, attended to and served his parents. His parents were blind and depended entirely on others. Therefore he served them.

"Ānanda, Nandipāla the potter, after the night had passed and at dawn, would go to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having arrived, he would pay homage and sit to one side. The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would teach him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, bringing him to delight. With countless skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight. Then he remained silent.

"Thereupon Nandipāla the potter, after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

"At that time, the young man Uttara, riding in a white horse-drawn chariot together with five hundred young men, after the night had passed and at dawn, went out from the village of Vebhaliṅga to a secluded place, intending to instruct various disciples who had come from many countries, having them recite the brahmin texts.

"Thereupon the young man Uttara, seeing Nandipāla the potter coming from a distance, asked upon seeing him: 'Nandipāla, where have you come from?' Nandipāla answered: 'I have just come from paying homage and making offerings to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Uttara, you should come with me to visit and pay homage to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

"Thereupon, the young man Uttara answered: 'Nandipāla, I do not wish to see a bald-headed ascetic. A bald ascetic should not attain the path, for the path is difficult to attain.'

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter seized the young man Uttara by the topknot of his hair and pulled him down from the chariot. Thereupon the young man Uttara had this thought: 'This Nandipāla the potter is normally not one to jest, nor is he mad or foolish. Now he has seized my topknot; there must certainly be a reason.' Having thought this, he said: 'Nandipāla, I will go with you. I will go with you.' Nandipāla was delighted and further said: 'It is very good that you go.'

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter and the young man Uttara went together to visit the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having arrived, they paid homage and sat to one side. Nandipāla the potter addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'World-Honored One, this young man Uttara is my friend. He is always dear to me, and he always delights in seeing me without satiation. However, he has no faith or reverence toward the World-Honored One. I only wish that the World-Honored One would kindly teach him the Dharma, causing him to rejoice and develop faith and reverence.'

"Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught the Dharma to Nandipāla the potter and the young man Uttara, encouraging and inspiring them, arousing their aspiration, bringing them to delight. With countless skillful means he taught them the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring them, arousing their aspiration, and bringing them to delight. Then he remained silent.

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter and the young man Uttara, after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had taught them the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring them, arousing their aspiration, and bringing them to delight, rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

"Thereupon, the young man Uttara, when they had not gone far on the return journey, asked: 'Nandipāla, having heard such subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, why do you remain at home? Are you unable to renounce and train in the holy path?'

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter answered: 'Uttara, you yourself know that I serve my parents for my entire life. My parents are blind and depend entirely on others. It is because I serve and attend to my parents.'

"Thereupon, the young man Uttara asked Nandipāla: 'Could I go forth from the home life and train in the path under the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life?'

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter and the young man Uttara returned from that place and went again to visit the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having arrived, they paid homage and sat to one side.

"Nandipāla the potter addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'World-Honored One, when this young man Uttara had not gone far on the return journey, he asked me: "Nandipāla, having heard such subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, why do you remain at home? Are you unable to renounce and train in the holy path?" World-Honored One, I answered him: "Uttara, you yourself know that I serve my parents for my entire life. My parents are blind and depend entirely on others. It is because I serve and attend to my parents." Uttara further asked me: "Nandipāla, could I go forth from the home life and train in the path under the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life?" I wish that the World-Honored One would ordain him, allowing him to go forth, train in the path, and grant him full ordination, so that he may become a bhikṣu.'

"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for Nandipāla's sake, silently accepted. Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter, knowing that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had silently accepted, rose from his seat, bowed his head in homage, circumambulated three times, and departed.

"Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not long after Nandipāla had departed, ordained the young man Uttara, allowing him to go forth and train in the path, and granted him full ordination. After granting him going forth and full ordination, he stayed in the village of Vebhaliṅga for several days, then gathered his robes and bowl, and together with a great assembly of bhikṣus set out traveling, intending to go to the city of Bārāṇasī in the country of Kāśi. Traveling from place to place, they arrived at the city of Bārāṇasī in the country of Kāśi, and stayed at the Deer Park in the Sages' Abode in Bārāṇasī.

"At that time, King Kiṃsuka heard that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was traveling in the country of Kāśi together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and had arrived at Bārāṇasī, staying at the Deer Park in the Sages' Abode. Having heard this, King Kiṃsuka told his charioteer: 'You should prepare the carriage. I now wish to visit the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.' The charioteer, having received the king's command, immediately prepared the carriage. When the preparation was complete, he reported back to the king: 'The fine carriage is prepared. May the Divine King proceed as he wishes.'

"Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka, having mounted the fine carriage, went out from Bārāṇasī to the Sages' Abode at the Deer Park. At that time, King Kiṃsuka, from a distance among the trees, saw the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, upright and beautiful, like the moon among stars, radiantly brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, replete with excellent marks, majestic in spiritual power, with faculties calm and settled, without any obstruction, having accomplished self-mastery, with a mind tranquil and silently at peace.

"Having seen this, he descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having arrived, he paid homage and sat to one side. After King Kiṃsuka had sat to one side, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, bringing him to delight. With countless skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight. Then he remained silent.

"Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka, after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'I only wish that the World-Honored One would accept my invitation tomorrow, together with the Sangha of bhikṣus.'

"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, silently accepted King Kiṃsuka's invitation. Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka, knowing that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had silently accepted, bowed his head in homage, circumambulated three times, and departed, returning to his home.

"During the night he prepared exceedingly fine, pure, and exquisite foods of various kinds in abundance, both hard and soft foods. When the night was over and the preparations were complete, at dawn he spread out seats and announced: 'World-Honored One, the time has come. The food is prepared. I only wish that the World-Honored One would grace us with his presence at this time.'

"Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, when the night had passed and at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and attended by the Sangha of bhikṣus, went to King Kiṃsuka's home. He sat down on the seat prepared for him at the head of the Sangha of bhikṣus.

"Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka, seeing the Buddha and the Sangha of bhikṣus seated, personally served water for hand-washing, and with exceedingly fine, pure, and exquisite foods of various kinds in abundance, both hard and soft, he personally ladled and served until all were satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels collected, and the water for hand-washing had been served, he set out a small seat and sat separately to hear the Dharma.

"After King Kiṃsuka had sat down, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, bringing him to delight. With countless skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight. Then he remained silent.

"Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka, after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'I only wish that the World-Honored One would accept my offering of the rains retreat here in Bārāṇasī, together with the Sangha of bhikṣus. I will build for the World-Honored One five hundred dwellings and five hundred beds and bedding, and I will offer fine white polished rice such as the king himself eats, with various flavors and dishes, to feed the World-Honored One and the Sangha of bhikṣus.'

"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, told King Kiṃsuka: 'Enough, enough, great king! Just be content at heart.'

"King Kiṃsuka, up to a second and third time, joined his palms and addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'I only wish that the World-Honored One would accept my offering of the rains retreat here in Bārāṇasī, together with the Sangha of bhikṣus. I will build for the World-Honored One five hundred dwellings and five hundred beds and bedding, and I will offer fine white polished rice such as the king himself eats, with various flavors and dishes, to feed the World-Honored One and the Sangha of bhikṣus.'

"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, also up to a second and third time told King Kiṃsuka: 'Enough, enough, great king! Just be content at heart.'

"Thereupon, King Kiṃsuka was discontent and displeased, and his heart was greatly distressed: 'The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, will not accept my offering of the rains retreat here in Bārāṇasī, together with the Sangha of bhikṣus.' Having thought thus, King Kiṃsuka addressed the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: 'World-Honored One, is there perhaps another lay person in white robes who serves the World-Honored One as I do?'

"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, told King Kiṃsuka: 'There is. Within your kingdom is the village of Vebhaliṅga, extremely prosperous and pleasant, with many people. Great king, in that village of Vebhaliṅga there is Nandipāla the potter.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter has taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus. He does not doubt the Three Honored Ones, is not confused about suffering, its origination, its cessation, and the path. He has attained faith, upholds the precepts, is broadly learned, generous in giving, and accomplished in wisdom. He abstains from killing and has abandoned killing, has cast aside knives and weapons, has shame and conscience, has a compassionate heart, and benefits all beings even down to insects. His mind is purified and freed from killing.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from taking what is not given and has abandoned taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, delights in taking what is given, always loves to give, is joyful and without stinginess, and does not hope for any return. His mind is purified and freed from taking what is not given.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from unchaste conduct and has abandoned unchaste conduct. He diligently cultivates the holy life, is energetic in excellent practice, pure and undefiled, free from desire and having abandoned sexual conduct. His mind is purified and freed from unchaste conduct.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from false speech and has abandoned false speech. He speaks truthfully, delights in truth, abides in truth without wavering, is entirely trustworthy, and does not deceive the world. His mind is purified and freed from false speech.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from divisive speech and has abandoned divisive speech. He practices non-divisive speech and does not cause the ruin of others. He does not hear something here and tell it there to cause ruin here, nor hear something there and tell it here to cause ruin there. He wishes to unite those who are separated, and those who are united he makes joyful. He does not form factions, does not delight in factions, and does not praise factions. His mind is purified and freed from divisive speech.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from harsh speech and has abandoned harsh speech. Whatever words are rough and coarse in manner, harsh-sounding and offensive to the ear, displeasing and unlovable to all, causing others suffering and distress, preventing concentration, such speech he abandons. Whatever he says is clear, gentle, and smooth, pleasing to the ear and entering the heart, agreeable and lovable, bringing others ease and comfort, his words being distinct and clear, not causing fear in others, enabling others to attain concentration; such is the speech he speaks. His mind is purified and freed from harsh speech.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from frivolous speech and has abandoned frivolous speech. He speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks of the Dharma, speaks of meaning, speaks of cessation, and delights in speaking of cessation. His words are appropriate to the occasion, well-instructing and well-admonishing. His mind is purified and freed from frivolous speech.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from trading and has abandoned trading. He has cast aside scales and measuring vessels, does not accept goods in trade, does not bind or restrain people, does not hope to cheat with false measures, and does not use small gains to encroach upon or deceive others. His mind is purified and freed from trading.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting widows and young girls, and has abandoned accepting widows and young girls. His mind is purified and freed from accepting widows and young girls.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting male and female slaves, and has abandoned accepting male and female slaves. His mind is purified and freed from accepting male and female slaves.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and has abandoned accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. His mind is purified and freed from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting chickens and pigs, and has abandoned accepting chickens and pigs. His mind is purified and freed from accepting chickens and pigs.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting farmlands and shops, and has abandoned accepting farmlands and shops. His mind is purified and freed from accepting farmlands and shops.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans, and has abandoned accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans. His mind is purified and freed from accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from alcohol and has abandoned alcohol. His mind is purified and freed from drinking alcohol.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from high and broad great beds and has abandoned high and broad great beds. His mind is purified and freed from high and broad great beds.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders, and has abandoned flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders. His mind is purified and freed from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumed ointments, and cosmetic powders.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them, and has abandoned singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them. His mind is purified and freed from singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to watch or listen to them.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting raw gold, silver, and precious jewels, and has abandoned accepting raw gold, silver, and precious jewels. His mind is purified and freed from raw gold, silver, and precious jewels.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter abstains from eating after midday and has abandoned eating after midday. He always eats one meal, does not eat at night, and trains in eating at the proper time. His mind is purified and freed from eating after midday.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter, for his entire life, keeps his hands away from plowshares and spades. He does not dig the ground himself, nor does he instruct others to do so. If riverbanks collapse or rats disturb the soil, he takes that earth and uses it to make vessels. He places them to one side and says to buyers: "If you have peas, rice, wheat, large or small hemp beans, cowpeas, or mustard seeds, pour them out and take the vessels away, as you wish."

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter, for his entire life, attends to and serves his parents. His parents are blind and depend entirely on others. Therefore he serves them.

"'Great king, I recall a former time when I was staying near the village of Vebhaliṅga. Great king, at that time, at dawn, I put on my robes, took my bowl, and entered the village of Vebhaliṅga to beg for food. Begging for food from house to house in order, I came to Nandipāla the potter's home. At that time, Nandipāla had gone out on a small errand and was not at home.

"'Great king, I asked Nandipāla the potter's parents: "Elders, where is the potter now?" They answered me: "World-Honored One, your attendant has gone out on a small errand and is temporarily away. Well-Gone One, your attendant has gone out on a small errand and is temporarily away. World-Honored One, in the basket there is barley rice, and in the pot there is bean soup. We only wish that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, would help himself as he pleases."

"'Great king, I then accepted in the manner of Uttarakuru, taking the soup and rice from the basket and pot, and departed.

"'When Nandipāla the potter later returned home, he saw that there was less rice in the basket and less soup in the pot, and he said to his parents: "Who took the soup and rice?" His parents answered: "Virtuous son, today the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, came here begging for food. He took soup and rice from the basket and pot and departed."

"'When Nandipāla the potter heard this, he had this thought: "I have gained good fortune! I have great merit! The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in my home has acted freely as he wished." With this joy he sat cross-legged, calmed his mind in silent meditation for seven days, and for fifteen days he experienced happiness. His parents at home also experienced happiness for seven days.

"'Furthermore, great king, I recall another former time when I was staying near the village of Vebhaliṅga. Great king, at that time, at dawn, I put on my robes, took my bowl, and entered the village of Vebhaliṅga to beg for food. Begging for food from house to house in order, I came to Nandipāla the potter's home. At that time, Nandipāla had gone out on a small errand and was not at home.

"'Great king, I asked Nandipāla the potter's parents: "Elders, where is the potter now?" They answered me: "World-Honored One, your attendant has gone out on a small errand and is temporarily away. Well-Gone One, your attendant has gone out on a small errand and is temporarily away. World-Honored One, in the large pot there is polished rice, and in the small pot there is soup. We only wish that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, would help himself as he pleases."

"'Great king, I then accepted in the manner of Uttarakuru, taking the soup and rice from the large and small pots, and departed.

"'When Nandipāla the potter later returned home, he saw that there was less rice in the large pot and less soup in the small pot, and he said to his parents: "Who took rice from the large pot and soup from the small pot?" His parents answered: "Virtuous son, today the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, came here begging for food. He took soup and rice from the large and small pots and departed."

"'When Nandipāla the potter heard this, he had this thought: "I have gained good fortune! I have great merit! The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in my home has acted freely as he wished." With this joy he sat cross-legged, calmed his mind in silent meditation for seven days, and for fifteen days he experienced happiness. His parents at home also experienced happiness for seven days.

"'Furthermore, great king, I recall a former time when I accepted the rains retreat near the village of Vebhaliṅga. Great king, at that time I had newly built a dwelling that was not yet roofed, while Nandipāla the potter's old pottery shed had a new roof.

"'Great king, I told the attendant bhikṣus: "You should go and dismantle the roof of Nandipāla the potter's old pottery shed, bring it here, and use it to roof my dwelling." The attendant bhikṣus received my instruction and went to Nandipāla the potter's home, pulled apart the old pottery shed, bundled the materials, and brought them to roof my dwelling.

"'Nandipāla the potter's parents heard the old pottery shed being dismantled, and upon hearing this, they asked: "Who is dismantling Nandipāla's old pottery shed?" The bhikṣus answered: "Elders, we are attendant bhikṣus of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. We are dismantling Nandipāla the potter's old pottery shed and bundling it to roof the dwelling of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One." Nandipāla's parents said: "Venerables, take it as you wish. There is no one to forbid you."

"'When Nandipāla the potter later returned home and saw that the old pottery shed had been dismantled, he said to his parents: "Who dismantled my old pottery shed?" His parents answered: "Virtuous son, today the attendant bhikṣus of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dismantled the old pottery shed, bundled the materials, and took them to roof the dwelling of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."

"'When Nandipāla the potter heard this, he had this thought: "I have gained good fortune! I have great merit! The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in my home has acted freely as he wished." With this joy he sat cross-legged, calmed his mind in silent meditation for seven days, and for fifteen days he experienced happiness. His parents at home also experienced happiness for seven days.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter's old pottery shed, throughout the entire summer of four months, never suffered any leaking at all. Why was this? Because of the awe-inspiring spiritual power of the Buddha.

"'Great king, Nandipāla the potter had no discontent, no displeasure, and no distress of heart that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in his home had acted freely as he wished. But you, great king, have discontent, displeasure, and great distress of heart because the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has not accepted your invitation for the rains retreat here in Bārāṇasī, together with the Sangha of bhikṣus.'

"Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught King Kiṃsuka the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, bringing him to delight. With countless skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, arousing his aspiration, and bringing him to delight. Then he rose from his seat and departed.

"At that time, King Kiṃsuka, not long after the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had departed, commanded his attendants: 'You should load five hundred carts full of white polished rice, with the various flavors and dishes such as the king himself eats, and transport them to the home of Nandipāla the potter. Tell him: "Nandipāla, these five hundred carts loaded with white polished rice, with the various flavors and dishes such as the king himself eats, are sent to you as a gift by King Kiṃsuka. Out of compassion, you should now accept them."'

"The attendants, having received the king's command, loaded five hundred carts full of white polished rice, with the various flavors and dishes such as the king himself eats, and sent them to the home of Nandipāla the potter. Having arrived, they said: 'Nandipāla the potter, these five hundred carts loaded with white polished rice, with the various flavors and dishes such as the king himself eats, are sent to you as a gift by King Kiṃsuka. Out of compassion, you should now accept them.'

"Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter declined and would not accept, saying to the attendants: 'Venerables, King Kiṃsuka has great affairs of state with many matters, and his expenditures are vast. I know this, and therefore I do not accept.'"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "What do you think? The young man Uttara at that time, do you suppose he was a different person? Do not think so. You should know that it was none other than myself. Ānanda, at that time I benefited myself and also benefited others, benefited many people, had compassion for the world, and for gods and humans sought meaning and benefit, sought peace and happiness. At that time my teaching of the Dharma had not yet reached its ultimate end, had not reached ultimate purity, had not reached the ultimate holy life, had not reached the fulfillment of the ultimate holy life. At that time I had not yet been freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow, nor had I yet been able to attain liberation from all suffering.

"Ānanda, now I have appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Now I benefit myself and also benefit others, benefit many people, have compassion for the world, and for gods and humans seek meaning and benefit, seek peace and happiness. Now my teaching of the Dharma has reached its ultimate end, reached ultimate purity, reached the ultimate holy life, reached the fulfillment of the ultimate holy life. Now I have been freed from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow. Now I have attained liberation from all suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had taught, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Vebhaliṅga, the Sixth.

## (64) The Sūtra on the Heavenly Messengers, Seventh in the Section on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are.

"If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"It is like when there is a great rain and bubbles on the water either arise or disappear. If a person with eyes stands in one place and observes their arising and disappearing, I am likewise. With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"It is like when there is a great rain and the raindrops either go up or come down. If a person with eyes stands in one place and observes their going up and coming down, I am likewise. With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"It is like a lapis lazuli gem, pure and natural, born without blemish, well-cut with eight facets, strung with a fine cord of blue, yellow, red, black, or white. If a person with eyes stands in one place and observes this lapis lazuli gem, pure and natural, born without blemish, well-cut with eight facets, strung with a fine cord of blue, yellow, red, black, or white, I am likewise. With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"It is like two houses sharing one door, with many people going in and out. If a person with eyes stands in one place and observes them going out and coming in, I am likewise. With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"If a person with eyes stands atop a high tower and observes the people below, coming and going, walking about, sitting, lying down, running, and leaping, I am likewise. With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance and bad appearance, in excellent states and unexcellent states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations. In accordance with the actions performed by these beings, I see them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of wrong views through wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely reach an evil destination and be born in a hell. If these beings have accomplished excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech and mind, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished the actions of right views through right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heaven.

"If there are beings who are born among humans but are not filial to their parents, do not know to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, do not practice what is true, do not perform meritorious deeds, and do not fear the consequences of sins in future lives, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are born in the realm of King Yama.

"King Yama's attendants seize them and bring them before the king, saying: 'Divine King, when this being was formerly a human, he was not filial to his parents, did not know to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, did not practice what is true, did not perform meritorious deeds, and did not fear the consequences of sins in future lives. We only wish that the Divine King would adjudge his punishment.'

"Thereupon, King Yama, with the first heavenly messenger, thoroughly questions, thoroughly examines, thoroughly instructs, and thoroughly admonishes: 'Have you perhaps ever seen the first heavenly messenger come?' That person answers: 'I have not seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Have you not formerly seen, in some village, a boy or a girl, a small infant, with a weak and soft body, lying on its back in its own urine and excrement, unable to speak to its parents, while the parents carry it away from the unclean place, wash its body, and make it clean?'

"That person answers: 'I have seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Why did you not later, when you had knowledge and understanding, have this thought: "I myself am subject to the law of birth and cannot escape from birth. I should practice excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind"?'

"That person says: 'Divine King, I was utterly ruined, forever lost?'

"King Yama says: 'You were utterly ruined, forever lost. Now you shall be punished, as one punishes a person of heedless conduct, a heedless person. This evil deed of yours was not done by your parents, not by a king, not by a god, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself formerly committed evil and unwholesome deeds. Therefore you must now receive the retribution.'

"After King Yama has thoroughly questioned, thoroughly examined, thoroughly instructed, and thoroughly admonished with this first heavenly messenger, he further thoroughly questions, thoroughly examines, thoroughly instructs, and thoroughly admonishes with the second heavenly messenger: 'Have you perhaps ever seen the second heavenly messenger come?'

"That person answers: 'I have not seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Have you not formerly seen, in some village, a man or a woman, extremely old in years, having passed through the extremity of suffering, with life nearly at its end, teeth fallen out, hair turned white, body bent and stooped, walking with a cane, the body trembling?'

"That person answers: 'I have seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Why did you not later, when you had knowledge and understanding, have this thought: "I myself am subject to the law of aging and cannot escape from aging. I should practice excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind"?'

"That person says: 'Divine King, I was utterly ruined, forever lost?'

"King Yama says: 'You were utterly ruined, forever lost. Now you shall be punished, as one punishes a person of heedless conduct, a heedless person. This evil deed of yours was not done by your parents, not by a king, not by a god, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself formerly committed evil and unwholesome deeds. Therefore you must now receive the retribution.'

"After King Yama has thoroughly questioned, thoroughly examined, thoroughly instructed, and thoroughly admonished with this second heavenly messenger, he further thoroughly questions, thoroughly examines, thoroughly instructs, and thoroughly admonishes with the third heavenly messenger: 'Have you perhaps ever seen the third heavenly messenger come?'

"That person answers: 'I have not seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Have you not formerly seen, in some village, a man or a woman, afflicted with serious illness, either sitting or lying on a bed, or sitting or lying on a couch, or sitting or lying on the ground, the body experiencing extreme suffering, very heavy suffering, disagreeable, shortening their life?'

"That person answers: 'I have seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Why did you not later, when you had knowledge and understanding, have this thought: "I myself am subject to the law of illness and cannot escape from illness. I should practice excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind"?'

"That person says: 'Divine King, I was utterly ruined, forever lost?'

"King Yama says: 'You were utterly ruined, forever lost. Now you shall be punished, as one punishes a person of heedless conduct, a heedless person. This evil deed of yours was not done by your parents, not by a king, not by a god, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself formerly committed evil and unwholesome deeds. Therefore you must now receive the retribution.'

"After King Yama has thoroughly questioned, thoroughly examined, thoroughly instructed, and thoroughly admonished with this third heavenly messenger, he further thoroughly questions, thoroughly examines, thoroughly instructs, and thoroughly admonishes with the fourth heavenly messenger: 'Have you perhaps ever seen the fourth heavenly messenger come?'

"That person answers: 'I have not seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Have you not formerly seen, in some village, a man or a woman, when they have died, after one, two, up to six or seven days, being pecked by crows and kites, eaten by jackals and wolves, or being burned by fire, or buried in the ground, or rotting and decaying?'

"That person answers: 'I have seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Why did you not later, when you had knowledge and understanding, have this thought: "I myself am subject to the law of death and cannot escape from death. I should practice excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind"?'

"That person says: 'Divine King, I was utterly ruined, forever lost?'

"King Yama says: 'You were utterly ruined, forever lost. Now you shall be punished, as one punishes a person of heedless conduct, a heedless person. This evil deed of yours was not done by your parents, not by a king, not by a god, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself formerly committed evil and unwholesome deeds. Therefore you must now receive the retribution.'

"After King Yama has thoroughly questioned, thoroughly examined, thoroughly instructed, and thoroughly admonished with this fourth heavenly messenger, he further thoroughly questions, thoroughly examines, thoroughly instructs, and thoroughly admonishes with the fifth heavenly messenger: 'Have you perhaps ever seen the fifth heavenly messenger come?'

"That person answers: 'I have not seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Have you not formerly seen the king's men seize a criminal and inflict various punishments: cutting off hands, cutting off feet, or cutting off both hands and feet; cutting off ears, cutting off noses, or cutting off both ears and noses; or slicing piece by piece; pulling out beard, pulling out hair, or pulling out both beard and hair; or placing in a cage and wrapping in cloth and burning; or burying in sand and wrapping in grass and burning; or placing inside an iron donkey; or placing in an iron pig's mouth; or placing in an iron tiger's mouth and burning; or placing in a bronze cauldron; or placing in an iron cauldron and boiling; or cutting into segments; or piercing with sharp tridents; or hooking with hooks; or laying on an iron bed and pouring boiling oil on them; or placing in an iron mortar and pounding with an iron pestle; or having dragons and snakes bite them; or whipping with whips; or striking with staffs; or beating with clubs; or impaling alive on high stakes; or severing the head?'

"That person answers: 'I have seen it, Divine King.'

"King Yama further asks: 'Why did you not later, when you had knowledge and understanding, have this thought: "I now see with my own eyes evil and unwholesome deeds"?'

"That person says: 'Divine King, I was utterly ruined, forever lost?'

"King Yama says: 'You were utterly ruined, forever lost. Now you shall be punished, as one punishes a person of heedless conduct, a heedless person. This evil deed of yours was not done by your parents, not by a king, not by a god, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself formerly committed evil and unwholesome deeds. Therefore you must now receive the retribution.'

"After King Yama has thoroughly questioned, thoroughly examined, thoroughly instructed, and thoroughly admonished with this fifth heavenly messenger, he hands them over to the hell wardens. The hell wardens then seize and cast them into the great hell with four gates. On this, there is a verse:

"'Four pillars with four gates,
The walls square with twelve edges,
Enclosed by iron ramparts,
With an iron cover above.
The ground inside the hell is iron,
Spread with blazing iron fire,
Immeasurably deep for many leagues,
Extending all the way to its foundation.
Extremely evil and unbearable,
Its fiery color terrible to behold;
Seeing it, the hairs of the body stand on end,
In fear and dread of its extreme suffering.
They fall into this hell,
Feet above, head below:
Those who slandered the noble ones,
The well-tamed, the virtuous, the good.'

"After an extremely long time has passed, for the sake of those beings, the east gate of the great hell with four gates opens. When the east gate opens, those beings come running toward it, seeking a safe place, seeking refuge. After countless hundreds of thousands have gathered there, the east gate of the hell closes again by itself. Within it, they experience extremely heavy suffering, weeping and crying out, fainting and falling to the ground, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"After an extremely long time, the south gate, the west gate, and the north gate also open. When the north gate opens, those beings come running toward it, seeking a safe place, seeking refuge. After countless hundreds of thousands have gathered there, the north gate of the hell closes again by itself. Within it, they experience extremely heavy suffering, weeping and crying out, fainting and falling to the ground, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Then, after an extremely long time, those beings emerge from the great hell with four gates. Adjacent to the great hell with four gates is the Hell of Burning Rocky Crags, filled with fire, without smoke or flames, and they are made to walk upon it, going back and forth. The skin, flesh, and blood of both their feet are destroyed when they step down, but grow back when they lift their feet, restored as before. They are punished in this way for countless hundreds of thousands of years, experiencing extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Then, after an extremely long time, those beings emerge from the Hell of Burning Rocky Crags. Adjacent to the Hell of Burning Rocky Crags is the Great Hell of Excrement and Filth, filled to the brim with excrement, immeasurably deep for hundreds of fathoms. All those beings fall completely into it. Within the Great Hell of Excrement and Filth are born many worms, worms named Liṅgu, with white bodies, black heads, and needle-like mouths. These worms bore into the feet of those beings, and having pierced their feet, they pierce their shin bones; having pierced the shin bones, they pierce the thigh bones; having pierced the thigh bones, they pierce the hip bones; having pierced the hip bones, they pierce the spine; having pierced the spine, they pierce the shoulder bones and neck bones and skull; having pierced the skull, they consume the brains completely. Those beings are thus tormented for countless hundreds of thousands of years, experiencing extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Then, after an extremely long time, those beings emerge from the Great Hell of Excrement and Filth. Adjacent to the Great Hell of Excrement and Filth is the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest. When those beings see it, they conceive the idea of coolness and have this thought: 'Let us go there and surely we will find cool relief.' Those beings come running toward it, seeking a safe place, seeking refuge. After countless hundreds of thousands have gathered, they enter the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest.

"Within the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest, from all four directions great hot winds come. When the hot winds come, iron leaves fall. When the iron leaves fall, they cut off hands, cut off feet, or cut off both hands and feet; cut off ears, cut off noses, or cut off both ears and noses, and other limbs and joints, cutting the body so that blood flows. For countless hundreds of thousands of years they experience extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Furthermore, within the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest are born extremely large dogs with exceedingly long fangs. They seize those beings and strip the skin from their feet up to their heads and devour it, or strip the skin from their heads down to their feet and devour it. Those beings are thus tormented for countless hundreds of thousands of years, experiencing extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Furthermore, within the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest are born great birds with two iron beaks. They perch on the beings' foreheads and, while they are alive, gouge out their eyes and swallow them, peck open their skulls, and eat their brains. Those beings are thus tormented for countless hundreds of thousands of years, experiencing extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Then, after an extremely long time, those beings emerge from the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest. Adjacent to the Great Hell of the Iron-Leaf Forest is the Great Hell of the Iron Sword-Tree Forest. The great sword-trees are one league in height, with thorns a foot and six inches long. The beings are made to climb up and down them. When they climb up the trees, the thorns point downward; when they descend the trees, the thorns point upward. The thorns of the sword-trees pierce and impale the beings, piercing their hands, piercing their feet, or piercing both hands and feet; piercing their ears, piercing their noses, or piercing both ears and noses, and other limbs and joints, piercing the body so that blood flows. For countless hundreds of thousands of years they experience extremely heavy suffering, yet they never die, until all of their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

"Then, after an extremely long time, those beings emerge from the Great Hell of the Iron Sword-Tree Forest. Adjacent to the Great Hell of the Iron Sword-Tree Forest is the Ash River. Its two banks are extremely high, and thorns grow everywhere along them. The river is full of boiling alkaline water. Within it is extreme darkness.

"When those beings see it, they conceive the idea of cold water, thinking there must be cold water. Having conceived this idea, they have this thought: 'Let us go there, and within it we can bathe, drink our fill as we please, and surely find cool refreshment.' Those beings race toward it and enter it, seeking a pleasant place, seeking refuge. After countless hundreds of thousands have gathered, they fall into the Ash River.

"Having fallen into the Ash River, they are carried downstream, upstream, or both downstream and upstream. As those beings are carried downstream, upstream, or both downstream and upstream, their skin cooks and falls off, their flesh cooks and falls off, or both skin and flesh cook and fall off together, leaving only the skeleton.

"On both banks of the Ash River stand hell wardens holding knives, swords, great clubs, and iron tridents. When those beings try to climb up onto the banks, the wardens push them back into the river.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama)

**(63) Sūtra on Bīja (The Parable of the Seed)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen well, listen well, and reflect upon it carefully. I will explain it for you. What is this teaching? It is the sūtra on the parable of the seed."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "If seeds are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, fresh and intact, and well preserved, but there is no earth element or water element, then can these seeds sprout, grow, and develop?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"If there is the earth element and the water element, but the seeds are broken, rotten, damaged by wind or sun, not fresh, not intact, and not well preserved, then can these seeds sprout, grow, and develop?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"If seeds are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, fresh and intact, and well preserved, and there is also the earth element and water element, then can these seeds sprout, grow, and develop?"

They answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"You should know that it is like the earth element: the four stations of consciousness should be understood in this way. You should know that it is like the water element: delight and craving should be understood in this way. You should know that it is like the seeds: consciousness together with its support should be understood in this way.

"If consciousness abides in the form element, being supported by the form element, being established upon the form element, being moistened by delight, it grows, increases, and expands. If consciousness abides in the feeling element, being supported by the feeling element, being established upon the feeling element, being moistened by delight, it grows, increases, and expands. If consciousness abides in the perception element, being supported by the perception element, being established upon the perception element, being moistened by delight, it grows, increases, and expands. If consciousness abides in the formations element, being supported by the formations element, being established upon the formations element, being moistened by delight, it grows, increases, and expands.

"Bhikṣus, if someone says: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will describe the coming and going of consciousness, its arising and passing away, its growth, increase, and expansion,' this is something that cannot be obtained.

"If a bhikṣu eliminates craving for the form element, then because craving is eliminated, the support is cut off, and consciousness has no ground upon which to stand. If a bhikṣu eliminates craving for the feeling element, then because craving is eliminated, the support is cut off, and consciousness has no ground upon which to stand. If a bhikṣu eliminates craving for the perception element, then because craving is eliminated, the support is cut off, and consciousness has no ground upon which to stand. If a bhikṣu eliminates craving for the formations element, then because craving is eliminated, the support is cut off, and consciousness has no ground upon which to stand.

"When consciousness has no ground upon which to stand, it does not increase, and having no activity, it is liberated. Being liberated, it is settled. Being settled, it is content. Being content, there is no anxiety. Having no anxiety, one naturally attains parinirvāṇa. One knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence.'"

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and put it into practice.

---

**(64) Sūtra on Heavenly Messengers**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will explain to you the parable of the three turning of the wheel by the king of hell against sinners. Listen well, listen well, and reflect upon it carefully. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, suppose the guardians of hell seize that sinner, bring him before King Yama, and say: 'Great king, this person did not act as a good son, did not show filial respect to father and mother, did not show respect to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, did not honor the elders of the clan. May the great king determine his punishment.'

"Then King Yama examines and questions him, interrogates and admonishes him about the first heavenly messenger, saying: 'Man, did you not see the first heavenly messenger appearing among humans?'

"He answers: 'I did not see it, Lord.'

"King Yama then says to him: 'Man, did you not see among humans a young infant, newly born, lying on its back, covered in its own filth, unable to take care of itself, dependent on its mother's breast for nourishment?'

"He answers: 'I did see this, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, you, being a person of intelligence and mature age, why did you not think thus: "I too am subject to birth, I have not transcended birth. I should do good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and good deeds of mind"?'

"He answers: 'Lord, I could not do this. It was because of negligence and laziness.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, it is through your own negligence that you did not do good deeds of body, speech, and mind. Truly, you will be dealt with according to your negligence. This evil action of yours was not done by your mother, not done by your father, not done by a king, not done by the gods, not done by anyone else. You yourself did this evil action, and you yourself must experience the results.'

"After King Yama has examined, questioned, interrogated, and admonished him about the first heavenly messenger, he then examines, questions, interrogates, and admonishes him about the second heavenly messenger, saying: 'Man, did you not see the second heavenly messenger appearing among humans?'

"He answers: 'I did not see it, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, did you not see among humans a woman or a man, aged eighty, ninety, or one hundred years, bent over and stooped, leaning on a staff when walking, the body afflicted and weakened, teeth broken and hair white, skin wrinkled and the body spotted, the limbs trembling?'

"He answers: 'I did see this, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, you, being a person of intelligence and mature age, why did you not think thus: "I too am subject to aging, I have not transcended aging. I should do good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and good deeds of mind"?'

"He answers: 'Lord, I could not do this. It was because of negligence and laziness.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, it is through your own negligence that you did not do good deeds of body, speech, and mind. Truly, you will be dealt with according to your negligence. This evil action of yours was not done by your mother, not done by your father, not done by a king, not done by the gods, not done by anyone else. You yourself did this evil action, and you yourself must experience the results.'

"After King Yama has examined, questioned, interrogated, and admonished him about the second heavenly messenger, he then examines, questions, interrogates, and admonishes him about the third heavenly messenger, saying: 'Man, did you not see the third heavenly messenger appearing among humans?'

"He answers: 'I did not see it, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, did you not see among humans a woman or a man who was sick, afflicted, gravely ill, lying in their own filth, unable to rise by themselves, requiring others to lift and turn them?'

"He answers: 'I did see this, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, you, being a person of intelligence and mature age, why did you not think thus: "I too am subject to illness, I have not transcended illness. I should do good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and good deeds of mind"?'

"He answers: 'Lord, I could not do this. It was because of negligence and laziness.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, it is through your own negligence that you did not do good deeds of body, speech, and mind. Truly, you will be dealt with according to your negligence. This evil action of yours was not done by your mother, not done by your father, not done by a king, not done by the gods, not done by anyone else. You yourself did this evil action, and you yourself must experience the results.'

"After King Yama has examined, questioned, interrogated, and admonished him about the third heavenly messenger, he then examines, questions, interrogates, and admonishes him about the fourth heavenly messenger, saying: 'Man, did you not see the fourth heavenly messenger appearing among humans?'

"He answers: 'I did not see it, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, did you not see among humans a woman or man who has committed a crime, being seized by the king, subjected to various kinds of punishment: being whipped, being beaten with rods, having hands cut off, having feet cut off, having both hands and feet cut off, having ears cut off, having the nose cut off, having ears and nose cut off, or subjected to various other cruel punishments?'

"He answers: 'I did see this, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, you, being a person of intelligence and mature age, why did you not think thus: "Truly, this person who did evil deeds has now received various punishments in the present life. What about the next life? I should do good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and good deeds of mind"?'

"He answers: 'Lord, I could not do this. It was because of negligence and laziness.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, it is through your own negligence that you did not do good deeds of body, speech, and mind. Truly, you will be dealt with according to your negligence. This evil action of yours was not done by your mother, not done by your father, not done by a king, not done by the gods, not done by anyone else.
