You yourself did this evil action, and you yourself must experience the results.'

"After King Yama has examined, questioned, interrogated, and admonished him about the fourth heavenly messenger, he then examines, questions, interrogates, and admonishes him about the fifth heavenly messenger, saying: 'Man, did you not see the fifth heavenly messenger appearing among humans?'

"He answers: 'I did not see it, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, did you not see among humans a woman or man who has died, after one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, the body swelling and bloating, putrefying and decaying, being devoured by worms?'

"He answers: 'I did see this, Lord.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, you, being a person of intelligence and mature age, why did you not think thus: "I too am subject to death, I have not transcended death. I should do good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and good deeds of mind"?'

"He answers: 'Lord, I could not do this. It was because of negligence and laziness.'

"King Yama says to him: 'Man, it is through your own negligence that you did not do good deeds of body, speech, and mind. Truly, you will be dealt with according to your negligence. This evil action of yours was not done by your mother, not done by your father, not done by a king, not done by the gods, not done by anyone else. You yourself did this evil action, and you yourself must experience the results.'

"After King Yama has examined, questioned, interrogated, and admonished him about the fifth heavenly messenger, he remains silent.

"Then the guardians of hell inflict various kinds of punishments upon that sinner. They take him to where there is heated iron ground. The entire ground is ablaze, burning and flaming, with fierce heat. They force that sinner to walk upon it, to stand upon it, to sit upon it, to lie upon it. Then they take heated iron and press it against his body. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"The guardians of hell then take that sinner and place him on heated iron ground, stretching him out face up, prying open his mouth with heated iron tongs, and placing heated iron balls into his mouth. Those heated iron balls burn his lips, burn his tongue, burn his palate, burn his throat, burn his chest, and pass through and exit below. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"The guardians of hell then take that sinner and place him on heated iron ground, stretching him out face up, prying open his mouth with heated iron tongs, and pouring molten copper into his mouth. That molten copper burns his lips, burns his tongue, burns his palate, burns his throat, burns his chest, and passes through and exits below. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"The guardians of hell then throw that sinner into a great hell. That great hell has four corners and four gates. It is divided equally into sections, with iron walls surrounding it and iron roofing over it. The ground is also made of iron. With heated iron joined at all sides, its extent is several hundred yojanas. It is always filled with blazing fire.

"That hell's eastern wall emits fire that burns the western wall. The western wall emits fire that burns the eastern wall. The southern wall emits fire that burns the northern wall. The northern wall emits fire that burns the southern wall. The upper part emits fire that burns the lower part. The lower part emits fire that burns the upper part. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"At some time, the eastern gate of the great hell opens. That sinner then runs quickly toward it. As he runs, his skin burns, his flesh burns, his sinews burn, and his bones burn, with smoke rising all around. When he reaches the gate, the gate closes again. If at some time the eastern gate opens and he passes through, there is another great hell just outside the gate.

"There is a hell of excrement. He falls into the hell of excrement. In the hell of excrement there are creatures with iron beaks that bore into his skin, bore into his flesh, bore into his sinews, bore into his bones, and suck out his marrow and eat it. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"Having passed through the hell of excrement, there is another great hell. There is a hell of hot ashes. He falls into the hell of hot ashes, where the ashes sink to his ankles, burning his skin, burning his flesh, burning his sinews, and burning his bones. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"Having passed through the hell of hot ashes, there is another great hell. There is a hell of an iron thorn forest. He enters the iron thorn forest and climbs the iron thorny trees. When climbing up, the thorns point downward; when climbing down, the thorns point upward. They pierce his hands, pierce his feet, pierce his body in all places. There are iron-beaked birds that perch on his head and peck at his eyes and eat them. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"Having passed through the iron thorn forest hell, there is another great hell. There is a hell of a sword-leaf forest. When the wind blows, the leaves fall and cut off his hands, cut off his feet, cut off his ears, and cut off his nose. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"Having passed through the sword-leaf forest hell, there is another great hell. There is a hell of a boiling river. That sinner falls into the boiling river. He is tossed up and down in it, sometimes sinking, sometimes floating, being boiled back and forth. The pain is extreme and unbearable. But he does not die, and he must wait until the evil karma is exhausted.

"Then the guardians of hell use iron hooks to hook that sinner out, place him on the bank, and ask him: 'Man, what do you want?'

"He answers: 'I am hungry.'

"Then the guardians of hell pry open his mouth with heated iron tongs and place heated iron balls into his mouth. Those heated iron balls burn his lips, burn his tongue, burn his palate, burn his throat, burn his chest, and pass through and exit below.

"They ask him again: 'What else do you want?'

"He answers: 'I am thirsty.'

"Then the guardians of hell pry open his mouth with heated iron tongs and pour molten copper into his mouth. That molten copper burns his lips, burns his tongue, burns his palate, burns his throat, burns his chest, and passes through and exits below.

"Then the guardians of hell throw that sinner back into the great hell again. In times long past, King Yama thought thus: 'All those beings in the world who do evil actions and unwholesome deeds will suffer these various kinds of punishments. I wish that I could obtain a human body, and that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One would appear in the world, and that I could serve that World-Honored One, and that the World-Honored One would teach me the Dharma, and that I could understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One.'

"Bhikṣus, I do not say this based on what I have heard from another śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa. I speak only of what I myself have known, what I myself have seen, and what I myself have realized."

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"Though warned by heavenly messengers,
Many people remain negligent.
Having arrived in the lower realms,
For a long time they grieve in sorrow.

But if good people in this world,
Are warned by heavenly messengers,
They never indulge in negligence,
Practicing the noble Dharma forever.

Seeing that attachment and clinging
Are the origin of birth and death,
By completely eradicating them,
They realize the cessation of birth and death.

Having attained peace and security,
In the present life they reach nirvāṇa.
Free from all fear and enmity,
They transcend all forms of suffering."

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and put it into practice.

---

**(65) Sūtra on Ūposatha (The Observance Day)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, the observance day, the World-Honored One sat in the open surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus. The World-Honored One silently surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus, then addressed them:

"Bhikṣus, should a practitioner not speak even a small amount of frivolous talk? Should a practitioner not engage even a small amount in frivolous discussion? I now address you bhikṣus: 'You should abandon frivolous talk and frivolous discussion. A bhikṣu should engage in the discussion of the Dharma, or maintain the noble silence. Do not be heedless.'

"Bhikṣus, there are eight kinds of observance. If a bhikṣu cultivates and practices them, they lead to great fruit and great benefit. What are the eight?

"Here, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned killing, have abstained from killing, have laid down the rod, have laid down weapons, with conscience and compassion, being kind and compassionate toward all living beings. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned killing, have abstained from killing, have laid down the rod, have laid down weapons, with conscience and compassion, being kind and compassionate toward all living beings. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the first branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned taking what is not given, practice only taking what is given, and delight in taking what is given. They are always generous, delighting in giving, without stinginess, and do not expect reward. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned taking what is not given, practice only taking what is given, and delight in taking what is given. I am generous, delighting in giving, without stinginess, and do not expect reward. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the second branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned the unchaste life, practice the chaste life, and live in purity, abandoning and departing from sexual desire. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned the unchaste life, practice the chaste life, and live in purity, abandoning and departing from sexual desire. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the third branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned false speech, practice speaking truth, and delight in speaking truth. They are established in truth, trustworthy and reliable, and do not deceive the world. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned false speech, practice speaking truth, and delight in speaking truth. I am established in truth, trustworthy and reliable, and do not deceive the world. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the fourth branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned intoxicating drinks, abstain from intoxicating drinks, and do not drink intoxicating drinks. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned intoxicating drinks, abstain from intoxicating drinks, and do not drink intoxicating drinks. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the fifth branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, eat only one meal a day, do not eat at improper times, eat at the proper time. I too, on this day and this night, eat only one meal, do not eat at improper times, and eat at the proper time. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the sixth branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned dancing, singing, music, and going to see entertainment, and have abandoned wearing garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics to adorn the body. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned dancing, singing, music, and going to see entertainment, and have abandoned wearing garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics to adorn the body. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the seventh branch of the observance.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu relies on the observance day, and reflects thus: 'The arahants, throughout their lives, have abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, and do not sit or lie on high and luxurious beds and seats, but use only low beds and grass mats. I too, on this day and this night, have abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, and do not sit or lie on high and luxurious beds and seats, but use only low beds and grass mats. By this practice, I imitate the arahants. This is called the observance.' This is the eighth branch of the observance.

"Bhikṣus, these are the eight branches of the observance. If cultivated and practiced, they lead to great fruit and great benefit."

"What sort of great fruit and great benefit? Bhikṣus, suppose someone were to exercise sovereignty over the sixteen great countries, namely, Aṅga, Magadha, Kāśī, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Cedi, Vaṃsa, Kuru, Pañcāla, Maccha, Sūrasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhāra, and Kamboja, with all their various treasures. Yet this would not be worth a sixteenth part of the eight-branched observance. Why is this? Because the sovereignty of human kings, compared to heavenly bliss, is insignificant and not worth mentioning.

"If a person observes the eight-branched observance, at the end of their life, they will be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings. Among the gods of the Four Great Kings, one day and one night is equivalent to fifty years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings is five hundred such years. Can an ordinary worldly person, who has not heard the Dharma, know or not know about this?

"Furthermore, the eight-branched observance can lead to rebirth among the gods of the Thirty-three. Among the gods of the Thirty-three, one day and one night is equivalent to one hundred years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three is one thousand such years.

"Furthermore, the eight-branched observance can lead to rebirth among the Yāma gods. Among the Yāma gods, one day and one night is equivalent to two hundred years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the Yāma gods is two thousand such years.

"Furthermore, the eight-branched observance can lead to rebirth among the Tuṣita gods. Among the Tuṣita gods, one day and one night is equivalent to four hundred years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the Tuṣita gods is four thousand such years.

"Furthermore, the eight-branched observance can lead to rebirth among the Nirmāṇarati gods. Among the Nirmāṇarati gods, one day and one night is equivalent to eight hundred years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati gods is eight thousand such years.

"Furthermore, the eight-branched observance can lead to rebirth among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. Among the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, one day and one night is equivalent to one thousand six hundred years among humans. Thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. The lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods is sixteen thousand such years."

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"Do not kill, do not steal,
Do not speak falsehood.
Do not drink intoxicants,
Abide in pure chaste conduct.

Do not eat at improper times,
Do not wear floral garlands.
Use a bed that is low and narrow;
These are called the eight branches.

The Buddha, the Destroyer of Suffering,
Taught these eight-branched observances.
Leading to the beautiful heavens,
They enable rebirth in places of bliss.

Having mastered the sixteen kingdoms,
Ruling over the entire great earth,
This is not equal to a sixteenth part
Of the merit of one observance day."

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and put it into practice.

---

**(66) Sūtra Spoken to Śuka**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, on Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.

At that time, Śuka Māṇava, the pupil of Todeyya, came to the place of the World-Honored One, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One asked him: "Śuka, how does the brāhmaṇa Todeyya instruct his disciples and teach the Dharma?"

Śuka Māṇava said: "The brāhmaṇa Todeyya instructs his disciples thus: 'One should see forms with the eyes, but one should not be attached to forms. One should hear sounds with the ears, but one should not be attached to sounds.' Gautama, the brāhmaṇa Todeyya instructs his disciples in this way and teaches the Dharma in this way."

The World-Honored One said: "Śuka, if as the brāhmaṇa Todeyya says, 'One should see forms with the eyes, but one should not be attached to forms; one should hear sounds with the ears, but one should not be attached to sounds,' then a blind person would be one who practices the teaching, and a deaf person would be one who practices the teaching. Why? Because a blind person does not see forms with the eyes, and a deaf person does not hear sounds with the ears."

When Śuka Māṇava heard this, he was silent and displeased.

The World-Honored One, knowing that Śuka Māṇava was silent and displeased, then addressed him: "Śuka, how does the brāhmaṇa Pokkharasāti instruct his disciples and teach the Dharma?"

Śuka Māṇava said: "The brāhmaṇa Pokkharasāti instructs his disciples thus: 'One should see forms with the eyes, but one should not give rise to craving for forms. One should hear sounds with the ears, but one should not give rise to craving for sounds.' Gautama, the brāhmaṇa Pokkharasāti instructs his disciples in this way and teaches the Dharma in this way."

The World-Honored One said: "Śuka, what the brāhmaṇa Pokkharasāti says is better than what the brāhmaṇa Todeyya says. But Śuka, I will explain to you the guarding of the sense faculties in the noble discipline. Listen well and pay careful attention. I will explain it for you."

Śuka Māṇava said: "Very well, Gautama. I wish to hear it."

The Buddha said: "Śuka, how does one guard the sense faculties in the noble discipline? Here, Śuka, a bhikṣu, having seen a form with the eyes, does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the eye faculty, he guards the eye faculty and achieves the guarding of the eye faculty.

"Having heard a sound with the ears, he does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the ear faculty, he guards the ear faculty and achieves the guarding of the ear faculty.

"Having smelled an odor with the nose, he does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the nose faculty, he guards the nose faculty and achieves the guarding of the nose faculty.

"Having tasted a flavor with the tongue, he does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the tongue faculty, he guards the tongue faculty and achieves the guarding of the tongue faculty.

"Having felt a tangible with the body, he does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the body faculty, he guards the body faculty and achieves the guarding of the body faculty.

"Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its marks or its secondary features. Because of what might flow in, namely, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and grief, if he were to dwell without guarding the mind faculty, he guards the mind faculty and achieves the guarding of the mind faculty.

"Śuka, this is called guarding the sense faculties in the noble discipline."

Śuka Māṇava, having heard what the Buddha said, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Not long after Śuka Māṇava left, he thought to himself: "The ascetic Gautama is truly extraordinary and remarkably wondrous, having such great wisdom and great supernatural power." He then returned and came again to the place of the World-Honored One, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One then gradually taught him the Dharma, illuminating it, making it joyful, explaining giving, morality, and the way to be reborn in heaven. He showed that desires are impure, defiled, and corrupt, and that leaving the household life brings great benefit. When the World-Honored One knew that Śuka Māṇava's mind was ready, softened, free from hindrances, uplifted, and joyful, he then explained what the Buddhas always teach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean white cloth, free from grime, can easily be dyed, so too did Śuka Māṇava, right there on that seat, see the Dharma, attain the Dharma, understand the Dharma, and penetrate the Dharma, crossing over doubt, free from confusion, attaining fearlessness, and not relying on others in the teaching of the Teacher. He then rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple who has taken the three refuges from this day until the end of my life."

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, Śuka Māṇava heard what the Buddha said, was delighted, and put it into practice.

---

**(67) Sūtra on the Great Heavenly Nārada Kassapa**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In the distant past, long, long ago, there was a king named Aṅgadinna, who ruled the city of Mithilā and governed the people of Videha. King Aṅgadinna had a brāhmaṇa priest named Govinda, who was his counselor and advisor, just as a father takes care of his son or as a son serves his father. King Aṅgadinna relied upon the brāhmaṇa Govinda, and the brāhmaṇa Govinda relied upon King Aṅgadinna.

"The brāhmaṇa Govinda had a son named Jotipāla. He was handsome and pleasing to look at, with excellent complexion. He was wise and intelligent, and could counsel and advise King Aṅgadinna on affairs of state and governance, just like his father, and could serve King Aṅgadinna in the same way his father had. King Aṅgadinna relied upon Jotipāla, and Jotipāla relied upon King Aṅgadinna.

"Bhikṣus, at a later time, the brāhmaṇa Govinda fell gravely ill. King Aṅgadinna went to visit him and said: 'Govinda, if something should happen to you, who could counsel and advise me on affairs of state and governance as you have done?'

"The brāhmaṇa Govinda answered: 'Great king, I have a son named Jotipāla. He is wise and intelligent, and can counsel and advise the great king on affairs of state and governance, just as I have done, and can serve the great king in the same way. May the great king appoint Jotipāla.'

"Not long after, the brāhmaṇa Govinda passed away. King Aṅgadinna mourned and grieved, then appointed Jotipāla as his counselor and called him the Great Steward. Jotipāla then counseled and advised King Aṅgadinna on affairs of state and governance, just as his father had done. Because of this, he was called Mahāgovinda, the Great Steward.

"Bhikṣus, at a later time, King Aṅgadinna also fell gravely ill. He summoned Prince Reṇu and said: 'Son, I am gravely ill. After my passing, you should be anointed as king. And you should rely upon the Great Steward Mahāgovinda, just as I have relied upon him.'

"Before long, King Aṅgadinna passed away. Prince Reṇu was anointed as king and ruled over the city of Mithilā, governing the people of Videha.

"Bhikṣus, King Reṇu had six companions who were princes. Those six princes heard that their companion Reṇu had been anointed as king, and they all came to visit King Reṇu. King Reṇu was delighted and said: 'Friends, since I have now received the great anointing and obtained the kingship, whatever I have shall be shared with you.'

"The six princes all said: 'Excellent, friend. We are well pleased.'

"Then King Reṇu summoned the Great Steward Mahāgovinda and said: 'Good sir, these six princes are my dear friends. They have now come to visit me. I wish to divide the kingdom into seven equal parts, giving each of them a portion. Please make it so.'

"Mahāgovinda replied: 'Very well, great king. I will do this.'

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda then divided the great land of India into seven equal parts. The first was the kingdom of Kāśī and Kosala, with Bārāṇasī as the capital, given to one prince. The second was the kingdom of the Kurus and the Pañcālas, with Indapatta as the capital. The third was the kingdom of the Maccha and the Sūrasenas, with Mathurā as the capital. The fourth was the kingdom of Avanti, with Māhissatī as the capital. The fifth was the kingdom of Assaka, with Potana as the capital. The sixth was the kingdom of Aṅga and Magadha, with Campā as the capital. The seventh was the kingdom of Videha, with Mithilā as the capital, retained by King Reṇu.

"Bhikṣus, the six princes, each having received their portions, were all satisfied and pleased, saying: 'What we wished for, what we desired and hoped for, has now been obtained.'

"Bhikṣus, at that time, those seven kings and the Great Steward Mahāgovinda, eight in total, were the most eminent, the greatest, the supreme among all people in the land of India. No one surpassed them.

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda counseled and advised these seven kings. He taught brāhmaṇas and householders to invoke blessings. After his death, he would be reborn in the Brahma world.

"Bhikṣus, at that time, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda thought: 'I counsel and advise these seven kings, and I teach brāhmaṇas and householders to invoke blessings. I should seek solitude and practice the Dharma in a secluded place.'

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda went to King Reṇu and said: 'Great king, I wish to go forth from the household life, shave my head and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and, with correct faith, leave the household life to practice the path.'

"King Reṇu said: 'Good sir, this is not the right time. You counsel and advise seven kings, and you teach brāhmaṇas and householders to invoke blessings. How can you go forth?'

"A second time, Mahāgovinda said: 'Great king, I wish to go forth.'

"King Reṇu again said: 'This is not the right time.'

"A third time, Mahāgovinda said: 'Great king, I wish to go forth.'

"King Reṇu said: 'Good sir, you may do as you wish. Do what you think is best.'

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda also went to the other six kings and asked leave to go forth. Each of the six kings also initially refused, but ultimately granted their permission.

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda also told his forty wives, saying: 'Ladies, whoever among you wishes to return to her family may do so, or you may each marry another husband.'

"All the wives said: 'You are our husband. Who else could be our husband? We wish to follow you and go forth to practice the path.'

"Bhikṣus, the Great Steward Mahāgovinda, together with his forty wives, many brāhmaṇas, and many others, in total several thousand people, all went forth, shaved their heads and beards, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with correct faith, left the household life to practice the path.

"The Great Steward Mahāgovinda abided in loving-kindness, pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, then the second, the third, and the fourth direction, and also above, below, and all around, everywhere pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, great, boundless, without enmity, without ill-will. He also abided in compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, pervading one direction, then the second, the third, and the fourth direction, and also above, below, and all around, everywhere pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, great, boundless, without enmity, without ill-will. He taught this to his disciples, and those among his disciples who practiced in this way were, after death, reborn in the Brahma world.

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? The Great Steward Mahāgovinda of that time, do you think he was someone else? You should not think so. You should know that he was I myself. At that time, I was the Great Steward Mahāgovinda. At that time, I taught people the path to be companions of the Brahma world. But that path was not the path to disgust, not the path to dispassion, not the path to cessation, not the path to tranquility, not the path to correct enlightenment, not the path to nirvāṇa. It was only the path to rebirth in the Brahma world.

"Now I teach people the path of the holy life that leads to complete disgust, to dispassion, to cessation, to tranquility, to correct enlightenment, to nirvāṇa. What is this path? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi. This is the path that leads to complete disgust, to dispassion, to cessation, to tranquility, to correct enlightenment, to nirvāṇa."

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and put it into practice.

---

**(68) Sūtra on the Great善見 (Mahāsudassana)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was at Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees of the Mallas, about to enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, please do not enter parinirvāṇa in this small, insignificant town, this wilderness town. There are other great cities, such as Campā, Rājagṛha, Sāvatthī, Sāketa, Kosambī, and Bārāṇasī. May the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa in one of these great cities, where there are many wealthy brāhmaṇas and householders who have faith in the Tathāgata, and they would make offerings for the Tathāgata's relics."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, do not say that this is a small, insignificant town, a wilderness town. Why? Ānanda, in the distant past, long, long ago, in this place there was a great city named Kuśāvatī, which was twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from north to south. It was prosperous, flourishing, and greatly populated.

"Ānanda, in the city of Kuśāvatī, there were seven rows of tāla trees. The trees were made of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, ruby, emerald, and all kinds of precious gems. The gold trees had gold roots, gold trunks, silver branches, silver leaves, silver flowers, and silver fruits. The silver trees had silver roots, silver trunks, gold branches, gold leaves, gold flowers, and gold fruits. The beryl trees had beryl roots, beryl trunks, crystal branches, crystal leaves, crystal flowers, and crystal fruits. The crystal trees had crystal roots, crystal trunks, beryl branches, beryl leaves, beryl flowers, and beryl fruits. The ruby trees had ruby roots, ruby trunks, emerald branches, emerald leaves, emerald flowers, and emerald fruits. The emerald trees had emerald roots, emerald trunks, ruby branches, ruby leaves, ruby flowers, and ruby fruits. The trees of all kinds of precious gems had roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all of various precious gems.

"Ānanda, between these seven rows of tāla trees, there were ponds with waters of eight qualities: clear, cool, sweet, soft, moisturizing, peaceful, capable of quenching thirst, and nourishing. These ponds were lined on all four sides with four kinds of precious materials: gold, silver, beryl, and crystal. There were gold stairs with silver railings, silver stairs with gold railings, beryl stairs with crystal railings, and crystal stairs with beryl railings. Around the ponds were seven rows of tāla trees, with each row being similarly adorned.

"Ānanda, in the city of Kuśāvatī, there was no sound of cows, no sound of horses, no sound of carriages, no wailing, and no weeping. Day and night one could always hear the sounds of drums, conches, singing, and music.

"Ānanda, at that time, in the city of Kuśāvatī, there was a king named Mahāsudassana, a wheel-turning sage king who possessed the four armies, had conquered the four quarters by the Dharma, had pacified the land, and possessed the seven treasures. He had the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the counselor treasure. He had a full one thousand sons, brave and heroic, able to conquer enemies. He ruled over this entire great earth up to the seas, without using rods or weapons, but by the Dharma.

"Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had a palace called Dhamma, which was eighty-four thousand yojanas in extent. It had eighty-four thousand pillars, all made of the seven precious materials. It had eighty-four thousand chambers, all covered with gold. In the gold chambers, there were silver couches, and on the silver couches were spread fine cloths, with beautiful coverings, and pillows at both ends.

"Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana had eighty-four thousand elephants, all adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, and covered with golden nets. He had eighty-four thousand horses, all adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, and covered with golden nets. He had eighty-four thousand chariots, covered with lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, and various fabrics, all adorned with gold ornaments, with gold banners and golden bells. He had eighty-four thousand jewels, all luminous, able to illuminate one yojana around. He had eighty-four thousand queens, all beautiful and charming as heavenly maidens.

"Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana thought: 'What previous actions of mine, what previous merit of mine, have caused me to now possess such great supernatural power and such great authority?' Then he reflected further: 'It is because of three things that I have obtained this: giving, self-control, and restraint.'

"Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana then went up to the great palace called Dhamma. He entered a golden chamber. He sat upon a silver couch and cultivated loving-kindness, pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, then the second, the third, and the fourth direction, and also above, below, and all around, everywhere pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, great, boundless, without enmity, without ill-will. He also cultivated compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity in the same way.

"Ānanda, at a later time, King Mahāsudassana fell gravely ill. His queen, Subhaddā, came to him and said: 'Great king, do not be attached to or cling to these eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Kuśāvatī as the chief. Do not be attached to or cling to these eighty-four thousand palaces, with the palace of Dhamma as the chief. Do not be attached to or cling to these eighty-four thousand chambers. Do not be attached to or cling to these eighty-four thousand couches. Do not be attached to or cling to these eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand jewels, and eighty-four thousand queens. Great king, abandon attachment, abandon clinging. Longing for life is suffering, and being greedy for life is suffering.'

"King Mahāsudassana said: 'Queen, for a long time your words have been kind, beneficial, comforting, and pleasant. But now, at the very end, your words are even more kind, beneficial, comforting, and pleasant.'

"Queen Subhaddā said: 'Great king, why do you say that my words at the very end are even more kind, beneficial, comforting, and pleasant?'

"King Mahāsudassana said: 'Queen, it is because you say to me: "Do not be attached, do not cling. Abandon attachment, abandon clinging." This is why I say your present words are even more kind, beneficial, comforting, and pleasant.'

"Ānanda, not long after, King Mahāsudassana passed away. Just as a householder who has eaten a fine meal feels satisfaction, so did King Mahāsudassana, after giving up this life, and was reborn in the Brahma world.

"Ānanda, what do you think? The King Mahāsudassana of that time, do you think he was someone else? You should not think so. You should know that he was I myself. At that time, I was King Mahāsudassana. At that time, I possessed eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Kuśāvatī as the chief. Now there remains only this Kuśinagara. At that time, I had eighty-four thousand palaces, with the palace of Dhamma as the chief. Now there remains only this hall of the Mallas. At that time, I had eighty-four thousand chambers. Now there remains only this single room made by Ānanda from bundled branches.

"Ānanda, in this way, all conditioned things are impermanent. They are things that arise and cease. Having arisen, they cease. Their peaceful cessation is bliss."

When the Buddha spoke this sūtra, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha said, were delighted, and put it into practice.

---

End of Fascicle 13 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 13

## Chapter on Kings, Part One

The Parable of the Crow; Speaking of Past Lives; the Celestial Nāḷi Grove; Sudarśana;
the Thirty Parables; the Wheel-Turning King; Vaiśālī comes last.

---

## (65) Sūtra on the Parable of the Crow, First of the Chapter on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Long ago, when a wheel-turning king wished to test his jewel-treasure, he assembled the four kinds of troops: elephant troops, horse troops, chariot troops, and foot soldiers. Having assembled the four kinds of troops, in the darkness of night he erected a tall banner, placed the jewel on top, and went out to the park. The radiance of the jewel illuminated the four kinds of troops, and the extent of its light reached half a yojana in every direction. At that time, there was a brahmin who had this thought: 'I should go and see the wheel-turning king and the four kinds of troops, and observe the lapis lazuli jewel.' Then that brahmin had another thought: 'Let me set aside seeing the wheel-turning king and the four kinds of troops and observing the lapis lazuli jewel. I should rather go to that grove over there.'

"Thereupon, the brahmin went to the grove. Having arrived, he entered it and went to the base of a tree. Not long after he had sat down, an otter came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, otter! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! This pond was formerly filled with clear springs overflowing, rich in lotus roots and abundant in flowers, full of fish and turtles. It was where I used to dwell, but now it has dried up. Brahmin, you should know: I wish to leave here and enter the great river. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.'

"At that time, the otter, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then a night heron came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, night heron! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! This pond was formerly filled with clear springs overflowing, rich in lotus roots and abundant in flowers, full of fish and turtles. It was where I used to dwell, but now it has dried up. Brahmin, you should know: I wish to leave here and roost at a place where dead cattle gather, or where dead donkeys gather, or where dead humans gather. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' The night heron, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then a vulture came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, vulture! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from one great cemetery to another, killing and destroying. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, the flesh of dead horses, dead cattle, and dead humans. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' At that time, the vulture, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then a vomit-eating bird came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, vomit-eating bird! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! Did you see the vulture that just left? I eat what it vomits up. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' The vomit-eating bird, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then a jackal came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, jackal! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from deep ravine to deep ravine, from thicket to thicket, from secluded place to secluded place. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, the flesh of dead horses, dead cattle, and dead humans. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' At that time, the jackal, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then a crow came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, crow! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! You stubborn, foolish madman! Why do you ask me, "Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?"' At that time, the crow, having reviled the brahmin to his face, departed and left. The brahmin remained sitting.

"Then an orangutan came. The brahmin, seeing it, asked: 'Welcome, orangutan! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' It answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from garden to garden, from park to park, from grove to grove, drinking clear spring water and eating fine fruits. I now wish to go, and I do not fear humans.' The orangutan, having discussed this with the brahmin, departed and left."

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "I have spoken this parable wishing you to understand its meaning. You should know that this teaching has meaning.

"At that time, the otter, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village. In the early morning, the bhikṣu dons his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food, but does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. He then teaches the Dharma, whether taught by the Buddha or taught by his disciples, and because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the otter, asked it: 'Welcome, otter! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! This pond was formerly filled with clear springs overflowing, rich in lotus roots and abundant in flowers, full of fish and turtles. It was where I used to dwell, but now it has dried up. Brahmin, you should know: I wish to leave here and enter the great river. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise: he enters into evil, unwholesome, defiled dharmas, which become the cause for future existence, the root of burning suffering and retribution, the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the otter; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"The night heron, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village. In the early morning, the bhikṣu dons his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food, but does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. He enters the homes of others to instruct and teach the Dharma, whether taught by the Buddha or taught by his disciples, and because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the night heron, asked it: 'Welcome, night heron! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! This pond was formerly filled with clear springs overflowing, rich in lotus roots and abundant in flowers, full of fish and turtles. It was where I used to dwell, but now it has dried up. Brahmin, you should know: I now wish to leave and roost at a place where dead cattle gather, or where dead donkeys gather, or where dead humans gather. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise: he depends on evil, unwholesome, defiled dharmas, which become the cause for future existence, the root of burning suffering and retribution, the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the night heron; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"At that time, the vulture, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village. In the early morning, the bhikṣu dons his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food, but does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. He enters the homes of others to instruct and teach the Dharma, whether taught by the Buddha or taught by his disciples, and because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the vulture, asked it: 'Welcome, vulture! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from one great cemetery to another, killing and destroying. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, the flesh of dead horses, dead cattle, and dead humans. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the vulture; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"The vomit-eating bird, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village. In the early morning, the bhikṣu dons his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food, but does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. He enters the quarters of bhikṣuṇīs to instruct and teach the Dharma, whether taught by the Buddha or taught by his disciples. Those bhikṣuṇīs then go into various households, speaking praise or blame, and receive offerings given in faith, which they bring to the bhikṣu. Because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the vomit-eating bird, asked it: 'Welcome, vomit-eating bird! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! Did you see the vulture that just left? I eat what it vomits up. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the vomit-eating bird; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"At that time, the jackal, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a poor village. If he learns that in a certain village or city there are many who are wise, diligent, and practicing the holy life, he immediately avoids that place. If he learns that in a certain village or city there are none who are wise, diligent, and practicing the holy life, he comes and dwells there, perhaps for nine months or ten months. When other bhikṣus see him, they ask: 'Venerable one, where have you been traveling?' He then answers: 'Venerables, I have been dwelling depending on such-and-such a poor village.' When the bhikṣus hear this, they think: 'This venerable one practices what is difficult to practice. Why is that? Because this venerable one is able to dwell depending on such-and-such a poor village.' The bhikṣus then together show him respect, honor, reverence, and offerings. Because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the jackal, asked it: 'Welcome, jackal! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from deep ravine to deep ravine, from thicket to thicket, from secluded place to secluded place. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, the flesh of dead horses, dead cattle, and dead humans. I now wish to go, but I only fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the jackal; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"At that time, the crow, having reviled the brahmin to his face, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a poor, secluded place and undertakes the summer retreat there. If he learns that in a certain village or city there are many who are wise, diligent, and practicing the holy life, he immediately avoids that place. If he learns that in a certain village or city there are none who are wise, diligent, and practicing the holy life, he comes and dwells there for two or three months. When other bhikṣus see him, they ask: 'Venerable one, where did you spend the summer retreat?' He answers: 'Venerables, I spent the summer retreat depending on such-and-such a poor, secluded place. I am not like those foolish fellows who make beds complete with the five comforts and dwell in them, going about from morning to midday and from midday to morning, with their mouths following their tastes and their tastes following their mouths, seeking and seeking, searching and searching.' When the bhikṣus hear this, they think: 'This venerable one practices what is difficult to practice. Why is that? Because this venerable one is able to spend the summer retreat depending on such-and-such a poor, secluded place.' The bhikṣus then together show him respect, honor, reverence, and offerings. Because of this he obtains gains: robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various requisites for livelihood. Having obtained these gains, he becomes attached, clinging and relying on them, not seeing the danger, unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases. That bhikṣu practices bad conduct, accomplished in evil dharmas, standing at the very edge, generating what is corrupt and rotten. He is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; he is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa. Just as the brahmin, having seen the crow, asked it: 'Welcome, crow! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! You stubborn, foolish madman! Why do you ask me, "Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?"' I say that bhikṣu is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the crow; do not rely on wrong dharmas to sustain your livelihood. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, dwell in a secluded place, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-begging, beg for food in due order, have few desires and know contentment, delight in dwelling in seclusion, practice diligence, establish right mindfulness, right knowledge, right concentration, and right wisdom, always dwelling in seclusion. You should train in this way.

"The orangutan, having discussed with the brahmin, departed and left. What is the meaning of this parable I have spoken? Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a village. In the early morning, the bhikṣu dons his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food, well guarding his body, restraining his sense faculties, and establishing right mindfulness. That bhikṣu, having finished begging for food in the village and having eaten, in the afternoon puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and goes either to a secluded place, or to the base of a tree, or to an empty room. He spreads out his sitting cloth, sits cross-legged, straightens his body, sets his aspiration right, turns his mindfulness inward, and cuts off covetousness. His mind is free from contention. Seeing the possessions and livelihood goods of others, he does not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for himself. He purifies his mind of covetousness. Likewise with ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse. He cuts off doubt and crosses beyond perplexity; regarding wholesome dharmas, he has no uncertainty. He purifies his mind of doubt and perplexity. Having cut off these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom, he separates from desires, separates from evil, unwholesome dharmas, and attains up to the fourth dhyāna, dwelling in its accomplishment. Having attained such concentration, his mind is pure, without defilement, without disturbance, supple, well-established, and has attained the imperturbable mind. He then turns toward the knowledge and realization of the destruction of the taints. He then knows 'this is suffering' as it truly is; he knows 'this is the origin of suffering'; he knows 'this is the cessation of suffering'; he knows 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' as it truly is. He knows 'these are the taints'; he knows 'this is the origin of the taints'; he knows 'this is the cessation of the taints'; he knows 'this is the path leading to the cessation of the taints' as it truly is. Knowing thus, seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence.' He knows this as it truly is. Just as the brahmin, having seen the orangutan, asked it: 'Welcome, orangutan! Where have you come from, and where do you wish to go?' And it answered: 'Brahmin! I have come from garden to garden, from park to park, from grove to grove, drinking clear spring water and eating fine fruits. I now wish to go, and I do not fear humans.' I say that bhikṣu is likewise.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the otter; do not act like the night heron; do not act like the vulture; do not act like the vomit-eating bird; do not act like the jackal; do not act like the crow. You should act like the orangutan. Why is that? Among beings in the world, the unattached true person is like the orangutan."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Parable of the Crow, the First.

---

## (66) Sūtra on Speaking of Past Lives, Second of the Chapter on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Vārāṇasī, staying in the Deer Park at the Dwelling Place of Seers.

At that time, after the midday meal, the bhikṣus gathered and sat in the assembly hall on account of a small matter, and together discussed this topic: "How is it, venerables? For a householder at home, which is more excellent: that a bhikṣu of excellent moral conduct and fine dharmas, accomplished in deportment, enters a household and receives food, or that every morning one gains profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand fold?"

Some bhikṣus spoke thus: "Venerables, what use is profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand fold? Only this is most essential: if a bhikṣu of excellent moral conduct and fine dharmas, accomplished in deportment, enters a household and receives food. This is not the same as gaining profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand fold every morning."

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was also sitting in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, what use is profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand fold? Even if it were more than that, only this is most essential: if a bhikṣu of excellent moral conduct and fine dharmas, accomplished in deportment, enters a household and receives food. This is not the same as gaining profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand fold every morning. Why is that? I recall that long ago in this land of Vārāṇasī, I was a poor person who lived only by gleaning and carrying loads for hire. At that time, the land of Vārāṇasī suffered from drought, early frost, and insect plagues; the crops did not ripen; the people were in famine, and things begged for were hard to obtain. At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha named Anupādrava, who dwelt depending on this Vārāṇasī. Then the pratyekabuddha Anupādrava, having spent the night, in the early morning donned his robes and took his bowl, and entered Vārāṇasī to beg for food. At that time, I had gone out of Vārāṇasī early in the morning to glean. Venerables, when I was just going out, I happened to see the pratyekabuddha Anupādrava entering the city. At that time, the pratyekabuddha Anupādrava carried his clean bowl in, and came out with his bowl as clean as before.

"Venerables, when I returned from gleaning and was entering Vārāṇasī, I again saw the pratyekabuddha Anupādrava coming out. When he saw me, he had this thought: 'When I entered this morning, I saw this person going out. Now that I am coming out, I again see this person coming in. Perhaps this person has not yet obtained food. I should follow this person.' Then the pratyekabuddha followed after me, like a shadow following a form. Venerables, carrying my gleanings, I returned home. Setting down my load, I turned and looked back, and saw the pratyekabuddha Anupādrava following behind me, like a shadow following a form. Seeing him, I had this thought: 'When I went out this morning, I saw this sage entering the city to beg for food. Perhaps this sage has not yet obtained food. I should forgo my own food and share it with this sage.' Having thought thus, I took my food and gave it to the pratyekabuddha, saying: 'Sage, you should know this food is my own portion. Out of compassion, I beg you to accept it.' At that time, the pratyekabuddha answered me: 'Householder, you should know that this year there is drought, early frost, and insect plagues; the five grains have not ripened; the people are in famine, and things begged for are hard to obtain. You may put half in my bowl and eat the other half yourself, so that we both may sustain our lives. That would be good.' I again said: 'Sage, you should know that in my household I have a cooking pot and stove, I have firewood, I have grain and rice, and as for food and drink, morning or evening, there is no fixed time. Sage, out of compassion for me, please accept all of this food.' Then the pratyekabuddha, out of compassion, accepted all of it.

"Venerables, because of the merit of offering that one bowl of food, for seven lifetimes I was reborn in heaven and became a heavenly king, and for seven lifetimes I was reborn among humans and became a human king. Venerables, because of the merit of offering that one bowl of food, I have been born in this Śākya clan, greatly wealthy and prosperous, with abundant livestock, townships, and fiefdoms, with immeasurable resources and complete in precious treasures. Venerables, because of the merit of offering that one bowl of food, I renounced a hundred thousand koṭis of gold coins as a prince and left the household life to study the Way, to say nothing of other various miscellaneous possessions. Venerables, because of the merit of offering that one bowl of food, I am recognized and treated with respect by kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and all the people, as well as by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Venerables, because of the merit of offering that one bowl of food, I am always invited by people to receive food and drink, robes, woolen blankets, felt rugs, bedding, fine cloth, medicines for illness, and various requisites for livelihood; I am never uninvited. Had I known at that time that the śramaṇa was an unattached true person, the merit I obtained would have been even greater, yielding a great fruit and reward, of the most marvelous virtue, with light shining thoroughly, extremely vast and great."

Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha, an unattached true person who had attained right liberation, spoke this verse:

"I recall when long ago I was poor,
Living only by gleaning for survival.
I gave up my own share for a śramaṇa,
Anupādrava, of supreme virtue.

Because of this I was born in the Śākya clan,
With the name Anuruddha.
Skilled in singing, dancing, and understanding,
Making music and always rejoicing.

I came to see the World-Honored One,
The Perfectly Awakened One, like sweet ambrosia.
Having seen him, faith and joy arose;
I renounced the household to study the Way.

I have come to know my past lives,
I know where I was formerly born.
Born in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three,
Seven times I dwelt there.

Seven here, seven there,
Receiving birth fourteen times in all,
Among humans and in heaven,
Never once falling into an evil destiny.

I now know death and rebirth,
The places where beings come and go.
I know the minds of others, right and wrong,
And the five pleasures of the noble ones.

Attaining the five-factored dhyāna concentration,
Always calming the mind in stillness,
Having attained stable, right abiding,
I then realized the purified divine eye.

What I set out to accomplish by leaving the household,
Renouncing and departing from home,
This purpose I have now fulfilled:
I have entered the domain of the Buddha.

I have no delight in death,
Nor do I wish for birth.
I go along with whatever comes at any time,
Establishing right mindfulness and wisdom.

At the Bamboo Grove near Vaijayantī,
My life will come to its end there.
Beneath the bamboo grove,
I shall attain final nirvāṇa without remainder."

At that time, the World-Honored One was in meditative seclusion and, with his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard the bhikṣus who, after the midday meal, had gathered and sat in the assembly hall discussing this matter.

Having heard this, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditative seclusion, went to the assembly hall, and before the assembly of bhikṣus, spread his seat and sat down. He asked the bhikṣus: "What matter has brought you together today to sit in the assembly hall?"

At that time, the bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One, today we gathered and sat in the assembly hall because the Venerable Anuruddha was teaching the Dharma based on past events."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Would you today like to hear the Buddha teach the Dharma based on future events?"

The bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One, now is the right time. Well-Gone One, now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus based on future events, the bhikṣus, having heard it, will well receive and uphold it."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus, listen carefully, listen carefully! Reflect well upon it. I shall explain it to you in detail." The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus, in the far distant future, there will come a time when human beings will live to eighty thousand years. When humans live to eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa will be extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people, and the villages and towns will be so close together that a chicken could fly from one to the next. Bhikṣus, when humans live to eighty thousand years, women will not marry until the age of five hundred. Bhikṣus, when humans live to eighty thousand years, there will be only these illnesses: cold, heat, the need for urination and defecation, desire, hunger and thirst, and old age. There will be no other ailments.

"Bhikṣus, when humans live to eighty thousand years, there will be a king named Śaṅkha, who will be a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing the four kinds of troops, governing the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma-king, he will be accomplished in the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military minister treasure, making seven. He will have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, able to vanquish all opponents. He will rule over this entire land up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma, instructing and commanding, bringing peace and happiness. He will have a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, raised a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference. He will erect it, and after erecting it, below it he will give gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who have come from afar to beg, giving them food and drink, robes, carriages, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, bedding, woolen blankets, fine cloth, servants, and lamps. Having made these gifts, he will then shave off his hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith, leave the household for the homeless life to study the Way. What that son of good family sets out to accomplish by shaving off his hair and beard, donning the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way, is solely the completion of the supreme holy life, so that in this very life he may know for himself, realize for himself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence.' He will know this as it truly is."

At that time, the Venerable Ajita was sitting in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Ajita rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, may I, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, become that king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing the four kinds of troops, governing the world under heaven, sovereign by my own authority. As a righteous Dharma-king, I would be accomplished in the seven treasures. Those seven treasures being: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military minister treasure, making seven. I would have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, able to vanquish all opponents. I would rule over this entire land up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma, instructing and commanding, bringing peace and happiness. I would have a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, raised a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference. I would erect it, and after erecting it, below it I would give gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who have come from afar to beg, giving them food and drink, robes, carriages, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, bedding, woolen blankets, fine cloth, servants, and lamps. Having made these gifts, I would then shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith, leave the household for the homeless life to study the Way. What I, as a son of good family, set out to accomplish by shaving off my hair and beard, donning the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way, would be solely the completion of the supreme holy life, so that in this very life I may know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence.' I would know this as it truly is."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One rebuked the Venerable Ajita: "You foolish person! You should be subject to only one death, yet you seek to die twice. Why is that? Because you have had this thought: 'World-Honored One, may I, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, become that king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing the four kinds of troops, governing the world under heaven, sovereign by my own authority. As a righteous Dharma-king, I would be accomplished in the seven treasures. Those seven treasures being: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military minister treasure, making seven. I would have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, able to vanquish all opponents. I would rule over this entire land up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma, instructing and commanding, bringing peace and happiness. I would have a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, raised a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference. I would erect it, and after erecting it, below it I would give gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who have come from afar to beg, giving them food and drink, robes, carriages, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, bedding, woolen blankets, fine cloth, servants, and lamps. Having made these gifts, I would then shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith, leave the household for the homeless life to study the Way. What I, as a son of good family, set out to accomplish by shaving off my hair and beard, donning the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way, would be solely the completion of the supreme holy life, so that in this very life I may know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment: Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence. I would know this as it truly is.'"

The World-Honored One then said: "Ajita, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, you will become that king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing the four kinds of troops, governing the world under heaven, sovereign by your own authority. As a righteous Dharma-king, you will be accomplished in the seven treasures. Those seven treasures being: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military minister treasure, making seven. You will have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, able to vanquish all opponents. You will rule over this entire land up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma, instructing and commanding, bringing peace and happiness. You will have a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, raised a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference. You will erect it, and after erecting it, below it you will give gifts to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who have come from afar to beg, giving them food and drink, robes, carriages, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, bedding, woolen blankets, fine cloth, servants, and lamps. Having made these gifts, you will then shave off your hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith, leave the household for the homeless life to study the Way. What you, as a son of good family, set out to accomplish by shaving off your hair and beard, donning the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way, will be solely the completion of the supreme holy life, so that in this very life you may know for yourself, realize for yourself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence.' You will know this as it truly is."

The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus: "In the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, there will be a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Just as I have now become a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. He, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, will know for himself, realize for himself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. Just as I now, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. He will teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. Just as I now teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life.
