He will widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. Just as I now widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. He will have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in his assembly, just as I now have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in my assembly."

At that time, the Venerable Maitreya was in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Maitreya rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, may I, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, become a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Just as the World-Honored One has now become a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. May I, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. Just as the World-Honored One now, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, knows for himself, realizes for himself, and dwells having personally witnessed attainment. May I teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. Just as the World-Honored One now teaches the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. May I widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. Just as the World-Honored One now widely expounds and disseminates the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. May I have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in my assembly, just as the World-Honored One now has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in his assembly."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya: "Excellent, excellent! Maitreya, your aspiration is most wonderful, in that you wish to lead a great assembly. Why is that? Because you have had this thought: 'World-Honored One, may I, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, become a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Just as the World-Honored One has now become a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. May I, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. Just as the World-Honored One now, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, knows for himself, realizes for himself, and dwells having personally witnessed attainment. May I teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. Just as the World-Honored One now teaches the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. May I widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. Just as the World-Honored One now widely expounds and disseminates the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it.'"

The Buddha further said: "Maitreya, in the far distant future when humans live to eighty thousand years, you will become a Buddha named Maitreya, a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. Just as I have now become a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Controller of the Dharma Way, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. You, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, will know for yourself, realize for yourself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. Just as I now, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, know for myself, realize for myself, and dwell having personally witnessed attainment. You will teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. Just as I now teach the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete in purity, revealing the holy life. You will widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. Just as I now widely expound and disseminate the holy life, with great assemblies beyond measure, from humans to gods, well proclaiming and revealing it. You will have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in your assembly, just as I now have immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus in my assembly."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was holding a whisk and attending the Buddha. Thereupon, the World-Honored One turned and said: "Ānanda, bring me the robe woven with golden thread. I now wish to give it to the bhikṣu Maitreya."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda received the World-Honored One's instruction, fetched the robe woven with golden thread, and presented it to the World-Honored One. Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having received the robe woven with golden thread from the Venerable Ānanda, said: "Maitreya, take this robe woven with golden thread from the Tathāgata, and offer it to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Why is that? Maitreya, all Tathāgatas, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are protectors of the world, seeking benefit and welfare, seeking peace and happiness."

Thereupon, the Venerable Maitreya took the robe woven with golden thread from the Tathāgata and offered it to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas had this thought: "This śramaṇa Gautama is traveling in Vārāṇasī at the Dwelling Place of Seers in the Deer Park. He is teaching the Dharma to his disciples based on future events. I should go and disturb him." Then Māra Pāpīyas went to where the Buddha was, and upon arriving, facing the Buddha, spoke this verse:

"He will certainly obtain
The most excellent appearance,
With flower garlands and jeweled ornaments on his body,
And bright pearls adorning his arms,
In the city of Ketumatī,
Within the realm of King Śaṅkha."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This Māra Pāpīyas has come to my presence wishing to disturb me." Having known this, the World-Honored One spoke this verse to Māra Pāpīyas:

"He will certainly obtain
Freedom from bondage, free from doubt and delusion,
Cutting off birth, old age, sickness, and death,
With taints exhausted and his task completed,
If he practices the holy life
Within the realm of Maitreya."

Thereupon, the Māra King again spoke this verse:

"He will certainly obtain
Fine robes and supreme garments,
Sandalwood anointing his body,
With a figure upright, beautiful, and tall,
In the city of Ketumatī,
Within the realm of King Śaṅkha."

At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke this verse:

"He will certainly obtain
Freedom from possessions and from home,
His hands not holding gold or treasures,
Without fabrication and without worry,
If he practices the holy life
Within the realm of Maitreya."

Thereupon, the Māra King again spoke this verse:

"He will certainly obtain
Famous wealth and fine food and drink,
Skilled in singing and dancing,
Making music and always rejoicing,
In the city of Ketumatī,
Within the realm of King Śaṅkha."

At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke this verse:

"He will certainly cross to the other shore,
Like a bird breaking free from a net.
Attaining dhyāna, he will roam freely,
Complete in bliss and always rejoicing.
You, Māra, should know for certain:
I have already vanquished you."

Thereupon, the Māra King had this thought: "The World-Honored One knows me; the Well-Gone One sees me." Grieved, troubled, and sorrowful, unable to remain, he suddenly vanished from that place and was seen no more.

Thus spoke the Buddha. Maitreya, Ajita, the Venerable Ānanda, and all the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgamas)
## Fascicle 14

---

**(63) Sūtra on the Parable of the Venomous Snake**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now explain a parable for you. A person of wisdom, by means of a parable, can understand the meaning. Suppose, bhikṣus, a person has four venomous snakes placed in a single basket, and there is a man who loves his life and fears death, who desires happiness and detests suffering. A second person then addresses him, saying: 'You must take this basket containing four venomous snakes and carry it. You must bathe them, feed them, and when they are angry, you must pacify them. If you do not do this, these four venomous snakes will certainly bring harm to you at any time. You should do what is proper regarding these four venomous snakes.'

"That man, out of fear of the four venomous snakes, flees in all directions. Another person then addresses him, saying: 'Sir, you should know that there are five enemies following behind you with drawn swords, wanting to kill you. If they catch up, they will certainly slay you. You should do what is proper.'

"That man, out of fear of both the four venomous snakes and the five enemies with swords, flees in all directions. Another person then addresses him, saying: 'Sir, you should know that there is also a sixth enemy, an internal murderer, who follows close behind with a drawn sword, wanting to kill you. If he catches up, he will certainly slay you. You should do what is proper.'

"That man, out of fear of the four venomous snakes, the five enemies with swords, and the sixth internal murderer, flees in all directions. As he flees, he comes upon an empty village. He enters a certain house and finds it deserted and in ruin, with all its vessels empty and hollow, with nothing substantial. Another person then addresses him, saying: 'Sir, you should know that there are bandits who will soon come and raid this empty village. You should do what is proper.'

"That man, out of fear of the four venomous snakes, the five enemies with swords, the sixth internal murderer, and the bandits who will raid the empty village, flees in all directions. As he flees, he comes upon a great flood of water. This shore is fraught with many dangers and terrors, while the other shore is safe, pleasant, and free from fear. However, there is no bridge or boat to cross over. Then that man thinks: 'This body of water is very wide. This shore is fraught with many dangers and terrors, while the other shore is safe, pleasant, and free from fear. There is no bridge or boat by which to cross. I should now gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves, bind them together into a raft, and using the raft, propel myself with hands and feet to safely cross to the other shore.'

"That man then gathers grass, wood, branches, and leaves, binds them together into a raft, and using the raft, propels himself with hands and feet to safely cross to the other shore. Having crossed over, he becomes a brahmin who has reached the other shore.

"Bhikṣus, I have explained this parable for you, and now I shall explain its meaning. The four venomous snakes represent the four great elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. The five enemies with swords represent the five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. The sixth internal murderer represents delight and craving. The empty village represents the six internal sense bases. Bhikṣus, suppose a wise person examines the eye base; it appears empty, hollow, impermanent, without a self, and without what belongs to a self. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases are likewise. The bandits who will raid the empty village represent the six external sense bases. Bhikṣus, when the eye encounters a pleasant form, it is harmed; when it encounters an unpleasant form, it is also harmed. The ear encountering sounds, the nose encountering smells, the tongue encountering tastes, the body encountering tangibles, and the mind encountering mental objects are likewise. The great flood of water represents the four flows: the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of views, and the flow of ignorance. The raft represents the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Propelling with hands and feet represents vigorous effort. Crossing to the other shore represents the cessation of suffering, which is nirvāṇa. Having crossed over, the brahmin who has reached the other shore represents the arahant."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(64) Sūtra on the Celestial Abodes**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain to you the four celestial abodes. Listen well and pay careful attention; I shall speak for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What are the four celestial abodes? A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial application and sustained application, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He pervades, fills, and saturates this body with joy and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that the joy and happiness born of seclusion does not reach. Just as a skilled bathhouse attendant or his apprentice, having placed bathing powder in a copper basin, sprinkles it with water and kneads it so that the moisture permeates it throughout, with no part that is not moistened, internally and externally pervading everything; in the same way, a bhikṣu pervades, fills, and saturates this body with joy and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that the joy and happiness born of seclusion does not reach. This is called the first celestial abode.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the stilling of initial application and sustained application, with internal purity and mental unification, without initial application and without sustained application, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He pervades, fills, and saturates this body with joy and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that the joy and happiness born of concentration does not reach. Just as a spring on a mountaintop, with clear, pure water that fills it to overflowing, water does not come from the east, west, south, or north, nor does it fall from the sky, but the spring of water naturally wells up from within and fills the entire pool, so that there is no part that is not pervaded by the cool water; in the same way, a bhikṣu pervades, fills, and saturates this body with joy and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that the joy and happiness born of concentration does not reach. This is called the second celestial abode.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body. As the noble ones describe: 'With equanimity, mindfulness, and dwelling in happiness,' he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He pervades, fills, and saturates this body with happiness free from joy, so that there is no part of his entire body that the happiness free from joy does not reach. Just as blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water and grown in the water, remain submerged within the water, and from root to tip are pervaded, saturated, and filled with cool water, so that there is no part that is not reached; in the same way, a bhikṣu pervades, fills, and saturates this body with happiness free from joy, so that there is no part of his entire body that the happiness free from joy does not reach. This is called the third celestial abode.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the prior cessation of gladness and sadness, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He sits, pervading this body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body that the pure and bright mind does not reach. Just as a person sitting down and covering himself with a white cloth from head to foot, so that there is no part of his entire body that the white cloth does not cover; in the same way, a bhikṣu sits, pervading this body with a pure and bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body that the pure and bright mind does not reach. This is called the fourth celestial abode.

"These are called the four celestial abodes."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(65) Sūtra on the Parable of the Cloth**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a mind has defilements, the mind is not well purified. If a mind is without defilements, the mind is well purified.

"Bhikṣus, just as a soiled, stained piece of cloth that a dyer dips into any kind of dye, whether blue, yellow, red, or black, the dyeing will not be good and the color will not be pure. Why is this? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, if a mind has defilements, one can expect a bad destination. Bhikṣus, just as a clean, pure piece of cloth that a dyer dips into any kind of dye, whether blue, yellow, red, or black, the dyeing will be good and the color will be pure. Why is this? Because the cloth is clean. In the same way, if a mind is without defilements, one can expect a good destination.

"What are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and wrongful greed are defilements of the mind. Ill will is a defilement of the mind. Anger is a defilement of the mind. Resentment is a defilement of the mind. Hostility is a defilement of the mind. Hypocrisy is a defilement of the mind. Malice is a defilement of the mind. Jealousy is a defilement of the mind. Miserliness is a defilement of the mind. Deceit is a defilement of the mind. Fraud is a defilement of the mind. Obstinacy is a defilement of the mind. Contentiousness is a defilement of the mind. Conceit is a defilement of the mind. Arrogance is a defilement of the mind. Pride is a defilement of the mind. Heedlessness is a defilement of the mind.

"If a bhikṣu knows that covetousness and wrongful greed are defilements of the mind, having known this, he abandons them. If a bhikṣu knows that ill will is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that anger is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that resentment is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that hostility is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that hypocrisy is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that malice is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that jealousy is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that miserliness is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that deceit is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that fraud is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that obstinacy is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that contentiousness is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that conceit is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that arrogance is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that pride is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it. If a bhikṣu knows that heedlessness is a defilement of the mind, having known this, he abandons it.

"When that bhikṣu has known that covetousness and wrongful greed are defilements of the mind and has abandoned them; has known that ill will is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that anger is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that resentment is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that hostility is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that hypocrisy is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that malice is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that jealousy is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that miserliness is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that deceit is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that fraud is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that obstinacy is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that contentiousness is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that conceit is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that arrogance is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that pride is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; has known that heedlessness is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; then that bhikṣu obtains unwavering faith in the Buddha, saying: 'The World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' He obtains unwavering faith in the Dharma, saying: 'The Dharma has been well expounded by the World-Honored One, is visible here and now, is not subject to time, can lead one upward, is to be personally known by the wise.' He obtains unwavering faith in the Sangha, saying: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples practices well, practices uprightly, practices in accord with the Dharma, practices with propriety; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'

"Having thus abandoned, having thus renounced, having thus liberated, having thus dissolved these defilements of the mind, he obtains the joy associated with the Dharma. Having obtained joy, he gives rise to delight. Having given rise to delight in the mind, the body becomes tranquil. With the body tranquil, he experiences happiness. Experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.

"He abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, and the four intermediate directions, above and below, all around and everywhere, to the whole world. He abides pervading everywhere with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, expansive, immeasurable, without hatred, without ill will. In the same way, he abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, and with a mind imbued with equanimity, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, and the four intermediate directions, above and below, all around and everywhere, to the whole world. He abides pervading everywhere with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, expansive, immeasurable, without hatred, without ill will.

"That bhikṣu then knows: 'There is this, there is the higher, there is the supreme, there is an escape transcending this entire realm of perception.' When he knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the defilement of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the defilement of existence, and the mind is liberated from the defilement of ignorance. Being liberated, there is the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'

"Bhikṣus, this is called a bhikṣu who has bathed with the inner bathing."

At that time, the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was seated in that assembly. Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja said to the World-Honored One: "Has the World-Honored One gone to bathe in the Bāhukā River?"

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, what has the Bāhukā River to do with anything? What can the Bāhukā River accomplish?"

The brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja said: "World-Honored One, many people believe that the Bāhukā River can grant liberation, that the Bāhukā River can grant merit. Many people have their evil deeds washed away in the Bāhukā River."

Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse to the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja:

"In the Bāhukā and Adhikakkā Rivers,
In the Gayā and Sundarikā,
In the Sarassatī and Payāga,
And in the Bāhumatī River,
A fool may constantly bathe therein,
But dark deeds cannot be cleansed.
What can the Sundarikā River accomplish?
What can the Payāga or Bāhukā do?
They cannot purify the evil-doer,
The person of harsh and wicked deeds.
For one who is pure, every day is auspicious,
For one who is pure, every day is blessed,
For one of pure deeds and pure conduct,
One's vows will always be fulfilled.
Brahmin, you should bathe right here,
And bring safety to all living beings.
If you do not speak falsehood,
If you do not kill living beings,
If you do not take what is not given,
If you live with faith and without miserliness,
What need to go to Gayā?
Any well can be your Gayā."

Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja said to the World-Honored One: "Excellent, Venerable Gautama! Excellent, Venerable Gautama! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, reveal what was hidden, point the way to one who was lost, or hold a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. In the same way, Venerable Gautama has explained the Dharma in various ways. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May Venerable Gautama accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(66) Sūtra on Explaining the Meaning**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain for you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, and that reveals the holy life. That is, the 'Sūtra on Explaining the Meaning.' Listen well and pay careful attention; I shall speak for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said:

"By eye and forms, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By ear and sounds, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By nose and smells, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By tongue and tastes, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By body and tangibles, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By mind and mental objects, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From contact, feeling comes to be;
From feeling, craving arises.
From craving, clinging comes to be;
From clinging, becoming arises.
From becoming, there is birth;
From birth come aging and death,
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair.
Such is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.

"By eye and forms, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

"By ear and sounds, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

"By nose and smells, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

"By tongue and tastes, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

"By body and tangibles, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

"By mind and mental objects, consciousness arises;
The three together are contact.
From the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
From the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
From the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
From the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases.
From the cessation of becoming, birth ceases.
From the cessation of birth, aging and death cease,
And sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
Distress, and despair all cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

**(67) Sūtra on the Great Chapter on Deeds**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain for you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, and that reveals the holy life. That is, the 'Great Chapter on Deeds.' Listen well and pay careful attention; I shall speak for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "There are four kinds of persons in this world. What are the four? There is a person who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views. After the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. 

"There is a person who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views. Yet after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.

"There is a person who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views. After the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.

"There is a person who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views. Yet after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell.

"Now, there is a certain ascetic or brahmin who, by ardor, by effort, by application, by diligence, by right mental attention, attains such a level of mental concentration that with the concentrated mind, which is purified, clear, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, workable, stable, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He then sees that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. Having seen this, he says: 'Indeed there are evil deeds, and there is the result of evil conduct. I have seen that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell.' He says: 'Whoever kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong.' He thus insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong.'

"Now, there is another ascetic or brahmin who, by ardor, by effort, by application, by diligence, by right mental attention, attains such a level of mental concentration that with the concentrated mind, which is purified, clear, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, workable, stable, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He then sees that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Having seen this, he says: 'Indeed there are no evil deeds, and there is no result of evil conduct. I have seen that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He says: 'Whoever kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong.' He thus insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong.'

"Now, there is another ascetic or brahmin who, by ardor, by effort, by application, by diligence, by right mental attention, attains such a level of mental concentration that with the concentrated mind, which is purified, clear, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, workable, stable, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He then sees that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Having seen this, he says: 'Indeed there are good deeds, and there is the result of good conduct. I have seen that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He says: 'Whoever abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong.' He thus insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong.'

"Now, there is another ascetic or brahmin who, by ardor, by effort, by application, by diligence, by right mental attention, attains such a level of mental concentration that with the concentrated mind, which is purified, clear, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, workable, stable, and having attained imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He then sees that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. Having seen this, he says: 'Indeed there are no good deeds, and there is no result of good conduct. I have seen that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell.' He says: 'Whoever abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong.' He thus insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong.'

"Bhikṣus, regarding the first ascetic or brahmin who says: 'Indeed there are evil deeds, and there is the result of evil conduct,' I grant him this much. When he says: 'I have seen that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell,' I also grant him this. But when he says: 'Whoever kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. When he insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great chapter on deeds is different.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the second ascetic or brahmin who says: 'Indeed there are no evil deeds, and there is no result of evil conduct,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'I have seen that person who killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world,' I grant him this. But when he says: 'Whoever kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. When he insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great chapter on deeds is different.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the third ascetic or brahmin who says: 'Indeed there are good deeds, and there is the result of good conduct,' I grant him this. When he says: 'I have seen that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world,' I also grant him this. But when he says: 'Whoever abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. When he insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great chapter on deeds is different.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the fourth ascetic or brahmin who says: 'Indeed there are no good deeds, and there is no result of good conduct,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'I have seen that person who abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, was reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell,' I grant him this. But when he says: 'Whoever abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, all of them after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell,' I do not grant him this. When he says: 'Whoever knows thus, they know correctly. Whoever knows otherwise, their knowledge is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. When he insists and clings to what he himself has known, has seen, and has understood, saying: 'Only this is true; anything else is wrong,' I also do not grant him this. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great chapter on deeds is different.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the person who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell: either in a former life he performed evil deeds that are to be experienced as suffering, and he fully experiences their result; or in a later life he performed evil deeds that are to be experienced as suffering, and he fully experiences their result; or at the time of death he generated and adopted wrong views. Because of this, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. Because he killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, he will experience its result either in this present life, or in a future life.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the person who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has ill will, and holds wrong views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world: either in a former life he performed good deeds that are to be experienced as happiness, and he fully experiences their result; or in a later life he performed good deeds that are to be experienced as happiness, and he fully experiences their result; or at the time of death he generated and adopted right views. Because of this, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. But because he killed living beings, took what is not given, engaged in sexual misconduct, spoke falsehood, spoke divisively, spoke harshly, engaged in idle chatter, was covetous, had ill will, and held wrong views, he will experience its result either in this present life, or in a future life.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the person who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, and who after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world: either in a former life he performed good deeds that are to be experienced as happiness, and he fully experiences their result; or in a later life he performed good deeds that are to be experienced as happiness, and he fully experiences their result; or at the time of death he generated and adopted right views. Because of this, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Because he abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, he will experience its result either in this present life, or in a future life.

"Bhikṣus, regarding the person who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from speaking divisively, abstains from speaking harshly, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views, yet after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell: either in a former life he performed evil deeds that are to be experienced as suffering, and he fully experiences their result; or in a later life he performed evil deeds that are to be experienced as suffering, and he fully experiences their result; or at the time of death he generated and adopted wrong views. Because of this, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. But because he abstained from killing living beings, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from speaking falsehood, abstained from speaking divisively, abstained from speaking harshly, abstained from idle chatter, was without covetousness, was without ill will, and held right views, he will experience its result either in this present life, or in a future life.

"Bhikṣus, thus, there are deeds that are worthless and appear worthless, there are deeds that are worthless but appear worthy, there are deeds that are worthy and appear worthy, and there are deeds that are worthy but appear worthless. Bhikṣus, this is the Tathāgata's knowledge of the great chapter on deeds."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(68) Sūtra on the Great Chapter on Deeds (Second)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, being alone in a quiet place and engaged in meditation, had this thought arise in his mind: "It is wonderful, indeed, that the World-Honored One has revealed, discerned, and explained the fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, the fragrance of liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation. These five fragrances are not blown by wind. Even against the wind, they spread far and wide. There are beings who know these five fragrances. Of such beings, there are extremely few. Most beings do not know them."

Then in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda rose from meditation, went to the World-Honored One, paid homage at his feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I was alone in a quiet place, engaged in meditation, when this thought arose in my mind: 'It is wonderful, indeed, that the World-Honored One has revealed, discerned, and explained the fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, the fragrance of liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation. These five fragrances are not blown by wind. Even against the wind, they spread far and wide. There are beings who know these five fragrances. Of such beings, there are extremely few. Most beings do not know them.'"

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is! Ānanda, these five fragrances are indeed not blown by wind, and even against the wind, they spread far and wide. There are beings who know these five fragrances. Of such beings, there are extremely few. Most beings do not know them.

"Ānanda, it is just as a person who is blind from birth and cannot see forms, whether white, black, blue, yellow, red, or purple, and cannot see what is level or uneven, and cannot see the stars, the sun, or the moon. Someone tells him: 'White looks like this, black like this, blue, yellow, red, purple look like this. Level looks like this, uneven like this. The stars look like this, the sun and moon look like this.' That person, blind from birth, cannot know or see any of them.

"In the same way, Ānanda, the Dharma-eye has not yet arisen in ordinary worldlings. The Dharma-eye not having arisen, they are just like those blind from birth; how could they know or see these five aggregates of dharma? Only a Tathāgata, a Worthy One, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Tathāgata's disciples who are well learned and well disciplined can know and see these five aggregates of dharma."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 14 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Fascicle Fourteen of the Madhyamāgama

---

## (67) Sūtra Three of the Chapter on Kings: The Sūtra of King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Videha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and proceeded to Mithilā, where he stayed in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One, while walking along the road, smiled with delight. Venerable Ānanda, seeing the World-Honored One smile, joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! For what reason do you smile? The Tathāgatas, the Unattached Ones, the Fully Enlightened Ones never smile without a reason. We wish to hear the meaning of this."

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! In the past, in a former time, in this very Mithilā Naiṣadha Grove, there was a king named Mahādeva. He was a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, who had four kinds of armies and ruled the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he was endowed with the seven treasures and obtained the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans. Ānanda! What were the seven treasures with which King Mahādeva was endowed? They were the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander-of-the-army treasure. These are called the seven.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the wheel treasure? Ānanda! At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of reciting the Prātimokṣa, King Mahādeva bathed and washed himself, then ascended to the main palace hall. A heavenly wheel treasure came from the east. The wheel had a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, its color like blazing fire, brilliantly radiant. When King Mahādeva saw it, he rejoiced and was elated, and thought to himself: 'A worthy wheel treasure has appeared, a marvelous wheel treasure has appeared! I have also heard from the ancients that if a head-anointed kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of reciting the Prātimokṣa, bathes and washes himself, ascends to the main palace hall, and a heavenly wheel treasure comes from the east, with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, its color like blazing fire, brilliantly radiant, then he shall surely become a wheel-turning king. Could it be that I shall become a wheel-turning king?'

"Ānanda! In the past, King Mahādeva wished to test the heavenly wheel treasure. At that time, he assembled the four kinds of armies: elephant army, horse army, chariot army, and infantry. Having assembled the four armies, he went to where the heavenly wheel treasure was, stroked the wheel with his left hand, turned it with his right hand, and spoke these words: 'Follow the heavenly wheel treasure, follow wherever the heavenly wheel treasure turns and goes.' Ānanda! The heavenly wheel treasure, having been turned, then set forth, heading toward the east. At that time, King Mahādeva himself followed behind it, along with the four kinds of armies. Wherever the heavenly wheel treasure came to rest, King Mahādeva would stop and lodge there, along with the four armies. Thereupon, the minor kings of the eastern regions all came to King Mahādeva's presence and said: 'Great King! Welcome! Great King! All these lands are exceedingly prosperous and happy, with many people, and all belong to the Great King. We humbly wish that the Great King govern them with the Dharma, and we shall assist the Great King.' Thereupon, King Mahādeva addressed the minor kings: 'Each of you shall govern your own territories. You should all govern with the Dharma, not with what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow evil deeds or those who are not of pure conduct in your kingdoms.'

"Ānanda! The heavenly wheel treasure passed through the east, crossed the great eastern ocean, and turned to the south, the west, and the north. Ānanda! Following the heavenly wheel treasure as it turned and traveled all around, King Mahādeva himself followed behind, along with the four armies. Wherever the heavenly wheel treasure came to rest, King Mahādeva would stop and lodge there, along with the four armies. Thereupon, the minor kings of the northern regions all came to King Mahādeva's presence and said: 'Great King! Welcome! Great King! All these lands are exceedingly prosperous and happy, with many people, and all belong to the Great King. We humbly wish that the Great King govern them with the Dharma, and we shall assist the Great King.' Thereupon, King Mahādeva addressed the minor kings: 'Each of you shall govern your own territories. You should all govern with the Dharma, not with what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow evil deeds or those who are not of pure conduct in your kingdoms.' Ānanda! The heavenly wheel treasure passed through the north, crossed the great northern ocean, and then swiftly returned to the original royal city. King Mahādeva sat in the main palace hall, adjudicating and managing affairs of property. At that time, the heavenly wheel treasure remained suspended in space. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the heavenly wheel treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the elephant treasure? Ānanda! At that time, an elephant treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That elephant was extremely white and had seven supports. The elephant was named Upasaha. When King Mahādeva saw it, he rejoiced and was elated, thinking that if it could be trained, it would be made supremely excellent. Ānanda! King Mahādeva then at a later time told the elephant trainer: 'You should quickly train the elephant and make it supremely well-trained. When the elephant is trained, come and report to me.' At that time, the elephant trainer, having received the king's command, went to the elephant treasure and quickly trained it, making it supremely well-trained. At that time, the elephant treasure, receiving thorough training, was swiftly well-trained, just as a fine elephant of old that lived for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years receiving thorough training, was swiftly well-trained. The elephant treasure was likewise: receiving thorough training, it was swiftly well-trained. Ānanda! At that time, the elephant trainer quickly trained the elephant treasure, making it supremely well-trained. When the elephant treasure was trained, he went to King Mahādeva's presence and said: 'Great King! You should know that I have thoroughly trained the elephant treasure. It is now trained and awaits the Great King's pleasure.' Ānanda! In the past, when King Mahādeva tested the elephant treasure, at dawn when the sun rose, he went to where the elephant treasure was, mounted the elephant treasure, and traveled over all the land as far as the great ocean, then swiftly returned to the original royal city. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the white elephant treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the horse treasure? Ānanda! At that time, a horse treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That horse treasure was of an extremely deep blue color, with a head shaped like a crow's, adorned with a mane upon its body, and was named the Mane Horse King. When the Great King saw it, he rejoiced and was elated, thinking that if it could be trained, it would be made supremely excellent. Ānanda! King Mahādeva then at a later time told the horse trainer: 'You should quickly train the horse and make it supremely well-trained. When the horse is trained, come and report to me.' At that time, the horse trainer, having received the king's command, went to the horse treasure and quickly trained it, making it supremely well-trained. At that time, the horse treasure, receiving thorough training, was swiftly well-trained, just as a fine horse of old that lived for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years receiving thorough training, was swiftly well-trained. The horse treasure was likewise: receiving thorough training, it was swiftly well-trained. Ānanda! At that time, the horse trainer quickly trained the horse treasure, making it supremely well-trained. When the horse treasure was trained, he went to King Mahādeva's presence and said: 'Great King! You should know that I have thoroughly trained the horse treasure. It is now trained and awaits the Great King's pleasure.' Ānanda! In the past, when King Mahādeva tested the horse treasure, at dawn when the sun rose, he went to where the horse treasure was, mounted the horse treasure, and traveled over all the land as far as the great ocean, then swiftly returned to the original royal city. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the dark blue horse treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the jewel treasure? Ānanda! At that time, a jewel treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That jewel treasure was luminous and pure by nature, with no maker. It was octagonal and without blemish, supremely well-polished, and strung with a five-colored cord: blue, yellow, red, white, and black. Ānanda! At that time, King Mahādeva, when he wished to have light inside the palace chambers, would simply use the jewel treasure. Ānanda! In the past, when King Mahādeva tested the jewel treasure, he assembled the four kinds of armies: elephant army, horse army, chariot army, and infantry. Having assembled the four armies, in the darkness of night he erected a tall banner, placed the jewel upon it, and went out to the park. The jewel's radiance illuminated the four armies, and the extent of its light reached half a yojana in every direction. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the luminous jewel treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the woman treasure? Ānanda! At that time, a woman treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That woman treasure had a body of lustrous radiance, bright and pure, with beauty surpassing that of humans, only slightly less than that of celestial beings, with a graceful and upright appearance, delighting all who saw her. From her mouth came the fragrance of blue lotus flowers, and from all the pores of her body emanated the scent of sandalwood. In winter her body was warm, and in summer her body was cool. That woman wholeheartedly served the king. Her words were pleasant and delightful, her actions swift and nimble. She was wise and intelligent, and joyfully practiced goodness. That woman's thoughts of the king never left her mind, let alone her actions of body and speech. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the beautiful woman treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the householder treasure? Ānanda! At that time, a householder treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That householder treasure was exceedingly wealthy, with immeasurable resources and possessions, many livestock, fiefs, and food-producing estates, complete with all kinds of things as the reward of meritorious deeds. He possessed the divine eye and could see all treasure stores, whether empty or full. He could see those with guardians and those without guardians, gold treasuries and coin treasuries, whether wrought or unwrought, seeing them all. Ānanda! The householder treasure went to King Mahādeva and said: 'Great King! If you wish to obtain gold or coin treasures, the Great King need not worry; I myself know the right time.' Ānanda! In the past, when King Mahādeva tested the householder treasure, the king boarded a boat and entered the Ganges River, then said: 'Householder! I wish to obtain gold and coin treasures.' The householder said: 'Great King! May the boat go to the shore.' At that time, King Mahādeva said: 'Householder! I wish to obtain them right here, right here!' The householder said: 'Great King! May the boat be stopped.' Ānanda! At that time, the householder treasure went to the bow of the boat, knelt down, extended his hands, and from the water brought up four treasuries: a gold treasury, a coin treasury, a wrought treasury, and an unwrought treasury. He said: 'Great King! Whatever you desire, gold and coin treasures, use them freely as you wish.' After using what was needed, the remainder was returned to the water. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the householder treasure.

"Ānanda! How was King Mahādeva endowed with the commander-of-the-army treasure? Ānanda! At that time, a commander-of-the-army treasure was born for King Mahādeva. That commander was wise and intelligent, eloquent and skillful in speech, well-informed and discerning. The commander treasure, for King Mahādeva, would set forth matters of benefit in this life and encourage and establish him in them, would set forth matters of benefit for the next life and encourage and establish him in them, and would set forth matters of benefit for both this life and the next and encourage and establish him in them. That commander, for King Mahādeva, when armies needed to be assembled, could assemble them; when they needed to be disbanded, could disband them. He could ensure that King Mahādeva's four kinds of armies were not fatigued, and he encouraged and assisted them. He treated the other ministers likewise. This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the commander-of-the-army treasure. Ānanda! This is how King Mahādeva was endowed with the seven treasures.

"Ānanda! How did King Mahādeva obtain the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans? King Mahādeva had an extremely long lifespan of eighty-four thousand years. For eighty-four thousand years he played as a youth, for eighty-four thousand years he served as a minor king, for eighty-four thousand years he served as a great king, and then he shaved off his beard and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, dwelling in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove. Ānanda! That King Mahādeva had an extremely long lifespan of eighty-four thousand years, for eighty-four thousand years played as a youth, for eighty-four thousand years served as a minor king, for eighty-four thousand years served as a great king, then shaved off his beard and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, dwelling in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove. This is called King Mahādeva's first gratifying virtue.

"Furthermore, Ānanda! King Mahādeva was free from illness and possessed an even and balanced digestive constitution, neither too cold nor too hot, peaceful and without disturbance. Because of this, whatever he ate and drank was safely digested. Ānanda! That King Mahādeva was free from illness and possessed an even and balanced digestive constitution, neither too cold nor too hot, peaceful and without disturbance, and because of this, whatever he ate and drank was safely digested. This is called King Mahādeva's second gratifying virtue.

"Furthermore, Ānanda! King Mahādeva's body was radiant, bright and pure, with beauty surpassing that of humans, only slightly less than that of celestial beings, upright and handsome, delighting all who saw him. Ānanda! That King Mahādeva's body was radiant, bright and pure, with beauty surpassing that of humans, only slightly less than that of celestial beings, upright and handsome, delighting all who saw him. This is called King Mahādeva's third gratifying virtue.

"Furthermore, Ānanda! King Mahādeva always regarded the brahmins and householders with affection and care, as a father cares for his children. The brahmins and householders likewise revered King Mahādeva, as children revere their father. Ānanda! In the past, when King Mahādeva was in the park, he told his charioteer: 'Drive the chariot slowly, for I wish to look upon the brahmins and householders for a long time.' The brahmins and householders also told their charioteers: 'Drive the chariot slowly, for we wish to look upon King Mahādeva for a long time.' Ānanda! That King Mahādeva always regarded the brahmins and householders with affection and care, as a father cares for his children, and the brahmins and householders likewise revered King Mahādeva, as children revere their father. This is called King Mahādeva's fourth gratifying virtue. Ānanda! This is how King Mahādeva obtained the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans.

"Ānanda! At a later time, King Mahādeva told his barber: 'If you see white hairs growing on my head, you should report this to me.' Thereupon, the barber, having received the king's command, at a later time was washing the king's head and saw white hairs growing. Having seen them, he reported: 'Great King! You should know that the heavenly messenger has arrived; white hairs have grown on your head.' King Mahādeva then told the barber: 'Take gold tweezers and gently pluck out the white hairs, and place them in my hand.' At that time, the barber, having heard the king's command, took gold tweezers and gently plucked the white hairs, placing them in the king's hand. Ānanda! King Mahādeva held the white hairs in his hands and spoke this verse:

"'White hairs have grown upon my head,
My lifespan now declines and wanes.
The heavenly messenger has arrived;
It is now time for me to practice the Way.'

"Ānanda! King Mahādeva, having seen the white hairs, told his crown prince: 'Crown Prince! Know that the heavenly messenger has arrived; white hairs have grown on my head. Crown Prince! I have already obtained the desires of the human realm. Now I should seek the desires of the heavenly realm. Crown Prince! I wish to shave off my beard and hair, don kāṣāya robes, and with faith, leave the household for the homeless life to practice the Way. Crown Prince! I now entrust the rule of these four continents to you. You should govern with the Dharma, not with what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow evil deeds or those who are not of pure conduct in your kingdom. Crown Prince! When you later see that the heavenly messenger has arrived and white hairs grow on your head, you should likewise entrust the governance of the kingdom to your own crown prince, instructing and admonishing him well. Having entrusted the kingdom to your crown prince, you too should shave off your beard and hair, don kāṣāya robes, and with faith, leave the household for the homeless life to practice the Way. Crown Prince! I now turn over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession. Do not let the people fall to the extreme limit. Crown Prince! What does it mean that I now turn over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession, so that the people do not fall to the extreme limit? Crown Prince! If in this kingdom the transmission of the Dharma ceases and is not continued, this is called the people falling to the extreme limit. Crown Prince! For this reason, I now turn it over to you. Crown Prince! I have turned over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession. Do not let the people fall to the extreme limit.'

"Ānanda! King Mahādeva, having entrusted the governance of the kingdom to the crown prince and having instructed and admonished him well, then shaved off his beard and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove. That one also became a wheel-turning king, endowed with the seven treasures and obtaining the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans. How was he endowed with the seven treasures and the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans? As previously described for the seven treasures and the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans.

"Ānanda! That wheel-turning king also, at a later time, told his barber: 'If you see white hairs growing on my head, you should report this to me.' Thereupon, the barber, having received the king's command, at a later time was washing the king's head and saw white hairs growing. Having seen them, he reported: 'Great King! You should know that the heavenly messenger has arrived; white hairs have grown on your head.' That wheel-turning king then told the barber: 'Take gold tweezers and gently pluck out the white hairs, and place them in my hand.' At that time, the barber, having heard the king's command, took gold tweezers and gently plucked the white hairs, placing them in the king's hand. Ānanda! That wheel-turning king held the white hairs in his hands and spoke this verse:

"'White hairs have grown upon my head,
My lifespan now declines and wanes.
The heavenly messenger has arrived;
It is now time for me to practice the Way.'

"Ānanda! That wheel-turning king, having seen the white hairs, told his crown prince: 'Crown Prince! Know that the heavenly messenger has arrived; white hairs have grown on my head. Crown Prince!
