I have already obtained the desires of the human realm. Now I should seek the desires of the heavenly realm. Crown Prince! I wish to shave off my beard and hair, don kāṣāya robes, and with faith, leave the household for the homeless life to practice the Way. I now entrust the rule of these four continents to you. You should govern with the Dharma, not with what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow evil deeds or those who are not of pure conduct in your kingdom. Crown Prince! When you later see that the heavenly messenger has arrived and white hairs grow on your head, you should likewise entrust the governance of the kingdom to your own crown prince, instructing and admonishing him well. Having entrusted the kingdom to your crown prince, you too should shave off your beard and hair, don kāṣāya robes, and with faith, leave the household for the homeless life to practice the Way. Crown Prince! I now turn over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession. Do not let the people fall to the extreme limit. Crown Prince! What does it mean that I now turn over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession, so that the people do not fall to the extreme limit? Crown Prince! If in this kingdom the transmission of the Dharma ceases and is not continued, this is called the people falling to the extreme limit. Crown Prince! For this reason, I now turn it over to you. Crown Prince! I have turned over to you this law of succession, and you too should turn over this law of succession. Do not let the people fall to the extreme limit.'

"Ānanda! That wheel-turning king, having entrusted the governance of the kingdom to the crown prince and having instructed and admonished him well, then shaved off his beard and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove.

"Ānanda! Thus, from son to son, from grandson to grandson, from clan member to clan member, from generation to generation, in succession, eighty-four thousand wheel-turning kings shaved off their beards and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove. The very last of these kings was named Nimi. He was a righteous Dharma King who practiced the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and for his crown princes, queens, court ladies, officials and subjects, śramaṇas and brahmins, down to the insects, he observed the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practiced giving, distributing to the destitute, śramaṇas and brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who came from afar begging, providing food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, perfumed ointments, dwellings, beds, woolen carpets, cotton blankets, servants, and lamps.

"At that time, the Thirty-Three Gods gathered and sat in the Hall of Good Dharma, praising and extolling King Nimi, saying: 'Gentlemen! The people of Videha have great good fortune, great merit. Why is this so? Their last king, named Nimi, is a righteous Dharma King who practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and for his crown princes, queens, court ladies, officials and subjects, śramaṇas and brahmins, down to the insects, he observes the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practices giving, distributing to the destitute, śramaṇas and brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who come from afar begging, providing food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, perfumed ointments, dwellings, beds, woolen carpets, cotton blankets, servants, and lamps.'

"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, was also among the assembly. Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, addressed the Thirty-Three Gods: 'Gentlemen! Do you wish to see King Nimi right here?' The Thirty-Three Gods replied: 'Kauśika! We wish to see King Nimi right here.' At that time, Śakra, just as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, vanished from among the Thirty-Three Gods above and appeared here in King Nimi's palace. Thereupon, King Nimi saw Śakra, Lord of the Gods. Having seen him, he asked: 'Who are you?' Śakra answered: 'Great King! Have you heard of Śakra, Lord of the Gods?' He answered: 'I have heard of Śakra.' Śakra said: 'I am he. Great King, you have great good fortune, great merit. Why is this so? The Thirty-Three Gods have gathered on your behalf and sat in the Hall of Good Dharma, praising and extolling you, saying: "Gentlemen! The people of Videha have great good fortune, great merit. Why is this so? Their last king, named Nimi, is a righteous Dharma King who practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and for his crown princes, queens, court ladies, officials and subjects, śramaṇas and brahmins, down to the insects, he observes the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practices giving, distributing to the destitute, śramaṇas and brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who come from afar begging, providing food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, perfumed ointments, dwellings, beds, woolen carpets, cotton blankets, servants, and lamps." Great King! Do you wish to see the Thirty-Three Gods?' He answered: 'I wish to see them.' Śakra then told King Nimi: 'I shall return to heaven and command that a chariot drawn by a thousand elephants be prepared. The Great King may ride the chariot for enjoyment and pleasure and ascend to heaven.' At that time, King Nimi silently assented to Śakra, Lord of the Gods.

"Thereupon, Śakra, knowing that King Nimi had silently assented, just as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, vanished from King Nimi's palace and returned to the Thirty-Three Gods' heaven. Having arrived, Śakra told his charioteer: 'You should quickly prepare the chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and go to welcome King Nimi. When you arrive, say: "Great King! You should know that Śakra, Lord of the Gods, has sent this chariot drawn by a thousand elephants to welcome the Great King. May you ride this chariot for enjoyment and pleasure and ascend to heaven." When the king has mounted the chariot, further say to the king: "By which road does the King wish me to convey him? Shall it be the road where the wicked receive wicked retribution, or the road where the virtuous receive virtuous retribution?"'

"Thereupon, the charioteer, having received Śakra's command, promptly prepared the chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and went to King Nimi's place. Having arrived, he said: 'Great King! You should know that Śakra has sent this chariot drawn by a thousand elephants to welcome the Great King. May you ride this chariot for enjoyment and pleasure and ascend to heaven.' At that time, King Nimi mounted the chariot. The charioteer then further said to the king: 'By which road does the King wish me to convey him? Shall it be the road where the wicked receive wicked retribution, or the road where the virtuous receive virtuous retribution?' At that time, King Nimi told the charioteer: 'Convey me between the two roads, where the wicked receive wicked retribution and the virtuous receive virtuous retribution.' Thereupon, the charioteer conveyed the king between the two roads, where the wicked receive wicked retribution and the virtuous receive virtuous retribution. Thereupon, the Thirty-Three Gods saw King Nimi approaching from afar. Having seen him, they called out in praise: 'Welcome, Great King! Welcome, Great King! May you dwell with the Thirty-Three Gods and enjoy yourself together.' At that time, King Nimi spoke this verse to the Thirty-Three Gods:

"'Just as one borrows a vehicle,
Temporarily seeking a chariot for a while,
This place too is likewise;
It is considered to belong to others.
I shall return to Mithilā
And perform immeasurable good deeds.
Through this I shall be born in heaven;
Making merit is the provision for the journey.'

"Ānanda! That King Mahādeva of old, do you think he was someone else? Do not think so. Know that he was none other than myself. Ānanda! In the past, from son to son, from grandson to grandson, from clan member to clan member, from myself in succession, eighty-four thousand wheel-turning kings shaved off their beards and hair, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faith, left the household for the homeless life to practice the Way, studying as the Sage-King and cultivating the holy life, here in Mithilā, in King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove. Ānanda! At that time, I acted for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people. Out of compassion for the world, for gods and humans, I sought meaning and benefit, sought peace and happiness. At that time, the Dharma I taught did not reach the ultimate, was not ultimately pure, was not ultimately the holy life, was not the completion of the holy life. At that time, I was not free from birth, old age, illness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow, nor had I yet been able to attain liberation from all suffering.

"Ānanda! Now I have appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Guide of the Dharma Path, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Now I act for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people. Out of compassion for the world, for gods and humans, I seek meaning and benefit, seek peace and happiness. Now the Dharma I teach has reached the ultimate, is ultimately pure, is ultimately the holy life, is the completion of the holy life. Now I am free from birth, old age, illness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow. Now I have attained liberation from all suffering.

"Ānanda! I now turn over to you the law of succession, and you too should turn over the law of succession. Do not let the Buddha-seed be cut off. Ānanda! What does it mean that I now turn over to you the law of succession, and you too should turn over the law of succession, so that the Buddha-seed is not cut off? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to right samādhi, making eight. Ānanda! This is what it means that I now turn over to you the law of succession, and you too should turn over the law of succession, so that the Buddha-seed is not cut off."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of "The Sūtra of King Mahādeva's Naiṣadha Grove," Sūtra Three.

---

## (68) Sūtra Four of the Chapter on Kings: The Sūtra of King Mahāsudassana

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the city of Kuśinagara, staying in the Mallas' sāla grove at Hiraññavatī.

At that time, the World-Honored One, when he was about to enter final nirvāṇa for the last time, said: "Ānanda! Go to the space between the twin sāla trees and prepare a bed for the Tathāgata with the head facing north. In the middle of the night, the Tathāgata shall enter final nirvāṇa."

Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Tathāgata's instruction, went to the twin trees and prepared a bed for the Tathāgata between the twin trees with the head facing north. Having finished preparing the bed, he returned to where the Buddha was, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, withdrew and stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I have prepared a bed for the Tathāgata between the twin trees with the head facing north. May the World-Honored One decide when the time is right." Thereupon, the World-Honored One, accompanied by Venerable Ānanda, went to the space between the twin trees. He folded his uttarāsaṅga in four layers and spread it upon the bed, folded his saṅghāṭī to make a pillow, lay down on his right side with his feet placed one upon the other, and was about to enter final nirvāṇa for the last time.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda held a whisk and attended to the Buddha. Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! There are other great cities: the first named Campā, the second Śrāvastī, the third Vaiśālī, the fourth Rājagṛha, the fifth Vārāṇasī, and the sixth Kapilavastu. Why does the World-Honored One not enter final nirvāṇa in one of those, but instead chooses this small mud-brick town, the most insignificant among all cities?"

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! You should not say that this is a small mud-brick town, the most insignificant among all cities. Why is that? In the past, this city of Kuśinagara was named the Royal City of Kuśinagara. It was exceedingly prosperous and happy, with many people. Ānanda! The Royal City of Kuśinagara was twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide. Ānanda! Towers and watchtowers were erected, as tall as one person, or two, three, four, up to seven persons high. Ānanda! Around the outer perimeter of the Royal City of Kuśinagara there were seven layers of moats. The moats were lined with bricks of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Their bottoms were spread with sand of four kinds of treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda! Around the outer perimeter of the Royal City of Kuśinagara there were seven layers of walls. The walls were also built with bricks of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda! Around the perimeter of the Royal City of Kuśinagara there were seven rows of tāla trees of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold tāla trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits. The silver tāla trees had gold leaves, flowers, and fruits. The lapis lazuli tāla trees had crystal leaves, flowers, and fruits. The crystal tāla trees had lapis lazuli leaves, flowers, and fruits.

"Ānanda! Between the tāla trees, various flower ponds were made: blue lotus flower ponds, and ponds of red lotuses, crimson lotuses, and white lotuses. Ānanda! The banks of those flower ponds were lined with bricks of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Their bottoms were spread with sand of four kinds of treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda! In those ponds there were stairways of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold stairways had silver steps, the silver stairways had gold steps, the lapis lazuli stairways had crystal steps, and the crystal stairways had lapis lazuli steps. Ānanda! Around those ponds were balustrades of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold railings had silver hooks, the silver railings had gold hooks, the lapis lazuli railings had crystal hooks, and the crystal railings had lapis lazuli hooks. Ānanda! Those ponds were covered with nets, and bells were suspended among them. The bells were of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold bells had silver clappers, the silver bells had gold clappers, the lapis lazuli bells had crystal clappers, and the crystal bells had lapis lazuli clappers.

"Ānanda! In those ponds were planted various water flowers: blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, and white lotuses. There was always water and always flowers, and there were no attendants guarding them; they were open to all people. Ānanda! On the banks of those ponds were planted various land flowers: sumanā flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mātuluṅga flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pārijāta flowers.

"Ānanda! On the banks of those flower ponds there were many women, their bodies radiant, bright and pure, with beauty surpassing that of humans, only slightly less than that of celestial beings, with graceful and upright appearances, delighting all who saw them. They were fully adorned with various jeweled ornaments. They practiced generosity, providing whatever was needed: food and drink, clothing, vehicles, dwellings, beds, woolen carpets, servants, and lamps, giving all of these.

"Ānanda! When the wind blew through the leaves of those tāla trees, there arose supremely wonderful musical sounds, like the harmonious music produced by five kinds of skilled musicians playing together, supremely wonderful and perfectly harmonious. Ānanda! When the wind blew through the leaves of those tāla trees, it was just like this. Ānanda! In the Royal City of Kuśinagara, even the lowliest and most humble of people, if they wished to enjoy the five kinds of music, would simply go to the space among the tāla trees, where they could indulge freely and enjoy themselves to their hearts' content. Ānanda! In the Royal City of Kuśinagara there were always twelve kinds of sounds that never ceased: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of infantry, the sound of conch shells blown, the sound of drums, the sound of hand drums, the sound of musical drums, the sound of singing, the sound of dancing, the sound of eating and drinking, and the sound of giving.

"Ānanda! In the city of Kuśinagara there was a king named Mahāsudassana. He was a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, who had four kinds of armies and ruled the world under heaven, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he was endowed with the seven treasures and obtained the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans. How was he endowed with the seven treasures and the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans? As previously described for the seven treasures and the four kinds of gratifying virtues among humans. Ānanda! Thereupon, the brahmins and householders of the Royal City of Kuśinagara gathered many jewels and kambala treasures, loaded them in carts, and brought them to King Mahāsudassana, saying: 'Great King! These many jewels and kambala treasures, may the Great King, out of compassion, deign to accept them.' King Mahāsudassana told the brahmins and householders: 'What you offer, I do not need. I already have my own.'

"Ānanda! Furthermore, eighty-four thousand minor kings came to King Mahāsudassana and said: 'Great King! We wish to build a palace for the Great King.' King Mahāsudassana told the minor kings: 'You wish to build a main palace for me, but I do not need it. I already have a main palace.' The eighty-four thousand minor kings all joined their palms, and entreated a second and third time: 'Great King! We wish to build a palace for the Great King. We wish to build a palace for the Great King.' Thereupon, King Mahāsudassana, for the sake of the eighty-four thousand minor kings, silently assented. At that time, the eighty-four thousand minor kings, knowing that King Mahāsudassana had silently assented, bowed, took their leave, circumambulated three times, and departed. Each returned to his own kingdom and, loading eighty-four thousand carts with gold of their own weight, together with coins both wrought and unwrought, and one by one with pillars of precious jewels, transported them to the city of Kuśinagara. Not far from the city, they built a great main palace.

"Ānanda! That great main palace was one yojana long and one yojana wide. Ānanda! That great main palace was built with bricks of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda! That great main palace had stairways of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold stairways had silver steps, the silver stairways had gold steps, the lapis lazuli stairways had crystal steps, and the crystal stairways had lapis lazuli steps. Ānanda! In the great main palace there were eighty-four thousand pillars, made of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold pillars had silver bases and capitals, the silver pillars had gold bases and capitals, the lapis lazuli pillars had crystal bases and capitals, and the crystal pillars had lapis lazuli bases and capitals. Ānanda! Within the great main palace were erected eighty-four thousand towers, made of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold towers had silver roofs, the silver towers had gold roofs, the lapis lazuli towers had crystal roofs, and the crystal towers had lapis lazuli roofs.

"Ānanda! In the great main palace were set up eighty-four thousand royal seats, also made of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. In the gold towers were placed silver royal seats, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Likewise, in the silver towers were placed gold royal seats, in the lapis lazuli towers were placed crystal royal seats, and in the crystal towers were placed lapis lazuli royal seats, each spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Ānanda! Around the perimeter of the great main palace were balustrades of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold railings had silver hooks, the silver railings had gold hooks, the lapis lazuli railings had crystal hooks, and the crystal railings had lapis lazuli hooks. Ānanda! The great main palace was covered with nets, and bells were suspended among them. The bells were of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold bells had silver clappers, the silver bells had gold clappers, the lapis lazuli bells had crystal clappers, and the crystal bells had lapis lazuli clappers.

"Ānanda! When the great main palace was completely finished, the eighty-four thousand minor kings, not far from the palace, built a great flower pond. Ānanda! That great flower pond was one yojana long and one yojana wide. Ānanda! That great flower pond was lined with bricks of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Its bottom was spread with sand of four kinds of treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda! That great flower pond had stairways of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold stairways had silver steps, the silver stairways had gold steps, the lapis lazuli stairways had crystal steps, and the crystal stairways had lapis lazuli steps.

"Ānanda! Around the perimeter of that great flower pond were balustrades of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold railings had silver hooks, the silver railings had gold hooks, the lapis lazuli railings had crystal hooks, and the crystal railings had lapis lazuli hooks. Ānanda! That great flower pond was covered with nets, and bells were suspended among them. The bells were of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold bells had silver clappers, the silver bells had gold clappers, the lapis lazuli bells had crystal clappers, and the crystal bells had lapis lazuli clappers.

"Ānanda! In that great flower pond were planted various water flowers: blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, and white lotuses. There was always water and always flowers, but there were attendants guarding them, and they were not open to all people. Ānanda! On the banks of that great flower pond were planted various land flowers: sumanā flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mātuluṅga flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pārijāta flowers.

"Ānanda! When the great palace and the great flower pond were completely finished, the eighty-four thousand minor kings, not far from the palace, built a tāla grove. Ānanda! That tāla grove was one yojana long and one yojana wide. Ānanda! In the tāla grove were planted eighty-four thousand tāla trees, made of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold tāla trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits. The silver tāla trees had gold leaves, flowers, and fruits. The lapis lazuli tāla trees had crystal leaves, flowers, and fruits. The crystal tāla trees had lapis lazuli leaves, flowers, and fruits. Ānanda! Around the perimeter of that tāla grove were balustrades of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold railings had silver hooks, the silver railings had gold hooks, the lapis lazuli railings had crystal hooks, and the crystal railings had lapis lazuli hooks. Ānanda! That tāla grove was covered with nets, and bells were suspended among them. The bells were of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold bells had silver clappers, the silver bells had gold clappers, the lapis lazuli bells had crystal clappers, and the crystal bells had lapis lazuli clappers.

"Ānanda! When the great palace, the flower pond, and the tāla grove were all completely finished, the eighty-four thousand minor kings together went to King Mahāsudassana and said: 'Great King! You should know that the great palace, the flower pond, and the tāla grove are all completely finished. May the Great King use them as he pleases.' Ānanda! At that time, King Mahāsudassana had this thought: 'I should not be the first to ascend this great palace. If there are venerable śramaṇas and brahmins dwelling in dependence upon this Royal City of Kuśinagara, I should rather invite them all to come and gather in this great palace, and serve them the finest and most delicious foods and delicacies, abundant and plentiful, both solid and liquid, with my own hands serving them until they are fully satisfied. When the meal is finished and the vessels are collected, and water for washing has been offered, I shall send them on their way.'

"Ānanda! Having had this thought, King Mahāsudassana then invited the venerable śramaṇas and brahmins dwelling in dependence upon the Royal City of Kuśinagara. All came and gathered, ascending to the great main palace. When all had gathered and sat down, he himself offered water for washing. Then he served the finest and most delicious foods and delicacies, abundant and plentiful, both solid and liquid, with his own hands serving them until they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels were collected, and water for washing had been offered, and their benedictions received, he sent them on their way.

"Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana then had another thought: 'Now I should not indulge in sensual pleasures in the great main palace. I should rather take only one attendant and ascend to the great palace to dwell.' Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana, at a later time, took one attendant and ascended to the great main palace. He entered the gold tower and sat upon the silver royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he was secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought, with sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, and attained and dwelled in the first dhyāna. Coming out of the gold tower, he next entered the silver tower and sat upon the gold royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he was secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought, with sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, and attained and dwelled in the first dhyāna. Coming out of the silver tower, he entered the lapis lazuli tower and sat upon the crystal royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he was secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought, with sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, and attained and dwelled in the first dhyāna. Coming out of the lapis lazuli tower, he entered the crystal tower and sat upon the lapis lazuli royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he was secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought, with sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, and attained and dwelled in the first dhyāna.

"Ānanda! At that time, the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, together having not seen King Mahāsudassana for a long time, all felt longing and yearned to see him. Thereupon, the eighty-four thousand consorts together went to the woman treasure and said: 'Queen! You should know that we have not had audience with the Great King for a long time. Queen! We now wish to see the Great King together.' When the woman treasure heard this, she told the commander-of-the-army: 'You should know! We have not had audience with the Great King for a long time. We now wish to go and see him.' When the commander heard this, he escorted the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure to the great main palace. Also, eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantry, and eighty-four thousand minor kings accompanied them to the great main palace. At the time of their arrival, the sound was great and loud, the noise reverberating. King Mahāsudassana heard the great and loud sound, the noise reverberating. Having heard it, he immediately asked the attendant beside him: 'Whose sound is this, so great and loud, reverberating?' The attendant replied: 'Great King! It is the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, who have all come together to the great main palace. Also, eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantry, and eighty-four thousand minor kings have also come together to the great main palace. Therefore the sound is great and loud, reverberating.' When King Mahāsudassana heard this, he told the attendant: 'Quickly go down from the palace and in the open ground swiftly prepare a golden seat. When it is done, come and report to me.' The attendant, receiving the command, went down from the palace and in the open ground swiftly prepared a golden seat. When it was done, he returned and reported: 'I have prepared a golden seat for the Great King in the open ground. May the Great King come at his pleasure.'

"Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana, together with the attendant, came down from the palace and ascended the golden seat, sitting in full cross-legged posture. Ānanda! At that time, the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure all came forward together to King Mahāsudassana. Ānanda! When King Mahāsudassana saw from afar the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, having seen them, he immediately closed and restrained his sense faculties. Thereupon, the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, seeing the king closing and restraining his sense faculties, had this thought: 'The Great King now surely has no use for us. Why is this so? As soon as the Great King saw us, he closed and restrained his sense faculties.'

"Ānanda! Thereupon, the woman treasure went forward to King Mahāsudassana. Having arrived, she said: 'Great King! You should know that these eighty-four thousand consorts and this woman treasure all belong to the Great King. May the Great King always remember us until the end of life. The eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantry, and eighty-four thousand minor kings all belong to the Great King. May the Great King always remember us until the end of life.'

"At that time, King Mahāsudassana, having heard these words, told the woman treasure: 'Sister! You have long been urging me to do evil and not urging me to practice loving-kindness. Sister! From now on, you should urge me to practice loving-kindness and not urge me to do evil.' Ānanda! The eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure withdrew and stood to one side, shedding tears and weeping, and spoke these words: 'We are not the Great King's sisters, yet now the Great King calls us sisters.'

"Ānanda! The eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure each wiped their tears with their garments, then went forward again to King Mahāsudassana. Having arrived, they said: 'Great King! How should we urge the Great King to practice loving-kindness and not do evil?' King Mahāsudassana answered: 'Sisters! You should speak to me thus: "Does the Great King know? Human life is short and fleeting; one must face the next world. One should cultivate the holy life. What is born must surely die. Great King! You should know that death, which is certain to come, is neither lovely nor pleasing; it destroys all the world. Therefore, Great King, whatever attachment or desire the Great King has for the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, may the Great King sever and abandon all of it, and not think of it unto the end. Whatever desire or attachment the Great King has for the eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantry, and eighty-four thousand minor kings, may the Great King sever and abandon all of it, and not think of it unto the end." Sisters, if you urge me thus to practice loving-kindness, you will not be urging me to do evil.'

"Ānanda! The eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure said: 'Great King! From now on, we shall urge the Great King to practice loving-kindness and not urge him to do evil. Great King! Human life is short and fleeting; one must face the next world. Death is certain to come; it is neither lovely nor pleasing; it destroys all the world. Therefore, Great King, whatever attachment or desire the Great King has for the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, may the Great King sever and abandon all of it, and not think of it unto the end. Whatever desire or attachment the Great King has for the eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantry, and eighty-four thousand minor kings, may the Great King sever and abandon all of it, and not think of it unto the end.' Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana taught the Dharma for the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing them in joy. With immeasurable skillful means he taught the Dharma for them, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing them in joy. Having done so, he dismissed them. Ānanda! The eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure, knowing that King Mahāsudassana had dismissed them, each bowed and took their leave.

"Ānanda! Not long after the eighty-four thousand consorts and the woman treasure had departed, King Mahāsudassana, together with his attendant, ascended the great palace once more. He entered the gold tower and sat upon the silver royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he contemplated thus: 'This is my final limit. Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, quarreling, mutual hatred, flattery, deceit, fraud, and false speech, and immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas: this is their final limit.' His mind pervaded with loving-kindness, he filled one direction and dwelled in it. Thus the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwelled in it.

"Coming out of the gold tower, he next entered the silver tower and sat upon the gold royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he contemplated thus: 'This is my final limit. Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, quarreling, mutual hatred, flattery, deceit, fraud, and false speech, and immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas: this is their final limit.' His mind pervaded with compassion, he filled one direction and dwelled in it. Thus the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwelled in it.

"Coming out of the silver tower, he entered the lapis lazuli tower and sat upon the crystal royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he contemplated thus: 'This is my final limit. Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, quarreling, mutual hatred, flattery, deceit, fraud, and false speech, and immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas: this is their final limit.' His mind pervaded with sympathetic joy, he filled one direction and dwelled in it. Thus the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwelled in it.

"Coming out of the lapis lazuli tower, he entered the crystal tower and sat upon the lapis lazuli royal seat, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silk, gauze, and thin silk, with quilted body covers and pillows at both ends, of kaliṅga fabric, pavarapaccattharaṇa. Having sat, he contemplated thus: 'This is my final limit. Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, quarreling, mutual hatred, flattery, deceit, fraud, and false speech, and immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas: this is their final limit.' His mind pervaded with equanimity, he filled one direction and dwelled in it. Thus the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwelled in it.

"Ānanda! At his very last moment, King Mahāsudassana experienced only the slightest, most subtle death-pain, just as a householder or a householder's son, after eating the finest of foods, might experience a slight discomfort. Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana at his very last moment experienced only the slightest, most subtle death-pain, just like that. Ānanda! At that time, King Mahāsudassana, having cultivated the four brahma-viharas and abandoned thoughts of desire, on the basis of this, at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahmā heaven.

"Ānanda! That King Mahāsudassana of old, in a former time, do you think he was someone else? Do not think so. Know that he was none other than myself. Ānanda! At that time, I acted for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people. Out of compassion for the world, for gods and humans, I sought meaning and benefit, sought peace and happiness. At that time, the Dharma I taught did not reach the ultimate, was not ultimately pure, was not ultimately the holy life, was not the completion of the holy life. At that time, I was not free from birth, old age, illness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow, nor had I yet been able to attain liberation from all suffering.

"Ānanda! Now I have appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Guide of the Dharma Path, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Now I act for my own benefit, and also for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people. Out of compassion for the world, for gods and humans, I seek meaning and benefit, seek peace and happiness. Now the Dharma I teach has reached the ultimate, is ultimately pure, is ultimately the holy life, is the completion of the holy life. Now I am free from birth, old age, illness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow. Now I have attained liberation from all suffering.

"Ānanda! From the city of Kuśinagara, from the Mallas' sāla grove at Hiraññavatī, from the Nairañjanā River, from the Kukuṭa River, from the Makuṭabandhana shrine, from the place where a bed was prepared for me, in the area between all these, I have cast off my body seven times. Among those, six times I was a wheel-turning king, and now, the seventh time, I am the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Fully Enlightened One.

"Ānanda! I do not see anyone in the world, including among gods, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brahmins, from gods to humans, who could cause me to cast off this body again. That situation is impossible. Ānanda! This is my final birth, my final existence, my final body, my final form, the attainment of my final self. I declare this to be the end of suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Venerable

# Middle-Length Āgama, Fascicle 29

Eastern Jin, translated by the tripiṭaka master Gautama Sanghadeva

---

## (121) Sūtra on "Request" (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from quiet sitting, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I was alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation, and this thought arose in my mind: 'It is rare indeed that Venerable Ānanda has obtained great good fortune: that the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has entered final nirvāṇa, and Venerable Ānanda is still a learner with tasks yet to accomplish. But the World-Honored One has personally given me a prediction.'"

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not say such things! Do not say such things! Ānanda, if you can diligently apply yourself and in a short time abandon desire, abandon unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, you will dwell having attained the first dhyāna. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by stilling initial thought and sustained thought, with inner purity and unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, you will dwell having attained the second dhyāna. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by being free from joy, dwelling in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness through the body, as the noble ones describe: 'With equanimity and mindfulness, one dwells in happiness,' you will dwell having attained the third dhyāna. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by abandoning happiness and abandoning suffering, with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, you will dwell having attained the fourth dhyāna. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with the thought 'Space is infinite,' you will dwell having attained the base of infinite space. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, with the thought 'Consciousness is infinite,' you will dwell having attained the base of infinite consciousness. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, with the thought 'There is nothing,' you will dwell having attained the base of nothingness. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, you will dwell having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, you will dwell having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. And having seen with wisdom, the outflows will be completely ended. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's teaching, the Tathāgata's instruction.

"Thus, Ānanda, I have shown you the path of sitting meditation, I have shown you the teaching, I have shown you the instruction. What a teacher should do out of compassion for his disciples, seeking their benefit, seeking their welfare, seeking their peace and happiness, I have already done for you. Ānanda, you should go to the foot of a tree or to an empty, quiet place, and practice sitting in meditation. Do not be negligent! Apply effort! Do not later have regrets! This is my instruction to you."

The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (122) Sūtra on "Request" (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you. What is it? It is the sūtra called 'Request.'"

The bhikṣus said: "We would be glad to hear it."

The Buddha said: "If there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the complete ending of three fetters, attain stream-entry, not falling into evil destinies, surely destined for right awakening, with at most seven more births in the heavens and among humans, and after seven returns, make an end of suffering.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the complete ending of three fetters, and with the diminishing of desire, anger, and delusion, become a once-returner, returning once more to this world, and then make an end of suffering.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the complete ending of the five lower fetters, attain birth by transformation, and attain final nirvāṇa there, not returning to this world.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me attain various kinds of supernormal powers: having been one, become many; having been many, become one; appearing and disappearing; passing through walls and barriers without obstruction, as if through empty space; sinking into the earth and rising from it, as if in water; walking on water without sinking, as if on earth; sitting cross-legged, traveling through the sky like a bird in flight; with the hand touching and stroking the sun and moon, which have such great power and majesty; and with the body reaching even up to the Brahmā world.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the purified divine ear element, surpassing that of humans, hear both kinds of sounds, those of devas and those of humans, whether far or near.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with my mind, know the minds of other beings, of other persons. A mind with desire, I know as a mind with desire. A mind without desire, I know as a mind without desire. A mind with anger, I know as a mind with anger. A mind without anger, I know as a mind without anger. A mind with delusion, I know as a mind with delusion. A mind without delusion, I know as a mind without delusion. A mind that is constricted, I know as a mind that is constricted. A mind that is distracted, I know as a mind that is distracted. A great mind, I know as a great mind. A mind that is not great, I know as a mind that is not great. A superior mind, I know as a superior mind. A mind that is not superior, I know as a mind that is not superior. A concentrated mind, I know as a concentrated mind. A mind that is not concentrated, I know as a mind that is not concentrated. A liberated mind, I know as a liberated mind. A mind that is not liberated, I know as a mind that is not liberated.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me recollect my many past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five births, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; the formation of countless world-cycles, the destruction of countless world-cycles, the formation and destruction of countless world-cycles. "I was in such and such a place, with such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food and drink, experiencing such happiness and suffering, with such a lifespan. Dying from that place, I was reborn in another place. In that place, I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food and drink, experiencing such happiness and suffering, with such a lifespan. Dying from that place, I was reborn here." Thus let me recollect the specific features and circumstances of my many past lives.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, see beings dying and being reborn, of good appearance or ugly appearance, in good destinies or bad destinies, noble or lowly, and know that beings fare according to their actions. "These beings have committed bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; they have reviled noble ones, held wrong views, and undertaken actions based on wrong views. Because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and they die, they are reborn in the evil destinies, falling into hell. Those other beings have performed good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct; they have not reviled noble ones, they have held right views, and have undertaken actions based on right views. Because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and they die, they are reborn in good destinies, born among the heavens."' Let me, with the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, see beings dying and being reborn, in good or bad destinies, noble or lowly, of good or ugly appearance, and know that beings fare according to their actions. This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, if there is a bhikṣu who has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom, then he would wish: 'Let me, with the ending of the outflows, in this very life, by my own direct knowledge, realize and dwell in the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.' This will certainly be so. Why? Because he has accomplished moral conduct, accomplished concentration, and accomplished wisdom."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (123) Sūtra on Śāriputra's "Request" (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Friends, I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus accepted the teaching and listened.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the complete ending of three fetters, attain stream-entry,' this is impossible. Why? Because he is not accomplished in moral conduct, and so it is impossible for him to attain stream-entry with the complete ending of three fetters.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the complete ending of three fetters, attain stream-entry, not falling into evil destinies, surely destined for right awakening, with at most seven more births, and after seven returns, make an end of suffering,' this will certainly be so. Why? Because he is accomplished in moral conduct.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the complete ending of three fetters, and with the diminishing of desire, anger, and delusion, become a once-returner,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to become a once-returner, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the complete ending of the five lower fetters, attain birth by transformation, and attain final nirvāṇa there, not returning to this world,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to become a non-returner, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me attain various kinds of supernormal powers: having been one, become many; having been many, become one; appearing and disappearing; passing through walls and barriers without obstruction, as if through empty space; sinking into the earth and rising from it, as if in water; walking on water without sinking, as if on earth; sitting cross-legged, traveling through the sky like a bird in flight; with the hand touching and stroking the sun and moon, which have such great power and majesty; and with the body reaching up to the Brahmā world,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to attain supernormal powers, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the purified divine ear element, surpassing that of humans, hear both kinds of sounds, those of devas and those of humans, whether far or near,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to attain the divine ear, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with my mind, know the minds of other beings, of other persons. A mind with desire, I know as a mind with desire. A mind without desire, I know as a mind without desire. A mind with anger, I know as a mind with anger. A mind without anger, I know as a mind without anger. A mind with delusion, I know as a mind with delusion. A mind without delusion, I know as a mind without delusion. A mind that is constricted, I know as a mind that is constricted. A mind that is distracted, I know as a mind that is distracted. A great mind, I know as a great mind. A mind that is not great, I know as a mind that is not great. A superior mind, I know as a superior mind. A mind that is not superior, I know as a mind that is not superior. A concentrated mind, I know as a concentrated mind. A mind that is not concentrated, I know as a mind that is not concentrated. A liberated mind, I know as a liberated mind. A mind that is not liberated, I know as a mind that is not liberated,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to attain knowledge of others' minds, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me recollect my many past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five births, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; the formation of countless world-cycles, the destruction of countless world-cycles, the formation and destruction of countless world-cycles. "I was in such and such a place, with such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food and drink, experiencing such happiness and suffering, with such a lifespan. Dying from that place, I was reborn in another place. In that place, I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food and drink, experiencing such happiness and suffering, with such a lifespan. Dying from that place, I was reborn here." Thus let me recollect the specific features and circumstances of my many past lives,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to recollect past lives, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, see beings dying and being reborn, of good appearance or ugly appearance, in good destinies or bad destinies, noble or lowly, and know that beings fare according to their actions. "These beings have committed bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; they have reviled noble ones, held wrong views, and undertaken actions based on wrong views. Because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and they die, they are reborn in the evil destinies, falling into hell. Those other beings have performed good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct; they have not reviled noble ones, have held right views, and have undertaken actions based on right views. Because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and they die, they are reborn in good destinies, born among the heavens." Let me, with the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, see beings dying and being reborn, in good or bad destinies, noble or lowly, of good or ugly appearance, and know that beings fare according to their actions,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes to attain the divine eye, this will certainly be so.

"If there is a bhikṣu who is not accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes: 'Let me, with the ending of the outflows, in this very life, by my own direct knowledge, realize and dwell in the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom,' this is impossible. If there is a bhikṣu who is accomplished in moral conduct, and he wishes for the ending of the outflows, this will certainly be so. Why? Because he is accomplished in moral conduct."

The Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (124) Sūtra on Śāriputra's "Request" (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Friends, I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus accepted the teaching and listened.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "If there is a bhikṣu who does not keep the precepts and is not accomplished in moral conduct, then for him to have concentration accomplished based on moral conduct, this is impossible.

"If there is no concentration, then for him to have seeing and knowing according to reality accomplished based on concentration, this is impossible.

"If there is no seeing and knowing according to reality, then for him to have revulsion and dispassion accomplished based on seeing and knowing according to reality, this is impossible.

"If there is no revulsion and dispassion, then for him to have liberation accomplished based on revulsion and dispassion, this is impossible.

"If there is no liberation, then for him to have the knowledge and vision of liberation accomplished based on liberation, this is impossible.

"Friends, it is just as when a tree does not have bark, then it cannot have sapwood; without sapwood, it cannot have heartwood. In the same way, if there is a bhikṣu who does not keep the precepts and is not accomplished in moral conduct, then for him to have concentration accomplished based on moral conduct, this is impossible. Without concentration, to have seeing and knowing according to reality, this is impossible. Without seeing and knowing according to reality, to have revulsion and dispassion, this is impossible. Without revulsion and dispassion, to have liberation, this is impossible. Without liberation, to have the knowledge and vision of liberation, this is impossible.

"If there is a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct, then for him to have concentration accomplished based on moral conduct, this is certainly possible.

"If there is concentration, then for him to have seeing and knowing according to reality accomplished based on concentration, this is certainly possible.

"If there is seeing and knowing according to reality, then for him to have revulsion and dispassion accomplished based on seeing and knowing according to reality, this is certainly possible.

"If there is revulsion and dispassion, then for him to have liberation accomplished based on revulsion and dispassion, this is certainly possible.

"If there is liberation, then for him to have the knowledge and vision of liberation accomplished based on liberation, this is certainly possible.

"Friends, it is just as when a tree has bark, then it can have sapwood; with sapwood, it can have heartwood. In the same way, if there is a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct, then for him to have concentration accomplished based on moral conduct, this is certainly possible. With concentration, to have seeing and knowing according to reality, this is certainly possible. With seeing and knowing according to reality, to have revulsion and dispassion, this is certainly possible. With revulsion and dispassion, to have liberation, this is certainly possible. With liberation, to have the knowledge and vision of liberation, this is certainly possible."

The Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (125) Sūtra on Śāriputra's "Request" (Third)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Friends, I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus accepted the teaching and listened.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "If an immoral bhikṣu, one not accomplished in moral conduct, wishes: 'Let me abandon desire, abandon unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, and dwell having attained the first dhyāna,' this is impossible. Why? Because this person does not keep the precepts and is not accomplished in moral conduct, and therefore it is impossible for him to attain the first dhyāna.

"If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes: 'Let me abandon desire, abandon unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, and dwell having attained the first dhyāna,' this will certainly be so. Why? Because this person keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct, and therefore it is possible for him to attain the first dhyāna.

"If an immoral bhikṣu, one not accomplished in moral conduct, wishes: 'Let me, by stilling initial thought and sustained thought, with inner purity and unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, dwell having attained the second dhyāna,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the second dhyāna, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, free from joy, dwelling in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness through the body, as the noble ones describe: "With equanimity and mindfulness, one dwells in happiness," dwell having attained the third dhyāna,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the third dhyāna, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by abandoning happiness and abandoning suffering, with the previous disappearance of joy and sorrow, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, dwell having attained the fourth dhyāna,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the fourth dhyāna, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with the thought "Space is infinite," dwell having attained the base of infinite space,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the base of infinite space, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, with the thought "Consciousness is infinite," dwell having attained the base of infinite consciousness,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the base of infinite consciousness, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, with the thought "There is nothing," dwell having attained the base of nothingness,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the base of nothingness, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, dwell having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this will certainly be so.

"If an immoral bhikṣu wishes: 'Let me, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwell having attained the cessation of perception and feeling, and having seen with wisdom, completely end the outflows,' this is impossible. If a bhikṣu who keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct wishes to attain the cessation of perception and feeling and the complete ending of outflows, this will certainly be so. Why? Because he keeps the precepts and is accomplished in moral conduct."

The Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (126) Sūtra on "Action" (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three kinds of unwholesome roots of action and three kinds of wholesome roots of action. What are the three kinds of unwholesome roots of action? They are desire, anger, and delusion. These are the three kinds of unwholesome roots of action.

"When one produces desire, what deeds does one commit? One commits deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk. These are the deeds committed through desire.

"When one produces anger, what deeds does one commit? One commits deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk. These are the deeds committed through anger.

"When one produces delusion, what deeds does one commit? One commits deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk. These are the deeds committed through delusion.

"Thus, bhikṣus, because of desire, arising from desire, born from desire, with desire as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Because of anger, arising from anger, born from anger, with anger as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Because of delusion, arising from delusion, born from delusion, with delusion as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

"It is just as a seed that is uninjured, not decomposed, not damaged by wind or heat, is fresh and well kept, and is planted in good soil with sufficient water. Will that seed grow and increase?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, because of desire, arising from desire, born from desire, with desire as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. This person, because of these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up and dies, is reborn in hell. Because of anger, arising from anger, born from anger, with anger as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. This person, because of these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up and dies, is reborn in hell. Because of delusion, arising from delusion, born from delusion, with delusion as the cause, one commits bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. This person, because of these causes and conditions, when the body breaks up and dies, is reborn in hell.

"What are the three kinds of wholesome roots of action? They are non-desire, non-anger, and non-delusion. These are the three kinds of wholesome roots of action.

"When one produces non-desire, what deeds does one commit? One abstains from killing, abstains from stealing, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from lying, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from frivolous talk.

"When one produces non-anger, what deeds does one commit? One abstains from killing, abstains from stealing, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from lying, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from frivolous talk.

"When one produces non-delusion, what deeds does one commit? One abstains from killing, abstains from stealing, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from lying, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from frivolous talk.

"Thus, bhikṣus, because of non-desire, arising from non-desire, born from non-desire, with non-desire as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Because of non-anger, arising from non-anger, born from non-anger, with non-anger as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Because of non-delusion, arising from non-delusion, born from non-delusion, with non-delusion as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct.

"It is just as a seed that is broken, decomposed, damaged by wind and heat, is not fresh, and is not well kept, and is cast onto open ground with insufficient water. Even if it rains, will that seed grow and increase?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, because of non-desire, arising from non-desire, born from non-desire, with non-desire as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Because of non-desire, the action is extinguished and does not grow. Because of non-anger, arising from non-anger, born from non-anger, with non-anger as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Because of non-anger, the action is extinguished and does not grow. Because of non-delusion, arising from non-delusion, born from non-delusion, with non-delusion as the cause, one practices good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Because of non-delusion, the action is extinguished and does not grow."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (127) Sūtra on "Action" (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three causes and conditions for the arising of actions. What are the three? They are desire, anger, and delusion.

"If an action is done through desire, arising from desire, born from desire, with desire as the cause, then that action is unwholesome, that action is blameworthy, the result of that action is suffering, that action leads to the further creation of action, and that action does not lead to the cessation of action.

"If an action is done through anger, arising from anger, born from anger, with anger as the cause, then that action is unwholesome, that action is blameworthy, the result of that action is suffering, that action leads to the further creation of action, and that action does not lead to the cessation of action.

"If an action is done through delusion, arising from delusion, born from delusion, with delusion as the cause, then that action is unwholesome, that action is blameworthy, the result of that action is suffering, that action leads to the further creation of action, and that action does not lead to the cessation of action.

"Furthermore, there are three causes and conditions for the arising of actions. What are the three? They are non-desire, non-anger, and non-delusion.

"If an action is done through non-desire, arising from non-desire, born from non-desire, with non-desire as the cause, then because desire is already gone, that action is abandoned, its root is cut off, like a tāla tree stump that cannot grow again and in the future will not arise.

"If an action is done through non-anger, arising from non-anger, born from non-anger, with non-anger as the cause, then because anger is already gone, that action is abandoned, its root is cut off, like a tāla tree stump that cannot grow again and in the future will not arise.

"If an action is done through non-delusion, arising from non-delusion, born from non-delusion, with non-delusion as the cause, then because delusion is already gone, that action is abandoned, its root is cut off, like a tāla tree stump that cannot grow again and in the future will not arise."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (128) Sūtra on the Qualities (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu achieves ten dharmas, he is called an 'accomplished one,' one who has attained the ultimate among men, an unshakeable śramaṇa. What are the ten? A bhikṣu accomplishes the right view of one beyond training, the right thought of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training, the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, the right concentration of one beyond training, the right knowledge of one beyond training, and the right liberation of one beyond training. If a bhikṣu achieves these ten dharmas, he is called an 'accomplished one,' one who has attained the ultimate among men, an unshakeable śramaṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (129) Sūtra on the Qualities (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu achieves ten dharmas, he is called an 'accomplished one,' one who has attained the ultimate among men, an unshakeable śramaṇa. What are the ten? A bhikṣu completely ends the five lower fetters and completely ends the five upper fetters. What are the five lower fetters? They are the view of a self in the body, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, desire, and ill will. These are the five lower fetters. What are the five upper fetters? They are desire for form, desire for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These are the five upper fetters.
