If a bhikṣu completely ends the five lower fetters and completely ends the five upper fetters, he is called an 'accomplished one,' one who has attained the ultimate among men, an unshakeable śramaṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (130) Sūtra on the Qualities (Third)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu who is a learner wants to proceed to the unsurpassed peace from bondage, then the internal conditions are as follows: There is nothing more important than right attention. If a bhikṣu who is a learner attends rightly, he can abandon unwholesomeness and cultivate wholesomeness.

"If a bhikṣu who is a learner possesses right attention, then he will accomplish right view. Having accomplished right view, he will accomplish right thought. Having accomplished right thought, he will accomplish right speech. Having accomplished right speech, he will accomplish right action. Having accomplished right action, he will accomplish right livelihood. Having accomplished right livelihood, he will accomplish right effort. Having accomplished right effort, he will accomplish right mindfulness. Having accomplished right mindfulness, he will accomplish right concentration. Having accomplished right concentration, he will accomplish right knowledge. Having accomplished right knowledge, he will accomplish right liberation.

"Thus, the bhikṣu who is a learner possesses eight branches, and the arahant possesses ten branches."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (131) Sūtra on the Qualities (Fourth)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu who is a learner wants to proceed to the unsurpassed peace from bondage, then the external conditions are as follows: There is nothing more important than associating with good friends. If a bhikṣu who is a learner associates with good friends, he can abandon unwholesomeness and cultivate wholesomeness.

"If a bhikṣu who is a learner associates with good friends, then he will accomplish right view. Having accomplished right view, he will accomplish right thought. Having accomplished right thought, he will accomplish right speech. Having accomplished right speech, he will accomplish right action. Having accomplished right action, he will accomplish right livelihood. Having accomplished right livelihood, he will accomplish right effort. Having accomplished right effort, he will accomplish right mindfulness. Having accomplished right mindfulness, he will accomplish right concentration. Having accomplished right concentration, he will accomplish right knowledge. Having accomplished right knowledge, he will accomplish right liberation.

"Thus, the bhikṣu who is a learner possesses eight branches, and the arahant possesses ten branches."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (132) Sūtra on the Qualities (Fifth)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Of all practices of unwholesomeness, wrong view is foremost. Of all practices of wholesomeness, right view is foremost.

"What is wrong view? It is to say: 'There is no giving, no ritual, no offering, no fruit or result of good and bad actions, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no beings who are spontaneously reborn, and in the world there are no śramaṇas or brahmins who are rightly practicing and rightly proceeding, who in this very life, by their own direct knowledge, realize and declare: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being."' This is called wrong view.

"What is right view? Right view is of two kinds. There is right view that has outflows, that has acquisitions, that ripens on the side of merit. There is right view that is noble, without outflows, transcendent, a factor of the path.

"What is right view that has outflows, that has acquisitions, that ripens on the side of merit? It is to say: 'There is giving, there is ritual, there is offering, there are fruits and results of good and bad actions, there is this world, there is the other world, there is mother, there is father, there are beings who are spontaneously reborn, and in the world there are śramaṇas and brahmins who are rightly practicing and rightly proceeding, who in this very life, by their own direct knowledge, realize and declare: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being."' This is called right view that has outflows, that has acquisitions, that ripens on the side of merit.

"What is right view that is noble, without outflows, transcendent, a factor of the path? It is the wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation of dharmas, the enlightenment factor of investigation of dharmas, the right view that is a factor of the path in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is without outflows, who possesses the noble path and is cultivating the noble path. This is called right view that is noble, without outflows, transcendent, a factor of the path.

"A person of wrong view, whatever bodily action, verbal action, or mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, and whatever intention, aspiration, vow, and conditioning: all these dharmas lead to what is undesirable, unwanted, disagreeable, to what is without benefit, and to suffering. Why is this? Because the view is bad. It is like a bitter gourd seed or a bitter oleander seed that is planted in moist soil. Whatever earth element and water element it draws upon, all of it leads to bitterness, pungency, and disagreeableness. Why is this? Because the seed is bad.

"A person of right view, whatever bodily action, verbal action, or mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, and whatever intention, aspiration, vow, and conditioning: all these dharmas lead to what is desirable, wanted, agreeable, to what is beneficial, and to happiness. Why is this? Because the view is good. It is like a sugarcane seed, a grape seed, or a seed of any sweet fruit that is planted in moist soil. Whatever earth element and water element it draws upon, all of it leads to sweetness and agreeableness. Why is this? Because the seed is good.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (133) Sūtra on the Qualities (Sixth)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom. What are the five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These are the five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom.

"If a bhikṣu does not abandon these five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom, then for him, with his weak and powerless mind, to know what is beneficial to himself, to know what is beneficial to others, to know what is beneficial to both, and to realize a superhuman dharma, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones: this is impossible.

"It is like a river flowing from a mountain, going far, with a swift current and carrying away everything. If a person then opens channels on both sides, when those channels on both sides are opened, then the current in the middle of the river will be disrupted, disturbed, and scattered, and it will not flow far, its current will not be swift, and it will not carry everything away. In the same way, if a bhikṣu does not abandon these five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom, then for him, with his weak and powerless mind, to know what is beneficial to himself, to know what is beneficial to others, to know what is beneficial to both, and to realize a superhuman dharma, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones: this is impossible.

"If a bhikṣu abandons these five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom, then for him, with his strong and powerful mind, to know what is beneficial to himself, to know what is beneficial to others, to know what is beneficial to both, and to realize a superhuman dharma, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones: this is certainly possible.

"It is like a river flowing from a mountain, going far, with a swift current and carrying away everything. If a person then closes up the channels on both sides, when those channels on both sides are closed, then the current in the middle of the river will not be disrupted, disturbed, or scattered, and it will flow far, its current will be swift, and it will carry everything away. In the same way, if a bhikṣu abandons these five hindrances and five covers that blind the mind and weaken wisdom, then for him, with his strong and powerful mind, to know what is beneficial to himself, to know what is beneficial to others, to know what is beneficial to both, and to realize a superhuman dharma, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones: this is certainly possible."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (134) Sūtra on the Qualities (Seventh)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about a person who resembles a wound, a person who resembles lightning, a person whose wisdom is like a diamond, a person who is darkened in wisdom, and a person who is broad in wisdom. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "We would be glad to hear it."

The Buddha said: "What is a person who resembles a wound? There is a person here who is often angry. When even slightly criticized, he becomes agitated and resentful, contentious and disputatious, producing anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction. Just as a rotten wound, when struck by a stick or a potsherd, will ooze out even more, in the same way there is a person who is often angry. When even slightly criticized, he becomes agitated and resentful, contentious and disputatious, producing anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction. This person is called one who resembles a wound.

"What is a person who resembles lightning? There is a person here who, as they really are, knows suffering, as it really is knows the arising of suffering, as it really is knows the cessation of suffering, and as it really is knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Just as a person with eyes, in the darkness of night when lightning flashes, can see forms by the lightning, in the same way there is a person who, as it really is, knows suffering, as it really is knows the arising of suffering, as it really is knows the cessation of suffering, and as it really is knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This person is called one who resembles lightning.

"What is a person whose wisdom is like a diamond? There is a person here who, with the ending of the outflows, in this very life, by their own direct knowledge, realizes and dwells in the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Just as there is nothing that a diamond cannot cut through, in the same way there is a person who, with the ending of the outflows, in this very life, by their own direct knowledge, realizes and dwells in the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. This person is called one whose wisdom is like a diamond.

"What is a person who is darkened in wisdom? There is a person here who, even when asked by another about certain things, cannot answer, much less without being asked. This person is called one who is darkened in wisdom.

"What is a person who is broad in wisdom? There is a person here who, when asked by another about certain things, can answer completely, and can explain their meaning in detail, much more so without being asked. This person is called one who is broad in wisdom."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (135) Sūtra on Good People and Bad People

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove, near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the qualities of a bad person and the qualities of a good person. Listen carefully and pay close attention. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus said: "We would be glad to hear it."

The Buddha said: "What are the qualities of a bad person? A bad person here is ungrateful and does not repay kindness. Being ungrateful and not repaying kindness is the quality of a bad person. What are the qualities of a good person? A good person here is grateful and repays kindness. Being grateful and repaying kindness is the quality of a good person.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

*End of Fascicle 29 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Fascicle Fifteen of the Madhyamāgama

---

## (69) Sūtra of the Thirty Similes, Fifth of the Chapter on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, collectively undertaking the summer retreat.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, during the recitation of the prātimokṣa, the World-Honored One spread a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. After the World-Honored One had seated himself, he entered concentrated meditation and observed the minds of the bhikṣus. Thereupon the World-Honored One saw that the assembly of bhikṣus sat in silence, in utmost silence, without any drowsiness, having removed the hindrances. The assembly of bhikṣus sat in a state that was profound, extremely profound; tranquil, extremely tranquil; subtle, extremely subtle.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also in the assembly. Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra! The assembly of bhikṣus sits in silence, in utmost silence, without any drowsiness, having removed the hindrances. The assembly of bhikṣus sits in a state that is profound, extremely profound; tranquil, extremely tranquil; subtle, extremely subtle. Śāriputra, who is able to revere and serve this assembly of bhikṣus?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! It is so. The assembly of bhikṣus sits in silence, in utmost silence, without any drowsiness, having removed the hindrances. The assembly of bhikṣus sits in a state that is profound, extremely profound; tranquil, extremely tranquil; subtle, extremely subtle. World-Honored One, no one is able to revere and serve this assembly of bhikṣus. Only the World-Honored One is able to revere and serve the Dharma and the Sangha, morality, diligence, generosity, and concentration. Only the World-Honored One is able to revere and serve them."

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra! It is so, it is so. No one is able to revere and serve this assembly of bhikṣus. Only the World-Honored One is able to revere and serve the Dharma and the Sangha, morality, diligence, generosity, and concentration. Only the World-Honored One is able to revere and serve them. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have various ornamental accessories: silks, brocades, and fine woolens; finger rings, arm bracelets, elbow ornaments, neck chains, and garlands of refined gold and jewels; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have moral virtue as their ornamental accessories. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish moral virtue as their ornamental accessories, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have five ceremonial items: a sword, a parasol, a heavenly crown, a jewel-handled whisk, and ornamental shoes, guarding their persons and keeping them safe and secure; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the observance of the precepts as protection of the holy life. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the observance of precepts as protection of the holy life, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have inner-chamber attendants; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the guarding of the six sense faculties as their inner-chamber attendants. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the guarding of the six sense faculties as their inner-chamber attendants, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a gate commander who is wise, intelligent, and discerning; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have right mindfulness as their gate commander. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish right mindfulness as their gate commander, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a fine bathing pool with clear springs, level and full; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have their own mind as their bathing pool and spring. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish their own mind as their bathing pool and spring, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have bathing attendants who regularly wash and bathe them; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have good spiritual friends as their bathing attendants. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish good spiritual friends as their bathing attendants, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have body-anointing fragrances: wood honey, aloeswood, sandalwood, storax, clove, and duliang; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have moral virtue as their anointing fragrance. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish moral virtue as their anointing fragrance, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have fine garments: fine cotton cloth, brocade and silk garments, white cotton garments, and Kaliṅga-pāvāra garments; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have a sense of shame and conscience as their garments. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish a sense of shame and conscience as their garments, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have fine beds and seats, extremely broad, high, and grand; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the four dhyānas as their beds and seats. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the four dhyānas as their beds and seats, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have skilled barbers who regularly wash and bathe them; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have right mindfulness as their barber. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish right mindfulness as their barber, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have delicacies and fine foods of various different flavors; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have joy as their food. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish joy as their food, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have various drinks: mango drink, campaka drink, sugarcane drink, grape drink, and mātsyandikā drink; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the taste of the Dharma as their drink. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the taste of the Dharma as their drink, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have beautiful flower garlands: blue lotus garlands, campaka flower garlands, sumanā flower garlands, vārṣika flower garlands, and atimuktaka flower garlands; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the three concentrations as their garlands: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the three concentrations as their garlands, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have various buildings, halls, pavilions, and towers; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the three chambers as their buildings: the heavenly chamber, the Brahma chamber, and the noble chamber. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the three chambers as their buildings, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have stewards, namely those who guard the chambers; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have wisdom as their chamber guardian. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish wisdom as their chamber guardian, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have four kinds of tax revenue from their various territories: the first portion provides for the king and supplies the queen and the women of the inner palace; the second portion supplies the crown prince and the ministers; the third portion supplies all the people of the nation; the fourth portion supplies śramaṇas and brahmins; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the four foundations of mindfulness as their tax revenue. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the four foundations of mindfulness as their tax revenue, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have four kinds of armies: elephant troops, cavalry troops, chariot troops, and infantry; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the four right efforts as their four kinds of armies. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the four right efforts as their four kinds of armies, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have various conveyances: elephant conveyances, horse conveyances, chariot conveyances, and palanquins; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the four bases of supernormal power as their conveyances. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the four bases of supernormal power as their conveyances, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have various chariot adornments, decorated with various fine skins of lions, tigers, and leopards with their spotted patterns, woven into multi-colored various ornaments; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have calm and insight as their chariot. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish calm and insight as their chariot, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a chariot driver, namely one who steers the chariot; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have right mindfulness as their chariot driver. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish right mindfulness as their chariot driver, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have an extremely tall banner; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have their own mind as their tall banner. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish their own mind as their tall banner, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a fine road, level, smooth, and even, leading only to gardens and pleasure parks; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the Noble Eightfold Path as their road, level, smooth, and even, leading only to nirvāṇa. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path as their road, level, smooth, and even, leading only to nirvāṇa, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a chief military minister who is wise, intelligent, and discerning; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have wisdom as their chief military minister. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish wisdom as their chief military minister, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a great main hall, extremely broad, high, and spacious; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have wisdom as their great main hall. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish wisdom as their great main hall, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers ascend to a high hall and from above observe people below going about, walking, running, jumping, standing, sitting, and lying down; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs ascend the high hall of unsurpassed wisdom to observe their own minds: upright, well-composed, gentle, joyful, and secluded. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the high hall of unsurpassed wisdom to observe their own minds as upright, well-composed, gentle, joyful, and secluded, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a minister of clan affairs who is well-versed in the genealogies of the clans; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the four noble lineages as their minister of clan affairs. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the four noble lineages as their minister of clan affairs, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a renowned good physician who can cure all diseases; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have right mindfulness as their good physician. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish right mindfulness as their good physician, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

"Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a proper royal couch, spread with rugs and carpets, covered with brocade, fine silk gauze, and thin silk, with soft body-cushions, pillows placed at both ends, and Kaliṅga-pāvāra and pracchastarāṇa coverings; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the unobstructed concentration as their proper royal couch. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the unobstructed concentration as their proper royal couch, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers have a renowned precious jewel; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the immovable liberation of mind as their renowned precious jewel. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the immovable liberation of mind as their renowned precious jewel, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra, just as a king and his great ministers, having bathed most thoroughly, anoint their bodies with fine fragrances, so that their bodies are utterly clean and pure; Śāriputra, in the same way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have the contemplation of their own minds as their utter bodily purity. Śāriputra, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs accomplish the contemplation of their own minds as their bodily purity, they are able to revere and serve the World-Honored One, the Dharma and the Sangha, morality, diligence, generosity, and concentration."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra of the Thirty Similes, the Fifth.

---

## (70) Sūtra of the Wheel-Turning King, Sixth of the Chapter on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Māthuran Kṣatriyas, on the bank of the swift river in the mango grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus! You should light the lamp of the Dharma for yourselves, take refuge in your own Dharma. Do not light another's lamp; do not take refuge in another's Dharma. Bhikṣus, if you light the lamp of the Dharma for yourselves and take refuge in your own Dharma, not lighting another's lamp, not taking refuge in another's Dharma, then you will be able to seek learning, gain benefit, and obtain immeasurable merit. Why is this? Bhikṣus, in the past there was a king named Daḷhanemi, a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, who had four kinds of armies and ruled the world, sovereign by his own authority. He was a righteous Dharma king, accomplished in the seven treasures, and possessed of four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues. How was he accomplished in the seven treasures and possessed of four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues? As previously described, he was accomplished in the seven treasures and possessed of four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues.

"Then, after some time, King Daḷhanemi's divine wheel-treasure moved and suddenly left its original place. Someone saw this and went to King Daḷhanemi and said: 'Your Majesty! You should know that the divine wheel-treasure has moved and left its original place.' When King Daḷhanemi heard this, he said: 'Crown Prince! My divine wheel-treasure has moved and left its original place. Crown Prince, I myself once heard from the elders of old: when a wheel-turning king's divine wheel-treasure moves and leaves its original place, that king will surely not remain long; his life will not last long. Crown Prince, I have already obtained human pleasures. Now I should seek heavenly pleasures. Crown Prince, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, leave the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path. Crown Prince, I now entrust to you these four continents. You should govern them according to the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma, and you must not allow evil deeds or those who act contrary to the holy life to exist in the kingdom. Crown Prince, if later you see the divine wheel-treasure move and leave its original place, you too should entrust the government to your own crown prince, instructing him well. After entrusting the kingdom to your crown prince, you too should shave off your hair and beard, don kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, leave the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path.' Thereupon King Daḷhanemi entrusted the kingdom to his crown prince, instructing him well, then shaved off his hair and beard, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, left the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path.

"Seven days after King Daḷhanemi had left the household life to train in the path, the divine wheel-treasure disappeared and was no longer visible. Having lost the divine wheel, the Kṣatriya crown prince became greatly worried, grieved, and unhappy. The Kṣatriya crown prince then went to where his father, the sage-recluse King Daḷhanemi, was staying. Having arrived, he said: 'Your Majesty! You should know that seven days after Your Majesty left the household to train in the path, the divine wheel-treasure disappeared and is no longer visible.' The sage-recluse father, King Daḷhanemi, said to his son, the Kṣatriya crown prince: 'Do not grieve over the loss of the divine wheel-treasure. Why is this? You did not inherit this divine wheel from your father.' The Kṣatriya crown prince then said to his father: 'Your Majesty, what should I do now?'

"The sage-recluse father, King Daḷhanemi, said to his son: 'You should learn the law of succession. If you learn the law of succession, then on the fifteenth day, at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant.' The Kṣatriya crown prince then said to his father: 'Your Majesty, what is this law of succession that you wish me to learn? Having learned it, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant?'

"The sage-recluse father, King Daḷhanemi, then said to his son: 'You should observe the Dharma according to the Dharma, practice the Dharma according to the Dharma, and for the sake of the crown prince, queens, palace women, ministers, people, śramaṇas, brahmins, and even down to insects, you should observe the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, and practice generosity. Give to the destitute, to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who come from afar to beg, providing them with food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, incense for anointing, shelter, bedding, rugs, woolen blankets, attendants, and lamps. If in your kingdom there are venerable and renowned śramaṇas and brahmins, you should go to visit them at the appropriate times, inquire about the Dharma, and receive the Dharma: "Venerable ones, what are wholesome dharmas? What are unwholesome dharmas? What constitutes sin? What constitutes merit? What is excellent? What is not excellent? What is dark? What is bright? From what do dark and bright dharmas arise? What benefits this present life? What benefits the next life? How should one act so as to receive what is wholesome and not receive what is evil?" Having heard from them, practice as they have taught. If in your kingdom there are those who are impoverished, you should provide wealth and goods to help and support them. Son, this is called the law of succession. You should learn it well. Having learned it well, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant.'

"The Kṣatriya crown prince then, in the time that followed, observed the Dharma according to the Dharma, practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma, and for the sake of the crown prince, queens, palace women, ministers, people, śramaṇas, brahmins, and even down to insects, observed the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, and practiced generosity. He gave to the destitute, to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who came from afar to beg, providing them with food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, incense for anointing, shelter, bedding, rugs, woolen blankets, attendants, and lamps. If in his kingdom there were venerable and renowned śramaṇas and brahmins, he would go to visit them at the appropriate times, inquire about the Dharma, and receive the Dharma: 'Venerable ones, what are wholesome dharmas? What are unwholesome dharmas? What constitutes sin? What constitutes merit? What is excellent? What is not excellent? What is dark? What is bright? From what do dark and bright dharmas arise? What benefits this present life? What benefits the next life? How should one act so as to receive what is wholesome and not receive what is evil?' Having heard from them, he practiced as they taught. If in his kingdom there were those who were impoverished, he provided wealth and goods, giving aid in due time. After some time, the Kṣatriya crown prince, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure came from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant. He too became a wheel-turning king, accomplished in the seven treasures, and possessed of four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues. How was he accomplished in the seven treasures and possessed of four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues? As previously described.

"After some time, that wheel-turning king's divine wheel-treasure moved and suddenly left its original place. Someone saw this and went to the wheel-turning king and said: 'Your Majesty! You should know that the divine wheel-treasure has moved and left its original place.' When the wheel-turning king heard this, he said: 'Crown Prince! My divine wheel-treasure has moved and left its original place. Crown Prince, I once heard from my father, the sage-recluse King Daḷhanemi: when a wheel-turning king's divine wheel-treasure moves and leaves its original place, that king will surely not remain long; his life will not last long. Crown Prince, I have already obtained human pleasures. Now I should seek heavenly pleasures. Crown Prince, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, leave the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path. Crown Prince, I now entrust to you these four continents. You should govern them according to the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma, and you must not allow evil deeds or those who act contrary to the holy life to exist in the kingdom. Crown Prince, if later you see the divine wheel-treasure move and leave its original place, you too should entrust the government to your own crown prince, instructing him well. After entrusting the kingdom to your crown prince, you too should shave off your hair and beard, don kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, leave the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path.' The wheel-turning king entrusted the kingdom to his crown prince, instructing him well, then shaved off his hair and beard, donned kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, left the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path.

"Seven days after that wheel-turning king had left the household life to train in the path, the divine wheel-treasure disappeared and was no longer visible. Having lost the divine wheel, the Kṣatriya crown prince did not grieve; instead, he was stained by desire, attached to desire, greedy for desire without satiation, bound by desire, afflicted by desire, driven by desire. He did not see the danger, and he did not know the way out. He then governed the kingdom according to his own ideas. Because he governed the kingdom according to his own ideas, the kingdom gradually declined and no longer increased, unlike in the past when the wheel-turning kings had learned the law of succession and the kingdom and its people continually increased and prospered without any decline. This Kṣatriya crown prince was also like this: he governed the kingdom according to his own ideas, and because he governed according to his own ideas, the kingdom gradually declined and no longer increased.

"Thereupon, the royal chaplain, a brahmin, touring the borders of the kingdom, saw that the people of the kingdom were gradually declining and no longer increasing. He then had this thought: 'The Kṣatriya crown prince governs the kingdom according to his own ideas. Because he governs according to his own ideas, the kingdom and its people are gradually declining and no longer increasing. In the past, the wheel-turning kings learned the law of succession, and the kingdom and its people continually increased and prospered without any decline. This Kṣatriya crown prince also governs the kingdom according to his own ideas, and because he governs according to his own ideas, the kingdom and its people are gradually declining and no longer increasing.'

"The royal chaplain, the brahmin, then went together to the Kṣatriya crown prince and said: 'Your Majesty! You should know that Your Majesty governs the kingdom according to your own ideas. Because you govern according to your own ideas, the kingdom and its people are gradually declining and no longer increasing. In the past, the wheel-turning kings learned the law of succession, and the kingdom and its people continually increased and prospered without any decline. Now Your Majesty also governs the kingdom according to your own ideas, and because you govern according to your own ideas, the kingdom and its people are gradually declining and no longer increasing.' The Kṣatriya crown prince, having heard this, said: 'Brahmin, what should I do?' The royal chaplain said: 'Your Majesty! In your kingdom there are wise and intelligent people, well-versed in calculations. Among the kingdom's great ministers and their retinues, there are those who have studied the scriptures, who know the scriptures well, who have recited, practiced, and upheld the law of succession, just as all of us in our retinue have. Your Majesty should learn the law of succession. Having learned the law of succession, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant.'

"The Kṣatriya crown prince then asked: 'Brahmin, what is this law of succession that you wish me to learn? Having learned it, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant?' The royal chaplain said: 'Your Majesty should observe the Dharma according to the Dharma, practice the Dharma according to the Dharma, and for the sake of the crown prince, queens, palace women, ministers, people, śramaṇas, brahmins, and even down to insects, observe the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, and practice generosity. Give to the destitute, to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who come from afar to beg, providing them with food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, incense for anointing, shelter, bedding, rugs, woolen blankets, attendants, and lamps. If in Your Majesty's kingdom there are venerable and renowned śramaṇas and brahmins, you should go to visit them at the appropriate times, inquire about the Dharma, and receive the Dharma: "Venerable ones, what are wholesome dharmas? What are unwholesome dharmas? What constitutes sin? What constitutes merit? What is excellent? What is not excellent? What is dark? What is bright? From what do dark and bright dharmas arise? What benefits this present life? What benefits the next life? How should one act so as to receive what is wholesome and not receive what is evil?" Having heard from them, practice as they have taught. If in Your Majesty's kingdom there are those who are impoverished, you should provide wealth and goods to help and support them. Your Majesty, this is called the law of succession. You should learn it well. Having learned it well, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the prātimokṣa, having bathed and washed, and ascended the main hall, the divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east, a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every way, pure and natural, not made by human hands, the color of a blazing fire, brilliantly radiant.'

"The Kṣatriya crown prince then, in the time that followed, observed the Dharma according to the Dharma, practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma, and for the sake of the crown prince, queens, palace women, ministers, people, śramaṇas, brahmins, and even down to insects, observed the Dharma fasting days on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, and practiced generosity. He gave to the destitute, to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the orphaned, and those who came from afar to beg, providing them with food and drink, clothing, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, incense for anointing, shelter, bedding, rugs, woolen blankets, attendants, and lamps. If in his kingdom there were venerable and renowned śramaṇas and brahmins, he would go to visit them at the appropriate times, inquire about the Dharma, and receive the Dharma: 'Venerable ones, what are wholesome dharmas? What are unwholesome dharmas? What constitutes sin? What constitutes merit? What is excellent? What is not excellent? What is dark? What is bright? From what do dark and bright dharmas arise? What benefits this present life? What benefits the next life? How should one act so as to receive what is wholesome and not receive what is evil?' Having heard from them, he practiced as they taught.

"However, when there were impoverished people in the kingdom, he was unable to provide wealth and goods to help and support them. Because the destitute poor who had no wealth could not be aided, the people grew increasingly impoverished. Because of the increasing poverty, they began to steal the property of others. Because of the stealing, the owners caught and seized and bound them, and brought them before the Kṣatriya crown prince, saying: 'Your Majesty! This person stole my property. We ask that Your Majesty administer punishment.' The Kṣatriya crown prince asked that person: 'Did you truly steal?' That person said: 'Your Majesty, I truly did steal. Why? Your Majesty, it was due to poverty and hardship. If I had not stolen, I would have had no means to sustain myself.' The Kṣatriya crown prince then provided him with wealth and goods, and said to the thief: 'You may go now, and do not do this again.' Thereupon, the people of the kingdom heard that the Kṣatriya crown prince, whenever someone in the kingdom committed theft, would provide them with wealth and goods. Because of this, people had this thought: 'We too should steal the property of others.' So the people of the kingdom all vied with one another to steal others' property. This was because the destitute poor who had no wealth could not be aided, and so the people grew increasingly impoverished. Because of the increasing poverty, theft grew ever more prevalent. Because theft grew ever more prevalent, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of forty thousand years. Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of forty thousand years, a person stole the property of others. The owner caught and seized and bound him, and brought him before the Kṣatriya crown prince, saying: 'Your Majesty! This person stole my property. We ask that Your Majesty administer punishment.' The Kṣatriya crown prince asked that person: 'Did you truly steal?' That person said: 'Your Majesty, I truly did steal. Why? It was due to poverty and hardship. If I had not stolen, I would have had no means to sustain myself.' When the Kṣatriya crown prince heard this, he had this thought: 'If whenever someone in my kingdom steals others' property, I keep providing more wealth and goods to give them, in this way I will vainly exhaust the national treasury, and theft will only grow worse. I should now have an extremely sharp sword made, and if anyone in my kingdom commits theft, I shall have them arrested, placed on a high stake, and beheaded.'

"Thereupon, the Kṣatriya crown prince later issued the command to have an extremely sharp sword made: 'If anyone in the kingdom steals others' property, they shall be arrested immediately, placed on a high stake, and beheaded.' The people of the kingdom heard that the Kṣatriya crown prince had commanded a sharp sword be made, and that if anyone in the kingdom stole others' property, they would be arrested, placed on a high stake, and beheaded. They thought: 'We too might as well make sharp swords ourselves, and carry them when robbing property. If someone resists the robbery, we shall seize the property owner and cut off their head.' Thereupon, those people later made sharp swords, carried them to rob property, and seized the property owners and cut off their heads. This was because the destitute poor who had no wealth could not be aided, and so the people grew increasingly impoverished. Because of the increasing poverty, theft grew ever more prevalent. Because theft grew ever more prevalent, killing with weapons increased. Because killing with weapons increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of forty thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of twenty thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of twenty thousand years, a person stole the property of others. The owner caught and seized and bound him, and brought him before the Kṣatriya crown prince, saying: 'Your Majesty! This person stole my property. We ask that Your Majesty administer punishment.' The Kṣatriya crown prince asked that person: 'Did you truly steal?' At that time, the thief had this thought: 'If the Kṣatriya crown prince learns the truth, he may bind me, whip me, cast me out, exile me, fine me, inflict various tortures on me, impale me on a stake, or cut off my head. Had I not better deceive the Kṣatriya crown prince with false speech?' Having thought thus, he said: 'Your Majesty, I did not steal.' This was because the destitute poor who had no wealth could not be aided, and so the people grew increasingly impoverished. Because of the increasing poverty, theft grew ever more prevalent. Because theft grew ever more prevalent, killing with weapons increased. Because killing with weapons increased, false speech and divisive speech further increased. Because false speech and divisive speech increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of twenty thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of ten thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of ten thousand years, among the people some had virtue and some lacked virtue. Those who lacked virtue, out of jealousy toward virtuous people, developed envious intentions and violated their wives. This was because the destitute poor who had no wealth could not be aided, and so the people grew increasingly impoverished. Because of the increasing poverty, theft grew ever more prevalent. Because theft grew ever more prevalent, killing with weapons increased. Because killing with weapons increased, false speech and divisive speech further increased. Because false speech and divisive speech increased, jealousy and sexual misconduct further increased. Because jealousy and sexual misconduct increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of ten thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of five thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of five thousand years, three things further increased: wrong conduct, lustful desire, and evil greed, and wrong teachings. Because these three things increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of five thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years. Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years, another three things further increased: divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. Because these three things increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years, the sons had a lifespan of one thousand years. Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of one thousand years, one thing further increased: wrong views. Because this one thing increased, the lifespan of those people decreased and their physical appearance deteriorated. As their lifespan decreased and their appearance deteriorated, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of one thousand years, the sons had a lifespan of five hundred years.

"Bhikṣus, when people had a lifespan of five hundred years, those people throughout their entire lives were unfilial to their parents, unable to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, did not practice what is proper and dutiful, did not perform meritorious deeds, and did not see the consequences of wrongdoing in the next life. Because of being unfilial to their parents, unable to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, not practicing what is proper and dutiful, not performing meritorious deeds, and not seeing the consequences of wrongdoing in the next life, bhikṣus, when the fathers had a lifespan of five hundred years, the sons had a lifespan of either two hundred fifty or two hundred years. Bhikṣus, nowadays if someone lives long, their lifespan is about a hundred years, or perhaps a bit more."

The Buddha then further said: "Bhikṣus, in the distant future, people will have a lifespan of ten years. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, a girl at five months of age will already be given in marriage. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, there will be a grain called barnyard millet, which will be considered the finest food, just as today people consider polished fragrant rice to be the finest meal. Bhikṣus, in the same way, when people have a lifespan of ten years, there will be a grain called barnyard millet, which will be considered the finest food. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, whatever fine flavors exist today, such as ghee, oil, salt, honey, sugarcane, and sugar, will all have completely disappeared. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, if someone practices the ten courses of unwholesome action, that person will be revered and respected by people, just as today one who practices the ten courses of wholesome action is revered and respected by people. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, it will also be the same: if someone practices the ten courses of unwholesome action, that person will be revered and respected by people. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, there will be utterly no reputation for virtue, let alone anyone who actually practices the ten courses of wholesome action.

"Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, there will be a person named 'the Punisher' who will go around everywhere, punishing from household to household. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, a mother will harbor extreme harmful intent toward her child, and a child will harbor extreme harmful intent toward its mother. Fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, relatives and kin will face one another with murderous intent, like a hunter who, seeing a deer, harbors extreme harmful intent. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, it will also be the same: a mother will harbor extreme harmful intent toward her child, and a child will harbor extreme harmful intent toward its mother. Fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, relatives and kin will face one another with murderous intent. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of ten years, there will be a seven-day calamity of weapons. Whenever they grasp grass, it will transform into a sword; whenever they grasp firewood, it will also transform into a sword. With these swords they will slaughter one another. During this seven-day calamity of weapons, after seven days it will cease.

"At that time, there will also be people who feel shame and embarrassment, who are disgusted and repelled by this. During the seven-day calamity of weapons, these people will enter the mountains and wilderness, hiding in secluded places. After the seven days have passed, they will come out from the mountains and wilderness, from their hidden places, and when they see one another again, they will give rise to compassionate hearts and feel the deepest affection, just as a loving mother with an only child, separated for a long time, who returns safely from a distant journey, comes home to a joyful reunion, giving rise to compassion and the deepest affection. In the same way, after the seven days have passed, those people will come out from the mountains and wilderness, from their hidden places, and when they see one another again, they will give rise to compassionate hearts and feel the deepest affection. After they have met, they will speak thus: 'Good people! We now see each other; we now have peace and safety. Because we gave rise to unwholesome dharmas, we have witnessed this: all our relatives have perished. We should now all practice wholesome dharmas together. How should we practice wholesome dharmas together? We have all been people who kill living beings. Let us now all abandon killing together, let us all refrain from killing. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of ten years will have children with a lifespan of twenty years. Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of twenty years will then have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing together, yet we still take what is not given. Let us now all abandon taking what is not given, let us all refrain from taking what is not given. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of twenty years will have children with a lifespan of forty years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of forty years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, yet we still engage in sexual misconduct. Let us now all abandon sexual misconduct, let us all refrain from sexual misconduct. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of forty years will have children with a lifespan of eighty years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of eighty years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, yet we still engage in false speech. Let us now all abandon false speech, let us all refrain from false speech. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of eighty years will have children with a lifespan of a hundred and sixty years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of a hundred and sixty years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, yet we still engage in divisive speech. Let us now all abandon divisive speech, let us all refrain from divisive speech. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of a hundred and sixty years will have children with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, yet we still engage in harsh speech. Let us now all abandon harsh speech, let us all refrain from harsh speech. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years will have children with a lifespan of six hundred and forty years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of six hundred and forty years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech, yet we still engage in frivolous speech. Let us now all abandon frivolous speech, let us all refrain from frivolous speech. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of six hundred and forty years will have children with a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech, abandoned frivolous speech and refrained from frivolous speech, yet we still engage in covetousness. Let us now all abandon covetousness, let us all refrain from covetousness. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years will have children with a lifespan of five thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of five thousand years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech, abandoned frivolous speech and refrained from frivolous speech, abandoned covetousness and refrained from covetousness, yet we still engage in ill will. Let us now all abandon ill will, let us all refrain from ill will. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of five thousand years will have children with a lifespan of ten thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of ten thousand years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech, abandoned frivolous speech and refrained from frivolous speech, abandoned covetousness and refrained from covetousness, abandoned ill will and refrained from ill will, yet we still hold wrong views. Let us now all abandon wrong views, let us all refrain from wrong views. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of ten thousand years will have children with a lifespan of twenty thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, those people with a lifespan of twenty thousand years will also have this thought: 'If one seeks to learn what is wholesome, one's lifespan increases and one's physical appearance improves. We should all further increase our practice of wholesome dharmas. How should we further increase our practice? We have already abandoned killing and refrained from killing, abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and refrained from sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech, abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech, abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech, abandoned frivolous speech and refrained from frivolous speech, abandoned covetousness and refrained from covetousness, abandoned ill will and refrained from ill will, abandoned wrong views and refrained from wrong views, yet we still have wrong conduct, lustful desire, evil greed, and wrong teachings. Let us now all abandon these three evil unwholesome dharmas, let us all refrain from these three evil unwholesome dharmas. We should all practice this wholesome dharma together.' They then all practice such wholesome dharma together. Having practiced wholesome dharma, their lifespans increase and their physical appearance improves. As their lifespans increase and their appearance improves, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of twenty thousand years will have children with a lifespan of forty thousand years.

"Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of forty thousand years, they will be filial to their parents, revere and honor śramaṇas and brahmins, practice what is proper and dutiful, cultivate meritorious deeds, and see the consequences of wrongdoing in the next life. Because of being filial to their parents, revering and honoring śramaṇas and brahmins, practicing what is proper and dutiful, cultivating meritorious deeds, and seeing the consequences of wrongdoing in the next life, bhikṣus, those with a lifespan of forty thousand years will have children with a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa will be extremely prosperous and joyful, with many people, and villages so close together that a chicken could fly from one to the next. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, a woman will not marry until she is five hundred years old. Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, the only illnesses will be cold, heat, the need for urination and defecation, desire, lack of appetite, and old age; there will be no other afflictions.

"Bhikṣus, when people have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will be a king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, who will have four kinds of armies and rule the world, sovereign by his own authority. He will be a righteous Dharma king, accomplished in the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the chief military minister-treasure; these are the seven. He will have a thousand sons, all of fine appearance, brave and fearless, able to subdue all adversaries. He will rule over all this land, up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but through Dharma teaching, bringing peace and happiness to all. Bhikṣus, the Kṣatriya kings of the line who gained sovereignty as human rulers, governing the world, traveled in their own domain, inherited from their fathers. Because they traveled in their own domain, inherited from their fathers, their lifespans did not decrease, their physical appearance did not deteriorate, they never lost happiness, and their strength did not decline. Bhikṣus, you too should be likewise: shave off your hair and beards, don kāṣāya robes, and with faithful conviction, leave the household life, becoming homeless, to train in the path, traveling in your own domain, inherited from your father. Bhikṣus, because you travel in your own domain, inherited from your father, your lifespans will not decrease, your physical appearance will not deteriorate, you will never lose happiness, and your strength will not decline.

"How does a bhikṣu travel in his own domain, inherited from his father? This bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body, contemplates feelings internally, mind, and dharmas as dharmas. This is called a bhikṣu traveling in his own domain, inherited from his father. How does a bhikṣu have longevity? This bhikṣu cultivates the base of supernormal power of concentration through desire, based on seclusion, based on non-attachment, based on cessation, tending toward relinquishment. He cultivates the base of supernormal power of concentration through effort; cultivates the base of supernormal power of concentration through mind; cultivates the base of supernormal power of concentration through investigation, based on seclusion, based on non-attachment, based on cessation, tending toward relinquishment. This is called a bhikṣu's longevity. How does a bhikṣu have good appearance? This bhikṣu cultivates and upholds the precepts, guards the prātimokṣa, and further well maintains proper deportment and etiquette. Seeing even the slightest transgression, he always harbors fearfulness. He upholds the training precepts. This is called a bhikṣu's good appearance. How does a bhikṣu have happiness? This bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna. This is called a bhikṣu's happiness. How does a bhikṣu have strength? This bhikṣu, all his outflows being exhausted, attains the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life knowing for himself, realizing for himself, personally witnessing and accomplishing this attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what needed to be done has been done, he will not receive further existence; he knows it as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu's strength.

"Bhikṣus, I do not see any other power that cannot be conquered like the power of Māra, the Evil One. Yet a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted can conquer it through the unsurpassed power of noble wisdom."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra of the Wheel-Turning King, the Sixth.

### (66) Sūtra on Instruction to Explain

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life. Listen well, listen well, and ponder it carefully. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "There are those who, having heard the Dharma, do not explain it to others. There are those who, having heard the Dharma, do explain it to others. What is meant by one who, having heard the Dharma, does not explain it to others?

"Suppose a person hears the Dharma and attains the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, or the fourth jhāna. Having attained these, that person dwells in ease and is self-satisfied, and does not explain it to others. This is called one who, having heard the Dharma, does not explain it to others.

"What is meant by one who, having heard the Dharma, explains it to others? Suppose a person hears the Dharma and thinks: 'I have heard this Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life. This Dharma should be explained to others, so that others may also hear it, and having heard it may gain faith, and having gained faith may practice accordingly.' This is called one who, having heard the Dharma, explains it to others.

"Among these two persons, the one who, having heard the Dharma, explains it to others is the more distinguished and the more excellent."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 16

## (71) The Sūtra on King Pāyāsi, Seventh of the Chapter on Kings

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa was traveling in the country of Kosala together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He went to Sethavyā and stayed in the Śiśapā Grove to the north of that village.

At that time, in Sethavyā there was a king named Pāyāsi, who was extremely wealthy and prosperous, with immeasurable resources and property, livestock and estates beyond reckoning. His fiefdoms and revenue villages were fully complete in every way. The springs, pools, grasses, and trees of the town of Sethavyā all belonged to the king, having been granted by King Prasenajit of Kosala.

Then the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā heard: "There is a śramaṇa named Kumāra Kāśyapa who is traveling in the country of Kosala together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He has come to this Sethavyā and is staying in the Śiśapā Grove to the north of the village. That śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has great renown, heard of in all ten directions. Kumāra Kāśyapa's eloquence is unobstructed and his teaching is subtle and wonderful. He is an Arhat of great learning. If anyone can see this Arhat and pay reverence and homage to him, that person swiftly obtains good fortune. We should go and see that śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa." The brahmins and householders of Sethavyā, each accompanied by their respective groups, set out from Sethavyā and together headed north to the Śiśapā Grove.

At that time, King Pāyāsi was on his upper palace hall and saw from afar the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā, each accompanied by their respective groups, setting out from Sethavyā and heading together northward to the Śiśapā Grove. Having seen this, King Pāyāsi said to his attendant: "Why are these brahmins and householders of Sethavyā today, each with their respective groups, setting out from Sethavyā and heading together northward to the Śiśapā Grove?"
