The attendant replied: "Your Majesty, those brahmins and householders of Sethavyā have heard that there is a śramaṇa named Kumāra Kāśyapa who is traveling in the country of Kosala together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He has come to this Sethavyā and is staying in the Śiśapā Grove to the north of the village. Your Majesty, that śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has great renown, heard of in all ten directions. Kumāra Kāśyapa's eloquence is unobstructed and his teaching is subtle and wonderful. He is an Arhat of great learning. If anyone can see this Arhat and pay reverence and homage to him, that person swiftly obtains good fortune. We should go and see that śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa. Your Majesty, that is why the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā, each with their respective groups, are setting out from Sethavyā and heading together northward to the Śiśapā Grove."

Having heard this, King Pāyāsi told his attendant: "Go to those brahmins and householders of Sethavyā and tell them: 'King Pāyāsi says to the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā: Good sirs, please wait. I will go together with you to see the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa. You are foolish! Do not be deceived by him into thinking there is a future life or that beings are reborn. My view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings.'"

The attendant received the order and went to the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā and told them: "King Pāyāsi says to the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā: 'Good sirs, please wait. I will go together with you to see the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa. You are foolish! Do not be deceived by him into thinking there is a future life or that beings are reborn. My view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings.'"

When the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā heard this order, they replied to the attendant: "We respectfully comply with the king's command."

The attendant returned and reported, having conveyed the king's command: "The brahmins and householders of Sethavyā are waiting for Your Majesty. May Your Majesty know that now is the time."

Then King Pāyāsi ordered his charioteer: "Quickly prepare the chariot. I wish to depart now."

The charioteer received the order and quickly prepared the chariot. When finished, he reported to the king: "The chariot is prepared. May Your Majesty proceed at will."

Then King Pāyāsi mounted the chariot and went to where the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā were, and together they traveled northward to the Śiśapā Grove. When King Pāyāsi saw the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa from afar among the trees in the grove, he descended from the chariot and proceeded on foot to where the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa was. They exchanged greetings with each other, and the king sat to one side and asked: "Kāśyapa, I wish to ask you a question. Would you be willing to listen?"

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, if you wish to ask, you may ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

Then King Pāyāsi asked: "Kāśyapa, my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings. Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa, what do you think about this?"

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, I shall now ask the king a question; answer as you understand. What do you think, O King? Are the sun and moon of this world, or of the next world?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I had relatives who were gravely ill. I went to them and said: 'You should know that my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings. Kinsmen, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and say: there is a future life, and there is rebirth of beings. I have never believed what they say. They also say this: "If there are men or women who perform evil deeds, who are not diligent, who are lazy and idle, jealous and miserly, who do not extend their hands in generosity, who do not aspire to good, and who are extremely attached to possessions, then because of these conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly fall into an evil realm and be reborn in hell." If what those śramaṇas and brahmins say is true, then you, my kinsmen, have performed evil deeds, have not been diligent, have been lazy and idle, jealous and miserly, have not extended your hands in generosity, have not aspired to good, and have been extremely attached to possessions. If, when your bodies break up and your lives end, you certainly fall into an evil realm and are reborn in hell, then come back and tell me: "Pāyāsi, in that hell there is such and such suffering." If you do so, then I will have seen it directly.' They heard my words and accepted my instruction, yet none of them has come to tell me: 'Pāyāsi, in that hell there is such and such suffering.' Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, I shall ask the king again; answer as you understand. Suppose there were officers of the king who seized a criminal and brought him before the king, saying: 'Your Majesty, this man has committed a crime. May the king punish him.' The king says to them: 'Take him away, bind his hands behind his back, make him ride a donkey, beat a broken drum whose sound is like a donkey's bray, and after proclaiming his crimes throughout the city, take him out through the south gate, seat him below a tall stake, and cut off his head.' They receive the order and bind the criminal's hands behind his back, make him ride a donkey, beat a broken drum whose sound is like a donkey's bray, proclaim his crimes throughout the city, take him out through the south gate, and seat him below a tall stake, about to cut off his head. This man, facing death, says to the executioner: 'Wait a moment. I wish to see my parents, wife and children, slaves and servants. Allow me to go briefly.' What do you think, O King? Would those executioners release this criminal and allow him to go briefly?"

Pāyāsi replied: "No, Kāśyapa."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, the case of the king's relatives is just like this. They performed evil deeds, were not diligent, were lazy and idle, jealous and miserly, did not extend their hands in generosity, did not aspire to good, and were extremely attached to possessions. Because of these conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, they certainly fell into an evil realm and were reborn in hell. When the hell wardens seize them and inflict extreme suffering upon them, they say to the wardens: 'Hell wardens, wait a moment! Do not torment me. I wish to go briefly to King Pāyāsi and tell him: "In that hell there is such and such suffering," so that he may see it directly.' What do you think, O King? Would those hell wardens release the king's relatives and allow them to come here briefly?"

Pāyāsi replied: "No, Kāśyapa."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the future life in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I had relatives who were gravely ill. I went to them and said: 'You should know that my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings. Kinsmen, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and say: there is a future life, and there is rebirth of beings. I have never believed what they say. They also say this: "If there are men or women who practice wholesome conduct with diligence, who are earnest and untiring, who are without jealousy and without miserliness, who extend their hands in generosity, who aspire to good, who are open-hearted and relinquishing, who provide for the orphaned and destitute, who always delight in giving, and who are not attached to possessions, then because of these conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly ascend to a good destination and be reborn in heaven." If what those śramaṇas and brahmins say is true, then you, my kinsmen, have practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, have been earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, have extended your hands in generosity, have aspired to good, have been open-hearted and relinquishing, have provided for the orphaned and destitute, have always delighted in giving, and have not been attached to possessions. If, when your bodies break up and your lives end, you certainly ascend to a good destination and are reborn in heaven, then come back and tell me: "Pāyāsi, in heaven there is such and such happiness." If you do so, then I will have seen it directly.' They heard my words and accepted my instruction, yet none of them has come to tell me: 'Pāyāsi, in heaven there is such and such happiness.' Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen to me explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose outside a village there was a public latrine pit, as deep as a person's height, filled with excrement. Suppose a man had fallen into the bottom of this pit. Then suppose another person, out of compassion for him, seeking his benefit and welfare, seeking his safety and happiness, gradually pulled him up from the pit, scraped him with bamboo strips, wiped him with tree leaves, and washed him with warm water. Then afterward, once he was completely bathed and cleaned, his body was anointed with fragrance. He ascended to the upper palace hall and was entertained with the five kinds of sensual pleasures. What do you think, O King? Would that man still remember the former pit, praise it with delight, and wish to see it again?"

Pāyāsi replied: "No, Kāśyapa. If any other person were to remember that pit, praise it with delight, and wish to see it, one would find that person repulsive. How much less would the man himself remember the former pit, praise it with delight, and wish to see it? That is impossible."

"Pāyāsi, if the king had relatives who practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, who were earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, who extended their hands in generosity, who aspired to good, who were open-hearted and relinquishing, who provided for the orphaned and destitute, who always delighted in giving, and who were not attached to possessions, then because of these conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, they certainly ascended to a good destination and were reborn in heaven. Having been reborn in heaven, they enjoy themselves with the five heavenly sensual pleasures. What do you think, O King? Would those heavenly sons abandon those five heavenly sensual pleasures, remember the five human sensual pleasures, praise them with delight, and wish to see them again?"

Pāyāsi replied: "No, Kāśyapa. Why? Human sensual pleasures are foul, impure, greatly repulsive, unapproachable, unlovable, coarse, rough, and impure. Kāśyapa, compared to human sensual pleasures, heavenly pleasures are supreme, most excellent, most beautiful, most wonderful, most superior. That a heavenly son would abandon the five heavenly pleasures and instead remember the five human pleasures, praise them with delight, and wish to see them again: that is impossible."

"Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the future life in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I had relatives who were gravely ill. I went to them and said: 'You should know that my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings. Kinsmen, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who hold this view and say: there is a future life, and there is rebirth of beings. I have never believed what they say. They also say this: "If there are men or women who practice wholesome conduct with diligence, who are earnest and untiring, who are without jealousy and without miserliness, who extend their hands in generosity, who aspire to good, who are open-hearted and relinquishing, who provide for the orphaned and destitute, who always delight in giving, and who are not attached to possessions, then because of these conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly ascend to a good destination and be reborn in heaven." If what those śramaṇas and brahmins say is true, then you, my kinsmen, have practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, have been earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, have extended your hands in generosity, have aspired to good, have been open-hearted and relinquishing, have provided for the orphaned and destitute, have always delighted in giving, and have not been attached to possessions. If, when your bodies break up and your lives end, you certainly ascend to a good destination and are reborn in heaven, then come back and tell me: "Pāyāsi, in heaven there is such and such happiness." If you think to yourselves in heaven: "If I were to return, what would I gain?" the household of King Pāyāsi has abundant wealth, and I will surely give it to you.' They heard my words and accepted my instruction, yet none of them has come to tell me: 'Pāyāsi, in heaven there is such and such happiness.' Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, the lifespan in heaven is long, while the human lifespan is short. One hundred years in the human world equals one day and one night in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods. With such days and nights, thirty days make a month, twelve months make a year, and the lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods is one thousand years. What do you think, O King? If your relatives who practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, who were earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, who extended their hands in generosity, who aspired to good, who were open-hearted and relinquishing, who provided for the orphaned and destitute, who always delighted in giving, and who were not attached to possessions, because of these conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, certainly ascended to a good destination and were reborn in heaven, and having been reborn in heaven they thought: 'Let us first enjoy ourselves with the five heavenly sensual pleasures for one day and one night, or two, three, four, up to six or seven days, and then we will go and tell King Pāyāsi: "In heaven there is such and such happiness," so that he may see it directly.' What do you think, O King? Would you still be alive by then?"

Pāyāsi asked: "Kāśyapa, who has come from the next world to report this? Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa says that the lifespan in heaven is long and the human lifespan is short, that one hundred years in the human world equals one day and one night in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods, with such days and nights, thirty days making a month, twelve months making a year, and the lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods being one thousand years."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen to me explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose there were a blind man who said: 'There is no black or white color, nor is there anyone who sees black or white color. There is no long or short form, nor is there anyone who sees long or short form. There is no near or far form, nor is there anyone who sees near or far form. There is no coarse or fine form, nor is there anyone who sees coarse or fine form. Why? Because I have never seen or known them; therefore there is no color.' Would what that blind man says be true?"

Pāyāsi replied: "No, Kāśyapa. Why? Kāśyapa, there is black and white color, and there are those who see black and white color. There is long and short form, and there are those who see long and short form. There is near and far form, and there are those who see near and far form. There is coarse and fine form, and there are those who see coarse and fine form. If the blind man says: 'I do not see or know them; therefore there is no color,' what he says is not true."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "King Pāyāsi is also like that blind man. When the king says: 'Who has come from the next world to report this? Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa says that the lifespan in heaven is long and the human lifespan is short, that one hundred years in the human world equals one day and one night in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods, with such days and nights, thirty days making a month, twelve months making a year, and the lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three Gods being one thousand years.'"

King Pāyāsi said: "Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa, this is most improper! You should not speak this way. Why? Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa, it is quite wrong to compare me to a blind man. Kāśyapa, if I knew, if I knew that my relatives had practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, had been earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, had extended their hands in generosity, had aspired to good, had been open-hearted and relinquishing, had provided for the orphaned and destitute, had always delighted in giving, and had not been attached to possessions, and that because of these conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, they certainly ascended to a good destination and were reborn in heaven, then, Kāśyapa, I would immediately practice generosity, cultivate merit, observe the fast and keep the precepts, and then kill myself with a knife, or take poison, or throw myself into a pit or well, or hang myself. Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa, it is quite wrong to compare me to a blind man."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose a brahmin had a young wife who had just become pregnant. He also had a son by his former wife. Then that brahmin died suddenly. After his death, the former wife's son said to his stepmother: 'Stepmother, you should know that all the property in this household should belong to me. I do not see anyone who should receive a share.' The stepmother replied: 'I am now pregnant. If I give birth to a boy, then you should share with him. If I give birth to a girl, then all the property shall be yours.' The former wife's son again said, a second and third time: 'All the property in this household should belong to me. I do not see anyone who should receive a share.' The stepmother also replied a second and third time: 'I am now pregnant. If I give birth to a boy, then you should share with him. If I give birth to a girl, then all the property shall be yours.' Thereupon, the stepmother, being foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking good discernment, lacking wisdom, wishing to preserve her life but instead harming herself, entered a room, took a sharp knife, and cut open her own belly to see whether it was a boy or a girl. That foolish one, lacking understanding, lacking good discernment, lacking wisdom, wishing to preserve her life, instead destroyed herself and the child in her womb. You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same: foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking good discernment, lacking wisdom, wishing to preserve your life, yet you think in the opposite way: 'Kāśyapa, if I knew, if I knew that my relatives had practiced wholesome conduct with diligence, had been earnest and untiring, without jealousy and without miserliness, had extended their hands in generosity, had aspired to good, had been open-hearted and relinquishing, had provided for the orphaned and destitute, had always delighted in giving, and had not been attached to possessions, and that because of these conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, they certainly ascended to a good destination and were reborn in heaven, then I would immediately practice generosity, cultivate merit, observe the fast and keep the precepts, and then kill myself with a knife, or take poison, or throw myself into a pit or well, or hang myself. Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa, it is quite wrong to compare me to a blind man.' Pāyāsi, if a diligent person lives long, then he gains great merit; if he gains great merit, then he is reborn in heaven with a long lifespan. Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the future life in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no future life, and there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I had relatives who were gravely ill. I went to them and offered consolation, and they also offered me consolation in return. But when they died, I went to them and offered consolation, yet they no longer offered me consolation, and I no longer offered them consolation. Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose there were a man who was skilled at blowing a conch shell. He went to a place where people had never heard the sound of a conch and, in the darkness of night, climbed to the top of a high mountain and blew the conch with all his might. The many people there who had never heard the sound of a conch, upon hearing it, thought: 'What is this sound? It is so extremely wonderful, so marvelous, truly delightful, pleasant to hear and listen to, making the heart joyful.' Then those people all went together to where the skilled conch-blower was. When they arrived, they asked: 'What is this sound? It is so extremely wonderful, so marvelous, truly delightful, pleasant to hear and listen to, making the heart joyful.' The skilled conch-blower threw the conch on the ground and told the people: 'Sirs, you should know that this was the sound of the conch.' Then the people kicked the conch with their feet, saying: 'Conch, make a sound! Conch, make a sound!' But it was completely silent. The skilled conch-blower then thought: 'These people are foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking wisdom. Why do they seek to obtain sound from a senseless object?' Then the skilled conch-blower picked up the conch again, washed it clean with water, raised it to his lips, and blew it with all his might. When those people heard it, they thought: 'The conch is truly marvelous. Why? Because it is through the hand, through the water, through the mouth and the blowing of breath that the beautiful sound is produced and fills all four directions.' In the same way, Pāyāsi, when a person is alive and his life persists, then he can speak and offer consolation to others. But when his life ends, he can no longer speak or offer consolation. Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the rebirth of beings in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I have officers who seized a criminal and brought him before me, saying: 'Your Majesty, this man has committed a crime. May the king punish him.' I told them: 'Take this criminal and weigh him alive. After weighing him alive, place him back on the ground and strangle him with a rope. After killing him, weigh him again. I wish to know: at which time is this man lightest, most supple and soft, with a radiant and beautiful complexion: when dead or when alive?' They received my order and took the criminal. They weighed him alive, then placed him back on the ground and strangled him with a rope. After killing him, they weighed him again. The criminal, when alive, was lighter, more supple and soft, with a radiant and beautiful complexion. After death, his body became heavier, harder and not supple, and his complexion was no longer radiant. Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose there were an iron ball or an iron plowshare that has been heated in fire all day long. At that time it would be extremely light, supple and soft, with a radiant and beautiful color. But after the fire goes out and it gradually cools, it becomes heavier, condensed, harder and not supple, and its color is no longer radiant. In the same way, Pāyāsi, when a person is alive, the body is extremely light, supple and soft, with a radiant and beautiful complexion. But after that person dies, the body becomes heavier, harder and not supple, and the complexion is no longer radiant. Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the rebirth of beings in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I have officers who seized a criminal and brought him before me, saying: 'Your Majesty, this man has committed a crime. May the king punish him.' I told them: 'Take this criminal and place him upside down in an iron pot, or a copper pot. Seal the mouth tightly, light a fire beneath, and after lighting the fire beneath, observe whether a being exits or enters, coming and going in any direction.' They received my order and took the criminal. They placed him upside down in an iron pot, or a copper pot, sealed the mouth tightly, lit a fire beneath, and after lighting the fire beneath, observed whether a being exited or entered, coming and going in any direction. Kāśyapa, despite these efforts, I did not see any rebirth of a being. Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, I shall now ask you a question; answer as you understand. What do you think? If you eat fine, extremely delicious food and take a nap on your bed during the day, have you ever recalled seeing in a dream gardens, parks, bathing pools, forests, trees, flowers and fruits, clear springs and flowing streams, enjoying yourself fully, going about here and there?"

Pāyāsi replied: "I recall that this has happened."

Kāśyapa further asked: "When you eat fine, extremely delicious food and take a nap on your bed during the day, at that time are there attendants on duty nearby?"

He answered: "There are."

Kāśyapa further asked: "When you eat fine, extremely delicious food and take a nap on your bed during the day, at that time can the attendants on duty nearby see you going out and coming back, moving about here and there?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Even other people cannot see it; how much less the attendants on duty nearby!"

"Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the rebirth of beings in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still my view and my teaching is this: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do you have yet further evidence worse than this?"

Pāyāsi replied: "Indeed, Kāśyapa, there is yet further evidence. Kāśyapa, I have officers who seized a criminal and brought him before me, saying: 'Your Majesty, this man has committed a crime. May the king punish him.' I told them: 'Take this criminal, flay his skin, cut his flesh, sever his sinews, break his bones, down to the marrow, and search for the rebirth of the being.' They received my order and took the criminal. They flayed his skin, cut his flesh, severed his sinews, broke his bones, down to the marrow, searching for the rebirth of the being. Kāśyapa, despite these efforts to search for the rebirth of the being, I never saw any rebirth of a being. Kāśyapa, because of this, I have concluded: there is no rebirth of beings."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose there was a fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin who lived near a road. Not far from him, some merchants made camp for the night. The merchants left hurriedly at dawn the next morning and forgot a small child. The fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin rose early and went to inspect the place where the merchants had camped. He saw a small child there alone, separated from its guardians. Having seen this, he thought: 'This small child has no one to depend on. If I do not care for it, it will surely die.' So he picked up the child, carried it back to his dwelling, and raised it. The child grew up and its faculties matured. At that time, the fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin had some small business to attend to among people. So the fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin instructed the young man: 'I have some small business to attend to and must go out briefly among people. You must tend the fire. Be sure not to let it go out. If the fire goes out, you can use this fire drill to rekindle it.'

"The fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin, having given these instructions properly, then went out among people. Afterward, the young man went out to play, and the fire went completely out. When he returned and sought to rekindle the fire, he took the fire drill and struck it against the ground, saying: 'Fire, come out! Fire, come out!' But no fire came out. He then struck it forcefully against a stone, saying: 'Fire, come out! Fire, come out!' But again no fire came out. Since no fire came out, he broke the fire drill into ten pieces, a hundred pieces, threw them away, sat on the ground, and said with distress: 'I cannot get fire. What shall I do?'

"At that time, the fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin finished his business among people and returned to his dwelling. When he arrived, he asked: 'Young man, did you not go out to play and then tend the fire so it would not go out?' The young man said: 'Venerable sir, I went out to play, and afterward the fire went out. When I returned and sought to rekindle it, I took the fire drill and struck it against the ground, saying: "Fire, come out! Fire, come out!" But no fire came out. I then struck it forcefully against a stone, saying: "Fire, come out! Fire, come out!" But again no fire came out. Since no fire came out, I broke the fire drill into ten pieces, a hundred pieces, and threw them away and sat on the ground. Venerable sir, I sought fire in this way but could not get it. What shall I do?'

"Then the fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin thought: 'This young man is very foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking wisdom. Why does he try to seek fire from a senseless fire drill in such a manner?' Then the fire-worshipping, dreadlock-wearing brahmin took a dry fire drill and fire-mother, placed them on the ground, and drilled. Fire immediately came out and grew into a blaze. He said to the young man: 'Young man, this is how one should seek fire. One should not be like you, foolish and unwise, lacking wisdom, trying to seek fire from a senseless fire drill in such a manner.' You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same: foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking good discernment, lacking wisdom, seeking the rebirth of beings from senseless dead flesh, down to the bones and marrow. Pāyāsi, you should contemplate the rebirth of beings in this way, and not merely through what the fleshly eye sees. Pāyāsi, if there are śramaṇas and brahmins who have completely abandoned and are freed from desire, who tend toward freedom from desire; who have completely abandoned and are freed from hatred, who tend toward freedom from hatred; who have completely abandoned and are freed from delusion, who tend toward freedom from delusion, they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, beautiful and ugly, going to good destinations and bad destinations. They see truly, according to the deeds performed by those beings."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it. Why? If people of other countries hear of it, they will say: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Kāśyapa, therefore this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen to me explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose two friends left home to earn their livelihood. While traveling on the road, they first saw a great quantity of hemp, lying unclaimed. One of them, seeing this, said to his companion: 'You should know that there is a great quantity of hemp here, unclaimed. I wish to join with you in taking it. Let us carry heavy loads back home, where it can provide for our needs.' So they took heavy loads. Then further along the road, they saw a great quantity of kapok thread and kapok cloth, also unclaimed. Then they saw much silver, also unclaimed. The one who saw it cast aside his hemp load and took a heavy load of silver. Then further along the road, they saw a great pile of gold, unclaimed. The one carrying silver said to the one carrying hemp: 'You should know that there is a great quantity of gold here, unclaimed. You should cast aside the hemp, and I will cast aside the silver. I wish to join with you in taking this gold. We can carry heavy loads home, where it can provide for our needs.' The hemp-carrier said to the silver-carrier: 'My hemp load is already well packed, firmly tied and bound. I have carried it from far away. I cannot cast it aside. You attend to your own affairs; do not worry about me.' Then the silver-carrier forcibly grabbed the hemp load, threw it on the ground, and tore it apart. The hemp-carrier said to the silver-carrier: 'You have already torn apart my load like this. My hemp load was firmly bound, and I have carried it from far away. I insist on carrying this hemp home. I will never abandon it. You attend to your own affairs; do not worry about me.'

"The silver-carrier then cast aside his silver load and took a heavy load of gold to carry home. When the gold-carrier returned home, his parents saw from afar that he was carrying gold home. Having seen this, they exclaimed: 'Welcome, worthy son! How wonderful that you have come, worthy son! With this gold you can live well, support your parents, provide for your wife, children, slaves, and servants, and furthermore you can make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, perform meritorious deeds for ascent to heaven, with good results and good rewards, and be reborn in heaven with a long lifespan.' When the hemp-carrier returned to his home, his parents saw from afar that he was carrying hemp home. Having seen this, they scolded: 'You criminal, you have come! You worthless person, you have come! With this hemp, you cannot live well, support your parents, provide for your wife, children, slaves, and servants, nor can you make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, perform meritorious deeds for ascent to heaven, with good results and good rewards, and be reborn in heaven with a long lifespan.' You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same. If you grasp this view through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion, and never abandon it, then you will receive immeasurable evil, and you will also be despised by the multitude."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it. Why? If people of other countries hear of it, they will say: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Kāśyapa, therefore this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose there were merchants together with a great company, having a thousand carts, traveling through a famine-stricken road. In this great company there were two leaders. They thought: 'How can we escape this difficulty?' They further thought: 'We should divide this great company into two groups, five hundred in each.' So the merchant company was divided into two groups, five hundred in each. Then one merchant leader set out with five hundred carts on the famine-stricken road. That merchant leader was always at the front, leading the way. He saw a man coming from a side road, his clothes all wet, his body dark, his hair yellow, his two eyes extremely red, wearing a garland of sweet-scented flowers, riding a donkey cart with mud on both wheel hubs. The merchant leader saw him and asked: 'Has there been rain on the famine-stricken road? Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?' The man answered: 'On the famine-stricken road a great rain has fallen. There is abundant fresh water and plentiful firewood and grass. Good sirs, you may discard your old water, firewood, and grass. Do not let your animals be burdened. Before long you will find fresh water and good firewood and grass.'

"The merchant leader, having heard this, returned to the merchants and told them: 'While I was traveling ahead, I saw a man coming from a side road. His clothes were all wet, his body dark, his hair yellow, his two eyes extremely red, wearing a garland of sweet-scented flowers, riding a donkey cart with mud on both wheel hubs. I asked him: "Has there been rain on the famine-stricken road? Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?" He answered me: "On the famine-stricken road a great rain has fallen. There is abundant fresh water and plentiful firewood and grass. Good sirs, you may discard your old water, firewood, and grass. Do not let your animals be burdened. Before long you will find fresh water and good firewood and grass." Merchants, let us discard our old water, firewood, and grass. Before long we will find fresh water, firewood, and grass. Do not let our animals be burdened.' Those merchants then discarded their old water, firewood, and grass. After one day of traveling they did not find fresh water, firewood, or grass. After two days, three days, up to seven days of traveling, they still did not find fresh water, firewood, or grass. After seven days had passed, they were all killed by man-eating demons.

"The second merchant leader then thought: 'The first merchant leader has already met with danger and calamity. By what means can we escape this difficulty?' Having thought thus, the second merchant leader set out with five hundred carts on the famine-stricken road. The second merchant leader was at the front, leading the way. He saw a man coming from a side road, his clothes all wet, his body dark, his hair yellow, his two eyes extremely red, wearing a garland of sweet-scented flowers, riding a donkey cart with mud on both wheel hubs. The second merchant leader saw him and asked: 'Has there been rain on the famine-stricken road? Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?' The man answered: 'On the famine-stricken road a great rain has fallen. There is abundant fresh water and plentiful firewood and grass. Good sirs, you may discard your old water, firewood, and grass. Do not let your animals be burdened. Before long you will find fresh water and good firewood and grass.'

"The second merchant leader, having heard this, returned to the merchants and told them: 'While I was traveling ahead, I saw a man coming from a side road. His clothes were all wet, his body dark, his hair yellow, his two eyes extremely red, wearing a garland of sweet-scented flowers, riding a donkey cart with mud on both wheel hubs. I asked him: "Has there been rain on the famine-stricken road? Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?" He answered me: "On the famine-stricken road a great rain has just fallen. There is abundant fresh water and plentiful firewood and grass. Good sirs, you may discard your old water, firewood, and grass. Do not let your animals be burdened. Before long you will find fresh water and good firewood and grass." Merchants, we should not yet discard our old water, firewood, and grass. If we find fresh water, firewood, and grass, then we shall discard the old.' They did not discard their old water, firewood, and grass. After one day of traveling they did not find fresh water, firewood, or grass. After two days, three days, up to seven days of traveling, they still did not find fresh water, firewood, or grass. As the second merchant leader was traveling ahead, he saw the first merchant leader and his merchants, all killed by the man-eating demons. Having seen this, the second merchant leader said to his merchants: 'Look at how the first merchant leader was foolish and unwise, lacking understanding, lacking good discernment, lacking wisdom. He not only killed himself but also killed all his people. Merchants, if you wish to take the possessions of the earlier merchants, help yourselves freely.' You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same. If you grasp this view through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion, and never abandon it, then you will receive immeasurable evil, and you will also be despised by the multitude, just like the first merchant leader and his merchants."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it. Why? If people of other countries hear of it, they will say: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Kāśyapa, therefore this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose two people agreed to play a gambling game with cakes as stakes. The first player secretly ate the cakes, eating one, two, three, or even many. The second player then thought: 'Playing with this person, he repeatedly cheats me and steals the cakes, eating one, two, three, or even many.' Having seen this, he said to his companion: 'I wish to rest now. We shall play again later.' Then the second player went away from that place and smeared poison on the cakes. Having done so, he returned and said to his companion: 'Come, let us play again.' So they played again. The first player again secretly ate the cakes, one, two, three, or even many. Having eaten the cakes, his eyes rolled back, he foamed at the mouth, and he was about to die. Then the second player spoke this verse to the first player:

"'These cakes were smeared with poison; you greedily ate without noticing.
Because you cheated me with the cakes, later you will surely suffer bitter consequences.'

"You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same. If you grasp this view through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion, and never abandon it, then you will receive immeasurable evil, and you will also be despised by the multitude. Just like the gambler who cheated others with cakes, he himself received the calamity."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it. Why? If people of other countries hear of it, they will say: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Kāśyapa, therefore this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain with a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi, suppose a pig-herder was traveling along a road and saw a great quantity of dried dung, unclaimed. He thought: 'This dung can be used to feed and fatten many pigs. I should take it and carry a heavy load on my way.' So he took it and carried it on his back. While on the road, a great rain from heaven fell upon him. The dung liquefied and ran all over him, soiling his body. Yet he still carried it and would not discard it. He then received immeasurable unpleasantness and was also despised by the multitude. You should know, Pāyāsi, that you are just the same. If you grasp this view through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion, and never abandon it, then you will receive immeasurable evil, and you will also be despised by the multitude, just like the pig-herder."

King Pāyāsi again said: "Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, still this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it. Why? If people of other countries hear of it, they will say: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Kāśyapa, therefore this view of mine is grasped by desire, grasped by hatred, grasped by fear, and grasped by delusion, and I can never abandon it."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, listen again as I explain one final simile. If you understand it, good. If you do not understand, I will teach the Dharma no further. Pāyāsi, suppose there was a great boar, king of five hundred boars, traveling along a dangerous road. Along the way it encountered a tiger. Seeing the tiger, the boar thought: 'If I fight it, the tiger will surely kill me. If I flee in fear, then all my relatives will look down on me. I do not know by what means I can escape this difficulty.' Having thought thus, it said to the tiger: 'If you wish to fight, then let us fight. If not, then lend me the road to pass.' The tiger, having heard this, said to the boar: 'I will fight you. I will not lend you the road.' The boar then said: 'Tiger, wait a moment. Let me put on my grandfather's armor, and then I will come back to fight you.' The tiger, having heard this, thought: 'Even without armor it is no match for me; how much less with its grandfather's armor?' So it said to the boar: 'Do as you wish.' The boar then went back to its latrine area, rolled about in the excrement, and smeared its body up to its eyes. Then it went to where the tiger was and said: 'If you wish to fight, then let us fight. If not, then lend me the road to pass.' The tiger, seeing the boar, thought again: 'I always avoid eating those infested with filthy vermin, out of care for my teeth. How much less would I go near this foul-smelling boar?' Having thought thus, the tiger said to the boar: 'I lend you the road. I will not fight you.' After the boar had passed, it turned back toward the tiger and spoke this verse:

"'Tiger, you have four feet, and I also have four feet.
Come and fight with me. Why do you flee in fear?'

"The tiger, having heard this, also spoke a verse in reply to the boar:

"'Your bristles stand on end, you are the lowest of all beasts.
Boar, be on your way quickly; the stench of dung is unbearable.'

"Then the boar, boasting, spoke another verse:

"'In the two kingdoms of Magadha and Aṅga, they will hear that I fought with you.
Come and battle with me. Why do you flee in fear?'

"The tiger, having heard this, spoke another verse:

"'Your entire body is soiled with filth. Boar, your stench assails me.
You fight seeking victory; I now grant you the victory.'"

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, I am like the tiger in this regard. If you grasp this view through desire, through hatred, through fear, and through delusion, and never abandon it, then you will receive immeasurable evil and will also be despised by the multitude, just as the tiger granted victory to the boar."

When King Pāyāsi heard this, he said: "Venerable one, when you first gave the simile of the sun and moon, I heard it and understood. I joyfully accepted it. However, I wished to hear from the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa ever higher and more wonderful teachings of wisdom. That is why I kept asking question after question. I now take refuge in the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, do not take refuge in me. The one in whom I take refuge is the Buddha. You too should take refuge in him."

King Pāyāsi said: "Venerable one, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I ask the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa to accept me on the Buddha's behalf as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my life. Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa, from this day forward I shall practice generosity and cultivate merit."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa asked: "Pāyāsi, if you wish to practice generosity and cultivate merit, to how many people will you give, and for how long?"

King Pāyāsi said: "I will give to a hundred people, or up to a thousand people, for one day, two days, or up to seven days."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "If the king practices generosity and cultivates merit, giving to a hundred people, or up to a thousand people, for one day, two days, or up to seven days, then śramaṇas and brahmins in all directions will hear: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Having heard this in all directions, they will all come from afar, and within those seven days they will not be in time for the king's offering. If they do not receive the king's faithful offering, then the king will have no merit and will not enjoy peace and happiness for a long time. Pāyāsi, it is like seeds that are unbroken, undamaged, unsplit, uncrushed, not harmed by wind or sun, not injured by water, and well stored in autumn. If a householder deeply plows a good field, thoroughly prepares the land, and plants the seeds at the proper time, yet the rain is not adequate, what do you think, Pāyāsi? Can those seeds grow and increase?"

He answered: "They cannot."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, you are also like this. If you practice generosity and cultivate merit, giving to a hundred people, or up to a thousand people, for one day, two days, or up to seven days, then śramaṇas and brahmins in all directions will hear: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa.' Having heard this in all directions, they will all come from afar, and within those seven days they will not be in time for the king's offering. If they do not receive the king's faithful offering, then the king will have no merit and will not enjoy peace and happiness for a long time."

King Pāyāsi again asked: "Venerable one, what should I do?"

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa answered: "Pāyāsi, you should practice generosity and cultivate merit by providing an ongoing, perpetual feast. If King Pāyāsi practices generosity and cultivates merit by providing an ongoing, perpetual feast, then when śramaṇas and brahmins in all directions hear: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa,' having heard this in all directions, they will all come from afar, and they will all be able to receive the king's faithful offering. The king will then have merit and will enjoy peace and happiness for a long time. Pāyāsi, it is like seeds that are unbroken, undamaged, unsplit, uncrushed, not harmed by wind or sun, not injured by water, and well stored in autumn. If a householder deeply plows a good field, thoroughly prepares the land, and plants the seeds at the proper time, and the rain is adequate, what do you think, Pāyāsi? Can those seeds grow and increase?"

He answered: "They will grow."

The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said: "Pāyāsi, you are also like this. If you practice generosity and cultivate merit by providing an ongoing, perpetual feast, then when śramaṇas and brahmins in all directions hear: 'King Pāyāsi had a view that he held for a long time, and he was defeated, subdued, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa,' having heard this in all directions, they will all come from afar, and they will all be able to receive the king's faithful offering. The king will then have merit and will enjoy peace and happiness for a long time."

Then King Pāyāsi said: "Venerable one, from this day forward I shall practice generosity and cultivate merit by providing an ongoing, perpetual feast."

At that time, the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa taught the Dharma for King Pāyāsi and the brahmins and householders of Sethavyā, encouraging and inspiring them, arousing their aspiration, and bringing them to delight. With

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama), Fascicle 17

---

## (68) Sūtra on the Great善 [Wholesome Condition]

*Third Day of Recitation*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, he then accomplishes and fulfills all wholesome dharmas. What is this one dharma? It is called diligence. What is diligence? A bhikṣu, regarding unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, for the sake of not giving rise to them, arouses desire, makes effort, generates energy, applies his mind, and strives. Regarding unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen, for the sake of abandoning them, arouses desire, makes effort, generates energy, applies his mind, and strives. Regarding wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, for the sake of giving rise to them, arouses desire, makes effort, generates energy, applies his mind, and strives. Regarding wholesome dharmas that have already arisen, for the sake of maintaining them, not losing them, increasing them, expanding them, cultivating them, and fulfilling them, arouses desire, makes effort, generates energy, applies his mind, and strives. This is called diligence.

"If a bhikṣu attains diligence and does not abandon it, then wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen will arise, and wholesome dharmas that have already arisen will increase and expand. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train thus: 'I shall attain diligence and not abandon it.' You should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (69) Sūtra on the Three Wisdoms

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three wisdoms. What are the three? They are: the wisdom of study, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of cultivation. What is the wisdom of study? A bhikṣu studies the many kinds of dharma: sūtras, verses, accounts, verses of causation, narratives of past lives, records of what was spoken, jātaka tales, extensive teachings, marvelous dharmas, and explanations. This is called the wisdom of study.

"What is the wisdom of reflection? A bhikṣu, having heard the dharma, reflects on it, examines it, and discerns it with wisdom. This is called the wisdom of reflection.

"What is the wisdom of cultivation? A bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body on the body, cultivates mindfulness of feelings on feelings, cultivates mindfulness of mind on the mind, and cultivates mindfulness of dharmas on dharmas. This is called the wisdom of cultivation.

"These are called the three wisdoms."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (70) Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of the Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus: "There are two extremes that those who have gone forth should not pursue. What are the two? One is attachment to desire and pleasure among desires; this is a base, common, worldly practice, unworthy, unprofitable, not the way to the goal. The other is attachment to self-mortification; this is painful, unworthy, and unprofitable, not the way to the goal. Abandoning both these extremes, the Tathāgata has realized the Middle Way, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to perfect awakening, to nirvāṇa.

"What is the Middle Way that the Tathāgata has realized, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to perfect awakening, to nirvāṇa? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi. This is the Middle Way that the Tathāgata has realized, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to perfect awakening, to nirvāṇa.

"This is the noble truth of suffering. Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is disliked is suffering, separation from what is loved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This noble truth of suffering is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This noble truth of suffering should be thoroughly known. This noble truth of suffering has been thoroughly known. This is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This noble truth of the origin of suffering is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be abandoned. This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned. This is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandoning, relinquishing, release, and letting go. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized. This is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. It is just this Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right samādhi. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering should be cultivated. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated. This is a dharma not heard before. When I properly attended to it, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, and light arose.

"As long as my knowledge and vision regarding these Four Noble Truths, with their three turnings and twelve aspects, was not perfectly pure, I did not claim to have realized the unsurpassed, perfect awakening in this world with its devas, Māra, Brahmā, with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, with its devas and humans.

"But when my knowledge and vision regarding these Four Noble Truths, with their three turnings and twelve aspects, was perfectly pure, then I claimed to have realized the unsurpassed, perfect awakening in this world with its devas, Māra, Brahmā, with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, with its devas and humans. Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Unshakable is my liberation of mind. This is my last birth. There is no further becoming.'"

When the World-Honored One spoke this discourse, the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas attained the pure, stainless Dharma-eye regarding dharmas: "Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya: "Kauṇḍinya, have you attained knowledge of the Dharma?" Kauṇḍinya replied: "World-Honored One, I have attained knowledge of the Dharma." And again he asked: "Kauṇḍinya, have you attained knowledge of the Dharma?" He replied: "Sugata, I have attained knowledge of the Dharma."

Because the Venerable Kauṇḍinya had attained knowledge, he was therefore named Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya ("Kauṇḍinya Who Has Attained Knowledge").

When the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya attained knowledge of the Dharma, the earth devas raised their voices and proclaimed: "The World-Honored One has turned the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dharma at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, which cannot be turned by any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

When the earth devas raised their voices, the devas of the Cāturmahārājika heaven heard them and also raised their voices, making the same proclamation. In this way, successively, the devas of Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, and the devas of the Brahma realm all raised their voices and proclaimed: "The World-Honored One has turned the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dharma at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, which cannot be turned by any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

In that instant, in that moment, the sound reached up to the Brahma realm. This world system quaked in six ways. A great, immeasurable, brilliant radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the radiance of the devas.

At that time, the World-Honored One declared: "Kauṇḍinya has truly attained knowledge. Kauṇḍinya has truly attained knowledge." Therefore, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya was named Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya and the five bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (71) Sūtra on the Example of the Bee

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you a Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, displaying the holy life. Listen well and pay close attention; I shall explain it."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is a dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, displaying the holy life? It is called the 'Sūtra on the Example of the Bee.' Listen and pay close attention.

"Bhikṣus, when a bhikṣu depends on a village or town and dwells, in the morning he dons his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village to beg for food. He guards his body well, guards his faculties well, and establishes mindfulness. Having begged for food, after the midday meal, he washes his bowl and puts away his robes, takes his sitting cloth, and goes to a forest, or to the base of a tree, or an empty and quiet place. He spreads his sitting cloth and sits cross-legged with body upright, establishing mindfulness before him.

"He abandons covetousness, abides with a mind free from covetousness, and purifies his mind of covetousness. He abandons ill will and hatred, abides with a mind of benevolence and compassion for all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. He abandons sloth and torpor, abides perceiving light, mindful and clearly aware, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. He abandons restlessness and remorse, without restlessness internally, with a mind at peace within, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. He abandons doubt, crosses beyond doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome dharmas, and purifies his mind of doubt.

"He abandons these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom. He abides contemplating the body as body, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world.

"Just as a bee gathers from flowers, taking the color and fragrance without harming the flower, so too a bhikṣu who depends on a village or town and dwells enters the village to beg for food. He guards his body well, guards his faculties well, and establishes mindfulness. Having begged for food, after the midday meal, he washes his bowl and puts away his robes, takes his sitting cloth, and goes to a forest, or to the base of a tree, or an empty and quiet place. He spreads his sitting cloth and sits cross-legged with body upright, establishing mindfulness before him. He abandons covetousness, abides with a mind free from covetousness, and purifies his mind of covetousness. He abandons ill will and hatred, abides with a mind of benevolence and compassion for all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. He abandons sloth and torpor, abides perceiving light, mindful and clearly aware, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. He abandons restlessness and remorse, without restlessness internally, with a mind at peace within, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. He abandons doubt, crosses beyond doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome dharmas, and purifies his mind of doubt. He abandons these five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom. He abides contemplating the body as body, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world."

The Buddha spoke thus:

"In a village, among householders,
The sage who goes and comes wisely,
Is like the bee among the flowers,
Not harming color or fragrance.

One need not observe others' faults,
Nor what they have or have not done;
One should observe only oneself,
What one has done and has not done."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (72) Sūtra on the Legend of King Udena

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī, in Ghosita's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was sitting cross-legged under a tree, having recently emerged from samādhi. Then King Udena, out riding for pleasure, went to the forest. Having arrived at the forest, he dismounted from his chariot, entered the forest on foot, and proceeded to where the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with him. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, King Udena asked the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: "Bhāradvāja, for what reason do young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time?"

The Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja replied: "Great King, the Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Who Knows and Sees, has declared: 'Come, bhikṣus, regard those women who are old enough to be your mothers as mothers, regard those old enough to be your elder sisters as elder sisters, and regard those young enough to be your daughters as daughters.' Great King, it is for this reason that young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time."

King Udena said: "Bhāradvāja, desire is of such a nature that sometimes one can give rise to lustful thoughts even toward those who are like one's mother, and give rise to lustful thoughts toward those who are like one's elder sisters, and give rise to lustful thoughts toward those who are like one's daughters. Bhāradvāja, is there another reason why young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time?"

The Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja replied: "Great King, the Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Who Knows and Sees, has declared: 'Come, bhikṣus, you should contemplate this body from the soles of the feet upward and from the crown of the head downward. It is enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities. In this body there are: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse skin, fine skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, undigested food, feces, brain, brain membrane, tears, sweat, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, mucus, phlegm, and urine.' Great King, it is for this reason that young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time."

King Udena said: "Bhāradvāja, for those bhikṣus whose bodies are cultivated, whose precepts are cultivated, whose minds are cultivated, and whose wisdom is cultivated, that is easy to do. But for those bhikṣus whose bodies are not cultivated, whose precepts are not cultivated, whose minds are not cultivated, and whose wisdom is not cultivated, that is difficult to do. Bhāradvāja, sometimes one intends to contemplate impurity, yet the mind turns to the pure aspects. Bhāradvāja, is there another reason why young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time?"

The Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja replied: "Great King, the Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Who Knows and Sees, has declared: 'Come, bhikṣus, you should guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp at its signs, do not grasp at its features. If one leaves the eye faculty unguarded, covetousness, grief, and unwholesome, evil dharmas will flow in. Therefore one should practice restraint, guarding the eye faculty and attaining its restraint. When the ear hears a sound, when the nose smells an odor, when the tongue tastes a flavor, when the body touches a tangible, when the mind cognizes a dharma, do not grasp at its signs, do not grasp at its features. If one leaves the mind faculty unguarded, covetousness, grief, and unwholesome, evil dharmas will flow in. Therefore one should practice restraint, guarding the mind faculty and attaining its restraint.' Great King, it is for this reason that young bhikṣus, of tender years, with dark hair, in the prime of life, who have not indulged in desires, practice the complete and pure holy life for the duration of their lives, and maintain it well for a long time."

King Udena said: "Excellent, Bhāradvāja! The Buddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Who Knows and Sees, has truly declared this. Bhāradvāja, for those whose bodies are cultivated, whose precepts are cultivated, whose minds are cultivated, and whose wisdom is cultivated, if they guard the sense faculties, that is easy. But for those whose bodies are not cultivated, whose precepts are not cultivated, whose minds are not cultivated, and whose wisdom is not cultivated, if they guard the sense faculties, that is difficult.

"Bhāradvāja, I have myself experienced this. At times when I enter the inner palace without guarding my body, without guarding my sense faculties, without establishing mindfulness, lustful thoughts arise abundantly in me. But at times when I enter the inner palace guarding my body, guarding my sense faculties, and establishing mindfulness, lustful thoughts do not arise so abundantly in me.

"Excellent, Bhāradvāja! Excellent! Bhāradvāja, you have well expounded the Dharma for me. Just as one might set upright what was overturned, reveal what was concealed, show the way to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes can see forms, in the same way the Venerable Bhāradvāja has expounded the Dharma in various ways. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the Venerable Bhāradvāja accept me as a lay disciple, from this day until the end of my life, taking refuge and keeping the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (73) Sūtra on the Deva
