Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, when the night was far advanced, a certain deva of surpassing radiance illuminated all of Jeta's Grove, came to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deva spoke a verse to the Buddha:

"Many devas and humans
Have reflected on what is auspicious,
Seeking peace and well-being.
Please explain what is the highest auspiciousness."

The World-Honored One replied in verse:

"Not associating with the foolish,
But associating with the wise,
Honoring those worthy of honor:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Living in a suitable place,
Having planted merit in the past,
Rightly directing oneself:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Broad learning and mastery of arts,
Well-trained in discipline and precepts,
And well-spoken words:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Attending to one's mother and father,
Cherishing one's wife and children,
Engaging in a livelihood without confusion:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Generosity and righteous conduct,
Caring for one's relatives,
Actions that are blameless:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Ceasing and abstaining from evil,
Refraining from intoxicants,
Not being negligent in dharmas:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Reverence and humility,
Contentment and gratitude,
Timely hearing of the Dharma:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Patience and obedient speech,
Meeting with śramaṇas,
Timely discussion of the Dharma:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Austerity and the holy life,
Seeing the Noble Truths,
Realization of nirvāṇa:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Though touched by worldly conditions,
The mind is not shaken,
Sorrowless, stainless, and secure:
This is the highest auspiciousness.

Those who accomplish such things,
Are everywhere undefeated,
Everywhere attaining well-being:
This is the highest auspiciousness."

The Buddha spoke thus. That deva, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted, venerated the Buddha, circumambulated him, and then vanished.

---

## (74) Sūtra on the Eight Thoughts

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are eight thoughts of a great person. This Dharma is for those who have few desires, not for those who have many desires; for the contented, not for the discontented; for those who delight in seclusion, not for those who delight in company; for the energetic, not for the lazy; for those who are mindful, not for those who are forgetful; for those who have attained samādhi, not for those who have not attained samādhi; for the wise, not for the foolish; for those who delight in non-proliferation, not for those who delight in proliferation.

"What are the eight thoughts of a great person?

"This Dharma is for those who have few desires, not for those who have many desires. This is the first thought of a great person. The contented, not the discontented: this is the second thought. Those who delight in seclusion, not those who delight in company: this is the third thought. The energetic, not the lazy: this is the fourth thought. Those who are mindful, not those who are forgetful: this is the fifth thought. Those who have attained samādhi, not those who have not attained samādhi: this is the sixth thought. The wise, not the foolish: this is the seventh thought. Those who delight in non-proliferation, who practice non-proliferation, not those who delight in proliferation: this is the eighth thought.

"How is the Dharma for those with few desires, not for those with many desires? A bhikṣu has few desires: he does not desire that others know 'I have few desires.' He is contented: he does not desire that others know 'I am contented.' He practices austerities: he does not desire that others know 'I practice austerities.' He has right mindfulness: he does not desire that others know 'I have right mindfulness.' He has attained samādhi: he does not desire that others know 'I have attained samādhi.' He is wise: he does not desire that others know 'I am wise.' He delights in non-proliferation: he does not desire that others know 'I delight in non-proliferation.' This is how the Dharma is for those with few desires, not for those with many desires.

"How is the Dharma for the contented, not for the discontented? A bhikṣu is contented with whatever robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness he receives. This is how the Dharma is for the contented.

"How is the Dharma for those who delight in seclusion, not for those who delight in company? A bhikṣu practices seclusion, delighting in secluded places. This is how the Dharma is for those who delight in seclusion.

"How is the Dharma for the energetic, not for the lazy? A bhikṣu practices with constant effort and energy, abandoning unwholesome dharmas and cultivating wholesome dharmas. He firmly exerts himself and does not neglect wholesome dharmas. This is how the Dharma is for the energetic.

"How is the Dharma for those who are mindful, not for those who are forgetful? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates the body as body externally and both internally and externally. He contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas, internally, externally, and both internally and externally, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. This is how the Dharma is for those who are mindful.

"How is the Dharma for those who have attained samādhi, not for those who have not attained samādhi? A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with examination and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of examination and sustained thought, with inner confidence and unification of mind, without examination and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of samādhi, he enters and abides in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, he abides equanimous, mindful, and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, he abides in happiness.' He enters and abides in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna. This is how the Dharma is for those who have attained samādhi.

"How is the Dharma for the wise, not for the foolish? A bhikṣu cultivates wisdom, contemplating the arising and passing away of dharmas, with noble and penetrating insight, correctly leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is how the Dharma is for the wise.

"How is the Dharma for those who delight in non-proliferation, who practice non-proliferation, not for those who delight in proliferation? A bhikṣu delights in nirvāṇa, takes joy in nirvāṇa, reflects on nirvāṇa, and mindfully contemplates nirvāṇa. This is how the Dharma is for those who delight in non-proliferation.

"Bhikṣus, these are the eight thoughts of a great person."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (75) Sūtra on the Pure Way to the Imperturbable

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the pure way to the imperturbable, the pure way to the realm of nothingness, the pure way to the realm of neither perception nor non-perception, and the noble liberation viewed as it really is. Listen well and pay close attention; I shall explain."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the pure way to the imperturbable? A bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the realm of desire, does not attend to the perception of the form realm, but attends only to the perception of oneness based on the perception of the imperturbable. His mind then flows toward the imperturbable, delights in it, has confidence in it, dwells in it, and is liberated in it. He then knows: 'In this state, the agitation of the desire realm is eliminated, and the agitation of the form realm is eliminated. There is only this disturbance, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the imperturbable.' He knows: 'This perception is empty of the perception of the desire realm. This perception is empty of the perception of the form realm. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the imperturbable.' Thus, what was not there he sees as empty; but what remains there, he truly knows as existing. This is called the purified, true, actual realization of emptiness.

"What is the pure way to the realm of nothingness? A bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the form realm, does not attend to the perception of the imperturbable, but attends only to the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of nothingness. His mind then flows toward the realm of nothingness, delights in it, has confidence in it, dwells in it, and is liberated in it. He then knows: 'In this state, the agitation of the desire realm is eliminated, the agitation of the form realm is eliminated, and the agitation of the imperturbable is eliminated. There is only this disturbance, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of nothingness.' He knows: 'This perception is empty of the perception of the form realm. This perception is empty of the perception of the imperturbable. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of nothingness.' Thus, what was not there he sees as empty; but what remains there, he truly knows as existing. This is called the purified, true, actual realization of emptiness.

"What is the pure way to the realm of neither perception nor non-perception? A bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the realm of nothingness but attends only to the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception. His mind then flows toward the realm of neither perception nor non-perception, delights in it, has confidence in it, dwells in it, and is liberated in it. He then knows: 'In this state, the agitation of the desire realm is eliminated, the agitation of the form realm is eliminated, the agitation of the imperturbable is eliminated, and the agitation of the realm of nothingness is eliminated. There is only this disturbance, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception.' He knows: 'This perception is empty of the perception of the realm of nothingness. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the perception of oneness based on the perception of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception.' Thus, what was not there he sees as empty; but what remains there, he truly knows as existing. This is called the purified, true, actual realization of emptiness.

"What is the noble liberation viewed as it really is? A bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the realm of nothingness, does not attend to the perception of the realm of neither perception nor non-perception, but attends to the perception of oneness based on the signless samādhi of mind. His mind then flows toward the signless samādhi of mind, delights in it, has confidence in it, dwells in it, and is liberated in it. He then knows: 'This signless samādhi of mind is conditioned, mentally generated.' He knows: 'Whatever is conditioned and mentally generated is impermanent and subject to cessation.' When he knows this and sees this, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, liberated from the outflow of existence, and liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, there arises the knowledge: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'

"He then knows: 'In this state, the agitation of the outflow of sensual desire is eliminated, the agitation of the outflow of existence is eliminated, and the agitation of the outflow of ignorance is eliminated. There is only this disturbance, namely, the six sense faculties that are dependent on this body and conditioned by life.' He knows: 'This perception is empty of the outflow of sensual desire. This perception is empty of the outflow of existence. This perception is empty of the outflow of ignorance. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the six sense faculties that are dependent on this body and conditioned by life.' Thus, what was not there he sees as empty; but what remains there, he truly knows as existing. This is called the purified, true, actual, unsurpassed realization of emptiness."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (76) Sūtra on [郁伽支羅] Ukkācelā

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Vajji and arrived at the village of Ukkācelā, where he stayed on the bank of the Gaṅgā River.

At that time, the World-Honored One knew that the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had recently passed away and entered parinirvāṇa. He addressed the bhikṣus: "In this assembly, I see it as empty. Because the Venerable Sāriputta and Mahāmaudgalyāyana have entered parinirvāṇa, this assembly appears empty to me. Before, wherever the Venerable Sāriputta and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were, that place was not empty; I was at ease in that place.

"Bhikṣus, the Buddhas of the past, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Worthy of Offerings, also had such a pair of disciples, just as I now have Sāriputta and Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The Buddhas of the future, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Worthy of Offerings, will also have such a pair of disciples, just as I now have Sāriputta and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

"Bhikṣus, it is marvelous and extraordinary! These disciples carry out the Teacher's teaching, follow the Teacher's instruction, serve as the assembly's comfort and support. It is marvelous and extraordinary!

"Bhikṣus, do not grieve and lament. Why? Is it not the case that all who are born, who come into being, who are formed and conditioned, are subject to destruction? To wish that what is formed and conditioned should not be destroyed: such a thing is impossible. It is as though the largest branch of a great tree standing firm were to break off. In the same way, among the great Sangha of the Tathāgata, who stands firm, Sāriputta and Mahāmaudgalyāyana have entered parinirvāṇa. Is it not the case that all who are born, who come into being, who are formed and conditioned, are subject to destruction? To wish that what is formed and conditioned should not be destroyed: such a thing is impossible.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, be your own island, be your own refuge, with no other refuge. Let the Dharma be your island, let the Dharma be your refuge, with no other refuge.

"How does a bhikṣu make himself his own island, make himself his own refuge, with no other refuge, make the Dharma his island, make the Dharma his refuge, with no other refuge? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas, with ardor, clearly aware, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief toward the world. This is how a bhikṣu makes himself his own island, makes himself his own refuge, with no other refuge, makes the Dharma his island, makes the Dharma his refuge, with no other refuge."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (77) Sūtra on the Three Groups of Elders

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, there were three groups of elder bhikṣus who were staying near the World-Honored One. The first group of elders practiced austerities: wearing rag-robes, begging for food, eating only one meal a day, sitting under trees, and dwelling in solitude. The second group of elders expounded the Dharma: they were expounders of sūtras, expounders of the Vinaya, expounders of the Abhidharma. The third group of elders practiced dhyāna meditation.

At that time, the first group of elders went to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, they said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we practice austerities: wearing rag-robes, begging for food, eating only one meal a day, sitting under trees, and dwelling in solitude."

Then the second group of elders went to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, they said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we are expounders of the Dharma: expounders of sūtras, expounders of the Vinaya, expounders of the Abhidharma."

Then the third group of elders went to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Having sat to one side, they said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, we practice dhyāna meditation."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the first group of elder bhikṣus: "Excellent, excellent! You should practice austerities. For what reason? Because for a long time it will be for your benefit and happiness."

The World-Honored One addressed the second group of elder bhikṣus: "Excellent, excellent! You should expound the Dharma. For what reason? Because for a long time it will be for your benefit and happiness."

The World-Honored One addressed the third group of elder bhikṣus: "Excellent, excellent! You should practice dhyāna meditation. For what reason? Because for a long time it will be for your benefit and happiness.

"However, among these three groups, if their outflows are not yet exhausted, of these three groups, the one that practices dhyāna meditation is the most distinguished and the most superior. For what reason? Because all the noble ones, from the time when their wisdom-eye first opens until they attain final nirvāṇa, throughout this time they must rely on samādhi. Therefore, among these three groups, if their outflows are not yet exhausted, the one that practices dhyāna meditation is the most distinguished and the most superior."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (78) Sūtra on Brahmā's Invitation to the Buddha

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. He was in the afternoon, after emerging from meditation.

At that time, the Brahmā named Sahāṃpati went to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Brahmā Sahāṃpati, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha in verse:

"In the clan of the Śākyas, well-born,
Abandoning all, seeking the way,
With valiant effort and diligence,
He attained the unsurpassed awakening.

I now entreat the World-Honored One:
Please turn the Wheel of the Dharma.
Deliver sentient beings from suffering,
Let many find the way to liberation."

At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Brahmā Sahāṃpati in verse:

"I have already considered this matter.
Because beings are deeply defiled,
This profound, subtle, and wonderful Dharma
Is difficult for those steeped in desire to comprehend."

Then the Brahmā Sahāṃpati further addressed the Buddha in verse:

"In the past, the defiled Dharma
That was preached in Magadha,
Was impure and came from wrong thinking.
Now please open the door to the deathless!

The Dharma realized by the Undefiled One:
Please let them hear the pure Dharma.
As one standing on a mountain peak
Can see the people all around,

So the All-Seeing Wise One,
Having ascended the palace of Dharma,
Himself free from sorrow,
Observes beings sunk in sorrow.

Arise, O hero who has won the battle!
O caravan leader, free from debt!
Walk through the world!
May the World-Honored One teach the Dharma;
There will be those who understand."

At that time, the World-Honored One knew the Brahmā Sahāṃpati's earnest request. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. The World-Honored One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw that among sentient beings, some had little dust in their eyes, some had much dust; some had keen faculties, some had dull faculties; some were of good disposition, some were of poor disposition; some were easy to teach, some were difficult to teach. Among those easy to teach, some had fear of wrongdoing and the other world.

Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged in the water; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and are level with the water's surface; some are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, unstained by the water. In the same way, the World-Honored One surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw that among sentient beings, some had little dust in their eyes, some had much dust; some had keen faculties, some had dull faculties; some were of good disposition, some were of poor disposition; some were easy to teach, some were difficult to teach.

Having seen this, he addressed the Brahmā Sahāṃpati in verse:

"I now open wide for them
The gate to the deathless Dharma.
Those who have ears, let them release faith.
I shall proclaim the excellent Dharma for them.

O Brahmā, because I perceived
The labor would be fruitless,
I did not wish to teach
This subtle, wonderful Dharma.

But now I shall proclaim it.
Where there is willingness to hear,
Beings with faith will attain liberation.
I now turn the Wheel of the wonderful Dharma."

At that time, the Brahmā Sahāṃpati knew that the World-Honored One had accepted his request and would turn the Wheel of the Dharma. He was delighted, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him, and then vanished.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

## (72) The Madhyamāgama, Long-Lived King Chapter: Sūtra on the Origin of King Long-Lived, First

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kauśāmbī, staying in Ghositārāma.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were repeatedly quarreling and disputing with one another. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, saying: "Bhikṣus! You should not quarrel with one another. Why is that?

"If with quarrels one tries to stop quarrels,
In the end one never sees them stopped;
Only through forbearance can quarrels be stopped:
This is a dharma worthy of reverence.

"Why is that? In the distant past, there was a king of the Kosala country named Long-Lived, and there was also a king of the Kāśī country named Brahmadatta. Those two kings were constantly waging war against each other. Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī raised four kinds of armies: an elephant army, a cavalry army, a chariot army, and an infantry army. Having raised these four kinds of armies, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī personally led his forces and went forth, wishing to do battle with King Long-Lived of Kosala. King Long-Lived of Kosala heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī had raised four kinds of armies: an elephant army, a cavalry army, a chariot army, and an infantry army, and having raised these four kinds of armies, was coming to wage war against him. Having heard this, King Long-Lived of Kosala also raised four kinds of armies: an elephant army, a cavalry army, a chariot army, and an infantry army. Having raised these four kinds of armies, King Long-Lived of Kosala personally led his forces out, went to the border, arrayed his troops, and joined battle, and immediately crushed and defeated them. Thereupon, King Long-Lived of Kosala completely seized Brahmadatta's four kinds of armies: the elephant army, the cavalry army, the chariot army, and the infantry army, and even captured King Brahmadatta of Kāśī alive. Having captured him, he released him and said to him: 'You are in desperate straits. Now I pardon and release you. Hereafter, do not do this again.'

"King Brahmadatta of Kāśī a second and third time raised four kinds of armies: an elephant army, a cavalry army, a chariot army, and an infantry army. Having raised these four kinds of armies, he again personally led his forces to do battle with King Long-Lived of Kosala. King Long-Lived of Kosala heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī had again raised four kinds of armies: an elephant army, a cavalry army, a chariot army, and an infantry army, and having raised these four kinds of armies, was coming to wage war against him. Having heard this, King Long-Lived of Kosala then had this thought: 'I have already defeated him; why should I defeat him again? I have already subdued him; why should I subdue him further? I have already vanquished him; why should I vanquish him again? With merely empty bows alone, I can subdue him.' Having had this thought, King Long-Lived of Kosala remained at ease and did not raise four kinds of armies: no elephant army, no cavalry army, no chariot army, no infantry army, nor did he go out himself. Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī was able to come and defeat him, completely seizing King Long-Lived of Kosala's four kinds of armies: the elephant army, the cavalry army, the chariot army, and the infantry army."

"Thereupon, King Long-Lived of Kosala heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī had come and completely seized his four kinds of armies: the elephant army, the cavalry army, the chariot army, and the infantry army. He then had this thought: 'Fighting is truly dreadful! Fighting is truly evil! Why is that? Having defeated, one will be defeated again; having subdued, one will be subdued again; having vanquished, one will be vanquished again. I should now take only my wife, and together riding in a single chariot, flee to Vārāṇasī.' Thereupon, King Long-Lived of Kosala took only his wife, and together riding in a single chariot, fled to Vārāṇasī. King Long-Lived of Kosala then had this thought: 'I should now go from village to village and town to town, to study and become widely learned.' Having had this thought, King Long-Lived of Kosala went from village to village and town to town, studying and becoming widely learned. Because of his wide learning, his name was changed to 'Long-Lived the Scholar.'

"Long-Lived the Scholar then had this thought: 'What I set out to learn, I have now attained. I should now go to the capital city of Vārāṇasī, dwell in every street and lane, and with a joyful countenance perform wondrous musical arts. In this way, the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī, hearing this, will be greatly delighted and entertained.' Having had this thought, Long-Lived the Scholar went to the capital city of Vārāṇasī, dwelt in every street and lane, and with a joyful countenance performed wondrous musical arts. In this way, the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī, hearing this, were greatly delighted and entertained. Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī's outer circle of attendants heard of this, then the middle circle of attendants, the inner circle of attendants, and the brahmin royal priest, all heard of it in succession. The brahmin royal priest, having heard, summoned him for an audience. Thereupon, Long-Lived the Scholar went to the brahmin royal priest's residence, stood before him, and with a joyful countenance performed wondrous musical arts. The brahmin royal priest, hearing this, was greatly delighted and entertained. Thereupon, the brahmin royal priest told Long-Lived the Scholar: 'From this day forth, you may stay with me. I shall provide for you.' Long-Lived the Scholar replied: 'Venerable sir! I have a wife. What shall be done about her?' The brahmin royal priest answered: 'Scholar! You may bring her to stay at my home. I shall provide for her as well.' Thereupon, Long-Lived the Scholar brought his wife to stay at the brahmin royal priest's home, and the brahmin royal priest provided for them.

"At a later time, Long-Lived the Scholar's wife became troubled at heart and had this thought: 'I wish to see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, so that I may observe them all. I also wish to drink water in which swords have been ground.' Having had this thought, the wife of Long-Lived the Scholar said to Long-Lived the Scholar: 'My heart is troubled and I have had this thought: "I wish to see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, so that I may observe them all. I also wish to drink water in which swords have been ground."' Long-Lived the Scholar immediately told his wife: 'You should not have such thoughts. Why is that? We have been defeated and ruined by King Brahmadatta. How could you possibly see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, so that you may observe them all, and also drink water in which swords have been ground?' His wife replied: 'My lord, if you can obtain this for me, I have hope of living. If you cannot obtain it, I will surely die without doubt.'

"Long-Lived the Scholar then went to the brahmin royal priest's residence, stood before him, his countenance sorrowful and distressed, and with a feeble, unpleasant voice performed various musical arts. The brahmin royal priest, hearing this, could not feel pleased. Thereupon, the brahmin royal priest asked: 'Scholar! Previously, when you stood before me, you performed wondrous musical arts with a joyful countenance, and hearing them, I was greatly delighted and entertained. Why is it that today you stand before me, your countenance sorrowful and distressed, performing musical arts with a feeble, unpleasant voice? Hearing them, I cannot feel pleased. Long-Lived the Scholar! Are you free from bodily illness and mental distress?' Long-Lived the Scholar replied: 'Venerable sir! I have no bodily illness, but I have mental distress. Venerable sir! My wife has become troubled at heart, having had this thought: "I wish to see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, so that I may observe them all. I also wish to drink water in which swords have been ground." I immediately told my wife: "You should not have such thoughts. Why is that? Given our present circumstances, how could you possibly see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, so that you may observe them all, and also drink water in which swords have been ground?" My wife replied to me: "My lord, if you can obtain this for me, I have hope of living. If you cannot obtain it, I will surely die without doubt." Venerable sir! If my wife does not survive, I too will have nothing to live for.'

"The brahmin royal priest asked: 'Scholar! May I see your wife?' He replied: 'Venerable sir! You may see her.' Thereupon, the brahmin royal priest took Long-Lived the Scholar to go visit his wife. At that time, Long-Lived the Scholar's wife was pregnant with a virtuous son. The brahmin royal priest, seeing that Long-Lived the Scholar's wife was pregnant with a virtuous son, knelt on his right knee on the ground, pressed his palms together facing Long-Lived the Scholar's wife, and three times proclaimed: 'Give birth to a King of Kosala! Give birth to a King of Kosala!' He ordered those around him: 'Do not let anyone know of this.' The brahmin royal priest then said: 'Scholar! Do not be distressed. I am able to arrange for your wife to see four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching slowly and ceremoniously past, and I can also arrange for her to drink water in which swords have been ground.'

"Thereupon, the brahmin royal priest went to King Brahmadatta of Kāśī. Having arrived, he said: 'Your Majesty! You should know that a virtuous star has appeared. May Your Majesty assemble the four kinds of armies in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching in slow and ceremonious procession, displaying military might, and grinding swords with water. May Your Majesty personally go out to observe. Your Majesty! If you do this, there will surely be an auspicious response.' King Brahmadatta of Kāśī immediately ordered his minister of war: 'Minister! You should know that a virtuous star has appeared. You should quickly assemble the four kinds of armies in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching in slow and ceremonious procession, displaying military might, and grinding swords with water. I shall personally go out to observe. If this is done, there will surely be an auspicious response.' At that time, the minister of war received the king's command, assembled the four kinds of armies in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching in slow and ceremonious procession, displaying military might, and grinding swords with water. Brahmadatta personally went out to observe.

"Because of this, the wife of Long-Lived the Scholar was able to see the four kinds of armies arrayed in full pageantry, with drawn white shining blades, marching in slow and ceremonious procession, displaying military might. She was also able to drink water in which swords had been ground. Having drunk the water in which swords had been ground, her distress was immediately dispelled. She soon gave birth to a virtuous son, and gave him the name 'Prince Long-Life.' He was entrusted to others to be raised in secret. Gradually he grew up. Prince Long-Life, like those kṣatriya kings born to royal consecration who govern the world and possess great kingdoms, mastered all manner of arts: riding elephants, riding horses, training and racing, archery, hand-to-hand combat, throwing lassos, throwing hooks, riding chariots, and sitting in palanquins. He was well-versed in all these various wondrous arts. In all manner of wondrous tactile matters he was exceptional. Brave, resolute, and surpassing the world, intelligent and outstanding, even regarding the subtle, hidden, and remote, there was nothing he had not thoroughly mastered.

"Thereupon, Brahmadatta heard that King Long-Lived of Kosala had become a scholar and was now going by a changed name and living in the city of Vārāṇasī. Brahmadatta immediately ordered his attendants: 'Go quickly and arrest King Long-Lived of Kosala! Bind his hands behind his back, make him ride a donkey, beat a broken drum making a sound like a donkey's bray. After this proclamation is made throughout the city, take him out through the south gate, seat him below a high stake, and interrogate him.' His attendants received the order, went and arrested King Long-Lived of Kosala, bound his hands behind his back, made him ride a donkey, beat a broken drum making a sound like a donkey's bray, and after this proclamation was made throughout the city, took him out through the south gate, seated him below a high stake, and interrogated him. At that time, Prince Long-Life followed behind his father, now on the left, now on the right, and said to his father: 'Your Majesty, do not be afraid! Your Majesty, do not be afraid! I am right here. I will surely be able to rescue you, I will surely be able to rescue you!' King Long-Lived of Kosala said: 'Child, you must endure! Child, you must endure! Do not give rise to enmity, but only practice kindness.' The people who heard King Long-Lived speak these words asked the king: 'What are you talking about?' The king replied to the crowd: 'This child is intelligent; he will surely understand my words.'

"At that time, Prince Long-Life exhorted the noble and wealthy families in the city of Vārāṇasī: 'Good sirs! Practice giving and cultivate merit. Make prayers for King Long-Lived of Kosala: "By the merit of this giving, may King Long-Lived of Kosala be safe and secure, and may he be liberated."' Thereupon, the noble and wealthy families in the city of Vārāṇasī, exhorted by Prince Long-Life, practiced giving and cultivated merit, making prayers for King Long-Lived of Kosala: 'By the merit of this giving, may King Long-Lived of Kosala be safe and secure, and may he be liberated.' King Brahmadatta of Kāśī heard that the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī were practicing giving and cultivating merit, making prayers for King Long-Lived of Kosala: 'By the merit of this giving, may King Long-Lived of Kosala be safe and secure, and may he be liberated.' Hearing this, he became greatly frightened, and his hair stood on end: 'Could it be that the noble and wealthy families of this city of Vārāṇasī will turn against me? Let that matter be set aside; I must now urgently put an end to this matter first.' Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī ordered his attendants: 'Go quickly and kill King Long-Lived of Kosala, and cut him into seven pieces.' The attendants received the order and immediately went and killed King Long-Lived, cutting him into seven pieces.

"Thereupon, Prince Long-Life exhorted the noble and wealthy families of the city of Vārāṇasī, saying these words: 'Good sirs, look at this! King Brahmadatta of Kāśī is cruel, violent, and without morality. He seized my father, King Long-Lived of Kosala, an innocent man, robbed him of his kingdom, treasury, and wealth, and cruelly and unjustly killed him, cutting him into seven pieces. Good sirs, please go and with new silk and fine cloth gather my father's remains, take the seven pieces of his body, heap together all manner of incense and fragrant wood, and cremate him. Erect a shrine for him. And compose a letter for me to Brahmadatta saying: "Prince Long-Life, son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, speaks thus: Do you not fear that in the future this will bring calamity upon your sons and grandsons?"' Thereupon, the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī, exhorted by Prince Long-Life, went with new silk and fine cloth to gather the remains, took the seven pieces of the body, heaped together all manner of incense and fragrant wood, and cremated him. They erected a shrine for him, and also composed a letter to Brahmadatta saying: 'Prince Long-Life, son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, speaks thus: Do you not fear that in the future this will bring calamity upon your sons and grandsons?'

"Thereupon, the wife of King Long-Lived told Prince Long-Life: 'You should know that this King Brahmadatta of Kāśī is cruel, violent, and without morality. He seized your father, King Long-Lived of Kosala, an innocent man, robbed him of his kingdom, treasury, and wealth, and cruelly and unjustly killed him, cutting him into seven pieces. Child, come! Let us ride together in a single chariot and flee from Vārāṇasī. If we do not leave, calamity will come upon you.' Thereupon, the wife of King Long-Lived and Prince Long-Life rode together in a single chariot and fled from Vārāṇasī. At that time, Prince Long-Life had this thought: 'I should now go from village to village and town to town, to study and become widely learned.' Having had this thought, Prince Long-Life went from village to village and town to town, studying and becoming widely learned. Because of his wide learning, his name was changed to 'Long-Life the Scholar.'

"Long-Life the Scholar then had this thought: 'What I set out to learn, I have now attained. I should now go to the capital city of Vārāṇasī, dwell in every street and lane, and with a joyful countenance perform wondrous musical arts. In this way, the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī, hearing this, will be greatly delighted and entertained.' Having had this thought, Long-Life the Scholar went to the capital city of Vārāṇasī, dwelt in every street and lane, and with a joyful countenance performed wondrous musical arts. In this way, the noble and wealthy families of Vārāṇasī, hearing this, were greatly delighted and entertained. Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī's outer circle of attendants heard of this, then the middle circle of attendants, the inner circle of attendants, the brahmin royal priest, and so on in succession until King Brahmadatta of Kāśī himself heard of it, and summoned him for an audience.

"Thereupon, Long-Life the Scholar went to King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, stood before him, and with a joyful countenance performed wondrous musical arts. King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, hearing this, was greatly delighted and entertained. Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī said: 'Scholar! From this day forth, you may stay with me. I shall provide for you.' Thereupon, Long-Life the Scholar stayed with him, and King Brahmadatta of Kāśī provided for him. Later he came to trust and rely on him, entrusting everything to him, and even handed his personal bodyguard sword to Long-Life the Scholar.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī ordered his charioteer: 'Prepare the chariot. I wish to go hunting.' The charioteer received the order and promptly prepared the chariot. When it was ready, he returned and reported: 'The chariot is prepared. It is at Your Majesty's pleasure.' Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī rode out in the chariot together with Long-Life the Scholar. Long-Life the Scholar then had this thought: 'This King Brahmadatta of Kāśī is cruel, violent, and without morality. He seized my father, King Long-Lived of Kosala, an innocent man, robbed him of his kingdom, treasury, and wealth, and cruelly and unjustly killed him, cutting him into seven pieces. I should now steer the chariot so that it becomes separated from the four kinds of armies, each going to a different place.' Having had this thought, Long-Life the Scholar steered the chariot away from the four kinds of armies, each going to a different place.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, having endured the hardships of the road, oppressed by wind and heat, tormented, thirsty, weary, and exhausted, wished to sleep. He dismounted from the chariot and lay down to sleep, resting his head on Long-Life the Scholar's lap. Thereupon, Long-Life the Scholar had this thought: 'This King Brahmadatta of Kāśī is cruel, violent, and without morality. He seized my father, an innocent man, robbed him of his kingdom, treasury, and wealth, and cruelly and unjustly killed him, cutting him into seven pieces. Yet today he is already in my hands. I should now take my revenge.' Having had this thought, Long-Life the Scholar drew the sharp sword and placed it at King Brahmadatta of Kāśī's neck, saying: 'I will now kill you! I will now kill you!' Long-Life the Scholar then had this thought: 'What I am doing is wrong. Why is that? I recall that my father, when he was below the stake long ago, said to me at the end of his life: "Child, you must endure! Child, you must endure! Do not give rise to enmity, but only practice kindness."' Remembering this, he lifted the sword and returned it to its sheath.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī dreamed that he saw the son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, Prince Long-Life, drawing a sharp sword and placing it at his neck, saying: 'I will now kill you! I will now kill you!' Seeing this, he was frightened and his hair stood on end. He quickly awoke in alarm, rose up, and said to Long-Life the Scholar: 'You should know, in my dream I saw the son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, Prince Long-Life, drawing a sharp sword and placing it at my neck, saying: "I will now kill you! I will now kill you!"' Long-Life the Scholar, hearing this, replied: 'Your Majesty, do not be afraid! Your Majesty, do not be afraid! Why is that? That son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, Prince Long-Life, is none other than myself. Your Majesty! I had this thought: "King Brahmadatta of Kāśī is cruel, violent, and without morality. He seized my father, an innocent man, robbed him of his kingdom, treasury, and wealth, and cruelly and unjustly killed him, cutting him into seven pieces. Yet today he is already in my hands. I should now take my revenge." Your Majesty! I drew the sharp sword and placed it at the king's neck, saying: "I will now kill you! I will now kill you!" Your Majesty! I then had this thought: "What I am doing is wrong. Why is that? I recall that my father, when he was below the stake long ago, said to me at the end of his life: 'Child, you must endure! Child, you must endure! Do not give rise to enmity, but only practice kindness.'" Remembering this, I lifted the sword and returned it to its sheath.'

"King Brahmadatta of Kāśī said: 'Child! When you say, "Child, you must endure! Child, you must endure!" I already understand this meaning. But when you also say, "Do not give rise to enmity, but only practice kindness," what does this mean?' Prince Long-Life answered: 'Your Majesty! "Do not give rise to enmity, but only practice kindness" refers precisely to this.' King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, hearing this, said: 'Child! From this day forth, all the territories under my rule I give entirely to you. Your father's original kingdom I return to you. Why is that? What you have done is exceedingly difficult: you have spared my life.' Prince Long-Life, hearing this, replied: 'Your Majesty's original kingdom still belongs to Your Majesty. My father's original kingdom, you may return to me.'

"Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī and Prince Long-Life rode back together to Vārāṇasī. Having entered the city of Vārāṇasī, he sat on the main throne and told his ministers: 'If you were to see the son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, Prince Long-Life, what would you do?' The ministers, hearing this, some replied: 'Your Majesty! If we saw him, we would cut off his hands.' Others said: 'Your Majesty! If we saw him, we would cut off his feet.' Others said: 'We would take his life.' King Brahmadatta of Kāśī told his ministers: 'If you wish to see the son of King Long-Lived of Kosala, Prince Long-Life, this is he. You must not harbor any ill will toward this young man. Why is that? What this young man has done is exceedingly difficult: he has spared my life.' Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśī bathed Prince Long-Life with a royal bath, anointed him with royal perfumes, dressed him in royal garments, seated him on a golden throne, gave him his daughter in marriage, and returned his original kingdom to him."

"Bhikṣus! Those kings, the kṣatriya consecrated rulers, being lords of great kingdoms, governing the world, themselves practiced forbearance and also praised forbearance; themselves practiced kindness and also praised kindness; themselves practiced generosity and also praised generosity. Bhikṣus! You too should be like this. Having gone forth in faith, having left the household to live the homeless life, training in the Way, you should practice forbearance and also praise forbearance; practice kindness and also praise kindness; practice generosity and also praise generosity."

Thereupon, the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had said, some said: "The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, should just leave us alone for now. Those ones disparage us; how can we not disparage them in return?"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One was not pleased with the conduct, manners, training, and practice of the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī. He rose from his seat and spoke these verses:

"With manifold words and speech,
They destroy the most honored community.
When the noble Sangha is being destroyed,
There is no one who can reprove and stop it.
Even when bodies are shattered unto death,
When elephants, cattle, horses, and wealth are seized,
When kingdoms are destroyed and utterly ruined,
They can still reconcile and make peace.
How much less for your petty insults,
Should you be unable to bring about harmony?
If one does not contemplate the true meaning,
How can enmity ever cease?
With reproach, blame, and harsh words of censure,
One who can bring about harmony:
If one contemplates the true meaning,
Enmity will surely cease.
If with quarrels one tries to stop quarrels,
In the end one never sees them stopped;
Only through forbearance can quarrels be stopped:
This is a dharma worthy of reverence.
Anger directed at the wise and true person,
Worthless words spoken from the mouth,
Slandering the sage and muni:
This is base and lowly, not wisdom.
'Others do not understand the meaning;
Only I alone can know.'
If there are those who understand the meaning,
Their anger will then be extinguished.
If one obtains calm companions,
Wise ones who cultivate good together,
Abandoning the views one formerly held,
One follows them joyfully at all times.
If one does not obtain calm companions,
A wise one cultivates good alone,
Like a king who rules his realm with stern justice,
Like an elephant dwelling alone in the wilds.
Going alone, do not commit evil,
Like an elephant alone in the wilds.
Going alone, doing good is superior;
Do not associate with the wicked.
If in one's training one does not find a good friend,
Nor one who is equal to oneself,
One should firmly resolve to dwell alone;
Do not associate with the wicked."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken these verses, using his supernatural power of psychic travel, rose through the air and departed, arriving at the village of Bālakaloṇakāra. In the village of Bālakaloṇakāra, there was the venerable Bhagu, a son of the Śākya clan, who day and night did not sleep, diligently practiced the Way, his conduct always settled, abiding in the factors of the path. The venerable son of the Śākya clan saw the Buddha coming from afar, and having seen him, went to greet him. He took the Buddha's robe and bowl, spread out a seat for the Buddha, and fetched water to wash his feet. After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat on the seat of the venerable Bhagu, son of the Śākya clan. Having sat, he asked: "Bhikṣu Bhagu! Are you always at ease and without wants?"

The venerable Bhagu, son of the Śākya clan, replied: "World-Honored One! I am always at ease and without wants."

The World-Honored One asked again: "Bhikṣu Bhagu! How are you at ease and without wants?"

The venerable Bhagu replied: "World-Honored One! I do not sleep day or night, diligently practice the Way, my conduct is always settled, and I abide in the factors of the path. World-Honored One! In this way I am always at ease and without wants."

The World-Honored One then thought: "This son of a good family travels in ease and happiness. I should now teach him the Dharma." Having had this thought, he taught the Dharma to the venerable Bhagu, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing him in joy. With immeasurable skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing him in joy. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed, going to the Protected Monastery Grove. Entering the Protected Monastery Grove, he went to the base of a tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged.

The World-Honored One then thought: "I am now free from those bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, who constantly quarrel, subdue one another, hate one another, are angry with one another, and dispute. I do not fondly think of that direction, namely the place where the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī dwell."

At that time, there was a great elephant, king of its herd, which had left the herd of elephants and wandered alone. It too came to the Protected Monastery Grove. Entering the Protected Monastery Grove, it went to a sāla tree and stood leaning against it. At that time, the great elephant had this thought: "I am now free from that herd of elephants: the female elephants, the male elephants, and the great and small young elephants. That herd of elephants always walks ahead, trampling the grass and muddying the water. At those times, I eat that trampled grass and drink that muddied water. Now I eat fresh grass and drink clear water."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, with the knowledge of others' minds, knew the thoughts in the great elephant's mind, and spoke this verse:

"One elephant and another elephant are alike,
With fully developed body and tusks.
Their minds are likewise in accord,
Both delighting in dwelling alone in the forest."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One departed from the Protected Monastery Grove, gathered his robe and took up his bowl, and went to the Pārileyyaka Monastery Grove. At that time, in the Pārileyyaka Monastery Grove there were three sons of good families dwelling together: the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila. The conduct of those venerable ones was as follows: Whichever one returned first from the alms round would spread out the seats, fetch water, set out the foot-washing basin, place the foot-washing step and the foot-wiping cloth, and set up the water jug and the hand-washing vessel. If the food obtained from the alms round could be entirely consumed, he would eat it all. If there was any left over, he would put it in a container, cover it, and set it aside. After eating, he would put away his bowl, wash his hands and feet, place his sitting cloth on his shoulder, and enter the room for quiet meditation. Whichever one returned later from the alms round, if he could eat all his food, he would eat it all. If it was not enough, he would take the previous leftovers to supplement his meal. If there was any left over, he would pour it out on clean ground or into water without insects. He would clean the food vessel, wash and wipe it, and put it away in its place. He would fold up the seats, put away the foot-washing step, put away the foot-wiping cloth, put away the foot-washing basin, the water jug, and the hand-washing vessel. He would sweep and sprinkle the dining hall, cleaning and removing refuse until it was clean. Then he would put away his robe and bowl, wash his hands and feet, place his sitting cloth on his shoulder, and enter the room for quiet meditation. Those venerable ones, when it came to the afternoon, whichever one first rose from quiet meditation, if he saw the water jug or hand-washing vessel empty and without water, he would carry it and go to fetch water. If he could carry it himself, he would lift it, bring it back, and place it to one side. If he could not carry it alone, he would beckon with his hand to another bhikṣu, and the two of them would carry it together and place it to one side. They did not speak to each other, nor did they question each other. Those venerable ones would assemble once every five days, either to discuss the Dharma together or to sit in noble silence.

Thereupon, the grove keeper, seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, called out to block him, saying: "Śramaṇa! Śramaṇa! Do not enter this grove. Why is that? In this grove there are now three sons of good families: the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila. If they see you, they might be displeased."

The World-Honored One said: "Grove keeper! If they see me, they will surely be pleased, not displeased."

Thereupon, the venerable Anuruddha, seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, immediately rebuked the grove keeper: "Grove keeper! Do not block the World-Honored One. Grove keeper! Do not stop the Well-Gone One. Why is that? It is our Master who has come, our Well-Gone One who has come." The venerable Anuruddha went out to welcome the World-Honored One and took the Buddha's robe and bowl. The venerable Nandiya spread out a seat for the Buddha. The venerable Kimbila fetched water for the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having washed his hands and feet, sat on the seat that the venerable ones had prepared. Having sat down, he asked: "Anuruddha! Are you always at ease and without wants?"

The venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One! I am always at ease and without wants."

The World-Honored One asked again: "Anuruddha! How are you at ease and without wants?"

The venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One! I have this thought: 'I have great good fortune, I have great merit, in that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.' World-Honored One! I constantly practice loving-kindness in bodily actions toward these fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they are present or not, equally without difference. I practice loving-kindness in verbal actions and loving-kindness in mental actions, whether they are present or not, equally without difference. World-Honored One! I have this thought: 'I should now abandon my own mind and follow the minds of these worthy ones.' World-Honored One! I then abandon my own mind and follow the minds of these worthy ones. World-Honored One! I have never had even a single thought of displeasure. World-Honored One! In this way I am always at ease and without wants." When the venerable Nandiya was asked, his answer was also the same.

He then asked the venerable Kimbila: "Are you always at ease and without wants?"

The venerable Kimbila replied: "World-Honored One! I am always at ease and without wants."

He asked: "Kimbila! How are you at ease and without wants?" The venerable Kimbila replied: "World-Honored One! I have this thought: 'I have great good fortune, I have great merit, in that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.' World-Honored One! I constantly practice loving-kindness in bodily actions toward these fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they are present or not, equally without difference. I practice loving-kindness in verbal actions and loving-kindness in mental actions, whether they are present or not, equally without difference. World-Honored One! I have this thought: 'I should now abandon my own mind and follow the minds of these worthy ones.' World-Honored One! I then abandon my own mind and follow the minds of these worthy ones. World-Honored One! I have never had even a single thought of displeasure. World-Honored One! In this way I am always at ease and without wants."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Anuruddha! If you all are always harmonious, at ease and without quarreling, of one mind and one teacher, blending together like water and milk, have you attained any superhuman state with progressive levels of peaceful abiding?"

The venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One! Indeed, we are always harmonious, at ease and without quarreling, of one mind and one teacher, blending together like water and milk, and we have attained a superhuman state with progressive levels of peaceful abiding. World-Honored One! We attain radiance and see forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away."

The World-Honored One said: "Anuruddha! You have not fully understood this characteristic, namely that you attain radiance and see forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away. Anuruddha! Before I had attained awakening to the unsurpassed, true, and perfect Way, I too attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I practiced with diligence and without laziness, my body was settled, I had right mindfulness and right knowledge, I was free of delusion, and I attained one-pointed concentration. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'I practice with diligence and without laziness, my body is settled, I have right mindfulness and right knowledge, I am free of delusion, and I have attained one-pointed concentration. If there is no path in the world, can I see and know it?' In my mind arose this affliction of doubt. Because of this affliction of doubt, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of inattention. Because of this affliction of inattention, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, nor shall I let the affliction of inattention arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of perception of bodily illness. Because of this affliction of perception of bodily illness, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, nor shall I let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of drowsiness. Because of this affliction of drowsiness, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, nor shall I let the affliction of drowsiness arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of excessive effort. Because of this affliction of excessive effort, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! It is just like a strong man who grasps a fly too tightly, and the fly immediately dies. Just so, Anuruddha! In my mind arose the affliction of excessive effort. Because of this affliction of excessive effort, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, nor shall I let the affliction of excessive effort arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of excessive laxity. Because of this affliction of excessive laxity, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! It is just like a strong man who grasps a fly too loosely, and the fly flies away. Anuruddha! In my mind arose the affliction of excessive laxity. Because of this affliction of excessive laxity, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, nor shall I let the affliction of excessive laxity arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of fear. Because of this affliction of fear, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! It is just like a person traveling on a road when hostile bandits come from all four directions. That person, seeing them, becomes fearful and terrified, and all the hair on his body stands on end. Just so, Anuruddha! In my mind arose the affliction of fear. Because of this affliction of fear, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive laxity arise, nor shall I let the affliction of fear arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of elation. Because of this affliction of elation, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! It is just like a person who originally sought one treasure trove and all at once found four treasure troves. Seeing them, he became elated and overjoyed. Just so, Anuruddha! In my mind arose the affliction of elation. Because of this affliction of elation, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away. Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive laxity arise, I shall not let the affliction of fear arise, nor shall I let the affliction of elation arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of conceit. Because of this affliction of conceit, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive laxity arise, I shall not let the affliction of fear arise, I shall not let the affliction of elation arise, nor shall I let the affliction of conceit arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of diverse perceptions. Because of this affliction of diverse perceptions, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive laxity arise, I shall not let the affliction of fear arise, I shall not let the affliction of elation arise, I shall not let the affliction of conceit arise, nor shall I let the affliction of diverse perceptions arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms, but that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.

"Anuruddha! I again had this thought: 'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose concentration and my eye to be extinguished, and once the eye is extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon fades away?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'In my mind arose the affliction of not observing forms. Because of this affliction of not observing forms, I lost concentration and my eye was extinguished, and once the eye was extinguished, the radiance I had previously attained and the seeing of forms, that radiance and seeing of forms soon faded away.' Anuruddha! I must now resolve: 'I shall not let doubt arise in my mind, I shall not let the affliction of inattention arise, I shall not let the affliction of perception of bodily illness arise, I shall not let the affliction of drowsiness arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive effort arise, I shall not let the affliction of excessive laxity arise, I shall not let the affliction of fear arise, I shall not let the affliction of elation arise, I shall not let the affliction of conceit arise, I shall not let the affliction of diverse perceptions arise, nor shall I let the affliction of not observing forms arise.' Anuruddha! Wishing not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practiced. Because of dwelling in seclusion alone, my mind without negligence, and diligently practicing, I attained radiance and saw forms. Anuruddha! If the affliction of doubt arose in my mind and was purified, the afflictions of inattention, perception of bodily illness, drowsiness, excessive effort, excessive laxity, fear, elation, conceit, diverse perceptions, and not observing forms were all likewise purified."

"Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'I should cultivate three kinds of concentration: I should cultivate concentration with initial and sustained application of thought, I should cultivate concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought, and I should cultivate concentration without initial or sustained application of thought.' Anuruddha! I then cultivated three kinds of concentration: I cultivated concentration with initial and sustained application of thought, I cultivated concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought, and I cultivated concentration without initial or sustained application of thought. When I cultivated concentration with initial and sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought. In this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration with initial and sustained application of thought. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct. When I cultivated concentration with initial and sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration without initial or sustained application of thought. In this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration with initial and sustained application of thought. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct.

"Anuruddha! When I cultivated concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration with initial and sustained application of thought. In this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct. When I cultivated concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration without initial or sustained application of thought. In this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct.

"Anuruddha! When I cultivated concentration without initial or sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration with initial and sustained application of thought. In this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration without initial or sustained application of thought. Anuruddha!
