At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct. When I cultivated concentration without initial or sustained application of thought, my mind would incline toward concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought. In this way, I would not lose this knowledge and vision. Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I cultivated concentration without initial or sustained application of thought. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct.

"Anuruddha! There were times when I knew radiance but did not see forms. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'What is the cause and condition by which I know radiance but do not see forms?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'If I attend to the characteristic of radiance but do not attend to the characteristic of form, then at that time I know radiance but do not see forms.' Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I knew radiance but did not see forms. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct. Anuruddha! There were times when I saw forms but did not know radiance. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'What is the cause and condition by which I see forms but do not know radiance?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'If I attend to the characteristic of form but do not attend to the characteristic of radiance, then at that time I know forms but do not know radiance.' Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I knew forms but did not know radiance. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct.

"Anuruddha! There were times when I knew radiance only slightly and also saw forms only slightly. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'What is the cause and condition by which I know radiance only slightly and also see forms only slightly?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'If I enter concentration only slightly, then because of entering concentration only slightly, my eye is only slightly purified. Because my eye is only slightly purified, I know radiance only slightly and also see forms only slightly.' Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I knew radiance only slightly and also saw forms only slightly. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct. Anuruddha! There were times when I knew radiance extensively and also saw forms extensively. Anuruddha! I had this thought: 'What is the cause and condition by which I know radiance extensively and also see forms extensively?' Anuruddha! I then had this thought: 'If I enter concentration extensively, then because of entering concentration extensively, my eye is extensively purified. Because my eye is extensively purified, I know radiance extensively and also see forms extensively.' Anuruddha! Knowing this to be so, for an entire day, an entire night, and an entire day-and-night, I knew radiance extensively and also saw forms extensively. Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct.

"Anuruddha! When the affliction of doubt arose in my mind and was purified, and the afflictions of inattention, perception of bodily illness, drowsiness, excessive effort, excessive laxity, fear, elation, conceit, diverse perceptions, and not observing forms arose in my mind and were all purified; when concentration with initial and sustained application of thought was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when concentration without initial application but with slight sustained application of thought was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when concentration without initial or sustained application of thought was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when one-pointed concentration was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when mixed concentration was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when limited concentration was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, when the vast and immeasurable concentration was cultivated and thoroughly cultivated; then my knowledge and vision were born, supremely pure. I was directed toward concentration, settled in it, and diligently cultivated the factors of the path. I knew as it truly is: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what needed to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming.' Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this abiding and conduct."

The Buddha spoke thus. The venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimbila heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, and respectfully practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on the Origin of King Long-Lived, First.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgamas)
## Fascicle 18

---

**(75) The Sūtra on the Pure Way of Life**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain to you the purification of the way of life. Listen well, listen well, and attend carefully. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the purification of the way of life? A bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening. This is called the purification of the way of life.

"How does a bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, cultivate and develop the seven factors of awakening? A bhikṣu cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, which depends on seclusion, depends on dispassion, depends on cessation, and issues in relinquishment. He cultivates the investigation-of-dharmas factor of awakening, the effort factor of awakening, the joy factor of awakening, the tranquility factor of awakening, the concentration factor of awakening, and the equanimity factor of awakening, each of which depends on seclusion, depends on dispassion, depends on cessation, and issues in relinquishment.

"This is how a bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(76) The Sūtra on [郁伽支羅] Ukkācelā**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Vajji, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and arrived at Ukkācelā, where he stayed on the bank of the Ganges River.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Suppose there was a person who was being carried away by the current of the Ganges River. He sang a song, hoping to cross to the other shore. What do you think, bhikṣus? Could that person, by singing a song, cross to the other shore of the Ganges?"

The bhikṣus replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "In the same way, there are some brahmins and śramaṇas who recite various mantras, various songs and chants, seeking thereby to attain the destruction of suffering. Can these brahmins and śramaṇas, through reciting various mantras, various songs and chants, attain the destruction of suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "No, World-Honored One."

"Suppose, bhikṣus, a person wishes to cross the Ganges River. Being wise, strong, and capable, he abandons this shore and swims across to the other shore. In the same way, if a bhikṣu depends on morality, is established in morality, and cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening, he can attain the destruction of suffering. This is called the purification of the way of life."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke verses:

"Some people recite prayers and mantras,
Seeking to cross the great flood.
But the flood cannot be crossed this way;
By cultivating the Way, one reaches the other shore.

"One who has right mindfulness and right concentration,
Who cultivates and practices the noble path,
Can destroy all bonds and fetters,
And surely attain the destruction of suffering.

"This person is not the same
As those who merely recite mantras and songs.
They are far removed from the deathless Dharma;
They cannot attain the end of suffering.

"A bhikṣu who, diligent and mindful,
Cultivates the seven factors of awakening,
Having abandoned all bonds and fetters,
Attains the unconditioned, nirvāṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(77) The Sūtra on the Three Clans**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three clans that are noble and supreme among devas and humans. What are the three?

"Bhikṣus, if a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Persons, Teacher of Devas and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, this is the first clan that is noble and supreme among devas and humans.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is well-proclaimed, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally known by the wise. This is the second clan that is noble and supreme among devas and humans.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, the Sangha of the Tathāgata's disciples is well-practiced, practiced on the straight path, practiced on the true path, practiced on the proper path: namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the third clan that is noble and supreme among devas and humans.

"Just as, bhikṣus, among all animals, the lion, king of beasts, is considered supreme; in the same way, these three clans are noble and supreme among devas and humans."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke verses:

"When one attains birth as a human,
The supreme clan among humans
Is the clan of the kṣatriyas.
Among devas and humans,
One perfect in knowledge and conduct is supreme.

"In the first watch of the day, in the middle watch,
Or in the last watch of the night,
One who arises and diligently practices,
Attains the supreme, peaceful bliss.

"The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,
These three are the supreme clans.
The Buddha is unsurpassed among beings;
The Dharma is the most excellent teaching;
The Sangha is the supreme field of merit.

"If one makes offerings to the Buddha,
The Dharma, and the Sangha,
One's merit is immeasurable,
Like the great ocean, deep and vast."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(78) The Sūtra on Brahmā's Request**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Once in the past, the Brahmā King Sahāmpati came to where I was, bowed his head at my feet, withdrew to one side, and said to me: 'World-Honored One, a bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, and who cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening, this is called the purification of the way of life.'

"After Brahmā King Sahāmpati said this, he bowed his head at my feet, circumambulated me three times, and departed.

"Bhikṣus, the Brahmā King Sahāmpati has right faith and is one who rightly speaks. A bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, and who cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening, this is called the purification of the way of life.

"How does a bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, cultivate and develop the seven factors of awakening? A bhikṣu cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, which depends on seclusion, depends on dispassion, depends on cessation, and issues in relinquishment. He cultivates the investigation-of-dharmas factor of awakening, the effort factor of awakening, the joy factor of awakening, the tranquility factor of awakening, the concentration factor of awakening, and the equanimity factor of awakening, each of which depends on seclusion, depends on dispassion, depends on cessation, and issues in relinquishment.

"This is how a bhikṣu who depends on morality, who is established in morality, cultivates and develops the seven factors of awakening."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(79) The Sūtra on the Sick [Greater]**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at the Pipphali Cave, and he was sick, afflicted, and suffering gravely.

Then the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to where the Venerable Mahākassapa was. He sat down on a prepared seat, and said to the Venerable Mahākassapa: "Kassapa, how are you? Is your sickness bearable? Are your painful feelings decreasing and not increasing? Are there signs of improvement?"

Mahākassapa replied: "World-Honored One, I cannot bear it. My painful feelings are great and ever increasing, not decreasing. There are no signs of improvement."

The Buddha said: "Kassapa, I have taught the seven factors of awakening, which when cultivated and developed, lead to knowledge and vision, lead to awakening, lead to nirvāṇa. What are the seven?

"The mindfulness factor of awakening, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of awakening, the effort factor of awakening, the joy factor of awakening, the tranquility factor of awakening, the concentration factor of awakening, and the equanimity factor of awakening. These are the seven factors of awakening, which when cultivated and developed, lead to knowledge and vision, lead to awakening, lead to nirvāṇa.

"Kassapa, these are the seven factors of awakening that I have truly taught. Do you agree?"

Mahākassapa said: "World-Honored One, these are truly the seven factors of awakening."

The Buddha said: "Kassapa, is it so?"

Mahākassapa replied: "World-Honored One, it is truly so."

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having heard the Buddha's teaching of the seven factors of awakening, was delighted and rejoiced. His sickness immediately diminished, and he recovered from that illness.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Mahākassapa, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(80) The Sūtra on the Sick [Lesser]**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Mahācunda was sick, afflicted, and suffering gravely.

Then the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to where the Venerable Mahācunda was. The World-Honored One sat down on a prepared seat, and said to the Venerable Mahācunda: "Cunda, how are you? Is your sickness bearable? Are your painful feelings decreasing and not increasing? Are there signs of improvement?"

Mahācunda replied: "World-Honored One, I cannot bear it. My painful feelings are great and ever increasing, not decreasing. There are no signs of improvement."

The Buddha said: "Cunda, I have taught the seven factors of awakening, which when cultivated and developed, lead to knowledge and vision, lead to awakening, lead to nirvāṇa. What are the seven?

"The mindfulness factor of awakening, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of awakening, the effort factor of awakening, the joy factor of awakening, the tranquility factor of awakening, the concentration factor of awakening, and the equanimity factor of awakening. These are the seven factors of awakening, which when cultivated and developed, lead to knowledge and vision, lead to awakening, lead to nirvāṇa.

"Cunda, these are the seven factors of awakening that I have truly taught. Do you agree?"

Mahācunda said: "World-Honored One, these are truly the seven factors of awakening."

The Buddha said: "Cunda, is it so?"

Mahācunda replied: "World-Honored One, it is truly so."

Then the Venerable Mahācunda, having heard the Buddha's teaching of the seven factors of awakening, was delighted and rejoiced. His sickness immediately diminished, and he recovered from that illness.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Mahācunda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(81) The Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Body**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after their midday meal, gathered in the assembly hall and discussed the following: "How marvelous, friends! Mindfulness of the body, when cultivated and developed, has great fruit and great benefit."

At that time, the World-Honored One was in quiet meditation, and with his purified divine ear, surpassing that of humans, heard the bhikṣus discussing this matter. The World-Honored One then rose from his meditation, went to the assembly hall, and sat down on a prepared seat. He addressed the bhikṣus: "What were you discussing just now?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One, after our midday meal, we gathered here and discussed: 'How marvelous, friends! Mindfulness of the body, when cultivated and developed, has great fruit and great benefit.' This was the discussion that had not yet concluded when the World-Honored One arrived."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, how does cultivating and developing mindfulness of the body have great fruit and great benefit?

"Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, while walking, knows that he is walking. While standing, he knows that he is standing. While sitting, he knows that he is sitting. While lying down, he knows that he is lying down. Whatever posture the body is in, he knows it as it actually is.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, or he contemplates the body externally, or he contemplates the body both internally and externally. He abides contemplating the arising nature of the body, or he abides contemplating the passing away nature of the body, or he abides contemplating both the arising and passing away nature of the body. His mindfulness that 'there is a body' is established in him to the extent necessary for knowledge and continuous mindfulness. He abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world. This is how a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, when breathing in a long breath, knows that he breathes in long. When breathing out a long breath, he knows that he breathes out long. When breathing in a short breath, he knows that he breathes in short. When breathing out a short breath, he knows that he breathes out short. He trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.' He trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains: 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation.' He trains: 'I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, diligent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure with regard to the world.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu clearly comprehends when going forth and when returning. He clearly comprehends when looking ahead and when looking aside. He clearly comprehends when bending and when stretching his limbs. He clearly comprehends when wearing his saṅghāṭī robe, his other robes, and carrying his bowl. He clearly comprehends when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting. He clearly comprehends when urinating and defecating. He clearly comprehends when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, fat, grease, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fluid of the joints, and urine.'

"Just as if there were a bag with two openings, full of various kinds of grain, such as rice, paddy, green beans, cow peas, sesame, and husked rice. A person with good eyesight, having opened it, would review it: 'This is rice, this is paddy, these are green beans, these are cow peas, this is sesame, this is husked rice.' In the same way, a bhikṣu reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, with regard to its elements: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'

"Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, were to sit at a crossroads and divide it into portions; in the same way, a bhikṣu reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, with regard to its elements: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, as though he were seeing a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and festering, compares this same body with that: 'This body of mine is of the same nature; it will become like that and cannot escape this fate.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, as though he were seeing a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, wild dogs, jackals, or various kinds of worms, compares this same body with that: 'This body of mine is of the same nature; it will become like that and cannot escape this fate.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, as though he were seeing a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, connected by sinews; or a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, connected by sinews; or a skeleton without flesh or blood, connected by sinews; or bones disconnected, scattered in all directions: here a hand bone, there a foot bone, here a shin bone, there a thigh bone, here a hip bone, there a spine bone, here a rib bone, there a chest bone, here an arm bone, there a shoulder bone, here a neck bone, there a jaw bone, here a skull; compares this same body with that: 'This body of mine is of the same nature; it will become like that and cannot escape this fate.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, as though he were seeing a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, bones white as shells, or bluish like pigeon feathers, or reduced to powder; compares this same body with that: 'This body of mine is of the same nature; it will become like that and cannot escape this fate.'

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first dhyāna.

"He permeates and suffuses this body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by the joy and happiness born of seclusion. Just as a skilled bathhouse attendant or his apprentice, having sprinkled bath powder into a metal basin, kneads it together with water, sprinkling it again and again, so that the ball of bath powder is pervaded, saturated, and suffused inside and out with moisture, yet does not drip. In the same way, a bhikṣu permeates and suffuses this body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, with the stilling of initial thought and sustained thought, with inner confidence and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and abides in the second dhyāna.

"He permeates and suffuses this body with the joy and happiness born of concentration. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by the joy and happiness born of concentration. Just as a spring-fed lake, with no inlet from the east, west, south, or north, and no replenishment from rainfall, yet the spring of cool water from within the lake wells up and permeates and suffuses the entire lake with cool water, so that there is no part of the lake that is not suffused. In the same way, a bhikṣu permeates and suffuses this body with the joy and happiness born of concentration. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by the joy and happiness born of concentration.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of joy, abides equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body. He enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as: 'Equanimous and mindful, one abides in happiness.'

"He permeates and suffuses this body with happiness free from joy. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by happiness free from joy. Just as in a lotus pond, the blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, not rising above the water, are nourished within the water, and from their roots to their tips are permeated and suffused by cool water, so that there is no part of them that is not suffused. In the same way, a bhikṣu permeates and suffuses this body with happiness free from joy. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by happiness free from joy.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the prior disappearance of elation and displeasure, enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

"He sits, suffusing his body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by a pure, bright mind. Just as a person might sit covered from head to foot with a white cloth, so that there is no part of his body that is not covered by the white cloth. In the same way, a bhikṣu sits, suffusing his body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by a pure, bright mind.

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way, and develops it repeatedly, he obtains the following eighteen merits:

"He is able to endure suffering, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, and harsh speech. He is able to endure bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and life-threatening. This is the first merit.

"He abandons sensual desire. Sensual desire does not overcome his mind. This is the second merit.

"He abandons ill will. Ill will does not overcome his mind. This is the third merit.

"He abandons sloth and torpor. Sloth and torpor do not overcome his mind. This is the fourth merit.

"He abandons restlessness and remorse. Restlessness and remorse do not overcome his mind. This is the fifth merit.

"He abandons doubt. Doubt does not overcome his mind. This is the sixth merit.

"He is courageous and not timid. This is the seventh merit.

"He is able to endure hardship. This is the eighth merit.

"He can enter the first dhyāna at will, without difficulty. This is the ninth merit.

"He can enter the second dhyāna at will, without difficulty. This is the tenth merit.

"He can enter the third dhyāna at will, without difficulty. This is the eleventh merit.

"He can enter the fourth dhyāna at will, without difficulty. This is the twelfth merit.

"He can exercise various supernormal powers: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one. He appears and vanishes. He goes unhindered through walls, through fences, through mountains, as though through space. He dives in and out of the earth as though it were water. He walks on water without sinking as though it were earth. Seated cross-legged, he travels through space like a bird. With his hand, he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. He exercises mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world. This is the thirteenth merit.

"With the divine ear element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds: divine and human, whether far or near. This is the fourteenth merit.

"He encompasses and knows the minds of other beings, of other persons, with his own mind. He knows a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust. He knows a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred. He knows a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion. He knows a contracted mind as contracted, a distracted mind as distracted. He knows a great mind as great, a narrow mind as narrow. He knows a surpassable mind as surpassable, an unsurpassable mind as unsurpassable. He knows a concentrated mind as concentrated, an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated. He knows a liberated mind as liberated, an unliberated mind as unliberated. This is the fifteenth merit.

"He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, the formation and dissolution of many eons of world-formation and dissolution: 'There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, ate such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, and had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance, ate such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, and had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and particulars. This is the sixteenth merit.

"With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings dying and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and in bad destinations. He understands how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings, who were endowed with wrong conduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions under the influence of wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell. But these beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions under the influence of right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings dying and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and in bad destinations, and he understands how beings fare according to their actions. This is the seventeenth merit.

"By the destruction of the taints, in this very life, he enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge. This is the eighteenth merit.

"Bhikṣus, these are the eighteen merits obtained by a bhikṣu who cultivates and develops mindfulness of the body. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train thus: 'We will cultivate mindfulness of the body and develop it repeatedly.' Bhikṣus, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(82) The Sūtra on Supporting**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu has faith but lacks morality, then for him it is incomplete on that side; he should make an aspiration: 'How can I attain both faith and morality?' If a bhikṣu has faith and morality but lacks learning, then for him it is incomplete on that side; he should make an aspiration: 'How can I attain faith, morality, and also learning?' If a bhikṣu has faith, morality, and learning but lacks generosity, then for him it is incomplete on that side; he should make an aspiration: 'How can I attain faith, morality, learning, and also generosity?' If a bhikṣu has faith, morality, learning, and generosity but lacks wisdom, then for him it is incomplete on that side; he should make an aspiration: 'How can I attain faith, morality, learning, generosity, and also wisdom?'

"Bhikṣus, it is just as when a bull has one foot but lacks the other three feet; for it, one side is incomplete. In the same way, if a bhikṣu has faith but lacks morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, then for him it is incomplete on that side.

"Bhikṣus, it is just as when a bull has four complete feet; in the same way, if a bhikṣu is endowed with faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, then for him all sides are complete."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(83) The Sūtra on the Long-Lived King (Part One)**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Kauśāmbī, at the Ghosita Monastery.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling and disputing, attacking each other with the weapons of the tongue, unable to reach reconciliation.

Then a certain bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and reported to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are quarreling and disputing, attacking each other with the weapons of the tongue, unable to reach reconciliation."

The World-Honored One then told a bhikṣu: "Go to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī and tell them: 'The World-Honored One calls you.'"

That bhikṣu received the instruction, went to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, and said: "The World-Honored One calls you."

The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī then went to the World-Honored One, bowed their heads at his feet, and sat down to one side. The World-Honored One addressed them: "Bhikṣus, stop! Do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not attack each other."

Among them, one bhikṣu said to the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One, the Lord of the Dharma, set this aside. May the World-Honored One dwell at ease in the present happiness of the Dharma. We shall be known on account of this quarreling, disputing, and mutual attacking."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus, stop! Do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not attack each other."

A second time, that bhikṣu said to the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One, the Lord of the Dharma, set this aside. May the World-Honored One dwell at ease in the present happiness of the Dharma. We shall be known on account of this quarreling, disputing, and mutual attacking."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣus, stop! Do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not attack each other."

A third time, that bhikṣu said to the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One, the Lord of the Dharma, set this aside. May the World-Honored One dwell at ease in the present happiness of the Dharma. We shall be known on account of this quarreling, disputing, and mutual attacking."

The World-Honored One then told the bhikṣus: "Once upon a time, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled the country of Kāśī, prosperous, wealthy, with abundant followers, and his land was vast and peaceful. King Brahmadatta possessed the four kinds of army: elephant forces, cavalry, chariot forces, and infantry. He was endowed with wisdom and all manner of skill.

"His minister, the prince Dīghāvu's father, King Dīghīti, ruled the country of Kośala, but was not prosperous, not wealthy, without abundant followers, and his land was not vast.

"King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, leading the four kinds of army, invaded and attacked King Dīghīti of Kośala. King Dīghīti heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, leading the four kinds of army, was coming to invade and attack. King Dīghīti knew that his own forces could not resist, so he took his chief queen and fled, abandoning his kingdom, and went into hiding, wandering from place to place.

"King Brahmadatta of Kāśī then conquered the country of Kośala and seized its territory and treasury.

"King Dīghīti, together with his queen, went into hiding in disguise and traveled to the city of Benares in the country of Kāśī. They lodged in a potter's dwelling on the outskirts of the city, living in concealment.

"After some time, King Dīghīti's queen became pregnant. She had a craving: she wished to see an army arrayed in formation at dawn, and to drink the water used to wash swords. She said to King Dīghīti: 'I am pregnant and have a craving. I wish to see an army arrayed in formation at dawn, and to drink the water used to wash swords. If I do not obtain this, I may die.'

"King Dīghīti said: 'You are in great distress. Where could I obtain such things? If we are discovered, both of us will die.'

"The queen replied: 'If I do not obtain this, I will surely die.'

"Then King Dīghīti went to King Brahmadatta's court brahmin and said to him: 'I tell you, sir, there is a woman who is pregnant and has a craving. She wishes to see an army arrayed in formation at dawn, and to drink the water used to wash swords. If she does not obtain this, she may die.'

"The court brahmin went to King Brahmadatta and said: 'Your Majesty should know that there is a woman who is pregnant and has a craving. She wishes to see an army arrayed in formation at dawn, and to drink the water used to wash swords. If she does not obtain this, she may die. May Your Majesty grant this.'

"King Brahmadatta then, at dawn, arrayed his army in formation and had swords washed. He allowed that woman to come, see the army, and drink the water used to wash swords.

"King Dīghīti brought his queen, who saw the army arrayed in formation at dawn and drank the water used to wash swords. Her craving was satisfied.

"Later, the queen gave birth to a son, handsome and fine in appearance. They named him Dīghāvu, meaning 'long-lived.' Not long after his birth, King Dīghīti thought: 'This place is perilous. If we are discovered, all three of us, father, mother, and son, will be killed.' He then sent Prince Dīghāvu away to be raised outside the city.

"Prince Dīghāvu grew up, and he was intelligent and wise, skilled in all manner of arts. He could learn an art after hearing it just once.

"At that time, King Dīghīti had a barber who later came to serve King Brahmadatta. This barber recognized King Dīghīti in the potter's dwelling and went to King Brahmadatta and said: 'Your Majesty should know that King Dīghīti of Kośala, together with his queen, is hiding in disguise in a potter's dwelling on the outskirts of Benares.'

"King Brahmadatta then ordered his men to seize King Dīghīti and his queen, bind them, place them on a donkey, lead them through the city, exit by the southern gate, and there, at the execution ground, cut them to pieces, in order to display his might.

"The men received the order, seized King Dīghīti and his queen, bound them tightly, placed them on a donkey, and led them through the streets of Benares, beating a drum and making proclamation, proceeding toward the southern gate.

"At that time, Prince Dīghāvu thought: 'It has been a long time since I have seen my father and mother. I shall go and visit them.' He then entered the city of Benares and saw, from a distance, his father and mother, bound, placed on a donkey, being paraded through the streets, about to be taken to the execution ground.

"Prince Dīghāvu went up close. King Dīghīti saw Prince Dīghāvu from afar and said: 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far, and do not look near. Enmity is not resolved by enmity. Enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity.'

"The people nearby said: 'This old man, placed on a donkey, has gone mad. Who is he talking to? Who is Dīghāvu? What does he mean by "do not look far, do not look near" and "enmity is not resolved by enmity, enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity"?'

"King Dīghīti said a second and a third time: 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far, and do not look near. Enmity is not resolved by enmity. Enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity.'

"King Brahmadatta's men then took King Dīghīti and his queen out by the southern gate, and at the execution ground, cut them to pieces.

"Prince Dīghāvu then went and bribed the executioners with wine, got them drunk, and when they were insensible, he recovered the bodies of his father and mother. He prepared a funeral pyre, cremated them, made offerings of flowers and incense, joined his palms, and circumambulated the pyre.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta was in the upper chamber of his palace. From afar, he saw Prince Dīghāvu in the charnel ground, making offerings of flowers and incense, joining his palms, and circumambulating the pyre. King Brahmadatta thought: 'That person must surely be a relative or family member of King Dīghīti. If he is not seized, there will be future trouble. Who could that be?'

"Prince Dīghāvu, filled with grief and sorrow, departed and went into the forest. He wept freely, wiped away his tears, and then returned to the city of Benares, going to the elephant stable. There he became an attendant to the elephant keeper, and early each morning he would rise and sing while grooming the elephants.

"King Brahmadatta heard the pleasant sound of singing early in the morning and asked: 'Who is singing so pleasantly early in the morning?'

"His attendants replied: 'Your Majesty, it is a young man, an attendant in the elephant stable, who sings pleasantly early in the morning while grooming the elephants.'

"King Brahmadatta then had that young man brought to serve him personally. Prince Dīghāvu was diligent and quick, rising before and sleeping after the king. He did whatever was required. He spoke gently and was agreeable in manner. Before long, King Brahmadatta appointed him to an intimate position of trust.

"Once, King Brahmadatta went out hunting with Prince Dīghāvu as his charioteer. In the course of the hunt, they became separated from the army and attendants. King Brahmadatta was weary and said to Dīghāvu: 'I am tired and wish to rest awhile. I shall lie down and sleep.' He then lay down, resting his head on Dīghāvu's lap, and fell asleep.

"Prince Dīghāvu thought: 'This King Brahmadatta brought great suffering upon us. He seized our kingdom, our territory, and our treasury. He killed my father and mother. This is my enemy. Now is the time for revenge.' He then drew his sword.

"But then Dīghāvu remembered his father's words: 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far, and do not look near. Enmity is not resolved by enmity. Enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity.' He thought about this and then sheathed his sword.

"A second time, he thought of taking revenge and drew his sword. Again he remembered his father's words and sheathed the sword. A third time, the same thing happened.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta, in his sleep, was seized by fear and suddenly awoke, trembling. Prince Dīghāvu asked: 'Your Majesty, why are you frightened? Why do you awaken trembling?'

"King Brahmadatta said: 'I had a dream. I dreamed that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti of Kośala, was about to kill me with a sword. That is why I am frightened.'

"Prince Dīghāvu then grasped the king's head with his left hand, drew his sword with his right hand, and said to King Brahmadatta: 'I am Dīghāvu, son of King Dīghīti of Kośala. You brought great suffering upon us. You seized our kingdom, our territory, and our treasury. You killed my father and mother. You are my enemy. Now is the time for revenge.'

"King Brahmadatta then fell at Prince Dīghāvu's feet and said: 'Dear Dīghāvu, spare my life! Dear Dīghāvu, spare my life!'

"Prince Dīghāvu said: 'I would not dare to harm Your Majesty. Rather, may Your Majesty spare my life!'

"King Brahmadatta said: 'I grant you your life. And you must grant me my life.'

"Thus they granted each other their lives and clasped hands and made a solemn oath.

"King Brahmadatta then said to Prince Dīghāvu: 'What did your father mean when, at the time of his death, he said to you: "Do not look far, and do not look near. Enmity is not resolved by enmity. Enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity"? What do these words mean?'

"Prince Dīghāvu replied: 'Your Majesty, my father's words "do not look far" mean "do not maintain prolonged enmity," because he did not want my enmity to continue long. His words "do not look near" mean "do not be hasty in breaking with friends," because he did not want me to alienate friends too quickly. His words "enmity is not resolved by enmity, enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity" mean this: Your Majesty killed my father and mother. If I were to take revenge on Your Majesty, then Your Majesty's supporters would want to kill me, and my supporters would want to kill them. Enmity would never cease. But now Your Majesty has granted me my life, and I have granted Your Majesty your life. This is the meaning of "enmity is not resolved by enmity, enmity is resolved only by the absence of enmity."'

"King Brahmadatta then thought: 'How marvelous! Prince Dīghāvu is so wise that he could understand the brief words of his father in their full meaning.' He was overjoyed. He returned Prince Dīghāvu's kingdom to him, returned his territory, and gave him his daughter in marriage. They became friends.

"The Buddha then said to the bhikṣus: 'These kings, who wielded the rod and wielded the sword, could still practice patience and gentleness toward each other. How much more should you, bhikṣus, who have gone forth in faith from the household life into homelessness in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya! You should practice patience and gentleness, shining brightly in this Dharma and Vinaya. Bhikṣus, stop! Do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not attack each other.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(84) The Sūtra on No Thorns**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Forest, at the Double-Roofed Hall.

At that time, the Licchavi Mahānāma came to where the World-Honored One was, bowed his head at the World-Honored One's feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I have long understood the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One in this way: concentration is disrupted by a thorn, and the lack of thorns is the absence of what disrupts concentration. World-Honored One, what are the thorns of concentration, and what is the absence of thorns?"

The World-Honored One said: "Mahānāma, for one who delights in company, who is pleased with company, who is devoted to the delight of company, who delights in crowds, who is pleased with crowds, who is devoted to the delight of crowds; company and crowds are a thorn to him. For one who delights in seclusion, the delight in seclusion is without thorns.

"For one who delights in talk, for one who delights in sleep, for one who delights in socializing, for one who is without restraint of the faculties, for one who is immoderate in eating, for one who is devoted to the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night; each of these is a thorn. Their absence is without thorns.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, the first dhyāna has thorns. What are the thorns of the first dhyāna? Sound is a thorn to the first dhyāna. For one who has entered the first dhyāna, sound is the thorn.

"The second dhyāna has thorns. What are the thorns of the second dhyāna? Initial thought and sustained thought are thorns to the second dhyāna.

"The third dhyāna has thorns. What are the thorns of the third dhyāna? Joy is a thorn to the third dhyāna.

"The fourth dhyāna has thorns. What are the thorns of the fourth dhyāna? Breathing in and breathing out are thorns to the fourth dhyāna.

"The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling has thorns. What are its thorns? Perception and feeling are thorns to the attainment of cessation.

"Sensual desire is a thorn. Ill will is a thorn. Delusion is a thorn. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train thus: 'We will be without the thorn of sensual desire, without the thorn of ill will, without the thorn of delusion.' Bhikṣus, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Licchavi Mahānāma and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(85) The Sūtra on the True Person**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall explain to you the dharma of one who is not a true person and the dharma of a true person. Listen well, listen well, and attend carefully. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the dharma of one who is not a true person? A person who is not a true person comes from a high-ranking family. Having come from a high-ranking family, he thinks: 'I come from a high-ranking family, but others do not come from high-ranking families.' He thereby exalts himself and disparages others. This is the dharma of one who is not a true person.

"A true person reflects thus: 'It is not on account of coming from a high-ranking family that one cuts off greed, hatred, and delusion. Even if a person does not come from a high-ranking family, if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma and practices on the right path, he should be honored and praised for that.' He thus places the practice of the path foremost and does not exalt himself or disparage others on account of family. This is the dharma of a true person.

"Furthermore, a person who is not a true person, being handsome in appearance, or wealthy, or learned in much, or being a keeper of the precepts, or being a forest-dweller, or being a wearer of refuse-rag robes, or being a beggar for alms, or practicing the dhūta austerities, or having attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, or having attained the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, the base of neither perception nor non-perception; on account of each of these, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is the dharma of one who is not a true person.

"A true person reflects thus: 'It is not on account of attaining the base of neither perception nor non-perception that one cuts off greed, hatred, and delusion. Even if a person has not attained the base of neither perception nor non-perception, if he practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma and practices on the right path, he should be honored and praised for that.' He thus places the practice of the path foremost and does not exalt himself or disparage others on account of any attainment. This is the dharma of a true person."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(86) The Sūtra on Explaining the Exposition**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good expression, complete and pure, the pure practice of the holy life. That is, the 'Exposition on the True Person and the Not True Person.' Listen well, listen well, and attend carefully. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is a person who is not a true person? There is a person who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, harbors ill will, and holds wrong views. This is called a person who is not a true person.

"What is a person who is a not-true-person yet even worse than a not-true-person? There is a person who himself kills living beings and also encourages others to kill living beings. He himself takes what is not given and also encourages others to take what is not given. He himself engages in sexual misconduct and also encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct. He himself speaks falsely and also encourages others to speak falsely. He himself speaks divisively and also encourages others to speak divisively. He himself speaks harshly and also encourages others to speak harshly. He himself engages in idle chatter and also encourages others to engage in idle chatter. He himself is covetous and also encourages others to be covetous. He himself harbors ill will and also encourages others to harbor ill will. He himself holds wrong views and also encourages others to hold wrong views. This is called a person who is a not-true-person yet even worse than a not-true-person.

"What is a true person? There is a person who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, is without ill will, and holds right views. This is called a true person.

"What is a true person who is even better than a true person? There is a person who himself abstains from killing living beings and also encourages others to abstain from killing living beings. He himself abstains from taking what is not given and also encourages others to abstain from taking what is not given. He himself abstains from sexual misconduct and also encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct. He himself abstains from false speech and also encourages others to abstain from false speech. He himself abstains from divisive speech and also encourages others to abstain from divisive speech. He himself abstains from harsh speech and also encourages others to abstain from harsh speech. He himself abstains from idle chatter and also encourages others to abstain from idle chatter. He himself is without covetousness and also encourages others to be without covetousness. He himself is without ill will and also encourages others to be without ill will. He himself holds right views and also encourages others to hold right views. This is called a true person who is even better than a true person."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 18 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Fascicle 18 of the Madhyamāgama

## (73) Sūtra on Devas, Second in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Cedi country, staying in the Jālini Grove by the waterside.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Before I had attained the awakening of the unsurpassed, true, and right path, I had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms. However, I had not yet assembled together with those devas, had not exchanged greetings with them, had not engaged in discourse with them, and had not had dialogue with them.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them. However, I did not know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, or their births.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births. However, I did not know what those devas ate, or how they experienced pleasure and pain.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also knew what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain. However, I did not know how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, or when their lives end.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also know how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also knew what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also knew how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end. However, I did not know that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also know how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also know that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also knew what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also knew how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also knew that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there. However, I did not know those devas among those various classes of devas.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also know how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also know that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there; and also know those devas among those various classes of devas. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also knew what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also knew how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also knew that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there; and also knew those devas among those various classes of devas. However, I did not know whether, among those heavens above, I had formerly been born there or had never been born there.

"I then had this thought: 'If only I could produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance perceive forms, and also assemble together with those devas, exchange greetings with them, engage in discourse with them, and have dialogue with them; and also know the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also know how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also know that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there; and also know those devas among those various classes of devas; and also know whether, among those heavens above, I had formerly been born there or had never been born there. In this way my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.' For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I then attained the radiance and perceived forms, and also assembled together with those devas, exchanged greetings with them, engaged in discourse with them, and had dialogue with them; and also knew the clan names of those devas, their personal names, and their births; and also knew what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain; and also knew how long-lived those devas are, how long they endure, and when their lives end; and also knew that those devas, having performed such and such deeds, died from here and were reborn there; and also knew those devas among those various classes of devas; and also knew whether, among those heavens above, I had formerly been born there or had never been born there.

"If I had not rightly known and attained these eight practices, then I could not have definitively declared that I had attained them, nor could I have known that I had awakened to the unsurpassed, true, and right path. I would not have been able to surpass in this world all the devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins. I would not have attained liberation and the various liberations. My mind would not have been free from all delusions. I would not have known as it truly is that birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further becoming. But because I rightly knew and attained these eight practices, I could definitively declare that I had attained them, and I knew that I had awakened to the unsurpassed, true, and right path. In this world, I have surpassed all devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins. I have attained liberation and the various liberations. My mind is free from all delusions. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming; this I know as it truly is."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Devas, Second

---

## (74) Sūtra on the Eight Thoughts, Third in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Bhagga country, at Crocodile Hill in the Bhesakalā Grove, the Deer Park.

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was in the Cedi country, in the Jālini Grove by the waterside. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, sitting quietly in a secluded place and contemplating, had these thoughts in his mind: "The path comes from desirelessness, not from having desires. The path comes from contentment, not from insatiability. The path comes from seclusion, not from delighting in gatherings, not from dwelling in gatherings, not from joining gatherings. The path comes from diligent effort, not from laziness. The path comes from right mindfulness, not from wrong mindfulness. The path comes from concentration of mind, not from a distracted mind. The path comes from wisdom, not from foolishness."

Then the World-Honored One, knowing through his knowledge of others' minds what the Venerable Anuruddha was thinking, contemplating, and practicing in his mind, entered the appropriate concentration. Through the appropriate concentration, just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, in that instant the World-Honored One disappeared from the Bhesakalā Grove at Crocodile Hill in the Bhagga country and appeared in the Jālini Grove by the waterside in the Cedi country, before the Venerable Anuruddha. Then the World-Honored One emerged from concentration and praised the Venerable Anuruddha, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Anuruddha! You were sitting quietly in a secluded place, contemplating, and had these thoughts in your mind: 'The path comes from desirelessness, not from having desires. The path comes from contentment, not from insatiability. The path comes from seclusion, not from delighting in gatherings, not from dwelling in gatherings, not from joining gatherings. The path comes from diligent effort, not from laziness. The path comes from right mindfulness, not from wrong mindfulness. The path comes from concentration of mind, not from a distracted mind. The path comes from wisdom, not from foolishness.'

"Anuruddha! You should receive from the Tathāgata an additional eighth thought of a great person. Having received it, you should contemplate: the path comes from non-frivolity, from delighting in non-frivolity, from practicing non-frivolity; not from frivolity, not from delighting in frivolity, not from practicing frivolity. Anuruddha! If you accomplish these eight thoughts of a great person, you will certainly be able to, separated from desires and separated from unwholesome states, attain up to the fourth jhāna and dwell therein. Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then just as a king or a king's minister has a fine chest filled with all kinds of garments, and in the morning if he wishes to put on certain clothes he takes them and puts them on, and at midday or in the afternoon if he wishes to put on clothes he takes them and puts them on, freely as he pleases; Anuruddha, you likewise, wearing rag-robes as your foremost garment, your mind free from desire, practicing and dwelling in this conduct.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then just as a king or a king's minister has a fine cook who prepares various pure, wonderful, sweet, and delicious dishes; Anuruddha, you likewise, always going on alms rounds as your foremost sustenance, your mind free from desire, practicing and dwelling in this conduct.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then just as a king or a king's minister has fine houses, or storied pavilions and palaces; Anuruddha, you likewise, dwelling at the foot of a tree as your foremost shelter, your mind free from desire, practicing and dwelling in this conduct.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then just as a king or a king's minister has a fine bed and seat, spread with woolen rugs and felt mats, covered with brocade and gauze, with a body-lining blanket, pillows at both ends, and coverings of kālinga, pavarapaccattharaṇa; Anuruddha, you likewise, with a grass seat or a leaf seat as your foremost seat, your mind free from desire, practicing and dwelling in this conduct.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then if you travel to the east, you will certainly find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction. If you travel to the south, west, or north, you will certainly find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, I would not even say that your wholesome qualities merely remain as they are, let alone say that they would decline. Rather, day and night your wholesome qualities will increase and not decline.

"Anuruddha! If you accomplish the eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, you will certainly attain one of two fruits: either in this present life you will attain final knowledge, or if there is a remainder, you will attain the state of a non-returner.

"Anuruddha! You should accomplish these eight thoughts of a great person and also obtain these four higher states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, and then undertake the summer retreat in the Jālini Grove by the waterside in the Cedi country."

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for the Venerable Anuruddha, encouraging and inspiring him, bringing about joy, and through immeasurable skillful means taught the Dharma for him, encouraging and inspiring him. Having brought about joy, he entered the appropriate concentration. Through the appropriate concentration, just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, in that instant the World-Honored One disappeared from the Jālini Grove by the waterside in the Cedi country and appeared at the Bhesakalā Grove at Crocodile Hill in the Bhagga country.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was holding a fan and attending the Buddha. Then the World-Honored One emerged from concentration, turned around, and said: "Ānanda! If there are any bhikṣus staying at Crocodile Hill in the Bhesakalā Grove, have all of them assemble in the lecture hall. Once they have assembled, come back and inform me."

The Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha's instruction, bowed at his feet, then went and proclaimed the order: "All bhikṣus staying at Crocodile Hill in the Bhesakalā Grove are to assemble in the lecture hall." When they had assembled, he went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! All the bhikṣus staying at Crocodile Hill in the Bhesakalā Grove have been assembled in the lecture hall. May the World-Honored One know that the time is appropriate."

Then the World-Honored One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the lecture hall. Before the assembly of bhikṣus, he arranged his seat and sat down. Having sat down, he said: "Bhikṣus! I will now teach you the eight thoughts of a great person. Listen carefully and reflect well upon them." The bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.

The Buddha said: "The eight thoughts of a great person are as follows: The path comes from desirelessness, not from having desires. The path comes from contentment, not from insatiability. The path comes from seclusion, not from delighting in gatherings, not from dwelling in gatherings, not from joining gatherings. The path comes from diligent effort, not from laziness. The path comes from right mindfulness, not from wrong mindfulness. The path comes from concentration of mind, not from a distracted mind. The path comes from wisdom, not from foolishness. The path comes from non-frivolity, from delighting in non-frivolity, from practicing non-frivolity; not from frivolity, not from delighting in frivolity, not from practicing frivolity.

"How does the path come from desirelessness, not from having desires? A bhikṣu attains desirelessness; he himself knows he has attained desirelessness, but does not make it known to others that he is desireless. He attains contentment, attains seclusion, attains diligent effort, attains right mindfulness, attains concentration of mind, attains wisdom, attains non-frivolity. He himself knows he has attained non-frivolity, but does not desire to make it known to others that he is desireless. This is called the path coming from desirelessness, not from having desires.

"How does the path come from contentment, not from insatiability? A bhikṣu practices contentment: in clothing, taking only enough to cover the body; in food, taking only enough to sustain the body. This is called the path coming from contentment, not from insatiability.

"How does the path come from seclusion, not from delighting in gatherings, not from dwelling in gatherings, not from joining gatherings? A bhikṣu practices seclusion, accomplishing two kinds of seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind. This is called the path coming from seclusion, not from delighting in gatherings, not from dwelling in gatherings, not from joining gatherings.

"How does the path come from diligent effort, not from laziness? A bhikṣu constantly practices diligent effort, abandoning what is unwholesome, cultivating wholesome states, always rousing his resolve, singleminded and firm, establishing the foundation of wholesome qualities, not abandoning skillful means. This is called the path coming from diligent effort, not from laziness.

"How does the path come from right mindfulness, not from wrong mindfulness? A bhikṣu contemplates the inner body as body, contemplates inner feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas. This is called the path coming from right mindfulness, not from wrong mindfulness.

"How does the path come from concentration of mind, not from a distracted mind? A bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from unwholesome states, attains up to the fourth jhāna and dwells therein. This is called the path coming from concentration of mind, not from a distracted mind.

"How does the path come from wisdom, not from foolishness? A bhikṣu cultivates wisdom, contemplating the dharma of arising and passing away, and attains such knowledge, noble wisdom that is bright and penetrating, clearly discerning and understanding, by which he rightly brings suffering to an end. This is called the path coming from wisdom, not from foolishness.

"How does the path come from non-frivolity, from delighting in non-frivolity, from practicing non-frivolity; not from frivolity, not from delighting in frivolity, not from practicing frivolity? A bhikṣu's mind constantly extinguishes frivolity, delighting in abiding in nirvāṇa without remainder, his mind always joyfully abiding, with gladness and mental resolution.
