This is called the path coming from non-frivolity, from delighting in non-frivolity, from practicing non-frivolity; not from frivolity, not from delighting in frivolity, not from practicing frivolity.

"Bhikṣus! The bhikṣu Anuruddha, having accomplished these eight thoughts of a great person, then undertook the summer retreat in the Jālini Grove by the waterside in the Cedi country. I taught him this instruction, and he dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Dwelling in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, that which a son of good family aims for when he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to train in the path, namely the unsurpassed completion of the holy life, he in this very life knew for himself, realized for himself, and personally witnessed, dwelling in its attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming'; this he knew as it truly is."

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha attained the state of an arhat, his mind rightly liberated. Having become a senior elder, he then at that time spoke these verses:

"From afar he knew my thoughts,
The unsurpassed teacher of the world.
With body upright, mind entering concentration,
Through space he suddenly arrived.
According to what was in my mind,
He taught and went beyond it;
All Buddhas delight in non-frivolity,
Far removed from all frivolity.
Having learned the Dharma from him,
I joyfully dwelt in the true Dharma.
Attaining the mastery of samādhi,
The task of the Buddha's Dharma is accomplished.
I do not yearn for death,
Nor do I wish for life;
Following the times, accepting what comes,
I stand in right mindfulness and right knowledge.
In the bamboo grove of Vesālī,
My life will end there.
Beneath the bamboo grove,
I will enter nirvāṇa without remainder."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Anuruddha and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Eight Thoughts, Third

---

## (75) Sūtra on the Path of Purification to the Imperturbable, Fourth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Kuru country, at the Kuru town of Kammāssadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Sensual desires are impermanent, false, and deceptive; they are the dharma of deception, being mere illusions, deceit, and foolishness. Whether sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether forms of this world or of the next world, all of these are Māra's domain; they are Māra's bait. Because of them, the mind gives rise to immeasurable unwholesome states, including covetousness, ill will, and quarreling, which create obstacles for noble disciples in their training. A well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'As the World-Honored One has said, sensual desires are impermanent, false, and deceptive; they are the dharma of deception, being mere illusions, deceit, and foolishness. Whether sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether forms of this world or of the next world, all of these are Māra's domain; they are Māra's bait. Because of them, the mind gives rise to immeasurable unwholesome states, including covetousness, ill will, and quarreling, which create obstacles for noble disciples in their training.' He then thinks: 'If I could attain a great mind, dwell therein, overcome the world, and master my mind. If I attain a great mind, dwell therein, overcome the world, and master my mind, then my mind would not give rise to immeasurable unwholesome states, including covetousness, ill will, and quarreling, which create obstacles for noble disciples in their training.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the imperturbable. This is called the first teaching of the path of purification to the imperturbable.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'Whatever has form, all of that is the four great elements and what is made from the four great elements. The four great elements are impermanent dharmas; they are suffering and subject to cessation.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the imperturbable. This is called the second teaching of the path of purification to the imperturbable.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'Whether sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether forms of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of forms of this world or of the next world, all such perceptions are impermanent dharmas; they are suffering and subject to cessation. At that time he necessarily attains the perception of the imperturbable.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the imperturbable. This is called the third teaching of the path of purification to the imperturbable.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'Whether perceptions of sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of forms of this world or of the next world, and the perception of the imperturbable, all such perceptions are impermanent dharmas; they are suffering and subject to cessation. At that time he attains the perception of the sphere of nothingness.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the imperturbable. This is called the first teaching of the path of purification to the sphere of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'This world is empty; empty of a self and what belongs to a self; empty of permanence; empty of constancy; empty of lasting endurance; empty of unchanging nature.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the sphere of nothingness here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of nothingness. This is called the second teaching of the path of purification to the sphere of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'I do not act for the sake of others, nor do I act for the sake of myself.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters the sphere of nothingness here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of nothingness. This is called the third teaching of the path of purification to the sphere of nothingness.

"Furthermore, a well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'Whether sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether forms of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of forms of this world or of the next world, and the perception of the imperturbable, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness, all such perceptions are impermanent dharmas; they are suffering and subject to cessation. At that time he attains non-perception.' Through this practice, this training, this cultivation broadly applied, he attains mental purity in that domain. Having attained mental purity in that domain, a bhikṣu either enters non-perception here, or is liberated through wisdom. Later, when his body perishes and life ends, because of his original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of non-perception. This is called the teaching of the path of purification to non-perception."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was holding a fan and attending the Buddha. Then the Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu practices thus, thinking 'There is no self, there is nothing belonging to a self; I shall not exist, what is mine shall not exist; if it previously existed, it is now completely relinquished,' World-Honored One, does a bhikṣu who practices thus completely attain nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! This matter is not definite. Some may attain it, and some may not."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! How does a bhikṣu practice and not attain nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! If a bhikṣu practices thus, thinking 'There is no self, there is nothing belonging to a self; I shall not exist, what is mine shall not exist; if it previously existed, it is now completely relinquished,' and if, Ānanda, that bhikṣu delights in that relinquishment, is attached to that relinquishment, and abides in that relinquishment, then, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who practices thus will certainly not attain nirvāṇa."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu has any grasping, he does not attain nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! If a bhikṣu has any grasping, he certainly will not attain nirvāṇa."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! What does that bhikṣu grasp?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! Among the formations there is a remainder, namely the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, which is the foremost among existences. That bhikṣu grasps this."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! Does that bhikṣu grasp a residual formation?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! Indeed, that bhikṣu grasps a residual formation."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! How does a bhikṣu practice to certainly attain nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! If a bhikṣu practices thus, thinking 'There is no self, there is nothing belonging to a self; I shall not exist, what is mine shall not exist; if it previously existed, it is now completely relinquished,' and if, Ānanda, that bhikṣu does not delight in that relinquishment, is not attached to that relinquishment, and does not abide in that relinquishment, then, Ānanda, a bhikṣu who practices thus will certainly attain nirvāṇa."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu has no grasping, will he certainly attain nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! If a bhikṣu has no grasping, he will certainly attain nirvāṇa."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "The World-Honored One has already taught the path of purification to the imperturbable, has already taught the path of purification to the sphere of nothingness, has already taught the path of purification to non-perception, and has already taught nirvāṇa without remainder. World-Honored One, what is the noble liberation?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! A well-learned noble disciple contemplates thus: 'Whether sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether forms of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of sensual desires of this world or of the next world, whether perceptions of forms of this world or of the next world, and the perception of the imperturbable, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness, and the perception of non-perception, all such perceptions are impermanent dharmas; they are suffering and subject to cessation. This is called one's own existence. Where there is one's own existence, there is birth, aging, sickness, and death. Ānanda! If there is a dharma by which all of this is completely extinguished without remainder and no longer exists, then there is no birth, no aging, no sickness, and no death. A noble one who contemplates thus, if there is that which exists, it is certainly the dharma of liberation. If there is nirvāṇa without remainder, it is called the sweet dew of immortality. Contemplating thus and seeing thus, he certainly attains liberation of mind from the outflow of sensual desire, liberation of mind from the outflow of existence, and liberation of mind from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming; this he knows as it truly is.

"Ānanda! I have now taught you the path of purification to the imperturbable, have taught the path of purification to the sphere of nothingness, have taught the path of purification to non-perception, have taught nirvāṇa without remainder, and have taught the noble liberation. What a venerable teacher should do for his disciples, arising from great compassion, with pity and sympathy, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their peace and happiness, I have already done. You should now do your own part further. Go to secluded places, to the foot of forest trees, to empty and quiet places. Sit in meditation and contemplate. Do not be negligent. Practice with diligent effort, lest you have regrets later. This is my teaching, this is my instruction."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Path of Purification to the Imperturbable, Fourth

---

## (76) Sūtra of Ukkacelā, Fifth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Ukkacelā, on the bank of the Ganges River.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, rising from meditation in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I wish that you would briefly teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, I will dwell in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because of dwelling in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, that which a son of good family aims for when he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to train in the path, namely the unsurpassed completion of the holy life, he will in this very life know for himself, realize for himself, and personally witness, dwelling in its attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming'; this I will know as it truly is."

The World-Honored One replied: "Bhikṣu! You should train as follows: make your mind settled, abiding inwardly without moving, with immeasurable wholesome cultivation. Then contemplate the inner body as body, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate the outer body as body, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate the inner and outer body as body, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Bhikṣu! Such concentration should be well cultivated when going and when coming, when standing, when sitting, when lying down, when sleeping, when waking, and when both sleeping and waking, it should also be cultivated. Furthermore, you should also cultivate the concentration with initial and sustained thought, the concentration without initial thought but with slight sustained thought, cultivate the concentration without initial or sustained thought, and also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by one-pointedness, and cultivate the concentration accompanied by equanimity.

"Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, then, bhikṣu, you should further cultivate contemplation of inner feelings as feelings, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate outer feelings as feelings, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate inner and outer feelings as feelings, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Bhikṣu! Such concentration should be well cultivated when going and when coming, when standing, when sitting, when lying down, when sleeping, when waking, and when both sleeping and waking, it should also be cultivated. Furthermore, you should also cultivate the concentration with initial and sustained thought, the concentration without initial thought but with slight sustained thought, cultivate the concentration without initial or sustained thought, and also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by one-pointedness, and cultivate the concentration accompanied by equanimity.

"Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, then, bhikṣu, you should further cultivate contemplation of the inner mind as mind, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate the outer mind as mind, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate the inner and outer mind as mind, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Bhikṣu! Such concentration should be well cultivated when going and when coming, when standing, when sitting, when lying down, when sleeping, when waking, and when both sleeping and waking, it should also be cultivated. Furthermore, you should also cultivate the concentration with initial and sustained thought, the concentration without initial thought but with slight sustained thought, cultivate the concentration without initial or sustained thought, and also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by one-pointedness, and cultivate the concentration accompanied by equanimity.

"Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, then, bhikṣu, you should further cultivate contemplation of inner dharmas as dharmas, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate outer dharmas as dharmas, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Then contemplate inner and outer dharmas as dharmas, practicing with utmost diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right knowledge, skillfully governing your mind, freeing it from covetousness, with no sorrow in the mind. Bhikṣu! Such concentration should be well cultivated when going and when coming, when standing, when sitting, when lying down, when sleeping, when waking, and when both sleeping and waking, it should also be cultivated. Furthermore, you should also cultivate the concentration with initial and sustained thought, the concentration without initial thought but with slight sustained thought, cultivate the concentration without initial or sustained thought, and also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by one-pointedness, and cultivate the concentration accompanied by equanimity.

"Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, then, bhikṣu, your mind should dwell together with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and dwelling therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely, your mind should dwell together with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein. Likewise with compassion, sympathetic joy, and your mind dwelling together with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein.

"Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, then if you travel to the east, you will certainly find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction. If you travel to the south, west, or north, you will certainly find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction. Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, I would not even say that your wholesome qualities merely remain as they are, let alone say that they would decline. Rather, day and night your wholesome qualities will increase and not decline. Bhikṣu! If you cultivate this concentration extremely well, you will certainly attain one of two fruits: either in this present life you will attain final knowledge, or if there is a remainder, you will attain the state of a non-returner."

Then that bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Receiving and upholding the Buddha's teaching, he dwelt in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because of dwelling in seclusion, alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, that which a son of good family aims for when he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to train in the path, namely the unsurpassed completion of the holy life, he in this very life knew for himself, realized for himself, and personally witnessed, dwelling in its attainment: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming"; this he knew as it truly is. That venerable one, having known the Dharma and reached its realization, attained the state of an arhat.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra of Ukkacelā, Fifth

---

## (77) Sūtra of the Three Clansmen of Sāketa, Sixth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Sāketa, staying in the Green Forest.

At that time, in Sāketa there were three sons of good family: the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila. All were young and had newly gone forth to train, having come to enter this true Dharma not long ago. At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "These three sons of good family are all young and have newly gone forth to train, having come to enter this true Dharma not long ago. Do these three sons of good family take delight in practicing the holy life in this true Dharma and Vinaya?" At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.

The World-Honored One again asked the bhikṣus a second and third time: "These three sons of good family are all young and have newly gone forth to train, having come to enter this true Dharma not long ago. Do these three sons of good family take delight in practicing the holy life in this true Dharma and Vinaya?" At that time, the bhikṣus again remained silent a second and third time and did not answer.

Then the World-Honored One himself asked the three sons of good family, addressing the Venerable Anuruddha: "You three sons of good family are all young and have newly gone forth to train, having come to enter this true Dharma not long ago. Anuruddha! Do you take delight in practicing the holy life in this true Dharma and Vinaya?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One! We delight in this true Dharma and practice the holy life."

The World-Honored One asked: "Anuruddha! When you were young, youthful boys with pure black hair, bodies strong and vigorous, delighting in play, delighting in frequent bathing, adorning and cherishing your bodies, afterward your relatives and parents all loved you dearly, wept and cried, and did not wish to let you go forth to train in the path. Yet you were still able to shave off your hair and beards, put on kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to train in the path. Anuruddha! You did not go forth to train in the path out of fear of kings, nor out of fear of bandits, nor out of fear of debt, nor out of fear and dread, nor because of poverty and inability to make a living. Rather, it was because of weariness with birth, aging, sickness, death, weeping, sorrow, and suffering, or perhaps wishing to reach the far shore of the great mass of suffering. Anuruddha! Did you not go forth to train in the path with such a mind?"

He answered: "Indeed so."

"Anuruddha! If a son of good family goes forth to train in the path with such a mind, do you know the means by which immeasurable wholesome qualities are attained?"

The Venerable Anuruddha said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. May you please teach it. Having heard it, we will come to understand the meaning broadly."

The Buddha then said: "Anuruddha! Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I will explain its meaning for you." Anuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Anuruddha! If one is overcome by desire and entangled in unwholesome states, one does not attain the bliss of equanimity and the supreme tranquility. His mind gives rise to increasing covetousness, ill will, and drowsiness; his mind gives rise to discontent; his body gives rise to restlessness; he eats excessively; and his mind becomes worried. That bhikṣu then cannot endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the oppression of wind and sun. He cannot endure harsh words or beating with sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point of life ending, all that is unpleasant he cannot bear. Why? Because he is overcome by desire, entangled in unwholesome states, and does not attain the bliss of equanimity and the supreme tranquility. If one is free from desire and not entangled in unwholesome states, one certainly attains the bliss of equanimity and the supreme tranquility. His mind does not give rise to increasing covetousness, ill will, or drowsiness; his mind does not give rise to discontent; his body does not give rise to restlessness; he does not eat excessively; and his mind is not worried. That bhikṣu then can endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the oppression of wind and sun. He can endure harsh words and beating with sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point of life ending, all that is unpleasant he can bear. Why? Because he is not overcome by desire, is not entangled in unwholesome states, and has attained the bliss of equanimity and the supreme tranquility."

The World-Honored One asked: "Anuruddha! For what purpose does the Tathāgata sometimes reject certain things, sometimes use certain things, sometimes endure certain things, sometimes stop certain things, and sometimes expel certain things?"

The Venerable Anuruddha said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. May you please teach it. Having heard it, we will come to understand the meaning broadly."

The Buddha then said: "Anuruddha! Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I will explain its meaning for you." Anuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Anuruddha! It is not because the Tathāgata has not exhausted or does not know the outflows that defile and pollute, that are the basis of future existence, that bring the bitter fruit of affliction, and that are the causes of birth, aging, sickness, and death, that he sometimes rejects, sometimes uses, sometimes endures, sometimes stops, and sometimes expels certain things. Anuruddha! The Tathāgata does so only because of this body, because of the six sense bases, and because of the life span that he sometimes rejects, sometimes uses, sometimes endures, sometimes stops, and sometimes expels certain things. Anuruddha! It is for this purpose that the Tathāgata sometimes rejects, sometimes uses, sometimes endures, sometimes stops, and sometimes expels certain things."

The World-Honored One asked: "Anuruddha! For what purpose does the Tathāgata dwell in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, without evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation?"

The Venerable Anuruddha said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. May you please teach it. Having heard it, we will come to understand the meaning broadly."

The Buddha then said: "Anuruddha! Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I will explain its meaning for you." Anuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Anuruddha! It is not because the Tathāgata has not yet obtained what he wishes to obtain, has not yet acquired what he wishes to acquire, or has not yet realized what he wishes to realize, that he dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, without evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation. Anuruddha! The Tathāgata dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, without evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation, for two purposes only: first, for his own present happy dwelling; second, out of compassion for people of future generations. There may be people of future generations who emulate the Tathāgata in dwelling in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, without evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation. Anuruddha! It is for this purpose that the Tathāgata dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, without evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation."

The World-Honored One asked: "Anuruddha! For what purpose does the Tathāgata, when a disciple has passed away, declare that such a one was reborn in such a place, that such a one was reborn in such a place?"

The Venerable Anuruddha said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. May you please teach it. Having heard it, we will come to understand the meaning broadly."

The Buddha then said: "Anuruddha! Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I will explain its meaning for you." Anuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Anuruddha! It is not merely for the sake of speaking to people, nor to deceive people, nor wishing to make people pleased, that the Tathāgata, when a disciple has passed away, declares that such a one was reborn in such a place, that such a one was reborn in such a place. Anuruddha! The Tathāgata does so only for the sake of faithful sons of good family and daughters of good family who have the utmost faith, the utmost love, and the utmost delight, so that after hearing this true Dharma and Vinaya, their minds may aspire to emulate such and such examples. Therefore, when a disciple has passed away, he declares that such a one was reborn in such a place, that such a one was reborn in such a place.

"If a bhikṣu hears that a certain venerable one has passed away in a certain place, and that the Buddha has declared of him that he attained final knowledge: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming'; this he knew as it truly is. Whether he has personally seen that venerable one or has repeatedly heard about him from others, he knows that venerable one had such faith, such morality, such learning, such generosity, and such wisdom. Having heard this, he recalls that venerable one's faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Having heard this true Dharma and Vinaya, his mind may aspire to emulate such and such examples. Anuruddha! Such a bhikṣu will certainly attain progressive improvement and happy dwelling.

# Fascicle 19 of the Madhyamāgama


## (78) Sūtra on Brahmā's Invitation to the Buddha, the Seventh of the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika.

At that time, there was a certain Brahmā dwelling in the Brahmā heaven who had given rise to such a wrong view: "This place is permanent, this place is eternal, this place is everlasting, this place is essential, this place is the dharma of no ending, this place is the way of escape, and beyond this way of escape there is no other way of escape that surpasses it; there is nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, through the knowledge of others' minds, knew what that Brahmā was thinking in his heart. He then entered a concentration of corresponding appearance. Through that concentration of corresponding appearance, just as a strong person might bend or extend an arm, he vanished from the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika in Śrāvastī, and appeared in the Brahmā heaven.

At that time, that Brahmā saw the World-Honored One coming and immediately invited the World-Honored One, saying: "Welcome, Great Sage! This place is permanent, this place is eternal, this place is everlasting, this place is essential, this place is the dharma of no ending, this place is the way of escape, and beyond this way of escape there is no other way of escape that surpasses it; there is nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! You declare what is impermanent to be permanent, what is not eternal to be eternal, what does not endure to endure, what is not essential to be essential, what is a dharma of ending to be a dharma of no ending, what is not the way of escape to be the way of escape, saying that beyond this way of escape there is no other way of escape that surpasses it, nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme. Brahmā! You have this ignorance. Brahmā! You have this ignorance."

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was present in that assembly. Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas said to the World-Honored One: "Bhikṣu! Do not contradict what this Brahmā says! Do not oppose what this Brahmā says! Bhikṣu! If you contradict what this Brahmā says, if you oppose what this Brahmā says, it would be as if, bhikṣu, an auspicious matter came to a person and he pushed it away. What you say, bhikṣu, is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣu, I tell you: do not contradict what this Brahmā says, do not oppose what this Brahmā says. Bhikṣu! If you contradict what this Brahmā says, if you oppose what this Brahmā says, it would be, bhikṣu, as if a person fell from a mountaintop and, though grasping with hands and feet at the empty air, could find nothing to hold onto. What you say, bhikṣu, is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣu, I tell you: do not contradict what this Brahmā says, do not oppose what this Brahmā says. Bhikṣu! If you contradict what this Brahmā says, if you oppose what this Brahmā says, it would be, bhikṣu, as if a person fell from a tree and, though grasping with hands and feet at the branches and leaves, could find nothing to hold onto. What you say, bhikṣu, is likewise. Therefore, bhikṣu, I tell you: do not contradict what this Brahmā says, do not oppose what this Brahmā says. Why is this? This Brahmā is Brahmā, blessed, able to transform, most honored, able to create, able to fashion, is the father; all beings that have been and will be are born from him. What he knows, he knows completely; what he sees, he sees completely.

"Great Sage! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who despise earth and revile earth, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who despise Brahmā and revile Brahmā, when their bodies break up and their lives end, will certainly be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Great Sage! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who delight in earth and praise earth, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly be reborn in the most supreme and honored Brahmā heaven. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā, when their bodies break up and their lives end, will certainly be reborn in the most supreme and honored Brahmā heaven. Great Sage! Do you not see this Brahmā with his great retinue seated, such as ourselves?"

That Māra Pāpīyas was neither Brahmā nor a member of Brahmā's retinue, yet he declared himself to be Brahmā. At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This Māra Pāpīyas is neither Brahmā nor a member of Brahmā's retinue, yet he declares himself to be Brahmā. If one speaks of Māra Pāpīyas, this is indeed Māra Pāpīyas."

Having known this, the World-Honored One said: "Māra Pāpīyas! You are not Brahmā, nor are you a member of Brahmā's retinue, yet you declare yourself to be Brahmā. If one speaks of Māra Pāpīyas, you are indeed Māra Pāpīyas." Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas had this thought: "The World-Honored One knows me, the Well-Gone One sees me." Knowing this, he became sorrowful and immediately vanished from that place.

At that time, that Brahmā invited the World-Honored One a second and a third time: "Welcome, Great Sage! This place is permanent, this place is eternal, this place is everlasting, this place is essential, this place is the dharma of no ending, this place is the way of escape, and beyond this way of escape there is no other way of escape that surpasses it; there is nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme."

The World-Honored One likewise said a second and a third time: "Brahmā! You declare what is impermanent to be permanent, what is not eternal to be eternal, what does not endure to endure, what is not essential to be essential, what is a dharma of ending to be a dharma of no ending, what is not the way of escape to be the way of escape, saying that beyond this way of escape there is no other way of escape that surpasses it, nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme. Brahmā! You have this ignorance. Brahmā! You have this ignorance."

Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! In the past there were śramaṇas and brahmins whose lifespans were extremely long and who dwelt for an exceedingly long time. Great Sage! Your lifespan is very short, not even equal to one period of seated meditation of those śramaṇas and brahmins. Why is this? What they knew, they knew completely; what they saw, they saw completely. If there truly is a way of escape, then there is no other way of escape that surpasses it, nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme. If there truly is no way of escape, then there is no other way of escape that surpasses it, nothing superior, nothing more excellent, nothing supreme. Great Sage! You perceive as the way of escape what is not the way of escape, and perceive as not the way of escape what is the way of escape. Thus you do not attain the way of escape and become greatly foolish. Why is this? Because you have no domain of knowledge. Great Sage! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who delight in earth and praise earth, they are under my authority, follow my desires, and obey my commands. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā are under my authority, follow my desires, and obey my commands. Great Sage! If you delight in earth and praise earth, you too would be under my authority, follow my desires, and obey my commands. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā, you too would be under my authority, follow my desires, and obey my commands."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! What you say is indeed true: 'If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who delight in earth and praise earth, they are under your authority, follow your desires, and obey your commands. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā are under your authority, follow your desires, and obey your commands.' Brahmā! If I were to delight in earth and praise earth, I too would be under your authority, follow your desires, and obey your commands. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and the Lord of Creatures: those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā, I too would be under your authority, follow your desires, and obey your commands.

"Brahmā! If with regard to these eight things I were to delight in and praise any of them accordingly, it would indeed be so for me. Brahmā! I know the place from which you came, the place to which you go, where you abide, where you come to an end, and where you are reborn. There is a Brahmā who has great psychic power, great authority, great blessedness, and great spiritual might."

Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! How do you know what I know and see what I see? How do you have complete understanding of me? Just as the sun is sovereign, illuminating all directions, this constitutes a thousand-world system. In this thousand-world system, do you have sovereignty? Do you know those various places where there is neither day nor night? Great Sage, have you ever been to and traversed those places, and have you repeatedly been through them?"

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! Just as the sun is sovereign, illuminating all directions, this constitutes a thousand-world system. In this thousand-world system, I have sovereignty, and I also know those various places where there is neither day nor night. Brahmā! I have been through them, and I have repeatedly traversed them. Brahmā! There are three kinds of devas: the Radiant Devas, the Pure Radiance Devas, and the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Brahmā! If those three kinds of devas have knowledge and vision, I also share that knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If those three kinds of devas lack knowledge and vision, I still have my own knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If those three kinds of devas together with their retinues have knowledge and vision, I also share that knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If those three kinds of devas together with their retinues lack knowledge and vision, I still have my own knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If you have knowledge and vision, I also share that knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If you lack knowledge and vision, I still have my own knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If you together with your retinue have knowledge and vision, I also share that knowledge and vision. Brahmā! If you together with your retinue lack knowledge and vision, I still have my own knowledge and vision. Brahmā! You do not equal me in all respects, you do not equal me in every way; rather, I am most supreme and most exalted above you."

Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! How is it that if those three kinds of devas have knowledge and vision, you also share that knowledge and vision; if those three kinds of devas lack knowledge and vision, you still have your own knowledge and vision; if those three kinds of devas together with their retinues have knowledge and vision, you also share that knowledge and vision; if those three kinds of devas together with their retinues lack knowledge and vision, you still have your own knowledge and vision? If I have knowledge and vision, you also share that knowledge and vision; if I lack knowledge and vision, you still have your own knowledge and vision; if I together with my retinue have knowledge and vision, you also share that knowledge and vision; if I together with my retinue lack knowledge and vision, you still have your own knowledge and vision. Great Sage! Are these not mere empty words? Having asked, you do not know, thus increasing your delusion. Why is this? Because consciousness has an immeasurable domain: immeasurable knowledge, immeasurable vision, immeasurable differentiation. I have distinct knowledge of each: earth, I know earth; water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, the Lord of Creatures; this is Brahmā, I know Brahmā."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding earth, have the perception of earth, thinking 'Earth is myself, earth is mine, I belong to earth'; having conceived earth as the self, they do not truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, the Untroubled, the Unscorched: regarding purity, they have the perception of purity, thinking 'Purity is myself, purity is mine, I belong to purity'; having conceived purity as the self, they do not truly know purity. Brahmā! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who know earth as earth, knowing 'Earth is not myself, earth is not mine, I do not belong to earth'; not conceiving earth as the self, they truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, the Untroubled, the Unscorched: knowing purity as purity, knowing 'Purity is not myself, purity is not mine, I do not belong to purity'; not conceiving purity as the self, they truly know purity. Brahmā! I know earth as earth, knowing 'Earth is not myself, earth is not mine, I do not belong to earth'; not conceiving earth as the self, I truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, the Untroubled, the Unscorched: knowing purity as purity, knowing 'Purity is not myself, purity is not mine, I do not belong to purity'; not conceiving purity as the self, I truly know purity."

Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! This being craves existence, delights in existence, and habituates to existence. You have already uprooted the root of existence. Why is this? Because you are the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One." He then spoke this verse:

"Seeing existence, there is fear;
Seeing non-existence, there is no fear.
Therefore, do not delight in existence;
In existence, what cannot be cut off?

"Great Sage! I now wish to conceal my form."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! If you wish to conceal your form, do as you please."

Thereupon, Brahmā attempted everywhere to conceal his form. The World-Honored One immediately knew: "Brahmā! You are there, you are here, you are in between."

Thereupon, Brahmā exhausted all his supernatural powers trying to conceal his form but was unable to hide, and remained standing in the Brahmā heaven. Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā! I now also wish to conceal my form."

Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! If you wish to conceal your form, do as you please."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One had this thought: "I should now manifest the supernatural power of the corresponding appearance, emitting supremely wondrous radiance illuminating the entire Brahmā heaven, while concealing myself, so that all the Brahmā devas and Brahmā's retinue only hear my voice but do not see my form." Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested the supernatural power of the corresponding appearance, emitting supremely wondrous radiance illuminating the entire Brahmā heaven, and concealed himself, so that all the Brahmā devas and Brahmā's retinue only heard his voice but did not see his form. Thereupon, Brahmā and Brahmā's retinue each had this thought: "The śramaṇa Gautama is truly remarkable! Truly extraordinary! He has great psychic power, great authority, great blessedness, and great spiritual might. Why is this? He emits supremely wondrous radiance illuminating the entire Brahmā heaven while concealing himself, so that we and our retinue only hear his voice but do not see his form."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One further had this thought: "I have already transformed this Brahmā and Brahmā's retinue. I should now withdraw my supernatural power." The World-Honored One then withdrew his supernatural power and remained standing in the Brahmā heaven.

At that time, the Māra King, also for a second and third time, was present in that assembly. At that time, the Māra King addressed the World-Honored One: "Great Sage, you see well, know well, and comprehend well. However, do not instruct, teach, or admonish your disciples; do not teach the Dharma for your disciples; do not be attached to your disciples. Do not, on account of attachment to your disciples, when your body breaks up and your life ends, be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Practice the unconditioned and receive comfort and happiness in this present life. Why is this? Great Sage! This is merely toiling in vain. Great Sage! In the past there were śramaṇas and brahmins who instructed their disciples, taught and admonished their disciples, taught the Dharma for their disciples, and were attached to their disciples. Because of their attachment to their disciples, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, they were reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Great Sage! Therefore I say to you: do not instruct, teach, or admonish your disciples; do not teach the Dharma for your disciples; do not be attached to your disciples. Do not, on account of attachment to your disciples, when your body breaks up and your life ends, be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Practice the unconditioned and receive comfort and happiness in this present life. Why is this? Great Sage! You merely toil in vain."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Māra Pāpīyas! You do not speak for my benefit, nor for my welfare, nor for my happiness, nor for my security, saying: 'Do not instruct, teach, or admonish your disciples; do not teach the Dharma for your disciples; do not be attached to your disciples. Do not, on account of attachment to your disciples, when your body breaks up and your life ends, be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Practice the unconditioned and receive comfort and happiness in this present life. Why is this? Great Sage! You merely toil in vain.' Māra Pāpīyas! You think: 'If this śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma for his disciples, those disciples, having heard the Dharma, will leave my domain.' Māra Pāpīyas! Therefore you now say to me: 'Do not instruct, teach, or admonish your disciples; do not teach the Dharma for your disciples; do not be attached to your disciples. Do not, on account of attachment to your disciples, when your body breaks up and your life ends, be reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians. Practice the unconditioned and receive comfort and happiness in this present life. Why is this? Great Sage! You merely toil in vain.'

"Māra Pāpīyas! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who instruct their disciples, teach and admonish their disciples, teach the Dharma for their disciples, and are attached to their disciples, and because of attachment to their disciples, when their bodies break up and their lives end, are reborn among the lesser, lowly classes of celestial musicians, those śramaṇas and brahmins are not true śramaṇas yet claim to be śramaṇas, are not true brahmins yet claim to be brahmins, are not true Arhats yet claim to be Arhats, are not truly Perfectly Enlightened yet claim to be Perfectly Enlightened. Māra Pāpīyas! I am truly a śramaṇa and declare myself a śramaṇa, truly a brahmin and declare myself a brahmin, truly an Arhat and declare myself an Arhat, truly Perfectly Enlightened and declare myself Perfectly Enlightened. Māra Pāpīyas! Whether I teach the Dharma to my disciples or do not teach it, you should simply go away. I myself know when I should teach the Dharma to my disciples and when I should not."

This was the invitation of Brahmā, and Māra Pāpīyas opposed the World-Honored One and spoke in his own way. Therefore this sūtra is called "Brahmā's Invitation to the Buddha."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Brahmā and Brahmā's retinue, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Brahmā's Invitation to the Buddha, the Seventh.

## (79) Sūtra on Superior Devas, the Eighth of the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika told a certain messenger: "Go to the Buddha and, on my behalf, bow your head in reverence, pay homage at the World-Honored One's feet, and inquire whether the World-Honored One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual. Speak thus: 'The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bows his head at the Buddha's feet and inquires whether the World-Honored One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual.' After you have made this inquiry of the Buddha on my behalf, go to the Venerable Anuruddha, bow your head in reverence and pay homage at his feet, and inquire whether the Venerable One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual. Speak thus: 'The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bows his head at the Venerable Anuruddha's feet and inquires whether the Venerable One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika invites the Venerable Anuruddha together with three others, making a group of four, to accept a meal offering tomorrow.' If he accepts the invitation, further say: 'Venerable Anuruddha! The householder Anāthapiṇḍika has many affairs and much to attend to, managing the king's official business and administering among the ministers. May the Venerable Anuruddha, out of compassion, together with the group of four, come early tomorrow morning to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika's home.'"

Thereupon, the messenger, having received the householder Anāthapiṇḍika's instructions, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bows his head at the Buddha's feet and inquires whether the World-Honored One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual."

At that time, the World-Honored One told the messenger: "May the householder Anāthapiṇḍika be safe and happy. May devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and other various kinds of beings be safe and happy."

Thereupon, the messenger, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to the Venerable Anuruddha, bowed his head and paid homage at his feet, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Anuruddha! The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bows his head at the Venerable Anuruddha's feet and inquires whether the Venerable One's sacred body is strong and healthy, well and free from illness, at ease in his movements, and with energy as usual. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika invites the Venerable Anuruddha together with three others, making a group of four, to accept a meal offering tomorrow."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was sitting in meditation not far from the Venerable Anuruddha. Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Worthy Kātyāyana! What I mentioned earlier, that tomorrow we would enter Śrāvastī for the sake of begging food, this is precisely it. Now the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has sent someone to invite the four of us to a meal offering tomorrow."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana immediately said: "May the Venerable Anuruddha, for that person's sake, silently accept the invitation. Tomorrow we will leave this dark forest and enter Śrāvastī for the sake of begging food." The Venerable Anuruddha, for that person's sake, silently accepted.

Thereupon, the messenger, knowing that the Venerable Anuruddha had silently accepted, further said: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍika wishes to inform the Venerable Anuruddha: the householder Anāthapiṇḍika has many affairs and much to attend to, managing the king's official business and administering among the ministers. May the Venerable Anuruddha, out of compassion, together with the group of four, come early tomorrow morning to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika's home."

The Venerable Anuruddha told the messenger: "You may return now. I myself will know the proper time." Thereupon, the messenger rose from his seat, bowed his head in reverence, circumambulated three times, and departed.

Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha, when the night had passed and it was early morning, put on his robes and took up his bowl. Together with the group of four, he went to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika's home. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, surrounded by his attendant women, was standing under the middle gate, waiting for the Venerable Anuruddha. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika saw the Venerable Anuruddha coming from afar. Having seen him, he joined his palms toward the Venerable Anuruddha and said in praise: "Welcome, Venerable Anuruddha! It has been long since the Venerable Anuruddha came here." Thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, with a respectful heart, supported and guided the Venerable Anuruddha, leading him into the house, where he prepared fine seats and invited him to sit.

The Venerable Anuruddha sat on the seat. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bowed his head at the Venerable Anuruddha's feet, sat to one side, and having sat, said: "Venerable Anuruddha! I wish to ask a question. May you be pleased to listen."

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "Householder! Ask whatever you wish. Having heard, I will consider it."

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika then asked the Venerable Anuruddha: "There are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who come to me and say: 'Householder! You should cultivate the great mind-liberation.' Venerable Anuruddha! There are also other śramaṇas and brahmins who come to me and say: 'Householder! You should cultivate the immeasurable mind-liberation.' Venerable Anuruddha! The great mind-liberation and the immeasurable mind-liberation: are these two liberations different in both word and meaning, or are they one in meaning but different in word?"

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "Householder! You have raised this question first; answer it yourself first, and I will answer afterward."

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika said: "Venerable Anuruddha! The great mind-liberation and the immeasurable mind-liberation: these two liberations are one in meaning but different in word. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika cannot answer this question properly."

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "Householder! Listen, and I will explain for you the great mind-liberation and the immeasurable mind-liberation. As for the great mind-liberation: if there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, and relying on one tree, with the mind resolved, pervade the great mind-liberation and dwell having accomplished it, that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. If not relying on one tree, they should rely on two or three trees, with the mind resolved, pervading the great mind-liberation and dwelling having accomplished it; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. If not relying on two or three trees, they should rely on one grove; if not relying on one grove, then on two or three groves; if not relying on two or three groves, then on one village; if not relying on one village, then on two or three villages; if not relying on two or three villages, then on one country; if not relying on one country, then on two or three countries; if not relying on two or three countries, then on this great earth extending to the great ocean. With the mind resolved, pervading the great mind-liberation and dwelling having accomplished it; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. This is called the great mind-liberation.

"Householder! What is the immeasurable mind-liberation? If there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, they pervade one direction and dwell having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally throughout all, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, pervading the entire world, they dwell having accomplished it. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy: with a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, pervading the entire world, they dwell having accomplished it. This is called the immeasurable mind-liberation. Householder! The great mind-liberation and the immeasurable mind-liberation: are these two liberations different in both meaning and word, or are they one in meaning but different in word?"

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika addressed the Venerable Anuruddha: "As I understand the meaning from what I have heard from the Venerable One, these two liberations are different in both meaning and word."

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "Householder! There are three kinds of devas: the Radiant Devas, the Pure Radiance Devas, and the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Among them, the Radiant Devas: they are born in one place and do not think: 'This is mine, that is mine.' The Radiant Devas simply go wherever they please and delight in that place. Householder! It is like a fly on a piece of meat that does not think: 'This is mine, that is mine.' The fly simply follows wherever the piece of meat goes and delights in it. Likewise, those Radiant Devas do not think: 'This is mine, that is mine.' The Radiant Devas simply go wherever they please and delight in that place. At times, the Radiant Devas gather together in one place; though their bodies are different, their radiance is not different. Householder! It is like someone who lights numerous lamps and places them in one room; though the lamps are different, their light is not different. Likewise, when those Radiant Devas gather together in one place, though their bodies are different, their radiance is not different. At times, the Radiant Devas each go their separate ways. When they separate, their bodies are different and their radiance is also different. Householder! It is like someone who takes the many lamps from one room and distributes them in various rooms; the lamps are then different, and their light is also different. Likewise, when those Radiant Devas each go their separate ways, when they separate, their bodies are different and their radiance is also different."

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Radiant Devas who are born in one place, can it be known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent among them?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! It can be said that among those Radiant Devas born in one place, it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Radiant Devas born in one place, what is the cause and condition by which it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, and relying on one tree, with the mind resolved, cultivate the perception of radiance and dwell having accomplished it, their mind making the perception of radiance extremely intense; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. If not relying on one tree, they rely on two or three trees, with the mind resolved, cultivating the perception of radiance and dwelling having accomplished it, their mind making the perception of radiance extremely intense; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. Worthy Kātyāyana! Of these two mind-liberations, which liberation is higher, superior, more excellent, and supreme?"

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied: "Venerable Anuruddha! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, not relying on one tree, rely on two or three trees, with the mind resolved, cultivating the perception of radiance and dwelling having accomplished it, their mind making the perception of radiance extremely intense; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. Venerable Anuruddha! Of the two liberations, this liberation is higher, superior, more excellent, and supreme."

The Venerable Anuruddha further asked: "Worthy Kātyāyana! If not relying on two or three trees, they rely on one grove; if not relying on one grove, then on two or three groves; if not relying on two or three groves, then on one village; if not relying on one village, then on two or three villages; if not relying on two or three villages, then on one country; if not relying on one country, then on two or three countries; if not relying on two or three countries, then on this great earth extending to the great ocean. With the mind resolved, cultivating the perception of radiance and dwelling having accomplished it, their mind making the perception of radiance extremely intense; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. Worthy Kātyāyana! Of these two liberations, which liberation is higher, superior, more excellent, and supreme?"

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana replied: "Venerable Anuruddha! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, not relying on two or three trees, rely on one grove; if not relying on one grove, then on two or three groves; if not relying on two or three groves, then on one village; if not relying on one village, then on two or three villages; if not relying on two or three villages, then on one country; if not relying on one country, then on two or three countries; if not relying on two or three countries, then on this great earth extending to the great ocean. With the mind resolved, cultivating the perception of radiance and dwelling having accomplished it, their mind making the perception of radiance extremely intense; that is the limit of this mind-liberation and does not go beyond it. Venerable Anuruddha! Of the two liberations, this liberation is higher, superior, more excellent, and supreme."

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "Kātyāyana! Because of this cause and this condition, those Radiant Devas born in one place are known to have those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent. Why is this? Because people's minds are superior or equal, their cultivation becomes either refined or coarse. Because cultivation is either refined or coarse, the persons who attain it are either superior or equal. Worthy Kātyāyana! The World-Honored One also says thus: among persons there are those who are superior or equal."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Pure Radiance Devas who are born in one place, can it be known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent among them?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! It can be said that among those Pure Radiance Devas born in one place, it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Pure Radiance Devas born in one place, what is the cause and condition by which it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. But if this concentration is not cultivated, not practiced, not broadened, and not fully accomplished, when their bodies later break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, they do not attain extreme tranquility, do not attain extreme serenity, and also do not live out the full span of their lifespan. Worthy Kātyāyana! It is like a blue lotus, a red lotus, a scarlet lotus, or a white lotus, which is born in water, grows in water, and while at the bottom of the water, its roots, stems, leaves, and flowers are all soaked by water, drenched by water, moistened by water, with no part not soaked. Worthy Kātyāyana! Likewise, if there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. But if this concentration is not cultivated, not practiced, not broadened, and not fully accomplished, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, they do not attain extreme tranquility, do not attain extreme serenity, and also do not live out the full span of their lifespan.

"Worthy Kātyāyana! Again, there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, with the mind resolved on the Pure Radiance Devas, pervade and dwell having accomplished it. If this concentration is repeatedly cultivated, repeatedly practiced, repeatedly broadened, and fully accomplished, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, they attain extreme tranquility, attain extreme serenity, and also live out the full span of their lifespan. Worthy Kātyāyana! It is like a blue lotus, a red lotus, a scarlet lotus, or a white lotus, which is born in water and grows in water, but rises above the water and stands there, not soaked by water. Worthy Kātyāyana! Likewise, again there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. If this concentration is repeatedly cultivated, repeatedly practiced, repeatedly broadened, and fully accomplished, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, they attain extreme tranquility, attain extreme serenity, and also live out the full span of their lifespan.

"Worthy Kātyāyana! Because of this cause and this condition, those Pure Radiance Devas born in one place are known to have those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent. Why is this? Because people's minds are superior or equal, their cultivation becomes either refined or coarse. Because cultivation is either refined or coarse, the persons who attain it are either superior or equal. Worthy Kātyāyana! The World-Honored One also says thus: among persons there are those who are superior or equal."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Universal Pure Radiance Devas who are born in one place, can it be known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent among them?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! It can be said that among those Universal Pure Radiance Devas born in one place, it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha! Those Universal Pure Radiance Devas born in one place, what is the cause and condition by which it is known that there are those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent?"

The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kātyāyana! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Universal Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. But they do not fully restrain drowsiness and sleep, and do not properly pacify and regulate restlessness and remorse. When their bodies later break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, their radiance is not extremely pure. Worthy Kātyāyana! It is like lighting a lamp, which depends on oil and a wick. If the oil has impurities and the wick is not clean, because of this the lamplight produced is not bright and pure. Worthy Kātyāyana! Likewise, if there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Universal Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. But they do not fully restrain drowsiness and sleep, and do not properly pacify and regulate restlessness and remorse. When their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, their radiance is not extremely pure.

"Worthy Kātyāyana! Again, there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Universal Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. They fully restrain drowsiness and sleep, and properly pacify and regulate restlessness and remorse. When their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, their radiance is extremely bright and pure. Worthy Kātyāyana! It is like lighting a lamp, which depends on oil and a wick. If the oil has no impurities and the wick is extremely clean, because of this the lamplight produced is extremely bright and pure.

"Worthy Kātyāyana! Likewise, again there are śramaṇas or brahmins in a secluded place, or who go to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, with the mind resolved on the Universal Pure Radiance Devas, they pervade and dwell having accomplished it. They fully restrain drowsiness and sleep, and properly pacify and regulate restlessness and remorse. When their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Universal Pure Radiance Devas. Having been reborn there, their radiance is extremely bright and pure.

"Worthy Kātyāyana! Because of this cause and this condition, those Universal Pure Radiance Devas born in one place are known to have those who are superior, equal, excellent, or not excellent. Why is this? Because people's minds are superior or equal, their cultivation becomes either refined or coarse. Because cultivation is either refined or coarse, the persons who attain it are either superior or equal. Worthy Kātyāyana! The World-Honored One also says thus: among persons there are those who are superior or equal."

Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana praised the householder Anāthapiṇḍika: "Excellent! Excellent! Householder! You have greatly benefited us. Why is this? You first asked the Venerable Anuruddha about the superior devas. We had never before heard such a teaching from the Venerable Anuruddha, namely that there are those devas, that those devas exist, and that those devas are as such."

Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Worthy Kātyāyana! There are many such devas. These sun and moon, which possess great psychic power, great authority, great blessedness, and great spiritual might, yet whose radiance does not compare to that radiance. They have gathered with me, exchanged greetings, engaged in discussion, and responded in conversation. Yet I do not say: 'Those devas are such, those devas exist, those devas are like this.'"

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, knowing that the venerable ones had finished speaking, rose from his seat, personally poured water for hand-washing, and with extremely pure and fine varieties of abundant food, things to eat, chew, suck, and drink, personally served and attended to them, filling them to satisfaction. When the meal was finished and the utensils were cleared away, and the water for hand-washing had been poured, he took a small seat and sat separately to listen to the Dharma. After the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was seated, the Venerable Anuruddha taught him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and filling him with joy.
