Through immeasurable skillful means he taught him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and filling him with joy, and then rose from his seat and departed.

Thus spoke the Venerable Anuruddha. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Superior Devas, the Eighth.


---


## (80) Sūtra on the Kaṭhina, the Ninth of the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍika.

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was also in Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain. Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha, when the night had passed and it was early morning, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food. The Venerable Ānanda also, early in the morning, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food.

The Venerable Anuruddha saw the Venerable Ānanda also going on his alms round. Having seen him, he said: "Worthy Ānanda! You should know that my three robes are coarse, worn, and completely tattered. Worthy one! Could you now ask the bhikṣus to make robes for me?" The Venerable Ānanda silently consented to ask on the Venerable Anuruddha's behalf.

Thereupon, when the Venerable Ānanda had finished begging food in Śrāvastī, after eating, in the afternoon he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth on his shoulder, took the door key in his hand, and went from room to room. Seeing the bhikṣus, he said to them: "Venerable ones! Let us go today to the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha."

Thereupon, the bhikṣus, hearing the Venerable Ānanda's words, all went to the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw the Venerable Ānanda with the door key in his hand going from room to room. Having seen this, he asked: "Ānanda! For what reason do you have a door key in your hand, going from room to room?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One! I am now asking the bhikṣus to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! Why did you not invite the Tathāgata to make robes for the bhikṣu Anuruddha?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda immediately joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One please go to the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha." The World-Honored One silently consented for the Venerable Ānanda's sake.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, taking the Venerable Ānanda with him, went to the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain, where a seat was prepared before the assembly of bhikṣus, and he sat down. At that time, eight hundred bhikṣus had gathered at the Sālaḷa Rocky Mountain together with the World-Honored One, sitting together to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also among the assembly. Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Maudgalyāyana! I can spread out and measure the cloth for Anuruddha's robes, cut it, piece it together, and sew it."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, arranged his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One please spread out and measure the cloth for the Worthy Anuruddha's robes, and the bhikṣus will together cut, piece together, and sew them."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spread out and measured the cloth for the Venerable Anuruddha's robes, and the bhikṣus together cut, pieced together, and sewed them. That very day, the three robes for the Venerable Anuruddha were completed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Venerable Anuruddha's three robes were completed, said: "Anuruddha! You should teach the bhikṣus the Kaṭhina Dharma. I now have a backache and wish to rest briefly."

The Venerable Anuruddha said: "So be it, World-Honored One."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One folded his uttarāsaṅga fourfold and spread it on the bed, folded his saṅghāṭī to make a pillow, lay down on his right side, placed foot upon foot, established the perception of radiance, set up right mindfulness and right awareness, and constantly maintained the intention to arise.

At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerable ones! When I had not yet left the household life to study the Way, I was disgusted with birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, sorrow, and distress, and wished to put an end to this great mass of suffering. Venerable ones! Being thus disgusted, I made this observation: 'The household life is exceedingly narrow, a place of dust and toil. Leaving home to study the Way is open and vast. Living at home now, I am bound as if by chains and cannot for the duration of my life cultivate the holy life. I should rather renounce a small amount of wealth and a great amount of wealth, leave behind few relatives and many relatives, shave my head and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household to be homeless and study the Way.' Venerable ones! Later, I did renounce a small amount of wealth and a great amount of wealth, left behind few relatives and many relatives, shaved my head and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household to be homeless and study the Way. Venerable ones! Having left the household to study the Way, having renounced my clan, I received the bhikṣu's training, practiced the precepts, guarded and followed the prātimokṣa, and further well restrained deportment and propriety. Seeing even the slightest fault, I constantly felt fearful, and I upheld and studied the precepts.

"Venerable ones! I abandoned killing, ceased killing, set aside weapons and clubs, had shame and conscience, had a compassionate heart, and benefited all beings down to insects. I purified my mind of killing. Venerable ones! I abandoned taking what is not given, ceased taking what is not given; I took only what was given and delighted in taking what was given. I was always fond of giving, joyful and ungrudging, without expectation of reward. I purified my mind of taking what is not given. Venerable ones! I abandoned unchastity, ceased unchastity, diligently cultivated the holy life, was a practitioner of the pure practice, clean and undefiled, free from desire and cutting off sexual misconduct. I purified my mind of unchastity.

"Venerable ones! I abandoned false speech, ceased false speech, spoke truthfully, delighted in truth, abided in truth, was unmoved, could be trusted by all, and did not deceive the world. I purified my mind of false speech. Venerable ones! I abandoned divisive speech, ceased divisive speech, and practiced non-divisive speech. I did not seek to break up others. I did not hear something here and report it there in order to break up those people, nor hear something there and report it here in order to break up these people. Those who were estranged I wished to reconcile; those already in harmony I rejoiced in. I did not form factions, did not delight in factions, did not praise factions. I purified my mind of divisive speech. Venerable ones! I abandoned harsh speech, ceased harsh speech. Whatever words were rough and coarse, with unpleasant sounds, grating to the ear, displeasing to the multitude, not loved by the multitude, causing others suffering and preventing concentration, I ceased such speech. Whatever I spoke was harmonious and gentle, pleasing to the ear and entering the heart, delightful and lovable, bringing comfort to others. My words were clear and complete, not causing others fear but enabling them to gain concentration. I spoke such words. I purified my mind of harsh speech. Venerable ones! I abandoned frivolous speech, ceased frivolous speech. I spoke at the right time, spoke truthfully, spoke of the Dharma, spoke of meaning, spoke words of cessation, delighted in words of cessation. My words were appropriate to the situation and timely, well-teaching and well-admonishing. I purified my mind of frivolous speech.

"Venerable ones! I abandoned trading, ceased trading, gave up weighing and measuring with scales and containers, did not accept goods, did not bind or coerce people, did not seek to cheat with short measures, and did not use small advantages to deceive others. I purified my mind of trading. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting widows and maidens, ceased accepting widows and maidens. I purified my mind of accepting widows and maidens. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting male and female servants, ceased accepting male and female servants. I purified my mind of accepting male and female servants. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, ceased accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. I purified my mind of accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting chickens and pigs, ceased accepting chickens and pigs. I purified my mind of accepting chickens and pigs. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting farmland and shops, ceased accepting farmland and shops. I purified my mind of accepting farmland and shops. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans, ceased accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans. I purified my mind of accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans.

"Venerable ones! I abandoned intoxicants, ceased intoxicants. I purified my mind of drinking intoxicants. Venerable ones! I abandoned high and broad beds, ceased high and broad beds. I purified my mind of high and broad beds. Venerable ones! I abandoned garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics, ceased garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics. I purified my mind of garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics. Venerable ones! I abandoned singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen, ceased singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen. I purified my mind of singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen. Venerable ones! I abandoned accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels, ceased accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels. I purified my mind of accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels. Venerable ones! I abandoned eating after midday, ceased eating after midday; I ate one meal a day, not eating at night, learning to eat at the proper time. I purified my mind of eating after midday.

"Venerable ones! Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, I further trained in extreme contentment: taking clothing only to cover the body, taking food only to sustain the frame, and wherever I traveled, I went with robes and bowl, journeying without attachment, just as a bird flies through the air together with its two wings. Venerable ones! I was likewise: wherever I traveled, I went with robes and bowl, journeying without attachment. Venerable ones! Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts and extreme contentment, I further trained in guarding the sense faculties, constantly mindful of closing and blocking them, aspiring to clear understanding, guarding the mindful heart to achieve it, and constantly arousing right awareness. When the eye sees forms, I did not grasp at signs nor relish forms, for the sake of preventing anger and contention. I guarded the eye faculty so that covetousness, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states would not arise in the mind, heading toward that end I guarded the eye faculty. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body; when the mind cognizes dharmas, I did not grasp at signs nor relish dharmas, for the sake of preventing anger and contention. I guarded the mind faculty so that covetousness, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states would not arise in the mind, heading toward that end I guarded the mind faculty.

"Venerable ones! Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, extreme contentment, and guarding the sense faculties, I further trained in right awareness of going out and coming in, skillfully observing and discerning: bending and extending, looking down and up, deportment and composure, properly wearing the saṅghāṭī and other robes and the bowl, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, being rightly aware of all these. Venerable ones! Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, extreme contentment, guarding the sense faculties, and right awareness of going out and coming in, I further trained in dwelling alone in solitude, in a secluded place, or going to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, a mountain cave or rocky shelter, open ground or a haystack, or in a forest, or among tombs. Venerable ones! Already being in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, I spread out my sitting cloth, sat cross-legged, straightened my body, set my face forward, and turned my mindfulness inward, free from outward direction. I abandoned covetousness. My mind was free from contention. Seeing others' possessions and means of livelihood, I did not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for myself. I purified my mind of covetousness. Likewise with anger, drowsiness, restlessness and remorse: I abandoned doubt and crossed over perplexity, and regarding wholesome dharmas I had no hesitation. I purified my mind of doubt and perplexity. Venerable ones! Having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weakeners of wisdom, free from desires, free from evil unwholesome states, I attained up to the fourth jhāna and dwelt therein.

"Venerable ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without defilement, without disturbance, soft, well-settled, and having gained an immovable mind, I trained to realize the knowledge of psychic power. Venerable ones! I attained immeasurable psychic powers, namely: dividing one into many, combining many into one, remaining in each as one, with knowledge and vision, passing through stone walls without obstruction as if moving through empty space, sinking into the earth as if into water, walking on water as if on earth, sitting cross-legged and ascending into the air like a bird in flight. These sun and moon, which possess great psychic power, great authority, great blessedness, and great spiritual might, I could touch and stroke with my hand, and my body reached up to the Brahmā heaven. Venerable ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without defilement, without disturbance, soft, well-settled, and having gained an immovable mind, I trained to realize the knowledge of the divine ear. Venerable ones! With the divine ear I heard the sounds of humans and non-humans, near and far, fine and coarse.

"Venerable ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without defilement, without disturbance, soft, well-settled, and having gained an immovable mind, I trained to realize the knowledge of others' minds. Venerable ones! I knew the thoughts, ideas, deeds, and actions of other beings. With the knowledge of others' minds, I knew others' minds as they truly are. A mind with desire I knew as a mind with desire, as it truly is. A mind without desire I knew as a mind without desire, as it truly is. A mind with anger, without anger; with delusion, without delusion; with defilement, without defilement; collected or scattered; elevated or lowly; small or great; cultivated or uncultivated; concentrated or unconcentrated; an unliberated mind I knew as an unliberated mind, as it truly is; a liberated mind I knew as a liberated mind, as it truly is.

"Venerable ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without defilement, without disturbance, soft, well-settled, and having gained an immovable mind, I trained to realize the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Venerable ones! With specific characteristics and appearances, I recalled innumerable past experiences, namely: one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, formation kalpas, destruction kalpas, innumerable formation and destruction kalpas. Those beings were named such-and-such, and in the past they experienced such things. I was born there, with such a clan name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, experiencing such suffering and happiness, with such a long life, dwelling for such a time, with such a lifespan. Dying there, they were born here; dying here, they were born there. I was born here, with such a clan name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, experiencing such suffering and happiness, with such a long life, dwelling for such a time, with such a lifespan.

"Venerable ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without defilement, without disturbance, soft, well-settled, and having gained an immovable mind, I trained to realize the knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings. Venerable ones

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama), Fascicle 19

---

## (77) The Sūtra on the Three Clans of Entertainers

*Second in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, a chief of entertainers named Tālapuṭa came to the World-Honored One. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have previously heard from senior and elder entertainers of former times who said: 'If an entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted, then after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn among the Laughing Heavenly Gods.' World-Honored One, what do you say about this?"

The World-Honored One said: "Stop, stop! Do not ask me about this matter."

The chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa asked a second time, saying: "World-Honored One, I have previously heard from senior and elder entertainers of former times who said: 'If an entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted, then after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn among the Laughing Heavenly Gods.' World-Honored One, what do you say about this?"

The World-Honored One again said: "Stop, stop! Do not ask me about this matter."

The chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa asked a third time, saying: "World-Honored One, I have previously heard from senior and elder entertainers of former times who said: 'If an entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted, then after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn among the Laughing Heavenly Gods.' World-Honored One, what do you say about this?"

The World-Honored One said: "I have already told you to stop, that you should not ask me about this matter. Yet you keep pressing me with questions, so I will now explain it for you.

"Chief of entertainers, what do you think? If an entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted: those sentient beings, not yet free from desire, are bound by the fetter of desire; not yet free from anger, are bound by the fetter of anger; not yet free from delusion, are bound by the fetter of delusion. And the entertainer, for these sentient beings who are already bound by desire, anger, and delusion, further increases their bonds of desire, further increases their bonds of anger, further increases their bonds of delusion. Chief of entertainers, it is like a person who is bound with ropes, and someone douses him with water, making the ropes tighter. Chief of entertainers, what do you think? Would that person who is bound, having been doused with water, have his bonds become tighter or looser?"

He answered: "World-Honored One, having been doused with water, the bonds would become tighter, not looser."

"Chief of entertainers, it is just so. Those sentient beings, not yet free from desire, are bound by the fetter of desire; not yet free from anger, are bound by the fetter of anger; not yet free from delusion, are bound by the fetter of delusion. And the entertainer, for these sentient beings who are already bound by desire, anger, and delusion, further increases their bonds of desire, further increases their bonds of anger, further increases their bonds of delusion. The entertainer himself, with a mind of wrong view, creates such unwholesome karma: in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causing the people to laugh and be delighted, increasing their bondage. Because of this karma, after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn in a hell called 'Laughing.' If he previously held this view, saying 'An entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted; after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn among the Laughing Heavenly Gods,' then this is wrong view. For a person of wrong view, I say there are only two destinations: either hell or the animal realm."

When this was spoken, the chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa wept and shed tears. The World-Honored One said: "Chief of entertainers, it is for this reason that I told you to stop, and that you should not ask me about this matter."

The chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa said: "World-Honored One, I am not weeping because of what the Buddha has said. Rather, I weep because I have been deceived and deluded for so long by those senior and elder entertainers of former times, who said: 'If an entertainer, in the midst of a great assembly, through various skills of singing, dancing, and theatrical performance, causes the people to laugh and be delighted, then after the body breaks up and life ends, he will be reborn among the Laughing Heavenly Gods.'

"World-Honored One, now I know! Now I understand! World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. From today forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge and become a lay disciple. World-Honored One, I wish to leave the household life and receive the full precepts under the World-Honored One, practicing the holy life."

Then the World-Honored One permitted the chief of entertainers Tālapuṭa to leave the household life and receive the full precepts. After he had left the household life and received the full precepts, the Venerable Tālapuṭa, dwelling alone in a secluded place, with diligent effort and an unrelaxed mind, practiced accordingly. He accomplished what a son of good family, having rightly left the household life to practice the way without a home, seeks as the supreme goal: in this very life, he himself realized with direct knowledge, attained, and dwelt in it. He knew: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further existence." The Venerable Tālapuṭa became an arhat.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Tālapuṭa, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (78) The Sūtra on Brahmā's Invitation

*Third in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Uruvelā, on the bank of the Nairañjanā River, beneath the Bodhi tree, having just attained right enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having attained right enlightenment, was seated cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation. After seven days had passed, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. The World-Honored One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw that sentient beings had their faculties either sharp or dull, their natures either keen or slow, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach, and among them some who feared the faults and transgressions of the other world, and some who did not. It was like a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses: some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged without emerging; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and are level with the water's surface; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, unstained by the water. In the same way, the World-Honored One surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw sentient beings with their faculties either sharp or dull, their natures either keen or slow, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach, and among them some who feared the faults and transgressions of the other world, and some who did not.

At that time, the World-Honored One understood this matter and thereupon spoke this verse:

"I have realized the profound, subtle, and marvelous Dharma,
Hard to see, hard to comprehend, calming all formations,
Beyond conceptual elaboration, extremely profound, difficult to perceive,
Subtle and fine, to be known only by the wise.
But sentient beings delight in attachment and are attached to objects of desire;
Sentient beings who delight in attachment and are attached to objects of desire
Cannot see such matters as conditioned arising and dependent origination.
Since all formations cease, desire is extinguished,
And since there is nirvāṇa, it is difficult for them to perceive this.
If I were to teach the Dharma, others would not understand;
If they do not understand, it would only cause me weariness.
I should rather remain silent."

At that time, the Brahmā King knew in his mind what the World-Honored One was thinking. He thought: "This world is about to be ruined, this world is about to perish! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One has attained right enlightenment but does not wish to teach the Dharma."

Then the Brahmā King, as quickly as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, disappeared from the Brahma world and appeared before the Buddha. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, please teach the Dharma! Well-Gone One, please teach the Dharma! There are sentient beings with little dust in their eyes who, without hearing the Dharma, will decline and fall. But there are those who can understand the Dharma. World-Honored One, may it be that the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma for them."

The Brahmā King then spoke in verse:

"In the land of Magadha, there has long arisen an impure Dharma
Devised by those of defiled minds.
Please open the gate of the deathless!
Let them hear the Dharma realized by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing atop a mountain peak
Can look out in all directions over the people below,
So too, the Wise One of All-Seeing Wisdom,
Please ascend the palace of Dharma
And look upon the multitude drowning in sorrow.
The One Free from Suffering, please look upon
Sentient beings oppressed by birth, old age, and death.
Rise up, O Hero who has conquered in battle!
Leader of the caravan, O Debtless One, walk through the world!
May the World-Honored One teach the Dharma;
There will surely be those who understand."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the request of the Brahmā King, and out of compassion for sentient beings, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. The World-Honored One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw that sentient beings had their faculties either sharp or dull, their natures either keen or slow, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach, and among them some who feared the faults and transgressions of the other world, and some who did not. It was like a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses: some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged without emerging; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and are level with the water's surface; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and rise above the water, unstained by the water. In the same way, the World-Honored One surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw sentient beings with their faculties either sharp or dull, their natures either keen or slow, some easy to teach and some difficult to teach, and among them some who feared the faults and transgressions of the other world, and some who did not.

At that time, the World-Honored One told the Brahmā King: "The gate of the deathless is open for them. Let those with ears release their faith. Brahmā, it was because I perceived difficulty and trouble that I did not wish to teach the Dharma that is sublime and wonderful for humans."

Then the Brahmā King thought: "The World-Honored One has consented to teach the Dharma!" He joyfully paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha, and then disappeared.

At that time, the World-Honored One thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" Then the World-Honored One further thought: "Ārāḍa Kālāma is wise, intelligent, and discerning. He has long had little dust in his eyes. I should first teach the Dharma to Ārāḍa Kālāma, and he will quickly understand it." Then a heavenly being appeared in the sky and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Ārāḍa Kālāma died seven days ago."

The World-Honored One also knew on his own that Ārāḍa Kālāma had died seven days ago, and the World-Honored One thought: "It is a great loss for Ārāḍa Kālāma. If he had heard my Dharma, he would have quickly understood it."

Then the World-Honored One further thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" The World-Honored One again thought: "Udraka Rāmaputra is wise, intelligent, and discerning. He has long had little dust in his eyes. I should first teach the Dharma to Udraka Rāmaputra, and he will quickly understand it." Then a heavenly being appeared in the sky and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, Udraka Rāmaputra died last evening."

The World-Honored One also knew on his own that Udraka Rāmaputra had died last evening, and the World-Honored One thought: "It is a great loss for Udraka Rāmaputra. If he had heard my Dharma, he would have quickly understood it."

Then the World-Honored One further thought: "To whom should I first teach the Dharma?" The World-Honored One again thought: "The group of five bhikṣus, who formerly attended upon me and served me while I practiced austerities, to them I should first teach the Dharma." The World-Honored One further thought: "Where are the group of five bhikṣus staying now?" The World-Honored One with his divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, saw the group of five bhikṣus staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī.

Then the World-Honored One, after staying at Uruvelā for as long as he wished, set out on the road toward Vārāṇasī. On the way, an Ājīvaka ascetic named Upaka saw the World-Honored One coming from afar. Seeing him, he approached and said to the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, your faculties are pure, your complexion is radiant and clear. Friend Gautama, under whom have you left the household life? Who is your teacher? Whose Dharma do you delight in?"

At that time, the World-Honored One answered the Ājīvaka Upaka in verse:

"I am the one who has conquered all, the one who knows all,
Among all dharmas I am undefiled.
I have abandoned all, and through the ending of craving I am liberated.
Having realized it myself, whom would I call my teacher?
I have no teacher;
There is none equal to me.
In the world with its gods,
There is no one who can rival me.
I am the Arhat of the world,
I am the unsurpassed teacher.
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One;
Having attained coolness, I have reached nirvāṇa.
I am now going to the city of Kāśī
To turn the wheel of the Dharma.
In a world that has become blind,
I shall beat the drum of the deathless."

Upaka said: "Friend Gautama, as you claim, you should indeed be the Victor of the Boundless."

The World-Honored One said: "Those like me who have attained the ending of the outflows are indeed victors. I have conquered all evil dharmas; therefore, Upaka, I am called 'the Victor.'"

When this was spoken, the Ājīvaka Upaka said: "Perhaps so, Friend Gautama." Shaking his head, he took another path and departed.

Then the World-Honored One, traveling by stages, arrived at the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī. The group of five bhikṣus saw the World-Honored One coming from afar, and seeing him, they made an agreement among themselves, saying: "Friends, this ascetic Gautama is coming. He is given to luxury and has abandoned his efforts. He has reverted to a life of abundance. We should not rise to greet him, should not pay homage to him, should not take his robe and bowl, should not offer him a seat. However, we may set a seat aside; if he wishes to sit, he may sit."

When the World-Honored One gradually approached the group of five bhikṣus, the group of five bhikṣus, upon seeing the World-Honored One approach, were unable to maintain their agreement. They all rose from their seats, went forward to welcome him: some took his robe and bowl, some offered him a seat, some prepared washing water for his feet. They addressed him as "Friend Gautama."

Then the World-Honored One told the group of five bhikṣus: "You should not address the Tathāgata by his clan name or call him 'Friend.' Why? The Tathāgata is an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well! The deathless has been attained, and I will instruct you. I will teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I instruct, you will before long, in this very life, through your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good families rightly leave the household life."

Then the group of five bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, formerly through your practices of austerity, through asceticism, through difficult practices, you did not attain the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision. Now how could you, having reverted to a life of luxury, having abandoned your efforts, having reverted to a life of abundance, have attained the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One then told the group of five bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata has not reverted to a life of luxury and has not abandoned his efforts. The Tathāgata is an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well! The deathless has been attained, and I will instruct you. I will teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I instruct, you will before long, in this very life, through your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good families rightly leave the household life."

A second time, the group of five bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, formerly through your practices of austerity, through asceticism, through difficult practices, you did not attain the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision. Now how could you, having reverted to a life of luxury, having abandoned your efforts, having reverted to a life of abundance, have attained the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One again told the group of five bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata has not reverted to a life of luxury and has not abandoned his efforts. The Tathāgata is an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well! The deathless has been attained, and I will instruct you. I will teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I instruct, you will before long, in this very life, through your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good families rightly leave the household life."

A third time, the group of five bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One: "Friend Gautama, formerly through your practices of austerity, through asceticism, through difficult practices, you did not attain the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision. Now how could you, having reverted to a life of luxury, having abandoned your efforts, having reverted to a life of abundance, have attained the superhuman Dharma, the noble and distinctive knowledge and vision?"

The World-Honored One then told the group of five bhikṣus: "Do you recall whether I have ever spoken to you in such a way before?"

The group of five bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"The Tathāgata is an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Listen well! The deathless has been attained, and I will instruct you. I will teach you the Dharma. If you practice as I instruct, you will before long, in this very life, through your own direct knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good families rightly leave the household life."

Then the group of five bhikṣus were able to listen to the World-Honored One and heeded his teaching.

The World-Honored One told them: "There are two extremes that those who have left the household life should not pursue. What are the two? One is attachment to desire and pleasure, which is low, common, vulgar, ignoble, and without benefit. The other is attachment to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and without benefit. By abandoning these two extremes, there is the middle path, which the Tathāgata has realized and attained by self-awakening, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to calm, to higher knowledge, to full enlightenment, to nirvāṇa.

"What is this middle path that the Tathāgata has realized and attained by self-awakening, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to calm, to higher knowledge, to full enlightenment, to nirvāṇa? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is the middle path that the Tathāgata has realized and attained by self-awakening, which gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, and leads to calm, to higher knowledge, to full enlightenment, to nirvāṇa."

The World-Honored One then said: "This is the noble truth of suffering. Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not obtaining what one wishes is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there, namely: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

"This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its abandoning, relinquishing, release, and non-attachment.

"This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

"'This is the noble truth of suffering': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be cultivated': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated': with regard to things not heard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, understanding, and light.

"As long as I had not thoroughly realized, in their true nature, with three turnings and twelve aspects, these Four Noble Truths in their complete purity, I did not claim to have attained the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in this world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, among the assemblages of ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans.

"But when I thoroughly realized, in their true nature, with three turnings and twelve aspects, these Four Noble Truths in their complete purity, then I claimed to have attained the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in this world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, among the assemblages of ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans.

"Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My liberation is unshakable. This is my last birth. There will be no further renewed existence.'"

When the World-Honored One taught this Dharma, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya attained the pure, stainless Dharma-eye with regard to all dharmas: "Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation."

When the World-Honored One had turned the wheel of the Dharma, the earth-dwelling gods raised a cry: "The World-Honored One, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, has turned the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma, which cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

Having heard the cry of the earth-dwelling gods, the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika heaven raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the gods of Trāyastriṃśa heaven raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the Yāma gods raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the Tuṣita gods raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the Nirmāṇarati gods raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods raised a cry. Having heard their cry, the gods of the Brahma world raised a cry: "The World-Honored One, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī, has turned the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma, which cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

In that instant, in that moment, the cry reached up to the Brahma world. This world of a billion realms trembled and shook in six ways, and an immeasurable, great radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine splendor of the gods.

Then the World-Honored One said: "Kauṇḍinya has understood! Kauṇḍinya has understood!" Therefore, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya received the name Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya ("Kauṇḍinya Who Has Understood").

Then the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having realized the Dharma, having penetrated the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, having cast off perplexity, having attained fearlessness, not relying on others in the Teacher's teaching, addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One, I wish to leave the household life under the World-Honored One and receive the full precepts, practicing the holy life."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣu! The Dharma is well proclaimed. Practice the holy life to make a complete end of suffering." This was the Venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya's full ordination.

Then the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the remaining bhikṣus. When the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the Venerable Vāṣpa and the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrika and the Venerable Aśvajit went on alms round. The food brought back by the Venerable Bhadrika and the Venerable Aśvajit was sufficient to feed all six of them.

When the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the Venerable Bhadrika and the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Vāṣpa and the Venerable Mahānāman went on alms round. The food brought back by the Venerable Vāṣpa and the Venerable Mahānāman was sufficient to feed all six of them.

Then the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, and the Venerable Aśvajit, when they heard the World-Honored One's teaching, attained the pure, stainless Dharma-eye with regard to all dharmas: "Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation."

Having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having realized the Dharma, having penetrated the Dharma, having crossed beyond doubt, having cast off perplexity, having attained fearlessness, not relying on others in the Teacher's teaching, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "World-Honored One, we wish to leave the household life under the World-Honored One and receive the full precepts, practicing the holy life."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣus! The Dharma is well proclaimed. Practice the holy life to make a complete end of suffering." This was their full ordination.

The World-Honored One further taught them the Dharma, saying: "Bhikṣus, form is not self. If form were self, form would not lead to affliction, and one could control form, saying 'Let my form be thus' or 'Let my form not be thus.' But because form is not self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot control form, saying 'Let my form be thus' or 'Let my form not be thus.'

"Feeling is not self. If feeling were self, feeling would not lead to affliction, and one could control feeling, saying 'Let my feeling be thus' or 'Let my feeling not be thus.' But because feeling is not self, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and one cannot control feeling.

"Perception is not self. If perception were self, perception would not lead to affliction, and one could control perception. But because perception is not self, therefore perception leads to affliction, and one cannot control perception.

"Mental formations are not self. If mental formations were self, mental formations would not lead to affliction, and one could control mental formations. But because mental formations are not self, therefore mental formations lead to affliction, and one cannot control mental formations.

"Consciousness is not self. If consciousness were self, consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could control consciousness. But because consciousness is not self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot control consciousness.

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

They answered: "It is impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

They answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard this as 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

They answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, is feeling permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard this as 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Is perception permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard this as 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Are mental formations permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent, are they suffering?"

"They are suffering, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard this as 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a learned noble disciple regard this as 'This is mine, this is I, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Therefore, bhikṣus, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever perception there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all perception should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever mental formations there are, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all mental formations should be seen as they really are with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether inferior or superior, whether far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this is not I, this is not my self.'

"Bhikṣus, a learned noble disciple who contemplates thus becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with mental formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further existence.'"

When the World-Honored One taught this Dharma, the minds of the group of five bhikṣus, through non-clinging, were liberated from the outflows. At that time, there were six arhats in the world.

The Buddha spoke thus. The group of five bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (79) The Sūtra on Having Causes

*Fourth in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If you are asked by wandering ascetics of other sects, 'Friends, does the ascetic Gautama have any particular distinction in terms of the highest knowledge and vision, different from all other ascetics and brahmins?' Being thus asked, you should answer those wandering ascetics of other sects as follows: 'Friends, our teacher, the World-Honored One, does have a particular distinction in terms of the highest knowledge and vision, different from all other ascetics and brahmins.'

"If they further ask, 'Friends, what is the particular distinction in the highest knowledge and vision that the ascetic Gautama has, different from all other ascetics and brahmins?' Being thus asked, you should answer those wandering ascetics of other sects as follows: 'Friends, our teacher, the World-Honored One, teaches that there are three types of distinction. What are the three? Our teacher, the World-Honored One, has supreme knowledge and vision regarding the past, our teacher, the World-Honored One, has supreme knowledge and vision regarding the future, and our teacher, the World-Honored One, has supreme knowledge and vision regarding the present. These are the three types of distinction in the highest knowledge and vision that our teacher, the World-Honored One, has, different from all other ascetics and brahmins.'

"Bhikṣus, whether or not they are present, I have knowledge and vision with regard to all conditioned things: 'This is so, this is not otherwise. It does not go beyond this. It is not deficient, it is not in excess.' All that the Tathāgata says is true, not false. It is factual, not unfactual. It is as it is, not otherwise.

"Bhikṣus, the Tathāgata's three turnings of the wheel of the Dharma cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. The first is that regarding all things, the Tathāgata has the supreme and perfect right knowledge, the supreme and perfect right vision, the supreme and perfect right enlightenment, the supreme and perfect right turning. The Tathāgata is called 'the Arhat,' 'the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

"The second is that the Tathāgata's disciples are well established in the right Dharma and practice the right Dharma, and their achievements are apparent to the world.

"The third is that the Tathāgata's disciples, following the Tathāgata's well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, practice accordingly, gain results, attain the fundamental goal, become self-witnesses, and dwell in realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further existence.'

"These are the Tathāgata's three turnings of the wheel of the Dharma that cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (80) The Sūtra on the Rough-Haired Cowherder

*Fifth in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, a rough-haired cowherder named Nanda came to the World-Honored One. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The rough-haired cowherder Nanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am now unable to leave the household life under the World-Honored One to practice the holy life. But from today I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and hold the precepts."

The World-Honored One told the rough-haired cowherder Nanda: "Do not take refuge in me. You should take refuge in the one in whom I took refuge."

The rough-haired cowherder Nanda asked: "World-Honored One, who is the one in whom the World-Honored One took refuge, in whom I should take refuge?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The rough-haired cowherder should know: I took refuge in the unsurpassed, right and perfect enlightenment. I took refuge in that and attained the right and perfect enlightenment. You should take refuge in that too."

The rough-haired cowherder Nanda said: "World-Honored One, from today I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and hold the precepts."

Then the rough-haired cowherder Nanda, shortly after taking refuge and receiving the precepts, needed to return the cattle to their owner. He said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I now have six hundred cattle that I must return to their owner. World-Honored One, please wait for me. After I have returned the cattle, I will come back."

The World-Honored One said: "The rough-haired cowherder should do as he sees fit."

Then the rough-haired cowherder Nanda returned the six hundred cattle to their owner. On the road back, he was gored to death by a bull.

At that time, a number of bhikṣus, having heard that the rough-haired cowherder Nanda, shortly after taking refuge under the World-Honored One and receiving the precepts, had been gored to death by a bull on the road, went to the World-Honored One, bowed their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and asked the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, where has the rough-haired cowherder Nanda been reborn, and what is his future destiny?"

The World-Honored One answered: "That good man had faith in the Dharma, accepted the Dharma, and practiced in accordance with the Dharma. He did not dispute about the Dharma. The rough-haired cowherder Nanda has ended the five lower fetters. He has been reborn by transformation and will attain parinirvāṇa there without returning to this world. Bhikṣus, if that good man had been able to spend more time with me, if he had stayed a bit longer, he would have known: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further existence,' and attained liberation in his very life."

At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is rare indeed that the rough-haired cowherder Nanda, in such a short time of taking refuge and receiving the precepts, should achieve such great benefit."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, bhikṣu. So it is. The rough-haired cowherder Nanda, in such a short time of taking refuge and receiving the precepts, achieved such great benefit."

Then the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "Among my excellent male lay disciples, the foremost in faith is the rough-haired cowherder Nanda."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (81) The Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Body

*Sixth in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There is one dharma that, when cultivated and practiced much, leads to great fear-stricken states being overcome, to the attainment of sweet dew and the realization of sweet dew. What is this one dharma? It is mindfulness of the body.

"How does a bhikṣu cultivate mindfulness of the body? A bhikṣu, whether walking, knows clearly 'I am walking'; whether standing, knows clearly 'I am standing'; whether sitting, knows clearly 'I am sitting'; whether lying down, knows clearly 'I am lying down.' Whatever posture the body may be in, he knows it clearly.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when going forward and returning, acts with clear comprehension. When looking ahead and looking behind, he acts with clear comprehension. When bending and extending his limbs, he acts with clear comprehension. When wearing his saṅghāṭī robe and carrying his bowl, he acts with clear comprehension. When eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, he acts with clear comprehension. When walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, and being silent, he acts with clear comprehension.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates this body from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities. In this body there are: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, rough skin, soft skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, fluid of the joints, and urine.

"Just as if there were a sack with two openings, full of various kinds of grain, such as rice, millet, sesame, and beans, and a man with good eyesight were to open it and examine it, saying, 'This is rice, this is millet, this is sesame, this is beans.' In the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates this body from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, rough skin, soft skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, fluid of the joints, and urine.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates this body with its elements as they exist, in their respective positions: 'In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'

"Just as a skilled butcher or butcher's apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, might lay out the parts at a crossroads, a bhikṣu likewise contemplates this body with its elements as they exist, in their respective positions: 'In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.'

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, as though he were viewing a corpse cast in a charnel ground, dead for one day, or two days, or three days, bloated, discolored, and festering, he compares his own body with it: 'My body too has this nature, has this destiny, and cannot escape it.'

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, as though he were viewing a corpse cast in a charnel ground, being eaten by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, wolves, and various kinds of insects, he compares his own body with it: 'My body too has this nature, has this destiny, and cannot escape it.'

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, as though he were viewing a corpse cast in a charnel ground: a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh or blood, held together by sinews; bones disconnected and scattered in all directions, here a hand bone, there a foot bone, here a shin bone, there a thigh bone, here a hip bone, there a spine bone, here a rib bone, there a breast bone, here an arm bone, there a shoulder bone, here a neck bone, there a jaw bone, here a skull bone, each in a different place, he compares his own body with it: 'My body too has this nature, has this destiny, and cannot escape it.'

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, as though he were viewing a corpse cast in a charnel ground: bones white as shells, or bluish like pigeons' color, or red like blood smears, or rotting and crumbling, or reduced to dust, he compares his own body with it: 'My body too has this nature, has this destiny, and cannot escape it.'

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with applied thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna. He pervades and fills this body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

"Just as a skilled bathhouse attendant or his apprentice, having placed fine bathing powder in a copper basin, sprinkles it again and again with water and kneads it, so that the ball of bath powder is thoroughly moistened, permeated inside and out with moisture, yet does not drip. In the same way, a bhikṣu pervades and fills this body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna. He pervades and fills this body with the joy and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of concentration.

"Just as a spring of water welling up from within, with no inflow from the east, west, south, or north, and no rain from the sky, but with a spring of pure water welling up from within the pool itself, pervading and filling the entire pool so that there is no part of the pool not pervaded by the cool water. In the same way, a bhikṣu pervades and fills this body with the joy and happiness born of concentration, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of concentration.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body. He enters and dwells in that which the noble ones describe as 'equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily' in the third dhyāna. He pervades and fills this body with happiness free from joy, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by happiness free from joy.

"Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged in the water, pervaded from root to tip by the cool water, so that there is no part not permeated by it. In the same way, a bhikṣu pervades and fills this body with happiness free from joy, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by happiness free from joy.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the previous disappearance of elation and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity and mindfulness purified. He sits pervading this body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the pure, bright mind.

"Just as a person sitting, covered from head to foot with a white cloth, so that there is no part of his body not covered by the white cloth. In the same way, a bhikṣu sits pervading this body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by the pure, bright mind.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates the perception of light, well taking hold of the perception, well maintaining the perception. As it is before, so it is after; as it is after, so it is before. As it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day. As it is above, so it is below; as it is below, so it is above. With an open, unobstructed mind, free from hindrances, he cultivates a mind pervaded by radiance.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu well takes hold of the reviewing sign. He well maintains in his mind the reviewing sign and well contemplates it. Just as one person observes another: a standing person observes a sitting person, or a sitting person observes a standing person. In the same way, a bhikṣu well takes hold of the reviewing sign, well maintains in his mind the reviewing sign, and well contemplates it.

"Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, living diligently, with clear comprehension and mindfulness, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world.

"If a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way, practicing it much, he will attain eighteen benefits. What are the eighteen?

"First, the bhikṣu is able to bear suffering. When suffering arises, his mind does not overwhelm him.

"Second, the bhikṣu is able to bear fear. When fear arises, his mind does not overwhelm him.

"Third, the bhikṣu is able to endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, bad odors, and being struck; he can endure painful bodily feelings that are sharp, intense, harsh, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening, and bear them patiently.

"Fourth, the bhikṣu can obtain the four dhyānas of the mind that pertain to the higher states of ease in this present life, obtaining them at will, without difficulty or trouble.

"Fifth, the bhikṣu exercises various kinds of supernormal powers: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he passes unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, as if through space; he sinks into the earth and emerges as if from water; he walks on water without sinking, as if on earth; seated cross-legged, he travels through space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he extends his bodily mastery even up to the Brahma world.

"Sixth, the bhikṣu, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing that of humans, hears both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near.

"Seventh, the bhikṣu, with his mind, knows the minds of other sentient beings and other persons: a mind with desire he knows as a mind with desire; a mind without desire he knows as a mind without desire; a mind with anger he knows as a mind with anger; a mind without anger he knows as a mind without anger; a mind with delusion he knows as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion he knows as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind he knows as a contracted mind; a distracted mind he knows as a distracted mind; a great mind he knows as a great mind; a mind that is not great he knows as a mind that is not great; a limited mind he knows as a limited mind; an unlimited mind he knows as an unlimited mind; a concentrated mind he knows as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind he knows as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind he knows as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind he knows as an unliberated mind.

"Eighth, the bhikṣu recollects the manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion: 'At that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, I experienced such pleasure and pain, I had such a lifespan. Dying from that place, I was reborn in another place. There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, I experienced such pleasure and pain, I had such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects the manifold past lives with their aspects and details.

"Ninth, the bhikṣu, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees sentient beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies, according to the karma of sentient beings: 'These sentient beings have done evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, evil deeds of mind; they reviled noble ones, held wrong views, and acted according to wrong views. Because of those causes and conditions, after the body breaks up and life ends, they are reborn in the evil destinies, in hell. These sentient beings have done good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, good deeds of mind; they did not revile noble ones, held right views, and acted according to right views. Because of those causes and conditions, after the body breaks up and life ends, they are reborn in good destinies, in the heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees sentient beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, in good destinies and bad destinies, and he knows them according to their karma.

"Tenth, the bhikṣu, through the destruction of the outflows, in this very life, through his own direct knowledge, realizes and dwells in the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further existence.'

"Bhikṣus, even if a person has not yet attained the ending of the outflows, there are still eight additional benefits from the cultivation of mindfulness of the body. What are the eight?

"Eleventh, his disenchantment and dispassion become sharper.

"Twelfth, he has no delight in worldly pleasures and pursues the practice of the holy life.

"Thirteenth, he is able to bear cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun, bad odors, and being struck; he can endure painful bodily feelings that are sharp, intense, harsh, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening, and bear them patiently.

"Fourteenth, he can obtain the four dhyānas.

"Fifteenth, he exercises various kinds of supernormal powers.

"Sixteenth, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds.

"Seventeenth, with his mind, he knows the minds of other sentient beings.

"Eighteenth, he recollects the manifold past lives.

"Even if a person has not yet attained the ending of the outflows, the above are the additional eight benefits from cultivating mindfulness of the body."

Then the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "If there is one dharma that is cultivated and practiced much, the body is at ease and the mind is at ease. With fear-stricken trembling overcome, it leads to the development of the mind, the development of wisdom, the attainment of great superknowledges, the attainment of the sweet dew, and the realization of the sweet dew. What is this one dharma? It is mindfulness of the body. If a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body and practices it much, the body is at ease and the mind is at ease. With fear-stricken trembling overcome, it leads to the development of the mind, the development of wisdom, the attainment of great superknowledges, the attainment of the sweet dew, and the realization of the sweet dew."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (82) The Sūtra on Cātumā

*Seventh in the series.*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the land of Cātumā, at a fig tree grove.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, came to the land of Cātumā to visit the World-Honored One. When the visiting bhikṣus exchanged greetings with the resident bhikṣus, arranged their bedding, and put away their robes and bowls, the noise was very great.

At that time, the World-Honored One asked the Venerable Ānanda: "What is this great noise? It sounds like fishermen hauling in fish."

The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, have come to the land of Cātumā to visit the World-Honored One. The visiting bhikṣus are exchanging greetings with the resident bhikṣus, arranging their bedding, and putting away their robes and bowls. That is the source of this great noise."

The World-Honored One told the Venerable Ānanda: "Go and tell those bhikṣus on my behalf: 'The Teacher summons you.'"

The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction. He went to those bhikṣus and said: "The World-Honored One summons you."

Those bhikṣus received the instruction and came to the World-Honored One. They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The World-Honored One then asked those bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, why is there such great noise? It sounds like fishermen hauling in fish."

Those bhikṣus addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, came to the land of Cātumā to visit the World-Honored One. The visiting bhikṣus were exchanging greetings with the resident bhikṣus, arranging their bedding, and putting away their robes and bowls. That was the source of the great noise."

The World-Honored One told those bhikṣus: "You may go! I dismiss you! You should not dwell near me."

Those bhikṣus replied: "Yes, World-Honored One." They rose from their seats, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, the people of the Cātumā land, the Śākyas, were assembled in the meeting hall for some business. They saw those bhikṣus coming from afar. Seeing them, they rose to greet them and asked: "Venerable Ones, where are you going?"

Those bhikṣus answered: "The World-Honored One has dismissed us from living near him."

The Śākyas of Cātumā said to those bhikṣus: "Venerable Ones, please wait here for a while. We will go and try to reconcile things."

Then the Śākyas of Cātumā went to the World-Honored One, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One accept those bhikṣus. World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One console those bhikṣus. Why? World-Honored One, among these bhikṣus there are those who are newly ordained and have only recently left the household life.
