If they do not get to see the World-Honored One, they may undergo change and deterioration. It is like a young seedling: if it does not get water, it will undergo change and deterioration. So too, World-Honored One, among these bhikṣus there are those who are newly ordained and have only recently left the household life. If they do not get to see the World-Honored One and receive his instruction, they may undergo change and deterioration. World-Honored One, please accept those bhikṣus and console them."

Then the Brahmā King also knew in his mind what the World-Honored One was thinking. As quickly as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, he disappeared from the Brahma world and appeared before the Buddha. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One accept those bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One console those bhikṣus. Why? World-Honored One, among these bhikṣus there are those who are newly ordained and have only recently left the household life. If they do not get to see the World-Honored One, they may

# Fascicle Twenty of the Madhyamāgama

## (81) Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Body, the Tenth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Aṅga together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and they proceeded to the dwelling place of Āpaṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, at dawn dressed in his robes, took his bowl, and entered Āpaṇa to beg for food. After eating, in the afternoon he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, went to a grove, entered that grove, arrived at the base of a tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after the midday meal, gathered and sat in the lecture hall, and together discussed this matter: "Venerables, the World-Honored One is truly extraordinary, truly remarkable! The cultivation of mindfulness of the body, analyzed and broadly expounded, thoroughly known, thoroughly contemplated, thoroughly cultivated, thoroughly guarded and managed, well accomplished, well practiced, abiding in unified mind. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body has great fruit and reward, gaining the eye, having vision, seeing the ultimate truth."

At that time, the World-Honored One was in meditative repose, and with his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, he heard the many bhikṣus after the midday meal gathered sitting in the lecture hall, together discussing this matter: "Venerables, the World-Honored One is truly extraordinary, truly remarkable! The cultivation of mindfulness of the body, analyzed and broadly expounded, thoroughly known, thoroughly contemplated, thoroughly cultivated, thoroughly guarded and managed, well accomplished, well practiced, abiding in unified mind. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body has great fruit and reward, gaining the eye, having vision, seeing the ultimate truth." Having heard this, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditative repose, went to the lecture hall, and sat down on a prepared seat before the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "What matter were you just discussing together? For what purpose did you gather and sit in the lecture hall?"

The bhikṣus then said: "World-Honored One, we bhikṣus, after the midday meal, gathered and sat in the lecture hall, and together discussed this matter: 'Venerables, the World-Honored One is truly extraordinary, truly remarkable! The cultivation of mindfulness of the body, analyzed and broadly expounded, thoroughly known, thoroughly contemplated, thoroughly cultivated, thoroughly guarded and managed, well accomplished, well practiced, abiding in unified mind. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body has great fruit and reward, gaining the eye, having vision, seeing the ultimate truth.' World-Honored One, we were just discussing this matter together; it was for this purpose that we gathered and sat in the lecture hall."

The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus again: "How do I teach the cultivation of mindfulness of the body, analyzed and broadly expounded, obtaining great fruit and reward?"

The bhikṣus then said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the World-Honored One is the lord of the Dharma, the Dharma comes from the World-Honored One. We pray that you will explain it; having heard it, we will come to broadly understand its meaning."

The Buddha then told them: "Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I shall analyze its meaning for you." The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "How does a bhikṣu cultivate mindfulness of the body? A bhikṣu, when walking, knows that he is walking; when standing, knows that he is standing; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; when lying down, knows that he is lying down; when sleeping, knows that he is sleeping; when awake, knows that he is awake; when between sleeping and waking, knows that he is between sleeping and waking. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu clearly knows going out and coming in, observes and discerns well bending and stretching, looking down and looking up; his deportment is composed and orderly; he properly wears his saṅghāṭī and other robes and his bowl; walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, he clearly knows all of these. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. When a bhikṣu gives rise to evil, unwholesome thoughts, he uses wholesome thoughts to cure, cut off, extinguish, and stop them. Just as a carpenter or a carpenter's apprentice holds a marking line to mark a piece of wood, and then with a sharp axe hews and straightens it. In the same way, when a bhikṣu gives rise to evil, unwholesome thoughts, he uses wholesome thoughts to cure, cut off, extinguish, and stop them. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu presses his teeth together, presses his tongue against the palate, and with mind controls mind, curing, cutting off, extinguishing, and stopping. Just as two strong men seize one weak person, grasping him everywhere, turning him about, freely striking and beating him. In the same way, a bhikṣu presses his teeth together, presses his tongue against the palate, and with mind controls mind, curing, cutting off, extinguishing, and stopping. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, being mindful of the in-breath, knows he is mindful of the in-breath; being mindful of the out-breath, knows he is mindful of the out-breath. Breathing in long, he knows he is breathing in long; breathing out long, he knows he is breathing out long. Breathing in short, he knows he is breathing in short; breathing out short, he knows he is breathing out short. He trains to breathe in experiencing the whole body; he trains to breathe out experiencing the whole body. He trains to breathe in calming bodily formations; he trains to breathe out calming verbal formations. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the joy and happiness born of seclusion permeate everywhere without exception. Just as a skilled bath attendant fills a vessel with bathing powder, mixes it with water into a ball, so that moisture drenches, pervades, and fills it throughout with no part untouched. In the same way, a bhikṣu, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the joy and happiness born of seclusion permeate everywhere without exception. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the joy and happiness born of concentration permeate everywhere without exception. Just as a mountain spring, extremely pure and limpid, full and overflowing, with water from the four directions having no way to enter, yet from the bottom of that spring water wells up of itself, overflowing outward, drenching the mountain, moistening it, pervading and filling it throughout with no part untouched. In the same way, a bhikṣu, with the joy and happiness born of concentration, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the joy and happiness born of concentration permeate everywhere without exception. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, with the happiness born of the absence of joy, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the happiness born of the absence of joy permeates everywhere without exception. Just as blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, and white lotuses, born in water and grown in water, resting at the bottom of the water, with their roots, stems, flowers, and leaves all drenched and moistened, pervaded and filled throughout with no part untouched. In the same way, a bhikṣu, with the happiness born of the absence of joy, drenches, moistens, pervades, and fills his entire body, so that the happiness born of the absence of joy permeates everywhere without exception. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, within this body, with a purified mind, mentally resolves and pervades it completely, accomplishing this and abiding therein. Within this body, the purified mind is everywhere without exception. Just as a person is covered with a cloth of seven or eight cubits, from head to foot, with no part of the body left uncovered. In the same way, a bhikṣu, within this body, with a purified mind, mentally resolves and pervades it completely, accomplishing this and abiding therein. Within this body, the purified mind is everywhere without exception. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu is mindful of the perception of light, well receives it, well maintains it, well establishes it in mind. As it is before, so too behind; as it is behind, so too before. As it is by day, so too by night; as it is by night, so too by day. As it is below, so too above; as it is above, so too below. Thus without inversion, with mind free from entanglement, he cultivates the mind of light, and his mind is never covered by darkness. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu contemplates the sign, well receives it, well maintains it, well establishes it in mind. Just as one person, sitting, observes another lying down, or lying down, observes another sitting. In the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates the sign, well receives it, well maintains it, well establishes it in mind. Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, with this body as it is positioned, regardless of whether it is in good or poor condition, from head to foot, contemplates and sees that it is filled with various kinds of impurities. He reflects: 'In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain and brain stem, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, phlegm, bile, and urine.' Just as a vessel filled with various kinds of seeds, which a person with eyes can see clearly and distinctly, namely, rice seeds, millet seeds, barley, wheat, large and small sesame seeds, and mustard seeds. In the same way, a bhikṣu, with this body as it is positioned, regardless of whether it is in good or poor condition, from head to foot, contemplates and sees that it is filled with various kinds of impurities. He reflects: 'In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain and brain stem, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, phlegm, bile, and urine.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu contemplates the elements of the body: 'In this body of mine there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.' Just as a butcher who has slaughtered an ox, removed its hide and spread it on the ground, and divided it into six portions. In the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates the elements of the body: 'In this body of mine there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu contemplates a dead corpse, one or two days dead, up to six or seven days, pecked by crows and kites, gnawed by jackals and dogs, burned by fire, buried in the earth, all rotten and decomposed. Having seen this, he compares it to himself: 'This body of mine is also just like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, as if he had previously seen on a charnel ground a skeleton turning blue, rotting, half-eaten, with the chain of bones lying on the ground, having seen this, compares it to himself: 'This body of mine is also just like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, as if he had previously seen on a charnel ground a corpse stripped of skin, flesh, and blood, with only sinews connecting the bones, having seen this, compares it to himself: 'This body of mine is also just like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, as if he had previously seen on a charnel ground the bone joints disarticulated, scattered in all directions: foot bones, shin bones, thigh bones, hip bones, spine bones, shoulder bones, neck bones, and skull, each in a different place. Having seen this, he compares it to himself: 'This body of mine is also just like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. A bhikṣu, as if he had previously seen on a charnel ground bones white as a conch shell, blue like the color of a pigeon, red as if smeared with blood, rotted and crumbled to powder. Having seen this, he compares it to himself: 'This body of mine is also just like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.' Thus a bhikṣu, in accordance with his bodily actions, knows the above as it truly is. If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with mind free from negligence, cultivating diligently, cutting off the afflictions of mind and attaining a concentrated mind, and having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the above as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating mindfulness of the body.

"If anyone cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, all wholesome dharmas are included within it, namely, the factors of the path. If one's mind is mentally resolved, pervading and filling all, it is like the great ocean, in which all the small rivers are contained. If anyone cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, all wholesome dharmas are included within it, namely, the factors of the path.

"If any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why is this? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. Just as there is a vessel, empty and without water, properly placed on the ground, and a person brings water to pour into the vessel. What do you bhikṣus think? Will that vessel receive the water?"

The bhikṣus answered: "It will, World-Honored One. Why? Because it is empty, without water, and properly placed on the ground; therefore it will certainly receive it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. If any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body. Just as there is a vessel, filled to the brim with water, properly placed on the ground, and a person brings water to pour into the vessel. What do you bhikṣus think? Will that vessel receive the water?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because that vessel is full of water and properly placed on the ground; therefore it will not receive it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body. If any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. Just as a strong man hurls a large heavy stone into soft mud. What do you bhikṣus think? Will the mud receive it?"

The bhikṣus answered: "It will, World-Honored One. Why? Because the mud is soft and the stone is heavy; therefore it will certainly receive it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. If any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body. Just as a strong man throws a light ball of feathers at a flat door panel. What do you bhikṣus think? Will it receive it?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because the feather ball is light and flimsy, and the door panel stands flat; therefore it will not receive it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body. If any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. Just as a person who seeks fire uses dry wood as the base and drills with a dry drill stick. What do you bhikṣus think? Will that person obtain fire?"

The bhikṣus answered: "He will, World-Honored One. Why? Because he drills with a dry drill stick on dry wood; therefore he will certainly obtain it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin does not properly establish mindfulness of the body and goes about with a narrow mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity and will certainly be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is empty, without mindfulness of the body. If any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body. Just as a person who seeks fire uses wet wood as the base and drills with a wet drill stick. What do you bhikṣus think? Will that person obtain fire?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why? Because he drills with a wet drill stick on wet wood; therefore he will not obtain it."

"In the same way, if any śramaṇa or brahmin properly establishes mindfulness of the body and goes about with a boundless mind, then Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity but will never be able to find one. Why? Because that śramaṇa or brahmin is not empty but possesses mindfulness of the body."

"If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, one should know there are eighteen benefits. What are the eighteen? A bhikṣu is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies and fleas, the assault of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh words and beatings with sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses, extremely painful, even to the point where his life is about to end, all that is disagreeable he can bear and endure. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the first benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu can endure displeasure. If displeasure arises, his mind never becomes attached to it. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the second benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu can endure fear. If fear arises, his mind never becomes attached to it. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the third benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu gives rise to three evil thoughts: thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm. If these three evil thoughts arise, his mind never becomes attached to them. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, these are called the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh benefits.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from evil, unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining and abiding in the fourth jhāna. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the eighth benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the three fetters already exhausted, attains the fruit of stream-entry, no longer falling into evil destinies, certain to proceed toward right awakening, taking at most seven more existences. Having gone back and forth between heaven and the human realm, he reaches the end of suffering. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the ninth benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the three fetters already exhausted, with lust, anger, and delusion diminished, attains the state of once-returning, going back and forth once between heaven and the human realm, and having done so once, reaches the end of suffering. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the tenth benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the five lower fetters exhausted, is born in that realm, where he attains final nirvāṇa, attaining the dharma of non-return, never returning to this world. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the eleventh benefit.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, if there is the peaceful liberation, departing from form and attaining the formless, in accordance with that sign, he realizes with his own body and abides therein, and with wisdom contemplates and knows the outflows, cutting off the outflows. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, these are called the twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth benefits.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains the bases of supernatural power, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of birth and death, and with all outflows already exhausted, attains the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In the present life he knows for himself, realizes for himself, personally bears witness and abides therein: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming.' He knows this as it truly is. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, this is called the eighteenth benefit. If one cultivates mindfulness of the body in this way and broadly develops it thus, one should know there are these eighteen merits."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of Sūtra on Mindfulness of the Body, the Tenth.

The eighteen benefits internally regarding the sixth, seventh, eighth, and thirteenth through seventeenth should be subsumed within the fifth and eighteenth benefits. In the Southern recension they are grouped within the fourth and twelfth, but the reasoning is still difficult to understand.

---

## (82) Sūtra on Jīvaka Insects, the Eleventh in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after the midday meal, having some business to attend to, gathered and sat in the lecture hall, wishing to settle a dispute, discussing this Dharma and Vinaya, this teaching of the Buddha. At that time, the bhikṣu Citrahastī (Cittra the Elephant's Son) was also in the assembly. Now, when the many bhikṣus were discussing this Dharma and Vinaya, this teaching of the Buddha, Citrahastī the bhikṣu, in the midst of their discussion, competitively interjected his own words, not waiting for the bhikṣus to finish speaking on the Dharma, and without respect, without proper regard, he questioned the senior elder bhikṣus.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila was in that assembly. Then the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila addressed the bhikṣu Citrahastī: "Venerable, you should know that when the many bhikṣus are discussing this Dharma and Vinaya, this teaching of the Buddha, you should not competitively interject your own words in the middle of it. When the bhikṣus have finished speaking, then you may speak. You should with respect, and with proper regard, question the senior elder bhikṣus. Do not be disrespectful, do not be without proper regard when questioning the senior elder bhikṣus."

At that time, the friends and companions of the bhikṣu Citrahastī were all in the assembly. Then the friends and companions of the bhikṣu Citrahastī said to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila: "Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, please do not greatly reproach and admonish the bhikṣu Citrahastī. Why? The bhikṣu Citrahastī is endowed with virtue and is learned. He appears to be lax, but he is not arrogant. Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the bhikṣu Citrahastī is able to assist the bhikṣus whenever they have something to do."

Then the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila addressed the friends and companions of the bhikṣu Citrahastī: "Venerables, those who do not know another's mind should not rashly speak of whether someone is worthy or unworthy. Why? There may be a person who, when in the presence of the World-Honored One, and in the presence of the senior, elder, holy practitioners who are worthy of shame, embarrassment, love, and respect, conducts himself well and guards himself well. But afterward, when away from the presence of the World-Honored One, and away from the presence of the senior, elder, holy practitioners who are worthy of shame, embarrassment, love, and respect, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just like an ox that enters another person's field, and the field keeper catches it and either ties it with a rope or puts it in a pen. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'This ox will never again enter another person's field,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? Because that ox, being tied with a rope, might break or loosen it, or being confined in a pen, might break through it or jump out, and enter another's field again just as before."

"Venerables, there may be a person who, when in the presence of the World-Honored One, and in the presence of the senior, elder, holy practitioners who are worthy of shame, embarrassment, love, and respect, conducts himself well and guards himself well. But afterward, when away from the presence of the World-Honored One, and away from the presence of the holy practitioners who are worthy of shame, embarrassment, love, and respect, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person.

"Furthermore, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the first jhāna. Having attained the first jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just as during a great rain, when the ponds between the villages are filled to the brim with water, so that whatever was formerly visible, such as sand, stones, grass, trees, beetles, fish, turtles, frogs, and various aquatic creatures, going, coming, running, and staying, after the water is full can no longer be seen. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'In that pond, one will never again see sand, stones, grass, trees, beetles, fish, turtles, frogs, and various aquatic creatures, going, coming, running, and staying,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? Because the water of that pond may be drunk by elephants, horses, camels, cattle, donkeys, pigs, deer, and water buffalo, or taken by people for use, or blown by wind and dried by sun. Whatever was formerly not visible, such as sand, stones, grass, trees, beetles, fish, turtles, frogs, and various aquatic creatures, going, coming, running, and staying, after the water recedes, will be seen again as before."

"In the same way, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the first jhāna. Having attained the first jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person.

"Furthermore, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the second jhāna. Having attained the second jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just as during a great rain, when the dust at a crossroads is extinguished and turns to mud. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'The mud at this crossroads will never dry out and turn back to dust,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? Because at this crossroads, elephants walk, horses walk, camels, cattle, donkeys, pigs, deer, water buffalo, and people walk upon it, and the wind blows and the sun dries it. The mud at that crossroads, once dried, will turn back to dust again."

"In the same way, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the second jhāna. Having attained the second jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person.

"Furthermore, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the third jhāna. Having attained the third jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just like the water of a mountain spring lake, clear and limpid, with even banks, still and unmoving, without waves. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'The water of that mountain spring lake will never again move, nor will there be waves,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? If a great wind suddenly comes from the east, blowing that lake water, it will stir and surge with waves. Likewise if a great wind suddenly comes from the south, west, or north, blowing that lake water, it will stir and surge with waves."

"In the same way, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the third jhāna. Having attained the third jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person.

"Furthermore, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the fourth jhāna. Having attained the fourth jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just like a householder or a householder's son who has eaten fine food and is fully satisfied. Having eaten their fill, whatever food they previously desired, they no longer desire. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'That householder or householder's son will never again desire food,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? Because that householder or householder's son, after passing the night and becoming hungry, whatever food they previously did not want, they will desire again."

"In the same way, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the fourth jhāna. Having attained the fourth jhāna, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person.

"Furthermore, venerables, there may be a person who has attained the concentration of the perception of neither perception nor non-perception. Having attained the concentration of the perception of neither perception nor non-perception, he rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, it is just like a remote, uninhabited place where one hears the sound of cicadas. In that remote place, if a king or a king's chief minister lodges there for the night, with the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, footsteps, conch shells, drums, slender-waisted drums, music drums, dancing, singing, lutes, and eating and drinking, then the sound of the cicadas that was formerly heard can no longer be heard. Venerables, if someone were to say, 'In that remote place, one will never again hear the sound of the cicadas,' would that be a correct statement?"

They answered: "No, it would not. Why? Because once that king and the king's chief minister have passed the night and departed at dawn, each returning to their own place, then the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, footsteps, conch shells, drums, slender-waisted drums, music drums, dancing, singing, harps, and eating and drinking that formerly obscured the sound of the cicadas, once they have gone, one will hear it again as before."

"In the same way, venerables, one who has attained the concentration of the perception of neither perception nor non-perception, having attained it, rests content therein and does not further seek what has not been attained, wishing to attain it; what has not been obtained, wishing to obtain it; what has not been realized, wishing to realize it. After some time, he frequently associates with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk. Having frequently associated with householders, joking, being arrogant, and engaging in various kinds of frivolous talk, desire arises in his mind. When desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes heated and his mind becomes heated. When his body and mind become heated, he abandons the precepts and leaves the monastic life. Venerables, this is called one such person."

At that time, the bhikṣu Citrahastī soon afterward abandoned the precepts and left the monastic life. The friends and companions of the bhikṣu Citrahastī, having heard that Citrahastī had abandoned the precepts and left the monastic life, went to the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila. Having arrived, they said: "Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, did you know the mind of the bhikṣu Citrahastī, or did you know from other circumstances? Why do we ask? Because the bhikṣu Citrahastī has already abandoned the precepts and left the monastic life."

The Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila addressed those friends and companions: "Venerables, this matter is exactly as it should be. Why? Because he did not know as it truly is, did not see as it truly is. Why? Because of not knowing as it truly is, not seeing as it truly is."

Thus spoke the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Jīvaka Insects, the Eleventh.

---

## (83) Sūtra on Sleep for Senior Elders, the Twelfth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vajji, at Mount Crocodile, in the Fearful Grove Deer Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was traveling in the country of Magadha, in the village of Good Friends. There, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while dwelling alone in a quiet place, seated in meditative reflection, fell asleep. The World-Honored One knew from afar that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while dwelling alone in a quiet place, seated in meditative reflection, had fallen asleep. Having known this, the World-Honored One entered the appropriate concentration, and through that concentration, just as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Fearful Grove Deer Park at Mount Crocodile in Vajji and appeared before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in the village of Good Friends in Magadha. Then the World-Honored One emerged from that concentration and said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you are drowsy with sleep! Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you are drowsy with sleep!"

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the World-Honored One: "So it is, World-Honored One."

The Buddha then said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana, whatever sign is connected to drowsy sleep, do not cultivate that sign, and do not dwell extensively upon it. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should recollect the Dharma you have formerly heard, recollect and uphold it, broadly spread it, and recite it. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should recollect the Dharma you have formerly heard, recollect and uphold it, and broadly explain it for others. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should recollect the Dharma you have formerly heard, recollect and uphold it, reflect upon it with the mind, and think upon it with the mind. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should rub both ears with both hands. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated.

"If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should wash your face and eyes with cold water and sprinkle it on your body. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should go outside your room, gaze at the four directions, and look up at the stars. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should go outside your room, and at the head of the building, in the open air, practice walking meditation, guarding your sense faculties, with your mind settled inwardly, maintaining the perception of what lies ahead and behind. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should leave the walking meditation path, go to the end of the walking path, spread out your sitting cloth, and sit cross-legged. In this way, drowsiness and sleep can be eliminated. If your drowsiness and sleep are still not eliminated, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should return to your room, fold your uttarāsaṅga in four layers and spread it on the bed, fold your saṅghāṭī to make a pillow, lie on your right side with feet placed one upon the other, establish the perception of light in your mind, set up right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and always maintain the intention to arise.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, do not take delight in the comfort of lying on your bed and the pleasure of sleep. Do not covet material gain, and do not cling to fame and reputation. Why? I say that not all dharmas should be associated with, yet I also say that some may be associated with. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, which dharmas do I say should not be associated with? Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the path and worldly dharmas are combined together, I say these dharmas should not be associated with. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the path and worldly dharmas are combined together, there will be much speaking. If there is much speaking, there will be agitation. If there is agitation, the mind will not be at rest. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the mind is not at rest, the mind departs from concentration. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, therefore I say one should not associate with these. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, which dharmas do I say may be associated with? Mahāmaudgalyāyana, those remote, uninhabited places, I say these dharmas may be associated with: mountain forests, beneath trees, empty and quiet places, high cliff caves that are silent and without sound, remote and secluded, free from harm, without people, suitable for meditative repose. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I say these dharmas may be associated with.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when you enter a village to beg for food, you should cultivate weariness toward gains, weariness toward offerings and reverence. When your mind has established weariness toward gains, offerings, and reverence, then enter the village to beg for food. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, do not enter a village to beg for food with a proud and haughty mind. Why? Among householder families there are such situations: when a bhikṣu comes to beg for food, the householder may pay no attention. The bhikṣu then thinks: 'Who has turned this householder family against me? Why is it that when I enter the householder's home, the householder pays me no attention?' Because of this, anxiety arises; because of anxiety, agitation arises; because of agitation, the mind does not rest; because the mind does not rest, the mind departs from concentration. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when you teach the Dharma, do not teach with contention. If one teaches with contention, there will be much speaking. Because of much speaking, agitation arises. Because agitation arises, the mind does not rest. Because the mind does not rest, the mind departs from concentration. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when you teach the Dharma, do not force it, teaching the Dharma like a lion. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when you teach the Dharma, teach with a humble mind, relinquishing force, extinguishing force, destroying force, and without forcing it, teach the Dharma like a lion. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should train in this way."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, how does a bhikṣu reach the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate completion of the holy life?"

The World-Honored One said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when a bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling, a painful feeling, or a feeling that is neither pleasant nor painful, he contemplates that feeling as impermanent, contemplates its arising and passing away, contemplates its cessation, contemplates dispassion, contemplates extinction, contemplates relinquishment. Having contemplated that feeling as impermanent, contemplated its arising and passing away, contemplated its cessation, contemplated dispassion, contemplated extinction, and contemplated relinquishment, he does not cling to this world. Because he does not cling to this world, he is not wearied. Because he is not wearied, he attains nirvāṇa. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. He knows this as it truly is. Mahāmaudgalyāyana, thus does a bhikṣu reach the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate completion of the holy life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Sleep for Senior Elders, the Twelfth.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Collection)
## Fascicle 21

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva during the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

---

### (87) Discourse on the Parable of the Raft

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "There was once a man traveling on a long road who came upon a great expanse of water. The near shore was dangerous and terrifying, while the far shore was safe and without fear. There was no boat or bridge by which to cross to the far shore. That man then thought: 'This great expanse of water has a near shore that is dangerous and terrifying, while the far shore is safe and without fear. There is no boat or bridge by which to cross to the far shore. I should now gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves and bind them into a raft. Riding this raft, using my hands and feet to propel myself, I shall safely cross to the far shore.'

"That man then gathered grass, wood, branches, and leaves and bound them into a raft. Riding this raft, using his hands and feet to propel himself, he safely crossed to the far shore. Having crossed to the far shore, that man then thought: 'This raft has been of great benefit to me. Riding this raft, using my hands and feet to propel myself, I safely crossed from the dangerous and terrifying near shore to the safe far shore without fear. I should now place this raft upon my head or carry it on my shoulders, and go wherever I wish.'

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? If that man does this with the raft, does he do what should be done with it?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, what should that man do to properly handle the raft? After that man has crossed to the far shore, he should think: 'This raft has been of great benefit to me. Riding this raft, using my hands and feet to propel myself, I safely crossed from the dangerous and terrifying near shore to the safe far shore without fear. I should now pull this raft up onto dry ground, or push it back into the water, and then go wherever I wish.' Bhikṣus, if that man does this, he does what should be done with the raft.

"In the same way, I have taught you the Dharma as being like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. If you understand the Dharma as being like a raft, you should let go even of the Dharma, how much more so what is not the Dharma.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are six views. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain them for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, there are ignorant ordinary people who have not met noble ones, are unskilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and are not trained in the Dharma of noble ones; who have not met good people, are unskilled in the Dharma of good people, and are not trained in the Dharma of good people. They regard form as self, or regard self as possessing form, or regard form as being in self, or regard self as being in form.

"They regard feeling as self, or regard self as possessing feeling, or regard feeling as being in self, or regard self as being in feeling.

"They regard perception as self, or regard self as possessing perception, or regard perception as being in self, or regard self as being in perception.

"They regard formations as self, or regard self as possessing formations, or regard formations as being in self, or regard self as being in formations.

"They regard consciousness as self, or regard self as possessing consciousness, or regard consciousness as being in self, or regard self as being in consciousness.

"They say: 'This is self, this is the world. After death, I shall be permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I shall abide thus forever.' This is the view of eternalism. What is called the view of eternalism is a view, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a deception of views, the agitation of views, the bondage of views. The ignorant ordinary person, bound by views, is subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, sorrow, suffering, and lamentation, and thus is not liberated from suffering. I say this.

"Bhikṣus, the learned noble disciple has met noble ones, is skilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and is well trained in the Dharma of noble ones; has met good people, is skilled in the Dharma of good people, and is well trained in the Dharma of good people. He does not regard form as self, does not regard self as possessing form, does not regard form as being in self, does not regard self as being in form.

"He does not regard feeling as self, does not regard self as possessing feeling, does not regard feeling as being in self, does not regard self as being in feeling.

"He does not regard perception as self, does not regard self as possessing perception, does not regard perception as being in self, does not regard self as being in perception.

"He does not regard formations as self, does not regard self as possessing formations, does not regard formations as being in self, does not regard self as being in formations.

"He does not regard consciousness as self, does not regard self as possessing consciousness, does not regard consciousness as being in self, does not regard self as being in consciousness.

"He does not say: 'This is self, this is the world. After death, I shall be permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I shall abide thus forever.' He does not hold the view of eternalism. What is called the view of eternalism is a view, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a deception of views, the agitation of views, the bondage of views. The learned noble disciple, being unbound by views, is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, sorrow, suffering, and lamentation, and thus is liberated from suffering. I say this.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, the ignorant ordinary person who has not met noble ones, is unskilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and is not trained in the Dharma of noble ones; who has not met good people, is unskilled in the Dharma of good people, and is not trained in the Dharma of good people. He says: 'There is no self, there is no self's possessions.' Such a person grasps at what does not exist. This person then worries and grieves, weeping and beating his breast, falling into confusion. Bhikṣus, this is how one is disturbed by what does not exist internally.

"Bhikṣus, how is one not disturbed by what does not exist internally? The bhikṣu does not regard form as self, does not regard self as possessing form, does not regard form as being in self, does not regard self as being in form. He does not regard feeling as self, does not regard self as possessing feeling, does not regard feeling as being in self, does not regard self as being in feeling. He does not regard perception as self, does not regard self as possessing perception, does not regard perception as being in self, does not regard self as being in perception. He does not regard formations as self, does not regard self as possessing formations, does not regard formations as being in self, does not regard self as being in formations. He does not regard consciousness as self, does not regard self as possessing consciousness, does not regard consciousness as being in self, does not regard self as being in consciousness. He does not grasp at what does not exist, and not grasping at what does not exist, he does not worry. Not worrying, he individually attains nirvāṇa: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; there is no more becoming, I know it as it really is.'

"Furthermore, bhikṣus, the ignorant ordinary person who has not met noble ones, is unskilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and is not trained in the Dharma of noble ones; who has not met good people, is unskilled in the Dharma of good people, and is not trained in the Dharma of good people. He is afraid and alarmed. Why? He hears the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples teaching the Dharma to bring the mind to peace and tranquility, to teach tending toward nirvāṇa, bringing all formations to extinction, abandoning all defilements, extinguishing craving, and attaining cessation, nirvāṇa. That ignorant ordinary person then thinks: 'I shall surely be annihilated, I shall surely perish, I shall surely not exist. Previously I existed, but now I shall not exist.' He then grieves, worries, weeps, and beats his breast, falling into confusion.

"Bhikṣus, this is how one is disturbed by what does not exist externally.

"Bhikṣus, how is one not disturbed by what does not exist externally? The bhikṣu hears the Tathāgata or the Tathāgata's disciples teaching the Dharma to bring the mind to peace and tranquility, to teach tending toward nirvāṇa, bringing all formations to extinction, abandoning all defilements, extinguishing craving, and attaining cessation, nirvāṇa. That bhikṣu does not then think: 'I shall surely be annihilated, I shall surely perish, I shall surely not exist. Previously I existed, but now I shall not exist.' He does not grieve, does not worry, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.

"Bhikṣus, this is how one is not disturbed by what does not exist externally.

"Bhikṣus, you may grasp at possessions that are permanent, eternal, not subject to change, and that abide thus forever. Bhikṣus, do you see any such possession that is permanent, eternal, not subject to change, and that abides thus forever?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Good, good, bhikṣus. I also do not see any possession that is permanent, eternal, not subject to change, and that abides thus forever.

"Bhikṣus, you may cling to the self-theory, whereby when clinging to the self-theory, no suffering arises, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow arises. Bhikṣus, do you see any such self-theory that, when clung to, brings about no suffering, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Good, good, bhikṣus. I also do not see any self-theory that, when clung to, brings about no suffering, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow.

"Bhikṣus, you may rely on a view as a support, whereby when relying on a view as a support, no suffering arises, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow arises. Bhikṣus, do you see any such view as a support that, when relied upon, brings about no suffering, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Good, good, bhikṣus. I also do not see any view as a support that, when relied upon, brings about no suffering, no grief, lamentation, pain, or sorrow.

"Bhikṣus, if there were a self, would there be 'belonging to self'?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, if there were things belonging to self, would there be a self?"

"Yes, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, self and things belonging to self, both being truly and actually unobtainable, then this view, namely, 'This is self, this is the world. After death, I shall be permanent, eternal, not subject to change. I shall abide thus forever,' is this not an utterly and completely foolish teaching?"

"It is so, World-Honored One. This is indeed an utterly and completely foolish teaching."

"Bhikṣus, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can the learned noble disciple regard this as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, is feeling permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can the learned noble disciple regard this as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, is perception permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can the learned noble disciple regard this as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, are formations permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent, are they suffering?"

"They are suffering, World-Honored One."

"If they are impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can the learned noble disciple regard this as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, is consciousness permanent or impermanent?"

"Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

"It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"If it is impermanent and suffering, subject to change, can the learned noble disciple regard this as: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

"No, World-Honored One."

"Therefore, bhikṣus, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether near or far, all form is not self, not other than self, and both do not abide together. This should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.

"Whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether near or far, all feeling is not self, not other than self, and both do not abide together. This should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.

"Whatever perception there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether near or far, all perception is not self, not other than self, and both do not abide together. This should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.

"Whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether near or far, all formations are not self, not other than self, and both do not abide together. This should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.

"Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether near or far, all consciousness is not self, not other than self, and both do not abide together. This should be seen as it really is with right wisdom.

"Bhikṣus, the learned noble disciple who sees thus becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; there is no more becoming, I know it as it really is.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (88) Discourse on the Parable of the Snake

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, gave rise to an evil wrong view such as this: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them."

A number of bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, had given rise to an evil wrong view such as this: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them." Those bhikṣus then went to the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha and asked him: "Ariṭṭha, did you really give rise to such a view as this: 'As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them'?"

The bhikṣu Ariṭṭha answered: "Indeed so. As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them."

At that time, those bhikṣus admonished the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, trying to make him abandon this evil wrong view: "Ariṭṭha, do not say this. Do not slander the World-Honored One. It is not good to slander the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One would never say such a thing. Ariṭṭha, the World-Honored One has in many ways taught that obstructive dharmas are indeed obstructive to the one who practices them." Although those bhikṣus admonished him thus, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha stubbornly held to this evil wrong view, insisting and maintaining: "This alone is true; everything else is false."

They admonished him three times but were unable to make him abandon this evil wrong view. Those bhikṣus then rose from their seats and went to the World-Honored One. They bowed their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a vulture trainer, has given rise to an evil wrong view such as this: 'As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them.' World-Honored One, we heard that the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha had given rise to such an evil wrong view, so we went to him and asked: 'Ariṭṭha, did you really give rise to such a view?' Ariṭṭha answered us: 'Indeed so. As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them.' World-Honored One, we then admonished the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, trying to make him abandon this evil wrong view: 'Ariṭṭha, do not say this. Do not slander the World-Honored One. It is not good to slander the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One would never say such a thing. Ariṭṭha, the World-Honored One has in many ways taught that obstructive dharmas are indeed obstructive to the one who practices them.' Although we admonished him three times, we were unable to make him abandon this evil wrong view. Therefore, World-Honored One, we have come to report this matter to you."

At that time, the World-Honored One told a certain bhikṣu: "Go to the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha and say: 'The World-Honored One calls you.'"

That bhikṣu received the instruction, went to the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, and said: "The World-Honored One calls you."

The bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, hearing that the World-Honored One was calling him, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at his feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked him: "Ariṭṭha, did you really give rise to such a view as this: 'As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them'?"

The bhikṣu Ariṭṭha answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One. As I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them."

The World-Honored One rebuked him: "Ariṭṭha, how do you understand my teaching of the Dharma in this way? Ariṭṭha, from whose mouth have you heard me teach the Dharma thus? You foolish man! I have in many ways taught that obstructive dharmas are indeed obstructive to the one who practices them. I have said that sensual pleasures give little satisfaction but much suffering and much trouble, and in them the danger is even greater. I have said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton, that sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat, that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch, that sensual pleasures are like a pit of fire, that sensual pleasures are like a venomous snake, that sensual pleasures are like a dream, that sensual pleasures are like borrowed goods, that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree. Thus have I in many ways taught that sensual pleasures give little satisfaction but much suffering and much trouble, and in them the danger is even greater. Yet you, foolish man, misunderstand my teaching and slander me. You harm yourself and accumulate much demerit. This will bring you long-lasting suffering and unhappiness."

The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus: "What do you think? Has this bhikṣu Ariṭṭha generated even a spark of wisdom in this right Dharma and discipline?"

"How could he, World-Honored One? No, World-Honored One."

When this was said, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha remained silent, ashamed, with drooping shoulders, head bowed, downcast, unable to speak.

The World-Honored One, seeing that the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha remained silent, ashamed, with drooping shoulders, head bowed, downcast, unable to speak, said to him: "You foolish man, you will be known by your own evil wrong view. I shall now question the bhikṣus about this matter."

The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you also understand my teaching of the Dharma in this way: 'Those dharmas that are said to be obstructive are not actually capable of obstructing the one who practices them'?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Then how do you understand my teaching of the Dharma?"

The bhikṣus answered: "We understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One thus: 'Obstructive dharmas are indeed obstructive to the one who practices them.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures give little satisfaction but much suffering and much trouble, and in them the danger is even greater."
