"Good, good, bhikṣus. You understand my teaching of the Dharma correctly. Why? Because I have indeed in many ways taught that obstructive dharmas are indeed obstructive to the one who practices them. I have taught that sensual pleasures give little satisfaction but much suffering and much trouble, and in them the danger is even greater.

"However, bhikṣus, if there are foolish people who do not understand the meaning and learn the sūtras, that is, learn the extensive discourses, verses, explanations, narrative verses, passages from other sūtras, original occurrences, stories based on existing events, birth stories, extensive teachings, unprecedented teachings, and instructions on principles, although they learn these sūtras, they do not examine the meaning with wisdom. Because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, they do not accept the Dharma through reflection. They learn the Dharma only for the sake of criticizing others and winning arguments, and do not achieve the goal for which one should learn the Dharma. Those dharmas, having been wrongly grasped by them, will bring these foolish people long-lasting suffering and unhappiness. Why? Because the dharmas have been wrongly grasped.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a man who desires a snake, seeks a snake, and goes about looking for a snake. He sees a large snake and grasps it by the body or tail. That snake then turns around and bites his hand, arm, or other limb. Because of this, he meets with death or suffering close to death. Why? Because he wrongly grasped the snake.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if there are foolish people who do not understand the meaning and learn the sūtras, that is, learn the extensive discourses, verses, explanations, narrative verses, passages from other sūtras, original occurrences, stories based on existing events, birth stories, extensive teachings, unprecedented teachings, and instructions on principles, although they learn these sūtras, they do not examine the meaning with wisdom. Because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, they do not accept the Dharma through reflection. They learn the Dharma only for the sake of criticizing others and winning arguments, and do not achieve the goal for which one should learn the Dharma. Those dharmas, having been wrongly grasped by them, will bring these foolish people long-lasting suffering and unhappiness. Why? Because the dharmas have been wrongly grasped.

"Bhikṣus, if there are good men who understand the meaning and learn the sūtras, that is, learn the extensive discourses, verses, explanations, narrative verses, passages from other sūtras, original occurrences, stories based on existing events, birth stories, extensive teachings, unprecedented teachings, and instructions on principles, having learned these sūtras, they examine the meaning with wisdom. Because they examine the meaning with wisdom, they accept the Dharma through reflection. They do not learn the Dharma for the sake of criticizing others and winning arguments, but they achieve the goal for which one should learn the Dharma. Those dharmas, having been correctly grasped by them, will bring these good men long-lasting benefit and happiness. Why? Because the dharmas have been correctly grasped.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a man who desires a snake, seeks a snake, and goes about looking for a snake. He sees a large snake and uses an iron fork to press down on its head. Having pressed down on its head with the iron fork, he firmly grasps its neck with his hand. Although that snake may coil its body around his hand, arm, or other limb, he will not therefore meet with death or suffering close to death. Why? Because he correctly grasped the snake.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if there are good men who understand the meaning and learn the sūtras, that is, learn the extensive discourses, verses, explanations, narrative verses, passages from other sūtras, original occurrences, stories based on existing events, birth stories, extensive teachings, unprecedented teachings, and instructions on principles, having learned these sūtras, they examine the meaning with wisdom. Because they examine the meaning with wisdom, they accept the Dharma through reflection. They do not learn the Dharma for the sake of criticizing others and winning arguments, but they achieve the goal for which one should learn the Dharma. Those dharmas, having been correctly grasped by them, will bring these good men long-lasting benefit and happiness. Why? Because the dharmas have been correctly grasped.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should understand the meaning of what I have taught. Practice according to the meaning. Why? Practice according to the meaning, and you will gain great benefit.

"Bhikṣus, I have taught you the Dharma as being like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping. If you understand the Dharma as being like a raft, you should let go even of the Dharma, how much more so what is not the Dharma."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (89) The Bhikṣu's Request Sūtra

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, in the evening, rose from his quiet meditation, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at his feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "May the World-Honored One briefly teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I will dwell alone in a quiet place, practicing diligently without negligence. Having dwelt alone in a quiet place, practicing diligently without negligence, I will then think: 'The purpose for which a person of good family shaves his head and beard, puts on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith goes forth from the household life into homelessness, to learn the Way and practice the holy life; the supreme end of the holy life is to know and see in the present life: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; there is no more becoming, I know it as it really is."'"

The World-Honored One told him: "Bhikṣu, if there is anything that is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self, then you should abandon it. If you abandon it, it will be for your long-lasting benefit and happiness."

That bhikṣu said to the World-Honored One: "I understand, World-Honored One. I understand, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One asked: "Bhikṣu, how do you understand the detailed meaning of what I have briefly taught?"

That bhikṣu answered: "World-Honored One, form is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Feeling is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Perception is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Formations are not the root of the self and are not connected to the root of the self; they should be abandoned. Consciousness is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. If I abandon them, it will be for my long-lasting benefit and happiness. World-Honored One, this is how I understand the detailed meaning of what the World-Honored One has briefly taught."

The World-Honored One told him: "Good, good, bhikṣu. You understand well the detailed meaning of what I have briefly taught. Why? Because form is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Feeling is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Perception is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. Formations are not the root of the self and are not connected to the root of the self; they should be abandoned. Consciousness is not the root of the self and is not connected to the root of the self; it should be abandoned. If you abandon them, it will be for your long-lasting benefit and happiness."

That bhikṣu, having heard the Buddha's teaching, was well pleased and delighted. He rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He dwelt alone in a quiet place, practicing diligently without negligence. Having dwelt alone in a quiet place, practicing diligently without negligence, the purpose for which that person of good family shaved his head and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith went forth from the household life into homelessness, to learn the Way, was to know and see in the present life the supreme end of the holy life: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done; there is no more becoming, I know it as it really is."

That bhikṣu knew the Dharma and, knowing the Dharma, became an arhat.

The Buddha spoke thus. That bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (90) Discourse on Understanding

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If bhikṣus, you do not know the self and do not see the self, then regarding that which is 'not self' and 'not belonging to self,' you should abandon it."

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robes to bare one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, what is that which, if one does not know the self and does not see the self, then regarding that which is 'not self' and 'not belonging to self,' should be abandoned?"

The World-Honored One told him: "Bhikṣu, listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

That bhikṣu received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Form is impermanent. What is impermanent, that is suffering. What is suffering, that is not self. What is not self, that is not belonging to self. If one sees this with right wisdom as it really is, this is called right liberation. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are impermanent. What is impermanent, that is suffering. What is suffering, that is not self. What is not self, that is not belonging to self. If one sees this with right wisdom as it really is, this is called right liberation.

"Bhikṣus, if bhikṣus see these five aggregates of clinging as not self and as not belonging to self, then they are called bhikṣus who have cut through the fetter of the view of self-identity, who have torn asunder the veil of conceit, who have correctly transcended the veil of conceit, and who have attained the end of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (91) Discourse on Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the First

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the land of the Śākyans, at Kapilavastu, in Nigrodha's Park.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to the World-Honored One, bowed her head at his feet, stood to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, it would be good if women could be allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way."

The World-Honored One told her: "Gautamī, stop, stop! Do not wish for women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. Gautamī, you should shave your hair but keep it at two finger-breadths, wear the kāṣāya robes, go forth into homelessness, and for your entire life practice the holy life."

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī again said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, it would be good if women could be allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way."

The World-Honored One told her a second time: "Gautamī, stop, stop! Do not wish for women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. Gautamī, you should shave your hair but keep it at two finger-breadths, wear the kāṣāya robes, go forth into homelessness, and for your entire life practice the holy life."

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī again said to the World-Honored One for a third time: "World-Honored One, it would be good if women could be allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way."

The World-Honored One told her a third time: "Gautamī, stop, stop! Do not wish for women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. Gautamī, you should shave your hair but keep it at two finger-breadths, wear the kāṣāya robes, go forth into homelessness, and for your entire life practice the holy life."

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been refused three times by the World-Honored One, who would not allow women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, was unable to contain her tears. She wept and bowed her head at the World-Honored One's feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, not long after, departed from the land of the Śākyans and journeyed among the people, arriving at Vaiśālī. He stayed at the Great Forest, in the Kūṭāgāra Hall.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī shaved her hair, keeping it at two finger-breadths, put on the kāṣāya robes, together with many Śākyan women, followed behind the World-Honored One, journeying among the people, and arrived at Vaiśālī.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī arrived at the Great Forest, in the Kūṭāgāra Hall. Her feet were swollen, her body covered with dust, her face tearful and distressed. She stood outside the gate, weeping.

The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing outside the gate with swollen feet, her body covered with dust, her face tearful and distressed, weeping. Seeing this, he asked: "Gautamī, why do you stand outside the gate with swollen feet, your body covered with dust, your face tearful and distressed, weeping?"

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī answered: "Venerable Ānanda, it is because the World-Honored One does not allow women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way."

The Venerable Ānanda told her: "Gautamī, wait here a moment. I shall enter and request the World-Honored One on your behalf."

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī replied: "Very well, Venerable Ānanda."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda entered, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at his feet, stood to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is now standing outside the gate with swollen feet, her body covered with dust, her face tearful and distressed, weeping, because the World-Honored One does not allow women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. May the World-Honored One allow women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way."

The World-Honored One told him: "Ānanda, stop, stop! Do not wish for women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. Ānanda, if women go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way, then this right Dharma will not endure long."

The Venerable Ānanda again said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was of great benefit to the World-Honored One. When the World-Honored One's mother passed away, she was the one who raised him with milk and nourished him, giving him all that was needed."

The World-Honored One told him: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was indeed of great benefit to me. When my mother passed away, she raised me with milk and nourished me, giving me all that was needed. Ānanda, I also was of great benefit to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Why? Ānanda, it is because of me that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī took refuge in the Buddha, took refuge in the Dharma, took refuge in the Sangha, and gave rise to faith without doubt in suffering, in the arising of suffering, in the cessation of suffering, and in the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Because of me, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī accomplished the precept of not killing, the precept of not stealing, the precept of not committing sexual misconduct, the precept of not lying, and the precept of not drinking alcohol.

"Ānanda, if anyone takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, takes refuge in the Sangha, and gives rise to faith without doubt in suffering, in the arising of suffering, in the cessation of suffering, and in the path leading to the cessation of suffering, Ānanda, that person need not repay any benefactor. Why? Because in this world, there is no greater repayment than this. Even if, Ānanda, one were to give garlands and perfumes, incense and cosmetics, clothing, food, drinks, bedding, medical supplies, and all manner of things in return, one still could not repay such a benefactor.

"Ānanda, if women go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, the right Dharma, which would otherwise endure for a thousand years, will now last only five hundred years. Ānanda, just as a household where there are many women and few men is easily invaded and plundered by thieves, in the same way, Ānanda, if women go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, this right Dharma will not endure long. Ānanda, just as a person who builds an embankment for a large pond of water in advance so that the water does not overflow, in the same way, Ānanda, I now set forth in advance eight rules of respect for bhikṣuṇīs, which they are not to transgress for their entire lives.

"What are the eight? First, a bhikṣuṇī, even if she has been ordained for a hundred years, must rise, bow, and respectfully greet a bhikṣu who has just been ordained that very day. She should respectfully worship him and invite him to sit. This is the first rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Second, a bhikṣuṇī must not spend the rains retreat in a place where there is no bhikṣu. This is the second rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Third, a bhikṣuṇī must every half-month seek two things from the bhikṣu Sangha: to ask about the date of the Upoṣadha observance, and to come to receive instruction and exhortation. This is the third rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Fourth, when the rains retreat is completed, a bhikṣuṇī must perform the pravāraṇā ceremony in both Sanghas, the bhikṣu Sangha and the bhikṣuṇī Sangha, asking whether anything was seen, heard, or suspected. This is the fourth rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Fifth, if a bhikṣuṇī transgresses a Sangha-remainder offense, she must practice the mānatva discipline for half a month in both Sanghas. This is the fifth rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Sixth, a female trainee, after studying the six rules for two years, must seek full ordination from both Sanghas. This is the sixth rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Seventh, a bhikṣuṇī must never, for any reason, abuse or revile a bhikṣu. This is the seventh rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Eighth, from this day forward, a bhikṣuṇī is not permitted to admonish a bhikṣu, but a bhikṣu is permitted to admonish a bhikṣuṇī. This is the eighth rule that bhikṣuṇīs should revere, honor, observe, and not transgress for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, if Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī accepts these eight rules of respect, that shall serve as her ordination."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received this teaching from the World-Honored One, came to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and told her: "Gautamī, the World-Honored One now allows women to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata, to learn the Way. The World-Honored One has said that if Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī accepts these eight rules of respect, that shall serve as her ordination."

He then fully explained the eight rules of respect.

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, just as a young woman or young man, freshly bathed and with head washed, is given a garland of utpala flowers or a garland of jasmine flowers, and receives it with both hands and places it on top of her head, in the same way, Venerable Ānanda, I accept these eight rules of respect and will observe them without transgression for my entire life."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda returned to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at his feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has accepted the eight rules of respect."

The World-Honored One told him: "Ānanda, if women had not been allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, then after the Buddha's passing, lay men of right faith, wearing white robes, would come to the Buddha's stūpa and prostrate themselves with the utmost reverence. But because women have been allowed to go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, Ānanda, after the Buddha's passing, lay men of right faith, wearing white robes, will not come to the Buddha's stūpa and prostrate themselves with the utmost reverence.

"Ānanda, just as a household where there are many women and few men is easily invaded and plundered by thieves, in the same way, Ānanda, if women go forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dharma and discipline of the Tathāgata to learn the Way, this right Dharma will not endure long.

"Ānanda, just as a person who builds an embankment for a large pond of water in advance so that the water does not overflow, in the same way, I now set forth in advance the eight rules of respect for bhikṣuṇīs, which they are not to transgress for their entire lives."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (92) Discourse on Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Second

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Great Forest, in the Kūṭāgāra Hall.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were former Śākyan women, all of whom had become arhats, went to the World-Honored One, bowed her head at his feet, stood to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, teach the bhikṣuṇīs, and give the bhikṣuṇīs a discourse on the Dharma."

The World-Honored One told her: "Gautamī, you should know the right time for this. Gautamī, you should know the right time for this."

A second time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, teach the bhikṣuṇīs, and give the bhikṣuṇīs a discourse on the Dharma."

The World-Honored One told her a second time: "Gautamī, you should know the right time for this. Gautamī, you should know the right time for this."

A third time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, teach the bhikṣuṇīs, and give the bhikṣuṇīs a discourse on the Dharma."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Gautamī, regarding whatever dharmas you know, if they lead to desires and not to lack of desires, if they lead to bondage and not to freedom from bondage, if they lead to accumulation and not to non-accumulation, if they lead to much wanting and not to little wanting, if they lead to discontent and not to contentment, if they lead to association with groups and not to solitude, if they lead to laziness and not to diligent effort, if they lead to difficulty in being supported and not to ease of being supported, then, Gautamī, you should definitely know: 'This is not the Dharma, this is not the discipline, this is not the teaching of the Master.'

"Gautamī, regarding whatever dharmas you know, if they lead to lack of desires and not to desires, if they lead to freedom from bondage and not to bondage, if they lead to non-accumulation and not to accumulation, if they lead to little wanting and not to much wanting, if they lead to contentment and not to discontent, if they lead to solitude and not to association with groups, if they lead to diligent effort and not to laziness, if they lead to ease of being supported and not to difficulty in being supported, then, Gautamī, you should definitely know: 'This is the Dharma, this is the discipline, this is the teaching of the Master.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (93) Discourse on the River of Water

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In autumn, during the rainy season, when a great rain falls, the water in the river increases and overflows, filling from bank to bank. Just as the river flows eastward toward the sea, at that time, on the near shore, there is a man whose body is bound and shackled. He cannot see the near shore and cannot see the far shore, cannot see the depths of the water, cannot see islands or sandbanks, cannot see shallows, cannot see the place for ferry crossings, cannot see the bridge, cannot see the man, and cannot see the man's shadow.

"At that time, on the far shore, there is a man who can see the near shore and can see the far shore, can see the depths of the water, can see islands and sandbanks, can see shallows, can see the place for ferry crossings, can see the bridge, can see the man, and can see the man's shadow.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, the ignorant ordinary person who has not met noble ones, is unskilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and is not trained in the Dharma of noble ones; who has not met good people, is unskilled in the Dharma of good people, and is not trained in the Dharma of good people, does not know form as it really is, does not know the arising of form, does not know the cessation of form, does not know the path leading to the cessation of form.

"Because he does not know form as it really is, does not know the arising of form, does not know the cessation of form, does not know the path leading to the cessation of form, he then regards form as self, or regards self as possessing form, or regards form as being in self, or regards self as being in form. He says: 'Form is mine. I am form.' Having grasped this, when form changes and transforms, his mind is then bound by it, and because his mind is bound, fear arises, and there is obstruction, concern, and worry, arising from grasping.

"He does not know feeling as it really is, does not know the arising of feeling, does not know the cessation of feeling, does not know the path leading to the cessation of feeling. Because he does not know feeling as it really is, does not know the arising of feeling, does not know the cessation of feeling, does not know the path leading to the cessation of feeling, he then regards feeling as self, or regards self as possessing feeling, or regards feeling as being in self, or regards self as being in feeling. He says: 'Feeling is mine. I am feeling.' Having grasped this, when feeling changes and transforms, his mind is then bound by it, and because his mind is bound, fear arises, and there is obstruction, concern, and worry, arising from grasping.

"He does not know perception as it really is, does not know the arising of perception, does not know the cessation of perception, does not know the path leading to the cessation of perception. Because he does not know perception as it really is, does not know the arising of perception, does not know the cessation of perception, does not know the path leading to the cessation of perception, he then regards perception as self, or regards self as possessing perception, or regards perception as being in self, or regards self as being in perception. He says: 'Perception is mine. I am perception.' Having grasped this, when perception changes and transforms, his mind is then bound by it, and because his mind is bound, fear arises, and there is obstruction, concern, and worry, arising from grasping.

"He does not know formations as they really are, does not know the arising of formations, does not know the cessation of formations, does not know the path leading to the cessation of formations. Because he does not know formations as they really are, does not know the arising of formations, does not know the cessation of formations, does not know the path leading to the cessation of formations, he then regards formations as self, or regards self as possessing formations, or regards formations as being in self, or regards self as being in formations. He says: 'Formations are mine. I am formations.' Having grasped this, when formations change and transform, his mind is then bound by them, and because his mind is bound, fear arises, and there is obstruction, concern, and worry, arising from grasping.

"He does not know consciousness as it really is, does not know the arising of consciousness, does not know the cessation of consciousness, does not know the path leading to the cessation of consciousness. Because he does not know consciousness as it really is, does not know the arising of consciousness, does not know the cessation of consciousness, does not know the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, he then regards consciousness as self, or regards self as possessing consciousness, or regards consciousness as being in self, or regards self as being in consciousness. He says: 'Consciousness is mine. I am consciousness.' Having grasped this, when consciousness changes and transforms, his mind is then bound by it, and because his mind is bound, fear arises, and there is obstruction, concern, and worry, arising from grasping.

"This is called 'does not see,' meaning: does not see the near shore and does not see the far shore, does not see the depths of the water, does not see islands or sandbanks, does not see shallows, does not see the place for ferry crossings, does not see the bridge, does not see the man, and does not see the man's shadow.

"Bhikṣus, the learned noble disciple who has met noble ones, is skilled in the Dharma of noble ones, and is well trained in the Dharma of noble ones; who has met good people, is skilled in the Dharma of good people, and is well trained in the Dharma of good people, knows form as it really is, knows the arising of form, knows the cessation of form, knows the path leading to the cessation of form.

"Because he knows form as it really is, knows the arising of form, knows the cessation of form, knows the path leading to the cessation of form, he does not regard form as self, does not regard self as possessing form, does not regard form as being in self, does not regard self as being in form. He does not say: 'Form is mine. I am form.' Not having grasped this, when form changes and transforms, his mind is not bound by it, and because his mind is not bound, fear does not arise, and there is no obstruction, concern, or worry, as there is no grasping.

"He knows feeling as it really is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling. Because he knows feeling as it really is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling, he does not regard feeling as self, does not regard self as possessing feeling, does not regard feeling as being in self, does not regard self as being in feeling. He does not say: 'Feeling is mine. I am feeling.' Not having grasped this, when feeling changes and transforms, his mind is not bound by it, and because his mind is not bound, fear does not arise, and there is no obstruction, concern, or worry, as there is no grasping.

"He knows perception as it really is, knows the arising of perception, knows the cessation of perception, knows the path leading to the cessation of perception. Because he knows perception as it really is, knows the arising of perception, knows the cessation of perception, knows the path leading to the cessation of perception, he does not regard perception as self, does not regard self as possessing perception, does not regard perception as being in self, does not regard self as being in perception. He does not say: 'Perception is mine. I am perception.' Not having grasped this, when perception changes and transforms, his mind is not bound by it, and because his mind is not bound, fear does not arise, and there is no obstruction, concern, or worry, as there is no grasping.

"He knows formations as they really are, knows the arising of formations, knows the cessation of formations, knows the path leading to the cessation of formations. Because he knows formations as they really are, knows the arising of formations, knows the cessation of formations, knows the path leading to the cessation of formations, he does not regard formations as self, does not regard self as possessing formations, does not regard formations as being in self, does not regard self as being in formations. He does not say: 'Formations are mine. I am formations.' Not having grasped this, when formations change and transform, his mind is not bound by them, and because his mind is not bound, fear does not arise, and there is no obstruction, concern, or worry, as there is no grasping.

"He knows consciousness as it really is, knows the arising of consciousness, knows the cessation of consciousness, knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness. Because he knows consciousness as it really is, knows the arising of consciousness, knows the cessation of consciousness, knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, he does not regard consciousness as self, does not regard self as possessing consciousness, does not regard consciousness as being in self, does not regard self as being in consciousness. He does not say: 'Consciousness is mine. I am consciousness.' Not having grasped this, when consciousness changes and transforms, his mind is not bound by it, and because his mind is not bound, fear does not arise, and there is no obstruction, concern, or worry, as there is no grasping.

"This is called 'sees,' meaning: sees the near shore and sees the far shore, sees the depths of the water, sees islands and sandbanks, sees shallows, sees the place for ferry crossings, sees the bridge, sees the man, and sees the man's shadow."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (94) Discourse on Black and White

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are two views. What are the two? The view of existence and the view of non-existence. Some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas grasp and cling to the view of existence, being obstructed by and attached to the view of existence; some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas grasp and cling to the view of non-existence, being obstructed by and attached to the view of non-existence.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the view of existence as it really is, do not know the arising of the view of existence, do not know the cessation of the view of existence, do not know the sweetness, do not know the danger, do not know the escape regarding the view of existence, they cannot cut off craving for the view of existence, cannot universally know the view of existence, and I say these persons do not see. Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the view of non-existence as it really is, do not know the arising of the view of non-existence, do not know the cessation of the view of non-existence, do not know the sweetness, do not know the danger, do not know the escape regarding the view of non-existence, they cannot cut off craving for the view of non-existence, cannot universally know the view of non-existence, and I say these persons do not see.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the view of existence as it really is, do not know the arising of the view of existence, do not know the cessation of the view of existence, do not know the sweetness, do not know the danger, do not know the escape regarding the view of existence, they are beings with craving, with attachment, with bondage, with defilements, with clinging, and I say they are not liberated from suffering.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not know the view of non-existence as it really is, do not know the arising of the view of non-existence, do not know the cessation of the view of non-existence, do not know the sweetness, do not know the danger, do not know the escape regarding the view of non-existence, they are beings with craving, with attachment, with bondage, with defilements, with clinging, and I say they are not liberated from suffering.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the view of existence as it really is, know the arising of the view of existence, know the cessation of the view of existence, know the sweetness, know the danger, know the escape regarding the view of existence, they can cut off craving for the view of existence, can universally know the view of existence, and I say these persons can see. Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the view of non-existence as it really is, know the arising of the view of non-existence, know the cessation of the view of non-existence, know the sweetness, know the danger, know the escape regarding the view of non-existence, they can cut off craving for the view of non-existence, can universally know the view of non-existence, and I say these persons can see.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the view of existence as it really is, know the arising of the view of existence, know the cessation of the view of existence, know the sweetness, know the danger, know the escape regarding the view of existence, they are beings without craving, without attachment, without bondage, without defilements, without clinging, and I say they are liberated from suffering.

"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the view of non-existence as it really is, know the arising of the view of non-existence, know the cessation of the view of non-existence, know the sweetness, know the danger, know the escape regarding the view of non-existence, they are beings without craving, without attachment, without bondage, without defilements, without clinging, and I say they are liberated from suffering.

"If a bhikṣu knows these

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle Twenty-One
