## (84) Sūtra on Thorns, the Thirteenth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in Vesālī, at the Gabled Pavilion in the Markaṭa River bank. Various well-known, senior, and honored great disciples were there, namely Cāla, Upacāla, Bhadda, Bhaddasena, Anupama, and Yaśas the Supremely Renowned. Such well-known, senior, and honored great disciples as these were also staying in Vesālī at the Gabled Pavilion by the Markaṭa River bank, all dwelling near the Buddha's leaf hut.

The Licchavi people of Vesālī heard that the World-Honored One was staying in Vesālī at the Gabled Pavilion by the Markaṭa River bank. They had this thought: "We should prepare a great display of splendor, assume royal majesty, and with loud proclamations, depart from Vesālī and go to the place of the Buddha to make offerings and pay respects."

At that time, the well-known, senior, and honored great disciples heard that the Licchavi people of Vesālī were preparing a great display of splendor, assuming royal majesty, and with loud proclamations, departing from Vesālī to come to the place of the Buddha to make offerings and pay respects. They had this thought: "Sound is a thorn to meditation. The World-Honored One has also said that sound is a thorn to meditation. We should go to the Gosiṅga Sāla Forest and dwell there undisturbed, in remote seclusion, dwelling alone in quiet retreat, sitting in meditation and contemplation." Thereupon, the well-known, senior, and honored great disciples went to the Gosiṅga Sāla Forest and dwelt there undisturbed, in remote seclusion, dwelling alone in quiet retreat, sitting in meditation and contemplation.

At that time, the many Licchavi people of Vesālī, having prepared a great display of splendor, assuming royal majesty, with loud proclamations, departed from Vesālī and went to the place of the Buddha to make offerings and pay respects. Some of the Licchavi people of Vesālī prostrated at the Buddha's feet and then sat to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and then sat to one side. Some joined their palms toward the Buddha and then sat to one side. Some, upon seeing the Buddha from afar, sat down in silence.

At that time, when the many Licchavi people of Vesālī had each settled in their seats, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for them, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them. With immeasurable skillful means he taught the Dharma for them, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them, and then he sat in silence. Thereupon, the many Licchavi people of Vesālī, after the World-Honored One had taught the Dharma for them, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening them, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Not long after the Licchavi people of Vesālī had departed, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Where have the senior, honored great disciples gone?"

The bhikṣus replied: "World-Honored One, the senior, honored great disciples heard that the Licchavi people of Vesālī were preparing a great display of splendor, assuming royal majesty, and with loud proclamations, departing from Vesālī to come to the place of the Buddha to make offerings and pay respects. They had this thought: 'Sound is a thorn to meditation. The World-Honored One has also said that sound is a thorn to meditation. We should go to the Gosiṅga Sāla Forest and dwell there undisturbed, in remote seclusion, dwelling alone in quiet retreat, sitting in meditation and contemplation.' World-Honored One, the senior, honored great disciples went there together."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having heard this, praised them saying: "Good! Good! The senior, honored great disciples should indeed speak thus: 'Sound is a thorn to meditation. The World-Honored One has also said that sound is a thorn to meditation.' Why is this? I have indeed said thus: meditation has thorns. For one who upholds the precepts, breaking the precepts is a thorn. For one who guards the sense faculties, adorning the body is a thorn. For one who cultivates contemplation of the impure, the perception of attractiveness is a thorn. For one who cultivates loving-kindness, anger is a thorn. For one who abstains from alcohol, drinking alcohol is a thorn. For one practicing celibacy, seeing the female form is a thorn. For one entering the first dhyāna, sound is a thorn. For one entering the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought is a thorn. For one entering the third dhyāna, rapture is a thorn. For one entering the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation is a thorn. For one entering the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form is a thorn. For one entering the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space is a thorn. For one entering the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is a thorn. For one entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is a thorn. For one entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling are thorns.

"Furthermore, there are three thorns: the thorn of desire, the thorn of anger, and the thorn of delusion. These three thorns have been cut off and fully known by the Arahant whose taints are exhausted; they have been uprooted and destroyed, never to arise again. This is why the Arahant is without thorns, the Arahant is separated from thorns, the Arahant is both without thorns and separated from thorns."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Thorns, the Thirteenth.

---

## (85) Sūtra on the True Person, the Fourteenth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will now explain to you the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon this."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the qualities of one who is not a true person? There may be a certain person who has gone forth from a noble and eminent family to study the Way, while others have not. Because he comes from such a noble and eminent family, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of being from a noble and eminent family that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who has not gone forth from a noble and eminent family, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who is handsome and attractive, while others are not. Because he is handsome and attractive, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of being handsome and attractive that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who is not handsome and attractive, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who is gifted in eloquent speech, while others are not. Because he is gifted in eloquent speech, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of being gifted in eloquent speech that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who is not gifted in eloquent speech, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who is a senior elder, known to kings and recognized by the people, and possessed of great merit, while others are not. Because he is a senior elder, known to kings and recognized by the people, and possessed of great merit, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of being a senior elder, known to kings and recognized by the people, and possessed of great merit that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who is not a senior elder, not known to kings or recognized by the people, and not possessed of great merit, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who recites the sūtras, upholds the Vinaya, and studies the Abhidharma; he is well-versed in the Āgamas and has studied many scriptures, while others are not. Because he is well-versed in the Āgamas and has studied many scriptures, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of being well-versed in the Āgamas and having studied many scriptures that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who is not well-versed in the Āgamas and has not studied many scriptures, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who wears rag-robes, possesses only the three robes, and holds to the robe of non-conceit, while others do not. Because he holds to the robe of non-conceit, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of holding to the robe of non-conceit that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who does not hold to the robe of non-conceit, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who always practices alms-begging, limits his food to five measures, restricts himself to seven houses for food, or eats only one meal, and does not drink juices after midday, while others do not. Because he does not drink juices after midday, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of not drinking juices after midday that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who does not abstain from drinking juices after midday, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who dwells in a secluded place, in mountain forests under trees, or lives on high cliffs, or stays in the open air, or dwells among charnel grounds, or is able to observe the proper times, while others are not. Because of observing the proper times, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'It is not because of observing the proper times that one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion.' There may be a certain person who does not observe the proper times, yet he practices the Dharma in accord with the Dharma, follows the Dharma accordingly, and proceeds in the proper sequence of the Dharma. Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who has attained the first dhyāna. Because of having attained the first dhyāna, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'Regarding the first dhyāna, the World-Honored One has spoken of immeasurable kinds. If anyone makes calculations about it, that is called craving.' Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who has attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, while others have not. Because of having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he exalts himself and disparages others. This is called the quality of one who is not a true person. The true person reflects thus: 'Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the World-Honored One has spoken of immeasurable kinds. If anyone makes calculations about it, that is called craving.' Because of this, he gains offerings and reverence. One who thus progresses toward and attains the true Dharma does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. This is called the quality of a true person.

"Bhikṣus, these are called the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person. You should know the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person. Having known the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person, abandon the qualities of one who is not a true person and study the qualities of a true person. You should train in this way."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Summary verses:
Noble birth, handsomeness, eloquence, seniority, reciting scriptures,
Robes, food, seclusion, the dhyānas, and the four formless realms at the end.

End of the Sūtra on the True Person, the Fourteenth.

---

## (86) Sūtra on the Topics of Instruction, the Fifteenth in the Chapter on King Long Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from his meditation and, bringing the junior bhikṣus with him, went to the place of the Buddha. He prostrated at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. The junior bhikṣus also prostrated at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, how should I admonish these junior bhikṣus? How should I instruct them? How should I teach the Dharma for them?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, you should explain the topics of instruction and teach the topics of instruction to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach the topics of instruction to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives."

The Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, now is the right time. Well-Gone One, now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would explain and teach the topics of instruction for the junior bhikṣus, I and the junior bhikṣus, having heard from the World-Honored One, will well receive and uphold them."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, listen carefully and reflect well upon this. I will explain in detail for you and the junior bhikṣus." The Venerable Ānanda and the others received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five aggregates of clinging to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five aggregates of clinging to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six internal sense bases: the eye sense base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind sense bases. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six internal sense bases to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six internal sense bases to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six external sense bases: the form sense base, the sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma sense bases. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six external sense bases to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six external sense bases to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of consciousness: eye consciousness, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of consciousness to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of consciousness to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of contact: eye contact, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind contact. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of contact to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of contact to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of feeling: eye feeling, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind feeling. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of feeling to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of feeling to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of perception: eye perception, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind perception. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of perception to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of perception to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of intention: eye intention, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind intention. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of intention to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of intention to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six bodies of craving: eye craving, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind craving. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six bodies of craving to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six bodies of craving to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the six elements: the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these six elements to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six elements to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you dependent origination and the phenomena produced by dependent origination. When this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that does not exist. When this arises, that arises; when this ceases, that ceases. Conditioned by ignorance, there are formations. Conditioned by formations, there is consciousness. Conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form. Conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases. Conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact. Conditioned by contact, there is feeling. Conditioned by feeling, there is craving. Conditioned by craving, there is clinging. Conditioned by clinging, there is becoming. Conditioned by becoming, there is birth. Conditioned by birth, there is aging and death. When ignorance ceases, then formations cease. When formations cease, then consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, then name-and-form ceases. When name-and-form ceases, then the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases. When contact ceases, then feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, then craving ceases. When craving ceases, then clinging ceases. When clinging ceases, then becoming ceases. When becoming ceases, then birth ceases. When birth ceases, then aging and death cease. Ānanda, you should explain and teach this dependent origination and the phenomena produced by dependent origination to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach this dependent origination and the phenomena produced by dependent origination to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four foundations of mindfulness: contemplating the body as body, contemplating feelings, the mind, and dharmas as dharmas. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four foundations of mindfulness to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four foundations of mindfulness to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four right efforts. A bhikṣu, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of preventing the arising of evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of giving rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of maintaining wholesome states that have already arisen, so that they are not forgotten, do not decline, but increase and expand, are fully developed and perfected, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four right efforts to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four right efforts to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four bases of spiritual power. A bhikṣu develops the base of spiritual power that possesses concentration due to desire together with the effort of elimination, cultivating the base of spiritual power based on non-desire, based on detachment, based on cessation, tending toward relinquishment. Likewise with the base of spiritual power of concentration due to effort, concentration due to mind, and that which possesses concentration due to investigation together with the effort of elimination, cultivating the base of spiritual power based on non-desire, based on detachment, based on cessation, tending toward relinquishment. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four bases of spiritual power to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four bases of spiritual power to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four dhyānas. A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome states, up to attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four dhyānas to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four dhyānas to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four noble truths: the noble truth of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four noble truths to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four noble truths to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four perceptions. A bhikṣu has the perception of the limited, the perception of the expansive, the perception of the immeasurable, and the perception of nothingness. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four perceptions to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four perceptions to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four immeasurables. A bhikṣu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction, dwells having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere throughout all directions. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four immeasurables to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four immeasurables to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four formless attainments. A bhikṣu, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, up to attaining and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four formless attainments to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four formless attainments to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four noble lineages. A bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, having obtained coarse and simple robes, knows contentment and does not seek to fulfill desires for robes. If he has not yet obtained robes, he does not grieve, lament, beat his breast, or become confused. If he obtains robes, he does not become defiled, attached, desirous, greedy, clinging, or calculating. He sees the danger and knows the escape, and uses robes accordingly. One who is not negligent in this matter and possesses right knowledge is called a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who rightly abides in the ancient noble lineage. Likewise with food and dwelling places. One who desires to abandon and delights in abandoning, desires to cultivate and delights in cultivating: because of desiring to abandon and delighting in abandoning, desiring to cultivate and delighting in cultivating, one does not exalt oneself and does not disparage others. One who is not negligent in this matter and possesses right knowledge is called a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who rightly abides in the ancient noble lineage. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four noble lineages to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four noble lineages to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the four fruits of the ascetic life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit of Arahantship. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these four fruits of the ascetic life to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these four fruits of the ascetic life to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five perceptions that ripen in liberation: the perception of impermanence, the perception that what is impermanent is suffering, the perception that what is suffering is not-self, the perception of impurity and foulness, and the perception that all the world is undesirable. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five perceptions that ripen in liberation to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five perceptions that ripen in liberation to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five bases of liberation. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, because of these, attains liberation of mind that was not yet liberated, attains the exhaustion of taints that were not yet exhausted, and attains the unsurpassed nirvāṇa that was not yet attained, what are these five? Ānanda, when the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and when wise practitioners of the holy life also teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs: Ānanda, when the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and when wise practitioners of the holy life also teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, having heard the Dharma, they come to understand the Dharma and comprehend its meaning. Because they understand the Dharma and comprehend its meaning, they experience delight. Because of delight, they experience joy. Because of joy, there is tranquility of body. Because of tranquility of body, they experience pleasure. Because of pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. Ānanda, because the mind of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī is concentrated, they come to see things as they really are and know them as they truly are. Because of seeing things as they really are and knowing them as they truly are, they experience revulsion. Because of revulsion, they become dispassionate. Because of dispassion, they attain liberation. Because of liberation, they know they are liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming.' They know this as it truly is. Ānanda, this is called the first basis of liberation. Because of this, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī whose mind was not yet liberated attains liberation, whose taints were not yet exhausted attains their complete exhaustion, and who had not yet attained the unsurpassed nirvāṇa attains the unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, when the World-Honored One does not teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and wise practitioners of the holy life also do not teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, but one extensively recites the Dharma as previously heard and studied. If one does not extensively recite the Dharma as previously heard and studied, then one extensively explains the Dharma as previously heard and studied to others. If one does not extensively explain the Dharma as previously heard and studied to others, then one mentally reflects upon and discerns the Dharma as previously heard and studied. If one does not mentally reflect upon and discern the Dharma as previously heard and studied, then one well maintains the various signs of samādhi. Ānanda, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī well maintains the various signs of samādhi, then they come to understand the Dharma and comprehend its meaning. Because they understand the Dharma and comprehend its meaning, they experience delight. Because of delight, they experience joy. Because of joy, there is tranquility of body. Because of tranquility of body, they experience pleasure. Because of pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. Ānanda, because the mind of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī is concentrated, they come to see things as they really are and know them as they truly are. Because of seeing things as they really are and knowing them as they truly are, they experience revulsion. Because of revulsion, they become dispassionate. Because of dispassion, they attain liberation. Because of liberation, they know they are liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further becoming.' They know this as it truly is. Ānanda, this is called the fifth basis of liberation. Because of this, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī whose mind was not yet liberated attains liberation, whose taints were not yet exhausted attains their complete exhaustion, and who had not yet attained the unsurpassed nirvāṇa attains the unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five bases of liberation to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five bases of liberation to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculties of effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five faculties to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five faculties to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five powers: the power of faith, the powers of effort, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five powers to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five powers to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the five elements of escape. What are the five? Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and well contemplates desire. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating desire, the mind does not incline toward desire, does not delight in desire, does not approach desire, does not place confidence in desire. If a mind of desire arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in desire, and is repelled by and disgusted with desire. Ānanda, just as a chicken feather or a sinew, when held in fire, immediately melts, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple likewise thoroughly and well contemplates desire. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating desire, the mind does not incline toward desire, does not delight in desire, does not approach desire, does not place confidence in desire. If a mind of desire arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in desire, and is repelled by and disgusted with desire. Contemplating non-desire, the mind inclines toward non-desire, delights in non-desire, approaches non-desire, places confidence in non-desire. The mind is unobstructed, the mind is unclouded, the mind attains happiness and can bring about happiness. One is far removed from all desire and from the taints, afflictions, and sorrows that arise because of desire. One is released from them, liberated from them, and further liberated from them. One no longer experiences those feelings that arise because of desire. This is the escape from desire. Ānanda, this is called the first element of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and well contemplates anger. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating anger, the mind does not incline toward anger, does not delight in anger, does not approach anger, does not place confidence in anger. If a mind of anger arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in anger, and is repelled by and disgusted with anger. Ānanda, just as a chicken feather or a sinew, when held in fire, immediately melts, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple likewise thoroughly and well contemplates anger. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating anger, the mind does not incline toward anger, does not delight in anger, does not approach anger, does not place confidence in anger. If a mind of anger arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in anger, and is repelled by and disgusted with anger. Contemplating non-anger, the mind inclines toward non-anger, delights in non-anger, approaches non-anger, places confidence in non-anger. The mind is unobstructed, the mind is unclouded, the mind attains happiness and can bring about happiness. One is far removed from all anger and from the taints, afflictions, and sorrows that arise because of anger. One is released from them, liberated from them, and further liberated from them. One no longer experiences those feelings that arise because of anger. This is the escape from anger. Ānanda, this is called the second element of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and well contemplates harmfulness. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating harmfulness, the mind does not incline toward harmfulness, does not delight in harmfulness, does not approach harmfulness, does not place confidence in harmfulness. If a mind of harmfulness arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in harmfulness, and is repelled by and disgusted with harmfulness. Ānanda, just as a chicken feather or a sinew, when held in fire, immediately melts, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple likewise thoroughly and well contemplates harmfulness. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating harmfulness, the mind does not incline toward harmfulness, does not delight in harmfulness, does not approach harmfulness, does not place confidence in harmfulness. If a mind of harmfulness arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in harmfulness, and is repelled by and disgusted with harmfulness. Contemplating non-harmfulness, the mind inclines toward non-harmfulness, delights in non-harmfulness, approaches non-harmfulness, places confidence in non-harmfulness. The mind is unobstructed, the mind is unclouded, the mind attains happiness and can bring about happiness. One is far removed from all harmfulness and from the taints, afflictions, and sorrows that arise because of harmfulness. One is released from them, liberated from them, and further liberated from them. One no longer experiences those feelings that arise because of harmfulness. This is the escape from harmfulness. Ānanda, this is called the third element of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and well contemplates form. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating form, the mind does not incline toward form, does not delight in form, does not approach form, does not place confidence in form. If a mind directed toward form arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in form, and is repelled by and disgusted with form. Ānanda, just as a chicken feather or a sinew, when held in fire, immediately melts, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple likewise thoroughly and well contemplates form. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating form, the mind does not incline toward form, does not delight in form, does not approach form, does not place confidence in form. If a mind directed toward form arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in form, and is repelled by and disgusted with form. Contemplating formlessness, the mind inclines toward formlessness, delights in formlessness, approaches formlessness, places confidence in formlessness. The mind is unobstructed, the mind is unclouded, the mind attains happiness and can bring about happiness. One is far removed from all form and from the taints, afflictions, and sorrows that arise because of form. One is released from them, liberated from them, and further liberated from them. One no longer experiences those feelings that arise because of form. This is the escape from form. Ānanda, this is called the fourth element of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and well contemplates one's own body. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating one's own body, the mind does not incline toward one's own body, does not delight in one's own body, does not approach one's own body, does not place confidence in one's own body. If a mind directed toward one's own body arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in one's own body, and is repelled by and disgusted with one's own body. Ānanda, just as a chicken feather or a sinew, when held in fire, immediately melts, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple likewise thoroughly and well contemplates one's own body. Because of thoroughly and well contemplating one's own body, the mind does not incline toward one's own body, does not delight in one's own body, does not approach one's own body, does not place confidence in one's own body. If a mind directed toward one's own body arises, it immediately melts away, shrivels up, turns back, and cannot spread out. One abandons and does not abide in one's own body, and is repelled by and disgusted with one's own body. Contemplating the absence of self-identity, the mind inclines toward the absence of self-identity, delights in the absence of self-identity, approaches the absence of self-identity, places confidence in the absence of self-identity. The mind is unobstructed, the mind is unclouded, the mind attains happiness and can bring about happiness. One is far removed from all self-identity and from the taints, afflictions, and sorrows that arise because of self-identity. One is released from them, liberated from them, and further liberated from them. One no longer experiences those feelings that arise because of self-identity. This is the escape from self-identity. Ānanda, this is called the fifth element of escape.

"Ānanda, you should explain and teach these five elements of escape to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five elements of escape to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the seven treasures: the treasure of faith, the treasures of morality, conscience, shame, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these seven treasures to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these seven treasures to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the seven powers: the power of faith, the powers of effort, conscience, shame, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these seven powers to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these seven powers to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the seven factors of awakening: the factor of mindfulness, the factors of investigation of dharmas, effort, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Ānanda, you should explain and teach these seven factors of awakening to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these seven factors of awakening to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have previously explained to you the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are the eight. Ānanda, you should explain and teach this noble eightfold path to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach this noble eightfold path to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, how extraordinary! How remarkable! The World-Honored One has explained and taught the topics of instruction for the junior bhikṣus."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, so it is, so it is. How extraordinary! How remarkable! I have explained and taught the topics of instruction for the junior bhikṣus. Ānanda, if you were to further ask the Tathāgata about the summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma, you would gain extreme faith and joy in the Tathāgata."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, now is the right time. Well-Gone One, now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would explain and teach the summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma for the junior bhikṣus, I and the junior bhikṣus, having heard from the World-Honored One, will well receive and uphold it."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, listen carefully and reflect well upon this. I will explain the summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma for you and the junior bhikṣus." The Venerable Ānanda and the others received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple, based on a mind of genuine truth, reflects, weighs, well contemplates, and discerns impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. As he thus reflects, weighs, well contemplates, and discerns, there arises acceptance, delight, and desire; desire to hear, desire to contemplate, desire to investigate. Ānanda, this is called the summit Dharma. Ānanda, if, having attained this summit Dharma, one then loses and declines from it, not cultivating or guarding it, not practicing with diligence, Ānanda, this is called declining from the summit Dharma. Likewise with the internal and external sense bases, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, intention, craving, the elements, and dependent origination. Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple reflects, weighs, well contemplates, and discerns dependent origination and phenomena produced by dependent origination as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. As he thus reflects, weighs, well contemplates, and discerns, there arises acceptance, delight, and desire; desire to hear, desire to contemplate, desire to investigate. Ānanda, this is called the summit Dharma. Ānanda, if, having attained this summit Dharma, one then loses and declines from it, not cultivating or guarding it, not practicing with diligence, Ānanda, this is called declining from the summit Dharma. Ānanda, you should explain and teach this summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma to the junior bhikṣus. If you explain and teach this summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma to the junior bhikṣus, they will gain security, gain strength, gain happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from affliction, and they will practice the holy life for their entire lives.

"Ānanda, I have explained for you the topics of instruction and taught the topics of instruction, and the summit Dharma and the decline from the summit Dharma. What an honorable teacher, out of great compassion and pity, seeking benefit and welfare, seeking security and happiness for his disciples, should do, I have already done. You should now continue to practice on your own. Go to secluded places, mountain forests, under trees, and empty, peaceful places to sit in meditation and contemplation. Do not be negligent. Apply yourselves with diligence, lest you have regrets later. This is my instruction; this is my admonition."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the junior bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Aggregates, internal, external, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, intention, craving, elements,
Dependent origination, mindfulness, right efforts, spiritual powers, dhyānas, truths, perceptions,
Immeasurables, formless attainments, noble lineages, fruits of the ascetic life, liberation,
Bases, faculties, powers, elements of escape, treasures, powers, awakening factors, the path, and the summit.

End of the Sūtra on the Topics of Instruction, the Fifteenth.
