## (87) Sūtra on Defilements, First of the Defilements Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Bhagga, staying in the Bhesakalā Forest Deer Park on Mount Crocodile.

At that time, Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, there are four kinds of people in the world. What are the four? There may be a person who actually has defilements within but does not know it himself; having defilements within, he does not know it as it truly is. There may be a person who actually has defilements within and knows it himself; having defilements within, he knows it as it truly is. There may be a person who actually has no defilements within but does not know it himself; having no defilements within, he does not know it as it truly is. There may be a person who actually has no defilements within and knows it himself; having no defilements within, he knows it as it truly is.

"Venerables, if there is a person who actually has defilements within but does not know it himself, having defilements within and not knowing it as it truly is, this person is the most inferior among people. If there is a person who actually has defilements within and knows it himself, having defilements within and knowing it as it truly is, this person is the most superior among people. If there is a person who actually has no defilements within but does not know it himself, having no defilements within and not knowing it as it truly is, this person is the most inferior among people. If there is a person who actually has no defilements within and knows it himself, having no defilements within and knowing it as it truly is, this person is the most superior among people."

Then a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward Venerable Śāriputra, and said: "Venerable Śāriputra, for what reason and what cause do you say that of the first two persons who both have defilements and defiled minds, one is inferior and one is most superior? And again, for what reason and cause do you say that of the latter two persons who both have no defilements and undefiled minds, one is inferior and one is most superior?"

Venerable Śāriputra then answered that bhikṣu: "Venerable, if there is a person who actually has defilements within but does not know it himself, having defilements within and not knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person does not wish to abandon the defilements, does not seek skillful means, and does not diligently train. He then dies with defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies with defilements and a defiled mind at the time of death, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unwholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies with defilements and a defiled mind at the time of death. Venerable, it is like a person who buys a copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, and it is covered with dust and grime. After bringing it home, he does not repeatedly wash off the dust, does not repeatedly scrub and wipe it, does not dry it in the sun, and moreover places it in a dusty place. In this way the copper bowl accumulates more dust and grime. Venerable, in the same way, if there is a person who actually has defilements within but does not know it himself, having defilements within and not knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person does not wish to abandon the defilements, does not seek skillful means, and does not diligently train. He then dies with defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies with defilements and a defiled mind at the time of death, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unwholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies with defilements and a defiled mind at the time of death.

"Venerable, if there is a person who knows, 'I have defilements within; I actually do have these defilements within,' knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person wishes to abandon these defilements, seeks skillful means, and diligently trains. He then dies without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies without defilements and with an undefiled mind at the time of death, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a wholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies without defilements and with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Venerable, it is like a person who buys a copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, and it is covered with dust and grime. After bringing it home, he repeatedly washes off the dust, repeatedly scrubs and wipes it, repeatedly dries it in the sun, and does not place it in a dusty place. In this way the copper bowl becomes extremely clean and pure. Venerable, in the same way, if there is a person who knows, 'I have defilements within; I actually do have these defilements within,' knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person wishes to abandon these defilements, seeks skillful means, and diligently trains. He then dies without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies without defilements and with an undefiled mind at the time of death, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a wholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies without defilements and with an undefiled mind at the time of death.

"Venerable, if there is a person who does not know, 'I have no defilements within; I actually have no defilements within,' not knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person does not guard the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because he does not guard the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear, he becomes entangled by the mind of desire. He then has desire and defilements, and dies with a defiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies having desire and defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unwholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies having desire and defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death. Venerable, it is like a person who buys a copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, and it is without grime and clean and pure. After bringing it home, he does not repeatedly wash off dust, does not repeatedly scrub and wipe it, does not repeatedly dry it in the sun, and places it in a dusty place. In this way the copper bowl will certainly accumulate dust and grime. Venerable, in the same way, if there is a person who does not know, 'I have no defilements within; I actually have no defilements within,' not knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person does not guard the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because he does not guard the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear, he becomes entangled by the mind of desire. He then has desire and defilements, and dies with a defiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies having desire and defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unwholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies having desire and defilements, with a defiled mind at the time of death.

"Venerable, if there is a person who knows, 'I have no defilements within; I actually have no defilements within,' knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person guards the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because he guards the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear, he is not entangled by the mind of desire. He then has no desire and no defilements, and dies with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies without desire and without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a wholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies without desire and without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Venerable, it is like a person who buys a copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, and it is without grime and clean and pure. After bringing it home, he repeatedly washes and polishes it, repeatedly scrubs and wipes it, repeatedly dries it in the sun, and does not place it in a dusty place. In this way the copper bowl becomes extremely clean and pure. Venerable, in the same way, if there is a person who knows, 'I have no defilements within; I actually have no defilements within,' knowing it as it truly is, you should know that this person guards the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because he guards the mental phenomena known through the eye and ear, he is not entangled by the mind of desire. He then has no desire and no defilements, and dies with an undefiled mind at the time of death. Because he dies without desire and without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a wholesome state. Why is that? Because he dies without desire and without defilements, with an undefiled mind at the time of death.

"Venerable, for this reason and this cause, it is said that of the first two persons who both have defilements and defiled minds, one is inferior and one is most superior. For this reason and this cause, it is said that of the latter two persons who both have no defilements and undefiled minds, one is inferior and one is most superior."

Then another bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward Venerable Śāriputra, and said: "Venerable Śāriputra, you speak of 'defilements'; what are these defilements?"

Venerable Śāriputra answered the bhikṣu: "Venerable, immeasurable unwholesome and evil dharmas arise from desire; these are called defilements. Why is this so? There may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'May no one else know of the precepts I have transgressed.' Venerable, but perhaps others do know of his transgression of the precepts. Because others know of his transgression of the precepts, his mind then gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome. Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'If I have transgressed the precepts, let others admonish me in private, and not admonish me for my transgressions in the midst of the assembly.' Venerable, but perhaps others admonish him in the midst of the assembly and not in private. Because others admonish him in the midst of the assembly and not in private, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome. Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'If I have transgressed the precepts, let a superior person admonish me, and not let an inferior person admonish me for my transgressions.' Venerable, but perhaps an inferior person admonishes him for his transgression of the precepts, and it is not a superior person. Because an inferior person admonishes him and it is not a superior person, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'Let me sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus. Let not other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus. Because other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome. Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus enter a house, let me be at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying me as we enter. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, be at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, are at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, are at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus have already entered a house, let me have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, let me teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'When householders come to visit the monastery garden, let me meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them. Let not other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them. Because other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'Let me be known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country. Let not other bhikṣus be known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus are known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country. Because other bhikṣus are known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'Let me be revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Let not other bhikṣus be revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus are revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Because other bhikṣus are revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind such a desire arises: 'Let me obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life. Let not other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life.' Venerable, but perhaps other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life. Because other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life, his mind gives rise to ill will. If that person's mind gives rise to ill will and his mind gives rise to such desire, both are unwholesome.

"Venerable, regarding such a person, if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do not know that he gives rise to such immeasurable unwholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is not a śramaṇa as a śramaṇa, perceive one who is not a wise śramaṇa as a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has not attained right knowledge as having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has not attained right mindfulness as having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is not pure as being pure. Venerable, but if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do know that he gives rise to such immeasurable unwholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is not a śramaṇa as not being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is not a wise śramaṇa as not being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has not attained right knowledge as not having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has not attained right mindfulness as not having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is not pure as not being pure.

"Venerable, it is like a person who buys a covered copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, fills it completely with excrement, covers the top, and carries it away, passing through shops and walking among the crowd. The crowd, seeing it, all wish to eat from it, with minds of great fondness, feeling no aversion, and giving rise to the perception of purity. But after he carries it to a certain place and opens it to show them, the crowd, seeing it, all do not wish to eat, have no fondness, are greatly disgusted, and give rise to the perception of impurity. Even those who wished to eat no longer want to; how much less those who originally did not wish to eat?

"Venerable, in the same way, regarding such a person, if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do not know that he gives rise to such immeasurable unwholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is not a śramaṇa as a śramaṇa, perceive one who is not a wise śramaṇa as a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has not attained right knowledge as having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has not attained right mindfulness as having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is not pure as being pure. Venerable, but if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do know that he gives rise to such immeasurable unwholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is not a śramaṇa as not being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is not a wise śramaṇa as not being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has not attained right knowledge as not having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has not attained right mindfulness as not having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is not pure as not being pure. Venerable, you should know that such a person should not be associated with, should not be honored, revered, or served. If a bhikṣu associates with one who should not be associated with, and honors, reveres, and serves one who should not be honored, revered, and served, then throughout the long night he will obtain no benefit and no welfare, and will not gain advantage, security, or happiness, but will produce suffering, grief, and sorrow.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'May no one else know of the precepts I have transgressed.' Venerable, and perhaps others do know of his transgression of the precepts. Because others know of his transgression of the precepts, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome. Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'If I have transgressed the precepts, let others admonish me in private, and not admonish me in the midst of the assembly.' Venerable, and perhaps others admonish him in the midst of the assembly and not in private. Because others admonish him in the midst of the assembly and not in private, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome. Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'If I have transgressed the precepts, let a superior person admonish me, and not let an inferior person admonish me.' Venerable, and perhaps an inferior person admonishes him for his transgression of the precepts, and it is not a superior person. Because an inferior person admonishes him and it is not a superior person, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'Let me sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus. Let not other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus. Because other bhikṣus sit before the Buddha, ask the World-Honored One about the Dharma, and expound it to the bhikṣus, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus enter a house, let me be at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying me as we enter. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, be at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, are at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus enter a house, are at the very front, with the bhikṣus attending and accompanying them as they enter, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus have already entered a house, let me have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have already entered the house, have the highest seat, obtain the first seat, the first hand-washing water, and obtain the first food, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'When the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, let me teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight. Let not other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight. Because other bhikṣus, when the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been put away, and the hand-washing water has been distributed, teach the Dharma to the householders, inspiring and arousing their aspiration, and accomplishing their delight, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'When householders come to visit the monastery garden, let me meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them. Let not other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them. Because other bhikṣus, when householders come to visit the monastery garden, meet with them, gather with them, sit with them, and converse with them, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'Let me be known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country. Let not other bhikṣus be known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus are known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country. Because other bhikṣus are known and recognized by kings, and by royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'Let me be revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Let not other bhikṣus be revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus are revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Because other bhikṣus are revered and honored by the four assemblies: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, there may be a person in whose mind no such desire arises: 'Let me obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life. Let not other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life.' Venerable, and perhaps other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life. Because other bhikṣus obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites of life, his mind does not give rise to ill will. If that person's mind has no ill will and his mind does not give rise to such desire, both are wholesome.

"Venerable, regarding such a person, if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do not know that he gives rise to such immeasurable wholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is a śramaṇa as not being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is a wise śramaṇa as not being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has attained right knowledge as not having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has attained right mindfulness as not having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is pure as not being pure. Venerable, but if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do know that he gives rise to such immeasurable wholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is a śramaṇa as being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is a wise śramaṇa as being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has attained right knowledge as having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has attained right mindfulness as having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is pure as being pure.

"Venerable, it is like a person who buys a covered copper bowl from a marketplace or from a coppersmith's shop, fills it completely with various kinds of pure and fine foods and drinks, covers the top, and carries it away, passing through shops and walking among the crowd. The crowd, seeing it, all do not wish to eat from it, have no fondness, are greatly disgusted, and give rise to the perception of impurity, saying: 'Take that excrement away! Take that excrement away!' But after he carries it to a certain place and opens it to show them, the crowd, seeing it, all wish to eat, with minds of great fondness, feeling no aversion, and giving rise to the perception of purity. Even those who originally did not wish to eat now wish to eat upon seeing it; how much more those who originally wished to eat?

"Venerable, in the same way, regarding such a person, if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do not know that he gives rise to such immeasurable wholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is a śramaṇa as not being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is a wise śramaṇa as not being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has attained right knowledge as not having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has attained right mindfulness as not having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is pure as not being pure. Venerable, but if wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do know that he gives rise to such immeasurable wholesome mental desires, then they perceive one who is a śramaṇa as being a śramaṇa, perceive one who is a wise śramaṇa as being a wise śramaṇa, perceive one who has attained right knowledge as having attained right knowledge, perceive one who has attained right mindfulness as having attained right mindfulness, and perceive one who is pure as being pure. Venerable, you should know that such a person should be associated with, honored, revered, and served. If a bhikṣu associates with one who should be associated with, and honors, reveres, and serves one who should be honored, revered, and served, then throughout the long night he will obtain benefit and welfare, and will gain advantage, security, and happiness, and will be free from suffering, grief, and sorrow."

At that time, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also in that assembly. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I now wish to use a simile regarding this matter. Will you permit me to speak?"

Venerable Śāriputra said: "Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if you wish to use a simile, please do so."

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I recall that once I was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the mountain caves. At that time, after the night had passed and early morning had come, I put on my robe, took my bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. I went to the house of the old chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūrṇa. At that time, next door to his house there was another chariot-maker working on a chariot axle. At that time, the old chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūrṇa, went to that other house. Then the old chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūrṇa, watched him working on the axle and thought to himself: 'If that chariot-maker would take his axe and chop off such-and-such bad spots, then this axle would be extremely good.' That chariot-maker then, just as the old chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūrṇa, had thought in his mind, took his axe and chopped off those very bad spots. At this, the old chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūrṇa, was extremely delighted and said: 'Chariot-maker's son! Your mind is such that you know my mind. Why is this? Because you took the axe and chopped the axle at those very bad spots, just as I intended.' In the same way, Venerable Śāriputra, if there are those who are flattering, deceitful, envious, without faith, lazy, lacking right mindfulness and right knowledge, without concentration and without wisdom, with confused minds, not guarding their faculties, not cultivating the śramaṇa way, and making no distinctions, Venerable Śāriputra, knowing their minds, has taught this Dharma for them. But, Venerable Śāriputra, if there are people who are not flattering, not deceitful, without envy, with faith, diligent and not lazy, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, cultivating concentration and cultivating wisdom, with unconfused minds, guarding their faculties, broadly cultivating the śramaṇa way and making good distinctions, when they hear Venerable Śāriputra's teaching of the Dharma, it is as if the hungry wish to obtain food and the thirsty wish to obtain drink, with their mouths and minds both.

"Venerable Śāriputra, it is like a kṣatriya woman, or a brahmin, householder, or artisan woman, who is beautiful and lovely, having bathed thoroughly, anointed her body with fragrance, wearing bright and clean garments, adorned with various ornaments to embellish her appearance. If someone, thinking of that woman and wishing to bring her benefit and well-being, wishing for her security and happiness, were to bring her a garland of blue lotus flowers, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of sumanā flowers, or a garland of vārṣika flowers, or a garland of atimukta flowers, and present it to her, that woman would joyfully receive it with both hands and adorn her head with it. Venerable Śāriputra, in the same way, if there are people who are not flattering, not deceitful, without envy, with faith, diligent and not lazy, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, cultivating concentration and cultivating wisdom, with unconfused minds, guarding their faculties, broadly cultivating the śramaṇa way and making good distinctions, when they hear Venerable Śāriputra's teaching of the Dharma, it is as if the hungry wish to eat and the thirsty wish to drink, with their mouths and minds both. Venerable Śāriputra, how wonderful! How extraordinary! Venerable Śāriputra constantly rescues and saves fellow practitioners of the holy life, causing them to leave behind what is unwholesome and establishing them in what is wholesome."

Thus the two venerables praised each other and then rose from their seats and departed.

What Venerable Śāriputra spoke was thus. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the bhikṣus, having heard what Venerable Śāriputra said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Defilements, First

---

## (88) Sūtra on Seeking the Dharma, Second of the Defilements Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and they went to the Śiṃśapā forest north of the village of Pañcasāla. Various renowned and honored senior elders, great disciples, were also there: Venerable Śāriputra, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, Venerable Ānanda, and other such renowned and honored senior elders and great disciples. They were also in the village of Pañcasāla, all staying near the Buddha's leaf hut.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "All of you should practice seeking the Dharma, and not practice seeking food and drink. Why is this? Out of compassion for my disciples, I wish them to practice seeking the Dharma and not to practice seeking food and drink. If you practice seeking food and drink and do not practice seeking the Dharma, you yourselves will be flawed, and I too will be without good reputation. If you practice seeking the Dharma and do not practice seeking food and drink, you yourselves will be good, and I too will have good reputation.

"How is it that disciples follow the Buddha seeking food and drink rather than seeking the Dharma? Suppose I have eaten my fill, the meal is finished, and there is leftover food. Afterward, two bhikṣus come who are hungry, thirsty, and weak. I say to them: 'I have eaten my fill, the meal is finished, and there is leftover food. If you wish to eat, take it and eat. If you do not take it, I will take it and discard it on clean ground, or pour it into water free of living creatures.' Of those two bhikṣus, the first bhikṣu thinks: 'The World-Honored One has eaten his fill, the meal is finished, and there is leftover food. If I do not take it, the World-Honored One will certainly discard it on clean ground or pour it into water free of living creatures. I should take it and eat.' He then takes and eats it.

"Although that bhikṣu, having taken this food, is comfortable and at ease for one day and one night, yet because that bhikṣu took this food, it does not please the Buddha. Why is this? Because that bhikṣu, having taken this food, does not attain fewness of desires, does not know contentment, is not easy to support, is not easy to satisfy, does not know the proper time, does not know moderation, does not attain diligence, does not attain meditative stillness, does not attain pure conduct, does not attain seclusion, does not attain one-pointedness of mind, does not attain zealous effort, and also does not attain nirvāṇa. Therefore, because that bhikṣu took this food, it does not please the Buddha. This is what it means for disciples to follow the Buddha seeking food and drink rather than seeking the Dharma.

"How is it that disciples practice seeking the Dharma and not seeking food and drink? Of those two bhikṣus, the second bhikṣu thinks: 'The World-Honored One has eaten his fill, the meal is finished, and there is leftover food. If I do not take it, the World-Honored One will certainly discard it on clean ground or pour it into water free of living creatures. Moreover, the World-Honored One has said that among foods, the lowest and most base is leftover food. I should not take this food.' Having thought thus, he does not take it.

"Although that bhikṣu, not having taken this food, endures hardship and is not at ease for one day and one night, yet because that bhikṣu did not take this food, it pleases the Buddha. Why is this? Because that bhikṣu, not having taken this food, attains fewness of desires, attains contentment, is easy to support, is easy to satisfy, knows the proper time, knows moderation, attains diligence, attains meditative stillness, attains pure conduct, attains seclusion, attains one-pointedness of mind, attains zealous effort, and also attains nirvāṇa. Therefore, because that bhikṣu did not take this food, it pleases the Buddha. This is what it means for disciples to practice seeking the Dharma and to follow the Buddha, not seeking food and drink."

Then the World-Honored One addressed the disciples: "If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people, many people do not attain happiness, it is not for compassion toward the world, nor for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the middle and junior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people, many people do not attain happiness, it is not for compassion toward the world, nor for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people, many people attain happiness, it is for compassion toward the world, and for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people, many people attain happiness, it is for compassion toward the world, and for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness."

At that time, Venerable Śāriputra was also in the assembly. The World-Honored One then said: "Śāriputra, you should teach the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma for the bhikṣus. I have a pain in my back and now wish to rest briefly."

Venerable Śāriputra accepted the Buddha's instruction: "Yes, World-Honored One." Thereupon the World-Honored One folded his uttarāsaṅga cloth four times and spread it on the bed, rolled up his saṅghāṭī robe to make a pillow, lay down on his right side, placed one foot upon the other, created the perception of light, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, and constantly kept in mind the intention to arise.

At that time, Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, you should know that the World-Honored One just now briefly taught the Dharma: 'If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people, many people do not attain happiness, it is not for compassion toward the world, nor for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the middle and junior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people, many people do not attain happiness, it is not for compassion toward the world, nor for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people, many people attain happiness, it is for compassion toward the world, and for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people, many people attain happiness, it is for compassion toward the world, and for the sake of gods and humans seeking welfare and benefit, seeking security and happiness.' However, the World-Honored One taught this Dharma very briefly. How do you understand its meaning? How would you explain it in detail?"

At that time, among the assembly, some bhikṣus spoke thus: "Venerable Śāriputra, if senior and honored elders themselves declare: 'I have attained ultimate knowledge. I know as it truly is that birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there will be no further existence,' then fellow practitioners of the holy life, hearing that bhikṣu's own declaration of having attained ultimate knowledge, are delighted."

Other bhikṣus spoke thus: "Venerable Śāriputra, if the middle and junior disciples aspire to the unsurpassed nirvāṇa, and fellow practitioners of the holy life see their practice, they are delighted." Thus those bhikṣus explained this meaning, but it did not accord with Venerable Śāriputra's intention.

Venerable Śāriputra addressed those bhikṣus: "Venerables, listen, and I will explain to you. Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, the senior disciples are blameworthy in three respects. What are the three? When the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the senior disciples do not train in renunciation, the senior disciples are blameworthy in this. When the teacher teaches dharmas that should be abandoned, but the senior disciples do not abandon those dharmas, the senior disciples are blameworthy in this. When there are attainments to be realized, but the senior disciples abandon the effort, the senior disciples are blameworthy in this. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, the senior disciples have these three grounds for blame. Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the middle and junior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, the middle and junior disciples are blameworthy in three respects. What are the three? When the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the middle and junior disciples do not train in renunciation, the middle and junior disciples are blameworthy in this. When the teacher teaches dharmas that should be abandoned, but the middle and junior disciples do not abandon those dharmas, the middle and junior disciples are blameworthy in this. When there are attainments to be realized, but the middle and junior disciples abandon the effort, the middle and junior disciples are blameworthy in this. If in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, but the middle and junior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, the middle and junior disciples have these three grounds for blame.

"Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, the senior disciples are praiseworthy in three respects. What are the three? When the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also train in renunciation, the senior disciples are praiseworthy in this. When the teacher teaches dharmas that should be abandoned, and the senior disciples abandon those dharmas, the senior disciples are praiseworthy in this. When there are attainments to be realized, and the senior disciples make diligent effort and do not abandon the practice, the senior disciples are praiseworthy in this. Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, the senior disciples have these three grounds for praise. Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, the middle and junior disciples are praiseworthy in three respects. What are the three? When the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also train in renunciation, the middle and junior disciples are praiseworthy in this. When the teacher teaches dharmas that should be abandoned, and the middle and junior disciples abandon those dharmas, the middle and junior disciples are praiseworthy in this. When there are attainments to be realized, and the middle and junior disciples make diligent effort and do not abandon the practice, the middle and junior disciples are praiseworthy in this. Venerables, if in any Dharma and Vinaya the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, the middle and junior disciples have these three grounds for praise."

Venerable Śāriputra further addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, there is a middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa. Venerables, what is this middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa? Venerables, desire is evil, and evil desire for desire is also evil; one should abandon desire and also abandon evil desire for desire. Likewise with anger, resentment, miserliness and jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, conceit, extreme conceit, arrogance, heedlessness, pride, and contentiousness. Venerables, craving is also evil, and attachment is also evil; one should abandon craving and also abandon attachment. Venerables, this is the middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa.

"Venerables, there is furthermore a middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa. Venerables, what is this further middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to right concentration; these are the eight. Venerables, this is the further middle path that can bring about mental stability, attainment of concentration and happiness, following the Dharma in proper sequence, attaining penetration and awakening, and also attaining nirvāṇa."

At that time, the World-Honored One's ailment subsided and he regained comfort. Rising from his rest, he sat cross-legged and praised Venerable Śāriputra: "Excellent! Excellent! Śāriputra, you have taught the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma for the bhikṣus. Śāriputra, you should continue to teach the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma for the bhikṣus. Śāriputra, you should repeatedly teach the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma for the bhikṣus."

Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "All of you should together receive the Dharma that accords with the Dharma, recite it, study it, and uphold it. Why is this? This Dharma that accords with the Dharma has both Dharma and meaning, is the foundation of the holy life, leads to penetration and awakening, and also leads to nirvāṇa. When sons and daughters of good family shave off their hair and beards, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with sincere faith leave the household life to live without a home and train in the Way, this Dharma that accords with the Dharma should be well received and upheld."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Seeking the Dharma, Second
