## (89) Sūtra on the Bhikṣu's Request, Third of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, undertaking the summer retreat.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables! If there is a bhikṣu who requests of the bhikṣus, 'Venerables, speak to me, teach me, admonish me, and do not make it difficult for me,' why is this? Venerables, there may be a person who is of perverse speech, who is accomplished in the qualities of perverse speech. Because of being accomplished in the qualities of perverse speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life will not speak to him, will not teach him, will not admonish him, but rather make it difficult for that person. Venerables, what are the qualities of perverse speech? If one is accomplished in the qualities of perverse speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life will not speak to him, will not teach him, will not admonish him, but rather make it difficult for that person. Venerables, there may be a person who has evil desires and harbors evil desires. Venerables, if a person has evil desires and harbors evil desires, this is called a quality of perverse speech. Likewise: engaging in defiled conduct, being defiled; maintaining the bond of silence and remaining in it; being deceitful, flattering, and fawning; being stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious; being without shame and without remorse; having anger, depravity, and ill will; speaking with angry, resentful words; retorting when admonished by bhikṣus; treating with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus; making counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults; mutually avoiding each other and speaking of irrelevant matters; maintaining silence, being wrathful, having hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely; having bad friends and bad companions; being ungrateful and not recognizing kindness. Venerables, if a person is ungrateful and does not recognize kindness, this is called a quality of perverse speech. Venerables, these are called the qualities of perverse speech. If one is accomplished in the qualities of perverse speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life will not speak to him, will not teach him, will not admonish him, but rather make it difficult for that person. Venerables, a bhikṣu should reflect upon himself.

"Venerables, if there is a person who has evil desires and harbors evil desires, I would not love that person. If I had evil desires and harbored evil desires, that person likewise would not love me. A bhikṣu, observing thus, should train to not practice evil desires and not harbor evil desires. Likewise with engaging in defiled conduct and being defiled; maintaining the bond of silence and remaining in it; being deceitful, flattering, and fawning; being stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious; being without shame and without remorse; having anger, depravity, and ill will; speaking with angry, wrathful words; retorting when admonished by bhikṣus; treating with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus; making counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults; mutually avoiding each other and speaking of irrelevant matters; maintaining silence, being wrathful, having hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely; having bad friends and bad companions; being ungrateful and not recognizing kindness. Venerables, if a person is ungrateful and does not recognize kindness, I would not love that person. If I were ungrateful and did not recognize kindness, that person likewise would not love me. A bhikṣu, observing thus, should train to not be ungrateful and to not fail to recognize kindness.

"Venerables, if a bhikṣu does not request of the bhikṣus, 'Venerables, speak to me, teach me, admonish me, and do not make it difficult for me,' why is this? Venerables, there may be a person who speaks well, who is accomplished in the qualities of good speech. Because of being accomplished in the qualities of good speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life speak well to him, teach him well, admonish him well, and do not make it difficult for that person. Venerables, what are the qualities of good speech? If one is accomplished in the qualities of good speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life speak well to him, teach him well, admonish him well, and do not make it difficult for that person. Venerables, there may be a person who is without evil desires and does not harbor evil desires. Venerables, if a person is without evil desires and does not harbor evil desires, this is called a quality of good speech. Likewise: not engaging in defiled conduct or being defiled; not maintaining the bond of silence and remaining in it; not being deceitful, flattering, or fawning; not being stingy, greedy, jealous, or envious; not being without shame and without remorse; not having anger, depravity, or ill will; not speaking with angry, wrathful words; not retorting when admonished by bhikṣus; not treating with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus; not making counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults; not mutually avoiding each other and speaking of irrelevant matters; not maintaining silence, being wrathful, or having hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely; not having bad friends or bad companions; not being ungrateful and not failing to recognize kindness. Venerables, if a person is not ungrateful and does not fail to recognize kindness, this is called a quality of good speech. Venerables, these are called the qualities of good speech. If one is accomplished in the qualities of good speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life speak well to him, teach him well, admonish him well, and do not make it difficult for that person. Venerables, a bhikṣu should reflect upon himself.

"Venerables, if there is a person who is without evil desires and does not harbor evil desires, I would love that person. If I were without evil desires and did not harbor evil desires, that person likewise would love me. A bhikṣu, observing thus, should train to not practice evil desires and not harbor evil desires. Likewise: not engaging in defiled conduct or being defiled; not maintaining the bond of silence and remaining in it; not being deceitful, flattering, or fawning; not being stingy, greedy, jealous, or envious; not being without shame and without remorse; not having anger, depravity, or ill will; not speaking with angry, wrathful words; not retorting when admonished by bhikṣus; not treating with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus; not making counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults; not mutually avoiding each other and speaking of irrelevant matters; not maintaining silence, being wrathful, or having hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely; not having bad friends or bad companions; not being ungrateful and not failing to recognize kindness. Venerables, if a person is not ungrateful and does not fail to recognize kindness, I would love that person. If I were not ungrateful and did not fail to recognize kindness, that person likewise would love me. A bhikṣu, observing thus, should train to not be ungrateful and to not fail to recognize kindness.

"Venerables, if a bhikṣu observes in this way, it will certainly bring great benefit: 'Am I one who has evil desires and harbors evil desires, or am I one who is without evil desires and does not harbor evil desires?' Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I have evil desires and harbor evil desires,' then he is not pleased and seeks to abandon them. Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I am without evil desires and do not harbor evil desires,' then he is pleased: 'I am myself pure, and I seek to train in the noble Dharma.' Because of this he is pleased. Venerables, it is like a person with eyes who uses a mirror to look at his own face and sees whether it is clean or unclean. Venerables, if the person with eyes sees dirt on his face, he is not pleased and seeks to wash it off. Venerables, if the person with eyes sees no dirt on his face, he is pleased: 'My face is clean.' Because of this he is pleased.

"Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I practice evil desires and harbor evil desires,' then he is not pleased and seeks to abandon them. Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I do not practice evil desires and do not harbor evil desires,' then he is pleased: 'I am myself pure, and I seek to train in the noble Dharma.' Because of this he is pleased. Likewise: 'Am I one who engages in defiled conduct and is defiled, or one who does not engage in defiled conduct and is not defiled? Am I one who maintains the bond of silence and remains in it, or one who does not maintain the bond of silence and remain in it? Am I one who is deceitful, flattering, and fawning, or one who is not deceitful, flattering, or fawning? Am I one who is stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious, or one who is not stingy, greedy, jealous, or envious? Am I one who is without shame and without remorse, or one who is not without shame and without remorse? Am I one who has anger, depravity, and ill will, or one who does not have anger, depravity, or ill will? Am I one who speaks with angry, wrathful words, or one who does not speak with angry, wrathful words? Am I one who retorts when admonished by bhikṣus, or one who does not retort when admonished by bhikṣus? Am I one who treats with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus, or one who does not treat with contempt when admonished by bhikṣus? Am I one who makes counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults, or one who does not make counter-accusations when bhikṣus expose faults? Am I one who mutually avoids, or one who does not mutually avoid? Am I one who speaks of irrelevant matters, or one who does not speak of irrelevant matters? Am I one who maintains silence, is wrathful, and has hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely, or one who does not maintain silence, is not wrathful, and does not have hatred and jealousy blazing fiercely? Am I one who has bad friends and bad companions, or one who does not have bad friends or bad companions? Am I one who is ungrateful and does not recognize kindness, or one who is not ungrateful and does not fail to recognize kindness?' Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I am ungrateful and do not recognize kindness,' then he is not pleased and seeks to abandon this. Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I am not ungrateful and do not fail to recognize kindness,' then he is pleased: 'I am myself pure, and I seek to train in the noble Dharma.' Because of this he is pleased. Venerables, it is like a person with eyes who uses a mirror to look at his own face and sees whether it is clean or unclean. Venerables, if the person with eyes sees dirt on his face, he is not pleased and seeks to wash it off. Venerables, if the person with eyes sees no dirt on his face, he is pleased: 'My face is clean.' Because of this he is pleased.

"Venerables, likewise, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I am ungrateful and do not recognize kindness,' then he is not pleased and seeks to abandon this. Venerables, if when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I am not ungrateful and do not fail to recognize kindness,' then he is pleased: 'I am myself pure, and I seek to train in the noble Dharma.' Because of this he is pleased. Because of being pleased, he attains joy. Because of joy, he attains tranquility of body. Because of tranquility of body, he experiences bliss. Because of experiencing bliss, he attains concentration of mind. Venerables, a learned noble disciple, because of attaining concentration of mind, sees things as they really are and knows them as they truly are. Because of seeing things as they really are and knowing them as they truly are, he attains disenchantment. Because of disenchantment, he attains dispassion. Because of dispassion, he attains liberation. Because of liberation, he knows that he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more becoming.' He knows this as it truly is."

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (90) Sūtra on Knowing the Dharma, Fourth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Kauśāmbī, in the Ghośitārāma Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Cunda addressed the bhikṣus: "If there is a bhikṣu who says, 'I know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, and I am without covetousness,' yet that worthy one's mind gives rise to evil covetousness and he abides in it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views; yet that worthy one's mind gives rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides in them. Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that worthy one does not truly know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, free from covetousness. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind gives rise to covetousness and he abides in it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind gives rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides in them.

"Venerables, it is like a person who is not wealthy yet claims to be wealthy, who has no royal estates yet says he has royal estates, who has no livestock yet says he has livestock. When he wants to use them, he has no gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, or amber; no livestock, grain, or rice; and no servants. His relatives and friends go to him and say: 'You are truly not wealthy yet claim to be wealthy, you have no royal estates yet say you have royal estates, you have no livestock yet say you have livestock. Yet when you want to use them, you have no gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, or amber; no livestock, grain, or rice; and no servants.' In the same way, venerables, if there is a bhikṣu who says, 'I know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, and I am without covetousness,' yet that worthy one's mind gives rise to evil covetousness and he abides in it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views; yet that worthy one's mind gives rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides in them. Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that worthy one does not truly know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, free from covetousness. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind is not directed toward the complete exhaustion of covetousness, toward nirvāṇa without remainder; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind is not directed toward the complete exhaustion of the dharma of evil views, toward nirvāṇa without remainder.

"Venerables, there may be a bhikṣu who does not say, 'I know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, and I am without covetousness,' yet that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil covetousness and he abides without it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views; that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides without them. Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that worthy one truly knows the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, free from covetousness. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil covetousness and he abides without it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides without them.

"Venerables, it is like a person who is greatly wealthy yet says he is not wealthy, who has royal estates yet says he has no royal estates, who has livestock yet says he has no livestock. When he wants to use them, he has gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, and amber; livestock, grain, and rice; and also servants. His relatives and friends go to him and say: 'You are truly wealthy yet say you are not wealthy, you have royal estates yet say you have no royal estates, you have livestock yet say you have no livestock. Yet when you want to use them, you have gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, and amber; livestock, grain, and rice; and also servants.' In the same way, venerables, if there is a bhikṣu who does not say, 'I know the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, and I am without covetousness,' yet that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil covetousness and he abides without it; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views; that worthy one's mind does not give rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides without them. Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that worthy one truly knows the dharmas, those dharmas that can be known, free from covetousness. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind is directed toward the complete exhaustion of covetousness, toward nirvāṇa without remainder; likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views. Why is this? Because that worthy one's mind is directed toward the complete exhaustion of the dharma of evil views, toward nirvāṇa without remainder."

The Venerable Cunda spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Cunda said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Knowing the Dharma, Fourth

---

## (91) Sūtra on Cunda's Question about Views, Fifth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Kauśāmbī, in the Ghośitārāma Garden.

Then the Venerable Mahācunda, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, among the various views that arise in the world, there are views calculating a self, calculating beings, calculating persons, calculating a life span, calculating a vital force, and calculating a world. World-Honored One, how should one know, how should one see, so that these views may be extinguished and abandoned, and so that other views do not continue and are not grasped?"

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Cunda, among the various views that arise in the world, there are views calculating a self, calculating beings, calculating persons, calculating a life span, calculating a vital force, and calculating a world. Cunda, if all dharmas are extinguished completely without remainder, by knowing thus and seeing thus, these views are extinguished and abandoned, and other views do not continue and are not grasped. One should train in gradual diminishing.

"Cunda, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, what is gradual diminishing? A bhikṣu, detached from desires, detached from evil and unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining the fourth dhyāna and abiding in its accomplishment. He thinks: 'I practice gradual diminishing.' Cunda, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, this alone is not gradual diminishing. There are the four higher states of mind that are blissful abidings in the present life. A practitioner, having arisen from these, then returns to enter them again. He thinks: 'I practice gradual diminishing.' Cunda, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, this alone is not gradual diminishing. A bhikṣu, transcending all perceptions of form, up to attaining the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and abiding in its accomplishment. He thinks: 'I practice gradual diminishing.' Cunda, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, this alone is not gradual diminishing. There are the four peaceful liberations: having left form, one attains the formless. A practitioner, having arisen from these, should explain them to others. He thinks: 'I practice gradual diminishing.'

"Cunda, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya, this alone is not gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have evil desires and harbor evil desires; I shall be without evil desires and not harbor evil desires': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have harmful intentions and anger; I shall be without harmful intentions and anger': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others engage in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct; I shall be without unchaste conduct': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have covetousness, a quarrelsome mind, are entangled by sloth, are restless and proud, and have doubt; I shall be without doubt': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, shamelessness, and lack of remorse; I shall have shame and remorse': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have conceit; I shall be without conceit': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have excessive conceit; I shall be without excessive conceit': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others are not learned; I shall be learned': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others do not contemplate wholesome dharmas; I shall contemplate wholesome dharmas': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others practice unrighteous and evil conduct; I shall practice righteous and excellent conduct': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and bad morality; I shall be without bad morality': one should train in gradual diminishing. Cunda, 'Others have no faith, are lazy, lack mindfulness, lack concentration, and have evil wisdom; I shall be without evil wisdom': one should train in gradual diminishing.

"Cunda, if one merely arouses the mental intention and desire to train in wholesome dharmas, this already brings great benefit, how much more so acting with body and speech in wholesome dharmas! Cunda, 'Others have evil desires and harbor evil desires; I shall be without evil desires and not harbor evil desires': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have harmful intentions and anger; I shall be without harmful intentions and anger': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others engage in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct; I shall be without unchaste conduct': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have covetousness, a quarrelsome mind, are entangled by sloth, are restless and proud, and have doubt; I shall be without doubt': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, shamelessness, and lack of remorse; I shall have shame and remorse': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have conceit; I shall be without conceit': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have excessive conceit; I shall be without excessive conceit': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others are not learned; I shall be learned': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others do not contemplate wholesome dharmas; I shall contemplate wholesome dharmas': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others practice unrighteous and evil conduct; I shall practice righteous and excellent conduct': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and bad morality; I shall be without bad morality': one should arouse this intention. Cunda, 'Others have no faith, are lazy, lack mindfulness, lack concentration, and have evil wisdom; I shall be without evil wisdom': one should arouse this intention.

"Cunda, just as an evil road is opposed by a right road, just as a bad crossing is opposed by a good crossing, in the same way, Cunda, one who has evil desires is opposed by being without evil desires. One who has harmful intentions and anger is opposed by being without harmful intentions and anger. One who engages in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct is opposed by chaste conduct. One who has covetousness, a quarrelsome mind, sloth, restlessness and pride, and doubt is opposed by being without doubt. One who has the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, shamelessness, and lack of remorse is opposed by having shame and remorse. One who has conceit is opposed by being without conceit. One who has excessive conceit is opposed by being without excessive conceit. One who is not learned is opposed by being learned. One who does not contemplate wholesome dharmas is opposed by contemplating wholesome dharmas. One who practices unrighteous and evil conduct is opposed by practicing righteous and excellent conduct. One who has false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and bad morality is opposed by good morality. One who has no faith, is lazy, lacks mindfulness, lacks concentration, and has evil wisdom is opposed by good wisdom.

"Cunda, there are dharmas that are dark with dark results, leading to evil destinations. There are dharmas that are bright with bright results, leading upward. In this way, Cunda, one who has evil desires ascends by being without evil desires. One who has harmful intentions and anger ascends by being without harmful intentions and anger. One who engages in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct ascends by chaste conduct. One who has covetousness, a quarrelsome mind, sloth, restlessness and pride, and doubt ascends by being without doubt. One who has the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, shamelessness, and lack of remorse ascends by having shame and remorse. One who has conceit ascends by being without conceit. One who has excessive conceit ascends by being without excessive conceit. One who is not learned ascends by being learned. One who does not contemplate wholesome dharmas ascends by contemplating wholesome dharmas. One who practices unrighteous and evil conduct ascends by practicing righteous and excellent conduct. One who has false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and bad morality ascends by good morality. One who has no faith, is lazy, lacks mindfulness, lacks concentration, and has evil wisdom ascends by good wisdom.

"Cunda, if one has not tamed oneself and wishes to tame others who are untamed, that is simply impossible. If one is oneself drowning and wishes to pull out others who are drowning, that is simply impossible. If one has not oneself attained parinirvāṇa and wishes to cause others who have not attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa, that is simply impossible. Cunda, if one has tamed oneself and wishes to tame others who are untamed, that is certainly possible. If one is oneself not drowning and wishes to pull out others who are drowning, that is certainly possible. If one has oneself attained parinirvāṇa and wishes to cause others who have not attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa, that is certainly possible. In this way, Cunda, one who has evil desires attains parinirvāṇa through being without evil desires. One who has harmful intentions and anger attains parinirvāṇa through being without harmful intentions and anger. One who engages in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct attains parinirvāṇa through chaste conduct. One who has covetousness, a quarrelsome mind, sloth, restlessness and pride, and doubt attains parinirvāṇa through being without doubt. One who has the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, shamelessness, and lack of remorse attains parinirvāṇa through having shame and remorse. One who has conceit attains parinirvāṇa through being without conceit. One who has excessive conceit attains parinirvāṇa through being without excessive conceit. One who is not learned attains parinirvāṇa through being learned. One who does not contemplate wholesome dharmas attains parinirvāṇa through contemplating wholesome dharmas. One who practices unrighteous and evil conduct attains parinirvāṇa through practicing righteous and excellent conduct. One who has false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, and bad morality attains parinirvāṇa through good morality. One who has no faith, is lazy, lacks mindfulness, lacks concentration, and has evil wisdom attains parinirvāṇa through good wisdom.

"Thus, Cunda, I have explained to you the teaching of gradual diminishing, I have explained the teaching of arousing intention, I have explained the teaching of opposition, I have explained the teaching of ascending, and I have explained the teaching of parinirvāṇa. What a revered teacher should do for disciples, arising from great compassion, sympathy, pity, and concern, seeking their benefit, seeking their welfare, seeking their ease and happiness, I have now done. You should also do your own part. Go to secluded places, mountain forests, under trees, in empty and quiet places. Sit in meditation and contemplation. Do not be negligent. Be diligent and energetic. Do not let yourselves have regrets afterward. This is my instruction; this is my admonition."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Mahācunda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Cunda's Question about Views, Fifth

---

## (92) Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, Sixth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are dharmas that are extinguished through the body, not through speech. There are dharmas that are extinguished through speech, not through the body. There are dharmas that are not extinguished through body or speech, but are extinguished only by seeing with wisdom.

"How are dharmas extinguished through the body, not through speech? A bhikṣu who is full of unwholesome bodily conduct, thoroughly engaging in and clinging to bodily actions: when other bhikṣus see this, they admonish that bhikṣu, saying, 'Worthy one, you are full of unwholesome bodily conduct, thoroughly engaging in and clinging to it; why do you cling to such bodily actions? Worthy one, you should abandon unwholesome bodily conduct and cultivate wholesome bodily conduct.' Afterward, that person abandons unwholesome bodily conduct and cultivates wholesome bodily conduct. This is called dharmas extinguished through the body, not through speech.

"How are dharmas extinguished through speech, not through the body? A bhikṣu who is full of unwholesome verbal conduct, thoroughly engaging in and clinging to verbal actions: when other bhikṣus see this, they admonish that bhikṣu, saying, 'Worthy one, you are full of unwholesome verbal conduct, thoroughly engaging in and clinging to it; why do you cling to such verbal actions? Worthy one, you should abandon unwholesome verbal conduct and cultivate wholesome verbal conduct.' Afterward, that person abandons unwholesome verbal conduct and cultivates wholesome verbal conduct. This is called dharmas extinguished through speech, not through the body.

"How are dharmas not extinguished through body or speech, but extinguished only by seeing with wisdom? Covetousness is not extinguished through body or speech, but only by seeing with wisdom. Likewise, quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views are not extinguished through body or speech, but only by seeing with wisdom. These are called dharmas not extinguished through body or speech, but extinguished only by seeing with wisdom.

"The Tathāgata, with a certain kind of observation, observes the minds of other people and knows: 'This person does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate morality, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom in such a way as to extinguish covetousness through cultivating body, morality, mind, and wisdom.' Why is this? Because this person's mind gives rise to evil covetousness and he abides in it. Likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, and lack of remorse; he is able to extinguish evil desires and evil views. Why is this? Because this person's mind gives rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides in them. He knows: 'This person cultivates the body, cultivates morality, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom in such a way as to extinguish covetousness through cultivating body, morality, mind, and wisdom.' Why is this? Because this person's mind does not give rise to evil covetousness and he abides without it. Likewise with quarreling, resentment, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, jealousy, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, and lack of remorse; he is able to extinguish evil desires and evil views. Why is this? Because this person's mind does not give rise to evil desires and evil views and he abides without them. Just as a blue lotus, a red lotus, a crimson lotus, or a white lotus is born in the water, grows in the water, rises above the water, and is not stained by the water; in the same way, the Tathāgata was born in the world, grew in the world, transcends the world in his conduct, and is not stained by worldly dharmas. Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has transcended the entire world."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was holding a fan and attending the Buddha. Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined facing the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, what should this sūtra be called? How should it be received and upheld?"

Then the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, this sūtra is called 'The Simile of the Blue and White Lotus.' You should well receive, uphold, and recite it."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "You should all together receive this Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, recite it, study it, and uphold it. Why is this? This Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus accords with the Dharma, is meaningful, is the foundation of the holy life, leads to penetrative knowledge, leads to awakening, and also leads to nirvāṇa. If a son of good family shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household for the homeless life to train in the Way, he should receive this Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, well recite it, and uphold it."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, Sixth

---

## (93) Sūtra on the Water-Purification Brahmin, Seventh of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Uruvelā, on the bank of the Nairañjanā River, beneath the Ajapāla Nyagrodha tree, shortly after first attaining the Way.

At that time, there was a water-purification brahmin who, in the afternoon, was strolling about and came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One saw the water-purification brahmin coming from afar, and on account of the water-purification brahmin, he addressed the bhikṣus: "If there are twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell. What are the twenty-one defilements? Wrong views as a defilement of the mind; unwholesome desires as a defilement of the mind; evil greed as a defilement of the mind; wrong dharmas as a defilement of the mind; desire as a defilement of the mind; anger as a defilement of the mind; sloth as a defilement of the mind; restlessness and regret as a defilement of the mind; doubt as a defilement of the mind; the fetter of anger as a defilement of the mind; the bond of silence as a defilement of the mind; stinginess as a defilement of the mind; jealousy as a defilement of the mind; deceit as a defilement of the mind; flattery as a defilement of the mind; shamelessness as a defilement of the mind; lack of remorse as a defilement of the mind; conceit as a defilement of the mind; great conceit as a defilement of the mind; arrogance as a defilement of the mind; heedlessness as a defilement of the mind. If there are these twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell. It is like a soiled and greasy garment given to a dyer. The dyer, having received it, treats it with pure lye, or with washing powder, or soaks it in earth and washes it thoroughly to make it clean. Although the dyer treats it with pure lye, or with washing powder, or soaks it in earth and washes it thoroughly to make it clean, that soiled garment still retains its stained color. In the same way, if there are twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell. What are the twenty-one defilements? Wrong views as a defilement of the mind; unwholesome desires as a defilement of the mind; evil greed as a defilement of the mind; wrong dharmas as a defilement of the mind; desire as a defilement of the mind; anger as a defilement of the mind; sloth as a defilement of the mind; restlessness and regret as a defilement of the mind; doubt as a defilement of the mind; the fetter of anger as a defilement of the mind; the bond of silence as a defilement of the mind; stinginess as a defilement of the mind; jealousy as a defilement of the mind; deceit as a defilement of the mind; flattery as a defilement of the mind; shamelessness as a defilement of the mind; lack of remorse as a defilement of the mind; conceit as a defilement of the mind; great conceit as a defilement of the mind; arrogance as a defilement of the mind; heedlessness as a defilement of the mind. If there are these twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

"If there are twenty-one defilements that do not pollute the mind, one will certainly go to a good destination and be born in heaven. What are the twenty-one defilements? Wrong views as a defilement of the mind; unwholesome desires as a defilement of the mind; evil greed as a defilement of the mind; wrong dharmas as a defilement of the mind; desire as a defilement of the mind; anger as a defilement of the mind; sloth as a defilement of the mind; restlessness and regret as a defilement of the mind; doubt as a defilement of the mind; the fetter of anger as a defilement of the mind; the bond of silence as a defilement of the mind; stinginess as a defilement of the mind; jealousy as a defilement of the mind; deceit as a defilement of the mind; flattery as a defilement of the mind; shamelessness as a defilement of the mind; lack of remorse as a defilement of the mind; conceit as a defilement of the mind; great conceit as a defilement of the mind; arrogance as a defilement of the mind; heedlessness as a defilement of the mind. If these twenty-one defilements do not pollute the mind, one will certainly go to a good destination and be born in heaven. It is like a pure white Bārāṇasī cloth given to a dyer. The dyer, having received it, treats it with pure lye, or with washing powder, or soaks it in earth and washes it thoroughly to make it clean. Although the dyer treats that pure white Bārāṇasī cloth with pure lye, or with washing powder, or soaks it in earth and washes it thoroughly to make it clean, that pure white Bārāṇasī cloth was already clean and becomes even cleaner. In the same way, if there are twenty-one defilements that do not pollute the mind, one will certainly go to a good destination and be born in heaven. What are the twenty-one defilements? Wrong views as a defilement of the mind; unwholesome desires as a defilement of the mind; evil greed as a defilement of the mind; wrong dharmas as a defilement of the mind; desire as a defilement of the mind; anger as a defilement of the mind; sloth as a defilement of the mind; restlessness and regret as a defilement of the mind; doubt as a defilement of the mind; the fetter of anger as a defilement of the mind; the bond of silence as a defilement of the mind; stinginess as a defilement of the mind; jealousy as a defilement of the mind; deceit as a defilement of the mind; flattery as a defilement of the mind; shamelessness as a defilement of the mind; lack of remorse as a defilement of the mind; conceit as a defilement of the mind; great conceit as a defilement of the mind; arrogance as a defilement of the mind; heedlessness as a defilement of the mind. If these twenty-one defilements do not pollute the mind, one will certainly go to a good destination and be born in heaven.

"If one knows that wrong views are a defilement of the mind, having known this, one abandons them. Likewise with unwholesome desires as a defilement of the mind; evil greed as a defilement of the mind; wrong dharmas as a defilement of the mind; desire as a defilement of the mind; anger as a defilement of the mind; sloth as a defilement of the mind; restlessness and regret as a defilement of the mind; doubt as a defilement of the mind; the fetter of anger as a defilement of the mind; the bond of silence as a defilement of the mind; stinginess as a defilement of the mind; jealousy as a defilement of the mind; deceit as a defilement of the mind; flattery as a defilement of the mind; shamelessness as a defilement of the mind; lack of remorse as a defilement of the mind; conceit as a defilement of the mind; great conceit as a defilement of the mind; arrogance as a defilement of the mind; if one knows that heedlessness is a defilement of the mind, having known this, one abandons it. Then, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, one pervades all ten directions and abides in its accomplishment. Thus toward the first direction, the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely throughout all, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and exceedingly great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, one abides in its accomplishment. Likewise with compassion, sympathetic joy, and with a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and exceedingly great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, one abides in its accomplishment. Brahmin, this is called the bathing that cleanses the inner mind, not the bathing of the outer body."

At that time, the brahmin said to the World-Honored One: "Gotama, you should go to the Bahukā River to bathe."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, if one goes to the Bahukā River to bathe, what does one gain from it?"

The brahmin replied: "Gotama, that Bahukā River is the mark of purification in the world, the mark of crossing over, the mark of merit. Gotama, if one goes to the Bahukā River to bathe, one cleanses and removes all evils."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for that brahmin:

"O brahmin of excellent head, if one enters the Bahukā River,
This is the sport of fools, and it cannot purify dark deeds.
O excellent head, why go to a spring? What is the purpose of the Bahukā River?
When a person has done unwholesome deeds, how can clear water benefit him?
The pure one is without stain or impurity; the pure one always upholds morality.
The pure one has bright and pure deeds and always attains pure conduct.
If you do not kill living beings, and never take what is not given,
Speak truth without false speech, and always have right mindfulness and right knowledge,
Brahmin, training in this way, all beings will be at peace.
Brahmin, why return home? The home spring cannot purify.
Brahmin, you should train: purify and wash with wholesome dharmas.
What need is there for foul water that only removes dirt from the body?"

The brahmin said to the Buddha: "I also have this thought:
One should purify and wash with wholesome dharmas; what need is there for foul water?"

The brahmin, hearing the Buddha's teaching,
With great joy in his heart,
Immediately bowed at the Buddha's feet
And took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

The brahmin said: "World-Honored One, I now know. Well-Gone One, I now understand. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

The Buddha spoke thus. The good-headed water-purification brahmin and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Water-Purification Brahmin, Seventh

---

## (94) Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Kāla, Eighth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Eastern Park, the Hall of Mṛgāra's Mother.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kāla, son of Mṛgāra's Mother, was constantly fond of quarreling and fighting, and he came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One saw the bhikṣu Kāla coming from afar, and on account of the bhikṣu Kāla, he addressed the bhikṣus: "There may be a person who is constantly fond of quarreling and fighting and does not approve of stopping quarrels. If a person is constantly fond of quarreling and fighting and does not approve of stopping quarrels, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who has evil desires and does not approve of stopping evil desires. If a person has evil desires and does not approve of stopping evil desires, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who violates the precepts, transgresses the precepts, has gaps in the precepts, has holes in the precepts, and stains the precepts, and does not approve of keeping the precepts. If a person violates the precepts, transgresses the precepts, has gaps in the precepts, has holes in the precepts, and stains the precepts, and does not approve of keeping the precepts, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who has the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess and jealousy, flattery and deceit, shamelessness and lack of remorse, and does not approve of shame and remorse. If a person has the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess and jealousy, flattery and deceit, shamelessness and lack of remorse, and does not approve of shame and remorse, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who does not serve fellow practitioners of the holy life and does not approve of serving fellow practitioners of the holy life. If a person does not serve fellow practitioners of the holy life and does not approve of serving fellow practitioners of the holy life, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who does not contemplate dharmas and does not approve of contemplating dharmas. If a person does not contemplate dharmas and does not approve of contemplating dharmas, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who does not practice seated meditation and does not approve of seated meditation. If a person does not practice seated meditation and does not approve of seated meditation, this quality is not pleasing, not lovable or delightful, cannot bring about affection, cannot bring about respect, cannot bring about cultivation, cannot bring about self-restraint, cannot lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to attaining nirvāṇa. Though such a person may think, 'May my fellow practitioners of the holy life make offerings to me, respect me, venerate me, and serve me,' nevertheless his fellow practitioners of the holy life will not make offerings to, respect, venerate, or serve that person. Why is this? Because that person has these immeasurable evil qualities, and on account of these immeasurable evil qualities, his fellow practitioners of the holy life will not make offerings to, respect, venerate, or serve that person. It is like a vicious horse tied up in a stable for feeding. Though the horse may think, 'May people tie me in a safe place, give me good food and drink, and look after me well,' nevertheless people will not tie it in a safe place, will not give it good food and drink, and will not look after it well. Why is this? Because that horse has evil qualities, being extremely coarse and not gentle, people will not tie it in a safe place, will not give it good food and drink, and will not look after it well. In the same way, though such a person may think, 'May my fellow practitioners of the holy life make offerings to me, respect me, venerate me, and serve me,' nevertheless his fellow practitioners of the holy life will not make offerings to, respect, venerate, or serve that person. Why is this? Because that person has these immeasurable evil qualities, and on account of these immeasurable evil qualities, his fellow practitioners of the holy life will not make offerings to, respect, venerate, or serve that person.

"There may be a person who does not delight in quarreling and fighting and praises the stopping of quarrels. If a person does not delight in quarreling and fighting and praises the stopping of quarrels, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who is without evil desires and praises the stopping of evil desires. If a person is without evil desires and praises the stopping of evil desires, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who does not violate the precepts, does not transgress the precepts, has no gaps in the precepts, has no holes in the precepts, does not stain the precepts, and praises keeping the precepts. If a person does not violate the precepts, does not transgress the precepts, has no gaps in the precepts, has no holes in the precepts, does not stain the precepts, and praises keeping the precepts, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who is without the fetter of anger, without the bond of silence, without stinginess and jealousy, without flattery and deceit, without shamelessness and lack of remorse, and praises shame and remorse. If a person is without the fetter of anger, without the bond of silence, without stinginess and jealousy, without flattery and deceit, without shamelessness and lack of remorse, and praises shame and remorse, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who serves fellow practitioners of the holy life and praises serving fellow practitioners of the holy life. If a person serves fellow practitioners of the holy life and praises serving fellow practitioners of the holy life, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who contemplates dharmas and praises contemplating dharmas. If a person contemplates dharmas and praises contemplating dharmas, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who practices seated meditation and praises seated meditation. If a person practices seated meditation and praises seated meditation, this quality is pleasing, lovable and delightful, can bring about affection, can bring about respect, can bring about cultivation, can bring about self-restraint, can lead to attaining the life of a śramaṇa, can lead to attaining one-pointedness of mind, and can lead to attaining nirvāṇa. Though such a person may not think, 'May my fellow practitioners of the holy life make offerings to me, respect me, venerate me, and serve me,' nevertheless his fellow practitioners of the holy life will make offerings to, respect, venerate, and serve that person. Why is this? Because that person has these immeasurable wholesome qualities, and on account of these immeasurable wholesome qualities, his fellow practitioners of the holy life will make offerings to, respect, venerate, and serve that person. It is like a fine horse tied up in a stable for feeding. Though the horse may not think, 'May people tie me in a safe place, give me good food and drink, and look after me well,' nevertheless people will tie it in a safe place, give it good food and drink, and look after it well. Why is this? Because that horse has good qualities, being gentle, well-trained, and extremely mild-tempered, people will tie it in a safe place, give it good food and drink, and look after it well. In the same way, though such a person may not think, 'May my fellow practitioners of the holy life make offerings to me, respect me, venerate me, and serve me,' nevertheless his fellow practitioners of the holy life will make offerings to, respect, venerate, and serve that person."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Kāla, Eighth

## (95) Sūtra on Abiding in Dharmas, Ninth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I speak of the decline of wholesome dharmas as neither abiding nor increasing. I speak of the abiding of wholesome dharmas as neither declining nor increasing. I speak of the increase of wholesome dharmas as neither declining nor abiding. How does one decline in wholesome dharmas, neither abiding nor increasing? A bhikṣu may have firm faith, moral discipline, broad learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, the scriptures and their attainments. If that person declines in these dharmas, neither abiding in nor increasing them, this is called declining in wholesome dharmas, neither abiding nor increasing. How does one abide in wholesome dharmas, neither declining nor increasing? A bhikṣu may have firm faith, moral discipline, broad learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, the scriptures and their attainments. If that person abides in these dharmas, neither declining in nor increasing them, this is called abiding in wholesome dharmas, neither declining nor increasing. How does one increase in wholesome dharmas, neither declining nor abiding? A bhikṣu may have firm faith, moral discipline, broad learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, the scriptures and their attainments. If that person increases in these dharmas, neither declining in nor abiding in them, this is called increasing in wholesome dharmas, neither declining nor abiding.

"A bhikṣu who examines himself in this way will certainly gain great benefit: 'Am I one who mostly practices covetousness, or one who mostly practices non-covetousness? Am I one who mostly practices an angry mind, or one who mostly practices a mind without anger? Am I one who mostly entangled by sloth, or one who mostly practices without entanglement by sloth? Am I one who mostly practices restlessness and pride, or one who mostly practices without restlessness and pride? Am I one who mostly practices doubt, or one who mostly practices without doubt? Am I one who mostly practices bodily contention, or one who mostly practices without bodily contention? Am I one who mostly practices a defiled mind, or one who mostly practices a mind without defilement? Am I one who mostly practices faith, or one who mostly practices without faith? Am I one who mostly practices diligence, or one who mostly practices laziness? Am I one who mostly practices mindfulness, or one who mostly practices without mindfulness? Am I one who mostly practices concentration, or one who mostly practices without concentration? Am I one who mostly practices evil wisdom, or one who mostly practices without evil wisdom?'

"If when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I mostly practice covetousness, an angry mind, entanglement by sloth, restlessness and pride, doubt, bodily contention, a defiled mind, lack of faith, laziness, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and mostly practice evil wisdom,' that bhikṣu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome dharmas, should quickly seek skillful means, train with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, enduring without retreat. It is like a person whose head or clothes are on fire, who urgently seeks skillful means to save his head and clothes. In the same way, a bhikṣu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome dharmas, should quickly seek skillful means, train with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, enduring without retreat.

"If when a bhikṣu examines himself, he knows, 'I mostly practice non-covetousness, a mind without anger, freedom from entanglement by sloth, freedom from restlessness and pride, freedom from doubt, freedom from bodily contention, a mind without defilement, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and mostly practice without evil wisdom,' that bhikṣu, desiring to abide in these wholesome dharmas without forgetting or declining, and to cultivate and spread them widely, should quickly seek skillful means, train with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, enduring without retreat. It is like a person whose head or clothes are on fire, who urgently seeks skillful means to save his head and clothes. In the same way, a bhikṣu, desiring to abide in these wholesome dharmas without forgetting or declining, and to cultivate and spread them widely, should quickly seek skillful means, train with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, enduring without retreat."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Abiding in Dharmas, Ninth

---

## (96) Sūtra on Having and Not Having, Tenth of the Defilement Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have not heard the Dharma and do not get to hear it, and who have already heard the Dharma but then forget it, and if there are dharmas previously cultivated, widely practiced, recited, and studied, comprehended by wisdom, which they no longer remember, knowing yet no longer knowing: venerables, this is called the decline of the pure dharmas of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

"Venerables, if there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have not heard the Dharma and now get to hear it, and who have already heard the Dharma and do not forget it, and if there are dharmas previously cultivated, widely practiced, recited, and studied, comprehended by wisdom, which they always remember, knowing and continuing to know: this is called the increase of the pure dharmas of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

"Venerables, a bhikṣu should examine himself in this way: 'Do I have covetousness, or am I without covetousness? Do I have an angry mind, or am I without an angry mind? Do I have entanglement by sloth, or am I without entanglement by sloth? Do I have restlessness and pride, or am I without restlessness and pride? Do I have doubt, or am I without doubt? Do I have bodily contention, or am I without bodily contention? Do I have a defiled mind, or am I without a defiled mind? Do I have faith, or am I without faith? Do I have diligence, or am I without diligence? Do I have mindfulness, or am I without mindfulness? Do I have concentration, or am I without concentration? Do I have evil

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgama)
## Fascicle 24

*(Note: The Taishō edition labels this as part of the collection starting from Fascicle 23, continuing into Fascicle 24. I will translate the complete contents of this fascicle.)*

**(97) Sūtra on the Great Cause**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Kurus, in the Kuru town called Kammāsadhamma.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was alone in a quiet place, meditating in repose. He had this thought: "It is marvelous, it is extraordinary! This dependent origination is so profound and appears so profound. Yet to me it seems as clear as if seen directly before my eyes."

Then the Venerable Ānanda arose from meditation in the evening, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and sat down. He said to the World-Honored One: "I was alone in a quiet place, meditating in repose, and I had this thought: 'It is marvelous, it is extraordinary! This dependent origination is so profound and appears so profound. Yet to me it seems as clear as if seen directly before my eyes.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, do not speak thus! Do not speak thus! This dependent origination is extremely profound and appears extremely profound. Ānanda, it is because of not understanding, not penetrating this Dharma that sentient beings become like entangled threads, like a tangled ball of yarn, like muñja grass and babaja reeds, and cannot escape from the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, death, and rebirth. Ānanda, do not speak thus: that it seems as clear as if seen directly before your eyes."

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for aging and death?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for aging and death?', you should answer, 'Birth is the condition for aging and death.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for birth?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for birth?', you should answer, 'Existence is the condition for birth.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for existence?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for existence?', you should answer, 'Clinging is the condition for existence.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for clinging?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for clinging?', you should answer, 'Craving is the condition for clinging.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for craving?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for craving?', you should answer, 'Feeling is the condition for craving.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for feeling?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for feeling?', you should answer, 'Contact is the condition for feeling.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for contact?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for contact?', you should answer, 'Name-and-form is the condition for contact.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for name-and-form?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for name-and-form?', you should answer, 'Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.'

"Ānanda, if you are asked, 'Is there a condition for consciousness?', you should answer, 'There is.' If asked, 'What is the condition for consciousness?', you should answer, 'Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.'

"Ānanda, thus consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions consciousness; name-and-form conditions contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering.

"Ānanda, I have said that birth is the condition for aging and death. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no birth at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: if there were no birth for devas as devas, no birth for Brahmā beings as Brahmā beings, no birth for Māras as Māras, no birth for śramaṇas as śramaṇas, no birth for brahmins as brahmins, no birth for householders as householders, if there were no birth at all for any beings in any state of existence, then with the complete absence of birth, with the cessation of birth, could aging and death be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, they could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of aging and death, namely, birth. Birth is the condition for aging and death.

"Ānanda, I have said that existence is the condition for birth. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no existence at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: no existence in the desire realm, no existence in the form realm, no existence in the formless realm, if there were no existence at all, then with the complete absence of existence, with the cessation of existence, could birth be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of birth, namely, existence. Existence is the condition for birth.

"Ānanda, I have said that clinging is the condition for existence. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no clinging at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: no clinging to sensual desires, no clinging to views, no clinging to precepts and observances, no clinging to a doctrine of self, if there were no clinging at all, then with the complete absence of clinging, with the cessation of clinging, could existence be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of existence, namely, clinging. Clinging is the condition for existence.

"Ānanda, I have said that craving is the condition for clinging. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no craving at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: no craving for forms, no craving for sounds, no craving for smells, no craving for tastes, no craving for tangibles, no craving for dharmas, if there were no craving at all, then with the complete absence of craving, with the cessation of craving, could clinging be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of clinging, namely, craving. Craving is the condition for clinging.

"Ānanda, I have said that feeling is the condition for craving. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no feeling at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: no feeling born of eye-contact, no feeling born of ear-contact, no feeling born of nose-contact, no feeling born of tongue-contact, no feeling born of body-contact, no feeling born of mind-contact, if there were no feeling at all, then with the complete absence of feeling, with the cessation of feeling, could craving be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of craving, namely, feeling. Feeling is the condition for craving.

"Ānanda, I have said that contact is the condition for feeling. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no contact at all, in any form whatsoever, for anyone anywhere: no eye-contact, no ear-contact, no nose-contact, no tongue-contact, no body-contact, no mind-contact, if there were no contact at all, then with the complete absence of contact, with the cessation of contact, could feeling be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of feeling, namely, contact. Contact is the condition for feeling.

"Ānanda, I have said that name-and-form is the condition for contact. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no name at all, no signs of name, no designation of name, no manifestation of name, then in this name-body, could bodily contact be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Ānanda, if there were no form at all, no signs of form, no designation of form, no manifestation of form, then in this form-body, could counterpart-contact be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Ānanda, if there were no name and no form at all, no signs of name, no designation of name, no manifestation of name, no signs of form, no designation of form, no manifestation of form, then could contact be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of contact, namely, name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for contact.

"Ānanda, I have said that consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if consciousness did not enter the mother's womb, would name-and-form come to be consolidated in the mother's womb?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Ānanda, if consciousness, having entered the mother's womb, were to depart, would name-and-form be produced for this present existence?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or young girl were cut off and extinguished, would name-and-form be able to grow, increase, and develop?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of name-and-form, namely, consciousness. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.

"Ānanda, I have said that name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. You should know that this meaning is as follows. Ānanda, if consciousness did not obtain a basis in name-and-form, then could consciousness have a basis for the arising of future suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition of consciousness, namely, name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.

"Ānanda, for this reason, name-and-form conditions consciousness, and consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering.

"Ānanda, in regard to the self, there are these views that posit a self. Either one regards feeling as the self, saying 'Feeling is my self'; or one regards the self as having no feeling, saying 'My self has no feeling'; or one regards the self as neither having feeling nor not having feeling, saying 'My self feels, and my self possesses the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, as for one who says 'Feeling is my self,' one should say to him: 'There are three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. Of these three feelings, which one do you regard as the self?' Ānanda, when one experiences pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience painful feeling or neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling; one experiences only pleasant feeling. Ānanda, when one experiences painful feeling, at that time one does not experience pleasant feeling or neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling; one experiences only painful feeling. Ānanda, when one experiences neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, at that time one does not experience pleasant feeling or painful feeling; one experiences only neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling.

"Ānanda, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, and arises through dependent origination; it is subject to wearing away, subject to fading, subject to cessation, subject to extinction. Ānanda, painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, and arises through dependent origination; it is subject to wearing away, subject to fading, subject to cessation, subject to extinction. Ānanda, neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, and arises through dependent origination; it is subject to wearing away, subject to fading, subject to cessation, subject to extinction.

"Ānanda, when experiencing pleasant feeling, one thinks, 'This is my self.' When pleasant feeling ceases, one thinks, 'My self has perished.' Ānanda, when experiencing painful feeling, one thinks, 'This is my self.' When painful feeling ceases, one thinks, 'My self has perished.' Ānanda, when experiencing neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one thinks, 'This is my self.' When neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling ceases, one thinks, 'My self has perished.'

"Ānanda, one who says 'Feeling is my self' falls, in this present life, into the perception of impermanence, of both pleasure and pain, of arising and cessation. Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard feeling as the self.

"Ānanda, as for one who says, 'My self has no feeling; my self does not feel,' one should say to him: 'If there were no feeling at all, anywhere, of any kind, with the complete absence of feeling, could one say "This is mine"?'"

Ānanda answered: "No, one could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard the self as having no feeling.

"Ānanda, as for one who says, 'My self feels; my self possesses the dharma of feeling,' one should say to him: 'If feelings were to completely cease without remainder, with the total absence of feeling, when feeling does not exist, could one still say "This is mine"?'"

Ānanda answered: "No, one could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason it is not fitting to regard the self as possessing the dharma of feeling.

"Ānanda, when a bhikṣu does not regard feeling as the self, does not regard the self as having no feeling, and does not regard the self as possessing the dharma of feeling, then he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not anxious. Not being anxious, he personally attains nirvāṇa: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there will be no more existence after this.' He knows it as it really is.

"Ānanda, if anyone should say to a bhikṣu whose mind is thus liberated, 'You hold the view that after the Tathāgata's death he exists,' this would not be fitting. If they say, 'You hold the view that after the Tathāgata's death he does not exist,' this would not be fitting. If they say, 'You hold the view that after the Tathāgata's death he both exists and does not exist,' this would not be fitting. If they say, 'You hold the view that after the Tathāgata's death he neither exists nor does not exist,' this would not be fitting. What is the reason? Ānanda, whatever can be designated by name, whatever can be designated by language, whatever can be designated by concepts, whatever can be designated by conventional usage, whatever is in the domain of knowledge, whatever is in the sphere of knowledge, the cycle that is cycled through: all of this the bhikṣu has abandoned by thorough knowledge. What the bhikṣu has abandoned by thorough knowledge has been cut off at the root, like a palm tree stump, such that it will never arise again in the future. Ānanda, a bhikṣu who is liberated through the destruction of craving is supreme, most excellent, the highest, the most outstanding.

"Ānanda, there are seven stations of consciousness and two bases. What are the seven?
