Thus a bhikṣu contemplates inner feelings as feelings, contemplates outer feelings as feelings, establishes mindfulness on feelings, with knowing and seeing, with clarity and comprehension. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating feelings as feelings. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī thus even to a small degree contemplates feelings as feelings, this is called contemplating feelings as feelings, the foundation of mindfulness.

"How does one contemplate the mind as mind, the foundation of mindfulness? A bhikṣu, when the mind has desire, knows the mind has desire as it truly is; when the mind is without desire, knows the mind is without desire as it truly is. When it has aversion, when it is without aversion; when it has delusion, when it is without delusion; when it is defiled, when it is undefiled. When it is collected, when it is scattered; when it is lowly, when it is lofty; when it is limited, when it is expansive. When it is cultivated, when it is uncultivated; when it is concentrated, when it is unconcentrated. When the mind is not liberated, he knows the mind is not liberated as it truly is; when the mind is liberated, he knows the mind is liberated as it truly is. Thus a bhikṣu contemplates the inner mind as mind, contemplates the outer mind as mind, establishes mindfulness on the mind, with knowing and seeing, with clarity and comprehension. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the mind as mind. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī thus even to a small degree contemplates the mind as mind, this is called contemplating the mind as mind, the foundation of mindfulness.

"How does one contemplate dharmas as dharmas, the foundation of mindfulness? The eye, in dependence on forms, gives rise to an internal fetter. A bhikṣu, when there actually is an internal fetter, knows there is an internal fetter as it truly is; when there actually is no internal fetter, knows there is no internal fetter as it truly is. When an internal fetter that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When an internal fetter that has already arisen is extinguished and does not arise again, he knows it as it truly is. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. The mind, in dependence on dharmas, gives rise to an internal fetter. A bhikṣu, when there actually is an internal fetter, knows there is an internal fetter as it truly is; when there actually is no internal fetter, knows there is no internal fetter as it truly is. When an internal fetter that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When an internal fetter that has already arisen is extinguished and does not arise again, he knows it as it truly is. Thus a bhikṣu contemplates inner dharmas as dharmas, contemplates outer dharmas as dharmas, establishes mindfulness on dharmas, with knowing and seeing, with clarity and comprehension. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating dharmas as dharmas, namely the internal six sense bases.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplating dharmas as dharmas: a bhikṣu, when there actually is desire internally, knows there is desire as it truly is; when there actually is no desire internally, knows there is no desire as it truly is. When desire that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When desire that has already arisen is extinguished and does not arise again, he knows it as it truly is. Likewise with aversion, sloth and torpor, and restlessness and remorse. When there actually is doubt internally, he knows there is doubt as it truly is; when there actually is no doubt internally, he knows there is no doubt as it truly is. When doubt that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When doubt that has already arisen is extinguished and does not arise again, he knows it as it truly is. Thus a bhikṣu contemplates inner dharmas as dharmas, contemplates outer dharmas as dharmas, establishes mindfulness on dharmas, with knowing and seeing, with clarity and comprehension. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating dharmas as dharmas, namely the five hindrances.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplating dharmas as dharmas: a bhikṣu, when there actually is the mindfulness awakening factor internally, he knows there is the mindfulness awakening factor as it truly is; when there actually is no mindfulness awakening factor internally, he knows there is no mindfulness awakening factor as it truly is. When the mindfulness awakening factor that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When the mindfulness awakening factor that has already arisen remains, is not forgotten, does not decline, but is further cultivated, increased, and broadened, he knows it as it truly is. Likewise with the investigation of dharmas, energy, joy, and tranquility awakening factors, and concentration. A bhikṣu, when there actually is the equanimity awakening factor internally, he knows there is the equanimity awakening factor as it truly is; when there actually is no equanimity awakening factor internally, he knows there is no equanimity awakening factor as it truly is. When the equanimity awakening factor that has not yet arisen arises, he knows it as it truly is. When the equanimity awakening factor that has already arisen remains, is not forgotten, does not decline, but is further cultivated, increased, and broadened, he knows it as it truly is. Thus a bhikṣu contemplates inner dharmas as dharmas, contemplates outer dharmas as dharmas, establishes mindfulness on dharmas, with knowing and seeing, with clarity and comprehension. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating dharmas as dharmas, namely the seven factors of awakening. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī thus even to a small degree contemplates dharmas as dharmas, this is called contemplating dharmas as dharmas, the foundation of mindfulness.

"If any bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī for seven years establishes the mind correctly abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, that person will certainly obtain one of two fruits: either in this present life attain ultimate knowledge, or with remainder attain the state of non-returner. Setting aside seven years: six, five, four, three, two, or one year. If any bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī for seven months establishes the mind correctly abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, that person will certainly obtain one of two fruits: either in this present life attain ultimate knowledge, or with remainder attain the state of non-returner. Setting aside seven months: six, five, four, three, two, or one month. If any bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī for seven days and seven nights establishes the mind correctly abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, that person will certainly obtain one of two fruits: either in this present life attain ultimate knowledge, or with remainder attain the state of non-returner. Setting aside seven days and seven nights: six, five, four, three, or two. Setting aside one day and one night, if any bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī even for a small, brief moment establishes the mind correctly abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, if that person practices thus in the morning, by evening that person will certainly attain advancement; if that person practices thus in the evening, by morning that person will certainly attain advancement."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on the Foundations of Mindfulness, Second.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 25

---

## (99) Sūtra on the Mass of Suffering, Third in the Cause Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, after the midday meal, the bhikṣus had some minor matters and gathered together sitting in the lecture hall. Then numerous adherents of other doctrines, wandering about in the afternoon, went to where the bhikṣus were. They exchanged greetings with one another, sat down to one side, and said to the bhikṣus: "Sirs! The ascetic Gautama teaches the knowledge and abandoning of desires; he teaches the knowledge and abandoning of form; he teaches the knowledge and abandoning of feelings. Sirs! We also teach the knowledge and abandoning of desires; we also teach the knowledge and abandoning of form; we also teach the knowledge and abandoning of feelings. Between the ascetic Gautama and us, regarding these two kinds of knowledge and two kinds of abandoning, what superiority is there? What difference is there?"

Then the bhikṣus, having heard what those numerous adherents of other doctrines said, neither affirmed nor denied it, but silently rose and departed, all thinking: "Regarding what has been said, we should learn from the World-Honored One." They then went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads in homage, sat down to one side, and fully reported to the Buddha the discussion they had shared with the numerous adherents of other doctrines.

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus: "You should immediately question those numerous adherents of other doctrines as follows: 'Sirs! What is the gratification of desires? What is the danger of desires? What is the escape from desires? What is the gratification of form? What is the danger of form? What is the escape from form? What is the gratification of feelings? What is the danger of feelings? What is the escape from feelings?' Bhikṣus! If you question them thus, upon hearing it they will merely dispute among themselves and speak of extraneous matters. Their anger and contention will only increase, and they will surely rise from their seats and depart silently. Why is this? I do not see anyone in this world, among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, or any other beings, who can understand this meaning and expound it, except for the Tathāgata, the disciples of the Tathāgata, or those who have heard it from them."

The Buddha said: "What is the gratification of desires? It is the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. This is the utmost gratification of desires, and there is nothing beyond this; yet the dangers are extremely numerous.

"What is the danger of desires? A clansman sustains his livelihood according to his skills and craft: perhaps through farming, or through trade, or through study of writing, or through mastery of arithmetic, or through knowledge of craftsmanship and calculation, or through skillful seal-carving, or through composing literature, or through calligraphy, or through expertise in scriptures, or through serving as a brave general, or through attending upon a king. In the cold he endures cold; in the heat he endures heat. He suffers hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the stinging of mosquitoes and gadflies. Performing such labors, he seeks to acquire wealth. If that clansman, having made such efforts, carried out such actions, and made such endeavors, does not obtain wealth, he then gives rise to sorrow, grief, distress, and vexation. His mind becomes deluded, and he says: 'In vain I have toiled, in vain I have suffered; my efforts have borne no fruit.' If that clansman, having made such efforts, carried out such actions, and made such endeavors, does obtain wealth, he then cherishes it, guards it, and stores it secretly. Why? 'May my wealth not be seized by kings, stolen by robbers, burned by fire, spoiled by decay, or simply lost; may my investments not fail, or may my undertakings not come to naught.' Yet even though he guards and stores it secretly in this way, if it is seized by kings, stolen by robbers, burned by fire, spoiled by decay, or lost, he then gives rise to sorrow, grief, distress, and vexation. His mind becomes deluded, and he says: 'That which through the long night I cherished and held dear has now been lost.' This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, mothers quarrel with children, children quarrel with mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, and relatives all quarrel with one another. Having fought and quarreled in this way, mothers speak ill of children, children speak ill of mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, and relatives all speak ill of one another, how much more so with strangers! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, kings quarrel with kings, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, commoners with commoners, and nations with nations. Because of fighting and quarreling, and mutual hatred, they inflict harm on each other with various weapons, striking with fists, grappling, throwing stones, beating with sticks, or slashing with swords. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and enter into battle formations. They fight with elephants, with horses, with chariots, with infantry, or with men and women in combat. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and go to seize other kingdoms, attacking cities and destroying fortresses. They engage in fierce combat, beating drums and blowing horns, shouting with loud voices, striking with hammers, thrusting with halberds, hurling sharp wheels, shooting arrows, raining down stones, firing great crossbows, or spraying them with molten copper pellets. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and enter villages, towns, kingdoms, and cities. They break through walls, plunder storehouses, rob wealth and possessions, block the king's roads, invade others' quarters, destroy villages, ravage towns, annihilate kingdoms, and demolish cities. Among these, some are caught by the king's men and subjected to various punishments: hands cut off, feet cut off, or both hands and feet cut off; ears cut off, noses cut off, or both ears and noses cut off; or they are sliced piece by piece. Their beards are torn out, their hair is torn out, or both beard and hair are torn out. Or they are placed in cages, wrapped in cloth and set on fire. Or they are smothered with sand, bound with grass, and set ablaze. Or they are placed inside iron donkeys, or put into the mouths of iron pigs, or placed in the mouths of iron tigers and burned. Or they are put into copper cauldrons, or placed in iron cauldrons and boiled. Or they are chopped into pieces, or pierced with sharp tridents, or hooked with iron hooks. Or they are laid on iron beds and doused with boiling oil, or seated in iron mortars and pounded with iron pestles. Or they are bitten by dragons and snakes, or whipped with lashes, or struck with staffs, or beaten with clubs. Or they are impaled alive on high stakes, or beheaded. Those among them either die or are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they engage in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind. Then later they fall ill, bedridden, or sit or lie on the ground, with suffering pressing upon their bodies, undergoing extremely heavy suffering that is not to be desired or enjoyed. If they have committed evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, at the time of their death these deeds stand before them as obstructions, just as when the sun is about to set, the shadows of great mountain ridges obstruct and cover the ground. In the same way, if they have committed evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, these stand before them as obstructions. They think: 'My past evil deeds now obstruct me. I did not perform meritorious deeds but performed many evil deeds. If there is a place where those who do evil and act viciously, who commit only sins, who do no merit, who practice no good, who have nothing to fear, nothing to rely on, nothing to take refuge in, are reborn, I shall surely be born there.' From this arises remorse. One who has remorse does not die well and ends life without merit. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they engage in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind. Because of this evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, on account of this, conditioned by this, when the body breaks up and life ends, they surely fall into evil destinies and are born in hell. This is called the mass of suffering in future lives, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root. This is called the danger of desires.

"What is the escape from desires? If one cuts off desires, relinquishes desires, extinguishes desires until desires are exhausted, and transcends desires, that is the escape from desires. If any ascetics or brahmins do not know as it truly is the gratification of desires, the danger of desires, and the escape from desires, they will never be able to cut off their own desires, how much less be able to cut off the desires of others! If any ascetics or brahmins know as it truly is the gratification of desires, the danger of desires, and the escape from desires, they can themselves eliminate desires, and they can also cut off the desires of others.

"What is the gratification of form? Consider a maiden of the warrior, brahmin, householder, or artisan class, aged fourteen or fifteen. At that time, her beauty is at its most sublime. If, because of that beauty, conditioned by that beauty, pleasure and joy arise, that is the utmost gratification of form, and there is nothing beyond this; yet the dangers are extremely numerous.

"What is the danger of form? If one sees that same beautiful maiden at a later time, extremely aged and decrepit, her hair white, teeth fallen out, back bent, legs crooked, walking with a cane, her youthful vigor daily declining, her lifespan nearly exhausted, her body trembling, her faculties deteriorated and decayed. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees that same beautiful maiden fallen ill, bedridden, or sitting or lying on the ground, with suffering pressing upon her body, undergoing extremely heavy suffering. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?" They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees that same beautiful maiden dead, after one, two, or up to six or seven days, pecked at by crows and owls, eaten by jackals and wolves, burned by fire, buried in the ground, completely putrid and decomposed. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees the remains of that same beautiful maiden on a charnel ground, the skeleton blue-colored and putrid, half eaten away, the bones scattered on the ground. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees the remains of that same beautiful maiden on a charnel ground, stripped of skin, flesh, and blood, with only sinews holding the bones together. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees the remains of that same beautiful maiden on a charnel ground, the joints disarticulated and scattered in all directions: foot bones, shin bones, thigh bones, hip bones, spine bones, shoulder bones, neck bones, and skull each in a separate place. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"Furthermore, if one sees the remains of that same beautiful maiden on a charnel ground, the bones white as a conch shell, bluish like the color of a pigeon, reddish as if smeared with blood, or decayed and crumbled into dust. What do you think? Has her former beauty perished, and has danger arisen?"

They answered: "So it is."

"This is called the danger of form."

"What is the escape from form? If one cuts off form, relinquishes form, extinguishes form until form is exhausted, and transcends form, that is the escape from form. If any ascetics or brahmins do not know as it truly is the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form, they will never be able to cut off their own attachment to form, how much less be able to cut off others' attachment to form! If any ascetics or brahmins know as it truly is the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form, they can themselves eliminate it, and they can also cut off others' attachment to form.

"What is the gratification of feelings? A bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome states, up to attaining the fourth dhyāna, dwells having accomplished it. At that time, he has no thought of harming himself, nor any thought of harming others. If there is no thought of harm, this is called the pleasant gratification of feelings. Why? Having no thought of harm, one accomplishes this pleasure. This is called the gratification of feelings.

"What is the danger of feelings? Feelings are subject to the law of impermanence, the law of suffering, the law of cessation. This is called the danger of feelings.

"What is the escape from feelings? If one cuts off feelings, relinquishes feelings, extinguishes feelings until feelings are exhausted, and transcends feelings, that is the escape from feelings. If any ascetics or brahmins do not know as it truly is the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings, they will never be able to cut off their own feelings, how much less be able to cut off the feelings of others! If any ascetics or brahmins know as it truly is the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings, they can themselves eliminate them, and they can also cut off the feelings of others."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Mass of Suffering, Third

---

## (100) Sūtra on the Mass of Suffering, Fourth in the Cause Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyans, staying in Kapilavatthu at the Nigrodha Park.

At that time, the Śākyan Mahānāma, wandering about in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I understand the Dharma of the World-Honored One such that it should cause the three defilements in my mind to be extinguished: the defilement of desire in the mind, the defilement of anger in the mind, and the defilement of delusion in the mind. World-Honored One! Although I understand this Dharma in this way, yet in my mind there again arise states of desire, states of anger, and states of delusion. World-Honored One! I have this thought: 'What quality within me has not been extinguished, such that states of desire, states of anger, and states of delusion again arise in my mind?'"

The World-Honored One said: "Mahānāma! There is one quality in you that has not been extinguished, namely, that you still dwell in the household life, and have not yet gone forth in faith, leaving home and homelessness, to train in the Way. Mahānāma! If you were to extinguish this one quality, you would certainly not dwell in the household life, but would go forth in faith, leaving home and homelessness, to train in the Way. Because this one quality has not been extinguished, you dwell in the household life and have not gone forth in faith, leaving home and homelessness, to train in the Way."

Thereupon the Śākyan Mahānāma rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to the World-Honored One: "I humbly pray that the World-Honored One will teach me the Dharma, so that my mind may be purified, doubts removed, and the Way attained."

The World-Honored One said: "Mahānāma! There are five strands of sensual pleasure that are lovable, memorable, joyful, associated with desire, and cause people delight. What are the five? They are forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, scents known by the nose, flavors known by the tongue, and tactile sensations known by the body. Through these, kings and their retinues obtain comfort, joy, and happiness. Mahānāma! This is the utmost gratification of desires, and there is nothing beyond this; yet the dangers are extremely numerous.

"Mahānāma! What is the danger of desires? Mahānāma! A clansman sustains his livelihood according to his skills and craft: perhaps through farming, or through trade, or through study of writing, or through mastery of arithmetic, or through knowledge of craftsmanship and calculation, or through skillful seal-carving, or through composing literature, or through calligraphy, or through expertise in scriptures, or through serving as a brave general, or through attending upon a king. In the cold he endures cold; in the heat he endures heat. He suffers hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the stinging of mosquitoes and gadflies. Performing such labors, he seeks to acquire wealth. Mahānāma! If this clansman, having made such efforts, carried out such actions, and made such endeavors, does not obtain wealth, he then gives rise to sorrow, grief, distress, and vexation. His mind becomes deluded, and he says: 'In vain I have toiled, in vain I have suffered; my efforts have borne no fruit.' Mahānāma! If that clansman, having made such efforts, carried out such actions, and made such endeavors, does obtain wealth, he then cherishes it, guards it, and stores it secretly. Why? 'May my wealth not be seized by kings, stolen by robbers, burned by fire, spoiled by decay, or simply lost; may my investments not fail, or may my undertakings not come to naught.' Yet even though he guards and stores it secretly in this way, if it is seized by kings, stolen by robbers, burned by fire, spoiled by decay, or lost, he then gives rise to sorrow, grief, distress, and vexation. His mind becomes deluded, and he says: 'That which through the long night I cherished and held dear has now been lost.' Mahānāma! This is the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, mothers quarrel with children, children quarrel with mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, and relatives all quarrel with one another. Having fought and quarreled in this way, mothers speak ill of children, children speak ill of mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, and relatives all speak ill of one another, how much more so with strangers! Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, kings quarrel with kings, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, commoners with commoners, and nations with nations. Because of fighting and quarreling, and mutual hatred, they inflict harm on each other with various weapons, striking with fists, grappling, throwing stones, beating with sticks, or slashing with swords. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and enter into battle formations. They fight with elephants, with horses, with chariots, with infantry, or with men and women in combat. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and go to seize other kingdoms, attacking cities and destroying fortresses. They engage in fierce combat, beating drums and blowing horns, shouting with loud voices, striking with hammers, thrusting with halberds, hurling sharp wheels, shooting arrows, raining down stones, firing great crossbows, or spraying them with molten copper pellets. In the midst of battle, some die, some are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields, and enter villages, towns, kingdoms, and cities. They break through walls, plunder storehouses, rob wealth and possessions, block the king's roads, invade others' quarters, destroy villages, ravage towns, annihilate kingdoms, and demolish cities. Among these, some are caught by the king's men and subjected to various punishments: hands cut off, feet cut off, or both hands and feet cut off; ears cut off, noses cut off, or both ears and noses cut off; or they are sliced piece by piece. Their beards are torn out, their hair is torn out, or both beard and hair are torn out. Or they are placed in cages, wrapped in cloth and set on fire. Or they are smothered with sand, bound with grass, and set ablaze. Or they are placed inside iron donkeys, or put into the mouths of iron pigs, or placed in the mouths of iron tigers and burned. Or they are put into copper cauldrons, or placed in iron cauldrons and boiled. Or they are chopped into pieces, or pierced with sharp tridents, or hooked with iron hooks. Or they are laid on iron beds and doused with boiling oil, or seated in iron mortars and pounded with iron pestles. Or they are bitten by dragons and snakes, or whipped with lashes, or struck with staffs, or beaten with clubs. Or they are impaled alive on high stakes, or beheaded. Those among them either die or are terrified, and they undergo extremely heavy suffering. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they engage in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind. Then later they fall ill, bedridden, or sit or lie on the ground, with suffering pressing upon their bodies, undergoing extremely heavy suffering that is not to be desired or enjoyed. If they have committed evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, at the time of their death these deeds stand before them as obstructions, just as when the sun is about to set, the shadows of great mountain ridges obstruct and cover the ground. In the same way, if they have committed evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, these stand before them as obstructions. They think: 'My past evil deeds now obstruct me. I did not perform meritorious deeds but performed many evil deeds. If there is a place where those who do evil and act viciously, who commit only sins, who do no merit, who practice no good, who have nothing to fear, nothing to rely on, nothing to take refuge in, are reborn, I shall surely be born there.' From this arises remorse. One who has remorse does not die well and ends life without merit. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because beings are caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as their root, they engage in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind. Because of this evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, on account of this, conditioned by this, when the body breaks up and life ends, they surely fall into evil destinies and are born in hell. Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in future lives, caused by desires, conditioned by desires, with desires as its root.

"Mahānāma! Therefore one should know that desires are entirely devoid of pleasure and are accompanied by immeasurable suffering and danger. If a learned noble disciple does not see this as it truly is, he is covered over by desires, entangled by evil and unwholesome states, and cannot obtain the pleasure of renunciation or the supreme peace. Mahānāma! In this way, that learned noble disciple regresses because of desires. Mahānāma! I know that desires are devoid of pleasure and are accompanied by immeasurable suffering and danger. Having known this as it truly is, Mahānāma, I am not covered over by desires, nor entangled by evil, and I thus obtain the pleasure of renunciation and the supreme peace. Mahānāma! Therefore I do not regress because of desires.

"Mahānāma! At one time I was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying on Mount Vaiḍūrya at the Saptaparṇa Cave of the Sages. Mahānāma! In the late afternoon, I rose from quiet meditation and went to the Broad Mountain. There I saw numerous Nigaṇṭhas practicing the non-sitting practice, constantly standing and never sitting, undergoing extremely heavy suffering. I went and asked them: 'Nigaṇṭhas! Why do you practice this non-sitting practice, constantly standing and never sitting, undergoing such suffering?' They said in this way: 'Gautama! We have a venerable teacher, the Nigaṇṭha called Nātaputta. He instructs us, saying: "Nigaṇṭhas! If in your past lives there was unwholesome karma, through this austerity it shall surely be exhausted. If in this present body you guard wholesome conduct of body, guard wholesome conduct of speech and mind, then because of this, on account of this, you will no longer create evil and unwholesome karma."'

"Mahānāma! I then asked them: 'Nigaṇṭhas! Do you believe your venerable teacher without any doubt?' They answered me: 'So it is, Gautama! We believe our venerable teacher without any doubt or hesitation.' Mahānāma! I then asked: 'Nigaṇṭhas! If that is so, then your venerable teacher, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, in past lives committed grave evil and unwholesome karma. He was formerly a Nigaṇṭha who died and was reborn in the human realm, where he went forth as a Nigaṇṭha, practicing the non-sitting practice, constantly standing and never sitting, undergoing such suffering, just like you and your fellow disciples.' They then said to me: 'Gautama! Happiness does not come from happiness; happiness must come from suffering. For example, the happiness of King Bimbisāra, the ascetic Gautama does not equal it.'

"I then said: 'You are foolish and deluded; what you say is meaningless. Why is this? Without skill and without understanding, and not knowing the proper occasion, you make such a statement: "The happiness of King Bimbisāra, the ascetic Gautama does not equal it." Nigaṇṭhas! You should first have asked this: "Whose happiness is superior, King Bimbisāra's or the ascetic Gautama's?" Nigaṇṭhas! If I were to say that my happiness is superior and that King Bimbisāra does not equal it, then, Nigaṇṭhas, you could make the statement: "The happiness of King Bimbisāra, the ascetic Gautama does not equal it."' Those Nigaṇṭhas then said: 'Gautama! We now ask the ascetic Gautama: whose happiness is superior, King Bimbisāra's or the ascetic Gautama's?' I then said: 'Nigaṇṭhas! I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Nigaṇṭhas, what do you think? Can King Bimbisāra, at will, remain silently without speaking, and because of this experience joyful happiness for seven days and seven nights?' The Nigaṇṭhas answered: 'No, Gautama!' 'For six, five, four, three, or two days, or for one day and one night, can he experience joyful happiness?' The Nigaṇṭhas answered: 'No, Gautama!' I further asked: 'Nigaṇṭhas! Can I, at will, remain silently without speaking, and because of this experience joyful happiness for one day and one night?' The Nigaṇṭhas answered: 'Yes, Gautama!' 'For two, three, four, five, six, or seven days and seven nights, can I experience joyful happiness?' The Nigaṇṭhas answered: 'Yes, Gautama!' I further asked: 'Nigaṇṭhas, what do you think? Whose happiness is superior, King Bimbisāra's or mine?' The Nigaṇṭhas answered: 'Gautama! As we understand the ascetic Gautama's words, Gautama's happiness is superior, and King Bimbisāra does not equal it.'

"Mahānāma! Because of this, one should know that desires are devoid of pleasure and are accompanied by immeasurable suffering and danger. If a learned noble disciple does not see this as it truly is, he is covered over by desires, entangled by evil and unwholesome states, and cannot obtain the pleasure of renunciation or the supreme peace. Mahānāma! In this way, that learned noble disciple regresses because of desires. Mahānāma! I know that desires are devoid of pleasure and are accompanied by immeasurable suffering and danger. Having known this as it truly is, I am not covered over by desires, nor entangled by evil and unwholesome states, and I thus obtain the pleasure of renunciation and the supreme peace. Mahānāma! Therefore I do not regress because of desires."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Śākyan Mahānāma and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Mass of Suffering, Fourth

---

## (101) Sūtra on the Higher Mind, Fifth in the Cause Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate five signs. Having repeatedly contemplated the five signs, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"What are the five? When a bhikṣu contemplates a sign associated with what is wholesome, if unwholesome thoughts arise, he should, because of that sign, further contemplate a different sign associated with what is wholesome, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise. Having, because of that sign, further contemplated a different sign associated with what is wholesome, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. It is like a carpenter or carpenter's apprentice who holds a chalk line and snaps it upon wood, then with a sharp axe chops and trims it straight. In the same way, when a bhikṣu, because of that sign, further contemplates a different sign associated with what is wholesome, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise, having, because of that sign, further contemplated a different sign associated with what is wholesome, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this first sign. Having contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates a sign associated with what is wholesome and unwholesome thoughts arise, he should examine the danger of those thoughts: 'These thoughts are evil and have calamitous consequences. These thoughts are unwholesome. These thoughts are evil. These thoughts are despised by the wise. If these thoughts were to be fulfilled, one would not attain penetration, would not attain awakening and the Way, would not attain nirvāṇa, for they cause the arising of evil and unwholesome thoughts.' Having thus examined the evil, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. It is like a young person, beautiful and attractive, who has bathed and washed, put on clean and bright clothing, anointed the body with fragrance, trimmed the beard and hair to extreme neatness, and then has a dead snake, a dead dog, or a half-eaten dead human corpse, blue-colored, bloated, foul-smelling, putrid, with impure fluids oozing out, hung around their neck. They would feel disgusted, displeased, and unhappy. In the same way, the bhikṣu examines the danger of those thoughts: 'These thoughts are evil and have calamitous consequences. These thoughts are unwholesome. These thoughts are evil. These thoughts are despised by the wise. If these thoughts were to be fulfilled, one would not attain penetration, would not attain awakening and the Way, would not attain nirvāṇa, for they cause the arising of evil and unwholesome thoughts.' Having thus examined the evil, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this second sign. Having contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu, while contemplating a sign associated with what is wholesome, has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while examining the danger of those thoughts, still has unwholesome thoughts arise, that bhikṣu should not attend to those thoughts, because they cause the arising of evil and unwholesome thoughts. By not attending to those thoughts, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. It is like a person with eyes, in a place with visible forms in the light, who does not wish to see them, and so either closes their eyes or turns their body away. What do you think? With the visible forms in the light, can that person perceive the characteristics of those forms?"

They answered: "No."

"In the same way, the bhikṣu should not attend to those thoughts, because they cause the arising of evil and unwholesome thoughts. By not attending to those thoughts, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this third sign. Having contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu, while contemplating a sign associated with what is wholesome, has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while examining the danger of those thoughts also has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while not attending to those thoughts still has unwholesome thoughts arise, that bhikṣu, regarding those thoughts, should use deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise. By using deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. It is like a person walking on a road, moving along quickly. That person thinks: 'Why am I going so fast? I should rather walk slowly.' They then walk slowly. They further think: 'Why am I walking slowly? I should rather stop.' They then stop. They further think: 'Why am I standing? I should rather sit down.' They then sit down. They further think: 'Why am I sitting? I should rather lie down.' They then lie down. In this way, that person gradually calms the coarse activities of the body. One should know that a bhikṣu is also like this. Regarding those thoughts, he should use deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise. By using deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this fourth sign. Having contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu, while contemplating a sign associated with what is wholesome, has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while examining the danger of those thoughts also has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while not attending to those thoughts also has unwholesome thoughts arise, and while using deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts still has unwholesome thoughts arise, that bhikṣu should examine as follows: because of these thoughts, unwholesome thoughts arise. That bhikṣu should then clench his teeth together, press his tongue against the palate, and with the mind subdue the mind, seize and overpower it, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise. Having with the mind subdued the mind, seized and overpowered it, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. It is like two strong men seizing one weak person and subduing and overpowering him. In the same way, the bhikṣu clenches his teeth together, presses his tongue against the palate, and with the mind subdues the mind, seizes and overpowers it, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise. Having with the mind subdued the mind, seized and overpowered it, the unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this fifth sign. Having contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration.

"If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate these five signs. Having repeatedly contemplated the five signs, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are then eliminated. When evil thoughts are eliminated, the mind constantly abides, internally calmed, unified, and attains concentration. If, when a bhikṣu contemplates a sign associated with what is wholesome, no evil thoughts arise; and when examining the danger of those thoughts, no evil thoughts arise; and when not attending to those thoughts, no evil thoughts arise; and when using deliberate mental effort to gradually diminish those thoughts, no evil thoughts arise; and when with the mind subduing the mind, seizing and overpowering it, no evil thoughts arise; then he gains mastery: when he wishes to think, he thinks; when he does not wish to think, he does not think. If a bhikṣu can think when he wishes to think and not think when he does not wish to think, this is called a bhikṣu who has mastery over all thoughts and is autonomous over the tracks of thought."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Higher Mind, Fifth

---

## (102) Sūtra on Thoughts, Sixth in the Cause Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus: "Before I had awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, I had this thought: 'I should divide my thoughts into two categories. Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm I shall place in one category. Thoughts free from desire, thoughts free from ill will, and thoughts free from harm I shall place in the other category.' Afterwards, I then divided my thoughts into two categories: thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm in one category; thoughts free from desire, thoughts free from ill will, and thoughts free from harm in the other category. While I was thus practicing, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, my mind free from negligence, cultivating practice with diligence, thoughts of desire arose. I immediately recognized: 'Thoughts of desire have arisen. They harm myself, harm others, and harm both. They destroy wisdom, cause much trouble, and do not lead to nirvāṇa.' Recognizing that they harm myself, harm others, and harm both, destroy wisdom, cause much trouble, and do not lead to nirvāṇa, they quickly ceased. Again, thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm arose. I immediately recognized: 'Thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm have arisen. They harm myself, harm others, and harm both. They destroy wisdom, cause much trouble, and do not lead to nirvāṇa.' Recognizing that they harm myself, harm others, and harm both, destroy wisdom, cause much trouble, and do not lead to nirvāṇa, they quickly ceased.

"When thoughts of desire arose in me, I did not accept them but cut them off, eliminated them, and expelled them. When thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm arose, I did not accept them but cut them off, eliminated them, and expelled them. Why? Because I saw that on account of these, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states would surely arise. It is like the later month of spring when, because the crops have been planted, the grazing land is not extensive. A cowherd who lets his cattle roam in the open fields finds that the cattle stray into others' fields. The cowherd immediately takes up a stick and goes to drive them back. Why? Because the cowherd knows that on account of this, there will surely be scolding, beating, binding, and punishment. Therefore the cowherd takes up a stick and drives them back. I was the same: when thoughts of desire arose, I did not accept them but cut them off, eliminated them, and expelled them. When thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm arose, I did not accept them but cut them off, eliminated them, and expelled them. Why? Because I saw that on account of these, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states would surely arise.

"Whatever a bhikṣu thinks about and ponders, the mind tends to incline in that direction. If a bhikṣu frequently thinks thoughts of desire, he abandons thoughts free from desire. Because he frequently thinks thoughts of desire, the mind inclines in that direction. If a bhikṣu frequently thinks thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm, he abandons thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm. Because he frequently thinks thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm, the mind inclines in that direction. In this way, a bhikṣu who does not abandon thoughts of desire, does not abandon thoughts of ill will, does not abandon thoughts of harm, cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and weeping, nor can he escape all suffering. While I was thus practicing, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, my mind free from negligence, cultivating practice with diligence, thoughts free from desire arose. I immediately recognized: 'Thoughts free from desire have arisen. They do not harm myself, do not harm others, and do not harm both. They cultivate wisdom, do not cause trouble, and lead to nirvāṇa.' Recognizing that they do not harm myself, do not harm others, and do not harm both, cultivate wisdom, do not cause trouble, and lead to nirvāṇa, I quickly cultivated, practiced, and spread them widely. Again, thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm arose. I immediately recognized: 'Thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm have arisen. They do not harm myself, do not harm others, and do not harm both. They cultivate wisdom, do not cause trouble, and lead to nirvāṇa.' Recognizing that they do not harm myself, do not harm others, and do not harm both, cultivate wisdom, do not cause trouble, and lead to nirvāṇa, I quickly cultivated, practiced, and spread them widely."

"When thoughts free from desire arose in me, and I pondered on them extensively; when thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm arose, and I pondered on them extensively; I then had this thought: 'If I ponder excessively, my body will become weary and forgetful concerning concentration, and this will impair the mind. I should rather settle the inner mind, constantly abide internally calmed, unified, and attain concentration, so as not to impair the mind.' Afterwards, I then settled the inner mind, constantly abiding internally calmed, unified, and attaining concentration, without impairing the mind. When thoughts free from desire arose in me, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. When thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm arose, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. Why? Because I did not see that on account of these, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states would arise. It is like the later month of autumn when, after all the grain has been harvested, a cowherd lets his cattle roam in the open fields and at that time thinks: 'My cattle are within the herd.' Why? Because the cowherd does not see that on account of this there would be scolding, beating, binding, or punishment. Therefore he thinks: 'My cattle are within the herd.' I was the same: when thoughts free from desire arose in me, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. When thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm arose, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. Why? Because I did not see that on account of these, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states would arise.

"Whatever a bhikṣu thinks about and ponders, the mind tends to incline in that direction. If a bhikṣu frequently thinks thoughts free from desire, he abandons thoughts of desire. Because he frequently thinks thoughts free from desire, the mind inclines in that direction. If a bhikṣu frequently thinks thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm, he abandons thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm. Because he frequently thinks thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm, the mind inclines in that direction. When his initial and sustained thought has ceased, internally calmed and with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains the second dhyāna and dwells having accomplished it. Separated from joy and desire, dwelling with equanimity, without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, and bodily experiencing happiness, as the noble ones describe: 'One who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells in happiness,' he attains the third dhyāna and dwells having accomplished it. When happiness ceases and suffering ceases, and when previous joy and sorrow have already ceased, without suffering and without pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he attains the fourth dhyāna and dwells having accomplished it.

"With the mind thus concentrated, purified, without defilement, without affliction, pliant, well-established, having attained imperturbability, he directs the mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows and the realization through direct knowledge. He then knows 'This is suffering' as it truly is. He knows 'This is the origin of suffering,' knows 'This is the cessation of suffering,' knows 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' as it truly is. He also knows 'These are the outflows' as it truly is. He knows 'This is the origin of the outflows,' knows 'This is the cessation of the outflows,' knows 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the outflows' as it truly is. Having known thus and seen thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire, from the outflow of existence, from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming into any state of being.' He knows this as it truly is. This bhikṣu, having abandoned thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm, is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and weeping, and is separated from all suffering. It is like an uninhabited place with a great pool of water, and a herd of deer dwelling and roaming there. A person comes along who does not seek the benefit and welfare of that herd of deer, nor seek their safety and happiness. He blocks the straight path, opens up an evil road, digs a great pit, and stations a person to keep watch. In this way, the entire herd of deer perishes. Then another person comes along who seeks the benefit and welfare of that herd of deer, who seeks their safety and happiness. He opens the straight path, closes off the evil road, dismisses the watchman, and in this way the entire herd of deer is safely delivered.

"Bhikṣus! You should know that I have spoken this parable so that you may understand its meaning. Those with wisdom, upon hearing the parable, will comprehend its purport. This parable has meaning: the great pool of water refers to the five sensual pleasures that are lovable, memorable, and joyful. What are the five? Forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, scents known by the nose, flavors known by the tongue, and tactile sensations known by the body. The great pool of water should be understood as these five sensual pleasures. The great herd of deer should be understood as ascetics and brahmins. The person who comes along not seeking their benefit and welfare, nor their safety and happiness, should be understood as Māra, the Evil One. Blocking the straight path and opening up an evil road refers to the three evil and unwholesome thoughts: thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm. The evil road should be understood as the three evil and unwholesome thoughts. There is yet another evil road, namely the eightfold wrong path: wrong view, up to wrong concentration, these being eight. Digging a great pit should be understood as ignorance. Stationing a person to keep watch should be understood as the retinue of Māra, the Evil One. The other person who comes along seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their safety and happiness, should be understood as the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Closing off the evil road and opening the straight path refers to the three wholesome thoughts: thoughts free from desire, thoughts free from ill will, and thoughts free from harm. The path should be understood as the three wholesome thoughts. There is yet another path, namely the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to right concentration, these being eight.

"Bhikṣus! I have opened the straight path for you, closed off the evil road, filled in the pit, and dismissed the watchman. What a teacher should do out of great compassion for his disciples, out of sympathy and concern, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their safety and happiness, I have already done. You should also do your part: go to secluded places, among mountain forests, under trees, in empty and quiet places. Sit in meditation and reflect. Do not be negligent. Strive diligently, so that you will have no regret later. This is my instruction; this is my admonition."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on Thoughts, Sixth
