## (103) Sūtra on the Lion's Roar, Seventh of the Chapter on Causes

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kuru, at the Kuru town of Kammāssadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Herein there is the first śramaṇa, the second, third, and fourth śramaṇa. Outside of this, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. The paths of other traditions are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins. You should, wherever you are among assemblies, make this correct lion's roar. Bhikṣus, there may be followers of other doctrines who come and ask you: 'Venerables, what practice do you have, what power do you have, what wisdom do you have, that causes you to make such a statement: "Herein there is the first śramaṇa, the second, third, and fourth śramaṇa. Outside of this, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. The paths of other traditions are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins. You, wherever you are among assemblies, make this correct lion's roar"?'

"Bhikṣus, you should answer the followers of other doctrines thus: 'Venerables, our World-Honored One, who has knowledge and vision, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught four dharmas. Because of these four dharmas, we make such a statement: "Herein there is the first śramaṇa, the second, third, and fourth śramaṇa. Outside of this, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. The paths of other traditions are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins. We, wherever we are among assemblies, make this correct lion's roar." What are the four? Venerables, we have faith in our Teacher, faith in the Dharma, faith in the complete fulfillment of moral virtue, and we cherish and respect our companions on the path, reverently attending to them. Venerables, our World-Honored One, who has knowledge and vision, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught these four dharmas. Because of these four dharmas, we make such a statement: "Herein there is the first śramaṇa, the second, third, and fourth śramaṇa. Outside of this, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. The paths of other traditions are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins. We, wherever we are among assemblies, make this correct lion's roar."'

"Bhikṣus, the followers of other doctrines may then say: 'Venerables, we too have faith in our teacher, namely our teacher. We have faith in our teaching, namely our teaching. We have fulfillment of moral virtue, namely our precepts. We cherish and respect our companions on the path, reverently attending to them, namely our companions who have gone forth and those who are householders. Venerables, between the śramaṇa Gautama and us, regarding these two kinds of statements, what is superior, what is the meaning, and what is the difference?' Bhikṣus, you should then ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is there one ultimate goal, or are there many ultimate goals?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'Venerables, there is one ultimate goal, not many ultimate goals.' Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one with desire who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one without desire who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'One without desire attains the ultimate goal; it is not one with desire who attains the ultimate goal.' Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one with hatred who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one without hatred who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'One without hatred attains the ultimate goal; it is not one with hatred who attains the ultimate goal.' Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one with delusion who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one without delusion who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'Venerables, one without delusion attains the ultimate goal; it is not one with delusion who attains the ultimate goal.'

"Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one with craving and clinging who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one without craving and without clinging who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'Venerables, one without craving and without clinging attains the ultimate goal; it is not one with craving and with clinging who attains the ultimate goal.' Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one without wisdom, who does not speak of wisdom, who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one with wisdom, who speaks of wisdom, who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'Venerables, one with wisdom, who speaks of wisdom, attains the ultimate goal; it is not one without wisdom, who does not speak of wisdom, who attains the ultimate goal.' Bhikṣus, you should further ask the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, is it one with aversion and contention who attains the ultimate goal, or is it one without aversion and without contention who attains the ultimate goal?' Bhikṣus, if the followers of other doctrines answer thus: 'Venerables, one without aversion and without contention attains the ultimate goal; it is not one with aversion and with contention who attains the ultimate goal.'

"Bhikṣus, you should then say to the followers of other doctrines: 'Venerables, it is as you say: there is one ultimate goal, not many ultimate goals. One without desire attains the ultimate goal, not one with desire. One without hatred attains the ultimate goal, not one with hatred. One without delusion attains the ultimate goal, not one with delusion. One without craving and without clinging attains the ultimate goal, not one with craving and with clinging. One with wisdom, who speaks of wisdom, attains the ultimate goal, not one without wisdom, who does not speak of wisdom. One without aversion and without contention attains the ultimate goal, not one with aversion and with contention. If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who rely on immeasurable views, all of them rely on two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. If one relies on the view of existence, then one becomes attached to the view of existence, depends on the view of existence, rests upon and abides in the view of existence, and has aversion and contention toward the view of non-existence. If one relies on the view of non-existence, then one becomes attached to the view of non-existence, depends on the view of non-existence, rests upon and abides in the view of non-existence, and has aversion and contention toward the view of existence.

"'If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who do not know the cause as it truly is, do not know the arising, do not know the cessation, do not know the ending, do not know the gratification, do not know the danger, do not know the escape, then all of them have desire, have hatred, have delusion, have craving, have clinging, are without wisdom, do not speak of wisdom, have aversion, and have contention. They are not freed from birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor can they escape from sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and vexation; they do not reach the end of suffering. If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who, regarding these two views, know the cause as it truly is, know the arising, know the cessation, know the ending, know the gratification, know the danger, and know the escape, then all of them are without desire, without hatred, without delusion, without craving, without clinging, have wisdom, speak of wisdom, are without aversion, and without contention. They are freed from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and they can escape from sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and vexation; they reach the end of suffering.

"'There are some śramaṇas and brahmins who posit the abandonment of clinging, yet do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. They posit the abandonment of sensual clinging, but do not posit the abandonment of clinging to precepts and rituals, clinging to views, and clinging to a doctrine of self. Why is that? Those śramaṇas and brahmins do not know three areas as they truly are. Therefore, although they posit the abandonment of clinging, they do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who posit the abandonment of clinging, yet do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. They posit the abandonment of sensual clinging and clinging to precepts and rituals, but do not posit the abandonment of clinging to views and clinging to a doctrine of self. Why is that? Those śramaṇas and brahmins do not know two areas as they truly are. Therefore, although they posit the abandonment of clinging, they do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who posit the abandonment of clinging, yet do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. They posit the abandonment of sensual clinging, clinging to precepts and rituals, and clinging to views, but do not posit the abandonment of clinging to a doctrine of self. Why is that? Those śramaṇas and brahmins do not know one area as it truly is. Therefore, although they posit the abandonment of clinging, they do not posit the abandonment of all clinging. In such a Dharma and Vinaya, if one has faith in the teacher, that is neither correct nor foremost. If one has faith in the teaching, it is also neither correct nor foremost. If one has complete fulfillment of moral virtue, it is also neither correct nor foremost. If one cherishes and respects companions on the path, reverently attending to them, it is also neither correct nor foremost.

"'If a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Unattached One, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma Path, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called a Buddha, the World-Honored One, he posits the abandonment of clinging, and in the present life he posits the abandonment of all clinging: the abandonment of sensual clinging, clinging to precepts and rituals, clinging to views, and clinging to a doctrine of self. What is the cause, what is the arising of these four kinds of clinging, from what do they arise, and what is their root? These four kinds of clinging have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their arising; they arise from ignorance, and ignorance is their root. If a bhikṣu has exhausted ignorance and generated knowledge, then from this he no longer takes up sensual clinging, clinging to precepts and rituals, clinging to views, or clinging to a doctrine of self. Not clinging, he is not frightened. Not being frightened, he cuts off the conditions and necessarily attains nirvāṇa. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, he will not receive further existence; he knows it as it truly is. In such a correct Dharma and Vinaya, if one has faith in the teacher, that is correct and foremost. If one has faith in the teaching, that is correct and foremost. If one has complete fulfillment of moral virtue, that is correct and foremost. If one cherishes and respects companions on the path, reverently attending to them, that is correct and foremost.'

"'Venerables, we have this practice, this power, and this wisdom. Because of this, we make such a statement: herein there is the first śramaṇa, the second, third, and fourth śramaṇa. Outside of this, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. The paths of other traditions are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins. Therefore, wherever we are among assemblies, we make this correct lion's roar.'"

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Lion's Roar Sūtra, Seventh.

---

## (104) The Udumbārikā Sūtra, Eighth of the Chapter on Causes, in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, there was a householder named Santuṭṭha (True Intention). Early in the morning he departed from Rājagṛha, intending to go and visit the Buddha, to pay homage and attend upon him. Then the householder Santuṭṭha had this thought: "Let me postpone visiting the Buddha. The World-Honored One may be in quiet meditation, as well as the venerable bhikṣus. I might as well go to the Udumbārikā Grove to visit the garden of the followers of other doctrines." Thereupon the householder Santuṭṭha went to the Udumbārikā Grove to visit the garden of the followers of other doctrines.

At that time, in the Udumbārikā Grove garden of the followers of other doctrines, there was a follower of another doctrine named Nigrodha (No Anger). He was the senior teacher among them, respected by the assembly, having defeated many in debate. He was the leader revered by five hundred followers of other doctrines. In that assembly there was commotion, with loud and clamorous voices, discussing various kinds of idle talk: talk of animals, talk of speeches, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of fighting and disputes, talk of food and drink, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of maidens, talk of courtesans, talk of worldly matters, talk of wrong paths, talk of the sea, talk of nations. Such various kinds of idle talk were being discussed; they were all gathered there sitting together. Then the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, seeing the householder Santuṭṭha coming from afar, immediately instructed his assembly to be silent: "Venerables, do not speak; be silent, be pleased with silence; each restrain yourselves. Why is that? The householder Santuṭṭha is coming. He is a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama. Among the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama who are householders of great renown and fame, worthy of respect, dwelling and residing in Rājagṛha, he is foremost. He is one who values silence, is pleased with silence, and is self-restrained. If he perceives that this assembly is abiding in silence, he may come over." Thereupon the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, having silenced the assembly, himself also became silent.

Then the householder Santuṭṭha went to where the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, was. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. The householder Santuṭṭha said: "Nigrodha, my Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or resides on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation. This is what the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is like: dwelling in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or residing on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation. In those remote places he constantly delights in quiet meditation, peaceful and joyful. That Buddha, the World-Honored One, never spends a single day and night gathered in assembly as you do today with your retinue."

Thereupon the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, said: "Householder, enough! Enough! How can you know? The śramaṇa Gautama has empty wisdom and liberation. This is not worth discussing. Whether it is fitting or not fitting, whether it follows or does not follow, that śramaṇa Gautama walks to the periphery, delights in the periphery, dwells in the periphery. Just as a blind cow grazes in the borderlands, walks to the periphery, delights in the periphery, and dwells in the periphery, so too is the śramaṇa Gautama. Householder, if that śramaṇa Gautama were to come to this assembly, I would with a single argument destroy him, like tipping an empty pot. I would also tell him the simile of the blind cow."

Thereupon the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, addressed his assembly: "Venerables, if the śramaṇa Gautama should come to this assembly, and should he certainly come, you should not respectfully rise from your seats, nor put your palms together toward him, nor invite him to sit. Just reserve a seat beforehand. When he arrives here, say thus: 'Gautama, there is a seat; if you wish to sit, sit as you please.'"

At that time, the World-Honored One, while in quiet meditation, with his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard the householder Santuṭṭha and the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, discussing in this manner. Then, in the late afternoon, he rose from quiet meditation and went to the Udumbārikā Grove, the garden of the followers of other doctrines. The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, seeing the World-Honored One coming from afar, immediately rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, put his palms together toward the Buddha, and praised him, saying: "Welcome, śramaṇa Gautama! It has been long since you came here. Please be seated on this seat."

At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This foolish person has violated his own agreement." Knowing this, the World-Honored One sat on that seat. The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, then exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side. The World-Honored One asked: "Nigrodha, what matter were you just discussing with the householder Santuṭṭha? For what reason were you all gathered here sitting together?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Gautama, we were having this thought: 'What kind of teaching does the śramaṇa Gautama have with which he trains his disciples? His disciples, having received training, attain peace for the rest of their lives, purely cultivate the holy life, and also teach it to others.' Gautama, this is what we were just discussing with the householder Santuṭṭha. For this reason, we were gathered here sitting together."

When the householder Santuṭṭha heard these words, he had this thought: "How strange that this follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, speaks falsely! Why is that? He is deceiving the World-Honored One right in front of the Buddha."

The World-Honored One, knowing this, said: "Nigrodha, my Dharma is extremely profound, extremely rare, extremely extraordinary, difficult to perceive and difficult to know, difficult to see and difficult to attain, namely the training I give my disciples. My disciples, having received this training, for the rest of their lives purely cultivate the holy life and also teach it to others. Nigrodha, if there is something unclear and objectionable in the doctrines of your teacher's tradition, you may ask me about it. I will certainly be able to answer to your satisfaction."

Thereupon the clamorous assembly of followers of other doctrines all called out in unison with great and loud voices: "The śramaṇa Gautama is extraordinary! Most extraordinary! He has great supernatural powers, great dignity and virtue, great merit, great supernatural authority. Why is that? He can set aside his own tradition and, following another's tradition, invite questions from others."

Then the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, having himself instructed his assembly to be silent, asked: "Gautama, the practice that is unclear and objectionable: how is it fulfilled? And how is it not fulfilled?"

Thereupon the World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who go naked without clothing, or use their hands as clothing, or use leaves as clothing, or use beads as clothing. They do not take water with a vessel, do not take water with a ladle. They do not eat food obtained by violence, robbery, or plunder. They do not eat food obtained by deception. They do not go themselves to receive food, do not send messengers, do not seek food to come to them. They do not stand honored, do not dwell honored in well-regarded places. If two people are eating together, they do not eat among them. They do not eat in the house of a pregnant woman, do not eat in a house where dogs are kept. If at a house there are dung-flies flying about, they do not eat there. They do not eat fish, do not eat meat, do not drink liquor, do not drink foul water, or drink nothing at all, practicing the asceticism of drinking nothing. Or they eat one mouthful, regarding one mouthful as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, regarding seven mouthfuls as sufficient. Or they eat one portion received, regarding one portion as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven portions, regarding seven portions as sufficient. Or they eat once a day, regarding one meal as sufficient; or once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once a fortnight, or once a month, regarding one meal as sufficient.

"Or they eat vegetables and herbs, or eat millet, or eat rough rice, or eat mixed coarse grains, or eat daddula food, or eat coarse food. Or they go to uninhabited places and dwell relying on seclusion. Or they eat roots, or eat fruits, or eat fruit that has fallen by itself. Or they wear joined-cloth garments, or wear woolen garments, or wear head-covering garments, or wear woolen head-covering garments, or wear whole hides, or wear perforated hides, or wear whole-and-perforated hides. Or they wear their hair loose, or wear their hair braided, or wear their hair both loose and braided. Or they shave their head, or shave their beard, or shave both beard and head. Or they pluck out their head hair, or pluck out their beard, or pluck out both beard and head hair. Or they stand and refuse to sit. Or they practice squatting. Or they sleep on thorns, making thorns their bed. Or they sleep on fruit, making fruit their bed. Or they worship water, dipping their hands in it day and night. Or they worship fire, keeping it burning all night long. Or they worship the sun and moon as venerable and greatly virtuous, putting their palms together toward them. In this manner and the like, they endure immeasurable suffering and practice austerities of self-mortification. Nigrodha, what do you think? Is such an unclear and objectionable practice fulfilled or not fulfilled?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Gautama, such an unclear and objectionable practice is fulfilled, not unfulfilled."

The World-Honored One further said: "Nigrodha, I will explain to you how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is polluted by immeasurable defilements."

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, asked: "Gautama, how do you explain that this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is polluted by immeasurable defilements?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this practice of pure austerity and asceticism, he has evil desires and craves desires. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this practice of pure austerity and asceticism, he has evil desires and craves desires, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity. Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this practice, he gazes upward at the sunlight and absorbs the sun's essence. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he gazes upward at the sunlight and absorbs the sun's essence, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity. Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he becomes proud and arrogant. Having attained the practice of pure austerity and asceticism, his mind becomes attached to it. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he becomes proud and arrogant, and having attained the practice of pure austerity and asceticism, his mind becomes attached to it, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he exalts himself and disparages others. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he exalts himself and disparages others, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity. Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he goes from house to house proclaiming: 'I practice pure austerity; my practice is extremely difficult.' Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he goes from house to house proclaiming: 'I practice pure austerity; my practice is extremely difficult,' this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he becomes jealous and says: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon that śramaṇa or brahmin? They should respect, honor, and attend upon me. Why? Because I practice austerity.' Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he becomes jealous and says: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon that śramaṇa or brahmin? They should respect, honor, and attend upon me. Why? Because I practice austerity,' this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he confronts and rebukes that śramaṇa or brahmin, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon you? You are full of desires, full of demands, always eating. You eat root seeds, tree seeds, fruit seeds, joint seeds, and kernel seeds, these five. Just like a violent storm that greatly damages the five grain seeds and disturbs livestock and people,' so too, he says, those śramaṇas and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others are likewise. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he confronts and rebukes that śramaṇa or brahmin, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon you? You are full of desires, full of demands, always eating. You eat root seeds, tree seeds, fruit seeds, joint seeds, and kernel seeds, these five. Just like a violent storm that greatly damages the five grain seeds and disturbs livestock and people,' so too, he says, those śramaṇas and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others are likewise, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he has grief, folly, and fear; he dreads secret conduct, suspects and fears the loss of his reputation, and increases in covetous observation and heedlessness. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he has grief, folly, and fear, dreads secret conduct, suspects and fears the loss of his reputation, and increases in covetous observation and heedlessness, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he gives rise to the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, and attachment to views. He is difficult to deal with, his mind has no moderation, and regarding dharmas that can be understood by śramaṇas and brahmins, he does not understand them. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he gives rise to the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, and attachment to views, is difficult to deal with, his mind has no moderation, and regarding dharmas that can be understood by śramaṇas and brahmins, he does not understand them, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he has anger, enmity, silence born of resentment, miserliness, jealousy, flattery, deception, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he has anger, enmity, silence born of resentment, miserliness, jealousy, flattery, deception, shamelessness, and lack of moral dread, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he speaks falsehood, engages in divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk, and possesses evil conduct. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he speaks falsehood, engages in divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk, and possesses evil conduct, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is without faith, is indolent, lacks right mindfulness and right understanding, and possesses evil wisdom. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is without faith, is indolent, lacks right mindfulness and right understanding, and possesses evil wisdom, this, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the practitioner of austerity. Nigrodha, have I not explained to you how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is polluted by immeasurable defilements?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Indeed, Gautama has explained to me how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is polluted by immeasurable defilements."

"Nigrodha, I will further explain to you how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is not polluted by immeasurable defilements."

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, asked again: "How does Gautama explain that this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is not polluted by immeasurable defilements?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this practice, he does not have evil desires and does not crave desires. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not have evil desires and does not crave desires, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not gaze at the sunlight and does not absorb the sun's essence. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not gaze at the sunlight and does not absorb the sun's essence, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is not proud or arrogant. Having attained the practice of pure austerity and asceticism, his mind does not become attached to it. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is not proud or arrogant, and having attained the practice of pure austerity and asceticism, his mind does not become attached to it, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not exalt himself and does not disparage others. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not exalt himself and does not disparage others, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, if there is one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not go from house to house proclaiming: 'I practice pure austerity; my practice is extremely difficult.' Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not go from house to house proclaiming: 'I practice pure austerity; my practice is extremely difficult,' this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he does not become jealous, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon that śramaṇa or brahmin? They should respect, honor, and attend upon me. Why? Because I practice austerity.' Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he does not become jealous, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon that śramaṇa or brahmin? They should respect, honor, and attend upon me. Why? Because I practice austerity,' this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he does not confront and rebuke that śramaṇa or brahmin, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon you? You are full of desires, full of demands, always eating. You eat root seeds, tree seeds, fruit seeds, joint seeds, and kernel seeds, these five. Just like a violent storm that greatly damages the five grain seeds and disturbs livestock and people,' so too, those śramaṇas and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others are likewise. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, when he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and attended upon by others, he does not confront and rebuke that śramaṇa or brahmin, saying: 'Why do they respect, honor, and attend upon you? You are full of desires, full of demands, always eating. You eat root seeds, tree seeds, fruit seeds, joint seeds, and kernel seeds, these five. Just like a violent storm that greatly damages the five grain seeds and disturbs livestock and people,' so too, those śramaṇas and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others are likewise, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not have grief, folly, or fear; he does not dread secret conduct, does not suspect and fear the loss of his reputation, and does not increase in covetous observation and heedlessness. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not have grief, folly, or fear, does not dread secret conduct, does not suspect and fear the loss of his reputation, and does not increase in covetous observation and heedlessness, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not give rise to the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, or attachment to views; he is not difficult to deal with, his mind is without excessive limits, and regarding dharmas that can be understood by śramaṇas and brahmins, he understands them. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not give rise to the view of self, extreme views, wrong views, or attachment to views, is not difficult to deal with, his mind is without excessive limits, and regarding dharmas that can be understood by śramaṇas and brahmins, he understands them, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is without anger, enmity, silence born of resentment, miserliness, jealousy, flattery, deception, shamelessness, or lack of moral dread. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is without anger, enmity, silence born of resentment, miserliness, jealousy, flattery, deception, shamelessness, or lack of moral dread, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not speak falsehood, does not engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous talk, and does not possess evil conduct. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he does not speak falsehood, does not engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous talk, and does not possess evil conduct, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement.

"Furthermore, Nigrodha, there may be one who practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is not without faith, not indolent, has right mindfulness and right understanding, and does not possess evil wisdom. Nigrodha, if one practices pure austerity and asceticism, and because of this, he is not without faith, not indolent, has right mindfulness and right understanding, and does not possess evil wisdom, this, Nigrodha, means the practitioner of austerity is without defilement. Nigrodha, have I not explained to you how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is not polluted by immeasurable defilements?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Indeed, Gautama has explained to me how this fulfilled practice that is unclear and objectionable is not polluted by immeasurable defilements."

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, asked: "Gautama, does this unclear and objectionable practice attain the foremost, attain the truly real?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, this unclear and objectionable practice does not attain the foremost, does not attain the truly real. However, it has two levels of attainment: attaining the bark and attaining the sapwood."

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, asked again: "Gautama, how does this unclear and objectionable practice attain the outer bark?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, here there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four kinds of conduct: not killing living beings, not instructing others to kill, not being complicit in killing; not stealing, not instructing others to steal, not being complicit in stealing; not taking another's wife, not instructing others to take another's wife, not being complicit in taking another's wife; not speaking falsehood, not instructing others to speak falsehood, not being complicit in speaking falsehood. He practices these four kinds of conduct, content and not striving further. His mind, together with loving-kindness, pervades one direction and dwells in it. In the same way, the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely, his mind together with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without hatred, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells in it. In the same way, with compassion, sympathetic joy, and his mind together with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without hatred, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells in it. Nigrodha, what do you think? Is this how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the outer bark?"

Nigrodha answered: "Gautama, indeed, this is how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the outer bark. Gautama, how does this unclear and objectionable practice attain the sapwood?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, here there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four kinds of conduct: not killing living beings, not instructing others to kill, not being complicit in killing; not stealing, not instructing others to steal, not being complicit in stealing; not taking another's wife, not instructing others to take another's wife, not being complicit in taking another's wife; not speaking falsehood, not instructing others to speak falsehood, not being complicit in speaking falsehood. He practices these four kinds of conduct, content and not striving further. He has practices and characteristics, and he recollects immeasurable past existences: one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births, eons of formation, eons of destruction, immeasurable eons of formation and destruction. Those beings were named such-and-such, those beings experienced thus in the past: 'I was once born there, with such a family name, such a given name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and happiness, such longevity, such duration of life, such a lifespan's end. Dying there, I was reborn here; dying here, I was reborn there. I was born here with such a family name, such a given name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and happiness, such longevity, such duration of life, such a lifespan's end.' Nigrodha, what do you think? Is this how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the sapwood?"

Nigrodha answered: "Gautama, indeed, this is how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the sapwood. Gautama, how does this unclear and objectionable practice attain the foremost, attain the truly real?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, here there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four kinds of conduct: not killing living beings, not instructing others to kill, not being complicit in killing; not stealing, not instructing others to steal, not being complicit in stealing; not taking another's wife, not instructing others to take another's wife, not being complicit in taking another's wife; not speaking falsehood, not instructing others to speak falsehood, not being complicit in speaking falsehood. He practices these four kinds of conduct, content and not striving further. With the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees beings dying and being reborn, of good complexion and bad complexion, beautiful and not beautiful, going to favorable destinations and unfavorable destinations, according to the deeds these beings have performed; he sees it as it truly is. If these beings have accomplished evil bodily conduct, evil verbal conduct, evil mental conduct, have slandered noble ones, and have accomplished wrong views and the karma of wrong views, then because of these conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they necessarily fall to evil destinations and are reborn in the hells. If these beings have accomplished wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, wholesome mental conduct, have not slandered noble ones, and have accomplished right views and the karma of right views, then because of these conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they necessarily ascend to favorable destinations and are reborn in the heavens. Nigrodha, what do you think? Is this how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the foremost, attains the truly real?"

Nigrodha answered: "Gautama, indeed, this is how the unclear and objectionable practice attains the foremost, attains the truly real. Gautama, is it for the realization of this unclear and objectionable practice that the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama rely on the śramaṇa to practice the holy life?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, it is not for the realization of this unclear and objectionable practice that my disciples rely on me to practice the holy life. Nigrodha, there is something else, most supreme, most wonderful, most excellent. It is for the realization of that that my disciples rely on me to practice the holy life."

Thereupon the clamorous assembly of followers of other doctrines raised their loud, great voices: "So it is, so it is! It is for the realization of that that the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama rely on the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life."

Then the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, having instructed his own assembly to be silent, addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, what is this other thing, most supreme, most wonderful, most excellent, for the realization of which the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama rely on the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life?"

Thereupon the World-Honored One answered: "Nigrodha, when a Tathāgata, Unattached One, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma Path, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called a Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world, he abandons the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, he attains up to the fourth dhyāna and dwells in it. With his mind thus concentrated, pure, without stain, without affliction, pliant, well settled, and having attained an imperturbable mind, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, realizing it directly. He knows this is suffering as it truly is, knows this is the arising of suffering, knows this is the cessation of suffering, knows this is the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. He also knows these are the outflows, knows this is the arising of the outflows, knows this is the cessation of the outflows, knows this is the path to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, liberated from the outflow of existence, and liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, he will not receive further existence; he knows it as it truly is. Nigrodha, this is what is other, most supreme, most wonderful, most excellent. It is for the realization of this that my disciples rely on me to practice the holy life."

Thereupon the householder Santuṭṭha said: "Nigrodha, the World-Honored One is here. Can you now with a single argument destroy him, like tipping an empty pot, and tell the simile of the blind cow grazing in the borderlands?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, addressed the follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha: "Did you really say such a thing?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "I truly did say such a thing, Gautama."

The World-Honored One further asked: "Nigrodha, have you ever heard from elder, senior teachers something like this: that past Tathāgatas, Unattached Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, dwelt in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or resided on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation? Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwelling in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or residing on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation, in those remote places they constantly delighted in quiet meditation, peaceful and joyful. They never spent a single day and night gathered in assembly, as you do today with your retinue?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Gautama, I have heard from elder, senior teachers something like this: that past Tathāgatas, Unattached Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, dwelt in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or resided on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation. Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwelling in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or residing on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation, in those remote places they constantly delighted in quiet meditation, peaceful and joyful. They never spent a single day and night gathered in assembly, as I do today with my retinue."

"Nigrodha, did you not have this thought: that World-Honored One, dwelling in secluded places in the mountains and forests beneath trees, or residing on high cliffs, silent without sound, remote and free from evil, without people, suitable for quiet meditation, in those remote places constantly delighting in quiet meditation, peaceful and joyful; is not the śramaṇa Gautama cultivating the path to perfect enlightenment?"

The follower of another doctrine, Nigrodha, answered: "Gautama, had I known this, how would I have said that with a single argument I could destroy him, like tipping an empty pot, and told the simile of the blind cow grazing in the borderlands?"

The World-Honored One said: "Nigrodha, I now have a Dharma that is well and rightly taught, with various liberation phrases that can be directly realized. With this, the Tathāgata himself declares fearlessness. My bhikṣu disciples come to me without flattery, without deception, honest and without pretense. Having trained according to my instruction, they will certainly attain the ultimate knowledge. Nigrodha, if you think: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma because he is greedy for being a teacher,' you should not think this. I return the role of teacher to you; I will still teach you the Dharma. Nigrodha, if you think: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma because he is greedy for disciples,' you should not think this. I return the disciples to you; I will still teach you the Dharma. Nigrodha, if you think: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma because he is greedy for offerings,' you should not think this. I return the offerings to you; I will still teach you the Dharma. Nigrodha, if you think: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma because he is greedy for praise and reputation,' you should not think this. I return the praise and reputation to you; I will still teach you the Dharma. Nigrodha, if you think: 'If I have a Dharma that is well and rightly taught, with various liberation phrases that can be directly realized, the śramaṇa Gautama will seize it from me and destroy it,' you should not think this. I return the Dharma to you; I will still teach you the Dharma."

Thereupon the great assembly remained silent. Why was that? Because they were controlled and held by Māra, the Evil One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Santuṭṭha: "Look at this great assembly, remaining silent. Why is that? Because they are controlled and held by Māra, the Evil One. He causes it so that among the assembly of followers of other doctrines, not a single one has the thought: 'Let me try to cultivate the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama.'"

The World-Honored One, knowing this, taught the Dharma for the householder Santuṭṭha, inspiring, encouraging, uplifting, and filling him with joy. Having in immeasurable ways taught the Dharma, inspiring, encouraging, uplifting, and filling him with joy, he then rose from his seat, took the householder Santuṭṭha by the arm, and with supernatural power flew up and departed through the sky.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The householder Santuṭṭha, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Udumbārikā Sūtra, Eighth.

---

## (105) The Sūtra on Aspirations, Ninth of the Chapter on Causes, in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was in a remote, secluded dwelling place, in a quiet location. While sitting in meditation and contemplation, he had this thought in his mind: "If only the World-Honored One would console me, speak with me, and teach me the Dharma, so that I might fulfill the precepts, not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places." Then, after having this thought, in the late afternoon he rose from meditation and went to where the Buddha was.

The World-Honored One saw that bhikṣu coming from afar. Because of that bhikṣu, he addressed the bhikṣus: "You should aspire: 'May the World-Honored One console me, speak with me, and teach me the Dharma, so that I may fulfill the precepts, not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places.' Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May my relatives, because of me, when their bodies break up and their lives end, necessarily ascend to favorable destinations and be reborn in the heavens.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May those who give me robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine and the necessities of life, may their offerings be of great merit, great radiance, and obtain great fruit and reward.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places.

"Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I be able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies and fleas, the oppression of wind and sun; may I also endure harsh words and beatings; when my body encounters various illnesses, extremely painful, even to the point where life is about to end, all that is unpleasant may I be able to bear.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I be able to endure displeasure; if displeasure arises, may my mind never become attached to it.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I be able to endure fear and terror; if fear and terror arise, may my mind never become attached to them.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'If the three evil, unwholesome thoughts arise in me, thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harming, may my mind never become attached to these three evil, unwholesome thoughts.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places.

"Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I be separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, and attain up to the fourth dhyāna and dwell in it.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May the three fetters be entirely exhausted in me, so that I attain stream-entry, never falling into evil destinies, certain to proceed toward right enlightenment, receiving at most seven existences, passing through the heavens and the human world seven times, and then reaching the end of suffering.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May the three fetters be entirely exhausted in me, with lust, anger, and delusion attenuated, so that I become a once-returner, passing through the heavens and the human world once, and after that one return, reaching the end of suffering.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May the five lower fetters be entirely exhausted in me, so that I am reborn in that realm and there attain nirvāṇa, attaining the state of non-return, never returning to this world.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places.

"Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I experience the peaceful liberations, and transcending form, attain the formless absorptions, and in accordance with those states, realize them with my own body and dwell in them, and with wisdom contemplate and cut off the outflows and know them.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places. Bhikṣus, you should aspire: 'May I attain the bases of supernatural power, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of birth and death; with all outflows exhausted, attaining the outflow-free liberation of mind, liberation of wisdom; in the present life, knowing for myself, realizing for myself, directly witnessing and dwelling in it: birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence; knowing it as it truly is.' Fulfill the precepts, do not neglect meditation, accomplish the practice of insight, and dwell in empty, quiet places."

Thereupon that bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, well received and well retained it. He rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. That bhikṣu, having received this instruction from the Buddha, in a secluded dwelling place, in a quiet location, sat in meditation and contemplation, practicing with diligence, his mind without heedlessness. Because of dwelling in seclusion, sitting in meditation and contemplation, practicing with diligence and his mind without heedlessness, that which a son of good family aspires to when he shaves off his beard and hair, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, namely the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, in the present life he knew for himself, realized for himself, directly witnessed and dwelt in it: birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence; he knew it as it truly is. That venerable one, having realized the Dharma, attained the state of an arhat.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Aspirations, Ninth.

---

## (106) The Sūtra on Perception, Tenth of the Chapter on Causes, in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, with regard to earth, have the perception of earth, thinking 'earth is the self,' 'earth belongs to the self,' 'the self belongs to earth'; having conceived that earth is the self, they do not truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirit beings, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the gods free from affliction, and the gods free from torment. With regard to purity, they have the perception of purity, thinking 'purity is the self,' 'purity belongs to the self,' 'the self belongs to purity'; having conceived that purity is the self, they do not truly know purity. The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; the one, the distinct, the manifold; the seen, the heard, the cognized, the known; that which is attained, contemplated, thought upon by the mind, conceived by the mind. From this world to that world, from that world to this world. With regard to the totality, they have the perception of totality, thinking 'the totality is the self,' 'the totality belongs to the self,' 'the self belongs to the totality'; having conceived that the totality is the self, they do not truly know the totality."

"If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, with regard to earth, truly know earth, knowing 'earth is not the self,' 'earth does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to earth'; not having conceived that earth is the self, they truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirit beings, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the gods free from affliction, and the gods free from torment. With regard to purity, they truly know purity, knowing 'purity is not the self,' 'purity does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to purity'; not having conceived that purity is the self, they truly know purity. The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; the one, the distinct, the manifold; the seen, the heard, the cognized, the known; that which is attained, contemplated, thought upon by the mind, conceived by the mind. From this world to that world, from that world to this world. With regard to the totality, they truly know the totality, knowing 'the totality is not the self,' 'the totality does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to the totality'; not having conceived that the totality is the self, they truly know the totality.

"With regard to earth, I truly know earth, knowing 'earth is not the self,' 'earth does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to earth'; not having conceived that earth is the self, I truly know earth. Likewise with water, fire, wind, spirit beings, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the gods free from affliction, and the gods free from torment. With regard to purity, I truly know purity, knowing 'purity is not the self,' 'purity does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to purity'; not having conceived that purity is the self, I truly know purity. The sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; the one, the distinct, the manifold; the seen, the heard, the cognized, the known; that which is attained, contemplated, thought upon by the mind, conceived by the mind. From this world to that world, from that world to this world. With regard to the totality, I truly know the totality, knowing 'the totality is not the self,' 'the totality does not belong to the self,' 'the self does not belong to the totality'; not having conceived that the totality is the self, I truly know the totality."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Perception, Tenth.

**(107) Sūtra on Forests**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu depends on a certain forest to dwell, and while dwelling in that forest, his mindfulness that was not yet established becomes established, his mind that was not yet concentrated becomes concentrated, his taints that were not yet ended become ended, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that he had not yet attained; and furthermore, the necessities of life that a renunciant requires: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for illness, these are all obtained without difficulty. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I depend on this forest to dwell. While dwelling in this forest, my mindfulness that was not yet established has become established, my mind that was not yet concentrated has become concentrated, my taints that were not yet ended have become ended, and I have attained the unsurpassed security from bondage that I had not yet attained. Furthermore, the necessities of life that a renunciant requires: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for illness, I obtain all these without difficulty.' That bhikṣu should dwell in that forest for the rest of his life and not leave it.

"If a bhikṣu depends on a certain forest to dwell, and while dwelling in that forest, his mindfulness that was not yet established becomes established, his mind that was not yet concentrated becomes concentrated, his taints that were not yet ended become ended, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that he had not yet attained; but the necessities of life that a renunciant requires: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for illness, these are all obtained with difficulty. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I depend on this forest to dwell. While dwelling in this forest, my mindfulness that was not yet established has become established, my mind that was not yet concentrated has become concentrated, my taints that were not yet ended have become ended, and I have attained the unsurpassed security from bondage that I had not yet attained. But the necessities of life that a renunciant requires: robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for illness, I obtain all these with difficulty. However, I did not leave the household life for the sake of robes, nor for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicines for illness. Rather, my mindfulness that was not yet established has become established, my mind that was not yet concentrated has become concentrated, my taints that were not yet ended have become ended, and I have attained the unsurpassed security from bondage that I had not yet attained.' **(109) Sūtra on Self-Contemplation of the Mind**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is unable to skillfully contemplate another's mind, he should skillfully contemplate his own mind. He should train in this way.

"How does a bhikṣu skillfully contemplate his own mind? A bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'Do I often practice covetous thoughts for acquiring things that are not mine? Do I often practice thoughts of ill will? Do I often practice sloth and torpor? Do I often practice restlessness? Do I often practice doubt? Do I often practice anger? Do I often practice defiled thoughts? Do I often practice bodily fatigue? Do I often practice laziness? Do I often practice a mind that is not concentrated?'

"If a bhikṣu, upon self-reflection, knows: 'I often practice covetous thoughts for acquiring things that are not mine. I often practice thoughts of ill will. I often practice sloth and torpor. I often practice restlessness. I often practice doubt. I often practice anger. I often practice defiled thoughts. I often practice bodily fatigue. I often practice laziness. I often practice a mind that is not concentrated,' then that bhikṣu should, for the sake of abandoning these evil, unwholesome states, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation. It is just as when a person whose clothes or head are on fire would, for the sake of extinguishing that fire, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort to extinguish it. In the same way, that bhikṣu should, for the sake of abandoning these evil, unwholesome states, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation.

"If a bhikṣu, upon self-reflection, knows: 'I do not often practice covetous thoughts for acquiring things that are not mine. I do not often practice thoughts of ill will. I do not often practice sloth and torpor. I do not often practice restlessness. I do not often practice doubt. I do not often practice anger. I do not often practice defiled thoughts. I do not often practice bodily fatigue. I do not often practice laziness. I do not often practice a mind that is not concentrated,' then that bhikṣu should, based on these wholesome states, train his mind further in the eradication of the taints. He should develop aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation."

The Buddha spoke thus: "It is just as a person who, looking at their reflection in a clear, bright mirror or a basin of pure water, sees a blemish and strives to remove it, or sees no blemish and is pleased, saying: 'How fortunate for me! I am clean!' In the same way, if a bhikṣu reflects and knows: 'I often practice covetous thoughts for acquiring things that are not mine, thoughts of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness, doubt, anger, defiled thoughts, bodily fatigue, laziness, and a mind that is not concentrated,' then that bhikṣu should, for the sake of abandoning these evil, unwholesome states, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation. It is just as when a person whose clothes or head are on fire would, for the sake of extinguishing that fire, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort to extinguish it. In the same way, that bhikṣu should, for the sake of abandoning these evil, unwholesome states, arouse an extremely strong aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation.

"If a bhikṣu reflects and knows: 'I do not often practice covetous thoughts for acquiring things that are not mine, thoughts of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness, doubt, anger, defiled thoughts, bodily fatigue, laziness, or a mind that is not concentrated,' then that bhikṣu should, based on these wholesome states, train his mind further in the eradication of the taints. He should develop aspiration, practice, strive with diligence, apply his mind, and exert effort without cessation."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

**(110) Sūtra on the Occasion of Affliction**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the Dharma concerning affliction and purification. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we will listen."

The Buddha said: "What is affliction, and how does affliction arise? Bhikṣus, there is a person whose body performs evil deeds, and he does not use skillful means to remove those evil bodily deeds. His mouth speaks evil speech, and he does not use skillful means to remove that evil speech. His mind thinks evil thoughts, and he does not use skillful means to remove those evil mental thoughts. For such a person, when evil bodily deeds have been done and not removed, when evil speech has been spoken and not removed, when evil mental thoughts have been thought and not removed, then his bodily evil deeds, verbal evil speech, and mental evil thoughts pollute his future body, verbal, and mental actions. Since his bodily, verbal, and mental actions are polluted, his death and the circumstances of his death are polluted. Since his death and the circumstances of his death are polluted, after his body breaks down and his life ends, he will be born in an evil destination. This is called affliction, and this is how affliction arises.

"It is like an unclean cloth that is further stained with dirt. Its master does not use skillful means to wash it. That cloth, which was already unclean, is further stained with dirt, and since its master does not use skillful means to wash it, it becomes increasingly dirty and impure. In the same way, there is a person whose body performs evil deeds, and he does not use skillful means to remove those evil bodily deeds. His mouth speaks evil speech, and he does not use skillful means to remove that evil speech. His mind thinks evil thoughts, and he does not use skillful means to remove those evil mental thoughts. For such a person, when evil bodily deeds have been done and not removed, when evil speech has been spoken and not removed, when evil mental thoughts have been thought and not removed, then his bodily evil deeds, verbal evil speech, and mental evil thoughts pollute his future bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Since his bodily, verbal, and mental actions are polluted, his death and the circumstances of his death are polluted. Since his death and the circumstances of his death are polluted, after his body breaks down and his life ends, he will be born in an evil destination. This is called affliction, and this is how affliction arises.

"What is purification, and how does purification arise? Bhikṣus, there is a person whose body performs evil deeds, and he uses skillful means to remove those evil bodily deeds. His mouth speaks evil speech, and he uses skillful means to remove that evil speech. His mind thinks evil thoughts, and he uses skillful means to remove those evil mental thoughts. For such a person, when evil bodily deeds have been done and are removed, when evil speech has been spoken and is removed, when evil mental thoughts have been thought and are removed, then his evil bodily deeds, evil verbal speech, and evil mental thoughts do not pollute his future bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Since his bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not polluted, his death and the circumstances of his death are not polluted. Since his death and the circumstances of his death are not polluted, after his body breaks down and his life ends, he will be born in a good destination. This is called purification, and this is how purification arises.

"It is like a clean cloth that is stained with dirt. Its master uses skillful means to wash it. That cloth, though it was stained with dirt, since its master uses skillful means to wash it, becomes clean and pure. In the same way, there is a person whose body performs evil deeds, and he uses skillful means to remove those evil bodily deeds. His mouth speaks evil speech, and he uses skillful means to remove that evil speech. His mind thinks evil thoughts, and he uses skillful means to remove those evil mental thoughts. For such a person, when evil bodily deeds have been done and are removed, when evil speech has been spoken and is removed, when evil mental thoughts have been thought and are removed, then his evil bodily deeds, evil verbal speech, and evil mental thoughts do not pollute his future bodily, verbal, and mental actions. Since his bodily, verbal, and mental actions are not polluted, his death and the circumstances of his death are not polluted. Since his death and the circumstances of his death are not polluted, after his body breaks down and his life ends, he will be born in a good destination. This is called purification, and this is how purification arises.

"This is the Dharma concerning affliction and purification."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If someone with a defiled mind dies, I say there is no way for that person to be reborn in a good destination. Why? Because one with a defiled mind who dies will certainly be reborn in an evil destination. It is like a vessel that is overturned: any water in it is spilled out and cannot be retained. In the same way, if someone with a defiled mind dies, I say there is no way for that person to be reborn in a good destination. Why? Because one with a defiled mind who dies will certainly be reborn in an evil destination.

"If someone with a pure mind dies, I say there is no way for that person to be reborn in an evil destination. Why? Because one with a pure mind who dies will certainly be reborn in a good destination. It is like a vessel that is upright: any water poured into it is retained and does not leak out. In the same way, if someone with a pure mind dies, I say there is no way for that person to be reborn in an evil destination. Why? Because one with a pure mind who dies will certainly be reborn in a good destination."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.
