**(111) Sūtra on Attaining the Way Through Progressive Training**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. What does one who knows and sees destroy the taints through? It is by knowing and seeing: 'This is suffering.' By knowing and seeing: 'This is the origin of suffering.' By knowing and seeing: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' By knowing and seeing: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' Thus knowing, thus seeing, one destroys the taints.

"I say that right view also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right view? It should be said: It is learning. Learning also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for learning? It should be said: It is using one's ears. Using one's ears also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for using one's ears? It should be said: It is listening. Listening also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for listening? It should be said: It is practicing respect. Practicing respect also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for practicing respect? It should be said: It is approaching. Approaching also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for approaching? It should be said: It is faith.

"Faith also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for faith? It should be said: It is suffering. Suffering also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for suffering? It should be said: It is old age and death. Old age and death also have their causes and conditions; they are not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for old age and death? It should be said: It is birth. Birth also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for birth? It should be said: It is existence. Existence also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for existence? It should be said: It is clinging. Clinging also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for clinging? It should be said: It is craving. Craving also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for craving? It should be said: It is feeling. Feeling also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for feeling? It should be said: It is contact. Contact also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for contact? It should be said: It is the six sense bases. The six sense bases also have their causes and conditions; they are not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for the six sense bases? It should be said: It is name-and-form. Name-and-form also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for name-and-form? It should be said: It is consciousness. Consciousness also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for consciousness? It should be said: It is formations. Formations also have their causes and conditions; they are not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for formations? It should be said: It is ignorance.

"In this way, because of ignorance there are formations; because of formations there is consciousness; because of consciousness there is name-and-form; because of name-and-form there are the six sense bases; because of the six sense bases there is contact; because of contact there is feeling; because of feeling there is craving; because of craving there is clinging; because of clinging there is existence; because of existence there is birth; because of birth there is old age and death. Because of old age and death there is suffering. Because of suffering there is faith. Because of faith there is approaching. Because of approaching there is practicing respect. Because of practicing respect there is listening. Because of listening there is using one's ears. Because of using one's ears there is learning. Because of learning there is right view. Because of right view there is right intention. Because of right intention there is right speech. Because of right speech there is right action. Because of right action there is right livelihood. Because of right livelihood there is right effort. Because of right effort there is right mindfulness. Because of right mindfulness there is right concentration. Because of right concentration there is right knowledge. Because of right knowledge there is right liberation.

"In this way, by progressive training, by progressive action, by progressive practice, one reaches right liberation. It is just like the vast ocean, which gradually slopes, gradually deepens, and does not suddenly become an abyss. In the same way, in this Dharma and Vinaya, by progressive training, by progressive action, by progressive practice, one attains right liberation, and it is not suddenly attained all at once.

"I say that right view also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right view? It should be said: It is right intention. Right intention also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right intention? It should be said: It is right speech. Right speech also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right speech? It should be said: It is right action. Right action also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right action? It should be said: It is right livelihood. Right livelihood also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right livelihood? It should be said: It is right effort. Right effort also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right effort? It should be said: It is right mindfulness. Right mindfulness also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right mindfulness? It should be said: It is right concentration. Right concentration also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right concentration? It should be said: It is right knowledge. Right knowledge also has its causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions. What are the causes and conditions for right knowledge? It should be said: It is right liberation.

"In this way, the disciple who is a learner possesses eight factors, and the arahant possesses ten factors."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(112) Sūtra on Blemishes**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you about the blemishes of the mind. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain them for you."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What are the blemishes of the mind? Covetousness and ill will are blemishes of the mind. Anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, stubbornness, impetuosity, arrogance, haughtiness, conceit, and heedlessness are blemishes of the mind.

"If a bhikṣu knows that covetousness and ill will are blemishes of the mind, and he abandons them; if he knows that anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, stubbornness, impetuosity, arrogance, haughtiness, conceit, and heedlessness are blemishes of the mind, and he abandons them, then that bhikṣu who has thus abandoned covetousness and ill will as blemishes of the mind, and who has abandoned anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, stubbornness, impetuosity, arrogance, haughtiness, conceit, and heedlessness as blemishes of the mind, that bhikṣu gains unwavering faith in the Buddha: 'This is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' He gains unwavering faith in the Dharma: 'The Dharma is well-expounded by the World-Honored One, visible here and now, not subject to time, inviting one to come and see, leading onwards, to be individually known by the wise.' He gains unwavering faith in the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples practices well, practices directly, practices truly, practices properly. These are the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This is the Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverence with joined palms, an unsurpassed field of merit in the world.'

"Having thus abandoned these blemishes of the mind, that bhikṣu gains unwavering faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. He gains the joy associated with meaning, the joy associated with the Dharma. When there is joy, delight arises. When the mind is delighted, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When there is happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.

"When the mind is concentrated, that bhikṣu abides pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions; above, below, and all around, he pervades the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, expansive, immeasurable, free from enmity and ill will.

"In the same way, with compassion, he pervades one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions; above, below, and all around, he pervades the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion, vast, expansive, immeasurable, free from enmity and ill will.

"With sympathetic joy, he pervades one direction with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions; above, below, and all around, he pervades the entire world with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy, vast, expansive, immeasurable, free from enmity and ill will.

"With equanimity, he pervades one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth directions; above, below, and all around, he pervades the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, expansive, immeasurable, free from enmity and ill will.

"That bhikṣu knows thus: 'There is this, there is what is inferior, there is what is superior, and there is the escape beyond this entire range of perception.'

"When he knows and sees in this way, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of existence, and liberated from the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'

"It is just as a cloth that is dirty and stained, and its master gives it to a dyer. The dyer soaks it in various dyes, whether blue, yellow, red, or black, and it always takes the color poorly. Why? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, if the mind is defiled, an evil destination can be expected.

"It is just as a cloth that is very clean and pure, and its master gives it to a dyer. The dyer soaks it in various dyes, whether blue, yellow, red, or black, and it always takes the color well. Why? Because the cloth is clean. In the same way, if the mind is pure, a good destination can be expected."

"If those who are well-born and not well-born both practice water purification rites to wash away evil, what purification can that give? For water always has fish, turtles, crocodiles, and various aquatic creatures. If water purification could remove evil, then the fisherman, the catcher of fish and turtles, the butcher of deer, the trapper, and all who commit evil deeds would also thereby remove their evil. If water could wash away evil, it would also wash away one's merit and good deeds. Therefore, I say it is not so.

"If water could wash away evil, those who are well-born and not well-born would both benefit. But the evil deeds done by oneself are not washed away by water. One who upholds the precepts, who is pure, who is clean, can always be pure."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 27 of the Madhyamāgama

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 27

## Chapter 5: The Forest Chapter

Two Forest Sūtras, two Observing the Mind Sūtras, Penetrating the Holy Life, Anupama, The Basis of Dharma, Udāra, The Honey Ball, Gotamī comes last.

## (107) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: First Sūtra on the Forest

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. If I am without right mindfulness, I shall attain right mindfulness. If my mind is not concentrated, I shall attain a concentrated mind. If I am not liberated, I shall attain liberation. If the taints are not exhausted, I shall attain the exhaustion of taints. If I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I shall attain nirvāṇa.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, if he is without right mindfulness and does not attain right mindfulness, if his mind is not concentrated and he does not attain a concentrated mind, if he is not liberated and does not attain liberation, if the taints are not exhausted and he does not attain the exhaustion of taints, if he has not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and still does not attain nirvāṇa; yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I left home to practice the path not for the sake of robes, not for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicines, nor for the sake of various necessities of life. Yet dwelling depending on this forest, if I am without right mindfulness and do not attain right mindfulness, if my mind is not concentrated and I do not attain a concentrated mind, if I am not liberated and do not attain liberation, if the taints are not exhausted and I do not attain the exhaustion of taints, if I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and still do not attain nirvāṇa; yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, may leave this forest and depart.

"Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. If I am without right mindfulness, I shall attain right mindfulness. If my mind is not concentrated, I shall attain a concentrated mind. If I am not liberated, I shall attain liberation. If the taints are not exhausted, I shall attain the exhaustion of taints. If I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I shall attain nirvāṇa.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, if he was without right mindfulness and attains right mindfulness, if his mind was not concentrated and he attains a concentrated mind, if he was not liberated and attains liberation, if the taints were not exhausted and he attains the exhaustion of taints, if he had not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and attains nirvāṇa; yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I left home to practice the path not for the sake of robes, not for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicines, nor for the sake of various necessities of life. Yet dwelling depending on this forest, if I was without right mindfulness, I attain right mindfulness. If my mind was not concentrated, I attain a concentrated mind. If I was not liberated, I attain liberation. If the taints were not exhausted, I attain the exhaustion of taints. If I had not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I attain nirvāṇa. Yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, should remain in this forest.

"Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. If I am without right mindfulness, I shall attain right mindfulness. If my mind is not concentrated, I shall attain a concentrated mind. If I am not liberated, I shall attain liberation. If the taints are not exhausted, I shall attain the exhaustion of taints. If I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I shall attain nirvāṇa.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, if he is without right mindfulness and does not attain right mindfulness, if his mind is not concentrated and he does not attain a concentrated mind, if he is not liberated and does not attain liberation, if the taints are not exhausted and he does not attain the exhaustion of taints, if he has not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and still does not attain nirvāṇa; and the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I dwell depending on this forest, yet I am without right mindfulness and do not attain right mindfulness, my mind is not concentrated and I do not attain a concentrated mind, I am not liberated and do not attain liberation, the taints are not exhausted and I do not attain the exhaustion of taints, I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and still do not attain nirvāṇa. And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, should immediately leave this forest, departing at midnight, without taking leave of anyone.

"Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. If I am without right mindfulness, I shall attain right mindfulness. If my mind is not concentrated, I shall attain a concentrated mind. If I am not liberated, I shall attain liberation. If the taints are not exhausted, I shall attain the exhaustion of taints. If I have not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I shall attain nirvāṇa.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, if he was without right mindfulness and attains right mindfulness, if his mind was not concentrated and he attains a concentrated mind, if he was not liberated and attains liberation, if the taints were not exhausted and he attains the exhaustion of taints, if he had not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa and attains nirvāṇa; and the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I dwell depending on this forest, and if I was without right mindfulness, I attain right mindfulness. If my mind was not concentrated, I attain a concentrated mind. If I was not liberated, I attain liberation. If the taints were not exhausted, I attain the exhaustion of taints. If I had not attained the supreme, secure nirvāṇa, I attain nirvāṇa. And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, should dwell in this forest for the rest of his life until his life's end. Just as with dwelling depending on a forest, so too with charnel grounds, villages, and dwelling depending on a person, it is likewise the same."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the First Sūtra on the Forest.

## (108) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: Second Sūtra on the Forest

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. The purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, may that goal be attained by me.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, the purpose for which he left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, that goal is not attained by him. Yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I left home to practice the path not for the sake of robes, not for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicines, nor for the sake of various necessities of life. Yet I dwell depending on this forest, and the purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, that goal is not attained by me. The requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, may leave this forest and depart.

"Suppose a bhikṣu dwells depending on a certain forest, thinking: 'I shall dwell depending on this forest. The purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, may that goal be attained by me.' That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest. Having dwelt depending on this forest, the purpose for which he left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, that goal is attained by him. Yet the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain. That bhikṣu should reflect thus: 'I left home to practice the path not for the sake of robes, not for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicines, nor for the sake of various necessities of life. Yet I dwell depending on this forest, and the purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, that goal is attained by me. The requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, should remain in this forest.

The purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, may that goal be attained by me.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all very difficult to obtain.' That bhikṣu, having reflected thus, should immediately leave this forest, departing at midnight, without taking leave of anyone.

The purpose for which I left home to practice the path, wishing to attain the goal of the ascetic life, may that goal be attained by me.' And the requisites needed by one practicing the path, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various necessities of life, are all easy to seek and not difficult to obtain.' Just as with dwelling depending on a forest, so too with charnel grounds, villages, and dwelling depending on a person, it is likewise the same."

## (109) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: Third Sūtra on Observing One's Own Mind

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is unable to skillfully observe the minds of others, he should skillfully observe and examine his own mind. He should train in this way. How does a bhikṣu skillfully observe his own mind? If a bhikṣu has this kind of observation, it will surely bring great benefit. He should reflect: 'Have I attained inner calm but not attained the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas? Have I attained the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas but not attained inner calm? Have I attained neither inner calm nor the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas? Have I attained both inner calm and the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas?'

"If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he has attained inner calm but has not attained the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas, then that bhikṣu, having established inner calm, should seek the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas. At a later time, he will attain both inner calm and the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas. If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he has attained the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas but has not attained inner calm, then that bhikṣu, having established the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas, should seek inner calm. At a later time, he will attain both the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas and inner calm. If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he has attained neither inner calm nor the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas, then such a bhikṣu, not having attained these wholesome dharmas, wishing to attain them, should quickly seek the means with expedient methods, training with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, persevering without allowing regression. Just as a person whose head or clothes are on fire urgently seeks the means to save his head or save his clothes, so too, a bhikṣu who has not attained these wholesome dharmas, wishing to attain them, should quickly seek the means with expedient methods, training with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, persevering without allowing regression. At a later time, he will attain both inner calm and the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas. If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he has attained both inner calm and the supreme wisdom of insight into dharmas, then that bhikṣu, having established these wholesome dharmas, should seek the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of taints through direct knowledge. Why is this? I say that one should not keep all robes, and I also say that one may keep all robes. What kind of robes do I say should not be kept? If keeping certain robes would increase unwholesome dharmas and cause wholesome dharmas to decline, such robes I say should not be kept. What kind of robes do I say may be kept? If keeping certain robes would increase wholesome dharmas and cause unwholesome dharmas to decline, such robes I say may be kept. As with robes, so too with food and drink, bedding, and villages, it is likewise the same. I say one should not associate closely with all persons, and I also say one may associate closely with all persons. What kind of persons do I say one should not associate closely with? If associating closely with certain persons would increase unwholesome dharmas and cause wholesome dharmas to decline, such persons I say one should not associate closely with. What kind of persons do I say one may associate closely with? If associating closely with certain persons would increase wholesome dharmas and cause unwholesome dharmas to decline, such persons I say one may associate closely with.

"One should know as it truly is what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. Having known as it truly is what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced, one does not practice what is not to be practiced, and one practices what is to be practiced. Not practicing what is not to be practiced, and practicing what is to be practiced, wholesome dharmas increase and unwholesome dharmas decline. This is called a bhikṣu who skillfully observes his own mind, skillfully knows his own mind, and skillfully takes up and skillfully abandons."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Third Sūtra on Observing One's Own Mind.

---

## (110) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: Fourth Sūtra on Observing One's Own Mind

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu is unable to skillfully observe the minds of others, he should skillfully observe and examine his own mind. He should train in this way. How does a bhikṣu skillfully observe his own mind? If a bhikṣu has this kind of observation, it will surely bring great benefit. He should reflect: 'Do I often practice with covetousness, or do I often practice without covetousness? Do I often practice with a mind of ill will, or do I often practice without a mind of ill will? Do I often practice with the fetter of sloth and torpor, or do I often practice free from the fetter of sloth and torpor? Do I often practice with restlessness and conceit, or do I often practice without restlessness and conceit? Do I often practice with doubt and confusion, or do I often practice without doubt and confusion? Do I often practice with bodily quarreling, or do I often practice without bodily quarreling? Do I often practice with a defiled mind, or do I often practice without a defiled mind? Do I often practice with faith, or do I often practice without faith? Do I often practice with diligence, or do I often practice with laziness? Do I often practice with mindfulness, or do I often practice without mindfulness? Do I often practice with concentration, or do I often practice without concentration? Do I often practice with unwholesome wisdom, or do I often practice without unwholesome wisdom?'

"If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he often practices with covetousness, with a mind of ill will, with the fetter of sloth and torpor, with restlessness and conceit, with doubt and confusion, with bodily quarreling, with a defiled mind, without faith, with laziness, without mindfulness, without concentration, and often practices with unwholesome wisdom, then that bhikṣu, wishing to eliminate these unwholesome dharmas, should quickly seek the means with expedient methods, training with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, persevering without allowing regression. Just as a person whose head or clothes are on fire urgently seeks the means to save his head or save his clothes, so too, a bhikṣu wishing to eliminate these unwholesome dharmas should quickly seek the means with expedient methods, training with utmost diligence, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, persevering without allowing regression. If, upon observing, a bhikṣu knows that he often practices without covetousness, without a mind of ill will, free from the fetter of sloth and torpor, without restlessness and conceit, without doubt and confusion, without bodily quarreling, without a defiled mind, with faith, with diligence, with mindfulness, with concentration, and often practices without unwholesome wisdom, then that bhikṣu, having established these wholesome dharmas, should seek the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of taints through direct knowledge. Why is this? I say that one should not keep all robes, and I also say that one may keep all robes. What kind of robes do I say should not be kept? If keeping certain robes would increase unwholesome dharmas and cause wholesome dharmas to decline, such robes I say should not be kept. What kind of robes do I say may be kept? If keeping certain robes would increase wholesome dharmas and cause unwholesome dharmas to decline, such robes I say may be kept. As with robes, so too with food and drink, bedding, and villages, it is likewise the same. I say one should not associate closely with all persons, and I also say one may associate closely with all persons. What kind of persons do I say one should not associate closely with? If associating closely with certain persons would increase unwholesome dharmas and cause wholesome dharmas to decline, such persons I say one should not associate closely with. What kind of persons do I say one may associate closely with? If associating closely with certain persons would increase wholesome dharmas and cause unwholesome dharmas to decline, such persons I say one may associate closely with.

"One should know as it truly is what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. Having known as it truly is what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced, one does not practice what is not to be practiced, and one practices what is to be practiced. Not practicing what is not to be practiced, and practicing what is to be practiced, wholesome dharmas increase and unwholesome dharmas decline. This is called a bhikṣu who skillfully observes his own mind, skillfully knows his own mind, and skillfully takes up and skillfully abandons."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Fourth Sūtra on Observing One's Own Mind.

## (111) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: Fifth Sūtra on Penetrating the Holy Life

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Kurus, in Kammāssadhamma, a town of the Kurus.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you a Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life, called 'Penetrating the Holy Life,' which can exhaust all taints. Listen carefully and reflect well upon it." At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "You should know the taints, know the cause from which taints arise, know that taints have consequences, know the distinctions among taints, know the complete cessation of taints, and know the path to the cessation of taints. You should know feelings, know the cause from which feelings arise, know that feelings have consequences, know the distinctions among feelings, know the complete cessation of feelings, and know the path to the cessation of feelings. You should know perceptions, know the cause from which perceptions arise, know that perceptions have consequences, know the distinctions among perceptions, know the complete cessation of perceptions, and know the path to the cessation of perceptions. You should know desires, know the cause from which desires arise, know that desires have consequences, know the distinctions among desires, know the complete cessation of desires, and know the path to the cessation of desires. You should know actions, know the cause from which actions arise, know that actions have consequences, know the distinctions among actions, know the complete cessation of actions, and know the path to the cessation of actions. You should know suffering, know the cause from which suffering arises, know that suffering has consequences, know the distinctions among suffering, know the complete cessation of suffering, and know the path to the cessation of suffering.

"How does one know the taints? There are three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. This is called knowing the taints. How does one know the cause from which taints arise? It is ignorance. Because of ignorance, there are taints. This is called knowing the cause from which taints arise. How does one know that taints have consequences? One who is fettered by ignorance is stained by the various taints, and because of this receives consequences, obtaining either a good destination or a bad destination. This is called knowing that taints have consequences. How does one know the distinctions among taints? There are taints that lead to rebirth in the hells, there are taints that lead to rebirth among animals, there are taints that lead to rebirth among hungry ghosts, there are taints that lead to rebirth in the heavens, and there are taints that lead to rebirth in the human realm. This is called knowing the distinctions among taints. How does one know the complete cessation of taints? When ignorance ceases, the taints cease. This is called knowing the complete cessation of taints. How does one know the path to the cessation of taints? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of taints. If a bhikṣu knows the taints in this way, knows the cause from which taints arise, knows the consequences of taints, knows the distinctions among taints, knows the complete cessation of taints, and knows the path to the cessation of taints, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all taints.

"How does one know feelings? There are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. This is called knowing feelings. How does one know the cause from which feelings arise? It is contact. Because of contact, there are feelings. This is called knowing the cause from which feelings arise. How does one know that feelings have consequences? It is craving. Craving is the consequence of feelings. This is called knowing that feelings have consequences. How does one know the distinctions among feelings? A bhikṣu, when experiencing a pleasant feeling, knows he is experiencing a pleasant feeling; when experiencing a painful feeling, knows he is experiencing a painful feeling; when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, knows he is experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant bodily, painful bodily, neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily; pleasant mental, painful mental, neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental; pleasant with material nutriment, painful with material nutriment, neither-painful-nor-pleasant with material nutriment; pleasant without material nutriment, painful without material nutriment, neither-painful-nor-pleasant without material nutriment; pleasant connected with desire, painful connected with desire, neither-painful-nor-pleasant connected with desire; pleasant free from desire, painful free from desire; and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling free from desire, he knows he is experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling free from desire. This is called knowing the distinctions among feelings. How does one know the complete cessation of feelings? When contact ceases, feelings cease. This is called knowing the complete cessation of feelings. How does one know the path to the cessation of feelings? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of feelings. If a bhikṣu knows feelings in this way, knows the cause from which feelings arise, knows the consequences of feelings, knows the distinctions among feelings, knows the complete cessation of feelings, and knows the path to the cessation of feelings, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all feelings.

"How does one know perceptions? There are four perceptions. A bhikṣu knows small perception, knows great perception, knows boundless perception, and knows the perception of the base of nothingness. This is called knowing perceptions. How does one know the cause from which perceptions arise? It is contact. Because of contact, there are perceptions. This is called knowing the cause from which perceptions arise. How does one know that perceptions have consequences? It is speech. According to one's perceptions, one speaks accordingly. This is called knowing that perceptions have consequences. How does one know the distinctions among perceptions? There are perceptions that perceive forms, there are perceptions that perceive sounds, there are perceptions that perceive smells, there are perceptions that perceive tastes, and there are perceptions that perceive tangible objects. This is called knowing the distinctions among perceptions. How does one know the complete cessation of perceptions? When contact ceases, perceptions cease. This is called knowing the complete cessation of perceptions. How does one know the path to the cessation of perceptions? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of perceptions. If a bhikṣu knows perceptions in this way, knows the cause from which perceptions arise, knows the consequences of perceptions, knows the distinctions among perceptions, knows the complete cessation of perceptions, and knows the path to the cessation of perceptions, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all perceptions.

"How does one know desires? There are the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are lovely, pleasing, of beautiful appearance, connected with desire, and very delightful. What are the five? Forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, smells known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangible objects known by the body. This is called knowing desires. How does one know the cause from which desires arise? It is contact. Because of contact, there are desires. This is called knowing the cause from which desires arise. How does one know that desires have consequences? According to the kinds of desire, one becomes attached to and abides in them with love and delight, and because of this receives consequences in places of merit, places of demerit, or places of imperturbability. This is called knowing that desires have consequences. How does one know the distinctions among desires? There are desires that desire forms, there are desires that desire sounds, there are desires that desire smells, there are desires that desire tastes, and there are desires that desire tangible objects. This is called knowing the distinctions among desires. How does one know the complete cessation of desires? When contact ceases, desires cease. This is called knowing the complete cessation of desires. How does one know the path to the cessation of desires? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of desires. If a bhikṣu knows desires in this way, knows the cause from which desires arise, knows the consequences of desires, knows the distinctions among desires, knows the complete cessation of desires, and knows the path to the cessation of desires, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all desires.

"How does one know actions? There are two kinds of action: volition and what has been willed. This is called knowing actions. How does one know the cause from which actions arise? It is contact. Because of contact, there are actions. This is called knowing the cause from which actions arise. How does one know that actions have consequences? There are actions that are dark with dark consequences, there are actions that are bright with bright consequences, there are actions that are both dark and bright with both dark and bright consequences, and there are actions that are neither dark nor bright, without consequences, actions that lead to the exhaustion of actions. This is called knowing that actions have consequences. How does one know the distinctions among actions? There are actions that lead to rebirth in the hells, there are actions that lead to rebirth among animals, there are actions that lead to rebirth among hungry ghosts, there are actions that lead to rebirth in the heavens, and there are actions that lead to rebirth in the human realm. This is called knowing the distinctions among actions. How does one know the complete cessation of actions? When contact ceases, actions cease. This is called knowing the complete cessation of actions. How does one know the path to the cessation of actions? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of actions. If a bhikṣu knows actions in this way, knows the cause from which actions arise, knows the consequences of actions, knows the distinctions among actions, knows the complete cessation of actions, and knows the path to the cessation of actions, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all actions.

"How does one know suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with what is hateful is suffering, separation from what is loved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering, and in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This is called knowing suffering. How does one know the cause from which suffering arises? It is craving. Because of craving, suffering arises. This is called knowing the cause from which suffering arises. How does one know that suffering has consequences? There is suffering that is slight and slow to cease, there is suffering that is slight and quick to cease, there is suffering that is intense and slow to cease, and there is suffering that is intense and quick to cease; suffering upon suffering comes to an end. This is called knowing that suffering has consequences. How does one know the distinctions among suffering? An unlearned, ignorant ordinary person who has not encountered good spiritual friends and who has not been guided by the noble Dharma, when a feeling of extreme pain arises in his body, exceedingly severe, as if his life were about to end, seeks externally outside of this, looking elsewhere. Perhaps there are certain ascetics or brahmins who hold one-verse spells, or two, three, four, or many-verse spells, or who hold hundred-verse spells, thinking: 'They can cure my suffering.' In this way, because of seeking, the suffering of birth arises; because of habitual practice, the suffering of birth arises; and suffering ceases. This is called knowing the distinctions among suffering. How does one know the complete cessation of suffering? When craving ceases, suffering ceases. This is called knowing the complete cessation of suffering. How does one know the path to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. This is called knowing the path to the cessation of suffering. If a bhikṣu knows suffering in this way, knows the cause from which suffering arises, knows the consequences of suffering, knows the distinctions among suffering, knows the complete cessation of suffering, and knows the path to the cessation of suffering, this is called penetrating the holy life, which can exhaust all suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Fifth Sūtra on Penetrating the Holy Life.

---

## (112) Madhyamāgama, Forest Chapter: Sixth Sūtra on Anupama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Vajjians, in Anupiya, a town of the Vajjians.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditative sitting, came down from the hall, and said: "Ānanda, come with me to the Aciravatī River to bathe."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, certainly."

Thereupon the World-Honored One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Aciravatī River. He removed his robes on the bank and entered the water to bathe. After bathing, he came out, dried his body, and put on his robes. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda held a fan and fanned the Buddha. Then the World-Honored One turned his head and said: "Ānanda, because of Devadatta's heedlessness, he has fallen into extreme suffering and difficulty. He is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue. Ānanda, have you not heard from the bhikṣus that I have definitively declared that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes, indeed."

At that time, a certain bhikṣu said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Did the World-Honored One, through the knowledge of others' minds, know Devadatta's mind, and therefore definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, that bhikṣu may be junior, or middle-ranking, or senior, or young and not knowing himself. Why is this? Because since the Tathāgata has already definitively declared it, there is doubt and confusion about it. Ānanda, I do not see anyone in this world, whether among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, or from humans to celestials, who could definitively declare as I have declared regarding Devadatta. Why is this? Ānanda, I definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue. Ānanda, if I had seen in Devadatta even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality, I would not have definitively declared that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue. Ānanda, because I do not see in Devadatta even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality, therefore I definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue.

"Ānanda, suppose not far from a village there is a great, deep cesspit, and a person falls into it, sinking to the bottom. If someone comes, motivated by great compassion, caring and sympathizing, seeking benefit and welfare, seeking peace and happiness for that person, and upon arriving, looks around and says: 'Is there on this person a single clean spot, even as small as a hair's breadth, not stained by filth, so that I might grasp it and pull him out?' And looking all around, he does not see on this person a single clean spot, even as small as a hair's breadth, not stained by filth, that he could grasp to pull him out. Likewise, Ānanda, if I had seen in Devadatta even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality, I would not have definitively declared that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue. Ānanda, because I do not see in Devadatta even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality, therefore I definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue."

At this, the Venerable Ānanda wept and, wiping his tears with his hand, said: "World-Honored One! How remarkable! How extraordinary! That the World-Honored One should definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda! I definitively declare that Devadatta is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell, where he will remain for an entire kalpa, beyond rescue. Ānanda, if you were to hear from the Tathāgata the discernment of the great person's faculties through wisdom, you would surely gain supreme faith in the Tathāgata and feel joy."

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! Now is the right time. Well-Gone One! Now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus the discernment of the great person's faculties through wisdom, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the World-Honored One, will well receive and uphold it."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I shall now teach you the discernment of the great person's faculties through wisdom." The Venerable Ānanda received the teaching and listened.

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen, yet there remain wholesome roots that have not been cut off. From these wholesome roots, wholesome dharmas will again arise. Thus this person attains the dharma of purification. Ānanda, it is just as at dawn when the sun first rises, darkness is extinguished and light arises. Ānanda, what do you think? As the sun continues to rise until mealtime, has the darkness been extinguished and has the light arisen?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes indeed, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen, yet there remain wholesome roots that have not been cut off. From these wholesome roots, wholesome dharmas will again arise. Thus this person attains the dharma of purification. Ānanda, it is just as seeds of grain that are not damaged, not broken, not rotten, not split, not harmed by wind or heat, well stored in autumn. If a householder prepares good, fertile fields and sows the seeds in them, and rain irrigates them in due season. Ānanda, what do you think? Would those seeds be able to further grow and develop?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes indeed, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen, yet there remain wholesome roots that have not been cut off. From these wholesome roots, wholesome dharmas will again arise. Thus this person attains the dharma of purification. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen; there remain wholesome roots that have not yet been cut off, but they will certainly be cut off. Thus this person attains the dharma of decline. Ānanda, it is just as in the late afternoon when the sun is about to set, light is extinguished and darkness arises. Ānanda, what do you think? When the sun has already set, has the light been extinguished and has the darkness arisen?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes indeed, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen; there remain wholesome roots that have not yet been cut off, but they will certainly be cut off. Thus this person attains the dharma of decline. Ānanda, it is just as seeds of grain that are not damaged, not broken, not rotten, not split, not harmed by wind or heat, well stored in autumn. If a householder prepares good, fertile fields and sows the seeds in them, but rain does not come in due season. Ānanda, what do you think? Would those seeds be able to further grow and develop?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with wholesome dharmas and also endowed with unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's wholesome dharmas have been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's wholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and unwholesome dharmas have already arisen; there remain wholesome roots that have not yet been cut off, but they will certainly be cut off. Thus this person attains the dharma of decline. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind: 'I do not see in this person even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality. this person is completely filled in every direction with unwholesome dharmas, impure and defiled, which are the root of future existence, the cause of affliction, heat, suffering, and of birth, old age, illness, and death. Thus, when this person's body is destroyed and life ends, he is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell.' Ānanda, it is just as seeds that are rotten, damaged, broken, and split, harmed by wind and heat, not well stored in autumn. If a householder's field is not good soil, and it is not well prepared, and the seeds are sown in it, and rain does not come in due season. Ānanda, what do you think? Would those seeds be able to further grow and develop?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind: 'I do not see in this person even as much as a single hair's breadth of pure, wholesome quality; this person is completely filled in every direction with unwholesome dharmas, impure and defiled, which are the root of future existence, the cause of affliction, heat, suffering, and of birth, old age, illness, and death. Thus, when this person's body is destroyed and life ends, he is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell.' Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas."

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! You have already explained these three types of persons. Could you further explain three other types of persons?"

The World-Honored One said: "It can be explained. Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with unwholesome dharmas and also endowed with wholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's unwholesome dharmas have been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's unwholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have already arisen, yet there remain unwholesome roots that have not been cut off. From these unwholesome roots, unwholesome dharmas will again arise. Thus this person attains the dharma of decline. Ānanda, it is just as when a fire has just been kindled, completely burning through a pile of embers, and someone adds dry grass and supplies it with dry wood. Ānanda, what do you think? Would that fire grow further in intensity?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Yes indeed, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with unwholesome dharmas and also endowed with wholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's unwholesome dharmas have been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's unwholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have already arisen, yet there remain unwholesome roots that have not been cut off. From these unwholesome roots, unwholesome dharmas will again arise. Thus this person attains the dharma of decline. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with unwholesome dharmas and also endowed with wholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's unwholesome dharmas have been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's unwholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have already arisen; there remain unwholesome roots that have not yet been cut off, but they will certainly be cut off. Thus this person attains the dharma of purification. Ānanda, it is just as when a fire is burning intensely, completely burning through a pile of embers, and someone takes embers from this blazing fire and places them on flat, clean ground, or upon a rock. Ānanda, what do you think? Would that fire grow further in intensity?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind and knows that this person is endowed with unwholesome dharmas and also endowed with wholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, again observes this person's mind and knows that this person's unwholesome dharmas have been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have arisen. This person's unwholesome dharmas have already been extinguished and wholesome dharmas have already arisen; there remain unwholesome roots that have not yet been cut off, but they will certainly be cut off. Thus this person attains the dharma of purification. Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind: 'I do not see in this person even as much as a single hair's breadth of dark action. This person is completely filled in every direction with wholesome dharmas, giving happiness and happy consequences, certain to be reborn in a happy destination and attain long life. Thus, this person in this very present life is certain to attain parinirvāṇa.' Ānanda, it is just as charcoal that has long been extinguished and has become cold. Even if someone were to add dry grass and supply it with dry wood, Ānanda, what do you think? Could that dead charcoal be made to blaze again?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "No, World-Honored One!"

"Likewise, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, with the knowledge of others' minds, observes another person's mind: 'I do not see in this person even as much as a single hair's breadth of dark action. This person is completely filled in every direction with wholesome dharmas, giving happiness and happy consequences, certain to be reborn in a happy destination and attain long life. Thus, this person in this very present life is certain to attain parinirvāṇa.' Ānanda, this is called the Tathāgata's great person's discernment of faculties through wisdom. Thus the Tathāgata rightly knows the roots of all dharmas.

"Ānanda, of the first three persons spoken of earlier, the first person attains the dharma of purification, the second person attains the dharma of decline, and the third person, when his body is destroyed and life ends, is certain to reach a bad destination, to be reborn in hell. Of the latter three persons, the first person attains the dharma of decline, the second person attains the dharma of purification, and the third person in this very present life attains parinirvāṇa. Ānanda, I have now taught you the discernment of the great person's faculties through wisdom. As a respected teacher, out of great compassion for his disciples, caring and sympathizing, seeking benefit and welfare, seeking peace and happiness, I have now done this. You should further practice on your own. Go to secluded places, mountain forests, under trees, to empty and quiet places. Sit in meditation and reflect. Do not be heedless. Strive with diligence, so as not to have regret later. This is my instruction, this is my exhortation."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sixth Sūtra on Anupama.

## (113) Sūtra on the Root of All Dharmas, Seventh of the Forest Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If various non-Buddhist wanderers come and ask you, 'What is the root of all dharmas?' you should answer them thus: 'Desire is the root of all dharmas.' If they further ask, 'What is their conjunction?' you should answer thus: 'Contact is their conjunction.' If they further ask, 'What is their arising?' you should answer thus: 'Feeling is their arising.' If they further ask, 'What is their existence?' you should answer thus: 'Perception is their existence.' If they further ask, 'What is their chief ruler?' you should answer thus: 'Mindfulness is their chief ruler.' If they further ask, 'What is their forerunner?' you should answer thus: 'Concentration is their forerunner.' If they further ask, 'What is their supreme quality?' you should answer thus: 'Wisdom is their supreme quality.' If they further ask, 'What is their true essence?' you should answer thus: 'Liberation is their true essence.' If they further ask, 'What is their final end?' you should answer thus: 'Nirvāṇa is their final end.' Thus, bhikṣus, desire is the root of all dharmas, contact is the conjunction of all dharmas, feeling is the arising of all dharmas, perception is the existence of all dharmas, mindfulness is the chief ruler of all dharmas, concentration is the forerunner of all dharmas, wisdom is the supreme quality of all dharmas, liberation is the true essence of all dharmas, and nirvāṇa is the final end of all dharmas. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train in this way.

"Cultivate the mind of going forth from home to study the Way. Cultivate the perception of impermanence. Cultivate the perception that impermanence is suffering. Cultivate the perception that suffering is without self. Cultivate the perception of impurity. Cultivate the perception that food is loathsome. Cultivate the perception that nothing in the entire world is delightful. Cultivate the perception of death. Know the good and evil of the world, and cultivate such perceptions in the mind. Know the arising and existence of the world, and cultivate such perceptions in the mind. Know the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape from the world as they truly are, and cultivate such perceptions in the mind. If a bhikṣu succeeds in cultivating the mind of going forth from home to study the Way, succeeds in cultivating the perception of impermanence, succeeds in cultivating the perception that impermanence is suffering, succeeds in cultivating the perception that suffering is without self, succeeds in cultivating the perception of impurity, succeeds in cultivating the perception that food is loathsome, succeeds in cultivating the perception that nothing in the entire world is delightful, succeeds in cultivating the perception of death; knows the good and evil of the world and succeeds in cultivating such perceptions in the mind; knows the arising and existence of the world and succeeds in cultivating such perceptions in the mind; knows the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape from the world as they truly are and succeeds in cultivating such perceptions in the mind; this is called a bhikṣu who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and through right knowledge and right contemplation of all dharmas, has reached the end of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Root of All Dharmas, Seventh.

## (114) Sūtra on Uddaka, Eighth of the Forest Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Uddaka Rāmaputta, while among his assembly, frequently spoke thus: 'In this life, one observes this, one perceives this, yet does not know the root of the boil; afterward, one thoroughly knows the root of the boil.' Uddaka Rāmaputta did not possess omniscience, yet he claimed omniscience; he truly had no realization, yet he claimed realization. Uddaka Rāmaputta held this view and taught thus: 'Existence is a disease, a boil, a thorn. But if one is without perception, that is foolishness. If there is any perception at all, that is tranquility, that is the most excellent,' referring to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He took delight in himself, received within himself, and being attached to himself, he cultivated up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. When his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn among the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. When his lifespan there was exhausted, he returned to this world and was reborn among wildcats. This bhikṣu who speaks rightly says: 'In this life, one observes this, one perceives this, yet does not know the root of the boil; afterward, one thoroughly knows the root of the boil.'

"How does a bhikṣu rightly observe? A bhikṣu knows the six kinds of contact, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, knows the escape from them, and knows them as they truly are through wisdom. This is called a bhikṣu's right observation. How does a bhikṣu perceive? A bhikṣu knows the three feelings, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, knows the escape from them, and knows them as they truly are through wisdom. This is called a bhikṣu's perception. How does a bhikṣu not know the root of the boil and afterward thoroughly know the root of the boil? A bhikṣu knows that craving for existence has ceased, has uprooted its root, and it will ultimately never arise again. This is called a bhikṣu who did not know the root of the boil and afterward thoroughly knows the root of the boil. The 'boil' refers to this body. It is composed of coarse form from the four great elements, born from father and mother, nourished by food and drink, dependent on clothing and bedding, massage, bathing, and forceful endurance. It is subject to the law of impermanence, destruction, and dissolution. This is called the boil. The 'root of the boil' refers to the three types of craving: craving for sensual desire, craving for form, and craving for formlessness. These are called the root of the boil. The 'all the outflows of the boil' refer to the six bases of contact. The eye has outflows through seeing forms, the ear has outflows through hearing sounds, the nose has outflows through smelling odors, the tongue has outflows through tasting flavors, the body has outflows through sensing touches, and the mind has outflows through cognizing dharmas. These are called all the outflows of the boil.

"Bhikṣus! I have already explained for you the boil and explained the root of the boil, as a worthy teacher who acts with great compassion for his disciples, with sympathetic concern and pity, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their peace and happiness. I have now already done this. You also should do your own part. Go to secluded places, to mountain forests, under trees, to empty and quiet places, sit in meditation and contemplate. Do not be negligent. Diligently apply effort so that you will not have regret later. This is my instruction; this is my admonition."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Uddaka, Eighth.
