## (115) Sūtra on the Simile of the Honey Ball, Ninth of the Forest Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyans, at Kapilavastu.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, at dawn dressed in his robes, took his bowl, and entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. After eating, in the afternoon he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and went to the Bamboo Grove, the Śākya temple. Entering that great forest, he reached a tree, spread his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged.

Then the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, walking with his staff, strolling about in the afternoon, came to where the Buddha was. They exchanged greetings, and leaning on his staff, he stood before the Buddha and asked the World-Honored One: "Ascetic Gautama! What is your fundamental doctrine? What dharma do you teach?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Śākyan! Such that in all the world, among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, there is no conflict; cultivating the practice of separation from desire, the pure brahmin practice, abandoning flattery and crookedness, removing regret, not being attached to existence or non-existence, and also being free from perception. This is my fundamental doctrine; what I teach is likewise."

Then the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, having heard what the Buddha said, neither affirmed nor denied it. He shook his head and left.

Then the World-Honored One, not long after the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi had left, in the late afternoon arose from meditation, went to the assembly hall, spread a seat before the community of bhikṣus and sat down, and addressed the bhikṣus: "This morning I dressed in my robes, took my bowl, and entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. After eating, in the afternoon I put away my robes and bowl, washed my hands and feet, placed my sitting cloth upon my shoulder, and went to the Bamboo Grove, the Śākya temple. Entering that great forest, I reached a tree, spread my sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged. Then the Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, walking with his staff, strolling about in the afternoon, came to where I was. We exchanged greetings, and leaning on his staff, he stood before me and asked me: 'Ascetic Gautama! What is your fundamental doctrine? What dharma do you teach?' I answered: 'Śākyan! Such that in all the world, among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, there is no conflict; cultivating the practice of separation from desire, the pure brahmin practice, abandoning flattery and crookedness, removing regret, not being attached to existence or non-existence, and also being free from perception. This is my fundamental doctrine; what I teach is likewise.' That Śākyan Daṇḍapāṇi, having heard what I said, neither affirmed nor denied it. He shook his head and left."

Then a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! How is it that in all the world, among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, there is no conflict? How does one cultivate the practice of separation from desire to attain the pure brahmin practice? How does one abandon flattery and crookedness, remove regret, not be attached to existence or non-existence, and also be free from perception?"

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu! Whatever is the basis through which a person's thoughts arise regarding going forth from home to study the Way, mental cultivation and practice, and dharmas of the past, future, and present, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus, then rose from his seat and entered his room to meditate.

Then the bhikṣus had this thought: "Venerables! You should know that the World-Honored One has briefly stated this meaning without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to meditate: 'Whatever is the basis through which a person's thoughts arise regarding going forth from home to study the Way, mental cultivation and practice, and dharmas of the past, future, and present, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering.'" They further thought: "Venerables! Who is able to explain in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?" They further thought: "The Venerable Mahākaccāna is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise ones living the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. Venerables! Let us go together to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and request that he explain this meaning. If the Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it in detail, we shall well receive and retain it."

Then the bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was. They exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Mahākaccāna! You should know that the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to meditate: 'Bhikṣu! Whatever is the basis through which a person's thoughts arise regarding going forth from home to study the Way, mental cultivation and practice, and dharmas of the past, future, and present, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering.' We then had this thought: 'Venerables! Who is able to explain in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?' We further thought: 'The Venerable Mahākaccāna is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise ones living the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated.' We wish that the Venerable Mahākaccāna, out of compassion, would explain it in full."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said: "Venerables! Listen to my simile. The wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Venerables! It is as if a person wished to find the heartwood. Seeking the heartwood, he took an axe and entered the forest. He saw a great tree complete with roots, trunk, knots, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. That person did not touch the roots, trunk, knots, or fruit, but only touched the branches and leaves. What you venerables have done is just like this. The World-Honored One is present, yet you set him aside and come to me to ask about this meaning. Why is that? Venerables! You should know that the World-Honored One is the eye, is wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma, is the lord of the Dharma, is the general of the Dharma. He speaks the meaning of true truth, and all meanings are revealed through that World-Honored One. You venerables should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning: 'World-Honored One! What is this? What is the meaning of this?' As the World-Honored One explains, you venerables should well receive and retain it."

Then the bhikṣus said: "Yes, indeed. Venerable Mahākaccāna! The World-Honored One is the eye, is wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma, is the lord of the Dharma, is the general of the Dharma. He speaks the meaning of true truth, and all meanings are revealed through that World-Honored One. We should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning: 'World-Honored One! What is this? What is the meaning of this?' As the World-Honored One explains, we shall well receive and retain it. However, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise ones living the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. We wish that the Venerable Mahākaccāna, out of compassion, would explain it in full."

The Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, all of you listen to what I have to say. Venerables! Dependent on the eye and on form, eye-consciousness arises. When these three come together, there is contact. Dependent on contact, there is feeling. What is felt is then perceived. What is perceived is then thought about. What is thought about is then given rise to in thought. What is given rise to in thought is then proliferated. A bhikṣu, based on such thought, goes forth from home to study the Way, engaging in mental cultivation and practice. Regarding past, future, and present dharmas herein, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. Dependent on the mind and on dharmas, mind-consciousness arises. When these three come together, there is contact. Dependent on contact, there is feeling. What is felt is then perceived. What is perceived is then thought about. What is thought about is then given rise to in thought. What is given rise to in thought is then proliferated. A bhikṣu, based on such thought, goes forth from home to study the Way, engaging in mental cultivation and practice. Regarding past, future, and present dharmas herein, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering.

"Venerables! If a bhikṣu, apart from the eye, apart from form, apart from eye-consciousness, were to designate contact while there is contact, such a situation is impossible. If contact is not designated, yet one were to designate feeling while there is feeling, such a situation is impossible. If feeling is not designated, yet one were to designate thought, going forth from home to study the Way, and mental cultivation and practice, such a situation is impossible. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If, apart from the mind, apart from dharmas, apart from mind-consciousness, one were to designate contact while there is contact, such a situation is impossible. If contact is not designated, yet one were to designate feeling while there is feeling, such a situation is impossible. If feeling is not designated, yet one were to designate thought, going forth from home to study the Way, and mental cultivation and practice, such a situation is impossible.

"Venerables! If a bhikṣu, based on the eye, based on form, based on eye-consciousness, designates contact while there is contact, such a situation necessarily exists. Based on the designation of contact, one designates feeling while there is feeling; such a situation necessarily exists. Based on the designation of feeling, one designates thought, going forth from home to study the Way, and mental cultivation and practice; such a situation necessarily exists. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. Based on the mind, based on dharmas, based on mind-consciousness, one designates contact while there is contact; such a situation necessarily exists. Based on the designation of contact, one designates feeling while there is feeling; such a situation necessarily exists. Based on the designation of feeling, one designates thought, going forth from home to study the Way, and mental cultivation and practice; such a situation necessarily exists. Venerables! This is what the World-Honored One briefly stated without explaining in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to meditate: 'Bhikṣu! Whatever is the basis through which a person's thoughts arise regarding going forth from home to study the Way, mental cultivation and practice, and dharmas of the past, future, and present, if one does not love them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, does not dwell in them, this is called the end of suffering. The tendency of desire, the tendency of aversion, the tendency of existence, the tendency of conceit, the tendency of ignorance, the tendency of views, the tendency of doubt, conflict, enmity, flattery, deceit, false speech, divisive speech, and immeasurable evil unwholesome dharmas; this is called the end of suffering.' This meaning that the World-Honored One briefly stated without explaining in detail, I have now explained in full with these phrases and this text. Venerables! You may go and present this to the Buddha. If it accords with the meaning as the World-Honored One would explain it, then you venerables may receive and retain it."

Then the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahākaccāna said, well received and recited it, rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Mahākaccāna three times, and departed. They went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads in salutation, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Earlier, the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to meditate. The Venerable Mahākaccāna has explained it in full with these phrases and this text."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Among my disciples there is one who has the eye, who has wisdom, who has the Dharma, who has the meaning. Why is that? When the teacher briefly states the meaning for his disciples without explaining it in detail, that disciple explains it in full with these phrases and this text. Just as the bhikṣu Kaccāna has explained it, you should receive and retain it accordingly. Why is that? Because when one contemplates and explains the meaning, it should be thus. Bhikṣus! It is as if a person, while walking in a desolate place, among mountains, forests, and trees, suddenly found a honey ball. Whatever part of it he tasted, he would experience its flavor. In the same way, a son of good family, in this right Dharma and discipline of mine, whatever part he contemplates, he experiences its flavor: contemplating the eye, he experiences its flavor; contemplating the ear, nose, tongue, body; contemplating the mind, he experiences its flavor."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a whisk. Then the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! What is the name of this teaching? How should I receive and retain it?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda! This teaching is called the Simile of the Honey Ball. You should receive and retain it."

Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "All of you, receive this teaching of the Simile of the Honey Ball and recite and study it. Why is that? Bhikṣus! This Simile of the Honey Ball contains the Dharma and the meaning. It is the foundation of the holy life, leading to penetration, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. If a son of good family has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, he should well receive and retain this Simile of the Honey Ball."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Simile of the Honey Ball, Ninth.

## (116) Sūtra on Gautamī, Tenth of the Forest Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyans, at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, together with a great community of bhikṣus, observing the summer retreat.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of the ascetic life? For this reason, can a woman, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way?"

The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop! Gautamī! Do not form such a thought: 'A woman may, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way.' Gautamī! Rather, you should shave your head, don the kāṣāya robes, and for the rest of your life purely cultivate the holy life."

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been refused by the Buddha, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, the bhikṣus were mending robes for the Buddha, as the World-Honored One would soon finish the summer retreat among the Śākyans, complete the mending of robes, and after the three months had passed, would take up his robes and bowl and travel among the people. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī heard that the bhikṣus were mending robes for the Buddha, that the World-Honored One would soon finish the summer retreat among the Śākyans, complete the mending of robes, and after the three months had passed, would take up his robes and bowl and travel among the people. Having heard this, she again went to where the Buddha was, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of the ascetic life? For this reason, can a woman, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way?"

The World-Honored One again said a second time: "Stop! Stop! Gautamī! Do not form such a thought: 'A woman may, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way.' Gautamī! Rather, you should shave your head, don the kāṣāya robes, and for the rest of your life purely cultivate the holy life."

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been refused by the Buddha a second time, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished the summer retreat among the Śākyans, completed the mending of robes, and after the three months had passed, took up his robes and bowl and traveled among the people. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī heard that the World-Honored One had finished the summer retreat among the Śākyans, completed the mending of robes, and after the three months had passed, had taken up his robes and bowl and was traveling among the people. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then, together with the elder Śākya women, followed after the Buddha, traveling gradually until she reached Nāmadika, and stayed at the Kuṇḍikā Monastery in Nāmadika. Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī again went to where the Buddha was, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of the ascetic life? For this reason, can a woman, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way?"

The World-Honored One said a third time: "Stop! Stop! Gautamī! Do not form such a thought: 'A woman may, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way.' Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī! Rather, you should shave your head, don the kāṣāya robes, and for the rest of your life purely cultivate the holy life."

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been refused by the World-Honored One a third time, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī stood outside the gate, barefoot and soiled, her body covered with dust, exhausted and weeping. The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing outside the gate, barefoot and soiled, her body covered with dust, exhausted and weeping. Having seen this, he asked: "Gautamī! For what reason are you standing outside the gate, barefoot and soiled, your body covered with dust, exhausted and weeping?"

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī answered: "Venerable Ānanda! Women are not permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Gautamī! Please wait here for now. I will go to the Buddha and report this matter."

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said: "Very well, Venerable Ānanda."

Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of the ascetic life? For this reason, can a woman, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way?"

The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop! Ānanda! Do not form such a thought: 'A woman may, in this right Dharma and discipline, with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way.' Ānanda! If women were permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, it would cause the holy life to not endure long. Ānanda! It is as if a household with many women and few men; can that household continue to flourish and prosper?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise, Ānanda! If women were permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, it would cause the holy life to not endure long. Ānanda! It is as if in a rice field or a wheat field, when blight arises, it will surely ruin that field. Likewise, Ānanda! If women were permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, it would cause the holy life to not endure long."

The Venerable Ānanda further said: "World-Honored One! Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to the World-Honored One. Why is that? After the World-Honored One's mother passed away, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī nurtured and raised the World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda! Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to me, having nurtured and raised me after my mother passed away. Ānanda! I have also been of great benefit to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Why is that? Ānanda! Because of me, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, taken refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus, is free from doubt regarding the Three Jewels and regarding suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path, has accomplished faith, upholds the precepts, has cultivated learning and broad hearing, has accomplished generosity, and has attained wisdom. She refrains from killing and has abandoned killing, refrains from taking what is not given and has abandoned taking what is not given, refrains from sexual misconduct and has abandoned sexual misconduct, refrains from false speech and has abandoned false speech, refrains from intoxicants and has abandoned intoxicants. Ānanda! If any person, because of another person, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, takes refuge in the Sangha of bhikṣus, is free from doubt regarding the Three Jewels and regarding suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path, accomplishes faith, upholds the precepts, cultivates learning and broad hearing, accomplishes generosity, and attains wisdom, refrains from killing and abandons killing, refrains from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given, refrains from sexual misconduct and abandons sexual misconduct, refrains from false speech and abandons false speech, refrains from intoxicants and abandons intoxicants, Ānanda, even if that person were to provide that other person with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all the necessities of life for the rest of their life, they still could not fully repay the debt of gratitude.

"Ānanda! I now establish for women eight rules of respect for the teacher, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives. Ānanda! It is as if a fisherman or a fisherman's apprentice builds a dam in deep water to guard and protect the water, not allowing it to flow out. Likewise, Ānanda, I now establish for women eight rules of respect for the teacher, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives. What are the eight? Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī must seek full ordination from bhikṣus. Ānanda! I establish this as the first rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī must go to bhikṣus every half month to receive instruction. Ānanda! I establish this as the second rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! If there is a place of residence where there are no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs must not observe the summer retreat there. Ānanda! I establish this as the third rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! After a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat, she must, before both communities, invite criticism on three matters: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected. Ānanda! I establish this as the fourth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! If a bhikṣu does not permit a bhikṣuṇī to ask questions, then the bhikṣuṇī must not ask a bhikṣu about the sūtras, the vinaya, or the abhidharma. If permission is given to ask, the bhikṣuṇī may ask about the sūtras, the vinaya, or the abhidharma. Ānanda! I establish this as the fifth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of the transgressions of a bhikṣu, but a bhikṣu may speak of the transgressions of a bhikṣuṇī. Ānanda! I establish this as the sixth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! If a bhikṣuṇī commits a Sangha-remainder offense, she must undergo a fifteen-day mānatta discipline before both communities. Ānanda! I establish this as the seventh rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been fully ordained for a hundred years, she must still bow her head in salutation with the utmost humility toward a bhikṣu who has just received full ordination, respectfully attend to him, and greet him with joined palms. Ānanda! I establish this as the eighth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Ānanda! I establish for women these eight rules of respect for the teacher, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives. Ānanda! If Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī upholds these eight rules of respect for the teacher, she may, in this right Dharma and discipline, go forth from home to study the Way, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, well received and retained it, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, departed, and went to where Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was. He said: "Gautamī! Women are permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī! The World-Honored One has established for women these eight rules of respect for the teacher, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives. What are the eight? Gautamī! A bhikṣuṇī must seek full ordination from bhikṣus. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the first rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! A bhikṣuṇī must go to bhikṣus every half month to receive instruction. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the second rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! If there is a place of residence where there are no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs must not observe the summer retreat there. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the third rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! After a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat, she must, before both communities, invite criticism on three matters: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the fourth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! If a bhikṣu does not permit a bhikṣuṇī to ask questions, then the bhikṣuṇī must not ask a bhikṣu about the sūtras, the vinaya, or the abhidharma. If permission is given to ask, the bhikṣuṇī may ask about the sūtras, the vinaya, or the abhidharma. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the fifth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of the transgressions of a bhikṣu, but a bhikṣu may speak of the transgressions of a bhikṣuṇī. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the sixth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! If a bhikṣuṇī commits a Sangha-remainder offense, she must undergo a fifteen-day mānatta discipline before both communities. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the seventh rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been fully ordained for a hundred years, she must still bow her head in salutation with the utmost humility toward a bhikṣu who has just received full ordination, respectfully attend to him, and greet him with joined palms. Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes this as the eighth rule of respect for the teacher for women, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives.

"Gautamī! The World-Honored One establishes for women these eight rules of respect for the teacher, which women must not transgress, which women are to uphold for the rest of their lives. Gautamī! The World-Honored One has said thus: 'If Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī upholds these eight rules of respect for the teacher, she may, in this right Dharma and discipline, go forth from home to study the Way, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī.'"

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said: "Venerable Ānanda! Listen to my simile. The wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Venerable Ānanda! It is as if a kṣatriya maiden, or a brahmin, householder, or artisan maiden, who is beautiful and graceful, has thoroughly bathed, anointed her body with fragrance, donned bright clean garments, and adorned herself with various ornaments. Or suppose someone, thinking of that maiden, seeking her benefit and welfare, seeking her peace and happiness, were to offer her a garland of blue lotus petals, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of sumanā flowers, or a garland of vārṣika flowers, or a garland of atimukta flowers. That maiden would joyfully receive them with both hands and place them upon her head as adornment. Likewise, Venerable Ānanda! The World-Honored One has established for women these eight rules of respect for the teacher. For the rest of my life, I reverently receive them upon my head and will uphold them."

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, in the right Dharma and discipline, went forth from home to study the Way, received full ordination, and became a bhikṣuṇī. Later, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī became a great elder bhikṣuṇī, and together with senior, eminent bhikṣuṇīs who were known by kings and had long cultivated the holy life, she went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, bowed in salutation, stood to one side, and said: "Venerable Ānanda! You should know that these bhikṣuṇīs are senior, eminent, known by kings, and have long cultivated the holy life. Yet those bhikṣus are junior, newly trained, who went forth later and entered this right Dharma and discipline only recently. We wish that those bhikṣus would bow in salutation to the bhikṣuṇīs according to seniority, respectfully attend to them, and greet them with joined palms."

Then the Venerable Ānanda said: "Gautamī! Please wait here for now. I will go to the Buddha and report this matter."

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said: "Very well, Venerable Ānanda."

Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Today, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with senior, eminent bhikṣuṇīs who are known by kings and have long cultivated the holy life, came to where I was, bowed at my feet, stood to one side, joined her palms, and said to me: 'Venerable Ānanda! These bhikṣuṇīs are senior, eminent, known by kings, and have long cultivated the holy life. Yet those bhikṣus are junior, newly trained, who went forth later and entered this right Dharma and discipline only recently. We wish that those bhikṣus would bow in salutation to the bhikṣuṇīs according to seniority, respectfully attend to them, and greet them with joined palms.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop! Ānanda! Guard this speech and do not speak thus. Ānanda! If you knew as I know, you should not speak even a single sentence, let alone speak like this. Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, brahmins and householders would spread their garments on the ground and say: 'May the diligent ascetics walk upon this. The diligent ascetics practice what is difficult to practice. May we gain benefit and welfare for the long night, peace and happiness.' Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, brahmins and householders would spread their hair on the ground and say: 'May the diligent ascetics walk upon this. The diligent ascetics practice what is difficult to practice. May we gain benefit and welfare for the long night, peace and happiness.'

"Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, brahmins and householders, upon seeing ascetics, would offer them various foods and drinks with their hands, wait by the roadside, and say: 'Venerables! Please accept this, eat this, take this and go; use it as you wish. May we gain benefit and welfare for the long night, peace and happiness.' Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, faithful brahmins, upon seeing diligent ascetics, would respectfully embrace them, lead them inside, and offer various possessions to the diligent ascetics, saying: 'Venerables! Please accept this, take this and go; use it as you wish. May we gain benefit and welfare for the long night, peace and happiness.'

"Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, then the sun and moon, though possessing great power of accomplishment, great majesty, great blessings, and great spiritual power, would still not match the majestic spiritual virtue of the diligent ascetics, let alone the emaciated non-Buddhist wanderers! Ānanda! If women had not been permitted, in this right Dharma and discipline, to with faith leave the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, the right Dharma would have endured for a thousand years. Now five hundred years have been lost, and only five hundred years remain. Ānanda! You should know that women cannot accomplish five things. If a woman were to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, or a wheel-turning king, or Indra lord of the gods, or the king of Māras, or a Great Brahmā, such a situation is utterly impossible. You should know that men can accomplish five things. If a man were to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, or a wheel-turning king, or Indra lord of the gods, or the king of Māras, or a Great Brahmā, such a situation is certainly possible."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Gautamī, Tenth.

### (113) Sūtra on the Various Wholesome Dharmas

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada's Park in Jeta's Grove near Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is not being negligent in wholesome dharmas. If a bhikṣu is not negligent in wholesome dharmas, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is being skillful in observing and contemplating dharmas. If a bhikṣu is skillful in observing and contemplating dharmas, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is eagerness of aspiration. If a bhikṣu has eagerness of aspiration, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is the ability to guard oneself. If a bhikṣu is able to guard himself, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is vigor. If a bhikṣu has vigor, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is mindfulness. If a bhikṣu has mindfulness, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is concentration. If a bhikṣu has concentration, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu accomplishes one dharma, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant. What is this one dharma? It is wisdom. If a bhikṣu has wisdom, then he will attain the arising of what has not yet arisen, and what has already arisen will increase and become abundant."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

## (117) Sūtra on Softness, First of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Since in the past I left home and studied the Way, I came from a life of ease, leisure, comfort, and the utmost softness. When I was in the home of my father, King Śuddhodana, palaces of various kinds were built for me: a spring palace, a summer palace, and a winter palace, all for my pleasant amusement. Not far from the palaces, various lotus pools of many kinds were also constructed: blue lotus pools, pink lotus pools, red lotus pools, and white lotus pools. In those pools were planted various water flowers: blue lotuses, pink lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses, with water always present and flowers always blooming, and people were assigned to guard them, not permitting anyone else access, all for my pleasant amusement. On the banks of those pools were planted various land flowers: sumanā flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mātuluṅga flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pāṭali flowers, all for my pleasant amusement. Four attendants would bathe me. After bathing me, red sandalwood fragrance was applied to my body. After the fragrance was applied to my body, I would put on new silk garments; upper and lower, inner and outer, every layer was new. Day and night, a parasol was constantly held over me, so that the prince would not be dampened by dew at night or scorched by the sun during the day. In ordinary households, coarse flour, barley rice, bean soup, and ginger vegetables were considered the finest food; yet in my father Śuddhodana's household, even the lowest servants had polished rice and delicacies as their finest food.

"Furthermore, as for wild game, the finest game birds such as tittira, kapinjala, and various other delicacies, such finest wild game was always prepared and set out as food for me.

"I recall that in the past, in my father Śuddhodana's household, during the four months of summer, I would ascend to the main palace, where there were no men, only female musicians for my entertainment, and I never came down at all. When I wished to go out to the park for an excursion, thirty renowned riders on specially selected superior mounts would form a procession before and behind, attending and escorting me, to say nothing of the rest. I had such a state of comfort; this was the utmost softness.

"I further recall that once, while watching the field workers resting in the fields, I went to a jambu tree, sat cross-legged, and, separated from desires, separated from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of separation, I attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna. I then had this thought: 'The unlearned, foolish ordinary person, who himself is subject to the dharma of illness and not free from illness, upon seeing another person who is ill, feels aversion, contempt, and dislike, without examining himself.' I further had this thought: 'I myself am subject to the dharma of illness and not free from illness. If, upon seeing another who is ill, I feel aversion, contempt, and dislike, that would not be fitting for me, for I too am subject to this dharma.' Having contemplated thus, whatever pride arising on account of being free from illness was immediately extinguished. I further had this thought: 'The unlearned, foolish ordinary person, who himself is subject to the dharma of aging and not free from aging, upon seeing another person who is old, feels aversion, contempt, and dislike, without examining himself.'

"I further had this thought: 'I myself am subject to the dharma of aging and not free from aging. If, upon seeing another who is old, I feel aversion, contempt, and dislike, that would not be fitting for me, for I too am subject to this dharma.' Having contemplated thus, whatever pride arising on account of youth was immediately extinguished. The unlearned, foolish ordinary person, being proud, arrogant, and heedless on account of being free from illness, produces delusion through desires and does not practice the holy life. The unlearned, foolish ordinary person, being proud, arrogant, and heedless on account of youth, produces delusion through desires and does not practice the holy life. The unlearned, foolish ordinary person, being proud, arrogant, and heedless on account of being alive, produces delusion through desires and does not practice the holy life."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"The dharma of illness, the dharma of aging,
And the dharma of death:
These dharmas are inherent in oneself,
Yet ordinary people find them hateful in others.
If I were to feel aversion,
Not transcending these dharmas,
That would not be fitting for me,
For I too am subject to these dharmas.
When one practices thus, knowing the dharma and transcending birth,
Pride in being free from illness, in youth, and in being alive
Is entirely cut off.
Seeing the peace of desirelessness,
One thus awakens, free from fear regarding desires,
Attaining the perception of nonexistence,
Practicing the pure holy life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on Softness, the First
