## (118) Sūtra on the Dragon-Elephant, Second of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the World-Honored One, during the afternoon, rose from his meditative rest, came down from the hall, and said: "Udāyin! Come with me to the eastern river to bathe."

The Venerable Udāyin replied: "Yes, indeed."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One took the Venerable Udāyin and went to the eastern river, removed his robes on the bank, and entered the water to bathe. After bathing, he came out, dried his body, and put on his robes.

At that time, King Prasenajit had a dragon-elephant named Nianyi (Recollection), which was parading with all kinds of musical performances across the eastern river. When the crowd saw it, they exclaimed: "This is a dragon among dragons, a great dragon-king! Who could this be?"

The Venerable Udāyin, with palms joined facing the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! The elephant has received a great body, and the crowd, seeing it, exclaims: 'This is a dragon among dragons, a great dragon-king! Who could this be?'"

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Udāyin! So it is, Udāyin! The elephant has received a great body, and the crowd, seeing it, exclaims: 'This is a dragon among dragons, a great dragon-king! Who could this be?' Udāyin, when a horse, camel, bull, donkey, serpent, human, or tree is born with a great form, Udāyin, the crowd, seeing it, exclaims: 'This is a dragon among dragons, a great dragon-king! Who could this be?' Udāyin, if there is anyone in the world, including devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, from humans to heavenly beings, who does not harm with body, speech, or mind, I call that one a dragon. Udāyin, the Tathāgata, in the world, including devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, from humans to heavenly beings, does not harm with body, speech, or mind; therefore I am called a dragon."

Thereupon, the Venerable Udāyin, with palms joined facing the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! I pray that the World-Honored One grant me his power, that the Well-Gone One grant me his power, that I may, in the Buddha's presence, praise the World-Honored One with verses befitting the dragon."

The World-Honored One said: "Do as you wish."

Thereupon, the Venerable Udāyin, in the Buddha's presence, praised the World-Honored One with verses befitting the dragon:

"The Perfectly Enlightened One, born among humans,
Self-controlled, attained right samādhi,
Cultivating and practicing the path of Brahmā,
With stilled mind, able to delight in oneself.
Revered and honored by people,
Having surpassed all dharmas,
Also revered by the devas,
The unattached, truly realized one.
Having crossed over all fetters,
From the forest, gone beyond the forest,
Abandoning desire, delighting in desirelessness,
Like gold refined from stone.
Renowned as the Perfectly and Fully Enlightened One,
Like the sun rising in the sky,
The highest among all dragons,
Like a peak among all mountains.
Called by the name 'Great Dragon,'
Yet causing no harm whatsoever,
The dragon among all dragons,
The true and unsurpassed dragon.
Gentle warmth and harmlessness:
These two are the dragon's feet.
Austerity and the holy life:
These are called the dragon's conduct.
The great dragon's hands are faith;
The two tusks are meritorious virtues;
The neck is mindfulness, the head is wisdom;
Contemplation discriminates the Dharma.
Upholding all dharmas is the belly;
Delighting in seclusion, the two arms;
Dwelling in the good cessation of in-breath and out-breath,
Inwardly the mind reaches excellent samādhi.
The dragon in movement is in samādhi;
When still, also in samādhi;
Sitting in samādhi, lying also in samādhi;
The dragon is in samādhi at all times:
This is called the dragon's constant dharma.
At a pure household, he accepts food;
Where there is impurity, he does not accept.
Receiving bad or impure food,
He discards it like a lion.
What offerings he receives,
He accepts out of compassion for others.
The dragon eats the faithful offerings of others,
Sustaining life without attachment.
Having cut off all great and small fetters,
Liberated from all bonds,
Wherever he goes and roams,
His mind has no attachment.
Just as the white lotus flower,
Born in water, nourished by water,
Is not stained by muddy water,
With wondrous fragrance and lovely color;
So the supreme enlightened one,
Born in the world, moving in the world,
Is not defiled by desires,
Like the flower unstained by water.
Just as a blazing fire,
If not fed with fuel, ceases;
Without fuel, the fire does not spread:
This fire is called extinguished.
The wise use this simile,
Wishing to make the meaning understood.
This is what the dragon knows,
What the dragon among dragons has spoken.
Far removed from lust and anger,
Having cut off delusion and attained freedom from defilements,
When the dragon relinquishes his body,
This dragon is said to be extinguished."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Udāyin, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Dragon-Elephant, the Second

---

## (119) Sūtra on Topics of Discussion, Third of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three topics of discussion, no four and no five. If a bhikṣu, having seen something, on that basis speaks, saying 'I have seen, heard, cognized, or known,' the bhikṣu speaks what he declares to be his own knowledge. What are the three? A bhikṣu speaks on the basis of the past, saying 'Thus it was in the past.' A bhikṣu speaks on the basis of the future, saying 'Thus it will be in the future.' A bhikṣu speaks on the basis of the present, saying 'Thus it is in the present.' These are the three topics of discussion, no four and no five. If a bhikṣu, having seen something, on that basis speaks, saying 'I have seen, heard, cognized, or known,' the bhikṣu speaks what he declares to be his own knowledge. Through what is spoken, one skillfully grasps the meaning; through what is not spoken, one does not skillfully grasp the meaning.

"When a noble disciple listens to the Dharma with both ears and a unified mind, having listened to the Dharma with both ears and a unified mind, he abandons one dharma, cultivates one dharma, and realizes one dharma. Having abandoned one dharma, cultivated one dharma, and realized one dharma, he attains right samādhi. When a noble disciple's mind has attained right samādhi, he cuts off all lust, anger, and delusion. When a noble disciple has thus attained liberation of mind, being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. Based on what is spoken, there are four bases by which one should examine a person, to determine whether this worthy one can be spoken with or cannot be spoken with. If this worthy one, when presented with a categorical question, does not give a categorical answer; when presented with an analytical question, does not give an analytical answer; when presented with a counter-question, does not respond with a counter-question; when presented with a question to be set aside, does not set it aside; then this worthy one cannot be spoken with, nor can one engage in discussion with him. If this worthy one, when presented with a categorical question, gives a categorical answer; when presented with an analytical question, gives an analytical answer; when presented with a counter-question, responds with a counter-question; when presented with a question to be set aside, sets it aside; then this worthy one can be spoken with, and one can engage in discussion with him.

"Furthermore, based on what is spoken, there are another four bases by which one should examine a person, to determine whether this worthy one can be spoken with or cannot be spoken with. If this worthy one does not abide in what is possible and impossible, does not abide in what is known, does not abide in the use of similes, and does not abide in the path of practice, then this worthy one cannot be spoken with, nor can one engage in discussion with him. If this worthy one abides in what is possible and impossible, abides in what is known, abides in the use of similes, and abides in the path of practice, then this worthy one can be spoken with, and one can engage in discussion with him. When speaking based on these, one should still the activities of speech, relinquish one's own views, relinquish enmity and resentment, relinquish desire, relinquish anger, relinquish delusion, relinquish pride, relinquish silence born of stubbornness, relinquish jealousy and stinginess, not seeking victory, not subduing others, and not seizing upon the other's mistakes. One should speak of meaning and speak of Dharma. Having spoken of meaning and spoken of Dharma, one should instruct and then cease instructing, rejoice oneself and cause the other to rejoice. Speaking of meaning in this way, speaking of matters in this way, this is the noble way of speaking of meaning, this is the noble way of speaking of matters, which leads to the ultimate end of all defilements."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"If there are disputatious debates,
With mixed intentions harboring pride,
Ignoble, slandering virtue,
Each seeking the other's faults;
Only seeking the other's mistakes,
Intending to subdue the other,
Competing to overcome each other:
The noble ones do not speak thus.
If one wishes to engage in discussion,
The wise should know the right time.
There is Dharma and there is meaning:
The noble ones discuss in this way.
The wise speak in this manner,
Without contention, without pride,
The mind never weary,
Without fetters, without defilements.
Following along without perversion,
Speaking with right knowledge,
Approving of what is well spoken,
And never speaking ill oneself.
Not engaging in disputatious debate,
Nor accepting contention from others,
Knowing the basis and the topic of discussion:
This is what they discuss.
Thus do the noble ones speak;
The wise together gain the meaning,
For the happiness of the present life,
And also for the well-being of the future.
Know the one who is intelligent and discerning:
He does not speak in a perverted or habitual way."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Topics of Discussion, the Third

---

## (120) Sūtra on Impermanence, Fourth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. Feeling is also impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. Perception is also impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. Mental formations are also impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. Consciousness is also impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. Thus, form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not self. A learned noble disciple, contemplating thus, cultivates the seven factors of the path, with unobstructed right thought and right mindfulness. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the defilement of desire, liberated from the defilement of existence, liberated from the defilement of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. Among all sentient beings and the nine abodes of sentient beings, up to and including the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the remaining foremost existence, among all of these, the first, the great, the supreme, the highest, the most honored, the most excellent is the arahant in the world. Why is this? Because the arahant in the world has attained the peace, comfort, and happiness of security."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"The unattached one has the foremost happiness;
Having cut off desire, without craving,
Forever abandoning the conceit of 'I,'
Tearing apart the net of ignorance.
He attains the immovable;
In his mind there is no impurity.
Not attached to the world,
The holy life attains freedom from defilements.
Having fully understood the five aggregates,
With the seven wholesome dharmas as his domain,
Where the great hero roams,
Separated from all fears.
Accomplished in the seven jewels of awakening,
Complete in the three trainings,
With excellent reputation and noble companions,
The Buddha's foremost true son.
Accomplished in the tenfold path,
The great dragon with deeply concentrated mind:
He is the foremost in the world,
And in him there is no craving.
Unmoved by all things,
Liberated from future existence,
Having cut off birth, old age, sickness, and death,
His task accomplished, his defilements extinguished.
He arouses the wisdom of the non-learner,
Having obtained the final body,
Fully endowed with the foremost holy life;
His mind does not depend on others.
Above, below, and in all directions,
He has no delight or pleasure in them.
He is able to roar the lion's roar:
The unsurpassed awakened one of the world."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Impermanence, the Fourth

---

## (121) The Invitation Sūtra, Fifth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, collectively undertaking the rains retreat.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, the World-Honored One, at the time of speaking the invitation for liberation, spread his seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus: "I am a brāhmaṇa who has attained complete cessation, the unsurpassed physician-king. The body I now receive is the very last. I am a brāhmaṇa who, having attained complete cessation, is the unsurpassed physician-king. The body I now receive is the very last. You all are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed through the Dharma. You all are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed through the Dharma. You should instruct one another, admonish one another in turn."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Just now you said: 'I am a brāhmaṇa who has attained complete cessation, the unsurpassed physician-king. The body I now receive is the very last. I am a brāhmaṇa who, having attained complete cessation, is the unsurpassed physician-king. The body I now receive is the very last. You all are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed through the Dharma. You all are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed through the Dharma. You should instruct one another, admonish one another in turn.' World-Honored One! Those who are untamed, you cause to be tamed; those who are not at peace, you cause to be at peace; those who have not crossed over, you cause to cross over; those who are not liberated, you cause to be liberated; those who have not attained complete cessation, you cause to attain complete cessation; those who have not attained the path, you cause to attain the path. You have established the holy life where it was not established. You know the path, you are awakened to the path, you discern the path, you teach the path. The World-Honored One's disciples afterward attain the Dharma; having received instruction and admonishment, having received instruction and admonishment, they follow the World-Honored One's words, immediately proceed to practice, and attain what accords with their intention, coming to rightly know the true Dharma. Now then, World-Honored One, do you find fault with my actions of body, speech, or mind?"

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra! I do not find fault with your actions of body, speech, or mind. Why is this? Śāriputra, you possess quick wisdom, great wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, keen wisdom, vast wisdom, profound wisdom, wisdom of liberation, and penetrating wisdom. Śāriputra, you have accomplished true wisdom. Śāriputra, just as a wheel-turning king has a crown prince who, not transgressing the instructions, is then anointed to receive what the father-king has transmitted, and is himself able to transmit it further, so too, Śāriputra, I have turned the Dharma-wheel, and you are able to turn it again. Śāriputra, therefore I do not find fault with your actions of body, speech, or mind."

The Venerable Śāriputra again joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "Indeed, the World-Honored One does not find fault with my actions of body, speech, or mind. Does the World-Honored One find fault with the actions of body, speech, or mind of these five hundred bhikṣus?"

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra! I also do not find fault with the actions of body, speech, or mind of these five hundred bhikṣus. Why is this? Śāriputra, these five hundred bhikṣus have all attained non-attachment; all their defilements are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, the heavy burden has been set down, the fetters of existence have been exhausted, and they have attained the good meaning through right knowledge and right liberation. There is only one bhikṣu whom I have already previously declared will, in this present life, attain ultimate knowledge: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. Śāriputra, therefore I do not find fault with the actions of body, speech, or mind of these five hundred bhikṣus."

The Venerable Śāriputra, for a third time, joined his palms facing the Buddha and said: "Indeed, the World-Honored One does not find fault with my actions of body, speech, or mind, nor does he find fault with the actions of body, speech, or mind of these five hundred bhikṣus. World-Honored One, among these five hundred bhikṣus, how many have attained the three knowledges? How many have attained both-ways liberation? How many have attained wisdom-liberation?"

The World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra! Among these five hundred bhikṣus, ninety have attained the three knowledges, ninety have attained both-ways liberation, and the remaining bhikṣus have attained wisdom-liberation. Śāriputra, this assembly is without branches, without leaves, and without knots or crookedness; it is pure and true, rightly established and standing firm."

At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was also in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "Indeed, may the World-Honored One grant me his power! May the Well-Gone One grant me his power, that I may, in the presence of the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, compose praising verses that accord with the meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Vaṅgīsa! Do as you wish."

Thereupon, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, in the presence of the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, praised in verses that accorded with the meaning:

"Today is the fifteenth, the day of invitation;
Assembled and seated are five hundred.
All fetters and bonds are severed;
These are sages who have exhausted all existence, free from obstruction.
Pure, with radiant illumination,
Liberated from all forms of existence;
Birth, old age, sickness, and death are ended;
Defilements extinguished, their task accomplished.
Remorse, regret, the fetter of doubt,
Pride, and defilements of existence are all ended;
The thorn of the fetter of craving is uprooted;
The supreme physician has nothing more to do.
Brave and valiant like lions,
All fears and terrors removed;
Having crossed beyond birth and death,
All defilements are completely extinguished.
Just as a wheel-turning king,
Surrounded by his ministers,
Rules over all the lands,
Even to the great ocean;
So the brave and victorious conqueror,
The unsurpassed caravan-leader,
Whose disciples joyfully pay homage:
Those with the three knowledges, free from the fear of death.
All are sons of the Buddha,
Forever rid of branches, leaves, and knots.
He who turns the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel:
I bow my head to the foremost honored one."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Invitation Sūtra, the Fifth

---

## (122) The Campā Sūtra, Sixth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Campā, by the bank of the Gaṅgā Pool.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of speaking the liberation, the World-Honored One spread his seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. After the World-Honored One had sat down, he entered samādhi and with the knowledge of others' minds surveyed the minds of the assembly. Having surveyed the minds of the assembly, he sat silently until the end of the first watch of the night. Thereupon, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! The first watch of the night has ended. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for a long time. May the World-Honored One please speak the liberation." At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer. Then the World-Honored One again sat silently through the middle watch of the night.

That bhikṣu rose from his seat a second time, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! The first watch has passed, and the middle watch is about to end. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for a long time. May the World-Honored One please speak the liberation." The World-Honored One again remained silent and did not answer. Then the World-Honored One again sat silently through the last watch of the night.

That bhikṣu rose from his seat a third time, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms facing the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! The first watch has already passed, the middle watch has also ended, and the last watch is nearly finished. Dawn is approaching, and daylight will soon appear. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for an exceedingly long time. May the World-Honored One please speak the liberation."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed that bhikṣu: "Within this assembly, there is one bhikṣu who has become impure."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had this thought: "For the sake of which bhikṣu did the World-Honored One say that within this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure? I should now enter into a samādhi of such a form, and with the knowledge of others' minds in such a samādhi, survey the minds of the assembly."

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then entered into a samādhi of such a form, and with the knowledge of others' minds in such a samādhi, surveyed the minds of the assembly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew for the sake of which bhikṣu the World-Honored One had said that within this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure. Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana emerged from samādhi, went before that bhikṣu, took him by the arm and led him out, opened the door and placed him outside, saying: "Foolish man, go far away! Do not remain here. You may no longer assemble with the community of bhikṣus. From this day forth, you are no longer a bhikṣu." He closed the door, locked it, and returned to the Buddha's presence, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! The bhikṣu for whose sake you said that within this assembly there is one bhikṣu who has become impure, I have already expelled him. World-Honored One! The first watch has already passed, the middle watch has also ended, the last watch is nearly finished, dawn is approaching, and daylight will soon appear. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for an exceedingly long time. May the World-Honored One please speak the liberation."

The World-Honored One said: "Mahāmaudgalyāyana! That foolish person will obtain great blame, for he has vexed and troubled the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus. Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If the Tathāgata were to speak the liberation in an impure assembly, that person's head would then split into seven pieces. Therefore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, from now on, you all shall speak the liberation. The Tathāgata will no longer speak the liberation. Why is this? In this way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there may be a foolish person who goes in and out with full awareness, who skillfully observes and discriminates, who bends and stretches, looks down and up with proper deportment, who properly wears the saṅghāṭī and other robes and carries his bowl, who in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and silence is fully aware of all, appearing like one who truly practices the holy life, going among those who truly practice the holy life, yet they may not know him. Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If those who practice the holy life come to know him, they will have this thought: 'This one is a stain on the śramaṇas, a disgrace to the śramaṇas, one the śramaṇas detest, a thorn among the śramaṇas.' Having known this, they should together expel and discard him. Why? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! It is like a householder who has a fine rice paddy, or a wheat field, in which there grows a weed called false wheat. Its roots resemble wheat, and its stems, nodes, leaves, and flowers all resemble wheat as well. But when it later produces grain, the householder sees it and has this thought: 'This is a stain on the wheat, a disgrace to the wheat, detested by the wheat, a thorn among the wheat.' Having recognized it, he pulls it out and casts it away outside. Why? So that it does not defile the remaining true, good wheat. In the same way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there may be a foolish person who goes in and out with full awareness, who skillfully observes and discriminates, who bends and stretches, looks down and up with proper deportment, who properly wears the saṅghāṭī and other robes and carries his bowl, who in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and silence is fully aware of all, appearing like one who truly practices the holy life, going among those who truly practice the holy life, yet they may not know him. Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If those who practice the holy life come to know him, they will have this thought: 'This one is a stain on the śramaṇas, a disgrace to the śramaṇas, one the śramaṇas detest, a thorn among the śramaṇas.' Having known this, they should together expel and discard him. Why? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! It is like a householder who, in autumn, winnows grain. Within a heap of grain, those that are full and substantial stay in place when winnowed, while those that are empty and mere chaff are blown away by the wind. The householder, seeing this, takes a broom and sweeps the area clean. Why? So that the remaining pure, good rice is not contaminated. In the same way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there may be a foolish person who goes in and out with full awareness, who skillfully observes and discriminates, who bends and stretches, looks down and up with proper deportment, who properly wears the saṅghāṭī and other robes and carries his bowl, who in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and silence is fully aware of all, appearing like one who truly practices the holy life, going among those who truly practice the holy life, yet they may not know him. Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If those who practice the holy life come to know him, they will have this thought: 'This one is a stain on the śramaṇas, a disgrace to the śramaṇas, one the śramaṇas detest, a thorn among the śramaṇas.' Having known this, they should together expel and discard him. Why? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life.

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! It is like a householder who, in order to channel spring water, makes a water trough. He takes an axe and enters the forest, tapping and striking various trees. Those that are solid and substantial give a small sound; those that are hollow inside give a loud sound. The householder, knowing this, then cuts and trims the nodes, intending to make a water trough from it. In the same way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there may be a foolish person who goes in and out with full awareness, who skillfully observes and discriminates, who bends and stretches, looks down and up with proper deportment, who properly wears the saṅghāṭī and other robes and carries his bowl, who in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and silence is fully aware of all, appearing like one who truly practices the holy life, going among those who truly practice the holy life, yet they may not know him. Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If those who practice the holy life come to know him, they will have this thought: 'This one is a stain on the śramaṇas, a disgrace to the śramaṇas, one the śramaṇas detest, a thorn among the śramaṇas.' Having known this, they should together expel and discard him. Why? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"When assembled together, one should recognize
Evil desires, hatred, jealousy, and anger,
Reticence, resentment, and stinginess,
Jealousy, flattery, deceit, and fraud.
In the assembly, he falsely claims to be at peace;
In private, he calls himself a śramaṇa.
Secretly performing all manner of evil deeds,
With wrong views and without self-restraint,
Deceitful and speaking false words:
Thus should one recognize him.
Coming to the assembly, do not associate with him;
Expel and discard him, do not dwell together.
Deceitful, fraudulent, speaking many lies,
Not at peace yet claiming to be at peace.
Knowing the time, endowed with pure conduct,
Expel and separate far from him.
The pure together with the pure
Should always dwell in harmony.
In harmony they attain peace and security;
Thus they reach the end of suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Campā Sūtra, the Sixth

---

## (123) Sūtra on the Śramaṇa Twenty Billion, Seventh of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti was also travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Dark Forest, practicing without sleep in the first and last watches of the night, with diligent effort, rightly established, cultivating the factors of the path. Thereupon, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti, dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, in calm contemplation and reflection, had this thought in his mind: "Among the World-Honored One's disciples who diligently study the true Dharma and Vinaya, I am the foremost. Yet my mind has not attained liberation from the defilements. My parents' household is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with abundant riches. Shall I now abandon the precepts, give up the path, return to lay life, enjoy desires, give generously, and cultivate various meritorious deeds?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, with the knowledge of others' minds, knew the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti. He then addressed a certain bhikṣu: "Go to that place and call Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti to come here."

That bhikṣu replied: "Yes, indeed." He rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti and said to him: "The World-Honored One is calling you."

The Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti, hearing the bhikṣu's words, immediately went to the Buddha's presence, bowed his head in homage, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One said: "Śramaṇa! Is it true that, dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, in calm contemplation and reflection, you had this thought in your mind: 'Among the World-Honored One's disciples who diligently study the true Dharma and Vinaya, I am the foremost. Yet my mind has not attained liberation from the defilements. My parents' household is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with abundant riches. Shall I now abandon the precepts, give up the path, return to lay life, enjoy desires, give generously, and cultivate various meritorious deeds?'"

At that time, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti felt ashamed and embarrassed, and was without boldness. "The World-Honored One knows the thoughts in my mind." He joined his palms facing the Buddha and said: "It is truly so."

The World-Honored One said: "Śramaṇa! I will now ask you; answer as you understand. What do you think? When you were a layperson, were you skilled at tuning and playing the vīṇā, with the vīṇā following the song and the song following the vīṇā?"

The Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti replied: "So it was, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further asked: "What do you think? If, when playing the vīṇā, the strings are too tight, will there be a harmonious sound that is pleasing?"

Śramaṇa replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further asked: "What do you think? If, when playing the vīṇā, the strings are too loose, will there be a harmonious sound that is pleasing?"

Śramaṇa replied: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further asked: "What do you think? If, when playing the vīṇā, the strings are tuned neither too tight nor too loose, but exactly in the middle, will there be a harmonious sound that is pleasing?"

Śramaṇa replied: "So it is, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Just so, Śramaṇa. Extreme effort causes the mind to become agitated and confused; insufficient effort causes the mind to become lax. Therefore, you should discern this occasion, observe this characteristic, and not be heedless."

At that time, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti, having heard what the Buddha said, received it well and retained it well. He rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. Having received the Buddha's teaching of the vīṇā simile, he dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from heedlessness, diligently practicing. Having dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from heedlessness, diligently practicing, this son of good family, for whose sake he had shaved off his hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household life for homelessness to study the path, the sole purpose being the completion of the unsurpassed holy life, in this present life he himself knew, himself realized, himself attained and dwelt in the attainment: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being." He knew it as it truly is. The Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti, having known the Dharma, attained the state of an arahant. At that time, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti, having attained the state of an arahant, had this thought: "Now is the right time. Should I not go to the World-Honored One's presence and declare my attainment of ultimate knowledge?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti went to the Buddha's presence, bowed his head in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! If there is a bhikṣu who has attained non-attachment, whose defilements are all ended, whose holy life has been established, whose task has been accomplished, whose heavy burden has been set down, whose fetters of existence have been severed, who has himself attained the good meaning through right knowledge and right liberation, at that time he delights in these six things: he delights in desirelessness, delights in seclusion, delights in non-contention, delights in the ending of craving, delights in the ending of clinging, and delights in the immovability of mind. World-Honored One! There may be someone who thinks: 'This worthy one, relying on faith, delights in desirelessness.' One should not regard it this way. Rather, it is the ending of desire, the ending of anger, and the ending of delusion that is the delight in desirelessness. World-Honored One! There may be someone who thinks: 'This worthy one, coveting gain, praise, renown, and offerings, delights in seclusion.' One should not regard it this way. Rather, it is the ending of desire, the ending of anger, and the ending of delusion that is the delight in seclusion. World-Honored One! There may be someone who thinks: 'This worthy one, relying on precepts, delights in non-contention.' One should not regard it this way. Rather, it is the ending of desire, the ending of anger, and the ending of delusion that is the delight in non-contention, the delight in the ending of craving, the delight in the ending of clinging, and the delight in the immovability of mind. World-Honored One! If there is a bhikṣu who has attained non-attachment, whose defilements are all ended, whose holy life has been established, whose task has been accomplished, whose heavy burden has been set down, whose fetters of existence have been severed, who has himself attained the good meaning through right knowledge and right liberation, at that time he delights in these six things.

"World-Honored One! If there is a bhikṣu who is still a learner, who has not yet attained his aspiration, who seeks and aspires to the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, at that time he has accomplished the faculties of a learner and the precepts of a learner. Later, when his defilements are all ended and he has attained freedom from defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life he himself knows, himself realizes, himself attains and dwells in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. At that time, he has accomplished the faculties of a non-learner and the precepts of a non-learner. World-Honored One! It is like a young child: at that time, he has accomplished the small faculties and the small precepts. Later, when he is fully endowed with the faculties of a learner, at that time he has accomplished the faculties of a learner and the precepts of a learner.

"In the same way, World-Honored One, if there is a bhikṣu who is still a learner, who has not yet attained his aspiration, who seeks and aspires to the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, at that time he has accomplished the faculties of a learner and the precepts of a learner. Later, when his defilements are all ended and he has attained freedom from defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life he himself knows, himself realizes, himself attains and dwells in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. At that time, he has accomplished the faculties of a non-learner and the precepts of a non-learner. If there are forms cognizable by the eye that confront the eye, they cannot cause him to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; his mind abides inwardly, well-controlled and guarded, observing the dharma of arising and passing away. If there are sounds cognizable by the ear, scents cognizable by the nose, tastes cognizable by the tongue, tangibles cognizable by the body, or dharmas cognizable by the mind that confront the mind, they cannot cause him to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; his mind abides inwardly, well-controlled and guarded, observing the dharma of arising and passing away.

"World-Honored One! It is like a great stone mountain, not far from a village, unbroken, without gaps, not brittle, solidly standing, not hollow, and of one piece. If a great wind and rain comes from the east, it cannot cause it to shake, move, shift, or be displaced; nor does the eastern wind push it to the south. If a great wind and rain comes from the south, it cannot cause it to shake, move, shift, or be displaced; nor does the southern wind push it to the west. If a great wind and rain comes from the west, it cannot cause it to shake, move, shift, or be displaced; nor does the western wind push it to the north. If a great wind and rain comes from the north, it cannot cause it to shake, move, shift, or be displaced; nor does the northern wind push it to any other direction. In the same way, if there are forms cognizable by the eye that confront the eye, they cannot cause him to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; his mind abides inwardly, well-controlled and guarded, observing the dharma of arising and passing away. If there are sounds cognizable by the ear, scents cognizable by the nose, tastes cognizable by the tongue, tangibles cognizable by the body, or dharmas cognizable by the mind that confront the mind, they cannot cause him to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; his mind abides inwardly, well-controlled and guarded, observing the dharma of arising and passing away."

Thereupon, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti spoke this verse:

"Delighting in desirelessness,
The mind abiding in seclusion,
Rejoicing in non-contention,
Joyful in the ending of clinging.
Also delighting in the ending of clinging,
With mind immovable,
Having known as it truly is,
From this the mind is liberated.
Having attained liberation of mind,
The bhikṣu's faculties are at rest;
What was to be done is done, and he looks not back,
With nothing more to seek or to do.
Just as a stone mountain
Cannot be moved by the wind,
So too with form, sound, scent, taste,
And tangibles as well:
Neither pleasing nor displeasing dharmas
Can move his mind."

After the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti had declared his attainment of ultimate knowledge before the Buddha, he rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, not long after the Venerable Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti had left, addressed the bhikṣus: "Sons of good families should come before me and declare their attainment of ultimate knowledge in this manner, just as Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti came before me and declared his attainment of ultimate knowledge, without praising himself, without showing contempt for others, speaking of meaning in accord with the present Dharma and following the various bases. Do not be like the foolish ones, bound by the conceits of the overestimation of attainment, who come before me and declare their attainment of ultimate knowledge. They do not attain the meaning, but only cause great vexation. Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoti came before me and declared his attainment of ultimate knowledge, without praising himself, without showing contempt for others, speaking of meaning in accord with the present Dharma and following the various bases."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Śramaṇa Twenty Billion, the Seventh

## (124) Sūtra on Eight Difficulties, Eighth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "For a person practicing the holy life, there are eight difficulties and eight inopportune times. What are the eight? At a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person is born in hell. This is called the first difficulty for practicing the holy life, the first inopportune time.

"Furthermore, at a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person is born among animals, born among hungry ghosts, born in the long-lived heavens, or born in the border regions among the barbarians, where there is no faith, no gratitude, no reciprocity, and where there are no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. This is called the fifth difficulty for practicing the holy life, the fifth inopportune time.

"Furthermore, at a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person, although born in the central lands, is deaf and mute, bleating like a sheep, always communicating with hand gestures, and unable to understand or explain the meaning of good and evil. This is called the sixth difficulty for practicing the holy life, the sixth inopportune time.

"Furthermore, at a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person, although born in the central lands, and not deaf, not mute, not bleating like a sheep, not communicating with hand gestures, and able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil, nevertheless holds wrong views and inverted views, seeing thus and declaring thus: 'There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there are no invocations, there are no wholesome or unwholesome deeds, there are no fruits or results of wholesome or unwholesome deeds, there is no this world or other world, there is no father and no mother, and in the world there are no true persons who go to good destinations, who have gone well, who go in the right direction, who in this world or the other world know and realize for themselves, attain and dwell in the attainment.' This is called the seventh difficulty for practicing the holy life, the seventh inopportune time.

"Furthermore, at a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not appear in the world, and does not teach the Dharma tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person is born in the central lands, is not deaf, not mute, not bleating like a sheep, does not communicate with hand gestures, and is able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil, and holds right views, not inverted views, seeing thus and declaring thus: 'There is giving, there is sacrifice, there are invocations; there are wholesome and unwholesome deeds, there are fruits and results of wholesome and unwholesome deeds; there is this world and other world; there is father and mother; and in the world there are true persons who go to good destinations, who have gone well, who go in the right direction, who in this world and the other world know and realize for themselves, attain and dwell in the attainment.' This is called the eighth difficulty for practicing the holy life, the eighth inopportune time.

"For a person practicing the holy life, there is one non-difficulty and one opportune time. What is the one non-difficulty and one opportune time for a person practicing the holy life? At a time when the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, tending toward peace, tending toward cessation, tending toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One, at that time, that person is born in the central lands, is not deaf, not mute, not bleating like a sheep, does not communicate with hand gestures, and is able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil, and holds right views, not inverted views, seeing thus and declaring thus: 'There is giving, there is sacrifice, there are invocations; there are wholesome and unwholesome deeds, there are fruits and results of wholesome and unwholesome deeds; there is this world and other world; there is father and mother; and in the world there are true persons who go to good destinations, who have gone well, who go in the right direction, who in this world and the other world know and realize for themselves, attain and dwell in the attainment.' This is called the one non-difficulty for practicing the holy life, and the one opportune time."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"If one obtains a human body,
And the most subtle and wondrous Dharma is taught,
If one does not attain the fruit,
It must be that one has not met the right time.
It is often said that the holy life is difficult;
A person may exist in future lives,
But if one encounters the right time,
That is extremely rare in the world.
If one wishes to regain a human body,
And to hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma,
One should study with diligence,
Out of compassion for oneself.
Discussing and hearing the good Dharma,
Do not let the time be lost;
If one loses this time,
One will certainly grieve, falling into hell.
If one does not meet the right time,
And does not hear the good Dharma taught,
It is like a merchant who has lost his goods:
One undergoes immeasurable births and deaths.
If one obtains a human body,
And hears the right and good Dharma taught,
Following the World-Honored One's teaching,
One surely encounters the right time.
If one encounters this time,
And is capable of the right holy life,
One accomplishes the unsurpassed eye,
As proclaimed by the Kinsman of the Sun.
Such a one always protects himself,
Advancing and departing from the latent tendencies,
Cutting off and extinguishing all fetters,
Subduing Māra and Māra's retinue.
Such a one crosses beyond the world,
Having completely exhausted all defilements."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Eight Difficulties, the Eighth

---

## (125) Sūtra on Poverty, Ninth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In the world, for a person with desires, is poverty a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person with desires, being poor, borrows property from another household, is borrowing property from another household in the world a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person with desires, having borrowed property, cannot repay it on time and says, 'Let the interest grow,' is the accrual of interest in the world a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person with desires, whose interest has grown and he still does not repay, and the creditor demands repayment, is the creditor's demand for repayment in the world a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person with desires, whose creditor demands repayment, and he cannot repay, and the creditor repeatedly comes to him to demand payment, is the creditor's repeated coming to demand payment in the world a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person with desires, whose creditor repeatedly comes to demand payment, and he still does not repay, and he is then seized and bound by the creditor, is being seized and bound by a creditor in the world a great suffering?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

"Thus, in the world, for a person with desires, poverty is a great suffering; in the world, for a person with desires, borrowing property is a great suffering; in the world, for a person with desires, the accrual of interest on borrowed property is a great suffering; in the world, for a person with desires, the creditor's demand for repayment is a great suffering; in the world, for a person with desires, the creditor's repeated coming to demand payment is a great suffering; in the world, for a person with desires, being seized and bound by a creditor is a great suffering. In the same way, if within this noble Dharma one has no faith in wholesome dharmas, no moral restraint, no learning, no generosity, and no wisdom regarding wholesome dharmas, then even though one may possess abundant gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, maṇi jewels, white conch, cowrie shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, giant clam shells, jade, red stone, and precious pearls, one is still poor and without power. This is what in my noble Dharma is called unwholesome poverty.

"His evil deeds of body, and evil deeds of speech and mind: this is what in my noble Dharma is called unwholesome borrowing. His wishing to conceal his evil deeds of body, not confessing them, not wanting them to be spoken of, not wanting others to reproach him, not being receptive; and his wishing to conceal his evil deeds of speech and mind, not confessing them, not wanting

### (121) Sūtra on Request

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from meditation, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, today I was alone in a quiet place, meditating, and this thought arose in my mind: 'It is extraordinary that the World-Honored One has said that for one who has a good friend, a good companion, and good associates, this is the entire practice of the holy life. Through relying on me as a good friend, sentient beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; sentient beings subject to old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are liberated from old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.' World-Honored One, how should we understand the meaning of this statement?"

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, what you have said is true. What you have said is true. A good friend, a good companion, and good associates: this is the entire practice of the holy life. Why is this? Because if sentient beings rely on me as a good friend, those subject to birth are liberated from birth; those subject to old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are liberated from old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.

"Ānanda, if I were not in this world, who would be a good friend for sentient beings? Because I am in this world, I serve as a good friend for sentient beings, and sentient beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; sentient beings subject to old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress are liberated from old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress.

"Ānanda, the Tathāgata, as a good friend for sentient beings, causes sentient beings subject to birth to be liberated from birth, and causes sentient beings subject to old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress to be liberated from old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress. Ānanda, with this meaning, you should know that a good friend, a good companion, and good associates: this is the entire practice of the holy life."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

### (122) Sūtra on Recitation

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much desire and often dwell in a state of desire,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little desire and do not often dwell in a state of desire,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much ill-will and often dwell in a state of ill-will,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little ill-will and do not often dwell in a state of ill-will,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much sloth and torpor and often dwell in a state of sloth and torpor,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little sloth and torpor and do not often dwell in a state of sloth and torpor,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much restlessness and remorse and often dwell in a state of restlessness and remorse,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little restlessness and remorse and do not often dwell in a state of restlessness and remorse,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much doubt and often dwell in a state of doubt,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little doubt and do not often dwell in a state of doubt,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much anger and often dwell in a state of anger,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little anger and do not often dwell in a state of anger,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much defilement and often dwell in a state of defilement,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little defilement and do not often dwell in a state of defilement,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'My mind has much distraction and I often dwell in a distracted state,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'My mind has little distraction and I do not often dwell in a distracted state,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Furthermore, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much unwholesome faith and often dwell in a state of unwholesome faith,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have wholesome faith and do not often dwell in a state of unwholesome faith,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it.

"Suppose a woman or a man, young and fond of adornment, having bathed and cleansed their head, obtains a bright, clean mirror or a bowl of clear water and examines their own face in it. If they see any dirt or blemish, they seek to remove it. If they see no dirt or blemish, they are pleased and delighted, saying: 'How fortunate I am; I am truly clean!' In the same way, if a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have much desire and often dwell in a state of desire,' then that monk or nun should dwell in a higher and more excellent Dharma, making effort to abandon these states. If a monk or a nun, through the mind, examines the mind and knows: 'I have little desire and do not often dwell in a state of desire,' then that monk or nun should dwell in that Dharma with joy and delight, day and night studying and practicing it. So too with ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt, anger, defilement, distraction, and unwholesome faith: it is likewise as above."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.
