### (123) Sūtra on Equality

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyans, in the city of Kapilavastu, in the Nigrodha Park.

At that time, the Śākyan Mahānāma went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does a disciple of the noble ones who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching frequently dwell?"

The Buddha said: "Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching frequently dwells in this way: Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Tathāgata: 'The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' When recollecting the Tathāgata thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Tathāgata, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through the Tathāgata. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Dharma: 'The Dharma of the World-Honored One is well expounded, visible here and now, not subject to time, leading one who practices it to attainment, each knowing for themselves through wise examination.' When recollecting the Dharma thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Dharma, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through the Dharma. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Sangha: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples has good practice, right practice, true practice, and upright practice. It consists of the four pairs and eight types of individuals. This Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, and is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' When recollecting the Sangha thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects the Sangha, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through the Sangha. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects one's own moral conduct: 'My moral conduct is unbroken, unfractured, unspotted, unblemished, practiced freely, praised by the wise, not grasped at, and conducive to concentration.' When recollecting moral conduct thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects moral conduct, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through moral conduct. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects one's own generosity: 'How fortunate I am! Among people afflicted by the stain of miserliness, I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of miserliness, freely giving, delighting in giving, equally distributing, and delighting in giving to others.' When recollecting generosity thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects generosity, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through generosity. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Furthermore, Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones recollects the devas: 'There are the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Transformation of Others' Enjoyments, and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations. If sentient beings have accomplished faith, moral conduct, learning, generosity, and wisdom, after the breakup of the body at death, they are born among the devas. I too have accomplished faith, moral conduct, learning, generosity, and wisdom.' When recollecting the devas thus, if there are any unwholesome desires, they are all eliminated. And whatever defilements, worries, and sufferings there are, they also do not arise. Mahānāma, when a disciple of the noble ones recollects the devas, at that time, the mind is not entangled by desire, not entangled by ill-will, not entangled by delusion. At that time, the mind is upright, having attained equanimity through the devas. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones whose mind is upright then attains the meaning of the Dharma, attains joy in the Dharma, attains bliss through the Dharma. When there is bliss, there is joy. When the mind has joy, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness. When one is happy, the mind attains concentration. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones who attains concentration then, amid sentient beings who have enmity and are armed, dwells with a mind of equality and without enmity, and cultivates extensively and practices widely. Mahānāma, a disciple of the noble ones should frequently cultivate this recollection.

"Mahānāma, this is how a disciple of the noble ones who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching frequently dwells."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Śākyan Mahānāma and the monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (124) Sūtra on Ānāpānasati (Mindfulness of Breathing)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "Cultivate mindfulness of breathing. If a monk cultivates mindfulness of breathing, practices it extensively and often, one can attain the cessation of perceiving and feeling.

"How does a monk cultivate mindfulness of breathing? A monk goes to a forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet place. He sits cross-legged with body upright, establishing mindfulness before him. Without confused thoughts, he mindfully breathes in; without confused thoughts, he mindfully breathes out.

"Breathing in long, one knows 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, one knows 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, one knows 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, one knows 'I breathe out short.'

"One trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.'

"One trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing joy.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing joy.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing bliss.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing bliss.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in calming the mental formation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out calming the mental formation.'

"One trains: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out gladdening the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in concentrating the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in liberating the mind.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out liberating the mind.'

"One trains: 'I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in contemplating dispassion.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out contemplating dispassion.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in contemplating cessation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out contemplating cessation.' One trains: 'I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment.' One trains: 'I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.'

"This is how a monk cultivates mindfulness of breathing.

"How does a monk who cultivates mindfulness of breathing fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness? When a monk breathes in long, one knows 'I breathe in long'; when breathing out long, one knows 'I breathe out long'; when breathing in short, one knows 'I breathe in short'; when breathing out short, one knows 'I breathe out short.' One trains experiencing the whole body while breathing in; one trains experiencing the whole body while breathing out. One trains calming the bodily formation while breathing in; one trains calming the bodily formation while breathing out. At that time, the monk contemplates the body as body, being diligent, not negligent, with right mindfulness and right comprehension, removing covetousness and sorrow from the world.

"When one trains experiencing joy while breathing in, one trains experiencing joy while breathing out. When one trains experiencing bliss while breathing in, one trains experiencing bliss while breathing out. When one trains experiencing the mental formation while breathing in, one trains experiencing the mental formation while breathing out. When one trains calming the mental formation while breathing in, one trains calming the mental formation while breathing out. At that time, the monk contemplates feelings as feelings, being diligent, not negligent, with right mindfulness and right comprehension, removing covetousness and sorrow from the world.

"When one trains experiencing the mind while breathing in, one trains experiencing the mind while breathing out. When one trains gladdening the mind while breathing in, one trains gladdening the mind while breathing out. When one trains concentrating the mind while breathing in, one trains concentrating the mind while breathing out. When one trains liberating the mind while breathing in, one trains liberating the mind while breathing out. At that time, the monk contemplates mind as mind, being diligent, not negligent, with right mindfulness and right comprehension, removing covetousness and sorrow from the world.

"When one trains contemplating impermanence while breathing in, one trains contemplating impermanence while breathing out. When one trains contemplating dispassion while breathing in, one trains contemplating dispassion while breathing out. When one trains contemplating cessation while breathing in, one trains contemplating cessation while breathing out. When one trains contemplating relinquishment while breathing in, one trains contemplating relinquishment while breathing out. At that time, the monk contemplates dharmas as dharmas, being diligent, not negligent, with right mindfulness and right comprehension, removing covetousness and sorrow from the world.

"This is how a monk who cultivates mindfulness of breathing fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.

"How does a monk who cultivates the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of awakening? When a monk contemplates the body as body and dwells in mindfulness, not forgetting, at that time, the monk has already given rise to mindfulness; having given rise to mindfulness, it is fulfilled. This is the mindfulness factor of awakening. When the monk is mindful and recollecting, one then wisely investigates, discriminates, and examines that Dharma. At that time, the monk has already given rise to the investigation of dharmas; having given rise to the investigation of dharmas, it is fulfilled. This is the investigation of dharmas factor of awakening. When the monk wisely investigates, discriminates, and examines that Dharma, then one gives rise to unremitting energy. At that time, the monk has already given rise to energy; having given rise to energy, it is fulfilled. This is the energy factor of awakening. When the monk gives rise to energy, one then gives rise to joy that transcends the worldly. At that time, the monk has already given rise to joy; having given rise to joy, it is fulfilled. This is the joy factor of awakening. When the monk's mind has joy, the body and mind become tranquil. At that time, the monk has already given rise to tranquility; having given rise to tranquility, it is fulfilled. This is the tranquility factor of awakening. When the monk's body is tranquil and at ease, one then experiences happiness, and the mind attains concentration. At that time, the monk has already given rise to concentration; having given rise to concentration, it is fulfilled. This is the concentration factor of awakening. When the monk's mind is concentrated, one well relinquishes and contemplates with equanimity. At that time, the monk has already given rise to equanimity; having given rise to equanimity, it is fulfilled. This is the equanimity factor of awakening.

"So too with contemplating feelings as feelings, contemplating mind as mind, and contemplating dharmas as dharmas: when the monk dwells in mindfulness, not forgetting, at that time, the monk has already given rise to mindfulness; having given rise to mindfulness, it is fulfilled. This is the mindfulness factor of awakening. When the monk is mindful and recollecting, one then wisely investigates, discriminates, and examines that Dharma. At that time, the monk has already given rise to the investigation of dharmas; having given rise to the investigation of dharmas, it is fulfilled. This is the investigation of dharmas factor of awakening. When the monk wisely investigates, discriminates, and examines that Dharma, then one gives rise to unremitting energy. At that time, the monk has already given rise to energy; having given rise to energy, it is fulfilled. This is the energy factor of awakening. When the monk gives rise to energy, one then gives rise to joy that transcends the worldly. At that time, the monk has already given rise to joy; having given rise to joy, it is fulfilled. This is the joy factor of awakening. When the monk's mind has joy, the body and mind become tranquil. At that time, the monk has already given rise to tranquility; having given rise to tranquility, it is fulfilled. This is the tranquility factor of awakening. When the monk's body is tranquil and at ease, one then experiences happiness, and the mind attains concentration. At that time, the monk has already given rise to concentration; having given rise to concentration, it is fulfilled. This is the concentration factor of awakening. When the monk's mind is concentrated, one well relinquishes and contemplates with equanimity. At that time, the monk has already given rise to equanimity; having given rise to equanimity, it is fulfilled. This is the equanimity factor of awakening.

"This is how a monk who cultivates the four establishments of mindfulness fulfills the seven factors of awakening.

"How does a monk who cultivates the seven factors of awakening fulfill understanding and liberation? A monk cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and leading to relinquishment. One cultivates the investigation of dharmas factor of awakening, the energy factor of awakening, the joy factor of awakening, the tranquility factor of awakening, the concentration factor of awakening, and the equanimity factor of awakening, each relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and leading to relinquishment.

"This is how a monk who cultivates the seven factors of awakening fulfills understanding and liberation."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (125) Sūtra on Contemplation of Impurity

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "If the contemplation of impurity is cultivated and practiced extensively, it will bear great fruit and bring great benefit. How does a monk cultivate the contemplation of impurity, and how does it bear great fruit and bring great benefit?

"A monk contemplates this body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, as enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, rough and smooth epidermis, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, fat, grease, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fluid in the joints, and urine.'

"It is like a two-mouthed sack filled with various kinds of grains, such as rice, millet, barley, wheat, sesame, beans, and various seeds. A person with eyes can open it and observe: 'This is rice, this is millet, this is barley, this is wheat, this is sesame, these are beans, and these are various seeds.' In the same way, a monk contemplates this body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the top of the head downward, as enclosed by skin and filled with various kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, rough and smooth epidermis, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, fat, grease, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fluid in the joints, and urine.'

"This is how a monk cultivates the contemplation of impurity. Cultivating it extensively, it bears great fruit and brings great benefit. It is for the purpose of attaining one of two fruits: either the attainment of arahantship in this very life, or if there is any remainder, the attainment of non-return."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (126) Sūtra on Contemplation of Repulsiveness in Food

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "If the contemplation of repulsiveness in food is cultivated and practiced extensively, it will bear great fruit and bring great benefit. How does a monk cultivate the contemplation of repulsiveness in food, and how does it bear great fruit and bring great benefit?

"A monk, when eating food, does not do so for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of sustaining this body, for avoiding harm, for supporting the holy life, thinking: 'I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings. I shall have continuation of life, be without fault, and dwell at ease.'

"It is like a man and woman whose skin has been wounded and who apply ointment to the wound, not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of healing the wound. In the same way, a monk, when eating food, does not do so for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of sustaining this body, for avoiding harm, for supporting the holy life, thinking: 'I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings. I shall have continuation of life, be without fault, and dwell at ease.'

"It is like a person who greases an axle, not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of carrying loads and making the journey. In the same way, a monk, when eating food, does not do so for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of sustaining this body, for avoiding harm, for supporting the holy life, thinking: 'I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings. I shall have continuation of life, be without fault, and dwell at ease.'

"This is how a monk cultivates the contemplation of repulsiveness in food. Cultivating it extensively, it bears great fruit and brings great benefit."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (127) Sūtra on Contemplation of Non-delight in the Entire World

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "If the perception of non-delight in the entire world is cultivated and practiced extensively, it will bear great fruit and bring great benefit. How does a monk cultivate the perception of non-delight in the entire world, and how does it bear great fruit and bring great benefit?

"A monk, whatever there is of grasping, attachment, determination of mind, fixation, and underlying tendencies in the world, all these one does not pursue, does not grasp, and abandons them. This is how a monk cultivates the perception of non-delight in the entire world. Cultivating it extensively, it bears great fruit and brings great benefit."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (128) Sūtra on the Perception of Impermanence

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the monks: "If the perception of impermanence is cultivated and practiced extensively, it will bear great fruit and bring great benefit. How does a monk cultivate the perception of impermanence, and how does it bear great fruit and bring great benefit?

"A monk contemplates thus: 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.'

"This is how a monk cultivates the perception of impermanence. If one cultivates the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively, it eliminates all sensual desire, it eliminates all desire for form, it eliminates all desire for existence, it eliminates all ignorance, and it eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like a farmer who, in the autumn, plows the field with a large plow, cutting through all the roots. In the same way, a monk who cultivates the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like a person who cuts down bamboo grass: taking the bamboo grass, bending it back and shaking it, all the leaves fall off. In the same way, a monk who cultivates the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like mango fruits on a stem: when the stem is severed, all the fruits connected to it fall down together. In the same way, a monk who cultivates the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like the ridge-beam of a peaked roof: the ridge-beam is supreme, being the highest and covering all the rafters. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like among all root-fragrances, black agarwood is considered supreme. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like among all heartwood-fragrances, red sandalwood is considered supreme. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like among all flower-fragrances, jasmine is considered supreme. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like among all kings, the wheel-turning king is considered supreme. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like among all the lights of the stars, the light of the moon is considered supreme. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"It is like when the sun appears after the rains have passed and the skies are clear of clouds and mist, the sun rises into the sky, dispelling all darkness with its great brightness. In the same way, the perception of impermanence, when cultivated and practiced extensively, eliminates all sensual desire, eliminates all desire for form, eliminates all desire for existence, eliminates all ignorance, and eliminates all conceit of 'I am.'

"This is how a monk cultivates the perception of impermanence. Cultivating it extensively, it bears great fruit and brings great benefit."

The Buddha spoke thus. The monks, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 30

---

## (126) Sūtra on Pursuing Desires, Tenth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, how many types of people in the world pursue desires?"

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, in the world there are ten types of people who pursue desires. What are the ten? Householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods. Having sought wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods, he does not provide for himself in comfort and security, nor for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. Nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods. Having sought wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. But he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods. Having sought wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. He also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, he does not provide for himself in comfort and security, nor for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. Nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. But he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. He also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires."

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through lawful means and by proper methods. Having sought wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, he does not provide for himself in comfort and security, nor for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. Nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through lawful means and by proper methods. Having sought wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. But he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through lawful means and by proper methods. Having sought wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. He also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Yet having obtained wealth, he is defiled, attached, bound, and entangled; being entangled, he is defiled and attached. He does not see the danger and does not know the way of escape, and yet he uses it. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Furthermore, householder, there is one type of person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through lawful means and by proper methods. Having sought wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, he is able to provide for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers. He also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life. Having obtained wealth, he is not defiled, not attached, not bound, not entangled; not being entangled, he is not defiled or attached. He sees the danger and knows the way of escape, and so he uses it. Such is one type of person who pursues desires.

"Householder, if there is a person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods, and having sought wealth through unlawful means and without proper methods, does not provide for himself in comfort and security, nor for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers, and does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life, this person who pursues desires is the lowest among all who pursue desires.

"Householder, if there is a person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, and having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, provides for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers, and also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life, this person who pursues desires is the highest among all who pursue desires [in those categories].

"Householder, if there is a person who pursues desires and seeks wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, and having sought wealth through lawful means and by proper methods, provides for himself in comfort and security, and for his parents, wife and children, servants and workers, and also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so as to ascend upward, and with happiness receive happy reward, be reborn in heaven, and attain long life, and having obtained wealth, is not defiled, not attached, not bound, not entangled, not being entangled is not defiled or attached, sees the danger, and knows the way of escape, and so uses it; this person who pursues desires, among all who pursue desires, is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime. Just as from the cow comes milk, from milk comes curds, from curds comes fresh butter, from fresh butter comes clarified butter, from clarified butter comes the essence of ghee, and the essence of ghee is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime. So too, householder, this person who pursues desires, among all who pursue desires, is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"If one seeks wealth unlawfully,
Or through both lawful and unlawful means,
Neither makes offerings nor uses it oneself,
Nor gives in charity to make merit,
Both aspects are equally evil;
Among those who pursue desires, this is the lowest.

If one seeks wealth lawfully,
Obtained through one's own diligent effort,
Makes offerings to others and uses it oneself,
And also gives in charity to make merit,
Both aspects are equally meritorious;
Among those who pursue desires, this is the highest.

If one attains the wisdom of renunciation,
While pursuing desires and dwelling as a householder,
Seeing danger and knowing contentment,
Using wealth with frugality and restraint,
That one who attains the wisdom of transcending desires
Is the highest among those who pursue desires."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Pursuing Desires, Tenth.

---

## (127) Sūtra on Fields of Merit, Eleventh of the Great Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, how many types of persons who are fields of merit are there in the world?"

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, in the world there are two types of persons who are fields of merit. What are the two? First, there are learners; second, there are those beyond learning. There are eighteen types of learners and nine types of those beyond learning.

"Householder, what are the eighteen learners? Those who proceed by faith, those who proceed by Dharma, those liberated by faith, those who have arrived at right view, those who have attained bodily realization, the family-to-family attainer, the one-seed attainer, those on the path toward stream-entry, those who have attained stream-entry, those on the path toward once-returning, those who have attained once-returning, those on the path toward non-returning, those who have attained non-returning, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion, and those who stream upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. These are called the eighteen learners.

"Householder, what are the nine persons beyond learning? Those of the nature to contemplate the Dharma, those of the nature to progress, those of the immovable nature, those of the nature to decline, those of the nature not to decline, those of the guarding nature who do not decline if they guard but decline if they do not guard, those of the nature to abide steadfastly, those liberated by wisdom, and those liberated in both ways. These are called the nine persons beyond learning."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"Learners and those beyond learning in the world
Are worthy of respect and worthy of reverence.
They are able to rectify their bodies,
And likewise their speech and minds.
Householder, they are excellent fields;
Giving to them yields great merit."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Fields of Merit, Eleventh.

---

## (128) Sūtra on the Lay Disciple, Twelfth of the Great Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of five hundred lay disciples, went to visit the Venerable Śāriputra, bowed in respect, and sat to one side. The five hundred lay disciples also paid their respects and sat to one side. After the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the five hundred lay disciples had sat to one side, the Venerable Śāriputra taught them the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring them, bringing them to joyful accomplishment, and through countless skillful means taught them the Dharma. Having encouraged and inspired them and brought them to joyful accomplishment, he then rose from his seat and went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. Not long after the Venerable Śāriputra had departed, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the five hundred lay disciples also went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

After the Venerable Śāriputra and the assembly had settled in their seats, the World-Honored One said: "Śāriputra, if you know that a white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices the five precepts and has obtained the four superior states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then, Śāriputra, you should declare that this noble disciple has exhausted the destinies of hell, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and all evil states of existence; that he has attained stream-entry, will not fall into evil destinies, is certain to proceed toward right enlightenment, and will undergo at most seven existences, passing back and forth seven times between heaven and the human realm before reaching the end of suffering.

"Śāriputra, how does a white-clad noble disciple well guard and practice the five precepts? A white-clad noble disciple abandons killing, ceases from killing, puts aside the sword and the staff, has a sense of shame and conscience, has a heart of kindness and compassion, and benefits all beings down to insects and worms. He purifies his mind with regard to killing. The white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices this first precept.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple abandons taking what is not given, ceases from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given and delights in taking what is given. He is always fond of generosity, gives joyfully and without stinginess, does not expect any reward, does not conceal anything through theft, and always protects himself. He purifies his mind with regard to taking what is not given. The white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices this second precept.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple abandons sexual misconduct, ceases from sexual misconduct. He does not transgress with women who are protected by their father, or protected by their mother, or protected by both father and mother, or protected by their brothers, or protected by their sisters, or protected by their parents-in-law, or protected by relatives, or protected by those of the same clan, or who are the wives of other men, or who are under the threat of punishment and intimidation, or including those who have been betrothed with a garland. He does not violate such women. He purifies his mind with regard to sexual misconduct. The white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices this third precept.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple abandons false speech, ceases from false speech. He speaks truthfully, delights in truth, abides in truth without wavering, and is entirely trustworthy, not deceiving the world. He purifies his mind with regard to false speech. The white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices this fourth precept.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple abandons intoxicants, ceases from intoxicants. He purifies his mind with regard to drinking intoxicants. The white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices this fifth precept.

"Śāriputra, how does a white-clad noble disciple obtain the four superior states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty? A white-clad noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata: 'That Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' Having thus recollected the Tathāgata, if there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple, by taking the Tathāgata as the object of contemplation, calms the mind and attains joy. If there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple attains the first superior state of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple recollects the Dharma: 'The Dharma well taught by the World-Honored One certainly leads to the ultimate goal; it is without affliction, without fever, eternally present and immovable.' Having thus contemplated, perceived, known, and recollected the Dharma, if there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple, by taking the Dharma as the object of contemplation, calms the mind and attains joy. If there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple attains this second superior state of mind.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple recollects the Sangha: 'The noble Sangha of the Tathāgata is of good conduct, of upright conduct, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, practicing the proper method, practicing in conformity with the Dharma. In that assembly there are truly Arhats and those progressing toward Arhatship, Non-returners and those progressing toward Non-returning, Once-returners and those progressing toward Once-returning, Stream-enterers and those progressing toward Stream-entry. These are called the four pairs and eight classes. The Tathāgata's Sangha has accomplished moral discipline, accomplished samādhi, accomplished prajñā, accomplished liberation, accomplished the knowledge and vision of liberation. They are worthy of respect, worthy of reverence, worthy of offerings, worthy of service; they are the world's excellent field of merit.' Having thus recollected the Tathāgata's Sangha, if there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple, by taking the Tathāgata's Sangha as the object of contemplation, calms the mind and attains joy. If there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. This is called the white-clad noble disciple attaining the third superior state of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a white-clad noble disciple recollects his own moral discipline: 'This moral discipline is unbroken, unperforated, without blemish, without impurity, abiding like the earth, not false, praised by the noble ones, well upheld and fully maintained.' Having thus recollected his own moral discipline, if there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. The white-clad noble disciple, by taking moral discipline as the object of contemplation, calms the mind and attains joy. If there are any evil desires, they are immediately eliminated; if there are unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts in the mind, they too are eliminated. This is called the white-clad noble disciple attaining the fourth superior state of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty.

"Śāriputra, if you know that a white-clad noble disciple well guards and practices these five precepts and has obtained these four superior states of mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then, Śāriputra, you should declare that this white-clad noble disciple has exhausted the destinies of hell, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and all evil states of existence; that he has attained stream-entry, will not fall into evil destinies, is certain to proceed toward right enlightenment, and will undergo at most seven existences, passing back and forth seven times between heaven and the human realm before reaching the end of suffering."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"The wise one dwelling as a householder,
Seeing the terror of hell,
Takes up and maintains the noble Dharma,
And removes all evil.

Not killing or harming living beings,
Knowing and able to relinquish,
Speaking truthfully without false speech,
Not stealing the property of others.

Content with one's own wife,
Not delighting in the wives of others,
Abandoning and ceasing from intoxicants,
The root of confused and deluded minds.

Always recollecting the Perfectly Enlightened One,
Contemplating the wholesome Dharma,
Recollecting the Sangha and observing moral discipline,
From this one obtains joy.

Wishing to practice generosity,
One should hope for its merit.
First give to those who have stilled their minds;
In this way the fruition is accomplished.

I shall now speak of those who have stilled their minds;
Śāriputra, listen well.
Whether there are black ones or white ones,
Red-colored or yellow,

Dappled, lovely-colored,
Cattle and various doves and birds,
Whatever the place of their birth,
The well-trained bull stands at the fore.

With bodily strength fully developed,
Swift and excellent in coming and going,
Take that one for its ability;
Do not reject it for its color.

So too among human beings,
Whatever the place of their birth,
Whether Kṣatriya, Brahmin,
Householder, or artisan,

Whatever the place of their birth,
The elder who purely upholds the precepts,
The Unattached One, the Well-Gone One,
Giving to such a one yields great fruit.

The foolish who know nothing,
Without wisdom, without learning,
Giving to them yields little fruit,
Without light, without illumination.

But those who have light and illumination,
Who have wisdom, disciples of the Buddha,
Who have faith directed toward the Well-Gone One,
Whose roots are well established and firm,

They are born in good destinations;
According to their wish they go to human families.
At last they attain nirvāṇa;
Thus each has their own conditions."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Śāriputra and the bhikṣus, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and the five hundred lay disciples, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Lay Disciple, Twelfth.

---

## (129) Sūtra on Enemies, Thirteenth of the Great Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are seven things characteristic of an enemy that create enmity, which come upon men and women when they are angry. What are the seven?

"An enemy does not wish for his enemy to have a good complexion. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to have a good complexion. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then even though he may bathe well and anoint his body with fine fragrances, his complexion remains ugly. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the first characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to sleep in comfort. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to sleep in comfort. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then even though he may lie on a royal bed, spread with woolen carpets and felt rugs, covered with brocade, fine silks, and gauze, with inner sheets, pillows at both ends, and coverings of Kaliṅga, Pavarā, and Pacasittaranā, still he sleeps in misery. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the second characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to obtain great profit. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to obtain great profit. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then what should have brought profit does not bring profit, and what should not have brought profit does bring profit. These two things are mutually contradictory, and he greatly incurs loss. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the third characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to have friends. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to have friends. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then whatever relatives and friends he has will forsake him and avoid him. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the fourth characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to have a good reputation. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to have a good reputation. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then his bad name and ugly reputation spread throughout all directions. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the fifth characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to be extremely wealthy. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to be extremely wealthy. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, then he engages in such bodily, verbal, and mental conduct that causes him to greatly lose his wealth. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the sixth characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry.

"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy, when the body breaks up and life comes to an end, to surely reach a good destination and be reborn in heaven. Why is that? An enemy does not desire his enemy to go to a good destination. When a person has anger, cultivates anger, is covered by anger, and does not abandon anger in his mind, he engages in evil conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, when the body breaks up and life comes to an end, he will surely reach an evil destination and be reborn in hell. Why is that? Because he is covered by anger and does not abandon anger in his mind. This is called the seventh characteristic of an enemy that creates enmity, which comes upon men and women when they are angry. These are the seven things characteristic of an enemy that create enmity, which come upon men and women when they are angry."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"The angry one gets an ugly complexion;
He sleeps in suffering and without peace.
What should have brought great wealth
Instead brings him loss.

Relatives and good friends
Distance themselves from the angry person.
One who repeatedly cultivates anger
Has an evil reputation spread throughout all directions.

Anger creates actions of body and speech;
Bound by resentment, one acts with the mind.
A person covered by anger
Loses all his wealth.

Anger gives rise to loss;
Anger produces mental defilement.
The terror that arises within
Is something others cannot perceive.

The angry one does not know what is right;
The angry one does not comprehend the Dharma.
Without eyes, blind in darkness,
Such is the person who delights in anger.

When anger first arises, it shows an ugly face,
Like smoke when fire first starts.
From this arises hatred and jealousy;
Because of this, people become enraged.

Whatever the angry one does,
Whether good deeds or bad,
Afterwards, when the anger subsides,
He burns with anguish like fire.

What is called the burning of karma,
And the entanglement by various mental states,
These things I now declare;
Listen well with wholesome minds.

The angry one may rebel against and harm his father,
And his brothers too.
He also kills sisters,
For the angry one causes much destruction.

She who gave birth and nurtured him,
Enabling him to see this world,
She by whom he was sustained in life,
Even this mother the angry one may kill.

Without shame, without conscience,
Bound by anger, there is nothing he will not say.
A person covered by anger
Will say anything from his mouth.

Committing foolish, sinful, and rebellious acts,
He even takes his own life.
While doing so, he is not aware;
From anger arises terror.

Attached to his own self,
Having loved without limit,
Though he loves and cherishes his own body,
The angry one even harms himself.

With a knife he stabs himself,
Or throws himself from a cliff,
Or hangs himself with a rope,
Or takes various poisons.

Such is the nature of anger;
Death depends upon anger.
All these things should be cut off;
Through wisdom one can fully comprehend.

Even small unwholesome deeds
The wise one can comprehend and remove.
One should endure such practices,
So as not to have an ugly complexion.

Without anger, without sorrow,
Free from arrogance, without conceit,
Having tamed and severed anger,
Extinguished, with no more outflows."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Enemies, Thirteenth.

---

## (130) Sūtra of Teaching Dhammika, Fourteenth of the Great Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Dhammika was a respected elder of a place called "Birth Land," and served as the superintendent of a Buddhist temple. He was honored by the people, yet he was violent, harsh, and extremely coarse and evil, abusing and scolding the bhikṣus. Because of this, the bhikṣus of Birth Land all left and departed, not wishing to stay there. Thereupon, the lay disciples of Birth Land, seeing that the bhikṣus of Birth Land had all left and departed, not wishing to stay there, thought: "For what reason have the bhikṣus of Birth Land all left and departed, not wishing to stay here?" The lay disciples of Birth Land heard that the Venerable Dhammika, the respected elder of Birth Land who was superintendent of the Buddhist temple and honored by the people, was violent, harsh, and extremely coarse and evil, abusing and scolding the bhikṣus, and that because of this the bhikṣus of Birth Land had all left and departed, not wishing to stay there. Having heard this, the lay disciples of Birth Land went together to the Venerable Dhammika and drove Dhammika out, expelling him from all the monasteries of Birth Land.

Thereupon, the Venerable Dhammika, having been driven out by the lay disciples of Birth Land and expelled from the monasteries of Birth Land, gathered his robes, took his bowl, and traveled until he arrived at the state of Śrāvastī, gradually making his way to Śrāvastī, and stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. Then the Venerable Dhammika went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, I have committed no offense, made no accusations, and done no wrong to the lay disciples of Birth Land. Yet the lay disciples of Birth Land have wrongfully driven me out and expelled me from the monasteries of Birth Land."

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Enough, enough, Dhammika! Why speak of this?"

The Venerable Dhammika, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said again: "World-Honored One, I have committed no offense, made no accusations, and done no wrong to the lay disciples of Birth Land. Yet the lay disciples of Birth Land have wrongfully driven me out and expelled me from the monasteries of Birth Land."

The World-Honored One also said a second time: "Dhammika, in ancient times, the merchants of this Jambudvīpa would board ships to enter the sea, bringing with them a shore-sighting hawk. When they had not yet gone far into the great ocean, they would release the shore-sighting hawk. If the shore-sighting hawk could reach the shore of the great ocean, it would never return to the ship. If the shore-sighting hawk could not reach the shore of the great ocean, it would come back to the ship. So too, Dhammika, having been driven out by the lay disciples of Birth Land and expelled from the monasteries of Birth Land, you have come back to where I am. Enough, enough, Dhammika! Why speak of this again?"

The Venerable Dhammika said a third time: "World-Honored One, I have committed no offense, made no accusations, and done no wrong to the lay disciples of Birth Land. Yet the lay disciples of Birth Land have wrongfully driven me out and expelled me from the monasteries of Birth Land."

The World-Honored One also said a third time: "Dhammika, did you abide in the way of a śramaṇa as befitting a śramaṇa, and were you still driven out by the lay disciples of Birth Land and expelled from the monasteries of Birth Land?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Dhammika rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, what is it for a śramaṇa to abide in the way befitting a śramaṇa?"

The World-Honored One said: "Dhammika, in ancient times, people had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Dhammika, when people had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa was extremely prosperous and happy, with many people, and villages were so close together that a rooster could fly from one to the next. Dhammika, when people had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, girls did not marry until the age of five hundred. Dhammika, when people had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there were only these illnesses: defecation, urination, desire, lack of appetite, and old age. Dhammika, when people had a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there was a king named Gaurava, who was wise and intelligent, a wheel-turning king with four kinds of armies, who governed the world justly, a righteous Dharma king endowed with the seven treasures. Those seven treasures were: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the general treasure; these are the seven. He had a thousand sons, of handsome appearance, courageous and fearless, able to subdue rival forces. He ruled over all the land up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but governing through the Dharma, bringing peace and security.

"Dhammika, King Gaurava had a tree called the King of Nyagrodha Trees, named 'Good Abode.' Dhammika, the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, had five branches. The first branch was for the king and the queen to eat from. The second branch was for the crown prince and the ministers to eat from. The third branch was for the common people to eat from. The fourth branch was for śramaṇas and brahmins to eat from. The fifth branch was for birds and animals to eat from. Dhammika, the fruit of the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, was as large as a two-measure jug, and its taste was like that of pure honey balls. Dhammika, the fruit of the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, had no one guarding it, nor did anyone steal from it.

"Then a certain man came, famished, thirsty, extremely emaciated, and haggard in appearance, wanting to eat the fruit. He went to the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode. After eating his fill of the fruit, he broke off one of its branches and took the fruit away with him. There was a deity who dwelt in the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode. That deity thought: 'How ungrateful and without reciprocity are the people of Jambudvīpa! Why is this? After eating his fill from the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, he broke off its branch and took the fruit away. I would rather that the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, should bear no fruit and produce no fruit.' The King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, then bore no fruit and produced no fruit."

"Another man came, famished, thirsty, extremely emaciated, and haggard in appearance, wanting to eat fruit. He went to the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, and saw that the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, bore no fruit and produced no fruit. He then went to King Gaurava and said: 'Your Majesty, you should know that the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, bears no fruit and produces no fruit.' When King Gaurava heard this, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, King Gaurava disappeared from Kuru and appeared in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. He stood before Śakra, Lord of the Gods, and said: 'Kauśika, you should know that the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, bears no fruit and produces no fruit.' Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, and King Gaurava, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, disappeared from the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and appeared in Kuru. Standing not far from the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, exercised his supernormal power in the appropriate manner, and with his supernormal power conjured a great flood and violent windstorm. Having conjured the great flood and violent windstorm, the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, was uprooted and overturned.

"Thereupon, the tree deity who dwelt in the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, because of this, became sorrowful, grieved, and wept with tears, standing before Śakra, Lord of the Gods. Śakra, Lord of the Gods, asked: 'Deity, why are you sorrowful, grieved, weeping with tears, standing before me?' The deity said: 'Kauśika, you should know that the great flood and violent windstorm uprooted and overturned the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode.' Then Śakra, Lord of the Gods, said to that tree deity: 'Deity, did you, as a tree deity, abide in the way befitting a tree deity when the great flood and violent windstorm uprooted and overturned the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode?' The tree deity said: 'Kauśika, what is it for a tree deity to abide in the way befitting a tree deity?' Śakra, Lord of the Gods, said: 'Deity, if someone wants the roots of the tree and takes the roots away, or wants the trunk, the branches, the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit and takes them away, the tree deity should not become angry, should not become hateful, and should not harbor resentment in the mind. The tree deity should dwell with equanimity; thus does a tree deity abide in the way befitting a tree deity.'

"The deity then said: 'Kauśika, I, as a tree deity, have not abided in the way befitting a tree deity. From this day forward, the tree deity shall abide in the way befitting a tree deity. May the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, be restored to its former state.' Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, exercised his supernormal power in the appropriate manner. Having exercised his supernormal power in the appropriate manner, he conjured another great flood and violent windstorm. Having conjured the great flood and violent windstorm, the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Good Abode, was immediately restored to its former state.

"In the same way, Dhammika, if a bhikṣu is reviled, he does not revile in return; if another is angry with him, he does not become angry in return; if another attacks him, he does not attack in return; if another strikes him, he does not strike in return. In this way, Dhammika, does a śramaṇa abide in the way befitting a śramaṇa."

Thereupon, the Venerable Dhammika rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and with tears streaming said: "World-Honored One, I have not abided as a śramaṇa in the way befitting a śramaṇa. From this day forward, I shall abide as a śramaṇa in the way befitting a śramaṇa."

The World-Honored One said: "Dhammika, in ancient times there was a great teacher named Sunetta, who was revered as a teacher by non-Buddhist sages. He had abandoned attachment to desires and attained supernormal powers. Dhammika, the great teacher Sunetta had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. Dhammika, the great teacher Sunetta taught his disciples the way to the Brahmā world. Dhammika, when the great teacher Sunetta was teaching the way to the Brahmā world, those among his disciples who did not fully practice the teaching, when their lives ended, were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. Dhammika, when the great teacher Sunetta was teaching the way to the Brahmā world, those among his disciples who did fully practice the teaching cultivated the four Brahmā abodes, abandoned desires, and when their lives ended, were reborn in the Brahmā world. Dhammika, at that time the great teacher Sunetta thought: 'I should not go together with my disciples to the next world, being reborn in the same place. I should now further cultivate a superior form of loving-kindness. Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, when my life ends, I shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.'

"Dhammika, at that time the great teacher Sunetta subsequently cultivated a superior form of loving-kindness. Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Dhammika, the great teacher Sunetta and his disciples did not practice the path in vain but obtained great fruition. Just as with the great teacher Sunetta, so too with Mūlī-Parganya, Āranyaka the Brahmin, Gaudariśata, Haitibalā the young Brahmin, Joti-Māli-Jyotividāla, and Saptapurohita.

"Dhammika, the seven Purohita teachers also each had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. Dhammika, the seven Purohita teachers taught their disciples the way to the Brahmā world. When the seven Purohita teachers were teaching the way to the Brahmā world, those among their disciples who did not fully practice the teaching, when their lives ended, were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. When the seven Purohita teachers were teaching the way to the Brahmā world, those among their disciples who did fully practice the teaching cultivated the four Brahmā abodes, abandoned desires, and when their lives ended, were reborn in the Brahmā world. Dhammika, the seven Purohita teachers thought: 'We should not go together with our disciples to the next world, being reborn in the same place. We should now further cultivate a superior form of loving-kindness. Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, when our lives end, we shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.'

"Dhammika, at that time the seven Purohita teachers subsequently cultivated a superior form of loving-kindness. Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, when their lives ended, they were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Dhammika, the seven Purohita teachers and their disciples did not practice the path in vain but obtained great fruition.

"Dhammika, if someone were to revile, strike, attack, become angry at, and scold those seven teachers and their immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers, they would surely incur immeasurable wrongdoing. If someone were to revile, strike, attack, become angry at, and scold even one bhikṣu, a disciple of the Buddha, who has attained even the smallest fruit with right view, the wrongdoing incurred would be far greater than the former. Therefore, Dhammika, you should each mutually protect one another. Why is this? Apart from this transgression, there is no greater fault."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"Sunetta, Mūlī-Parganya, Āranyaka the Brahmin, Gaudariśata, Haitibalā the young Brahmin, Joti-Māli-Jyotividāla, and Saptapurohita.

"These, in ages past,
Were seven teachers of renowned virtue.
Free from the bonds of attachment, delighting in compassion,
They passed beyond the fetters of desire.

They had disciples
Of immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
They too were free from the fetters of desire,
Yet were not ultimately complete.

If toward those non-Buddhist sages,
Who well practiced austere conduct,
One harbors hatred and jealousy in the heart,
The one who reviles them incurs great wrongdoing.

If toward even one who has attained right view,
A son of the Buddha abiding in even the smallest fruit,
One reviles, scolds, strikes, or attacks,
The wrongdoing is far greater than the former.

Therefore, Dhammika,
You should each mutually protect one another.
The reason for mutually protecting one another
Is that there is no heavier wrongdoing than this.

Such extremely heavy suffering
Is also despised by the noble ones.
One will surely receive an ugly form
And wrongly grasp erroneous views.

This is the lowest of persons,
As declared in the noble Dharma:
Those who have not yet left behind sensual desire
Yet attain the subtle five faculties.

Faith, energy, mindfulness,
Right samādhi, and right contemplation;
Such is the suffering obtained,
The retribution received before.

Having first received one's own retribution,
Afterwards one will harm others.
If one can protect oneself,
Then one is able to protect what is outside.

Therefore one should protect oneself;
The wise one will have boundless happiness."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Dhammika and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra of Teaching Dhammika, Fourteenth.

---

## (131) Sūtra on Subduing Māra, Fifteenth of the Great Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Bharga, in the Bhīṣaṇavana Deer Park on Mount Suṃsumāragiri.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was teaching and building a meditation hut for the Buddha. He was walking in meditation on open ground. At that time, Māra the Evil One transformed himself into a minute form and entered the belly of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana. Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought: "My belly now feels as if I have eaten beans. I should enter the appropriate form of samādhi and with that samādhi examine my own belly." At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the end of the walking meditation path, spread out his sitting cloth, sat cross-legged, entered the appropriate form of samādhi, and with that samādhi examined his own belly. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew that Māra the Evil One was inside his belly.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately emerged from samādhi and said to Māra the Evil One: "Come out, Pāpīyas! Come out, Pāpīyas! Do not trouble the Tathāgata, and do not trouble the Tathāgata's disciples. Do not bring about what is without benefit, without welfare over the long night; you will surely be reborn in an evil destination and suffer immeasurable pain."

At that time, Māra the Evil One thought: "This śramaṇa does not see and does not know, and yet he speaks thus: 'Come out, Pāpīyas! Come out, Pāpīyas! Do not trouble the Tathāgata, and do not trouble the Tathāgata's disciples. Do not bring about what is without benefit, without welfare over the long night; you will surely be reborn in an evil destination and suffer immeasurable pain.' Even your teacher, who has great supernormal powers, great majesty, great blessings, and great divine might, could not quickly know or quickly see this. How much less could a disciple know and see it?"

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then said again to Māra the Evil One: "I also know your thoughts. You think thus: 'This śramaṇa does not know and does not see, and yet he speaks thus: "Come out, Pāpīyas! Come out, Pāpīyas!
