Do not trouble the Tathāgata, and do not trouble the Tathāgata's disciples. Do not bring about what is without benefit, without welfare over the long night; you will surely be reborn in an evil destination and suffer immeasurable pain. Even your teacher, who has great supernormal powers, great majesty, great blessings, and great divine might, could not thus quickly know or quickly see this. How much less could a disciple know and see it?"'"

Māra Pāpīyas then thought: "This śramaṇa speaks thus because he knows and sees me." Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas transformed himself into a minute form, came out from the mouth, and stood before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Pāpīyas, in ancient times there was a Tathāgata named Kakusandha, a Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One. At that time, I was a Māra named 'Evil One,' and I had a sister named 'Dark.' You are her son. Pāpīyas, because of this, you are my nephew.

"Pāpīyas, the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, had two great disciples. The first was named Sound, and the second was named Perception. Pāpīyas, for what reason was the Venerable Sound called 'Sound'? Pāpīyas, the Venerable Sound, dwelling in the Brahmā world, with his ordinary voice could fill a thousand world-systems. There was no other disciple whose voice equaled his, resembled his, or surpassed his. Pāpīyas, for this reason, the Venerable Sound was called 'Sound.'

"Pāpīyas, for what reason was the Venerable Perception called 'Perception'? Pāpīyas, the Venerable Perception, when traveling and staying in the villages he frequented, would rise in the morning, put on his robes, take his bowl, and enter the village to beg for food, well guarding his body, well restraining his sense faculties, and establishing himself in right mindfulness. After begging for food and finishing his meal, in the afternoon, he would put away his robes and bowl, wash his hands and feet, place his sitting cloth on his shoulder, and go to a secluded place, or to a mountain forest beneath a tree, or to a quiet, solitary place. He would spread out his sitting cloth, sit cross-legged, and quickly enter the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. At that time, if there were cowherds, shepherds, woodcutters, grass-gatherers, or travelers who entered that mountain forest, they would see him sitting in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and would think: 'This śramaṇa has died while sitting in this secluded place. We should gather dry wood and grass, pile it up, cover his body with it, and cremate him.' They then gathered wood and grass, piled it over his body, set it on fire, and departed.

"The Venerable Perception, rising the next morning, emerged from samādhi, shook out his robes, and as was his custom when traveling in the villages he frequented, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food, well guarding his body, well restraining his sense faculties, and establishing himself in right mindfulness. Those cowherds, shepherds, woodcutters, grass-gatherers, or travelers who had entered that mountain forest and had seen him before would then think: 'This śramaṇa who was sitting in the secluded place and had died, for whom we gathered dry wood and grass, piled it over his body, set it on fire, and departed; yet this worthy one has consciousness again!' Pāpīyas, for this reason, the Venerable Perception was called 'Perception.'

"Pāpīyas, at that time, the evil Māra thought: 'These bald-headed śramaṇas, bound by the Dark One, their lineage cut off and without progeny, they practice meditation; they watch, intensely watch, again and again watch. Just as a donkey who carries heavy loads all day, tied to a manger and unable to get grain to eat, watches for that grain, intensely watches, again and again watches. So too, these bald-headed śramaṇas, bound by the Dark One, their lineage cut off and without progeny, practice meditation; they watch, intensely watch, again and again watch. Just as a cat sits by a mouse hole, wanting to catch a mouse, watching, intensely watching, again and again watching. So too, these bald-headed śramaṇas, bound by the Dark One, their lineage cut off and without progeny, practice meditation; they watch, intensely watch, again and again watch. Just as an owl sits among dry wood-piles, wanting to catch a mouse, watching, intensely watching, again and again watching. So too, these bald-headed śramaṇas, bound by the Dark One, their lineage cut off and without progeny, practice meditation; they watch, intensely watch, again and again watch. Just as a heron stands by the water's edge, wanting to catch fish, watching, intensely watching, again and again watching. So too, these bald-headed śramaṇas, bound by the Dark One, their lineage cut off and without progeny, practice meditation; they watch, intensely watch, again and again watch. What are they watching for? For what purpose do they watch? What are they seeking in watching? Those deranged, maddened, and confused ones; I do not know where they come from, nor where they go, nor where they abide, nor where they die, nor where they are reborn. I should now instruct the brahmins and householders: come, all of you, revile, strike, attack, become angry at, and scold the diligent śramaṇas. Why? Perhaps when being reviled, struck, attacked, and scolded, they might give rise to evil thoughts, and I will gain an opportunity against them.'

"Pāpīyas, at that time, the evil Māra then instructed the brahmins and householders, and those brahmins and householders reviled, struck, attacked, became angry at, and scolded the diligent śramaṇas. Those brahmins and householders struck them with wood, pelted them with stones, beat them with staffs, wounded the heads of the diligent śramaṇas, tore their robes, and broke their alms bowls. At that time, those among the brahmins and householders who died, because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, surely went to an evil destination and were reborn in hell. Having been reborn there, they thought: 'I deserve to suffer this pain, but I shall have to endure suffering even more extreme than this. Why? Because we acted with evil conduct toward the diligent śramaṇas.'

"Pāpīyas, the disciples of the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, having had their heads wounded, their robes torn, and their bowls broken, went to where the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, was. At that time, the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers as he taught the Dharma. The Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, saw from afar that his disciples' heads were wounded, bleeding and staining their faces, their robes were torn, and their bowls were broken as they came. Seeing this, he addressed the bhikṣus: 'Do you see? The evil Māra instructed the brahmins and householders: "Come, all of you, revile, strike, attack, become angry at, and scold the diligent śramaṇas. Why? Perhaps when being reviled, struck, attacked, and scolded, they might give rise to evil thoughts, and I will gain an opportunity against them." Bhikṣus, you should pervade one direction with a mind of loving-kindness and dwell therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere, with a mind of loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy; with a mind of equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein. This will prevent the evil Māra from finding any opportunity against you.'

"Pāpīyas, the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, taught his disciples with this instruction, and they received the teaching. They pervaded one direction with a mind of loving-kindness and dwelt therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading everywhere, with a mind of loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy; with a mind of equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling therein. Because of this, the evil Māra sought an opportunity against them but could not find one.

"Pāpīyas, at that time, the evil Māra again thought: 'By these means I sought an opportunity against the diligent śramaṇas but could not find one. I should now instruct the brahmins and householders: come, all of you, honor, make offerings to, and serve the diligent śramaṇas. Perhaps through honoring, making offerings to, and serving the diligent śramaṇas, they might give rise to evil thoughts, and I will gain an opportunity against them.' Pāpīyas, after those brahmins and householders were instructed by the evil Māra, they together honored, made offerings to, and served the diligent śramaṇas. They spread their garments on the ground and said: 'Let the diligent śramaṇas walk upon them. The diligent śramaṇas have practiced what is difficult to practice. May we gain benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for a long time.' The brahmins and householders spread their hair on the ground and said: 'Let the diligent śramaṇas walk upon them. The diligent śramaṇas have practiced what is difficult to practice. May we gain benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for a long time.' The brahmins and householders held various foods and drinks in their hands, stood by the roadside waiting, and said: 'May the diligent śramaṇas accept this food, eat this, take this away, and use it as they wish. May we gain benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for a long time.' The faithful brahmins and householders, upon seeing the diligent śramaṇas, embraced them with reverent hearts, brought them into their homes, offered them various kinds of property, and said to the diligent śramaṇas: 'Accept this, use this, take this away, and use it as you wish.' At that time, those among the brahmins and householders who died, because of these causes and conditions, when their bodies broke up and their lives ended, surely went to a good destination and were reborn in heaven. Having been reborn there, they thought: 'I deserve to enjoy this happiness, but I shall receive happiness even more excellent than this. Why? Because we acted with good conduct toward the diligent śramaṇas.'

"Pāpīyas, the disciples of the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, having received honor, offerings, and service, went to where the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, was. At that time, the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers as he taught the Dharma. The Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, saw from afar that his disciples had received honor, offerings, and service and were coming. Seeing this, he addressed the bhikṣus: 'Do you see? The evil Māra instructed the brahmins and householders: "Come, all of you, honor, make offerings to, and serve the diligent śramaṇas. Perhaps through honoring, making offerings to, and serving the diligent śramaṇas, they might give rise to evil thoughts, and I will gain an opportunity against them." Bhikṣus, you should contemplate that all conditioned things are impermanent, contemplate the nature of arising and passing away, contemplate dispassion, contemplate abandonment, contemplate cessation, contemplate cutting off. This will prevent the evil Māra from finding any opportunity against you.' Pāpīyas, the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, taught his disciples with this instruction, and they received the teaching. They contemplated that all conditioned things are impermanent, contemplated the nature of arising and passing away, contemplated dispassion, contemplated abandonment, contemplated cessation, contemplated cutting off. Because of this, the evil Māra sought an opportunity against them but could not find one.

"Pāpīyas, at that time, the evil Māra again thought: 'By these means I sought an opportunity against the diligent śramaṇas but could not find one. I should now transform myself into the form of a young man, take a great staff in hand, stand by the roadside, and strike the Venerable Sound on the head until it breaks and blood flows, staining his face.' Pāpīyas, subsequently the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, was traveling in the villages he frequented. In the morning, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. The Venerable Sound followed behind, attending him. Pāpīyas, at that time, the evil Māra transformed himself into the form of a young man, took a great staff in hand, stood by the roadside, and struck the Venerable Sound on the head until it broke and blood flowed, staining his face. Pāpīyas, the Venerable Sound, with his head broken and blood flowing, followed behind the Tathāgata Kakusandha, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, like a shadow that does not de

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgamas)
## Fascicle 31

---

**(131) The Sūtra on Descending [into the Womb]**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kuru, in the town of the Kurus called Kammāsadhamma (Jiandu).

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "I shall explain to you the teaching on descending into the womb. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall speak."

The bhikṣus replied, "Yes, World-Honored One, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of beings who descend into the womb. What are the three?

"Here, there is a being who, when descending into the mother's womb, does not know; while dwelling in the womb, does not know; and when emerging from the womb, does not know. This is the first kind of descending into the womb.

"Furthermore, there is a being who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; but while dwelling in the womb, does not know; and when emerging from the womb, does not know. This is the second kind of descending into the womb.

"Furthermore, there is a being who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; while dwelling in the womb, knows; but when emerging from the womb, does not know. This is the third kind of descending into the womb.

"Furthermore, there is a being who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; while dwelling in the womb, knows; and when emerging from the womb, also knows. This is the fourth kind of descending into the womb.

"Of these, who is the one who, when descending into the mother's womb, does not know; while dwelling in the womb, does not know; and when emerging from the womb, does not know? There are beings who, possessing much unwholesomeness, much ignorance, and little merit, when descending into the mother's womb, do not know; while dwelling in the womb, do not know; and when emerging from the womb, do not know. This is the first kind of descending into the womb.

"Who is the one who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; but while dwelling in the womb, does not know; and when emerging from the womb, does not know? There are beings who possess a small amount of merit and wisdom, and when descending into the mother's womb, they know; but while dwelling in the womb, do not know; and when emerging from the womb, do not know. This is the second kind of descending into the womb.

"Who is the one who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; while dwelling in the womb, knows; but when emerging from the womb, does not know? There are beings who possess a greater amount of merit and wisdom, and when descending into the mother's womb, they know; while dwelling in the womb, they know; but when emerging from the womb, they do not know. This is the third kind of descending into the womb.

"Who is the one who, when descending into the mother's womb, knows; while dwelling in the womb, knows; and when emerging from the womb, also knows? This refers to the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva descends into the mother's womb, he knows; while dwelling in the womb, he knows; and when emerging from the womb, he also knows. This is the fourth kind of descending into the womb.

"When the Bodhisattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita heaven, he manifests five omens. What are the five? First, the flowers on his garland wither. Second, his garments become soiled. Third, sweat flows from his armpits. Fourth, his body loses its radiance. Fifth, he takes no pleasure in his heavenly seat.

"When the Bodhisattva is about to descend from the Tuṣita heaven, the devas of the Tuṣita heaven, knowing that the Bodhisattva will soon descend to be born among humans, accompany and follow him, saying: 'May you be born in a place that is central, not on the frontier. May you be born in a good family, either a kṣatriya great clan or a brahmin great clan, one that is wealthy and prosperous, with many treasuries and storehouses, with many servants and retainers, with great authority and power.'

"When the Bodhisattva descends into his mother's womb, at the moment of his descent, a great, immeasurable, brilliant light appears throughout the world, surpassing the radiance of the devas. Even in those spaces between the worlds, in the perpetual darkness where the sun and moon, however powerful and majestic, cannot illuminate with their light, in those places a great, immeasurable, brilliant light also appears. The beings born in those places, by this light, can see one another and know that there are other beings existing there. They say: 'There are also other beings born in this place.' At that time, this great thousandfold world system shakes and quakes in six ways. This immeasurable, brilliant light appears throughout the world. This is the manifestation of the Bodhisattva's great spiritual power and great merit.

"When the Bodhisattva first descends into his mother's womb, the mother's body is at ease, without illness or suffering. The mother naturally upholds the five precepts: she does not kill living beings, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not drink alcohol. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva first descends into his mother's womb, his mother has no thoughts of desire toward men, and no man is able to violate the Bodhisattva's mother. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva first descends into his mother's womb, his mother obtains the five kinds of sensual pleasures and is well provided for, enjoying and playing with them. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva first descends into his mother's womb, his mother has no illness whatsoever. She is happy and at peace in body and mind, and she can see the Bodhisattva within her womb, complete in all his limbs and faculties. Just as a pure maṇi gem, well polished, of the finest quality, strung on a blue, yellow, red, or white thread, is placed on a clear surface, and a person with good eyesight can clearly see through it; in the same way, the Bodhisattva's mother can see the Bodhisattva within her womb, complete in all limbs and faculties. This is a natural dharma.

"After the Bodhisattva's mother gives birth to the Bodhisattva, within seven days the mother passes away and is reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. This is a natural dharma.

"While other women give birth after nine or ten months, the Bodhisattva's mother does not do so. The Bodhisattva's mother carries the Bodhisattva for exactly ten months and then gives birth. This is a natural dharma.

"While other women give birth either sitting or lying down, the Bodhisattva's mother does not do so. The Bodhisattva's mother gives birth standing. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb, the devas receive him first, and afterward humans receive him. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb, before he reaches the ground, four devas receive the Bodhisattva and place him before his mother, saying: 'Rejoice, for you have given birth to a son of great merit and great power.' This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb, he comes out clean and pure, without being defiled by any impurities, without being stained by blood, without being stained by pus, without any unclean substance, clean and pure. Just as placing a gem on Kāśi silk, neither the gem stains the silk nor does the silk stain the gem, and why? Because both are pure. In the same way, the Bodhisattva emerges clean and pure. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb, two streams of water descend from the sky, one warm and one cool, to bathe the Bodhisattva. This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva is first born, he stands firmly with both feet on the ground, faces north, takes seven steps, with a white parasol held above him, and surveys all directions. He speaks with the voice of a bull among men, saying: 'In heaven and on earth, I alone am to be honored. I will bring to an end birth, old age, sickness, and death.' This is a natural dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva emerges from his mother's womb, at the moment of his birth, a great, immeasurable, brilliant light appears throughout the world, surpassing the radiance of the devas. Even in those spaces between the worlds, in the perpetual darkness where the sun and moon, however powerful and majestic, cannot illuminate with their light, in those places a great, immeasurable, brilliant light also appears. The beings born in those places, by this light, can see one another and know that there are other beings existing there. They say: 'There are also other beings born in this place.' At that time, this great thousandfold world system shakes and quakes in six ways. This immeasurable, brilliant light appears throughout the world. This is the manifestation of the Bodhisattva's great spiritual power and great merit.

"When the Bodhisattva is born, in this world the devas, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, and all the people, along with the various beings, have not seen nor heard what has never before been seen or heard. At that time, people conceive this thought: 'The devas, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, and all the people of this world, along with the various beings, have not seen nor heard what has never before been seen or heard.'

"When the Bodhisattva is born, his father, the king, summons physiognomists to examine the prince's features. The physiognomists examine the prince and report to the king: 'Great king, you should rejoice! This prince is endowed with great merit. He possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man. A person endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man will have one of two destinies, and no other. If he remains as a householder, he will become a wheel-turning sage king, a just and righteous Dharma king, ruling over the four quarters, who brings peace to the land, who possesses the seven treasures. The seven treasures are: the golden wheel treasure, the white elephant treasure, the blue horse treasure, the divine pearl treasure, the maiden treasure, the householder treasure, and the commander treasure. These are the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, brave and heroic in appearance, able to vanquish enemy armies. He will rule over this entire earth, up to the ocean's edge, without using knife or club, but by means of the Dharma, and he will rule in peace and equality. If he leaves home and goes forth from the household life, shaving off his hair and beard, putting on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith, leaving home to study the Way, he will attain the supreme and perfect enlightenment, and his fame will fill the entire world.'

"'What are the thirty-two marks of a great man?'

"'First, the soles of his feet are flat and firmly planted. Second, on the soles of his feet are wheels with a thousand spokes, with hub and rim, natural and fully formed. Third, his fingers are long and slender. Fourth, his heels are broad and full. Fifth, between his fingers and toes are webbed membranes like those of a royal goose. Sixth, his hands and feet are soft and delicate. Seventh, the tops of his feet are high and full. Eighth, his calves are like those of an eṇeya deer. Ninth, when standing upright and not bending, the palms of both hands can touch and rub his knees. Tenth, his male organ is concealed in a sheath. Eleventh, his body is proportioned like a banyan tree, the span of his outstretched arms equaling his height. Twelfth, each of his body hairs curls to the right. Thirteenth, his body hairs grow upward, each one individually, blue-black in color, curling to the right. Fourteenth, his body is golden in color. Fifteenth, he radiates light for one full fathom around his body. Sixteenth, his skin is fine and smooth. Seventeenth, the seven parts of his body are full and rounded. These seven are: both hands, both feet, both shoulders, and the neck. Eighteenth, the area below his armpits is full. Nineteenth, his upper body is like a lion's. Twentieth, his body is tall and straight. Twenty-first, his shoulders are round and full. Twenty-second, he has forty teeth. Twenty-third, his teeth are even and uniform. Twenty-fourth, his teeth are without gaps. Twenty-fifth, his teeth are white and lustrous. Twenty-sixth, he has the taste of the supreme flavor. Twenty-seventh, his tongue is long and broad. Twenty-eighth, his voice is like that of Brahmā, like the cry of a kalaviṅka bird. Twenty-ninth, his eyes are deep blue. Thirtieth, his eyelashes are like those of a royal bull. Thirty-first, between his eyebrows there is a white tuft of hair, soft and fine, like cotton. Thirty-second, on his head there is a fleshy protuberance.'

"'These are the thirty-two marks of a great man. A person endowed with these thirty-two marks of a great man will have one of two destinies, and no other. If he remains as a householder, he will become a wheel-turning sage king. If he leaves home, he will attain the supreme and perfect enlightenment.'

"At that time, the father king, in order to keep the prince and prevent him from going forth to leave the household life, provides the five kinds of sensual pleasures for his enjoyment. He provides the prince with beautiful forms, sounds, fragrances, flavors, and tangibles for his pleasure. He builds for him three palaces: one for winter, one for summer, and one for the rainy season. He provides him with the five kinds of sensual pleasures, and for four months during the rainy season, the prince stays in the upper palace, surrounded by female musicians, without any men in attendance, and he does not descend from the palace.

"When the Bodhisattva sees an old person, a sick person, a dead person, and a renunciant, he then goes forth, shaving off his hair and beard, putting on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith, leaves the household life to study the Way.

"After going forth, he cultivates and studies the practices of the ascetic path. He abides in a remote and solitary place, constantly practicing diligence, not being negligent. Having cultivated and studied the practices of the ascetic path, abiding in a remote and solitary place, and constantly practicing diligence without negligence, before long he realizes the supreme, unexcelled Brahma-conduct for which sons of good families rightly leave the household life to go forth to study the Way. In this very life, he himself knows, realizes, and personally attains the fruit: 'Birth is ended, the Brahma-conduct has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more return to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is.

"Having attained the supreme and perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata accomplishes the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. He turns the unsurpassed Dharma wheel, which cannot be turned by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. He extensively teaches the Dharma: this is suffering, this is the arising of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(132) The Sūtra on Kāśyapa the Youth**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at the city of Rājagṛha, on the mountain called Kālaka, at the place of the Ibex.

At that time, Kāśyapa the Youth went to visit the World-Honored One. Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, Kāśyapa the Youth said to the World-Honored One:

"Venerable Gautama, I once heard: 'The ascetic Gautama does not pay respect to aged, senior brahmins who are old, advanced in years, of great age and long life, who have reached the final stage; he does not rise for them, does not invite them to sit, and does not converse with them.' Venerable Gautama, this is truly so, for Venerable Gautama does not pay respect to aged, senior brahmins who are old, advanced in years, of great age and long life, who have reached the final stage; he does not rise for them, does not invite them to sit, and does not converse with them. This is not good."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, in this world of devas, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from devas to humans, I do not see anyone whom I should pay respect to, or for whom I should rise, or whom I should invite to sit, or with whom I should converse. Kāśyapa, if the Tathāgata were to pay respect to someone, rise for them, invite them to sit, or converse with them, that person's head would shatter."

Kāśyapa the Youth said to the World-Honored One: "Venerable Gautama speaks without restraint."

The World-Honored One said: "It is true, it could be said that I speak without restraint. But it is not for the reason you think. Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata is the one who has no fear. A lion, the king of beasts, in whatever assembly he enters, he is without fear. Kāśyapa, in the same way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, in whatever assembly he enters, he is without fear. But it is not for the reason you think. Therefore, Kāśyapa, it can be said that I speak without restraint."

Kāśyapa the Youth said to the World-Honored One: "Venerable Gautama, there is speaking, and there is conversing. Speaking and conversing are different, Venerable Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, in what way is speaking different from conversing?"

Kāśyapa the Youth was silent and did not answer.

The World-Honored One asked a second time: "Kāśyapa, in what way is speaking different from conversing?"

Kāśyapa the Youth was again silent and did not answer.

The World-Honored One asked a third time: "Kāśyapa, in what way is speaking different from conversing? Kāśyapa, you should answer now. If you are asked three times and do not answer, your head will split into seven pieces."

At that time, the Vajrapāṇi yakṣa, holding a great flaming iron vajra, was hovering in the air above Kāśyapa the Youth. If Kāśyapa the Youth did not answer the World-Honored One's question after the third time, the Vajrapāṇi would split his head into seven pieces. The World-Honored One saw the Vajrapāṇi yakṣa holding a great flaming iron vajra, hovering in the air above Kāśyapa the Youth, and said to Kāśyapa the Youth: "Kāśyapa, look up and see."

Kāśyapa the Youth looked up and saw the Vajrapāṇi yakṣa holding a great flaming iron vajra hovering in the air above him. Seeing this, he was greatly frightened and terrified, his hair standing on end. He moved close to the World-Honored One, seeking the World-Honored One's protection and refuge. He sat to one side and said to the World-Honored One: "Venerable Gautama, please ask me. I will answer."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, what do you think? When the noble, learned disciples hear this, what would they say? Would it be proper for the elder Kāśyapa the Youth to engage in discussion and debate with the ascetic Gautama?"

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Venerable Gautama, those noble, learned ones would say: 'How could the elder Kāśyapa the Youth engage in discussion and debate with the ascetic Gautama? Just as a man who, having lost his eyes, wants to follow the tracks of birds in the sky, similarly, the elder Kāśyapa the Youth wants to engage in discussion and debate with the ascetic Gautama.'"

Kāśyapa the Youth then said to the World-Honored One: "I have heard from aged, senior brahmins who are old, advanced in years, of great age and long life, who have reached the final stage, who are teachers and teachers of teachers, who say: 'In the past, the world was empty of Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, just as it is now.' I do not know whether this statement is true or false."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, those aged, senior brahmins who are old, advanced in years, of great age and long life, who have reached the final stage, who are teachers and teachers of teachers, who say: 'In the past, the world was empty of Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, just as it is now,' this statement is false. Why? Because in the past there have been Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and in the future there will also be Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Kāśyapa, I am now the Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One.

"Kāśyapa, there are ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past as it truly is, do not know the future as it truly is, and do not know the present as it truly is. They think to themselves: 'We know everything, we see everything.' Kāśyapa, what do you think? Do these ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past as it truly is, do not know the future as it truly is, and do not know the present as it truly is, yet say 'We know everything, we see everything,' do they speak truly or falsely?"

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Venerable Gautama, those ascetics and brahmins speak falsely."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, it is like a man who says: 'I desire and love the most beautiful woman in this land.' Others ask him: 'Good man, do you know who she is? Is she a kṣatriya woman, a brahmin woman, a merchant woman, or a śūdra woman?' He answers: 'I do not know.' They further ask: 'Good man, do you know that woman's name, her clan name, whether she is tall or short, dark or fair, what village, town, or city she lives in?' He answers: 'I do not know.' Others then say: 'Good man, do you desire and love a woman you have never known or seen?' He answers: 'Yes.'

"Kāśyapa, what do you think? Given this, is not that man's speech foolish talk?"

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Indeed, Venerable Gautama, that man's speech is foolish talk."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, in the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past as it truly is, do not know the future as it truly is, and do not know the present as it truly is, yet they say 'We know everything, we see everything.' This is also foolish talk.

"Kāśyapa, it is like a man who, at a crossroads, builds a staircase, intending to climb up to a palace. Others ask him: 'Good man, the palace you want to climb up to, do you know whether it is in the east, south, west, or north? Do you know whether it is high or low, broad or narrow?' He answers: 'I do not know.' Others then say: 'Good man, you want to build a staircase to climb up to a palace that you do not know and have never seen?' He answers: 'Yes.'

"Kāśyapa, what do you think? Given this, is not that man's speech foolish talk?"

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Indeed, Venerable Gautama, that man's speech is foolish talk."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, in the same way, there are ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past as it truly is, do not know the future as it truly is, and do not know the present as it truly is, yet they say 'We know everything, we see everything.' This is also foolish talk."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, what do you think? The earth element: do you know the earth element as it truly is?"

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Venerable Gautama, the earth element: I know the earth element as it truly is."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, what is the earth element? How do you know the earth element as it truly is?"

At that time, Kāśyapa the Youth pointed to a small clod of earth and said: "Venerable Gautama, this is the earth element. This is how I know the earth element as it truly is."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, this small clod of earth is a small amount. It cannot be called knowing the earth element as it truly is. Kāśyapa, what is the earth element? The earth element has two kinds: the internal earth element and the external earth element.

"What is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, belonging to the self, that is solid and firm: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, large intestine, small intestine, stomach, and other things internal, belonging to the self, that are solid and firm. This is called the internal earth element.

"The internal earth element and the external earth element are both the earth element. One should contemplate with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having contemplated thus with right wisdom as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element, and the mind becomes liberated from the earth element.

"Kāśyapa, what is the water element? The water element also has two kinds: the internal water element and the external water element.

"What is the internal water element? Whatever is internal, belonging to the self, that is liquid and moist: tears, sweat, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, phlegm, bile, urine, and other things internal, belonging to the self, that are liquid and moist. This is called the internal water element.

"The internal water element and the external water element are both the water element. One should contemplate with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having contemplated thus with right wisdom as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted with the water element, and the mind becomes liberated from the water element.

"Kāśyapa, what is the fire element? The fire element also has two kinds: the internal fire element and the external fire element.

"What is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, belonging to the self, that is hot and warming: that which heats the body, that which ages the body, that which burns the body, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested, and other things internal, belonging to the self, that are hot and warming. This is called the internal fire element.

"The internal fire element and the external fire element are both the fire element. One should contemplate with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having contemplated thus with right wisdom as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element, and the mind becomes liberated from the fire element.

"Kāśyapa, what is the wind element? The wind element also has two kinds: the internal wind element and the external wind element.

"What is the internal wind element? Whatever is internal, belonging to the self, that is moving and stirring: upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds that pervade the limbs, in-breath, out-breath, and other things internal, belonging to the self, that are moving and stirring. This is called the internal wind element.

"The internal wind element and the external wind element are both the wind element. One should contemplate with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having contemplated thus with right wisdom as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted with the wind element, and the mind becomes liberated from the wind element.

"Kāśyapa, what is the space element? The space element also has two kinds: the internal space element and the external space element.

"What is the internal space element? Whatever is internal, belonging to the self, that is space and is empty: the ear holes, the nose holes, the mouth cavity, that by which food and drink are swallowed and the space where they reside, and that through which food and drink pass downward and are expelled, and other things internal, belonging to the self, that are space and empty. This is called the internal space element.

"The internal space element and the external space element are both the space element. One should contemplate with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having contemplated thus with right wisdom as it truly is, one becomes disenchanted with the space element, and the mind becomes liberated from the space element.

"Kāśyapa, if a bhikṣu does not take the earth element as self, does not take self as possessing the earth element, does not take the earth element as being in the self, and does not take the self as being in the earth element; does not take the water element, fire element, wind element, or space element as self, does not take self as possessing them, does not take them as being in the self, and does not take the self as being in them; then Kāśyapa, this bhikṣu does not take the earth element and the other elements as self.

"A bhikṣu who does not take the earth element and the other elements as self: his consciousness does not cling to them, is not bound to them, is not attached to them. Being unattached, he is not frightened. Not being frightened, he personally attains nirvāṇa. He knows: 'Birth is ended, the Brahma-conduct has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more return to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is.

"Kāśyapa, this is the teaching that the Tathāgata teaches. If one practices it, one will attain the fruit of the supreme Brahma-conduct."

Kāśyapa the Youth heard the Buddha's teaching and was delighted and faithful. He said to the World-Honored One: "Venerable Gautama, it is like overturning what was overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes can see forms. In the same way, Venerable Gautama has used various methods to explain the Dharma for me. I now take refuge in the World-Honored One, in the Dharma, and in the Sangha of bhikṣus. May Venerable Gautama accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa, do not be hasty. A person of your fame should investigate carefully and then decide."

Kāśyapa the Youth said: "Venerable Gautama, by saying this, you make me even more delighted and faithful. Why? If other heretical teachers had obtained me as a disciple, they would have carried banners throughout the city of Rājagṛha, proclaiming: 'Kāśyapa the Youth has become my disciple!' But Venerable Gautama instead tells me: 'Kāśyapa, do not be hasty. A person of your fame should investigate carefully and then decide.'

"Venerable Gautama, a second time I take refuge in the World-Honored One, in the Dharma, and in the Sangha of bhikṣus. May Venerable Gautama accept me as a lay disciple. From today until the end of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. Kāśyapa the Youth, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(133) The Sūtra on Excellence**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Nālandā, in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.

At that time, the householder Kevaṭṭa went to visit the World-Honored One. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, then sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Kevaṭṭa said to the World-Honored One:

"World-Honored One, Nālandā is a prosperous and flourishing city, with a large population. Would it not be good if the World-Honored One were to instruct one bhikṣu to perform supernatural powers and miraculous transformations, showing feats surpassing those of ordinary humans? Then the people of Nālandā would have even greater faith in the World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Kevaṭṭa, I do not teach the Dharma to bhikṣus in this way, saying: 'Go, display supernatural powers and miraculous transformations surpassing those of ordinary humans to the white-robed householders.'"

A second time, the householder Kevaṭṭa said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, Nālandā is a prosperous and flourishing city, with a large population. Would it not be good if the World-Honored One were to instruct one bhikṣu to perform supernatural powers and miraculous transformations, showing feats surpassing those of ordinary humans? Then the people of Nālandā would have even greater faith in the World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said a second time: "Kevaṭṭa, I do not teach the Dharma to bhikṣus in this way, saying: 'Go, display supernatural powers and miraculous transformations surpassing those of ordinary humans to the white-robed householders.'"

A third time, the householder Kevaṭṭa said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, Nālandā is a prosperous and flourishing city, with a large population. Would it not be good if the World-Honored One were to instruct one bhikṣu to perform supernatural powers and miraculous transformations, showing feats surpassing those of ordinary humans? Then the people of Nālandā would have even greater faith in the World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Kevaṭṭa, there are three kinds of miraculous powers. What are the three? The first is the miraculous power of supernatural abilities. The second is the miraculous power of knowing others' minds. The third is the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Kevaṭṭa, what is the miraculous power of supernatural abilities? Here, a bhikṣu performs various supernatural transformations: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one. He appears and disappears. He passes through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, without obstruction, as if through empty space. He plunges in and out of the earth as if it were water. He walks on water without sinking, as if on earth. Sitting cross-legged, he travels through the air like a bird in flight. With his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. He exerts mastery with his body as far as the Brahmā world.

"If a faithful and devoted person sees this, he then tells an unfaithful and undevoted person: 'Marvelous! Extraordinary! The supernatural power of that ascetic is extremely great and marvelous! I myself saw him perform various supernatural transformations: being one, becoming many; being many, becoming one; appearing and disappearing; passing through walls, ramparts, and mountains without obstruction; plunging in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water without sinking; sitting cross-legged, traveling through the air; with his hand touching the sun and moon; exerting mastery with his body as far as the Brahmā world.'

"The unfaithful and undevoted person would then say: 'There is a charm called the Gandhāra charm. It is by means of this charm that he can perform various supernatural transformations: being one, becoming many, and so forth.'

"Kevaṭṭa, what do you think? Would not the unfaithful and undevoted person say such a thing?"

Kevaṭṭa said: "He would say so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Kevaṭṭa, I see such a fault in the miraculous power of supernatural abilities. That is why I am disgusted, ashamed, and do not practice it.

"Kevaṭṭa, what is the miraculous power of knowing others' minds? Here, a bhikṣu reads the minds of other beings, of other persons: if there is a mind with desire, he knows it as a mind with desire; if there is a mind without desire, he knows it as a mind without desire; if there is a mind with anger, he knows it as a mind with anger; if there is a mind without anger, he knows it as a mind without anger; if there is a mind with delusion, he knows it as a mind with delusion; if there is a mind without delusion, he knows it as a mind without delusion; if there is a contracted mind, he knows it as a contracted mind; if there is an expansive mind, he knows it as an expansive mind; if there is a limited mind, he knows it as a limited mind; if there is an unlimited mind, he knows it as an unlimited mind; if there is a concentrated mind, he knows it as a concentrated mind; if there is an unconcentrated mind, he knows it as an unconcentrated mind; if there is a liberated mind, he knows it as a liberated mind; if there is an unliberated mind, he knows it as an unliberated mind.

"If a faithful and devoted person sees this, he then tells an unfaithful and undevoted person: 'Marvelous! Extraordinary! The supernatural power of that ascetic is extremely great and marvelous! He can read the minds of other beings, of other persons.'

"The unfaithful and undevoted person would then say: 'There is a charm called the Maṇikā charm. It is by means of this charm that he can read the minds of other beings, of other persons.'

"Kevaṭṭa, what do you think? Would not the unfaithful and undevoted person say such a thing?"

Kevaṭṭa said: "He would say so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Kevaṭṭa, I see such a fault in the miraculous power of knowing others' minds. That is why I am disgusted, ashamed, and do not practice it.

"Kevaṭṭa, what is the miraculous power of teaching and instruction? Here, a bhikṣu teaches others thus: 'You should think in this way, not in that way. You should attend to this, not to that. You should abandon this, and attain and abide in that.' Kevaṭṭa, this is called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Kevaṭṭa, here a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Persons to Be Tamed, Teacher of Devas and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. Among devas and humans, among Māra and Brahmā, among ascetics and brahmins, he himself knows and realizes, and teaches others. He teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with meaning and phrasing complete, proclaiming the pure Brahma-conduct.

"A householder or householder's son hears this Dharma. Having heard this Dharma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, he reflects thus: 'The household life is constricting and dusty; going forth is like the open air. Living at home, I cannot practice the Brahma-conduct in its complete fullness and purity, like a polished conch shell. Let me shave off my hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith, leave the household life to go forth to study the Way.'

"He then abandons his wealth, whether small or great, abandons his circle of relatives, whether small or great. He shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith, leaves the household life and goes forth.

"Having gone forth, he keeps the precepts and the rules of conduct, abandoning the killing of living beings, refraining from killing living beings, discarding knife and club, being conscientious, being compassionate, and being kind and beneficial to all living beings. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons taking what is not given, refraining from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given and expects only what is given. He lives with a pure self, without theft. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons unchastity, practicing chastity and purity, living apart from lewdness, abandoning the village dharma of sexual intercourse. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons false speech, refraining from false speech. He speaks truth, delights in truth, abides in truth, is trustworthy, and does not deceive the world. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons divisive speech, refraining from divisive speech. He does not, having heard something here, repeat it there to cause division; nor, having heard something there, repeat it here to cause division. He reconciles those who are divided and strengthens those who are united. He delights in harmony, takes pleasure in harmony, rejoices in harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons harsh speech, refraining from harsh speech. Whatever speech is gentle, pleasing to the ear, loving, going to the heart, courteous, dear and agreeable to many people, he speaks such words. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons idle chatter, refraining from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks about the Dharma, speaks about the Vinaya. His speech is timely and has a reason, is measured and is beneficial. This is how he keeps the precepts.

"He abandons injuring seeds and plants. He eats once a day, not at night, keeping to the proper time. He does not watch dancing, singing, music, or shows. He does not wear garlands, perfumes, or ornaments. He does not use high or broad beds. He does not accept gold or silver. He does not accept raw grain. He does not accept raw meat. He does not accept women or girls. He does not accept male or female servants. He does not accept elephants, horses, cattle, or sheep. He does not accept chickens or pigs. He does not accept fields or estates. He does not send others on errands or deliver messages. He does not engage in buying and selling. He does not cheat with false measures and weights. He does not practice bribery, deception, or fraud. He does not injure, kill, bind, ambush, plunder, or oppress.

"He is content with robes that cover his body and with food that sustains his belly. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies only with its wings, so too this bhikṣu, wherever he goes, takes only his robes and alms bowl with him.

"He, keeping these precepts and this noble aggregate of moral conduct, inwardly experiences the blameless bliss.

"When he sees a form with his eyes, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Because if he were to dwell without restraining the eye faculty, evil and unwholesome states, covetousness and grief, would flow into him. He practices restraint for the sake of that. He guards the eye faculty, and he attains restraint of the eye faculty. In the same way, when he hears a sound with his ears, smells an odor with his nose, tastes a flavor with his tongue, feels a tangible with his body, or cognizes a mental object with his mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Because if he were to dwell without restraining the mind faculty, evil and unwholesome states, covetousness and grief, would flow into him. He practices restraint for the sake of that. He guards the mind faculty, and he attains restraint of the mind faculty.

"He, possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, inwardly experiences unblemished bliss.

"He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning, when looking ahead and looking around, when bending and stretching, when wearing his robes and carrying his bowl, when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, when walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, speaking, and being silent, he acts with clear comprehension.

"He, possessing this noble aggregate of moral conduct, this noble restraint of the faculties, and this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, resorts to a secluded dwelling place: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a cave, a hillside, a wilderness, an open space, or a haystack.

"After his meal, returning from his alms round, he sits down, crossing his legs, keeping his body upright, and establishing mindfulness in front of him.

"He abandons covetousness with regard to the world. He dwells with a mind free from covetousness. He purifies his mind of covetousness.

"He abandons ill will and hatred. He dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. He purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.

"He abandons sloth and torpor. He dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending. He purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.

"He abandons restlessness and remorse. He dwells without restlessness, with inward peace of mind. He purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.

"He abandons doubt. He has crossed beyond doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome dharmas. He purifies his mind of doubt.

"He, having abandoned these five hindrances, these defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with applied thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters and abides in the first dhyāna.

"Kevaṭṭa, this is called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Furthermore, with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, with inner confidence and unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters and abides in the second dhyāna. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Furthermore, with the fading away of joy, he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and he experiences happiness with the body. That which the noble ones describe as: 'Equanimous and mindful, one abides in happiness,' he enters and abides in the third dhyāna. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Furthermore, with the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of pleasure and pain, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna, which has neither suffering nor happiness and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"He, with his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, the formations of many world-cycles, the dissolutions of many world-cycles, the formations and dissolutions of many world-cycles. 'There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn there. There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"He, with his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings as they pass away and are reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations. He understands how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings who were endowed with bad conduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, who held wrong views and undertook actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a lower realm, in hell. But these beings who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views and undertook actions based on right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings as they pass away and are reborn, and he understands how beings fare according to their actions. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"He, with his mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, free from defilements, pliant, malleable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it truly is: 'This is suffering.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the arising of suffering.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it truly is: 'These are the taints.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the arising of the taints.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the cessation of the taints.' He understands as it truly is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the taints.'

"Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of becoming, his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is ended, the Brahma-conduct has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more return to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is. Kevaṭṭa, this is also called the miraculous power of teaching and instruction.

"Kevaṭṭa, these are the three kinds of miraculous powers. Among these three, which one do you consider the most excellent, the most wonderful?"

Kevaṭṭa said: "World-Honored One, of the first two kinds, in which a person performs them himself and experiences them himself, I consider these to be like a magical illusion. I am not pleased with them. But the third kind, the miraculous power of teaching and instruction, this I consider to be the most excellent and most wonderful. Why? Because a bhikṣu, having been instructed thus: 'You should think in this way, not in that way; attend to this, not that; abandon this, and attain and abide in that,' and in sequence he accomplishes each stage, up to and including the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. Therefore, World-Honored One, of these three kinds of miraculous powers, the miraculous power of teaching and instruction I consider to be the most excellent and most wonderful."

The World-Honored One said: "Good, good! Kevaṭṭa, it is as you say."

The World-Honored One then said: "Kevaṭṭa, once in the past, in this assembly, a bhikṣu conceived this thought: 'Where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?' That bhikṣu then entered into such a samādhi that, with his mind concentrated, the path leading to the devas appeared before him.

"He then went to the realm of the Four Great Kings and asked the devas of the Four Great Kings: 'Friends, where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?' The devas of the Four Great Kings said to the bhikṣu: 'We do not know where the four great elements cease without remainder. But there are the Four Great Kings, who are superior to us and more eminent. They would know.'

"The bhikṣu then went to the Four Great Kings and asked: 'Friends, where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?' The Four Great Kings said to the bhikṣu: 'We do not know where the four great elements cease without remainder. But there is the Trāyastriṃśa heaven above us, and the devas there are superior to us and more eminent. They would know.'

"The bhikṣu then went to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and asked those devas the same question. The devas said: 'We do not know. But there is Lord Śakra, who is superior to us. He would know.'

"The bhikṣu then went to Lord Śakra and asked the same question. Lord Śakra said: 'I do not know. But there is the Yāma heaven above. The devas there would know.'

"The bhikṣu went to the Yāma heaven, and those devas referred him to the Yāma lord. The Yāma lord said he did not know, and referred him to the Tuṣita heaven.

"The bhikṣu went to the Tuṣita heaven, and those devas referred him to the Tuṣita lord. The Tuṣita lord said he did not know, and referred him to the Nirmāṇarati heaven.

"The bhikṣu went to the Nirmāṇarati heaven, and those devas referred him to the Nirmāṇarati lord. The Nirmāṇarati lord said he did not know, and referred him to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven.

"The bhikṣu went to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, and those devas referred him to the Paranirmitavaśavartin lord. The Paranirmitavaśavartin lord said he did not know, and referred him to the Brahmā heaven, saying: 'There are the Brahmā devas above. They are superior to us and more eminent. They would know.'

"The bhikṣu then entered into such a samādhi that, with his mind concentrated, the path leading to the Brahmā world appeared before him. He went to the Brahmā world and asked those Brahmā devas: 'Friends, where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?' The Brahmā devas said: 'We do not know. But there is the Great Brahmā, the Lord and Creator, who created us and this world. He is all-seeing, all-powerful. He would know.'

"The bhikṣu said: 'Where is the Great Brahmā now?'

"The Brahmā devas said: 'We do not know where the Great Brahmā is or in what direction he may be found. But when signs appear, when light appears and radiance manifests, then the Great Brahmā will appear. These are the signs of the Great Brahmā's coming: light appears and radiance manifests before his coming.'

"Before long, the Great Brahmā appeared. The bhikṣu went to the Great Brahmā and asked: 'Friend, where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?'

"The Great Brahmā said to the bhikṣu: 'Bhikṣu, I am the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Appointer, the Father of all that have been and will be.'

"The bhikṣu said: 'I did not ask you this. I asked: where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?'

"A second time, the Great Brahmā said to the bhikṣu: 'Bhikṣu, I am the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Appointer, the Father of all that have been and will be.'

"The bhikṣu again said: 'I did not ask you this. I asked: where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?'

"A third time, the Great Brahmā said the same.

"The bhikṣu again said: 'I did not ask you this. I asked: where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?'

"Then the Great Brahmā took the bhikṣu by the hand, led him aside, and said to him: 'Bhikṣu, the Brahmā devas all believe that the Great Brahmā is all-knowing, all-seeing, all-powerful. That is why, in their presence, I did not answer. Bhikṣu, I too do not know where the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder. Bhikṣu, you have done wrong in that you bypassed the World-Honored One and came here seeking an answer to this question. Bhikṣu, you should go back to the World-Honored One and ask him this question. As the World-Honored One explains it, so you should accept it.'

"The bhikṣu then, as swiftly as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, disappeared from the Brahmā world and appeared before the World-Honored One. He bowed his head at the World-Honored One's feet and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the bhikṣu said to the World-Honored One:

"'World-Honored One, where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?'

"The World-Honored One said: 'Bhikṣu, it is as if there were a merchant who had a bird, and while traveling on the great ocean, when the ship was out of sight of land, he released the bird. The bird flew in all four directions, in all the intermediate directions, upward and downward. If it found land, it would alight there. If it could not find land, it would return to the ship. Bhikṣu, in the same way, you have searched everywhere, up to the Brahmā world, and could not obtain an answer to your question, and so you have returned to me. Bhikṣu, you should not ask the question in this way: "Where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, cease without remainder?" Rather, you should ask:

"'"Where is it that earth, water, fire, and wind find no footing? Where is it that long and short, fine and coarse, beautiful and ugly, name and form completely cease without remainder?"

"'The answer to this is: In the consciousness that is invisible, infinite, and luminous in all directions. It is here that earth, water, fire, and wind find no footing. It is here that long and short, fine and coarse, beautiful and ugly, name and form completely cease without remainder. With the cessation of consciousness, all of these cease.'"

The World-Honored One spoke thus. The householder Kevaṭṭa, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 31

## Sūtra 132: The Great Chapter, Raṭṭhapāla Sūtra, Number Sixteen

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Kuru country, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He went to Thullakoṭṭhika and stayed in the Śiśapā Grove north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhika.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika heard: "The ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan who left the Śākya lineage to go forth from home and study the Way, is traveling in the Kuru country together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He has come to this Thullakoṭṭhika and is staying in the Śiśapā Grove north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhika. That ascetic Gautama has great renown, known throughout the ten directions. The ascetic Gautama is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Dharma, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. He, in this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics and brahmins, from humans to gods, has himself known, himself realized, himself attained realization and abides therein. When he teaches the Dharma, it is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. If one can see the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, pay reverence and respect, make offerings and attend upon him, one will quickly obtain great benefit. We should all go together to see the ascetic Gautama, pay reverence and make offerings."

After the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika heard this, each with their respective retinues and companions following, they went out from Thullakoṭṭhika, heading north to the Śiśapā Grove, wishing to see the World-Honored One, pay reverence, and make offerings. Having gone to the Buddha, the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika, some bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side; some greeted the Buddha with inquiries and sat to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down silently. At that time, after the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika had all settled in their seats, the Buddha taught them the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring thirst and longing, bringing about joy. With immeasurable skillful means he taught them the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring thirst and longing, bringing about joy, and then remained silent. At that time, after the Buddha had taught the Dharma to the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika, exhorting and inspiring thirst and longing, bringing about joy, each arose from their seats, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.

At that time, Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, remained seated and did not rise. Then Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, not long after the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika had departed, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder and arranged his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I remain at home, bound by fetters, I cannot for the rest of my life practice the pure holy life. World-Honored One! I wish to be allowed to go forth from the World-Honored One and study the Way, to receive the full precepts, to become a bhikṣu, and to purely cultivate the holy life."

The World-Honored One asked: "Householder's son! Have your parents given permission for you to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way?"

Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, said: "World-Honored One! My parents have not yet given permission for me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder's son! If your parents have not given permission for you to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way, then I cannot ordain you to go forth and study the Way, nor can I grant you the full precepts."

Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, said: "World-Honored One! I shall use skillful means to seek permission from my parents, and I will surely cause them to permit me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder's son! Do as you wish."

Thereupon Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, having heard the Buddha's words, received and upheld them well, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and returned home. He said: "Dear parents! As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I remain at home, bound by fetters, I cannot for the rest of my life practice the pure holy life. I sincerely wish that my parents would permit me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way."

Raṭṭhapāla's parents told him: "Raṭṭhapāla! We now have only you as our one son. We love and cherish you dearly, our hearts always rejoice in you, and we never tire of seeing you. If you were to die, we would still not wish to be separated from you. How much less could we bear to be parted from you while you are alive and not see you?"

Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, again asked a second and third time, saying: "Dear parents! As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I remain at home, bound by fetters, I cannot for the rest of my life practice the pure holy life. I sincerely wish that my parents would permit me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way."

Raṭṭhapāla's parents also replied a second and third time, saying: "Raṭṭhapāla! We now have only you as our one son. We love and cherish you dearly, our hearts always rejoice in you, and we never tire of seeing you. If you were to die, we would still not wish to be separated from you. How much less could we bear to be parted from you while you are alive and not see you?"

Then Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, immediately lay down on the ground: "From now on I will not rise, I will not drink and I will not eat, until my parents permit me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way." Thereupon Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, did not eat for one day, then for two, three, four, and many days he did not eat.

Then Raṭṭhapāla's parents went to their son and said: "Raṭṭhapāla! You are so delicate, your body is extremely fine, you always sit and lie on fine beds. Do you not know suffering now? Raṭṭhapāla! You should quickly get up, enjoy pleasures, give generously, and happily cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this? Raṭṭhapāla! The realm of the World-Honored One is extremely difficult, extremely difficult. Going forth and studying the Way is also extremely difficult." At that time, Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, remained silent and did not answer.

Then Raṭṭhapāla's parents went to Raṭṭhapāla's relatives and ministers, and said: "All of you, come together to Raṭṭhapāla's place and urge him to get up from the ground."

Raṭṭhapāla's relatives and ministers then all went together to Raṭṭhapāla's place and said: "Raṭṭhapāla! You are so delicate, your body is extremely fine, you always sit and lie on fine beds. Do you not know suffering now? Raṭṭhapāla! You should quickly get up, enjoy pleasures, give generously, and happily cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this? The realm of the World-Honored One is extremely difficult, extremely difficult. Going forth and studying the Way is also extremely difficult." At that time, Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, remained silent and did not answer.

Then Raṭṭhapāla's parents went to Raṭṭhapāla's good friends, companions, and contemporaries, and said: "All of you, come together to Raṭṭhapāla's place and urge him to get up from the ground."

Then Raṭṭhapāla's good friends, companions, and contemporaries all went together to Raṭṭhapāla's place and said: "Raṭṭhapāla! You are so delicate, your body is extremely fine, you always sit and lie on fine beds. Do you not know suffering now? Raṭṭhapāla! You should quickly get up, enjoy pleasures, give generously, and happily cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this? Raṭṭhapāla! The realm of the World-Honored One is extremely difficult, extremely difficult. Going forth and studying the Way is also extremely difficult." At that time, Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, remained silent and did not answer.

Then Raṭṭhapāla's good friends, companions, and contemporaries went to Raṭṭhapāla's parents and said: "You should permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way. If he finds joy in it, then in this very life you may still see each other. If he does not find joy in it, he will certainly return of his own accord to his parents. If you do not permit him now, he will surely die without doubt. What benefit would that bring?"
