Then Raṭṭhapāla's parents, having heard this, said to Raṭṭhapāla's good friends, companions, and contemporaries: "We now permit Raṭṭhapāla to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way. If after studying the Way he comes back, we may still see him."

Raṭṭhapāla's good friends, companions, and contemporaries then all went together to Raṭṭhapāla's place and said: "Householder's son! Your parents have permitted you to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way. After studying the Way, you should return to see your parents."

When Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, heard these words, he was greatly delighted, filled with love and joy. He rose from the ground, gradually nourished his body, and when his body had recovered, he went out from Thullakoṭṭhika to the Buddha's place, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One! My parents have permitted me to go forth with full faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya, to leave home and become homeless, and to study the Way. I sincerely wish the World-Honored One would allow me to go forth from the World-Honored One and study the Way, to receive the full precepts, and to become a bhikṣu."

Thereupon the World-Honored One ordained Raṭṭhapāla, the householder's son, granting him the going forth and the full precepts. After receiving the full precepts, he stayed for some time in Thullakoṭṭhika, and afterward he gathered his robes, took his bowl, and traveled on, arriving at Śrāvastī, where he stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. After the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had gone forth and received the full precepts, he dwelt in seclusion alone, his mind free from negligence, cultivating with diligence. Having dwelt in seclusion alone, his mind free from negligence, cultivating with diligence, the purpose for which sons of good families shave off their hair and beards, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness to study the Way, namely the unsurpassed completion of the holy life, he in this present life himself knew, himself realized, himself attained realization and abided therein: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence." He knew it as it truly is. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having known the Dharma, had attained arhatship.

Then after the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had attained arhatship, after nine or ten years, he had this thought: "I previously made a promise that after going forth and studying the Way I would return to see my parents. I should now go back to fulfill that promise." Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla went to the Buddha's place, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I previously made a promise that after going forth and studying the Way I would return to see my parents. World-Honored One! I now take my leave to go see my parents and fulfill that promise."

At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This son of good family Raṭṭhapāla, if he were to abandon the precepts, leave the Way, and return to sensual pleasures as before, there is certainly no possibility of that." The World-Honored One, having understood this, said: "Go! Those who have not yet been delivered, deliver them. Those who have not yet been liberated, cause them to be liberated. Those whose nirvāṇa has not yet been completed, cause them to complete it. Raṭṭhapāla! Go now as you wish."

At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having heard the Buddha's words, received and upheld them well, then rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to his own room, put away his bedding, put on his robes and took his bowl, and traveled on until he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika, where he stayed in the Śiśapā Grove north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhika. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having passed the night, at dawn put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika to beg for food. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had this thought: "The World-Honored One praises begging for alms in sequence from house to house. I should now beg for alms in sequence in this Thullakoṭṭhika." The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla then begged for alms in sequence in Thullakoṭṭhika, and in due course arrived at his former home.

At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was standing at the middle gate, having his hair and beard trimmed. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar and said: "This bald ascetic, bound by darkness, has cut off our lineage and left us without an heir, destroying our family. I had one son whom I loved and cherished dearly, my heart always delighted in him, and I never tired of seeing him. He took him away and ordained him. Do not give him food!"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, at his own father's house, received no offering but only scolding: "This bald ascetic, bound by darkness, has cut off our lineage and left us without an heir, destroying our family. I had one son whom I loved and cherished dearly, my heart always delighted in him, and I never tired of seeing him. He took him away and ordained him. Do not give him food!" The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having understood this, quickly departed.

At that time, a female servant of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father's household had put foul and rotten food scraps into a winnowing basket and was about to discard them in the rubbish heap. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, seeing his father's servant putting foul and rotten food scraps into a winnowing basket about to discard them in the rubbish heap, said: "Sister! If this rotten food is to be thrown away, please put it in my bowl and I shall eat it."

At that time, the female servant of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father's household poured the foul and rotten food scraps from the basket into his bowl. As she poured them into the bowl, she noted two distinguishing features: she recognized his voice and his hands and feet. Having noted these two features, she immediately went to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father and said: "Sir, you should know that your son Raṭṭhapāla has returned to this Thullakoṭṭhika. You should go see him." When the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father heard this, he was greatly delighted and overjoyed. He gathered up his robe with his left hand, smoothed his hair and beard with his right hand, and hastened to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's place.

At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was facing the wall eating this foul and rotten food. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, seeing the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla facing the wall eating this foul and rotten food, said: "Raṭṭhapāla! You are so delicate, your body is extremely fine, you always ate fine food. Raṭṭhapāla! How can you eat this foul and rotten food? Raṭṭhapāla! For what reason have you come to this Thullakoṭṭhika and yet not come to your parents' home?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Householder! I entered my father's house and received no offering but only scolding: 'This bald ascetic, bound by darkness, has cut off our lineage and left us without an heir, destroying our family. I had only one son whom I loved and cherished dearly, my heart always delighted in him, and I never tired of seeing him. He took him away and ordained him. Do not give him food!' When I heard this, I quickly departed."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father immediately apologized, saying: "Raṭṭhapāla, please forgive me! Raṭṭhapāla, please forgive me! I truly did not know that Raṭṭhapāla had returned and entered his father's house." Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father respectfully embraced the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla and led him inside, prepared a seat and invited him to sit. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla then took his seat.

Then the father, seeing the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla seated, went to his wife and said: "You should know that the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla has now returned home. Quickly prepare food and drink."

When the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother heard this, she was greatly delighted and overjoyed, and quickly prepared food and drink. After preparing the food and drink, she hurriedly brought out money on carts and placed it in the middle of the courtyard, heaped into a great pile. The great pile of money was so large that a person standing on one side could not see a person sitting on the other side. After making this great pile of money, she went to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla and said: "Raṭṭhapāla! This is the wealth and property from your mother's share. Your father's wealth is immeasurable, hundreds of thousands beyond counting. It is all now given to you. Raṭṭhapāla! You should abandon the precepts, leave the Way, enjoy pleasures, give generously, and happily cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this? The realm of the World-Honored One is extremely difficult, extremely difficult. Going forth and studying the Way is also extremely difficult."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his mother: "I now wish to say something. Will you be willing to listen?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother said: "Householder's son! Say what you wish, and I shall listen."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his mother: "You should make new cloth bags, fill them with money, load them onto carts, take them to the Ganges River, and pour them into the deepest part. Why is this? Because of this money, people are made to suffer worry, grief, weeping, and sorrow, and cannot attain happiness."

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother had this thought: "By this means I cannot cause my son Raṭṭhapāla to abandon the precepts and leave the Way. Perhaps I should go to his former wives and say: 'Daughters-in-law! You should adorn yourselves with the jewelry and ornaments you used to wear. When the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla was formerly at home, he was extremely fond of you. Having quickly adorned yourselves with these jewels, you should all go together to the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla, each embrace one of his feet, and say: "We wonder, dear husband, what heavenly maidens surpass us, that our dear husband would abandon us to cultivate the holy life for their sake?"'"

Then his mother went to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives and said: "Daughters-in-law! You should adorn yourselves with the jewelry and ornaments you used to wear. When the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla was formerly at home, he was extremely fond of you. Having quickly adorned yourselves with these jewels, you should all go together to the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla, each embrace one of his feet, and say: 'We wonder, dear husband, what heavenly maidens surpass us, that our dear husband would abandon us to cultivate the holy life for their sake?'"

At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives each adorned themselves with the jewelry and ornaments they used to wear, with which the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had been extremely fond of them when he was formerly at home. Having adorned themselves with these jewels, they went to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, each embraced one of his feet, and said: "We wonder, dear husband, what heavenly maidens surpass us, that our dear husband would abandon us to cultivate the holy life for their sake?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his former wives: "Sisters! You should know that I did not cultivate the holy life for the sake of heavenly maidens. The purpose for which I cultivated the holy life, that goal has been attained. What the Buddha's teaching required to be done has now been accomplished."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's wives withdrew to one side, weeping and shedding tears, and said: "We are not our dear husband's sisters, yet our dear husband calls us sisters."

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla turned back and looked at his parents, saying: "Householder! If you wish to offer food, then offer it at the proper time. Why do you trouble me?"

At that time, his parents rose from their seats and personally brought water for washing hands, and with the finest delicacies and a rich variety of food, things to eat, chew, lick, and drink, they personally served him, filling him completely. When the meal was finished and the vessels cleared away, and the hand-washing completed, he took a small seat and sat separately to listen to the Dharma. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla taught his parents the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring thirst and longing, bringing about joy. With immeasurable skillful means he taught them the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring thirst and longing, bringing about joy. Then he rose from his seat, stood, and spoke these verses:

"Behold this adorned form, with precious jewels and ornaments,
Right-coiled hair upon the head, dark kohl painted on the brows.
This deceives the foolish, but does not fool those who have crossed beyond.
With many fine colors and fabrics, they adorn the foul-smelling body.
This deceives the foolish, but does not fool those who have crossed beyond.
Various fragrances rubbed all over the body, turmeric yellowing the feet.
This deceives the foolish, but does not fool those who have crossed beyond.
The body dressed in pure and wondrous garments, adorned like an illusion.
This deceives the foolish, but does not fool those who have crossed beyond.
Having broken the deer-trap's bonds, and shattered the deer enclosure's gate,
I have cast off the bait and departed. Who would delight in the deer's snare?"

After the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla spoke these verses, he rose into the sky by means of supernormal power and departed, arriving at the Thullakoṭṭhika forest. Entering that forest, he spread out his sitting cloth beneath a Vilva tree and sat cross-legged. At that time, King Koravya, surrounded by his ministers in front and behind, was seated in his main hall, praising and extolling the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: "If I hear that the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla has come to this Thullakoṭṭhika, I shall certainly go to see him."

Then King Koravya ordered his huntsman: "Go and inspect the Thullakoṭṭhika forest. I wish to go hunting." The huntsman received the order and went to inspect the Thullakoṭṭhika forest. While inspecting the Thullakoṭṭhika forest, the huntsman saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla beneath the Vilva tree, seated cross-legged on his sitting cloth, and had this thought: "The very one for whom King Koravya and his ministers, seated in the main hall, praised and extolled, is now here."

At that time, the huntsman, having finished inspecting the Thullakoṭṭhika forest, returned to King Koravya's place and said: "Great King! You should know that I have inspected the Thullakoṭṭhika forest, as the Great King wished. The one for whom the Great King, together with his ministers, sat in the main hall praising and extolling the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, saying: 'If I hear that the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla has come to this Thullakoṭṭhika, I shall certainly go to see him,' the son of good family, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, is now in the Thullakoṭṭhika forest beneath a Vilva tree, seated cross-legged on his sitting cloth. If the Great King wishes to see him, he may go now."

When King Koravya heard this, he ordered his charioteer: "Quickly prepare the carriage. I now wish to go see Raṭṭhapāla."

The charioteer received the order and quickly prepared the carriage. When it was ready, he reported: "Great King! You should know that the carriage is prepared. It is at the Great King's pleasure."

Then King Koravya mounted the carriage and went to the Thullakoṭṭhika forest. Seeing the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla from afar, he descended from the carriage, proceeded on foot to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's place. The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, seeing King Koravya approach, said: "Great King! You have come. Would you like to sit?"

King Koravya said: "Though I have arrived in my own territory, I wish for the son of good family Raṭṭhapāla to invite me to sit."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla then invited King Koravya, saying: "There is a separate seat here. Great King, please be seated."

Then King Koravya and the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla exchanged greetings. He sat to one side and said to Raṭṭhapāla: "Did you go forth and study the Way because of decline in your household? If you went forth because of lack of wealth, Raṭṭhapāla, King Koravya's household has abundant wealth. I will provide wealth to Raṭṭhapāla and urge Raṭṭhapāla to abandon the precepts, leave the Way, enjoy pleasures, give generously, and happily cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this? Raṭṭhapāla! The teacher's realm is extremely difficult. Going forth and studying the Way is also extremely difficult."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having heard this, said: "Great King! You have now made an impure request of me, not a pure request."

King Koravya, hearing this, asked: "How should I make a pure request of Raṭṭhapāla, and not an impure one?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! You should speak thus: 'Raṭṭhapāla! The people of my country are peaceful and happy, without fear, without conflict, without thorns, without bitter forced labor. Grain and rice are abundant, and alms food is easy to obtain. Raṭṭhapāla, dwell in my country, and I shall protect you according to the Dharma.' Great King! In this way you make a pure request of me, not an impure one."

King Koravya, having heard this, said: "I now make a pure request of Raṭṭhapāla, not an impure one. The people of my country are peaceful and happy, without fear, without conflict, without thorns, without bitter forced labor. Grain and rice are abundant, and alms food is easy to obtain. Raṭṭhapāla, dwell in my country, and I shall protect you according to the Dharma.

"Furthermore, Raṭṭhapāla! There are four kinds of decline, and it is because of these declines that people shave off their hair and beards, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way. What are the four? Decline through illness, decline through old age, decline of wealth, and decline of relatives. Raṭṭhapāla! What is decline through illness? There may be a person who has a long illness and ailment, extremely heavy and painful. He thinks: 'I have a long illness and ailment, extremely heavy and painful. Though I truly have desires, I cannot fulfill them. I should now shave off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way.' He then, because of decline through illness, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, goes forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studies the Way. This is decline through illness.

"Raṭṭhapāla! What is decline through old age? There may be a person who is aged, his faculties worn, his lifespan nearly spent. He thinks: 'I am aged, my faculties worn, my lifespan nearly spent. Though I truly have desires, I cannot fulfill them. I should now shave off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way.' He then, because of decline through old age, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, goes forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studies the Way. This is decline through old age.

"Raṭṭhapāla! What is decline of wealth? There may be a person who is poor and without resources. He thinks: 'I am poor and without resources. I should now shave off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way.' He then, because of decline of wealth, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, goes forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studies the Way. This is decline of wealth.

"Raṭṭhapāla! What is decline of relatives? There may be a person whose relatives and kin are all gone, dead and perished. He thinks: 'My relatives and kin are all gone, dead and perished. I should now shave off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way.' He then, because of decline of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, goes forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studies the Way. This is decline of relatives.

"Raṭṭhapāla, in former times, was free from illness, healthy and well, with a balanced digestive system, neither too cold nor too hot, balanced, comfortable, and harmonious, and therefore all that he ate, chewed, licked, and drank was digested with ease. Raṭṭhapāla did not shave off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way because of decline through illness.

"In former times, Raṭṭhapāla was a young man, with black and lustrous hair, his body strong and vigorous. At that time he engaged in music and entertainment, greatly amusing himself, adorning his body, always delighting in play. At that time, his relatives all did not wish him to go forth. His parents wept with grief, worry, and sorrow, and also did not permit you to go forth and study the Way. Yet you shaved off your hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way. Raṭṭhapāla did not shave off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way because of decline through old age.

"Raṭṭhapāla! In this Thullakoṭṭhika, yours is the foremost family, the greatest family, the most excellent family, the highest family, in terms of wealth and property. Raṭṭhapāla did not shave off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way because of decline of wealth.

"Raṭṭhapāla! In this Thullakoṭṭhika forest and surroundings, your great and powerful relatives and kin are all still living. Raṭṭhapāla did not shave off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way because of decline of relatives.

"Raṭṭhapāla, these are the four kinds of decline, and some who have such decline shave off their hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way. I see that Raṭṭhapāla has none of these declines that would cause Raṭṭhapāla to shave off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way. Raṭṭhapāla! What did you know and see? What did you hear that caused you to shave off your hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, go forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and study the Way?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla answered: "Great King! The World-Honored One who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught me four things, which I accepted and delighted in. I knew, saw, and heard these, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way. What are the four? Great King! First, this world is without protection, without anything to rely upon. Second, this world entirely tends toward the dharma of aging. Third, this world is impermanent, and must certainly be relinquished. Fourth, this world is never satisfied, never has enough, and is driven by craving."

King Koravya asked: "Raṭṭhapāla! Regarding what you said: 'Great King! This world is without protection, without anything to rely upon.' Raṭṭhapāla! I have sons and grandsons, brothers and kinsmen, elephant troops, chariot troops, cavalry, and infantry, all skilled in archery and chariot-driving, stern and courageous, princes, warriors, Prākṛtamahānāga experts, those with divination skills, those with strategic planning, those with calculation skills, those skilled in writing, those skilled in debate, ministers and retainers, those who know and hold mantras. They can subdue any direction from which danger arises. If Raṭṭhapāla says: 'Great King! This world is without protection, without anything to rely upon,' Raṭṭhapāla, what is the meaning of what you said?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla answered: "Great King! I now ask the King, and please answer as you understand. Great King! Does your body ever have illness?"

King Koravya answered: "Raṭṭhapāla! My body constantly suffers from wind disease."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla asked: "Great King! When the wind disease flares up and you experience extremely heavy and painful suffering, Great King, at that time can you tell those sons and grandsons, brothers, elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, infantry skilled in archery and chariot-driving, stern and courageous, princes, warriors, Prākṛtamahānāga experts, diviners, strategists, calculators, scribes, skilled debaters, ministers and retainers, those who know and hold mantras, 'All of you come and temporarily bear this extremely heavy and painful suffering in my place, so that I may be free of illness and at ease'?"

King Koravya answered: "No. Why is this? I myself created this karma, and by reason of karma and conditions of karma, I alone endure this extremely heavy, painful suffering."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! For this reason, the World-Honored One said that this world is without protection, without anything to rely upon. I accepted and delighted in this. I knew, saw, and heard this, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way."

King Koravya said: "If Raṭṭhapāla says: 'Great King! This world is without protection, without anything to rely upon,' I too accept this and delight in it. Why is this? This world is truly without protection, without anything to rely upon."

King Koravya further asked: "Regarding what Raṭṭhapāla said: 'Great King! This world entirely tends toward the dharma of aging.' Raṭṭhapāla, what is the meaning of what you said?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla answered: "Great King! I now ask the King, and please answer as you understand. When the Great King was perhaps twenty-four or twenty-five years old, what do you think? At that time, how was your swiftness compared to now? At that time, how were your strength, physique, and complexion compared to now?"

King Koravya answered: "Raṭṭhapāla! When I was perhaps twenty-four or twenty-five years old, I recall that at that time, in swiftness, strength, physique, and complexion, none surpassed me. Raṭṭhapāla! I am now extremely old, my faculties are withered, my lifespan nearly spent. I am now eighty years old and can no longer stand up."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! For this reason, the World-Honored One said that this world entirely tends toward the dharma of aging. I accepted and delighted in this. I knew, saw, and heard this, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way."

King Koravya said: "If Raṭṭhapāla says: 'Great King! This world entirely tends toward the dharma of aging,' I too accept this and delight in it. Why is this? This world truly, entirely tends toward the dharma of aging."

King Koravya further asked: "Regarding what Raṭṭhapāla said: 'Great King! This world is impermanent, and must certainly be relinquished.' Raṭṭhapāla, what is the meaning of what you said?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! I now ask the King, and please answer as you understand. Great King! Do you possess the prosperous Kuru country, a prosperous harem, and prosperous treasuries?"

King Koravya answered: "Yes, indeed."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla further asked: "Great King! Having the prosperous Kuru country, a prosperous harem, and prosperous treasuries, when the time comes that death arrives, which cannot be relied upon, which is beyond one's tolerance, which destroys everything, and none in this world can escape death, at that time, the prosperous Kuru country, the prosperous harem, and the prosperous treasuries, can you take them from this world to the next world?"

King Koravya answered: "No. Why is this? I go alone without a second, without companions, from this world to the next world."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! For this reason, the World-Honored One said that this world is impermanent, and must certainly be relinquished. I accepted and delighted in this. I knew, saw, and heard this, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way."

King Koravya said: "If Raṭṭhapāla says: 'Great King! This world is impermanent, and must certainly be relinquished,' I too accept this and delight in it. Why is this? This world is truly impermanent, and must certainly be relinquished."

King Koravya further asked: "Regarding what Raṭṭhapāla said: 'Great King! This world is never satisfied, never has enough, and is driven by craving.' Raṭṭhapāla, what is the meaning of what you said?"

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla answered: "Great King! I now ask the King, and please answer as you understand. Great King! Do you possess the prosperous Kuru country, a prosperous harem, and prosperous treasuries?"

King Koravya answered: "Yes, indeed."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla further asked: "Great King! Having the prosperous Kuru country, a prosperous harem, and prosperous treasuries, suppose from the east a man came, trustworthy and reliable, who does not deceive the world, and said to the King: 'I have come from the east. I have seen a country there that is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people. Great King! You could obtain that country's wealth, people, and labor. Would you wish to conquer and rule that country?'"

King Koravya answered: "Raṭṭhapāla! If I knew there were such a prosperous country, with such wealth, people, and labor, and could conquer its people and govern it, I would certainly take it."

"Likewise, from the south, from the west, from the north, or from the other shore of the great sea, if a man came, trustworthy and reliable, who does not deceive the world, and said to the King: 'I have come from the other shore of the great sea. I have seen a country there that is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people. Great King! You could obtain that country's wealth, people, and labor. Would you wish to conquer and rule that country?'"

King Koravya answered: "Raṭṭhapāla! If I knew there were such a prosperous country, with such wealth, people, and labor, and could conquer its people and govern it, I would certainly take it."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! For this reason, the World-Honored One said that this world is never satisfied, never has enough, and is driven by craving. I accepted and delighted in this. I knew, saw, and heard this, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way."

King Koravya said: "If Raṭṭhapāla says: 'Great King! This world is never satisfied, never has enough, and is driven by craving,' I too accept this and delight in it. Why is this? This world is truly never satisfied, never has enough, and is driven by craving."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King! The World-Honored One who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught me these four things. I accepted and delighted in them. I knew, saw, and heard them, and therefore I shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, went forth with full faith from home to homelessness, and studied the Way."

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla spoke these verses:

"I see people in this world, who, having wealth, are foolish and do not give.
Having obtained wealth, they seek yet more, stingy and greedy, hoarding their goods.
Kings who gain the whole world, ruling and governing as far as their power extends,
Within the seas are not yet satisfied, and seek yet further beyond the seas.
Kings and all their people, before departing desire their lives come to an end.
With hair unbound, wives and children weep, crying 'Alas! This suffering is hard to bear.'
Wrapped in cloth and buried, or piled on wood and burned by fire.
Passing on to the next world, once burned, without wisdom or thought.
After death, wealth does not follow, nor wives, children, or servants.
Rich and poor are alike in this, foolish and wise are also the same.
The wise do not harbor grief; only the foolish embrace sorrow.
Therefore wisdom is supreme, leading to attainment of the path of perfect awakening.
Deeply attached to existence upon existence, the foolish commit evil deeds,
Acting contrary to Dharma, using force to seize from others.
Those of little wisdom follow and imitate others; the foolish mostly commit evil deeds.
Entering the womb to the next world, again and again they undergo birth and death.
Having been born into this world, alone they commit many evil deeds.
Like a thief bound by others, by one's own evil deeds one is harmed.
Thus these beings, arriving at the next world,
Are harmed by their own deeds, harmed by the evil they themselves have done.
Like ripe fruit that falls of itself, so too the old and the young.
Desiring adornment, beauty, love, and delight, the mind pursues pleasing and ugly forms.
Bound and harmed by desire, from desire fear arises.
O King! I have seen this and awakened, knowing that the path of the ascetic is excellent."

The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla spoke thus. King Koravya, hearing what the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had spoken, was delighted and put it into practice.

End of the Raṭṭhapāla Sūtra, Number Sixteen.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtra)
## Fascicle 32

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva during the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

---

## Chapter on Great Categories (continued)

### (131) Sūtra on Subduing Pride

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma that is good at the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, that is complete and pure, declaring the practice of the holy life. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you. It is called 'Subduing Pride.'

"What is 'Subduing Pride'? A bhikṣu, relying on a certain village or town, dwells there. He reflects thus: 'For what purpose did I come to dwell in this village or town? Was it not for the sake of subduing pride?'

"He then reflects: 'Am I now dwelling here with pride subdued or not? If a bhikṣu has not yet eliminated the defilements of desire, and in dependence on this village or town, dwelling here, the defilements of desire are eliminated, then this bhikṣu should dwell in dependence on this village or town, and should not depart.'

"If a bhikṣu has not yet eliminated the defilements of desire, and in dependence on this village or town, dwelling here, the defilements of desire are not eliminated, this bhikṣu should reflect: 'For what purpose do I dwell in dependence on this village or town? Is it not for the sake of subduing pride?'

"He then reflects: 'If while dwelling here in dependence on this village or town, the defilements of desire are not eliminated, then I should depart from this village or town.'

"This bhikṣu should depart from this village or town and should not remain.

"It is like a deer in the wilderness. It walks on the path freely, stands freely, sits freely, and lies down freely. Why is this? Because it has gone beyond the hunter's domain. In the same way, this bhikṣu should depart from this village or town and should not remain. Why is this? Because he has already gone beyond Māra's domain.

"If a bhikṣu has already eliminated the defilements of desire, and in dependence on this village or town, dwelling here, the defilements of desire have been eliminated, this bhikṣu should dwell in dependence on this village or town and should not depart. Why is this? Because the defilements of desire have been eliminated.

"It is like a deer that has been captured and bound. It lies on the pile of nets, unable to walk freely, stand freely, sit freely, or lie down freely. Why is this? Because it has not gone beyond the hunter's domain. In the same way, if a bhikṣu's defilements of desire have not yet been eliminated, and in dependence on this village or town, the defilements are not eliminated, yet he does not depart, this is not to be praised. Why is this? Because he has not gone beyond Māra's domain.

"If a bhikṣu has already eliminated the defilements of desire, and in dependence on this village or town, dwelling here, the defilements of desire have already been eliminated, this bhikṣu may dwell here or may depart; either way is suitable. Why is this? Because his defilements have already been eliminated.

"It is like a deer in the wilderness that walks on the path freely, stands freely, sits freely, and lies down freely. Even if a hunter comes, it can go where it wishes. Why is this? Because it has already gone beyond the hunter's domain. In the same way, this bhikṣu's defilements have been eliminated, so whether dwelling or departing, both are suitable."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (132) Sūtra on Kalāma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and they arrived at a brahmin village of the Kālāmas called Kesamutti.

The Kālāma brahmins of Kesamutti heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama, son of the Śākya clan, who had left the Śākya household to go forth and attain the path, was traveling in Kosala with a great assembly of bhikṣus and had arrived at Kesamutti. That Śramaṇa Gautama had a great reputation, and was known thus: "He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Among gods, Māra, Brahmā, and among śramaṇas, brahmins, from gods to humans, he has himself realized, attained, and declared it. He teaches the Dharma that is good at the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, that is complete and pure, declaring the practice of the holy life. It would be good to see such an Arhat."

Then the Kālāma brahmins of Kesamutti, each with their retinue, proceeded toward the World-Honored One. Some bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Some joined their palms toward the World-Honored One and sat to one side. Some announced their name and clan from afar and sat to one side. Some remained silent and sat to one side.

The Kālāma brahmins of Kesamutti then addressed the Buddha: "Gautama, there are some śramaṇas and brahmins who come to Kesamutti. They expound and praise only their own doctrines, but disparage, defame, criticize, and reject the doctrines of others. Gautama, then other śramaṇas and brahmins also come to Kesamutti. They too expound and praise only their own doctrines, but disparage, defame, criticize, and reject the doctrines of others. Gautama, regarding these various teachers, we have doubts and perplexity: among these śramaṇas and brahmins, who speaks truth and who speaks falsehood?"

The Buddha addressed the Kālāmas: "You should indeed have doubts, you should indeed be perplexed. When doubts arise, perplexity naturally arises. Kālāmas, you should not accept something merely because of repeated hearing. You should not accept something merely because of tradition. You should not accept something merely because of rumor. You should not accept something merely because it is in a scripture. You should not accept something merely because of logical reasoning. You should not accept something merely because of inference. You should not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons. You should not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view. You should not accept something merely because of the speaker's seeming competence. You should not accept something merely because 'this śramaṇa is our teacher.'

"Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are unwholesome; these dharmas are blameworthy; these dharmas are criticized by the wise; if these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to non-benefit and suffering.' If so, then you should abandon them.

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When greed arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For non-benefit."

"Kālāmas, this greedy person, overcome by greed, with mind enveloped by greed, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term non-benefit and suffering?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When hatred arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For non-benefit."

"Kālāmas, this hateful person, overcome by hatred, with mind enveloped by hatred, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term non-benefit and suffering?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When delusion arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For non-benefit."

"Kālāmas, this deluded person, overcome by delusion, with mind enveloped by delusion, kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term non-benefit and suffering?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these dharmas wholesome or unwholesome?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Unwholesome."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Blameworthy."

"Are they criticized by the wise or praised by the wise?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Criticized by the wise."

"If these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, do they lead to non-benefit and suffering, or not?"

The Kālāmas replied: "If these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to non-benefit and suffering."

"Therefore, Kālāmas, I said earlier: You should not accept something merely because of repeated hearing, not merely because of tradition, not merely because of rumor, not merely because it is in a scripture, not merely because of logical reasoning, not merely because of inference, not merely because of reflection on reasons, not merely because it agrees with your considered view, not merely because of the speaker's seeming competence, not merely because 'this śramaṇa is our teacher.' Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are unwholesome; these dharmas are blameworthy; these dharmas are criticized by the wise; if these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to non-benefit and suffering.' If so, then you should abandon them. That is why I said this.

"Kālāmas, you should not accept something merely because of repeated hearing. You should not accept something merely because of tradition. You should not accept something merely because of rumor. You should not accept something merely because it is in a scripture. You should not accept something merely because of logical reasoning. You should not accept something merely because of inference. You should not accept something merely because of reflection on reasons. You should not accept something merely because it agrees with your considered view. You should not accept something merely because of the speaker's seeming competence. You should not accept something merely because 'this śramaṇa is our teacher.'

"Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are wholesome; these dharmas are blameless; these dharmas are praised by the wise; if these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to benefit and happiness.' If so, then you should undertake and abide in them.

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When non-greed arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For benefit."

"Kālāmas, this non-greedy person, not overcome by greed, with mind not enveloped by greed, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When non-hatred arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For benefit."

"Kālāmas, this non-hateful person, not overcome by hatred, with mind not enveloped by hatred, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? When non-delusion arises in a person, does it arise for their benefit or non-benefit?"

The Kālāmas replied: "For benefit."

"Kālāmas, this non-deluded person, not overcome by delusion, with mind not enveloped by delusion, does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise. Is this for their long-term benefit and happiness?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Yes, it is so."

"Kālāmas, what do you think? Are these dharmas wholesome or unwholesome?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Wholesome."

"Are they blameworthy or blameless?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Blameless."

"Are they criticized by the wise or praised by the wise?"

The Kālāmas replied: "Praised by the wise."

"If these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, do they lead to benefit and happiness, or not?"

The Kālāmas replied: "If these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to benefit and happiness."

"Therefore, Kālāmas, I said earlier: You should not accept something merely because of repeated hearing, not merely because of tradition, not merely because of rumor, not merely because it is in a scripture, not merely because of logical reasoning, not merely because of inference, not merely because of reflection on reasons, not merely because it agrees with your considered view, not merely because of the speaker's seeming competence, not merely because 'this śramaṇa is our teacher.' Kālāmas, you should know for yourselves: 'These dharmas are wholesome; these dharmas are blameless; these dharmas are praised by the wise; if these dharmas are undertaken and practiced, they lead to benefit and happiness.' If so, then you should undertake and abide in them. That is why I said this.

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple who is thus free from covetousness, free from malice, not deluded, with right mindfulness, right awareness, pervades one direction with a mind of loving-kindness and dwells thus. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; above, below, and all around; everywhere and in all respects, he pervades the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without malice, and dwells thus.

"In the same way, with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he pervades one direction and dwells thus. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; above, below, and all around; everywhere and in all respects, he pervades the entire world with a mind of equanimity that is vast, great, boundless, without hatred, without malice, and dwells thus.

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from malice, pure and undefiled, in this present life obtains four comforts.

"The first comfort is this: 'If there is an afterlife, and if there are fruitions of good and evil actions, then at the dissolution of the body after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He obtains this first comfort.

"The second comfort is this: 'If there is no afterlife, and if there are no fruitions of good and evil actions, then in this present life, I dwell in happiness, free from enmity, free from malice.' He obtains this second comfort.

"The third comfort is this: 'If evil befalls the evildoer, then since I have no evil intentions toward anyone, and since I do no evil deeds, how can suffering befall me?' He obtains this third comfort.

"The fourth comfort is this: 'If evil does not befall the evildoer, then I see myself as pure in both respects.' He obtains this fourth comfort.

"Kālāmas, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from malice, pure and undefiled, in this present life obtains these four comforts."

The Kālāmas addressed the Buddha: "So it is, World-Honored One! The noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from malice, pure and undefiled, in this present life obtains four comforts.

"The first comfort is this: 'If there is an afterlife, and if there are fruitions of good and evil actions, then at the dissolution of the body after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' He obtains this first comfort.

"The second comfort is this: 'If there is no afterlife, and if there are no fruitions of good and evil actions, then in this present life, I dwell in happiness, free from enmity, free from malice.' He obtains this second comfort.

"The third comfort is this: 'If evil befalls the evildoer, then since I have no evil intentions toward anyone, and since I do no evil deeds, how can suffering befall me?' He obtains this third comfort.

"The fourth comfort is this: 'If evil does not befall the evildoer, then I see myself as pure in both respects.' He obtains this fourth comfort.

"World-Honored One, the noble disciple whose mind is thus free from enmity, free from malice, pure and undefiled, in this present life obtains these four comforts.

"Excellent, World-Honored One! Excellent! It is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or point the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms. In the same way, the World-Honored One has, through various methods, illuminated the Dharma. We now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Sangha. May the World-Honored One accept us as lay disciples. From this day forth, for the rest of our lives, we take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Kālāma brahmins of Kesamutti, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (133) Sūtra on Excellence

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If sentient beings were to know, as I know, the fruit of giving and sharing, even if it were their last morsel of food, if they had not yet given or shared it, they would not eat it by themselves, and the stain of stinginess would not cover and envelop their minds. Even if it were their last morsel of food, they would not eat it alone without sharing. Because sentient beings do not know, as I know, the fruit of giving and sharing, therefore they eat by themselves without sharing, and the stain of stinginess covers and envelops their minds."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (134) Sūtra on Releasing Cattle

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you a comparison. A wise person, through this comparison, understands the meaning. It is like a cowherd who is foolish, without wisdom, and without skill. In the autumn harvest season, when the crops on this side of the river have been reaped but the crops on the far side are still standing, he drives the herd of cattle to cross from this bank to the far bank of the Ganges River, to seek the land of Videha. But he does not examine the near bank and the far bank, and does not seek a ford. He drives the cattle to enter the middle of the stream. Because this foolish cowherd has no skill and no wisdom, the cattle come to harm in the middle of the Ganges River and cannot cross to reach the far bank.

"In the same way, if there is any śramaṇa or brahmin who is not skilled regarding this world, not skilled regarding the other world, not skilled regarding Māra's domain, not skilled regarding what is not Māra's domain, not skilled regarding the domain of Death, not skilled regarding what is not the domain of Death; if someone thinks that they should listen to and believe such a person, it will be for their long-term non-benefit and suffering.

"It is like a cowherd who is wise, has wisdom, and has skill. In the autumn harvest season, when the crops on this side of the river have been reaped but the crops on the far side are still standing, he drives the herd of cattle to cross from this bank to the far bank of the Ganges River, to seek the land of Videha. He carefully examines the near bank and the far bank, and seeks a ford. He first drives the strong bulls and the leading cattle to enter the water. They cut across the stream of the Ganges and safely reach the far bank. Next he drives the moderately strong cattle to enter the water. They too cut across the stream and safely reach the far bank. Next he drives the young calves and the weak cattle to enter the water. They too cut across the stream and safely reach the far bank. At that time, there was a young calf that had just been born. Following its mother's lowing, it too cut across the Ganges stream and safely reached the far bank. Why is this? Because this wise cowherd has skill and wisdom, and carefully examines the near bank and the far bank, and seeks a ford; therefore all the cattle safely cross to the far bank.

"In the same way, if there is any śramaṇa or brahmin who is skilled regarding this world, skilled regarding the other world, skilled regarding Māra's domain, skilled regarding what is not Māra's domain, skilled regarding the domain of Death, skilled regarding what is not the domain of Death; if someone thinks that they should listen to and believe such a person, it will be for their long-term benefit and happiness.

"Just as those strong bulls and leading cattle cut across the Ganges stream and safely reached the far bank, in the same way, those bhikṣus who have exhausted the outflows, accomplished the task of the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, obtained their own benefit, completely severed the fetters of existence, and been liberated through right wisdom; they too cut across Māra's stream and safely reach the far bank.

"Just as those moderately strong cattle cut across the Ganges stream and safely reached the far bank, in the same way, those bhikṣus who have severed the five lower fetters and attained intermediate parinirvāṇa, not returning to this world; they too cut across Māra's stream and safely reach the far bank.

"Just as those young calves and weak cattle cut across the Ganges stream and safely reached the far bank, in the same way, those bhikṣus who have severed the three fetters, with greed, hatred, and delusion weakened, are once-returners who return to this world once more and then make an end of suffering; they too cut across Māra's stream and safely reach the far bank.

"Just as that young calf that had just been born, following its mother's lowing, cut across the Ganges stream and safely reached the far bank, in the same way, those bhikṣus who have severed the three fetters and are stream-enterers, no longer subject to falling into evil states, surely destined for enlightenment, with at most seven more existences among gods and humans before making an end of suffering; they too cut across Māra's stream and safely reach the far bank."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"This world and the other world,
The wise one has well declared both;
What is within Māra's reach,
And what is not reached by Death.

The All-Knowing Buddha
Who comprehends the entire world,
Has opened the door of the deathless,
For safely reaching the land of security.

Having cut across Māra's stream,
Having destroyed and shattered it,
The bhikṣus, with joy overflowing,
Have reached the place beyond."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (135) Sūtra on Good People and Evil People

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the dharmas of evil people and the dharmas of good people. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you.

"What are the dharmas of evil people? An evil person is ungrateful and does not acknowledge favors. This ingratitude and non-acknowledgment of favors is a dharma of evil people. Why is this? An evil person is ungrateful and does not acknowledge favors. Therefore the dharma of evil people is spoken of as being ungrateful and not acknowledging favors.

"What are the dharmas of good people? A good person is grateful and acknowledges favors. This gratitude and acknowledgment of favors is a dharma of good people. Why is this? A good person is grateful and acknowledges favors. Therefore the dharma of good people is spoken of as being grateful and acknowledging favors.

"Bhikṣus, if anyone should show gratitude and acknowledgment of favors, even in small matters, let alone in great matters."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (136) Sūtra on the Businessman's Request

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.

At that time, the householder Ugga of Rājagṛha went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The householder Ugga then addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, may the World-Honored One accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal, together with the assembly of bhikṣus."

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted in silence. The householder Ugga, knowing that the Buddha had accepted, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

The householder Ugga returned home, and during that night prepared various exquisite foods and drinks. When morning came, he spread out his seat, set out clean water, and then sent a messenger to announce the time to the Buddha: "The food is ready. May the World-Honored One know that it is time."

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the early morning, put on his robe, took his bowl, and went to the householder Ugga's home. He sat on the seat that had been prepared. The assembly of bhikṣus also sat down in order.

The householder Ugga, seeing that the Buddha and the bhikṣus were seated, personally served various exquisite foods and drinks, satisfying them fully. After the meal was finished, when the Buddha had put down his bowl and washed his hands, the householder Ugga took a low seat and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.

The householder Ugga then addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I shall make eight requests to the Buddha. May the World-Honored One grant them."

The Buddha told Ugga: "In the present time, it is not the occasion for granting requests."

Ugga addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what I request is wholesome, not unwholesome; it is blameless, not blameworthy."

The Buddha said: "Speak then, Ugga."

The householder Ugga then addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide food for the Sangha. This is my first request to the Buddha. May the World-Honored One grant it.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide food for bhikṣus who come from outside. This is my second request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide food for bhikṣus who are departing on journeys. This is my third request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide food for sick bhikṣus. This is my fourth request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide food for bhikṣus who attend the sick. This is my fifth request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide medicine for sick bhikṣus. This is my sixth request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to constantly provide rice gruel for the Sangha. This is my seventh request.

"World-Honored One, from this day forth, for the rest of my life, I wish to provide bathing garments for the bhikṣunī Sangha. This is my eighth request.

"World-Honored One, these are the eight requests I make to the Buddha. May the World-Honored One grant them."

The Buddha said: "Very good, Ugga! You have made these eight requests, all of which are pure in mind. You give with faith, and you give with purity of mind. Ugga, I now grant your eight requests."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a verse of blessing for the householder Ugga:

"The person who joyfully gives food,
Will be given food in return.
One who gives clothing, conveyances, and garlands,
Will have these things in return.

One who gives the best things,
Will obtain the best in return.
One who gives the finest things,
Will obtain the finest in return.

The person who gives the best and finest,
Will be reborn in a long-lived heaven;
Having obtained the best and finest,
Will rejoice in the heavenly realm."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken the Dharma for the householder Ugga, instructing, benefiting, and delighting him, rose from his seat and departed.

The Buddha spoke thus. The householder Ugga of Rājagṛha, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (137) Sūtra on the World

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the arising of the world and the cessation of the world. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you.

"What is the arising of the world? One sees with the eye, cognizes forms, and is bound by desire for pleasing forms. Because one is bound by desire for pleasing forms, consciousness that delights in them arises. Because consciousness delights in them, there is attachment. Because of attachment, there is craving. Because of craving, there is clinging. Because of clinging, there is becoming. Because of becoming, there is birth. Because of birth, there arise aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. This is called the arising of the world.

"One hears with the ear, cognizes sounds... One smells with the nose, cognizes odors... One tastes with the tongue, cognizes flavors... One touches with the body, cognizes tangibles... One cognizes with the mind, cognizes dharmas, and is bound by desire for pleasing dharmas. Because one is bound by desire for pleasing dharmas, consciousness that delights in them arises. Because consciousness delights in them, there is attachment. Because of attachment, there is craving. Because of craving, there is clinging. Because of clinging, there is becoming. Because of becoming, there is birth. Because of birth, there arise aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. This is called the arising of the world.

"What is the cessation of the world? One sees with the eye, cognizes forms, and is not bound by desire for pleasing forms. Because one is not bound by desire for pleasing forms, consciousness that delights in them does not arise. Because consciousness does not delight in them, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, there is no craving. Because there is no craving, there is no clinging. Because there is no clinging, there is no becoming. Because there is no becoming, there is no birth. Because there is no birth, aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease. This is called the cessation of the world.

"One hears with the ear, cognizes sounds... One smells with the nose, cognizes odors... One tastes with the tongue, cognizes flavors... One touches with the body, cognizes tangibles... One cognizes with the mind, cognizes dharmas, and is not bound by desire for pleasing dharmas. Because one is not bound by desire for pleasing dharmas, consciousness that delights in them does not arise. Because consciousness does not delight in them, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, there is no craving. Because there is no craving, there is no clinging. Because there is no clinging, there is no becoming. Because there is no becoming, there is no birth. Because there is no birth, aging, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease. This is called the cessation of the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (138) Sūtra on Welfare

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are four dharmas that lead to the welfare and happiness of a good man in the present life. What are the four? They are: accomplishment in diligence, accomplishment in guarding, association with good friends, and balanced livelihood.

"What is accomplishment in diligence? A good man, whatever his occupation, whether farming, trade, herding cattle, archery, service to a king, or any other skill, is diligent and not lazy, and is endowed with discernment regarding means, able to manage and arrange his affairs. This is called accomplishment in diligence.

"What is accomplishment in guarding? A good man, whatever wealth and grain he has acquired through his own effort and diligence, gathered by the strength of his arms, obtained by his own sweat, rightfully and according to Dharma, guards and protects them well, thinking: 'Let not kings seize it, let not thieves plunder it, let not fire burn it, let not water sweep it away, let not unfavorable heirs waste it.' This is called accomplishment in guarding.

"What is association with good friends? A good man who resides in a village or town associates with householders or their sons, whether young or old, who are endowed with faith, endowed with morality, endowed with generosity, and endowed with wisdom; he shares their conduct and consults with them, and in faith, morality, generosity, and wisdom, he trains along with them. This is called association with good friends.

"What is balanced livelihood? A good man knows his income and knows his expenditure, and maintains his livelihood in balance, not too extravagant and not too miserly. He knows that his income exceeds his expenditure, and his expenditure does not exceed his income. It is like a scale-holder or his apprentice who, holding the scale, knows: 'This has decreased by so much, this has increased by so much.' In the same way, a good man knows his income and knows his expenditure, and maintains his livelihood in balance, not too extravagant and not too miserly. If a good man has little income but lives extravagantly, people will say: 'This good man's wealth flows away like the udumbara fig tree which has fruit but no flowers.' If a good man has great income but lives miserably, people will say: 'This good man dies like a pauper.' Therefore a good man should know his income and know his expenditure, and maintain his livelihood in balance, not too extravagant and not too miserly. This is called balanced livelihood.

"Such wealth as is thus obtained has four outlets of loss. What are the four? Indulgence in women, indulgence in drinking, indulgence in gambling, and association with evil friends. It is like a great pond with four inlets and four outlets; if someone blocks the inlets and opens the outlets, and there is no rainfall, then that great pond will only decrease and not increase. In the same way, such wealth has four outlets of loss: indulgence in women, indulgence in drinking, indulgence in gambling, and association with evil friends.

"Such wealth as is thus obtained has four inlets of increase. What are the four? Not indulging in women, not indulging in drinking, not indulging in gambling, and association with good friends. It is like a great pond with four inlets and four outlets; if someone opens the inlets and blocks the outlets, and there is also rainfall, then that great pond will only increase and not decrease. In the same way, such wealth has four inlets of increase: not indulging in women, not indulging in drinking, not indulging in gambling, and association with good friends.

"Bhikṣus, these are the four dharmas that lead to the welfare and happiness of a good man in the present life.

"There are four dharmas that lead to the welfare and happiness of a good man in the future life. What are the four? They are: accomplishment in faith, accomplishment in morality, accomplishment in generosity, and accomplishment in wisdom.

"What is accomplishment in faith? A good man has faith, believes in the wisdom of the Tathāgata: 'He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' This is called accomplishment in faith.

"What is accomplishment in morality? A good man does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, does not drink alcohol. This is called accomplishment in morality.

"What is accomplishment in generosity? A good man dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, constantly delighting in giving, with hands open in generosity, delighting in renunciation, taking pleasure in giving equally, and taking pleasure in giving and sharing. This is called accomplishment in generosity.

"What is accomplishment in wisdom? A good man possesses the wisdom of the noble ones that penetrates and discerns, that rightly leads to the complete ending of suffering. This is called accomplishment in wisdom.

"These are the four dharmas that lead to the welfare and happiness of a good man in the future life."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"Accomplishment in diligence and guarding,
Association with good friends and balanced livelihood;
Faith, morality, generosity, and wisdom:
These eight dharmas bring happiness.

Diligence leads to acquiring wealth,
And thus one gains great fame.
If one goes to a gathering of people,
One is honored and respected.

If one is accomplished in morality,
And accomplished in generosity,
One who practices these beneficial dharmas
Will be born in a heavenly realm.

A wise person seeks merit,
Accomplishing these four dharmas;
In truth, obtaining great fame,
One is praised and goes to heaven."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (139) Sūtra on the Sākyan

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of the Śākyans, in a town of the Śākyans called Kapilavatthu, in the Banyan Tree Park.

At that time, Mahānāma the Śākyan went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. Mahānāma the Śākyan then addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one become a lay disciple?"

The Buddha told Mahānāma: "One who has taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Sangha is called a lay disciple."

Mahānāma again asked: "World-Honored One, how does a lay disciple accomplish morality?"

The Buddha told Mahānāma: "A lay disciple does not kill living beings, does not take what is not given, does not commit adultery, does not speak falsehood, and does not drink alcohol. Mahānāma, this is how a lay disciple accomplishes morality."

Mahānāma again asked: "World-Honored One, how does a lay disciple accomplish faith?"

The Buddha told Mahānāma: "A lay disciple has faith, believes in the wisdom of the Tathāgata: 'He is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' Mahānāma, this is how a lay disciple accomplishes faith."

Mahānāma again asked: "World-Honored One, how does a lay disciple accomplish generosity?"

The Buddha told Mahānāma: "A lay disciple dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, constantly delighting in giving, with hands open in generosity, delighting in renunciation, taking pleasure in giving equally, and taking pleasure in giving and sharing. Mahānāma, this is how a lay disciple accomplishes generosity."

Mahānāma again asked: "World-Honored One, how does a lay disciple accomplish wisdom?"

The Buddha told Mahānāma: "A lay disciple possesses the wisdom of the noble ones that penetrates and discerns, that rightly leads to the complete ending of suffering. Mahānāma, this is how a lay disciple accomplishes wisdom."

The Buddha spoke thus. Mahānāma the Śākyan, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (140) Sūtra on Supreme

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the supreme in each category. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you.

"What is the supreme in each category? Among all conditioned dharmas, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared supreme.

"Among all footprints, the elephant's footprint is declared supreme. Among all contemplations, mindfulness of the body is declared supreme.

"Among all conditioned dharmas, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared supreme. Among the paths, the Eightfold Path is supreme: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.

"Among all dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared supreme. That is, the subduing of pride and arrogance, the ending of thirst, the eradication of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle, the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.

"Those who have faith in the supreme Dharma, that is, faith in the supreme; for those who have faith in the supreme Dharma, the fruition is also supreme. Those who have faith and have gone forth will obtain the supreme benefit; they will be reborn in a heavenly realm or attain nirvāṇa."

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"Having faith in the supreme Dharma,
Knowing the supreme and profound Dharma,
Having faith in the Buddha, supreme and unsurpassed,
Worthy of receiving offerings;

Having faith in the supreme Dharma,
In dispassion, peace, and happiness;
Having faith in the supreme Sangha,
The field of merit, unsurpassed;

Giving gifts to the supreme,
Supreme merit increases;
Supreme life, supreme complexion,
Supreme fame, supreme peace.

The wise one who gives to the supreme,
Concentrated on the supreme Dharma,
Whether born as a god or human,
Attaining the supreme, rejoices."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

*End of Fascicle 32 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 32

## Sūtra 133: The Upāli Sūtra, Number Seventeen of the Great Division

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering in Nālandā, staying in Pāvārika's mango grove.

At that time, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha, in the afternoon, went strolling to visit the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked: "Ascetic, how many courses of conduct does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Gotama, my revered teacher Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta does not prescribe courses of conduct for us so that we do not practice evil actions and do not perform evil actions. Rather, he prescribes punishments for us so that we do not practice evil actions and do not perform evil actions."

The World-Honored One again asked: "Ascetic, how many punishments does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Gotama, my revered teacher Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribes three punishments for us so that we do not practice evil actions and do not perform evil actions. What are the three? Bodily punishment, verbal punishment, and mental punishment."

The World-Honored One again asked: "Ascetic, are bodily punishment, verbal punishment, and mental punishment each different from one another?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Gotama, our bodily punishment is different, verbal punishment is different, and mental punishment is different."

The World-Honored One again asked: "Ascetic, among these three punishments, which are thus distinct, which punishment does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions? Is it bodily punishment, verbal punishment, or mental punishment?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Gotama, among these three punishments, which are thus distinct, my revered teacher Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribes bodily punishment as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions. Verbal punishment is not so, and mental punishment is the least, not comparable to bodily punishment, which is extremely great and very serious."

The World-Honored One again asked: "Ascetic, do you say that bodily punishment is the most serious?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Gotama, bodily punishment is the most serious."

The World-Honored One asked again a second and third time: "Ascetic, do you say that bodily punishment is the most serious?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha also replied a second and third time: "Gotama, bodily punishment is the most serious." Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having confirmed this matter with the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha three times, remained silent.

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked: "What does the ascetic Gotama prescribe as punishments so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions?"

At that time, the World-Honored One replied: "Ascetic, I do not prescribe punishments so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions. I prescribe actions so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked: "How many actions does Gotama prescribe so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions?"
