The World-Honored One again replied: "Ascetic, I prescribe three actions so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions. What are the three? Bodily action, verbal action, and mental action."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked: "Gotama, are bodily action, verbal action, and mental action each different from one another?"

The World-Honored One again replied: "Ascetic, my bodily action is different, verbal action is different, and mental action is different."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked: "Gotama, among these three actions, which are thus distinct, which action do you prescribe as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions? Is it bodily action, verbal action, or mental action?"

The World-Honored One again replied: "Ascetic, among these three actions, which are thus distinct, I prescribe mental action as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions. Bodily action and verbal action are not so."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked: "Does Gotama prescribe mental action as the most serious?"

The World-Honored One again replied: "Ascetic, I prescribe mental action as the most serious."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked again a second and third time: "Does Gotama prescribe mental action as the most serious?" The World-Honored One also replied a second and third time: "Ascetic, I prescribe mental action as the most serious." Thereupon, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha, having confirmed this matter with the World-Honored One three times, rose from his seat, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, and departed, going to where Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was.

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta saw the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha coming from afar and immediately asked: "Ascetic, where have you come from?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Venerable one, I have come from the ascetic Gotama's place at Pāvārika's mango grove in Nālandā."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked: "Ascetic, did you have any discussion with the ascetic Gotama?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "We did discuss."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, if you had any discussion with the ascetic Gotama, tell me all of it. Perhaps I can understand the points of that discussion."

Thereupon, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha recounted in full everything he had discussed with the World-Honored One. Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, upon hearing, praised him: "Excellent, Ascetic! You have practiced the disciple's duty toward your teacher, acting with wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness, secure and fearless, accomplished in training, having attained great eloquence, having obtained the banner of the deathless, having personally realized and attained the realm of the deathless. Why is this? Because you declared to the ascetic Gotama that bodily punishment is prescribed as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions, that verbal punishment is not so, and that mental punishment is the least, not comparable to bodily punishment, which is extremely great and very serious."

At that time, the householder Upāli, together with five hundred householders, was gathered in the assembly, with palms joined toward Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. Thereupon, the householder Upāli said to the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha: "Has the venerable one already confirmed this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Householder, I have already confirmed this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times."

The householder Upāli said to the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha: "I too can go and confirm this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times, and then drag him about as I please. Just as a strong man seizes a long-haired ram and drags it wherever he wishes, so too can I confirm this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times and drag him about as I please. Just as a strong man takes a hairy fleece and shakes it to remove the dust, so too can I confirm this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times and drag him about as I please. Just as a liquor-seller or a liquor-seller's apprentice takes a straining bag and puts it in deep water, moving it wherever he wishes, so too can I confirm this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times and drag him about as I please. Just as a great bull elephant, fully sixty years old, with proud and majestic tusks, legs, and body complete, its sinews and strength blazing, when a strong man takes it to wash its haunches, wash its back, wash its flanks, wash its belly, wash its tusks, wash its head, and play in the water, so too can I confirm this matter with the ascetic Gotama three times and wash him as I please. I shall go to the ascetic Gotama, engage him in discussion, defeat him, and return."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said to the householder Upāli: "I too can defeat the ascetic Gotama, you can too, and the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha can as well."

Thereupon, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha said to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: "I would not wish the householder Upāli to go to the ascetic Gotama. Why? The ascetic Gotama knows magical enchantments and can enchant people to become his disciples, whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. I fear that the householder Upāli may be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple is utterly impossible. But that the ascetic Gotama would be enchanted by the householder Upāli and turned into his disciple, that is certainly possible."

The householder Upāli said to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta three times: "I shall now go to the ascetic Gotama, engage him in discussion, defeat him, and return."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta also replied three times: "You may go quickly! I too can defeat the ascetic Gotama, you can too, and the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha can as well."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha again said three times: "I would not wish the householder Upāli to go to the ascetic Gotama. Why? The ascetic Gotama knows magical enchantments and can enchant people to become his disciples, whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. I fear that the householder Upāli may be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple is utterly impossible. But that the ascetic Gotama would be enchanted by the householder Upāli and turned into his disciple, that is certainly possible. Householder Upāli, you may go as you wish."

Thereupon, the householder Upāli bowed at the feet of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings, sat down to one side, and asked: "Gotama, did the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha come here today?"

The World-Honored One replied: "He did, householder."

The householder Upāli asked: "Gotama, did you have any discussion with the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha?"

The World-Honored One replied: "There was a discussion."

The householder Upāli said: "Gotama, if you had any discussion with the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha, please tell me all of it. If I hear it, perhaps I can understand it." Thereupon, the World-Honored One recounted in full everything he had discussed with the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha.

At that time, the householder Upāli, upon hearing, praised: "Excellent, Ascetic! He has practiced the disciple's duty toward his revered teacher, acting with wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness, secure and fearless, accomplished in training, having attained great eloquence, having obtained the banner of the deathless, having personally realized and attained the realm of the deathless. Why is this? Because he declared to the ascetic Gotama that bodily punishment is prescribed as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions, that verbal punishment is not so, and that mental punishment is the least, not comparable to bodily punishment, which is extremely great and very serious."

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Householder, I wish to discuss this matter with you. If you abide in truth, answer with truth."

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, I abide in truth and will answer with truth. Ascetic Gotama, just discuss this matter with me."

The World-Honored One asked: "Householder, what do you think? Suppose a Nigaṇṭha comes who delights in giving, who joyfully practices giving, who is without frivolity and delights in non-frivolity, who is extremely pure and practices extreme austerities. When that one walks about, he kills many small creatures. What about this, householder? Does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta prescribe retribution for this killing of living beings?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, if there is intention, there is great guilt. If there is no intention, there is no great guilt."

The World-Honored One asked: "Householder, what do you call intention?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, it is mental action."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, you should reflect before answering. What you have said earlier contradicts what comes later, and what comes later contradicts what came earlier; they are inconsistent. Householder, you yourself said in this assembly: 'Gotama, I abide in truth and will answer with truth. Ascetic Gotama, just discuss this matter with me.' Householder, what do you think? Suppose a Nigaṇṭha comes who drinks hot water and abstains from cold water. When he has no hot water, he then desires cold water. Not obtaining cold water, he dies. Householder, what does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta say about where that Nigaṇṭha is reborn?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, there is a heaven called 'Attached by Mind.' When that Nigaṇṭha dies, if he dies with mental attachment, he will certainly be reborn in that place."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, you should reflect before answering. What you have said earlier contradicts what comes later, and what comes later contradicts what came earlier; they are inconsistent. You yourself said in this assembly: 'Gotama, I abide in truth and will answer with truth. Ascetic Gotama, just discuss this matter with me.' Householder, what do you think? Suppose a person comes with a sharp sword and says: 'I will take all the living beings within this Nālandā, and in a single day, hack, chop, slash, cut, flay, slice, and scrape them, making them into one heap of flesh, one pile of flesh.' Householder, what do you think? Could that person take all the living beings within this Nālandā, and in a single day, hack, chop, slash, cut, flay, slice, and scrape them, making them into one heap of flesh, one pile of flesh?"

The householder Upāli replied: "No. Why? This Nālandā is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people. Therefore, that person could never, in a single day, hack, chop, slash, cut, flay, slice, and scrape all the living beings within this Nālandā, making them into one heap of flesh, one pile of flesh. Gotama, that person would merely exhaust himself with great toil."

"Householder, what do you think? Suppose an ascetic or brahmin comes who possesses great psychic power, great spiritual authority, great merit and blessings, great supernatural abilities, and whose mind has attained mastery. He says: 'With one thought of anger, I will cause all of this Nālandā to burn to ashes.' Householder, what do you think? Could that ascetic or brahmin cause all of this Nālandā to burn to ashes?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, how could it be just one Nālandā? How could it be just two, three, or four? Gotama, if that ascetic or brahmin possesses great psychic power, great spiritual authority, great merit and blessings, great supernatural abilities, and his mind has attained mastery, then with one thought of anger he could cause all countries and all peoples to burn to ashes, let alone one Nālandā!"

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, you should reflect before answering. What you have said earlier contradicts what comes later, and what comes later contradicts what came earlier; they are inconsistent. You yourself said in this assembly: 'Gotama, I abide in truth and will answer with truth. Ascetic Gotama, just discuss this matter with me.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Householder, have you ever heard of the great marshes becoming desolate, the qilin becoming desolate, the deer becoming desolate, the tranquil places becoming desolate, the empty wilderness becoming desolate, the desolate becoming desolate?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Gotama, I have heard of such things."

"Householder, what do you think? Who caused those great marshes to become desolate, the qilin to become desolate, the deer to become desolate, the tranquil places to become desolate, the empty wilderness to become desolate, the desolate to become desolate?"

The householder Upāli remained silent without answering. The World-Honored One said: "Householder, answer quickly! Householder, answer quickly! Now is not the time for silence. You yourself said in this assembly: 'Gotama, I abide in truth and will answer with truth. Ascetic Gotama, just discuss this matter with me.'"

Thereupon, the householder Upāli, after a moment of silence, said: "Gotama, I was not being silent; I was merely reflecting on this meaning. Gotama, those foolish Nigaṇṭhas, who do not understand well, who cannot comprehend, who do not recognize good fields, and who do not examine themselves, have throughout the long night deceived me. I have been misled by them, saying that bodily punishment was declared to the ascetic Gotama as the most serious, so that one does not practice evil actions and does not perform evil actions, and that verbal and mental punishments are not comparable. But as I understand the meaning from what the ascetic Gotama has said, a sage with one thought of anger can cause great marshes to become desolate, cause the qilin to become desolate, cause the deer to become desolate, cause the tranquil places to become desolate, cause the empty wilderness to become desolate, cause the desolate to become desolate. World-Honored One, I have understood! Well-Gone One, I have comprehended! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka, from this day onward taking refuge for the rest of my life, until the end of my days."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, act in silence and do not proclaim it publicly. For such a distinguished person, silence is good."

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, for this very reason I am even more greatly delighted in the World-Honored One. Why? Because the World-Honored One said: 'Householder, act in silence and do not proclaim it publicly. For such a distinguished person, silence is good.' World-Honored One, if I were to become a disciple of some other ascetic or brahmin, they would carry banners, pennants, and canopies and parade throughout Nālandā, proclaiming: 'The householder Upāli has become my disciple! The householder Upāli has become my disciple!' Yet the World-Honored One says: 'Householder, act in silence and do not proclaim it publicly. For such a distinguished person, silence is good.'"

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, from this day forward, I will not permit any Nigaṇṭhas to enter my household gate. I will only permit the World-Honored One's fourfold community of disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, those Nigaṇṭhas have been respected by your family throughout the long night. If they come, you should provide offerings to them according to your ability."

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, for this very reason I am even more greatly delighted in the World-Honored One. Why? Because the World-Honored One said: 'Householder, those Nigaṇṭhas have been respected by your family throughout the long night. If they come, you should provide offerings to them according to your ability.' World-Honored One, I formerly heard that the World-Honored One said: 'Give to me, do not give to others. Give to my disciples, do not give to the disciples of others. If you give to me, you will gain great merit; if you give to others, you will not gain great merit. If you give to my disciples, you will gain great merit; if you give to the disciples of others, you will not gain great merit.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, I did not say: 'Give to me, do not give to others. Give to my disciples, do not give to the disciples of others. If you give to me, you will gain great merit; if you give to others, you will not gain great merit. If you give to my disciples, you will gain great merit; if you give to the disciples of others, you will not gain great merit.' Householder, I say this: give to all, following what makes the mind joyful. However, giving to those who are not diligent does not produce great merit, while giving to those who are diligent produces great merit."

The householder Upāli said: "World-Honored One, please do not trouble yourself about this. I myself know whether to give to Nigaṇṭhas or not to give to Nigaṇṭhas. World-Honored One, I now take refuge a second time in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka, from this day onward taking refuge for the rest of my life, until the end of my days."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Upāli, exhorting, inspiring, and filling him with longing, accomplishing joy. With immeasurable skillful means he taught the Dharma for him, exhorting, inspiring, and filling him with longing, accomplishing joy. As is the method of all Buddhas, he first taught the proper and upright Dharma so that hearers would be delighted, namely, teaching about giving, teaching about morality, teaching about rebirth in heaven, criticizing desire as calamitous, birth-and-death as defiling, and praising desirelessness as sublime, with the factors of the path being pure and white. After the World-Honored One had taught such Dharma for him, the Buddha knew that he had a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a gentle mind, a receptive mind, an elevated mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free from doubt, a mind free from hindrances, and had the capacity and power to receive the true Dharma. As all Buddhas teach what is essential and correct, the World-Honored One then taught him suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The householder Upāli, right there on his seat, saw the four noble truths: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. Just as white silk is easily dyed with color, so the householder Upāli, right there on his seat, saw the four noble truths: suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Thereupon, the householder Upāli saw the Dharma, obtained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, cut off doubt, crossed beyond perplexity, had no other teacher, no longer followed others, was without hesitation, had already abided in the fruit of realization, and attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma. He rose from his seat and bowed to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I now take refuge a third time in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka, from this day onward taking refuge for the rest of my life, until the end of my days."

Thereupon, the householder Upāli, having heard what the Buddha taught, received and upheld it well, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned home. He commanded the gatekeepers: "You should know that I am now a disciple of the World-Honored One. From this day forward, when Nigaṇṭhas come, do not allow them to enter the gate. Only permit the World-Honored One's fourfold community of disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter. If Nigaṇṭhas come, tell them: 'Venerable ones, the householder Upāli has now been converted by the Buddha and has become his disciple. He no longer permits Nigaṇṭhas to enter the gate. He only permits the World-Honored One's fourfold community of disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter. If you need food, you may wait here and food will be brought out to you.'"

Thereupon, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha heard that the householder Upāli had been converted by the ascetic Gotama and had become his disciple, and that he no longer permitted Nigaṇṭhas to enter his gate, only permitting the ascetic Gotama's disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter. Having heard this, the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha went to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said: "Venerable one, this is what I originally said."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked: "Ascetic, what is it that you originally said?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Venerable one, I originally said that I did not wish the householder Upāli to go to the ascetic Gotama. Why? The ascetic Gotama knows magical enchantments and can enchant people to become his disciples, whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. I feared that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple. Venerable one, the householder Upāli has now been enchanted by the ascetic Gotama. Having been turned into his disciple, he no longer permits Nigaṇṭhas to enter his gate, only permitting the ascetic Gotama's disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple is utterly impossible. But that the ascetic Gotama would be enchanted by the householder Upāli and turned into his disciple, that is certainly possible."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha again said: "Venerable one, if you do not believe what I have said, you may go yourself, or you may also send a messenger."

Thereupon, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, you may go yourself to see whether the householder Upāli has been enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple, or whether the ascetic Gotama has been enchanted by the householder Upāli and turned into his disciple."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha, having received Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's instruction, went to the household of the householder Upāli. The gatekeeper, seeing the elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha coming from afar, spoke thus: "Venerable one, the householder Upāli has now been converted by the Buddha and has become his disciple. He no longer permits Nigaṇṭhas to enter the gate. He only permits the World-Honored One's fourfold community of disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter. If you want food, you may wait here and food will be brought out to you."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha said: "Gatekeeper, I do not need food."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha, having ascertained this matter, shook his head and departed. He went to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said: "Venerable one, this is exactly what I originally said."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked: "Ascetic, what is it that you originally said?"

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha replied: "Venerable one, I originally said that I did not wish the householder Upāli to go to the ascetic Gotama. Why? The ascetic Gotama knows magical enchantments and can enchant people to become his disciples, whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. I feared that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple. Venerable one, the householder Upāli has now been enchanted by the ascetic Gotama. Having been turned into his disciple, he no longer permits Nigaṇṭhas to enter his gate, only permitting the ascetic Gotama's disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Ascetic, that the householder Upāli would be enchanted by the ascetic Gotama and turned into his disciple is utterly impossible. But that the ascetic Gotama would be enchanted by the householder Upāli and turned into his disciple, that is certainly possible."

The elder ascetic Nigaṇṭha said: "Venerable one, if you do not believe what I have said, may the venerable one go himself."

Thereupon, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a great Nigaṇṭha assembly of five hundred, went to the household of the householder Upāli. The gatekeeper, seeing Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming from afar with a great Nigaṇṭha assembly of five hundred, spoke thus: "Venerable one, the householder Upāli has now been converted by the Buddha and has become his disciple. He no longer permits Nigaṇṭhas to enter the gate. He only permits the World-Honored One's fourfold community of disciples, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, to enter. If you want food, you may wait here and food will be brought out to you."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Gatekeeper, I do not need food. I only wish to see the householder Upāli."

The gatekeeper said: "May the venerable one wait here. I shall go in and inform the venerable householder Upāli."

The gatekeeper then went in and reported: "Householder, you should know that Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a great Nigaṇṭha assembly of five hundred, is standing outside the gate, saying: 'I wish to see the householder Upāli.'"

The householder Upāli instructed the gatekeeper: "Go to the middle gate, arrange seats and beds, and when finished, come back and tell me."

The gatekeeper, receiving the instruction, went to the middle gate, arranged the seats and beds, and when finished, came back and reported: "Householder, you should know that the beds and seats are arranged. May the householder decide as he sees fit."

The householder Upāli, taking the gatekeeper along, went to the middle gate. There was a seat, extremely high, broad, and great, extremely clean and well-prepared, which was the very seat on which the householder Upāli had formerly held Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and asked him to sit. The householder Upāli seated himself upon it, sitting cross-legged, and instructed the gatekeeper: "Go out to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and say: 'Sir, the householder Upāli says: "If the sir wishes to enter, he may do so as he pleases."'"

The gatekeeper, receiving the instruction, went out to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said: "Sir, the householder Upāli says: 'If the sir wishes to enter, he may do so as he pleases.'" Thereupon, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with the great Nigaṇṭha assembly of five hundred, entered the middle gate.

The householder Upāli, seeing from afar Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta coming in with the great Nigaṇṭha assembly of five hundred, spoke: "Sir, there are seats. If you wish to sit, please do so as you please."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Householder, is this proper? You sit yourself upon a high seat, cross-legged, and speak with people, no different from a renunciant who has left home to practice the way."

The householder Upāli said: "Sir, these are my own possessions. If I wish to give, I give; if I do not wish to give, I do not give. This seat is mine, therefore I say: 'There are seats. If you wish to sit, please do so as you please.'"

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta arranged a seat and sat down, then said: "Householder, why is it like this? You wished to defeat the ascetic Gotama, but instead came back defeated yourself. It is as if a person went into the forest seeking eyes but returned having lost his eyes. Just so, householder, you wished to go and defeat the ascetic Gotama, but instead were defeated by the ascetic Gotama and came back. It is as if a person entered a pool because of thirst but came back still thirsty. Just so, householder, you wished to go and defeat the ascetic Gotama, but instead came back defeated yourself. Householder, why is it like this?"

The householder Upāli said: "Sir, listen to my simile. The wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Sir, suppose there was a brahmin who had a young wife. That wife became pregnant and said to her husband: 'I am now pregnant. Husband, go to the market and buy some fine toys for the child.' At that time, the brahmin said to his wife: 'Just let me wait until you have safely given birth; what worry then? If you give birth to a boy, I will buy toys for a boy. If you give birth to a girl, I will buy toys for a girl.' The wife again said two and three times to her husband: 'I am now pregnant. Husband, go to the market and quickly buy some fine toys for the child.' The brahmin also said two and three times to his wife: 'Just let me wait until you have safely given birth; what worry then? If you give birth to a boy, I will buy toys for a boy. If you give birth to a girl, I will buy toys for a girl.'

"The brahmin, being extremely fond of his wife, then asked: 'What kind of toy do you want me to buy for the child?' The wife answered: 'Husband, go and buy a toy monkey for the child to play with.' The brahmin, having heard, went to the market and bought a toy monkey. He brought it back and told his wife: 'I have bought a toy monkey for the child and returned.' The wife, upon seeing it, disliked its color, finding it unattractive. She then said to her husband: 'Husband, take this toy monkey to the dyer's shop and have it dyed yellow, making it extremely lovely, and pound it to make it lustrous.' The brahmin, having heard, immediately took the toy monkey to the dyer's shop and said to the dyer: 'Dye this toy monkey for me in a fine yellow color, making it extremely lovely, and pound it to make it lustrous.' At that time, the dyer said to the brahmin: 'This toy monkey can be dyed yellow and made extremely lovely, that is possible. However, it cannot be pounded to make it lustrous.' Thereupon, the dyer spoke this verse:

"'The monkey can endure the dye,
But cannot endure the pounding.
If pounded, it will die.
It can never be beaten smooth,
For it is a foul-smelling sack,
A monkey full of impurity.'

"Sir, you should know that the teachings of the Nigaṇṭhas are just like this. They cannot endure being questioned and challenged by others, nor can they bear investigation and contemplation. They can only be dyed with foolishness, not dyed with wisdom. Sir, listen further. It is like a pure cloth of Bārāṇasī. The owner takes it to the dyer's shop and says: 'Dye this cloth for me in the finest color, making it lovely. Also pound it well to make it lustrous.' At that time, the dyer says to the cloth's owner: 'This cloth can be dyed in the finest color and made lovely. It can also be pounded well to make it lustrous.' Thereupon, the dyer spoke this verse:

"'Like a cloth of Bārāṇasī,
White and pure, it endures the dye.
When pounded, it becomes soft,
Its luster and color increase in beauty.'

"Sir, you should know that the teachings of the Tathāgatas, the Worthy Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are just like this. They can supremely endure being questioned and challenged by others, and can well bear investigation and contemplation. They can only be dyed with wisdom, not dyed with foolishness."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Householder, you have been enchanted by the ascetic Gotama's magical spells."

The householder Upāli said: "Sir, it is a good enchantment, an extremely good enchantment! Sir, that enchantment causes my father and mother to gain benefit and advantage throughout the long night, to be at ease and happy, and also my wife and children, servants and laborers, and the king of Nālandā, and all the world, devas, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics and brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, causing them to gain benefit and advantage throughout the long night, to be at ease and happy."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said: "Householder, all of Nālandā knows that the householder Upāli is a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas. Whose disciple are you now?"

Thereupon, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, knelt on his right knee, and with palms joined toward wherever the Buddha was, said: "Sir, listen to what I say:

"The heroic one, free from delusion,
Who has cut off defilement, is well-tamed and subdued,
Without rival, of subtle thought,
Trained in morality, meditation, and wisdom,
At ease and without stain:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"The Great Sage, having cultivated well,
Attains virtue and speaks with mastery,
With good mindfulness and right contemplation,
Neither high nor low,
Unshakable and always self-possessed:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Without crookedness, always content,
Having abandoned miserliness and attained fullness,
Having accomplished the ascetic path and attained awakening,
In his final body, the honored great being,
Without comparison, without dust:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Without affliction, immeasurable,
Profound, having attained the state of a sage,
Always at ease and courageous,
Abiding in the Dharma with subtle thought,
The trainer, always without frivolity:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"The great dragon delighting in lofty abodes,
Whose fetters are ended and who has attained liberation,
Responsive, eloquent, and pure,
Wisdom born, free from sorrow and grief,
A non-returner, a Śākya:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Rightly gone, absorbed in meditation,
Without disturbance, pure,
Always smiling, without anger,
Delighting in detachment, attaining the foremost,
Fearless, always focused:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"The Seventh Sage, without equal,
Of threefold knowledge, having attained the Brahma state,
Bathed in purity like a bright lamp,
Having attained cessation and ended enmity,
Heroic and supremely pure:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Having attained cessation, wise as the earth,
Of great wisdom, removing worldly greed,
Worthy of offerings, the unsurpassed eye,
The highest being, without equal,
The charioteer, without anger:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Having cut off longing, unsurpassedly good,
Well-tamed, the peerless charioteer,
Unsurpassed, always joyful,
Without doubt, possessing radiance,
Having cut off conceit, the unsurpassed awakened one:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"Having cut off craving, the incomparable awakened one,
Without smoke, without flame,
The Thus-Gone, the Well-Gone,
Without comparison, without equal,
Whose fame has already attained what is right:
Upāli is a disciple of the Buddha.

"These are a hundred praises of the Buddha,
Never before contemplated,
Spoken by Upāli.
The devas came to that place,
Kindly assisting and adding eloquence.
In accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the person,
When questioned by Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta,
The disciple of the Buddha of Ten Powers replied."

Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked: "Householder, with what intention do you praise the ascetic Gotama?"

The householder Upāli replied: "Sir, listen to my simile. The wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Just as a skilled garland-maker or a garland-maker's apprentice gathers various flowers and, with a long thread, strings them into various garlands, so too, sir, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has immeasurable praises. He is the one I revere, and therefore I praise him."

When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Upāli, far removed from dust, free from defilement, the Dharma-eye concerning all dharmas arose in him. Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta then vomited hot blood and went to the country of Pāvā. Due to this evil affliction, he soon died.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The householder Upāli, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Upāli Sūtra, Number Seventeen.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgama)
## Fascicle 33

---

**(133) Sūtra on Preferring Goodness**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life? It is called 'Preferring Goodness.'

"What is 'preferring goodness'? Bhikṣus, there are people in the world who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a person who has been bound and imprisoned. If at a later time they are released from prison and freed from bondage, they attain peace and happiness. In the same way, bhikṣus, there are people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a person who is sick and afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, who cannot eat or drink and whose strength is diminishing and waning. If at a later time they recover from their illness, can eat and drink, and their strength is restored and increased, they attain peace and happiness. In the same way, bhikṣus, there are people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a person who is imprisoned in jail. If at a later time they are released from jail and attain peace and safety, with nothing to fear, they attain peace and happiness. In the same way, bhikṣus, there are people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a person who is a slave, not self-governing, dependent on others, unable to go where they wish. If at a later time they are freed from slavery and become self-governing, no longer dependent on others, able to go freely wherever they wish, they think to themselves: 'Previously I was a slave, not self-governing, dependent on others, unable to go where I wished. Now I have been freed from slavery, am self-governing, no longer dependent on others, and can go freely wherever I wish.' Because of this, they attain joy and happiness. In the same way, bhikṣus, there are people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, it is like a person carrying wealth and treasures who travels on a long road through wilderness and desolate lands, where there is much fear and danger. If at a later time they cross through the wilderness, reach a place of peace and safety with nothing to fear, they attain peace and happiness. In the same way, bhikṣus, there are people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. If, at a later time, they come to prefer goodness, they become endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

"Bhikṣus, people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind should be regarded as one who is bound and imprisoned, as one who is sick and afflicted, as one in jail, as a slave, and as one traveling through wilderness. Why is that? Bhikṣus, people who are endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind will, because of this cause, at the breaking up of the body after death, surely fall into an evil destination, being reborn in hell.

"Bhikṣus, people who are endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind should be regarded as one freed from bondage, as one recovered from illness, as one released from jail, as one freed from slavery, and as one who has crossed through the wilderness to safety. Why is that? Bhikṣus, people who are endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind will, because of this cause, at the breaking up of the body after death, surely go to a good destination, being reborn in heaven.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should learn thus: 'We shall abandon bad conduct of body and cultivate good conduct of body. We shall abandon bad conduct of speech and cultivate good conduct of speech. We shall abandon bad conduct of mind and cultivate good conduct of mind.' Bhikṣus, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(134) Sūtra on Releasing Cattle**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life? It is called 'Releasing Cattle.'

"Bhikṣus, if a cowherd has eleven bad qualities, he is unable to tend and grow his herd. What are the eleven? The cowherd does not know physical form, does not know characteristics, does not remove insects, does not bind wounds, does not make smoke, does not know the ford, does not know the watering place, does not know the road, does not know the pasturing grounds, milks without leaving any, and does not show special respect to the bull that is the leader and father of the herd. Bhikṣus, if a cowherd has these eleven bad qualities, he is unable to tend and grow his herd.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has eleven bad qualities, he is unable to grow in this Dharma and discipline, unable to develop, and unable to reach fulfillment. What are the eleven? The bhikṣu does not know physical form, does not know characteristics, does not remove insects, does not bind wounds, does not make smoke, does not know the ford, does not know the watering place, does not know the road, does not know the pasturing grounds, milks without leaving any, and does not show special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice.

"How does a bhikṣu not know physical form? A bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, that all form whatsoever, all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, is physical form. If a bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, that all form whatsoever, all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, is physical form, then such a bhikṣu does not know physical form.

"How does a bhikṣu not know characteristics? A bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, that fools are characterized by their deeds, and wise people are also characterized by their deeds. If a bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, that fools are characterized by their deeds and wise people are also characterized by their deeds, then such a bhikṣu does not know characteristics.

"How does a bhikṣu not remove insects? A bhikṣu, when a thought of desire arises, accepts it and does not abandon it, does not vomit it out, does not put an end to it. When a thought of ill-will arises, or a thought of harmfulness arises, he accepts it and does not abandon it, does not vomit it out, does not put an end to it. Whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he accepts them and does not abandon them, does not vomit them out, does not put an end to them. If a bhikṣu, whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, accepts them and does not abandon them, does not vomit them out, does not put an end to them, then such a bhikṣu does not remove insects.

"How does a bhikṣu not bind wounds? A bhikṣu, when the eye sees a form, grasps at its signs and grasps at its features. Because he does not guard the eye faculty, covetousness, grief, evil, and unwholesome states flow into his mind. He does not restrain himself, does not guard the eye faculty, and does not cultivate the guarding of the eye faculty. When the ear hears a sound, the nose smells an odor, the tongue tastes a flavor, the body touches a tangible, and the mind cognizes a mental object, he grasps at its signs and grasps at its features. Because he does not guard the mind faculty, covetousness, grief, evil, and unwholesome states flow into his mind. He does not restrain himself, does not guard the mind faculty, and does not cultivate the guarding of the mind faculty. If a bhikṣu does not guard the six faculties, then such a bhikṣu does not bind wounds.

"How does a bhikṣu not make smoke? A bhikṣu does not teach others in detail the Dharma he has heard and the Dharma he has learned. If a bhikṣu does not teach others in detail the Dharma he has heard and the Dharma he has learned, then such a bhikṣu does not make smoke.

"How does a bhikṣu not know the ford? A bhikṣu does not from time to time go to learned and accomplished bhikṣus who have broadly heard and understood the Dharma, who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the summaries, to ask and inquire of them: 'Venerable one, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What actions, when I perform them, will bring about long-lasting harm and suffering? What actions, when I perform them, will bring about long-lasting benefit and happiness?' If a bhikṣu does not from time to time go to learned and accomplished bhikṣus to ask and inquire, then such a bhikṣu does not know the ford.

"How does a bhikṣu not know the watering place? A bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, does not attain understanding of the meaning, does not attain understanding of the Dharma, does not attain joy connected with the Dharma. If a bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, does not attain understanding of the meaning, does not attain understanding of the Dharma, does not attain joy connected with the Dharma, then such a bhikṣu does not know the watering place.

"How does a bhikṣu not know the road? A bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, the Noble Eightfold Path. If a bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, the Noble Eightfold Path, then such a bhikṣu does not know the road.

"How does a bhikṣu not know the pasturing grounds? A bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. If a bhikṣu does not truly know, in accordance with reality, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, then such a bhikṣu does not know the pasturing grounds.

"How does a bhikṣu milk without leaving any? When faithful householders generously offer robes, alms food, bedding, and medicines for illness, the bhikṣu does not know moderation in accepting them. If the bhikṣu does not know moderation in accepting offerings from faithful householders, then such a bhikṣu milks without leaving any.

"How does a bhikṣu not show special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice? A bhikṣu does not establish bodily acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen, toward elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice. He does not establish verbal acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen. He does not establish mental acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen. If a bhikṣu does not establish acts of loving-kindness in body, speech, and mind, whether seen or unseen, toward elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice, then such a bhikṣu does not show special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has these eleven bad qualities, he is unable to grow in this Dharma and discipline, unable to develop, and unable to reach fulfillment.

"Bhikṣus, if a cowherd has eleven good qualities, he is able to tend and grow his herd. What are the eleven? The cowherd knows physical form, knows characteristics, removes insects, binds wounds, makes smoke, knows the ford, knows the watering place, knows the road, knows the pasturing grounds, milks while leaving some, and shows special respect to the bull that is the leader and father of the herd. Bhikṣus, if a cowherd has these eleven good qualities, he is able to tend and grow his herd.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has eleven good qualities, he is able to grow in this Dharma and discipline, able to develop, and able to reach fulfillment. What are the eleven? The bhikṣu knows physical form, knows characteristics, removes insects, binds wounds, makes smoke, knows the ford, knows the watering place, knows the road, knows the pasturing grounds, milks while leaving some, and shows special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice.

"How does a bhikṣu know physical form? A bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, that all form whatsoever, all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, is physical form. If a bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, that all form whatsoever, all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, is physical form, then such a bhikṣu knows physical form.

"How does a bhikṣu know characteristics? A bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, that fools are characterized by their deeds, and wise people are also characterized by their deeds. If a bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, that fools are characterized by their deeds and wise people are also characterized by their deeds, then such a bhikṣu knows characteristics.

"How does a bhikṣu remove insects? A bhikṣu, when a thought of desire arises, does not accept it but abandons it, vomits it out, and puts an end to it. When a thought of ill-will arises, or a thought of harmfulness arises, he does not accept it but abandons it, vomits it out, and puts an end to it. Whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not accept them but abandons them, vomits them out, and puts an end to them. If a bhikṣu, whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, does not accept them but abandons them, vomits them out, and puts an end to them, then such a bhikṣu removes insects.

"How does a bhikṣu bind wounds? A bhikṣu, when the eye sees a form, does not grasp at its signs and does not grasp at its features. Because he guards the eye faculty, covetousness, grief, evil, and unwholesome states do not flow into his mind. He restrains himself, guards the eye faculty, and cultivates the guarding of the eye faculty. When the ear hears a sound, the nose smells an odor, the tongue tastes a flavor, the body touches a tangible, and the mind cognizes a mental object, he does not grasp at its signs and does not grasp at its features. Because he guards the mind faculty, covetousness, grief, evil, and unwholesome states do not flow into his mind. He restrains himself, guards the mind faculty, and cultivates the guarding of the mind faculty. If a bhikṣu guards the six faculties, then such a bhikṣu binds wounds.

"How does a bhikṣu make smoke? A bhikṣu teaches others in detail the Dharma he has heard and the Dharma he has learned. If a bhikṣu teaches others in detail the Dharma he has heard and the Dharma he has learned, then such a bhikṣu makes smoke.

"How does a bhikṣu know the ford? A bhikṣu from time to time goes to learned and accomplished bhikṣus who have broadly heard and understood the Dharma, who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the summaries, to ask and inquire of them: 'Venerable one, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What actions, when I perform them, will bring about long-lasting harm and suffering? What actions, when I perform them, will bring about long-lasting benefit and happiness?' If a bhikṣu from time to time goes to learned and accomplished bhikṣus to ask and inquire, then such a bhikṣu knows the ford.

"How does a bhikṣu know the watering place? A bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, attains understanding of the meaning, attains understanding of the Dharma, and attains joy connected with the Dharma. If a bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, attains understanding of the meaning, attains understanding of the Dharma, and attains joy connected with the Dharma, then such a bhikṣu knows the watering place.

"How does a bhikṣu know the road? A bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, the Noble Eightfold Path. If a bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, the Noble Eightfold Path, then such a bhikṣu knows the road.

"How does a bhikṣu know the pasturing grounds? A bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. If a bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, then such a bhikṣu knows the pasturing grounds.

"How does a bhikṣu milk while leaving some? When faithful householders generously offer robes, alms food, bedding, and medicines for illness, the bhikṣu knows moderation in accepting them. If the bhikṣu knows moderation in accepting offerings from faithful householders, then such a bhikṣu milks while leaving some.

"How does a bhikṣu show special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice? A bhikṣu establishes bodily acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen, toward elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice. He establishes verbal acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen. He establishes mental acts of loving-kindness, whether seen or unseen. If a bhikṣu establishes acts of loving-kindness in body, speech, and mind, whether seen or unseen, toward elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice, then such a bhikṣu shows special respect to elder bhikṣus of great virtue who have long been in the practice.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has these eleven good qualities, he is able to grow in this Dharma and discipline, able to develop, and able to reach fulfillment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(135) Sūtra on Good Persons**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about a person who is like darkness heading toward darkness, a person who is like darkness heading toward light, a person who is like light heading toward darkness, and a person who is like light heading toward light. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is a person who is like darkness heading toward darkness? There is a person here who is reborn in a lowly family, either a caṇḍāla family, a family of bamboo-workers, a family of hunters, a family of chariot-makers, or a family of flower-scavengers, a poor and destitute family that lacks food and drink and is difficult to sustain, a place where food and clothing are hard to obtain. Moreover, this person is ugly in appearance, unpleasant to look at, short and squat, with many illnesses, being blind, crippled, lame, or half-paralyzed. He obtains neither food, nor drink, nor clothing, nor vehicles, nor garlands and fragrances, nor bedding, nor dwellings, nor lamps. He performs bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. Having performed bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he goes to an evil destination, being reborn in hell. It is as if a person goes from darkness to darkness, from gloom to gloom, from defilement to defilement. This person is said to be like this. This is called a person who is like darkness heading toward darkness.

"What is a person who is like darkness heading toward light? There is a person here who is reborn in a lowly family, either a caṇḍāla family, a family of bamboo-workers, a family of hunters, a family of chariot-makers, or a family of flower-scavengers, a poor and destitute family that lacks food and drink and is difficult to sustain, a place where food and clothing are hard to obtain. Moreover, this person is ugly in appearance, unpleasant to look at, short and squat, with many illnesses, being blind, crippled, lame, or half-paralyzed. He obtains neither food, nor drink, nor clothing, nor vehicles, nor garlands and fragrances, nor bedding, nor dwellings, nor lamps. He performs good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. Having performed good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he goes to a good destination, being reborn in heaven. It is as if a person ascends from the ground onto a bed, or from a bed onto horseback, or from horseback onto an elephant, or from an elephant onto a building. This person is said to be like this. This is called a person who is like darkness heading toward light.

"What is a person who is like light heading toward darkness? There is a person here who is reborn in a noble family, either a kṣatriya great family, a brahmin great family, a householder great family, or any other wealthy and prosperous great family with much property, many treasures and possessions, an abundance of livestock, servants, and attendants. Moreover, this person is handsome in appearance, pleasant to look at, with a fine complexion. He obtains food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands and fragrances, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. He performs bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. Having performed bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he goes to an evil destination, being reborn in hell. It is as if a person descends from a building onto an elephant, or from an elephant onto horseback, or from horseback onto a bed, or from a bed down to the ground, or from the ground into darkness. This person is said to be like this. This is called a person who is like light heading toward darkness.

"What is a person who is like light heading toward light? There is a person here who is reborn in a noble family, either a kṣatriya great family, a brahmin great family, a householder great family, or any other wealthy and prosperous great family with much property, many treasures and possessions, an abundance of livestock, servants, and attendants. Moreover, this person is handsome in appearance, pleasant to look at, with a fine complexion. He obtains food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands and fragrances, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. He performs good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. Having performed good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, he goes to a good destination, being reborn in heaven. It is as if a person goes from a bed onto a bed, or from horseback onto horseback, or from an elephant onto an elephant, or from a building onto a building. This person is said to be like this. This is called a person who is like light heading toward light.

"These are the four kinds of persons existing in the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(136) Sūtra on Merchants**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a merchant has three qualities, he cannot achieve gains he has not yet achieved, and gains already achieved will diminish. What are the three? Here, a merchant does not attend to his business in the morning, does not attend to his business at midday, and does not attend to his business in the evening. If a merchant has these three qualities, he cannot achieve gains he has not yet achieved, and gains already achieved will diminish.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has three qualities, he cannot achieve wholesome states he has not yet achieved, and wholesome states already achieved will decline. What are the three? Here, a bhikṣu does not attend to the sign of samādhi in the morning, does not attend to the sign of samādhi at midday, and does not attend to the sign of samādhi in the evening. If a bhikṣu has these three qualities, he cannot achieve wholesome states he has not yet achieved, and wholesome states already achieved will decline.

"If a merchant has three qualities, he can achieve gains he has not yet achieved, and gains already achieved will not diminish. What are the three? Here, a merchant attends to his business in the morning, attends to his business at midday, and attends to his business in the evening. If a merchant has these three qualities, he can achieve gains he has not yet achieved, and gains already achieved will not diminish.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has three qualities, he can achieve wholesome states he has not yet achieved, and wholesome states already achieved will not decline. What are the three? Here, a bhikṣu attends to the sign of samādhi in the morning, attends to the sign of samādhi at midday, and attends to the sign of samādhi in the evening. If a bhikṣu has these three qualities, he can achieve wholesome states he has not yet achieved, and wholesome states already achieved will not decline."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(137) Sūtra on the World**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The world has three dharmas that are not lovable, not pleasing, and not delightful. What are the three? They are old age, illness, and death. Bhikṣus, if there were no old age, illness, and death in the world, the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, would not appear in the world, and the Dharma and discipline taught by the Tathāgata would not shine in the world. Because there are old age, illness, and death in the world, therefore the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, appears in the world, and the Dharma and discipline taught by the Tathāgata shines in the world.

"If one does not first cut down the tree, one cannot cut the branches and leaves. In the same way, if the Tathāgata does not first attain the supreme, complete enlightenment, he cannot bring about an abundance of wholesome Dharma for śrāvakas.

"It is like a great mountain of stone, without cracks, without holes, solid throughout, a single mass. Even if wind and rain come from the east, they cannot move it. Even if wind and rain come from the south, the west, or the north, they cannot move it. In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu abandons the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and his mind is well established in the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, and he cultivates the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, then even if a great mass of earth comes, it cannot shake him.

"What is a bhikṣu who abandons the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, whose mind is well established in the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, and who cultivates the Seven Factors of Enlightenment? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligence and effort, right mindfulness and right comprehension, not forgetting, removing covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates the body as body externally. He contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligence and effort, right mindfulness and right comprehension, not forgetting, removing covetousness and grief toward the world. In the same way, he contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas internally, externally, and both internally and externally, with diligence and effort, right mindfulness and right comprehension, not forgetting, removing covetousness and grief toward the world.

"He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, leading to release. He cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of dharmas, the factor of enlightenment that is energy, the factor of enlightenment that is joy, the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility, the factor of enlightenment that is samādhi, and the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, leading to release.

"This is a bhikṣu who abandons the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, whose mind is well established in the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, and who cultivates the Seven Factors of Enlightenment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(138) Sūtra on Welfare**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu has accomplished seven dharmas and also attains the four increased states of mind that bring happiness in the present life, easily attaining them without difficulty, then this bhikṣu is called one who abides in the unshakable in this very life, and has attained the exhaustion of the outflows.

"What are the seven dharmas that a bhikṣu accomplishes? Here, a bhikṣu truly knows, in accordance with reality, that this is suffering. He truly knows, in accordance with reality, that this is the origin of suffering. He truly knows, in accordance with reality, that this is the cessation of suffering. He truly knows, in accordance with reality, that this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects on and examines the Dharma with his own wisdom and knowledge, investigating its meaning. He thinks thus: 'This is the meaning, this is the Dharma.' He attains joy connected with the Dharma. Furthermore, a bhikṣu is not one who speaks much idle talk, who speaks about kings, speaks about bandits, speaks about disputes, speaks about food and drink, speaks about clothing, speaks about women, speaks about towns and villages, speaks about men, speaks about evil people, speaks about the wilderness, speaks about rivers and seas, or speaks other kinds of meaningless talk. He can restrain himself from such talk. Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates spiritual faculties, keeps the precepts perfectly, guards the doors of the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, practices wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night, constantly delights in abiding in elevated practices, cultivates mindfulness and wisdom, is ever diligent and not lazy, and does not fail in his duty.

"These are the seven dharmas that a bhikṣu accomplishes.

"What are the four increased states of mind that bring happiness in the present life, easily attained without difficulty? Here, a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from evil, unwholesome states, with initial application and sustained application, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and abides in the first dhyāna. With the subsiding of initial application and sustained application, with inner serenity and unification of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with joy and happiness born of samādhi, he enters and abides in the second dhyāna. With the fading of joy, he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones declare: 'One who is equanimous and mindful abides in happiness.' He enters and abides in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the previous disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna.

"These are the four increased states of mind that bring happiness in the present life, easily attained without difficulty.

"If a bhikṣu has accomplished these seven dharmas and also attains these four increased states of mind that bring happiness in the present life, easily attaining them without difficulty, then this bhikṣu is called one who abides in the unshakable in this very life, and has attained the exhaustion of the outflows."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(139) Sūtra on Quietude**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, there are five things that are most difficult to obtain in the world. What are the five?

"First, one who has lost wealth and seeks to regain it; this is most difficult to obtain in the world. Second, one who is born into a family of good standing, being handsome in appearance, and who also learns broadly and has much knowledge; this is most difficult to obtain in the world. Third, one who is able to maintain the precepts purely and without blemish in the Buddha's teaching; this is most difficult to obtain in the world. Fourth, one who, having left the household life, is able to cultivate the holy life and complete it to the end; this is most difficult to obtain in the world. Fifth, that a Buddha should appear in the world; this is the most difficult to obtain.

"These are the five things that are most difficult to obtain in the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(140) Sūtra on the Supreme**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are five things that cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. What are the five?

"'May what is subject to aging not age': this cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. 'May what is subject to illness not become ill': this cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. 'May what is subject to death not die': this cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. 'May what is subject to decay and destruction not decay and be destroyed': this cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. 'May what is subject to loss not be lost': this cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world.

"Bhikṣus, the ordinary worldling who has not learned, when encountering what is subject to aging, illness, death, decay and destruction, or loss, is distressed and grieved, beats his breast, wails and weeps, becomes confused, and loses his mind. He does not reflect thus: 'It is not only I who am subject to aging, illness, death, decay and destruction, and loss. All beings who come, go, pass away, and are reborn, all of them are subject to aging; what is subject to aging will age. All of them are subject to illness; what is subject to illness will become ill. All of them are subject to death; what is subject to death will die. All of them are subject to decay and destruction; what is subject to decay and destruction will decay and be destroyed. All of them are subject to loss; what is subject to loss will be lost. If, when I encounter what is subject to aging, illness, death, decay and destruction, and loss, I alone am distressed and grieved, beat my breast, wail and weep, become confused, and lose my mind, then I will not desire food, my body will become ugly, my work will not be accomplished, my enemies will be pleased, and my friends and relatives will be saddened.'

"When encountering what is subject to aging, illness, death, decay and destruction, and loss, the worldling is distressed and grieved, beats his breast, wails and weeps, becomes confused, and loses his mind. This is called an ordinary worldling who has not learned, who is struck by the poisoned arrow of sorrow and grief, and who harms himself.

"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple, when encountering what is subject to aging, illness, death, decay and destruction, and loss, is not distressed and grieved, does not beat his breast, does not wail and weep, does not become confused, and does not lose his mind. This is called a learned noble disciple who has pulled out the poisoned arrow of sorrow and grief with which the ordinary worldling strikes himself, harming himself. The noble disciple, without sorrow and without the poisoned arrow, attains self-extinguishment of nirvāṇa.

"These are the five things that cannot be obtained by a śramaṇa, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(141) Sūtra on Joy**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu accomplishes precepts, accomplishes samādhi, accomplishes wisdom, then in this very life he frequently enters and abides in the liberation of the exhaustion of the outflows, with the mind liberated and with the liberation by wisdom. He truly knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' I say that this bhikṣu's walking is not in vain, and how much more so his sitting, lying down, and standing. Why is that?

"Because, bhikṣus, what I have said should happen for a bhikṣu who has left home and shaved his head, donning the kāṣāya robe and with right faith leaving the household life for homelessness to learn the Way, the supreme goal of the holy life, the bhikṣu in this very life has himself realized through direct knowledge, attaining and abiding in it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'"

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"If one does not delight in the holy life,
And does not reach the stilling of the mind,
Grasping at everything as it comes,
Such a person is tied and bound by Māra.

If one does delight in the holy life,
And also reaches the stilling of the mind,
Not grasping at anything as it comes,
Such a person is freed from the bonds of Māra.

One should not delight in evil dharmas,
Nor place the mind in a state of negligence.
One should not embrace wrong views,
Nor increase worldly attachments."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

**(142) Sūtra on Rain**

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about three kinds of days. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What are the three kinds of days? They are hot days, cold days, and rainy days.

"What are hot days? When the fire element becomes agitated and the wind element does not blow and rain does not fall, these are called hot days. What are cold days? When the wind element blows excessively, rain falls heavily, the fire element subsides, and it becomes extremely cold, these are called cold days. What are rainy days? When the earth becomes moist, rain falls, and water gathers, these are called rainy days.

"Bhikṣus, I have taught you about three kinds of days. Now I shall teach you about three other kinds of days. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What are the three kinds of days? They are hot days, cold days, and rainy days.

"What are hot days? When a thought of desire arises, these are called hot days. Why is that? Bhikṣus, if one is defiled by desire, the mind becomes heated. Therefore, these are called hot days.

"What are cold days? When a thought of ill-will arises, these are called cold days. Why is that? Bhikṣus, if one has a mind of ill-will, one destroys the good. Therefore, these are called cold days.

"What are rainy days? When a thought of delusion arises, these are called rainy days. Why is that? Bhikṣus, if one is covered by delusion, one cannot see the truth. Therefore, these are called rainy days.

"These three kinds of days can be eliminated. The hot days of desire can be eliminated, the cold days of ill-will can be eliminated, and the rainy days of delusion can be eliminated."

The World-Honored One then spoke in verse:

"Desire is called the hot days,
Ill-will is called the cold days,
Delusion is called the rainy days;
The fire, wind, and rain of the three poisons.

The hot days of desire can burn,
The cold days of ill-will can freeze,
The rainy days of delusion can flood;
The wind, rain, and fire of these three.

Desire, ill-will, and delusion,
These three are not form or feeling;
They defile sentient beings,
And cause one to fall into the evil destinies.

Therefore one should abandon these,
As one who takes a thorn from one's flesh.
Having pulled out these three,
The bhikṣu attains nirvāṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 33 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 33

## (134) Sūtra on Sakka's Questions, Eighteenth of the Great Division

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Magadha, staying east of Rājagṛha, north of the village of the mango grove, in the Indra Cave on Mount Vediyaka.

At that time, Sakka, King of the Gods, heard that the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Magadha, staying east of Rājagṛha, north of the village of the mango grove, in the Indra Cave on Mount Vediyaka. Then Sakka, King of the Gods, addressed Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas: "I have heard that the World-Honored One is traveling in the kingdom of Magadha, staying east of Rājagṛha, north of the village of the mango grove, in the Indra Cave on Mount Vediyaka. Pañcaśikha! Come, let us go together to see the Buddha."

Pañcaśikha replied: "Very well." Thereupon Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, took up his lapis lazuli lute and followed Sakka, King of the Gods.
