The gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens, hearing that Sakka, King of the Gods, with utmost sincerity wished to go see the Buddha, also attended and followed Sakka, King of the Gods. Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, just as a strong man might stretch or bend his arm, vanished from the Thirty-Three Heavens and appeared in the kingdom of Magadha, east of Rājagṛha, north of the village of the mango grove, on Mount Vediyaka, not far from the stone cave.

At that time, Mount Vediyaka was brilliantly illuminated and radiant, bright as a blazing fire. The residents dwelling around that mountain, seeing this, had this thought: "Mount Vediyaka is ablaze with fire burning everywhere."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having stopped in one place, said: "Pañcaśikha! The World-Honored One dwells thus in secluded places, in mountain forests beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, without people, suitable for meditative sitting. He possesses great majestic power, and the gods accompany him together, delighting in that seclusion, sitting in meditation, peaceful, comfortable, and wandering happily. We have not yet announced ourselves and should not simply go forward. Pañcaśikha! You go first to announce us, and afterward we shall proceed."

Pañcaśikha replied: "Very well." Thereupon Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, having received Sakka's instruction, took up his lapis lazuli lute and went first to the Indra Cave. He then thought: "I know the place that is neither too near nor too far from the Buddha, so that the Buddha will notice me and hear the sound of my music." Having stationed himself at that place, he tuned his lapis lazuli lute and composed verses connected with desire, verses connected with dragons, verses connected with śramaṇas, and verses connected with arhats. He sang these verses:

"O Worthy One, I salute your father and mother,
Moon and Timbaru,
Who begot you so wonderfully,
Making my heart burst with joy.

As one burning with heat seeks a cool breeze,
As one thirsting desires cold water,
Just so do I love you,
As an arhat loves the Dharma.

As it is most difficult to collect water that has been poured out,
So too is it with attachment to desire;
Through countless births we may come together,
Like giving without attachment.

The pool water is clear and cool,
With golden sand at the bottom;
Like a lordly elephant oppressed by heat,
Entering this pool to bathe.

Just as a hook leads an elephant,
My mind is subdued by you;
You do not know my conduct,
O graceful one, I have not yet won you.

My mind clings deeply to you,
Anguish and affliction burn my heart,
Therefore I find no joy,
Like a person entering a tiger's mouth.

Like a son of the Śākyas contemplating in meditation,
Always delighting in oneness,
Like a sage who attains awakening,
Attaining you would be wondrously pure and radiant.

As the sage delights
In unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening,
Just so do I delight,
Always seeking to obtain you.

As the sick desire medicine,
As the hungry desire food,
O Worthy One, quench my heart,
As water extinguishes fire.

Whatever merit I have performed,
Offerings made to those without attachment,
All that is completely pure and wonderful,
May I share the fruit with you.

I wish to end my days with you,
Not to live apart from you alone,
I would rather die together with you,
Than live separated from you.

O Sakka, grant me my wish,
Most honored of the Thirty-Three Gods,
You, the supreme among people,
This is my firmest vow.

Therefore I bow to the Great Hero,
I prostrate before the foremost among people,
Who has severed all thorns of craving;
I bow to the Kinsman of the Sun."

Thereupon the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and praised Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas: "Excellent! Excellent! Pañcaśikha! Your singing voice harmonizes with the sound of the lute, and the sound of the lute harmonizes with your singing voice. The singing voice does not go beyond the lute sound, and the lute sound does not go beyond the singing voice. Pañcaśikha! Do you recall when in the past you once sang these verses connected with desire, verses connected with dragons, verses connected with śramaṇas, and verses connected with arhats?"

Pañcaśikha replied: "World-Honored One! Only the Great Sage himself should know this. Great Sage! In the past, when the World-Honored One had first attained the Way of Awakening and was traveling on the bank of the Nerañjarā River in Uruvelā, beneath the Ajapāla Nigrodha tree, at that time, Timbaru the Gandharva King had a daughter named Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā. There was a deva named Sikhandhi, son of Mātali the charioteer, who was seeking that maiden. Great Sage! At the time when he was seeking that maiden, I too was seeking to obtain her. However, Great Sage, when I sought that maiden, I ultimately could not win her. At that time I stood behind that maiden and sang these verses connected with desire, verses connected with dragons, verses connected with śramaṇas, and verses connected with arhats. Great Sage! When I sang these verses, that maiden turned around and, with a gentle smile, said to me: 'Pañcaśikha! I have never seen that Buddha, the World-Honored One, but I have already heard from the Thirty-Three Gods about that World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, known as the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Pañcaśikha! If you can repeatedly praise the World-Honored One, then I will be willing to be together with you, O Great Sage.' We were together only once, and thereafter I never saw her again."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, had this thought: "Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, has already caused the World-Honored One to awaken from concentration and has announced me to the Well-Gone One." At that time, Sakka, King of the Gods, said: "Pañcaśikha! Go there now and on my behalf bow your head at the Buddha's feet, inquire about the World-Honored One, and ask: 'Is the World-Honored One's sacred body strong and well, in good health, free from illness, light and comfortable in daily activities, with energy as usual?' Speak thus: 'Great Sage! Sakka, King of the Gods, bows his head at the Buddha's feet and inquires: Is the World-Honored One's sacred body strong and well, in good health, free from illness, light and comfortable in daily activities, with energy as usual? Great Sage! Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens, wishes to see the World-Honored One!'"

Pañcaśikha replied: "Very well."

Thereupon Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, set aside his lapis lazuli lute, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Great Sage! Sakka, King of the Gods, bows his head at the Buddha's feet and inquires: Is the World-Honored One's sacred body strong and well, in good health, free from illness, light and comfortable in daily activities, with energy as usual? Great Sage! Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens, wishes to see the World-Honored One!"

At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Pañcaśikha! May Sakka, King of the Gods, now be peaceful and happy, and may all the gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings be peaceful and happy. Pañcaśikha! If Sakka, King of the Gods, wishes to see me, let him come as he pleases."

Thereupon Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to where Sakka, King of the Gods, was and said: "Your Majesty! I have already announced you to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One now awaits Your Majesty. May Your Majesty know it is the proper time."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, went to where the Buddha was. Then Sakka, King of the Gods, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and three times announced his own name and clan, saying: "Great Sage! I am Sakka, King of the Gods! I am Sakka, King of the Gods!"

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is, Kausika! You are Sakka, King of the Gods."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having three times announced his own name and clan, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. The gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, also bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. Then Sakka, King of the Gods, said: "Great Sage! Shall I sit near to or far from the World-Honored One?"

The World-Honored One said: "You may sit near me. Why? Because you have a great retinue of gods." Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, also bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. At that time, the Indra Cave suddenly became vast and spacious. Why was this? It was due to the Buddha's majestic spiritual power and the majestic virtue of the gods.

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having been seated, said: "Great Sage! Throughout the long night I have wished to see the World-Honored One and wished to ask about the Dharma. Great Sage! Once in the past, the World-Honored One was traveling in the country of Śrāvastī, staying in a stone cave. Great Sage! At that time, on my own behalf and on behalf of the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens, I mounted my chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and went to the house of King Vaiśravaṇa. At that time, in King Vaiśravaṇa's household there was a concubine named Pañcanā. At that time, the World-Honored One had entered concentration and was in stillness, and that concubine, with palms joined, was paying homage at the World-Honored One's feet. Great Sage! I spoke to her saying: 'Sister! Now is not the time for me to visit the World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has entered concentration. If the World-Honored One awakens from concentration, sister, please on my behalf bow your head at the Buddha's feet and inquire about the World-Honored One: Is his sacred body strong and well, in good health, free from illness, light and comfortable in daily activities, with energy as usual? Speak thus: "Great Sage! Sakka, King of the Gods, bows his head at the Buddha's feet and inquires: Is the World-Honored One's sacred body strong and well, in good health, free from illness, light and comfortable in daily activities, with energy as usual?"' Great Sage! Did that sister bow her head at the Buddha's feet on my behalf, inquire about the World-Honored One? Does the World-Honored One remember this?"

The World-Honored One said: "Kausika! That sister did bow her head at my feet on your behalf, conveyed your message fully, and inquired about me. I do remember it. Kausika! When you departed, I heard the sound and then awakened from concentration."

"Great Sage! In the past I heard that when a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, known as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world, the hosts of gods increase and the hosts of asuras decrease. Great Sage! I have seen with my own eyes that the World-Honored One's disciple bhikṣus, who have cultivated the holy life under the World-Honored One, having abandoned desire and become free from desire, when their bodies decay and their lives end, attain a good destination and are reborn among the gods. Great Sage! Gopikā, a Śākya woman, was a disciple of the World-Honored One and also cultivated the holy life under the World-Honored One. She loathed her female body and loved the male form. She transformed her female body and received a male form. Having abandoned desire and become free from desire, when her body decayed and her life ended, she was reborn in the wonderful realm of the Thirty-Three Heavens and became my son. After he was born, all the gods knew him: Gopaka the deva son possesses great magical powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed fortune, and great spiritual authority.

"Great Sage! I also saw that there were three bhikṣu disciples of the World-Honored One who also cultivated the holy life under the World-Honored One, but who did not abandon desire. When their bodies decayed and their lives ended, they were reborn in the lowly palace of the gandharva musicians. After they were born there, they came daily to the Thirty-Three Heavens to serve the gods and attend upon Gopaka the deva son. When the deva son saw them, he spoke these verses:

"'I am the laywoman Gopikā,
Who made offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma,
And with a pure mind made offerings to the Sangha.
I have already received the Buddha's grace;
Being a Śākya daughter of great blessed virtue,
Wonderfully reborn among the Thirty-Three,
I am known as Gopaka the deva son.

I see those who were formerly bhikṣus,
Now reborn as gandharva spirits,
Standing before me with palms joined;
Gopaka speaks these verses for them:

These were formerly sons of Gautama;
When I was formerly a human being,
They came to my household,
Where I served them food and drink with fine hospitality.

These formerly dwelled with the holy ones,
Practicing the unsurpassed holy life,
But now they serve others,
Coming daily to attend upon the gods.

I formerly served and waited on you,
Hearing the noble, well-spoken Dharma;
Having attained faith and accomplished in precepts,
I was wonderfully reborn among the Thirty-Three.

You who formerly received offerings,
Practicing the unsurpassed holy life,
Now serve others,
Coming daily to attend upon the gods.

How can you show your faces?
Having upheld the Buddha's Dharma,
You then turned your backs and departed from the Dharma.
This is what the Eye of Awakening has well proclaimed.

I, who formerly saw you all,
Now see you born among the lowly gandharva musicians;
You yourselves practiced unlawful conduct,
You yourselves were born in an unlawful state.

I was formerly a laywoman at home;
Observe my present superior virtue:
Transforming from female into a deva son,
Freely enjoying the five sensual pleasures.'

"Having admonished those sons of Gautama, and they being ashamed, he praised Gautama:
"'We shall now strive forward; the deva son speaks the truth.'

"Two of them thereupon strove diligently, recollecting the Dharma and discipline of Gautama, knowing the danger and disaster of desires, and immediately abandoned and departed from desire. Having been bound by the fetter of desire, they then attained liberation and departed far from it, like elephants breaking their bonds and chains, they transcended the Thirty-Three Heavens. Indra, the Brahmā gods, and all came together, and from those very seats they ascended, heroically casting off the dust of desire.

"Sakka, seeing this, was amazed; the most excellent god, god among gods:
"'Those who were formerly born in a lowly state have now transcended the Thirty-Three Heavens.'
Having been amazed, the Wonderful Pacifier spoke. Gopaka then said:

"'Among humans there is the Buddha, the supreme one, the Śākya sage who knows desires. Those disciples lost their mindfulness, but I admonished them and they recovered it. Of the three, one was reborn among the gandharva musicians. Two accomplished the right path, among the gods established in the bliss of meditative absorption. You teach such Dharma that your disciples are without confusion. Transcending the outflows, cutting off wrong doubt, I bow to the Buddha, the supreme one who conquers the faculties. When they awakened to all dharmas, the two attained a place of advancement. Having attained advancement, they were reborn in the Brahmā heavens. We understand this Dharma; the Great Sage has come to this place.'"

At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This spirit has throughout the long night been without flattery, without deception, without guile, and is straightforward. Whatever he asks, he asks entirely from a wish to know, not from a desire to vex or disturb. Whatever he asks is just like this. I should therefore explain the profound Abhidharma." The World-Honored One, knowing this, spoke this verse for Sakka, King of the Gods:

"For the sake of happiness in the present life,
And also for happiness in future lives,
Kausika, ask freely as you wish,
Whatever your heart desires;
For each and every question,
I shall make a complete determination.
The World-Honored One has already granted permission;
The Lord of Day seeks to see the meaning,
In the land of Magadha,
Vāsava now asks."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, said: "World-Honored One! Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings, how many fetters does each have?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings each have two fetters: stinginess and jealousy. Each of them has this thought: 'May I be without violence, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without quarreling, without fighting, without suffering, and may I wander in peace and happiness.' Although they have such thoughts, they still experience violence, bondage, enmity, anger, quarreling, fighting, and suffering, and do not wander in peace and happiness."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings each have two fetters. They have this thought: 'May I be without violence, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without quarreling, without fighting, without suffering, and may I wander in peace and happiness.' Although they have such thoughts, they still experience violence, bondage, enmity, anger, quarreling, fighting, and suffering, and do not wander in peace and happiness. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Stinginess and jealousy, what is their cause, what is their condition, from what do they arise, and by what do they come to exist? Furthermore, due to what cause are stinginess and jealousy absent?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Stinginess and jealousy have liking and disliking as their cause, liking and disliking as their condition; they arise from liking and disliking and exist due to liking and disliking. If there were no liking and disliking, then there would be no stinginess and jealousy."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! Stinginess and jealousy have liking and disliking as their cause, liking and disliking as their condition; they arise from liking and disliking and exist due to liking and disliking. If there were no liking and disliking, then there would be no stinginess and jealousy. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Liking and disliking, what is their cause, what is their condition, from what do they arise, and by what do they come to exist? Furthermore, due to what cause are liking and disliking absent?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Liking and disliking have desire as their cause and desire as their condition; they arise from desire and exist due to desire. If there were no desire, then there would be no liking and disliking."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! Liking and disliking have desire as their cause and desire as their condition; they arise from desire and exist due to desire. If there were no desire, then there would be no liking and disliking. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Desire, what is its cause, what is its condition, from what does it arise, and by what does it come to exist? Furthermore, due to what cause is desire absent?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Desire has thought as its cause and thought as its condition; it arises from thought and exists due to thought. If there were no thought, then there would be no desire."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! Desire has thought as its cause and thought as its condition; it arises from thought and exists due to thought. If there were no thought, then there would be no desire. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Thought, what is its cause, what is its condition, from what does it arise, and by what does it come to exist? Furthermore, due to what cause is thought absent?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Thought has mental proliferation as its cause and mental proliferation as its condition; it arises from mental proliferation and exists due to mental proliferation. If there were no mental proliferation, then there would be no thought. Due to thought there is desire; due to desire there is liking and disliking; due to liking and disliking there is stinginess and jealousy; due to stinginess and jealousy there arise weapons and fighting, quarreling, jealousy, flattery, deception, false speech, and divisive speech; in the mind arise immeasurable evil, unwholesome dharmas. Thus this entire great mass of suffering arises. If there is no mental proliferation, then there is no thought; if there is no thought, then there is no desire; if there is no desire, then there is no liking and disliking; if there is no liking and disliking, then there is no stinginess and jealousy; if there is no stinginess and jealousy, then there are no weapons and fighting, quarreling, jealousy, flattery, deception, false speech, and divisive speech; in the mind do not arise immeasurable evil, unwholesome dharmas. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! Thought has mental proliferation as its cause and mental proliferation as its condition; it arises from mental proliferation and exists due to mental proliferation. If there were no mental proliferation, then there would be no thought. Due to thought there is desire; due to desire there is liking and disliking; due to liking and disliking there is stinginess and jealousy; due to stinginess and jealousy there arise weapons and fighting, quarreling, jealousy, flattery, deception, false speech, and divisive speech; in the mind arise immeasurable evil, unwholesome dharmas. Thus this entire great mass of suffering arises. If there is no mental proliferation, then there is no thought; if there is no thought, then there is no desire; if there is no desire, then there is no liking and disliking; if there is no liking and disliking, then there is no stinginess and jealousy; if there is no stinginess and jealousy, then there are no weapons and fighting, quarreling, jealousy, flattery, deception, false speech, and divisive speech; in the mind do not arise immeasurable evil, unwholesome dharmas. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! What is the path leading to the cessation of mental proliferation? What practice does a bhikṣu follow that leads toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! The path leading to the cessation of mental proliferation is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. Kausika, this is called the path leading to the cessation of mental proliferation. A bhikṣu practices this, heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! The path leading to the cessation of mental proliferation is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, making eight. Great Sage! This is the path leading to the cessation of mental proliferation. A bhikṣu practices this, heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation, how many things does he abandon and how many things does he practice?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation abandons three things and cultivates three things. What are the three? First, thought; second, speech; third, seeking. Kausika, regarding thought, I say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If a thought is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If a thought is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that thought. Speech is likewise. Kausika, regarding seeking, I also say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If a seeking is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If a seeking is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that seeking."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation abandons three things and cultivates three things. What are the three? First, thought; second, speech; third, seeking. The Great Sage says that regarding thought there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If a thought increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage then cuts it off. If a thought diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that thought. Speech is likewise. The Great Sage says that regarding seeking there are also two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If a seeking increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage then cuts it off. If a seeking diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that seeking. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation, in how many things does he exercise restraint, and from how many things does he seek liberation through practice?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation exercises restraint in six things and seeks liberation through practice of six things. What are the six? The eye seeing forms, the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, the body sensing tactile objects, and the mind cognizing dharmas. Kausika, regarding the eye seeing forms, I say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If the eye seeing forms is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If the eye seeing forms is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. Likewise for the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, the body sensing tactile objects, and the mind cognizing dharmas. I also say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If the mind cognizing dharmas is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If the mind cognizing dharmas is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation exercises restraint in six things and seeks liberation through practice of six things. What are the six? The eye seeing forms, the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, the body sensing tactile objects, and the mind cognizing dharmas. The Great Sage says regarding the eye seeing forms, there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If the eye seeing forms increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage cuts it off. If the eye seeing forms diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. Likewise for the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling scents, the tongue tasting flavors, and the body sensing tactile objects. The Great Sage says regarding the mind cognizing dharmas, there are also two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If the mind cognizing dharmas increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage cuts it off. If the mind cognizing dharmas diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation, even if his life were to last but a single moment, how many more things does he abandon and how many more things does he practice?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation, even if his life were to last but a single moment, further abandons three things and practices three things. What are the three? First, joy; second, sorrow; third, equanimity. Kausika, regarding joy, I say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If a joy is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If a joy is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. Sorrow is likewise. Kausika, regarding equanimity, I also say there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If equanimity is not to be practiced, I cut it off. If equanimity is to be practiced, I discern the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! A bhikṣu heading toward the path of the cessation of mental proliferation, even if his life were to last but a single moment, abandons three things and practices three things. What are the three? First, joy; second, sorrow; third, equanimity. The Great Sage says that regarding joy there are two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If joy increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage cuts it off. If joy diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. Sorrow is likewise. The Great Sage says that regarding equanimity there are also two kinds: what is to be practiced and what is not to be practiced. If equanimity increases evil, unwholesome dharmas and diminishes wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage cuts it off. If equanimity diminishes evil, unwholesome dharmas and increases wholesome dharmas, the Great Sage discerns the right time for it, with mindfulness and wisdom, in order to fulfill that. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Do all śramaṇas and brahmins share one teaching, one desire, one love, one delight, and one intention?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Not all śramaṇas and brahmins share one teaching, one desire, one love, one delight, and one intention."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, further asked: "Great Sage! For what reason do not all śramaṇas and brahmins share one teaching, one desire, one love, one delight, and one intention?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! In this world there are various kinds of elements, immeasurable elements. According to whichever element they come to know, in accordance with that element, according to their capacity and according to their means, they declare definitively: 'This is the truth; all else is false.' Kausika, for this reason, not all śramaṇas and brahmins share one teaching, one desire, one love, one delight, and one intention."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! In this world there are various kinds of elements, immeasurable elements. According to whichever element they come to know, in accordance with that element, according to their capacity and according to their means, they declare definitively: 'This is the truth; all else is false.' Great Sage! For this reason, not all śramaṇas and brahmins share one teaching, one desire, one love, one delight, and one intention. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

He further asked: "Great Sage! Do all śramaṇas and brahmins reach the ultimate, the ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, the completion of the ultimate holy life?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! Not necessarily do all śramaṇas and brahmins reach the ultimate, the ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, the completion of the ultimate holy life."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, further asked: "Great Sage! For what reason do not necessarily all śramaṇas and brahmins reach the ultimate, the ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, the completion of the ultimate holy life?"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, answered: "Kausika! If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, have not properly and well liberated their minds, they do not reach the ultimate, do not reach the ultimately pure, do not reach the ultimate holy life, and do not reach the completion of the ultimate holy life. Kausika! If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, have properly and well liberated their minds, they reach the ultimate, the ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, the completion of the ultimate holy life."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard this, said: "So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, have not properly and well liberated their minds, they do not reach the ultimate, do not reach the ultimately pure, do not reach the ultimate holy life, and do not reach the completion of the ultimate holy life. Great Sage! If there are śramaṇas and brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, have properly and well liberated their minds, they reach the ultimate, the ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, the completion of the ultimate holy life. So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Well-Gone One! So it is, Great Sage! As the Buddha has taught the Dharma, I fully understand it. I have cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, and have no more hesitation, having heard what the Buddha has taught."

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, and said: "Great Sage! Throughout the long night I have had the thorn of doubt and perplexity, and the World-Honored One has today pulled it out. Why? Because of the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kausika! Do you recall whether in the past you ever asked other śramaṇas or brahmins about such matters?"

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, answered: "World-Honored One! Only the Great Sage himself should know this. Great Sage! The gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens gathered in the Hall of Dharma, each harboring grief and anxiety, and repeatedly lamented and said: 'If we were to encounter a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One, we would surely go to see him.' Great Sage! However, not having encountered a Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One, we then engaged fully in the five kinds of sensual pleasures. Great Sage! We became heedless, and having acted heedlessly, gods of great majestic virtue in the most excellent realms then met their end. Great Sage! When I saw gods of great majestic virtue in the most excellent realms meeting their end, I was filled with extreme aversion, with my body hair standing on end, thinking: 'May I not swiftly meet my end in this place!'

"Great Sage! Because of this aversion and this grief, whenever I saw other śramaṇas or brahmins dwelling in secluded places, in mountain forests beneath trees, delighting in lofty cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, without people, suitable for meditative sitting, delighting in seclusion, sitting in meditation, peaceful, comfortable, and wandering happily, when I saw them, I would think they were Tathāgatas, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and I would go to pay my respects. But they did not recognize me and would ask me: 'Who are you?' I would answer them: 'Great Sage! I am Sakka, King of the Gods! Great Sage! I am Sakka, King of the Gods!' They would then ask me: 'I have heard of Sakka, and also of the Śākya clan. For what reason are you called Sakka? For what reason do you belong to the Śākya clan?' I would answer them: 'Great Sage! If anyone comes to ask me about matters, I answer them according to my ability and my capacity. Therefore I am called Sakka.' They would then say: 'If we ask Sakka about matters, Sakka will also answer us about those matters. They ask me about matters, but I do not ask them. They take refuge in me, but I do not take refuge in them.' Great Sage! From those śramaṇas and brahmins I never received any proper teaching on conduct and Dharma; how much less could I have received answers to questions like these?"

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, spoke these verses:

"Sakka went, and having gone,
Sakka now speaks thus:
In seclusion, as the mind contemplated,
Doubts and hesitations were removed.

Long have I traveled through the world,
Searching and seeking the Tathāgata;
Seeing śramaṇas and brahmins
Sitting in secluded meditation,

I thought they were Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
And went to pay respects and honor;
'How does one attain advancement?'
Thus I asked them.

Having asked, they could not know
The holy path or the path's way.
World-Honored One, now for me,
Whatever doubt may be in my mind,

Whatever is thought and contemplated,
Whatever the mind's ways,
Knowing the hidden and manifest of the heart,
O Wise One, explain them for me.

Honored is the Buddha, honored as Teacher,
Honored is the unattached Sage,
Honored is he who has cut off all fetters,
Who has himself crossed over and leads beings across.

The Awakened One has the foremost awakening,
The Tamer is the supreme tamer,
The Pacifier has the most excellent peace;
The Great Sage has himself crossed over and leads others across.

Therefore I bow to the Lord of Gods,
I prostrate before the foremost among humans;
Who has severed all thorns of craving,
I bow to the Kinsman of the Sun."

Thereupon the World-Honored One asked: "Kausika! Do you recall whether in the past you ever attained such freedom from defilement, such joy as this, namely the joy of Dharma that you have obtained from me?"

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, answered: "World-Honored One! Only the Great Sage himself should know this. Great Sage! Once in the past, the gods and the asuras were at war with each other. Great Sage! When the gods and asuras were at war, I had this thought: 'May the gods be victorious and defeat the asuras, and may the food of the gods and the food of the asuras all be consumed by the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens.' Great Sage! When the gods and asuras were at war, the gods were indeed victorious and defeated the asuras, and the food of the gods and the food of the asuras were all consumed by the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens. Great Sage! At that time there was freedom from defilement and there was joy, but it was mixed with weapons, bondage, enmity, quarreling, and jealousy, and did not lead to spiritual penetration, did not lead to awakening, and did not lead to nirvāṇa. Great Sage! Today the freedom from defilement and joy that I have attained are not mixed with weapons, bondage, enmity, quarreling, or jealousy, and they lead to penetration, lead to awakening, and also lead to nirvāṇa."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kausika! What is the cause by which you attain this freedom from defilement and joy? Is it the joy of Dharma that you have obtained from me?"

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, answered: "Great Sage! I have this thought: 'When I pass away from this life, I shall be reborn in the human world. If there is a clan that is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with immeasurable resources and possessions, with livestock and properties beyond reckoning, with estates and villages abundantly provided, whether it be a kṣatriya elder's clan, a brahmin elder's clan, a householder elder's clan, or another clan that is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with immeasurable resources and possessions, with livestock and properties beyond reckoning, with estates and villages abundantly provided. Having been born into such a clan, with my faculties complete, if there are those who gain faith in the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata, having gained faith, I shall shave off my hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with sincere faith, leave the household life to live without a home and train in the Way. I shall train in wisdom. Having trained in wisdom, if I attain wisdom, then I shall attain the ultimate wisdom, reaching the final limit. Training in wisdom, having trained in wisdom, if I attain wisdom but do not attain the ultimate wisdom, then among the gods who possess great blessed fortune, whose forms are majestic and whose radiance is brilliant, who possess extreme authority, who are peaceful and happy, who dwell long in their palaces, born in the highest realms, I shall be reborn among them.'"

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, spoke these verses:

"Abandoning the divine body,
Coming down to be born in the human world,
Not foolishly entering the womb,
But according to my heart's desire.

Having obtained a complete body,
Attaining the straight and right path,
Practicing the holy life fully,
Always delighting in living on alms food.

"Training in wisdom, having trained in wisdom, if I attain wisdom, then I shall attain the ultimate wisdom, reaching the final limit. Training in wisdom, having trained in wisdom, if I attain wisdom but do not attain the ultimate wisdom, I shall become one of the highest, most excellent gods, the gods known by name as the Akaniṣṭha gods, and be reborn among them. Great Sage! I wish to attain the state of a non-returner. Great Sage! I am now certain of having attained the fruit of stream-entry."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kausika! What is the cause by which you have attained this extremely good, extremely lofty, extremely vast and graduated distinction, and you declare yourself to have attained stream-entry?"

Then Sakka, King of the Gods, answered with this verse:

"There is no other honored one;
It is only the World-Honored One's domain.
I have attained the highest graduated distinction;
Never before has there been such a place.

Great Sage, while I sit here,
Right in this divine body,
I have further gained an increase of life.
This I have seen with my own eyes."

When this Dharma was being taught, Sakka, King of the Gods, became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas. Also, eighty thousand gods likewise became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas. Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the pure and white Dharma, cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, with no other honored one to rely upon, no longer following others, without any hesitation, having established himself in the fruit, and having attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma, he rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One! Today I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I pray the World-Honored One will accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forth, throughout my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, praised Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Pañcaśikha, you have been of great benefit to me. Why? Because of you, the Buddha awakened from concentration. Because you first caused the World-Honored One to awaken from concentration, we were afterward able to see the Buddha. Pañcaśikha! From now on I shall give you Bhaddā Suriyavaccasā, the daughter of Timbaru the Gandharva King, in marriage as your wife, and I shall also bestow upon you her father's, the Music King's, homeland, and install you as the Gandharva King."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens: "All of you, come! Whatever reverence we formerly showed to Brahmā, the King, dwelling in the Brahmā heaven, bowing three times in respectful service, all that reverence we shall now show to the World-Honored One in respectful service. Why? The World-Honored One is Brahmā. Brahmā creates and is the most honored one who gives birth to beings. Regarding beings that exist and that shall exist, all that can be known he fully knows, and all that can be seen he fully sees."

Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, whatever reverence they formerly showed to Brahmā, dwelling in the Brahmā heaven, bowing three times in respectful service, they all now showed to the World-Honored One in respectful service, bowing their heads before the Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened One. Thereupon Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, paid reverence twice more to the World-Honored One in respectful service, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and right there vanished from sight.

At that time, Brahmā, whose form was majestic and whose radiance was brilliant, as the night was turning toward dawn, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and then spoke this verse to the World-Honored One:

"For the benefit and welfare of many,
Seeing benefit and meaning, called 'God,'
The Worthy One, dwelling in the land of Magadha,
Vāsava asked about matters.

"Great Sage! When you taught this Dharma, Sakka, King of the Gods, became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas. Also, eighty thousand gods likewise became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas." Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed Brahmā: "So it is, so it is. What Brahmā has said:

"'For the benefit and welfare of many,
Seeing benefit and meaning, called "God,"
The Worthy One, dwelling in the land of Magadha,
Vāsava asked about matters.'

"Brahmā! When I taught the Dharma, Sakka, King of the Gods, became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas. Also, eighty thousand gods likewise became free from dust and stain, and the Dharma-eye arose regarding all dharmas."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Sakka, King of the Gods, together with the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens, Pañcaśikha, Son of the Gandharvas, and the Great Brahmā, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

End of the Eighteenth Sūtra: Sakka's Questions

## (135) Sūtra on Śāṇakavāsin (善生), Nineteenth of the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Forest Abounding in Frogs.

At that time, Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, when his father was on his deathbed, because of the six directions, left instructions for his son, teaching and admonishing him well, saying: "Siṅgālaka! After I die, you should join your palms and bow to the six directions, saying: 'If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me.'"

Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, having heard his father's instructions, replied to his father: "Yes, I shall follow your honored command."

Thereupon Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, after his father's death, at dawn bathed himself, put on new silk garments, and with fresh kuśa grass in his hand, went to the water's edge, joined his palms, and bowed to the six directions, saying: "If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, at dawn dressed in his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for alms. As the World-Honored One was entering Rājagṛha to beg for alms, he saw from afar Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, who at dawn had bathed himself, put on new silk garments, and with fresh kuśa grass in his hand, had gone to the water's edge, joined his palms, and was bowing to the six directions, saying: "If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me."

The World-Honored One, having seen this, went to where Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, was and asked: "Householder's son! From what śramaṇa or brahmin did you receive instruction, teaching you to revere, make offerings, and honor, bathing at dawn, putting on new silk garments, with fresh kuśa grass in hand, going to the water's edge, joining your palms, and bowing to the six directions, saying: 'If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me'?"

Siṅgālaka, the householder's son, answered: "World-Honored One! I did not receive instruction from any other śramaṇa or brahmin. World-Honored One! When my father was on his deathbed, because of the six directions, he left instructions for me, teaching and admonishing me well, saying: 'Siṅgālaka! After I die, you should join your palms and bow to the six directions, saying: "If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me."' World-Honored One! I received my father's dying instructions, and out of reverence, making offerings, and honor, I bathed at dawn, put on new silk garments, and with fresh kuśa grass in hand, went to the water's edge, joined my palms, and bowed to the six directions, saying: 'If there are any beings in the eastern direction, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me. Likewise for the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the lower direction, and the upper direction. If there are any beings there, I shall completely revere, make offerings to, and honor them. Having completely revered, made offerings to, and honored them, they too shall revere, make offerings to, and honor me.'"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, said: "Householder's son! I teach that there are six directions; I do not say there are none. Householder's son! If a person properly distinguishes the six directions, abandons the evil, unwholesome deeds and defilements of the four directions, that person in this present life is worthy of respect and regard, and when his body decays and his life ends, he will surely reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavens. Householder's son! Beings have four kinds of deeds and four kinds of defilements. What are the four? Householder's son! Killing living beings is a deed-seed and defilement-seed of beings. Taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech are deed-seeds and defilement-seeds of beings." Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"Killing, taking what is not given,
Sexual misconduct, violating others' spouses,
Speaking what is not true:
The wise do not praise these.

"Householder's son! Due to four things, a person obtains much wrongdoing. What are the four? Acting from desire, acting from anger, acting from fear, and acting from delusion." Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"Desire, anger, fear, and delusion:
Whoever does evil and unlawful deeds,
That person's fame and reputation will surely fade,
Like the moon waning toward its end.

"Householder's son! Due to four things, a person obtains much merit. What are the four? Not acting from desire, not acting from anger, not acting from fear, and not acting from delusion." Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"Cutting off desire, free from anger and fear,
Free from delusion, acting in accord with the Dharma:
That person's fame and reputation spread everywhere,
Like the moon gradually waxing to fullness.

"Householder's son! One who seeks wealth should know there are six wrong paths. What are the six? First, seeking wealth through various kinds of gambling is a wrong path. Second, seeking wealth by going out at improper times is a wrong path. Third, seeking wealth through drinking and heedlessness is a wrong path. Fourth, seeking wealth by associating with bad companions is a wrong path. Fifth, seeking wealth by constantly delighting in entertainment and music is a wrong path. Sixth, seeking wealth by being lazy is a wrong path.

"Householder's son! If a person engages in various kinds of gambling, one should know there are six calamities. What are the six? First, when one loses, one generates enmity. Second, when one loses, one generates shame. Third, when one loses, one cannot sleep peacefully. Fourth, it causes one's enemies to rejoice. Fifth, it causes one's kinsmen to grieve. Sixth, what one says in the assembly, people do not trust. Householder's son! A person who gambles does not manage his affairs. If affairs are not managed, then undertakings are not accomplished. Wealth not yet obtained cannot be obtained, and wealth already possessed will gradually be consumed.

"Householder's son! If a person goes out at improper times, one should know there are six calamities. What are the six? First, one does not protect oneself. Second, one does not protect one's wealth. Third, one does not protect one's wife and children. Fourth, one becomes suspected by others. Fifth, many sufferings and troubles arise. Sixth, one is slandered by others. Householder's son! A person who goes out at improper times does not manage his affairs. If affairs are not managed, then undertakings are not accomplished. Wealth not yet obtained cannot be obtained, and wealth already possessed will gradually be consumed.

## (136) Sūtra on Merchants Seeking Wealth, the Twentieth in the Great Division

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Long ago in the past, the merchants of Jambudvīpa all gathered together in the merchants' hall and had this thought: 'We should outfit ships and sail into the great ocean to obtain treasures and wealth to supply our households.' They further thought: 'Sirs, when entering the ocean, one cannot know in advance whether it will be safe or unsafe. We should each prepare implements for crossing the sea, namely goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts.' Afterward, they each prepared implements for crossing the sea: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, and then entered the great ocean. While they were at sea, the makara fish-king destroyed their ship. Those merchants each clung to their own sea-crossing implements: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, floating off in various directions.

"At that time, a great east wind suddenly arose over the sea and blew the merchants to the western shore of the ocean. There they encountered a group of women, exceedingly beautiful and lovely, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament. Those women, seeing them, spoke thus: 'Welcome, sirs! Come quickly, sirs! This place is supremely delightful and wonderful, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. There is much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems. All of this we give to you, sirs. You should enjoy yourselves with us. Do not let the merchants of Jambudvīpa go south, not even in their dreams.' Those merchants all enjoyed themselves together with the women. Because of their union with the women, sons and daughters were born to them. Later, one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa went to a quiet place by himself and had this thought: 'For what reason do these women forbid us from going south? I should watch the woman I live with, and when I know she is asleep, I will rise gently and secretly go south.'

"That one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa then watched the woman he lived with, and when he knew she was asleep, he rose gently and secretly went south. After that one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa had gone south, he heard from afar a great sound of loud calling and crying, the voices of many people weeping and lamenting, calling for their fathers and mothers, calling for their wives, children, and all their beloved relatives and friends: 'Beautiful Jambudvīpa, safe and happy, we shall never see you again!' When that merchant heard this, he was extremely frightened, his hair standing on end, thinking: 'Let no human or nonhuman being harm me!' Thereupon, that one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa controlled his fear and continued south. After he had gone further south, he suddenly saw to the east a great iron city. Having seen it, he looked all around but could not find any gate, not even an opening large enough for a kitten to pass through.

"That one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa saw to the north of the iron city a great thicket of trees. He went to that great thicket and climbed up gently. Having climbed up, he asked the great crowd of people: 'Sirs! Why are you weeping and lamenting, calling for your fathers and mothers, calling for your wives, children, and all your beloved relatives and friends? Will you never again see beautiful Jambudvīpa, safe and happy?' Then the great crowd of people answered him: 'Sir! We are merchants of Jambudvīpa. We all gathered together in the merchants' hall and had this thought: "We should outfit ships and sail into the great ocean to obtain treasures and wealth to supply our households." Sir, we further thought: "Sirs, when entering the ocean, one cannot know in advance whether it will be safe or unsafe. We should each prepare implements for crossing the sea, namely goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts." Sir, afterward we each prepared implements for crossing the sea: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, and then entered the great ocean. Sir, while we were at sea, the makara fish-king destroyed our ship. Sir, we merchants each clung to our own sea-crossing implements: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, floating off in various directions. At that time, a great east wind suddenly arose over the sea and blew us merchants to the western shore of the ocean. There we encountered a group of women, exceedingly beautiful and lovely, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament. Those women, seeing us, spoke thus: "Welcome, sirs! Come quickly, sirs! This place is supremely delightful and wonderful, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. There is much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems. All of this we give to you, sirs. You should enjoy yourselves with us. Do not let the merchants of Jambudvīpa go south, not even in their dreams."

"'Sir, we enjoyed ourselves together with those women. Because of our union with the women, sons and daughters were born to us. Sir, when those women did not hear that other merchants of Jambudvīpa were at sea and had their ships destroyed by the makara fish-king, they would enjoy themselves with us. Sir, but when those women heard that merchants of Jambudvīpa were at sea and had their ships destroyed by the makara fish-king, they would devour us, and we were severely oppressed. When devouring people, if there remained any hair or nails or teeth, those women would consume all of it. When devouring people, if any blood dripped to the ground, those women would dig into the earth four inches deep with their fingernails and consume it. Sir, you should know that we merchants of Jambudvīpa originally numbered five hundred. Among us, two hundred and fifty have already been devoured, and the remaining two hundred and fifty are now all inside this great iron city. Sir, do not believe those women's words. They are not real humans; they are rākṣasī demons!'

"Thereupon, that one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa climbed gently down from the great thicket of trees and returned along the path to the place where the women lived, to where he had previously resided with his woman. He knew that his woman was still asleep and had not yet awakened. That very night, the one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa quickly went to where the other merchants of Jambudvīpa were and spoke thus: 'Come together with me! We should go to a quiet place. Each of you go alone; do not bring your children. We shall gather there to discuss something in secret.' The merchants of Jambudvīpa went together to a quiet place, each going alone without bringing their children.

"Thereupon, the one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa said: 'Fellow merchants! I went to a quiet place alone and had this thought: "For what reason do these women forbid us from going south? I should watch the woman I live with, and when I know she is asleep, I will rise gently and secretly go south." So I watched the woman I lived with, and when I knew she was asleep, I rose gently and secretly went south. After going south, I heard from afar a great sound of loud calling and crying, the voices of many people weeping and lamenting, calling for their fathers and mothers, calling for their wives, children, and all their beloved relatives and friends: "Beautiful Jambudvīpa, safe and happy, we shall never see you again." When I heard this, I was extremely frightened, my hair standing on end, thinking: "Let no human or nonhuman being harm me!" So I controlled my fear and continued south. After going further south, I suddenly saw to the east a great iron city. Having seen it, I looked all around but could not find any gate, not even an opening large enough for a kitten to pass through.

"'I also saw to the north of the great iron city a great thicket of trees. I went to that great thicket and climbed up gently. Having climbed up, I asked the great crowd of people: "Sirs! Why are you weeping and lamenting, calling for your fathers and mothers, calling for your wives, children, and all your beloved relatives and friends? Will you never again see beautiful Jambudvīpa, safe and happy?" The great crowd of people answered me: "Sir! We are merchants of Jambudvīpa. We all gathered together in the merchants' hall and had this thought: 'We should outfit ships and sail into the great ocean to obtain treasures and wealth to supply our households.' Sir, we further thought: 'Sirs, when entering the ocean, one cannot know in advance whether it will be safe or unsafe. We should each prepare implements for crossing the sea, namely goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts.' Sir, afterward we each prepared implements for crossing the sea: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, and then entered the great ocean. Sir, while we were at sea, the makara fish-king destroyed our ship. Sir, we merchants each clung to our own sea-crossing implements: goatskin floats, large gourds, and log rafts, floating off in various directions. At that time, a great east wind suddenly arose over the sea and blew us merchants to the western shore of the ocean. There we encountered a group of women, exceedingly beautiful and lovely, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament. Those women, seeing us, spoke thus: 'Welcome, sirs! Come quickly, sirs! This place is supremely delightful and wonderful, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. There is much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems. All of this we give to you, sirs. You should enjoy yourselves with us. Do not let the merchants of Jambudvīpa go south, not even in their dreams.' Sir, we enjoyed ourselves together with those women. Because of our union with the women, sons and daughters were born to us. Sir, when those women did not hear that other merchants of Jambudvīpa were at sea and had their ships destroyed by the makara fish-king, they would enjoy themselves with us. Sir, but when those women heard that other merchants of Jambudvīpa were at sea and had their ships destroyed by the makara fish-king, they would devour us, and we were severely oppressed. When devouring people, if there remained any hair or nails or teeth, those women would consume all of it. When devouring people, if any blood dripped to the ground, those women would dig into the earth four inches deep with their fingernails and consume it. Sir, you should know that we merchants of Jambudvīpa originally numbered five hundred. Among us, two hundred and fifty have already been devoured, and the remaining two hundred and fifty are now all inside this great iron city. Sir, do not believe those women's words. They are not real humans; they are rākṣasī demons!"'

"Thereupon, the merchants of Jambudvīpa asked that one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa: 'Sir! Did you not ask those people: "Sirs, is there some means by which we and you may safely cross over to Jambudvīpa?"' The one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa replied: 'Sirs, at that time I neglected to ask that question.' Then the merchants of Jambudvīpa said: 'Sir! Go back to the place where you live with the woman, watch for when she is asleep, rise gently, secretly go south again, go to those people, and ask: "Sirs, is there some means by which we and you may safely cross over to Jambudvīpa?"' Thereupon, the one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa silently accepted on behalf of the merchants.

"At that time, the one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa returned to the place where his woman lived, watched for when she was asleep, rose gently, and secretly went south. He went again to those people and asked: 'Sirs, is there some means by which we and you may safely cross over to Jambudvīpa?' The crowd of people answered: 'Sir, there is no other means by which we can safely cross over to Jambudvīpa. Sir, we had this thought: "We should break through and dig through this wall together and return to our homeland." But as soon as we had that thought, this wall grew to twice its usual height. Sir, this is why there is no means for us to safely cross over to Jambudvīpa. Sir, there is another means by which you may safely cross over to Jambudvīpa, but for us there is no means at all. Sirs, we heard a voice from the sky proclaiming: "The merchants of Jambudvīpa are foolish, irresolute, and lack good understanding. Why? Because they cannot, on the fifteenth day, at the time of the Prātimokṣa recitation, go south. There is a Valāhaka Horse-King who feeds on naturally grown rice, is peaceful and happy, with all his faculties fulfilled. He calls out three times: 'Who wishes to cross to the other shore? Who wishes me to liberate them? Who wishes me to carry them safely from here to Jambudvīpa?' You should go together to the Valāhaka Horse-King and say: 'We wish to cross to the other shore. Please liberate us. Please carry us safely from here to Jambudvīpa.'"' Sir, this is the means by which you may safely cross over to Jambudvīpa. Merchants, come! You should go to the Valāhaka Horse-King and say: "We wish to cross to the other shore. Please liberate us. Please carry us safely from here to Jambudvīpa."'

"Thereupon, the one wise merchant of Jambudvīpa said: 'Fellow merchants! Now is the time to go to the Valāhaka Horse-King and say: "We wish to cross to the other shore. Please liberate us. Please carry us safely from here to Jambudvīpa." Fellow merchants, follow the devas' instructions. Fellow merchants, on the fifteenth day, at the time of the Prātimokṣa recitation, the Valāhaka Horse-King, having fed on naturally grown rice, peaceful and happy, with all his faculties fulfilled, will call out three times: "Who wishes to cross to the other shore? Who wishes me to liberate them? Who wishes me to carry them safely from here to Jambudvīpa?" At that time we shall go to him and say: "We wish to cross to the other shore. Please liberate us. Please carry us safely from here to Jambudvīpa."'

"Thereupon, on the fifteenth day, at the time of the Prātimokṣa recitation, the Valāhaka Horse-King, having fed on naturally grown rice, peaceful and happy, with all his faculties fulfilled, called out three times: 'Who wishes to cross to the other shore? I shall liberate them. I shall carry them safely from here to Jambudvīpa.' The merchants of Jambudvīpa, hearing this, immediately went to the Valāhaka Horse-King and said: 'We wish to cross to the other shore. Please liberate us. Please carry us safely from here to Jambudvīpa.' Then the Valāhaka Horse-King said: 'Merchants! Those women will certainly come carrying their children and speak thus: "Sirs! Welcome, please come back! This place is supremely delightful and wonderful, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. There is much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems. All of this we give to you, sirs. You should enjoy yourselves with us. If you do not care for us, then at least have pity on your children." If any merchant has this thought: "I have sons and daughters. I have a supremely delightful and wonderful place, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. I have much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems," then even though he rides squarely upon the middle of my back, he will surely topple upside down and fall into the water. He will then be devoured by those women and severely oppressed. When they devour people, if there remain any hair or nails or teeth, those women will consume all of it. Furthermore, when devouring people, if any blood drips to the ground, those women will dig into the earth four inches deep with their fingernails and consume it. If a merchant does not have this thought: "I have sons and daughters. I have a supremely delightful and wonderful place, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. I have much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems," then even if he holds onto only a single hair of my body, he will surely cross safely to Jambudvīpa.'"

Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Those women came carrying their children and spoke thus: 'Sirs! Welcome, please come back! This place is supremely delightful and wonderful, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. There is much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems. All of this we give to you, sirs. You should enjoy yourselves with us.' If any merchant had this thought: 'I have sons and daughters. I have a supremely delightful and wonderful place, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests. I have much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems,' then even though he rode squarely on the Valāhaka Horse-King's spine upon the middle of his back, he would surely topple upside down and fall into the water. He would then be devoured by those women and severely oppressed. When they devoured people, if there remained any hair or nails or teeth, those women would consume all of it. Furthermore, when devouring those people, if any blood dripped to the ground, those women would dig into the earth four inches deep with their fingernails and consume it. If a merchant did not have this thought: 'I have sons and daughters. I have a supremely delightful and wonderful place, with parks, pools for bathing, sleeping quarters, and dense forests.
