I have much wealth: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch shells, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoiseshell, red stone, and whirling gems,' then even if he held onto only a single hair of the Valāhaka Horse-King, he would surely cross safely to Jambudvīpa.

"Bhikṣus! I have spoken this parable so that you may understand the meaning. This is the meaning I declare. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans.

"If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'The eye is myself, I possess the eye; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are myself, I possess the mind,' that bhikṣu will certainly be destroyed, just as the merchants were devoured by the rākṣasīs. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'The eye is not myself, I do not possess the eye; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not myself, I do not possess the mind,' that bhikṣu will depart safely, just as the merchants rode the Valāhaka Horse-King and crossed safely. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans.

"If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'Form is myself, I possess form; sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas are myself, I possess dharmas,' that bhikṣu will certainly be destroyed, just as the merchants were devoured by the rākṣasīs. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'Form is not myself, I do not possess form; sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas are not myself, I do not possess dharmas,' that bhikṣu will depart safely, just as the merchants rode the Valāhaka Horse-King and crossed safely. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans.

"If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'The aggregate of form is myself, I possess the aggregate of form; the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are myself, I possess the aggregate of consciousness,' that bhikṣu will certainly be destroyed, just as the merchants were devoured by the rākṣasīs. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'The aggregate of form is not myself, I do not possess the aggregate of form; the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are not myself, I do not possess the aggregate of consciousness,' that bhikṣu will depart safely, just as the merchants rode the Valāhaka Horse-King and crossed safely. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans.

"If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'Earth is myself, I possess earth; water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are myself, I possess consciousness,' that bhikṣu will certainly be destroyed, just as the merchants were devoured by the rākṣasīs. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed, extremely vast, well guarded with no gaps, like a bridge, a raft, a floating device, pervading and spreading everywhere, reaching to devas and humans. If a bhikṣu has this thought: 'Earth is not myself, I do not possess earth; water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are not myself, I do not possess consciousness,' that bhikṣu will depart safely, just as the merchants rode the Valāhaka Horse-King and crossed safely."

Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse:

"If one has no faith in
The true Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha,
That person will certainly be destroyed,
As if devoured by rākṣasīs.
If one has faith in
The true Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha,
That person will cross safely,
As if riding the Valāhaka Horse-King."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Merchants Seeking Wealth, the Twentieth.

---

## (137) Sūtra on the World, the Twenty-first in the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The Tathāgata has himself realized the world and also teaches others about it; the Tathāgata knows the world. The Tathāgata has himself realized the arising of the world and also teaches others about it; the Tathāgata has cut off the arising of the world. The Tathāgata has himself realized the cessation of the world and also teaches others about it; the Tathāgata has realized the cessation of the world. The Tathāgata has himself realized the path leading to the cessation of the world and also teaches others about it; the Tathāgata cultivates the path leading to the cessation of the world.

"Whatever exists in its entirety, all of that the Tathāgata knows, sees, realizes, and attains. Why is this? From the night when the Tathāgata awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, until this very day and night, when in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder he will attain final cessation, during the entire time in between, whatever the Tathāgata has spoken with his mouth, whatever he has responded to, all of it is true, not false, not deviating from suchness, and not inverted. It is true, authentic, and real. If one speaks of a lion's roar, one should speak thus of the Tathāgata. Why is this? The Tathāgata, when teaching among assemblies, roars the lion's roar. In all the world, among devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, from humans to devas: the Tathāgata is Brahmā-become; the Tathāgata has arrived at coolness; he is free from affliction and free from fever; he is truly existent, not falsely existent."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"Knowing the entire world,
Transcending the entire world,
Teaching about the entire world,
Knowing the entire world as it truly is.
He is the supreme and heroic one,
Who can release all bonds,
Who has exhausted all karmic actions,
And is completely liberated from birth and death.
He is deva and also human;
If any being takes refuge in the Buddha,
Bowing in homage to the Tathāgata,
Vast and deep like the great ocean.
Having known, they also cultivate reverence;
The devas, gandharvas, and kinnaras
Also bow in homage,
Following him who has transcended death.
Bowing in homage to the wise one,
Taking refuge in the highest among humans,
Free from sorrow, free from defilement, at peace,
Unobstructed in all liberations.
Therefore one should delight in meditation,
Dwelling in seclusion and deep concentration.
One should make oneself a lamp;
Without a self, one will surely lose the opportunity.
When the opportunity is lost, there is grief,
Which means falling into the hells."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the World, the Twenty-first.

---

## (138) Sūtra on Merit, the Twenty-second in the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Do not fear merit; it is pleasant and agreeable to the mind. Why is this? Merit is a term for happiness. Fear what is not meritorious; it is unpleasant and disagreeable to the mind. Why is this? Non-merit is a term for suffering. For what reason? I recall that in the distant past, I performed meritorious deeds for a long time and received their results for a long time, pleasant and agreeable to the mind. In the past, for seven years I practiced loving-kindness. For seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction, I did not return to this world. When the world was destroyed, I was born in the Ābhāsvara heaven. When the world was re-established, I descended and was born in an empty Brahmā palace. In that Brahmā realm, I became a Great Brahmā. One thousand times in other places I became a Lord of the Freely-Creating devas. Thirty-six times I became Śakra, the lord of devas. And countless times I became a noble wheel-turning king.

"Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand great elephants, fitted with fine harnesses, adorned with many jewels, covered with white pearl necklaces, with the elephant Uposatha as the foremost. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand horses, fitted with fine harnesses, adorned with many jewels, covered with nets of gold and silver, with the Valāhaka Horse-King as the foremost. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with four kinds of decorations, beautifully appointed, covered with skins of lions, tigers, and leopards woven in variegated colors, with various decorations, the swiftest named the Chariot of Delightful Sound as the foremost. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand great cities, extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people, with the royal city of Kuśāvatī as the foremost. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand pavilions, pavilions of four kinds of jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, with the Hall of the True Dharma as the foremost.

"Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand thrones, thrones of four kinds of jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, covered with woolen carpets and rugs, overlaid with brocade, silk gauze, and fine cloth, with body-fitting coverlets and pillows at both ends, made of Kaliṅga and Pāvāra fabrics and Pacasītarana cloth. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand pairs of garments: the finest silk garments, brocade garments, cotton garments, and Kaliṅga-Pāvāra garments. Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand women, with bodies radiant and luminous, of pure and bright complexion, their beauty surpassing humans yet slightly less than devas, graceful and lovely, a delight to behold, fully adorned with various jeweled ornaments, all of the kṣatriya caste, with innumerable others from other families.

"Bhikṣus! When I was a noble wheel-turning king, I had eighty-four thousand kinds of food, constantly provided day and night, prepared for me, wishing me to eat. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand kinds of food, there was one kind of food, supremely delicious, pure and clean, with innumerable flavors, which I always ate. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand women, there was one kṣatriya woman, the most graceful and beautiful, who always attended me. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand pairs of garments, there was one pair, whether of the finest silk, brocade, cotton, or Kaliṅga-Pāvāra fabric, which I always wore. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand thrones, there was one throne, either of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal, covered with woolen carpets and rugs, overlaid with brocade, silk gauze, and fine cloth, with body-fitting coverlets and pillows at both ends, made of Kaliṅga-Pāvāra and Pacasītarana cloth, upon which I always reclined.

"Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand pavilions, there was one pavilion, either of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal, named the Hall of the True Dharma, where I always dwelt. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand great cities, there was one city, extremely wealthy and prosperous, with many people, named Kuśāvatī, where I always resided. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was one chariot, beautifully appointed, covered with skins of lions, tigers, and leopards woven in variegated colors, with various decorations, the swiftest named the Chariot of Delightful Sound, which I always rode when visiting parks and gardens. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was one horse, with a body of deep blue color and a head shaped like a crow's, named the Valāhaka Horse-King, which I always rode when visiting parks and gardens. Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand great elephants, there was one elephant, entirely white, with all seven limbs perfectly proportioned, named the Uposatha Elephant-King, which I always mounted when visiting parks and gardens.

"Bhikṣus! I had this thought: 'What action has borne this fruit? What action has brought this reward, that today I have such great miraculous power, such great majesty, such great blessings, and such great supernatural authority?' Bhikṣus! I further had this thought: 'It is the fruit of three actions, the reward of three actions, that today I have such great miraculous power, such great majesty, such great blessings, and such great supernatural authority. The first is generosity. The second is self-discipline. The third is self-restraint.'"

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"Observe this reward of merit,
Wonderfully good and abundantly beneficial.
Bhikṣus, in the past I
Cultivated the mind of loving-kindness for seven years.
For seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction
I did not return to this world.
When the world was destroyed,
I was born in the Ābhāsvara heaven.
When the world was being re-established,
I was born in the Brahmā realm.
In the Brahmā realm I was Great Brahmā;
A thousand times a Lord of Freely-Creating devas.
Thirty-six times I was Śakra;
Countless hundreds of times a wheel-turning king.
As a noble wheel-turning king,
The most honored among people,
Ruling the world by Dharma, not by sword or rod,
Governing the entire world.
By Dharma, without wrongful punishment,
Rightly instructing in peace and happiness,
By Dharma, transmitting from one to another
Throughout the entire great earth.
Greatly wealthy with much treasure,
Born into such a clan,
With grain and wealth fully abundant,
Accomplished in the seven jeweled treasures.
Because of this great merit and blessing,
In each life I attained sovereignty.
The Buddhas who govern the world,
What those Buddhas have taught:
Knowing this most wondrous and extraordinary,
Seeing the spiritual powers are not few.
Who, knowing this, would not believe?
Such a one is born into darkness.
Therefore one should work for one's own benefit;
If one desires to seek great merit and blessing,
One should revere the Dharma,
And always be mindful of the Buddha's Dharma and Vinaya."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Merit, the Twenty-second.

---

## (139) Sūtra on the Path to the Charnel Ground, the Twenty-third in the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "A young bhikṣu who has just completed his training in morality should frequently go to the charnel ground to contemplate the signs: the sign of bones, the sign of blueness, the sign of decomposition, the sign of being eaten, and the sign of a skeleton. Having well received and well retained these signs, he should return to his dwelling place, wash his hands and feet, spread out his sitting cloth, sit cross-legged upon his seat, and then contemplate these signs: the sign of bones, the sign of blueness, the sign of decomposition, the sign of being eaten, and the sign of a skeleton. Why is this? If a bhikṣu cultivates these signs, he will quickly remove the afflictions of desire and anger from his mind."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"If a young bhikṣu
Has awakened but not yet attained the higher mind,
He should go to the charnel ground
In order to remove his sensual desires.
With no anger or contention in the mind,
With compassion for all beings,
Pervading all directions,
He goes to observe the various bodies.
He should contemplate the sign of blueness,
And the rotting and decaying,
Observe what is eaten by birds and insects,
And bones linked joint to joint.
Having cultivated such signs,
He returns to his original dwelling,
Washes his hands and feet,
Spreads his mat, and sits upright on his seat.
He should contemplate as it truly is
The internal body and the external body,
Filled with excrement and urine,
Heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, and so forth.
When wishing to go on alms round
And entering a village or town,
Like one encased in armor,
He should always keep right mindfulness at the fore.
If he sees a pleasing form,
Pure and associated with desire,
Having seen it, he contemplates it as it truly is,
Rightly mindful of the Buddha's Dharma and Vinaya.
In this there are no bones or sinews,
No flesh and no blood,
No kidneys, heart, liver, or lungs,
No mucus, saliva, or brain.
All earth elements are empty,
And likewise the water elements;
Empty are all fire elements,
And the wind elements are also empty.
Whatever feelings there are
That are pure and associated with desire,
All of them are brought to cessation,
As wisdom contemplates them.
Practicing thus with diligence,
Always mindful of the perception of impurity,
He permanently cuts off lust, anger, and delusion,
And removes all ignorance.
He gives rise to pure illumination,
And the bhikṣu reaches the end of suffering."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Path to the Charnel Ground, the Twenty-third.

---

## (140) Sūtra on Reaching the Limit, the Twenty-fourth in the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Among livelihoods, the lowest and most extreme is begging for food. It is a great curse in the world to be called a shaven-headed one who walks about carrying a bowl in hand. Yet sons of good families accept this for the sake of a higher purpose. Why is this? Because of revulsion toward birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and vexation, so as to perhaps reach the limit of this entire great mass of suffering. Did you not go forth from the household life to train in the path with such a mind?"

The bhikṣus replied: "Indeed so."

The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus: "That foolish person, having gone forth with such a mind to train in the path, yet practices sensual thoughts, is deeply stained by attachment, is muddled and entangled in mind, is resentful and faithless, is lazy and loses right mindfulness, lacks right concentration, has perverted wisdom and a deranged mind, with disordered faculties, keeps his moral discipline extremely lax, does not cultivate the śramaṇa practice, and does not develop it further. It is like trying to wash soot with ink, trying to remove blood with blood, trying to clean filth with filth, trying to purify turbidity with turbidity, or trying to clean a latrine with a latrine; one only increases the foulness. Going from darkness into darkness, from obscurity into obscurity. I say that the practice of the śramaṇa discipline by that foolish person is also like this: that person who practices sensual thoughts, is deeply stained by attachment, is muddled and entangled in mind, is resentful and faithless, is lazy and loses right mindfulness, lacks right concentration, has perverted wisdom and a deranged mind, with disordered faculties, keeps his moral discipline extremely lax, does not cultivate the śramaṇa practice, and does not develop it further. It is like a cremation log at an uninhabited place where corpses are burned; that charred remnant is of no use to the uninhabited place, nor is it of any use to a village. I say that the practice of the śramaṇa discipline by that foolish person is also like this: that person who practices sensual thoughts, is deeply stained by attachment, is muddled and entangled in mind, is resentful and faithless, is lazy and loses right mindfulness, lacks right concentration, has perverted wisdom and a deranged mind, with disordered faculties, keeps his moral discipline extremely lax, does not cultivate the śramaṇa practice, and does not develop it further."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"The fool has lost sensual pleasures,
And has also lost the purpose of the śramaṇa life.
He has lost both sides,
Like a burnt-out cremation log.
Just as in an uninhabited place,
A burnt-out cremation log from a corpse
Is of no use to the wilderness or the village,
So too is one attached to desires:
Like a burnt-out cremation log,
He has lost both sides."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Reaching the Limit, the Twenty-fourth.

---

## (141) Sūtra on Similes, the Twenty-fifth in the Great Division of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there are innumerable wholesome dharmas to be attained, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their cause, are born from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost. Heedfulness is the very first among all wholesome dharmas. Just as in farming, all such work depends on the ground, relies on the ground, and is established on the ground, and thereby farming can be done, so too, if there are innumerable wholesome dharmas to be attained, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their cause, are born from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost. Heedfulness is the very first among all wholesome dharmas. Just as seed-villages and spirit-villages, and all grains and medicinal plants grow and are nourished, all of them depend on the ground, rely on the ground, and are established on the ground, and thereby they grow and are nourished;

"So too, if there are innumerable wholesome dharmas to be attained, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their cause, are born from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost. Heedfulness is the very first among all wholesome dharmas. Just as among all root fragrances, aloeswood is the foremost. Just as among all tree fragrances, red sandalwood is the foremost. Just as among all water flowers, the blue lotus is the foremost. Just as among all land flowers, the sumanā flower is the foremost. Just as among all animal tracks, all of them fit within the elephant's track, and the elephant's track contains them all; the elephant's track is the very first, because it is the widest. So too, if there are innumerable wholesome dharmas to be attained, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their cause, are born from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost. Heedfulness is the very first among all wholesome dharmas. Just as among all beasts, the lion king is the very first. Just as in battle formation when engaging in combat, the battle oath alone is the foremost. Just as the rafters of a pavilion all depend on and are supported by the ridgepole; the ridgepole supports them all, and the ridgepole is the very first, because it holds them all together.

"So too, if there are innumerable wholesome dharmas to be attained, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their cause, are born from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost. Heedfulness is the very first among all wholesome dharmas. Just as among all mountains, Mount Sumeru is the foremost. Just as among all springs and great bodies of water, the great ocean is the foremost. Just as among all great-bodied beings, the Asura king is the foremost. Just as among all those who keep watch, the King of Māras is the foremost. Just as among all who pursue desires, the wheel-turning king is the foremost. Just as among all lesser kings, the wheel-turning king is the foremost. Just as among the stars and constellations in the sky, the moon's palace is the foremost. Just as among all colored garments, white silk is the foremost. Just as among all radiances, the radiance of wisdom is the foremost. Just as among all assemblies, the assembly of the Tathāgata's disciples is the foremost. Just as among all dharmas, conditioned and unconditioned, the exhaustion of craving, the absence of desire, complete cessation, and nirvāṇa are the foremost. Just as among all beings, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed, with form or without form, with perception or without perception, including neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the Tathāgata is the very first among them, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime. Just as from the cow comes milk, from milk comes curds, from curds comes fresh butter, from fresh butter comes clarified butter, and from clarified butter comes the essence of butter, and the essence of butter is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime; so too, among all beings, whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed, with form or without form, with perception or without perception, including neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the Tathāgata is the very first among them, the greatest, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime."

Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"If one seeks wealth and possessions,
Exceedingly fine and ever-increasing,
Praise heedfulness.
In all matters, the wise proclaim it so.
One who is heedful
Will surely obtain both kinds of benefit:
What can be gained in this very world,
And what can also be gained in the next.
The heroic one who contemplates all meanings,
The wise one, will surely attain liberation."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Similes, the Twenty-fifth.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Collection)
## Fascicle 35

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva during the Eastern Jin dynasty*

---

### (145) The Sūtra on Gaveṣin

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling among the Bhaggas, at the Deer Park of Bhesakaḷā Grove in the Crocodile Mountain.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from sitting meditation, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew and sat to one side. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Do you know Gaveṣin, the lay follower?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Yes, I know him, World-Honored One."

The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the past, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, practiced the holy life in the time of the Buddha Kassapa. Gaveṣin, the lay follower, was the leader of five hundred lay followers. Gaveṣin, the lay follower, did not keep the precepts, and the five hundred lay followers also did not keep the precepts.

"At that time, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, thought: 'I am the leader of five hundred lay followers. I do not keep the precepts, and the five hundred lay followers also do not keep the precepts. In this way, we are all the same, with no distinction between us. I should now seek what is superior and excellent.'

"Then Gaveṣin, the lay follower, went to the five hundred lay followers and said: 'You should know, from today onward I will keep the precepts. You may address me as one who keeps the precepts.'

"At that time, the five hundred lay followers thought: 'Gaveṣin, the lay follower, is our leader. He now keeps the precepts. Why should we not do likewise?' Then the five hundred lay followers went to Gaveṣin, the lay follower, and said: 'We too, from today onward, will keep the precepts. You may address us as those who keep the precepts.'

"At that time, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, thought: 'I am the leader of five hundred lay followers. I keep the precepts, and the five hundred lay followers also keep the precepts. In this way, we are all the same, with no distinction between us. I should now seek what is superior and excellent.'

"Then Gaveṣin, the lay follower, went to the five hundred lay followers and said: 'You should know, from today onward I will practice the celibate life, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct. You may address me as one who practices celibacy.'

"At that time, the five hundred lay followers thought: 'Gaveṣin, the lay follower, is our leader. He now practices celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct. Why should we not do likewise?' Then the five hundred lay followers went to Gaveṣin, the lay follower, and said: 'We too, from today onward, will practice celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct. You may address us as those who practice celibacy.'

"At that time, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, thought: 'I am the leader of five hundred lay followers. I keep the precepts, and the five hundred lay followers also keep the precepts. I practice celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct, and the five hundred lay followers also practice celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct. In this way, we are all the same, with no distinction between us. I should now seek what is superior and excellent.'

"Then Gaveṣin, the lay follower, went to the five hundred lay followers and said: 'You should know, from today onward I will eat one meal a day, not eating at night, and will not eat at improper times. You may address me as one who eats one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times.'

"At that time, the five hundred lay followers thought: 'Gaveṣin, the lay follower, is our leader. He now eats one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times. Why should we not do likewise?' Then the five hundred lay followers went to Gaveṣin, the lay follower, and said: 'We too, from today onward, will eat one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times. You may address us as those who eat one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times.'

"At that time, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, thought: 'I am the leader of five hundred lay followers. I keep the precepts, and the five hundred lay followers also keep the precepts. I practice celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct, and the five hundred lay followers also practice celibacy, keeping away from the impure act, renouncing sexual conduct. I eat one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times, and the five hundred lay followers also eat one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times. In this way, we are all the same, with no distinction between us. I should now seek what is superior and excellent.'

"Then Gaveṣin, the lay follower, went to the five hundred lay followers and said: 'You should know, from today onward I will leave the household life, shave my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leave home to practice the Way.'

"At that time, the five hundred lay followers thought: 'Gaveṣin, the lay follower, is our leader. He now wishes to leave the household life, shave his hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leave home to practice the Way. Why should we not do likewise?' Then the five hundred lay followers went to Gaveṣin, the lay follower, and said: 'We too wish to leave the household life, shave our hair and beards, don the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leave home to practice the Way. If Gaveṣin leaves the household life, we will follow and also leave the household life.'

"Then Gaveṣin, the lay follower, together with the five hundred lay followers, went to the Sangha of the Buddha Kassapa's time and requested to leave the household life, to receive the full ordination, and to become bhikṣus. Then Gaveṣin and the five hundred lay followers left the household life, shaved their hair and beards, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith left home to practice the Way, receiving the full ordination and becoming bhikṣus.

"At that time, the Venerable Gaveṣin thought: 'I am the leader of five hundred bhikṣus. I have left the household life, and the five hundred bhikṣus have also left the household life. In this way, we are all the same, with no distinction between us. I should now seek what is superior and excellent.'

"Then the Venerable Gaveṣin, secluded and alone, in a quiet place, practiced diligently and assiduously, not neglecting his practice. Having secluded himself, alone, in a quiet place, practicing diligently and assiduously, not neglecting his practice, he before long attained what a son of good family seeks when he shaves his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leaves home to practice the Way: the unsurpassed completion of the holy life. In the present life, he realized it himself, dwelt in its attainment, and knew: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence.' The Venerable Gaveṣin attained arhatship.

"At that time, the five hundred bhikṣus heard: 'The Venerable Gaveṣin, our leader, has realized the highest knowledge.' The five hundred bhikṣus thought: 'The Venerable Gaveṣin is our leader. He has now realized the highest knowledge. Why should we not do likewise?'

"Then the five hundred bhikṣus, secluded and alone, in quiet places, practiced diligently and assiduously, not neglecting their practice. Having secluded themselves, alone, in quiet places, practicing diligently and assiduously, not neglecting their practice, they before long attained what sons of good families seek when they shave their hair and beards, don the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leave home to practice the Way: the unsurpassed completion of the holy life. In the present life, they realized it themselves, dwelt in its attainment, and knew: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence.' Those five hundred bhikṣus all attained arhatship.

"Thus, Ānanda, Gaveṣin, the lay follower, always sought what is superior and excellent, and was never content with what is inferior. Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus: 'We too should always seek what is superior and excellent, and never be content with what is inferior.' Ānanda, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (146) The Sūtra on the Elephant's Footprint Simile (象跡喻經)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a skilled elephant tracker who enters a forest and sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, he should not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why? Because in the forest there are female elephants that are called 'big-footed'; this could be their footprint.

"If he further sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, and also sees marks of rubbing against high places, he should not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why? Because in the forest there are female elephants that are called 'tall-shouldered'; this could be their footprint.

"If he further sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, sees marks of rubbing against high places, and also sees marks of tusks scraping high places, he should not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.' Why? Because in the forest there are female elephants that are called 'having tusks'; this could be their footprint.

"If he further sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, sees marks of rubbing against high places, sees marks of tusks scraping high places, and also sees that the branches in high places are broken, then he may conclude: 'This is certainly a great bull elephant.'

"In the same way, if a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Men to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One, and his disciples hear these teachings but do not yet have complete faith in the Tathāgata's most profound and supreme enlightenment, saying: 'This World-Honored One is indeed a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One.'

"What are those teachings? The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples: 'You, bhikṣus, should abandon the five hindrances: desire and covetousness, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.'

"When a disciple hears the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of abandoning desire and covetousness, he does not yet have complete faith in the Tathāgata. This is like the skilled elephant tracker who sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, but does not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.'

"Again, the Tathāgata further teaches the Dharma to his disciples, explaining a more profound teaching. What is this teaching? It is abandoning ill will, abandoning sloth and torpor, abandoning restlessness and remorse, abandoning doubt. When a disciple hears the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of abandoning ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt, he does not yet have complete faith in the Tathāgata. This is like the skilled elephant tracker who further sees in the forest marks of rubbing against high places but does not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.'

"Again, the Tathāgata further teaches the Dharma to his disciples, explaining a yet more profound teaching. What is this teaching? There are internal forms; one contemplates external forms, whether few or many, good-looking or ugly. Transcending them, one knows and sees. This is the first liberation. Internal formlessness; one contemplates external forms, whether few or many, good-looking or ugly. Transcending them, one knows and sees. This is the second liberation. The liberation of purity; one directly experiences it with the body and dwells in its attainment. This is the third liberation. By transcending all perception of forms, by the cessation of perception of resistance, by non-attention to the perception of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space, knowing 'space is infinite,' and dwells therein. This is the fourth liberation. By transcending all the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness, knowing 'consciousness is infinite,' and dwells therein. This is the fifth liberation. By transcending all the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness, knowing 'there is nothing,' and dwells therein. This is the sixth liberation. By transcending all the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception and dwells therein. This is the seventh liberation. By transcending all the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, one enters the cessation of perception and feeling and dwells therein. Having seen with wisdom, the outflows are completely ended. This is the eighth liberation.

"When a disciple hears the Tathāgata teach the Dharma of these eight liberations, he does not yet have complete faith in the Tathāgata. This is like the skilled elephant tracker who further sees in the forest marks of tusks scraping high places but does not yet conclude: 'This is certainly the footprint of a great bull elephant.'

"Again, the Tathāgata further teaches the Dharma to his disciples, explaining a supremely profound teaching. What is this teaching? A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of initial thought and sustained thought, with inner tranquility, with one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in happiness,' and he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"Having thus attained a concentrated mind, purified, bright, without blemish, free from defilements, soft, workable, established, and immovable, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects his manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five births, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty births, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand births, countless births, the formation of eons, the dissolution of eons, the formation and dissolution of eons: 'In such a place I had such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, experienced such happiness and suffering, had such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their details and circumstances.

"When a disciple hears the Tathāgata teach such a Dharma, he still does not yet have complete faith in the Tathāgata.

"Again, the Tathāgata further teaches the Dharma, explaining a yet more supremely profound teaching. With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, without blemish, free from defilements, soft, workable, established, and immovable, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human eye, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, in good destinations and bad destinations, of beautiful appearance and ugly appearance, in fortunate and unfortunate states, and he knows that beings fare according to their karma: 'These beings, possessing wrong bodily conduct, wrong verbal conduct, wrong mental conduct, reviling noble ones, holding wrong views, undertaking actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a lower realm, in hell. But these beings, possessing right bodily conduct, right verbal conduct, right mental conduct, not reviling noble ones, holding right views, undertaking actions based on right views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human eye, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, in good destinations and bad destinations, of beautiful appearance and ugly appearance, in fortunate and unfortunate states, and knows that beings fare according to their karma.

"When a disciple hears the Tathāgata teach such a Dharma, he then has complete faith in the Tathāgata, and he has no doubts about the Tathāgata's most profound and supreme enlightenment, saying: 'The World-Honored One is indeed a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Men to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One.' This is like the skilled elephant tracker who sees in the forest a large elephant footprint, both long and wide, sees marks of rubbing against high places, sees marks of tusks scraping high places, and also sees that the branches in high places are broken. He then concludes: 'This is certainly a great bull elephant.'

"In the same way, when a Tathāgata's disciple hears the Tathāgata teach such a Dharma, he then has complete faith in the Tathāgata, and he has no doubts about the Tathāgata's most profound and supreme enlightenment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (147) The Sūtra Addressed to Heard

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Heard addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Friends, the World-Honored One has spoken of four kinds of persons existing in the world. What are the four? The first kind torments himself, pursues the practice of self-torment. The second kind torments others, pursues the practice of tormenting others. The third kind torments himself and also torments others, pursues the practice of tormenting self and others. The fourth kind neither torments himself nor torments others; he does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others. In the present life, he has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and his self becomes Brahman. Friends, which of these four kinds of persons do your minds delight in?"

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the first kind, who torments himself and pursues the practice of self-torment, our minds delight in this."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the second kind, who torments others and pursues the practice of tormenting others, our minds delight in this."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the third kind, who torments himself and also torments others and pursues the practice of tormenting self and others, our minds delight in this."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the fourth kind, who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others, who in the present life has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and whose self becomes Brahman, our minds delight in this."

At that time, the Venerable Heard addressed the bhikṣus: "Friends, I shall again ask you. Answer as you see fit. Friends, which of these four kinds of persons is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme?"

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the first kind, who torments himself and pursues the practice of self-torment, is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the second kind, who torments others and pursues the practice of tormenting others, is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the third kind, who torments himself and also torments others and pursues the practice of tormenting self and others, is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme."

Some bhikṣus replied: "Venerable Heard, the fourth kind, who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others, who in the present life has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and whose self becomes Brahman, is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme."

At that time, the Venerable Heard, each answering according to their own view, and unable to settle the matter among themselves, said to the bhikṣus: "Friends, let us go together to the World-Honored One, present this matter, and as the World-Honored One explains, we shall remember it."

The bhikṣus replied: "Very well."

Then the Venerable Heard, together with the bhikṣus, went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side. The Venerable Heard then told the Buddha the entire matter, saying: "World-Honored One, which of these four kinds of persons is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme?"

The World-Honored One told the Venerable Heard: "Among those four kinds of persons, the fourth kind, who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others, who in the present life has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and whose self becomes Brahman, this one is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme among the four. It is like when a cow produces milk, from milk comes cream, from cream comes butter, from butter comes clarified butter, from clarified butter comes the finest essence of clarified butter. The finest essence of clarified butter is declared the supreme among them. In the same way, among these four kinds of persons, the fourth kind is the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme. Why is that? The fourth kind is superior to the other three."

The Venerable Heard asked: "World-Honored One, for what reason, on what basis, does the World-Honored One declare the fourth kind of person, who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others, who in the present life has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and whose self becomes Brahman, to be the most subtle, the most wonderful, the highest, and the most supreme among the four?"

The World-Honored One said: "Listen carefully and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The Venerable Heard replied: "Yes, I will listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the person who torments himself, who pursues the practice of self-torment? There is a person who goes naked, without clothing, who uses his hand as a bowl, does not accept food that comes to him, does not accept food specially prepared for him, does not accept invitations, does not receive food from a pot, does not receive food from a bowl, does not receive food across a threshold, does not receive food across a stick, does not receive food across a pestle, does not eat food where two are eating together, does not eat food from a pregnant woman, does not eat food from a nursing woman, does not eat food from a woman living with a man, does not eat food from a place where there is a dog, does not eat where flies swarm, does not eat fish, does not eat meat, does not drink liquor, does not drink fermented drinks. He may observe the practice of accepting food from one house only, eating one mouthful; or accepting food from two houses, eating two mouthfuls; up to accepting food from seven houses, eating seven mouthfuls. He may eat from one small plate of food, or from two, or up to seven small plates. He may eat once a day, or once every two days, or up to once every seven days. Thus he may practice the eating of food at set intervals up to once every half month. He may eat herbs, or eat rice, or eat wild rice, or eat Darbha grass, or eat husks, or eat rice bran, or eat rice scum, or eat sesame cake, or eat grass, or eat cow dung. He eats forest roots and fruits; he eats fallen fruits for his sustenance.

"He wears coarse hemp, or wears mixed coarse cloth, or wears cloth from a corpse, or wears rags from a refuse heap, or wears tree bark, or covers himself with an antelope skin, or with strips of antelope skin, or wears a grass garment, or wears a bark garment, or wears a wooden-chip garment, or covers himself with head-hair woven into cloth, or with tail-hair woven into cloth, or wears an owl-wing garment.

"He pulls out his hair and beard, practicing the pulling out of hair and beard. He practices standing only, not sitting. He squats, practicing squatting. He lies on thorns, making thorns his bed. He lies on a bed of fruit husks. He sleeps on bare ground. He sleeps on one side only. He smears his body with dust and filth. He practices staying in the open air. He sits wherever he happens to be. He eats impure food, practicing the eating of impure food. He practices not drinking water, or practices bathing in water three times a day, practicing the entering of water by day and night. Thus in many ways he practices tormenting and afflicting this body. This is called the person who torments himself, who pursues the practice of self-torment.

"What is the person who torments others, who pursues the practice of tormenting others? There is a person who is a butcher of sheep, or a butcher of pigs, or a bird catcher, or a trapper of wild animals, or a hunter, or a fisherman, or a thief, or an executioner, or a jailer, or any other such person engaged in cruel occupations. This is called the person who torments others, who pursues the practice of tormenting others.

"What is the person who torments himself and also torments others, who pursues the practice of tormenting self and others? There is a person who is a king, a ruler of a realm, a kṣatriya who has been consecrated on the head, or a wealthy brahmin. To the east of the city, he has a new sacrificial hall built. He shaves his hair and beard, puts on a rough hide, smears his body with ghee and sesame oil, scratches his back with a deer horn, and enters the sacrificial hall together with his chief queen and the brahmin who presides over the sacrifice. There in the hall, he lies on bare ground smeared with cow dung. The king drinks the milk from the udder of a cow that has a calf of the same color; the chief queen drinks the milk from the udder of a second such cow; the presiding brahmin drinks from a third. For the remaining milk, it is poured onto the fire. Those calves live on what milk remains.

"He declares: 'For this sacrifice, slaughter so many bulls, so many young bulls, so many heifers, so many goats, so many sheep. Cut down so many trees for sacrificial posts. Mow so much grass for the sacrificial ground.' The servants and workers, driven by punishment and fear, crying with tear-streaked faces, perform their tasks. This is called the person who torments himself and also torments others, who pursues the practice of tormenting self and others.

"What is the person who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others, who in the present life has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and whose self becomes Brahman? A Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of Men to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One. In this world with its gods, Māra, Brahmā, with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, he realizes through his own higher knowledge and proclaims it. He teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with right meaning and right phrasing, complete and pure, proclaiming the holy life.

"A householder or householder's son, or one born in some other clan, hears this Dharma. Having heard it, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, he reflects: 'The household life is confining, a dusty path. Leaving home is open like the sky. Dwelling in a household, one cannot practice the holy life in complete purity and perfection, like a polished shell. Let me now shave my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leave home to practice the Way.'

"He then abandons his wealth, whether small or great, abandons his circle of relatives, whether small or great, shaves his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith leaves home to practice the Way. After leaving home, he keeps the precepts, guarding the precept of the Prātimokṣa, with proper conduct, proper deportment, and proper domain. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, he trains in the rules of training that he has undertaken.

"He abandons killing and refrains from killing. Laying down the rod, laying down the knife, he has a sense of shame and kindness, and is compassionate toward all living beings.

"He abandons taking what is not given and refrains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and does not commit theft. He keeps himself pure.

"He abandons the non-celibate life and practices the celibate life. He practices detachment, renouncing the impure act of sexual intercourse.

"He abandons false speech and refrains from false speech. He speaks truth, is devoted to truth, is reliable, is trustworthy, does not deceive the world.

"He abandons divisive speech and refrains from divisive speech. He does not tell what he has heard here to those there in order to divide them from those here, nor does he tell what he has heard there to those here in order to divide them from those there. He reconciles the divided, encourages the united, delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, and speaks words that promote harmony.

"He abandons harsh speech and refrains from harsh speech. Whatever speech is gentle, pleasant to the ear, loving, going to the heart, courteous, dear to many, pleasing to many, such speech he speaks.

"He abandons idle chatter and refrains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks about the Dharma, speaks about the Vinaya. He speaks words worth treasuring, timely, with reason, well-defined, and connected with the goal.

"He refrains from damaging seeds and growing plants. He eats one meal a day, not eating at night, not eating at improper times. He refrains from watching dancing, singing, music, and performances. He refrains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and cosmetics to beautify himself. He refrains from high and luxurious beds. He refrains from accepting gold and silver. He refrains from accepting raw grain. He refrains from accepting raw meat. He refrains from accepting women and girls. He refrains from accepting male and female servants. He refrains from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, chickens, and pigs. He refrains from accepting fields and estates. He refrains from carrying messages and running errands. He refrains from buying and selling. He refrains from false weights and measures. He refrains from crookedness, deception, and fraud. He refrains from cutting, beating, binding, ambushing, and plundering.

"He is content with robes to cover his body and with almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he carries only his bowl and robes. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, carries only its wings, so too the bhikṣu, wherever he goes, carries only his bowl and robes.

"He is endowed with this aggregate of noble morality. Because of being endowed with this aggregate of noble morality, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.

"When his eye sees a form, he does not grasp at its signs, does not grasp at its features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of desire and grief might invade him, he practices restraint, guards the eye faculty, and attains the restraint of the eye faculty. When his ear hears a sound, when his nose smells an odor, when his tongue tastes a flavor, when his body touches a tangible, when his mind cognizes a mental object, he does not grasp at its signs, does not grasp at its features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of desire and grief might invade him, he practices restraint, guards the mind faculty, and attains the restraint of the mind faculty.

"He is endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties. Because of being endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an unpolluted happiness.

"When going forward and returning, he acts with clear comprehension. When looking ahead and looking around, he acts with clear comprehension. When bending and stretching, he acts with clear comprehension. When putting on his saṅghāṭī robe and carrying his bowl, he acts with clear comprehension. When eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, he acts with clear comprehension. When walking, standing, sitting, lying down, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and remaining silent, he acts with clear comprehension.

"He is endowed with this noble aggregate of morality, endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension. He resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, under a tree, a mountain, a cave, a gorge, a charnel ground, a grove, the open air, or a haystack.

"After his meal, returning from the almsround, he sits down cross-legged, setting his body upright and establishing mindfulness before him. He abandons desire and covetousness for the world, and dwells with a mind free from desire and covetousness. He purifies his mind of desire and covetousness. He abandons ill will and hatred. With a mind free from ill will, compassionate toward all living beings, he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. He abandons sloth and torpor. With the perception of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. He abandons restlessness and remorse. Inwardly calm, he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. He abandons doubt. Having crossed over doubt, no longer uncertain about wholesome states, he purifies his mind of doubt.

"Having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weaken wisdom, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of initial thought and sustained thought, with inner tranquility, with one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in happiness,' and he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"Having thus attained a concentrated mind, purified, bright, without blemish, free from defilements, soft, workable, established, and immovable, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. He knows as it really is: 'This is suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the arising of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it really is: 'These are the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the arising of the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the outflows.' He knows as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the outflows.'

"Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the outflow of existence, his mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence.'

"This is called the person who neither torments himself nor torments others, who does not pursue the practice of tormenting self or others. In the present life, he has extinguished craving, attained cessation, experienced coolness, feels happiness, and his self becomes Brahman."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Heard and the bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (148) The Sūtra Addressed to Heard (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Heard went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One told him: "Heard, what in the world do ascetics and brahmins declare? What views do they hold, what do they proclaim?"

The Venerable Heard said: "World-Honored One, there are five kinds of views that ascetics and brahmins in the world declare, hold, and proclaim. What are the five? Some ascetics and brahmins make this declaration and hold this view: 'Pleasure is the self; after death, the self truly exists; this alone is true, anything else is wrong.' Some ascetics and brahmins make this declaration and hold this view: 'Suffering is the self; after death, the self truly exists; this alone is true, anything else is wrong.' Some ascetics and brahmins make this declaration and hold this view: 'Both pleasure and suffering are the self; after death, the self truly exists; this alone is true, anything else is wrong.' Some ascetics and brahmins make this declaration and hold this view: 'Neither pleasure nor suffering is the self; after death, the self truly exists; this alone is true, anything else is wrong.' Some ascetics and brahmins make this declaration and hold this view: 'The self has the nature of perception; after death, the self truly exists; this alone is true, anything else is wrong.' World-Honored One, these are the five kinds of views that ascetics and brahmins in the world declare, hold, and proclaim."

The World-Honored One told the Venerable Heard: "Those ascetics and brahmins who make this declaration and hold this view that 'pleasure is the self; after death, the self truly exists,' I go to them and ask: 'Is it really so? Do you truly declare and hold the view that pleasure is the self, and that after death, the self truly exists?' They reply: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know the entire world to be wholly pleasure?' They are unable to reply. I further ask them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know from one day to the next, or from one night to the next, nothing but pleasure?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'Do you know whether there exists a state that is pleasure or one that is not pleasure? Do you know whether form is the self or the self is apart from form? Do you know whether feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are the self, or the self is apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'If one does not know and does not see, and yet declares "pleasure is the self," this is not reasonable.'

"Heard, those ascetics and brahmins who make this declaration and hold this view that 'suffering is the self; after death, the self truly exists,' I go to them and ask: 'Is it really so? Do you truly declare and hold the view that suffering is the self, and that after death, the self truly exists?' They reply: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know the entire world to be wholly suffering?' They are unable to reply. I further ask them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know from one day to the next, or from one night to the next, nothing but suffering?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'Do you know whether there exists a state that is suffering or one that is not suffering? Do you know whether form is the self or the self is apart from form? Do you know whether feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are the self, or the self is apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'If one does not know and does not see, and yet declares "suffering is the self," this is not reasonable.'

"Heard, those ascetics and brahmins who make this declaration and hold this view that 'both pleasure and suffering are the self; after death, the self truly exists,' I go to them and ask: 'Is it really so? Do you truly declare and hold the view that both pleasure and suffering are the self, and that after death, the self truly exists?' They reply: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know the entire world to be wholly both pleasure and suffering?' They are unable to reply. I further ask them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know from one day to the next, or from one night to the next, nothing but both pleasure and suffering?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'Do you know whether there exists a state that is both pleasure and suffering, or one that is not? Do you know whether form is the self or the self is apart from form? Do you know whether feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are the self, or the self is apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'If one does not know and does not see, and yet declares "both pleasure and suffering are the self," this is not reasonable.'

"Heard, those ascetics and brahmins who make this declaration and hold this view that 'neither pleasure nor suffering is the self; after death, the self truly exists,' I go to them and ask: 'Is it really so? Do you truly declare and hold the view that neither pleasure nor suffering is the self, and that after death, the self truly exists?' They reply: 'Yes.' I then say to them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know the entire world to be wholly neither pleasure nor suffering?' They are unable to reply. I further ask them: 'While you dwell in the world, do you know from one day to the next, or from one night to the next, nothing but neither pleasure nor suffering?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'Do you know whether there exists a state that is neither pleasure nor suffering, or one that is not? Do you know whether form is the self or the self is apart from form? Do you know whether feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are the self, or the self is apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?' They are still unable to reply.

"I further say to them: 'If one does not know and does not see, and yet declares "neither pleasure nor suffering is the self," this is not reasonable.'

"Heard, if an ascetic or brahmin makes this declaration and holds this view: 'The self has the nature of perception; after death, the self truly exists,' there are three kinds of perceptions: pleasant perception, painful perception, and neither pleasant nor painful perception. These three perceptions are impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering; it is impermanent and of the nature of suffering. Can one say of this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'? This is not reasonable.

"If someone says: 'I abandon pleasant perception and painful perception, and the neither pleasant nor painful perception ceases; this neither pleasure nor suffering is the self,' I say to them: 'If pleasant perception ceases, when pleasant perception ceases, would one then perceive "this is my self"?' They are unable to reply. I further say to them: 'If painful perception ceases, when painful perception ceases, would one then perceive "this is my self"?' They are unable to reply. I further say to them: 'If neither pleasant nor painful perception ceases, when neither pleasant nor painful perception ceases, would one then perceive "this is my self"?' They are unable to reply.

"Heard, this bhikṣu, when he does not perceive pleasant perception as self, does not perceive painful perception as self, does not perceive neither pleasant nor painful perception as self, because he does not perceive thus, he does not grasp at anything in the world. Not grasping, he is not agitated. Not being agitated, he personally attains nirvāṇa. He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence.'

"Heard, if someone were to say to this bhikṣu whose mind is thus liberated: 'Do you hold the view that the Tathāgata exists after death?' This is not reasonable. 'Do you hold the view that the Tathāgata does not exist after death?' This is not reasonable. 'Do you hold the view that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death?' This is not reasonable. 'Do you hold the view that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?' This is not reasonable.

"Why? Because what can be designated by name, what can be described by language, what can be expressed by words, what can be made the object of knowledge, what can be encompassed by the sphere of cognition, in this bhikṣu's case, all of this has been transcended, all of this has been cut off, all of this has been uprooted, so that it will never arise again in the future. Heard, this bhikṣu who has transcended perception and designation is vast and immeasurable, and he has abandoned everything."

The Venerable Heard asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does a bhikṣu's mind become liberated and reach a state where he does not decline?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Heard, a bhikṣu who, regarding the earth element, is not earth, not dependent on earth, not delighting in earth. Regarding the water element, is not water, not dependent on water, not delighting in water. Regarding the fire element, is not fire, not dependent on fire, not delighting in fire. Regarding the wind element, is not wind, not dependent on wind, not delighting in wind. Regarding the sphere of infinite space, is not the sphere of infinite space, not dependent on the sphere of infinite space, not delighting in the sphere of infinite space. Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness, is not the sphere of infinite consciousness, not dependent on the sphere of infinite consciousness, not delighting in the sphere of infinite consciousness. Regarding the sphere of nothingness, is not the sphere of nothingness, not dependent on the sphere of nothingness, not delighting in the sphere of nothingness. Regarding the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, is not the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, not dependent on the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, not delighting in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Regarding this world, is not this world, not dependent on this world, not delighting in this world. Regarding the other world, is not the other world, not dependent on the other world, not delighting in the other world. Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or mentally considered, regarding all of these, he is not that, not dependent on that, not delighting in that. A bhikṣu whose mind is thus liberated is one who does not decline."

The Venerable Heard then asked: "World-Honored One, how does a bhikṣu's mind become liberated and reach a state of supreme, peerless excellence?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Heard, a bhikṣu who, regarding the earth element, is not earth, not dependent on earth, not delighting in earth, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the water element, is not water, not dependent on water, not delighting in water, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the fire element, is not fire, not dependent on fire, not delighting in fire, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the wind element, is not wind, not dependent on wind, not delighting in wind, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the sphere of infinite space, is not the sphere of infinite space, not dependent on the sphere of infinite space, not delighting in the sphere of infinite space, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the sphere of infinite consciousness, is not the sphere of infinite consciousness, not dependent on the sphere of infinite consciousness, not delighting in the sphere of infinite consciousness, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the sphere of nothingness, is not the sphere of nothingness, not dependent on the sphere of nothingness, not delighting in the sphere of nothingness, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, is not the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, not dependent on the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, not delighting in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding this world, is not this world, not dependent on this world, not delighting in this world, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Regarding the other world, is not the other world, not dependent on the other world, not delighting in the other world, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom.
