Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or mentally considered, regarding all of these, he is not that, not dependent on that, not delighting in that, and has exhausted the outflows, freed the mind, and attained liberation through wisdom. Heard, a bhikṣu whose mind is thus liberated, even if all the gods, including Brahmā, were to seek the consciousness of this bhikṣu, wondering 'Where is this bhikṣu's consciousness established?', they would be unable to find it. Why? I say that in the present life this person cannot be traced."

The Venerable Heard then asked: "World-Honored One, how does a bhikṣu who has thus transcended perception and designation have a vast and immeasurable mind, having abandoned everything?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Heard, a bhikṣu who, regarding the earth element, generates a perception. Regarding the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, this world, the other world, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or mentally considered, regarding all of these, if he generates a perception, this is a tied-down state. Heard, a bhikṣu who, regarding the earth element, does not generate a perception. Regarding the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, this world, the other world, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, or mentally considered, regarding all of these, if he does not generate a perception, Heard, this is the bhikṣu who has transcended perception and designation, whose mind is vast and immeasurable, and who has abandoned everything."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Heard, hearing what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

## (142) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Brahmins: The Sūtra on Vassakāra, Number One

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha was hostile toward the Vajjians, and constantly declared among his retinue: "The Vajjian people possess great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might. I shall annihilate the Vajjian race, destroy the Vajjians, and cause the Vajjian people to encounter immeasurable calamity."

Then King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha heard that the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. He addressed the great minister Vassakāra, saying: "I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is staying in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. Vassakāra, go to the śramaṇa Gautama and, bearing my name, inquire whether his sacred body is well and free from illness, and whether his strength is as usual. Speak thus: 'Gautama, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha inquires whether your sacred body is well and free from illness, and whether your strength is as usual. Gautama, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha is hostile toward the Vajjians, and constantly declares among his retinue: "The Vajjian people possess great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might. I shall annihilate the Vajjian race, destroy the Vajjians, and cause the Vajjian people to encounter immeasurable calamity." What does the śramaṇa Gautama say to this?' Vassakāra, whatever the śramaṇa Gautama says, retain it well. Why? Such a person never speaks falsely."

The great minister Vassakāra, having received the king's instruction, mounted the finest carriage and, together with five hundred carriages, departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain. He ascended Vulture Peak Mountain, alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot to the Buddha's presence. He exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, sat to one side, and said: "Gautama, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha inquires whether your sacred body is well and free from illness, and whether your strength is as usual. Gautama, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha is hostile toward the Vajjians, and constantly declares among his retinue: 'The Vajjian people possess great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might. I shall annihilate the Vajjian race, destroy the Vajjians, and cause the Vajjian people to encounter immeasurable calamity.' What does the śramaṇa Gautama say to this?"

Having heard this, the World-Honored One said: "Vassakāra, I once traveled in the Vajjian country, where there is a monastery called Cāpāla. Vassakāra, at that time I taught the Vajjian people seven conditions of non-decline, and the Vajjian people were able to receive and practice these seven conditions of non-decline. Vassakāra, if the Vajjian people practice these seven conditions of non-decline without transgressing them, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The great minister Vassakāra addressed the World-Honored One: "The śramaṇa Gautama has stated this matter briefly without explaining it in detail. We cannot understand the meaning. May the śramaṇa Gautama explain it in detail so that we may understand."

The World-Honored One said: "Vassakāra, listen carefully and consider it well. I shall explain this meaning in detail for you." The great minister Vassakāra received the teaching and listened.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fan. The World-Honored One turned around and asked: "Ānanda, have you heard that the Vajjians hold frequent assemblies and gather together in large numbers?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that the Vajjians hold frequent assemblies and gather together in large numbers."

The World-Honored One then told the great minister Vassakāra: "If the Vajjians hold frequent assemblies and gather together in large numbers, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that the Vajjians assemble together in harmony, conduct Vajjian affairs together, and rise together?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that the Vajjians assemble together in harmony, conduct Vajjian affairs together, and rise together."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If the Vajjians assemble together in harmony, conduct Vajjian affairs together, and rise together, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established, do not alter what has previously been established, and properly follow the ancient Vajjian laws?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established, do not alter what has previously been established, and properly follow the ancient Vajjian laws."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If the Vajjians do not establish what has not been established, do not alter what has previously been established, and properly follow the ancient Vajjian laws, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that the Vajjians do not forcibly violate the wives or daughters of others?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that the Vajjians do not forcibly violate the wives or daughters of others."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If the Vajjians do not forcibly violate the wives or daughters of others, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that when there are those of renowned virtue and seniority among the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to them, and heed their counsel when they hear it?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that when there are those of renowned virtue and seniority among the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to them, and heed their counsel when they hear it."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If when there are those of renowned virtue and seniority among the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to them, and heed their counsel when they hear it, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that regarding the ancient shrines of the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together maintain and adorn them, follow, make offerings to, and worship at them, that the original provisions are always maintained and never abandoned, and the original practices are not diminished?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that regarding the ancient shrines of the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together maintain and adorn them, follow, make offerings to, and worship at them, that the original provisions are always maintained and never abandoned, and the original practices are not diminished."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If regarding the ancient shrines of the Vajjians, all the Vajjians together maintain and adorn them, follow, make offerings to, and worship at them, the original provisions are always maintained and never abandoned, and the original practices are not diminished, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

The World-Honored One again asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Have you heard that the Vajjians all together protect the arahants, with utmost love and respect, always wishing that arahants who have not yet come will come, that those who have already come will be happy to stay permanently, and ensuring they never lack robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, I have heard that the Vajjians all together protect the arahants, with utmost love and respect, always wishing that arahants who have not yet come will come, that those who have already come will be happy to stay permanently, and ensuring they never lack robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life."

The World-Honored One again told the great minister Vassakāra: "If the Vajjians all together protect the arahants, with utmost love and respect, always wishing that arahants who have not yet come will come, that those who have already come will be happy to stay permanently, and ensuring they never lack robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline. Vassakāra, if the Vajjians practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold these seven conditions of non-decline, the Vajjians will surely prevail and will not decline."

Thereupon, the great minister Vassakāra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Gautama, if the Vajjians accomplish even one condition of non-decline, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha would be unable to subdue them, let alone all seven conditions of non-decline! Gautama, I have many state affairs to attend to and request permission to withdraw and return."

The World-Honored One replied: "Go as you wish."

Thereupon, the great minister Vassakāra, having heard what the Buddha said, properly retained it, rose, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, and departed.

Not long after the great minister Vassakāra had departed, the World-Honored One turned around and said: "Ānanda, if there are any bhikṣus residing in various places near Vulture Peak Mountain, proclaim that they should all gather in the lecture hall. When all have gathered, come and inform me."

The Venerable Ānanda received the Buddha's instruction: "Yes, World-Honored One." At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went and proclaimed: "If there are any bhikṣus residing in various places near Vulture Peak Mountain, all are now to gather in the lecture hall." When all had gathered, he went to the Buddha's presence, bowed his head in reverence, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, I have proclaimed: 'If there are any bhikṣus residing in various places near Vulture Peak Mountain, all are to gather in the lecture hall.' They have now all gathered. May the World-Honored One proceed at the appropriate time."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the lecture hall. He had a seat arranged before the assembly of bhikṣus, sat down, and addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now teach you seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus hold frequent assemblies and gather together in large numbers, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus assemble together in harmony, conduct Sangha affairs together, and rise together, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus do not establish what has not been established, do not alter what has been previously established, and properly follow the precepts I have taught, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If, regarding this 'craving for future existence, accompanied by delight and desire, taking pleasure in this and that,' bhikṣus do not follow such craving when it arises, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If there are elder, senior bhikṣus who are companions in the holy life, and all bhikṣus revere, honor, serve, and make offerings to them, and heed their counsel when they hear it, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If there are secluded places, forests, high cliffs, quiet and tranquil dwellings, places without sound, remote, free from evil, without people, suitable for meditation, and bhikṣus delight in dwelling there and do not leave, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus all together protect their companions in the holy life, with utmost love and respect, always wishing that those practicing the holy life who have not yet come will come, that those who have already come will be happy to stay permanently, and ensuring they never lack robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus revere the teacher, respectfully making great offerings and serving him, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus revere the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, heedfulness, generosity, and concentration, respectfully making great offerings and serving them, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus do not engage in worldly activities, do not delight in worldly activities, and do not habituate themselves to worldly activities, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If they do not engage in idle chatter, do not delight in idle chatter, and do not habituate themselves to idle chatter; if they do not engage in socializing, do not delight in socializing, and do not habituate themselves to socializing; if they do not engage in mingling with crowds, do not delight in mingling with crowds, and do not habituate themselves to mingling with crowds; if they do not engage in sleeping, do not delight in sleeping, and do not habituate themselves to sleeping; if they do not practice the holy life for gain, not for fame, and not for the sake of others; if they do not stop their efforts prematurely, and do not give up striving for the sake of minor attainments, but continue their efforts to achieve supreme attainment; the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus accomplish the treasure of faith, the treasure of morality, the treasure of conscience, the treasure of shame, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and accomplish the treasure of wisdom, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus accomplish the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of conscience, the power of shame, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and accomplish the power of wisdom, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus cultivate the awakening factor of mindfulness, based on relinquishment, based on the absence of desire, based on cessation, tending toward the way of release; and likewise cultivate the awakening factors of investigation of dharmas, energy, joy, tranquility, and concentration; and cultivate the awakening factor of equanimity, based on relinquishment, based on the absence of desire, based on cessation, tending toward the way of release, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you another set of seven conditions of non-decline. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the seven? If bhikṣus, when the rule of face-to-face settlement should be applied, apply the rule of face-to-face settlement; when the rule of recollection should be applied, apply the rule of recollection; when the rule of non-insanity should be applied, apply the rule of non-insanity; when the rule of voluntary confession should be applied, apply the rule of voluntary confession; when the rule of majority decision should be applied, apply the rule of majority decision; when the rule of successive referral should be applied, apply the rule of successive referral; and when a dispute arises in the Sangha, settle it by the method of sweeping away as if sweeping refuse, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline. If bhikṣus practice these seven conditions of non-decline and uphold them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely prevail and the Dharma will not decline."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now teach you six principles of cordiality. Listen carefully and consider them well."

At that time, the bhikṣus replied: "Yes, indeed."

The Buddha said: "What are the six? Acting toward one's companions in the holy life with bodily actions of loving-kindness: this is a principle of cordiality, a principle of love and joy, that causes love and respect, that causes reverence and esteem, that causes cultivation and restraint, that leads to the attainment of the śramaṇa life, to single-mindedness, to diligence, and to nirvāṇa. Likewise, acting with verbal actions of loving-kindness and mental actions of loving-kindness. If there are rightful material gains, gains obtained in accordance with the Dharma, even food received in one's own bowl, sharing such gains and distributing them among one's companions in the holy life: this is a principle of cordiality, a principle of love and joy, that causes love and respect, that causes reverence and esteem, that causes cultivation and restraint, that leads to the attainment of the śramaṇa life, to single-mindedness, to diligence, and to nirvāṇa. If there are precepts that are unbroken, unpierced, unstained, unblemished, liberating like the earth, not dependent on others, praised by the noble ones, well undertaken and perfectly maintained, sharing such moral conduct with one's companions in the holy life: this is a principle of cordiality, a principle of love and joy, that causes love and respect, that causes reverence and esteem, that causes cultivation and restraint, that leads to the attainment of the śramaṇa life, to single-mindedness, to diligence, and to nirvāṇa. If there is right view that is noble, leading to liberation, clearly understood and deeply penetrated, capable of rightly ending suffering, sharing such view with one's companions in the holy life: this is a principle of cordiality, a principle of love and joy, that causes love and respect, that causes reverence and esteem, that causes cultivation and restraint, that leads to the attainment of the śramaṇa life, to single-mindedness, to diligence, and to nirvāṇa. What I previously spoke of as six principles of cordiality was said on account of this."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Vassakāra, Number One.

---

## (143) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Brahmins: The Sūtra on Saṅgārava, Number Two

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the young brahmin Saṅgārava, wandering in the afternoon, went to the Buddha's presence. They exchanged greetings, and he sat to one side and said: "Gautama, I wish to ask a question. Will you permit me to speak?"

The World-Honored One said: "Young man, if you have a doubt, ask as you wish."

The young brahmin Saṅgārava then asked: "Gautama, when a brahmin lawfully seeks wealth through begging, and either personally performs a sacrifice or has others perform a sacrifice; Gautama, when he personally performs a sacrifice or has others perform it, he thereby walks the path of immeasurable merit, because of the sacrifice. But the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama, who shave off their hair and beard according to their clan, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave home to be homeless and study the Way, taming themselves, calming themselves, and bringing themselves to final cessation: thus the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama walk only one path of merit, not the path of immeasurable merit, because of their studying the Way."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fan. The Venerable Ānanda then asked: "Young man, of these two paths, which is the highest, finest, and most excellent?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava said: "Ānanda, I equally revere, respect, and venerate both the śramaṇa Gautama and Ānanda."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Young man, I am not asking you whom you revere, respect, and venerate. I am only asking you: of these two paths, which is the highest, finest, and most excellent?"

The Venerable Ānanda asked a second and third time: "Young man, of these two paths, which is the highest, finest, and most excellent?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava likewise replied a second and third time: "Ānanda, I equally revere, respect, and venerate both the śramaṇa Gautama and Ānanda."

The Venerable Ānanda again said: "Young man, I am not asking you whom you revere, respect, and venerate. I am only asking you: of these two paths, which is the highest, finest, and most excellent?"

Then the World-Honored One had this thought: "This young brahmin Saṅgārava is being pressed by Ānanda. I should rescue him."

Having realized this, the World-Honored One said: "Young man, the other day when the king and his ministers gathered in a great assembly, what matter did they discuss? For what matter did they gather?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava answered: "Gautama, the other day the king and his ministers gathered in a great assembly and discussed this matter: 'What is the cause and condition that formerly the śramaṇa Gautama established few precepts, yet many bhikṣus attained the Way? And what is the cause and condition that now the śramaṇa Gautama has established many precepts, yet few bhikṣus attain the Way?' Gautama, the other day the king and his ministers gathered in a great assembly to discuss this matter; it was for this matter that they gathered."

Then the World-Honored One said: "Young man, I shall now ask you a question; answer as you understand. What do you think? Suppose there were a śramaṇa or brahmin who himself practiced such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all his defilements were exhausted, he attained the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for himself, realizing and abiding in the attainment, knowing: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence,' knowing it as it truly is. He then tells others: 'I myself practiced such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all my defilements were exhausted, I attained the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for myself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. Come, all of you, and likewise practice such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all your defilements will be exhausted, you will attain the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for yourself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is.' Those others also practice such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all their defilements are exhausted, they attain the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for themselves, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. They then tell others, and those others tell yet others, and so on by turns, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds and thousands. What do you think, young man? Are the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama, who shave off their hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave home to be homeless and study the Way, walking only one path of merit, not walking the path of immeasurable merit, because of their studying the Way?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava answered: "Gautama, as I understand the meaning of what the śramaṇa Gautama has said, the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama, who shave off their hair and beard according to their clan, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave home to be homeless and study the Way, walk the path of immeasurable merit, not merely one path of merit, because of their studying the Way."

The World-Honored One further told Saṅgārava: "There are three kinds of demonstrations: the demonstration of supernatural power, the demonstration of mind-reading, and the demonstration of instruction. Young man, what is the demonstration of supernatural power? There is a śramaṇa or brahmin who possesses great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might, whose mind has mastery over supernatural powers, and who performs immeasurable feats of supernatural power: dividing one body into many, merging many into one, remaining in one place with knowledge and vision, passing unobstructed through walls and rocks as if moving through space, sinking into the earth as into water, walking on water as on land, sitting cross-legged and rising into the sky like a bird in flight. This sun and moon, which possess great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might, he touches and strokes with his hand, and reaches with his body as far as the Brahmā heaven. Young man, this is called the demonstration of supernatural power.

"Young man, what is the demonstration of mind-reading? There is a śramaṇa or brahmin who reads others' minds by their physical signs, knowing: 'Your mind is thus, it is like this, it truly is like this,' reading countless minds with not a few readings, all of which are true without any error. Even without reading others' minds by their physical signs, but hearing the voices of heavenly beings or non-human beings, he reads others' minds, knowing: 'Your mind is thus, it is like this, it truly is like this,' reading countless minds with not a few readings, all of which are true without any error. Even without reading others' minds by their physical signs, and without hearing the voices of heavenly beings or non-human beings, but by hearing the thoughts, reflections, and speech of others, having heard these sounds, he reads others' minds, knowing: 'Your mind is thus, it is like this, it truly is like this,' reading countless minds with not a few readings, all of which are true without any error. Even without reading others' minds by their physical signs, without hearing the voices of heavenly beings or non-human beings, and without hearing the thoughts, reflections, and speech of others, but seeing another enter the concentration without initial and sustained application of thought, and having seen this, he thinks: 'This worthy one is not thinking or reflecting; as his mind wills it, so it is.' When that worthy one emerges from this concentration, he thinks in such and such a way. When he emerges from this concentration, he indeed thinks in exactly that way. He also reads the past, reads the future, reads the present, reads what was done and said long ago, and reads peaceful abodes and those dwelling in peaceful abodes, and reads the mind and mental factors. Young man, this is called the demonstration of mind-reading.

"Young man, what is the demonstration of instruction? There is a śramaṇa or brahmin who himself practices such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all his defilements are exhausted, he attains the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for himself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. He then tells others: 'I myself practiced such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all my defilements were exhausted, I attained the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for myself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. Come, all of you, and likewise practice such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all your defilements will be exhausted, you will attain the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for yourself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is.' Those others also practice such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all their defilements are exhausted, they attain the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for themselves, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. They tell others, and those others tell yet others, and so on by turns, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds and thousands. Young man, this is called the demonstration of instruction. Of these three demonstrations, which demonstration is the highest, finest, and most excellent?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava answered: "Gautama, if a śramaṇa or brahmin possesses great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might, with mastery of mind over supernatural powers, and reaches with his body even to the Brahmā heaven; Gautama, this is something he does himself and possesses himself, and he himself receives the fruit. Gautama, among the demonstrations, this demonstrates a great principle. Gautama, if a śramaṇa or brahmin reads others' minds by their physical signs, and so on, reading even the mind and mental factors; Gautama, this is also something he does himself and possesses himself, and he himself receives the fruit. Gautama, among the demonstrations, this also demonstrates a great principle. Gautama, if a śramaṇa or brahmin himself practices such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all his defilements are exhausted, he attains the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for himself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. He tells others, and those others tell yet others, and so on by turns, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds and thousands. Gautama, of the three demonstrations, this demonstration is the highest, finest, and most excellent."

The World-Honored One further asked Saṅgārava: "Of the three demonstrations, which demonstration do you praise?"

The young brahmin Saṅgārava answered: "Gautama, of the three demonstrations, I praise the śramaṇa Gautama. Why? The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might, with mastery of mind, and reaches with his body even to the Brahmā heaven. The śramaṇa Gautama reads others' minds by their physical signs, and reads even the mind and mental factors. The śramaṇa Gautama demonstrates such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all his defilements are exhausted, he attains the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for himself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. The śramaṇa Gautama tells others, and those others tell yet others, and so on by turns, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds and thousands. Gautama, therefore, of the three demonstrations, I praise the śramaṇa Gautama!"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Young man, you have well understood this discourse. Why? I do possess great supernatural power, great majesty, great fortune, and great spiritual might, with mastery of mind over supernatural powers, and reach with my body even to the Brahmā heaven. Young man, I do read others' minds by their physical signs, and read even the mind and mental factors. Young man, I myself have practiced such a path, such a way, and having practiced this path and this way, all my defilements are exhausted, I have attained the state without defilements, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and seeing for myself, realizing and abiding in the attainment. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence, knowing it as it truly is. I tell others, and those others tell yet others, and so on by turns, numbering in the immeasurable hundreds and thousands. Young man, therefore you have well understood this discourse. You should thus receive and retain it well. Why? The meaning that has been stated should indeed be thus."

Thereupon, the young brahmin Saṅgārava said: "World-Honored One, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The young brahmin Saṅgārava, the Venerable Ānanda, and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Saṅgārava, Number Two.

---

## (144) Madhyamāgama, Chapter on Brahmins: The Sūtra on Gaṇaka Moggallāna, Number Three

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Śrāvastī, at the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the brahmin Gaṇaka Moggallāna, the arithmetician, wandering in the afternoon, went to the Buddha's presence. They exchanged greetings, and he sat to one side and said: "Gautama, I wish to ask a question. Will you permit me to speak?"

The World-Honored One said: "Moggallāna, ask as you wish; do not hesitate."

The arithmetician Moggallāna then asked: "Gautama, this Hall of Migāra's Mother was built gradually, step by step, until it was finally completed. Gautama, this Hall of Migāra's Mother has stairs: first one ascends the first step, then the second, third, and fourth. Gautama, thus this Hall of Migāra's Mother was gradually ascended step by step. Gautama, elephant trainers also gradually train and complete their training of elephants, namely by means of the hook. Gautama, horse trainers also gradually train and complete their training of horses, namely by means of the bridle. Gautama, warriors also gradually progress to completion, namely through the practice of bows and arrows. Gautama, brahmins also gradually progress to completion, namely through the study of scriptures. Gautama, we who study arithmetic and make our living by arithmetic also gradually progress to completion. When we have students, whether male or female, we first teach them to count by ones, then by twos, threes, tens, hundreds, thousands, and ten-thousands, progressing step by step upward. Gautama, thus we who study arithmetic and make our living by arithmetic gradually progress to completion. In the Dharma and Vinaya of the śramaṇa Gautama, how does one gradually progress step by step to completion?"

The World-Honored One said: "Moggallāna, if there is a correct description of gradual, step-by-step progress to completion, it is in my Dharma and Vinaya that such a correct description applies. Why? Moggallāna, in my Dharma and Vinaya there is gradual, step-by-step progress to completion. Moggallāna, when a young bhikṣu first comes to study the Way and newly enters this Dharma and Vinaya, the Tathāgata first teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! Guard your bodily conduct and keep it pure, and guard your verbal and mental conduct and keep them pure.' Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu guards his bodily conduct and keeps it pure, and guards his verbal and mental conduct and keeps them pure, the Tathāgata further teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! Contemplate the body internally as body, and contemplate feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas.' Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body, and contemplates feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas, the Tathāgata further teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! Contemplate the body internally as body, and do not give rise to thoughts connected with desire. Contemplate feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas, and do not give rise to thoughts connected with unwholesome states.'

"Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body and does not give rise to thoughts connected with desire, and contemplates feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas and does not give rise to thoughts connected with unwholesome states, the Tathāgata further teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! Guard the sense faculties, always being mindful and restrained, with mindfulness directed toward clear understanding, guarding the mindful mind and achieving accomplishment, constantly maintaining clear comprehension. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp at its sign, nor relish the form. Because of contention and anger, guard the eye faculty. Do not let covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind, and for that reason guard the eye faculty. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognizes a mental object, do not grasp at its sign, nor relish the object. Because of contention and anger, guard the mind faculty. Do not let covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind, and for that reason guard the mind faculty.'

"Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu guards the sense faculties, is always mindful and restrained, with mindfulness directed toward clear understanding, guarding the mindful mind and achieving accomplishment, constantly maintaining clear comprehension, when the eye sees a form, does not grasp at its sign, does not relish the form, because of contention and anger guards the eye faculty, does not let covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind, and for that reason guards the eye faculty; likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body; when the mind cognizes a mental object, does not grasp at its sign, does not relish the object, because of contention and anger guards the mind faculty, does not let covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind, and for that reason guards the mind faculty, the Tathāgata further teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! With clear comprehension when going out and coming in, well observing and discerning, bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, with dignified and composed deportment, properly wearing the saṅghāṭī robe and other robes and bowl, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and being silent, in all things maintain clear comprehension.'

"Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu maintains clear comprehension when going out and coming in, well observing and discerning, bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, with dignified and composed deportment, properly wearing the saṅghāṭī robe and other robes and bowl, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and being silent, in all things maintaining clear comprehension, the Tathāgata further teaches him: 'Bhikṣu, come! Dwell alone in seclusion, in a secluded place, whether at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet place, in a mountain cave or rock shelter, in the open air, or among haystacks, or in a forest, or dwelling among graves. Having gone to a secluded place, or to an empty and quiet place at the foot of a tree, spread out your sitting mat, sit cross-legged with body upright, set your aspiration correctly, direct your mindfulness, and abandon covetousness: let your mind be free of contention. Seeing others' property and the various necessities of life, do not give rise to covetousness wishing them to be yours. Purify your mind of covetousness. Likewise with anger, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse; abandon doubt, cross over perplexity. Regarding wholesome states, have no uncertainty. Purify your mind of doubt and perplexity. Having abandoned these five hindrances, which are mental defilements that weaken wisdom, secluded from desires, secluded from evil unwholesome states, attain and abide in the fourth jhāna.' Moggallāna, when a bhikṣu is secluded from desires, secluded from evil unwholesome states, and attains and abides in the fourth jhāna; Moggallāna, the Tathāgata greatly benefits the young bhikṣus through this training and instruction. Moggallāna, for those bhikṣus who are elders, seniors, and long-trained in the holy life, the Tathāgata further teaches them the ultimate, namely the complete exhaustion of all defilements."

The arithmetician Moggallāna then further asked: "Śramaṇa Gautama, do all your disciples, being thus trained and instructed, attain the ultimate knowledge and surely reach nirvāṇa?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Moggallāna, not all necessarily attain it. Some attain it, and some do not."

The arithmetician Moggallāna further asked: "Gautama, what is the cause and condition here? There exists nirvāṇa, and there exists the path to nirvāṇa. The śramaṇa Gautama is the present guide. Yet some bhikṣus, being thus trained and instructed, attain the ultimate nirvāṇa, while some do not?"

The World-Honored One said: "Moggallāna, I shall ask you in return; answer as you understand. Moggallāna, what do you think? Do you know where the city of Rājagṛha is, and are you familiar with the road there?"

The arithmetician Moggallāna answered: "Indeed, I know where the city of Rājagṛha is, and I am familiar with the road there."

The World-Honored One asked: "Moggallāna, suppose someone came wishing to see the king and go to Rājagṛha. That person asks you: 'I wish to see the king and go to Rājagṛha. The arithmetician Moggallāna knows where Rājagṛha is and is familiar with the roads and paths. Can you show me the way?' You tell that person: 'Going east from here, you will reach such-and-such a village. From that village, you will reach such-and-such a town. Thus proceeding successively, you will reach Rājagṛha. Outside of Rājagṛha there are beautiful gardens, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and also clear springs; you will see and know all of this.' That person, having heard your words and received your instruction, sets out eastward, but before long abandons the correct road and takes a wrong path back. He does not see or know any of the beautiful gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs.

"Suppose another person comes wishing to see the king and go to Rājagṛha. That person asks you: 'I wish to see the king and go to Rājagṛha. The arithmetician Moggallāna knows where Rājagṛha is and is familiar with the roads and paths. Can you show me the way?' You tell that person: 'Going east from here, you will reach such-and-such a village. From that village, you will reach such-and-such a town. Thus proceeding successively, you will reach Rājagṛha. Outside of Rājagṛha there are beautiful gardens, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and also clear springs; you will see and know all of this.' That person, having heard your words and received your instruction, sets out eastward and reaches such-and-such a village. From that village he proceeds to such-and-such a town. Thus proceeding successively, he reaches Rājagṛha. Outside of Rājagṛha there are beautiful gardens, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs; he sees and knows all of this.

"Moggallāna, what is the cause and condition here? There exists the city of Rājagṛha, and there exists the road to Rājagṛha. You are the present guide. Yet the first person, following your instruction, before long abandons the level road and takes a wrong path back, and does not see or know the beautiful gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs. While the second person, following your instruction, proceeds along the level road and successively reaches Rājagṛha, and sees and knows all the beautiful gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs?"

The arithmetician Moggallāna answered: "Gautama, I have nothing to do with it. There exists the city of Rājagṛha, and there exists the road to Rājagṛha. I am the present guide. The first person did not follow my instruction, abandoned the level road, and took a wrong path back, and did not see or know the beautiful gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs. The second person followed my instruction, proceeded along the level road, and successively reached Rājagṛha, and saw and knew all the beautiful gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long river, and clear springs."

The World-Honored One said: "Just so, Moggallāna. I likewise have nothing to do with it. There exists nirvāṇa, and there exists the path to nirvāṇa. I am the guide. I train and instruct the bhikṣus thus, and some attain the ultimate nirvāṇa while some do not. Moggallāna, each simply follows the path that each bhikṣu walks. At that time, the World-Honored One then confirmed the practice of those who attain the ultimate exhaustion of all defilements."

The arithmetician Moggallāna said: "Gautama, I have understood. Gautama, I have comprehended. Gautama, it is like good soil with a sāla forest, and in that forest there is a keeper of the sāla forest who is wise, capable, and untiring. He digs around the sāla roots at the proper time, levels the high places and fills in the low, fertilizes and irrigates them without missing the right time. If foul and unwholesome weeds grow nearby, he pulls them all out and discards them. If there are crooked and misshapen trees that are not straight, he trims them all. If there are excellent, straight trees growing in the center, he carefully nurtures and protects them, digging, fertilizing, and irrigating at the proper time, never missing the right time. Thus the sāla forest on good soil grows ever more flourishing and beautiful. Gautama, likewise, if there are people who are flattering, deceitful, dishonest, thoroughly unaspiring, faithless, lazy, lacking mindfulness, lacking concentration, with poor wisdom, with distracted minds and uncontrolled faculties, who are lax in observing the precepts and do not broadly cultivate the śramaṇa life; Gautama, one cannot work together with such people. Why? Gautama, such people defile the holy life. Gautama, if there are people who are not flattering, not deceitful, who are aspiring and faithful, diligent and untiring, mindful, concentrated, and also wise, who greatly revere the precepts and broadly cultivate the śramaṇa life; Gautama, one can work together with such people. Why? Gautama, such people purify the holy life.

"Gautama, just as among all root fragrances, aloeswood is the foremost. Why? Gautama, because aloeswood is supreme among all root fragrances. Gautama, just as among all heartwood fragrances, red sandalwood is the foremost. Why? Gautama, because red sandalwood is supreme among all heartwood fragrances. Gautama, just as among all water flowers, the blue lotus is the foremost. Why? Gautama, because the blue lotus is supreme among all water flowers. Gautama, just as among all land flowers, the sumanā flower is the foremost. Why? Gautama, because the sumanā flower is supreme among all land flowers. Gautama, just as among all debaters in the world, the śramaṇa Gautama is the foremost. Why? Because the śramaṇa Gautama, as a debater, is able to overcome all the various non-Buddhist schools. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The arithmetician Moggallāna and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Gaṇaka Moggallāna, Number Three.
