## (145) Sūtra on Gopaka Moggallāna, Fourth of the Brahmin Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, not long after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra was governing Rājagṛha, on account of guarding against the Vajjians. Thereupon, the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra dispatched the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna as an overseer of field-workers to the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having passed the night, at dawn dressed in his robes and took up his bowl, intending to enter Rājagṛha for alms. Then the Venerable Ānanda had this thought: "Let me set aside begging for alms in Rājagṛha for now. I should rather go to the place where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna oversees the field-workers." Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda went to the place of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, the overseer of field-workers.

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, seeing the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar, immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his garment, joined his palms toward the Venerable Ānanda, and said: "Welcome, Ānanda! It has been long since you came here. Please sit on this seat." The Venerable Ānanda then sat on that seat.

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda and, sitting to one side, said: "Ānanda, I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Moggallāna, you may ask. Having heard, I shall consider."

He then asked: "Ānanda, is there a single bhikṣu who is equal to the ascetic Gotama?"

While the Venerable Ānanda and the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna were discussing this matter, at that time the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra, while visiting the field-workers to encourage them, came to the place of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, the overseer of field-workers.

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra, seeing from afar the Venerable Ānanda seated among the field-workers of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, went to the Venerable Ānanda, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and asked: "Ānanda, what matter are you discussing with the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna? For what reason have you gathered here?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna asked me: 'Ānanda, is there a single bhikṣu who is equal to the ascetic Gotama?'"

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, how did you answer him?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, there is no single bhikṣu who is fully equal to the World-Honored One."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Indeed, Ānanda, there is no single bhikṣu fully equal to the World-Honored One. But is there a single bhikṣu whom the ascetic Gotama, while he was alive, appointed, saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus,' whom you now rely upon?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, there is no single bhikṣu who was known and seen by the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, whom he appointed while alive, saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus,' whom we now rely upon."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, indeed, there is no single bhikṣu fully equal to the ascetic Gotama; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the ascetic Gotama, while alive, appointed, saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus,' whom you now rely upon. But is there a single bhikṣu whom the Sangha has harmoniously assembled and selected, so that after the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu serves as the refuge for the bhikṣus, whom you now rely upon?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, there is also no single bhikṣu whom the Sangha has harmoniously assembled and selected, so that after the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu serves as the refuge for the bhikṣus, whom we now rely upon."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, indeed, there is no single bhikṣu fully equal to the ascetic Gotama; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the ascetic Gotama, while alive, appointed, saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus,' whom you now rely upon; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the Sangha has harmoniously assembled and selected, so that after the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu serves as the refuge for the bhikṣus, whom you now rely upon. Ānanda, if this is so, then having no refuge, how do you dwell in harmony, without contention, in safety, with a unified teaching, blended as water and milk, traveling happily, as when the ascetic Gotama was alive?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Vassakāra, do not speak thus, saying that we have no refuge. Why is this? We do have a refuge."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda, how is it that your earlier and later statements do not accord? Ānanda, you previously said: 'There is no single bhikṣu fully equal to the World-Honored One; nor is there a single bhikṣu who was known and seen by the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, whom he appointed while alive, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus," whom we now rely upon; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the Sangha has harmoniously assembled and selected, so that after the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu serves as the refuge for the bhikṣus, whom we now rely upon.' Ānanda, for what cause and reason do you now say you have a refuge?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, we do not rely upon a person but rely upon the Dharma. Vassakāra, when we travel among villages and towns, on the fifteenth day, at the time of reciting the Prātimokṣa, we gather and sit together in one place. If there is a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, we request that bhikṣu to expound the Dharma for us. If the assembly is pure, we all joyfully practice what that bhikṣu teaches. If the assembly is not pure, according to what the Dharma prescribes, we instruct that it be done accordingly."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda, it is not you who instruct that it be done so; rather, it is the Dharma that instructs it be done so. Ānanda, if even a little Dharma, or much Dharma, can endure for a long time, then in this way the Venerable Ānanda and his companions dwell in harmony, without contention, in safety, with a unified teaching, blended as water and milk, traveling happily, as when the ascetic Gotama was alive."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, is there something worthy of veneration?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, there is something worthy of veneration."

Vassakāra said: "Ānanda, how is it that your earlier and later statements do not accord? Ānanda, you previously said: 'There is no single bhikṣu fully equal to the World-Honored One; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the World-Honored One, while alive, appointed, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu shall be the refuge for the bhikṣus," whom we now rely upon; nor is there a single bhikṣu whom the Sangha has harmoniously assembled and selected, so that after the World-Honored One's parinirvāṇa, this bhikṣu serves as the refuge for the bhikṣus, whom we now rely upon.' Ānanda, for what cause and reason do you now say there is something worthy of veneration?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught ten qualities that are worthy of veneration. If we see a bhikṣu possessing these ten qualities, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies. What are the ten?

"Vassakāra, a bhikṣu cultivates and practices the precepts, guards the Prātimokṣa, and further, well governs deportment and propriety. Seeing even the slightest offense, he constantly harbors fear and dread. He upholds and trains in the precepts. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in the practice of the higher precepts, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu is broadly learned and much heard, retains what he has learned and does not forget, and accumulates extensive learning. The teachings that are called the Dharma are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and text, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life. Such teachings he broadly learns, much hears, recites and studies to the thousands, reflects upon them with his mind, and clearly perceives their profound depth. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in broad learning, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu is a good spiritual friend, a good companion, and a good associate. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in being a good spiritual friend, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu delights in dwelling in seclusion and achieves two kinds of seclusion: of body and of mind. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in delighting in seclusion, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu delights in quiet meditation, inwardly practices right concentration, and does not abandon investigation. He achieves contemplation and increases the practice of emptiness. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in delighting in quiet meditation, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu is content. His robes serve only to cover his body; his food serves only to sustain his frame. Wherever he travels, he goes with his robes and bowl, moving without attachment. Just as a hawk or bird, with its two wings, soars through the sky, so too a bhikṣu is content. His robes serve only to cover his body; his food serves only to sustain his frame. Wherever he travels, he goes with his robes and bowl, moving without attachment. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in contentment, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu constantly practices mindfulness and achieves right mindfulness. What was long ago practiced and long ago heard, he always remembers and does not forget. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in right mindfulness, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome states. He constantly arouses his intention, focused and firm, establishing the roots of wholesomeness, never abandoning skillful means. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in energetic diligence, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu cultivates wisdom, contemplating the nature of arising and ceasing. He attains such knowledge, noble wisdom that is clear and penetrating, discerning and understanding, so as to rightly put an end to suffering. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who excels in practicing wisdom, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, a bhikṣu whose outflows are entirely exhausted, having attained the outflow-free state, liberated in mind and liberated in wisdom, knows for himself and realizes for himself, accomplishing and abiding in the realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence'; he knows it as it truly is. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies.

"Vassakāra, the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, taught these ten qualities as worthy of veneration. Vassakāra, if we see a bhikṣu who practices these ten qualities, we together cherish, respect, honor, support, revere, and serve that bhikṣu with ceremonies."

Thereupon, that great assembly raised a loud, great voice: "The straight path can indeed be cultivated, it is not impossible to cultivate. If one cultivates the straight path and it is not impossible to cultivate, one follows the Arahants in the world with cherishing, respect, honor, support, and ceremonial service. If the venerables can indeed cultivate the straight path and are able to cultivate it, therefore the Arahants in the world are cherished, respected, honored, supported, and served with ceremonies."

Then the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra and his retinue asked: "Ānanda, where are you staying now?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "I am now staying in this Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park in Rājagṛha."

"Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park, is extremely delightful, neat and pleasing. In the daytime it is not noisy; at night it is quiet and still. There are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor flies or fleas. It is neither cold nor hot. Ānanda, do you enjoy dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "So it is, Vassakāra. So it is, Vassakāra. The Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park, is extremely delightful, neat and pleasing. In the daytime it is not noisy; at night it is quiet and still. There are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor flies or fleas. It is neither cold nor hot. Vassakāra, I enjoy dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park. Why is this? Because of the World-Honored One's protection."

At that time, General Upananda was in that assembly. General Upananda said: "So it is, Vassakāra. So it is, Vassakāra. The Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park, is extremely delightful, neat and pleasing. In the daytime it is not noisy; at night it is quiet and still. There are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor flies or fleas. It is neither cold nor hot. The venerable one enjoys dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park. Why is this? Because this venerable one practices jhāna and delights in jhāna."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra, having heard this, said: "General Upananda! The ascetic Gotama formerly traveled in the Jīvaka Mango Grove. General Upananda! At that time, I frequently went to visit him and saw the ascetic Gotama. Why is this? The ascetic Gotama practiced jhāna and delighted in jhāna, and he praised all jhāna."

The Venerable Ānanda, having heard this, said: "Vassakāra, do not speak thus, that the ascetic Gotama praised all jhāna. Why is this? The World-Honored One sometimes praised jhāna and sometimes did not praise jhāna."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, when the ascetic Gotama did not praise jhāna, what kind of jhāna did he not praise?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, suppose someone is entangled by sensual desire and gives rise to sensual desire, not knowing the escape from it as it truly is. Because he is obstructed by sensual desire, he dwells in jhāna, intensifies jhāna, and deepens jhāna. Vassakāra, this is called the first kind of jhāna that the World-Honored One did not praise.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, suppose someone is entangled by ill-will and gives rise to ill-will, not knowing the escape from it as it truly is. Because he is obstructed by ill-will, he dwells in jhāna, intensifies jhāna, and deepens jhāna. Vassakāra, this is called the second kind of jhāna that the World-Honored One did not praise.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, suppose someone is entangled by sloth-and-torpor and gives rise to sloth-and-torpor, not knowing the escape from it as it truly is. Because he is obstructed by sloth-and-torpor, he dwells in jhāna, intensifies jhāna, and deepens jhāna. Vassakāra, this is called the third kind of jhāna that the World-Honored One did not praise.

"Furthermore, Vassakāra, suppose someone is entangled by doubt and gives rise to doubt, not knowing the escape from it as it truly is. Because he is obstructed by doubt, he dwells in jhāna, intensifies jhāna, and deepens jhāna. Vassakāra, this is called the fourth kind of jhāna that the World-Honored One did not praise.

"Vassakāra, the World-Honored One did not praise these four kinds of jhāna."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda, these four kinds of jhāna are subject to increase and subject to conditions for increase. The ascetic Gotama did not praise them. Why is this? Because he was perfectly and fully enlightened."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra further asked: "Ānanda, what kinds of jhāna did the ascetic Gotama praise?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra, when a bhikṣu, secluded from desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains up to the fourth jhāna and abides in its accomplishment, Vassakāra, the World-Honored One praised these four jhānas."

The Magadhan great minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda, these four jhānas are worthy of praise and are conditions for praise. The ascetic Gotama praised them. Why is this? Because he was perfectly and fully enlightened. Ānanda, I have many pressing affairs and beg leave to return."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "You may return as you wish."

Thereupon, the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, well received and well retained it. He rose from his seat, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda three times, and departed.

At that time, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, not long after the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra had departed, said: "Ānanda, you have not at all answered the question I asked you?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Moggallāna, indeed I did not answer."

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said: "Ānanda, I have another question to ask. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Moggallāna, you may ask. Having heard, I shall consider."

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna then asked: "Ānanda, regarding the liberation of the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the liberation of the wisdom-liberated one, and the liberation of the Arahant: is there any difference among these three liberations? Is there any superiority or inferiority?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Moggallāna, regarding the liberation of the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the liberation of the wisdom-liberated one, and the liberation of the Arahant: among these three liberations there is no difference, nor any superiority or inferiority."

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said: "Ānanda, please take your meal here." The Venerable Ānanda accepted in silence.

The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, knowing he had silently accepted, immediately rose from his seat and personally carried the washing water. Extremely fine, pure, and exquisite, with abundant and various foods to eat, chew, and swallow, he personally ladled and served until the Venerable Ānanda was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels removed, and the washing water had been served, the brahmin took a small seat and sat separately to hear the Dharma.

The Venerable Ānanda expounded the Dharma for him, encouraging and inspiring him, establishing him in joy. With immeasurable skillful means he expounded the Dharma for him, encouraging and inspiring him, establishing him in joy. The Venerable Ānanda spoke thus. The retinue of the Magadhan great minister Vassakāra and the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Gopaka Moggallāna, Fourth.

---

## (146) Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint, Fifth of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the wanderer Pilotika, early in the morning, went out from Śrāvastī to the Buddha's abode, bowed his head in salutation, and sat to one side. The Buddha expounded the Dharma for him, encouraging and inspiring him, establishing him in joy. With immeasurable skillful means he expounded the Dharma for him, encouraging and inspiring him, establishing him in joy, and then remained silent. The wanderer Pilotika, after the Buddha had expounded the Dharma, encouraging and inspiring him, establishing him in joy, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, riding an extremely fine white chariot, together with five hundred disciples, in the early morning went out from Śrāvastī to a secluded place, intending to teach his disciples the chanting and study of scriptures. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, seeing the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar, asked him: "Vaccha! Where have you come from so early in the morning?"

The wanderer Pilotika answered: "Brahmin, I have come from seeing the World-Honored One, paying respects and making offerings."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Vaccha, do you happen to know the wisdom learned by the ascetic Gotama in empty, tranquil places?"

The wanderer Pilotika answered: "Brahmin, what kind of person could know the wisdom the World-Honored One learned in empty, tranquil places? Brahmin, if one could know the wisdom the World-Honored One learned in empty, tranquil places, that person would have to be like him. However, brahmin, in the texts I have studied there are four points of reasoning. Because of these four points, I am certain in my faith that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Brahmin, it is like a skilled elephant tracker roaming in the wilderness who, in a forest, sees a large elephant footprint. Having seen it, he is certain that the elephant must be extremely large to leave such a footprint. Brahmin, I too am like this. In the texts I have studied there are four points of reasoning, and because of these four points, I am certain in my faith that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"What are the four points? Brahmin, there are wise kṣatriya debaters, broadly learned and decisive, able to vanquish people of the world, with nothing they do not know. With their various views they compose treatises and circulate them in the world. They think: 'I shall go to the ascetic Gotama and ask such and such questions. If he can answer, I shall question him further. If he cannot answer, I shall defeat him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is traveling in a certain village or town and go there. Having seen the World-Honored One, they do not even dare to ask, let alone defeat him. Brahmin, in the texts I have studied, I obtained this first point of reasoning. Because of this point, I am certain in my faith that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Likewise, there are wise brahmin debaters, wise householder debaters, and wise ascetic debaters, broadly learned and decisive, able to vanquish people of the world, with nothing they do not know. With their various views they compose treatises and circulate them in the world. They think: 'I shall go to the ascetic Gotama and ask such and such questions. If he can answer, I shall question him further. If he cannot answer, I shall defeat him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is traveling in a certain village or town and go there. Having seen the World-Honored One, they do not even dare to ask, let alone defeat him. Brahmin, in the texts I have studied, I obtained this fourth point of reasoning. Because of this point, I am certain in my faith that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Brahmin, in the texts I have studied there are these four points of reasoning. Because of these four points, I am certain in my faith that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said: "Vaccha, you greatly honor and serve the ascetic Gotama. Whatever the cause and condition, you rejoice and practice accordingly."

The wanderer Pilotika replied: "Brahmin, so it is, so it is. I greatly honor and serve that World-Honored One and greatly praise him. All the world should likewise make offerings."

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, having heard this meaning, immediately descended from his chariot, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park, and three times made salutation: "Homage to the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One." Having done so three times, he mounted his fine white chariot again and went to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. Arriving at the place for dismounting, he dismounted and walked forward to the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat to one side.

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi related in full to the Buddha the discussion he had previously had with the wanderer Pilotika. The World-Honored One, having heard it, said: "Brahmin, the wanderer Pilotika's simile of the elephant's footprint was not well made, nor was it complete. As for a well-made and complete simile of the elephant's footprint, I shall now teach it to you. Listen well.

"Brahmin, suppose a skilled elephant tracker, roaming in the wilderness, sees in a forest a large elephant footprint. Having seen it, he is certain that the elephant must be extremely large to leave such a footprint.

"Brahmin, that skilled elephant tracker might not yet be convinced, thinking: 'In this forest there is also a female elephant named Kāliṇī, whose body is extremely tall and large. She might have made this footprint.' He follows this footprint and again sees a large elephant footprint. Having seen it, he is certain that the elephant must be extremely large to leave such a footprint.

"Brahmin, that skilled elephant tracker might still not be convinced, thinking: 'In this forest there is also another female elephant named Kāḷārikā, whose body is extremely tall and large. She might have made this footprint.' He follows this footprint and again sees a large elephant footprint. Having seen it, he is certain that the elephant must be extremely large to leave such a footprint.

"Brahmin, that skilled elephant tracker might still not be convinced, thinking: 'In this forest there is yet another female elephant named Vāmaṇī, whose body is extremely tall and large. She might have made this footprint.' He follows this footprint and again sees a large elephant footprint. Having seen it, he is certain that the elephant must be extremely large to leave such a footprint.

"Having followed this footprint, he sees a great elephant's track: the footprints are square, extremely long and extremely broad, pressed all around, deeply sunk into the earth. And he sees that elephant, either going or coming, standing or running, standing still or lying down. Having seen that elephant, he thinks: 'With such footprints, it must be a great elephant.'

"Brahmin, in the same way, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Persons, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, he, in this world, among gods and Māra, Brahmā, ascetics and brahmins, and among gods and humans, knows for himself, realizes for himself, accomplishes and abides in the realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence'; he knows it as it truly is.

"He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and text, complete and pure, manifesting the holy life.

"The Dharma that he teaches, a householder or householder's son, having heard it, gains faith in the Tathāgata's right Dharma and discipline. Having gained faith, he thinks: 'The household life is confined and narrow, a place of dust and toil. Going forth into homelessness to train in the path is open and vast. Now while I live at home, I am bound by shackles and cannot, for the span of my life, purely cultivate the holy life. I should rather abandon a small or large amount of wealth, leave behind a small or large circle of relatives, shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leave home for the homeless life to train in the path.'

"At a later time, he abandons a small or large amount of wealth, leaves behind a small or large circle of relatives, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaves home for the homeless life to train in the path. Having gone forth, he leaves behind the signs of the householder's life and receives the essentials of the bhikṣu. He cultivates and practices the precepts, guards the Prātimokṣa, and further well governs deportment and propriety. Seeing even the slightest offense, he constantly harbors fear and dread. He upholds and trains in the precepts.

"He abstains from killing and abandons killing. He gives up the knife and club, has a sense of shame and conscience, has a compassionate heart, and benefits all beings, even insects. His mind is purified regarding killing.

"He abstains from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given. He takes only what is given and delights in taking what is given. He constantly enjoys giving, is joyful and generous without stinginess, and does not expect reward. His mind is purified regarding taking what is not given.

"He abstains from unchastity and abandons unchastity. He diligently cultivates the holy life, striving in the excellent practice, pure and undefiled, free from desire and abandoning sexual conduct. His mind is purified regarding unchastity.

"He abstains from false speech and abandons false speech. He speaks truth, delights in truth, abides in truth, is unwavering. All his words are trustworthy and he does not deceive the world. His mind is purified regarding false speech.

"He abstains from divisive speech and abandons divisive speech. He does not practice divisive speech. He does not break up others. He does not hear words here and report them there, wishing to break up these people; he does not hear words there and report them here, wishing to break up those people. Those who are separated he wishes to reconcile; those who are united he causes to rejoice. He does not form factions, does not delight in factions, and does not speak in praise of factional matters. His mind is purified regarding divisive speech.

"He abstains from harsh speech and abandons harsh speech. Whatever words are coarse and rough in tone, with ugly sound offensive to the ear, displeasing to all, unloved by all, causing others pain and preventing concentration, he abandons such speech. Whatever words are gentle, harmonious, and soft, pleasing to the ear and entering the heart, delightful and beloved, bringing peace to others, with clear and complete voice that does not frighten people, enabling others to gain concentration, he speaks such words. His mind is purified regarding harsh speech.

"He abstains from frivolous speech and abandons frivolous speech. He speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks on the Dharma, speaks on the meaning, speaks on cessation, and delights in speaking on cessation. His words are timely and appropriate, with good instruction and good admonition. His mind is purified regarding frivolous speech.

"He abstains from trading and abandons trading. He gives up weighing and measuring with scales and bushels. He does not accept bribes, does not bind and constrain people, does not hope to gain by short-changing in measures, and does not use small advantages to cheat others. His mind is purified regarding trading.

"He abstains from accepting widows and young girls and abandons accepting widows and young girls. His mind is purified regarding accepting widows and young girls.

"He abstains from accepting male and female slaves and abandons accepting male and female slaves. His mind is purified regarding accepting male and female slaves.

"He abstains from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and abandons accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. His mind is purified regarding accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep.

"He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs, and abandons accepting chickens and pigs. His mind is purified regarding accepting chickens and pigs.

"He abstains from accepting farmland and shops, and abandons accepting farmland and shops. His mind is purified regarding accepting farmland and shops.

"He abstains from accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans, and abandons accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans. His mind is purified regarding accepting raw rice, wheat, and beans.

"He abstains from alcohol and abandons alcohol. His mind is purified regarding drinking alcohol.

"He abstains from high and broad beds and abandons high and broad beds. His mind is purified regarding high and broad beds.

"He abstains from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics, and abandons flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics. His mind is purified regarding flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics.

"He abstains from singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen to them, and abandons singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen to them. His mind is purified regarding singing, dancing, performances, and going to watch and listen to them.

"He abstains from accepting gold, silver, and precious gems, and abandons accepting gold, silver, and precious gems. His mind is purified regarding accepting gold, silver, and precious gems.

"He abstains from eating after midday and abandons eating after midday. He eats one meal, does not eat at night, and trains in eating at the proper time. His mind is purified regarding eating after midday.

"Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, he further practices extreme contentment. His robes serve only to cover his body; his food serves only to sustain his frame. Wherever he travels, he goes with his robes and bowl, moving without attachment, just as a hawk or bird, with its two wings, soars through the sky.

"Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts and extreme contentment, he further guards the sense faculties. He is constantly mindful to close and block them, with the aspiration for clear understanding. Guarding mindful awareness and achieving its accomplishment, he constantly maintains clear knowing. When the eye sees a form, he does not grasp at its sign, nor does he relish the form. Because contention and strife might arise, he guards the eye faculty. So that covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states might not arise in his mind and tend toward those objects, he guards the eye faculty. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognizes a mental object, he does not grasp at its sign, nor does he relish the mental object. Because contention and strife might arise, he guards the mind faculty. So that covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states might not arise in his mind and tend toward those objects, he guards the mind faculty.

"Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, extreme contentment, and guarding of the sense faculties, he further maintains clear knowing in going out and coming in, well observing and distinguishing. In bending and stretching, looking down and up, his bearing is composed and orderly. He properly wears the saṅghāṭī and all robes and the bowl. In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in sleeping and waking, in speaking and being silent, he maintains clear knowing of all.

"Having accomplished this aggregate of noble precepts, extreme contentment, guarding of the sense faculties, and clear knowing in going out and coming in, he further dwells alone in seclusion, in an uninhabited place: beneath a tree, in a quiet, empty spot, in a mountain cave or rock chamber, in the open air or among straw heaps, in a forest, or among tombs.

"Having already gone to an uninhabited place, beneath a tree, in a quiet, empty spot, he spreads his sitting cloth, sits cross-legged, holds his body upright, sets up right aspiration, and turns his mindfulness inward. He abandons covetousness; his mind is without contention. Seeing others' possessions and means of livelihood, he does not give rise to covetousness wishing he might obtain them. His mind is purified regarding covetousness.

"Likewise regarding ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse: he abandons doubt and overcomes perplexity. Regarding all wholesome states, he has no hesitation. His mind is purified regarding doubt.

"Having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind and weakeners of wisdom, secluded from desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains the first jhāna and abides in its accomplishment.

"Brahmin, this is what the Tathāgata has trodden, where the Tathāgata has walked, and what the Tathāgata has experienced. Yet he does not take this as the end, concluding that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"With initial thought and sustained thought having subsided, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains the second jhāna and abides in its accomplishment.

"Brahmin, this is what the Tathāgata has trodden, where the Tathāgata has walked, and what the Tathāgata has experienced. Yet he does not take this as the end, concluding that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Having separated from joy and desire, he abides with equanimity, without craving, mindful and clearly knowing, and the body experiences happiness. As the noble ones describe it: 'With equanimity and mindfulness he dwells in happiness.' He attains the third jhāna and abides in its accomplishment.

"Brahmin, this is what the Tathāgata has trodden, where the Tathāgata has walked, and what the Tathāgata has experienced. Yet he does not take this as the end, concluding that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"With the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, and with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, he attains the fourth jhāna and abides in its accomplishment.

"Brahmin, this is what the Tathāgata has trodden, where the Tathāgata has walked, and what the Tathāgata has experienced. Yet he does not take this as the end, concluding that the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and that the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure and without defilement, free from afflictions, pliant, well-settled, and having attained the immovable mind, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows and the realization of direct knowledge. He knows this is suffering as it truly is. He knows this is the origin of suffering. He knows this is the cessation of suffering. He knows this is the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. He knows these are the outflows as they truly are. He knows this is the origin of the outflows. He knows this is the cessation of the outflows. He knows this is the path to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is.

"Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence'; he knows it as it truly is.

"Brahmin, this is what the Tathāgata has trodden, where the Tathāgata has walked, and what the Tathāgata has experienced. He takes this as the end, concluding: the World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Unattached One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One is excellent; and the Tathāgata's assembly of disciples is well-directed.

"Brahmin, what do you think? Is such a simile of the elephant's footprint well made and complete?"

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi answered: "Indeed so, Gotama. Such a simile of the elephant's footprint is well made and complete."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said: "World-Honored One, I have understood! Well-Gone One, I have comprehended! World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forth, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until my life ends."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi and the wanderer Pilotika, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint, Fifth.

---

## (147) Sūtra on the Merit of Learning, Sixth of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, in the afternoon while strolling, went to the Buddha's abode, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Gotama, I wish to ask something. Only if you permit do I dare to present it."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, ask as you wish."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi then asked: "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, whether they are householders or those who have gone forth to train in the path, for what purpose do they engage in broad learning and recitation?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, my disciples, whether householders or those who have gone forth to train in the path, engage in broad learning and recitation because they wish to tame themselves, wish to calm themselves, and seek their own complete cessation. Brahmin, my disciples, whether householders or those who have gone forth to train in the path, engage in broad learning and recitation for this purpose."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, is there a distinction in broad learning and recitation? Is there merit in broad learning and recitation?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, there is a distinction in broad learning and recitation, and there is merit in broad learning and recitation."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, what distinctions and what merits does broad learning and recitation have?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple performs work during the day, wishing to gain profit from it. If his work fails and does not succeed, after the failure and non-success of his work, he nevertheless does not grieve, worry, lament, or cry, does not beat his chest in anguish, nor does he go mad. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple performs work during the day, wishing to gain profit, and his work fails and does not succeed, yet after the failure and non-success of his work he nevertheless does not grieve, worry, lament, or cry, does not beat his chest in anguish, nor go mad, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, when all that a well-learned noble disciple loves and cherishes changes, dissolves, and is no longer in accord, and he is separated from it, he nevertheless does not grieve, worry, lament, or cry, does not beat his chest in anguish, nor does he go mad. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, when all that he loves and cherishes changes, dissolves, and is no longer in accord, and he is separated from it, nevertheless does not grieve, worry, lament, or cry, does not beat his chest in anguish, nor go mad, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, knowing that all possessions are impermanent, contemplates going forth to train in the path. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, knowing that all possessions are impermanent, contemplates going forth to train in the path, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, knowing that all possessions are impermanent, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaves home for the homeless life to train in the path. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, knowing that all possessions are impermanent, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with full faith leaves home for the homeless life to train in the path, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas, the oppression of wind and sun. He is also able to endure harsh words and beatings. When his body encounters various illnesses, extremely painful, even to the point of life-threatening, and all that is disagreeable, he is able to bear them all. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas, the oppression of wind and sun, is also able to endure harsh words and beatings, and when his body encounters various illnesses, extremely painful, even to the point of life-threatening, and all that is disagreeable, he is able to bear them all, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple can endure displeasure. When displeasure arises, his mind never clings to it. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple can endure displeasure, and when displeasure arises, his mind never clings to it, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple can endure fear. When fear arises, his mind never clings to it. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple can endure fear, and when fear arises, his mind never clings to it, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, if three evil, unwholesome thoughts arise in a well-learned noble disciple: thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of harm, and because of these three evil, unwholesome thoughts, his mind never clings to them. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, when three evil, unwholesome thoughts arise: thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of harm, and because of these three evil, unwholesome thoughts, his mind never clings to them, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, secluded from desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains up to the fourth jhāna and abides in its accomplishment. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, secluded from desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, attains up to the fourth jhāna and abides in its accomplishment, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, with the three fetters having been exhausted, attains stream-entry. He does not fall into evil states, is certain to progress toward perfect enlightenment, and at most undergoes seven more existences. Having gone back and forth seven times between the heavenly and human realms, he reaches the end of suffering. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, with the three fetters having been exhausted, attains stream-entry, does not fall into evil states, is certain to progress toward perfect enlightenment, and at most undergoes seven more existences, having gone back and forth seven times between the heavenly and human realms reaches the end of suffering, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, with the three fetters having been exhausted, and with sensual desire, anger, and delusion attenuated, attains the state of once-returning. Having gone once to the heavenly realm and once to the human realm, he reaches the end of suffering. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, with the three fetters having been exhausted, and with sensual desire, anger, and delusion attenuated, attains the state of once-returning, having gone once to the heavenly realm and once to the human realm reaches the end of suffering, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple, with the five lower fetters exhausted, is born in that realm and there attains parinirvāṇa, attaining the state of non-returning and not returning to this world. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple, with the five lower fetters exhausted, is born in that realm and there attains parinirvāṇa, attaining the state of non-returning and not returning to this world, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple has the tranquil liberation. Having left behind form and attained the formless concentration corresponding to its characteristic, he realizes it with his own body and abides in its accomplishment. Through wisdom's contemplation he severs the outflows and knows the outflows. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple has the tranquil liberation, having left behind form and attained the formless concentration corresponding to its characteristic, realizes it with his own body and abides in its accomplishment, and through wisdom's contemplation severs the outflows and knows the outflows, brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple attains the bases of supernormal power, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the outflows entirely exhausted, having attained the outflow-free state, liberated in mind and liberated in wisdom, in this present life he knows for himself, realizes for himself, accomplishes and abides in the realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence'; he knows it as it truly is. Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple attains the bases of supernormal power, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, with the outflows entirely exhausted, having attained the outflow-free state, liberated in mind and liberated in wisdom, in this present life knows for himself, realizes for himself, accomplishes and abides in the realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more future existence'; he knows it as it truly is; brahmin, this is a distinction and merit of broad learning and recitation."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked the World-Honored One: "This broad learning and recitation has these distinctions and these merits. Are there any further distinctions, further merits, that are supreme, most excellent, and most superior?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, this broad learning and recitation has these distinctions and these merits. There are no further distinctions, no further merits that are supreme, most excellent, or most superior."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said: "World-Honored One, I have understood! Well-Gone One, I have comprehended! World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forth, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until my life ends."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Merit of Learning, Sixth.

## (148) Sūtra on What is Suffering, Seventh of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, in the afternoon while strolling, went to the Buddha's abode, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Gotama, I wish to ask something. Only if you permit do I dare to present it."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, ask as you wish."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi then asked: "Gotama, what is the suffering of a householder? What is the suffering of one who has gone forth to train in the path?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, for a householder, the suffering lies in lack of control. For one who has gone forth to train in the path, the suffering lies in having control."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how is it that for a householder the suffering lies in lack of control? How is it that for one who has gone forth to train in the path the suffering lies in having control?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, if a householder's wealth does not increase, if gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, and crystal all do not increase, if livestock, grain, and male and female servants also do not increase, then at that time the householder grieves, worries, and is troubled. Because of this, a householder has much grief, worry, and trouble. Brahmin, if one who has gone forth to train in the path acts according to his desires, acts according to anger and delusion, then at that time the one who has gone forth grieves, worries, and is troubled. Because of this, one who has gone forth to train in the path has much grief, worry, and trouble. Brahmin, thus for a householder the suffering lies in lack of control, and for one who has gone forth to train in the path the suffering lies in having control."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, what is the happiness of a householder? What is the happiness of one who has gone forth to train in the path?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, for a householder, the happiness lies in having control. For one who has gone forth to train in the path, the happiness lies in lack of control."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how is it that for a householder the happiness lies in having control? How is it that for one who has gone forth to train in the path the happiness lies in lack of control?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, if a householder's wealth increases, if gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, and crystal all increase, if livestock, grain, and male and female servants also increase, then at that time the householder is happy and joyful. Because of this, a householder is very happy and joyful. Brahmin, if one who has gone forth to train in the path does not act according to desire, does not act according to anger and delusion, then at that time the one who has gone forth is happy and joyful. Because of this, one who has gone forth to train in the path is very happy and joyful. Brahmin, thus for a householder the happiness lies in having control, and for one who has gone forth to train in the path the happiness lies in lack of control."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, on account of what are gods and humans certain to have no benefit? On account of what are gods and humans certain to have benefit?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, if gods and humans quarrel with each other, there is certainly no benefit. If gods and humans do not quarrel with each other, there is certainly benefit."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how is it that when gods and humans quarrel with each other there is certainly no benefit? How is it that when gods and humans do not quarrel with each other there is certainly benefit?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, when gods and humans fight, quarrel, and bear enmity toward each other, at that time gods and humans grieve, worry, and are troubled. Because of this, gods and humans have much grief, worry, and trouble. Brahmin, when gods and humans do not fight, do not quarrel, and do not bear enmity toward each other, at that time gods and humans are happy and joyful. Because of this, gods and humans are very happy and joyful. Brahmin, thus when gods and humans quarrel with each other there is certainly no benefit, and when gods and humans do not quarrel with each other there is certainly benefit."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, on account of what are gods and humans certain not to obtain welfare and certain to obtain suffering? On account of what are gods and humans certain to obtain welfare and certain to obtain happiness?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, if gods and humans practice what is contrary to the Dharma and practice evil, they will certainly not obtain welfare and will certainly obtain suffering. If gods and humans practice in accord with the Dharma and do not practice evil, they will certainly obtain welfare and will certainly obtain happiness."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how is it that when gods and humans practice what is contrary to the Dharma and practice evil, they will certainly not obtain welfare and will certainly obtain suffering? How is it that when gods and humans practice in accord with the Dharma and do not practice evil, they will certainly obtain welfare and will certainly obtain happiness?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, when gods and humans practice with their bodies what is contrary to the Dharma and practice evil, and when their speech and minds practice what is contrary to the Dharma and practice evil, at that time gods and humans will certainly decline, and the asuras will certainly flourish.

"Brahmin, when gods and humans practice with their bodies in accord with the Dharma and guard their bodies, and when their speech and minds practice in accord with the Dharma and they guard their speech and minds, at that time gods and humans will certainly flourish, and the asuras will certainly decline.

"Brahmin, thus when gods and humans practice what is contrary to the Dharma and practice evil, they certainly do not obtain welfare and certainly obtain suffering. Brahmin, thus when gods and humans practice in accord with the Dharma and do not practice evil, they certainly obtain welfare and certainly obtain happiness."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how should one view a bad friend?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, one should view a bad friend as being like the moon."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi further asked: "Gotama, how should one view a bad friend as being like the moon?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmin, just as the waning moon day by day gradually diminishes: its palace also diminishes, its light also diminishes, its form and color also diminish, and it dwindles day by day. Brahmin, there comes a time when the moon completely disappears and is no longer seen at all.

"Brahmin, a person who is a bad friend may gain faith in the Tathāgata's right Dharma and discipline. But having gained faith, at a later time he becomes unfilial and disrespectful. His conduct is not in accordance, he does not establish right knowledge, and he does not progress toward the Dharma in due order. Then he loses his faith, and his morality, learning, aspiration, and wisdom are also lost. Brahmin, there comes a time when this bad friend's wholesome qualities are entirely extinguished, just as the moon disappears completely. Brahmin

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtra), Fascicle 37

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva of the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

## (147) Sūtra on Hearing in Accordance with the Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you. What is the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life? It is called 'hearing in accordance with the Dharma.'

"What is hearing in accordance with the Dharma? It is knowing the self and knowing the self as it truly is. How does one know the self and know the self as it truly is?

"A bhikṣu who knows the eye, knows forms, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the ear, knows sounds, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the nose, knows odors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the tongue, knows flavors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the body, knows tangibles, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the mind, knows mental objects, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the eye? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the eye-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the eye.

"What are forms? It is called the external four great elements and the forms derived from the four great elements, being forms that can be seen and are resistant. This is called form.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the eye faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the eye faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the ear? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the ear-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the ear.

"What are sounds? It is called the external four great elements and the sounds derived from the four great elements, being sounds that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called sound.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the ear faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the ear faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the nose? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the nose-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the nose.

"What are odors? It is called the external four great elements and the odors derived from the four great elements, being odors that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called odor.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the nose faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the nose faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the tongue? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the tongue-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the tongue.

"What are flavors? It is called the external four great elements and the flavors derived from the four great elements, being flavors that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called flavor.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the tongue faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the tongue faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the body? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the body-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the body.

"What are tangibles? It is called the external four great elements and the tangibles derived from the four great elements, being tangibles that cannot be seen and are resistant. This is called tangible.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the body faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the body faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the mind? It is called the mind, the intention, the consciousness. This is called the mind.

"What are mental objects? It is called the external mental objects that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called mental objects.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the mind faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the mind faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"This is called hearing in accordance with the Dharma."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.
