## (148) Sūtra on the Explanation of What Was Said

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you. What is the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life?

"There is a verse whose meaning has not yet been explained. I will now explain it for you. What is it?

"'Examining the inner,
And examining the outer,
In examination one attains firm abiding,
This is what should be known.'

"What is examining the inner? A bhikṣu who knows the eye, knows forms, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the ear, knows sounds, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the nose, knows odors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the tongue, knows flavors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the body, knows tangibles, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the mind, knows mental objects, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"This is called examining the inner.

"What is examining the outer? A bhikṣu who knows the eye, knows forms, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the ear, knows sounds, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the nose, knows odors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the tongue, knows flavors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the body, knows tangibles, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the mind, knows mental objects, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"This is called examining the outer.

"What is 'in examination one attains firm abiding'? A bhikṣu who with the body, in one's experience, practices recollection and is not forgetful, this is called 'in examination one attains firm abiding.'

"This is the explanation of the verse:

"'Examining the inner,
And examining the outer,
In examination one attains firm abiding,
This is what should be known.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the mind, knows mental objects, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"This is called examining the inner.

"What is examining the outer? A bhikṣu who knows the eye, knows forms, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the ear, knows sounds, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the nose, knows odors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the tongue, knows flavors, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the body, knows tangibles, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"One knows the mind, knows mental objects, knows the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"This is called examining the outer.

"What is 'in examination one attains firm abiding'? A bhikṣu who with the body, in one's experience, practices recollection and is not forgetful, this is called 'in examination one attains firm abiding.'

"This is the verse:

"'Examining the inner,
And examining the outer,
In examination one attains firm abiding,
This is what should be known.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

## (150) Sūtra on the Yoke

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you. What is the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good words, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life? It is the teaching of the six pairs of sense-bases.

"What are the six pairs of sense-bases? Knowing the eye, knowing forms, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"Knowing the ear, knowing sounds, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"Knowing the nose, knowing odors, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"Knowing the tongue, knowing flavors, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"Knowing the body, knowing tangibles, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"Knowing the mind, knowing mental objects, knowing the bondage arising dependent on the two. That bondage which has not yet arisen, one knows how it comes to arise. That bondage which has already arisen, one knows how it comes to be abandoned. That bondage which has been abandoned, one knows how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the eye? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the eye-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the eye.

"What are forms? It is called the external four great elements and the forms derived from the four great elements, being forms that can be seen and are resistant. This is called form.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the eye faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise. This is called: the bondage which has not yet arisen, how it comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the eye faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned. This is called: the bondage which has already arisen, how it comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the eye and forms, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future. This is called: the bondage which has been abandoned, how it does not arise again in the future.

"What is the ear? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the ear-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the ear.

"What are sounds? It is called the external four great elements and the sounds derived from the four great elements, being sounds that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called sound.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the ear faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the ear faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the ear and sounds, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future.

"What is the nose? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the nose-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the nose.

"What are odors? It is called the external four great elements and the odors derived from the four great elements, being odors that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called odor.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the nose faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the nose faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the nose and odors, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future.

"What is the tongue? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the tongue-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the tongue.

"What are flavors? It is called the external four great elements and the flavors derived from the four great elements, being flavors that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called flavor.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the tongue faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the tongue faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the tongue and flavors, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future.

"What is the body? It is called the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements, being the body-organ that cannot be seen and is resistant. This is called the body.

"What are tangibles? It is called the external four great elements and the tangibles derived from the four great elements, being tangibles that cannot be seen and are resistant. This is called tangible.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the body faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the body faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the body and tangibles, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future.

"What is the mind? It is called the mind, the intention, the consciousness. This is called the mind.

"What are mental objects? It is called the external mental objects that cannot be seen and are not resistant. This is called mental objects.

"What is the bondage? It is called desire and lust. In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that arise are called the bondage.

"That bondage which has not yet arisen, how does it come to arise? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have not yet arisen: when one does not guard the mind faculty, dwelling with a mind that is unrestrained, then the bondage that has not yet arisen comes to arise.

"That bondage which has already arisen, how does it come to be abandoned? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have already arisen: when one guards the mind faculty, dwelling with a mind that is restrained, then the bondage that has already arisen comes to be abandoned.

"That bondage which has been abandoned, how does it not arise again in the future? In dependence on the mind and mental objects, the desire and lust that have been abandoned: when one cultivates mindfulness, the awakening factor, cultivates investigation of dharmas, the awakening factor, cultivates energy, the awakening factor, cultivates joy, the awakening factor, cultivates tranquility, the awakening factor, cultivates concentration, the awakening factor, cultivates equanimity, the awakening factor, being dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, directed toward renunciation, then the bondage that has been abandoned does not arise again in the future.

"This is called the teaching of the six pairs of sense-bases."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

## (151) Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Sense-Bases

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the analysis of the six sense-bases. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the analysis of the six sense-bases? The eye is one sense-base, forms are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"The ear is one sense-base, sounds are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"The nose is one sense-base, odors are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the nose and odors, nose-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"The tongue is one sense-base, flavors are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the tongue and flavors, tongue-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"The body is one sense-base, tangibles are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"The mind is one sense-base, mental objects are another sense-base; these two are dependent on each other. In dependence on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition, feeling arises. From feeling as condition, craving arises. This is the true arising of suffering, as it truly is. If in dependence on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises, and the coming together of the three is contact, from contact as condition, feeling arises, from feeling as condition, craving arises, then with the complete and remainderless cessation and abandoning of that craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and anguish cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases. This is the true cessation of suffering, as it truly is.

"This is called the analysis of the six sense-bases."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

## (152) Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Sense-Bases (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the analysis of the six sense-bases. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you."

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the analysis of the six sense-bases? There are internal sense-bases, and there are external sense-bases. What are the internal sense-bases? The eye is one sense-base, the ear is one sense-base, the nose is one sense-base, the tongue is one sense-base, the body is one sense-base, the mind is one sense-base. If someone asks, 'What reason and what conditions are there for these to be called the internal sense-bases?' one should answer: 'Because each of these is a self-contained sense-base, therefore they are called the internal sense-bases.'

"If someone asks, 'What reason and what conditions are there for these sense-bases to each be a self-contained sense-base?' one should answer: 'Because the eye is a sense-base in which one's own consciousness arises and one's own consciousness dwells, therefore the eye is a self-contained sense-base. Because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are each sense-bases in which one's own consciousness arises and one's own consciousness dwells, therefore the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are each self-contained sense-bases. Because each of these is a self-contained sense-base, therefore they are called the internal sense-bases.'

"What are the external sense-bases? Forms are one sense-base, sounds are one sense-base, odors are one sense-base, flavors are one sense-base, tangibles are one sense-base, mental objects are one sense-base. If someone asks, 'What reason and what conditions are there for these to be called the external sense-bases?' one should answer: 'Because each of these is the object of another's consciousness, therefore they are called the external sense-bases.'

"If someone asks, 'What reason and what conditions are there for these sense-bases to each be the object of another's consciousness?' one should answer: 'Because forms are the object of the eye-consciousness, therefore forms are the object of another's consciousness. Because sounds are the object of the ear-consciousness, odors are the object of the nose-consciousness, flavors are the object of the tongue-consciousness, tangibles are the object of the body-consciousness, and mental objects are the object of the mind-consciousness, therefore sounds, odors, flavors, tangibles, and mental objects are each the object of another's consciousness. Because each of these is the object of another's consciousness, therefore they are called the external sense-bases.'

"In dependence on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition there arises feeling, either pleasant, or painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. If one experiences pleasant feeling, one delights in it, welcomes it, and continues bound to it. Therein the latent tendency to lust lies dormant. If one experiences painful feeling, one is sorrowful, grieved, lamenting, beating one's breast, bewildered, and deluded. Therein the latent tendency to aversion lies dormant. If one experiences neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one does not know as it truly is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling. Therein the latent tendency to ignorance lies dormant.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not continue bound to it, then the latent tendency to lust does not lie dormant therein. If due to painful feeling, one is not sorrowful, not grieved, not lamenting, not beating one's breast, not bewildered, not deluded, then the latent tendency to aversion does not lie dormant therein. If due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one knows as it truly is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling, then the latent tendency to ignorance does not lie dormant therein.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, is without the latent tendency to lust lying dormant, due to painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to aversion lying dormant, and due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to ignorance lying dormant, this is called a bhikṣu who is free from the bondage of all feeling, who sees clearly. This is called a bhikṣu who has cut off craving, who has removed the fetter, who, through the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering.
