Therein the latent tendency to ignorance lies dormant.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not continue bound to it, then the latent tendency to lust does not lie dormant therein. If due to painful feeling, one is not sorrowful, not grieved, not lamenting, not beating one's breast, not bewildered, not deluded, then the latent tendency to aversion does not lie dormant therein. If due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one knows as it truly is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling, then the latent tendency to ignorance does not lie dormant therein.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, is without the latent tendency to lust lying dormant, due to painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to aversion lying dormant, and due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to ignorance lying dormant, this is called a bhikṣu who is free from the bondage of all feeling, who sees clearly. This is called a bhikṣu who has cut off craving, who has removed the fetter, who, through the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering.

"In dependence on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. From contact as condition there arises feeling, either pleasant, or painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. If one experiences pleasant feeling, one delights in it, welcomes it, and continues bound to it. Therein the latent tendency to lust lies dormant. If one experiences painful feeling, one is sorrowful, grieved, lamenting, beating one's breast, bewildered, and deluded. Therein the latent tendency to aversion lies dormant. If one experiences neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one does not know as it truly is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling. Therein the latent tendency to ignorance lies dormant.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not continue bound to it, then the latent tendency to lust does not lie dormant therein. If due to painful feeling, one is not sorrowful, not grieved, not lamenting, not beating one's breast, not bewildered, not deluded, then the latent tendency to aversion does not lie dormant therein. If due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one knows as it truly is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding that feeling, then the latent tendency to ignorance does not lie dormant therein.

"If a bhikṣu, due to pleasant feeling, is without the latent tendency to lust lying dormant, due to painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to aversion lying dormant, and due to neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, is without the latent tendency to ignorance lying dormant, this is called a bhikṣu who is free from the bondage of all feeling, who sees clearly. This is called a bhikṣu who has cut off craving, who has removed the fetter, who, through the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering.

"This is called the analysis of the six sense-bases."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (153) Sūtra Given to the Bhikṣu Named Pūrṇa

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and sat down. He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it would be good if the World-Honored One would briefly teach me the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, I will dwell alone in a secluded place, without negligence, practicing diligently. The reason for dwelling alone in a secluded place, without negligence, practicing diligently is that a clansman who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith has gone forth from the household to the homeless life, that he might study the unsurpassed end of the holy life, and in this very life, with his own higher knowledge, realize, attain, and dwell in it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, I know that there is no more existence to come.'"

The World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa: "Very good, very good! Pūrṇa, it is excellent that you are able to come to the Tathāgata and ask such a question. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and ponder it well. I will explain it for you."

The Venerable Pūrṇa received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Pūrṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with desire, and enticing. If a bhikṣu delights in, welcomes, and continues bound to such forms, then because he delights in, welcomes, and continues bound to them, delight arises. Pūrṇa, I say that from the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering. Pūrṇa, there are sounds cognizable by the ear, odors cognizable by the nose, flavors cognizable by the tongue, tangibles cognizable by the body, and mental objects cognizable by the mind that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with desire, and enticing. If a bhikṣu delights in, welcomes, and continues bound to such mental objects, then because he delights in, welcomes, and continues bound to them, delight arises. Pūrṇa, I say that from the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering.

"Pūrṇa, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with desire, and enticing. If a bhikṣu does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not continue bound to such forms, then because he does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not continue bound to them, delight ceases. Pūrṇa, I say that from the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering. Pūrṇa, there are sounds cognizable by the ear, odors cognizable by the nose, flavors cognizable by the tongue, tangibles cognizable by the body, and mental objects cognizable by the mind that are wished for, desired, agreeable, connected with desire, and enticing. If a bhikṣu does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not continue bound to such mental objects, then because he does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not continue bound to them, delight ceases. Pūrṇa, I say that from the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering.

"Pūrṇa, I have now briefly taught you the Dharma. Where do you wish to go to dwell?"

The Venerable Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have now already heard the brief teaching of the Dharma. I wish to go to the western region, to the land of the Sunāparanta people, and dwell there."

The World-Honored One said: "Pūrṇa, the people of the western region, the Sunāparanta people, are violent and fierce. Pūrṇa, if those people revile and abuse you with foul words, what will you think then?"

The Venerable Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if those people revile and abuse me with foul words, at that time I will think: 'These Sunāparanta people are truly good, truly well-behaved, because they only revile and abuse me with foul words and do not strike me with their hands or stones.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Pūrṇa, if the Sunāparanta people strike you with their hands or stones, what will you think then?"

Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if those people strike me with their hands or stones, at that time I will think: 'These Sunāparanta people are truly good, truly well-behaved, because they only strike me with their hands or stones and do not strike me with knives or staves.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Pūrṇa, if the Sunāparanta people strike you with knives or staves, what will you think then?"

Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if those people strike me with knives or staves, at that time I will think: 'These Sunāparanta people are truly good, truly well-behaved, because they only strike me with knives or staves and do not kill me.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Pūrṇa, if the Sunāparanta people kill you, what will you think then?"

Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if those people kill me, at that time I will think: 'There are disciples of the World-Honored One who, weary and disgusted with the body and with life, seek a knife with which to end their lives. I have now, without seeking it, obtained it. These Sunāparanta people are truly good, truly well-behaved, because they have freed me from this vile and filthy body with so little trouble.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Very good, very good! Pūrṇa, you can, with the attainment of such forbearance and gentleness, dwell in the land of the Sunāparanta people. Go now, Pūrṇa. Having been liberated, liberate others. Having crossed over, help others cross over. Having been comforted, comfort others. Having attained nirvāṇa, lead others to attain nirvāṇa."

Thereupon, the Venerable Pūrṇa, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted. He rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

He then put his dwelling in

# Fascicle 37 of the Madhyamāgama

---

## (149) Sūtra on What Is Desired, Eighth of the Brahmin Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, wandering about in the afternoon, went to visit the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. He said: "Gautama, I wish to ask a question. If you permit, I shall venture to state it."

The World-Honored One said: "Ask whatever you wish."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama, what do kṣatriyas desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Kṣatriyas desire to obtain wealth. They practice wisdom. They establish themselves upon the sword. They depend upon the people. Their final goal is sovereignty."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Gautama, what do householders desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Householders desire to obtain wealth. They practice wisdom. They establish themselves upon skilled crafts. They depend upon their occupations. Their final goal is the completion of their work."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Gautama, what do women desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Women desire to obtain a husband. They practice adornment. They establish themselves upon having children. They depend upon having no rival. Their final goal is sovereignty."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Gautama, what do thieves and robbers desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Thieves and robbers desire to take what is not given. They practice in hidden places. They establish themselves upon the sword. They depend upon darkness. Their final goal is not being seen."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Gautama, what do brahmins desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Brahmins desire to obtain wealth. They practice wisdom. They establish themselves upon the scriptures. They depend upon observing fasts and precepts. Their final goal is Brahmā's heaven."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: "Gautama, what do śramaṇas desire, what do they practice, what do they establish themselves upon, what do they depend on, and what is their final goal?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Śramaṇas desire to attain the true truth. They practice wisdom. They establish themselves upon moral precepts. They depend upon having no attachments. Their final goal is nirvāṇa."

The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said: "World-Honored One, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on What Is Desired, Eighth

---

## (150) Sūtra on Uḍḍaka Rāma, Ninth of the Brahmin Section of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.

At that time, the brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma, wandering about in the afternoon, went to visit the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. He said: "Gautama, I wish to ask a question. If you permit, I shall venture to state it."

The World-Honored One said: "Ask whatever you wish."

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma then asked: "Gautama, brahmins prescribe four kinds of service for the four castes: they prescribe service for brahmins, and they prescribe service for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans. Gautama, brahmins prescribe that brahmins should serve brahmins, and that kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans should also serve brahmins. Gautama, these four castes should serve brahmins. Gautama, brahmins prescribe that kṣatriyas should serve kṣatriyas, and that householders and artisans should also serve kṣatriyas. Gautama, these three castes should serve kṣatriyas. Gautama, brahmins prescribe that householders should serve householders, and that artisans should also serve householders. Gautama, these two castes should serve householders. Gautama, brahmins prescribe that artisans should serve artisans. Who else is lower that service should be prescribed for artisans? Only artisans serve artisans."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, do the brahmins themselves actually know that they prescribe four kinds of service for the four castes: prescribing service for brahmins, and prescribing service for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "They do not know. Gautama, but the brahmins themselves make this claim. In this world, among devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brahmins, from humans to devas, the brahmins do not themselves know that they prescribe four kinds of service for the four castes: prescribing service for brahmins, and prescribing service for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, it is like a man who forces meat upon another and says: 'Good man, you must eat this, and you must pay me for it.' Brahmin, what you say on behalf of the brahmins is just like this. Why? Because the brahmins do not themselves know that they prescribe four kinds of service for the four castes: prescribing service for brahmins, and prescribing service for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you mean by service? If there is service, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? If there is service, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, if I serve someone, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve that person. If I serve someone, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve that person. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve them. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve them."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, suppose another brahmin were to come, one who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, whose mind is not confused, who is free and independent. I would ask that brahmin: 'What do you think? If there is service, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? If there is service, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, is that true service?'

"Brahmin, that brahmin, who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, whose mind is not confused, who is free and independent, would answer me saying: 'Gautama, if I serve someone, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve that person. If I serve someone, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve that person. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are only equals and none superior, I should not serve them. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service there are superiors and none equal, I should serve them.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? If there is service, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If there is service, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, if I serve someone, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve that person. If I serve someone, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve that person. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve them. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve them."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, suppose another brahmin were to come, one who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, whose mind is not confused, who is free and independent. I would ask that brahmin: 'What do you think? If there is service, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If there is service, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service one loses faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? Brahmin, if one serves brahmins, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service? If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service one increases in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, is that true service?'

"Brahmin, that brahmin, who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, whose mind is not confused, who is free and independent, would also answer me in the same way, saying: 'Gautama, if I serve someone, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve that person. If I serve someone, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve that person. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service I lose faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should not serve them. Gautama, if I serve brahmins, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve them. If I serve kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans, and because of that service I increase in faith, morality, broad learning, aspiration, and wisdom, I should serve them.'"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma said: "Gautama, brahmins prescribe four kinds of personal property for the four castes: they prescribe personal property for brahmins, and they prescribe personal property for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans. Gautama, regarding the personal property that brahmins prescribe for brahmins: Gautama, brahmins prescribe that begging is the personal property of brahmins. If a brahmin looks down upon begging, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss. Just as a cowherd who cannot properly watch over his cattle incurs loss, so too, Gautama, brahmins prescribe that begging is the personal property of brahmins. If a brahmin looks down upon begging, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss.

"Gautama, regarding the personal property that brahmins prescribe for kṣatriyas: Gautama, brahmins prescribe that bows and arrows are the personal property of kṣatriyas. If a kṣatriya looks down upon bows and arrows, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss. Just as a cowherd who cannot properly watch over his cattle incurs loss, so too, Gautama, brahmins prescribe that bows and arrows are the personal property of kṣatriyas. If a kṣatriya looks down upon bows and arrows, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss.

"Gautama, regarding the personal property that brahmins prescribe for householders: Gautama, brahmins prescribe that farming is the personal property of householders. If a householder looks down upon farming, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss. Just as a cowherd who cannot properly watch over his cattle incurs loss, so too, Gautama, brahmins prescribe that farming is the personal property of householders. If a householder looks down upon farming, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss.

"Gautama, regarding the personal property that brahmins prescribe for artisans: Gautama, brahmins prescribe that hemp-work is the personal property of artisans. If an artisan looks down upon hemp-work, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss. Just as a cowherd who cannot properly watch over his cattle incurs loss, so too, Gautama, brahmins prescribe that hemp-work is the personal property of artisans. If an artisan looks down upon hemp-work, then he looks down upon his own personal property. Having looked down upon his own personal property, he incurs loss."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, do the brahmins themselves actually know that they prescribe four kinds of personal property for the four castes: prescribing personal property for brahmins, and prescribing personal property for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "They do not know. Gautama, but the brahmins themselves say that in this world, among devas, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brahmins, from humans to devas, they do not themselves know that they prescribe four kinds of personal property for the four castes: prescribing personal property for brahmins, and prescribing personal property for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, it is like a man who forces meat upon another and says: 'Good man, you must eat this, and you must pay me for it.' Brahmin, what you say on behalf of the brahmins is just like this. Why? Because the brahmins do not themselves know that they prescribe four kinds of personal property for the four castes: prescribing personal property for brahmins, and prescribing personal property for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans. In this way, brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? Is there any brahmin who alone is unattached, unbound, untouched, and unobstructed in this space, while kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans are not so?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, brahmins are unattached, unbound, untouched, and unobstructed in this space, and kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans are likewise."

"Brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? Is there any brahmin who alone can practice the mind of loving-kindness, without bonds, without enmity, without anger, without contention, while kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans cannot?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, brahmins can practice the mind of loving-kindness, without bonds, without enmity, without anger, without contention, and kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans can likewise."

"Brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? Suppose a hundred kinds of people came, and one person said to them: 'Come, all of you! If there are those born into kṣatriya clans or brahmin clans, only they can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean.' Brahmin, what do you think? Is it that only those of kṣatriya clans and brahmin clans can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean? Is it that those of householder clans and artisan clans cannot take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean? Or can all of the hundred kinds of people take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, all of the hundred kinds of people can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean."

"Just so. Brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? Suppose a hundred kinds of people came, and one person said to them: 'Come, all of you! If there are those born into kṣatriya clans or brahmin clans, only they can use extremely dry sāla and sandalwood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it.' Brahmin, what do you think? Is it that only those of kṣatriya clans and brahmin clans can use extremely dry sāla and sandalwood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it? Is it that those of householder clans and artisan clans must use dry pig troughs, dog troughs, eranda wood, and other inferior wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it? Or can all of the hundred kinds of people use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, all of the hundred kinds of people can use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it."

"Just so. Brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? If those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, do all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire? Or does only that fire have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can perform the functions of fire? Or does only that fire lack flame, lack color, lack heat, and lack light, and cannot perform the functions of fire? Or do all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, if those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, then all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire. That only that fire should have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and be able to perform the functions of fire: that is impossible. That only that fire should lack flame, lack color, lack heat, and lack light, and not be able to perform the functions of fire: that too is impossible. Rather, Gautama, all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire."

"Just so. Brahmin, I myself well understand and well know the dharmas. I prescribe for people the Dharma of cessation, the Dharma of extinguishing, the Dharma of the path of awakening, the Dharma of the good destination. I prescribe personal property."

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, what do you think? If those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, and then someone puts dry grass and wood into those fires, producing flame, producing color, producing heat, producing smoke, are there any differences among the flame, color, heat, and smoke of those fires?"

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma answered: "Gautama, if those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, and then someone puts dry grass and wood into those fires, producing flame, producing color, producing heat, producing smoke, I am unable to establish that there are any differences among the flame, color, heat, and smoke of those fires."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin, in the same way, the fire I have obtained, the diligence I have obtained, can extinguish heedlessness and pride and arrogance. I too cannot establish that there are any differences among those fires."

The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma said: "World-Honored One, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The brahmin Uḍḍaka Rāma, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Uḍḍaka Rāma, Ninth

---

## (151) Sūtra on Assalāyana, Tenth of the Brahmin Section of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada.

At that time, a great number of brahmins in Kosala gathered in a study hall and discussed this matter together: "The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā. Yet the śramaṇa Gautama proclaims and teaches that all four castes are equally pure." They thought: "Sirs, who among us has the ability to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason?" They further thought: "The young man Assalāyana has been acknowledged by his parents as being of pure birth, with an unbroken lineage of parents for seven generations, generation after generation without fault. He is broadly learned, retentive of memory, and has mastered the four Vedas, deeply versed in the five explanatory methods of etymology, ritual, correct grammar, phonetics, and narrative. The young man Assalāyana has the ability to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason." "Sirs, let us go together to the young man Assalāyana, explain this matter to him, and whatever the young man Assalāyana says, we shall accept."

Thereupon, the many brahmins of Kosala went to the young man Assalāyana. They exchanged greetings, sat down to one side, and said: "Young man, we, the many brahmins of Kosala, gathered in a study hall and discussed this matter together: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā. Yet the śramaṇa Gautama proclaims and teaches that all four castes are equally pure.' We thought: 'Sirs, who among us has the ability to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason?' We further thought: 'The young man Assalāyana has been acknowledged by his parents as being of pure birth, with an unbroken lineage of parents for seven generations, generation after generation without fault. He is broadly learned, retentive of memory, and has mastered the four Vedas, deeply versed in the five explanatory methods of etymology, ritual, correct grammar, phonetics, and narrative. The young man Assalāyana has the ability to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason.' May the young man Assalāyana go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason."

The young man Assalāyana said to the brahmins: "Sirs, the śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. If one teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, he cannot be challenged."

The many brahmins of Kosala said: "Young man, you have not yet been defeated. You should not submit in advance. Why? The young man Assalāyana has been acknowledged by his parents as being of pure birth, with an unbroken lineage of parents for seven generations, generation after generation without fault. He is broadly learned, retentive of memory, and has mastered the four Vedas, deeply versed in the five explanatory methods of etymology, ritual, correct grammar, phonetics, and narrative. The young man Assalāyana has the ability to go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason. May the young man Assalāyana go to the śramaṇa Gautama and challenge him on this matter in accordance with reason." The young man Assalāyana silently accepted the request of the many brahmins of Kosala.

Thereupon, the young man Assalāyana, together with the many brahmins of Kosala, went to visit the Buddha. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side. He said: "Gautama, I wish to ask a question. Will you allow me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Young man, ask whatever you wish."

Assalāyana then asked: "Gautama, the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.' What does the śramaṇa Gautama say about this?"

The World-Honored One said: "I shall now ask you; answer as you understand. Young man, have you heard that in other regions and in the continent of Jambudvīpa there are two classes, masters and servants, and that masters can become servants, and servants can become masters?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, I have heard that in other regions and in the continent of Jambudvīpa there are two classes, masters and servants, and that masters can become servants, and servants can become masters."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? Is it that only brahmins alone are unattached, unbound, untouched, and unobstructed in this space, while kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans are not so?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, brahmins are unattached, unbound, untouched, and unobstructed in this space, and kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans are likewise."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? Is it that only brahmins alone can practice the mind of loving-kindness, without bonds, without enmity, without anger, without contention, while kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans cannot?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, brahmins can practice the mind of loving-kindness, without bonds, without enmity, without anger, without contention, and kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans can likewise."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? Suppose a hundred kinds of people came, and one person said to them: 'Come, all of you! If there are those born into kṣatriya clans or brahmin clans, only they can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean.' Young man, what do you think? Is it that only those of kṣatriya clans and brahmin clans can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean? Is it that those of householder clans and artisan clans cannot take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean? Or can all of the hundred kinds of people take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, all of the hundred kinds of people can take bath-powder and go to the water to wash and bathe, removing all dirt until completely clean."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? Suppose a hundred kinds of people came, and one person said to them: 'Come, all of you! If there are those born into kṣatriya clans or brahmin clans, only they can use extremely dry sāla and sandalwood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it.' Young man, what do you think? Is it that only those of kṣatriya clans and brahmin clans can use extremely dry sāla and sandalwood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it? Is it that those of householder clans and artisan clans must use dry pig troughs, dog troughs, eranda wood, and other inferior wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it? Or can all of the hundred kinds of people use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, all of the hundred kinds of people can use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? If those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, do all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire? Or does only that fire have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can perform the functions of fire? Or does only that fire lack flame, lack color, lack heat, and lack light, and cannot perform the functions of fire? Or do all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire?"

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, if those hundred kinds of people all use various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drill them with a fire-drill, produce fire, and nurture it, then all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire. That only that fire should have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and be able to perform the functions of fire: that is impossible. That only that fire should lack flame, lack color, lack heat, and lack light, and not be able to perform the functions of fire: that too is impossible. Gautama, rather, all those fires have flame, have color, have heat, and have light, and can all perform the functions of fire."

"Just so. Young man, if a brahmin rightly directs himself, he attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma. If a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan rightly directs himself, he also attains good understanding and knows for himself what is in accordance with the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana said: "Gautama, how wondrous! How extraordinary! How well you have spoken this simile. But the brahmins make this claim: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Young man, this body is reckoned according to wherever it is born. If born into a brahmin clan, it is reckoned as of the brahmin clan. If born into a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan clan, it is reckoned as of the artisan clan. Young man, it is like fire: it is reckoned according to wherever it originates. If it originates from wood, it is reckoned as a wood fire. If it originates from grass, dung, or kindling, it is reckoned as a kindling fire. In the same way, young man, this body is reckoned according to wherever it is born. If born into a brahmin clan, it is reckoned as of the brahmin clan. If born into a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan clan, it is reckoned as of the artisan clan."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? If a kṣatriya woman and a brahmin man unite together, and because of that union a child is later born, who may resemble the father, or resemble the mother, or resemble neither parent, what would you say? Would that child be a kṣatriya or a brahmin?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, if a kṣatriya woman and a brahmin man unite together, and because of that union a child is later born, who may resemble the father, or resemble the mother, or resemble neither parent, I would not call that child a kṣatriya, nor would I call it a brahmin. Gautama, I would merely call it a person of mixed birth."

"Just so. Young man, this body is reckoned according to wherever it is born. If born into a brahmin clan, it is reckoned as of the brahmin clan. If born into a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan clan, it is reckoned as of the artisan clan."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, if a brahmin woman and a kṣatriya man unite together, and because of that union a child is later born, who may resemble the father, or resemble the mother, or resemble neither parent, what would you say? Would that child be a brahmin or a kṣatriya?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, if a brahmin woman and a kṣatriya man unite together, and because of that union a child is later born, who may resemble the father, or resemble the mother, or resemble neither parent, I would not call that child a brahmin, nor would I call it a kṣatriya. Gautama, I would merely call it a person of mixed birth."

"Just so. Young man, this body is reckoned according to wherever it is born. If born into a brahmin clan, it is reckoned as of the brahmin clan. If born into a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan clan, it is reckoned as of the artisan clan."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young man, what do you think? If a person has many mares and releases one male donkey among them, and one mare unites with the male donkey, and because of that union a foal is later born, what would you say? Would that be a donkey or a horse?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, if a mare and a donkey unite together, and because of that union a foal is later born, I would not call it a donkey, nor would I call it a horse. Gautama, I would merely call it a mule."

"Just so. Young man, this body is reckoned according to wherever it is born. If born into a brahmin clan, it is reckoned as of the brahmin clan. If born into a kṣatriya, householder, or artisan clan, it is reckoned as of the artisan clan."

The World-Honored One said: "Young man, long ago in the past, there were many sages who lived together in a secluded and elevated place, and they generated this wrong view: 'The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā.' At that time, the sage Asita Devala heard that many sages living together in a secluded and elevated place had generated this wrong view. He put on a kāṣāya robe, wrapped his head with a kāṣāya cloth, took a staff and parasol, dressed in a white garment as a disguise, did not enter through the gate, and arrived at the quiet meditation path of the sages' dwelling.

"At that time, one of the sages dwelling together in that secluded and elevated place saw the sage Asita Devala wearing a kāṣāya robe, with his head wrapped in a kāṣāya cloth, carrying a staff and parasol, dressed in a white garment as a disguise, not entering through the gate, arriving at the quiet meditation path of the sages' dwelling. Having seen him, he went to the many sages dwelling together in that secluded and elevated place and spoke thus: 'Sirs, there is now a man wearing a kāṣāya robe, with his head wrapped in a kāṣāya cloth, carrying a staff and parasol, dressed in a white garment as a disguise, not entering through the gate, arriving at the quiet meditation path of the sages' dwelling. Should we not go together and curse him: "Become ashes! Become ashes!"?'

"Thereupon, the many sages dwelling together in that secluded and elevated place went to the sage Asita Devala and, having arrived, cursed him together: 'Become ashes! Become ashes!' Although they cursed him according to their cursing method, saying 'Become ashes! Become ashes!', the more they cursed him, the more radiant his complexion became, and the more well-nourished his body. Those many sages then thought: 'In the past, when we cursed others saying "Become ashes! Become ashes!", they indeed became ashes. Now we are cursing this person saying "Become ashes! Become ashes!", and we are cursing him according to our cursing method, yet this person's complexion only becomes more radiant and his body more well-nourished. We should ask him.' They then asked him: 'Who are you?' The sage Asita Devala answered: 'Sirs, have you perchance heard of the sage Asita Devala?' They answered: 'We have heard of the sage Asita Devala.' He further said: 'I am that very person.' Those many sages then apologized and begged forgiveness of the sage Asita Devala, saying: 'May you be forbearing and forgiving. We did not know that you, venerable one, are the sage Asita Devala.'

"Thereupon, the sage Asita Devala said to the sages: 'I have forgiven you. Did you truly generate this wrong view: "The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā"?' Those sages answered: 'That is so.' Asita further asked the sages: 'Do you know your own fathers?' Those sages answered: 'We do. Those brahmins married brahmin wives and not non-brahmin wives. Their fathers, and their fathers' fathers, for seven generations, those brahmins married brahmin wives and not non-brahmin wives.' Asita further asked the sages: 'Do you know your own mothers?' Those sages answered: 'We do. Those brahmin women married brahmin husbands and not non-brahmin husbands. Their mothers, and their mothers' mothers, for seven generations, those brahmin women married brahmin husbands and not non-brahmin husbands.' Asita further asked the sages: 'Do you actually know how conception takes place?' Those sages answered: 'We do. Conception takes place through the equal meeting of three things: the father and mother unite, the mother is fertile and able to conceive, and the gandharva has arrived. Asita, when these conditions equally meet, the being enters the mother's womb.'

"Asita further asked the sages: 'Do you know whether the being conceived will be male or female? Do you know where it comes from? Does it come from a kṣatriya clan, a brahmin, householder, or artisan clan? Does it come from the east, the south, the west, or the north?' Those sages answered: 'We do not know.' Asita further said to the sages: 'Sirs, since you neither see nor know these things, since you do not know from where or from whom the conceived being comes, whether it will be male or female, whether it comes from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or artisans, whether it comes from the east, the south, the west, or the north, yet you make this claim: "The brahmin caste is superior; the others are not as good. The brahmin caste is white; the others are all dark. Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity. Brahmins are sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created and transformed by Brahmā."' Young man, those many sages dwelling in a secluded and elevated place were so well taught and well rebuked by the sage Asita Devala, yet even they could not establish the purity of brahmins. How much less can you, a teacher with your disciples, clad in hides and grass garments?"

At this, the young man Assalāyana, having been directly rebuked and challenged by the World-Honored One, was inwardly distressed, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence, and had no words to say.

Then the World-Honored One, having directly rebuked and challenged the young man Assalāyana, further caused him to rejoice and said: "Young man, suppose a brahmin held a feast and made offerings, and he had four sons, two who were fond of learning and two who were not fond of learning. What do you think, young man? To which of them would that brahmin first give the foremost seat, the first washing water, and the first food?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, if that brahmin had two sons who were fond of learning, he would certainly first give them the foremost seat, the first washing water, and the first food."

The World-Honored One further asked: "Young man, suppose a brahmin held a feast and made offerings, and he had four sons. Two were fond of learning but were not diligent and delighted in practicing evil deeds. Two were not fond of learning but were diligent and delighted in practicing good deeds. What do you think, young man? To which of them would that brahmin first give the foremost seat, the first washing water, and the first food?"

The young man Assalāyana answered: "Gautama, if that brahmin had two sons who, though not fond of learning, were diligent and delighted in practicing good deeds, he would certainly first give them the foremost seat, the first washing water, and the first food."

The World-Honored One said: "Young man, you first praised learning, and afterward you praised keeping the precepts. Young man, I proclaim and teach that all four castes are equally pure, and you too proclaim and teach that all four castes are equally pure."

At this, the young man Assalāyana rose from his seat and was about to bow at the Buddha's feet. At that time, that great assembly called out in a loud, great voice: "The śramaṇa Gautama is truly wondrous! Truly extraordinary! He possesses great psychic powers, great majesty, great blessings, and great spiritual authority. Why is that? Just as the śramaṇa Gautama proclaims and teaches that all four castes are equally pure, he has caused the young man Assalāyana also to proclaim and teach that all four castes are equally pure."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of that great assembly, said: "Enough, enough, Assalāyana! Simply be satisfied in your heart. You may sit down again. I shall teach you the Dharma."

The young man Assalāyana bowed at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side. The World-Honored One taught him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and filling him with joy, using immeasurable skillful means to teach him the Dharma, encouraging, inspiring, and filling him with joy. Having done so, he fell silent.

Then the young man Assalāyana, having been taught the Dharma by the Buddha, encouraged, inspired, and filled with joy, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. At that time, the many brahmins of Kosala, who had departed and were not far away, rebuked the young man Assalāyana with various words: "What were you trying to do? You went to defeat the śramaṇa Gautama, but instead you were defeated by the śramaṇa Gautama and came back. It is like a man who enters a forest seeking eyes but instead loses his eyes and comes back. Assalāyana, you are just like that. You went to defeat the śramaṇa Gautama, but instead you were defeated by the śramaṇa Gautama and came back. It is like a man who goes to a pond seeking drink but instead comes back thirsty. Assalāyana, you are just like that. You went to defeat the śramaṇa Gautama, but instead you were defeated by the śramaṇa Gautama and came back. Assalāyana, what were you trying to do?"

Thereupon, the young man Assalāyana said to the many brahmins of Kosala: "Sirs, I told you before: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. If one teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, he cannot be challenged.'"

Thus spoke the Buddha. The young man Assalāyana, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Assalāyana, Tenth

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 38

## Chapter on Brahmins, Part One

Parrot, Sukhanti, Devapāla's Wandering Hall,
Sudatta, Brahmapāla, Yellow Reed Garden, Dhona,
Agārahāna, Araṇa, Brahmā.

## (152) The Parrot Sūtra, First of the Chapter on Brahmins

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the young brahmin Parrot, son of Todeya, having some business to attend to, went to Rājagṛha and lodged at a householder's residence. Thereupon, the young brahmin Parrot, son of Todeya, asked the householder at whose home he was lodging: "Is there a śramaṇa or brahmin who is the head of a community, the teacher of a multitude, who leads a great assembly and is honored by people, whom I might visit and pay respects to at a suitable time, and through paying such respects, might I obtain joy?"

The householder answered: "There is indeed, World-Honored One! The śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, who left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, and awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. World-Honored One, you may visit him at a suitable time, go to him and pay respects; perhaps through paying such respects, your mind may obtain joy."

The young brahmin Parrot then asked: "Where is the śramaṇa Gautama now? I wish to see him."

The householder answered: "The śramaṇa Gautama is here in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandaka Garden. You may go there to see him."

Thereupon, the young brahmin Parrot departed from the householder's residence where he was lodging and went to the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. The young brahmin Parrot saw the World-Honored One from afar among the trees, upright and beautiful in appearance, like the moon among the stars, radiantly brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, complete in marks of excellence, majestic in spiritual power, with faculties calm and settled, without obstruction, having accomplished mastery and self-control, with a mind at peace and in silent tranquility. Having seen him, he went forward to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Gautama, I wish to ask something. If you will permit me, I shall speak."

The World-Honored One said: "Ask as you wish."

The young brahmin Parrot asked: "Gautama, as I have heard, those who remain as householders attain good understanding and know what accords with the Dharma, but those who leave home to study the Way do not. I ask Gautama: how is this matter?"

The World-Honored One said: "This matter is not fixed."

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, I wish that you would now distinguish this matter for me."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, listen carefully and consider it well. I shall explain it to you in full." The young brahmin Parrot received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Young brahmin, if there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice wrong conduct, I do not praise them. Why is that? If there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice wrong conduct, they do not attain good understanding and do not know what accords with the Dharma. Therefore, young brahmin, if there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice wrong conduct, I do not praise them. Young brahmin, if there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice right conduct, I praise them. Why is that? If there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice right conduct, they certainly attain good understanding and know what accords with the Dharma. Therefore, young brahmin, if there are householders and those who have left home to study the Way who practice right conduct, I praise them. Young brahmin, I speak thus, explaining these two categories of dharma, distinguishing them thus, showing them thus. If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, strong and firm, deeply entrenched, one-sidedly attached, say that only this is true and all else is false."

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, as I have heard, those who remain as householders have great benefit and great merit, but those who leave home to study the Way do not. I ask Gautama: how is this matter?"

The World-Honored One said: "This matter is not fixed."

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, I wish that you would again distinguish this matter for me."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, listen carefully and consider it well. I shall explain it to you in full." The young brahmin Parrot received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Young brahmin, if a householder has great calamities, great quarrels, and great enmities, and practices wrong conduct, he does not obtain great fruit and has no great merit. It is like farming: there are great calamities, great quarrels, and great enmities, and one who practices wrong conduct does not obtain great fruit and has no great merit. Likewise, young brahmin, the householder is also like this. Young brahmin, one who leaves home to study the Way has few calamities, few quarrels, and few enmities; but if one practices wrong conduct, one does not obtain great fruit and has no great merit. It is like trading: there are few calamities, few quarrels, and few enmities, but one who practices wrong conduct does not obtain great fruit and has no great merit. Likewise, young brahmin, one who leaves home to study the Way is also like this.

"Young brahmin, if a householder has great calamities, great quarrels, and great enmities, but practices right conduct, he obtains great reward and has great merit. It is like farming: there are great calamities, great quarrels, and great enmities, but one who practices right conduct obtains great reward and has great merit. Likewise, young brahmin, the householder is also like this. Young brahmin, one who leaves home to study the Way has few calamities, few quarrels, and few enmities, and if one practices right conduct, one obtains great reward and has great merit. It is like trading: there are few calamities, few quarrels, and few enmities, and one who practices right conduct obtains great reward and has great merit. Likewise, young brahmin, one who leaves home to study the Way is also like this. Young brahmin, I speak thus, explaining these two categories of dharma, distinguishing them thus, showing them thus. If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, strong and firm, deeply entrenched, one-sidedly attached, say that only this is true and all else is false."

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds."

The World-Honored One said: "If the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds, can you, being in this assembly, now explain them?"

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, there is nothing I cannot say. Why is that? Gautama, you are now sitting right here in this assembly."

The World-Honored One said: "Then please explain."

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, please listen well. Gautama, the brahmins establish the first dharma, truthfulness, as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds. The second is recitation and study. The third is austerity. The fourth is ascetic practice. Gautama, the brahmins establish the fifth, the holy life, as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds."

The World-Honored One said: "If the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds, is there among those brahmins even one brahmin who says: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits'?"

The young brahmin Parrot said to the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Is there any teacher, or teacher's teacher, going back seven generations of ancestors, who has said: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits'?"

The young brahmin Parrot said to the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

At that time, the World-Honored One asked: "Young brahmin, were there brahmins of old, who lived and passed away, who upheld and transmitted scriptures, who disseminated scriptures, who recited and studied the canonical texts: first, Aṭṭaka; second, Vāmaka; third, Vāmadeva; fourth, Viśvāmitra; fifth, Yamataggi; sixth, Aṅgirasa; seventh, Vasiṣṭha; eighth, Kāśyapa; ninth, Bhāradvāja; tenth, Bhṛgu? The brahmins of today recite, study, and learn those very same complete scriptures. Did any of them say: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits'?"

The young brahmin Parrot said to the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. But the brahmins accept and uphold them based on faith."

The World-Honored One said: "If among all the brahmins there is not a single brahmin who says: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits and rewards'; and there is no teacher or teacher's teacher, going back seven generations of ancestors, who says: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits and rewards'; and if there were brahmins of old who lived and passed away, who upheld and transmitted scriptures, who disseminated scriptures, who recited and studied the canonical texts: first, Aṭṭaka; second, Vāmaka; third, Vāmadeva; fourth, Viśvāmitra; fifth, Yamataggi; sixth, Aṅgirasa; seventh, Vasiṣṭha; eighth, Kāśyapa; ninth, Bhāradvāja; tenth, Bhṛgu; and the brahmins of today recite, study, and learn those very same complete scriptures, yet none of them says: 'Regarding these five dharmas, in this present life I have myself known, myself realized, and having myself borne witness, established their fruits and rewards.' Young brahmin, do not those brahmins, for this reason, have no foundation in their faith?"

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, truly there is no foundation. But the brahmins accept and uphold what they have heard."

The World-Honored One said: "It is like a line of blind men, each supporting the one before him. The one in front cannot see what is behind, nor can he see the middle. The one in the middle cannot see what is in front, nor can he see what is behind. The one in the rear cannot see the middle, nor can he see the front. Young brahmin, the brahmins you speak of are likewise. Young brahmin, first you spoke of faith, and now you speak again of hearsay."

The young brahmin Parrot became angry at the World-Honored One, resentful and displeased, slandering the World-Honored One, pointing at the World-Honored One, and reviling the World-Honored One: "One should slander Gautama! One should point at Gautama! One should denounce Gautama!" He said to the World-Honored One: "There is a brahmin named Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent. He says thus: 'If any śramaṇa or brahmin claims to have knowledge and vision regarding superhuman dharmas, claiming "I have now attained it," when I hear this, I laugh greatly at it, finding it unacceptable, false and untrue, and not in accord with the Dharma. How can a human, born among humans, claim to have attained superhuman dharmas? If one claims regarding superhuman dharmas "I know, I see," this is impossible.'"

Then the World-Honored One had this thought: "The young brahmin Parrot, son of Todeya, is angry at me, resentful and displeased, slandering me, pointing at me, and reviling me: 'One should slander Gautama! One should point at Gautama! One should denounce Gautama!' And he says to me: 'Gautama, there is a brahmin named Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent. He says thus: "If any śramaṇa or brahmin claims to have knowledge and vision regarding superhuman dharmas, claiming 'I have now attained it,' when I hear this, I laugh greatly at it, finding it unacceptable, false and untrue, and not in accord with the Dharma. How can a human, born among humans, claim to have attained superhuman dharmas? If one claims regarding superhuman dharmas 'I know, I see,' this is impossible."'"

Having understood this, the World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, does the brahmin Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent, know the minds and thoughts of all śramaṇas and brahmins, and then make this statement: 'If any śramaṇa or brahmin claims to have knowledge and vision regarding superhuman dharmas, claiming "I have now attained it," when I hear this, I laugh greatly at it, finding it unacceptable, false and untrue, and not in accord with the Dharma. How can a human, born among humans, claim to have attained superhuman dharmas? If one claims regarding superhuman dharmas "I know, I see," this is impossible'?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered: "Gautama, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent, has a serving woman named Punī, and he cannot even know her mind and thoughts, how much less could he know the minds and thoughts of all śramaṇas and brahmins? If he claims to know, that is utterly impossible."

The World-Honored One said: "It is like a person born blind who says: 'There are no dark and light colors, nor are there those who see dark and light colors. There are no beautiful and ugly colors, nor are there those who see beautiful and ugly colors. There are no long and short shapes, nor are there those who see long and short shapes. There are no near and far things, nor are there those who see near and far things. There are no coarse and fine things, nor are there those who see coarse and fine things. I have never seen or known them; therefore there are no visible forms.' If that person born blind speaks thus, is it truthful?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. Why is that? There are dark and light colors, and there are those who see dark and light colors. There are beautiful and ugly colors, and there are those who see beautiful and ugly colors. There are long and short shapes, and there are those who see long and short shapes. There are near and far things, and there are those who see near and far things. There are coarse and fine things, and there are those who see coarse and fine things. If one says 'I have never seen or known them; therefore there are no visible forms,' then that person born blind who speaks thus does not speak truthfully."

"Young brahmin, is not the brahmin Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent, like a person born blind and without eyes in what he says?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "Like a blind person, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, what do you think? Were there brahmins of old who lived and passed away, who upheld and transmitted scriptures, who disseminated scriptures, who recited and studied the canonical texts, namely the brahmin Soṅka, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, and your father Todeya? Whether what they said was acceptable or unacceptable, true or untrue, exalted or lowly?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "If there were brahmins of old who lived and passed away, who upheld and transmitted scriptures, who disseminated scriptures, who recited and studied the canonical texts, namely the brahmin Soṅka, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, and my father Todeya, regarding what they said, in my mind I would wish it to be acceptable and not unacceptable, wish it to be true and not untrue, wish it to be exalted and not lowly."

At that time, the World-Honored One asked: "Young brahmin, is not what the brahmin Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent, said, in fact unacceptable and without acceptability? In fact untrue and without truth? In fact lowly and without exaltedness?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "It is truly so, Gautama."

"Furthermore, young brahmin, there are five dharmas that create obstruction, create covering, create blindness and lack of vision, that can destroy wisdom, cause pointless weariness, and prevent the attainment of nirvāṇa. What are the five? Young brahmin, desire is the first dharma that creates obstruction, creates covering, creates blindness and lack of vision, that can destroy wisdom, causes pointless weariness, and prevents the attainment of nirvāṇa. Young brahmin, anger, attachment to self-view, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt is the fifth dharma that creates obstruction, creates covering, creates blindness and lack of vision, that can destroy wisdom, causes pointless weariness, and prevents the attainment of nirvāṇa. Young brahmin, what do you think? If one is obstructed, covered, and entangled by these five dharmas, could one ever hope to observe one's own benefit, observe others' benefit, observe the benefit of both, and know the minds and thoughts of all śramaṇas and brahmins? That would be utterly impossible. Young brahmin, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, of the Opamañña lineage, pure by direct descent, is stained by desire, defiled by desire, touched by desire and leaning on desire, attached to desire and immersed in desire, not seeing its danger, not knowing the escape, and yet practicing desire. Being obstructed, covered, and entangled by these five dharmas, if he wished to observe his own benefit, observe others' benefit, observe the benefit of both, and know the minds and thoughts of all śramaṇas and brahmins, that would be utterly impossible.

"Furthermore, young brahmin, there are five strands of sensual pleasure, lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and extremely delightful. What are the five? The eye cognizes forms, the ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes smells, the tongue cognizes tastes, the body cognizes tangibles. Young brahmin, what do you think? Do beings, on account of these five strands of sensual pleasure, produce pleasure and joy, and is there nothing beyond this?"

The young brahmin Parrot said to the World-Honored One: "It is so, Gautama."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young brahmin, what do you think? If fire is kindled dependent on grass and wood, and if fire is kindled independent of grass and wood, which fire has the greatest, most wonderful, most supreme radiance?"
