The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, if fire were to be kindled independent of grass and wood, that would be utterly impossible, unless by the power of psychic abilities. Gautama, if fire were kindled independent of grass and wood, that radiance would be the greatest, most wonderful, and most supreme."

The World-Honored One said: "Just so, just so, young brahmin. If fire were to be kindled independent of grass and wood, that would be utterly impossible, unless by the power of psychic abilities. If fire were kindled independent of grass and wood, that radiance would be the greatest, most wonderful, and most supreme. I now use this analogy. Young brahmin, as fire kindled dependent on grass and wood: so is the joy and pleasure of beings that arises dependent on desires and unwholesome dharmas, without attaining the pleasure of equanimity and calm cessation. Young brahmin, as fire kindled independent of grass and wood: so is the equanimous pleasure of beings that arises dependent on being free from desires, from wholesome dharmas, attaining the pleasure of equanimity and calm cessation."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, what do you think? Suppose a brahmin performs a sacrificial feast and gives gifts. From the east comes a young kṣatriya who says: 'I should receive the first seat, the first ablution water, and the first food among them.' But he does not receive the first seat, the first ablution water, and the first food, and so he generates resentment and harbors enmity. From the south comes a young brahmin who says: 'I should receive the finest food among them.' But he does not receive the finest food, and so he generates resentment and harbors enmity. From the west comes a young householder who says: 'I should receive abundant food among them.' But he does not receive abundant food, and so he generates resentment and harbors enmity. From the north comes a young artisan who says: 'I should receive plentiful food among them.' But he does not receive plentiful food, and so he generates resentment and harbors enmity. Young brahmin, when those brahmins perform such gifts, what kind of reward do they establish?"

The young brahmin Parrot said: "Gautama, brahmins do not give gifts with such a mind as to cause others to generate resentment and harbor enmity. Gautama, you should know that brahmins give gifts with a mind of compassion and sympathy. Having given gifts with a mind of compassion and sympathy, they obtain great merit."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, have not the brahmins then established a sixth dharma as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "It is so, Gautama."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young brahmin, if the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds, do you see these dharmas as being found more often among householders or among those who have left home to study the Way?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered: "Gautama, if the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds, I see these dharmas as being found more often among those who have left home to study the Way, and not among householders. Why is that? Householders have many affairs, much to do, many grudges and resentments, and many quarrels and conflicts; they cannot maintain and guard truthfulness. Gautama, those who have left home to study the Way have few affairs, little to do, few grudges and resentments, and few quarrels and conflicts; they can certainly maintain and guard truthfulness. Gautama, as for truthfulness, I see it as being found more often among those who have left home to study the Way, and not among householders. Why is that? Householders have many affairs, much to do, many grudges and resentments, and many quarrels and conflicts; they cannot practice giving, cannot practice recitation and study, cannot practice austerity, and cannot practice the holy life. Gautama, those who have left home to study the Way have few affairs, little to do, few grudges and resentments, and few quarrels and conflicts; they can practice giving, they can practice recitation and study, practice austerity, and practice the holy life. Gautama, as for practicing the holy life, I see this dharma as being found more often among those who have left home to study the Way, and not among householders."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, if the brahmins have established five dharmas as having great reward, great merit, and producing good fortune through meritorious deeds, I say these arise from the mind. What is this mind? It is a mind without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention; it is for the cultivation of these. Young brahmin, what do you think? If a bhikṣu maintains and guards truthfulness, and because of maintaining and guarding truthfulness, he obtains joy and gladness. Young brahmin, if there is joy and gladness, well associated with goodness, I say these arise from the mind. What is this mind? It is a mind without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention; it is for the cultivation of these. Likewise he can practice giving, practice recitation and study, practice austerity, and practice the holy life. Because of practicing the holy life, he obtains joy and gladness. Young brahmin, if there is joy and gladness, well associated with goodness, I say these arise from the mind. What is this mind? It is a mind without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention. His mind, together with loving-kindness, pervades one direction and dwells having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally throughout all, his mind together with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it. Likewise with compassion, sympathetic joy, and his mind together with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it.

"Young brahmin, it is like a person who is skilled at blowing a conch. If there is a region where it has never been heard, he ascends a high mountain in the middle of the night and blows the conch with all his strength, producing a subtle and wonderful sound that pervades the four directions. In this way, a bhikṣu, his mind together with loving-kindness, pervades one direction and dwells having accomplished it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally throughout all, his mind together with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it. Likewise with compassion, sympathetic joy, and his mind together with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely broad and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading the entire world, he dwells having accomplished it. Young brahmin, what do you think? If someone seeking rebirth in heaven, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in heaven, dwells with a mind associated with covetousness, wishing: 'May I become a deva or be among other devas.' And if someone seeking rebirth in heaven, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in heaven, dwells without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, immeasurable, extremely broad, well cultivated, with mind concentrated and intention resolved, pervading all and dwelling having accomplished it, wishing: 'May I become a deva or be among other devas.' Looking at both of them, which one would attain becoming a deva or being among other devas?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered: "Gautama, if this one seeking rebirth in heaven, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in heaven, dwells without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, immeasurable, extremely broad, well cultivated, with mind concentrated and intention resolved, pervading all and dwelling having accomplished it, I see that this one would certainly attain becoming a deva or being among other devas."

The World-Honored One asked: "Young brahmin, what do you think? If someone seeking rebirth in the Brahmā world, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in the Brahmā world, dwells with a mind associated with covetousness, wishing: 'May I become Brahmā or be among other Brahmās.' And if someone seeking rebirth in the Brahmā world, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in the Brahmā world, dwells without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, immeasurable, extremely broad, well cultivated, with mind concentrated and intention resolved, pervading all and dwelling having accomplished it, wishing: 'May I become Brahmā or be among other Brahmās.' Looking at both of them, which one would attain becoming Brahmā or being among other Brahmās?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered: "Gautama, if this one seeking rebirth in the Brahmā world, expressly for the purpose of being reborn in the Brahmā world, dwells without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, immeasurable, extremely broad, well cultivated, with mind concentrated and intention resolved, pervading all and dwelling having accomplished it, I see that this one would attain becoming Brahmā or being among other Brahmās."

The young brahmin Parrot asked: "Does Gautama know the path leading to Brahmā?"

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, I shall now ask you; answer as you understand. Young brahmin, what do you think? Is the village of Nālakagāma far from this assembly or not?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered: "Not far."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, what do you think? If here in this assembly you tell a person: 'Go to the village of Nālakagāma and return as soon as you arrive.' That person, receiving your instruction, goes swiftly to the village of Nālakagāma and returns as soon as he arrives. After his round trip, you ask him about the road, about the affairs of going and returning, entering and leaving the village of Nālakagāma. Would that person stand there unable to answer?"

The young brahmin Parrot answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Young brahmin, that person who made the round trip to the village of Nālakagāma, when asked about the road, might possibly stand there unable to answer. But if someone asks the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One about the path leading to Brahmā, he would never for a moment stand there unable to answer."

The young brahmin Parrot said to the World-Honored One: "The śramaṇa Gautama, without attachment, is a heavenly temple! This matter is fully evident, for when asked about the path leading to Brahmā, he can answer immediately. World-Honored One, I have understood. Well-Gone One, I have comprehended. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I wish that the World-Honored One would accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my days."

The Buddha spoke thus. The young brahmin Parrot, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Parrot Sūtra, the first.

---

## (153) The Māgandiya Sūtra, Second of the Chapter on Brahmins

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Kuru country, at the Bhāradvāja First Hermitage, sitting on a grass seat.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night at dawn, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the town of Kammāssadhamma to beg for food in sequence. After eating, in the afternoon he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth over his shoulder, went to a forest, and arrived at a place for daytime abiding. Then the World-Honored One entered that forest, went to the base of a tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged.

Then the wanderer Māgandiya, wandering about in the afternoon, went to the Bhāradvāja First Hermitage. The wanderer Māgandiya saw from afar that in the Bhāradvāja First Hermitage there was a grass seat with a one-sided resting place, resembling the resting place of a lion, resembling the resting place of a śramaṇa, resembling the resting place of a practitioner of the holy life. Having seen it, the wanderer Māgandiya asked: "In the Bhāradvāja First Hermitage, whose grass seat with a one-sided resting place is this, resembling the resting place of a lion, resembling the resting place of a śramaṇa, resembling the resting place of a practitioner of the holy life?"

The brahmin Bhāradvāja answered: "Māgandiya, there is the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, who left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way, and awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. This First Hermitage has this grass seat with a one-sided resting place, resembling the resting place of a lion, resembling the resting place of a śramaṇa, resembling the resting place of a practitioner of the holy life."

The wanderer Māgandiya said: "Bhāradvāja! Today I have seen what should not be seen and heard what should not be heard, that I should see the resting place of the śramaṇa Gautama. Why is that? That śramaṇa Gautama is a destroyer of what is productive; one who destroys what is productive is of no use."

Bhāradvāja said: "Māgandiya, you should not revile the śramaṇa Gautama with such words. Why is that? That śramaṇa Gautama possesses much wisdom: the wisdom of kṣatriyas, the wisdom of brahmins, the wisdom of householders, the wisdom of śramaṇas. If one speaks of wisdom, all can attain noble knowledge. Māgandiya, I wish to report this matter to the śramaṇa Gautama. Is that acceptable?"

Māgandiya said: "Bhāradvāja, if you wish to report it, then do as you please; I have no objection. Bhāradvāja, if I see the śramaṇa Gautama, I will also state this matter. Why is that? That śramaṇa Gautama is a destroyer of what is productive; one who destroys what is productive is of no use."

At that time, the World-Honored One, at his daytime abiding place, with his pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard the brahmin Bhāradvāja and the wanderer Māgandiya discussing this matter. Having heard it, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his quiet sitting and went to the Bhāradvāja brahmin's First Hermitage. On the grass seat he spread his sitting cloth and sat cross-legged. The brahmin Bhāradvāja, seeing the World-Honored One from afar among the trees, upright and beautiful in appearance, like the moon among the stars, radiantly brilliant, shining like a golden mountain, complete in marks of excellence, majestic in spiritual power, with faculties calm and settled, without obstruction, having accomplished mastery and self-control, with a mind at peace and in silent tranquility. Having seen him, he went forward to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Bhāradvāja, did you discuss this grass seat with the wanderer Māgandiya?"

The brahmin Bhāradvāja answered the World-Honored One: "It is so, Gautama. I also wished to report this matter to the śramaṇa Gautama, but the śramaṇa Gautama already knew before I spoke. Why is that? Because he is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."

While the World-Honored One was discussing this matter with the brahmin Bhāradvāja, the wanderer Māgandiya, wandering about afterward, came to the Bhāradvāja First Hermitage. The World-Honored One, seeing the wanderer Māgandiya coming from afar, said: "Māgandiya, one who does not discipline the eye faculty, who does not closely guard it and does not cultivate it, will surely receive painful results. The śramaṇa Gautama, who well disciplines himself, well guards closely, and well cultivates, surely obtains pleasant results. Māgandiya, is it because of this that you say the śramaṇa Gautama is a destroyer of what is productive, that one who destroys what is productive is of no use?"

The wanderer Māgandiya answered the World-Honored One: "It is so, Gautama."

"Māgandiya, likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties; one who does not discipline the mind faculty, who does not closely guard it and does not cultivate it, will surely receive painful results. The śramaṇa Gautama, who well disciplines himself, well guards closely, and well cultivates, surely obtains pleasant results. Māgandiya, is it because of this that you say the śramaṇa Gautama is a destroyer of what is productive, that one who destroys what is productive is of no use?"

The wanderer Māgandiya answered the World-Honored One: "It is so, Gautama."

The World-Honored One asked: "Māgandiya, what do you think? Suppose a person, before leaving home to study the Way, whose eye cognizes forms that are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful. Later he gives up the eye's cognizing of forms, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Regarding the eye's cognizing of forms, he sees as they truly are their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and dwells with an inwardly peaceful mind. If he sees a person who has not yet been freed from desire for forms, who is consumed by craving for forms, who burns with the fever of forms, whose eye cognizes forms that are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful; seeing such a person while going about, he does not praise him and does not delight in him. Māgandiya, what do you think? If there is this pleasure, arising from craving and from forms, and when taking pleasure in this pleasure, one disdains it and therefore does not praise it, disdains it and therefore does not delight in it, can anything be said against him for this?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

"Māgandiya, what do you think? Suppose a person, before leaving home to study the Way, likewise with the ear cognizing sounds, the nose cognizing smells, the tongue cognizing tastes, the body cognizing tangibles that are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful. Later he gives up the body's cognizing of tangibles, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Regarding the body's cognizing of tangibles, he sees as they truly are their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and dwells with an inwardly peaceful mind. If he sees a person who has not yet been freed from desire for tangibles, who is consumed by craving for tangibles, who burns with the fever of tangibles, whose body cognizes tangibles that are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful; seeing such a person while going about, he does not praise him and does not delight in him. Māgandiya, what do you think? If there is this pleasure, arising from craving and from tangibles, and when one who takes pleasure in this pleasure disdains it and therefore does not praise it, disdains it and therefore does not delight in it, can anything be said against him for this?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

The World-Honored One asked: "Māgandiya, what do you think? Suppose a person, before leaving home to study the Way, possessed the five strands of sensual pleasure that are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful. Later he gives up the five strands of sensual pleasure, shaves off his hair and beard, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure, he sees as they truly are their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and dwells with an inwardly peaceful mind. If he sees a person who has not yet been freed from desires, who is consumed by craving for desires, who burns with the fever of desires, whose five strands of sensual pleasure are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful; seeing such a person while going about, he does not praise him and does not delight in him. Māgandiya, what do you think? If there is this pleasure, arising from desires and from craving for desires, and when one who takes pleasure in this pleasure disdains it and therefore does not praise it, disdains it and therefore does not delight in it, can anything be said against him for this?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

"Māgandiya, before I left home to study the Way, I obtained the five strands of sensual pleasure easily and without difficulty, lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful. Later I gave up the five strands of sensual pleasure, shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure, I saw as they truly are their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and I dwelt with an inwardly peaceful mind. When I see a person who has not yet been freed from desires, who is consumed by craving for desires, who burns with the fever of desires, whose five strands of sensual pleasure are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful; seeing such a person while going about, I do not praise him and I do not delight in him. Māgandiya, what do you think? If there is this pleasure, arising from desires and from craving for desires, and when one who takes pleasure in this pleasure disdains it and therefore does not praise it, disdains it and therefore does not delight in it, can anything be said against me for this?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Māgandiya, it is like a householder or householder's son, extremely rich and prosperous, with immeasurable wealth, many herds of livestock, fiefs, and estates, with all manner of abundant livelihood provisions. He obtains the five desires easily and without difficulty. Having accomplished bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct, at the time of death he does not delight in giving up the five strands of sensual pleasure, and when his body breaks apart and his life ends, he rises to a good destination and is reborn in heaven, fully enjoying the five strands of heavenly sensual pleasure. Māgandiya, would this deva or heavenly son then give up the five strands of heavenly sensual pleasure and delight in human desires, cherishing them with joy?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. Why is that? Human desires are foul, impure, extremely defiled and repulsive to the mind, and not to be approached; they involve quarrels and extreme suffering. Gautama, compared to human desires, heavenly desires are the highest, most wonderful, and most supreme. If that deva or heavenly son were to give up the five strands of heavenly sensual pleasure and delight in human desires, cherishing them with joy, that would be utterly impossible."

"Just so, Māgandiya. I have cut off human desires, transcended heavenly desires, shaved off my hair and beard, put on kāṣāya robes, and with complete faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the Way. Regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure, I saw as they truly are their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, and I dwelt with an inwardly peaceful mind. When I see a person who has not yet been freed from desires, who is consumed by craving for desires, who burns with the fever of desires, whose five strands of sensual pleasure are lovable, pleasant, associated with desire, and delightful; seeing such a person while going about, I do not praise him and I do not delight in him. Māgandiya, what do you think? If there is this pleasure, arising from desires and from craving for desires, and when one who takes pleasure in this pleasure disdains it and therefore does not praise it, disdains it and therefore does not delight in it, can anything be said against me for this?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Māgandiya, it is like a person afflicted with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, who scratches open his sores with his nails and holds himself near a fire pit to warm himself. Māgandiya, what do you think? If the person afflicted with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, who scratches open his sores with his nails and holds himself near a fire pit to warm himself, would doing this eliminate the disease, give him strength, preserve his faculties, free him from the leprosy, make his body whole and healthy, restore him as before, and return him to his original place?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. Why is that? If the person afflicted with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, who scratches open his sores with his nails and holds himself near a fire pit to warm himself, this only causes new sores to increase and the original sores to grow larger. Yet he takes the leprosy sores as pleasure."

"Māgandiya, just as the person afflicted with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, who scratches open his sores with his nails and holds himself near a fire pit to warm himself, this only causes new sores to increase and the original sores to grow larger, yet he takes the leprosy sores as pleasure. Māgandiya, in the same way, beings who have not yet been freed from desires, who are consumed by craving for desires, who burn with the fever of desires, practice desires. Māgandiya, in this way, beings who have not yet been freed from desires, who are consumed by craving for desires, who burn with the fever of desires, practice desires, and their desires only increase further, their craving for desires only expands further, yet they take craving for desires as pleasure. If, without cutting off desires and without being freed from craving for desires, they could achieve inward peace of mind, whether in the past, the future, or the present, that would be utterly impossible. Why is that? It is not in accordance with reason that one could cut off desires and be freed from craving for desires while still practicing desires."

The World-Honored One said: "Māgandiya, it is like a king or great minister who obtains the five desired things easily and without difficulty. If, without cutting off desires and without being freed from craving for desires, he could achieve inward peace of mind, whether in the past, the future, or the present, that would be utterly impossible. Why is that? It is not in accordance with reason that one could cut off desires and be freed from craving for desires while still practicing desires. Just so, Māgandiya, beings who have not yet been freed from desires, who are consumed by craving for desires, who burn with the fever of desires, practice desires. Māgandiya, if beings who have not yet been freed from desires, who are consumed by craving for desires, who burn with the fever of desires, practice desires, their desires only increase further, their craving for desires only expands further, yet they take craving for desires as pleasure. If, without cutting off desires and without being freed from craving for desires, they could achieve inward peace of mind, whether in the past, the future, or the present, that would be utterly impossible. Why is that? It is not in accordance with reason that one could cut off desires and be freed from craving for desires while still practicing desires.

"Māgandiya, it is like the person afflicted with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, who scratches open his sores with his nails and holds himself near a fire pit to warm himself. Suppose someone for his sake, out of compassion and sympathy, seeking his benefit and welfare, seeking his peace and happiness, gives him appropriate good medicine. Having given him appropriate good medicine, his disease is eliminated, he gains strength, his faculties are unimpaired, he is freed from the leprosy, his body is whole and healthy, restored as before, and he returns to his original place. If he then sees another person with leprosy, whose body is festering, eaten by worms, scratching open his sores with nails, holding himself near a fire pit to warm himself. Māgandiya, seeing this, would that person take delight in it, praise it, or find joy in it?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. Why is that? When there is disease, medicine is needed; when there is no disease, medicine is not needed."

"Māgandiya, what do you think? If that person, whose disease has been eliminated, who has gained strength, whose faculties are unimpaired, who is freed from the leprosy, whose body is whole and healthy, restored as before, and who has returned to his original place, and two strong men were to forcibly seize him and hold him near the fire pit to warm him, he would panic and struggle to escape, and his body would produce intense heat. Māgandiya, what do you think? Is this fire pit now hotter, with greater suffering and worse affliction, than before?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama. Previously, when he was still afflicted with leprosy, his body festering, eaten by worms, scratching open his sores with his nails, holding himself near a fire pit to warm himself, he had the perception of great pleasure in what was actually great suffering, his mind was confused, and he had inverted perceptions. Gautama, that person now, with his disease eliminated, having gained strength, with faculties unimpaired, freed from the leprosy, with body whole and healthy, restored as before, having returned to his original place, he now has the perception of great suffering in what is great suffering, his mind is calm, and he has no inverted perceptions."

"Māgandiya, just as the person afflicted with leprosy, whose body was festering, eaten by worms, who scratched open his sores with his nails and held himself near a fire pit to warm himself, had the perception of great pleasure in what was actually great suffering, his mind was confused, and he had inverted perceptions. Just so, Māgandiya, beings who have not been freed from desires, who are consumed by craving for desires, who burn with the fever of desires, practice desires. They have the perception of pleasure in desires that are actually suffering, their minds are confused, and they have inverted perceptions. Māgandiya, just as that person, whose disease has been eliminated, who has gained strength, whose faculties are unimpaired, who is freed from the leprosy, whose body is whole and healthy, restored as before, and who has returned to his original place, he has the perception of great suffering in what is great suffering, his mind is calm, and he has no inverted perceptions. Just so, Māgandiya, I have the perception of suffering in desires that are suffering, perceiving them as they truly are, without inverted perceptions. Why is that? Māgandiya, past desires are foul, impure, extremely defiled and repulsive to the mind, not to be approached, involving quarrels, suffering, and painful contact. Future and present desires are also foul, impure, extremely defiled and repulsive to the mind, not to be approached, involving quarrels, suffering, and painful contact. Māgandiya, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One declares: freedom from disease is the foremost gain, and nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss."

The wanderer Māgandiya said to the World-Honored One: "Gautama, I too have previously heard from elder, venerable, senior teachers who have long practiced the holy life: 'Freedom from disease is the foremost gain, and nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Māgandiya, if you have previously heard from elder, venerable, senior teachers who have long practiced the holy life: 'Freedom from disease is the foremost gain, and nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss,' then Māgandiya, what is freedom from disease? What is nirvāṇa?"

Thereupon, the wanderer Māgandiya, whose body itself is disease, is a tumor, is an arrow, is a serpent, is impermanent, is suffering, is empty, is not-self, rubbed and stroked it with both hands and said: "Gautama, this is freedom from disease; this is nirvāṇa."

The World-Honored One said: "Māgandiya, it is like a person born blind, who, hearing from a sighted person what he says: 'Pure white and spotless, pure white and spotless,' upon hearing this, seeks the pure white. There is a deceitful person who, not seeking his benefit or welfare, not seeking his peace and happiness, takes a grimy, filthy, impure garment, brings it to him and says: 'You should know, this is a pure white, spotless garment. Receive it respectfully with both hands and wear it on your body.' That blind man, delighted, respectfully receives it with both hands and wears it on his body, saying: 'Pure white and spotless, pure white and spotless.' Māgandiya, does that person speak from his own knowledge, or does he speak without knowledge? Does he speak from his own seeing, or does he speak without seeing?"

The wanderer Māgandiya answered: "Gautama, one who speaks thus truly does not know or see."

The World-Honored One said: "Just so, Māgandiya. Like one blind and without eyes, whose body itself is disease, is a tumor, is an arrow, is a serpent, is impermanent, is suffering, is empty, is not-self, rubbing and stroking it with both hands, saying: 'Gautama, this is freedom from disease; this is nirvāṇa.' Māgandiya, you do not yet even recognize freedom from disease; how much less could you know or see nirvāṇa? To claim knowledge and vision of it would be utterly impossible. Māgandiya, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One has declared:

'Freedom from disease is the foremost gain, nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss;
Among all paths, the Eightfold Noble Path leads to dwelling in secure, deathless peace.'

"Many people have all heard this together, and many wanderers, having heard this verse, transmitted it to one another, yet cannot understand its meaning. Having heard it, they wish to seek its teaching, but being foolish, they deceive one another. They manifest their own bodies of the four great elements, born from father and mother, nourished by food and drink, constantly covered, massaged, bathed, and endured, subject to breaking, wearing away, disintegration, and dispersal. Yet they see a self as experiencing, and conditioned by experience there is existence, conditioned by existence there is birth, conditioned by birth there is old age and death, conditioned by old age and death there is grief, lamentation, suffering, sorrow, and vexation. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering."

Thereupon, the wanderer Māgandiya rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Gautama, I now have the utmost faith in the śramaṇa Gautama. I wish that Gautama would skillfully teach me the Dharma, so that I may know what is freedom from disease and what is nirvāṇa."

The World-Honored One said: "Māgandiya, if your noble wisdom eye is not yet purified and I teach you about freedom from disease and nirvāṇa, you will never be able to understand it; it would only be a pointless trouble to me. Māgandiya, it is like a person born blind for whom another person says: 'You should know, this is blue color, yellow, red, white color.' Māgandiya, could that person born blind, through what another person tells him, know what is blue color, yellow, red, or white color?"

He answered the World-Honored One: "No, Gautama."

"Just so, Māgandiya. If your noble wisdom eye is not yet purified and I teach you about freedom from disease and nirvāṇa, you will never be able to understand it; it would only be a pointless trouble to me. Māgandiya, I shall teach you an appropriate wonderful medicine that will purify the noble wisdom eye that is not yet purified. Māgandiya, if your noble wisdom eye becomes purified, you will yourself know what is freedom from disease and what is nirvāṇa. Māgandiya, it is like a person born blind whose relatives, out of compassion and sympathy for him, seeking his benefit and welfare, seeking his peace and happiness, seek an eye doctor for him. That eye doctor applies various treatments: sometimes causing vomiting, sometimes purging, sometimes nasal drops, sometimes purging below, sometimes lancing a vein, sometimes inducing tears. Māgandiya, perhaps through this, both eyes can be cleared. Māgandiya, if both his eyes become clear, then he himself sees what is blue, yellow, red, and white color. Seeing that grimy, filthy, impure garment, he then thinks: 'That person was indeed my enemy, who for a long time deceived me with a grimy, filthy garment.' He then harbors resentment. Māgandiya, that person might even kill him. Just so, Māgandiya, I shall teach you an appropriate wonderful medicine that will purify the noble wisdom eye that is not yet purified. Māgandiya, if your noble wisdom eye becomes purified, you will yourself know what is freedom from disease and what is nirvāṇa.

"Māgandiya, there are four kinds of dharma that purify the noble wisdom eye that is not yet purified. What are the four? Drawing near to good spiritual friends, showing respect and serving them; hearing the good Dharma; reflecting well; and practicing in accordance with the Dharma in proper sequence. Māgandiya, you should train in this way: draw near to good spiritual friends, show respect and serve them; hear the good Dharma; reflect well; and practice in accordance with the Dharma in proper sequence. Māgandiya, train in this way. Māgandiya, when you draw near to good spiritual friends and show respect and serve them, you will then hear the good Dharma. Having heard the good Dharma, you will then reflect well. Having reflected well, you will then practice in accordance with the Dharma in proper sequence. Having practiced in accordance with the Dharma in proper sequence, you will then know this suffering as it truly is, know this origin of suffering, know this cessation of suffering, and know the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.

"How does one know suffering as it truly is? It is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of meeting with what one resents, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and in brief the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. Thus one knows suffering as it truly is. How does one know the origin of suffering as it truly is? It is this craving that leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and desire, seeking delight here and there. Thus one knows the origin of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the cessation of suffering as it truly is? It is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of this craving that leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and desire, seeking delight here and there: its abandonment, its relinquishment, its release, its exhaustion, its fading away, its cessation, its stilling. Thus one knows the cessation of suffering as it truly is. How does one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to right concentration; these are called the eight. Thus one knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is."

When this Dharma had been taught, the wanderer Māgandiya became free from dust, free from defilement, and the Dharma eye arose in him regarding all dharmas. Thereupon, the wanderer Māgandiya, having seen the Dharma, having attained the Dharma, having realized the pure white Dharma, having cut off doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, needing no other teacher, no longer following others, without hesitation, having established himself in the fruit, and having attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma, immediately rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One, I wish to be allowed to leave home, study the Way, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu."

The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣu! Practice the holy life."

The wanderer Māgandiya thereupon left home, studied the Way, received full ordination, and became a bhikṣu. Having left home, studied the Way, received full ordination, and understood the Dharma, he attained the state of an arahant.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Māgandiya, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama), Fascicle 39

---

## (154) Sūtra on Bhaddāli

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I wish to eat food at one sitting [i.e., eating only one meal a day]. Eating food at one sitting, I find my body free from illness and affliction, and I am vigorous, strong, and at ease. You too should eat food at one sitting. Eating food at one sitting, your bodies will be free from illness and affliction, and you will be vigorous, strong, and at ease."

At that time, among the bhikṣus there was one named Bhaddāli, who rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One, and said: "World-Honored One, I am unable to eat food at one sitting. Why? Because if I eat food at one sitting, my mind will have regret and worry."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, if you cannot eat at one sitting, then when invited somewhere, you may eat part and bring back the rest to eat. In this way, you too should eat properly."

Bhaddāli again said: "World-Honored One, I am unable to do even this. Why? Because if I do this, my mind will still have regret and worry."

At that time, when the World-Honored One had the multitude of bhikṣus present and was establishing a training rule, only the bhikṣu Bhaddāli publicly declared that he could not practice it. Then the bhikṣu Bhaddāli, for an entire quarter of the year, did not dare to come into the presence of the World-Honored One. Why? Because he had not practiced the training rule.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Rammaka who was mending robes. The bhikṣu Bhaddāli went to where the bhikṣu Rammaka was, and having arrived, sat down together to one side.

The bhikṣu Bhaddāli said to the bhikṣu Rammaka: "Venerable one, you should know that when the World-Honored One had the multitude of bhikṣus present and established a training rule, I alone publicly declared that I could not practice it. For an entire quarter of the year, I have not dared to come into the presence of the World-Honored One. Why? Because I have not practiced the training rule."

The bhikṣu Rammaka said to the bhikṣu Bhaddāli: "If so, Venerable Bhaddāli, this is indeed a serious matter! You should go before the World-Honored One, confess your fault, repent of your transgression, and reform yourself. Why? The World-Honored One is compassionate and has sympathy and pity. He will certainly accept your confession and repentance so that you may reform yourself."

The bhikṣu Bhaddāli replied: "Venerable Rammaka, I wish to go to the World-Honored One to confess my fault and repent, but I feel ashamed."

At that time, the bhikṣu Rammaka accompanied the bhikṣu Bhaddāli, and together they went to the World-Honored One's abode. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.

The bhikṣu Bhaddāli then said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, I have committed an offense. What I did was foolish, ignorant, confused, and unwise. When the World-Honored One had the multitude of bhikṣus present and established a training rule, I alone publicly declared that I could not practice it. I now confess my fault before the World-Honored One, repent of my transgression, and wish to reform myself."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, you indeed committed an offense. What you did was foolish, ignorant, confused, and unwise. When I had the multitude of bhikṣus present and established a training rule, you alone publicly declared that you could not practice it. Bhaddāli, you did not at that time know this: 'The World-Honored One is staying at Sāvatthī. The World-Honored One will recognize me thus: "Among the bhikṣus, there is one named Bhaddāli who does not practice the training rule."' You did not understand this at that time."

"That is so, World-Honored One. I committed that offense."

"Bhaddāli, you also did not at that time know this: 'Many bhikṣus have come to Sāvatthī for the rains retreat. They will recognize me thus: "The bhikṣu Bhaddāli does not practice the training rule established by the World-Honored One."' You did not understand this at that time."

"That is so, World-Honored One. I committed that offense."

"Bhaddāli, you also did not at that time know this: 'Many bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās will recognize me thus: "The bhikṣu Bhaddāli does not practice the training rule established by the World-Honored One."' You did not understand this at that time."

"That is so, World-Honored One. I committed that offense."

"Bhaddāli, you also did not at that time know this: 'Various heterodox wanderers and brahmins of other sects will also recognize me thus: "The bhikṣu Bhaddāli, a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, does not practice the training rule."' You did not understand this at that time."

"That is so, World-Honored One. I committed that offense. What I did was foolish, ignorant, confused, and unwise. I now confess my fault before the World-Honored One, repent of my transgression, and wish to reform myself."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, you indeed committed an offense. What you did was foolish, ignorant, confused, and unwise. Nevertheless, since you now recognize your offense as an offense, recognize your transgression as a transgression, and are able to confess and repent, wishing to reform yourself, I accept your confession. Why? Bhaddāli, if a person recognizes an offense as an offense, recognizes a transgression as a transgression, is able to confess and repent, and wishes to reform, this increases and does not diminish the noble discipline.

"Bhaddāli, suppose there is a bhikṣu who does not practice the training rules and precepts but says: 'I shall practice the higher mind and the practices of insight and wisdom.' This is not the proper way. It is like a person whose hands and feet have been cut off who says: 'I wish to walk.' This is not the proper way.

"Just so, Bhaddāli, a bhikṣu who does not practice the training rules and precepts but says: 'I shall practice the higher mind and the practices of insight and wisdom,' this is not the proper way. Why? Because it is impossible to reach there without these [basic practices].

"Bhaddāli, suppose there is a bhikṣu who practices the training rules and precepts well and says: 'I shall practice the higher mind and the practices of insight and wisdom.' This is the proper way. It is like a person whose hands and feet are sound and complete who says: 'I wish to walk.' This is the proper way.

"Just so, Bhaddāli, a bhikṣu who practices the training rules and precepts well and says: 'I shall practice the higher mind and the practices of insight and wisdom,' this is the proper way. Why? Because it is possible to reach there with these [basic practices].

"Bhaddāli, I shall now speak a parable for you, and wise people through a parable are able to understand the meaning of what is said.

"Bhaddāli, it is like a person who owns horses. He has a fine, good horse, and he entrusts it to a horse trainer, saying: 'Please tame this horse for me according to proper methods. I wish it to be able to wear a harness, to walk and stop at the right time, to gallop, to run swiftly, to be well-trained in all equestrian skills, and to be suitable as a royal horse.'

"That excellent horse trainer receives the horse and uses various methods to train it. When it should walk, he trains it to walk. When it should stand, he trains it to stand. When it should turn, he trains it to turn. He sometimes uses gentle methods, sometimes uses harsh methods, and sometimes uses both gentle and harsh methods. In this way, the horse is gradually trained, and in time it becomes fit for the king's use.

"Bhaddāli, in just the same way, if a bhikṣu has these ten qualities, then the Tathāgata considers him worthy of being taught and led further. What are the ten? The bhikṣu has supreme precepts, supreme concentration, supreme wisdom, supreme liberation, and supreme knowledge and vision of liberation. He is one who can listen, one who can retain what he has heard, one who accumulates what he has heard, one who stores up what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, that have good meaning and good phrasing, that are complete, pure, and clarify the holy life: he has heard such teachings extensively, has retained them, has recited them verbally, has investigated them mentally, and has penetrated them well with right view. These are the ten qualities.

"If a bhikṣu has these ten qualities, then the Tathāgata considers him worthy of being taught and guides him. How does he guide him? He says: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should guard the precepts, guard the discipline of the Prātimokṣa, and practice the deportment and domain of the Prātimokṣa. Having received and upheld the training rules, practice them well. With regard to the slightest offenses, see danger in them. Having received the training rules, practice them.'

"When the bhikṣu has guarded the precepts and the discipline of the Prātimokṣa and practiced the deportment and domain of the Prātimokṣa well, the Tathāgata then guides him further: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees forms, do not grasp at signs or secondary characteristics. If you do not guard the faculty of the eye, then covetousness and grief, unwholesome states, will flow in. Practice guarding it, guard the faculty of the eye. Likewise for the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling odors, the tongue tasting flavors, the body experiencing contacts, and the mind knowing mental objects: do not grasp at signs or secondary characteristics. If you do not guard the faculty of the mind, then covetousness and grief, unwholesome states, will flow in. Practice guarding it, guard the faculty of the mind.'

"When the bhikṣu has guarded the sense faculties, the Tathāgata then guides him further: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should be moderate in eating. Take food with right reflection, not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of maintaining this body, to sustain life, to eliminate old suffering and not give rise to new suffering, so that one may practice the holy life and live long. It is like a person who anoints a wound for the sake of healing it, or like one who greases an axle solely for the purpose of transporting goods. Just so, bhikṣu, take food with right reflection, not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the purpose of maintaining this body.'

"When the bhikṣu is moderate in eating, the Tathāgata then guides him further: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should practice wakefulness. During the day, whether walking or sitting, purify the mind of obstructive states. In the first watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, purify the mind of obstructive states. In the middle watch of the night, lie down on the right side in the lion's posture, one foot upon the other, with mindful awareness, keeping in mind the thought of rising. In the last watch of the night, rise early and, whether walking or sitting, purify the mind of obstructive states.'

"When the bhikṣu practices wakefulness, the Tathāgata then guides him further: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should practice right mindfulness and right awareness. When going forward or coming back, look straight ahead with full awareness. When bending or stretching, when looking down or gazing around, when folding the robe or carrying the bowl, when eating, drinking, and tasting, when walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent: always practice with right mindfulness and right awareness.'

"When the bhikṣu practices right mindfulness and right awareness, the Tathāgata then guides him further: 'Bhikṣu, come! You should stay in a remote place, in a forest, under a tree, in an empty quiet place, a mountain cave, an open space, a field, or on a straw mat. In the afternoon, after the meal, sit cross-legged, keep the body upright, and establish mindfulness before you. Abandon covetousness and dwell with a mind free from covetousness. Purify the mind of covetousness. In the same way, abandon ill will, abandon sloth and torpor, abandon restlessness and remorse, and abandon doubt. Having cut off doubt, dwell without perplexity regarding wholesome states. Purify the mind of doubt.'

"Having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, he, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna.

"With the stilling of initial and sustained thought, with inner confidence, with the mind unified, without initial thought, without sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna.

"With the fading away of rapture, he dwells with equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, and he experiences happiness with the body. As the noble ones describe: 'Equanimous and mindful, he dwells in happiness.' He enters and dwells in the third dhyāna.

"Having abandoned happiness and abandoned suffering, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, without suffering and without happiness, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"Bhaddāli, this is how the Tathāgata trains a bhikṣu who is still in the stage of training and has not yet attained the goal. With such instruction and guidance, the bhikṣu who has been well trained attains supreme peace.

"Bhaddāli, as for those bhikṣus who are arahants, who have ended the defilements, who have completed the holy life, who have done what was to be done, who have laid down the burden, who have attained their own goal, who have completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and who are liberated by right knowledge: for them, these teachings serve as their pleasant abiding in the present life and as [a cause for] mindfulness and right awareness."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣu Bhaddāli, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (155) Sūtra on the Parable of the Mustard Seed

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall speak to you the parable of 'the impure and the pure.' Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we wish to hear."

The Buddha said: "What is meant by 'the impure'? It is like a sesame seed that has a mustard seed within it, or a mustard seed that has a sesame seed within it. A person of wisdom would say: 'This sesame seed has a mustard seed within it, or this mustard seed has a sesame seed within it.' Why would they say this? Because each contaminates the other.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu whose bodily conduct is impure, whose verbal conduct is impure, whose mental conduct is impure, and whose livelihood is impure: I say this person is impure. Why? Because this bhikṣu's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and livelihood, are all impure.

"It is like a white cloth that has become soiled and stained. Even if one dips it in dye, the color will not be bright and vivid. Why? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, when a bhikṣu's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and livelihood, are impure, the result one can expect is unhappy.

"What is meant by 'the pure'? It is like a sesame seed that is clean and free from mustard seeds, or a mustard seed that is clean and free from sesame seeds. A person of wisdom would say: 'This sesame seed is clean and free from mustard seeds, or this mustard seed is clean and free from sesame seeds.' Why? Because each is pure on its own.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu whose bodily conduct is pure, whose verbal conduct is pure, whose mental conduct is pure, and whose livelihood is pure: I say this person is pure. Why? Because this bhikṣu's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and livelihood, are all pure.

"It is like a white cloth that is clean and spotless. If one dips it in dye, the color will be bright and vivid. Why? Because the cloth is clean. In the same way, when a bhikṣu's bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and livelihood, are pure, the result one can expect is happy.

"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should learn thus: 'We shall purify our bodily conduct, purify our verbal conduct, purify our mental conduct, and purify our livelihood.' You should train in this way."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (156) Sūtra on the Parable of the Dirty Cloth

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu's mind is defiled, the destination will be bad. It is like a dirty cloth that is dyed: even if you dip it in blue, yellow, red, or purple dye, the color will not be bright. Why? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, if a bhikṣu's mind is defiled, the destination will be bad.

"If a bhikṣu's mind is not defiled, the destination will be good. It is like a clean cloth that is dyed: if you dip it in blue, yellow, red, or purple dye, the color will be bright and vivid. Why? Because the cloth is clean. In the same way, if a bhikṣu's mind is not defiled, the destination will be good.

"What are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unlawful greed is a defilement of the mind. Ill will is a defilement of the mind. Anger is a defilement of the mind. Resentment is a defilement of the mind. Covering up one's faults is a defilement of the mind. Dominating others is a defilement of the mind. Jealousy is a defilement of the mind. Stinginess is a defilement of the mind. Deceit is a defilement of the mind. Flattery is a defilement of the mind. Shamelessness is a defilement of the mind. Lack of moral dread is a defilement of the mind. Inertia is a defilement of the mind. Agitation is a defilement of the mind. Disputatiousness is a defilement of the mind. Holding to one's own views, clinging tenaciously, and being difficult to dissuade is a defilement of the mind.

"If a bhikṣu knows that covetousness and unlawful greed is a defilement of the mind, knowing this, he abandons it. If he knows that ill will, anger, resentment, covering up faults, dominating others, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, inertia, agitation, disputatiousness, holding to one's own views, clinging tenaciously, and being difficult to dissuade are defilements of the mind, knowing these, he abandons them.

"When this bhikṣu has known that covetousness and unlawful greed is a defilement of the mind and has abandoned it; when he has known that ill will, anger, resentment, covering up faults, dominating others, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, flattery, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, inertia, agitation, disputatiousness, holding to one's own views, clinging tenaciously, and being difficult to dissuade are defilements of the mind and has abandoned them: then he attains unwavering faith in the Buddha, saying: 'The World-Honored One is the Accomplished One, the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Persons, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.'

"He also attains unwavering faith in the Dharma, saying: 'The Dharma has been well expounded by the World-Honored One, is visible here and now, is not subject to time, is verifiable by the wise, and leads onward to nirvāṇa.'

"He also attains unwavering faith in the Sangha, saying: 'The Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is well practiced, practices the straight path, practices the true path, practices the proper path. These are the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Sangha of the World-Honored One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms; it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'

"At that time, the bhikṣu has abandoned, has expelled, has let go, has freed himself, and has detached from these defilements. He then thinks thus: 'I have attained unwavering faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.' He thereby gains joy. Having gained joy, he gains delight. With a delighted mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he experiences happiness. Experiencing happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.

"Having a concentrated mind, he practices pervading one direction with a mind of loving-kindness. In the same way, he pervades the second direction, the third direction, and the fourth direction, as well as above, below, and all around. Everywhere and in every way, with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, great, boundless, free from enmity and ill will, he pervades the entire world and dwells in it.

"In the same way, with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he pervades one direction, the second direction, the third direction, the fourth direction, above, below, and all around. Everywhere and in every way, with a mind of equanimity that is vast, great, boundless, free from enmity and ill will, he pervades the entire world and dwells in it.

"It is like a bathing pool of clear, clean water. If a person comes from the east, oppressed by heat, weary and thirsty, and arrives at the pool, the water removes his thirst and heat, and he is refreshed. Likewise if someone comes from the south, the west, or the north, oppressed by heat, weary and thirsty, and arrives at the pool, the water removes his thirst and heat, and he is refreshed.

"In the same way, if a kṣatriya shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith leaves the household to practice the path, with right mindfulness and right awareness abandoning these mental defilements and cultivating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he thereby gains inner peace. How does he gain inner peace? It is because he has abandoned and purified these defilements. Likewise if a brahmin, a vaiśya, or a śūdra shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the kāṣāya robes, and with right faith leaves the household to practice the path, with right mindfulness and right awareness abandoning these mental defilements and cultivating loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he thereby gains inner peace. This is called the 'liberation of the four castes,' where all four attain the supreme purification."

At that time, a bhikṣu in the assembly said to the World-Honored One: "Truly, World-Honored One, these four castes all attain purification."

The World-Honored One said: "Indeed, it is just as I have explained. These four castes all attain purification. Why? It is like water from different rivers: whether from the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Sarabhū, or the Aciravatī, once they flow into the great ocean, they all lose their former names and are simply called 'the great ocean.' In the same way, when these four castes, the kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, and śūdras, all leave the household with right faith to practice the path under the Tathāgata's teaching, they all abandon their former clan names and are simply called 'śramaṇas, disciples of the son of the Śākyas.' "

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (157) Sūtra at the Residence of Brahmā

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Campā, on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the full moon, on the upoṣadha day, the World-Honored One sat in the open surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus. The World-Honored One silently surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus and then addressed them:

"Bhikṣus, there is no idle talk here. Bhikṣus, this assembly is free from idle talk. It is entirely pure and established in the essence. Bhikṣus, this assembly is such an assembly: it is an assembly worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms. It is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This assembly is such that a small gift given to it becomes great, and a great gift becomes even greater. This assembly is such that it is worthy of being visited from far away to pay respect.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who are arahants, who have ended the defilements, who have completed the holy life, who have done what was to be done, who have laid down the burden, who have attained their own goal, who have completely destroyed the fetters of existence, and who are liberated by right knowledge. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who have eliminated the five lower fetters and will be spontaneously reborn, will attain final nirvāṇa there, and will not return to this world. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who have eliminated the three fetters and have weakened desire, hatred, and delusion, becoming once-returners who will return once more to this world and then make an end of suffering. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who have eliminated the three fetters and have become stream-enterers, who will never fall into bad destinies, who are certain to attain supreme awakening, and who will pass through at most seven more existences among gods and humans before making an end of suffering. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who practice the four foundations of mindfulness. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly. There are bhikṣus who practice the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"In this assembly, there are bhikṣus who practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly. There are bhikṣus who practice the contemplation of impurity, the mindfulness of breathing. Such bhikṣus exist in this assembly.

"Bhikṣus, there is no idle talk here. Bhikṣus, this assembly is free from idle talk. It is entirely pure and established in the essence."

Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:

"On this supreme full-moon night,
The sky is free from all clouds.
All the people look upward,
Wanting to see this beautiful moon.
Even more so is this assembly:
It shines with no idle talk.
If you wish to cut off birth and death,
You must seek the path of cessation.
This auspicious assembly
Has nothing to be ashamed of.
Bhikṣus, I now tell you:
Rise and depart, the assembly is dismissed."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (158) Sūtra on the Parable of the Head Being on Fire

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a person's turban or head were on fire, what should that person do?"

The bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, if a person's turban or head were on fire, that person should urgently seek to extinguish it."

The World-Honored One said: "A person whose turban or head is on fire can set that aside for the moment. But one should urgently seek to eradicate the defilements, with diligent effort, mindfulness, and right awareness. Why?

"From time without beginning, you have transmigrated through birth and death, and countless heads and bodies have been burnt by fire. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train thus: 'We shall practice diligently with effort, mindfulness, and right awareness, to eradicate the defilements.' You should train in this way.

"How does a bhikṣu practice diligently with effort, mindfulness, and right awareness, to eradicate the defilements? Here, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body, being diligent, with right awareness and right mindfulness, removing covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas, being diligent, with right awareness and right mindfulness, removing covetousness and grief toward the world.

"In this way, a bhikṣu practices diligently with effort, mindfulness, and right awareness, to eradicate the defilements."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (159) Sūtra on Ājānīya (The Noble Horse)

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "A noble horse of the king possesses eight qualities and is worthy of the king's use, having great regal power and being dignified in the king's procession. What are the eight?

"Here, a noble horse is well-born on both the sire's and dam's side, being from a land of fine horses. This is the first quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse eats fine fodder, whether fresh grass or dried grain, and never refuses it. This is the second quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is disgusted by sitting or lying in filth. This is the third quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is gentle in nature and can dwell harmoniously with other horses, not startling or harming them. This is the fourth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse, whatever pretenses or deceptions it may have, whatever faults or fears, will reveal them all to the horse trainer, who can then correct them. This is the fifth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse, when yoked to a carriage, thinks thus: 'The other horses, whether they pull or not, I alone shall pull, and I shall not abandon the effort.' This is the sixth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse always goes along the proper road and never strays from the path. This is the seventh quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is strong and enduring. Even if it falls ill, it still exerts itself and does not abandon its task. This is the eighth quality.

"A king's noble horse possessing these eight qualities is worthy of the king's use, having great regal power and being dignified in the king's procession.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu possessing eight qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms, and is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the eight?

"Here, a bhikṣu upholds the precepts and the discipline of the Prātimokṣa, his deportment and domain are perfect, and regarding the slightest offenses, he sees danger in them. Having received the training rules, he practices them. Just as that noble horse is well-born on both sides, this is the bhikṣu's first quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, whether receiving coarse or fine food, whether good or bad, he eats it equally without complaint or dissatisfaction. Just as that noble horse eats fine fodder and never refuses it, this is the bhikṣu's second quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu is disgusted by evil, unwholesome deeds: bodily evil conduct, verbal evil conduct, and mental evil conduct. He is disgusted by evil, unwholesome states. Just as that noble horse is disgusted by filth, this is the bhikṣu's third quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu is of gentle nature and can dwell harmoniously with other bhikṣus, not quarreling. Just as that noble horse is gentle and dwells harmoniously with other horses, this is the bhikṣu's fourth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, whatever pretenses or deceptions he may have, whatever faults or fears, will reveal them all before the teacher or wise companions in the holy life, who can then correct them. Just as that noble horse reveals all its faults to the trainer, this is the bhikṣu's fifth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu thinks thus: 'Whether the other bhikṣus practice or not, I alone shall practice diligently.' Just as that noble horse, whether other horses pull or not, pulls on its own, this is the bhikṣu's sixth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu always goes along the right path, and the right path is the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Just as that noble horse always goes along the proper road, this is the bhikṣu's seventh quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu is strong and enduring. Even if he falls ill, he still exerts his energy and does not abandon his effort, enduring suffering and not retreating. Just as that noble horse is strong and enduring even in illness, this is the bhikṣu's eighth quality.

"A bhikṣu possessing these eight qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms, and is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

## (160) Sūtra on Ājānīya (The Noble Horse), Second

*Thus have I heard.* At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "A noble horse of the king possesses eight qualities and is worthy of the king's use, having great regal power and being dignified in the king's procession. What are the eight?

"Here, a noble horse is well-born on both the sire's and dam's side, being from a land of fine horses. This is the first quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse eats fine fodder, whether fresh grass or dried grain, and never refuses it. This is the second quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is disgusted by sitting or lying in filth. This is the third quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is gentle in nature and can dwell harmoniously with other horses, not startling or harming them. This is the fourth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse, whatever pretenses or deceptions it may have, whatever faults or fears, will reveal them all to the horse trainer, who can then correct them. This is the fifth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse, when yoked to a carriage, thinks thus: 'The other horses, whether they pull or not, I alone shall pull, and I shall not abandon the effort.' This is the sixth quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse always goes along the proper road and never strays from the path. This is the seventh quality.

"Furthermore, this noble horse is strong and enduring. Even if it falls ill, it still exerts itself and does not abandon its task. This is the eighth quality.

"A king's noble horse possessing these eight qualities is worthy of the king's use, having great regal power and being dignified in the king's procession.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu possessing eight qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms, and is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the eight?

"Here, a bhikṣu upholds the precepts and the discipline of the Prātimokṣa, his deportment and domain are perfect, and regarding the slightest offenses, he sees danger in them. Having received the training rules, he practices them. Just as that noble horse is well-born on both sides, this is the bhikṣu's first quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, whether receiving coarse or fine food, whether good or bad, he eats it equally without complaint or dissatisfaction. Just as that noble horse eats fine fodder and never refuses it, this is the bhikṣu's second quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu is disgusted by evil, unwholesome deeds: bodily evil conduct, verbal evil conduct, and mental evil conduct. He is disgusted by evil, unwholesome states. Just as that noble horse is disgusted by filth, this is the bhikṣu's third quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu is of gentle nature and can dwell harmoniously with other bhikṣus, not quarreling. Just as that noble horse is gentle and dwells harmoniously with other horses, this is the bhikṣu's fourth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu, whatever pretenses or deceptions he may have, whatever faults or fears, will reveal them all before the teacher or wise companions in the holy life, who can then correct them. Just as that noble horse reveals all its faults to the trainer, this is the bhikṣu's fifth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu thinks thus: 'Whether the other bhikṣus practice or not, I alone shall practice diligently.' Just as that noble horse, whether other horses pull or not, pulls on its own, this is the bhikṣu's sixth quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu always goes along the right path, and the right path is the noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Just as that noble horse always goes along the proper road, this is the bhikṣu's seventh quality.

"Furthermore, the bhikṣu exerts his energy, abandoning unwholesome states and cultivating wholesome states. In wholesome states, he is ever striving, vigorous, and unrelenting, and does not abandon the task. Even with his body of flesh and blood, his flesh and blood may wither away until only skin, sinews, and bones remain, yet he does not abandon his effort until he has attained what should be attained by manly vigor and manly strength. Just as that noble horse is strong and enduring, this is the bhikṣu's eighth quality.

"A bhikṣu possessing these eight qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of being honored with joined palms, and is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

When the World-Honored One had spoken this teaching, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.
