## (157) Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Garden, Sixth of the Brahmin Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Verañjā, staying in the Yellow Reed Garden.

At that time, there was a brahmin of Verañjā who was aged and elderly, whose life was about to end, whose lifespan was nearly exhausted. He was one hundred and twenty years old and walked leaning on a staff. In the afternoon, wandering about, he went to visit the Buddha. After exchanging greetings, he stood before the Buddha leaning on his staff and said: "Gautama! I have heard that the ascetic Gautama is young and of tender age, newly gone forth to study the path. When renowned and virtuous ascetics and brahmins come personally to visit, he does not bow to them in respect, does not show them reverence, does not rise from his seat, and does not invite them to sit. Gautama! This is greatly improper."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin! I do not see anyone among gods, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, who, having come to visit, could cause the Tathāgata to bow in respect and reverence, to rise from his seat and invite them to sit. Brahmin! If anyone were to come wishing to make the Tathāgata bow in respect and reverence, rise from his seat and invite them to sit, that person's head would surely split into seven pieces."

The brahmin then said: "Gautama is without relish."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin! There is a reason I am without relish, but it is not as you mean. If there is relish in form, relish in sound, relish in smell, relish in touch, the Tathāgata has severed these with knowledge, extinguished them, uprooted them so they will never arise again. This is the reason I am without relish, but it is not as you mean."

The brahmin then said: "Gautama is without fear."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin! There is a reason I am without fear, but it is not as you mean. If there is fear from form, fear from sound, smell, taste, and touch, the Tathāgata has severed these with knowledge, extinguished them, uprooted them so they will never arise again. This is the reason I am without fear, but it is not as you mean."

The brahmin then said: "Gautama does not enter the womb."

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin! There is a reason I do not enter the womb, but it is not as you mean. If there are ascetics or brahmins for whom the bed of future birth has been severed with knowledge, extinguished, uprooted so it will never arise again, I say they do not enter the womb. The Tathāgata's bed of future birth has been severed with knowledge, extinguished, uprooted so it will never arise again; therefore I do not enter the womb. This is the reason I do not enter the womb, but it is not as you mean.

"Brahmin! Among these beings who come from ignorance, delight in ignorance, are covered by ignorance, and are wrapped in the egg of ignorance, I was the first to perceive the Dharma, and among all beings I am the foremost. Just as a hen lays eggs, whether ten or twelve, and she constantly watches over them, constantly covers them, constantly warms them, constantly protects them; afterward, even if the hen is negligent, among those chicks there will be one that uses its beak or its claws to peck through and break its shell, emerging safely. That one is the foremost among the chicks. So too am I: among these beings who come from ignorance, delight in ignorance, are covered by ignorance, and are wrapped in the egg of ignorance, I was the first to perceive the Dharma, and among all beings I am the foremost.

"Brahmin! I took kuśa grass and went to the tree of awakening, spread the grass beneath the tree, laid out my sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged. I resolved not to break my upright sitting posture until I had exhausted the outflows. I resolved not to break my upright sitting posture until I had exhausted the outflows. Having sat upright, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, I attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna. This is how at that time I gained the first supreme state of mind, attaining peaceful dwelling in the present life, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in security and bliss, leading toward nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, brahmin, when my initial thought and sustained thought had ceased, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, I attained and dwelt in the second dhyāna. This is how at that time I gained the second supreme state of mind, attaining peaceful dwelling in the present life, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in security and bliss, leading toward nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, brahmin, being free from joy, desiring equanimity, dwelling without craving, with right mindfulness and right awareness, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness,' I attained and dwelt in the third dhyāna. This is how at that time I gained the third supreme state of mind, attaining peaceful dwelling in the present life, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in security and bliss, leading toward nirvāṇa. Furthermore, brahmin, with the cessation of pleasure and the cessation of pain, and with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, I attained and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna. This is how at that time I gained the fourth supreme state of mind, attaining peaceful dwelling in the present life, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in security and bliss, leading toward nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, brahmin, having attained such a concentrated mind, purified, without defilement, without affliction, pliant, well-established, having attained an immovable mind, I realized the knowledge and supernatural power of recollecting past lives. With dispositions and characteristics, I recalled immeasurable past experiences: one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, kalpas of formation, kalpas of destruction, immeasurable kalpas of formation and destruction. Those beings were named such-and-such, with such-and-such past experiences. I had been born there, with such a clan name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and happiness, such a lifespan, such a duration of life, such an end of life. Dying there, I was reborn here; dying here, I was reborn there. I was born here, with such a clan name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and happiness, such a lifespan, such a duration of life, such an end of life. This is how at that time, in the first watch of the night, I attained this first clear knowledge. Because originally I was without negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and cultivated diligent practice, ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose, darkness was shattered and light appeared, the destruction of ignorance gave rise to light: the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

"Furthermore, brahmin, having attained such a concentrated mind, purified, without defilement, without affliction, pliant, well-established, having attained an immovable mind, I studied and realized the knowledge and supernatural power concerning birth and death. With the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I saw these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, with good appearance or bad appearance, in favorable or unfavorable conditions, going to good destinies or bad destinies, according to the actions these beings had performed, seeing them as they truly are. If these beings had accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech and mind, slandered noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished the karma of wrong views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were certain to go to an evil destiny, being reborn in hell. If these beings had accomplished good conduct of body, good conduct of speech and mind, did not slander noble ones, held right views, and accomplished the karma of right views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were certain to ascend to a good destiny, being reborn in heaven. This is how at that time, in the middle watch of the night, I attained this second clear knowledge. Because originally I was without negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and cultivated diligent practice, ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose, darkness was shattered and light appeared, the destruction of ignorance gave rise to light: the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of birth and death.

"Furthermore, brahmin, having attained such a concentrated mind, purified, without defilement, without affliction, pliant, well-established, having attained an immovable mind, I studied and realized the knowledge and supernatural power of the exhaustion of outflows. I knew this suffering as it truly is; I knew the origin of this suffering, I knew the cessation of this suffering, I knew the path to the cessation of this suffering as it truly is. I knew these outflows as they truly are; I knew the origin of these outflows, I knew the cessation of these outflows, I knew the path to the cessation of these outflows as it truly is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the outflow of desire, liberated from the outflow of existence, liberated from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, I knew I was liberated: birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of existence; I knew this as it truly is. This is how at that time, in the last watch of the night, I attained this third clear knowledge. Because originally I was without negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and cultivated diligent practice, ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose, darkness was shattered and light appeared, the destruction of ignorance gave rise to light: the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

"Furthermore, brahmin, if anyone were to speak correctly, saying there is a teaching of non-delusion, and that among beings born in the world, among all beings, there is one who is the most supreme, not overcome by suffering or pleasure, then know that the one rightly spoken of is none other than I. Why? Because I teach the Dharma of non-delusion; among beings born in the world, among all beings, I am the most supreme, not overcome by suffering or pleasure."

Thereupon, the brahmin of Verañjā immediately set aside his staff, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said to the World-Honored One: "The World-Honored One is the foremost, the World-Honored One is the great, the World-Honored One is the highest, the World-Honored One is the supreme, the World-Honored One is the equal, the World-Honored One is the unequaled, the World-Honored One has no one equal to him, the World-Honored One is without obstruction, the World-Honored One is a person without obstruction. World-Honored One! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, I take refuge for my entire life, until the end of my days."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin of Verañjā and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Garden, Sixth.

---

## (158) Sūtra on Doṇa, Seventh of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the brahmin Doṇa, wandering about in the afternoon, went to visit the Buddha. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side. The World-Honored One asked: "Doṇa! If someone were to ask you, 'Are you a brahmin?' you, being a brahmin, would declare yourself so."

The brahmin Doṇa replied: "Gautama! If one were to correctly describe a brahmin, it would be one who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach, broadly learned and retaining all knowledge, having recited and mastered the four Vedic scriptures, deeply comprehending the five modes of discourse: causes, conditions, proper meaning, grammar, and exposition. Gautama! The one correctly described as such a brahmin is none other than I. Why? Because I was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach, broadly learned and retaining all knowledge, having recited and mastered the four Vedic scriptures, deeply comprehending the five modes of discourse: causes, conditions, proper meaning, grammar, and exposition."

The World-Honored One said: "Doṇa! I shall now ask you; answer as you understand. Doṇa! What do you think? In the past, there were brahmins who ended their lives and passed away, who recited and preserved scriptures, transmitted scriptures, recited and studied the canonical texts, namely Yājña, Vāma, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, Yatakārṇi, Aṅgirasa, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Bhṛgu. These established five kinds of brahmins: there is a brahmin who is like Brahmā; there is a brahmin who resembles a deva; there is a brahmin who does not transgress the boundary; there is a brahmin who transgresses the boundary; and there is a brahmin who is a brahmin-caṇḍāla, the fifth. Doṇa! Among these five kinds of brahmins, which do you resemble?"

Doṇa said: "Gautama! You have stated this meaning briefly without elaborating in detail; I cannot understand it. I wish the ascetic Gautama would explain it well so that I may understand the meaning."

The World-Honored One said: "Doṇa! Listen carefully, think well upon it, and I shall explain it for you in detail."

Doṇa said: "Indeed, Gautama!" The brahmin Doṇa received the instruction and listened.

The Buddha said: "Doṇa! What is a brahmin who is like Brahmā? If there is a brahmin who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, seeking to obtain the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts. Having obtained the scriptures and recited and studied the canonical texts, he seeks and begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher, doing so lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? Not by farming, not by commerce, not by writing, not by accounting, not by mathematics, not by seal-making, not by calligraphy, not by literary composition, not by sūtra recitation, not by poetry, not by sword and staff, not by serving the king. He lawfully begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher. Having given wealth in offering, his mind dwells with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and abiding therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all; his mind dwells with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and his mind dwells with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein. Doṇa! Such is the brahmin who is like Brahmā.

"Doṇa! What is a brahmin who resembles a deva? If there is a brahmin who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, seeking to obtain the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts. Having obtained the scriptures and recited and studied the canonical texts, he seeks and begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher, doing so lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? Not by farming, not by commerce, not by writing, not by accounting, not by mathematics, not by seal-making, not by calligraphy, not by literary composition, not by sūtra recitation, not by poetry, not by sword and staff, not by serving the king. He lawfully begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher. Having given wealth in offering, he practices good conduct of body, good conduct of speech and mind. Having practiced good conduct of body, good conduct of speech and mind, because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is certain to ascend to a good destiny, being reborn in heaven. Doṇa! Such is the brahmin who resembles a deva.

"Doṇa! What is a brahmin who does not transgress the boundary? If there is a brahmin who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, seeking to obtain the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts. Having obtained the scriptures and recited and studied the canonical texts, he seeks and begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher, doing so lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? Not by farming, not by commerce, not by writing, not by accounting, not by mathematics, not by seal-making, not by calligraphy, not by literary composition, not by sūtra recitation, not by poetry, not by sword and staff, not by serving the king. He lawfully begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher. Having given wealth in offering, he seeks a wife for himself, lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? A brahmin does not act thus: directing his mind toward a brahmin woman, causing mutual love and attraction to bring about union. He goes only to a brahmin woman, not to a non-brahmin woman, nor to a kṣatriya woman, not to one who is pregnant, not to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who is pregnant? Lest that man and woman be called impure through lust; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who is pregnant. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who has just given birth? Lest that man and woman be called impure through anger; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! In his purpose and intent, it is not for wealth, not for pride, not for adornment, not for decoration, but solely for the sake of children. After his children are born, whatever boundaries and restrictions were established by the ancient brahmin vows, he abides in them, upholds them, and does not transgress them. Doṇa! Such is the brahmin who does not transgress the boundary.

"Doṇa! What is a brahmin who transgresses the boundary? If there is a brahmin who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, seeking to obtain the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts. Having obtained the scriptures and recited and studied the canonical texts, he seeks and begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher, doing so lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? Not by farming, not by commerce, not by writing, not by accounting, not by mathematics, not by seal-making, not by calligraphy, not by literary composition, not by sūtra recitation, not by poetry, not by sword and staff, not by serving the king. He lawfully begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher. Having given wealth in offering, he seeks a wife for himself, lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? A brahmin does not act thus: directing his mind toward a brahmin woman, causing mutual love and attraction to bring about union. He goes only to a brahmin woman, not to a non-brahmin woman, nor to a kṣatriya woman, not to one who is pregnant, not to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who is pregnant? Lest that man and woman be called impure through lust; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who is pregnant. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who has just given birth? Lest that man and woman be called impure through anger; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! In his purpose and intent, it is not for wealth, not for pride, not for adornment, not for decoration, but solely for the sake of children. After his children are born, whatever boundaries and restrictions were established by the ancient brahmin vows, he does not abide in them, does not uphold them, and transgresses them. Doṇa! Such is the brahmin who transgresses the boundary.

"Doṇa! What is the brahmin who is a brahmin-caṇḍāla? If there is a brahmin who was acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, seeking to obtain the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts. Having obtained the scriptures and recited and studied the canonical texts, he seeks and begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher, doing so lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? Not by farming, not by commerce, not by writing, not by accounting, not by mathematics, not by seal-making, not by calligraphy, not by literary composition, not by sūtra recitation, not by poetry, not by sword and staff, not by serving the king. He lawfully begs for wealth to make offerings to his teacher. Having given wealth in offering, he seeks a wife for himself, lawfully, not unlawfully. What is unlawful? A brahmin does not act thus: directing his mind toward a brahmin woman, causing mutual love and attraction to bring about union. He goes only to a brahmin woman, not to a non-brahmin woman, nor to a kṣatriya woman, not to one who is pregnant, not to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who is pregnant? Lest that man and woman be called impure through lust; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who is pregnant. Doṇa! For what reason does a brahmin not go to one who has just given birth? Lest that man and woman be called impure through anger; therefore the brahmin does not go to one who has just given birth. Doṇa! In his purpose and intent, it is not for wealth, not for pride, not for adornment, not for decoration, but solely for the sake of children. After his children are born, he engages in affairs befitting a king, in affairs befitting a thief, and in affairs befitting the wrong path, and speaks thus: 'A brahmin should engage in all affairs. A brahmin is not defiled by this, nor polluted. Just as fire burns what is clean and also burns what is unclean, so a brahmin, no matter what affair he engages in, is not defiled by this, nor polluted.' Doṇa! Such is the brahmin who is a brahmin-caṇḍāla. Doṇa! Among these five kinds of brahmins, which do you resemble?"

Doṇa said: "Gautama! Even this last one, the brahmin-caṇḍāla that you have described, I do not even measure up to, let alone the others! World-Honored One! I have understood. Well-Gone One! I have comprehended. World-Honored One! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, I take refuge for my entire life, until the end of my days."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Doṇa, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Doṇa, Seventh.

---

## (159) Sūtra on Aggarahana, Eighth of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the brahmin Aggarahana, wandering about in the afternoon, went to visit the Buddha. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and said: "Gautama! I wish to ask something; I will speak only if permitted."

The World-Honored One said: "Ask whatever you wish."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what do the brahmin scriptures depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The brahmin scriptures depend upon people and abide."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what do people depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "People depend upon rice and wheat and abide."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what do rice and wheat depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Rice and wheat depend upon the earth and abide."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the earth depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The earth depends upon water and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does water depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Water depends upon wind and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does wind depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Wind depends upon space and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does space depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Space depends upon nothing, but because of the sun and moon, there is space."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what do the sun and moon depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The sun and moon depend upon the Four Great Kings' Heaven and abide."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Four Great Kings' Heaven depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Four Great Kings' Heaven depends upon the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Heaven of the Thirty-Three depends upon the Yāma Heaven and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Yāma Heaven depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Yāma Heaven depends upon the Tuṣita Heaven and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Tuṣita Heaven depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Tuṣita Heaven depends upon the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Nirmāṇarati Heaven depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Nirmāṇarati Heaven depends upon the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven depends upon the Brahmā world and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does the Brahmā world depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "The Brahmā world depends upon Great Brahmā and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does Great Brahmā depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Great Brahmā depends upon patience and gentleness and abides."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what do patience and gentleness depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Patience and gentleness depend upon nirvāṇa and abide."

The brahmin then asked: "Gautama! Upon what does nirvāṇa depend and abide?"

The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin! You wish to pursue an endless chain of dependencies. You have received from me a boundless series of questions, yet nirvāṇa depends upon nothing and abides in nothing. Nirvāṇa is simply complete cessation; nirvāṇa is the ultimate. Brahmin! It is for this purpose that one practices the holy life under me."

The brahmin said: "World-Honored One! I have understood. Well-Gone One! I have comprehended. World-Honored One! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, I take refuge for my entire life, until the end of my days."

The Buddha spoke thus. The brahmin Aggarahana, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Aggarahana, Eighth.

---

## (160) Sūtra on Āraṇya, Ninth of the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the bhikṣus, after the midday meal, gathered and sat in the lecture hall, discussing this matter: "Venerables! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct."

At that time, the World-Honored One was in his daytime resting place. With his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, he heard the bhikṣus who, after the midday meal, had gathered and sat in the lecture hall, discussing this matter: "Venerables! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct."

Having heard this, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation, went to the lecture hall, spread a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. He asked the bhikṣus: "What were you discussing? For what reason did you gather and sit in the lecture hall?"

At that time, the bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One! We bhikṣus, after the midday meal, gathered and sat in the lecture hall, discussing this matter: 'Venerables! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct.' World-Honored One! We were discussing this matter together; it was for this reason that we gathered and sat in the lecture hall."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Good! Good! Bhikṣus, that you should speak thus: 'Venerables! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct.' Why is that? I too say the same: 'How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct.' Why is that? In the distant past, there were beings whose lifespan was eighty thousand years. Bhikṣus! When humans lived eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa was extremely prosperous and happy, rich in wealth and treasures. Villages were so close together that a chicken could fly from one to the next. Bhikṣus! When humans lived eighty thousand years, women did not marry until the age of five hundred. Bhikṣus! When humans lived eighty thousand years, there were only these illnesses: cold, heat, need for urination and defecation, desire, lack of appetite, and old age. There were no other ailments.

"Bhikṣus! When humans lived eighty thousand years, there was a king named Kururāja, who was a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, possessing four kinds of armies, ruling the land under heaven by his own authority, a righteous Dharma King, endowed with the seven treasures. Those seven treasures were: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister of war treasure; these are the seven. He was endowed with a thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, able to conquer other hosts. He was certain to rule over all this land to the shores of the great ocean, not by sword and staff, but teaching and ordering through the Dharma, causing all to dwell in peace.

"Bhikṣus! King Kururāja had a brahmin named Āraṇya, a great elder, acknowledged by both father and mother, of pure birth, whose lineage through seven generations of parents was unbroken, born generation after generation without reproach, broadly learned and retaining all knowledge, having recited and mastered the four Vedic scriptures, deeply comprehending the five modes of discourse: causes, conditions, proper meaning, grammar, and exposition. Bhikṣus! The brahmin Āraṇya had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of young students. The brahmin Āraṇya, for the sake of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of young students, dwelt in a secluded place and taught them the scriptures.

"At that time, the brahmin Āraṇya, dwelling alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, had this thought in his mind: 'How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct. It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness to study the path.' Thereupon, the brahmin Āraṇya went to the place where his many young students from various countries were gathered and said to them: 'Young students! I was dwelling alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and this thought arose in my mind: "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct. I now wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness to study the path." Young students! I now wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness to study the path. What will you do?'

"Those many young students from various countries said: 'Honored teacher! All that we know, we owe to the teacher's grace. If the honored teacher shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with faith goes forth from the household life into homelessness to study the path, then we too shall shave off our hair and beards, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness, and under that honored teacher study the path.' Thereupon, the brahmin Āraṇya subsequently shaved off his hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith went forth from the household life into homelessness to study the path. Those many young students from various countries also shaved off their hair and beards, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith went forth from the household life into homelessness, and under their honored teacher, the brahmin Āraṇya, went forth to study the path. Thus he was the Teacher Āraṇya; thus was the origin of the name of the Teacher Āraṇya's disciples.

"At that time, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct.' At that time, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! How extraordinary! How extraordinary! Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death. Yet people in the present world make no effort and seek nothing regarding righteous conduct, meaningful conduct, wholesome conduct, and excellent conduct.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as morning dew drops on the grass are evaporated when the sun comes out, existing only briefly and not for long; so too, young students, human life is like morning dew, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as during a great rain, the drops of water form bubbles that arise and disappear; so too, young students, human life is like a bubble, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a stick thrown into water quickly comes out again; so too, young students, human life is like a stick thrown into water that quickly re-emerges, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a new clay pot, when dipped in water and then placed in wind and heat, dries out extremely quickly; so too, young students, human life is like a new clay pot that dries quickly after being soaked in water, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a small piece of meat placed in a large cauldron of water with a fierce fire underneath is quickly consumed; so too, young students, human life is like meat being consumed, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a criminal bound and led to the execution stake: with every step he raises his foot, step by step he approaches death, step by step he approaches the end of life; so too, young students, human life is like a criminal bound and led to the execution stake, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a butcher leads an ox to slaughter: with every step it raises its foot, step by step it approaches death, step by step it approaches the end of life; so too, young students, human life is like an ox being led to slaughter, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as weaving on a loom: with each passing of the shuttle, the fabric nears completion, nears its end; so too, young students, human life is like a loom nearing the end of its weaving, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples. Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as a mountain torrent, rushing and flowing swiftly, sweeping away much in its path, the water flowing rapidly without a moment's pause; so too, young students, the course of human life passes swiftly, going without stopping even for an instant. Thus, young students, human life is like swift-flowing water, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! Just as in the darkness of night, a stick is thrown to the ground, and it may land head-down, or it may land tail-down, or it may land lying flat, or it may fall in a clean place, or it may fall in an unclean place; so too, young students, beings covered by ignorance and bound by craving may be born in hell, may be born as animals, may be born as hungry ghosts, may be born in heaven, or may be born among humans. Thus, young students, human life is like a stick thrown to the ground in darkness, extremely hard to obtain, with the least bit of savor, yet great in suffering and calamity, with calamities exceedingly numerous.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! I have in the world abandoned covetousness, my mind free from contention. Seeing others' wealth and possessions, the various means of livelihood, I do not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for myself. I have purified my mind of covetousness. Likewise with anger, drowsiness, restlessness and worry. I have in the world abandoned doubt and passed beyond confusion. Regarding all wholesome dharmas, I am without hesitation. I have purified my mind of doubt and confusion. Young students! You too should in the world abandon covetousness, with minds free from contention. Seeing others' wealth and possessions, the various means of livelihood, do not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for yourselves. You should purify your minds of covetousness. Likewise with anger, drowsiness, restlessness and worry. You should in the world abandon doubt and pass beyond confusion. Regarding all wholesome dharmas, be without hesitation.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples: 'Young students! My mind dwells with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and abiding therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all; my mind dwells with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and my mind dwells with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein. Young students! You too should have your minds dwell with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and abiding therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally encompassing all; your minds should dwell with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and your minds should dwell with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurable and well cultivated, pervading the entire world and abiding therein.' Thus the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma to his disciples.

"Furthermore, the Teacher Āraṇya taught his disciples the Dharma of the Brahmā world. When the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma of the Brahmā world, those among his disciples who did not fully practice the Dharma, after death, were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. When the Teacher Āraṇya taught the Dharma of the Brahmā world, those among his disciples who fully practiced the Dharma, cultivating the four Brahmā-abodes and abandoning desire, after death were reborn in the Brahmā heaven. At that time, the Teacher Āraṇya had this thought: 'I should not go together with my disciples to the same place in the next world, sharing the same rebirth. I should now further cultivate the higher loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher loving-kindness, after death I shall be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.' The Teacher Āraṇya subsequently further cultivated the higher loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher loving-kindness, after death he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. The Teacher Āraṇya and his disciples did not practice the path in vain; they attained great fruition.

"Bhikṣus! What do you think? That Teacher Āraṇya of long ago, do you think he was a different person? Do not think so. Why? Bhikṣus, you should know that it was none other than I. At that time, I was named the Teacher Āraṇya. At that time, I had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. At that time, I taught my disciples the Dharma of the Brahmā world.

"When I taught the Dharma of the Brahmā world, those among my disciples who did not fully practice the Dharma, after death, were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. When I taught the Dharma of the Brahmā world, those among my disciples who fully practiced the Dharma, cultivating the four Brahmā-abodes and abandoning desire, after death were reborn in the Brahmā heaven. At that time, I had this thought: 'I should not go together with my disciples to the same place in the next world, sharing the same rebirth. I should now further cultivate the higher loving-kindness.' Having cultivated the higher loving-kindness, after death I was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Subsequently I further cultivated the higher loving-kindness. Having cultivated the higher loving-kindness, after death I was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. At that time, I and my disciples did not practice the path in vain; we attained great fruition.

"At that time, I benefited myself and also benefited others, benefiting many people, having compassion for the world, seeking meaning and benefit for gods and humans, seeking peace, security, and happiness. At that time, the Dharma I taught did not reach the ultimate, was not ultimately pure, was not the ultimate holy life, was not the ultimate completion of the holy life. At that time, I had not separated from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow, nor had I been able to attain liberation from all suffering. Bhikṣus! Now I have appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer and Guide of the Dharma, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Now I benefit myself and also benefit others, benefiting many people, having compassion for the world, seeking meaning and benefit for gods and humans, seeking peace, security, and happiness. Now I teach the Dharma that reaches the ultimate, that is ultimately pure, that is the ultimate holy life, that is the ultimate completion of the holy life. Now I have separated from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, grief, and sorrow. Now I have attained liberation from all suffering.

"Bhikṣus! If anyone were to speak correctly: 'Human life is extremely brief. One must go to the next world. One should do good deeds, one should practice the holy life. No one who is born escapes death.' Bhikṣus, now is the time for that correct statement. Why? If there are those of long life now, they reach at most a hundred years, or perhaps slightly more. If there are those of long life, they live through three hundred seasons: one hundred spring seasons, one hundred summer seasons, one hundred winter seasons. Those who live through one thousand two hundred months: four hundred spring months, four hundred summer months, four hundred winter months. Those who live through one thousand two hundred months live through two thousand four hundred half-months: eight hundred spring half-months, eight hundred summer half-months, eight hundred winter half-months. Those who live through two thousand four hundred half-months live through thirty-six thousand days and nights: twelve thousand spring days and nights, twelve thousand summer days and nights, twelve thousand winter days and nights. Those who live through thirty-six thousand days and nights consume seventy-two thousand meals, including obstacles and mother's milk. Among the obstacles to eating: not eating because of cold, not eating because of anger, not eating because of illness, not eating because of business, not eating while traveling, not eating when attending the king, not eating on fast days, and not eating when food cannot be obtained. These are the calculations for the bhikṣu who lives one hundred years: the count of years, the count of seasons, the count of months per season, the count of months, the count of half-months, the count of half-months per month, the count of days, the count of nights, the count of days and nights, the count of meals, the count of obstacles, and the count of meals with obstacles.

"Bhikṣus! If there is a teacher who, for the sake of his disciples, arises from great loving-kindness and compassion, caring for and pitying them, seeking their meaning and benefit, seeking their peace, security, and happiness, then what I have already done, you too should do. Go to secluded places, in mountain forests, under trees, in empty and tranquil places, sit in meditation and contemplation. Do not be negligent. Strive with diligent effort. Do not let there be later regret. This is my instruction; this is my teaching."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Āraṇya, Ninth.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 41

*Translated from Chinese*

---

## (163) The Sūtra on Analysis of the Six Realms

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with good meaning and good phrasing, pure and complete, the pure practice of the holy life. Listen well, listen well, and contemplate it carefully. I shall speak it for you. It is called 'Analysis of the Six Realms.'"

The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is 'Analysis of the Six Realms'? There are six realms of a person: the earth realm, the water realm, the fire realm, the wind realm, the space realm, and the consciousness realm. These are the six realms of a person.

"When I said 'there are six realms of a person,' with regard to what was this said? What is the earth realm of a person? There is an internal earth realm and an external earth realm. What is the internal earth realm? It is the internal elements that belong to oneself, that are solid, that are hard, that are grasped and held. What are they? They are hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, rough and fine skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, spleen, intestines, stomach, feces, and other such things within the body that are solid, that are hard, that are grasped and held by oneself. These are called the internal earth realm.

"Both the internal earth realm and the external earth realm are simply the earth realm. One should with right wisdom observe it as it really is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having observed it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with the earth realm and causes the mind to be free from attachment to the earth realm.

"What is the water realm of a person? There is an internal water realm and an external water realm. What is the internal water realm? It is the internal elements that belong to oneself, that are water, that are moist, that are grasped and held. What are they? They are tears, sweat, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, mucus, phlegm, urine, and other such things within the body that are water, that are moist, that are grasped and held by oneself. These are called the internal water realm.

"Both the internal water realm and the external water realm are simply the water realm. One should with right wisdom observe it as it really is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having observed it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with the water realm and causes the mind to be free from attachment to the water realm.

"What is the fire realm of a person? There is an internal fire realm and an external fire realm. What is the internal fire realm? It is the internal elements that belong to oneself, that are fire, that are heat, that are grasped and held. What are they? They are that by which the body is warmed, that by which there is aging, that by which there is burning, that by which food and drink are properly digested, and other such things within the body that are fire, that are heat, that are grasped and held by oneself. These are called the internal fire realm.

"Both the internal fire realm and the external fire realm are simply the fire realm. One should with right wisdom observe it as it really is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having observed it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with the fire realm and causes the mind to be free from attachment to the fire realm.

"What is the wind realm of a person? There is an internal wind realm and an external wind realm. What is the internal wind realm? It is the internal elements that belong to oneself, that are wind, that are light and moving, that are grasped and held. What are they? They are the upward-moving winds, the downward-moving winds, the winds in the belly, the winds that move through the limbs, the in-breath, the out-breath, and other such things within the body that are wind, that are light and moving, that are grasped and held by oneself. These are called the internal wind realm.

"Both the internal wind realm and the external wind realm are simply the wind realm. One should with right wisdom observe it as it really is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having observed it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with the wind realm and causes the mind to be free from attachment to the wind realm.

"What is the space realm of a person? There is an internal space realm and an external space realm. What is the internal space realm? It is the internal elements that belong to oneself, that are space, that are empty, that are grasped and held. What are they? They are the openings of the eyes, the openings of the ears, the openings of the nose, the opening of the mouth, and that by which food and drink enter and pass through, that in which food and drink accumulate, and that from below which food and drink are expelled. These are called the internal space realm.

"Both the internal space realm and the external space realm are simply the space realm. One should with right wisdom observe it as it really is: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Having observed it thus with right wisdom as it really is, one becomes disenchanted with the space realm and causes the mind to be free from attachment to the space realm.

"What remains then is only consciousness, which is purified and bright. What does one cognize with this consciousness? One cognizes pleasure, one cognizes pain, one cognizes neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

"Dependent on a contact that is experienced as pleasant, there arises a pleasant feeling. When one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows: 'I experience a pleasant feeling.' When that contact experienced as pleasant ceases, then the feeling produced by that contact, the pleasant feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as pleasant, also ceases and comes to rest.

"Dependent on a contact that is experienced as painful, there arises a painful feeling. When one experiences a painful feeling, one knows: 'I experience a painful feeling.' When that contact experienced as painful ceases, then the feeling produced by that contact, the painful feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as painful, also ceases and comes to rest.

"Dependent on a contact that is experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. When one experiences a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows: 'I experience a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.' When that contact experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant ceases, then the feeling produced by that contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, also ceases and comes to rest.

"Just as when two pieces of wood are rubbed together, heat arises and fire is produced from the contact, and when those two pieces of wood are separated from each other, the heat arising from that also ceases and comes to rest. In the same way, dependent on a contact that is experienced as pleasant, there arises a pleasant feeling. When one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows: 'I experience a pleasant feeling.' When that contact experienced as pleasant ceases, the feeling produced by that contact, the pleasant feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as pleasant, also ceases and comes to rest.

"Dependent on a contact that is experienced as painful, there arises a painful feeling. When one experiences a painful feeling, one knows: 'I experience a painful feeling.' When that contact experienced as painful ceases, the feeling produced by that contact, the painful feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as painful, also ceases and comes to rest.

"Dependent on a contact that is experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. When one experiences a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows: 'I experience a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.' When that contact experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant ceases, the feeling produced by that contact, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising dependent on that contact experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, also ceases and comes to rest.

"What remains then is only equanimity, which is purified and bright, soft and supple, radiant and luminous. Just as a skilled goldsmith or goldsmith's apprentice lights a furnace, and having lit the furnace, puts gold into the crucible and from time to time blows on it, from time to time sprinkles water on it, and from time to time examines it closely. That gold then becomes refined, its impurities all removed, becoming soft, supple, radiant, and luminous, and can be freely worked. Whatever ornament the goldsmith wishes to make, whether a bracelet, an earring, a necklace, or a golden garland, all can be accomplished as desired.

"In the same way, what remains is only equanimity, which is purified and bright, soft and supple, radiant and luminous. One then knows: 'If I direct this equanimity, which is purified and bright, to the base of boundless space and cultivate the mind accordingly, then relying on this equanimity, abiding in this equanimity, this equanimity becomes established in the base of boundless space and is maintained there. One knows as it really is: "This is conditioned, this is volitionally produced." That which is conditioned, that which is volitionally produced, is impermanent and subject to cessation.' One knows this.

"One knows: 'If I direct this equanimity, which is purified and bright, to the base of boundless consciousness and cultivate the mind accordingly, then relying on this equanimity, abiding in this equanimity, this equanimity becomes established in the base of boundless consciousness and is maintained there. One knows as it really is: "This is conditioned, this is volitionally produced." That which is conditioned, that which is volitionally produced, is impermanent and subject to cessation.' One knows this.

"One knows: 'If I direct this equanimity, which is purified and bright, to the base of nothingness and cultivate the mind accordingly, then relying on this equanimity, abiding in this equanimity, this equanimity becomes established in the base of nothingness and is maintained there. One knows as it really is: "This is conditioned, this is volitionally produced." That which is conditioned, that which is volitionally produced, is impermanent and subject to cessation.' One knows this.

"One knows: 'If I direct this equanimity, which is purified and bright, to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and cultivate the mind accordingly, then relying on this equanimity, abiding in this equanimity, this equanimity becomes established in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is maintained there. One knows as it really is: "This is conditioned, this is volitionally produced." That which is conditioned, that which is volitionally produced, is impermanent and subject to cessation.' One knows this.

"One knows: 'If I direct this equanimity, which is purified and bright, to the signless concentration of mind and cultivate the mind accordingly, then relying on this equanimity, abiding in this equanimity, this equanimity becomes established in the signless concentration of mind and is maintained there. One knows as it really is: "This is conditioned, this is volitionally produced." That which is conditioned, that which is volitionally produced, is impermanent and subject to cessation.' One knows this.

"That bhikṣu neither fabricates the conditioned formation for existence, nor fabricates the conditioned formation for non-existence. Because of neither fabricating the conditioned formation for existence nor for non-existence, one does not grasp at anything in the world. Not grasping, one is not anxious. Not being anxious, one individually attains parinirvāṇa. One knows as it really is: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence.'

"If that bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows it is impermanent, one knows it should not be attached to, one knows it should not be delighted in. If one experiences a painful feeling, one knows it is impermanent, one knows it should not be attached to, one knows it should not be delighted in. If one experiences a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one knows it is impermanent, one knows it should not be attached to, one knows it should not be delighted in.

"If one experiences a pleasant feeling, one experiences it as detached. If one experiences a painful feeling, one experiences it as detached. If one experiences a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, one experiences it as detached.

"When one experiences a feeling limited to the body, one knows: 'I experience a feeling limited to the body.' When one experiences a feeling limited to life, one knows: 'I experience a feeling limited to life.' One knows: 'When the body breaks up and life ends, after life has ceased, all that is experienced, in which one does not delight, will become cool right here.'

"Just as a potter or potter's apprentice shapes a vessel on the wheel. If given a great push, it turns for a long time, knowing: 'A great push was given, so it turns for a long time.' If given a small push, it turns for a short time, knowing: 'A small push was given, so it turns for a short time.' When the force is exhausted, it gradually stops and turns no more, knowing: 'The force is exhausted, so the turning gradually stops.'

"In the same way, that bhikṣu, when experiencing a feeling limited to the body, knows: 'I experience a feeling limited to the body.' When experiencing a feeling limited to life, knows: 'I experience a feeling limited to life.' One knows: 'When the body breaks up and life ends, after life has ceased, all that is experienced, in which one does not delight, will become cool right here.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

## (164) The Sūtra on Ox Dung

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there were even as much as a fingertip of existence and coming to be that were permanent, unchanging, eternal, and not subject to transformation, then living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering would not be discernible. However, because even as much as a fingertip of existence and coming to be is not permanent, not unchanging, not eternal, and is subject to transformation, therefore living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering is discernible.

"Just as in this land of Rājagṛha, those whose homes have much ox dung pile it up in heaps. One person takes it to spread over a field. Having spread it, they might say: 'This ox dung that was spread has already been used; this ox dung cannot return to the ox dung heap, and neither is it ox dung anymore, but has lost its original nature.' In the same way, if there were even as much as a fingertip of existence and coming to be that were permanent, unchanging, eternal, and not subject to transformation, then living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering would not be discernible. However, because even as much as a fingertip of existence and coming to be is not permanent, not unchanging, not eternal, and is subject to transformation, therefore living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering is discernible.

"I do not see even a single form in which, if a being were to be attached to and remain in it, there would be no sorrow, no lamentation, no suffering, no distress, and no despair. However, when a being is attached to and remains in form, there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair."

At that time, the World-Honored One grasped a small piece of ox dung with his fingernail and addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, you do not even have this much of a self or anything belonging to a self. If there were this much of a self or anything belonging to a self, then living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering would not be discernible. Because there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, not even this much, therefore living the holy life for the right and complete ending of suffering is discernible."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

## (165) The Sūtra on the Simile of the Warm Springs

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there were no gratification in the world, then beings would not become defiled by the world. Because there is gratification in the world, therefore beings become defiled by the world.

"If there were no danger in the world, then beings would not become disenchanted with the world. Because there is danger in the world, therefore beings become disenchanted with the world.

"If there were no escape from the world, then beings could not escape from the world. Because there is escape from the world, therefore beings can escape from the world.

"If I had not with right wisdom known as it really is the gratification in the world as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, then I would not have attained unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, Brahmā, its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, its devas and humans. Because I with right wisdom knew as it really is the gratification in the world as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, therefore I attained unsurpassed, right, and complete enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māra, Brahmā, its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, its devas and humans.

"What is the gratification of the world? The world has five qualities of sensual pleasure. The eye cognizes forms that are wished for, desired, delightful, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. The ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes smells, the tongue cognizes tastes, and the body cognizes tactile objects that are wished for, desired, delightful, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on these five qualities of sensual pleasure: this is the gratification of the world.

"What is the danger of the world? If a person works at a craft, whether tilling the land, keeping accounts, calculating, writing, being an archer, serving a king, or practicing any other such craft, suffering cold, suffering heat, being bitten by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and sun, being hungry and thirsty, and working hard in various ways to seek a livelihood: this is the danger of the world.

"If that person works hard in this way, makes effort in this way, seeking a livelihood, but does not obtain wealth, that person then sorrows, grieves, beats their breast, weeps and cries, becomes confused and deranged, saying: 'I work hard in vain, my efforts achieve nothing.' This is the danger of the world.

"If that person works hard in this way, makes effort in this way, seeking a livelihood, and does obtain wealth, that person then suffers from guarding and protecting it, fearing that the king will seize it, fearing that thieves will rob it, fearing fire will burn it, fearing floods will wash it away, fearing that unfilial children will scatter it and waste it. Even though one guards and protects it, the wealth is still lost. That person then sorrows, grieves, beats their breast, weeps and cries, becomes confused and deranged, saying: 'What I formerly owned, now I have lost it all.' This is the danger of the world.

"Furthermore, because of craving for sensual pleasures, because sensual pleasures are the cause, because sensual pleasures are the condition, kings quarrel with kings, brāhmaṇas quarrel with brāhmaṇas, householders quarrel with householders, mothers quarrel with children, children quarrel with mothers, fathers quarrel with children, children quarrel with fathers, brothers quarrel with brothers, brothers quarrel with sisters, sisters quarrel with brothers, friends quarrel with friends. Because they quarrel and fight with each other, they attack each other with fists, stones, knives, and sticks, and from this they suffer injury and death. This is the danger of the world.

"Furthermore, because of craving for sensual pleasures, because sensual pleasures are the cause, because sensual pleasures are the condition, people don armor, take up weapons, bows, arrows, and various sharp blades, and charge into battle. Or they climb elephants, or mount horses, or ride chariots, and charge forward to attack. At that time, elephants clash with elephants, horses clash with horses, chariots clash with chariots, infantry clashes with infantry, elephants clash with horses, horses clash with chariots, chariots clash with infantry. They attack each other with arrows, knives, spears, sharp swords, and round stones, and from this they suffer injury and death. This is the danger of the world.

"Furthermore, because of craving for sensual pleasures, because sensual pleasures are the cause, because sensual pleasures are the condition, people don armor, take up weapons, bows, arrows, and various sharp blades, and go to attack fortified cities and towns. They attack each other with arrows, knives, spears, boiling butter, and great stones, and from this they suffer injury and death. This is the danger of the world.

"Furthermore, because of craving for sensual pleasures, because sensual pleasures are the cause, because sensual pleasures are the condition, people don armor, take up weapons, bows, arrows, and various sharp blades, and go to rob on the road, plundering villages and towns, breaking into houses, committing banditry, and standing at crossroads to steal from and violate others' wives. The king then captures such people and subjects them to various punishments: cutting off hands, cutting off feet, or cutting off both hands and feet, cutting off ears, cutting off nose, or cutting off both ears and nose, or they are placed in a cauldron and boiled, or their hair is plucked out, or they are wrapped in grass and set on fire, or wrapped in bark and set on fire, or made to lie in an iron bed and have boiling oil poured on them, or placed in a stone mortar and pounded, or made a living target for shooting. Various such punishments are inflicted, and from this they suffer injury and death. This is the danger of the world.

"Furthermore, beings engage in evil bodily conduct, evil verbal conduct, and evil mental conduct. Because of engaging in evil bodily conduct, evil verbal conduct, and evil mental conduct, when the body breaks up and life ends, they surely fall into evil destinies, being reborn in hell. This is the danger of the world.

"What is the escape from the world? If one is able to subdue and abandon desire and craving for the five qualities of sensual pleasure, removing desire and craving: this is the escape from the world.

"It is just as at Rājagṛha there are hot springs. There is water flowing from the east, and there is water flowing from the west. There is hot water and there is cold water. Suppose the hot water in the hot springs were to think: 'Where does my heat come from?' The heat of the hot water in the hot springs comes from the fire realm. If the fire realm ceases, the water would become cold. In the same way, pleasure and joy arise dependent on the five qualities of sensual pleasure. If one is able to subdue and abandon this desire and craving, removing desire and craving, then there is no more pleasure and joy arising dependent on the five qualities of sensual pleasure."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

## (166) The Sūtra on Releasing [the Lump of] Foam

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "It is just as if there were a great downpour of rain and water formed bubbles on the surface. A person with good eyesight would observe those bubbles, examine them, and analyze them. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing them, one would find them to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in water bubbles? In the same way, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near, a bhikṣu observes it, examines it, and analyzes it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one finds it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in form?

"It is just as in the autumn months, when rain is falling, water bubbles arise and burst on the surface of the water. A person with good eyesight would observe them, examine them, and analyze them. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing them, one would find them to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in water bubbles? In the same way, whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near, a bhikṣu observes it, examines it, and analyzes it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one finds it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in feeling?

"It is just as in the last month of spring when a mirage shimmers at midday. A person with good eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one would find it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in a mirage? In the same way, whatever perception there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near, a bhikṣu observes it, examines it, and analyzes it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one finds it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in perception?

"It is just as if a person needing heartwood were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There one sees a great plantain tree, straight and tall, young and without any knots. One would cut it down at the root and chop off the top, and then peel away the leaves one by one. As one peels the leaves, one cannot even find the pith, let alone heartwood. A person with good eyesight would observe it, examine it, and analyze it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one would find it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in a plantain tree? In the same way, whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near, a bhikṣu observes them, examines them, and analyzes them. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing them, one finds them to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in formations?
