"It is just as if a master magician or a magician's apprentice were to perform an illusion at a crossroads. A person with good eyesight would observe the illusion, examine it, and analyze it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one would find it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in a magical illusion? In the same way, whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether gross or subtle, whether beautiful or ugly, whether far or near, a bhikṣu observes it, examines it, and analyzes it. Upon observing, examining, and analyzing it, one finds it to be empty, without substance, without solidity. How could there be substance in consciousness?"

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, saying:

"Form is like a lump of foam,
Feeling like a water bubble,
Perception like a mirage,
Formations like a plantain tree,
And consciousness like a magical illusion:
So has the Kinsman of the Sun taught.

"If one examines and analyzes them,
Observing well with proper attention,
Whoever sees them as they really are
Finds them to be empty, without substance.

"Regarding this body,
The One of Broad Wisdom has taught
That when three things are abandoned,
One sees that form is cast off:

"When life-warmth and consciousness
Depart from this body,
Then it is discarded and cast aside,
Lying there, senseless as a log.

"Such is the nature of this body:
It is a deceit that deludes the foolish.
It is like a murderer,
And in it no core can be found.

"A bhikṣu who is energetic
Should contemplate the aggregates in this way,
Whether by day or by night,
Always with right mindfulness and clear comprehension.

"One should abandon all fetters
And make a refuge for oneself,
Practicing as if one's head were on fire,
Aspiring to the state that does not decline."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

## (167) The Sūtra on Aḥnanda (The Discourse on Aḥnanda's Questions)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation, and this thought arose in his mind: "Wonderful! Marvelous! This dependent origination is truly profound, and its appearance is also profound. But to my observation, it appears to be extremely clear and simple."

Then the Venerable Ānanda arose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and sat down. He then said to the World-Honored One: "I was alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation, and this thought arose in my mind: 'Wonderful! Marvelous! This dependent origination is truly profound, and its appearance is also profound. But to my observation, it appears to be extremely clear and simple.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, do not speak in this way! Do not speak in this way! This dependent origination is extremely profound, and its appearance is also profound. Ānanda, it is because of not understanding, not penetrating this dharma that sentient beings are like tangled thread, like a knotted ball of yarn, like muñja grass and babbaja grass, and cannot escape from saṃsāra, the rounds of rebirth, being reborn in this world and the next. Ānanda, this is speaking of the suffering in the world.

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for old age and death?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for old age and death?' one should answer: 'Birth is the condition for old age and death.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for birth?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for birth?' one should answer: 'Existence is the condition for birth.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for existence?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for existence?' one should answer: 'Clinging is the condition for existence.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for clinging?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for clinging?' one should answer: 'Craving is the condition for clinging.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for craving?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for craving?' one should answer: 'Feeling is the condition for craving.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for feeling?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for feeling?' one should answer: 'Contact is the condition for feeling.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for contact?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for contact?' one should answer: 'Name-and-form is the condition for contact.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for name-and-form?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for name-and-form?' one should answer: 'Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.'

"Ānanda, if one asks: 'Is there a condition for consciousness?' one should answer: 'There is.' If one asks: 'What is the condition for consciousness?' one should answer: 'Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.'

"Ānanda, thus consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, and name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. Name-and-form is the condition for contact, contact is the condition for feeling, feeling is the condition for craving, craving is the condition for clinging, clinging is the condition for existence, existence is the condition for birth, and birth is the condition for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. In this way the entire great mass of suffering arises.

"Ānanda, I have said that birth is the condition for old age and death. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no birth at all, of any kind whatsoever, of any being whatsoever, such as the birth of devas among devas, the birth of humans among humans, and so on for each kind of being in their respective realms, if there were absolutely no birth anywhere at all, then when there is no birth, could old age and death be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, they could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for old age and death, namely birth. Birth is the condition for old age and death.

"Ānanda, I have said that existence is the condition for birth. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no existence at all, of any kind whatsoever, such as existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, or existence in the formless realm, if there were absolutely no existence at all, then when there is no existence, could birth be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for birth, namely existence. Existence is the condition for birth.

"Ānanda, I have said that clinging is the condition for existence. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no clinging at all, of any kind whatsoever, such as clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and observances, or clinging to a doctrine of self, if there were absolutely no clinging at all, then when there is no clinging, could existence be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for existence, namely clinging. Clinging is the condition for existence.

"Ānanda, I have said that craving is the condition for clinging. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no craving at all, of any kind whatsoever, such as craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tactile objects, or craving for dharmas, if there were absolutely no craving at all, then when there is no craving, could clinging be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for clinging, namely craving. Craving is the condition for clinging.

"Ānanda, I have said that feeling is the condition for craving. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no feeling at all, of any kind whatsoever, such as feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, or feeling born of mind-contact, if there were absolutely no feeling at all, then when there is no feeling, could craving be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for craving, namely feeling. Feeling is the condition for craving.

"Ānanda, you should know that feeling arises from craving, craving arises from feeling. It is because of feeling that there is craving, and because of craving that there is feeling. If there were no feeling, there would be no craving, and if there were no craving, there would be no feeling. These two dharmas, feeling and craving, are therefore the cause, the origin, the arising, and the condition for clinging.

"Ānanda, I have said that contact is the condition for feeling. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no contact at all, of any kind whatsoever, such as eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, if there were absolutely no contact at all, then when there is no contact, could feeling be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for feeling, namely contact. Contact is the condition for feeling.

"Ānanda, I have said that name-and-form is the condition for contact. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if there were no name at all, of any kind whatsoever, no designation, no concept, no convention for name, then when there is no name, could contact by the mental body be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Ānanda, if there were no form at all, of any kind whatsoever, no shape, no appearance, no convention for form, then when there is no form, could resistance-contact be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Ānanda, if there were no name and no form, then could contact be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for contact, namely name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for contact.

"Ānanda, I have said that consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if consciousness did not enter the mother's womb, would name-and-form develop in the mother's womb?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Ānanda, if consciousness, having entered the mother's womb, were then to depart, would name-and-form come to be in this present existence?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or young girl were cut off and ceased prematurely, would name-and-form grow, develop, and mature?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for name-and-form, namely consciousness. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.

"Ānanda, I have said that name-and-form is the condition for consciousness. You should know that the meaning of this is as follows. Ānanda, if consciousness did not obtain a foothold in name-and-form, then could consciousness have a basis, and could the arising of birth, old age, sickness, death, and suffering in the future be discerned?"

Ānanda answered: "No, it could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the arising, this is the condition for consciousness, namely name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.

"Ānanda, for this reason, name-and-form is the condition for consciousness, and consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for contact, contact is the condition for feeling, feeling is the condition for craving, craving is the condition for clinging, clinging is the condition for existence, existence is the condition for birth, and birth is the condition for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. In this way the entire great mass of suffering arises.

"Ānanda, what is the designation of a self? What is the designation that is held? The designation of a self is when one holds thus: 'The self has form, is finite.' Or one holds: 'The self has form, is infinite.' Or one holds: 'The self is formless, is finite.' Or one holds: 'The self is formless, is infinite.' Ānanda, among those who designate the self as having form and finite, they designate it as being so at present, or they designate it as naturally being so, or they designate it as intending to make it so, saying: 'I shall make it become so.' Among those who designate the self as having form and infinite, having no form and finite, or having no form and infinite, they designate it as being so at present, or as naturally being so, or as intending to make it so.

"Ānanda, among those who designate the self, how many designate the self as having form and finite? How many designate the self as having form and infinite? How many designate the self as formless and finite? How many designate the self as formless and infinite? Ānanda, those who designate the self either designate it as having form or as formless, either as finite or as infinite, or as neither finite nor infinite. If so, then is it the case that anyone in the world who designates a self does not designate it in any of these ways? One cannot find such a case.

"Ānanda, what is the non-designation of a self? Those who do not designate the self as having form and finite, do not designate it as having form and infinite, do not designate it as formless and finite, do not designate it as formless and infinite. Ānanda, among those who do not designate the self, how many do not designate the self as having form and finite? How many do not designate it as having form and infinite? How many do not designate it as formless and finite? How many do not designate it as formless and infinite? Ānanda, those who do not designate the self neither designate it as having form nor as formless, neither as finite nor as infinite, nor as neither finite nor infinite. If so, then is it the case that anyone in the world who does not designate a self still designates it in any of these ways? One cannot find such a case.

"Ānanda, what is the view of a self? What is the view that is held? For example, one who considers feeling to be the self holds: 'Feeling is my self.' Or one holds: 'Feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling.' Or one holds: 'Feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling, but rather my self feels; my self has the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, the one who holds 'feeling is my self' should be asked: 'Feeling has three kinds: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Among these three feelings, which one do you consider to be the self?' Ānanda, whenever one experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; one only experiences a pleasant feeling. Whenever one experiences a painful feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; one only experiences a painful feeling. Whenever one experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience a pleasant feeling or a painful feeling; one only experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

"Ānanda, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decline, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Painful feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decline, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decline, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.

"If when experiencing a pleasant feeling one thinks 'this is my self,' then when that pleasant feeling ceases, one would think 'my self has departed.' If when experiencing a painful feeling one thinks 'this is my self,' then when that painful feeling ceases, one would think 'my self has departed.' If when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling one thinks 'this is my self,' then when that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases, one would think 'my self has departed.'

"Therefore, whoever holds that 'feeling is my self' falls into the view of a self that is impermanent in this very life, a mixture of pleasure and pain, arising and ceasing by nature. Therefore, Ānanda, it is for this reason that it is not appropriate to hold that 'feeling is my self.'

"Ānanda, the one who holds 'feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling' should be asked: 'In a realm where there is absolutely no feeling of any kind, could one say "this is my being"?'"

Ānanda answered: "No, one could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, it is for this reason that it is not appropriate to hold that 'feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling.'

"Ānanda, the one who holds 'feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling, but rather my self feels; my self has the dharma of feeling' should be asked: 'If feeling were to completely cease without any remainder, and there were absolutely no feeling at all, then when feeling has ceased, could one say "this is my being"?'"

Ānanda answered: "No, one could not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, it is for this reason that it is not appropriate to hold that 'feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling, but rather my self feels; my self has the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu does not hold that 'feeling is my self,' does not hold that 'my self has no feeling,' does not hold that 'my self feels; my self has the dharma of feeling,' then one does not grasp at anything in the world. Not grasping, one is not anxious. Not being anxious, one individually attains parinirvāṇa. One knows as it really is: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more existence.'

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu's mind has been liberated in this way, and if someone asks this bhikṣu: 'After the Tathāgata dies, does the Tathāgata exist?' this is not appropriate. 'After the Tathāgata dies, does the Tathāgata not exist?' this is not appropriate. 'After the Tathāgata dies, does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist?' this is not appropriate. 'After the Tathāgata dies, does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist?' this is not appropriate. Why? Because this is beyond the scope of designation, beyond the path of designation, beyond the range of designation. What is the range of designation? It is that all designation is from the range of designation. A bhikṣu's mind has been liberated in this way, through the dharma of deeply knowing and deeply seeing, which is beyond the range of designation."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the World-Honored One: "World-Honored One, if a bhikṣu's mind has been liberated in this way, after the body breaks up and life ends, where does one go?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, this question should not be asked. Why? Because I do not speak of going anywhere. If I were to speak of a place of going, then you could ask about a place of going. I do not speak of this. Why? This is beyond the scope of designation, beyond the path of designation, beyond the range of designation. All designation is from the range of designation. A bhikṣu's mind has been liberated in this way, through the dharma of deeply knowing and deeply seeing, which is beyond the range of designation.

"Ānanda, in the range of seven consciousnesses and two abodes, how does a being stand, how does a being go, how does a being remain, how does a being move? What are the seven consciousnesses and two abodes?

"Ānanda, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the lower realms. This is called the first consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings with diverse bodies and unified perception, such as the Brahmā gods who are born there for the first time and those devas of the Brahmā retinue. This is called the second consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara devas. This is called the third consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings with unified bodies and unified perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna devas. This is called the fourth consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings who have completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, and who enter into and abide in boundless space, thinking 'space is boundless.' This is the base of boundless space. This is called the fifth consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings who have completely transcended the base of boundless space and enter into and abide in boundless consciousness, thinking 'consciousness is boundless.' This is the base of boundless consciousness. This is called the sixth consciousness abode.

"Ānanda, there are beings who have completely transcended the base of boundless consciousness and enter into and abide in nothingness, thinking 'there is nothing.' This is the base of nothingness. This is called the seventh consciousness abode.

"Furthermore, the two abodes: the first is the base of non-percipient beings, and the second is the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"Ānanda, the first consciousness abode, with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the lower realms: if a being knows this consciousness abode, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that being delight in it?"

Ānanda answered: "No, one should not."

"Ānanda, the second consciousness abode, the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh consciousness abodes, and the two abodes, the base of non-percipient beings and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: if a being knows these abodes, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, and knows the escape from them, should that being delight in them?"

Ānanda answered: "No, one should not."

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, with regard to these seven consciousnesses and two abodes, knows them as they really are, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, and knows the escape from them, and is liberated through non-attachment, then this bhikṣu is called one liberated by wisdom.

"Ānanda, there are eight liberations. What are the eight?

"Having form within, one sees forms externally. This is the first liberation.

"Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally. This is the second liberation.

"The pure liberation. This is the third liberation.

"Having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters into and abides in boundless space, thinking 'space is boundless.' This is the base of boundless space. This is the fourth liberation.

"Having completely transcended the base of boundless space, one enters into and abides in boundless consciousness, thinking 'consciousness is boundless.' This is the base of boundless consciousness. This is the fifth liberation.

"Having completely transcended the base of boundless consciousness, one enters into and abides in nothingness, thinking 'there is nothing.' This is the base of nothingness. This is the sixth liberation.

"Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters into and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the seventh liberation.

"Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters into and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the eighth liberation.

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, with regard to these eight liberations, can enter and emerge in both forward and reverse order, entering and emerging at will, and with regard to the seven consciousnesses and two abodes, knows them as they really are, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, and knows the escape from them, and is liberated through non-attachment, then this bhikṣu is called liberated in both ways."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

## (168) The Sūtra on Intention

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there is intention, if there is planning, if there is latent tendency, then there is a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a foothold for consciousness. When consciousness has a foothold and grows, there is the production of future renewed existence. When there is the production of future renewed existence, then in the future there is birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. In this way the entire great mass of suffering arises.

"If there is no intention, if there is no planning, but there are still latent tendencies, then there is a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a foothold for consciousness. When consciousness has a foothold and grows, there is the production of future renewed existence. When there is the production of future renewed existence, then in the future there is birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. In this way the entire great mass of suffering arises.

"If there is no intention, if there is no planning, and if there are no latent tendencies, then there is no basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is no basis, there is no foothold for consciousness. When consciousness has no foothold and does not grow, there is no production of future renewed existence. When there is no production of future renewed existence, then in the future, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease. In this way the entire great mass of suffering ceases."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it respectfully.

---

*End of Fascicle 41 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Fascicle 41 of the Madhyamāgama

## Sūtra 161: The Brahmāyu Sūtra, Tenth of the Brahmin Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Videha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, in Mithilā there was a brahmin named Brahmāyu, who was extremely wealthy and prosperous, with immeasurable assets. His livestock, estates, and enterprises were incalculable. He had fiefdoms and food-granting villages, fully equipped with all manner of abundant provisions. Mithilā, down to its water, grasses, and trees, had been specially granted to him as a brahminical fief by King Ajātaśatru Vaidehi-putra of Magadha. The brahmin Brahmāyu had a young student named Uttara, who was esteemed by his father and mother, whose birth-lineage was pure going back through seven generations of parents with an unbroken clan, generation after generation without fault. He was broadly learned and retentive, having recited and mastered the four Vedic scriptures, deeply versed in the five modes of explanation: causation, correlation, proper text, grammar, and narrative.

The brahmin Brahmāyu heard that there was a śramaṇa named Gotama, a son of the Śākya clan, who had left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his beard and hair, put on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith had left the household life for homelessness to study the Way. He was traveling in the country of Videha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. That śramaṇa Gotama had a great reputation that was heard in all ten directions. That śramaṇa Gotama was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as Buddha, the World-Honored One. In this world, among gods and Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, he had known and realized for himself, and having attained realization, he dwelt accordingly. He taught the Dharma that was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life.

Furthermore, he had heard that the śramaṇa Gotama was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions.

The brahmin Brahmāyu, having heard this, said: "Uttara! I have heard thus: 'That śramaṇa Gotama, a son of the Śākya clan, has left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his beard and hair, put on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith has left the household life for homelessness to study the Way. He is traveling in the country of Videha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.' Uttara! 'That śramaṇa Gotama has a great reputation, heard in all ten directions. That śramaṇa Gotama is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as Buddha, the World-Honored One. In this world, among gods and Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, he has known and realized for himself, and having attained realization, he dwells accordingly. He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life.'

"Furthermore, Uttara! 'That śramaṇa Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions.'

"Uttara! You have studied and retained the scriptures concerning the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions."

Uttara replied: "Just so, Venerable One! I have studied and retained the scriptures concerning the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions."

The brahmin Brahmāyu said: "Uttara! Go to that śramaṇa Gotama and observe whether that śramaṇa Gotama is as described or not. Does he truly possess the thirty-two marks of a great person?"

The young student Uttara, having heard this, bowed at the feet of the brahmin Brahmāyu, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and observed the World-Honored One's body for the thirty-two marks. He saw that the World-Honored One's body had thirty marks, but regarding two marks he had doubts: the mark of the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue. The World-Honored One thought: "This Uttara has been observing my body for the thirty-two marks. He has seen thirty marks but has doubts about two: the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue. I should now dispel his doubts." The World-Honored One, having known this, exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner. Having exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner, he caused the young student Uttara to see his sheathed male organ and his broad, long tongue.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner. Having exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner, the young student Uttara saw the World-Honored One's sheathed male organ and his broad, long tongue. The broad, long tongue: from his mouth the tongue emerged and completely covered his entire face. The young student Uttara, having seen this, thought: "The śramaṇa Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions."

The young student Uttara further thought: "I should thoroughly observe his deportment and manners, and also observe his conduct and movements." Thereupon, the young student Uttara followed along with the Buddha, and for the four months of the summer he observed his deportment and manners, and also observed his conduct and movements. After those four months of summer had passed, the young student Uttara was delighted with the World-Honored One's deportment and manners, and having observed his conduct and movements, he said: "Gotama! I now have matters to attend to and wish to take my leave."

The World-Honored One said: "Uttara! Go as you please."

The young student Uttara, having heard what the World-Honored One said and having well received and well retained it, rose from his seat, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to where the brahmin Brahmāyu was, bowed at the feet of the brahmin Brahmāyu, and sat down to one side.

The brahmin Brahmāyu asked: "Uttara! Is it truly as we heard, that the śramaṇa Gotama has a great reputation heard in all ten directions? Is it so or not? Does he truly possess the thirty-two marks of a great person?"

The young student Uttara replied: "Just so, Venerable One! It is truly as we heard. The śramaṇa Gotama has a great reputation heard in all ten directions. The śramaṇa Gotama is as described, not otherwise, and he truly possesses the thirty-two marks. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's feet are evenly flat when standing. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has wheels on the soles of his feet, the wheels having a thousand spokes, all complete. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's toes are long and slender. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's feet are symmetrical and straight. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's heels and ankles are evenly full on both sides. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's two ankles are even. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's body hair curls upward. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's hands and feet are webbed, like a royal goose. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama.

"Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's hands and feet are extremely fine, soft and delicate, like the tūla flower. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's skin is smooth and fine, so that dust and water do not adhere to it. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, each of the śramaṇa Gotama's hairs grows singly, one hair from each pore, its color like dark blue, like a conch spiraling to the right. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has calves like those of a deer king. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has his male organ sheathed, like a fine stallion king. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's body is well-rounded, like the nyagrodha tree, proportional above and below. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's body is not bent; his body not being bent means that standing upright with arms extended he can touch his knees. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama.

"Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's body is the color of golden yellow, like refined purple-gold. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's body is full in seven places; the seven places being full means the two hands, two feet, two shoulders, and neck. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's upper body is large, like a lion. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has lion-like jaws. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's spine is straight and even. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's two shoulders are connected, joining the neck evenly and fully. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has forty teeth, the teeth are not spaced apart, the teeth are white, and the teeth convey the foremost taste. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has a Brahmā-voice that is pleasing, his voice being like that of the kalaviṅka bird. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama.

"Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has a broad, long tongue; the broad, long tongue being such that the tongue emerges from his mouth and completely covers his face. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's eye sockets are full, like a bull king. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's eyes are dark blue in color. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has a fleshy protuberance on the crown of his head, round and symmetrical, with hair spiraling to the right. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. Furthermore, Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama has a tuft of hair growing between his eyebrows, pure white and curling to the right. This is, Venerable One, a mark of a great person of the śramaṇa Gotama. These, Venerable One, are the thirty-two marks of a great person that the śramaṇa Gotama possesses.

"If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world, sovereign by his own authority. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions.

"Furthermore, Venerable One, I observed the śramaṇa Gotama putting on his robe, having put on his robe; donning his outer garment, having donned his outer garment; leaving his room, having left his room; leaving the park, having left the park; walking along the path to a village; entering the village, having entered the village; being in the lanes; entering a house, having entered a house; arranging his seat, having arranged his seat; sitting down, having sat down; washing his hands, having washed his hands; receiving food and drink, having received food and drink; eating, having eaten; washing his hands and giving a benediction; rising from his seat; leaving the house, having left the house; being in the lanes; leaving the village, having left the village; entering the park, having entered the park; entering his room, having entered his room. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama puts on his robe evenly, neither too high nor too low; his robe does not cling to his body, yet the wind cannot cause the robe to separate far from his body. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama dons his outer garment evenly, neither too high nor too low; his garment does not cling to his body, yet the wind cannot cause the garment to separate far from his body. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama always wears a fresh robe, conforming to the noble ones, cut with a knife, dyed in muted colors, thus dyed in the muted colors of the noble ones. He who holds this robe does so not for wealth, not for pride, not for personal adornment, not for embellishment, but only for protection from mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, and sun, and for the sake of modesty, to cover his body.

"When he leaves his room, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when leaving his room, never stoops his body. Venerable One, when the śramaṇa Gotama wishes to walk, he first raises his right foot, lifts it properly and sets it down properly; his walking is untroubled and without disturbance. When walking, his two ankles never knock together. Venerable One, when the śramaṇa Gotama walks, he is not soiled by dust. Why is this? Because of his originally wholesome conduct. When he leaves the park, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when leaving the park, never stoops his body. Arriving at the approach to the village, his body turns fully to the right, and he surveys like a dragon, looking all around without fear, without terror, without alarm, observing all directions. Why is this? Because he is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One. When he enters the village, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when entering the village, never stoops his body. When in the lanes, he does not look down, nor does he look up; he only gazes straight ahead, and in this his knowing and seeing are unobstructed.

"Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's sense faculties are always composed. Why is this? Because of his originally wholesome conduct. When he enters a house, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when entering a house, never stoops his body. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama turns his body to the right, arranges his seat, and sits down. On the seat he does not sit down with full force, nor does he press his hands on his thighs to sit on the seat. Having sat on the seat, he is not depressed, not agitated, and also not elated. When receiving water for washing, it is neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little. When he receives food and drink, it is neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama receives food with his bowl level, with curry and food in equal portions. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama forms his morsels evenly and places them slowly in his mouth. Before a morsel reaches his mouth, he does not open it prematurely. Once in his mouth, he chews three times before swallowing. No rice or curry is left broken up, nor does he put a subsequent morsel in while there is still some remaining in his mouth.

"Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama eats in three kinds of purity, desiring to obtain the taste of food but not wishing to be attached to the taste. He eats not for wealth, not for pride, not for personal adornment, not for embellishment, but only to sustain the body, to endure long without ailment, to stop old diseases and not give rise to new ones, to preserve life without ailment, with strength and well-being. When the meal is finished, when he receives water for washing his hands, it is neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little. When he receives water for washing his bowl, it is neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little. When he has washed his hands clean, his bowl is also clean; when he has washed the bowl clean, his hands are also clean. Having wiped his hands, he then wipes his bowl; having wiped his bowl, he then wipes his hands. Having washed and wiped his bowl, he sets it aside in one place, not too near and not too far. He does not keep looking at the bowl, nor is his mind on the bowl. He does not disparage this food, nor does he praise that food, but sits in modest silence. He then teaches the Dharma for the householders, inspiring them with eagerness, accomplishing their delight. Having by immeasurable skillful means taught the Dharma, inspiring eagerness and accomplishing delight, he then rises from his seat and withdraws to return. When he leaves the house, his body is neither stooped nor raised.

"Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when leaving the house, never stoops his body. When in the lanes, he does not look down, nor does he look up; he only gazes straight ahead, and in this his knowing and seeing are unobstructed. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's sense faculties are always composed. Why is this? Because of his originally wholesome conduct. When he leaves the village, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when leaving the village, never stoops his body. When he enters the park, his body is neither stooped nor raised. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, when entering the park, never stoops his body. After the midday meal, he puts away his robe and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, enters his room, and sits in meditation. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama enters his room and sits in meditation for the benefit of the world. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama, at the afternoon time, rises from his meditation with a radiant complexion. Why is this? Because he is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One.

"Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's mouth produces eight kinds of voice: the first is profound, the second is resonant, the third is penetrating to the heart, the fourth is pleasing, the fifth is full, the sixth is unfailing, the seventh is clear and distinct, the eighth is wise. It is loved by many, enjoyed by many, cherished by many, and causes the mind to become composed. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama teaches the Dharma in accordance with the assembly, his voice not going beyond the assembly but remaining within it. He teaches the Dharma for them, inspiring eagerness, accomplishing delight. Having by immeasurable skillful means taught the Dharma, inspiring eagerness and accomplishing delight, he then rises from his seat and returns to his dwelling. Venerable One, the śramaṇa Gotama's manner is as I have described, but in fact there is even more that surpasses this. Venerable One, I wish to go to that śramaṇa Gotama and practice the holy life under him."

The brahmin Brahmāyu said: "As you wish."

Thereupon, the young student Uttara bowed at the feet of the brahmin Brahmāyu, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, bowed at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! I wish to study the Way under the World-Honored One and receive full ordination, to become a bhikṣu and practice the holy life under the World-Honored One."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One ordained the young student Uttara, allowing him to enter training and receive full ordination. Having ordained the young student Uttara and given him the training and full ordination, the Buddha continued traveling in the country of Videha, together with the great assembly of bhikṣus, and proceeding forward, arrived at Mithilā, where he stayed in the Great Heavenly Nāla Grove in Mithilā.

The brahmins and householders of that Mithilā heard that the śramaṇa Gotama, a son of the Śākya clan who had left the Śākya lineage and gone forth to study the Way, was traveling in the country of Videha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and had progressively come to this Mithilā, staying in the Great Heavenly Nāla Grove. The śramaṇa Gotama had a great reputation heard in all ten directions. The śramaṇa Gotama was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as Buddha, the World-Honored One. In this world, among gods and Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, he had known and realized for himself, and having attained realization, he dwelt accordingly. He taught the Dharma that was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. If one could see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, and respectfully bow, make offerings, and attend upon him, one would obtain the finest benefit. "We should all go together to see that śramaṇa Gotama, bow to him and make offerings!"

Those brahmins and householders of Mithilā, each with their respective retinues following, departed from Mithilā, went north to the Great Heavenly Nāla Grove, wishing to see the World-Honored One, bow to him and make offerings. Having arrived before the Buddha, some of the brahmins and householders of Mithilā bowed at the Buddha's feet and then sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and then sat down to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and then sat down to one side; some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down in silence. After those brahmins and householders of Mithilā had each taken their seats, the Buddha taught the Dharma for them, inspiring eagerness, accomplishing delight. Having by immeasurable skillful means taught the Dharma, inspiring eagerness and accomplishing delight, he then sat in silence.

The brahmin Brahmāyu heard that the śramaṇa Gotama, a son of the Śākya clan who had left the Śākya lineage and gone forth to study the Way, was traveling in the country of Videha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and had progressively come to this country of Mithilā, staying in the Great Heavenly Nāla Grove. That śramaṇa Gotama had a great reputation heard in all ten directions. That śramaṇa Gotama was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Master of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, honored as Buddha, the World-Honored One. In this world, among gods and Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans to celestial beings, he had known and realized for himself, and having attained realization, he dwelt accordingly. He taught the Dharma that was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent at the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. If one could see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, and respectfully bow, make offerings, and attend upon him, one would obtain the finest benefit. "I should go to see the śramaṇa Gotama, bow to him and make offerings!"

The brahmin Brahmāyu told his charioteer: "Quickly harness the carriage! I now wish to go to the śramaṇa Gotama."

The charioteer received the order, quickly harnessed the carriage, and returned to announce: "The carriage is ready. May the Venerable One proceed at his pleasure." Thereupon, Brahmāyu mounted an exceedingly fine and excellent carriage, departed from Mithilā, and went north to the Great Heavenly Nāla Grove, wishing to see the World-Honored One, bow to him, and make offerings.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a measureless assembly, before and behind, and was teaching the Dharma for them. The brahmin Brahmāyu saw from afar the World-Honored One surrounded by a measureless assembly, before and behind, teaching the Dharma for them. Seeing this, he was filled with awe. Thereupon, Brahmāyu turned aside to the edge of the road and stopped at a tree. He told a young student: "Go to that śramaṇa Gotama and on my behalf inquire whether his sacred person is strong and well, free from illness, at ease in rising and resting, with energy as usual. Speak thus: 'Gotama! My teacher Brahmāyu inquires whether your sacred person is strong and well, free from illness, at ease in rising and resting, with energy as usual. Gotama! My teacher Brahmāyu wishes to come and see the śramaṇa Gotama.'"

Thereupon, the young student received the instruction, went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said: "Gotama! My teacher Brahmāyu inquires whether your sacred person is strong and well, free from illness, at ease in rising and resting, with energy as usual. Gotama! My teacher Brahmāyu wishes to come and see the śramaṇa Gotama."

The World-Honored One said: "Young student! May the brahmin Brahmāyu be at peace and well. May the gods and humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other kinds of beings be at peace and well. Young student, if the brahmin Brahmāyu wishes to come, let him do so as he pleases."

Thereupon, the young student, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. He returned to where the brahmin Brahmāyu was and reported: "Venerable One! I have conveyed the message to the śramaṇa Gotama. That śramaṇa Gotama now awaits the Venerable One. May the Venerable One proceed at his convenience."

The brahmin Brahmāyu then descended from his carriage and walked to where the Buddha was. The assembly, seeing the brahmin Brahmāyu coming from afar, immediately rose from their seats and made way for him. Why? Because he was renowned and widely recognized.

The brahmin Brahmāyu told that assembly: "Good sirs! Each of you please sit back down. I wish to go directly to see the śramaṇa Gotama." Thereupon, Brahmāyu went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.

At that time, Brahmāyu's two faculties were unimpaired: the eye faculty and the ear faculty. The brahmin Brahmāyu, having seated himself, carefully observed the Buddha's body for the thirty-two marks. He saw thirty marks but had doubts about two: the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue. The brahmin Brahmāyu then questioned the World-Honored One in verse:

"As I have heard in the past,
Of the thirty-two marks of a great person,
Among them I cannot find two
On the body of the honored śramaṇa Gotama.
Does he have the sheathed male organ?
Most honored among all people, it is deeply concealed.
How can this most honored of humans
Not display the subtle and wondrous tongue?
If the Honored One has the broad, long tongue,
May he please allow me to see it.
I now truly have a doubting mind;
May the Tamer of Beings resolve my doubt."

The World-Honored One thought: "This brahmin Brahmāyu seeks the thirty-two marks on my body. He has seen thirty but has doubts about two: the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue. I should now dispel his doubt." The World-Honored One, having known this, exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner. Having exercised his psychic power in the appropriate manner, the brahmin Brahmāyu saw the World-Honored One's sheathed male organ and his broad, long tongue. The broad, long tongue: the tongue emerged from his mouth and completely covered his entire face. The World-Honored One then ceased his psychic power and spoke these verses for the brahmin Brahmāyu:

"What you have heard in the past,
The thirty-two marks of a great person,
All of them are on my body,
Complete, fulfilled, and supremely correct.
The Tamer of Beings has cut off your doubt;
Brahmin, give rise to subtle and wondrous faith.
The one most difficult to see and hear,
The Supremely Correct, Fully Enlightened One.
Appearing in the world is extremely rare,
The Supremely Correct, Fully Enlightened One.
Brahmin, I am the Perfectly Enlightened One,
The Unsurpassed, Correct Dharma King."

The brahmin Brahmāyu, having heard this, thought: "This śramaṇa Gotama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great person. If one is endowed with the marks of a great person, there are necessarily two destinies, truthful and not false. If he remains as a householder, he will surely become a wheel-turning king, wise and intelligent, with four kinds of armies, governing the world. As a righteous Dharma King, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the army-commander treasure; these are called the seven. He will have a full thousand sons, of handsome appearance, valiant and fearless, able to subdue all opponents. He will surely rule this entire earth up to the great ocean, not by sword or staff, but by the Dharma's instruction, causing all to dwell in peace. If he shaves off his beard and hair, puts on kāṣāya robes, and with perfect faith leaves the household life for homelessness to study the Way, he will surely attain the state of Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Enlightened One, with his renown spreading and being heard in all ten directions."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought: "This brahmin Brahmāyu has long been without flattery or deceit. Whatever he wishes to ask, it is entirely from a desire to know, not to cause annoyance. He is indeed thus. I should now teach him the profound Abhidharma." The World-Honored One, having known this, spoke these verses for the brahmin Brahmāyu:

"For the sake of happiness in the present life,
And benefit for the world to come,
Brahmin, ask whatever you wish,
According to whatever is in your mind.
Whatever questions you may have,
I will resolve your doubts for you."

The World-Honored One having already permitted questions,
The brahmin Brahmāyu therefore
Asked the World-Honored One,
According to whatever was in his mind:

"What makes one a brahmin?
What is the meaning of the three knowledges?
By what is one called 'unattached'?
What is it to be 'perfectly and fully enlightened'?"

At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:

"One who has extinguished evil and unwholesome dharmas,
Who stands firm, having chosen the holy life,
Who cultivates and practices the brahmin's rectitude,
By this one is called a brahmin.
One who clearly knows the past,
Who sees the realms of bliss and woe,
Who has attained the end of ignorance and can explain it,
Know that this establishes the sage.
One who well knows the purified mind,
Who has completely freed himself from lust, anger, and delusion,
Who has accomplished the three knowledges,
By this one is called 'possessing the three knowledges.'
One who is far removed from unwholesome dharmas,
Who rightly abides in the ultimate meaning,
The foremost, honored by the world,
By this one is called 'unattached.'
One who benefits gods and humans,
Who gives the eye and extinguishes harmful disputes,
Who completely knows and sees the end of all things in the present,
By this one is 'perfectly and fully enlightened.'"

Thereupon, Brahmāyu rose from his seat, wishing to bow at the Buddha's feet. At that time, the great assembly simultaneously raised a great and mighty sound: "The śramaṇa Gotama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He has great psychic powers, great might, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this? Of all the brahmins and householders in this country of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost among them in terms of birth. The brahmin Brahmāyu was esteemed by his father and mother, his birth-lineage pure going back through seven generations of parents with an unbroken clan, generation after generation without fault. Yet he most humbly shows respect, bows, makes offerings, and attends upon the śramaṇa Gotama. The śramaṇa Gotama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He has great psychic powers, great might, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this? Of all the brahmins and householders in this country of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost among them in terms of learning. The brahmin Brahmāyu is broadly learned and retentive, having recited and mastered the four Vedic scriptures, deeply versed in the five modes of explanation: causation, correlation, proper text, grammar, and narrative. Yet he most humbly shows respect, bows, makes offerings, and attends upon the śramaṇa Gotama.

"The śramaṇa Gotama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He has great psychic powers, great might, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this? Of all the brahmins and householders in this country of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost among them in terms of wealth. The brahmin Brahmāyu is extremely wealthy and prosperous, with immeasurable assets. His livestock, estates, and enterprises are incalculable. He has fiefdoms and food-granting villages, fully equipped with all manner of abundant provisions. Mithilā, down to its water, grasses, and trees, was specially granted to him as a brahminical fief by King Ajātaśatru Vaidehi-putra of Magadha. Yet he most humbly shows respect, bows, makes offerings, and attends upon the śramaṇa Gotama. The śramaṇa Gotama is truly extraordinary! Truly remarkable! He has great psychic powers, great might, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this? Of all the brahmins and householders in this country of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost among them in terms of longevity. The brahmin Brahmāyu is a great elder of extreme old age, with a full lifespan of one hundred and twenty-six years. Yet he most humbly shows respect, bows, makes offerings, and attends upon the śramaṇa Gotama."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing with his knowledge of others' minds what that great assembly was thinking, told the brahmin Brahmāyu: "Enough, enough, brahmin! Simply rejoice in your mind and be content. Please sit back down, and I will teach the Dharma for you."

The brahmin Brahmāyu bowed at the Buddha's feet and then sat down to one side. The World-Honored One taught the Dharma for him, inspiring eagerness, accomplishing delight. Having by immeasurable skillful means taught the Dharma, inspiring eagerness and accomplishing delight, then, as is the way of all Buddhas, he first spoke of the upright Dharma, hearing which brings joy: he spoke of giving, spoke of morality, and spoke of the Dharma for being born in heaven. He censured desire as a calamity, birth and death as defilement, and praised desirelessness as sublime and the factors of the path as pure and clean. Having taught this, the Buddha knew that Brahmāyu had a joyful mind, a receptive mind, a soft mind, an enduring mind, an aspiring mind, a focused mind, a mind without doubt, a mind without hindrances, and was capable and able to receive the Buddha's correct Dharma. Then, as all Buddhas teach the essential and correct teaching, the World-Honored One fully taught him suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path. The brahmin Brahmāyu, right there on his seat, saw the four noble truths: suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path. Just as white silk is easily dyed with color, so too Brahmāyu, right there on his seat, saw the four noble truths: suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path.

Thereupon, Brahmāyu saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, cut off doubt, crossed beyond perplexity, had no other teacher, was no longer dependent on others, was free from hesitation, had already dwelt in the fruit and realization, and in the World-Honored One's Dharma attained fearlessness. He then rose from his seat and bowed at the Buddha's feet: "World-Honored One! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forth, for as long as I live, I take refuge, until the end of my life."

Then the brahmin Brahmāyu joined his palms toward the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One! May you kindly grace me by accepting my invitation tomorrow, together with the assembly of bhikṣus." The World-Honored One, for the sake of the brahmin Brahmāyu, accepted in silence.

The brahmin Brahmāyu, knowing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He returned to his home. That very night he prepared delicacies of the finest and most excellent flavors, abundantly varied, both food and drink, both chewable and soft. Having finished the preparations, at dawn he arranged seats and at the appropriate time announced: "World-Honored One! The meal is ready. May the Sage proceed at his convenience."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed, at dawn dressed in his robes and took up his bowl. With the bhikṣus flanking him, the World-Honored One in front, he went to the home of the brahmin Brahmāyu, and before the assembly of bhikṣus spread his seat and sat down. The brahmin Brahmāyu, knowing that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus were settled in their seats, personally served the water for washing hands, and with the finest delicacies, abundantly varied, both food and drink, both chewable and soft, he personally ladled and served until they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished, the vessels were collected, water for washing hands was served, and he took a small seat and sat to receive the benediction.

After the brahmin Brahmāyu was seated, the World-Honored One spoke the benediction for him:

"The fire offering is the foremost of rites;
The syllable is the source of all sounds.
The king is the most honored among humans;
The ocean is the chief of rivers.
The moon is brightest among the stars;
In radiance none surpasses the sun.
Above, below, and in all directions,
Throughout all the world,
From humans up to celestial beings,
Only the Buddha is the most supreme."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having spoken the benediction for the brahmin Brahmāyu, rose from his seat and departed. He stayed for several days in the country of Mithilā, then gathered his robes, took up his bowl, and journeyed onward to the country of Śrāvastī. Progressing forward, he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. At that time, many bhikṣus, while begging for food in Śrāvastī, heard that the brahmin Brahmāyu of Mithilā, who had questioned the Buddha in verse, had passed away. The bhikṣus, having heard this and having finished their meal, after the midday put away their robes and bowls, washed their hands and feet, placed their sitting cloths upon their shoulders, went to where the Buddha was, bowed in homage, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! We, a number of bhikṣus, this morning dressed in our robes, took up our bowls, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food. At that time we heard that the brahmin Brahmāyu of Mithilā, who had questioned the Buddha in verse, has passed away. World-Honored One! Where has he gone? Where was he reborn? What is his future state?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Bhikṣus! The brahmin Brahmāyu gained the greatest benefit. At the very end he came to know the Dharma, and for the sake of the Dharma he did not trouble me further. Bhikṣus! The brahmin Brahmāyu has exhausted the five lower fetters. He was born in that realm and will attain parinirvāṇa there. He has attained the state of non-returning and will not return to this world." At that time, the World-Honored One declared that Brahmāyu had attained the fruit of an anāgāmin.

Thus spoke the Buddha. The brahmin Brahmāyu and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Brahmāyu Sūtra, Tenth
