## Sūtra 162: Analysis of the Six Elements, First of the Chapter on Fundamental Analysis

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Magadha and went to the city of Rājagṛha to spend the night. Then the World-Honored One went to a potter's house and said: "Potter! I wish to lodge in your pottery shed for one night. Will you permit this?"

The potter replied: "I have no objection. However, there is a bhikṣu who has already taken up residence there. If he permits it, you may stay as you wish."

At that time, the Venerable Pukkusāti had already been dwelling in that pottery shed. Then the World-Honored One left the potter's house, entered the pottery shed, and said to the Venerable Pukkusāti: "Bhikṣu! I wish to lodge in this pottery shed for one night. Will you permit this?"

The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: "Sir! I have no objection. Moreover, a grass seat has already been spread in this pottery shed. If you wish to stay, please do so as you wish."

At that time, the World-Honored One went outside the pottery shed, washed his feet, returned inside, spread his sitting cloth upon the grass seat, sat cross-legged, and throughout the night sat silently in tranquil meditation with concentrated mind. The Venerable Pukkusāti also throughout the night sat silently in tranquil meditation with concentrated mind. At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This bhikṣu dwells in stillness and tranquility. How extraordinary! How remarkable! I should now ask this bhikṣu: 'Who is your teacher? Under whom did you go forth to study the path and receive the Dharma?'"

Having thought this, the World-Honored One asked: "Bhikṣu! Who is your teacher? Under whom did you go forth to study the path and receive the Dharma?"

The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: "Worthy one! There is the renunciant Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, who left the Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robe, and with faith left the household life for the homeless life to study the path. He awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He is my teacher. Under him I went forth to study the path and receive the Dharma."

The World-Honored One then asked again: "Bhikṣu! Have you ever seen your teacher?"

The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: "I have not seen him."

The World-Honored One asked: "If you were to see your teacher, would you recognize him?"

The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: "I would not recognize him. However, worthy one, I have heard that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Master of the Way, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, is called the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He is my teacher. Under him I went forth to study the path and receive the Dharma."

At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought: "This clansman went forth to study the path and receive the Dharma under me. I should now teach him the Dharma."

Having thought this, the World-Honored One said to the Venerable Pukkusāti: "Bhikṣu! I will teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which has meaning and phrasing, which is complete and pure, and which reveals the holy life. It is called the Analysis of the Six Elements. You should listen attentively and reflect well upon it."

The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: "Certainly."

The Buddha said to him: "Bhikṣu! A person has the collection of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental activities, and four abodes. If one abides in these without hearing of distressing matters, and having not heard of distressing matters, the mind does not hate, does not grieve, does not become weary, and does not become fearful. Such is the teaching: non-negligence in wisdom, guarding of truth, cultivating generosity. Bhikṣu! One should train in the supreme; one should train toward complete peace. Analyze the six elements. Thus, bhikṣu, a person has the collection of six elements. For what reason is this said? They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. That a person has the collection of six elements is said for this reason.

"Bhikṣu! A person has six bases of contact. For what reason is this said? The eye contacts and sees forms, the ear contacts and hears sounds, the nose contacts and smells odors, the tongue contacts and tastes flavors, the body contacts and feels tangibles, the mind contacts and knows dharmas. That a person has six bases of contact is said for this reason.

"Bhikṣu! A person has eighteen mental activities. For what reason is this said? When a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he abides contemplating forms with joy, abides contemplating forms with sorrow, or abides contemplating forms with equanimity. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind knows dharmas, one abides contemplating dharmas with joy, abides contemplating dharmas with sorrow, or abides contemplating dharmas with equanimity. Bhikṣu! These six contemplations with joy, six contemplations with sorrow, and six contemplations with equanimity, combined together, make eighteen activities. That a person has eighteen mental activities is said for this reason.

"Bhikṣu! A person has four abodes. For what reason is this said? They are the abode of truth, the abode of wisdom, the abode of generosity, and the abode of peace. That a person has four abodes is said for this reason.

"How is a bhikṣu non-negligent in wisdom? If a bhikṣu analyzes the elements of the body, thinking: 'Now this body of mine has the internal earth element, received at birth,' what does this refer to? It refers to hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, flesh, bones, sinews, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, large intestine, stomach, and feces. In this way, whatever else within this body is internal, belongs to the internal, is solid, of a solid nature, abides internally, and was received at birth: this is called the bhikṣu's internal earth element. Bhikṣu! Whether there is the internal earth element or the external earth element, all of it is collectively called the earth element. All of it is not mine, I am not its, nor is it a self. Contemplating thus with wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become attached to this earth element. This is called a bhikṣu's non-negligence in wisdom.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is non-negligent in wisdom. If a bhikṣu analyzes the elements of the body, thinking: 'Now this body of mine has the internal water element, received at birth,' what does this refer to? It refers to brain membrane, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, phlegm, bile, and urine. In this way, whatever else within this body is internal, belongs to the internal, is water, of a moist nature, moistens the internal, and was received at birth: this is called the bhikṣu's internal water element. Bhikṣu! Whether there is the internal water element or the external water element, all of it is collectively called the water element. All of it is not mine, I am not its, nor is it a self. Contemplating thus with wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become attached to this water element. This is called a bhikṣu's non-negligence in wisdom.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is non-negligent in wisdom. If a bhikṣu analyzes the elements of this body, thinking: 'Now this body of mine has the internal fire element, received at birth,' what does this refer to? It refers to that which heats the body, warms the body, causes distress and agitation in the body, that which warms and maintains the body, and that which digests food and drink. In this way, whatever else within this body is internal, belongs to the internal, is fire, of a heating nature, heats the internal, and was received at birth: this is called the bhikṣu's internal fire element. Bhikṣu! Whether there is the internal fire element or the external fire element, all of it is collectively called the fire element. All of it is not mine, I am not its, nor is it a self. Contemplating thus with wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become attached to this fire element. This is called a bhikṣu's non-negligence in wisdom.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is non-negligent in wisdom. If a bhikṣu analyzes the elements of the body, thinking: 'Now this body of mine has the internal wind element, received at birth,' what does this refer to? It refers to upward winds, downward winds, winds in the sides, convulsive winds, winds of the limbs, winds that go the wrong way, winds in the joints, the out-breath, and the in-breath. In this way, whatever else within this body is internal, belongs to the internal, is wind, of a moving nature, moves within, and was received at birth: this is called the bhikṣu's internal wind element. Bhikṣu! Whether there is the internal wind element or the external wind element, all of it is collectively called the wind element. All of it is not mine, I am not its, nor is it a self. Contemplating thus with wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become attached to this wind element. This is called a bhikṣu's non-negligence in wisdom.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is non-negligent in wisdom. If a bhikṣu analyzes the elements of the body, thinking: 'Now this body of mine has the internal space element, received at birth,' what does this refer to? It refers to the space of the eyes, the space of the ears, the space of the nose, the space of the mouth, the space of the throat through which movement occurs, that through which food that is eaten, chewed, and digested passes gently down and remains, and that through which it passes out below. In this way, whatever else within this body is internal, belongs to the internal, is space, being space that is not covered by flesh, skin, bone, or sinew: this is called the bhikṣu's internal space element. Bhikṣu! Whether there is the internal space element or the external space element, all of it is collectively called the space element. All of it is not mine, I am not its, nor is it a self. Contemplating thus with wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become attached to this space element. This is called a bhikṣu's non-negligence in wisdom.

"Bhikṣu! If a bhikṣu knows these five elements as they truly are, and having known them as they truly are, his mind does not become attached to them and is liberated, there remains only consciousness. What consciousness is this? It is pleasant consciousness, painful consciousness, joyful consciousness, sorrowful consciousness, and equanimous consciousness.

"Bhikṣu! Because of pleasant contact, a pleasant feeling arises. One feels a pleasant feeling, and having felt a pleasant feeling, one knows: 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' If a bhikṣu extinguishes this pleasant contact, and having extinguished this pleasant contact, whatever pleasant feeling arose from that pleasant contact also ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become cool.

"Bhikṣu! Because of painful contact, a painful feeling arises. One feels a painful feeling, and having felt a painful feeling, one knows: 'I feel a painful feeling.' If a bhikṣu extinguishes this painful contact, and having extinguished this painful contact, whatever painful feeling arose from that painful contact also ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become cool.

"Bhikṣu! Because of joyful contact, a joyful feeling arises. One feels a joyful feeling, and having felt a joyful feeling, one knows: 'I feel a joyful feeling.' If a bhikṣu extinguishes this joyful contact, and having extinguished this joyful contact, whatever joyful feeling arose from that joyful contact also ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become cool.

"Bhikṣu! Because of sorrowful contact, a sorrowful feeling arises. One feels a sorrowful feeling, and having felt a sorrowful feeling, one knows: 'I feel a sorrowful feeling.' If a bhikṣu extinguishes this sorrowful contact, and having extinguished this sorrowful contact, whatever sorrowful feeling arose from that sorrowful contact also ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become cool.

"Bhikṣu! Because of equanimous contact, an equanimous feeling arises. One feels an equanimous feeling, and having felt an equanimous feeling, one knows: 'I feel an equanimous feeling.' If a bhikṣu extinguishes this equanimous contact, and having extinguished this equanimous contact, whatever equanimous feeling arose from that equanimous contact also ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become cool.

"Bhikṣu! Because of this or that contact, this or that feeling arises. With the cessation of this or that contact, this or that feeling also ceases. One knows that this feeling comes from contact, has contact as its root, has contact as its origin, arises from contact, has contact as its foremost condition, and proceeds dependent on contact.

"Bhikṣu! It is like a fire-producing device: because of the drill, the stick, and a person's effort generating heat, fire is produced. Bhikṣu! When those many pieces of wood are separated and scattered apart, if the fire that arose from them repeatedly heats what it repeatedly receives from birth, it all ceases, subsides, and stops, and the firewood becomes cool. In the same way, bhikṣu, because of this or that contact, this or that feeling arises. With the cessation of this or that contact, this or that feeling also ceases. One knows that this feeling comes from contact, has contact as its root, has contact as its origin, arises from contact, has contact as its foremost condition, and proceeds dependent on contact.

"If a bhikṣu is not attached to these three feelings and is liberated from them, that bhikṣu abides only in equanimity, which is supremely pure. Bhikṣu! That bhikṣu then thinks: 'This pure equanimity of mine, I shall transfer it to the base of infinite space, cultivating such a mind, depending on it, abiding in it, established in it, conditioned by it, bound to it. This pure equanimity of mine, I shall transfer it to the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, cultivating such a mind, depending on it, abiding in it, established in it, conditioned by it, bound to it.'

"Bhikṣu! It is like a skilled goldsmith, a master craftsman of the finest gold, who burns the gold with fire, hammers it extremely thin, and again heats it with fire, repeatedly stoking the fire, refining and purifying it, making it extremely soft and lustrous. Bhikṣu! After this gold has been repeatedly stoked with fire, refined, and purified by the goldsmith, made extremely soft and lustrous, the goldsmith can then fashion it into whatever he wishes: whether winding it with silk thread, adorning new garments, making finger rings, arm bracelets, necklaces, or jeweled garlands, fashioning whatever he desires. In the same way, bhikṣu, that bhikṣu thinks: 'This pure equanimity of mine, I shall transfer it to the base of infinite space, cultivating such a mind, depending on it, abiding in it, established in it, conditioned by it, bound to it. This pure equanimity of mine, I shall transfer it to the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, cultivating such a mind, depending on it, abiding in it, established in it, conditioned by it, bound to it.'

"That bhikṣu then further thinks: 'This pure equanimity of mine, dependent on the base of infinite space, is still conditioned. If it is conditioned, then it is impermanent. If it is impermanent, then it is suffering. If it is suffering, then one knows suffering. Having known suffering, this equanimity no longer transfers to the base of infinite space. This pure equanimity of mine, dependent on the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is still conditioned. If it is conditioned, then it is impermanent. If it is impermanent, then it is suffering. If it is suffering, then one knows suffering. Having known suffering, this equanimity no longer transfers to the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.'

"Bhikṣu! If a bhikṣu contemplates these four abodes with wisdom, knows them as they truly are, and the mind does not become established in them and does not transfer to them, then at that time there is no more conditioning and no more thinking about existence or non-existence. One receives the final feeling of the body and knows: 'I receive the final feeling of the body.' One receives the final feeling of life and knows: 'I receive the final feeling of life.' When the body breaks apart and life ends, and the lifespan is exhausted, all that is felt ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become completely cool.

"Bhikṣu! It is like a burning lamp that depends on oil and a wick. If no one adds more oil or renews the wick, the previous fuel is already exhausted, and what follows does not continue; there is nothing more to receive. In the same way, bhikṣu, one receives the final feeling of the body and knows: 'I receive the final feeling of the body.' One receives the final feeling of life and knows: 'I receive the final feeling of life.' When the body breaks apart and life ends, and the lifespan is exhausted, all that is felt ceases, subsides, and stops, and one knows it has become completely cool.

"Bhikṣu! This is called the bhikṣu's foremost right wisdom, namely the ultimate extinction. The bhikṣu whose taints are exhausted accomplishes this, accomplishing the foremost place of right wisdom.

"Bhikṣu! This liberation abides in truth and is immovable. Truth means what accords with the Dharma. Falsehood means false dharmas. Bhikṣu! One who accomplishes this has attained the foremost place of truth.

"Bhikṣu! That bhikṣu who used to speak of giving and giving, which originally necessarily involved enmity, at that time relinquishes, discards, liberates, and completely extinguishes all of that. Bhikṣu! This is called the bhikṣu's foremost right generous giving, namely the complete abandonment of all worldly things: dispassion, cessation, stilling, and stopping. The bhikṣu who accomplishes this has attained the foremost place of generous giving.

"Bhikṣu! That bhikṣu whose mind was defiled by desire, aversion, and delusion and could not attain liberation: bhikṣu, when all of this lust, anger, and delusion is exhausted, with dispassion, cessation, stilling, and stopping, one attains the foremost peace. Bhikṣu! One who accomplishes this has attained the foremost place of peace.

"Bhikṣu! 'I' is self-exaltation. 'I shall exist' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall not exist and shall not not-exist' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall have form' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall be formless' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall be neither with form nor formless' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall have perception' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall be without perception' is also self-exaltation. 'I shall be neither with perception nor without perception' is also self-exaltation. This is conceit, this is pride, this is heedlessness.

"Bhikṣu! If there is none of all this self-exaltation, conceit, pride, and heedlessness, the mind is called at peace. Bhikṣu! When the mind is at peace, one does not hate, does not grieve, does not become weary, and does not become fearful. Why is this? Because that bhikṣu has accomplished the Dharma, there is nothing more that can be called hating. If one does not hate, then one does not grieve. If one does not grieve, then one does not sorrow. If one does not sorrow, then one does not become weary. If one does not become weary, then one does not become fearful. Because one does not become fearful, one will attain parinirvāṇa. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there is no more receiving of existence. One knows it as it truly is."

When this Dharma had been spoken, the Venerable Pukkusāti, far from dust and free from defilement, attained the Dharma-eye regarding all dharmas. Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, cut through doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, had no other teacher, no longer relied on others, was without hesitation, had already abided in the fruit and realization, and attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma. He immediately rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One! I repent and confess. Well-Gone One! I declare my fault. I was foolish, ignorant, unsteady, lacking in good understanding, unable to recognize the field of merit, and unable to know myself. Why? Because I addressed the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One as 'Sir.' I only wish that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance. Having repented, I will not do so again."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu! You were indeed foolish. You were indeed unsteady. You lacked good understanding, in that you addressed the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One as 'Sir.' Bhikṣu! If you can repent of your own accord, see your fault and confess it openly, and guard against doing it again, then, bhikṣu, in the noble Dharma and Vinaya this leads to growth and not to decline, namely being able to repent of one's own accord, see one's fault and confess it openly, and guard against doing it again."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Pukkusāti, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Elements, First

---

## Sūtra 163: Analysis of the Six Bases, Second of the Chapter on Fundamental Analysis

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which has meaning and phrasing, which is complete and pure, and which reveals the holy life. It is called the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Bases. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it."

At that time, the bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One! We will receive the teaching."

The Buddha said: "You should know the six bases internally. You should know the six bases of contact internally. You should know the eighteen mental activities internally. You should know the thirty-six kinds of feeling internally. Among these, abandon those and accomplish these. You should know the immeasurable teaching of the Dharma internally. There are three mental abodes that the noble ones practice. Having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed. The unsurpassed trainer of persons trains persons in all directions. This is the subject matter of the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Bases.

"'You should know the six bases internally': for what reason is this said? They are the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. That you should know the six bases internally is said for this reason.

"'You should know the six bases of contact internally': for what reason is this said? The eye contacts in order to see forms, the ear contacts in order to hear sounds, the nose contacts in order to smell odors, the tongue contacts in order to taste flavors, the body contacts in order to feel tangibles, the mind contacts in order to know dharmas. That you should know the six bases of contact internally is said for this reason.

"'You should know the eighteen mental activities internally': for what reason is this said? When a bhikṣu has seen forms with the eye, he analyzes and abides in forms with joy, analyzes and abides in forms with sorrow, or analyzes and abides in forms with equanimity. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind has known dharmas, one analyzes and abides in dharmas with joy, analyzes and abides in dharmas with sorrow, or analyzes and abides in dharmas with equanimity. These are called the analysis of six joys, the analysis of six sorrows, and the analysis of six equanimities, which together are called the eighteen mental activities. That you should know the eighteen mental activities internally is said for this reason.

"'You should know the thirty-six kinds of feeling internally': for what reason is this said? There are six joys dependent on attachment, six joys dependent on dispassion, six sorrows dependent on attachment, six sorrows dependent on dispassion, six equanimities dependent on attachment, and six equanimities dependent on dispassion.

"What are the six joys dependent on attachment? What are the six joys dependent on dispassion? Having seen forms with the eye, joy arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is joy dependent on attachment? The eye knows forms that are pleasing, that one thinks about, that one loves, forms associated with desire and pleasure. When one has not yet obtained them, one desires to obtain them. When one has already obtained them, one recollects them and joy arises. Such joy is called joy dependent on attachment. What is joy dependent on dispassion? Knowing that forms are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all forms, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, joy arises. Such joy is called joy dependent on dispassion. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind has known dharmas, joy arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is joy dependent on attachment? The mind knows dharmas that are pleasing, that one thinks about, that one loves, dharmas associated with desire and pleasure. When one has not yet obtained them, one desires to obtain them. When one has already obtained them, one recollects them and joy arises. Such joy is called joy dependent on attachment. What is joy dependent on dispassion? Knowing that dharmas are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all dharmas, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, joy arises. Such joy is called joy dependent on dispassion.

"What are the six sorrows dependent on attachment? What are the six sorrows dependent on dispassion? Having seen forms with the eye, sorrow arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is sorrow dependent on attachment? The eye knows forms that are pleasing, that one thinks about, that one loves, forms associated with desire and pleasure. When one has not yet obtained them and does not obtain them, or when one has already obtained them but they have passed away, scattered, decayed, ceased, and changed, sorrow arises. Such sorrow is called sorrow dependent on attachment. What is sorrow dependent on dispassion? Knowing that forms are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all forms, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, one has this thought: 'When shall I attain and dwell in that state in which the noble ones attain and dwell?' This is the supreme aspiration accompanied by longing and apprehension, knowing suffering. Sorrow arises from such sorrow. Such sorrow is called sorrow dependent on dispassion. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind has known dharmas, sorrow arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is sorrow dependent on attachment? The mind knows dharmas that are pleasing, that one thinks about, that one loves, dharmas associated with desire and pleasure. When one has not yet obtained them and does not obtain them, or when one has already obtained them but they have passed away, scattered, decayed, ceased, and changed, sorrow arises. Such sorrow is called sorrow dependent on attachment. What is sorrow dependent on dispassion? Knowing that dharmas are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all dharmas, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, one has this thought: 'When shall I attain and dwell in that state in which the noble ones attain and dwell?' This is the supreme aspiration accompanied by longing and apprehension, knowing suffering. Sorrow arises from such sorrow. Such sorrow is called sorrow dependent on dispassion.

"What are the six equanimities dependent on attachment? What are the six equanimities dependent on dispassion? Having seen forms with the eye, equanimity arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is equanimity dependent on attachment? The eye knows forms and equanimity arises, but that equanimity is level and neutral. One who is unlearned, lacking wisdom, foolish, deluded, and an ordinary person has equanimity regarding forms but does not become free from forms. This is called equanimity dependent on attachment. What is equanimity dependent on dispassion? Knowing that forms are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all forms, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, one abides in equanimity. If one cultivates this equanimity with focused attention, this is called equanimity dependent on dispassion. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind has known dharmas, equanimity arises. One should know it to be of two kinds: either dependent on attachment or dependent on dispassion. What is equanimity dependent on attachment? The mind knows dharmas and equanimity arises. It is level and neutral. One who is unlearned, lacking wisdom, foolish, deluded, and an ordinary person has equanimity regarding dharmas but does not become free from dharmas. This is called equanimity dependent on attachment. What is equanimity dependent on dispassion? The mind knows that dharmas are impermanent, subject to change, subject to exhaustion, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation and stilling; that all dharmas, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; recollecting this, one abides in equanimity. If one cultivates this equanimity with focused attention, this is called equanimity dependent on dispassion. These are the six joys dependent on attachment, six joys dependent on dispassion, six sorrows dependent on attachment, six sorrows dependent on dispassion, six equanimities dependent on attachment, and six equanimities dependent on dispassion, which together are called the thirty-six kinds of feeling. That you should know them internally is said for this reason.

"'Among these, abandon those and accomplish these': for what reason is this said? Take up these six joys dependent on dispassion, rely on them, and abide in them. As for these six joys dependent on attachment, extinguish them, remove them, and discard them. Thus one abandons those. Take up these six sorrows dependent on dispassion, rely on them, and abide in them. As for these six sorrows dependent on attachment, extinguish them, remove them, and discard them. Thus one abandons those. Take up these six equanimities dependent on dispassion, rely on them, and abide in them. As for these six equanimities dependent on attachment, extinguish them, remove them, and discard them. Thus one abandons those. Take up these six sorrows dependent on dispassion, rely on them, and abide in them. As for these six joys dependent on dispassion, extinguish them, remove them, and discard them. Thus one abandons those. Take up these six equanimities dependent on dispassion, rely on them, and abide in them. As for these six sorrows dependent on dispassion, extinguish them, remove them, and discard them. Thus one abandons those.

"There is equanimity with manifold contacts and various contacts, and there is equanimity with unified contact and not various contacts. What is equanimity with manifold contacts and various contacts? Equanimity that is directed toward forms, sounds, odors, flavors, and tangibles: this equanimity has manifold contacts and various contacts. What is equanimity with unified contact and not various contacts? Equanimity that depends on the base of infinite space, or depends on the base of infinite consciousness, or depends on the base of nothingness, or depends on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this equanimity has unified contact and not various contacts.

"Take up this equanimity with unified contact and not various contacts, rely on it, and abide in it. As for this equanimity with manifold contacts and various contacts, extinguish it, remove it, and discard it. Thus one abandons it. Take up the immeasurable, rely on the immeasurable, and abide in the immeasurable. As for this equanimity with unified contact and not various contacts, take it up, rely on it, and abide in it. As for this equanimity with manifold contacts and various contacts, extinguish it, remove it, and discard it. Thus one abandons it. 'Among these, abandon those and accomplish these' is said for this reason.

"'You should know the immeasurable teaching of the Dharma internally': for what reason is this said? Suppose the Tathāgata has four disciples who have superior conduct, superior intention, superior mindfulness, and superior wisdom, who have eloquence and have accomplished the foremost eloquence, and who live for a hundred years. If the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to them for a full hundred years, excluding the times for eating and drinking, for relieving themselves, for sleeping and resting, and for gathering together, then regarding the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, its phrases and Dharma phrases, contemplating their meaning, with wisdom they would quickly contemplate the meaning without needing to ask the Tathāgata further about the Dharma. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma is limitless and inexhaustible. Its phrases and Dharma phrases and the contemplation of their meaning would still remain even when the four disciples' lives ended. It is like four skilled archers who draw their powerful bows and release their arrows simultaneously, well-trained and well-knowing, with skillful means, swiftly piercing and passing through their targets. In the same way, the World-Honored One has four disciples who have superior conduct, superior intention, superior mindfulness, and superior wisdom, who have eloquence and have accomplished the foremost eloquence, and who live for a hundred years. If the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to them for a full hundred years, excluding the times for eating and drinking, for relieving themselves, for sleeping and resting, and for gathering together, then regarding the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, its phrases and Dharma phrases, contemplating their meaning, with wisdom they would quickly contemplate the meaning without needing to ask the Tathāgata further about the Dharma. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is limitless and inexhaustible. That you should know the immeasurable teaching of the Dharma internally is said for this reason.

"'Three mental abodes that the noble ones practice; having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed': for what reason is this said? If the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples with compassion and sympathy, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their peace, comfort, and happiness, arousing a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, saying 'This is for your benefit, this is for your happiness, this is for your welfare and happiness,' and if those disciples do not show respect, do not practice accordingly, do not establish themselves in knowledge, their minds do not turn toward the Dharma and the next Dharma, do not accept the correct Dharma, violate the World-Honored One's teaching, and cannot attain concentration, the World-Honored One does not become distressed by this. Rather, the World-Honored One remains in equanimity, without concern, ever mindful and ever wise. This is called the first mental abode that the noble ones practice. Having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed.

"Furthermore, if the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples with compassion and sympathy, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their peace, comfort, and happiness, arousing a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, saying 'This is for your benefit, this is for your happiness, this is for your welfare and happiness,' and if those disciples show respect, practice accordingly, and establish themselves in knowledge, their minds turn toward the Dharma and the next Dharma, accept and uphold the correct Dharma, do not violate the World-Honored One's teaching, and can attain concentration, the World-Honored One does not become delighted by this. Rather, the World-Honored One remains in equanimity, without concern, ever mindful and ever wise. This is called the second mental abode that the noble ones practice. Having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed.

"Furthermore, if the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples with compassion and sympathy, seeking their benefit and welfare, seeking their peace, comfort, and happiness, arousing a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, saying 'This is for your benefit, this is for your happiness, this is for your welfare and happiness,' and if some disciples do not show respect, do not practice accordingly, do not establish themselves in knowledge, their minds do not turn toward the Dharma and the next Dharma, do not accept the correct Dharma, violate the World-Honored One's teaching, and cannot attain concentration, while other disciples show respect, practice accordingly, and establish themselves in knowledge, their minds turn toward the Dharma and the next Dharma, accept and uphold the correct Dharma, do not violate the World-Honored One's teaching, and can attain concentration, the World-Honored One does not become distressed by this nor delighted by this. Rather, the World-Honored One remains in equanimity, without concern, ever mindful and ever wise. This is called the third mental abode. These are the three mental abodes that the noble ones practice. Having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed. That the three mental abodes are what the noble ones practice, and having practiced what the noble ones practice, the assembly can be instructed, is said for this reason.

"'The unsurpassed trainer of persons trains persons in all directions': for what reason is this said? A trainer of persons trains the person to go in one direction: either east, or south, or west, or north. A trainer of elephants trains the elephant to go in one direction: either east, or south, west, or north. A trainer of horses trains the horse to go in one direction: either east, or south, west, or north. A trainer of oxen trains the ox to go in one direction: either east, or south, west, or north. But the unsurpassed trainer of persons trains persons to go in all directions. Among these directions: contemplating form with reference to form, this is called the first direction. Having no perception of form internally, contemplating external forms, this is called the second direction. The liberation of purity, attaining and abiding in it with the body by direct contact, this is called the third direction. Completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with infinite space, one attains and abides in the base of infinite space. This is called the fourth direction. Completely transcending the base of infinite space, with infinite consciousness, one attains and abides in the base of infinite consciousness. This is called the fifth direction. Completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, with nothingness, one attains and abides in the base of nothingness. This is called the sixth direction. Completely transcending the base of nothingness, with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the seventh direction. Completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling, attaining and abiding in it with the body by direct contact, contemplating with wisdom, the taints are exhausted and cut off by knowledge. This is called the eighth direction. That the unsurpassed trainer of persons trains persons in all directions is said for this reason."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Bases, Second

---

## Sūtra 164: Analysis of the Contemplation of Dharmas, Third of the Chapter on Fundamental Analysis

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which has meaning and phrasing, which is complete and pure, and which reveals the holy life. It is called the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Contemplation of Dharmas. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it."

At that time, the bhikṣus said: "World-Honored One! We will receive the teaching."

The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind goes out externally and becomes scattered; the mind does not abide internally; not grasping, there is fear. Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind does not go out externally and is not scattered; the mind abides internally; not grasping, there is no fear. In this way, there is no more birth, old age, sickness, or death. This is called the end of suffering."

Having said this, the Buddha rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation.

Then the bhikṣus had this thought: "Worthies! You should know that the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation: 'Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind goes out externally and becomes scattered; the mind does not abide internally; not grasping, there is fear. Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind does not go out externally and is not scattered; the mind abides internally; not grasping, there is no fear. In this way, there is no more birth, old age, sickness, or death. This is called the end of suffering.'"

They further had this thought: "Worthies! Who can elaborate in detail on the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?" They further had this thought: "The Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the World-Honored One and by wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana can elaborate in detail on the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. Worthies! Let us go together to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana and request him to explain this meaning. If the Venerable Mahākātyāyana elaborates on it, we shall well receive and uphold it."

Then the bhikṣus went to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, exchanged greetings with him, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Mahākātyāyana! You should know that the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation: 'Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind goes out externally and becomes scattered; the mind does not abide internally; not grasping, there is fear. Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind does not go out externally and is not scattered; the mind abides internally; not grasping, there is no fear. In this way, there is no more birth, old age, sickness, or death. This is called the end of suffering.' We then had this thought: 'Worthies! Who can elaborate in detail on the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?' We further had this thought: 'The Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the World-Honored One and by wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana can elaborate in detail on the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated.' We only wish that the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion, would explain it in detail."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said: "Worthies! Listen to my simile, for the wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Worthies! It is like a person who wishes to find the heartwood and, seeking the heartwood, takes an axe into the forest. He sees a great tree complete with roots, trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. That person does not touch the roots, the trunk, the joints, or the fruit, but only touches the branches and leaves. What you worthies have done is also like this. The World-Honored One is present, yet you set him aside and come to me to ask about this meaning. Why is this? Worthies! You should know that the World-Honored One is the eye, the knowledge, the meaning, and the Dharma. He is the lord of the Dharma, the general of the Dharma. He speaks the meaning of truth and reveals all meanings. It is from that World-Honored One that you should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning, saying: 'World-Honored One! What does this mean? What is its significance?' As the World-Honored One explains it, you worthies should well receive and uphold it."

At that time, the bhikṣus said: "Indeed so, Venerable Mahākātyāyana! The World-Honored One is the eye, the knowledge, the meaning, and the Dharma. He is the lord of the Dharma, the general of the Dharma. He speaks the meaning of truth and reveals all meanings. It is from that World-Honored One that we should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning, saying: 'World-Honored One! What does this mean? What is its significance?' As the World-Honored One explains it, we should well receive and uphold it. However, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana is always praised by the World-Honored One and by wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana can elaborate in detail on the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. We only wish that the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, out of compassion, would explain it in detail."

The Venerable Mahākātyāyana addressed the bhikṣus: "Worthies! Listen together to what I have to say.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu's mind go out externally and become scattered? Worthies! When a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, consciousness feeds on the characteristic of forms, consciousness becomes attached to the pleasurable characteristic of forms, consciousness becomes bound to the pleasurable characteristic of forms. Through the relishing of the characteristic of forms, the mind is fettered, goes out externally, and becomes scattered. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind knows dharmas, consciousness feeds on the characteristic of dharmas, consciousness becomes attached to the pleasurable characteristic of dharmas, consciousness becomes bound to the pleasurable characteristic of dharmas. Through the relishing of the characteristic of dharmas, the mind is fettered, goes out externally, and becomes scattered. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu's mind goes out externally and becomes scattered.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu's mind not go out externally and not become scattered? Worthies! When a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, consciousness does not feed on the characteristic of forms, consciousness does not become attached to the pleasurable characteristic of forms, consciousness does not become bound to the pleasurable characteristic of forms. Through not relishing the characteristic of forms, the mind is not fettered, does not go out externally, and is not scattered. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind knows dharmas, consciousness does not feed on the characteristic of dharmas, consciousness does not become attached to the pleasurable characteristic of dharmas, consciousness does not become bound to the pleasurable characteristic of dharmas. Through not relishing the characteristic of dharmas, the mind is not fettered, does not go out externally, and is not scattered. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu's mind does not go out externally and is not scattered.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu's mind not abide internally? Worthies! A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and abides in the first dhyāna. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of seclusion, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, with initial and sustained thought having subsided, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial or sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and abides in the second dhyāna. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of concentration, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, having separated from the desire for joy, abiding in equanimity without craving, with right mindfulness, right knowledge, and bodily experience of happiness, which the noble ones describe as 'the equanimous one, mindful, happily abiding,' attains and abides in the third dhyāna. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of being without joy, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness, with the cessation of suffering, with joy and sorrow having already ceased, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and abides in the fourth dhyāna. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with infinite space, attains and abides in the base of infinite space. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of the knowledge of space, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of infinite space, with infinite consciousness, attains and abides in the base of infinite consciousness. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of the knowledge of consciousness, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, with nothingness, attains and abides in the base of nothingness. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of the knowledge of nothingness, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of nothingness, with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attains and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. His consciousness becomes attached to the taste of the knowledge of non-perception, depends on it, abides in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound to it. Consciousness does not abide internally. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu's mind does not abide internally.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu's mind abide internally? Worthies! A bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and abides in the first dhyāna. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of seclusion, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, with initial and sustained thought having subsided, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial or sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and abides in the second dhyāna. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of concentration, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, having separated from the desire for joy, abiding in equanimity without craving, with right mindfulness, right knowledge, and bodily experience of happiness, which the noble ones describe as 'the equanimous one, mindful, happily abiding,' attains and abides in the third dhyāna. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of being without joy, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness, with the cessation of suffering, with joy and sorrow having already ceased, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and abides in the fourth dhyāna. Consciousness does not become attached to the taste of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with infinite space, attains and abides in the base of infinite space. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of the knowledge of space, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of infinite space, with infinite consciousness, attains and abides in the base of infinite consciousness. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of the knowledge of consciousness, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, with nothingness, attains and abides in the base of nothingness. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of the knowledge of nothingness, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally.

"Furthermore, worthies, a bhikṣu, completely transcending the base of nothingness, with neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attains and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. His consciousness does not become attached to the taste of the knowledge of non-perception, does not depend on it, does not abide in it, is not conditioned by it, and is not bound to it. Consciousness abides internally. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu's mind abides internally.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu not grasp yet have fear? Worthies! A bhikṣu has not become free from the stain of form, has not become free from the desire for form, has not become free from the love of form, has not become free from the thirst for form. Worthies! If a bhikṣu has not become free from the stain of form, has not become free from the desire for form, has not become free from the love of form, has not become free from the thirst for form, he wishes to obtain form, seeks form, is attached to form, and dwells in form, regarding form as 'This is my self,' and form as 'This is mine.' Having wished to obtain form, being attached to form, and dwelling in form, regarding form as 'This is my self' and form as 'This is mine,' consciousness gropes at form. Having groped at form, when that form changes, consciousness turns with the form. When consciousness turns with the form, dharmas of fear arise, and the mind dwells within them. Because the mind does not know, there is fright, distress, and weariness: not grasping, yet there is fear. Likewise with feeling, perception, and formations.

"A bhikṣu has not become free from the stain of consciousness, has not become free from the desire for consciousness, has not become free from the love of consciousness, has not become free from the thirst for consciousness. Worthies! If a bhikṣu has not become free from the stain of consciousness, has not become free from the desire for consciousness, has not become free from the love of consciousness, has not become free from the thirst for consciousness, he wishes to obtain consciousness, seeks consciousness, is attached to consciousness, and dwells in consciousness, regarding consciousness as 'This is my self,' and consciousness as 'This is mine.' Having wished to obtain consciousness, sought consciousness, being attached to consciousness, and dwelling in consciousness, regarding consciousness as 'This is my self' and consciousness as 'This is mine,' consciousness gropes at consciousness. Having groped at consciousness, when that consciousness changes, consciousness turns with the consciousness. When consciousness turns with the consciousness, dharmas of fear arise, and the mind dwells within them. Because the mind does not know, there is fright, distress, and weariness: not grasping, yet there is fear. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu does not grasp yet has fear.

"Worthies! How does a bhikṣu not grasp and have no fear? Worthies! A bhikṣu has become free from the stain of form, has become free from the desire for form, has become free from the love of form, has become free from the thirst for form. Worthies! If a bhikṣu has become free from the stain of form, has become free from the desire for form, has become free from the love of form, has become free from the thirst for form, he does not wish to obtain form, does not seek form, is not attached to form, and does not dwell in form. Form is not his self, and form is not his. Not wishing to obtain form, not seeking form, not being attached to form, and not dwelling in form, with form not being his self and form not being his, consciousness does not grope at form. When consciousness does not grope at form, when that form changes, consciousness does not turn with the form. When consciousness does not turn with the form, dharmas of fear do not arise, and the mind does not dwell within them. Because the mind knows, there is no fright, no distress, no weariness: not grasping, and no fear. Likewise with feeling, perception, and formations.

"A bhikṣu has become free from the stain of consciousness, has become free from the desire for consciousness, has become free from the love of consciousness, has become free from the thirst for consciousness. Worthies! If a bhikṣu has become free from the stain of consciousness, has become free from the desire for consciousness, has become free from the love of consciousness, has become free from the thirst for consciousness, he does not wish to obtain consciousness, does not seek consciousness, is not attached to consciousness, and does not dwell in consciousness. Consciousness is not his self, and consciousness is not his. Not wishing to obtain consciousness, not seeking consciousness, not being attached to consciousness, and not dwelling in consciousness, with consciousness not being his self and consciousness not being his, consciousness does not grope at consciousness. When consciousness does not grope at consciousness, when that consciousness changes, consciousness does not turn with the consciousness. When consciousness does not turn with the consciousness, dharmas of fear do not arise, and the mind does not dwell within them. Because the mind knows, there is no fright, no distress, no weariness: not grasping, and no fear. Worthies! In this way a bhikṣu does not grasp and has no fear.

"Worthies! The World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation: 'Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind goes out externally and becomes scattered; the mind does not abide internally; not grasping, there is fear. Bhikṣus! Contemplating in such and such a way, as you have contemplated, bhikṣus, the mind does not go out externally and is not scattered; the mind abides internally; not grasping, there is no fear. In this way, there is no more birth, old age, sickness, or death. This is called the end of suffering.' This is the meaning that the World-Honored One briefly stated without elaborating in detail. I have now explained it in full with these phrases and this text. Worthies! You may go and present this to the Buddha in full. If it accords with the meaning as the World-Honored One would explain it, then you worthies should receive and uphold it."

Then the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahākātyāyana said, well received and recited it. They rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Mahākātyāyana three times, departed, went to the Buddha, bowed their heads in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Earlier, the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation. The Venerable Mahākātyāyana has explained it in detail with these phrases and this text."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, praised them, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Among my disciples there is one who has the eye, has knowledge, has the Dharma, and has the meaning. Why is this? When the teacher briefly states the meaning for his disciples without elaborating in detail, and that disciple can explain it in full with these phrases and this text, as the bhikṣu Kātyāyana has explained it, you should all receive and uphold it accordingly. Why is this? Because the explanation of the contemplated meaning should be just like this."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Contemplation of Dharmas, Third
