## (165) Sūtra on the Deva at the Hot Springs Grove, the Fourth in the Chapter on Root Distinctions

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Samiddhi was also traveling in Rājagṛha, dwelling at the Hot Springs Grove. Then the Venerable Samiddhi, as night was turning toward dawn, left his dwelling and went to the hot springs. He removed his clothing on the bank and entered the hot springs to bathe. After bathing he came back out, dried his body, and put on his clothing.

At that time, a certain deva of extremely fine form, majestic in appearance, as night was turning toward dawn, came to the Venerable Samiddhi, bowed in homage, and stood to one side. That deva's appearance and divine majesty were supremely fine, and his radiance illuminated the entire bank of the hot springs. That deva, having stood to one side, addressed the Venerable Samiddhi, saying: "Bhikṣu! Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse?"

The Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deva: "I do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse." He then asked that deva: "Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse?"

That deva answered: "I also do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse."

The Venerable Samiddhi again asked that deva: "Who retains the Bhaddekaratta verse?"

That deva answered: "The World-Honored One is traveling in this Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. He retains the Bhaddekaratta verse. Bhikṣu! You should go and face the World-Honored One directly to properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse. Why is that? The Bhaddekaratta verse has Dharma and has meaning. It is the foundation of the holy life, leading to knowledge, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. One of good family who, through faith, leaves the household for the homeless life to train in the Way should properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse." That deva, having spoken thus, bowed at the feet of the Venerable Samiddhi, circumambulated him three times, and vanished right there.

Then the Venerable Samiddhi, not long after the deva had vanished, went to the Buddha's presence, bowed in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Today, as night was turning toward dawn, I left my dwelling and went to the hot springs, removed my clothing on the bank, and entered the hot springs to bathe. After bathing I came out and stood on the bank drying my body. At that time, a certain deva of extremely fine form, majestic in appearance, as night was turning toward dawn, came to my presence, bowed in homage, and stood to one side. That deva's appearance and divine majesty were supremely fine, and his radiance illuminated the entire bank of the hot springs. That deva, having stood to one side, said to me: 'Bhikṣu! Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse?' I replied to that deva: 'I do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse.' I asked that deva: 'Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse?' That deva answered: 'I also do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse.' I again asked: 'Who retains the Bhaddekaratta verse?' That deva answered: 'The World-Honored One is traveling in this Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. He retains the Bhaddekaratta verse. Bhikṣu! You should go and face the World-Honored One directly to properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse. Why is that? The Bhaddekaratta verse has meaning and has Dharma. It is the foundation of the holy life, leading to knowledge, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. One of good family who, through faith, leaves the household for the homeless life to train in the Way should properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse.' That deva, having spoken thus, bowed at my feet, circumambulated me three times, and vanished right there."

The World-Honored One asked: "Samiddhi! Do you know where that deva came from? What is that deva's name?"

The Venerable Samiddhi answered: "World-Honored One! I do not know where that deva came from, nor do I know his name."

The World-Honored One said: "Samiddhi! That deva son is named Candana, and he is a general of the Thirty-Three Gods."

Then the Venerable Samiddhi said: "World-Honored One! Now is the proper time. Well-Gone One! Now is the proper time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus the Bhaddekaratta verse, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the World-Honored One, will properly retain it."

The World-Honored One said: "Samiddhi! Listen carefully, listen carefully, and consider it well. I shall teach it to you."

The Venerable Samiddhi said: "So be it." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha spoke:

"Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one practices the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse."

Having spoken thus, the Buddha rose from his seat and entered his chamber for quiet meditation. Then those bhikṣus had this thought: "Venerables! Know that the World-Honored One has given this teaching in brief without explaining it in detail, and then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for quiet meditation.

"'Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one practices the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse.'"

They then had this thought: "Venerables! Who is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the World-Honored One has just stated in brief?" They further thought: "The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the World-Honored One has just stated in brief. Venerables, let us go together to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and request him to explain this meaning. If the Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it for us, we shall properly retain it."

Then the bhikṣus went to the Venerable Mahākaccāna, exchanged greetings with him, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Mahākaccāna! Know that the World-Honored One gave this teaching in brief without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for quiet meditation.

"'Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one trains in the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse.'

"We then had this thought: 'Venerables! Who is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the World-Honored One has just stated in brief?' We further thought: 'The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the World-Honored One has just stated in brief.' We entreat the Venerable Mahākaccāna, out of compassion, to explain it in detail."

The Venerable Mahākaccāna said: "Venerables! Listen as I speak a simile, for the wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Venerables! It is like a person who desires to find heartwood and, seeking heartwood, takes an axe and enters a forest. He sees a great tree with roots, trunk, knots, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. That person does not touch the roots, trunk, knots, or fruit, but only touches the branches and leaves. What the venerables have done is just like this. The World-Honored One is present, yet you leave him aside and come to me to ask about this meaning. Why is that? Venerables! You should know that the World-Honored One is the eye, is the knowledge, is the meaning, is the Dharma. He is the Lord of the Dharma, the General of the Dharma. He reveals the meaning of truth, and the manifestation of all meaning comes from the World-Honored One. Venerables, you should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning: 'World-Honored One! What does this mean? What is its significance?' As the World-Honored One explains it, the venerables should properly retain it."

The bhikṣus then said: "So it is. Venerable Mahākaccāna! The World-Honored One is the eye, is the knowledge, is the meaning, is the Dharma. He is the Lord of the Dharma, the General of the Dharma. He reveals the meaning of truth, and the manifestation of all meaning comes from the World-Honored One. We should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning: 'World-Honored One! What does this mean? What is its significance?' As the World-Honored One explains it, we shall properly retain it. However, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the World-Honored One has just stated in brief. We entreat the Venerable Mahākaccāna, out of compassion, to explain it in detail."

The Venerable Mahākaccāna told the bhikṣus: "Venerables, all of you listen to what I shall say. Venerables! How does a bhikṣu dwell on the past? Venerables! A bhikṣu truly has the eye knowing forms that are agreeable and pleasing to the mind, forms connected with love and desire that delight the heart. He gropes after their origin, and that origin is the past. He desires to be attached to the consciousness regarding the past, and because of desiring attachment to that consciousness, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he dwells on the past. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. He truly has the mind knowing dharmas that are agreeable and pleasing to the mind, dharmas connected with love and desire that delight the heart. He gropes after their origin, and that origin is the past. He desires to be attached to the consciousness regarding the past, and because of desiring attachment to that consciousness, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he dwells on the past. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu dwell on the past.

"Venerables! How does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past? Venerables! A bhikṣu truly has the eye knowing forms that are agreeable and pleasing to the mind, forms connected with love and desire that delight the heart. He gropes after their origin, and that origin is the past. He does not desire to be attached to the consciousness regarding the past, and because of not desiring attachment to that consciousness, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not dwell on the past. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. He truly has the mind knowing dharmas that are agreeable and pleasing to the mind, dharmas connected with love and desire that delight the heart. He gropes after their origin, and that origin is the past. He does not desire to be attached to the consciousness regarding the past, and because of not desiring attachment to that consciousness, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not dwell on the past. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past.

"Venerables! How does a bhikṣu wish for the future? Venerables! If a bhikṣu has eye, form, and eye-consciousness pertaining to the future, then regarding what he has not yet obtained, he desires to obtain it; regarding what he has already obtained, his mind wishes for more. Because of his mind wishing, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he wishes for the future. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If there is mind, dharmas, and mind-consciousness pertaining to the future, regarding what he has not yet obtained, he desires to obtain it; regarding what he has already obtained, his mind wishes for more. Because of his mind wishing, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he wishes for the future. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu wish for the future.

"Venerables! How does a bhikṣu not wish for the future? Venerables! If a bhikṣu has eye, form, and eye-consciousness pertaining to the future, then regarding what he has not yet obtained, he does not desire to obtain it; regarding what he has already obtained, his mind does not wish for more. Because his mind does not wish, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not wish for the future. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If there is mind, dharmas, and mind-consciousness pertaining to the future, regarding what he has not yet obtained, he does not desire to obtain it; regarding what he has already obtained, his mind does not wish for more. Because his mind does not wish, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not wish for the future. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu not wish for the future.

"Venerables! How does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena? Venerables! If a bhikṣu has eye, form, and eye-consciousness in the present, he desires to be attached to the consciousness regarding the present. Because of desiring attachment to that consciousness, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he clings to present phenomena. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If there is mind, dharmas, and mind-consciousness in the present, he desires to be attached to the consciousness regarding the present. Because of desiring attachment to that consciousness, he delights in it. Because of delighting in it, he clings to present phenomena. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena.

"Venerables! How does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena? Venerables! If a bhikṣu has eye, form, and eye-consciousness in the present, he does not desire to be attached to the consciousness regarding the present. Because of not desiring attachment to that consciousness, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not cling to present phenomena. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If there is mind, dharmas, and mind-consciousness in the present, he does not desire to be attached to the consciousness regarding the present. Because of not desiring attachment to that consciousness, he does not delight in it. Because of not delighting in it, he does not cling to present phenomena. Venerables! Thus does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena.

"Venerables! The World-Honored One gave this teaching in brief without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for quiet meditation.

"'Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one trains in the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse.'

"This is what the World-Honored One stated in brief without explaining in detail. Using these phrases and this text, I have explained it in detail in this way. Venerables! You may go and present it to the Buddha. If it accords with the meaning as the World-Honored One would explain it, then the venerables may all retain it together."

Then the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Mahākaccāna said and having properly retained and recited it, rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Mahākaccāna three times, and departed. They went to the Buddha's presence, bowed in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Earlier the World-Honored One gave this teaching in brief without explaining it in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for quiet meditation. The Venerable Mahākaccāna, using these phrases and this text, explained it in detail."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, praised them saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Among my disciples there is one who has the eye, has the knowledge, has the Dharma, has the meaning. Why is that? When the teacher gives a teaching in brief to his disciples without explaining it in detail, and that disciple, using these phrases and this text, explains it in detail, just as the bhikṣu Mahākaccāna has explained it, you should retain it in this way. Why is that? Because explaining the meaning through contemplation should be like this."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully practiced in accord with it.

End of the Sūtra on the Deva at the Hot Springs Grove, the Fourth.

---

## (166) Sūtra of the Venerable One in the Meditation Chamber among the Śākyas, the Fifth in the Chapter on Root Distinctions of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya was traveling among the Śākyas, staying in a secluded meditation chamber. Then the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, as night was turning toward dawn, came out from that meditation chamber and sat in the shade of the open-air meditation hall on a rope-bed, having spread out his sitting cloth, sitting cross-legged.

At that time, a certain deva of extremely fine form, majestic in appearance, as night was turning toward dawn, came to the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, bowed in homage, and stood to one side. That deva's appearance and divine majesty were supremely fine, and his radiance illuminated the entire meditation chamber. That deva, having stood to one side, addressed the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, saying: "Bhikṣu! Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?"

The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya replied to that deva: "I do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, nor do I retain its meaning."

He then asked that deva: "Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?"

That deva answered: "I retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, but I do not retain its meaning."

The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya again asked that deva: "How is it that you retain the Bhaddekaratta verse but do not retain its meaning?"

That deva answered: "At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. At that time, the World-Honored One taught the bhikṣus the Bhaddekaratta verse:

"'Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one trains in the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse.'

"Bhikṣu! Thus do I retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, but I do not retain its meaning."

The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya again asked that deva: "Who retains the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?"

That deva answered: "The Buddha is traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. He retains the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning. Bhikṣu! You should go and face the World-Honored One directly to properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning. Why is that? The Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning have meaning and have Dharma. It is the foundation of the holy life, leading to knowledge, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. One of good family who, through faith, leaves the household for the homeless life to train in the Way should properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning." That deva, having spoken thus, bowed at the feet of the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, circumambulated him three times, and vanished right there.

Not long after the deva vanished, the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya, having completed his summer retreat among the Śākyas, after three months had passed, having mended his robes, took up his robes and bowl and traveled toward Śrāvastī, progressing forward stage by stage until he reached Śrāvastī and stayed in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya went to the Buddha's presence, bowed in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! At one time I was traveling among the Śākyas, staying in a secluded meditation chamber. World-Honored One! At that time, as night was turning toward dawn, I came out from that meditation chamber and sat in the shade of the open-air meditation hall on a rope-bed, having spread out my sitting cloth, sitting cross-legged. At that time, a certain deva of extremely fine form, majestic in appearance, as night was turning toward dawn, came to my presence, bowed in homage, and stood to one side. That deva's appearance and divine majesty were supremely fine, and his radiance illuminated the entire meditation chamber. That deva, having stood to one side, said to me: 'Bhikṣu! Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?' I replied to that deva: 'I do not retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, nor do I retain its meaning.' I then asked that deva: 'Do you retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?' That deva answered: 'I retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, but I do not retain its meaning.' I again asked the deva: 'How is it that you retain the Bhaddekaratta verse but do not retain its meaning?' The deva answered me: 'At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. At that time, the World-Honored One taught the bhikṣus the Bhaddekaratta verse:

"'"Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one trains in the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse."'

"'Bhikṣu! Thus do I retain the Bhaddekaratta verse, but I do not retain its meaning.' I again asked the deva: 'Who retains the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?' The deva answered me: 'The Buddha is traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park. He retains the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning. Bhikṣu! You should go and face the World-Honored One directly to properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning. Why is that? The Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning have meaning and have Dharma. It is the foundation of the holy life, leading to knowledge, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. One of good family who, through faith, leaves the household for the homeless life to train in the Way should properly retain and recite the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning.' That deva, having spoken thus, bowed at my feet, circumambulated me three times, and vanished right there."

Then the World-Honored One asked the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya: "Do you know where that deva came from? What is that deva's name?"

The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya answered: "World-Honored One! I do not know where that deva came from, nor do I know his name."

The World-Honored One said: "Kaṅgiya! That deva son is named Candana, and he is a general of the Thirty-Three Gods."

At that time, the Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya said: "World-Honored One! Now is the proper time. Well-Gone One! Now is the proper time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the World-Honored One, will properly retain it."

The World-Honored One said: "Kaṅgiya! Listen carefully, consider it well. I shall explain its meaning in detail for you."

The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya said: "So be it. I shall receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha spoke:

"Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one practices the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse.

"Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu dwell on the past? If a bhikṣu delights in past form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in past feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu dwell on the past. Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past? If a bhikṣu does not delight in past form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in past feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past. Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu wish for the future? If a bhikṣu delights in future form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu wish for the future. Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu not wish for the future? If a bhikṣu does not delight in future form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not wish for the future.

"Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena? If a bhikṣu delights in present form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in present feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena. Kaṅgiya! How does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena? If a bhikṣu does not delight in present form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in present feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Lomasakaṅgiya and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully practiced in accord with it.

End of the Sūtra of the Venerable One in the Meditation Chamber among the Śākyas, the Fifth.

---

## (167) Sūtra of Ānanda's Explanation, the Sixth in the Chapter on Root Distinctions of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, for the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall at night, was teaching the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, when the night had passed and the early morning came, went to the Buddha's presence, bowed in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! The Venerable Ānanda has been teaching the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall at night, explaining the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning."

Then the World-Honored One told a bhikṣu: "Go to the bhikṣu Ānanda and say thus: 'Ānanda! The World-Honored One is calling you.'"

That bhikṣu received the World-Honored One's instruction, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to the Venerable Ānanda and said: "The World-Honored One is calling the Venerable Ānanda!"

The Venerable Ānanda then went to the Buddha's presence, bowed in homage, and stood to one side. The World-Honored One asked: "Ānanda! Did you truly teach the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall at night, explaining the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "Indeed so."

The World-Honored One asked: "Ānanda! How did you teach the bhikṣus the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning?"

The Venerable Ānanda then spoke the verse:

"Be careful not to dwell on the past,
Nor wish for the future.
Past events have already perished,
And the future has not yet arrived.
Whatever phenomena exist in the present,
These too one should contemplate with wisdom.
Know that there is nothing firm or enduring;
The wise one awakens to this truth.
If one practices the conduct of noble ones,
Who then would grieve and worry about death?
I shall certainly not encounter
The end of that great suffering and calamity.
Thus practicing with diligence,
Day and night without slackening,
Therefore one should always recite
The Bhaddekaratta verse."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu dwell on the past?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu delights in past form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in past feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu dwell on the past."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu does not delight in past form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in past feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not dwell on the past."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu wish for the future?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu delights in future form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu wish for the future."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu not wish for the future?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu does not delight in future form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in future feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not wish for the future."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu delights in present form, with desire, attachment, and clinging; if he delights in present feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, with desire, attachment, and clinging; thus does a bhikṣu cling to present phenomena."

The World-Honored One then asked: "Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One! If a bhikṣu does not delight in present form, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; if he does not delight in present feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, without desire, without attachment, without clinging; thus does a bhikṣu not cling to present phenomena. World-Honored One! Thus did I teach the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall at night, explaining the Bhaddekaratta verse and its meaning."

Then the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "Excellent! Excellent! Among my disciples there is one who has the eye, has the knowledge, has the meaning, has the Dharma. Why is that? When a disciple, in the teacher's very presence, explains this meaning with such phrases and such text, it is truly as the bhikṣu Ānanda has explained it. You should all retain it in this way. Why is that? Because explaining the meaning through contemplation should be like this."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully practiced in accord with it.

End of the Sūtra of Ānanda's Explanation, the Sixth.

---

## (168) Sūtra on Mental Conduct, the Seventh in the Chapter on Root Distinctions of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "I shall now teach you the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, having meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. It is called the Sūtra on Distinguishing Mental Conduct, on how one is reborn according to mental conduct. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and consider it well." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "How does rebirth occur according to mental conduct? Suppose a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the Brahmā Body gods. Those Brahmā Body gods, born there and abiding there, experience the joy and happiness born of seclusion. And the bhikṣu abiding here, having entered the first dhyāna, experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion. These two kinds of joy and happiness born of seclusion are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the Brahmā Body gods. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu's initial thought and sustained thought have ceased, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the Ābhāsvara gods. Those Ābhāsvara gods, born there and abiding there, experience the joy and happiness born of concentration. And the bhikṣu abiding here, having entered the second dhyāna, experiences the joy and happiness born of concentration. These two kinds of joy and happiness born of concentration are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the Ābhāsvara gods. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu is separated from the desire for joy, abiding in equanimity, without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, he experiences happiness with the body. This is what the noble ones describe as 'dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness.' He attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the Śubhakṛtsna gods. Those Śubhakṛtsna gods, born there and abiding there, experience happiness without joy. And the bhikṣu abiding here, having entered the third dhyāna, experiences happiness without joy. These two kinds of happiness without joy are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the Śubhakṛtsna gods. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu's happiness has ceased and suffering has ceased, and joy and sorrow having already ceased before, with neither suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the Bṛhatphala gods. Those Bṛhatphala gods, born there and abiding there, experience the happiness of equanimity, mindfulness, and purity. And the bhikṣu abiding here, having entered the fourth dhyāna, experiences the happiness of equanimity, mindfulness, and purity. These two kinds of happiness of equanimity, mindfulness, and purity are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the Bṛhatphala gods. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, realizing 'Space is infinite,' he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the gods of the sphere of infinite space. Those gods of the sphere of infinite space, born there and abiding there, experience the perception of the sphere of infinite space. And the bhikṣu abiding here experiences the perception of the sphere of infinite space. These two perceptions of the sphere of infinite space are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the gods of the sphere of infinite space. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, realizing 'Consciousness is infinite,' he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Those gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness, born there and abiding there, experience the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. And the bhikṣu abiding here experiences the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. These two perceptions of the sphere of infinite consciousness are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, realizing 'There is nothing,' he attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the gods of the sphere of nothingness. Those gods of the sphere of nothingness, born there and abiding there, experience the perception of the sphere of nothingness. And the bhikṣu abiding here experiences the perception of the sphere of nothingness. These two perceptions of the sphere of nothingness are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the gods of the sphere of nothingness. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he enters neither perception nor non-perception, and attains and dwells in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. He delights in this concentration and wishes to abide in it. Having delighted in this concentration and wished to abide in it, there certainly is this result: abiding there and delighting there, at the end of life he is reborn among the gods of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Those gods of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, born there and abiding there, experience the perception of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. And the bhikṣu abiding here experiences the perception of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. These two perceptions are without difference; both are entirely equal. Why is that? First he practiced this concentration here, and afterward he was reborn there. This concentration, cultivated in this way, practiced in this way, spread widely in this way, leads to rebirth among the gods of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. Thus does rebirth occur according to mental conduct.

"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has completely transcended the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, with the cessation of perception and knowledge, he attains and dwells in the bodily realization of that cessation. Through wisdom he sees that all the contaminants are exhausted and severed. Among all those concentrations, this concentration is said to be the most supreme, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most subtle. Just as from the cow comes milk, from milk comes curds, from curds comes fresh butter, from fresh butter comes clarified butter, from clarified butter comes the finest ghee, and the finest ghee is said to be the most supreme, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most subtle, so too among all those concentrations, this concentration is said to be the most supreme, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most subtle. Having attained this concentration, relying on this concentration, and abiding in this concentration, one no longer undergoes the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death. This is called the end of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully practiced in accord with it.

End of the Sūtra on Mental Conduct, the Seventh.

## (169) Sūtra on Non-Contention at Kuru, the Eighth in the Chapter on Root Distinctions of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Bhagga country, at the Kuru town of Kammāssadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, having meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. It is called the Sūtra on Distinguishing Non-Contention. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and consider it well." The bhikṣus then received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "Do not seek the pleasure of desires, which is an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people. Nor seek the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit. Departing from these two extremes, there is a middle path that produces vision, produces knowledge, leads freely to concentration, leads to knowledge, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa. There is praise and blame; there is neither praise nor blame, and yet the Dharma is taught. Determine the limit, and having determined and known it, seek whatever inner happiness there is. Do not engage in misleading speech, nor praise face to face. Speak within proper limits, do not seek beyond proper limits. Following local customs, do not affirm and do not deny. These are the matters of the Sūtra on Distinguishing Non-Contention.

"'Do not seek the pleasure of desires, which is an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people; nor seek the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit.' Why was this said? 'Do not seek the pleasure of desires, which is an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people,' this speaks of one extreme. 'Nor seek the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit,' this speaks of the second extreme. 'Do not seek the pleasure of desires, which is an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people; nor seek the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit.' It was said for this reason.

"'Departing from these two extremes, there is a middle path that produces vision, produces knowledge, leads freely to concentration, leads to knowledge, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa.' Why was this said? There is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration. These are called the eight. 'Departing from these two extremes, there is a middle path that produces vision, produces knowledge, leads freely to concentration, leads to knowledge, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa.' It was said for this reason.

"'There is praise and blame; there is neither praise nor blame, and yet the Dharma is taught.' Why was this said? What is praise? What is blame? And yet not teaching the Dharma? If there is something associated with desires, accompanied by joy and happiness, an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then blames oneself. Why is that? Desires are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction. Having known the impermanence of desires, therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one blames oneself.

"Self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then blames oneself. Why is that? Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, with the suffering they so dread, shaved their hair and beards, put on kāṣāya robes, and through faith left the household for the homeless life to train in the Way, yet those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas again embrace this very suffering. Therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one blames oneself.

"When fetters are not exhausted, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then blames oneself. Why is that? If fetters are not exhausted, then existence is also not exhausted. Therefore all of it has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one blames oneself.

"When fetters are exhausted, this dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, one then praises oneself. Why is that? If fetters are exhausted, then existence is also exhausted. Therefore all of it has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, therefore one praises oneself.

"Not seeking inner happiness, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then blames oneself. Why is that? If one does not seek inner happiness, then one also does not seek what is within. Therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one blames oneself.

"Seeking inner happiness, this dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, one then praises oneself. Why is that? If one seeks inner happiness, then one also seeks what is within. Therefore all of it has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, therefore one praises oneself.

"Thus there is praise and blame, yet not teaching the Dharma. Neither praising nor blaming, yet teaching the Dharma.

"How is there neither praising nor blaming, yet teaching the Dharma? If something associated with desires, accompanied by joy and happiness, an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'Desires are impermanent, suffering, and subject to destruction; having known the impermanence of desires, therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma of suffering, with distress, with burning, with grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"Self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'Self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma of suffering, with distress, with burning, with grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"When fetters are not exhausted, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'If fetters are not exhausted, then existence is also not exhausted, therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma of suffering, with distress, with burning, with grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"When fetters are exhausted, this dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'If fetters are exhausted, then existence is also exhausted, therefore all of it has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma without suffering, without distress, without burning, without grievous wrong conduct, as right conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"Not seeking inner happiness, this dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'If one does not seek inner happiness, then one also does not seek what is within; therefore all of it has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma of suffering, with distress, with burning, with grievous wrong conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"Seeking inner happiness, this dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Having known this, one then teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Without saying it thus: 'If one seeks inner happiness, then one also seeks what is within; therefore all of it has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct,' without penetrating this dharma but only recognizing it as a dharma without suffering, without distress, without burning, without grievous wrong conduct, as right conduct. Having known this, therefore one teaches the Dharma.

"Thus there is neither praising nor blaming, yet teaching the Dharma. 'There is praise and blame; there is neither praise nor blame, and yet the Dharma is taught.' It was said for this reason.

"'Determine the limit, and having determined and known it, seek whatever inner happiness there is.' Why was this said? There is happiness that is not noble happiness but ordinary happiness, the root of illness, the root of abscesses, the root of arrow-wounds, which has nutriment and has birth and death, which should not be cultivated, not practiced, not spread widely. I say that it should not be cultivated. There is happiness that is noble happiness, desireless happiness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of right awakening, which is without nutriment and without birth and death, which can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely. I say that it can be cultivated.

"What is that happiness that is not noble happiness but ordinary happiness, the root of illness, the root of abscesses, the root of arrow-wounds, which has nutriment and has birth and death, which should not be cultivated, not practiced, not spread widely, and which I say should not be cultivated? If joy and happiness arise dependent on the five qualities of sensual pleasure, this happiness is not noble happiness but ordinary happiness, the root of illness, the root of abscesses, the root of arrow-wounds, which has nutriment and has birth and death, which should not be cultivated, not practiced, not spread widely. I say that it should not be cultivated.

"What is that happiness that is noble happiness, desireless happiness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of right awakening, which is without nutriment and without birth and death, which can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely, and which I say can be cultivated? If a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, up to attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna, this happiness is noble happiness, desireless happiness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of right awakening, which is without nutriment and without birth and death, which can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely. I say that it can be cultivated. 'Determine the limit, and having determined and known it, seek whatever inner happiness there is.' It was said for this reason.

"'Do not engage in misleading speech, nor praise face to face.' Why was this said? There is misleading speech that is untrue, false, and associated with no benefit. There is misleading speech that is true, not false, yet associated with no benefit. There is misleading speech that is true, not false, and associated with benefit. Among these, if the misleading speech is untrue, false, and associated with no benefit, this one should never speak. Among these, if the misleading speech is true, not false, yet associated with no benefit, one should train not to speak this either. Among these, if the misleading speech is true, not false, and associated with benefit, one should know the right time and, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, bring it to accomplishment. Thus regarding face-to-face praise: 'Do not engage in misleading speech, nor praise face to face.' It was said for this reason.

"'Speak within proper limits, do not go beyond proper limits.' Why was this said? Speaking without proper limits wearies the body, causes mindfulness to lapse into forgetfulness, tires the mind, ruins the voice, and one does not speak freely before the wise. Speaking within proper limits does not weary the body, does not cause mindfulness to lapse into forgetfulness, does not tire the mind, does not ruin the voice, and one speaks freely before the wise. 'Speak within proper limits, do not go beyond proper limits.' It was said for this reason.

"'Following local customs, do not affirm and do not deny.' Why was this said? How does one follow local customs and affirm or deny? In various regions, among various peoples, regarding various objects, some call it a 'basin,' some call it a 'bowl,' some call it a 'tub,' some call it a 'cup,' some call it a 'vessel.' Just as in various regions, among various peoples, regarding various objects, some call it a 'basin,' some call it a 'bowl,' some call it a 'tub,' some call it a 'cup,' some call it a 'vessel,' one who regarding those various objects forcefully insists in one direction, saying 'This alone is the truth, and all else is false,' this is how one follows local customs and affirms or denies.

"How does one follow local customs and neither affirm nor deny? In various regions, among various peoples, regarding various objects, some call it a 'basin,' some call it a 'bowl,' some call it a 'tub,' some call it a 'cup,' some call it a 'vessel.' Just as in various regions, among various peoples, regarding various objects, some call it a 'basin,' some call it a 'bowl,' some call it a 'tub,' some call it a 'cup,' some call it a 'vessel,' one who regarding those various objects does not forcefully insist in one direction, not saying 'This alone is the truth, and all else is false,' this is how one follows local customs and neither affirms nor denies. 'Following local customs, do not affirm and do not deny.' It was said for this reason.

"There are dharmas of contention and dharmas without contention. What are dharmas of contention? What are dharmas without contention?

"If something is associated with desires, accompanied by joy and happiness, an extremely low and base occupation, the practice of ordinary people, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"If one practices self-mortification, which is painful, not a noble practice, and associated with no benefit, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Departing from these two extremes, there is a middle path that produces vision, produces knowledge, leads freely to concentration, leads to knowledge, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa. This dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"When fetters are not exhausted, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"When fetters are completely exhausted, this dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"Not seeking inner happiness, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Seeking inner happiness, this dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"Among these, if there is happiness that is not noble happiness but ordinary happiness, the root of illness, the root of abscesses, the root of arrow-wounds, which has nutriment and has birth and death, which should not be cultivated, not practiced, not spread widely, and which I say should not be cultivated, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Among these, if there is happiness that is noble happiness, desireless happiness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of right awakening, which is without nutriment and without birth and death, which can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely, and which I say can be cultivated, this dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"Among these, if there is misleading speech that is untrue, false, and associated with no benefit, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Among these, if there is misleading speech that is true, not false, yet associated with no benefit, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Among these, if there is speech that is true, not false, and associated with benefit, this dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"Speaking without proper limits, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.

"Speaking within proper limits, this dharma is without contention. Why is this dharma without contention? This dharma has no suffering, no distress, no burning, no grievous wrong conduct. It is right conduct. Therefore this dharma is without contention.

"Following local customs and affirming or denying, this dharma involves contention. Why does this dharma involve contention? This dharma has suffering, has distress, has burning, has grievous wrong conduct. Therefore this dharma involves contention.
