### (172) Sūtra on the Mind

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If the mind of a bhikṣu is inclined toward attachment and craving, he should use the contemplation of impurity to regulate it. If the mind is inclined toward anger and hatred, he should use the contemplation of loving-kindness to regulate it. If the mind is inclined toward ignorance and delusion, he should use the contemplation of dependent origination to regulate it. If the mind is inclined toward excessive pride, he should use the contemplation of the divisions of the elements to regulate it. If the mind is inclined toward excessive thinking, he should use mindfulness of breathing to regulate it.

"It is like a skilled carpenter or carpenter's apprentice who uses a straight line to correct bent and crooked wood. In the same way, a bhikṣu whose mind is inclined toward attachment should use the contemplation of impurity; one whose mind is inclined toward anger should use the contemplation of loving-kindness; one whose mind is inclined toward ignorance should use the contemplation of dependent origination; one whose mind is inclined toward pride should use the contemplation of the divisions of elements; and one whose mind is inclined toward excessive thinking should use mindfulness of breathing."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (173) Sūtra on Venerables

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are five things that cause a young bhikṣu, newly ordained, who has recently entered this Dharma and Vinaya, to attain growth, not deterioration, in the practice. What are the five?

"Here, a bhikṣu maintains the Prātimokṣa precepts, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the precepts, perfecting deportment and conduct, seeing danger in the slightest faults. He trains himself by receiving and upholding the training precepts. This is the first thing.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu has heard much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, that are endowed with meaning and phrasing, that are complete and pure, that reveal the holy life: such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, investigated with his mind, and thoroughly penetrated with right view. This is the second thing.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates. This is the third thing.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu speaks with ease, is amenable to instruction, has patience, and correctly accepts admonishment. This is the fourth thing.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, whatever tasks arise among his fellow practitioners, whether coarse or fine, is skilled and not lazy regarding them, using proper methods to accomplish them, being able to manage and arrange them. This is the fifth thing.

"These are the five things that cause a young bhikṣu to attain growth, not deterioration."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (174) Sūtra on the Bhikṣu's Petition

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda arose from his seat in the afternoon, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I was sitting alone in a quiet place, and this thought arose in my mind: 'It is said that half of the holy life consists of virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates.'"

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, do not speak thus. Do not say that half of the holy life consists of virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates. Why? Virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates are the entirety of the holy life. Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates, one should expect of him that he will cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path and practice the Noble Eightfold Path extensively.

"How does a bhikṣu who has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path and practice the Noble Eightfold Path extensively? Here, a bhikṣu cultivates right view, which depends on seclusion, depends on dispassion, depends on cessation, and tends toward relinquishment. He cultivates right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, which depend on seclusion, depend on dispassion, depend on cessation, and tend toward relinquishment. This is how a bhikṣu who has virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path and practices the Noble Eightfold Path extensively.

"Ānanda, you should know this through the following reasoning: it is by relying on me as a virtuous friend that sentient beings subject to birth are freed from birth, that sentient beings subject to aging are freed from aging, that sentient beings subject to illness are freed from illness, that sentient beings subject to death are freed from death, that sentient beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress are freed from sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. Ānanda, by this reasoning you should know that virtuous friends, virtuous companions, and virtuous associates are the entirety of the holy life."

The Buddha spoke thus. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (175) Sūtra on the Arising of Suffering

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the arising of suffering? Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of these three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Conditioned by feeling, craving arises. This is the arising of suffering. Conditioned by the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises. Conditioned by the nose and scents, nose-consciousness arises. Conditioned by the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. Conditioned by the body and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises. Conditioned by the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of these three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Conditioned by feeling, craving arises. This is the arising of suffering.

"What is the cessation of suffering? Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of these three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Conditioned by feeling, craving arises. When that craving ceases without remainder, through complete dispassion, clinging ceases. When clinging ceases, becoming ceases. When becoming ceases, birth ceases. When birth ceases, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress all cease. This is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Conditioned by the ear and sounds, conditioned by the nose and scents, conditioned by the tongue and tastes, conditioned by the body and tangible objects, conditioned by the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of these three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Conditioned by feeling, craving arises. When that craving ceases without remainder, through complete dispassion, clinging ceases. When clinging ceases, becoming ceases. When becoming ceases, birth ceases. When birth ceases, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress all cease. This is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (176) Sūtra on Conduct

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu possesses conduct and virtue, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I have no regret.' Bhikṣus, it is natural that one who possesses conduct and virtue will have no regret.

"If one has no regret, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I have delight.' It is natural that one who has no regret will have delight.

"If one has delight, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I have joy.' It is natural that one who has delight will have joy.

"If one has joy, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May my body be at ease.' It is natural that one who has joy will have a body at ease.

"If one's body is at ease, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I experience happiness.' It is natural that one whose body is at ease will experience happiness.

"If one experiences happiness, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May my mind be concentrated.' It is natural that one who experiences happiness will have a concentrated mind.

"If one's mind is concentrated, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I know and see according to reality.' It is natural that one whose mind is concentrated will know and see according to reality.

"If one knows and sees according to reality, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I have disenchantment and dispassion.' It is natural that one who knows and sees according to reality will have disenchantment and dispassion.

"If one has disenchantment and dispassion, there is no need to intentionally wish: 'May I realize the knowledge and vision of liberation.' It is natural that one who has disenchantment and dispassion will realize the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"Bhikṣus, this is how, step by step, this Dharma leads to the other shore, leads to liberation. That is to say, possessing conduct and virtue leads to having no regret; having no regret leads to delight; delight leads to joy; joy leads to bodily ease; bodily ease leads to happiness; happiness leads to concentration; concentration leads to knowing and seeing according to reality; knowing and seeing according to reality leads to disenchantment and dispassion; disenchantment and dispassion leads to the realization of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

"It is like a great tree whose roots have moisture. The roots having moisture, the bark becomes moist. The bark being moist, the branches become moist. The branches being moist, the twigs become moist. The twigs being moist, the leaves become moist. The leaves being moist, the flowers become moist. The flowers being moist, the fruit becomes moist. In the same way, possessing conduct and virtue leads to having no regret; having no regret leads to delight; delight leads to joy; joy leads to bodily ease; bodily ease leads to happiness; happiness leads to concentration; concentration leads to knowing and seeing according to reality; knowing and seeing according to reality leads to disenchantment and dispassion; disenchantment and dispassion leads to the realization of the knowledge and vision of liberation."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (177) Sūtra Spoken to Rāhula (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula: "Rāhula, how do you contemplate the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness?"

Rāhula said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I contemplate the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness as not self."

The Buddha said: "Excellent, Rāhula! It is just as you have said. One should contemplate the eye, forms, and eye-consciousness as not self with right wisdom as it really is. If one contemplates them thus with right wisdom as it really is, one will have no conceit of 'I' regarding eye-consciousness. This is called practice."

The Buddha said: "Rāhula, how do you contemplate the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness? How do you contemplate the nose, scents, and nose-consciousness? How do you contemplate the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness? How do you contemplate the body, tangible objects, and body-consciousness? How do you contemplate the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness?"

Rāhula said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I contemplate the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness as not self. I contemplate the nose, scents, and nose-consciousness as not self. I contemplate the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness as not self. I contemplate the body, tangible objects, and body-consciousness as not self. I contemplate the mind, mental objects, and mind-consciousness as not self."

The Buddha said: "Excellent, Rāhula! It is just as you have said. One should contemplate them with right wisdom as it really is as not self. If one contemplates them thus with right wisdom as it really is, one will have no conceit of 'I' regarding mind-consciousness. This is called practice. If you practice thus, this is called the practice of a bhikṣu who does not add anything, neither increasing nor decreasing. One who neither increases nor decreases already has parinirvāṇa."

The Buddha spoke thus. Rāhula and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (178) Sūtra Spoken to Rāhula (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula: "Rāhula, the eye is permanent or impermanent?"

Rāhula answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

Rāhula answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if it is impermanent and suffering, being subject to change, would a learned noble disciple contemplate this and regard it as self, as belonging to self, or as self being within it?"

Rāhula answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, forms are permanent or impermanent? Eye-consciousness is permanent or impermanent? Eye-contact is permanent or impermanent? The feelings, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant, that arise conditioned by eye-contact, are they permanent or impermanent?"

Rāhula answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if they are impermanent, are they suffering?"

Rāhula answered: "They are suffering, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if they are impermanent and suffering, being subject to change, would a learned noble disciple contemplate these and regard them as self, as belonging to self, or as self being within them?"

Rāhula answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"The ear, sounds, ear-consciousness, ear-contact, and the feelings that arise conditioned by ear-contact; the nose, scents, nose-consciousness, nose-contact, and the feelings that arise conditioned by nose-contact; the tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness, tongue-contact, and the feelings that arise conditioned by tongue-contact; the body, tangible objects, body-consciousness, body-contact, and the feelings that arise conditioned by body-contact; the mind, mental objects, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feelings, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant, that arise conditioned by mind-contact: are they permanent or impermanent?"

Rāhula answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if they are impermanent, are they suffering?"

Rāhula answered: "They are suffering, World-Honored One."

"Rāhula, if they are impermanent and suffering, being subject to change, would a learned noble disciple contemplate these and regard them as self, as belonging to self, or as self being within them?"

Rāhula answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "Excellent, Rāhula! A learned noble disciple who contemplates thus becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, and disenchanted with the feelings that arise conditioned by eye-contact, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant. He becomes disenchanted with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and disenchanted with the feelings that arise conditioned by mind-contact, whether pleasant, unpleasant, or neither pleasant nor unpleasant. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Being liberated, he knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further existence beyond this.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. While this teaching was being spoken, Rāhula's mind was liberated from the taints without clinging. And five hundred bhikṣus also attained the pure Dharma-eye with regard to all dharmas, being free from dust and stain.

The Buddha spoke thus. Venerable Rāhula and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (179) Sūtra on the Five Supports

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are five supports for right view, by which the mind's liberation that is not yet ripe becomes ripe, and the liberation by wisdom that is not yet ripe becomes ripe. What are the five?

"Here, a bhikṣu is supported by conduct and virtue. He is supported by learning. He is supported by discussion. He is supported by calm abiding. He is supported by insight.

"These are the five supports for right view, by which the mind's liberation that is not yet ripe becomes ripe, and the liberation by wisdom that is not yet ripe becomes ripe."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (180) Sūtra on the Gautamī

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyans, at Kapilavastu, in the Banyan Park.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, holding a new pair of garments, went to the Buddha, bowed her head at his feet, withdrew to one side, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, these new garments were personally spun and woven by me for the World-Honored One. May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accept them from me."

The Buddha said: "Gautamī, offer them to the Sangha. By offering to the Sangha, you will have made an offering to me and also to the Sangha."

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke to the Buddha a second time: "World-Honored One, these new garments were personally spun and woven by me for the World-Honored One. May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accept them from me."

The Buddha spoke to her a second time: "Gautamī, offer them to the Sangha. By offering to the Sangha, you will have made an offering to me and also to the Sangha."

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke to the Buddha a third time: "World-Honored One, these new garments were personally spun and woven by me for the World-Honored One. May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accept them from me."

The Buddha spoke to her a third time: "Gautamī, offer them to the Sangha. By offering to the Sangha, you will have made an offering to me and also to the Sangha."

At that time, Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him. Venerable Ānanda then said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, please accept these garments from Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to the World-Honored One. She is the World-Honored One's aunt, who served as his foster mother and nurse, giving him milk. After the World-Honored One's mother passed away, she nursed him with her own milk. The World-Honored One has also been of great benefit to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. It is because of the World-Honored One that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Sangha. It is because of the World-Honored One that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has abandoned killing, abandoned stealing, abandoned sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech, and abandoned drinking alcohol. It is because of the World-Honored One that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has attained unwavering faith in the Buddha, unwavering faith in the Dharma, unwavering faith in the Sangha, and has perfected the precepts cherished by the noble ones. It is because of the World-Honored One that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is free from doubt regarding suffering, free from doubt regarding the arising of suffering, free from doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and free from doubt regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering. World-Honored One, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to the World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Ānanda, if a person, because of another, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Sangha, I say it is not easy to repay that person's kindness through bowing, rising, welcoming, sending off, putting palms together in reverence, making offerings of robes, food, bedding, or medicines for illness.

"Ānanda, if a person, because of another, abandons killing, abandons stealing, abandons sexual misconduct, abandons false speech, and abandons drinking alcohol, I say it is not easy to repay that person's kindness through bowing, rising, welcoming, sending off, putting palms together in reverence, making offerings of robes, food, bedding, or medicines for illness.

"Ānanda, if a person, because of another, attains unwavering faith in the Buddha, unwavering faith in the Dharma, unwavering faith in the Sangha, and perfects the precepts cherished by the noble ones, I say it is not easy to repay that person's kindness through bowing, rising, welcoming, sending off, putting palms together in reverence, making offerings of robes, food, bedding, or medicines for illness.

"Ānanda, if a person, because of another, becomes free from doubt regarding suffering, free from doubt regarding the arising of suffering, free from doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and free from doubt regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering, I say it is not easy to repay that person's kindness through bowing, rising, welcoming, sending off, putting palms together in reverence, making offerings of robes, food, bedding, or medicines for illness.

"Ānanda, there are fourteen kinds of personal gifts. What are the fourteen? One makes an offering to the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: this is the first personal gift. One makes an offering to a pratyekabuddha: this is the second personal gift. One makes an offering to a disciple of the Tathāgata who is an arhat: this is the third. One makes an offering to one who is on the path to the realization of the fruit of an arhat: this is the fourth. One makes an offering to a non-returner: this is the fifth. One makes an offering to one who is on the path to the realization of the fruit of a non-returner: this is the sixth. One makes an offering to a once-returner: this is the seventh. One makes an offering to one who is on the path to the realization of the fruit of a once-returner: this is the eighth. One makes an offering to a stream-enterer: this is the ninth. One makes an offering to one who is on the path to the realization of the fruit of a stream-enterer: this is the tenth. One makes an offering to one outside the teaching who is free from desire: this is the eleventh. One makes an offering to a good ordinary person who keeps the precepts: this is the twelfth. One makes an offering to a bad ordinary person who does not keep the precepts: this is the thirteenth. One makes an offering to an animal: this is the fourteenth.

"Ānanda, if one makes an offering to an animal, one can expect to receive a reward a hundredfold. If one makes an offering to a bad ordinary person who does not keep the precepts, one can expect to receive a reward a thousandfold. If one makes an offering to a good ordinary person who keeps the precepts, one can expect to receive a reward of a hundred thousandfold. If one makes an offering to one outside the teaching who is free from desire, one can expect to receive a reward that is incalculable and immeasurable. How much more so if one makes an offering to a stream-enterer, to one on the path to the fruit of a stream-enterer, to a once-returner, to one on the path to the fruit of a once-returner, to a non-returner, to one on the path to the fruit of a non-returner, to an arhat, to one on the path to the fruit of an arhat, to a pratyekabuddha, or to the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!

"Ānanda, there are seven kinds of offerings to the Sangha. What are the seven? If one makes an offering to the Sangha of both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in the presence of the Buddha: this is the first offering to the Sangha. If one makes an offering to the Sangha of both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs after the Buddha's passing: this is the second offering to the Sangha. If one makes an offering to the Sangha of bhikṣus: this is the third. If one makes an offering to the Sangha of bhikṣuṇīs: this is the fourth. If one says, 'Please designate a certain number of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs from the Sangha, and I will make an offering to them': this is the fifth. If one says, 'Please designate a certain number of bhikṣus from the Sangha, and I will make an offering to them': this is the sixth. If one says, 'Please designate a certain number of bhikṣuṇīs from the Sangha, and I will make an offering to them': this is the seventh.

"Ānanda, in the future there will be those who wear the kāṣāya merely in name, who have poor conduct and virtue and are unwholesome. One may make an offering to such people of poor virtue for the sake of the Sangha. I say that this offering to the Sangha is still immeasurable, incalculable. I say it is always more beneficial to make an offering to the Sangha than to make a personal offering. Therefore, Ānanda, I say to you: offer to the Sangha. If you offer to the Sangha, you will have made offerings to me and also to the Sangha."

The Buddha spoke thus. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (181) Sūtra on Multiple Feelings (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about two kinds of feelings. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain them for you. What are two kinds of feelings? They are bodily feeling and mental feeling. These are called two kinds of feelings.

"There are also three kinds of feelings. What are three kinds of feelings? They are pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling. These are called three kinds of feelings.

"There are also four kinds of feelings. What are four kinds of feelings? They are the feeling of the sphere of the Desire Realm, the feeling of the sphere of the Form Realm, the feeling of the sphere of the Formless Realm, and the feeling of the sphere of cessation. These are called four kinds of feelings.

"There are also five kinds of feelings. What are five kinds of feelings? They are the pleasure faculty, the happiness faculty, the suffering faculty, the sorrow faculty, and the equanimity faculty. These are called five kinds of feelings.

"There are also six kinds of feelings. What are six kinds of feelings? They are the feeling arisen from eye-contact, the feeling arisen from ear-contact, the feeling arisen from nose-contact, the feeling arisen from tongue-contact, the feeling arisen from body-contact, and the feeling arisen from mind-contact. These are called six kinds of feelings.

"There are also eighteen kinds of feelings. What are eighteen kinds of feelings? They are the six kinds of feelings associated with joy, the six kinds of feelings associated with sorrow, and the six kinds of feelings associated with equanimity. These are called eighteen kinds of feelings.

"There are also thirty-six kinds of feelings. What are thirty-six kinds of feelings? They are the six kinds of joy based on the household life, the six kinds of joy based on renunciation, the six kinds of sorrow based on the household life, the six kinds of sorrow based on renunciation, the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life, and the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation. These are called thirty-six kinds of feelings.

"There are also one hundred and eight kinds of feelings. What are one hundred and eight kinds of feelings? They are the thirty-six kinds of feelings of the past, the thirty-six kinds of feelings of the future, and the thirty-six kinds of feelings of the present. These are called one hundred and eight kinds of feelings.

"These are the multiple feelings. They have been taught as two, as three, as four, as five, as six, as eighteen, as thirty-six, and as one hundred and eight feelings. They are all taught in dependence on contact."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (182) Sūtra on Multiple Feelings (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.

At that time, the Parivrājaka Uttiya went to the Buddha, exchanged courtesies with him, and sat down to one side. He then said to the Buddha: "Gautama, is it the case that you say there are only two kinds of feelings, pleasant and unpleasant, and no third feeling, the neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling?"

The Buddha said: "Uttiya, do not say this. I do indeed teach three kinds of feelings: pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling."

Uttiya said again to the Buddha: "Gautama, there are only two feelings, pleasant and unpleasant, and no third feeling. That which is the neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling, this is included in the subtle and supreme pleasant feeling."

The Buddha said: "Uttiya, do not say this. Do not say this. I do indeed teach three kinds of feelings: pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling." The Buddha spoke to him a second and third time in the same way.

Then the Parivrājaka Uttiya made the same assertion repeatedly, and the Buddha again told him repeatedly not to speak in this way.

Then the World-Honored One thought: "This foolish man is persistently obstinate and repeatedly expresses this view. I should now question him further." The Buddha then asked Uttiya: "Uttiya, when a bhikṣu has attained the first dhyāna, does he experience any unpleasant feeling?"

Uttiya answered: "No, Gautama."

"Why is that? Because having attained the first dhyāna, he has already transcended unpleasant feeling. This is why no unpleasant feeling arises.

"Uttiya, when a bhikṣu has attained the second dhyāna, does he experience any pleasant feeling that involves initial thought and sustained thought?"

Uttiya answered: "No, Gautama."

"Why is that? Because having attained the second dhyāna, he has already transcended the pleasant feeling that involves initial thought and sustained thought. This is why that pleasant feeling does not arise.

"Uttiya, when a bhikṣu has attained the third dhyāna, does he experience any feeling of joy?"

Uttiya answered: "No, Gautama."

"Why is that? Because having attained the third dhyāna, he has already transcended the feeling of joy. This is why the feeling of joy does not arise.

"Uttiya, when a bhikṣu has attained the fourth dhyāna, does he experience any feeling of happiness?"

Uttiya answered: "No, Gautama."

"Why is that? Because having attained the fourth dhyāna, he has already transcended the feeling of happiness. This is why the feeling of happiness does not arise.

"Uttiya, when a bhikṣu has attained the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, does he experience any perception?"

Uttiya answered: "No, Gautama."

"Why is that? Because having attained the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he has already transcended all perception. This is why perception does not arise.

"Uttiya, the Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of pleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of unpleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of the neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of pride. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of ignorance."

Then the Parivrājaka Uttiya heard the words of the Buddha, and he did not delight in them. He ridiculed them and left.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him. Then Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what was the meaning of what the World-Honored One taught? If any bhikṣus have not yet fully comprehended it, let them comprehend it after hearing the World-Honored One explain it."

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has attained the first dhyāna, he has transcended the unpleasant feeling. Since the first dhyāna transcends the unpleasant feeling, one should know that the Buddha teaches the abandonment of unpleasant feeling. When a bhikṣu has attained the second dhyāna, he has transcended the pleasant feeling that involves initial and sustained thought. Since the second dhyāna transcends that pleasant feeling, one should know that the Buddha teaches the abandonment of pleasant feeling. When a bhikṣu has attained the third dhyāna, he has transcended the joy of the second dhyāna. Since the third dhyāna transcends that joy, one should know that the Buddha teaches the abandonment of joy. When a bhikṣu has attained the fourth dhyāna, he has transcended the happiness of the third dhyāna. Since the fourth dhyāna transcends that happiness, one should know that the Buddha teaches the abandonment of happiness. When a bhikṣu has attained the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he has transcended all perception. Since this attainment transcends all perception, one should know that the Buddha teaches the abandonment of all perception.

"Ānanda, the Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of pleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of unpleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of the neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of pride. The Buddha indeed teaches the abandonment of ignorance.

"Ānanda, there is a method by which I teach the abandonment of pride: suppose a bhikṣu does not give rise to the conceit of self, knowing and seeing that all formations are impermanent, knowing and seeing that all formations are suffering, knowing and seeing that all dharmas are not self, knowing and seeing that 'this is the peaceful, this is the supreme, namely the cessation of all formations, the relinquishment of all substrates of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.' Having abided thus, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not anxious. Not being anxious, he personally attains parinirvāṇa. He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further existence beyond this.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (183) Sūtra on the Horse-Taming Metaphor

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.

At that time, there was a horse trainer named Kesi who went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to one side, and sat down. The World-Honored One said: "Kesi, you are indeed one skilled in training horses. How do you tame horses?"

Kesi said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I use both gentle methods and harsh methods to tame them. I also use both gentle and harsh methods simultaneously."

The Buddha said: "Kesi, if a horse does not submit to any of your gentle methods, your harsh methods, or the combination of gentle and harsh methods, what do you do with it?"

Kesi said: "World-Honored One, if it does not submit to gentle, harsh, or combined methods, then I kill it. Why? So as not to bring shame upon my teacher's lineage. But, World-Honored One, the World-Honored One is the unsurpassed trainer of persons. How does the World-Honored One train people?"

The Buddha said: "Kesi, I also use gentle methods, harsh methods, and the combination of gentle and harsh methods to train people. As for gentle methods: I teach them thus: 'This is good bodily conduct, this is the result of good bodily conduct. This is good verbal conduct, this is the result of good verbal conduct. This is good mental conduct, this is the result of good mental conduct. This is a deva, this is a human being.' As for harsh methods: I teach them thus: 'This is bad bodily conduct, this is the result of bad bodily conduct. This is bad verbal conduct, this is the result of bad verbal conduct. This is bad mental conduct, this is the result of bad mental conduct. This is a hell being, this is an animal, this is a hungry ghost.' As for the combination of gentle and harsh methods: I teach them thus: 'This is good bodily conduct, this is the result of good bodily conduct; this is bad bodily conduct, this is the result of bad bodily conduct. This is good verbal conduct, this is the result of good verbal conduct; this is bad verbal conduct, this is the result of bad verbal conduct. This is good mental conduct, this is the result of good mental conduct; this is bad mental conduct, this is the result of bad mental conduct. This is a deva, this is a human being; this is a hell being, this is an animal, this is a hungry ghost.'"

Kesi then asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a person does not submit to gentle, harsh, or combined methods, what does the World-Honored One do with such a person?"

The Buddha said: "Kesi, if a person does not submit to gentle, harsh, or combined methods, then I kill that person."

Kesi said: "World-Honored One, it is not fitting for the Buddha to kill a living being. Yet the World-Honored One says: 'I kill that person.' How should I understand this?"

The Buddha said: "So it is, Kesi, so it is. It is indeed not fitting for the Tathāgata to kill a living being. However, if a person does not submit to gentle, harsh, or combined methods, then the Tathāgata considers that person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed. The Tathāgata's wise fellow practitioners in the holy life also consider that person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed. Kesi, when the Tathāgata considers a person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed, and the wise fellow practitioners in the holy life also consider that person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed, is that not the killing and destruction of that person in the Dharma and Vinaya?"

Kesi said: "World-Honored One, indeed! When the Tathāgata considers a person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed, and the wise fellow practitioners also consider that person not worthy of being spoken to or instructed, that person is truly killed and destroyed in the Dharma and Vinaya. World-Honored One, this is wonderful! Just as the inferior skill of a horse-trainer has been compared with the supreme skill of the Tathāgata, please let me take refuge in the Buddha, in the Dharma, and in the Sangha. May I be accepted as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the rest of my life, I take refuge and uphold the precepts."

The Buddha spoke thus. The horse trainer Kesi and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (184) Sūtra on Oxen

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Suppose there is a bad ox, crooked-horned and violent, that bites people, kicks people, and breaks utensils. Its owner chains it and ties it to a stake, and it cannot move freely. Bhikṣus, what do you think? Can that ox free itself from the bonds?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if one does not abandon the fetters of the mind, one cannot be freed from suffering, cannot be freed from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress.

"Suppose there is a good ox, not crooked-horned, not violent, that does not bite people, does not kick people, and does not break utensils. Its owner ties it to a stake, but it can pull free and leave. Bhikṣus, what do you think? Can that ox free itself from the bonds?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if one has abandoned the fetters of the mind, one can be freed from suffering, freed from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress.

"Bhikṣus, there are five aggregates of clinging. What are the five? The form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the formations aggregate of clinging, and the consciousness aggregate of clinging. One should contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as an illness, as a tumor, as a thorn, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as not self. One who contemplates these five aggregates of clinging in this way can realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (185) Sūtra on the Cowherd

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a cowherd possesses eleven qualities, he is able to tend his herd, make it prosper, and maintain it. What are the eleven? Here, a cowherd knows form, knows characteristics, knows how to remove parasites, knows how to bandage wounds, knows how to make smoke to drive off insects, knows the fording places, knows where the cattle should drink, knows the paths, is skilled in selecting pastures, does not milk the cows completely dry, and gives special attention and care to the bull who leads the herd. These are the eleven qualities.

"In the same way, bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu possesses eleven qualities, he is able to dwell, make progress, and maintain himself in this Dharma and Vinaya. What are the eleven? Here, a bhikṣu knows form, knows characteristics, knows how to remove parasites, knows how to bandage wounds, knows how to make smoke, knows the fording places, knows what to drink, knows the path, is skilled in selecting pastures, does not drain completely, and gives special care to the senior elders.

"How does a bhikṣu know form? A bhikṣu knows as it really is that all form, whatever form there is, consists entirely of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements. This is how a bhikṣu knows form.

"How does a bhikṣu know characteristics? A bhikṣu knows as it really is that fools are characterized by their actions, and wise persons are characterized by their actions. This is how a bhikṣu knows characteristics.

"How does a bhikṣu know how to remove parasites? Here, when a thought of desire arises, a bhikṣu does not accept it, but abandons it, dispels it, puts an end to it, and makes it not arise again. When a thought of ill-will arises, or a thought of harmfulness arises, he does not accept it, but abandons it, dispels it, puts an end to it, and makes it not arise again. When any evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not accept them, but abandons them, dispels them, puts an end to them, and makes them not arise again. This is how a bhikṣu knows how to remove parasites.

"How does a bhikṣu know how to bandage wounds? Here, a bhikṣu guards the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, he does not grasp at its signs or its details. If he were to leave the eye-faculty unguarded, coveting and sorrow, evil unwholesome states would flow in. He practices restraint of the eye-faculty and guards it. When the ear hears sounds, when the nose smells scents, when the tongue tastes flavors, when the body contacts tangible objects, when the mind cognizes mental objects, he does not grasp at their signs or details. If he were to leave the mind-faculty unguarded, coveting and sorrow, evil unwholesome states would flow in. He practices restraint of the mind-faculty and guards it. This is how a bhikṣu knows how to bandage wounds.

"How does a bhikṣu know how to make smoke? Here, a bhikṣu teaches others the Dharma he has learned, just as he has heard it, just as he has received it. He expounds it extensively for others. This is how a bhikṣu knows how to make smoke.

"How does a bhikṣu know the fording places? Here, a bhikṣu, from time to time, approaches those who have heard much learning, who have thoroughly mastered the āgamas, who uphold the Dharma, who uphold the Vinaya, and who uphold the summaries. He respectfully questions them: 'Venerable ones, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What actions will lead to long-lasting suffering for me? What actions will lead to long-lasting benefit and happiness for me?' This is how a bhikṣu knows the fording places.

"How does a bhikṣu know what to drink? Here, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya, a bhikṣu attains the meaning, attains the Dharma, and practices the Dharma with delight. This is how a bhikṣu knows what to drink.

"How does a bhikṣu know the path? Here, a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it really is: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is how a bhikṣu knows the path.

"How is a bhikṣu skilled in selecting pastures? Here, a bhikṣu knows the four foundations of mindfulness as they really are. He dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, removing covetousness and sorrow regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, contemplating mind in mind, and contemplating dharmas in dharmas, ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, removing covetousness and sorrow regarding the world. This is how a bhikṣu is skilled in selecting pastures.

"How does a bhikṣu not drain completely? Here, when faithful householders invite a bhikṣu and wish to make offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness, the bhikṣu knows the measure in accepting. This is how a bhikṣu does not drain completely.

"How does a bhikṣu give special care to the senior elders? Here, a bhikṣu, toward those elder bhikṣus who have long been in the practice, who went forth long ago, who are the leaders and guides of the Sangha, serves them, respects them, honors them, and reveres them with bodily, verbal, and mental acts of kindness, whether in public or in private. This is how a bhikṣu gives special care to the senior elders.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu possesses these eleven qualities, he is able to dwell, make progress, and maintain himself in this Dharma and Vinaya."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (186) Sūtra on Seeking Dharma

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three kinds of people to be found in the world. What are three? Those who seek by wrong means, those who seek by right means, and those who have already obtained and completed their seeking.

"What is a person who seeks by wrong means? Here, a certain person has not yet attained freedom from bondage, has not yet been freed from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. He does not understand the escape from suffering as it really is. He seeks that which is subject to bondage, that which is subject to birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. What things are subject to bondage? Wife and children, servants and maids, elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, shops and dwellings, fields and estates, gold and silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, agate, crystal, coral, amber, jade, and other precious things. These things are subject to bondage. This person, being himself subject to bondage, seeks that which is subject to bondage. Being himself subject to birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress, he seeks that which is subject to birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. This is called a person who seeks by wrong means.

"What is a person who seeks by right means? Here, a certain person has not yet attained freedom from bondage, has not yet been freed from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. He understands the escape from suffering as it really is. Knowing the danger of being subject to bondage, to birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress, he seeks the unsurpassed peace of nirvāṇa, which is free from bondage, free from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress. This is called a person who seeks by right means.

"What is a person who has already obtained and completed their seeking? The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has already attained freedom from bondage, has been freed from birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress, and has obtained the unsurpassed peace of nirvāṇa. This is called a person who has already obtained and completed their seeking."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (187) Sūtra Spoken to Anomiya (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Even if a bhikṣu is not skilled in the mental dispositions of other beings, not skilled in the mental dispositions of other persons, he should still train himself in skill regarding his own mental dispositions, saying: 'I shall be skilled regarding my own mental dispositions.'

"Bhikṣus, how is a bhikṣu skilled regarding his own mental dispositions? It is just as when a young man or woman, adorning themselves, looks at their own face in a clean, bright mirror or in a vessel of clear water. If they see any dirt or blemish on their face, they strive to remove it. If they see no dirt or blemish on their face, they are pleased and think: 'How fortunate! My face is clean!'

"In the same way, bhikṣus, a bhikṣu's self-examination is most beneficial. He should ask himself: 'Do I often have covetous thoughts or not? Do I often have thoughts of ill-will or not? Do I often have sloth and torpor or not? Do I often have restlessness and regret or not? Do I often have doubt or not? Do I often have anger or not? Do I often have defiled thoughts or not? Is my body often agitated or not? Am I often lazy or not? Is my mind often unconcentrated or not?'

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, upon self-examination, finds that he often has covetousness, often has ill-will, often has sloth and torpor, often has restlessness and regret, often has doubt, often has anger, often has defiled thoughts, his body is often agitated, he is often lazy, and his mind is often unconcentrated, then that bhikṣu, in order to abandon these evil, unwholesome states, should arouse his desire, make effort, generate vigor, exert his mind, and strive with effort. It is just as when a person's clothing or head catches fire: in order to extinguish it, he quickly arouses effort, makes haste, exerts himself, and strives with effort. In the same way, that bhikṣu, in order to abandon these evil, unwholesome states, should arouse his desire, make effort, generate vigor, exert his mind, and strive with effort.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu, upon self-examination, finds that he does not often have covetousness, does not often have ill-will, does not often have sloth and torpor, does not often have restlessness and regret, does not often have doubt, does not often have anger, does not often have defiled thoughts, his body is not often agitated, he is not often lazy, and his mind is not often unconcentrated, then that bhikṣu, in order to maintain these wholesome states, should further arouse his desire, make effort, generate vigor, exert his mind, and strive to destroy the taints."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (188) Sūtra Spoken to Anomiya (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Even if a bhikṣu is not skilled in the mental dispositions of other beings, not skilled in the mental dispositions of other persons, he should still train himself in skill regarding his own mental dispositions, saying: 'I shall be skilled regarding my own mental dispositions.'

"Bhikṣus, how is a bhikṣu skilled regarding his own mental dispositions? He should ask himself: 'Have I obtained internal serenity of mind or not? Have I obtained the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas or not?'

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has obtained internal serenity of mind but has not obtained the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas, that bhikṣu, having established himself in internal serenity of mind, should make effort to attain the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas. After some time, he will obtain both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has obtained the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas but has not obtained internal serenity of mind, that bhikṣu, having established himself in the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas, should make effort to attain internal serenity of mind. After some time, he will obtain both the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas and internal serenity of mind.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has obtained neither internal serenity of mind nor the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas, that bhikṣu, in order to obtain these wholesome states, should arouse his desire, make effort, generate vigor, exert his mind, and strive with effort. It is just as when a person's clothing or head catches fire: in order to extinguish it, he quickly arouses effort, makes haste, exerts himself, and strives with effort. In the same way, that bhikṣu should arouse his desire, make effort, generate vigor, exert his mind, and strive with effort.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu has obtained both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into dharmas, that bhikṣu, having established himself in these wholesome states, should further make effort to destroy the taints."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (189) Sūtra on the Holy Path (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the path that is holy and leads to the correct direction. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you. What is the path that is holy and leads to the correct direction? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (190) Sūtra on the Holy Path (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the path that is wrong and does not lead to the correct direction, and the path that is holy and leads to the correct direction. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain them for you.

"What is the path that is wrong and does not lead to the correct direction? Wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. This is called the path that is wrong and does not lead to the correct direction.

"What is the path that is holy and leads to the correct direction? Right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the path that is holy and leads to the correct direction."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (191) Sūtra on the Great Emptiness (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the Dharma of great emptiness. Listen well and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we shall listen."

The Buddha said: "What is the Dharma of great emptiness? When the eye exists, eye-consciousness arises. The arising of eye-consciousness is not under the control of the eye, not under the control of forms, not under the control of the person. It arises from causes and conditions. It is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. When the ear exists, when the nose exists, when the tongue exists, when the body exists, when the mind exists, mind-consciousness arises. The arising of mind-consciousness is not under the control of the mind, not under the control of mental objects, not under the control of the person. It arises from causes and conditions. It is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen.

"When there are causes, there is arising; when there are no causes, there is no arising. This is how it should be known: because this exists, that exists. Because this arises, that arises. Conditioned by ignorance, formations arise. Conditioned by formations, consciousness arises. Conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises. Conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise. Conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Conditioned by feeling, craving arises. Conditioned by craving, clinging arises. Conditioned by clinging, becoming arises. Conditioned by becoming, birth arises. Conditioned by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress arise. Thus the entire mass of suffering arises.

"When ignorance ceases, formations cease. When formations cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases. When name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. When contact ceases, feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, craving ceases. When craving ceases, clinging ceases. When clinging ceases, becoming ceases. When becoming ceases, birth ceases. When birth ceases, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and distress cease. Thus the entire mass of suffering
