## (172) Sūtra on the Mind, First of the Mind Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, dwelling alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, had this thought arise in his mind: "Who leads the world away? Who is it that becomes attached? Who arises with sovereignty?"

At that time, the bhikṣu rose from his meditation in the afternoon and went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side, saying: "World-Honored One! Today I was dwelling alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and this thought arose in my mind: 'Who leads the world away? Who is it that becomes attached? Who arises with sovereignty?'"

Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu! You have a worthy path and worthy contemplation, supremely wonderful discernment, and good reflection. 'Who leads the world away? Who is it that becomes attached? Who arises with sovereignty?' Bhikṣu, is what you asked like this?"

The bhikṣu replied: "It is so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu, it is the mind that leads the world away; it is the mind that becomes attached; it is the mind that arises with sovereignty. Bhikṣu, it is that which leads the world away, it is that which becomes attached, it is that which arises with sovereignty. Bhikṣu, the well-learned noble disciple is not led away by the mind, not attached through the mind, not subject to the mind's sovereignty. Bhikṣu, the well-learned noble disciple does not follow the mind's sovereignty; rather, the mind follows the well-learned noble disciple."

The bhikṣu said: "Excellent! Excellent! Just so, World-Honored One." At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

He then asked: "World-Honored One, a 'bhikṣu of much learning' is spoken of. World-Honored One, what is a bhikṣu of much learning? How does one designate a bhikṣu of much learning?"

Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu! You have a worthy path and worthy contemplation, supremely wonderful discernment, and good reflection. 'World-Honored One, a bhikṣu of much learning is spoken of. World-Honored One, what is a bhikṣu of much learning? How does one designate a bhikṣu of much learning?' Bhikṣu, is what you asked like this?"

The bhikṣu replied: "It is so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu, what I have taught is very extensive, namely: sūtras, verses, explanations, stanzas, accounts of causes and conditions, compilations, stories of origins, 'thus-said' discourses, birth stories, extensive expositions, unprecedented teachings, and discourses on meaning. Bhikṣu, if a person of good family, regarding even a four-line verse that I have taught, understands its meaning, understands its Dharma, proceeds in accord with the Dharma, directs himself toward the Dharma, and proceeds in accord with the holy life, then, bhikṣu, one speaks of a bhikṣu of much learning; there is nothing beyond this. Bhikṣu, such is a bhikṣu of much learning; the Tathāgata thus designates a bhikṣu of much learning."

The bhikṣu said: "Excellent! Excellent! Just so, World-Honored One." At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

He then asked: "World-Honored One, a 'bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom' is spoken of. World-Honored One, what is a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom? How does one designate a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom?"

Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu! You have a worthy path and worthy contemplation, supremely wonderful discernment, and good reflection. 'World-Honored One, a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom is spoken of. World-Honored One, what is a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom? How does one designate a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom?' Bhikṣu, is what you asked like this?"

The bhikṣu replied: "It is so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu, if a bhikṣu has heard 'this is suffering,' and further with wisdom rightly sees suffering as it truly is; has heard the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path to the cessation of suffering, and further with wisdom rightly sees the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is; bhikṣu, such is a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom. The Tathāgata thus designates a bhikṣu of much learning who has penetrating wisdom."

The bhikṣu said: "Excellent! Excellent! Just so, World-Honored One." At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

He then asked: "World-Honored One, a 'wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom' is spoken of. World-Honored One, what is a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom? How does one designate a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom?"

Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu! You have a worthy path and worthy contemplation, supremely wonderful discernment, and good reflection. 'World-Honored One, what is a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom? How does one designate a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom?' Bhikṣu, is what you asked like this?"

The bhikṣu replied: "It is so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "If a bhikṣu does not intend harm to himself, does not intend harm to others, and does not intend harm to both; if the bhikṣu thinks only of benefiting himself and benefiting others, benefiting many people, having compassion for the world, seeking meaning and benefit for devas and humans, seeking peace and happiness; bhikṣu, such is a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom. Thus does the Tathāgata designate a wise bhikṣu of keen and broad wisdom."

The bhikṣu said: "Excellent! Excellent! Just so, World-Honored One."

At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha said, well received it, well retained it, and having well recited and studied it, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard the World-Honored One's teaching, dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, cultivating with diligence. Dwelling in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, cultivating with diligence, he realized that for which sons of good families shave their hair and beards, don kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household life for homelessness to train in the path. The unsurpassed holy life was completed. In the present life, he himself knew, himself realized, himself witnessed and attained: "Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no further existence." He knew it as it truly is. That venerable one, having known the Dharma, attained arhatship.

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Mind, the First.

---

## (173) Sūtra on Phūmiya, Second of the Mind Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.

At that time, the Venerable Phūmiya was also in Rājagṛha, in a secluded meditation chamber. Then the Venerable Phūmiya, when the night had passed and dawn had come, put on his robes and took his bowl, intending to enter Rājagṛha to beg for food. The Venerable Phūmiya then had this thought: "Let me set aside entering Rājagṛha to beg for food. I should rather go to the house of Prince Jīvaka Kumāra."

Thereupon, the Venerable Phūmiya went to the house of Prince Jīvaka Kumāra.

Prince Jīvaka Kumāra saw the Venerable Phūmiya coming from afar. He immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Phūmiya, and spoke thus: "Welcome, Venerable Phūmiya! It has been long since Venerable Phūmiya has come here. Please sit on this seat." The Venerable Phūmiya then took a seat.

Prince Jīvaka Kumāra bowed his head at the Venerable Phūmiya's feet, then sat to one side and said: "Venerable Phūmiya, I wish to ask a question. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Phūmiya replied: "Prince, if you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider."

The Prince then asked the Venerable Phūmiya: "There are some ascetics and brahmins who come to me and say: 'Prince! If a person practices the holy life with aspiration, he will surely obtain the fruit. Or without aspiration, or with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the holy life, he will surely obtain the fruit.' Venerable Phūmiya, what is your teacher's view? What does he say?"

The Venerable Phūmiya said: "Prince, I have not heard this directly from the World-Honored One, nor have I heard it from fellow practitioners of the holy life. Prince, the World-Honored One may speak thus: 'There are those who practice the holy life with aspiration, and they will surely obtain the fruit; or without aspiration, or with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit.'"

The Prince said: "If the Venerable Phūmiya's teacher holds such a view and speaks thus, then among all in the world, including devas, Māra, Brahmā, ascetics, brahmins, from humans to devas, he stands supreme above them all. Venerable Phūmiya, please eat here." The Venerable Phūmiya accepted in silence. The Prince, knowing that the Venerable Phūmiya had silently accepted, rose from his seat, personally brought washing water, and with extremely fine, pure, and excellent foods of various kinds in abundance, food to be chewed and swallowed, personally served and ladled for him until he was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels had been cleared away, and washing water had been brought, the Prince took a small seat and sat apart to hear the Dharma.

The Venerable Phūmiya taught the Dharma for him, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing in him delight. With countless skillful means, he taught the Dharma for him, encouraging, inspiring, and establishing delight. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.

He went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported in full to the Buddha everything he had discussed with the Prince.

Having heard this, the World-Honored One said: "Phūmiya, why did you not teach the Prince the four similes?"

The Venerable Phūmiya asked: "World-Honored One, what are the four similes?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain milk and milks the horn of a cow. He will surely not obtain milk. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain milk and milks the horn of a cow will surely not obtain milk. Why is this? Because he seeks milk in a wrong way, namely milking a cow's horn.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain milk, feeds and waters the cow well, and then milks the cow's udder. He will surely obtain milk. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain milk, feeds and waters the cow well, and then milks the cow's udder will surely obtain milk. Why is this? Because he seeks milk in the right way, namely milking the cow's udder.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain butter and fills a vessel with water and churns it. He will surely not obtain butter. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain butter and fills a vessel with water and churns it will surely not obtain butter. Why is this? Because he seeks butter in a wrong way, namely churning water.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain butter and fills a vessel with curds and churns it. He will surely obtain butter. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain butter and fills a vessel with curds and churns it will surely obtain butter. Why is this? Because he seeks butter in the right way, namely churning curds.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain oil and fills an oil press with sand, douses it with cold water, and presses it. He will surely not obtain oil. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain oil and fills an oil press with sand, douses it with cold water, and presses it will surely not obtain oil. Why is this? Because he seeks oil in a wrong way, namely pressing sand.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"It is like a person who wants to obtain oil and fills an oil press with sesame seeds, douses them with warm water, and presses them. He will surely obtain oil. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain oil and fills an oil press with sesame seeds, douses them with warm water, and presses them will surely obtain oil. Why is this? Because he seeks oil in the right way, namely pressing sesame seeds.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain fire and uses wet wood as the fire-board and drills with a wet drill. He will surely not obtain fire. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain fire and uses wet wood as the fire-board and drills with a wet drill will surely not obtain fire. Why is this? Because he seeks fire in a wrong way, namely drilling wet wood.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold wrong views and are established in wrong views, then whether they practice a wrong holy life with aspiration, they will surely not obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing a wrong holy life, they will surely not obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in a wrong way; this is not the path.

"Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, it is like a person who wants to obtain fire and uses dry wood as the fire-board and drills with a dry drill. He will surely obtain fire. Whether without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, a person who wants to obtain fire and uses dry wood as the fire-board and drills with a dry drill will surely obtain fire. Why is this? Because he seeks fire in the right way, namely drilling dry wood.

"Just so, Phūmiya, if there are ascetics and brahmins who hold right views and are established in right views, then whether they practice the right holy life with aspiration, they will surely obtain the fruit; without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, practicing the right holy life, they will surely obtain the fruit. Why is this? Because they seek the fruit in the right way; this is the path.

"Phūmiya, if you had taught the Prince these four similes, the Prince, upon hearing them, would have been greatly delighted and would have made offerings to you for the rest of his life, namely robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines, and various other requisites of livelihood."

The Venerable Phūmiya said: "World-Honored One, I had never before heard these four similes. How could I have taught them? Only now have I heard them from the World-Honored One."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Phūmiya and the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Phūmiya, the Second.

## (174) Sūtra on Undertaking Dharma, Third of the Mind Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In this world there are truly four kinds of undertaking dharma. What are the four? There is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result. There is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result. There is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result. And there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result? There are some ascetics and brahmins who sport together with beautifully adorned women, and they speak thus: 'These ascetics and brahmins, what future fear do they see in sensual desires? What calamity do they see, that they abandon sensual desires and teach the abandonment of sensual desires? The touch of these beautifully adorned women's bodies is pleasant and delightful.' They sport together with these women, playing among them. Having undertaken this dharma and fulfilled it, when their bodies break apart and life ends, they go to an evil destination and are born in hell. Then they think: 'Those ascetics and brahmins saw this future fear in sensual desires, saw this calamity, and therefore abandoned sensual desires and taught the abandonment of sensual desires. Because of desires, because of quarreling over desires, because of being conditioned by desires, we now suffer such extreme and grievous pain.'

"It is like this: in the last month of spring, when the midday sun is extremely hot, there are creeper seeds that, scorched by the sun, split open and fall at the base of a sāla tree. At that time, the spirit of the sāla tree becomes fearful because of this. Then the tree spirits who are neighbors, or village spirits of seeds, village spirits of grains and medicinal plants, or tree spirits who are relatives and friends, seeing the future fear and calamity in the seed, go to that tree spirit and console it, saying: 'Do not fear, tree spirit! Do not fear, tree spirit! This seed may be eaten by deer, eaten by peacocks, blown away by wind, burned by village fire, burned by wildfire, or it may decay and not become a viable seed. In that case, tree spirit, you will be safe. But if this seed is not eaten by deer, not eaten by peacocks, not blown away by wind, not burned by village fire, not burned by wildfire, and does not decay, and the seed is not defective, not hollow, not split, and is not damaged by wind, rain, or sun, and receives abundant rain, then it will quickly sprout.'

"That tree spirit then thinks: 'For what reason do those neighboring tree spirits, village spirits of seeds, village spirits of grains and medicinal plants, and relative and friend tree spirits see future fear and calamity in the seed, and come to console me, saying: "Do not fear, tree spirit! Do not fear, tree spirit! This seed may be eaten by deer, eaten by peacocks, blown away by wind, burned by village fire, burned by wildfire, or it may decay and not become a viable seed. In that case, tree spirit, you will be safe. But if this seed is not eaten by deer, not eaten by peacocks, not blown away by wind, not burned by village fire, not burned by wildfire, and does not decay, and the seed is not defective, not hollow, not split, and is not damaged by wind, rain, or sun, and receives abundant rain, then it will quickly sprout"?'

"It produces stems, branches, and leaves that are soft and form joints, and their touch is delightful to the body. These stems, branches, and leaves, soft with formed joints, are delightful and pleasant to touch. Then this creeper grows into great branches, joints, and leaves, wrapping around that tree, covering it from above. Once it covers the tree from above, that tree spirit then thinks: 'Those neighboring tree spirits, village spirits of seeds, village spirits of grains and medicinal plants, and relative and friend tree spirits saw this future fear and this calamity in the seed, and therefore came to console me, saying: "Do not fear, tree spirit! Do not fear, tree spirit! This seed may be eaten by deer, eaten by peacocks, blown away by wind, burned by village fire, burned by wildfire, or it may decay and not become a viable seed. In that case, tree spirit, you will be safe. But if this seed is not eaten by deer, not eaten by peacocks, not blown away by wind, not burned by village fire, not burned by wildfire, and does not decay, and the seed is not defective, not hollow, not split, and is not damaged by wind, rain, or sun, and receives abundant rain, then it will quickly sprout." Because of the seed, conditioned by the seed, I now suffer this extreme and grievous pain.'

"Just so, there are some ascetics and brahmins who sport together with beautifully adorned women, and they speak thus: 'These ascetics and brahmins, what future fear do they see in sensual desires? What calamity do they see, that they abandon sensual desires and teach the abandonment of sensual desires? The touch of these beautifully adorned women's bodies is pleasant and delightful.' They sport together with these women, playing among them. Having undertaken this dharma and fulfilled it, when their bodies break apart and life ends, they go to an evil destination and are born in hell. Then they think: 'Those ascetics and brahmins saw this future fear in sensual desires, saw this calamity, and therefore abandoned sensual desires and taught the abandonment of sensual desires. Because of desires, because of quarreling over desires, because of being conditioned by desires, we now suffer such extreme and grievous pain.' This is called the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result? There may be someone who by nature has heavy, turbid desire, heavy, turbid aversion, and heavy, turbid delusion. That person, frequently following the mind of desire, experiences suffering and grief; frequently following the mind of aversion and delusion, experiences suffering and grief. That person, with suffering and grief, for the entire span of life practices the holy life, even to the point of sobbing and shedding tears. Having undertaken this dharma and fulfilled it, when the body breaks apart and life ends, one surely ascends to a good destination and is born among the devas. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result? There are some ascetics and brahmins who go naked and without clothing, or use their hands as clothing, or use leaves as clothing, or use beads as clothing; they do not take water with a pot, they do not take water with a ladle; they do not eat food obtained by the knife or the staff, food obtained by robbery, or food obtained by deceit. They do not go themselves to receive food, they do not send messengers, they are not summoned to come. They do not honor the one who prepares food, they do not honor the one who cooks, they do not stand to honor. If two people are eating, they do not eat among them. They do not eat in the house of a pregnant woman, they do not eat in the house where a dog is kept, they do not eat where flies swarm over excrement. They do not eat fish, they do not eat meat, they do not drink liquor, they do not drink foul water. Some do not drink at all, practicing the way of not drinking. Some eat one mouthful, taking one mouthful as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, taking seven mouthfuls as sufficient. Some eat from one alms-offering, taking one offering as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven offerings, taking seven offerings as sufficient. Some eat once a day, taking one meal as sufficient; or once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once a fortnight, or once a month, taking one meal as sufficient. Some eat vegetables and greens, some eat millet, some eat wild rice, some eat mixed dregs, some eat tutthula fruits, some eat coarse food. Some go to a deserted place and dwell relying on solitude. Some eat roots, some eat fruits, some eat fruits that have fallen of their own accord.

"Some wear garments of hemp cloth, some wear garments of hair, some wear garments of head-hair cloth, some wear garments of mixed hair and head-hair cloth. Some wear whole skins, some wear perforated skins, some wear both whole and perforated skins. Some wear their hair loose, some wear their hair braided, some wear both loose and braided hair. Some shave their hair, some shave their beards, some shave both beards and hair. Some pull out their hair, some pull out their beards, some pull out both beards and hair. Some stand upright, refusing to sit. Some practice squatting. Some lie on thorns, using thorns as their bed. Some lie on grass, using grass as their bed. Some worship water, day and night scooping it with their hands. Some worship fire, keeping it burning through the night. Some worship the sun and moon, venerating them with great reverence, joining their palms toward them.

"Practices of this kind, enduring immeasurable suffering, training in austerities and burning practices, having undertaken this dharma and fulfilled it, when the body breaks apart and life ends, they surely go to an evil destination and are born in hell. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result? There may be someone who by nature does not have heavy, turbid desire, does not have heavy, turbid aversion, and does not have heavy, turbid delusion. That person does not frequently follow the mind of desire and experience suffering and grief; does not frequently follow the mind of aversion and delusion and experience suffering and grief. That person, with happiness and joy, for the entire span of life practices the holy life, to the point of delighting the mind. Having undertaken this dharma and fulfilled it, the five lower fetters being exhausted, one is reborn by transformation in that realm and there attains parinirvāṇa, attaining the dharma of non-regression, not returning to this world. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result.

"That there are truly in the world these four kinds of undertaking dharma, it is for this reason that I have spoken."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Undertaking Dharma, the Third.

---

## (175) Sūtra on Undertaking Dharma, Fourth of the Mind Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Kuru country, at the town of Kammāssadhamma among the Kurus.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "This world has such desires, such wishes, such loves, such pleasures, such intentions, and yet unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. With such desires, such wishes, such loves, such pleasures, such intentions, yet unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is the dharma of delusion. My Dharma is very profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, difficult to comprehend. Thus my Dharma is very profound, difficult to see, difficult to realize, difficult to comprehend: that unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise; this is the dharma of non-delusion.

"In the world there are truly four kinds of undertaking dharma. What are the four? There is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result. There is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result. There is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result. And there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result? There may be someone who takes pleasure and delight in killing living beings, and because of killing living beings, gives rise to pleasure and delight. That person takes pleasure and delight in taking what is not given, in sexual misconduct, in false speech, and so on up to wrong views, and because of wrong views, gives rise to pleasure and delight. Such bodily pleasure and mental pleasure, arising from the unwholesome and born of the unwholesome, do not tend toward wisdom, do not tend toward awakening, do not tend toward nirvāṇa. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result? There may be someone who suffers and grieves in abstaining from killing, and because of abstaining from killing, gives rise to suffering and grief. That person suffers and grieves in abstaining from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and so on up to abstaining from wrong views, and because of abstaining from wrong views, gives rise to suffering and grief. Such bodily suffering and mental suffering, arising from the wholesome and born of the wholesome, tend toward wisdom, tend toward awakening, tend toward nirvāṇa. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result? There may be someone who suffers and grieves while killing living beings, and because of killing living beings, gives rise to suffering and grief. That person suffers and grieves while taking what is not given, engaging in sexual misconduct, speaking falsely, and so on up to wrong views, and because of wrong views, gives rise to suffering and grief. Such bodily suffering and mental suffering, arising from the unwholesome and born of the unwholesome, do not tend toward wisdom, do not tend toward awakening, do not tend toward nirvāṇa. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result.

"What is the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result? There may be someone who takes pleasure and delight in abstaining from killing, and because of abstaining from killing, gives rise to pleasure and delight. That person takes pleasure and delight in abstaining from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and so on up to abstaining from wrong views, and because of abstaining from wrong views, gives rise to pleasure and delight. Such bodily pleasure and mental pleasure, arising from the wholesome and born of the wholesome, tend toward wisdom, tend toward awakening, tend toward nirvāṇa. This is called the undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish.

"It is like the āmalaka medicine, which has fine color, fragrance, and taste in one respect, but is mixed with poison. If there is a person who, because of illness, takes it, at the time of taking it, the color, fragrance, and taste are fine, it is pleasing to the mouth and does not hurt the throat, but after it enters the stomach it does not serve as medicine.

"Just so, this undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of delusion.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the deluded person does not practice it and abandons it. Not practicing it and abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of delusion.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish.

"It is like urine and feces, further mixed with poison. If there is a person who, because of illness, takes it, at the time of taking it, its color is bad, its smell is foul, it has no taste, it is displeasing to the mouth and hurts the throat, and after it enters the stomach it does not serve as medicine.

"Just so, this undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the deluded person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of delusion.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the deluded person does not practice it and abandons it. Not practicing it and abandoning it, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of delusion.

"The deluded person does not know as it truly is what should be practiced. The deluded person does not know as it truly is what should not be practiced. Not knowing as it truly is what should be practiced, not knowing as it truly is what should not be practiced, the deluded person then practices what should not be practiced and does not practice what should be practiced. Practicing what should not be practiced and not practicing what should be practiced, unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of delusion.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present but brings suffering as its future result, the wise person does not practice it and abandons it. Not practicing it and abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the wise person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish.

"It is like urine and feces mixed with various medicines. If there is a person who, because of illness, takes it, at the time of taking it, its color is bad, its smell is foul, it has no taste, it is displeasing to the mouth and hurts the throat, but after it enters the stomach it serves as medicine.

"Just so, this undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present but brings happiness as its future result, the wise person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is painful in the present and also brings suffering as its future result, the wise person does not practice it and abandons it. Not practicing it and abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"If there is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the wise person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish.

"It is like clarified butter and honey mixed with various medicines. If there is a person who, because of illness, takes it, at the time of taking it, the color, fragrance, and taste are fine, it is pleasing to the mouth and does not hurt the throat, and after it enters the stomach it serves as medicine.

"Just so, this undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the wise person knows it as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is that this undertaking of dharma is pleasant in the present and also brings happiness as its future result, the wise person continues to practice it and does not abandon it. Continuing to practice it without abandoning it, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"The wise person knows as it truly is what should be practiced. The wise person knows as it truly is what should not be practiced. Knowing as it truly is what should be practiced, knowing as it truly is what should not be practiced, the wise person then practices what should be practiced and does not practice what should not be practiced. Practicing what should be practiced and not practicing what should not be practiced, pleasant, lovely, and desirable dharmas arise, while unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable dharmas perish. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"That there are truly in the world these four kinds of undertaking dharma, it is for this reason that I have spoken."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Undertaking Dharma, the Fourth.

## (176) Sūtra on Practicing Dhyāna, Fifth of the Heart Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In the world there truly are four kinds of dhyāna practitioners. What are the four? There are dhyāna practitioners who are progressing brilliantly yet think they are declining. There are dhyāna practitioners who are declining yet think they are progressing brilliantly. There are dhyāna practitioners who, when declining, know they are declining as it truly is. And there are dhyāna practitioners who, when progressing brilliantly, know they are progressing brilliantly as it truly is.

"How is a dhyāna practitioner progressing brilliantly yet thinking he is declining? That dhyāna practitioner, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the first dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the second dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the third dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the fourth dhyāna toward the sphere of boundless space; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the fourth dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the fourth dhyāna toward the sphere of boundless space; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the sphere of boundless space toward the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of boundless space; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless space toward the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the sphere of boundless consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of boundless consciousness; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. His mind, cultivating right thought, proceeds from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of nothingness; my concentration has perished.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Not knowing as it truly is, he regresses from what is true, and his mind loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is progressing brilliantly yet thinks he is declining.

"How is a dhyāna practitioner declining yet thinking he is progressing brilliantly? That dhyāna practitioner, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the second dhyāna. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the first dhyāna, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the second dhyāna.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the third dhyāna. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the second dhyāna, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the third dhyāna.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the fourth dhyāna. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the third dhyāna, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the fourth dhyāna.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the sphere of boundless space. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the fourth dhyāna toward the sphere of boundless space; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the fourth dhyāna, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the sphere of boundless space.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the sphere of boundless consciousness. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless space toward the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the sphere of boundless space, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the sphere of boundless consciousness.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the sphere of nothingness. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the sphere of boundless consciousness, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the sphere of nothingness.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He thinks upon other, lesser perceptions and cultivates the path of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; this is a superior calming and stilling.' That dhyāna practitioner does not know as it truly is: 'It would be better to think perceptions associated with revulsion and enter the sphere of nothingness, rather than to think other, lesser perceptions and enter the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.' Not knowing as it truly is, he fails to be aware of his mind and loses concentration. Thus is a dhyāna practitioner who is declining yet thinks he is progressing brilliantly.

"How does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is? That dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, with neither perception nor non-perception, attains and dwells in the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of nothingness, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless consciousness, the original practice. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of nothingness; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless space, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of boundless consciousness; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with delight in form, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the sphere of boundless space; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the third dhyāna, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the fourth dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the second dhyāna, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the third dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the first dhyāna, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the second dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with sensual pleasure, the original requisites of regression. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind has departed from its original characteristic and moved toward another place. I have lost the first dhyāna; my concentration has perished.' Knowing as it truly is, he does not regress from what is true, and his mind does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know declining as declining, as it truly is.

"How does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is? That dhyāna practitioner, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the fourth dhyāna toward the sphere of boundless space; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the fourth dhyāna toward the sphere of boundless space; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless space toward the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless space toward the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of boundless consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the dhyāna practitioner, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. His mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; this is a superior calming and stilling. That dhyāna practitioner then has this thought: 'My mind, cultivating right thought, with happiness calmed and stilled, proceeds from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception; this is a superior calming and stilling.' Knowing as it truly is, he is then aware of his mind and does not lose concentration. Thus does a dhyāna practitioner know progressing brilliantly as progressing brilliantly, as it truly is. In the world there truly are these four kinds of dhyāna practitioners; it is for this reason that this is taught."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Practicing Dhyāna, the Fifth.

## (177) Sūtra on Exposition, Sixth of the Heart Chapter in the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Kuru country, in the Kuru town of Kammāssadhamma.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now teach you the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with words, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. It is called the Four Kinds of Exposition. I shall distinguish and explain the meaning of the Four Kinds of Exposition. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it. I shall now teach."

At that time, the bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "How are the Four Kinds of Exposition distinguished in their meaning? If a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, yet he does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, and only engages in mindful perceptions associated with sensual pleasure, the requisites of regression, that bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the second dhyāna, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the second dhyāna.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, secluded from desires, secluded from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.
