"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the first dhyāna, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the third dhyāna, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the third dhyāna.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with initial thought and sustained thought already stilled, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the second dhyāna, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the fourth dhyāna, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the fourth dhyāna.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily happiness, what the noble ones describe as 'noble equanimity, mindfulness, and happy dwelling,' attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the third dhyāna, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless space, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the sphere of boundless space.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, with happiness ceased, with suffering ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, neither in suffering nor happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with delight in form, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless consciousness, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the sphere of boundless consciousness.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with boundless space, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless space. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless space, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of nothingness, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the sphere of nothingness.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, with boundless consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with cessation and stilling, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion; thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of boundless consciousness, the requisites of regression. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me abide, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to regress; moreover, this concentration of mine will not endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He takes up this practice, attends to these signs and markers, establishes mindfulness in accordance with the Dharma, and causes his mind to abide in one-pointedness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me progress, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen enables me to abide; moreover, this concentration of mine will surely endure long.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, the requisites of progress upward. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not lead to revulsion. This state that has arisen causes me to progress upward; thus, before long, I shall attain the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu, through his practice, his signs, and his markers, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, with nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness. He does not take up this practice, does not attend to these signs and markers, but only engages in mindful perceptions associated with revulsion, the requisites of desirelessness. That bhikṣu should know: 'This state has arisen in me. It does not make me regress, does not make me abide, and does not make me progress upward. This state that has arisen leads me to revulsion. Thus, before long, I shall attain the ending of the outflows.' That bhikṣu should know thus.

"Where there is perception and knowledge, up to this extent one can know, reaching as far as the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception, which is the practice of the remaining foremost existence. For a bhikṣu who practices dhyāna, from this point onward, one should teach him accordingly."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Exposition, the Sixth.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama Sūtra), Fascicle 47

*Translated by Gautama Sanghadeva during the Eastern Jin Dynasty*

---

## Chapter on "The Great" (Part Three)

---

### (180) Sūtra on Gavampati

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Gavampati was dwelling in seclusion, in quiet meditation. He had this thought: "Can one know suffering without personally experiencing suffering? Can one know the origin of suffering without personally experiencing the origin of suffering? Can one know the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the cessation of suffering? Can one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the path leading to the cessation of suffering?"

Then in the evening, the Venerable Gavampati arose from his meditation, went to the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "Bhagavān, I was dwelling in seclusion, in quiet meditation, and had this thought: 'Can one know suffering without personally experiencing suffering? Can one know the origin of suffering without personally experiencing the origin of suffering? Can one know the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the cessation of suffering? Can one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the path leading to the cessation of suffering?'"

The World-Honored One said: "Gavampati, one can know suffering without personally experiencing suffering, can know the origin of suffering without personally experiencing the origin of suffering, can know the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the cessation of suffering, and can know the path leading to the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

Gavampati asked: "Bhagavān, how can one know suffering without personally experiencing suffering, know the origin of suffering without personally experiencing the origin of suffering, know the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the cessation of suffering, and know the path leading to the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the path leading to the cessation of suffering?"

The World-Honored One said: "Gavampati, suppose a bhikṣu, with respect to pleasant feelings, knows that pleasant feelings are impermanent, knows they are subject to destruction, knows they are subject to dispassion, knows they are subject to cessation. With respect to painful feelings, he knows that painful feelings are impermanent, knows they are subject to destruction, knows they are subject to dispassion, knows they are subject to cessation. With respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, he knows that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are impermanent, knows they are subject to destruction, knows they are subject to dispassion, knows they are subject to cessation.

"Thus, Gavampati, a bhikṣu can know suffering without personally experiencing suffering, can know the origin of suffering without personally experiencing the origin of suffering, can know the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the cessation of suffering, and can know the path leading to the cessation of suffering without personally experiencing the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Gavampati, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (181) Sūtra on Many Bhikṣus (First)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after their midday meal, having put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and then gathered in the assembly hall and sat together. They discussed this question: "Venerables, the Tathāgata, when he was about to enter final nirvāṇa, spoke to the Venerable Ānanda saying: 'Ānanda, after my passing, the Pratimokṣa shall be your teacher.' How should we understand the meaning of this? Should we understand it as the Tathāgata said it, or is there another meaning?"

Among them, some bhikṣus said: "The World-Honored One stated that there is one Dharma. This is the meaning that the World-Honored One spoke; there is no other meaning."

Some bhikṣus said: "The World-Honored One stated that there are two Dharmas. This is the meaning that the World-Honored One spoke; there is no other meaning."

Some bhikṣus said: "The World-Honored One stated that there are three Dharmas. This is the meaning that the World-Honored One spoke; there is no other meaning."

Some bhikṣus said: "The World-Honored One stated that there are four Dharmas. This is the meaning that the World-Honored One spoke; there is no other meaning."

Some said five, some said six, some said seven, some said eight, some said nine, some said ten, some said eleven, and some said twelve. "The World-Honored One stated that there are twelve Dharmas. This is the meaning that the World-Honored One spoke; there is no other meaning."

Then the Venerable Ānanda was also in the assembly. The Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, there is one Dharma correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What is that one Dharma correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? It is right mindfulness of the body. This is that one Dharma correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are two Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those two Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: samatha and vipaśyanā. These are those two Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are three Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those three Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the three samādhis: the empty samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi. These are those three Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are four Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those four Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right comprehension, overcoming covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates feelings as feelings, contemplates mind as mind, and contemplates dharmas as dharmas internally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right comprehension, overcoming covetousness and grief toward the world. These are those four Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are five Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those five Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the five faculties. What are the five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of effort, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These are those five Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are six Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those six Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the six subjects of recollection. What are the six? Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of moral discipline, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the devas. These are those six Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are seven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those seven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the seven factors of enlightenment. What are the seven? The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of dharmas, the factor of enlightenment of effort, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are those seven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are eight Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those eight Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the Noble Eightfold Path. What are the eight? Right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These are those eight Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are nine Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those nine Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the nine successive abodes of beings. What are the nine? There are beings with different bodies and different perceptions; this is the first abode of beings, namely humans and some devas. There are beings with different bodies but the same perception; this is the second abode of beings, namely the Brahmākāyika devas who are first born there. There are beings with the same body but different perceptions; this is the third abode of beings, namely the Ābhāsvara devas. There are beings with the same body and the same perception; this is the fourth abode of beings, namely the Śubhakṛtsna devas. There are beings without perception and without feeling; this is the fifth abode of beings, namely the unconscious beings. There are beings who have completely transcended all perceptions of form, who have eliminated perceptions of resistance, and who do not attend to perceptions of diversity, attaining boundless space and dwelling in the sphere of boundless space; this is the sixth abode of beings. There are beings who have completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, attaining boundless consciousness and dwelling in the sphere of boundless consciousness; this is the seventh abode of beings. There are beings who have completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, attaining nothingness and dwelling in the sphere of nothingness; this is the eighth abode of beings. There are beings who have completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, attaining neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the ninth abode of beings. These are those nine Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are ten Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those ten Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the ten wholesome courses of action. What are the ten? Abandoning killing, abandoning stealing, abandoning sexual misconduct, abandoning false speech, abandoning divisive speech, abandoning harsh speech, abandoning idle chatter, abandoning covetousness, abandoning ill will, and right view. These are those ten Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are eleven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those eleven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the eleven images of the mind of loving-kindness. What are the eleven? A bhikṣu, with a mind of loving-kindness, pervades one direction and dwells in it. In this way he pervades two directions, three directions, four directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading the entire world. With a mind of loving-kindness, free from resentment, free from ill will, free from anger, free from enmity, vast, great, boundless, well cultivated, he pervades it all and dwells in it. Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise practiced.

"Venerables, if a bhikṣu practices the mind of loving-kindness, develops it extensively, he gains eleven benefits. What are the eleven? He sleeps happily, he wakes happily, he does not have evil dreams, humans hold him dear, non-humans hold him dear, devas protect him, fire and poison and weapons do not approach him, his mind is easily concentrated, the expression of his face is serene, he dies without confusion, and if he does not penetrate to anything higher, he is reborn in the Brahma world.

"These are those eleven Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"There are twelve Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

"What are those twelve Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One? They are: the twelve links of dependent origination. What are the twelve? Conditioned by ignorance, there are volitional formations. Conditioned by volitional formations, there is consciousness. Conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form. Conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases. Conditioned by the six sense bases, there is contact. Conditioned by contact, there is feeling. Conditioned by feeling, there is craving. Conditioned by craving, there is clinging. Conditioned by clinging, there is becoming. Conditioned by becoming, there is birth. Conditioned by birth, there arise aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus this entire great mass of suffering arises. But with the complete cessation and fading away of ignorance, volitional formations cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all cease. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases.

"These are those twelve Dharmas correctly proclaimed by the World-Honored One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. We should all gather together, together recite and not dispute, so that this holy practice may long endure, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans."

The Venerable Ānanda spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (182) Sūtra on Many Bhikṣus (Second): The Parable of the Horse

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, many bhikṣus, after their midday meal, having put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and then gathered in the assembly hall and sat together. They discussed this question: "Venerables, there is a person: for his own benefit, not for the benefit of others. There is a person: for the benefit of others, not for his own benefit. There is a person: neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others. There is a person: both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. Among these four persons, who is the most superior and excellent, the most foremost and supreme?"

Among them, some bhikṣus said: "The person who is for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others is superior to the person who neither benefits himself nor benefits others. The person who benefits others but not himself is superior to the person who benefits himself but not others. The person who benefits both himself and others is superior to the person who benefits others but not himself. Among these four persons, the last one, who benefits both himself and others, is the most superior and excellent, the most foremost and supreme.

"Just as from a cow one gets milk, from milk one gets cream, from cream one gets butter, from butter one gets ghee, and from ghee one gets the finest ghee, and the finest ghee is declared the most supreme among them; in the same way, the person who benefits both himself and others is the most superior and excellent among these four persons."

Then the Venerable Ānanda was also in the assembly. The Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerables, now let us go together to see the World-Honored One and present this matter to him. As the World-Honored One explains it, so shall we remember it."

The bhikṣus replied: "Very well."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with the many bhikṣus, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported in full what had happened. He said: "Bhagavān, the many bhikṣus discussed this question. Among them, some bhikṣus gave this explanation. Bhagavān, among these four persons, who is the most superior and excellent, the most foremost and supreme?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, one cannot decide in a general way among these four persons which is most superior. Why? Because there may be a person who benefits himself but not others, who practices renunciation and becomes a renunciant; such a person is superior. If, however, a person who is said to benefit others but not himself brings others to complete moral discipline, this person is more difficult and more rare than the one who benefits himself alone.

"Ānanda, there may be a person who benefits neither himself nor others; such a person is to be pitied. There may be a person who benefits both himself and others, who himself practices renunciation and also establishes others in renunciation. Among these four persons, this person who benefits both himself and others is the most superior and excellent, the most foremost and supreme.

"Ānanda, it is like a bull leading cattle, or a stallion leading horses. Among these four persons, the person who benefits both himself and others is the most superior and excellent, the most foremost and supreme."

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, what do you think? Is there a person who, based on moral discipline, attains concentration of mind, who may or may not attain the destruction of the outflows?"

Ānanda replied: "Bhagavān, according to my understanding of the meaning of what the World-Honored One has taught, there is a person who, based on moral discipline, attains concentration of mind, and based on that concentration, may attain the destruction of the outflows."

The World-Honored One said: "Very good, very good, Ānanda! This is the meaning of what I said. Based on moral discipline, one attains concentration of mind, and based on concentration, one may attain the destruction of the outflows.

"Ānanda, in this way, moral discipline is the ground, moral discipline is the basis. Based on moral discipline, one attains concentration of mind, and based on concentration, one may attain the destruction of the outflows. This is what I call the greater benefit and the greater fruit.

"Ānanda, it is like a tree: depending on the ground, depending on the earth, it grows, develops, increases, and flourishes. Ānanda, in the same way, based on moral discipline, grounded in moral discipline, a bhikṣu attains concentration of mind, and based on concentration, may attain the destruction of the outflows."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, there are five things for accomplishment. What are the five? First, one should have faith and believe in the Tathāgata's enlightenment: 'The World-Honored One is indeed the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Beings, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' Second, one should be free from illness, in good health, with proper digestion, neither too cold nor too hot, suitable for practice. Third, one should not be deceitful or flattering but should sincerely reveal oneself as one truly is to the teacher and to wise companions in the holy life. Fourth, one should dwell with effort in abandoning unwholesome states and cultivating wholesome states, steadfast, firm in resolve, not shirking the task of cultivating wholesome states. Fifth, one should have wisdom, possessing the noble wisdom of arising and passing away that leads to the complete destruction of suffering.

"These are the five things for accomplishment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (183) Sūtra on the Horse

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are four good horses in the world. What are the four?

"There is a good horse: when the driver raises the whip and its shadow falls upon the horse, the horse is immediately startled and knows what the driver wishes, whether to go left or right, fast or slow, and it responds accordingly. This is the first good horse in the world.

"Furthermore, there is a good horse: when the shadow of the whip does not startle it, but when the whip touches its hair or the tip of its tail, it is then startled and knows what the driver wishes, whether to go left or right, fast or slow, and it responds accordingly. This is the second good horse in the world.

"Furthermore, there is a good horse: when the shadow of the whip does not startle it, and touching its hair does not startle it, but when the whip strikes its flesh, it is then startled and knows what the driver wishes, whether to go left or right, fast or slow, and it responds accordingly. This is the third good horse in the world.

"Furthermore, there is a good horse: when the shadow of the whip does not startle it, touching its hair does not startle it, and striking its flesh does not startle it, but when the whip strikes to the bone, it is then startled and deeply troubled. It then knows what the driver wishes, whether to go left or right, fast or slow, and it responds accordingly. This is the fourth good horse in the world.

"These are the four good horses in the world.

"In the same way, there are four good men in the world. What are the four?

"There is a good man who hears that in another village there is a person who is suffering from illness, is in great pain, or has died, and he is immediately alarmed and deeply moved, saying: 'That suffering that person has experienced, I too could experience such suffering.' He then practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, with correct practice. It is like that good horse that, upon seeing the shadow of the whip, is immediately startled and responds to the driver's wishes. I say this good man is also like that.

"Furthermore, there is a good man who does not hear about suffering in another village, but he himself sees in his own village a person who is suffering from illness, in great pain, or has died, and he is then alarmed and deeply moved, saying: 'That suffering that person has experienced, I too could experience such suffering.' He then practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, with correct practice. It is like that good horse that, upon the whip touching its hair, is startled and responds to the driver's wishes. I say this good man is also like that.

"Furthermore, there is a good man who neither hears about suffering in another village nor sees it in his own village, but he sees that his own relative or family member is suffering from illness, in great pain, or has died, and he is then alarmed and deeply moved, saying: 'That suffering my relative has experienced, I too could experience such suffering.' He then practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, with correct practice. It is like that good horse that, upon the whip striking its flesh, is startled and responds to the driver's wishes. I say this good man is also like that.

"Furthermore, there is a good man who neither hears about suffering in another village, nor sees it in his own village, nor sees his relatives suffering, but he himself experiences physical illness and extreme pain, his very life being imperiled. He is then alarmed and deeply moved, saying: 'I am now experiencing this suffering; I should urgently seek liberation from it.' He then practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, with correct practice. It is like that good horse that, upon the whip striking to the bone, is startled, deeply troubled, and responds to the driver's wishes. I say this good man is also like that.

"These are the four good men in the world."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (184) Sūtra on the Bull

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will now teach you the parable of the bull. Listen well, listen well, and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, Bhagavān, we wish to hear."

The Buddha said: "It is like a bull with six horns. The bull carries a heavy yoke on its neck. A man is unable to drive it, but the bull itself goes forward, and in going forward it moves the yoke along.

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, a bhikṣu depends on moral discipline, and based on moral discipline, he cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness.

"What are the four? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right comprehension, overcoming covetousness and grief toward the world. He contemplates the body as body externally. He contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right comprehension, overcoming covetousness and grief toward the world.

"In the same way, he contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas internally, externally, and both internally and externally, with diligent effort, right mindfulness, and right comprehension, overcoming covetousness and grief toward the world.

"Bhikṣus, this is how a bhikṣu depends on moral discipline, is grounded in moral discipline, and cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (185) Sūtra on the Bull Traces

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a cowherd wishes to move his herd of cattle to another place, he should first investigate the ford: where is it safe to cross, where can the cattle enter and emerge safely, without danger? Then he drives the cattle across.

"First, he drives the strong and prime bulls across. They go straight, do not care about the current, cross to the other shore safely, and reach the further bank.

"Next, he drives the middle-class cattle across. They too go straight, cross to the other shore safely, and reach the further bank.

"Then, even the young calves, following the lowing of their mothers, either swimming or being carried by the current, also cross over to the other shore safely and reach the further bank.

"Bhikṣus, in the same way, among the beings in the three existences who wish to cross over and escape, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is the first to cross. Having destroyed the five lower fetters, he has the power to transform beings. The Tathāgata is like those strong prime bulls that first crossed the ford.

"Those who have destroyed the five lower fetters and attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, never returning to this world, they are like those middle-class cattle that also cross over.

"Those who have destroyed the three fetters and weakened desire, hatred, and delusion, the once-returners who return once to this world and then make an end of suffering, and those who have destroyed the three fetters and become stream-enterers, certain of attaining enlightenment and never falling into evil destinies, with at most seven more returns among gods and humans before making an end of suffering, they are like those young calves that, following their mothers' calls, also cross to the other shore.

"Bhikṣus, for this reason, even those following the Dharma, following faith, they too cross over to the other shore."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (186) Sūtra on the Inquiry

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, if wanderers of other sects ask you: 'Venerables, the śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma to his disciples in this way: Bhikṣus, you should abandon the five hindrances that defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and with a mind of loving-kindness pervade one direction and dwell in it, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading the entire world. With a mind of loving-kindness, free from resentment, free from ill will, free from anger, free from enmity, vast, great, boundless, well cultivated, pervade it all and dwell in it. Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise. Venerables, we too teach our disciples in this way. What then is the distinction, what is the difference, between your teacher, the śramaṇa Gautama, and us, in terms of teaching, instruction, and cultivation?'

"Bhikṣus, if wanderers of other sects should speak thus, you should reply to them: 'Venerables, does the teaching of your master lead to a single or many states? And does the teaching of our World-Honored One also lead to a single or many states?'

"Bhikṣus, if the wanderers of other sects truly answer, they will say: 'Venerables, the teaching of our master also leads to a single state, not to many states. The teaching of your World-Honored One also leads to a single state, not to many states.'

"Then you should further ask them: 'Venerables, what is your one? Is it limited or unlimited?'

"Bhikṣus, if the wanderers of other sects truly answer, they will say: 'Venerables, the loving-kindness our master teaches leads to a limited state.'

"Then you should tell them: 'Venerables, the loving-kindness that our World-Honored One teaches leads to an unlimited state. This is the distinction, this is the difference, between our World-Honored One and your master.

"Furthermore, Venerables, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness: does it have an objective support or does it have no objective support?'

"Bhikṣus, if the wanderers of other sects truly answer, they will say: 'Venerables, the loving-kindness our master teaches has an objective support.'

"Then you should tell them: 'Venerables, the loving-kindness that our World-Honored One teaches has no objective support. It is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness without an objective support. This is the distinction, this is the difference, between our World-Honored One and your master.'

"Bhikṣus, how long does a bhikṣu practice the liberation of mind through loving-kindness? Having pervaded one direction and dwelling in it, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, pervading the entire world, with a mind of loving-kindness, free from resentment, free from ill will, free from anger, free from enmity, vast, great, boundless, well cultivated, pervading it all and dwelling in it, he knows: 'This liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been cultivated, is well cultivated, is ascending and rising, and is well liberated. This liberation of mind is incalculable, has been well accomplished, and is well established.'

"Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who knows thus and sees thus: should one say that after the body breaks up and life ends, he exists?"

The bhikṣus replied: "No, Bhagavān."

"Should one say he does not exist?"

"No, Bhagavān."

"Should one say he both exists and does not exist?"

"No, Bhagavān."

"Should one say he neither exists nor does not exist?"

"No, Bhagavān."

"Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu who knows thus and sees thus, who knows and sees the present world as it really is: should one say that after the body breaks up and life ends, he exists, does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist?"

"No, Bhagavān."

"Very good, very good, bhikṣus! It has been thus from the beginning: one cannot determine it, and it is inconceivable. It is the same with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (187) Sūtra Spoken to the Settled One

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I be loved and respected by my companions in the holy life,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I obtain robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May those donors who provide me with offerings obtain great fruit, great benefit, and great radiance,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May my relatives and family members who have passed away, when they recollect me with a faithful mind, obtain great fruit, great benefit, and great radiance,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I endure dissatisfaction and delight, and not be overcome by dissatisfaction but overcome it whenever it arises,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I endure fear and dread, and not be overcome by fear and dread but overcome them whenever they arise,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I obtain at will, without difficulty, the four jhānas, which are higher states of mind and pleasant abodes in this very life,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I, with the complete transcendence of all perceptions of form, the elimination of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, attain boundless space and dwell in the sphere of boundless space,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, attain boundless consciousness and dwell in the sphere of boundless consciousness,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, attain nothingness and dwell in the sphere of nothingness,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, attain neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"If a bhikṣu should wish: 'May I, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attain the cessation of perception and feeling and dwell in it, and with wisdom see that the outflows are completely destroyed,' then he should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.

"Bhikṣus, it was with this intention that I have said: 'You should fulfill moral discipline, be devoted to inner mental tranquility, not neglect meditation, be endowed with insight, and frequent empty dwellings.'"

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (188) Sūtra on Ānanda

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling in seclusion, in quiet meditation. He had this thought: "Can there be a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, yet is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains? If a bhikṣu, having ceased perception of form, could attain and dwell in the formless, that would be good."

Then in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda arose from his meditation, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "Bhagavān, I was dwelling in seclusion, in quiet meditation, and I had this thought: 'Can there be a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, yet is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains? If a bhikṣu, having ceased perception of form, could attain and dwell in the formless, that would be good.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, there is indeed a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains."

Ānanda asked: "Bhagavān, how is there a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, a bhikṣu may think: 'It would be good if I, with the complete transcendence of all perceptions of form, the elimination of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, could attain boundless space and dwell in the sphere of boundless space.' He practices accordingly, and attaining boundless space, he dwells in the sphere of boundless space. Having attained this, he contemplates what pertains to form in it, knowing it is impermanent, subject to cessation. He inclines his mind toward the deathless and considers: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.' Established therein, he attains the destruction of the outflows. If he does not attain the destruction of the outflows, then through that very delight in the Dharma, that joy in the Dharma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains intermediate nirvāṇa, or he attains nirvāṇa at landing, or he attains nirvāṇa without exertion, or he attains nirvāṇa with exertion, or he goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Ānanda, this is a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu may think: 'It would be good if I, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless space, could attain boundless consciousness and dwell in the sphere of boundless consciousness.' He practices accordingly, and attaining boundless consciousness, he dwells in the sphere of boundless consciousness. Having attained this, he contemplates what pertains to consciousness in it, knowing it is impermanent, subject to cessation. He inclines his mind toward the deathless and considers: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.' Established therein, he attains the destruction of the outflows. If he does not attain the destruction of the outflows, then through that very delight in the Dharma, that joy in the Dharma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains intermediate nirvāṇa, or he attains nirvāṇa at landing, or he attains nirvāṇa without exertion, or he attains nirvāṇa with exertion, or he goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu may think: 'It would be good if I, having completely transcended the sphere of boundless consciousness, could attain nothingness and dwell in the sphere of nothingness.' He practices accordingly, and attaining nothingness, he dwells in the sphere of nothingness. Having attained this, he contemplates what pertains to consciousness in it, knowing it is impermanent, subject to cessation. He inclines his mind toward the deathless and considers: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.' Established therein, he attains the destruction of the outflows. If he does not attain the destruction of the outflows, then through that very delight in the Dharma, that joy in the Dharma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains intermediate nirvāṇa, or he attains nirvāṇa at landing, or he attains nirvāṇa without exertion, or he attains nirvāṇa with exertion, or he goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Ānanda, this too is a person who has attained partial cessation of perception, is not attached to it, and continues to practice what remains.

"Ānanda, suppose a person were to shoot two arrows in succession, one after the other. Ānanda, such a bhikṣu is also like that. From this attainment, he progresses to the next, and from that attainment, he progresses further. Ānanda, this is what I call the gradual cessation of perception."

Ānanda asked: "Bhagavān, can a bhikṣu, from one attainment, progress to the next, and from that attainment, progress further, reaching the summit of existence, and standing at the summit, progress further?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, a bhikṣu can indeed, from one attainment, progress to the next, and from that attainment, progress further, reaching the summit of existence, and standing at the summit, progress further."

Ānanda asked: "Bhagavān, how can a bhikṣu, from one attainment, progress to the next, and from that attainment, progress further, reaching the summit of existence, and standing at the summit, progress further?"

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, a bhikṣu may think: 'It would be good if I, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, could attain neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' He practices accordingly, and attaining neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having attained this, he contemplates what pertains to consciousness in it, knowing it is impermanent, subject to cessation. He inclines his mind toward the deathless and considers: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nirvāṇa.' Established therein, he attains the destruction of the outflows. If he does not attain the destruction of the outflows, then through that very delight in the Dharma, that joy in the Dharma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he attains intermediate nirvāṇa, or he attains nirvāṇa at landing, or he attains nirvāṇa without exertion, or he attains nirvāṇa with exertion, or he goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Ānanda, this is how a bhikṣu, from one attainment, progresses to the next, and from that attainment, progresses further, reaching the summit of existence, and standing at the summit, progresses further."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (189) Sūtra on the Sage

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the Dharma of sages and the Dharma of non-sages. Listen well, listen well, and pay careful attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, Bhagavān, we wish to hear."

The Buddha said: "What is the Dharma of non-sages? An untaught ordinary person who has not attained the noble Dharma, who is not skilled in the noble Dharma, who has not been trained in the noble Dharma, who has not attained the Dharma of the true person, who is not skilled in the Dharma of the true person, who has not been trained in the Dharma of the true person, he, seeing form with the eye, grasps at signs and grasps at features. Because he dwells without restraining the eye faculty, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states flood into him. He does not practice restraint for the sake of its protection, and does not guard the eye faculty.

"Hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, knowing mental objects with the mind, he grasps at signs and grasps at features. Because he dwells without restraining the mind faculty, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states flood into him. He does not practice restraint for the sake of its protection, and does not guard the mind faculty.

"Having not restrained the six faculties, he gives rise to feeling. He experiences three kinds of feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

"When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he is delighted by it, welcomes it, and remains attached to it. Because of delighting in, welcoming, and remaining attached to it, the underlying tendency of desire arises.

"When he experiences a painful feeling, he is sorrowful, grieving, lamenting, beating his breast, and bewildered. Because of being sorrowful, grieving, and bewildered, the underlying tendency of aversion arises.

"When he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he does not know the arising, cessation, enjoyment, danger, and escape of that feeling as it really is. Because of not knowing the arising, cessation, enjoyment, danger, and escape of that feeling as it really is, the underlying tendency of ignorance arises.

"Bhikṣus, that person, because of not abandoning the underlying tendency of desire with respect to pleasant feeling, because of not abandoning the underlying tendency of aversion with respect to painful feeling, because of not abandoning the underlying tendency of ignorance with respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, because of not eradicating ignorance and not giving rise to knowledge, to make an end of suffering in this very life: this is impossible. This is called the Dharma of non-sages.

"What is the Dharma of sages? A well-taught noble disciple who has attained the noble Dharma, who is skilled in the noble Dharma, who has been trained in the noble Dharma, who has attained the Dharma of the true person, who is skilled in the Dharma of the true person, who has been trained in the Dharma of the true person, he, seeing form with the eye, does not grasp at signs and does not grasp at features. Because he dwells with the eye faculty restrained, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states do not flood into him. He practices restraint for the sake of its protection and guards the eye faculty.

"Hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, knowing mental objects with the mind, he does not grasp at signs and does not grasp at features. Because he dwells with the mind faculty restrained, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states do not flood into him. He practices restraint for the sake of its protection and guards the mind faculty.

"Having restrained the six faculties, he gives rise to feeling. He experiences three kinds of feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

"When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he is not delighted by it, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it. Because of not delighting in, not welcoming, and not remaining attached to it, the underlying tendency of desire with respect to pleasant feeling ceases.

"When he experiences a painful feeling, he is not sorrowful, not grieving, not lamenting, not beating his breast, and not bewildered. Because of not being sorrowful, not grieving, and not bewildered, the underlying tendency of aversion with respect to painful feeling ceases.

"When he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows the arising, cessation, enjoyment, danger, and escape of that feeling as it really is. Because of knowing the arising, cessation, enjoyment, danger, and escape of that feeling as it really is, the underlying tendency of ignorance with respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases.

"Bhikṣus, that person, because of abandoning the underlying tendency of desire with respect to pleasant feeling, because of abandoning the underlying tendency of aversion with respect to painful feeling, because of abandoning the underlying tendency of ignorance with respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, because of eradicating ignorance and giving rise to knowledge, to make an end of suffering in this very life: this is possible. This is called the Dharma of sages."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

End of Fascicle 47 of the Madhyamāgama.

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 47

---

## (178) Sūtra on the Hunter, Seventh of the Heart Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "When a hunter feeds deer, he does not have this intention: to make the deer become fat, gain good color, gain strength, gain happiness, or live long. When a hunter feeds deer, he has this intention in feeding them: he only desires that they come close to eat, and having come close to eat, that they become arrogant, indulgent, and heedless; and having become heedless, that they fall under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Such is the hunter's intention in feeding deer.

"The first herd of deer came close to eat the hunter's food. Having come close to eat, they became arrogant, indulgent, and heedless. Having become heedless, they fell under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Thus the first herd of deer did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue.

"The second herd of deer had this thought: 'The first herd of deer came close to eat the hunter's food. Having come close to eat, they became arrogant, indulgent, and heedless. Having become heedless, they fell under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Thus the first herd of deer did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Would it not be better for us to not eat the hunter's food, to depart from fear, to dwell in a secluded place, and to eat grass and drink water?' After the second herd of deer had this thought, they abandoned the hunter's food, departed from fear, dwelt in a secluded place, and ate grass and drank water. In the last month of spring, when all the grass and water were exhausted, their bodies became extremely emaciated and their strength declined. Then they fell under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Thus the second herd of deer also did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue.

"The third herd of deer also had this thought: 'The first and second herds of deer all did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Would it not be better for us to leave the hunter and the hunter's retinue and dwell not far away? Having dwelt not far away, we will not come close to eat the hunter's food. Not coming close to eat, we will not become arrogant, indulgent, and heedless. Not being heedless, we will not fall under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue.' After the third herd of deer had this thought, they left the hunter and the hunter's retinue and dwelt not far away. Having dwelt not far away, they did not come close to eat the hunter's food. Not coming close to eat, they did not become arrogant, indulgent, and heedless. Not being heedless, they did not fall under the power of the hunter and the hunter's retinue. Then the hunter and the hunter's retinue had this thought: 'The third herd of deer is remarkably cunning, extremely cunning. Why is this? They eat my food, yet cannot be caught. Would it not be better for us to make a large surrounding net?' After making the large surrounding net, they caught the third herd of deer at their dwelling place. After the hunter and the hunter's retinue had this thought, they made a large surrounding net. Having made the large surrounding net, they caught the third herd of deer at their dwelling place. Thus the third herd of deer also did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue.

"The fourth herd of deer also had this thought: 'The first, second, and third herds of deer all did not escape the domain of the hunter and the hunter's retinue.
