## (184) Madhyamāgama, Chapter of Pairs: Third Sūtra on the Gosinga Sāla Forest

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Vajjī country, in the Gosinga Sāla Forest, together with many well-known, senior bhikṣus who were great disciples. Venerable Śāriputra, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, and Venerable Ānanda: such bhikṣus, well-known senior bhikṣus who were great disciples, were also traveling in the Vajjī country, in the Gosinga Sāla Forest, all staying near the Buddha's leaf hut.

Then Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, and Venerable Anuruddha, at dawn after the night had passed, went to visit Venerable Śāriputra. Venerable Ānanda, seeing those venerable ones approaching from afar, said: "Worthy Revata! You should know that Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, and Venerable Anuruddha have come at dawn after the night to visit Venerable Śāriputra. Worthy Revata, let us now go together with those venerable ones to visit Venerable Śāriputra. Perhaps through them we may hear some Dharma from Venerable Śāriputra." Then Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, and Venerable Ānanda, at dawn after the night had passed, went to visit Venerable Śāriputra.

Venerable Śāriputra, seeing those venerable ones approaching from afar, because of them, said: "Welcome, Worthy Ānanda! Welcome, Ānanda! Welcome, Ānanda! The World-Honored One's attendant who understands the World-Honored One's mind, constantly praised by the World-Honored One and by wise practitioners of the holy life. I now ask Worthy Ānanda: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Ānanda, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Ānanda answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who is widely learned and of extensive knowledge, who retains what is learned and does not forget it, who has accumulated broad learning. The Dharma that is spoken is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, possessing meaning and expression, complete in purity, and manifesting the holy life. Such dharmas he has broadly learned and extensively studied, practiced and recited up to a thousand times, contemplated with the mind, clearly seen and deeply penetrated. His exposition of the Dharma is concise and swift, corresponding with what is right, aimed at severing all fetters. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then asked: "Worthy Revata, Worthy Ānanda the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Revata: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Revata, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Revata answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who delights in seated meditation, who internally practices calming, who does not neglect sitting in dhyāna, who accomplishes insight, who constantly prefers solitude and delights in peaceful and quiet places. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then asked: "Worthy Anuruddha, Worthy Revata the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Anuruddha: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Anuruddha, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who has attained the divine eye and accomplished the divine eye, and with only a slight effort can in an instant see throughout a thousand worlds. Venerable Śāriputra, just as a person with eyes standing on a high tower looks down at a thousand bricks on the open ground below, and with only a slight effort can in an instant see them all. Venerable Śāriputra, likewise if there were a bhikṣu who has attained the divine eye and accomplished the divine eye, and with only a slight effort can in an instant see throughout a thousand worlds. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then asked: "Worthy Kātyāyana, Worthy Anuruddha the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Kātyāyana: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Kātyāyana, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Mahākātyāyana answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, suppose two bhikṣu Dharma teachers were to discuss the profound Abhidharma. Whatever questions are asked, they understand and know them all, answering without obstruction, expounding the Dharma with eloquent swiftness. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then asked: "Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Worthy Kātyāyana the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Venerable Mahākāśyapa: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Mahākāśyapa answered: "Worthy Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who himself dwells in the practice of few desires and praises the practice of few desires, who himself has fewness of wishes and praises fewness of wishes, who himself has contentment and praises contentment, who himself delights in dwelling in seclusion and solitude and praises dwelling in seclusion and solitude, who himself cultivates energetic striving and praises the cultivation of energetic striving, who himself establishes right mindfulness and right comprehension and praises the establishment of right mindfulness and right comprehension, who himself attains concentration and praises the attainment of concentration, who himself possesses wisdom and praises wisdom, who himself has ended all āsravas and praises the ending of all āsravas, who himself encourages, inspires thirst and aspiration, accomplishes delight, and praises the encouragement, inspiration, thirst, aspiration, and accomplishment of delight. Worthy Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then asked: "Worthy Maudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Maudgalyāyana: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana answered: "Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority, with mastery over immeasurable supernormal powers. Exercising immeasurable supernormal powers, he transforms one into many, merges many into one, remains as one in one place, with knowledge and vision, passes through stone walls as if through empty space without obstruction, enters and emerges from the earth as if it were water, walks on water as on ground without sinking, ascends into empty space and sits cross-legged as if he were a bird, and with his hand touches and strokes this sun and moon that possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority, and his body reaches up to the Brahmā heaven. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then asked: "Venerable Śāriputra, I and all the venerable ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge. I now ask Venerable Śāriputra: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Venerable Śāriputra, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?"

Venerable Śāriputra answered: "Worthy Maudgalyāyana, if there were a bhikṣu who uses the mind at will and freely, rather than being controlled by the mind. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation in the morning, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation in the morning. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, just as a king or a king's minister who has very many garments of various wonderful colors: if he wishes to wear something in the morning, he takes it and puts it on. If he wishes to wear something at midday or in the afternoon, he takes it and puts it on. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, likewise, if there were a bhikṣu who uses the mind at will and freely, rather than being controlled by the mind. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation in the morning, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation in the morning. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Venerable Śāriputra then said: "Worthy Maudgalyāyana, I and all the worthy ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, should we not now go together with these worthy ones to visit the Buddha, and present this discussion before him, so that we may know whose answer was the best?" Then Venerable Śāriputra, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Venerable Mahākātyāyana, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, and Venerable Ānanda went to visit the Buddha. All the venerable ones paid homage at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. Venerable Ānanda also paid homage at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, today Worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Worthy Kātyāyana, Worthy Anuruddha, Worthy Revata, and Worthy Ānanda came to visit me at dawn after the night. When I saw those worthy ones approaching from afar, because of them I said: 'Welcome, Worthy Ānanda! Welcome, Ānanda! Welcome, Ānanda! The World-Honored One's attendant who understands the World-Honored One's mind, constantly praised by the World-Honored One and by wise practitioners of the holy life. I now ask Worthy Ānanda: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Ānanda, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Worthy Ānanda then answered me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who is widely learned and of extensive knowledge, who retains what is learned and does not forget it, who has accumulated broad learning. The Dharma that is spoken is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, possessing meaning and expression, complete in purity, and manifesting the holy life. Such dharmas he has broadly learned and extensively studied, practiced and recited up to a thousand times, contemplated with the mind, clearly seen and deeply penetrated. His exposition of the Dharma is concise and swift, corresponding with what is right, aimed at severing all fetters. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is truly as Ānanda the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Ānanda the bhikṣu has accomplished extensive learning."

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, after Worthy Ānanda spoke thus, I further asked: 'Worthy Revata, Worthy Ānanda the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Revata: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Revata, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Worthy Revata then answered me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who delights in seated meditation, who internally practices calming, who does not neglect sitting in dhyāna, who accomplishes insight, who constantly prefers solitude and delights in peaceful and quiet places. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is as Revata the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Revata the bhikṣu constantly delights in sitting in dhyāna."

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, after Worthy Revata spoke thus, I further asked: 'Worthy Anuruddha, Worthy Revata the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Anuruddha: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Anuruddha, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Worthy Anuruddha then answered me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who has attained the divine eye and accomplished the divine eye, and with only a slight effort can in an instant see throughout a thousand worlds. Venerable Śāriputra, just as a person with eyes standing on a high tower looks down at a thousand bricks on the open ground below, and with only a slight effort can in an instant see them all. Venerable Śāriputra, likewise if there were a bhikṣu who has attained the divine eye and accomplished the divine eye, and with only the slightest effort can in an instant see throughout a thousand worlds. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is as Anuruddha the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Anuruddha the bhikṣu has accomplished the divine eye."

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, after Worthy Anuruddha spoke thus, I further asked: 'Worthy Kātyāyana, Worthy Anuruddha the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Kātyāyana: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Kātyāyana, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Worthy Kātyāyana then answered me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, suppose two bhikṣu Dharma teachers were to discuss the profound Abhidharma. Whatever questions are asked, they understand and know them all, answering without obstruction, expounding the Dharma with eloquent swiftness. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is as Kātyāyana the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Kātyāyana the bhikṣu is an analytical Dharma teacher."

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, after Worthy Kātyāyana spoke thus, I further asked: 'Venerable Mahākāśyapa, Worthy Kātyāyana the bhikṣu has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Venerable Mahākāśyapa: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Venerable Mahākāśyapa, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Venerable Mahākāśyapa then answered me: 'Worthy Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who himself dwells in the practice of few desires and praises the practice of few desires, who himself has fewness of wishes and praises fewness of wishes, who himself has contentment and praises contentment, who himself delights in dwelling in seclusion and solitude and praises dwelling in seclusion and solitude, who himself cultivates energetic striving and praises the cultivation of energetic striving, who himself establishes right mindfulness and right comprehension and praises the establishment of right mindfulness and right comprehension, who himself attains concentration and praises the attainment of concentration, who himself possesses wisdom and praises wisdom, who himself has ended all āsravas and praises the ending of all āsravas, who himself encourages, inspires thirst and aspiration, accomplishes delight, and praises the encouragement, inspiration, thirst, aspiration, and accomplishment of delight. Worthy Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is as Kāśyapa the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Kāśyapa the bhikṣu constantly practices the ascetic qualities."

Venerable Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, after Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke thus, I further asked: 'Worthy Maudgalyāyana, Venerable Mahākāśyapa has spoken according to his knowledge. I now further ask Worthy Maudgalyāyana: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana then answered me: 'Venerable Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority, with mastery over immeasurable supernormal powers. Exercising immeasurable supernormal powers, he transforms one into many, merges many into one, remains as one in one place, with knowledge and vision, passes through stone walls as if through empty space without obstruction, enters and emerges from the earth as if it were water, walks on water as on ground without sinking, ascends into empty space and sits cross-legged as if he were a bird, and with his hand touches and strokes this sun and moon that possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority, and his body reaches up to the Brahmā heaven. Venerable Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra! It is as Maudgalyāyana the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Maudgalyāyana the bhikṣu possesses great supernormal powers."

Then Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, after I and the venerable ones had spoken thus, I said to Venerable Śāriputra: 'Venerable Śāriputra, I and the venerable ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge. I now ask Venerable Śāriputra: this Gosinga Sāla Forest is very delightful. The night has a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are diffusing wonderful fragrance, like heavenly flowers. Venerable Śāriputra, what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest?' Venerable Śāriputra then answered me: 'Worthy Maudgalyāyana, if there were a bhikṣu who uses the mind at will and freely, rather than being controlled by the mind. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation in the morning, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation in the morning. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, just as a king or a king's minister who has very many garments of various wonderful colors: if he wishes to wear something in the morning, he takes it and puts it on. If he wishes to wear something at midday or in the afternoon, he takes it and puts it on. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, likewise, if there were a bhikṣu who uses the mind at will and freely, rather than being controlled by the mind. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation in the morning, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation in the morning. If he wishes to dwell in whatever abode and practice walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon, then he dwells in that abode and practices walking meditation at midday or in the afternoon. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest.'"

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Maudgalyāyana! It is as Śāriputra the bhikṣu has spoken. Why is this? Because Śāriputra the bhikṣu uses the mind at will and freely."

Then Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, after I and the worthy ones had spoken thus, I said: 'Worthy Maudgalyāyana, I and the worthy ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge. Worthy Maudgalyāyana, should we not now go together with these worthy ones to visit the Buddha, and present this discussion before him, so that we may know whose answer was the best?' World-Honored One, which of us has spoken well?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Śāriputra, all have spoken well. Why is this? Because all these dharmas are what I have taught. Śāriputra, listen to what I say about what kind of bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest. Śāriputra, if there were a bhikṣu who, wherever he resides in a city, town, or village, at dawn after the night puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village to beg for food, well-guarding his body, well-restraining his sense faculties, well-establishing his mindfulness. After begging for food, past midday, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places the sitting cloth on his shoulder, and goes to a quiet place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty and peaceful place. He spreads out the sitting cloth, sits cross-legged, and does not unfold from the cross-legged position until the āsravas are ended. He does not unfold from the cross-legged position until the āsravas are ended. Śāriputra, such a bhikṣu would illuminate the Gosinga Sāla Forest."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

End of the Third Sūtra on the Gosinga Sāla Forest.

---

## (185) Madhyamāgama, Chapter of Pairs: Fourth Sūtra on the Gosinga Sāla Forest

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Nādika country, staying at the Brick Hall.

At that time, the World-Honored One, at dawn after the night, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Nādika to beg for food. After eating, past midday, he went to the Gosinga Sāla Forest.

At that time, in the Gosinga Sāla Forest there were three sons of good families dwelling together: Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila. The practice of those venerable ones was as follows: whichever one returned first from begging for food would set out the seats, draw water, bring out the foot-washing vessel, arrange the foot-washing stool, the foot-wiping cloth, the water jug, and the washing pitcher. If the food obtained from begging could be eaten entirely, he would eat it all. If there was a remainder, he would place it in a vessel and cover it for storage. After eating, he would put away his bowl, wash his hands and feet, place the sitting cloth on his shoulder, and enter his room for seated meditation. Whichever one returned last from begging for food: if he could eat all his food, he would eat it all. If it was insufficient, he would take the previous one's remainder and supplement his meal. If there was still a remainder, he would pour it on clean ground or into water free of insects. He would take the eating vessel, wash and wipe it clean, and put it away to one side. He would roll up and store the seats, put away the foot-washing stool, store the foot-wiping cloth, put away the foot-washing vessel, the water jug, and the washing pitcher, sweep and sprinkle the dining hall, clean out the refuse, then put away his robes and bowl, wash his hands and feet, place the sitting cloth on his shoulder, and enter his room for seated meditation. Those venerable ones, when it was the afternoon, whichever one rose first from seated meditation, if he saw that the water jug and washing pitcher were empty and without water, would take them and go to fetch water. If he could carry them, he would lift them and bring them back, placing them to one side. If he could not carry them, he would beckon another bhikṣu with his hand, and the two would carry them together and place them to one side. They did not speak to one another and did not ask one another about such matters. Those venerable ones would gather once every five days, either to discuss the Dharma together or to dwell in noble silence.

Then the forest keeper, seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, called out to stop him: "Śramaṇa! Śramaṇa! Do not enter this forest. Why is this? In this forest now there are three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila. If they see you, they may be displeased."

The World-Honored One said: "Forest keeper, if they see me, they will surely be pleased, and not displeased."

Then Venerable Anuruddha, seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, immediately called out to the forest keeper: "Forest keeper! Do not obstruct the World-Honored One! Forest keeper! Do not obstruct the Well-Gone One! Why is this? It is my honored teacher who comes, my Well-Gone One who comes."

Venerable Anuruddha went out to welcome the World-Honored One and took the Buddha's robes and bowl. Venerable Nandiya spread out a seat for the Buddha. Venerable Kimbila fetched water for the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having washed his hands and feet, sat on the seat that the venerable one had spread. Having sat, he asked: "Anuruddha, are you always at ease and without any lack?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, I am always at ease and without any lack."

The World-Honored One further asked: "Anuruddha, how are you at ease and without any lack?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, I think to myself: 'I have good fortune and great meritorious virtue, that I practice together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.' World-Honored One, I constantly direct kindly bodily actions toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether I see them or not, equally without difference. I direct kindly verbal actions and kindly mental actions toward them, whether I see them or not, equally without difference. World-Honored One, I think to myself: 'I should now set aside my own wishes and follow the wishes of these worthy ones.' I then set aside my own wishes and follow the wishes of those worthy ones. I have never had a single thought of displeasure. World-Honored One, thus I am always at ease and without any lack."

When Venerable Nandiya was asked, he answered likewise. Then Venerable Kimbila was asked: "Are you always at ease and without any lack?"

Venerable Kimbila replied: "World-Honored One, I am always at ease and without any lack."

He was asked: "Kimbila, how are you at ease and without any lack?"

Venerable Kimbila replied: "World-Honored One, I think to myself: 'I have good fortune and great meritorious virtue, that I practice together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.' World-Honored One, I constantly direct kindly bodily actions toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether I see them or not, equally without difference. I direct kindly verbal actions and kindly mental actions toward them, whether I see them or not, equally without difference. World-Honored One, I think to myself: 'I should now set aside my own wishes and follow the wishes of these worthy ones.' I then set aside my own wishes and follow the wishes of those worthy ones. I have never had a single thought of displeasure. World-Honored One, thus I am always at ease and without any lack."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Anuruddha! Since you all constantly dwell together in harmony, at ease and without contention, of one mind, with one teacher, blending together like water and milk, have you attained any states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, indeed we constantly dwell together in harmony, at ease and without contention, of one mind, with one teacher, blending together like water and milk, and we have attained states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding. World-Honored One, we have separated from desire, separated from evil unwholesome dharmas, and attained up to the fourth dhyāna, dwelling in its accomplishment. World-Honored One, thus we constantly dwell together in harmony, at ease and without contention, of one mind, with one teacher, blending together like water and milk, and we have attained these states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Anuruddha! Relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, are there yet other states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are yet further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding. World-Honored One, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, I pervade one direction and dwell in its accomplishment. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely in all directions, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without ill-will, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable and well-cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling in its accomplishment. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without ill-will, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable and well-cultivated, pervading the entire world and dwelling in its accomplishment. World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are indeed these further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Anuruddha! Relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, are there yet other states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are yet further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding. World-Honored One, we have transcended all perceptions of form, and attained up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwelling in its accomplishment. World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are indeed these further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Anuruddha! Relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, are there yet other states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are yet further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding. World-Honored One, we have attained the supernormal power of psychic abilities, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings. All āsravas have been ended; we have attained the āsrava-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this present life, we know for ourselves, realize for ourselves, and personally attain and dwell in the realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more becoming.' We know this as it truly is. World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are indeed these further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding."

The World-Honored One exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Anuruddha! Relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, are there yet other states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding?"

Venerable Anuruddha replied: "World-Honored One, relinquishing this abiding, going beyond it and surpassing it, there are no further states surpassing those of ordinary humans, with successive, elevated, and peaceful abiding."

Then the World-Honored One thought to himself: "These sons of good families practice and abide in ease and happiness. I should now teach them the Dharma." Having thought this, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila, encouraging them, inspiring their thirst and aspiration, and accomplishing their delight. With immeasurable skillful means he taught them the Dharma, encouraged them, inspired their thirst and aspiration, and accomplished their delight. Having done so, he rose from his seat and departed. Then Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila escorted the World-Honored One, each going as far as was appropriate, and then returned to their dwelling place.

Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila praised Venerable Anuruddha: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Anuruddha! We had never before heard Venerable Anuruddha say that we possess such great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority. Yet Venerable Anuruddha fully praised us before the World-Honored One."

Venerable Anuruddha praised Venerable Nandiya and Kimbila: "Excellent! Excellent, venerable ones! I likewise had never heard from you venerable ones that you possess such great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority. However, for a long time I have known your minds through my own mind: you venerable ones possess great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, great blessed merit, and great spiritual authority. That is why I spoke thus before the World-Honored One."

Then the yakṣa deva of lofty form and exceedingly wonderful appearance, with brilliant and majestic radiance, as the night was about to turn to dawn, went to visit the Buddha. He paid homage at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said to the World-Honored One: "Great Sage! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila."

The earth deities, having heard what the yakṣa deva said, raised a loud and great voice: "Great Sage! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila."

Hearing the voice of the earth deities, the devas of empty space, the Four Great Kings' Heaven, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, in an instant the sound reached up to the Brahmā Heaven: "Great Sage! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is, yakṣa deva! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila. Yakṣa deva, the earth deities, having heard your voice, raised a loud and great voice: 'Great Sage! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.' Hearing the voice of the earth deities, the devas of empty space, the Four Great Kings' Heaven, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, in an instant the sound reached up to the Brahmā Heaven: 'Great Sage! The Vajjī people have gained great good fortune, that the World-Honored One is now present here, along with three sons of good families: Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.' Yakṣa deva, if those three families from which these three sons of good families shaved off their hair and beards, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with firm faith left the household for the homeless life to train in the Way, if those three families remember these three sons of good families and the causes and practices by which they went forth, those families too will for a long time gain great good fortune, ease, and happiness. ## (187) Madhyamāgama, Pairs Chapter: Sūtra on Declaring Knowledge, Number One

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu comes to you and declares his attained knowledge, saying, 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is,' you, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! The World-Honored One has taught five aggregates of clinging: the form aggregate of clinging, the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness aggregates of clinging. Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see these five aggregates of clinging, such that one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! The form aggregate of clinging is without substance, empty, not to be desired, not permanently existing, not to be relied upon; it is a thing subject to change. I know it thus. If regarding the form aggregate of clinging there is desire, there is defilement, there is attachment, there is bondage, and bondage by the latent tendencies, when all these are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Likewise with the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness aggregates of clinging: they are without substance, empty, not to be desired, not permanently existing, not to be relied upon; they are things subject to change. I know it thus. If regarding the consciousness aggregate of clinging there is desire, there is defilement, there is attachment, there is bondage, and bondage by the latent tendencies, when all these are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing these five aggregates of clinging, I attain the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! The World-Honored One has taught four kinds of nutriment by which beings are sustained and nourished. What are the four? The first is material food, coarse or fine. The second is contact. The third is mental volition. The fourth is consciousness. Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see these four kinds of nutriment, such that one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! Regarding material food, my mind is neither elated nor depressed, neither reliant nor bound, neither defiled nor attached; I have gained release and freedom, completely gained release and freedom, my mind is free from inversion. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Likewise with contact, mental volition, and consciousness as nutriment: my mind is neither elated nor depressed, neither reliant nor bound, neither defiled nor attached; I have gained release and freedom, completely gained release and freedom, my mind is free from inversion. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing these four kinds of nutriment, I attain the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! The World-Honored One has taught four declarations. What are the four? The first is the declaration of what is seen as seen. The second is the declaration of what is heard as heard. The third is the declaration of what is sensed as sensed. The fourth is the declaration of what is cognized as cognized. Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see these four declarations, such that one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! Regarding the declaration of what is seen as seen, my mind is neither elated nor depressed, neither reliant nor bound, neither defiled nor attached; I have gained release and freedom, completely gained release and freedom, my mind is free from inversion. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Likewise with the declaration of what is heard as heard, what is sensed as sensed, and what is cognized as cognized: my mind is neither elated nor depressed, neither reliant nor bound, neither defiled nor attached; I have gained release and freedom, completely gained release and freedom, my mind is free from inversion. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing these four declarations, I attain the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! The World-Honored One has taught six internal sense-bases: the eye sense-base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind sense-bases. Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see these six internal sense-bases, such that one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! I know the eye together with eye-consciousness, and I know the phenomena cognized by eye-consciousness; having known these two things together: worthy ones, when regarding the eye together with eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognized by eye-consciousness, the pleasure therein is exhausted, when they are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind together with mind-consciousness: I know the phenomena cognized by mind-consciousness together; having known these two things together: worthy ones, when regarding the mind together with mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognized by mind-consciousness, the pleasure therein is exhausted, when they are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing these six internal sense-bases, I attain the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! The World-Honored One has taught six elements: the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element. Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see these six elements, such that one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! I do not regard the earth element as mine, nor myself as belonging to the earth element, nor the earth element as a self. However, I recognize that the three feelings depend upon and abide in the earth element, and are where the tendencies of consciousness attach. When they are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Likewise with the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements: they are not mine, I do not belong to the consciousness element, the consciousness element is not a self. However, I recognize that the three feelings depend upon and abide in the consciousness element, and are where the tendencies of consciousness attach. When they are exhausted, when desire is gone, when they are extinguished, calmed, and ceased, one attains the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing these six elements, I attain the knowledge of non-clinging, the ending of the taints, and the liberation of mind.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then question that bhikṣu thus: 'Worthy one! How does one know, how does one see, such that regarding this inner body together with consciousness and all external signs, the conceit of "I," the activity of "I," and the latent tendency of conceit are cut off and known, uprooted at their root, never to arise again?'

"A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus: 'Worthy ones! Before I had gone forth to study the path, I was weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping and lamentation, hardship, sorrow, vexation, and grief, and wished to put an end to this great mass of suffering. Worthy ones! Having become weary and disenchanted, I made this observation: household life is confining and a place of dust and toil; going forth to study the path is open and expansive. Now while I remain at home, I am bound by fetters and cannot for the whole of my life purely cultivate the holy life. I should rather relinquish small wealth and great wealth, leave behind few relatives and many relatives, shave off my hair and beard, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household for the homeless life to study the path. Worthy ones! At a later time, I relinquished small wealth and great wealth, left behind few relatives and many relatives, shaved off my hair and beard, donned the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household for the homeless life to study the path. Worthy ones! Having gone forth to study the path, having left behind the marks of clan, I received the bhikṣu precepts. I cultivated and practiced the training rules, guarded and upheld the code of liberation, and further well maintained my deportment and propriety. Seeing even the slightest transgression, I constantly harbored dread and fear. I received and upheld the rules of training.

"'Worthy ones! I abandoned killing and refrained from killing, cast aside knife and staff. Having shame and conscience, having a compassionate heart, I benefited all beings down to insects. Regarding killing, I purified my mind. I abandoned taking what is not given and refrained from taking what is not given; I took only what was given and delighted in taking what was given. I was always fond of generosity, joyful and without stinginess, not hoping for reward. Regarding taking what is not given, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned unchastity and refrained from unchastity. I diligently cultivated the holy life, practiced with vigor the excellent conduct, being pure and undefiled, abandoning desire and cutting off sexual conduct. Regarding unchastity, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned false speech and refrained from false speech. I spoke truthfully and delighted in truth, abided in truth without wavering. All my words were trustworthy, and I did not deceive the world. Regarding false speech, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned divisive speech and refrained from divisive speech. I practiced non-divisive speech and did not seek to break up others. I did not hear something here and tell it there to break up these people, nor hear something there and tell it here to break up those people. I sought to unite those who were divided, and I rejoiced with those who were united. I did not form factions, did not delight in factions, did not praise factions. Regarding divisive speech, I purified my mind.

"'Worthy ones! I abandoned harsh speech and refrained from harsh speech. Whatever words are rough and coarse, with an evil sound offensive to the ear, displeasing to the many, unloved by the many, causing others to suffer, preventing concentration, I refrained from such speech. Whatever words are pure, gentle, and smooth, pleasing to the ear and entering the heart, delightful and lovable, bringing comfort to others, whose sound is clear and does not cause fear, enabling others to attain concentration, I spoke such words. Regarding harsh speech, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned frivolous speech and refrained from frivolous speech. I spoke at the right time, spoke truthfully, spoke of the Dharma, spoke of meaning, spoke of cessation, and delighted in settling disputes. Speaking in accord with the occasion and as was fitting, I gave good instruction and good admonishment. Regarding frivolous speech, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned trading and refrained from trading. I cast aside scales and measures, bushels and pecks. I did not accept goods, did not bind or constrain people. I did not expect to gain by manipulating measures, nor did I cheat others for small profits. Regarding trading, I purified my mind.

"'Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting widows and young girls, and refrained from accepting widows and young girls. Regarding accepting widows and young girls, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting male and female servants, and refrained from accepting male and female servants. Regarding accepting male and female servants, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and refrained from accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep. Regarding accepting elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting chickens and pigs, and refrained from accepting chickens and pigs. Regarding accepting chickens and pigs, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting farmland and shops, and refrained from accepting farmland and shops. Regarding accepting farmland and shops, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans, and refrained from accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans. Regarding accepting raw grain, wheat, and beans, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned alcohol and refrained from alcohol. Regarding drinking alcohol, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned high and broad beds, and refrained from high and broad beds. Regarding high and broad beds, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics, and refrained from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics. Regarding flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and cosmetics, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned singing, dancing, performing, and attending such spectacles, and refrained from singing, dancing, performing, and attending such spectacles. Regarding singing, dancing, performing, and attending such spectacles, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels, and refrained from accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels. Regarding accepting gold, silver, and precious jewels, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! I abandoned eating after midday, and refrained from eating after midday. I ate one meal a day, did not eat at night, and learned to eat at the proper time. Regarding eating after midday, I purified my mind.

"'Worthy ones! Having accomplished this noble body of morality, I further practiced contentment. For clothing I took only enough to cover my body; for food I took only enough to sustain my frame. Wherever I went, my robes and bowl accompanied me, without any attachment. Just as a wild goose flies through the sky together with its two wings, so was I likewise. Worthy ones! Having accomplished this noble body of morality and extreme contentment, I further guarded my sense faculties, constantly mindful of closing and blocking them, desiring clear understanding, guarding the mindful heart. Having accomplished this, I constantly wished to arouse my intention. When the eye saw forms, I did not grasp at signs nor savored forms. Because of quarreling and contention, I guarded the eye faculty. Lest covetousness, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states arise in the mind and tend toward those objects, I guarded the eye faculty. Likewise with the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognized dharmas, I did not grasp at signs nor savored dharmas. Because of quarreling and contention, I guarded the mind faculty. Lest covetousness, sorrow, and evil unwholesome states arise in the mind and tend toward those objects, I guarded the mind faculty. Worthy ones! Having accomplished this noble body of morality, extreme contentment, and the noble guarding of the sense faculties, I practiced clear comprehension in going out and coming in, skillfully observing and discerning in bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, maintaining proper comportment, properly wearing the saṅghāṭī robe and other garments, and handling the bowl. In walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and being silent, I applied clear comprehension to all.

"'Worthy ones! Having accomplished this noble body of morality, extreme contentment, and the noble guarding of the sense faculties, and having attained clear comprehension in going out and coming in, I dwelt alone in a remote place, in a secluded location, or went to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet place, a mountain cave, an open ground, or a haystack, or went into a forest, or stayed among the tombs. Worthy ones! Having been in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree in an empty and quiet place, I spread out my sitting cloth, sat cross-legged with body upright and right aspiration, with mindfulness not directed outward. I abandoned covetousness, and my mind was without contention. Seeing others' possessions and various means of livelihood, I did not give rise to covetousness wishing to obtain them for myself. Regarding covetousness, I purified my mind. Likewise with ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse. I abandoned doubt, crossed over perplexity, and had no uncertainty regarding wholesome dharmas. Regarding doubt and perplexity, I purified my mind. Worthy ones! Having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of the mind, and weaknesses of wisdom, separated from desires and separated from evil unwholesome states, I attained and dwelt in the fourth jhāna. Worthy ones! Having attained such a concentrated mind, pure, without blemish, without defilement, soft, well-settled, and having attained an imperturbable mind, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

"'Worthy ones! I knew this is suffering as it truly is, knew this is the arising of suffering, knew this is the cessation of suffering, knew this is the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. I knew these are the taints, knew this is the arising of the taints, knew this is the cessation of the taints, knew this is the path to the cessation of the taints as it truly is. Knowing thus, seeing thus, the mind was liberated from the taint of desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, I knew I was liberated. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Worthy ones! Thus knowing, thus seeing, regarding this inner body together with consciousness and all external signs, the conceit of "I," the activity of "I," and the latent tendency of conceit are cut off and known, uprooted at their root, never to arise again.' A bhikṣu whose taints are ended and who has attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established should answer thus.

"You, upon hearing this, should rightly approve and joyfully accept his words. Having rightly approved and joyfully accepted, you should then say to that bhikṣu: 'Worthy one! From your first statement onward, we have been pleased and delighted. However, we wished to question you further and further, seeking wisdom and the capacity for discerning response. That is why we have questioned the worthy one again and again.'"

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on Declaring Knowledge, Number One.

---

## (188) Madhyamāgama, Pairs Chapter: The Ajina Sūtra, Number Two

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying at the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation, came down from the hall, and in the shadow of the hall, on open ground, walked back and forth, broadly teaching the bhikṣus the profound and subtle Dharma. At that time, the wanderer Ajina, a disciple of the ascetic Mantou, saw from afar the World-Honored One rise from his meditation, come down from the hall, and in the shadow of the hall, on open ground, walk back and forth, broadly teaching the bhikṣus the profound and subtle Dharma. The wanderer Ajina, a disciple of the ascetic Mantou, went to the Buddha, exchanged greetings, and walked alongside the Buddha on his walking path. The World-Honored One turned and asked: "Ajina! Does the ascetic Mantou truly think five hundred thoughts? That if any other ascetic or brahmin claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, declaring 'I have complete, exhaustive knowledge, exhaustive vision,' they have faults and declare themselves to have faults?"

The wanderer Ajina, a disciple of the ascetic Mantou, replied: "Gotama! The ascetic Mantou truly thinks five hundred thoughts. That if any other ascetic or brahmin claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, declaring 'I have complete, exhaustive knowledge, exhaustive vision,' they have faults and declare themselves to have faults."

The World-Honored One asked again: "Ajina! How does the ascetic Mantou think five hundred thoughts? That if any other ascetic or brahmin claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, declaring 'I have complete, exhaustive knowledge, exhaustive vision,' they have faults and declare themselves to have faults?"

The wanderer Ajina, a disciple of the ascetic Mantou, replied: "Gotama! The ascetic Mantou speaks thus: 'Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or waking, whether by day or by night, I constantly have unobstructed knowledge and vision. Yet sometimes I encounter a wild elephant, a bolting horse, a runaway chariot, rebellious soldiers, a fleeing man, or a fleeing woman. Or traveling on such a road, I encounter a vicious elephant, a vicious horse, a vicious ox, or a vicious dog. Or I come across a swarm of snakes, or I am hit by thrown clods of earth, or struck by a staff. Or I fall into a ditch, or fall into a latrine, or step upon a sleeping ox, or fall into a deep pit, or walk into thorns. Or I see a village and ask its name and the way. I see men and women and ask their clan names. Or I look into an empty house, or enter a family's dwelling in such a way. Having entered, they ask me: "Venerable one, from where have you come?" I answer them: "Worthy ones, I was heading along a bad road."' Gotama! The ascetic Mantou thinks five hundred such thoughts. That if any other ascetic or brahmin claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, declaring 'I have complete, exhaustive knowledge, exhaustive vision,' they have faults."

Thereupon the World-Honored One left the walking path, went to the head of the walking path, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged. He asked the bhikṣus: "The matters of wisdom that I have taught, have you retained them?"

The bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.

The World-Honored One asked again a second and a third time: "Bhikṣus! The matters of wisdom that I have taught, have you retained them?" The bhikṣus also remained silent a second and a third time without answering.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Now is the proper time. Well-Gone One! Now is the proper time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus about matters of wisdom, the bhikṣus, having heard from the World-Honored One, will well retain them."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu! Listen carefully and reflect well upon it. I shall explain it to you in full detail."

The bhikṣus then said: "Yes, we will receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha further said: "There are two kinds of assemblies: one is called a Dharma assembly, and the other is called a non-Dharma assembly. What is a non-Dharma assembly? If someone practices what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Dharma, and that assembly also practices what is not the Dharma and speaks what is not the Dharma, and that person of non-Dharma, standing before the non-Dharma assembly, speaks falsely and deceptively about his own knowledge, not truthfully and not genuinely, displaying, differentiating, establishing his practice, disseminating and teaching in an orderly manner, wishing to cut off others' arguments with wicked and difficult challenges that cannot be answered; and within the true Dharma and Vinaya, his own professed knowledge cannot be established; and that person of non-Dharma, standing before the non-Dharma assembly, declares 'I have all-pervading wisdom and knowledge,' and if among them there is someone who speaks about matters of wisdom in such a manner, this is called a non-Dharma assembly. What is a Dharma assembly? If someone practices the Dharma and speaks the Dharma, and that assembly also practices the Dharma and speaks the Dharma, and that person of the Dharma, standing before the Dharma assembly, speaks of his own knowledge without falsehood or deception, truthfully and genuinely, displaying, differentiating, establishing his practice, disseminating and teaching in an orderly manner, wishing to cut off others' arguments with wicked and difficult challenges that can be answered; and within the true Dharma his own professed knowledge can be established; and that person of the Dharma, standing before the Dharma assembly, declares 'I have all-pervading wisdom and knowledge,' and if among them there is someone who speaks about matters of wisdom in such a manner, this is called a Dharma assembly. Therefore, you should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is meaningful and what is not meaningful. Having known Dharma and non-Dharma, meaning and non-meaning, you should train in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning."

Thus spoke the Buddha. He then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation. Thereupon the bhikṣus had this thought: "Worthy ones! You should know that the World-Honored One has briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation: 'Therefore, you should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is meaningful and what is not meaningful. Having known Dharma and non-Dharma, meaning and non-meaning, you should train in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning.'" They further thought: "Worthy ones! Who can elaborate in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?" They further thought: "The Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha's attendant and knows the Buddha's intention. He is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda can elaborate in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. Worthy ones! Let us go together to the Venerable Ānanda and request him to explain this meaning. If the Venerable Ānanda explains it in detail, we shall well retain it."

Thereupon the bhikṣus went to the Venerable Ānanda, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Venerable Ānanda! You should know that the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation: 'You should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is meaningful and what is not meaningful. Having known Dharma and non-Dharma, meaning and non-meaning, you should train in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning.' We then had this thought: 'Worthy ones! Who can elaborate in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated?' We further thought: 'The Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha's attendant and knows the Buddha's intention. He is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda can elaborate in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated.' We pray that the Venerable Ānanda, out of compassion, will explain it in detail."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Worthy ones! Listen while I speak a simile, for the wise, upon hearing a simile, understand its meaning. Worthy ones! Suppose a person wished to find heartwood, and for the sake of finding heartwood took an axe and entered a forest. He saw a great tree complete with roots, trunk, knots, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. That person, instead of touching the roots, trunk, knots, or heartwood, only touched the branches and leaves. What you worthy ones propose is just like this. The World-Honored One is present right here, yet you bypass him and come to me to ask about this meaning. Why is that? Worthy ones! You should know that the World-Honored One is the eye, is the wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma. He is the Dharma master, the Dharma general. He speaks the true meaning and reveals all meanings, for they originate from the World-Honored One. You worthy ones should go to the World-Honored One and ask about this meaning: 'World-Honored One! What does this mean? What is its significance?' As the World-Honored One explains it, you worthy ones should well retain it."

The bhikṣus then said: "Indeed so, Venerable Ānanda! The World-Honored One is the eye, is the wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma. He is the Dharma master, the Dharma general. He speaks the true meaning and reveals all meanings, for they originate from the World-Honored One. However, the Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha's attendant and knows the Buddha's intention. He is always praised by the World-Honored One and by the wise practitioners of the holy life. The Venerable Ānanda can elaborate in detail the meaning that the World-Honored One has just briefly stated. We pray that the Venerable Ānanda, out of compassion, will explain it in detail."

The Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus: "Worthy ones! Listen together to what I shall say. Worthy ones! Wrong view is non-Dharma; right view is Dharma. If because of wrong view there arise innumerable evil unwholesome states, this is called non-meaning. If because of right view there arise innumerable wholesome states, this is called meaning. Worthy ones! Likewise, up to wrong knowledge is non-Dharma; right knowledge is Dharma. If because of wrong knowledge there arise innumerable evil unwholesome states, this is called non-meaning. If because of right knowledge there arise innumerable wholesome states, this is called meaning. Worthy ones! This is what the World-Honored One briefly stated without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation: 'Therefore, you should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is meaningful and what is not meaningful. Having known Dharma and non-Dharma, meaning and non-meaning, you should train in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning.' This meaning briefly stated by the World-Honored One without elaboration, I have now with these phrases and these words explained in detail in this way. Worthy ones, you may go and present this to the Buddha. If it accords with the meaning as the World-Honored One would explain it, then you worthy ones should accept and retain it."

Thereupon the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, well received and recited it. They rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda three times, departed, went to the Buddha, bowed their heads in homage, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Earlier, the World-Honored One briefly stated this meaning without elaborating in detail, then rose from his seat and entered his chamber for meditation. The Venerable Ānanda, with these phrases and these words, has explained it in detail."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Among my disciples there is one with the eye, with wisdom, with Dharma, with meaning. Why is that? When a teacher briefly states the meaning for his disciples without elaborating in detail, that disciple, with these phrases and these words, explains it in detail. As Ānanda has explained it, so should you accept and retain it. Why is that? Because when one examines the meaning through explanation, it should be thus."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Ajina Sūtra, Number Two.

---

## (189) Madhyamāgama, Pairs Chapter: The Noble Path Sūtra, Number Three

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Kurus, in the town called Kammāssadhamma in the Kuru country.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There is one path that enables beings to become purified, to be free from sorrow, lamentation, weeping, and crying, to extinguish grief, suffering, and vexation, and thereby to attain the true Dharma. This is called noble right concentration. It has its prerequisites, its supports, and its requisites, and there are seven factors. Regarding noble right concentration, I speak of its prerequisites, its supports, and its requisites. What are the seven? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness. If with these seven factors as prerequisites, supports, and requisites, one well directs the mind and attains its unification, this is called noble right concentration with its prerequisites, its supports, and its requisites. Why is this so? Right view gives rise to right intention, right intention gives rise to right speech, right speech gives rise to right action, right action gives rise to right livelihood, right livelihood gives rise to right effort, right effort gives rise to right mindfulness, right mindfulness gives rise to right concentration. When a noble disciple's mind is thus rightly concentrated, he at once exhausts lust, anger, and delusion. When a noble disciple's mind is thus rightly liberated, he at once knows: birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. Among these, right view is foremost.

"When one sees wrong view as wrong view, this is called right view. When one sees right view as right view, this is also called right view. What is wrong view? It is the view that there is no giving, no offering, no incantation, no good and evil actions, no results of good and evil actions, no this world or other world, no father, no mother, and that in the world there are no true persons who go to good destinations, who proceed well and are well-directed, who in this world and the other world know for themselves, realize for themselves, and dwell having directly witnessed it. This is called wrong view. What is right view? It is the view that there is giving, there is offering, and there is also incantation; there are good and evil actions, there are results of good and evil actions; there is this world and the other world; there is father, there is mother; in the world there are true persons who go to good destinations, who proceed well and are well-directed, who in this world and the other world know for themselves, realize for themselves, and dwell having directly witnessed it. This is called right view. Thus, seeing wrong view as wrong view is called right view; seeing right view as right view is also called right view. Having known thus, one then seeks to train, wishing to abandon wrong view and accomplish right view. This is called right effort. When a bhikṣu, with mindfulness, abandons wrong view and accomplishes right view, this is called right mindfulness. These three factors follow right view from the standpoint of view and effort. Therefore right view is foremost.

"When one sees wrong intention as wrong intention, this is called right intention. When one sees right intention as right intention, this is also called right intention. What is wrong intention? Thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of harm. This is called wrong intention. What is right intention? Thoughts free from desire, thoughts free from ill-will, thoughts free from harm. This is called right intention. Thus, seeing wrong intention as wrong intention is called right intention; seeing right intention as right intention is also called right intention. Having known thus, one then seeks to train, wishing to abandon wrong intention and accomplish right intention. This is called right effort. When a bhikṣu, with mindfulness, abandons wrong intention and accomplishes right intention, this is called right mindfulness. These three factors follow right intention from the standpoint of view and effort. Therefore right view is foremost.

"When one sees wrong speech as wrong speech, this is called right speech. When one sees right speech as right speech, this is also called right speech. What is wrong speech? False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech. This is called wrong speech. What is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech. This is called right speech. Thus, seeing wrong speech as wrong speech is called right speech; seeing right speech as right speech is also called right speech. Having known thus, one then seeks to train, wishing to abandon wrong speech and accomplish right speech. This is called right effort. When a bhikṣu, with mindfulness, abandons wrong speech and accomplishes right speech, this is called right mindfulness. These three factors follow right speech from the standpoint of view and effort. Therefore right view is foremost.

"When one sees wrong action as wrong action, this is called right action. When one sees right action as right action, this is also called right action. What is wrong action? Killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct. This is called wrong action. What is right action? Abstaining from killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. This is called right action. Thus, seeing wrong action as wrong action is called right action; seeing right action as right action is also called right action. Having known thus, one then seeks to train, wishing to abandon wrong action and accomplish right action. This is called right effort. When a bhikṣu, with mindfulness, abandons wrong action and accomplishes right action, this is called right mindfulness. These three factors follow right action from the standpoint of view and effort. Therefore right view is foremost.

"When one sees wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, this is called right livelihood. When one sees right livelihood as right livelihood, this is also called right livelihood. What is wrong livelihood? If one, seeking without satisfaction, by means of various animal spells and incantations, maintains a wrong livelihood for one's existence, not seeking robes in accordance with the Dharma, for it is unlawful, not seeking food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life in accordance with the Dharma, for it is unlawful.
