This is called wrong livelihood. What is right livelihood? If one does not seek without satisfaction, does not by means of various animal spells and incantations maintain a wrong livelihood for one's existence, and seeks robes in accordance with the Dharma, for it is lawful, and seeks food and drink, bedding, medicines, and the various necessities of life in accordance with the Dharma, for it is lawful. This is called right livelihood. Thus, seeing wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood is called right livelihood; seeing right livelihood as right livelihood is also called right livelihood. Having known thus, one then seeks to train, wishing to abandon wrong livelihood and accomplish right livelihood. This is called right effort. When a bhikṣu, with mindfulness, abandons wrong livelihood and accomplishes right livelihood, this is called right mindfulness. These three factors follow right livelihood from the standpoint of view and effort. Therefore right view is foremost.

"What is right effort? A bhikṣu, for the sake of abandoning evil states that have already arisen, generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of preventing evil states that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of generating wholesome states that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. For the sake of maintaining wholesome states that have already arisen so they do not fade, do not decline, but rather grow, expand, develop, and reach fulfillment, he generates desire, strives, makes effort, exerts the mind, and endeavors. This is called right effort.

"What is right mindfulness? A bhikṣu contemplates the inner body as body, contemplates feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas. This is called right mindfulness.

"What is right concentration? A bhikṣu, separated from desires and separated from evil unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This is called right concentration.

"What is right liberation? A bhikṣu's mind is liberated from desire, liberated from anger and delusion. This is called right liberation.

"What is right knowledge? A bhikṣu knows that the mind is liberated from desire, knows that the mind is liberated from anger and delusion. This is called right knowledge. Thus, a learner accomplishes eight factors, and an arahat whose taints are ended accomplishes ten factors.

"How does a learner accomplish eight factors? From the learner's right view up to the learner's right concentration: this is how a learner accomplishes eight factors. How does an arahat whose taints are ended accomplish ten factors? From the non-learner's right view up to the non-learner's right knowledge: this is how an arahat whose taints are ended accomplishes ten factors. Why is this so? With right view, one abandons wrong view. If because of wrong view there arise innumerable evil unwholesome states, those are also abandoned. If because of right view there arise innumerable wholesome states, one cultivates and develops them to complete fulfillment. Up to right knowledge, one abandons wrong knowledge. If because of wrong knowledge there arise innumerable evil unwholesome states, those are also abandoned. If because of right knowledge there arise innumerable wholesome states, one cultivates and develops them to complete fulfillment.

"Thus there are twenty wholesome qualities and twenty unwholesome qualities. This is called the teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma. No ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain it or say it is wrong. If any ascetic or brahmin were to claim that my teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or say is wrong, is wrong, there would be ten legitimate reproaches against them in accordance with the Dharma. What are the ten? If one disparages right view and praises wrong view; if there are ascetics or brahmins of wrong view, and one makes offerings to them and praises them; then if any ascetic or brahmin were to claim that my teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or say is wrong, is wrong, then in accordance with the Dharma this constitutes the first reproach.

"If one disparages right knowledge, up to right knowledge, and praises wrong knowledge; if there are ascetics or brahmins of wrong knowledge, and one makes offerings to them and praises them; then if any ascetic or brahmin were to claim that my teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or say is wrong, is wrong, then in accordance with the Dharma this constitutes the tenth reproach. If any ascetic or brahmin were to claim that my teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or say is wrong, is wrong, then in accordance with the Dharma there are these ten reproaches. If furthermore there are other ascetics or brahmins who, crouching, speak of crouching; who speak of nothingness regarding nothingness; who speak of no cause, no action, and no karma, establishing that all the good and evil deeds attributed to this or that person are cut off and destroyed, then regarding my teaching of the forty great Dharma qualities that turns the wheel of Brahma, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or say is wrong, they too will face reproach, sorrow, and fear."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Noble Path Sūtra, Number Three.

---

## (190) Madhyamāgama, Pairs Chapter: The Lesser Emptiness Sūtra, Number Four

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying at the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the late afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to the Buddha. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, then stood to one side and said: "World-Honored One! At one time the World-Honored One was traveling among the Śākyans, at a city called Śākyans' capital. At that time I heard from the World-Honored One this statement: 'Ānanda! I frequently abide in emptiness.' Did I well understand, well receive, and well retain what the World-Honored One said?"

At that time, the World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda! What I said, you have indeed well understood, well received, and well retained. Why is that? From that time until now, I have frequently abided in emptiness. Ānanda! Just as this Hall of Migāra's Mother is empty of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, possessions, grain, and servants, yet it is not empty of one thing only, namely the assembly of bhikṣus. Thus, Ānanda, if something is absent here, one therefore sees it as empty regarding that; if something else remains here, one sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion. Ānanda! If a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of a village, should not attend to the perception of people, but should frequently attend to the single perception of a wilderness. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of a village, empty of the perception of people, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single perception of a wilderness. If there is any weariness due to the perception of a village, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of people, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single perception of a wilderness. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of people, should not attend to the perception of a wilderness, but should frequently attend to the single perception of earth. If that bhikṣu sees that this earth has hills and hollows, has snake lairs, has thickets of thorns, has sand and stones, steep mountains, deep rivers, he should not attend to those. If he sees that this earth is level as the palm of the hand, a fine prospect to gaze upon, he should frequently attend to that. Ānanda! Just as a cowhide stretched taut with a hundred pegs, fully stretched out, with no wrinkles or creases. If he sees that this earth has hills and hollows, has snake lairs, has thickets of thorns, has sand and stones, steep mountains, deep rivers, he should not attend to those. If he sees that this earth is level as the palm of the hand, a fine prospect to gaze upon, he should frequently attend to that. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of people, empty of the perception of a wilderness, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single perception of earth. If there is any weariness due to the perception of people, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of a wilderness, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single perception of earth. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of a wilderness, should not attend to the perception of earth, but should frequently attend to the single perception of the sphere of infinite space. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of a wilderness, empty of the perception of earth, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single perception of the sphere of infinite space. If there is any weariness due to the perception of a wilderness, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of earth, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single perception of the sphere of infinite space. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of earth, should not attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite space, but should frequently attend to the single perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of earth, empty of the perception of the sphere of infinite space, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. If there is any weariness due to the perception of earth, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of the sphere of infinite space, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite space, should not attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, but should frequently attend to the single perception of the sphere of nothingness. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of the sphere of infinite space, empty of the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single perception of the sphere of nothingness. If there is any weariness due to the perception of the sphere of infinite space, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single perception of the sphere of nothingness. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, if a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, should not attend to the perception of the sphere of nothingness, but should frequently attend to the single signless concentration of mind. He then knows thus: it is empty of the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, empty of the perception of the sphere of nothingness, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely the single signless concentration of mind. If there is any weariness due to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the perception of the sphere of nothingness, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to the single signless concentration of mind. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion.

"He then reflects: 'This signless concentration of mind was originally conditioned and originally intended. Whatever was originally conditioned and originally intended, I do not delight in it, do not seek it, and should not abide in it.' Knowing thus, seeing thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated. Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not receive further existence, I know it as it truly is. He then knows thus: it is empty of the taint of desire, empty of the taint of existence, empty of the taint of ignorance, yet it is not empty of one thing, namely this body of mine with its six sense-bases that remain alive. If there is any weariness due to the taint of desire, I have none of that. If there is any weariness due to the taint of existence or the taint of ignorance, I also have none of that. There is only the weariness due to this body of mine with its six sense-bases that remain alive. What is absent therein, by that he sees it as empty; what remains therein, he sees it as truly existing. Ānanda! This is called practicing genuinely, in accordance with emptiness, without inversion; namely, the ending of the taints, the taintless, the unconditioned liberation of mind.

"Ānanda! All the Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, they all practiced this genuine emptiness, without inversion; namely, the ending of the taints, the taintless, the unconditioned liberation of mind. Ānanda! All the Tathāgatas, Worthy Ones, Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the future, they all will practice this genuine emptiness, without inversion; namely, the ending of the taints, the taintless, the unconditioned liberation of mind. Ānanda! Now in the present, I, the Tathāgata, Worthy One, Perfectly Enlightened One, I also practice this genuine emptiness, without inversion; namely, the ending of the taints, the taintless, the unconditioned liberation of mind. Ānanda! You should train thus: I also will practice this genuine emptiness, without inversion; namely, the ending of the taints, the taintless, the unconditioned liberation of mind. Therefore, Ānanda, you should train thus."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Lesser Emptiness Sūtra, Number Four.

---

## (191) Madhyamāgama, Pairs Chapter: The Greater Emptiness Sūtra, Number Five

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyans, at Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed and at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. After eating, in the afternoon, he went to the Kālakhemaka Śākyan's hermitage. At that time, the Kālakhemaka Śākyan's hermitage had many beds and seats laid out, and many bhikṣus were dwelling there. Then the World-Honored One left the Kālakhemaka Śākyan's hermitage and went to the Kāla Śākyan's hermitage. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, together with many bhikṣus, had gathered in the Kāla Śākyan's hermitage engaged in robe-making. The Venerable Ānanda saw the Buddha coming from afar. Seeing him, he went out to welcome him, took the Buddha's robes and bowl, returned and spread out a seat, and drew water for washing the feet. After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat on the seat that the Venerable Ānanda had prepared in the Kāla Śākyan's hermitage and said: "Ānanda! The Kālakhemaka Śākyan's hermitage has many beds and seats laid out, and many bhikṣus are dwelling there."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Indeed so, World-Honored One! The Kālakhemaka Śākyan's hermitage has many beds and seats laid out, and many bhikṣus are dwelling there. The reason is that we are now engaged in robe-making."

Then the World-Honored One further told Ānanda: "A bhikṣu should not desire noisy talk, delight in noisy talk, engage in noisy talk, desire crowds, delight in crowds, gather in crowds, not desire seclusion, and not delight in dwelling alone in remote places. If a bhikṣu desires noisy talk, delights in noisy talk, engages in noisy talk, desires crowds, delights in crowds, gathers in crowds, does not desire seclusion, and does not delight in dwelling alone in remote places, then that he should attain happiness, noble happiness, the happiness of desirelessness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, the happiness of perfect awakening, the happiness without sustenance, the happiness that is not the happiness of birth and death, and that he should easily and without difficulty attain such happiness: this is impossible. Ānanda! If a bhikṣu does not desire noisy talk, does not delight in noisy talk, does not engage in noisy talk, does not desire crowds, does not delight in crowds, does not gather in crowds, desires seclusion, and always delights in dwelling alone in remote places, then that he should attain happiness, noble happiness, the happiness of desirelessness, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, the happiness of perfect awakening, the happiness without sustenance, the happiness that is not the happiness of birth and death, and that he should easily and without difficulty attain such happiness: this is certainly possible.

"Ānanda! A bhikṣu should not desire noisy talk, delight in noisy talk, engage in noisy talk, desire crowds, delight in crowds, gather in crowds, not desire seclusion, and not delight in dwelling alone in remote places. If a bhikṣu desires noisy talk, delights in noisy talk, engages in noisy talk, desires crowds, delights in crowds, gathers in crowds, does not desire seclusion, and does not delight in dwelling alone in remote places, then that he should attain the timely pleasant liberation of mind and the non-temporal unshakeable liberation of mind: this is impossible. Ānanda! If a bhikṣu does not desire noisy talk, does not delight in noisy talk, does not engage in noisy talk, does not desire crowds, does not delight in crowds, does not gather in crowds, desires seclusion, and always delights in dwelling alone in remote places, then that he should attain the timely pleasant liberation of mind and the non-temporal unshakeable liberation of mind: this is certainly possible. Why is that? I do not see any single form that I would desire and delight in; for when that form deteriorates, changes, and becomes different, there arise sorrow, lamentation, weeping, grief, suffering, and vexation. For this reason, I abide in this other dwelling place, having perfectly and completely awakened to it. This means transcending all perceptions of form and abiding in external emptiness.

"Ānanda! Having abided in this dwelling place, joy arises in me. With this joy, through the entire body I experience right mindfulness and clear comprehension. Rapture arises, tranquility arises, happiness arises, concentration arises. With this concentration, through the entire body I experience right mindfulness and clear comprehension. Ānanda! If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās come to visit me, I then, on their behalf, practice such and such a state of mind, of seclusion, delighting in desirelessness, and I also teach them the Dharma, encouraging and assisting them. Ānanda! If a bhikṣu wishes to frequently abide in emptiness, that bhikṣu should hold the inner mind steady and make it unified in concentration. Having held the inner mind steady and made it unified in concentration, he should then contemplate inner emptiness. Ānanda! If a bhikṣu says 'I do not hold the inner mind steady, I do not make it unified in concentration, yet I contemplate inner emptiness,' you should know that bhikṣu greatly wearies himself.

"Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu hold the inner mind steady and make it unified in concentration? A bhikṣu's body, through seclusion, gives rise to rapture and happiness, which soak, drench, pervade, and fill it completely. There is no part of the body that the rapture and happiness born of seclusion do not pervade. Ānanda! Just as when a person bathes, a vessel is filled with bath powder, and water is poured and mixed with it, kneaded into a ball. The moisture soaks, drenches, pervades, and fills it completely, inside and out, thoroughly, with no seepage anywhere. Just so, Ānanda, the bhikṣu's body, through seclusion, gives rise to rapture and happiness, which soak, drench, pervade, and fill it completely. There is no part of the body that the rapture and happiness born of seclusion do not pervade. Ānanda! In this way the bhikṣu holds the inner mind steady and makes it unified in concentration. Having held the inner mind steady and made it unified in concentration, he should then contemplate inner emptiness. Having contemplated inner emptiness, if his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate inner emptiness; Ānanda, if the bhikṣu, upon observing, knows that contemplating inner emptiness, his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate inner emptiness, then that bhikṣu should contemplate external emptiness. Having contemplated external emptiness, if his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate external emptiness.

"Ānanda! If the bhikṣu, upon observing, knows that contemplating external emptiness, his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate external emptiness, then that bhikṣu should contemplate internal-external emptiness. Having contemplated internal-external emptiness, if his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate internal-external emptiness. Ānanda! If the bhikṣu, upon observing, knows that contemplating internal-external emptiness, his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate internal-external emptiness, then that bhikṣu should contemplate imperturbability. Having contemplated imperturbability, if his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate imperturbability.

"Ānanda! If the bhikṣu, upon observing, knows that contemplating imperturbability, his mind wanders, does not incline toward it, does not become clear and settled, does not abide in and does not penetrate imperturbability, then that bhikṣu should, with respect to each of those states of concentration, guide it again and again, train it again and again, soften it again and again, making it well-pliant, gentle, and harmonious, gathered in and delighting in seclusion. When the mind, with respect to each of those states of concentration, has been guided again and again, trained again and again, softened again and again, made well-pliant, gentle, and harmonious, gathered in and delighting in seclusion, then he should dwell accomplished in inner emptiness. Having dwelt accomplished in inner emptiness, the mind does not wander, inclines toward it, becomes clear and settled, abides in and penetrates inner emptiness. Ānanda! When such a bhikṣu, upon observing, knows that dwelling accomplished in inner emptiness, the

# Madhyamāgama (Middle-Length Āgama), Fascicle 49

---

## (190) Sūtra on the Lesser Discourse on the Full-Moon Night

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in Jīvaka's Mango Grove.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the full-moon night, the World-Honored One sat in the open, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus.

Then the World-Honored One surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus, which was completely silent. He addressed the bhikṣus: "If an outsider were to ask you: 'What do the śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, practice during the rainy season retreat?' you should answer thus: 'The śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, practice the four foundations of mindfulness during the rainy season retreat.' Why is this? Bhikṣus, I truly practice the four foundations of mindfulness. Because I practice the four foundations of mindfulness, I obtained the highest and most excellent fruit.

"What are the four? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. He contemplates the body as body externally. He contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world.

"In the same way, he contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas internally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. He contemplates dharmas as dharmas externally. He contemplates dharmas as dharmas both internally and externally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world.

"If an outsider were to ask you: 'Do the śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, have still further dharmas that they practice, cultivate, and develop?' you should answer thus: 'They do.' If they ask: 'What further dharmas do the śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, practice, cultivate, and develop?' you should answer: 'The śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, further practice, cultivate, and develop the seven factors of enlightenment.'

"What are the seven? The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of dharmas, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of joy, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

"If an outsider were to ask you: 'What benefit, what fruit, do the śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, obtain from practicing, cultivating, and developing the seven factors of enlightenment?' you should answer: 'The śramaṇas, disciples of the Śākyan son, by practicing, cultivating, and developing the seven factors of enlightenment, obtain the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of liberation.'

"How does a bhikṣu cultivate the enlightenment factor of mindfulness? A bhikṣu contemplates the body as body internally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. He contemplates the body as body externally. He contemplates the body as body both internally and externally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world.

"In the same way, he contemplates feelings as feelings, mind as mind, and dharmas as dharmas internally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. He contemplates dharmas as dharmas externally. He contemplates dharmas as dharmas both internally and externally, with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world.

"When a bhikṣu thus abides in contemplation of dharmas as dharmas, he carefully investigates, reflects upon, and discerns those dharmas with wisdom. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of investigation of dharmas.

"When a bhikṣu thus carefully investigates, reflects upon, and discerns dharmas with wisdom, he practices energy without indolence. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of energy.

"When a bhikṣu practices energy without indolence, joy arises that is not of the flesh. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of joy.

"When a bhikṣu has a mind of joy, his body and mind become tranquil. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of tranquility.

"When a bhikṣu's body is tranquil and at ease, he experiences happiness, and his mind attains concentration. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of concentration.

"When a bhikṣu's mind is concentrated, he well attains equanimity. This is called a bhikṣu cultivating the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

"These are the four foundations of mindfulness and the seven factors of enlightenment that I practice, cultivate, and develop, through which I obtained supreme, right, and complete enlightenment."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (191) Sūtra on the Greater Discourse on the Full-Moon Night

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the full-moon night, the World-Honored One sat in the open, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus.

Then the World-Honored One surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus, which was completely silent. He addressed the bhikṣus: "Is there a bhikṣu here who can affirm of himself: 'I have ended the defilements, accomplished the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained my own benefit, exhausted the bonds of existence, and by right knowledge am liberated'?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Musīla can affirm of himself that he has ended the defilements."

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "How does Musīla affirm of himself that he has ended the defilements?"

Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Musīla knows and sees as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations.' He also knows and sees as it truly is: 'With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. With formations as condition, there is consciousness. With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases. With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With contact as condition, there is feeling. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With feeling as condition, there is craving. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With craving as condition, there is clinging. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With clinging as condition, there is existence. With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With existence as condition, there is birth. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With birth as condition, there arise old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair all cease.' Because the Venerable Musīla thus knows and sees, he can affirm of himself that he has ended the defilements."

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "Stop, stop! Do not speak like this. If anyone can thus know and see as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,' and so on in full detail up to 'With birth as condition, there are old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease,' if this were sufficient, then he would be an arhat who has exhausted the defilements. But this is not necessarily so.

"Ānanda, it is as if there were a traveler in a wilderness who was tormented by thirst. He would seek water with energy. He would see a well with water in it. He would look into it and understand that there is water. But he would have no rope or bucket with which to draw the water. Though he sees the water and knows the water, he cannot touch it with his body.

"In the same way, Ānanda, though one may know and see as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,' and so on in full detail up to 'With birth as condition, there are old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease,' yet though he thus knows and sees, he is not necessarily an arhat who has exhausted the defilements."

Then the Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Nārada can affirm of himself that he has ended the defilements."

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "How does Nārada affirm of himself that he has ended the defilements?"

Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, the Venerable Nārada knows and sees as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease. With formations as condition, there is consciousness. With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases. With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. With contact as condition, there is feeling. With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With feeling as condition, there is craving. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With craving as condition, there is clinging. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. With clinging as condition, there is existence. With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With existence as condition, there is birth. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With birth as condition, there arise old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair all cease.' Furthermore, the Venerable Nārada has realized the cessation of existence, nirvāṇa, as it truly is, with right wisdom. Yet though he has not yet obtained the exhaustion of the defilements, he has attained partial realization. Because the Venerable Nārada thus knows and sees, he can affirm of himself accordingly."

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "So it is, so it is, Ānanda. The Venerable Nārada knows and sees as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,' and so on in full detail up to 'With birth as condition, there are old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair cease.' Furthermore, the Venerable Nārada has realized the cessation of existence, nirvāṇa, as it truly is, with right wisdom. Yet though he has not yet obtained the exhaustion of the defilements, he has attained partial realization.

"Ānanda, it is as if there were a traveler in a wilderness who was tormented by thirst. He would seek water with energy. He would see a well with water in it. He would look into it and understand that there is water. Though he has no rope or bucket, he exerts his strength and uses his hands to touch the water.

"In the same way, Ānanda, the Venerable Nārada knows and sees as it truly is: 'With ignorance as condition, there are formations. With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,' and so on in full detail. Furthermore, he has realized the cessation of existence, nirvāṇa, as it truly is, with right wisdom. Yet though he has not yet obtained the exhaustion of the defilements, he has attained partial realization."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (192) Sūtra on Kāśyapa, Lord of Vaijayanta

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling at the Vaijayanta Cave. Then, after remaining in solitary meditation for a long time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his meditation in the late afternoon and went to the World-Honored One. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One addressed him: "Kāśyapa, you should teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus, admonish the bhikṣus. Kāśyapa, you should teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus, admonish them. Why? I always teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and admonish them, and you should do likewise."

The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣus today are difficult to teach; they possess dharmas that make them hard to teach. They have no patience in receiving admonishment. World-Honored One, I have seen a bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Venerable Ānanda, named Dantika, and a bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, named Rāhuladattaka. These two bhikṣus competed with each other in learning, each saying: 'Come, let us see who can speak more, who can speak better, who can speak longer without stopping.'"

Then the Venerable Ānanda was nearby. The World-Honored One addressed Ānanda: "Is it true that a bhikṣu who is your disciple, named Dantika, and a bhikṣu who is a disciple of Maudgalyāyana, named Rāhuladattaka, compete with each other in learning, each saying: 'Come, let us see who can speak more, who can speak better, who can speak longer'?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, who am I to speak against the words of the senior elder?"

The World-Honored One addressed Ānanda: "What do you mean, Ānanda? Do you think: 'The Tathāgata is the senior elder'?"

Ānanda said: "I do not, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, what do you mean? Would the senior elder speak empty words? Kāśyapa admonishes out of compassion, out of kindness. Ānanda, if Kāśyapa did not admonish, who would admonish? Ānanda, you should not have such thoughts. You should call that bhikṣu Dantika. Maudgalyāyana should call the bhikṣu Rāhuladattaka."

The Venerable Ānanda then summoned the bhikṣu Dantika, and the Venerable Maudgalyāyana summoned the bhikṣu Rāhuladattaka. Both bhikṣus came.

Then the World-Honored One addressed the two bhikṣus: "Is it true that you two compete with each other in learning, each saying: 'Come, let us see who can speak more, who can speak better, who can speak longer'?"

The two bhikṣus answered: "It is so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Have you ever heard me teach such a dharma as this: 'Come, bhikṣus, you should compete with each other in learning, each seeing who can speak more, who can speak better, who can speak longer'? Have I taught this?"

The two bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "If you have not heard me teach such a dharma, then why do you, having gone forth into homelessness in the right Dharma, do such a thing? Foolish ones! This is not fitting."

The two bhikṣus, having heard the World-Honored One's rebuke, were fearful and ashamed, and repented. The World-Honored One, having rebuked them, remained silent.

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (193) Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana, the Oxherd

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "A cowherder who possesses eleven qualities is unable to tend and increase his herd. What are the eleven? A cowherder does not know form, does not know characteristics, does not remove insects, does not dress wounds, does not make smoke, does not know the ford, does not know where to drink, does not know the road, is not skilled in finding pasture, milks dry without leaving any, and does not especially care for the leading bulls among the herd.

"How does a cowherder not know form? A cowherder does not truly know as it is whether the ox is black, white, or mottled, or of whatever form. This is called a cowherder not knowing form.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not know form as it truly is. He does not truly know as it is that all form, whatever form there is, is composed entirely of the four great elements and that which depends on the four great elements. This is called a bhikṣu not knowing form.

"How does a cowherder not know characteristics? A cowherder does not truly know an ox by its characteristics, whether it is noble or base. This is called a cowherder not knowing characteristics.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not know characteristics as they truly are. He does not truly know as it is that the fool is known by his actions and the wise one is known by his actions. This is called a bhikṣu not knowing characteristics.

"How does a cowherder not remove insects? A cowherder does not remove the eggs of insects from the ox's body, and so flies and gnats devour it. This is called a cowherder not removing insects.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not remove the insects. When thoughts of sensual desire arise, he accepts and does not abandon them; he does not remove, spit out, or end them. When thoughts of ill will arise, when thoughts of harming arise, he accepts and does not abandon them; he does not remove, spit out, or end them. And whenever evil, unwholesome dharmas arise, he accepts and does not abandon them; he does not remove, spit out, or end them. This is called a bhikṣu not removing insects.

"How does a cowherder not dress wounds? A cowherder does not dress or treat the wounds of the ox. This is called a cowherder not dressing wounds.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not dress wounds. A bhikṣu, having seen form with the eye, grasps at signs and grasps at accompanying features. Because he does not guard the faculty of the eye, covetousness, sorrow, and evil, unwholesome dharmas follow and enter. He does not guard against this; he does not guard the faculty of the eye. Having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, known dharmas with the mind, he grasps at signs and grasps at accompanying features. Because he does not guard the faculty of the mind, covetousness, sorrow, and evil, unwholesome dharmas follow and enter. He does not guard against this; he does not guard the faculty of the mind. This is called a bhikṣu not dressing wounds.

"How does a cowherder not make smoke? A cowherder does not make smoke to drive away mosquitoes and gadflies from the ox. This is called not making smoke.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not make smoke. A bhikṣu does not teach to others in detail the Dharma he has learned. This is called a bhikṣu not making smoke.

"How does a cowherder not know the ford? A cowherder does not know the place where the ox should ford the river, whether there is a ford or not. This is called not knowing the ford.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not know the ford. A bhikṣu does not from time to time approach those who are well-learned, who have extensively heard the tradition, who uphold the Dharma, who uphold the Vinaya, who uphold the Mātṛkā, and question them: 'Venerable one, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be practiced? What should not be practiced? What actions, when I do them, will bring me long-lasting suffering and harm? What actions, when I do them, will bring me long-lasting benefit and happiness?' This is called a bhikṣu not knowing the ford.

"How does a cowherder not know where to drink? A cowherder does not know the good place where the ox should drink. This is called not knowing where to drink.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not know where to drink. A bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, does not obtain the meaning, does not obtain the Dharma, does not obtain joy that accords with the Dharma. This is called a bhikṣu not knowing where to drink.

"How does a cowherder not know the road? A cowherder does not know the road the ox should travel. This is called not knowing the road.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not know the road. A bhikṣu does not know as it truly is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called a bhikṣu not knowing the road.

"How is a cowherder not skilled in finding pasture? A cowherder does not know good pastureland where the ox can graze. This is called not being skilled in finding pasture.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu is not skilled in finding pasture. A bhikṣu does not know as they truly are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Contemplating the body as body with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. Contemplating feelings as feelings, mind as mind, dharmas as dharmas with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. This is called a bhikṣu not being skilled in finding pasture.

"How does a cowherder milk dry without leaving any? A cowherder milks the cow completely dry, leaving nothing for the calf to drink. This is called milking dry without leaving any.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu is greedy without measure. When faithful householders provide robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness, the bhikṣu does not know moderation in accepting them. This is called a bhikṣu milking dry without leaving any.

"How does a cowherder not especially care for the leading bulls among the herd? A cowherder does not especially provide for and attend to the leading bulls who guide the herd. This is called not especially caring for the leading bulls.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu does not especially care for the leading ones. In the Sangha, the elder bhikṣus who have been long ordained, who are senior, who are heads of the community, and who are leaders of the community, the bhikṣu does not make offerings to them with body, speech, and mind, or show respect and serve them. This is called a bhikṣu not especially caring for the leading ones.

"If a bhikṣu possesses these eleven dharmas, he is unable to grow and increase in this Dharma and Vinaya.

"If a cowherder possesses eleven qualities, he is able to tend and increase his herd. What are the eleven? A cowherder knows form, knows characteristics, removes insects, dresses wounds, makes smoke, knows the ford, knows where to drink, knows the road, is skilled in finding pasture, does not milk dry but leaves some, and especially cares for the leading bulls among the herd.

"How does a cowherder know form? A cowherder truly knows as it is whether the ox is black, white, or mottled, or of whatever form. This is called a cowherder knowing form.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows form as it truly is. He truly knows as it is that all form, whatever form there is, is composed entirely of the four great elements and that which depends on the four great elements. This is called a bhikṣu knowing form.

"How does a cowherder know characteristics? A cowherder truly knows an ox by its characteristics, whether it is noble or base. This is called a cowherder knowing characteristics.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows characteristics as they truly are. He truly knows as it is that the fool is known by his actions and the wise one is known by his actions. This is called a bhikṣu knowing characteristics.

"How does a cowherder remove insects? A cowherder removes the eggs of insects from the ox's body, so flies and gnats do not devour it. This is called a cowherder removing insects.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu removes insects. When thoughts of sensual desire arise, he does not accept them; he abandons, removes, spits out, and ends them. When thoughts of ill will arise, when thoughts of harming arise, he does not accept them; he abandons, removes, spits out, and ends them. Whenever evil, unwholesome dharmas arise, he does not accept them; he abandons, removes, spits out, and ends them. This is called a bhikṣu removing insects.

"How does a cowherder dress wounds? A cowherder dresses and treats the wounds of the ox. This is called a cowherder dressing wounds.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu dresses wounds. A bhikṣu, having seen form with the eye, does not grasp at signs and does not grasp at accompanying features. Because he guards the faculty of the eye, covetousness, sorrow, and evil, unwholesome dharmas do not follow and enter. He guards against this; he guards the faculty of the eye. Having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, felt tangibles with the body, known dharmas with the mind, he does not grasp at signs and does not grasp at accompanying features. Because he guards the faculty of the mind, covetousness, sorrow, and evil, unwholesome dharmas do not follow and enter. He guards against this; he guards the faculty of the mind. This is called a bhikṣu dressing wounds.

"How does a cowherder make smoke? A cowherder makes smoke to drive away mosquitoes and gadflies from the ox. This is called making smoke.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu makes smoke. A bhikṣu teaches to others in detail the Dharma he has learned. This is called a bhikṣu making smoke.

"How does a cowherder know the ford? A cowherder knows the place where the ox should ford the river, where there is a ford. This is called knowing the ford.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows the ford. A bhikṣu from time to time approaches those who are well-learned, who have extensively heard the tradition, who uphold the Dharma, who uphold the Vinaya, who uphold the Mātṛkā, and questions them: 'Venerable one, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be practiced? What should not be practiced? What actions, when I do them, will bring me long-lasting suffering and harm? What actions, when I do them, will bring me long-lasting benefit and happiness?' This is called a bhikṣu knowing the ford.

"How does a cowherder know where to drink? A cowherder knows the good place where the ox should drink. This is called knowing where to drink.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows where to drink. A bhikṣu, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and Vinaya for him, obtains the meaning, obtains the Dharma, obtains joy that accords with the Dharma. This is called a bhikṣu knowing where to drink.

"How does a cowherder know the road? A cowherder knows the road the ox should travel. This is called knowing the road.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows the road. A bhikṣu knows as it truly is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called a bhikṣu knowing the road.

"How is a cowherder skilled in finding pasture? A cowherder knows good pastureland where the ox can graze. This is called being skilled in finding pasture.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu is skilled in finding pasture. A bhikṣu knows as they truly are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Contemplating the body as body with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. Contemplating feelings as feelings, mind as mind, dharmas as dharmas with diligence, right mindfulness, and right knowledge, removing covetousness and sorrow toward the world. This is called a bhikṣu being skilled in finding pasture.

"How does a cowherder not milk dry but leave some? A cowherder does not milk the cow completely dry, but leaves some for the calf to drink. This is called not milking dry.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu knows moderation. When faithful householders provide robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness, the bhikṣu knows moderation in accepting them. This is called a bhikṣu not milking dry.

"How does a cowherder especially care for the leading bulls among the herd? A cowherder especially provides for and attends to the leading bulls who guide the herd. This is called especially caring for the leading bulls.

"In the same way, a bhikṣu especially cares for the leading ones. In the Sangha, the elder bhikṣus who have been long ordained, who are senior, who are heads of the community, and who are leaders of the community, the bhikṣu makes offerings to them with body, speech, and mind, and shows respect and serves them. This is called a bhikṣu especially caring for the leading ones.

"If a bhikṣu possesses these eleven dharmas, he is able to grow and increase in this Dharma and Vinaya."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (194) Sūtra on Bhikṣu Vekhanassa (跋陀和利)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I wish to eat one meal a day. Because I eat one meal a day, my body is without illness, without suffering, and is light, strong, and at ease. Bhikṣus, you also should eat one meal a day. Because you eat one meal a day, your bodies will be without illness, without suffering, and will be light, strong, and at ease."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Bhaddāli. He rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I am unable to eat just one meal a day. Why? If I eat only one meal a day, my mind will have doubts and regrets."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, then when you eat at the assembly's mealtime, you may separate out a portion and eat it at another time."

Bhaddāli said: "World-Honored One, I am also unable to do this. My mind will still have doubts and regrets."

Then the World-Honored One admonished sternly, saying: "This is not right, Bhaddāli. In the Sangha, when the Tathāgata establishes a rule, you alone say you are unable to follow it. Bhaddāli, I say that even with regard to a person of great wisdom, there will at times be some things that are more distinguished and some things that are lesser. How much more so for you! Bhaddāli, a foolish one who does not consent: it will be to his long-lasting harm and suffering."

Then the bhikṣu Bhaddāli, unable to comply with the rule established by the World-Honored One, for that entire rainy-season retreat did not appear before the Buddha. Why? Because he did not follow the training rule established by the World-Honored One.

At that time, many bhikṣus were making robes for the World-Honored One, saying: "When the robes are finished, after the three months, the World-Honored One will travel."

Then the bhikṣu Bhaddāli went to those bhikṣus of long standing whom he was close to, and said: "Venerable ones, I did not follow the training rule established by the World-Honored One, and for the entire rainy-season retreat I did not appear before him. Now, many bhikṣus are making robes for the World-Honored One, and when the robes are finished, the World-Honored One will travel. Venerable ones, I have not yet gone to repent before the World-Honored One. I wish that the venerable ones would escort me to the World-Honored One so that I may confess my fault."

Then those bhikṣus escorted the bhikṣu Bhaddāli to the World-Honored One. Having arrived, they bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The bhikṣu Bhaddāli also bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, then knelt before the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One, I transgressed. I was foolish, I was confused, I was unwise. The World-Honored One established the rule of eating one meal a day, and I alone said I could not follow it. World-Honored One, I now repent, confess, and censure myself for my transgression. I wish that the World-Honored One would accept my repentance so that I may exercise restraint in the future."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, indeed you transgressed. You were foolish, confused, and unwise. When I established the rule, you alone said you could not follow it. Bhaddāli, what do you think? If a bhikṣu has obtained liberation in both ways, and I tell him: 'Come, bhikṣu, build a bridge for me with your body across the mud,' would he not do it, or would he turn away, or would he show a contrary aspect?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Bhaddāli, what do you think? If a bhikṣu has attained liberation through wisdom, or has become a body-witness, or has attained the view, or has been liberated by faith, or follows the Dharma, or follows faith, or has planted seeds of goodness, and I tell him: 'Come, bhikṣu, build a bridge for me with your body across the mud,' would he not do it, or would he turn away, or would he show a contrary aspect?"

He answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Bhaddāli, what do you think? At that time, were you one liberated in both ways, or one liberated through wisdom, or a body-witness, or one who has attained the view, or one liberated by faith, or one who follows the Dharma, or one who follows faith, or one who has planted seeds of goodness?"

Bhaddāli answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, at that time you were empty, you were nothing, you had not attained anything. Being empty, being nothing, having not attained anything, yet you said: 'World-Honored One, I am unable to eat just one meal a day.' Was this not your transgression?"

Bhaddāli said: "It was so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, since you now know and see your transgression, confess it, censure yourself, and exercise restraint in the future, I accept your repentance. If someone in the Noble One's Vinaya can know and see his transgression, confess it, censure himself, and exercise restraint in the future, this will lead to his growth in the noble Dharma.

"Bhaddāli, I will now speak a parable for you. A wise person, through a parable, can understand the meaning. Bhaddāli, it is as if a king had a border town. The walls and ramparts were solid, the gates were properly fitted. It had six gates. The gatekeeper was wise, intelligent, and discerning. He would keep out those he did not know and allow in those he knew. If a pair of swift messengers came from the east, the gatekeeper would ask: 'Where have you come from? Where are you going?' They would answer: 'We have come from the east and wish to see the king.' The gatekeeper would say: 'Go, you may enter and see the king.' Likewise, messengers from the south, west, north, above, or below would all be directed to the king if they wished to see him. Bhaddāli, I speak this parable with a meaning.

"The town is a metaphor for the body. The six gates are a metaphor for the six internal sense bases. The gatekeeper is a metaphor for mindfulness. The pair of swift messengers is a metaphor for calm and insight. The king is a metaphor for consciousness."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhaddāli, there is a reason why a bhikṣu fails to complete the training, and there is a reason why a bhikṣu completes the training. What is the reason why a bhikṣu fails to complete the training? Bhaddāli, when a bhikṣu does not guard the doors of the sense faculties, does not know moderation in eating, does not apply himself to wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night, does not delight in practice, does not abide in right mindfulness and right knowledge, and does not cultivate the pure foundations of the holy life, and when the training rules established by the Tathāgata he does not desire to study, then the other bhikṣus will speak of him thus: 'This venerable one does not guard the doors of the sense faculties, does not know moderation in eating, does not apply himself to wakefulness, does not delight in practice, does not abide in right mindfulness and right knowledge, does not cultivate the pure foundations of the holy life, and when the training rules established by the Tathāgata, he does not desire to study.' This is the reason why a bhikṣu fails to complete the training.

"What is the reason why a bhikṣu completes the training? Bhaddāli, when a bhikṣu guards the doors of the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, applies himself to wakefulness in the first and last watches of the night, delights in practice, abides in right mindfulness and right knowledge, cultivates the pure foundations of the holy life, and when the training rules established by the Tathāgata he desires to study, then the other bhikṣus will speak of him thus: 'This venerable one guards the doors of the sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, applies himself to wakefulness, delights in practice, abides in right mindfulness and right knowledge, cultivates the pure foundations of the holy life, and when the training rules established by the Tathāgata, he desires to study.' This is the reason why a bhikṣu completes the training.

"Bhaddāli, if that bhikṣu is an elder, the other bhikṣus will speak of him in three ways: 'The elder guards the doors of the sense faculties,' and so forth as above, and 'the Tathāgata's training rules he desires to study. This is well. Why? Because we have never seen the elder violate the training rules.' Bhaddāli, hearing such praise, that elder bhikṣu is pleased.

"If that bhikṣu is of middle standing, the other bhikṣus will speak of him in three ways, as above.

"If that bhikṣu is a junior, the other bhikṣus will speak of him in three ways: 'The junior bhikṣu guards the doors of the sense faculties,' and so forth as above, and 'the Tathāgata's training rules he desires to study. This is well. Why? Because we have never seen this junior bhikṣu violate the training rules.' Bhaddāli, hearing such praise, that junior bhikṣu is pleased.

"That bhikṣu, pleased and joyful, so proceeding, secluded from desires, secluded from evil, unwholesome dharmas, with initial application and sustained application, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. With the stilling of initial application and sustained application, with inner clarity and one-pointedness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. With the fading away of joy, he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly knowing, experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily,' he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. With the abandoning of happiness and suffering, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, without suffering and without happiness, with the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, supple, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. He recollects manifold past lives: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, through the formation and dissolution of worlds, through many formations and dissolutions of worlds: 'There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of happiness and suffering, such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn there. There again I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of happiness and suffering, such a lifespan. Dying from there, I was reborn here.' Thus he recollects manifold past lives with their details and circumstances.

"With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, supple, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings dying and being reborn, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations, superior and inferior. He knows beings as they fare according to their actions: 'These beings, who were endowed with bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, bad conduct of mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, at the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in ruin, in hell. But these beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, good conduct of mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views, at the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings dying and being reborn, and knows beings as they fare according to their actions.

"With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, supple, workable, steady, and having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the defilements. He knows as it truly is: 'This is suffering.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the origin of suffering.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' He knows as it truly is: 'These are the defilements.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the origin of the defilements.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the cessation of the defilements.' He knows as it truly is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the defilements.' Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the defilement of sensual desire, liberated from the defilement of existence, and liberated from the defilement of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows: 'I am liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'

"Bhaddāli, this is the reason why a bhikṣu completes the training."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣu Bhaddāli, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

## (195) Sūtra on Atimuktaka

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the country of Aṅga, traveling among the Aṅgans, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and arrived at a town called Āpaṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I will teach you the dharma of analysis and the dharma of non-analysis. Listen well, pay close attention, and carefully consider it."

The bhikṣus responded: "We will, World-Honored One."

The Buddha said: "What is the dharma of analysis and the dharma of non-analysis? Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu dwells thus: depending on such-and-such a dwelling place, the unarisen defilements arise, and the arisen defilements increase, and the unarisen benefits do not arise, and the arisen benefits decline, then such a dwelling place should be abandoned. If a bhikṣu dwells thus: depending on such-and-such a dwelling place, the unarisen defilements do not arise, and the arisen defilements decline, and the unarisen benefits arise, and the arisen benefits increase, then such a dwelling place should not be abandoned.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu depends on a certain practice: depending on such a practice, the unarisen defilements arise, and the arisen defilements increase, and the unarisen benefits do not arise, and the arisen benefits decline, then such a practice should be abandoned. If depending on such a practice, the unarisen defilements do not arise, and the arisen defilements decline, and the unarisen benefits arise, and the arisen benefits increase, then such a practice should not be abandoned.

"Bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu depends on a certain person: depending on such a person, the unarisen defilements arise, and the arisen defilements increase, and the unarisen benefits do not arise, and the arisen benefits decline, then such a person should be left behind. If depending on such a person, the unarisen defilements do not arise, and the arisen defilements decline, and the unarisen benefits arise, and the arisen benefits increase, then one should follow such a person as a shadow follows a form, and that person should not be left.

"This is called the dharma of analysis and the dharma of non-analysis."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

*End of Fascicle 49 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 50

## Great Chapter, the Second

Kālodāyin, Mūḷasiri Puṇṇa (Moliyaphagguna),
Bhadda, Assaji, Cunda, Upāli,
Taming, Foolish and Wise, Earth, Ariṭṭha, Sāti


## (192) Madhyamāgama, Great Chapter: The Kālodāyin Sūtra, First

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the country of Aṅga, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He went to Āpaṇa and stayed at the Keṇiya hermitage.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, at early dawn put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Āpaṇa to beg for food. Having finished his meal in the afternoon, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and went to a grove, wishing to do walking meditation during the day. The Venerable Udāyin also, having passed the night, at early dawn put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Āpaṇa to beg for food. Having finished his meal in the afternoon, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and followed behind the Buddha, thinking: "If the World-Honored One goes for daytime practice today, I too will go there for daytime practice."

Thereupon the World-Honored One entered the grove, went to the foot of a tree, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat down cross-legged. The Venerable Udāyin also entered that grove, went to the foot of a tree not far from the Buddha, spread out his sitting cloth, and sat down cross-legged. At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, alone in a quiet place, sat in meditation and contemplation, and this thought arose in his mind: "The World-Honored One has greatly benefited us; the Well-Gone One has greatly brought us peace and security. The World-Honored One has for my sake removed the dharmas of various sufferings and increased the dharmas of happiness. The World-Honored One has for my sake removed immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas and increased immeasurable wholesome and excellent dharmas."

The Venerable Udāyin, at the time of late afternoon, rose from meditation and went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side. The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin! Are you without want, peaceful and happy, and is your strength as usual?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "Indeed so, World-Honored One! I am without want, peaceful and happy, and my strength is as usual."

The World-Honored One again asked: "Udāyin! How is it that you are without want, peaceful and happy, and your strength is as usual?"

The Venerable Udāyin answered: "World-Honored One! I was alone in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and contemplation, and this thought arose in my mind: 'The World-Honored One has greatly benefited us; the Well-Gone One has greatly brought us peace and security. The World-Honored One has for my sake removed the dharmas of various sufferings and increased the dharmas of happiness. The World-Honored One has for my sake removed immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas and increased immeasurable wholesome and excellent dharmas.' World-Honored One, formerly you told the bhikṣus: 'You should abandon eating after midday.' World-Honored One, when we heard this, we could not bear it, could not endure it, did not desire it, and were not pleased. When faithful brahmins and householders came to the community garden and extensively gave alms and made merit, we received food with our own hands. Yet the World-Honored One now teaches us to abandon this, the Well-Gone One teaches us to give up this. We also said: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' However, out of our reverence and inability to resist the World-Honored One's majestic power and wondrous virtue, we therefore abandoned eating after midday.

"Furthermore, formerly the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: 'You should abandon eating at night.' World-Honored One, when we heard this, we could not bear it, could not endure it, did not desire it, and were not pleased. Of the two meals, the supreme, most wonderful, most excellent, and most delicious one, the World-Honored One now teaches us to abandon this, the Well-Gone One teaches us to give up this. We also said: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' World-Honored One, formerly there was a householder who brought many kinds of pure and wonderful foods and drinks, returned to his home, and instructed his household, saying: 'You receive these and store them in one place. I shall gather everyone together for the evening meal; it is not for morning or midday.' World-Honored One, if among households there is arranged a supremely wonderful and finest meal, it is only the evening meal. It was for morning and midday that the World-Honored One now teaches us to abandon this, the Well-Gone One teaches us to give up this. We also said: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' However, out of our reverence and inability to resist the World-Honored One's majestic power and wondrous virtue, we therefore abandoned eating at night.

"World-Honored One, I further had this thought: 'If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time to beg for food, he might encounter bandits, whether they are actively engaged in their deeds or not. Or he might encounter a tiger, or a deer, or a tiger and deer, or a leopard, or a bear, or a leopard and bear. Or he might go to such places and encounter a vicious elephant, a vicious horse, a vicious bull, or a vicious dog. Or he might come upon a nest of snakes. Or he might be pelted with clods of earth, or struck with sticks. Or he might fall into a ditch or drain, or fall into a latrine. Or he might stumble over a sleeping ox, or fall into a deep pit, or get caught in thorns. Seeing an empty house, he might enter such a house, and if he enters, a woman seeing him might call him to engage in evil and impure conduct.'

"World-Honored One, once a bhikṣu, in darkness of night with light rain and flashing lightning, went at an improper time to beg for food at another's house. The woman of that house had gone outside at that time to wash and clean the food vessels. That woman, in the flash of lightning, saw the bhikṣu from afar and thought he was a ghost. Having seen him, she was terrified, her body hair stood on end, she cried out in a loud shriek, and she immediately miscarried. She said: 'You are a ghost! You are a ghost!' At that time, the bhikṣu said to the woman: 'Sister, I am not a ghost. I am a śramaṇa; I have come to beg for food.' Then the woman angrily cursed the bhikṣu with the most bitter and vile words, saying: 'May this śramaṇa's life-faculty be cut short! May this śramaṇa's father and mother die early! May this śramaṇa's clan be extinguished! May this śramaṇa's belly split open and be destroyed! Bald-headed śramaṇa wrapped in black, childless and without descendants! You would better take a sharp knife and cut open your own belly than go begging for food at night at an improper time. Because of this śramaṇa, I have miscarried!' World-Honored One, when I recalled this, I felt joyful. World-Honored One, because of this joy, my whole body was filled; with right mindfulness and right knowing, joy, tranquility, happiness, and concentration arose. World-Honored One, because of this concentration, my whole body was filled, with right mindfulness and right knowing. Thus, World-Honored One, I am without want, peaceful and happy, and my strength is as usual."

The World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Udāyin! You are not like those foolish people. Those foolish people, when I tell them: 'You should abandon this,' they say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' They also say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' They do not abandon it, and they only generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, they also generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, the bonds of those foolish people are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and they cannot attain liberation. Udāyin, it is like a fly caught in mucus or spittle; once trapped within it, it suffers or dies. Udāyin, if someone were to say that the fly's bonds are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and that it can attain liberation, would that be a correct statement?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A fly caught in mucus or spittle, trapped within it, suffers or dies. Therefore, World-Honored One, the fly's bonds are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and it cannot attain liberation."

"Udāyin, those foolish people, when I tell them: 'You should abandon this,' they say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' They also say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.'
