They do not abandon it, and they only generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, they also generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, the bonds of those foolish people are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and they cannot attain liberation. Udāyin, if a son of good family, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he does not say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also does not say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He then abandons it. He does not generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and uphold the precepts, he also does not generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, the bonds of that son of good family are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation. Udāyin, it is like a great elephant king who has reached the age of sixty, proud and noble, a great nāga, with complete tusks, feet, and body, overflowing with sinew and strength. When firmly bound, if in anger he turns his body with force, those firm bonds are then severed, and he returns to his former place. Udāyin, if someone were to say that the great elephant king who has reached the age of sixty, proud and noble, a great nāga, with complete tusks, feet, and body, overflowing with sinew and strength, that his bonds are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and that he cannot attain liberation, would that be a correct statement?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? That great elephant king who has reached the age of sixty, proud and noble, a great nāga, with complete tusks, feet, and body, overflowing with sinew and strength. When firmly bound, if in anger he turns his body with force, those firm bonds are then severed, and he returns to his former place. World-Honored One, therefore that great elephant king who has reached the age of sixty, proud and noble, a great nāga, with complete tusks, feet, and body, overflowing with sinew and strength, his bonds are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation."

"Just so, Udāyin, when I tell that son of good family: 'You should abandon this,' he does not say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also does not say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He then abandons it. He does not generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also does not generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, the bonds of that son of good family are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation. Udāyin, if there is a foolish person, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he says: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also says: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He does not abandon it, and he only generates displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also generates displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, the bonds of that foolish person are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and he cannot attain liberation.

"Udāyin, it is like a poor man without money or possessions, and also without power. He has one wife, and she is blind in her eyes, ugly and unlovable. He has only one house, and it is crumbling and ruined, with holes and leaks, roosted in by crows and birds, wretched and unfit to dwell in. He has one bed, and it too is broken and collapsed, wretched and unfit to lie on. He has only one pot, and it is cracked and unusable. He sees a bhikṣu who, having finished his meal in the afternoon, has washed his hands and feet, spread out his sitting cloth, and sits beneath a tree, cool and composed, cultivating the higher mind. Having seen this, he thinks: 'A śramaṇa is truly happy! A śramaṇa is like nirvāṇa! I am wretched and without virtue. Why is that? I have one wife who is blind in her eyes, ugly and unlovable, yet I cannot let her go. I have only one house that is crumbling and ruined, with holes and leaks, roosted in by crows and birds, wretched and unfit to dwell in, yet I cannot let it go. I have one bed that is broken and collapsed, wretched and unfit to lie on, yet I cannot let it go. I have only one pot that is cracked and unusable, yet I cannot let it go. I would love to be like a bhikṣu, shaving off my beard and hair, donning the kāṣāya robes, with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way.' Udāyin, if someone were to say: 'That poor man without money or possessions, and also without power, his bonds are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation,' would that be a correct statement?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? That poor man without money or possessions, and also without power, has one blind wife, ugly and unlovable, yet cannot let her go. He has only one house that is crumbling and ruined, with holes and leaks, roosted in by crows and birds, wretched and unfit to dwell in, yet cannot let it go. He has one bed that is broken and collapsed, wretched and unfit to lie on, yet cannot let it go. He has only one pot that is cracked and unusable, yet cannot let it go. He would love to be like a bhikṣu, shaving off his beard and hair, donning the kāṣāya robes, with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way. World-Honored One, therefore that poor man without money or possessions, and also without power, his bonds are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and he cannot attain liberation."

"Just so, Udāyin, if there is a foolish person, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he says: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also says: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He does not abandon it, and he only generates displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also generates displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, therefore the bonds of that foolish person are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and he cannot attain liberation. Udāyin, if a son of good family, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he does not say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also does not say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He then abandons it. He does not generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also does not generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, therefore the bonds of that son of good family are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation.

"Udāyin, it is like a householder or a householder's son, extremely wealthy and prosperous, with much money and possessions, herds and properties beyond reckoning, fiefs, revenues, abundant rice and grain, and all manner of life's provisions, servants, elephants, and horses, innumerable in count. He sees a bhikṣu who, having finished his meal in the afternoon, has washed his hands and feet, spread out his sitting cloth, and sits beneath a tree, cool and composed, cultivating the higher mind. Having seen this, he thinks: 'A śramaṇa is truly happy! A śramaṇa is like nirvāṇa! Would that I could abandon extreme wealth and prosperity, gold, treasures, property, grain, elephants, horses, and servants, and love to be like a bhikṣu, shaving off my beard and hair, donning the kāṣāya robes, with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way.' Udāyin, if someone were to say: 'That householder or householder's son, his bonds are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and he cannot attain liberation,' would that be a correct statement?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? That householder or householder's son, he is able to abandon extreme wealth and prosperity, gold, treasures, property, grain, elephants, horses, and servants, and loves to be like a bhikṣu, shaving off his beard and hair, donning the kāṣāya robes, with full faith leaving the household for the homeless life to study the Way. World-Honored One, therefore that householder or householder's son, his bonds are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation."

"Just so, Udāyin, if a son of good family, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he does not say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also does not say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He then abandons it. He does not generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also does not generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, therefore the bonds of that son of good family are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation. Udāyin, when a bhikṣu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, if there arise thoughts connected with desire, and he delights in, bonds to, and is fettered by them, and he takes pleasure in them, does not sever them, does not halt them, and does not expel them, Udāyin, I say this is bondage, not liberation. Why is that? Because the fetters are unwholesome. Udāyin, because the fetters are unwholesome, I say this is bondage, not liberation. Udāyin, when a bhikṣu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, if there arise thoughts connected with desire, and he delights in, bonds to, and is fettered by them, yet he takes no pleasure in them, severs them, halts them, and expels them, Udāyin, I say this too is bondage, not liberation. Why is that? Because the fetters are unwholesome. Udāyin, because the fetters are unwholesome, I say this is bondage, not liberation. Udāyin, when a bhikṣu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, if sometimes through unmindfulness there co-arise thoughts connected with desire, with delighting in, bonding to, and fettering, but the arising is slow and the cessation is swift, Udāyin, it is like an iron ball or an iron plowshare heated in fire all day long; if someone places two or three drops of water on it, the drops come slowly but the water quickly evaporates. Udāyin, just so, when a bhikṣu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, if sometimes through unmindfulness there co-arise thoughts connected with desire, with delighting in, bonding to, and fettering, the arising is slow and the cessation is swift. Udāyin, I say this too is bondage, not liberation. Why is that? Because the fetters are unwholesome. Udāyin, because the fetters are unwholesome, I say this is bondage, not liberation.

"Udāyin, when one dwells at the root of suffering, traveling without birth and death, in the unsurpassed complete exhaustion of craving, with the mind well liberated, Udāyin, I say this is liberation, not bondage. Why is that? Because all fetters are exhausted. Udāyin, because all fetters are exhausted, I say this is liberation, not bondage. Udāyin, there is happiness that is not noble happiness; it is the happiness of ordinary people, the root of illness, the root of boils, the root of arrows and thorns. It has nutriment, it involves birth and death. It should not be cultivated, should not be practiced, should not be spread widely. I say that one should not cultivate it. Udāyin, there is happiness that is noble happiness, the happiness of desirelessness, the happiness of separation, the happiness of cessation, the happiness of perfect awakening. It has no nutriment, it is without birth and death. It can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely. I say that one should cultivate it. Udāyin, what is this happiness that is not noble happiness, that is the happiness of ordinary people, the root of illness, the root of boils, the root of arrows and thorns, that has nutriment, that involves birth and death, that should not be cultivated, should not be practiced, should not be spread widely, that I say one should not cultivate? If because of the five sensual desires there arises happiness and what is called wholesome, this happiness is not noble happiness; it is the happiness of ordinary people, the root of illness, the root of boils, the root of arrows and thorns. It has nutriment, it involves birth and death. It should not be cultivated, should not be practiced, should not be spread widely. I say that one should not cultivate it.

"Udāyin, what is this happiness that is noble happiness, the happiness of desirelessness, the happiness of separation, the happiness of cessation, the happiness of perfect awakening, that has no nutriment, that is without birth and death, that can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely, that I say one should cultivate? Udāyin, if a bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining the fourth dhyāna and dwelling in its accomplishment, this happiness is noble happiness, the happiness of desirelessness, the happiness of separation, the happiness of cessation, the happiness of perfect awakening. It has no nutriment, it is without birth and death. It can be cultivated, can be practiced, can be spread widely. I say that one should cultivate it. Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of separation, attains the first dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, the Noble Ones say this is 'still subject to movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'movement'? Herein, the initial thought and sustained thought are what the Noble Ones call 'movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'movement'? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, with initial thought and sustained thought having ceased, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought, without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains the second dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, the Noble Ones say this is 'still subject to movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'movement'? The joy herein obtained is what the Noble Ones call 'movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'movement'? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, separated from the desire for joy, abiding in equanimity, without craving, with right mindfulness and right knowing, experiencing happiness with the body, as the Noble Ones describe it: 'one who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells in happiness,' attains the third dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, the Noble Ones say this is 'still subject to movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'movement'? The mental happiness herein described as 'movement' is what the Noble Ones call 'movement.' Herein, what do the Noble Ones call 'not subject to movement'? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, without suffering, without happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains the fourth dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, this is what the Noble Ones call 'not subject to movement.'

"Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of separation, attains the first dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, Udāyin, I say this should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, with initial thought and sustained thought having ceased, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought, without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, attains the second dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, separated from the desire for joy, abiding in equanimity, without craving, with right mindfulness and right knowing, experiencing happiness with the body, as the Noble Ones describe it: 'one who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells in happiness,' attains the third dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, with the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, without suffering, without happiness, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains the fourth dhyāna and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended.

"Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu transcends all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, with infinite space, attains the base of infinite space and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu transcends the entire base of infinite space, with infinite consciousness, attains the base of infinite consciousness and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu transcends the entire base of infinite consciousness, with nothingness, attains the base of nothingness and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say this too should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Herein, what is the transcendence? Udāyin, when a bhikṣu transcends the entire base of nothingness, with neither perception nor non-perception, attains the base of neither perception nor non-perception and dwells in its accomplishment, this is the transcendence herein. Udāyin, I say that even the base of neither perception nor non-perception should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, but should be transcended. Udāyin, is there any single fetter, whether large or small, that long abides, of which I say it should not be annihilated, should not be cut off, should not be transcended, meaning that I say it should not be severed?"

The Venerable Udāyin said: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Udāyin! You are not like those foolish people. Those foolish people, when I tell them: 'You should abandon this,' they say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' They also say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' They do not abandon it, and they only generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, they also generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, therefore the bonds of those foolish people are extremely firm and strong, ever tightening and increasing, impossible to sever, and they cannot attain liberation. Udāyin, if there is a son of good family, when I tell him: 'You should abandon this,' he does not say: 'This is a small matter; what need is there to abandon it? Yet the World-Honored One now teaches me to abandon this, the Well-Gone One commands me to give up this.' He also does not say: 'This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.' He then abandons it. He does not generate displeasure and intolerance toward me, and toward other bhikṣus who well guard and maintain the precepts, he also does not generate displeasure and intolerance. Udāyin, therefore the bonds of that son of good family are not firm, not strong, do not increasingly tighten, can be severed, and he can attain liberation."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Udāyin, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Kālodāyin Sūtra, First


---

## (193) Madhyamāgama, Great Chapter: The Moliyaphagguna Sūtra, Second

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna frequently gathered together with bhikṣuṇīs. If anyone spoke to the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna about the bhikṣuṇīs in his presence, upon hearing it he would become angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling. If anyone spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs about the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna in their presence, the bhikṣuṇīs upon hearing it would become angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling.

Many bhikṣus, having heard of this, went to the Buddha, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna frequently gathers together with bhikṣuṇīs. If anyone speaks to the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna about the bhikṣuṇīs, upon hearing it he becomes angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling. If anyone speaks to the bhikṣuṇīs about the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna, the bhikṣuṇīs upon hearing it become angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling."

The World-Honored One, having heard this, told a certain bhikṣu: "Go to where the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna is and tell him: 'The World-Honored One summons you.'"

That bhikṣu, having heard, said: "Indeed, World-Honored One!" He then rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to where the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna was and said to him: "The World-Honored One summons you." Moliyaphagguna, having heard, came to where the Buddha was, made obeisance to the Buddha, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One said: "Phagguna! Is it true that you frequently gather together with bhikṣuṇīs? If anyone speaks to you about the bhikṣuṇīs, upon hearing it you become angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling? If anyone speaks to the bhikṣuṇīs about you, the bhikṣuṇīs upon hearing it become angry, resentful, and jealous, to the point of quarreling? Phagguna, is this truly so?"

Phagguna answered: "It is true, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further asked: "Phagguna, did you not, with full faith, leave the household for the homeless life to study the Way?"

Phagguna answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Phagguna, since you have, with full faith, left the household for the homeless life to study the Way, you should train as follows. Whatever desires and thoughts that are dependent on the household life, sever them. Whatever desires and thoughts that are dependent on desirelessness, practice them, cultivate them, and spread them widely. Phagguna, you should train in this way."

At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Have you not, with full faith, left the household for the homeless life to study the Way?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One further told the bhikṣus: "Since you have, with full faith, left the household for the homeless life to study the Way, you should train as follows. Whatever desires and thoughts that are dependent on the household life, sever them. Whatever desires and thoughts that are dependent on desirelessness, practice them, cultivate them, and spread them widely. You should train in this way. Formerly I once told the bhikṣus: 'You all, whether bhikṣus of wide acquaintance or bhikṣus of few acquaintances, all should train in eating one meal a day. Having trained in eating one meal a day, you will be without concern, without seeking, without illness or affliction, the body will be light and nimble, strength will be vigorous, peaceful and happy.' Those bhikṣus of wide acquaintance and those of few acquaintances all trained in eating one meal a day. Having trained in eating one meal a day, they were without concern, without seeking, without illness or affliction, the body was light and nimble, strength was vigorous, peaceful and happy. Those bhikṣus were pleasing to my mind, and I did not need to instruct and admonish them much. The bhikṣus, because of this, generated mindfulness directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. It is like a horse-drawn chariot, whose driver mounts it, holding the reins in the left hand and the whip in the right hand, traveling along the eightfold road, going wherever the mind wishes. Just so, the bhikṣus were pleasing to my mind, and I did not need to instruct and admonish them much. The bhikṣus, because of this, generated mindfulness directed toward the Dharma in proper sequence. It is like good land with a sāla tree grove. The caretaker of that grove, being wise, clever, and diligent, tends the roots of the sāla trees at the proper time, repeatedly hoeing and fertilizing, irrigating with water, leveling the high ground and filling in the low places. If bad grass grows at the edges, he weeds and discards it. If trees growing alongside are crooked, twisted, bad, and not straight, he uproots them and casts them outside. If branches grow sideways and crooked, he trims and prunes them. If newly growing trees nearby are well-shaped, straight, and good, he tends them at the proper time, repeatedly hoeing and fertilizing, irrigating with water. Thus that sāla tree grove on good land grows ever more flourishing. Just so, the bhikṣus were pleasing to my mind, and I did not need to instruct and admonish them much. That which I praise as good speech and compliance does not mean doing so because of robes and bowls, food and drink, beds and mats, medicines, and the various necessities of life. Why is that? If a bhikṣu does not receive these, he will revert to bad speech and non-compliance, and will come to embody the dharma of bad speech and non-compliance.

"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of seclusion, relying on seclusion, dwelling in seclusion, practices good speech and compliance, and embodies the dharma of good speech and compliance, this is what I call good speech and compliance. Why is that? There may be one who well guards and practices the conduct of the Well-Gone One, meaning because others do not speak harsh words to him. If others do not speak harsh words, he does not become angry, nor resentful and jealous, does not dwell in sorrowful entanglement, does not harbor resentment and anger, and does not expose others' faults. The bhikṣus, seeing this, think: 'This worthy one is patient, gentle, tolerant, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed.' But if others speak harsh words to him, he becomes angry, resentful, and jealous, dwells in sorrowful entanglement, harbors resentment and anger, and exposes faults. The bhikṣus, seeing this, think: 'This worthy one is of bad temperament, hasty, crude, and rough, unsettled, uncontrolled, and uncalmed.' Why is that?

"Bhikṣus, long ago there was a householder's wife named Vedehikā. She was extremely wealthy and prosperous, with much money and possessions, herds and properties beyond reckoning, fiefs, revenues, abundant rice and grain, and all manner of life's provisions. At that time, the householder's wife Vedehikā had such a great reputation that spread throughout all directions: 'The householder's wife Vedehikā is patient, tolerant, gentle, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed.' At that time, the householder's wife Vedehikā had a maid named Kālī, who was her long-time attendant, with wonderfully good speech, and who somewhat conducted herself well. That maid Kālī had this thought: 'My mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, has such a great reputation that has spread throughout all directions: the householder's wife Vedehikā is patient, tolerant, gentle, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed. Let me now test my mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā: does she truly become angry or does she truly not become angry?'

"Thereupon, the maid Kālī lay in bed and did not rise early. The mistress called: 'Maid Kālī! Why do you not rise early?' The maid Kālī, hearing this, thought: 'My mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, truly does become angry; it is not that she does not become angry. But because I am skilled at managing the household affairs, skilled at conducting business, and skilled at maintaining things, my mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, has such an extremely great reputation that has spread throughout all directions: the householder's wife Vedehikā is patient, tolerant, gentle, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed. Let me now test my mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, even more greatly: does she truly become angry or does she truly not become angry?'

"Thereupon, the maid Kālī lay in bed until very late and did not rise. The mistress called: 'Maid Kālī! Why have you lain in bed until very late and not risen?' The maid Kālī, hearing this, thought: 'My mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, truly does become angry; it is not that she does not become angry. But because I am skilled at managing the household affairs, skilled at conducting business, and skilled at maintaining things, my mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, has such an extremely great reputation that has spread throughout all directions: the householder's wife Vedehikā is patient, tolerant, gentle, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed. Let me now test my mistress, the householder's wife Vedehikā, even more extremely: does she truly become angry or does she truly not become angry?'

"Thereupon, the maid Kālī lay in bed until late afternoon before rising. The mistress called: 'Maid Kālī! Why have you stayed in bed until late afternoon to rise? You neither do the work yourself nor instruct others to do it! This maid Kālī does not follow my instructions! This maid Kālī is disrespectful to me!' She then became greatly angry and resentful and jealous. Three veins stood up on her forehead, her face wrinkled, and she went herself, closed the door and fastened the bolt, took a large stick in her hand, and struck the maid on the head, cracking it open and causing blood to flow. Thereupon, the maid Kālī, with her head cracked open and blood flowing, went out and spoke to the neighbors, loudly complaining and widely telling everyone: 'Respected ones! Do you see this patient one, this tolerant one, this gentle one, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed in her conduct? She cursed me saying: "Maid Kālī! Why have you stayed in bed until late afternoon to rise? You neither do the work yourself nor instruct others to do it! This maid Kālī does not follow my instructions! This maid Kālī is disrespectful to me!" She then became greatly angry and resentful and jealous. Three veins stood up on her forehead, her face wrinkled, she came herself, closed the door and fastened the bolt, took a large stick in her hand, and struck my head, cracking it open and causing blood to flow.' At that time, the householder's wife Vedehikā thus came to have an extremely bad reputation that spread throughout all directions: 'The householder's wife Vedehikā is of bad temperament, hasty, crude, and rough, unsettled, uncontrolled, and uncalmed.'

"Just so, there may be one who well guards and practices the conduct of the Well-Gone One, meaning because others do not speak harsh words to him. If others do not speak harsh words, he does not become angry, nor resentful and jealous, does not dwell in sorrowful entanglement, does not harbor resentment and anger, and does not expose others' faults. The bhikṣus, seeing this, think: 'This worthy one is patient, gentle, tolerant, well-controlled, well-settled, and well-calmed.' But if others speak harsh words to him, he becomes angry, resentful, and jealous, dwells in sorrowful entanglement, harbors resentment and anger, and exposes faults. The bhikṣus, seeing this, think: 'This worthy one is of bad temperament, hasty, crude, and rough, unsettled, uncontrolled, and uncalmed.'

"Furthermore, there are five kinds of speech that others may use: sometimes timely, sometimes untimely; sometimes true, sometimes untrue; sometimes gentle, sometimes harsh; sometimes with kindness, sometimes with anger; sometimes meaningful, sometimes meaningless. You all, if when others use these five kinds of speech, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows regarding these five kinds of speech: when others speak thus, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the one who speaks to you, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, pervade one direction and dwell in its accomplishment. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwell in its accomplishment. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and with a mind accompanied by equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way. It is like a person who brings a great spade and hoe and says: 'I will make this great earth into non-earth.' He then digs here and there, digs again and again, spits and urinates on it to defile it, speaks evil words, and says: 'Let the great earth become non-earth.' What do you think? Can that person, by these means, make this great earth into non-earth?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? This great earth is extremely deep, extremely vast, and immeasurable. Therefore that person, by these means, cannot make this great earth into non-earth. World-Honored One, that person would only exhaust himself in vain."

"Just so, there are these five kinds of speech that others may use: sometimes timely, sometimes untimely; sometimes true, sometimes untrue; sometimes gentle, sometimes harsh; sometimes with kindness, sometimes with anger; sometimes meaningful, sometimes meaningless. You all, if when others use these five kinds of speech, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows regarding these five kinds of speech: when others speak thus, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the one who speaks, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. Let your mind's practice be like the earth, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, and dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way. It is like a person who brings a large bundle of burning grass and says: 'I will heat the water of the Ganges River with this burning grass and make it into boiling water.' What do you think? Can that person, by these means, heat the Ganges water and make it into boiling water?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? World-Honored One, the Ganges water is extremely deep, extremely vast, and immeasurable. Therefore that person, by these means, cannot heat the Ganges water and make it into boiling water. World-Honored One, that person would only exhaust himself in vain."

"Just so, there are these five kinds of speech that others may use: sometimes timely, sometimes untimely; sometimes true, sometimes untrue; sometimes gentle, sometimes harsh; sometimes with kindness, sometimes with anger; sometimes meaningful, sometimes meaningless. You all, if when others use these five kinds of speech, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows regarding these five kinds of speech: when others speak thus, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the one who speaks, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. Let your mind's practice be like the Ganges water, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, and dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way. It is like a painter or a painter's apprentice who brings various pigments and says: 'I will paint forms and images in empty space and adorn them with colors.' What do you think? Can that painter or painter's apprentice, by these means, paint forms and images in empty space and adorn them with colors?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? World-Honored One, this empty space is without form, invisible, and without resistance. Therefore that painter or painter's apprentice, by these means, cannot paint forms and images in empty space and adorn them with colors. World-Honored One, that painter or painter's apprentice would only exhaust themselves in vain."

"Just so, there are these five kinds of speech that others may use: sometimes timely, sometimes untimely; sometimes true, sometimes untrue; sometimes gentle, sometimes harsh; sometimes with kindness, sometimes with anger; sometimes meaningful, sometimes meaningless. You all, if when others use these five kinds of speech, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows regarding these five kinds of speech: when others speak thus, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the one who speaks, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. Let your mind's practice be like empty space, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, and dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way. It is like a cat-skin bag, softly tanned until extremely supple, with all crackling sounds removed, without any crackling sound. If someone punches it with a fist, or throws stones at it, or strikes it with a stick, or slashes it with a knife, or throws it on the ground. What do you think? That cat-skin bag, softly tanned until extremely supple, with all crackling sounds removed, without any crackling sound, would it still produce any crackling sound?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? World-Honored One, that cat-skin bag is softly tanned until extremely supple, with all crackling sounds removed, without any crackling sound. Therefore it would no longer produce any crackling sound."

"Just so, bhikṣus, if other people punch you with fists, throw stones at you, strike you with sticks, or slash you with knives. You all, if when other people punch you with fists, throw stones, strike with sticks, or slash with knives, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows: if when other people punch you with fists, throw stones, strike with sticks, or slash with knives, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the person who strikes you, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. Let your mind's practice be like a cat-skin bag, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, and dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way. If bandits come and sever your limbs joint by joint with a sharp saw, you all, if when bandits come and sever your limbs joint by joint with a sharp saw, your mind changes or your mouth utters evil words, I say you will surely decline because of this. You should train as follows: if bandits come and sever your limbs joint by joint with a sharp saw, your mind should not change, your mouth should not utter evil words. Toward the person who cuts and severs you, generate a mind of compassion on their behalf. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, pervade one direction and dwell in its accomplishment. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwell in its accomplishment. Likewise with compassion, with sympathetic joy, and with a mind accompanied by equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurably well cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwell in its accomplishment. You should train in this way."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! You should frequently reflect upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas. Having frequently reflected upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas, do you see any unpleasant or harsh speech directed at you by others that, upon hearing, you could not endure?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One again praised the bhikṣus, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! You should frequently reflect upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas. Having frequently reflected upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas, if you travel to the east, you will surely attain peace and happiness, without any suffering or affliction. If you travel to the south, the west, or the north, you will surely attain peace and happiness, without any suffering or affliction. Excellent! Excellent! You should frequently reflect upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas. Having frequently reflected upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas, I would not even say that your wholesome dharmas merely remain as they are, let alone say they decline. Rather, day and night your wholesome dharmas will increase and grow, without decline. Excellent! Excellent! You should frequently reflect upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas. Having frequently reflected upon the Simile of the Saw, the teaching for śramaṇas, you will surely attain one of two fruits: either the attainment of ultimate knowledge in this present life, or, if there is a remainder, the attainment of the state of a non-returner."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Moliyaphagguna Sūtra, Second
