## Sūtra 194: The Bhadrapāla Sūtra, Third of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the state of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, undertaking the summer retreat.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I eat one meal at a single sitting. Having eaten one meal at a single sitting, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also train in eating one meal at a single sitting. Having eaten one meal at a single sitting, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness."

At that time, the Venerable Bhadrapāla was also present in the assembly. Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting. Why is this? If I were to eat one meal at a single sitting, I would be unable to accomplish my tasks, and would feel distressed and regretful. World-Honored One! Therefore I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! If I receive an invitation and you accompany me, I will permit you to eat the invited meal and set aside the one-meal-at-a-single-sitting practice. Bhadrapāla! If it is like this, you can manage your livelihood well."

The Venerable Bhadrapāla again said: "World-Honored One! Even so, I am still unable to eat one meal at a single sitting. Why is this? If I were to eat one meal at a single sitting, I would be unable to accomplish my tasks, and would feel distressed and regretful. World-Honored One! Therefore I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting."

The World-Honored One again, up to a second and third time, addressed the bhikṣus: "I eat one meal at a single sitting. Having eaten one meal at a single sitting, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also train in eating one meal at a single sitting. Having eaten one meal at a single sitting, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness."

The Venerable Bhadrapāla also, up to a second and third time, rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting. Why is this? If I were to eat one meal at a single sitting, I would be unable to accomplish my tasks, and would feel distressed and regretful. World-Honored One! Therefore I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting."

The World-Honored One also, up to a second and third time, said: "Bhadrapāla! If I receive an invitation and you accompany me, I will permit you to eat the invited meal and set aside the one-meal-at-a-single-sitting practice. Bhadrapāla! If it is like this, you can manage your livelihood well."

The Venerable Bhadrapāla also, up to a second and third time, said: "World-Honored One! Even so, I am still unable to eat one meal at a single sitting. Why is this? If I were to eat one meal at a single sitting, I would be unable to accomplish my tasks, and would feel distressed and regretful. World-Honored One! Therefore I am unable to eat one meal at a single sitting."

At that time, the World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only the Venerable Bhadrapāla declared that he was unable, and rose from his seat and left. Why was this? Because he did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla went into hiding for the entire summer and did not see the World-Honored One. Why was this? Because he did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings.

At that time, the bhikṣus were making robes for the Buddha. The World-Honored One had completed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī, and after three months had passed, having finished mending and preparing his robes, he gathered his robes, took up his bowl, and was about to journey among the people. The Venerable Bhadrapāla heard that the bhikṣus were making robes for the Buddha, that the World-Honored One had completed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī, and that after three months had passed, having finished mending and preparing his robes, he had gathered his robes, taken up his bowl, and was about to journey among the people. Having heard this, the Venerable Bhadrapāla went to where the bhikṣus were. The bhikṣus saw the Venerable Bhadrapāla coming from afar and said to him: "Worthy Bhadrapāla! You should know that these robes have been made for the Buddha. The World-Honored One has completed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī, and after three months have passed, having finished mending and preparing his robes, he has gathered his robes, taken up his bowl, and is about to journey among the people. Bhadrapāla, you should go there and guard yourself well, lest later there be much trouble."

Having heard these words, the Venerable Bhadrapāla went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said: "World-Honored One! I truly have transgressed. I truly have transgressed. I was like a fool, like one deluded, like one who does not understand, like one who is not good. Why is this? The World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only I declared that I was unable and rose from my seat and left. Why was this? Because I did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! Did you not know at that time that many bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs were undertaking the summer retreat in Śrāvastī? They knew of me and saw me, and knew that there was a bhikṣu named Bhadrapāla, a disciple of the World-Honored One, who did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Bhadrapāla! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadrapāla! Did you not know at that time that many upāsakas and upāsikās were dwelling in Śrāvastī? They knew of me and saw me, and knew that there was a bhikṣu named Bhadrapāla, a disciple of the World-Honored One, who did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Bhadrapāla! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadrapāla! Did you not know at that time that many śramaṇas and brahmins of other schools were undertaking the summer retreat in Śrāvastī? They knew of me and saw me, and knew that there was a bhikṣu named Bhadrapāla, a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, of renowned virtue, who did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Bhadrapāla! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadrapāla! If there were a bhikṣu who had attained liberation in both ways, and I were to say to him: 'Come, enter the mud,' Bhadrapāla, what do you think? When I instruct that bhikṣu, would that bhikṣu be able to stand still and move aside?"

The Venerable Bhadrapāla answered: "No."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! If there were a bhikṣu who, even if not one liberated in both ways, had wisdom-liberation; even if not one with wisdom-liberation, had body-witness; even if not a body-witness, had vision-attainment; even if not one with vision-attainment, had faith-liberation; even if not one with faith-liberation, was a Dharma-follower; even if not a Dharma-follower, was a faith-follower; and I were to say to him: 'Come, enter the mud,' Bhadrapāla, what do you think? When I instruct that bhikṣu, would that bhikṣu be able to stand still and move aside?"

The Venerable Bhadrapāla answered: "No."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! What do you think? At that time, had you attained the status of a faith-follower, a Dharma-follower, faith-liberation, vision-attainment, body-witness, wisdom-liberation, or liberation in both ways?"

The Venerable Bhadrapāla answered: "No."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! Were you not at that time like an empty house?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla, having been admonished to his face by the World-Honored One, harbored inner sorrow and grief, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence and had no words, as if waiting for something.

Then the World-Honored One, having admonished the Venerable Bhadrapāla to his face, wished to make him joyful again and said to him: "Bhadrapāla! At that time, you had no faith-tranquility toward me, no love-tranquility, no tranquility-tranquility. Why was this? I established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only you declared that you were unable and rose from your seat and left. Why was this? Because you did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings."

The Venerable Bhadrapāla said: "It is truly so. Why? The World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only I declared that I was unable and rose from my seat and left. Why? Because I did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. I only wish that the World-Honored One would accept my confession of wrongdoing. Having seen my fault, I shall repent of it, and from now on guard against it and never commit it again."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! Indeed, you were truly like a fool, like one deluded, like one who does not understand, like one who is not good. Why is this? I established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only you declared that you were unable and rose from your seat and left. Why? Because you did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Bhadrapāla! If, having transgressed, you see your fault and repent of it, and from now on guard against it and do not commit it again, Bhadrapāla, then in the noble Dharma and Vinaya you will increase and not decline. If, having transgressed, you see your fault and repent of it, and from now on guard against it and do not commit it again, Bhadrapāla, what do you think? If a bhikṣu does not train in the full precepts, and he dwells in a secluded place in a mountain forest beneath trees, or on high cliffs, silent and without sounds, remote, without evil, without people, in accordance with quiet sitting; and dwelling in that remote place, practicing with diligence, he attains the higher mind and dwells in the happiness of the present Dharma; and dwelling in that remote place, practicing with diligence, in peace, ease, and happiness, he falsely slanders the World-Honored One's precepts, and falsely slanders the devas, the wise ones, and those who practice the holy life, and also falsely slanders his own precepts. Having falsely slandered the World-Honored One's precepts, having falsely slandered the devas, the wise ones, and those who practice the holy life, and having also falsely slandered his own precepts, he does not give rise to delight. Not having given rise to delight, he does not give rise to joy. Not having given rise to joy, his body is not tranquilized. His body not being tranquilized, he does not experience happiness. Not experiencing happiness, his mind is not concentrated. Bhadrapāla! When the mind of the noble disciple is not concentrated, he does not see as it really is and does not know as it truly is.

"Bhadrapāla! What do you think? If a bhikṣu trains in the full precepts, and he dwells in a secluded place in a mountain forest beneath trees, or on high cliffs, silent and without sounds, remote, without evil, without people, in accordance with quiet sitting; and dwelling in that remote place, practicing with diligence, he attains the higher mind and dwells in the happiness of the present Dharma; and dwelling in that remote place, practicing with diligence, in peace, ease, and happiness, he does not falsely slander the World-Honored One's precepts, does not falsely slander the devas, the wise ones, and those who practice the holy life, and also does not falsely slander his own precepts. Not having falsely slandered the World-Honored One's precepts, not having falsely slandered the devas, the wise ones, and those who practice the holy life, and also not having falsely slandered his own precepts, he gives rise to delight. Having given rise to delight, he gives rise to joy. Having given rise to joy, his body is tranquilized. His body being tranquilized, he experiences happiness. Experiencing happiness, his mind becomes concentrated.

"Bhadrapāla! When the mind of the noble disciple is concentrated, he sees as it really is and knows as it truly is. Having seen as it really is and having known as it truly is, he is separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome states, and with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the first higher mind, and in the present Dharma obtaining peaceful dwelling, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in peace, ease, and happiness, leading to the ascent to nirvāṇa. When initial thought and sustained thought have ceased, with inner tranquility, with unified mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the second higher mind, and in the present Dharma obtaining peaceful dwelling, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in peace, ease, and happiness, leading to the ascent to nirvāṇa. Having separated from joy and desire, dwelling with equanimity, without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, and experiencing bodily happiness, which the noble ones describe as dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the third higher mind, and in the present Dharma obtaining peaceful dwelling, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in peace, ease, and happiness, leading to the ascent to nirvāṇa. With the cessation of pleasure and the cessation of pain, and with joy and sorrow having already ceased, neither in pain nor in pleasure, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the fourth higher mind, and in the present Dharma obtaining peaceful dwelling, easily and without difficulty, dwelling in happiness without fear, in peace, ease, and happiness, leading to the ascent to nirvāṇa.

"Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, without defilement, without affliction, soft and pliant, well-settled, having attained an imperturbable mind, he realizes the knowledge and spiritual penetration of recollecting past lives. With actions and characteristics, he recollects innumerable past experiences: one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, aeons of formation, aeons of destruction, innumerable aeons of formation and destruction. Those beings had such names, and such past experiences. 'I was once born there, with such a family name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pain and pleasure, such a lifespan, such a length of dwelling, such an end of life. Dying here, I was born there; dying there, I was born here. I was born in this place, with such a family name, such a personal name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pain and pleasure, such a lifespan, such a length of dwelling, such an end of life.' Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the first clear knowledge, because originally being without heedlessness, delighting in dwelling in seclusion, practicing with diligence: ignorance is destroyed and knowledge arises, darkness is destroyed and light is produced, delusion is destroyed and illumination arises. This is the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

"Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, without defilement, without affliction, soft and pliant, well-settled, having attained an imperturbable mind, he trains in and realizes the knowledge and spiritual penetration of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the pure divine eye surpassing that of humans, he sees beings at the time of dying and at the time of being born, of good appearance and bad appearance, of fine destiny and poor destiny, going to fortunate places and unfortunate places, in accordance with the actions these beings have performed, seeing them as they truly are. If these beings have accomplished evil bodily conduct, evil verbal and mental conduct, have slandered noble ones, have accomplished wrong views and the karma of wrong views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they certainly go to an unfortunate place and are born in hell. If these beings have accomplished good bodily conduct, good verbal and mental conduct, have not slandered noble ones, have accomplished right views and the karma of right views, then by these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they certainly ascend to a fortunate place and are born above in heaven. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the second clear knowledge, because originally being without heedlessness, delighting in dwelling in seclusion, practicing with diligence: ignorance is destroyed and knowledge arises, darkness is destroyed and light is produced, delusion is destroyed and illumination arises. This is the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

"Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, without defilement, without affliction, soft and pliant, well-settled, having attained an imperturbable mind, he trains in and realizes the knowledge and spiritual penetration of the destruction of the outflows. He knows this is suffering as it truly is; he knows this is the origin of suffering, he knows this is the cessation of suffering, he knows this is the path to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. He knows these are the outflows as they truly are; he knows this is the origin of the outflows, he knows this is the cessation of the outflows, he knows this is the path to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire, from the outflow of existence, and from the outflow of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of existence.' He knows as it truly is. Bhadrapāla! This is called at that time obtaining the third clear knowledge, because originally being without heedlessness, delighting in dwelling in seclusion, practicing with diligence: ignorance is destroyed and knowledge arises, darkness is destroyed and light is produced, delusion is destroyed and illumination arises. This is the clear knowledge realized through the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows."

Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! What is the cause and what is the condition that, when bhikṣus commit the same transgression of precepts, some are treated harshly and some are not treated harshly?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhadrapāla! There may be a bhikṣu who repeatedly transgresses the precepts. Because of his repeated transgressions, he is admonished by those practicing the holy life, on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others. Having been admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others, he speaks various irrelevant discourses and other matters, becomes angry, hateful, and jealous, erupts in rage and widespread malice, disturbs the community, shows contempt for the community, and speaks thus: 'I shall now do what will make the community pleased and agreeable, and I shall form such an intention.' Bhadrapāla! The bhikṣus then think: 'This worthy one repeatedly transgresses the precepts. Because of his repeated transgressions, he is admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others. Having been admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others, he speaks various irrelevant discourses and other matters, becomes angry, hateful, and jealous, erupts in rage and widespread malice, disturbs the community, shows contempt for the community, and speaks thus: "I shall now do what will make the community pleased and agreeable." Having seen this, they say: "Venerables! Let us observe and make this matter last a long time."' Bhadrapāla! The bhikṣus thus observe and make the matter last a long time.

"There may be a bhikṣu who repeatedly transgresses the precepts. Because of his repeated transgressions, he is admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others. Having been admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others, he does not speak various irrelevant discourses and other matters, does not become angry, hateful, and jealous, does not erupt in rage and widespread malice, does not disturb the community, does not show contempt for the community, and does not speak thus: 'I shall now do what will make the community pleased and agreeable, and I do not form such an intention.' Bhadrapāla! The bhikṣus then think: 'This worthy one repeatedly transgresses the precepts. Because of his repeated transgressions, he is admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others. Having been admonished by those practicing the holy life on the basis of what is seen, heard, or suspected by others, he does not speak various irrelevant discourses and other matters, does not become angry, hateful, and jealous, does not erupt in rage and widespread malice, does not disturb the community, does not show contempt for the community, and does not speak thus: "I shall now do what will make the community pleased and agreeable." Having seen this, they say: "Venerables! Let us observe and bring this matter to an early end."' Bhadrapāla! The bhikṣus thus observe and bring the matter to an early end. The same applies for minor transgressions of the precepts.

"Bhadrapāla! There may be a bhikṣu who has faith, has love, and has tranquility. Now this bhikṣu has faith, has love, and has tranquility. 'If we treat this worthy one harshly, since this worthy one has faith, has love, and has tranquility, because of this he will certainly break away. We should rather carefully look after and protect this worthy one.' The bhikṣus then carefully look after and protect him. Bhadrapāla! It is like a person who has only one eye. His relatives, out of loving concern and compassionate pity, seeking his benefit and welfare, seeking his peace, ease, and happiness, carefully look after and protect him, saying: 'Do not let this person be exposed to cold, heat, hunger, thirst, illness, or grief. Do not let there be dust, smoke, or dust and smoke.' Why is this? They further fear that this person may lose his one remaining eye, and therefore the relatives carefully look after and protect him. Bhadrapāla! In the same way, when a bhikṣu has little faith, little love, and little tranquility, the bhikṣus think: 'Now this bhikṣu has little faith, little love, and little tranquility. If we treat this worthy one harshly, since this worthy one has little faith, little love, and little tranquility, because of this he will certainly break away. We should rather carefully look after and protect this worthy one.' Therefore the bhikṣus carefully look after and protect him, just as relatives protect a one-eyed person."

Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! What is the cause and what is the condition that in former times, few precepts were established, yet many bhikṣus observed and upheld them? What is the cause and what is the condition that now the World-Honored One establishes many precepts, yet few bhikṣus observe and uphold them?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhadrapāla! When the community of bhikṣus has not attained material gains, the community does not produce desirable states. When the community attains material gains, the community produces desirable states. Having produced desirable states, the World-Honored One, wishing to cut off these desirable states, then establishes precepts for his disciples. The same applies for fame, eminence, being known to kings, having great merit, and extensive learning. Bhadrapāla! When the community has not become widely learned, the community does not produce desirable states. When the community becomes widely learned, the community produces desirable states. Having produced desirable states, the World-Honored One, wishing to cut off these desirable states, then establishes precepts for his disciples. Bhadrapāla! It is not for the purpose of cutting off outflows in the present life that I establish precepts for my disciples. I establish precepts for my disciples for the purpose of cutting off outflows in future lives. Bhadrapāla! Therefore I establish precepts for my disciples to cut off outflows, so that they receive my teaching. Bhadrapāla! In former times I taught the bhikṣus the Dharma teaching of the simile of the thoroughbred horse. As for this matter, what was the reason? Do you remember?"

The Venerable Bhadrapāla said: "World-Honored One! There is a reason in this matter. Why is this? The World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal at a single sitting. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Only I declared that I was unable and rose from my seat and left, because I did not train in the full precepts and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. World-Honored One! This is the reason in this matter."

The World-Honored One further said: "Bhadrapāla! The reason in this matter is not only that. Bhadrapāla! If I were to teach the bhikṣus the Dharma teaching of the simile of the thoroughbred horse, you would certainly not have been single-minded, would not have been properly respectful, and would not have listened attentively. Bhadrapāla! This is the further reason in this matter."

Thereupon, the Venerable Bhadrapāla rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! Now is the right time. Well-Gone One! Now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus the Dharma teaching of the simile of the thoroughbred horse, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the World-Honored One, will well receive and uphold it."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhadrapāla! Just as a skilled horse-trainer obtains a pure thoroughbred horse, that trainer first works on its mouth. Having worked on its mouth, there is displeasure at the movements, whether willing or unwilling. Why is this? Because it has never been trained before. Bhadrapāla! When the thoroughbred horse, through the trainer's first training, achieves success, the horse-trainer then further trains it with the bit in its mouth and fetters on its feet, with fettered feet and bitted mouth, making it gallop, making it step over a threshold, so that it is fit for the king's chariot with supreme conduct and supreme restraint, training all its limbs and joints, fully training it to completion. There may be displeasure at the movements, whether willing or unwilling. Why is this? Because of the repeated training. Bhadrapāla! When the thoroughbred horse, through the trainer's repeated training, achieves success, at that time it is tamed, well-tamed, attains supreme tameness, attains the foremost supreme tameness, supreme conduct, attains the foremost conduct, and is then fit for the king's chariot, eats the king's grain, and is praised as the king's horse.

"Bhadrapāla! In the same way, when a wise and good person is endowed with the ten qualities of one beyond training: right view of one beyond training, up to right knowledge of one beyond training, at that time he is tamed, well-tamed, attains supreme tameness, attains the foremost supreme tameness, supreme calm, attains the foremost calm, has removed all crookedness, removed all defilement, removed all fear, removed all delusion, removed all deceit, stopped all dust, purified all stains, and is without attachment. He is worthy of respect, worthy of reverence, worthy of offerings, worthy of homage, and is a supreme field of merit for all devas and humans."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Bhadrapāla and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Bhadrapāla Sūtra, Third

---

## Sūtra 195: The Aśvajit Sūtra, Fourth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Kāśi, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, staying in a certain place. He addressed the bhikṣus: "I eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness."

At that time, the World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal per day. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Then the World-Honored One traveled on and arrived at Kālarāka, staying in the Śiśapā Forest north of the village of Kālarāka.

At that time, in Kālarāka there were two bhikṣus: one named Aśvajit and the other named Punarvasuka. They were established local landlords, monastery heads, and leaders of the community. They ate in the morning, ate in the evening, ate during the day, and ate after midday. Having eaten in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday, they were free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, their bodies were light and comfortable, their strength was vigorous and robust, and they abided in peace, ease, and happiness. Many bhikṣus, having heard this, went to where the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka were and said to them: "Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! The World-Honored One was traveling in the state of Kāśi, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, staying in a certain place, and he addressed the bhikṣus: 'I eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness.' At that time, the World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal per day. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should not go against the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus."

Having heard this, Aśvajit and Punarvasuka replied: "Worthy ones! We eat in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday. Having eaten in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday, we are free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, our bodies are light and comfortable, our strength is vigorous and robust, and we abide in peace, ease, and happiness. Why should we abandon what is present and wait for what comes later?" This happened up to three times.

The many bhikṣus were unable to make Aśvajit and Punarvasuka abandon their evil wrong views. They rose from their seats, left them, and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Here in Kālarāka there are two bhikṣus, one named Aśvajit and the other named Punarvasuka. They are established local landlords, monastery heads, and leaders of the community. They eat in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday. Having eaten in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday, they are free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, their bodies are light and comfortable, their strength is vigorous and robust, and they abide in peace, ease, and happiness. World-Honored One! We heard this and went to where the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka were, and said to them: 'Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! The World-Honored One was traveling in the state of Kāśi, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, staying in a certain place, and he addressed the bhikṣus: "I eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness." At that time, the World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal per day. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should not go against the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.'

"Having heard this, Aśvajit and Punarvasuka replied to us: 'Worthy ones! We eat in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday. Having eaten in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday, we are free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, our bodies are light and comfortable, our strength is vigorous and robust, and we abide in peace, ease, and happiness. Why should we abandon what is present and wait for what comes later?' This happened up to three times. World-Honored One! We were unable to make Aśvajit and Punarvasuka abandon their evil wrong views, so we rose from our seats, left them, and departed."

Having heard this, the World-Honored One told a certain bhikṣu: "Go to where the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka are and speak to them thus: 'Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! The World-Honored One summons you.'"

That bhikṣu, having heard this, said: "Yes, World-Honored One!" He then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka were and spoke to them thus: "Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! The World-Honored One summons you worthy ones."

Having heard this, Aśvajit and Punarvasuka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! Did the many bhikṣus truly say to you: 'The bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka, the World-Honored One was traveling in the state of Kāśi, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, staying in a certain place, and he addressed the bhikṣus: "I eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, I am free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, my body is light and comfortable, my strength is vigorous and robust, and I abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness." At that time, the World-Honored One established for the assembly of bhikṣus the precept of eating one meal per day. All the bhikṣus in the assembly respectfully trained in the precept and in the World-Honored One's domain of subtle and wonderful teachings. Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! You should also eat one meal per day. Having eaten one meal per day, you will be free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, your bodies will be light and comfortable, your strength vigorous and robust, and you will abide in peace, ease, and happiness. You should not go against the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.'

"Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! Having heard this, did you say to the bhikṣus: 'Worthy ones! We eat in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday. Having eaten in the morning, in the evening, during the day, and after midday, we are free from concerns and desires, without illness or pain, our bodies are light and comfortable, our strength is vigorous and robust, and we abide in peace, ease, and happiness. Why should we abandon what is present and wait for what comes later?' This happened up to three times. Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! Were the bhikṣus unable to make you abandon your evil wrong views, and did they rise from their seats, leave you, and depart?"

Aśvajit and Punarvasuka answered: "It is truly so."

The World-Honored One said: "Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! Do you understand that I teach the Dharma thus: If one experiences a pleasant feeling, having experienced that pleasant feeling, evil and unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease? If one experiences a painful feeling, having experienced that painful feeling, evil and unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase?"

Aśvajit and Punarvasuka answered: "Indeed so. We understand that the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma thus: If one experiences a pleasant feeling, having experienced that pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease. If one experiences a painful feeling, having experienced that painful feeling, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase."

The World-Honored One rebuked the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Punarvasuka: "You foolish ones! How do you know that I teach the Dharma thus? You foolish ones! From whose mouth have you heard that I teach the Dharma thus? You foolish ones! I did not teach in a one-sided way, yet you hold to it in a one-sided manner. You foolish ones! When the many bhikṣus spoke to you, you should have answered in accordance with the Dharma thus: 'We do not yet know. We shall ask the bhikṣus.'"

Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you also understand that I teach the Dharma thus: If one experiences a pleasant feeling, having experienced that pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease? If one experiences a painful feeling, having experienced that painful feeling, unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase?"

The many bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One further asked: "How then do you understand that I teach the Dharma?"

The many bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One! We understand that the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma thus: There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase. World-Honored One! We understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One in this way."

Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus: "Excellent! Excellent! If you say thus: There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase. Why is this? I also teach thus: There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a pleasant feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states increase while wholesome states decrease. There are cases where one experiences a painful feeling and evil unwholesome states decrease while wholesome states increase.

"If I did not know as it truly is, did not see, did not understand, did not attain, did not fully and perfectly awaken, that there are pleasant feelings where unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, I should not say to abandon those pleasant feelings. If I did not know as it truly is, did not see, did not understand, did not attain, did not fully and perfectly awaken, that there are pleasant feelings where evil unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, I should not say to cultivate those pleasant feelings. If I did not know as it truly is, did not see, did not understand, did not attain, did not fully and perfectly awaken, that there are painful feelings where evil unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, I should not say to abandon those painful feelings. If I did not know as it truly is, did not see, did not understand, did not attain, did not fully and perfectly awaken, that there are painful feelings where evil unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, I should not say to cultivate those painful feelings.

"Because I know as it truly is, see, understand, attain, and fully and perfectly awaken, that there are pleasant feelings where evil unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, therefore I say to abandon those pleasant feelings. Because I know as it truly is, see, understand, attain, and fully and perfectly awaken, that there are pleasant feelings where evil unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, therefore I say to cultivate those pleasant feelings. Because I know as it truly is, see, understand, attain, and fully and perfectly awaken, that there are painful feelings where evil unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decrease, therefore I say to abandon those painful feelings. Because I know as it truly is, see, understand, attain, and fully and perfectly awaken, that there are painful feelings where evil unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase, therefore I say to cultivate those painful feelings. Why is this? I do not say to cultivate all bodily pleasure, nor do I say not to cultivate all bodily pleasure. I do not say to cultivate all bodily pain, nor do I say not to cultivate all bodily pain. I do not say to cultivate all mental pleasure, nor do I say not to cultivate all mental pleasure. I do not say to cultivate all mental pain, nor do I say not to cultivate all mental pain.

"What bodily pleasure do I say not to cultivate? If cultivating bodily pleasure causes evil unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decrease, such bodily pleasure I say not to cultivate. What bodily pleasure do I say to cultivate? If cultivating bodily pleasure causes evil unwholesome states to decrease and wholesome states to increase, such bodily pleasure I say to cultivate. What bodily pain do I say not to cultivate? If cultivating bodily pain causes evil unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decrease, such bodily pain I say not to cultivate. What bodily pain do I say to cultivate? If cultivating bodily pain causes evil unwholesome states to decrease and wholesome states to increase, such bodily pain I say to cultivate. What mental pleasure do I say not to cultivate? If cultivating mental pleasure causes evil unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decrease, such mental pleasure I say not to cultivate. What mental pleasure do I say to cultivate? If cultivating mental pleasure causes evil unwholesome states to decrease and wholesome states to increase, such mental pleasure I say to cultivate. What mental pain do I say not to cultivate? If cultivating mental pain causes evil unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decrease, such mental pain I say not to cultivate. What mental pain do I say to cultivate? If cultivating mental pain causes evil unwholesome states to decrease and wholesome states to increase, such mental pain I say to cultivate. When one knows as it truly is what should be cultivated and also knows as it truly is what should not be cultivated; when one knows as it truly is what should be cultivated and also knows as it truly is what should not be cultivated, then one does not cultivate what should not be cultivated and cultivates what should be cultivated. Not cultivating what should not be cultivated and cultivating what should be cultivated, evil unwholesome states decrease and wholesome states increase.

"I do not say that all bhikṣus should practice heedfulness, nor do I say that all bhikṣus should not practice heedfulness. What bhikṣus do I say need not practice heedfulness? If there is a bhikṣu who has attained liberation in both ways. How does a bhikṣu have liberation in both ways? If there is a bhikṣu who has contacted and attained through his body the eight liberations, and through wisdom has seen that all outflows are ended and known, such a bhikṣu has liberation in both ways. This bhikṣu I say need not practice heedfulness. Why is this? This worthy one has already practiced heedfulness in the past. If this worthy one were to be heedless, that is simply impossible. Therefore I say this bhikṣu need not practice heedfulness. If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways but has wisdom-liberation, how does a bhikṣu have wisdom-liberation? If there is a bhikṣu who has not contacted and attained through his body the eight liberations, but through wisdom has seen that all outflows are ended and known, such a bhikṣu has wisdom-liberation. This bhikṣu I say need not practice heedfulness. Why is this? This worthy one has already practiced heedfulness in the past. If this worthy one were to be heedless, that is simply impossible. Therefore I say this bhikṣu need not practice heedfulness. These two kinds of bhikṣus I say need not practice heedfulness.

"What bhikṣus do I say should practice heedfulness? If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways and also does not have wisdom-liberation, but has body-witness. How does a bhikṣu have body-witness? If there is a bhikṣu who has contacted and attained through his body the eight liberations, but through wisdom has not seen that all outflows are ended and known, such a bhikṣu has body-witness. This bhikṣu I say should practice heedfulness. What fruit do I see from this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness, such that I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness? Perhaps this bhikṣu will seek to guard his faculties, associate with good friends, practice in accordance with appropriate dwelling and restraint, and all outflows being ended, he will attain the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and in the present life will himself know, himself realize, himself accomplish and dwell in it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of existence.' He will know as it truly is. I see this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness as having such fruit. Therefore I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness.

"If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways, does not have wisdom-liberation, and also does not have body-witness, but has vision-attainment. How does a bhikṣu have vision-attainment? If there is a bhikṣu who has single-minded, resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and according to whatever Dharma he hears, he contemplates with higher wisdom and accepts with higher patience, such a bhikṣu has vision-attainment. This bhikṣu I say should practice heedfulness. What fruit do I see from this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness, such that I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness? Perhaps this bhikṣu will seek to guard his faculties, associate with good friends, practice in accordance with appropriate dwelling and restraint, and all outflows being ended, he will attain the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and in the present life will himself know, himself realize, himself accomplish and dwell in it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of existence.' He will know as it truly is. I see this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness as having such fruit. Therefore I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness.

"If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways, does not have wisdom-liberation, does not have body-witness, and also does not have vision-attainment, but has faith-liberation. How does a bhikṣu have faith-liberation? If there is a bhikṣu who has single-minded, resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and according to whatever Dharma he hears, he contemplates with wisdom and accepts, but not to the degree of one with vision-attainment, such a bhikṣu has faith-liberation. This bhikṣu I say should practice heedfulness. What fruit do I see from this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness, such that I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness? Perhaps this bhikṣu will seek to guard his faculties, associate with good friends, practice in accordance with appropriate dwelling and restraint, and all outflows being ended, he will attain the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and in the present life will himself know, himself realize, himself accomplish and dwell in it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, there will be no more receiving of existence.' He will know as it truly is. I see this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness as having such fruit. Therefore I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness.

"If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways, does not have wisdom-liberation, does not have body-witness, does not have vision-attainment, and also does not have faith-liberation, but is a Dharma-follower. How is a bhikṣu a Dharma-follower? If there is a bhikṣu who has single-minded, resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and according to whatever Dharma he hears, he contemplates with higher wisdom and accepts with higher patience, such a bhikṣu is a Dharma-follower. This bhikṣu I say should practice heedfulness. What fruit do I see from this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness, such that I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness? Perhaps this bhikṣu will seek to guard his faculties, associate with good friends, practice in accordance with appropriate dwelling and restraint, and of two fruits he will certainly attain one: either in the present life he will attain ultimate knowledge, or if there is a remainder, he will attain the state of a non-returner. I see this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness as having such fruit. Therefore I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness.

"If there is a bhikṣu who does not have liberation in both ways, does not have wisdom-liberation, does not have body-witness, does not have vision-attainment, does not have faith-liberation, and is also not a Dharma-follower, but is a faith-follower. How is a bhikṣu a faith-follower? If there is a bhikṣu who has single-minded, resolute faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and according to whatever Dharma he hears, he contemplates with wisdom and accepts, but not to the degree of a Dharma-follower, such a bhikṣu is a faith-follower. This bhikṣu I say should practice heedfulness. What fruit do I see from this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness, such that I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness? Perhaps this bhikṣu will seek to guard his faculties, associate with good friends, practice in accordance with appropriate dwelling and restraint, and of two fruits he will certainly attain one: either in the present life he will attain ultimate knowledge, or if there is a remainder, he will attain the state of a non-returner. I see this bhikṣu's practice of heedfulness as having such fruit. Therefore I say this bhikṣu should practice heedfulness. These bhikṣus I say should practice heedfulness.

"I do not say that all bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge, nor do I say that all bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge from the very start. Rather, through gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress, receiving instruction and receiving admonishment, afterward the bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge. How is it that through gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress, receiving instruction and receiving admonishment, afterward the bhikṣus attain the ultimate knowledge they attain? When one has faith, one approaches. Having approached, one draws near and attends. Having drawn near and attended, one listens to the Dharma single-mindedly. Having listened to the Dharma single-mindedly, one retains the Dharma. Having retained the Dharma, one reflects upon it. Having reflected upon it, one weighs and examines it. Having weighed and examined it, one investigates it. When the noble disciple investigates, he realizes through his body the truth and contemplates with higher wisdom. He then thinks: 'This truth I had not previously realized through my body, nor had I contemplated it with higher wisdom. Now I realize this truth through my body and contemplate it with higher wisdom.' It is in this way that through gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress, receiving instruction and receiving admonishment, afterward the bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge, and this is the ultimate knowledge these bhikṣus attain."

Then the World-Honored One said: "Aśvajit! Punarvasuka! There is a teaching called the four propositions. I wish to explain it for you. Do you wish to know it?"

Aśvajit and Punarvasuka said: "World-Honored One! Who are we? How could we know the Dharma?"

Thereupon the World-Honored One had this thought: "These foolish people! They have gone far beyond this true Dharma and Vinaya of mine, extremely far away. If there were a teacher of Dharma and Vinaya who was attached to food and not free from food, even his disciples should not quickly practice heedlessness. How much more so when I am not attached to food and am far removed from food! A faithful disciple should speak thus: 'The World-Honored One is my teacher, and I am the World-Honored One's disciple. The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma for me, the Well-Gone One teaches the Dharma for me, enabling me to attain benefit, welfare, peace, ease, and happiness throughout the long night.'

"If a faithful disciple accomplishes much in the domain of the World-Honored One, benefits much in the domain of the World-Honored One, practices much in the domain of the World-Honored One, enters the domain of the World-Honored One, and abides in the domain of the World-Honored One, then whether he travels to the east, he will certainly attain peace and happiness without manifold sufferings and afflictions; whether he travels to the south, the west, or the north, he will certainly attain peace and happiness without manifold sufferings and afflictions. If a faithful disciple accomplishes much in the domain of the World-Honored One, benefits much in the domain of the World-Honored One, practices much in the domain of the World-Honored One, enters the domain of the World-Honored One, and abides in the domain of the World-Honored One, I do not even say that wholesome states will merely remain as they are, let alone say they will decline. Rather, day and night wholesome states will increase and not decline. If a faithful disciple accomplishes much in the domain of the World-Honored One, benefits much in the domain of the World-Honored One, practices much in the domain of the World-Honored One, enters the domain of the World-Honored One, and abides in the domain of the World-Honored One, of two fruits he will certainly attain one: either in the present life he will attain ultimate knowledge, or if there is a remainder, he will attain the state of a non-returner."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Aśvajit Sūtra, Fourth
