## (196) Sūtra on Cunda, Fifth of the Great Chapters

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the Vajji country, staying in the village of Sāmagāma.

At that time, the novice Cunda had spent the rains retreat in Pāvā. In that Pāvā there was a Nirgrantha named Jñātaputra, who had passed away there. Not long after his death, the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's disciples each broke apart and did not dwell in harmony together. They spoke of division and matters of disharmony, quarreling, binding one another in disputes, hating each other and contending: "I know this Dharma; you do not know it. What Dharma do you know that compares with what I know? I am well-ordered; you are not well-ordered. I am consistent; you are not consistent. What should be said first you say last; what should be said last you say first. I am superior; you are inferior. I question you on a matter, and you cannot answer. I have already defeated you; I shall question you further. If you stir, I shall bind you further." Mutually arrogant, they only sought to prevail in speech, and there was none to rebuke them. As for the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's lay white-robed disciples, they all became weary and disgusted with these disciples of the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra. Why was this? Because what they taught was a bad dharma and vinaya, not leading to liberation, not tending toward right awakening, and not taught by the Well-Gone One. It was collapsed and without pillars, without refuge or support, and their revered teacher was not a Tathāgata, an Unattached One, a Perfectly Enlightened One.

Thereupon, after the novice Cunda had completed the rains retreat, when the three months had passed and he had finished mending his robes, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled to the village of Sāmagāma, staying in the Śiśapā Grove north of the village of Sāmagāma. The novice Cunda went to the Venerable Ānanda's place. Having arrived, he bowed at his feet and sat to one side. The Venerable Ānanda asked: "Worthy Cunda, from where have you come? Where did you spend the rains retreat?"

The novice Cunda answered: "Venerable Ānanda, I have come from Pāvā, where I spent the rains retreat. Venerable Ānanda, in that Pāvā there was a Nirgrantha named Jñātaputra, who passed away there. Not long after his death, the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's disciples each broke apart and did not dwell in harmony together. They spoke of division and matters of disharmony, quarreling, binding one another in disputes, hating each other and contending: 'I know this Dharma; you do not know it. What Dharma do you know that compares with what I know? I am well-ordered; you are not well-ordered. I am consistent; you are not consistent. What should be said first you say last; what should be said last you say first. I am superior; you are inferior. I question you on a matter, and you cannot answer. I have already defeated you; I shall question you further. If you stir, I shall bind you further.' Mutually arrogant, they only sought to prevail in speech, and there was none to rebuke them. As for the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's lay white-robed disciples, they all became weary and disgusted with these disciples of the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra. Why was this? Because what they taught was a bad dharma and vinaya, not leading to liberation, not tending toward right awakening, and not taught by the Well-Gone One. It was collapsed and without pillars, without refuge or support, and their revered teacher was not a Tathāgata, an Unattached One, a Perfectly Enlightened One."

The Venerable Ānanda, having heard this, said: "Worthy Cunda, by reason of this matter, we should go to see the Buddha and offer this report to the World-Honored One. Worthy Cunda, let us now go together to the Buddha and fully relate this matter to the World-Honored One. Perhaps by this we may hear a different teaching from the World-Honored One."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went together to the Buddha. They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet. The Venerable Ānanda stood to one side, and the novice Cunda sat to one side.

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, today the novice Cunda came to my place, bowed his head at my feet, and sat to one side. I asked: 'Worthy Cunda, from where have you come? Where did you spend the rains retreat?' The novice Cunda answered me saying: 'Venerable Ānanda, I have come from Pāvā, where I spent the rains retreat. Venerable Ānanda, in that Pāvā there was a Nirgrantha named Jñātaputra, who passed away there. Not long after his death, the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's disciples each broke apart and did not dwell in harmony together. They spoke of division and matters of disharmony, quarreling, binding one another in disputes, hating each other and contending: "I know this Dharma; you do not know it. What Dharma do you know that compares with what I know? I am well-ordered; you are not well-ordered. I am consistent; you are not consistent. What should be said first you say last; what should be said last you say first. I am superior; you are inferior. I question you on a matter, and you cannot answer. I have already defeated you; I shall question you further. If you stir, I shall bind you further." Mutually arrogant, they only sought to prevail in speech, and there was none to rebuke them. As for the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra's lay white-robed disciples, they all became weary and disgusted with these disciples of the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra. Why was this? Because what they taught was a bad dharma and vinaya, not leading to liberation, not tending toward right awakening, and not taught by the Well-Gone One. It was collapsed and without pillars, without refuge or support, and their revered teacher was not a Tathāgata, an Unattached One, a Perfectly Enlightened One.'

"World-Honored One, when I heard this, I was fearful and alarmed, and the hairs of my body stood on end, thinking: 'Let there not be a bhikṣu who, after the World-Honored One's passing, gives rise to such quarrels in the community, for such quarrels do not benefit many people; many people will have suffering. They are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and they cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans.' World-Honored One, I saw a bhikṣu sitting before the World-Honored One, with a devoted mind deeply reverencing the World-Honored One, well-protecting the Well-Gone One. World-Honored One, seeing this, I thought: 'If this bhikṣu, after the World-Honored One's passing, gives rise to such quarrels in the community, such quarrels would not benefit many people; many people would have suffering. They would not be righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and they would cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans.'"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked: "Ānanda, what kind of quarrels do you see arising in the community that do not benefit many people, that cause many people to have suffering, that are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and that cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "World-Honored One, I refer to quarrels that arise in the community because of higher morality, higher mind, and higher insight. World-Honored One, such quarrels do not benefit many people; many people have suffering. They are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and they cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, such quarrels are quite minor, those arising because of higher morality, higher mind, and higher insight. Ānanda, if quarrels arise in the community because of the path and the way of the path, such quarrels do not benefit many people; many people have suffering. They are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness. Ānanda, do you see among them two bhikṣus, each with different views, giving rise to quarrels: 'This is Dharma; this is not Dharma. This is Vinaya; this is not Vinaya. This is an offense; this is not an offense. This is light; this is heavy. This can be repented; this cannot be repented. This can be guarded against; this cannot be guarded against. This has a remainder; this has no remainder. This arises; this does not arise.' Ānanda, what do you think? The collection of my Dharma, which I myself knew, myself awakened to, and myself realized and attained: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path. Ānanda, the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra truly was not omniscient, yet he claimed to be omniscient. Ānanda, if the Nirgrantha Jñātaputra were one of all-knowledge and all-seeing, he would have established for his disciples six roots of quarrels, which could be heard and thereby stopped."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, now is the right time. Well-Gone One, now is the right time. If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus about the six roots of quarrels, the bhikṣus, having heard from the World-Honored One, will well receive and uphold them."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, listen carefully and consider it well. I shall thoroughly explain it for you."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "So it shall be. I shall receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, suppose there is a person who is angry and resentful, bound by fetters. Ānanda, when a person is angry and resentful, bound by fetters, that person does not respect the teacher, does not see the Dharma, and does not guard the precepts. Not respecting the teacher, not seeing the Dharma, and not guarding the precepts, that person then gives rise to such quarrels in the community. Such quarrels do not benefit many people; many people have suffering. They are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and they cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans. Ānanda, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, are not yet exhausted, then to cut off these quarrels, you should quickly seek skillful means, practice with extreme diligence, right mindfulness and right wisdom, enduring without regression. Ānanda, just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire urgently seeks means to save the head or clothing, so too, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, are not yet exhausted, then to cut off these quarrels, you should quickly seek skillful means, practice with extreme diligence, right mindfulness and right wisdom, enduring without regression. Ānanda, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, have been exhausted, you should further guard that mind, ever without negligence, wishing to stop these quarrels, and thus you cut off the root of these quarrels. Ānanda, just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire urgently seeks means to save the head or clothing, so too, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, have been exhausted, you should further guard that mind, ever without negligence, wishing to stop these quarrels, and thus you cut off the root of these quarrels.

"Likewise with the fetter of silence, the fetter of miserliness, jealousy, flattery and deceit, shamelessness, lack of moral dread, evil desires, wrong views, and evil dispositions that are uncontrollable. Ānanda, if there is a person with evil desires, wrong views, and evil dispositions that are uncontrollable, that person does not respect the teacher, does not see the Dharma, and does not guard the precepts. Not respecting the teacher, not seeing the Dharma, and not guarding the precepts, that person then gives rise to such quarrels in the community. Such quarrels do not benefit many people; many people have suffering. They are not righteous, not beneficial, not for peace and happiness, and they cause extreme suffering and distress even for gods and humans. Ānanda, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, are not yet exhausted, then to cut off these quarrels, you should quickly seek skillful means, practice with extreme diligence, right mindfulness and right wisdom, enduring without regression. Ānanda, just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire urgently seeks means to save the head or clothing, so too, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, are not yet exhausted, then to cut off these quarrels, you should quickly seek skillful means, practice with extreme diligence, right mindfulness and right wisdom, enduring without regression. Ānanda, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, have been exhausted, you should further guard that mind, ever without negligence, wishing to stop these quarrels, and thus you cut off the root of these quarrels. Ānanda, just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire urgently seeks means to save the head or clothing, so too, if such quarrels, whether seen internally or externally, have been exhausted, you should further guard that mind, ever without negligence, wishing to stop these quarrels, and thus you cut off the root of these quarrels.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, there are seven methods for settling quarrels. First, one should apply the vinaya of settling in the presence. Second, one should apply the vinaya of settling by recollection. Third, one should apply the vinaya of settling by non-insanity. Fourth, one should apply the vinaya of settling by self-confession. Fifth, one should apply the vinaya of settling by majority decision. Sixth, one should apply the vinaya of settling by successive referral. Seventh, one should apply the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse. Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling in the presence? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling in the presence. Ānanda, one person admonishes and corrects one person, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. One person admonishes and corrects two persons; one person admonishes and corrects many persons; one person admonishes and corrects the assembly, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Two persons admonish and correct two persons, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Two persons admonish and correct many persons; two persons admonish and correct the assembly; two persons admonish and correct one person, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Many persons admonish and correct many persons, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Many persons admonish and correct the assembly; many persons admonish and correct one person; many persons admonish and correct two persons, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. The assembly admonishes and corrects the assembly, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. The assembly admonishes and corrects one person; the assembly admonishes and corrects two persons; the assembly admonishes and corrects many persons, guarding according to the Dharma and Vinaya as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling in the presence. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling in the presence.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling by recollection? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling by recollection. Ānanda, suppose there is a person who has violated the precepts but does not remember it. The bhikṣus, having seen this, say to that person: 'You have violated the precepts but do not yourself remember it. You should seek from the assembly the vinaya of recollection, and the assembly will jointly give the worthy one the vinaya of recollection.' Ānanda, wherever there is an assembly gathered in harmony, that bhikṣu should go there, bare one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, bow his head at the feet of the elder senior bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder senior bhikṣus saying: 'Venerables, hear me. I once violated the precepts but do not remember it. I now seek from the assembly the vinaya of recollection. May the assembly in harmony grant me the vinaya of recollection.' Ānanda, for the sake of that bhikṣu, the assembly gathers in harmony and should grant the vinaya of recollection, according to the Dharma and Vinaya, as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling by recollection. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling by recollection.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling by non-insanity? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling by non-insanity. Ānanda, suppose there is a person who became insane and whose mind was deranged. Having become insane and mentally deranged, that person committed many impure deeds, which were not the conduct of a renunciant, not in accordance with proper practice, and were spoken of as violations. Later, that person recovered his original mind. The bhikṣus, having seen this, say to that person: 'You became insane and your mind was deranged. Being insane and mentally deranged, you committed many impure deeds, which were not the conduct of a renunciant, not in accordance with proper practice, and were spoken of as violations. Later, the worthy one recovered his original mind. The worthy one may seek from the assembly the vinaya of non-insanity, and the assembly will jointly grant the worthy one the vinaya of non-insanity.' Ānanda, wherever there is an assembly gathered in harmony, that bhikṣu should go there, bare one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, bow his head at the feet of the elder senior bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder senior bhikṣus saying: 'Venerables, hear me. I once became insane and my mind was deranged. Being insane and mentally deranged, I committed many impure deeds, which were not the conduct of a renunciant, not in accordance with proper practice, and were spoken of as violations. Later I recovered my original mind. I now seek from the assembly the vinaya of non-insanity. May the assembly in harmony grant me the vinaya of non-insanity.' Ānanda, for the sake of that bhikṣu, the assembly gathers in harmony and should grant the vinaya of non-insanity, according to the Dharma and Vinaya, as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling by non-insanity. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling by non-insanity.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling by self-confession? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling by self-confession. Ānanda, suppose there is a person who has violated the precepts. There may be some who speak of it and some who do not; there may be some who remember it and some who do not. Ānanda, wherever there is an assembly gathered in harmony, that bhikṣu should go there, bare one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, bow his head at the feet of the elder senior bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder senior bhikṣus saying: 'Venerables, hear me. I have violated such-and-such a precept. I now, before the elder senior bhikṣus, sincerely confess and openly declare it, not daring to conceal it, and I shall guard the precepts well henceforth and not commit such offenses again.' Ānanda, the assembly of bhikṣus should then ask that bhikṣu: 'Worthy one, do you yourself see the offense you committed?' He should answer: 'I truly see the offense I committed.' The assembly should then tell him: 'Guard the precepts well henceforth and do not commit such offenses again.' Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling by self-confession. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling by self-confession.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling by majority decision? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling by majority decision. Ānanda, suppose there is a person who is shameless, who does not repent what is seen or heard, and who, based on suspicion from others, has evil desires. Having violated the precepts, he claims to know one thing, then claims to see another; having claimed to know, he then claims to see; having claimed to see, he then claims to know. In the assembly he claims to know one thing; in the assembly he claims to see another; having claimed to know, he then claims to see; having claimed to see, he then claims to know. Ānanda, for the sake of that bhikṣu, the assembly gathers in harmony and should apply the majority decision: the majority finds him without principle and without reason; the majority finds him evil and unwholesome. Why is this? Because having violated the precepts, he claimed to know one thing, then claimed to see another; having claimed to know, he claimed to see; having claimed to see, he claimed to know. In the assembly he claimed to know one thing; in the assembly he claimed to see another; having claimed to know, he claimed to see; having claimed to see, he claimed to know. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling by majority decision. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling by majority decision.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling by successive referral? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling by successive referral. Ānanda, suppose two bhikṣus have a quarrel arise between them over various views, namely: 'This is Dharma; this is not Dharma. This is Vinaya; this is not Vinaya. This is an offense; this is not an offense. This is light; this is heavy. This can be spoken of; this cannot be spoken of. This can be guarded against; this cannot be guarded against. This has a remainder; this has no remainder. This can be repented; this cannot be repented.' Ānanda, those bhikṣus should settle this quarrel in a private place. If it is settled in a private place, this quarrel should be called settled. If it is not settled in a private place, this quarrel should be brought before the assembly. If it is settled in the assembly, this quarrel should be called settled. If it is not settled in the assembly, Ānanda, among those dwelling nearby, if there are bhikṣus who uphold the sūtras, uphold the Vinaya, or uphold the Mātṛkā, these bhikṣus should go together to those persons and present the matter of this quarrel. If it is settled on the way, this quarrel should be called settled. If it is not settled on the way, this quarrel should be brought before the assembly again. If it is settled in the assembly, this quarrel should be called settled. If it is not settled in the assembly, Ānanda, those who have the greater number of supporters, who uphold the sūtras, uphold the Vinaya, or uphold the Mātṛkā, Ānanda, those bhikṣus who are correct should settle this quarrel, according to the Dharma and Vinaya, as the honored teacher instructed, bringing happiness face to face. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling by successive referral. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling by successive referral.

"Ānanda, how should one apply the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse? How is this quarrel resolved? It is by means of the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse. Ānanda, suppose in a certain dwelling place the bhikṣus of the community quarrel, hate, and are jealous of each other, hating and contending together. Ānanda, those bhikṣus divide and form two groups. Having divided into two groups, in one group there is an elder senior one, or there is a next in rank, or there is a group leader, or there is a next in rank. Ānanda, a bhikṣu of this group says to those bhikṣus: 'Worthies, hear me. We are without principle and without reason; we are evil and unwholesome. Why is this? In this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, having gone forth with faith, leaving the household life to train in the homeless life, we quarrel, hate, and are jealous, hating and contending together. Worthies, because of this quarrel, whatever precepts we have violated, excluding sthūlātyaya offenses and excluding offenses associated with the household life, I now, on my own behalf and on behalf of these worthies, sincerely confess before you, openly declare and display it, not daring to conceal it, and shall guard the precepts well henceforth and not commit such offenses again.'

"Ānanda, if in this group there is no bhikṣu who accepts, Ānanda, this bhikṣu should then go to the second group. Having arrived, he should bow his head at the feet of the elder senior bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder senior bhikṣus saying: 'Venerables, hear me. We are without principle and without reason; we are evil and unwholesome. Why is this? In this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, having gone forth with faith, leaving the household life to train in the homeless life, we quarrel, hate, and are jealous, hating and contending together. Worthies, because of this quarrel, whatever precepts we have violated, excluding sthūlātyaya offenses and excluding offenses associated with the household life, I now, on my own behalf and on behalf of those worthies, sincerely confess before the elder seniors, openly declare and display it, not daring to conceal it, and shall guard the precepts well henceforth and not commit such offenses again.' Ānanda, those bhikṣus should then say to this bhikṣu: 'Worthy one, do you yourself see the offenses against the precepts?' He should answer: 'I truly see the offenses I committed.' They should then tell him: 'Guard the precepts well henceforth and do not commit such offenses again.' The second group should likewise proceed in the same way. Ānanda, this is called applying the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse. Thus is this quarrel resolved, by means of the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse.

"Ānanda, I now charge you to teach the six principles of concord. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and consider them well."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "So it shall be. I shall receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha said: "What are the six? Compassionate bodily actions toward fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is a principle of concord, a principle of affection, a principle of joy, making for love, making for respect, making for reverence, making for esteem, making for cultivation and restraint, leading to the attainment of the life of a renunciant, leading to one-pointedness of mind, leading to diligent effort, leading to nirvāṇa. Compassionate verbal actions. Compassionate mental actions. Whatever rightful gains obtained in accordance with Dharma, even food received in one's own bowl, such gains are shared and distributed among fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is a principle of concord, a principle of affection, a principle of joy, making for love, making for respect, making for reverence, making for esteem, making for cultivation and restraint, leading to the attainment of the life of a renunciant, leading to one-pointedness of mind, leading to diligent effort, leading to nirvāṇa. Whatever precepts are unbroken, unpierced, unstained, unspotted, like the earth, not dependent on others, praised by the noble ones, well-received and perfectly upheld: such a share of precepts is distributed and given to fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is a principle of concord, a principle of affection, a principle of joy, making for love, making for respect, making for reverence, making for esteem, making for cultivation and restraint, leading to the attainment of the life of a renunciant, leading to one-pointedness of mind, leading to diligent effort, leading to nirvāṇa. Whatever noble view leading to liberation, with clear vision and deep penetration, able to rightly end suffering: such a share of view is distributed and given to fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is a principle of concord, a principle of affection, a principle of joy, making for love, making for respect, making for reverence, making for esteem, making for cultivation and restraint, leading to the attainment of the life of a renunciant, leading to one-pointedness of mind, leading to diligent effort, leading to nirvāṇa. Ānanda, what I previously spoke of as the six principles of concord, it is on account of this that I spoke.

"Ānanda, if you all cut off, terminate, and sever these six roots of quarrels, and if you settle quarrels arising in the community by applying these seven methods for settling quarrels, including the vinaya of settling as by sweeping away refuse, and if you further practice these six principles of concord, Ānanda, in this way, after my passing, you will all dwell together in harmony, joyful and without quarrels, of one mind, of one teaching, blended like water and milk, traveling happily as if I were still present."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Cunda Sūtra, Fifth.

---

## (197) Sūtra on Upāli, Sixth of the Great Chapters

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Campā, on the bank of the Gaṅgā Pool.

At that time, the Venerable Upāli, in the afternoon, rose from his quiet meditation and went to the Buddha's place. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony but performs a different action or speaks of a different matter, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when the vinaya of settling in the presence should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by recollection; or when the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling in the presence, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by non-insanity; or when the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by recollection, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by self-confession; or when the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by non-insanity, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by majority decision; or when the vinaya of settling by majority decision should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by self-confession, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when the majority decision should be applied, instead applies a formal censure; or when a formal censure should be applied, instead applies the majority decision, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a formal censure should be applied, instead applies a demotion; or when a demotion should be applied, instead applies a formal censure, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a demotion should be applied, instead applies a suspension; or when a suspension should be applied, instead applies a demotion, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a suspension should be applied, instead applies an expulsion; or when an expulsion should be applied, instead applies a suspension, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when an expulsion should be applied, instead applies a recollection procedure; or when a recollection procedure should be applied, instead applies an expulsion, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a recollection procedure should be applied, instead applies a proceeding from the root; or when a proceeding from the root should be applied, instead applies a recollection procedure, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a proceeding from the root should be applied, instead applies a banishment; or when a banishment should be applied, instead applies a proceeding from the root, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a banishment should be applied, instead applies a practice of non-arrogance; or when a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, instead applies a banishment, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli."

The Venerable Upāli further asked: "World-Honored One, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony, and when a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, instead applies rehabilitation; or when rehabilitation should be applied, instead applies a practice of non-arrogance, is that an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya?"

The World-Honored One answered: "No, Upāli. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony but performs a different action or speaks of a different matter, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the vinaya of settling in the presence should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by recollection; or when the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling in the presence, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by non-insanity; or when the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by recollection, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by self-confession; or when the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by non-insanity, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault.

"Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by majority decision; or when the vinaya of settling by majority decision should be applied, instead applies the vinaya of settling by self-confession, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the majority decision should be applied, instead applies a formal censure; or when a formal censure should be applied, instead applies the majority decision, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a formal censure should be applied, instead applies a demotion; or when a demotion should be applied, instead applies a formal censure, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a demotion should be applied, instead applies a suspension; or when a suspension should be applied, instead applies a demotion, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault.

"Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a suspension should be applied, instead applies an expulsion; or when an expulsion should be applied, instead applies a suspension, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when an expulsion should be applied, instead applies a recollection procedure; or when a recollection procedure should be applied, instead applies an expulsion, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a recollection procedure should be applied, instead applies a proceeding from the root; or when a proceeding from the root should be applied, instead applies a recollection procedure, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a proceeding from the root should be applied, instead applies a banishment; or when a banishment should be applied, instead applies a proceeding from the root, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a banishment should be applied, instead applies a practice of non-arrogance; or when a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, instead applies a banishment, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, instead applies rehabilitation; or when rehabilitation should be applied, instead applies a practice of non-arrogance, that is an action not in accordance with Dharma and not in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs fault.

"Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and whatever action should be performed is the very action that is spoken of, that is an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs no fault. Upāli, if the bhikṣu Sangha gathers in harmony and when the vinaya of settling in the presence should be applied, applies the vinaya of settling in the presence; when the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, applies the vinaya of settling by recollection; when the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, applies the vinaya of settling by non-insanity; when the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, applies the vinaya of settling by self-confession; when the vinaya of settling by majority decision should be applied, applies the vinaya of settling by majority decision; when a formal censure should be applied, applies a formal censure; when a demotion should be applied, applies a demotion; when a suspension should be applied, applies a suspension; when an expulsion should be applied, applies an expulsion; when a recollection procedure should be applied, applies a recollection procedure; when a proceeding from the root should be applied, applies a proceeding from the root; when a banishment should be applied, applies a banishment; when a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, applies a practice of non-arrogance; when rehabilitation should be applied, applies rehabilitation: that is an action in accordance with Dharma and in accordance with Vinaya, and the assembly incurs no fault.

"Upāli, you should train thus: whatever action should be performed is the very action that is spoken of. When the vinaya of settling in the presence should be applied, apply the vinaya of settling in the presence. When the vinaya of settling by recollection should be applied, apply the vinaya of settling by recollection. When the vinaya of settling by non-insanity should be applied, apply the vinaya of settling by non-insanity. When the vinaya of settling by self-confession should be applied, apply the vinaya of settling by self-confession. When the vinaya of settling by majority decision should be applied, apply the vinaya of settling by majority decision. When a formal censure should be applied, apply a formal censure. When a demotion should be applied, apply a demotion. When a suspension should be applied, apply a suspension. When an expulsion should be applied, apply an expulsion. When a recollection procedure should be applied, apply a recollection procedure. When a proceeding from the root should be applied, apply a proceeding from the root. When a banishment should be applied, apply a banishment. When a practice of non-arrogance should be applied, apply a practice of non-arrogance. When rehabilitation should be applied, apply rehabilitation. Upāli, you should train in this way."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The Venerable Upāli and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Upāli Sūtra, Sixth.

---

## (198) Sūtra on the Stages of Training, Seventh of the Great Chapters

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the novice Aggivessana was also staying in Rājagṛha, dwelling in a meditation hut in a secluded place. At that time, the prince Jayasena, wandering about in the afternoon, went to the novice Aggivessana's place. They exchanged greetings, and the prince sat to one side and said: "Worthy Aggivessana, I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The novice Aggivessana said: "Noble prince, if you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

The prince asked: "Aggivessana, is it truly the case that bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind?"

The novice answered: "Noble prince, it is truly the case that bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind."

The prince further asked: "Worthy Aggivessana, according to what you have heard and what you have studied and recited, please explain it all to me: how bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind."

The novice answered: "Noble prince, I am not able to fully explain to you, according to what I have heard and what I have studied and recited, how bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind. Noble prince, if I were to explain to you, according to what I have heard and what I have studied and recited, how bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind, perhaps the noble prince would not understand, and then my effort would be in vain."

The prince said to the novice: "Worthy Aggivessana, you have not been defeated by anyone. For what reason do you retreat on your own? Worthy Aggivessana, according to what you have heard and what you have studied and recited, please explain it to me: how bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind. If I understand, that will be good. If I do not understand, I shall simply not ask further about the Dharma."

Thereupon, the novice Aggivessana, according to what he had heard and what he had studied and recited, explained to the prince Jayasena how bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind.

Thereupon, the prince Jayasena said: "Worthy Aggivessana, that bhikṣus in this Dharma and Vinaya, being diligent and not negligent, practicing with effort, attain one-pointedness of mind: that can never be the case." Having declared that it could never be the case, he rose from his seat and departed without taking leave.

Not long after the prince Jayasena had departed, the novice Aggivessana went to the Buddha's place, bowed his head in salutation, sat to one side, and related in full what he and the prince Jayasena had discussed.

The World-Honored One, having heard this, told the novice: "Aggivessana, enough! How could the prince Jayasena, who pursues sensual pleasures, is attached to sensual pleasures, is consumed by desire for sensual pleasures, and is burned by sensual pleasures, know or see the stage where sensual desires are cut off, where the love of sensual desires is cut off, where the burning heat of sensual desires is cut off, where there is no knowledge of desire, no seeing of desire, and no perception of desire? That the prince could know or see this stage can never be the case. Why is that? Aggivessana, the prince Jayasena constantly pursues sensual pleasures.

"Aggivessana, just as there are four kinds of training subjects: elephant training, horse training, ox training, and human training. Among these, two training subjects cannot be trained, and two training subjects can be trained. Aggivessana, what do you think? If those two training subjects that cannot be trained, being untrained, at the untrained stage, were to receive and accept the tasks of training, that can never be the case. If those two training subjects that can be trained are well trained, then being trained, at the untrained stage, they receive and accept the tasks of training; that is certainly possible. In the same way, Aggivessana, enough! How could the prince Jayasena, who pursues sensual pleasures, is attached to sensual pleasures, is consumed by desire for sensual pleasures, and is burned by sensual pleasures, know or see the stage where sensual desires are cut off, where the love of sensual desires is cut off, where the burning heat of sensual desires is cut off, where there is no knowledge of desire, no seeing of desire, and no perception of desire? That the prince could know or see this stage can never be the case. Why is that? Aggivessana, the prince Jayasena constantly pursues sensual pleasures.

"Aggivessana, suppose not far from a village there is a great stone mountain, without gaps, without holes, solid and not hollow, firm and unmoving, all in one mass. Suppose two people wish to see what is beyond. One of them quickly ascends the mountain, while the second remains standing at the base. The person on top of the stone mountain sees that on the other side of the mountain there is a beautiful flat land, parks and gardens, groves of trees, clear springs, flower-covered ponds, and long flowing rivers. The person on top, having seen this, says to the person at the base: 'Do you see that on the other side of the mountain there is a beautiful flat land, parks and gardens, groves of trees, clear springs, flower-covered ponds, and long flowing rivers?' The person at the base answers: 'For me to see that on the other side of the mountain there is a beautiful flat land, parks and gardens, groves of trees, clear springs, flower-covered ponds, and long flowing rivers, that can never be the case.' Thereupon, the person on top of the stone mountain quickly descends, takes hold of the person at the base, and swiftly brings him up to the top of the stone mountain. Having arrived, he asks: 'Do you see that on the other side of the mountain there is a beautiful flat land, parks and gardens, groves of trees, clear springs, flower-covered ponds, and long flowing rivers?' That person answers: 'Now I see it.' He further asks that person: 'Previously you said "that can never be the case," and now you say you see it. What do you mean by this?' That person answers: 'Previously I was obstructed by the mountain, and therefore could not see.' In the same way, Aggivessana, enough! How could the prince Jayasena, who pursues sensual pleasures, is attached to sensual pleasures, is consumed by desire for sensual pleasures, and is burned by sensual pleasures, know or see the stage where sensual desires are cut off, where the love of sensual desires is cut off, where the burning heat of sensual desires is cut off, where there is no knowledge of desire, no seeing of desire, and no perception of desire? That the prince could know or see this stage can never be the case.

"Aggivessana, in former times the anointed warrior-king Mūrdhagata had an elephant catcher. The king commanded him: 'You, elephant catcher, go and catch a wild elephant for me and bring it back. When you have done so, report to me.' The elephant catcher, having received the king's command, mounted the king's elephant and went into the wilderness. That elephant catcher in the wilderness saw a great wild elephant. Having seen it, he captured and bound it to the neck of the king's elephant. At that time the king's elephant led the wild elephant out to open ground. The elephant catcher returned to the anointed warrior-king Mūrdhagata and reported: 'Your Majesty, the wild elephant has been caught and is tied in the open ground. May Your Majesty do as you wish.' The anointed warrior-king Mūrdhagata, having heard this, commanded: 'Skilled elephant trainer, you should now quickly train this wild elephant, tame it and make it well-trained. When it is well-trained, return and report to me.' Thereupon, the skilled elephant trainer, having received the king's command, took a very large staff, placed it on his right shoulder, and went to the wild elephant. He planted the staff in the ground and tied the wild elephant's neck, controlling its desire for the wilds, removing its longing for the wilderness, stopping its weariness from the wilderness, and making it enjoy the village and become accustomed to human company. The skilled elephant trainer first gave it food and drink.

"Aggivessana, when that wild elephant first accepted food and drink from the elephant trainer, the skilled elephant trainer thought: 'This wild elephant will certainly survive. Why is that? This great wild elephant has first accepted food and drink.' When that wild elephant first accepted food and drink from the elephant trainer, the skilled elephant trainer then addressed it with soft and pleasing words, commanding it to lie down, stand up, come, go, pick up, put down, bend, and stretch. When that wild elephant followed the elephant trainer's soft and pleasing words to lie down, stand up, come, go, pick up, put down, bend, and stretch, the wild elephant thus followed the elephant trainer's instructions. Aggivessana, when the wild elephant followed the elephant trainer's instructions, the skilled elephant trainer then bound its two front legs, its back legs, its two thighs, its two flanks, its tail, its back, its head, its forehead, its ears, its tusks, and bound its trunk, and had a man holding a hook mounted on its head. He then had many men standing before it holding swords, shields, spears, lances, halberds, axes, and battle-axes. The skilled elephant trainer, holding a sharp lance, stood before the wild elephant and spoke thus: 'I shall now discipline you so that you do not move. I discipline you: do not stir.' When that wild elephant, following the elephant trainer's discipline, did not move, it did not raise its front legs, nor move its back legs; its thighs, flanks, tail, back, head, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk all did not stir. Thus the wild elephant, following the elephant trainer, stood without moving.

"Aggivessana, when that wild elephant followed the elephant trainer and stood without moving, at that time it could endure swords, shields, spears, lances, halberds, axes, battle-axes, shouting and loud cries, whistling, blowing of conches, beating of drums, and striking of bells; it could endure them all. When that wild elephant could endure all these, at that time it was trained, well-trained, supremely trained, most supremely trained, supremely swift, unsurpassably swift, fit to serve as the king's mount, to receive food from the king's stores, and to be called a royal elephant.

"In the same way, Aggivessana, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Unattached One, a Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed One, a Guide for Those to Be Tamed, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, called a Buddha, the World-Honored One: he, in this world of gods, māras, brahmās, renunciants and brāhmaṇas, from humans to gods, himself knows, himself awakens, and himself realizes and attains the accomplishment and abides therein. He teaches a Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with meaning and with phrasing, complete and pure, displaying the holy life. When he teaches this Dharma, a householder's son hears it. Having heard it, the householder's son gains faith in the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata. Having gained faith, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leaves the household life for the homeless life to train in the path. Aggivessana, at that time the noble disciple has come out into the open, just like the king's wild elephant. Just as the wild elephant's attachment to pleasure was in the forest, so too, Aggivessana, the attachment of gods and humans to pleasures lies in the five kinds of sensual desire: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. The Tathāgata first trains that bhikṣu: 'You should guard your body and livelihood in purity. You should guard your speech, mind, and livelihood in purity.'

"When the noble disciple guards his body and livelihood in purity, guards his speech, mind, and livelihood in purity, the Tathāgata further trains the bhikṣu: 'You should contemplate the body internally as body, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas.' When the noble disciple contemplates the body internally as body, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas, these four foundations of mindfulness, being in the noble disciple's mind, bind his mind, control his desire for the household life, remove his longing for household desires, stop his weariness from household life, and make him delight in the true Dharma and cultivate the noble precepts. Aggivessana, just as the elephant trainer, having received the anointed warrior-king Mūrdhagata's command, took a very large staff, placed it on his right shoulder, went to the wild elephant, planted the staff in the ground, and tied the wild elephant's neck, controlling its desire for the wilds, removing its longing for the wilderness, stopping its weariness from the wilderness, and making it enjoy the village and become accustomed to human company; so too, Aggivessana, these four foundations of mindfulness, being in the noble disciple's mind, bind his mind, control his desire for the household life, remove his longing for household desires, stop his weariness from household life, and make him delight in the true Dharma and cultivate the noble precepts.

"When the noble disciple contemplates the body internally as body, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas, the Tathāgata further trains the bhikṣu: 'You should contemplate the body internally as body without thinking thoughts associated with sensual desire, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas without thinking thoughts associated with unwholesome dharmas.' When the noble disciple contemplates the body internally as body without thinking thoughts associated with sensual desire, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas without thinking thoughts associated with unwholesome dharmas, the noble disciple thus follows the Tathāgata's instructions. Aggivessana, just as the wild elephant followed the elephant trainer when addressed with soft and pleasing words, obeying commands to lie down, stand up, come, go, pick up, put down, bend, and stretch, and thus the wild elephant followed the elephant trainer's instructions; so too, Aggivessana, when the noble disciple contemplates the body internally as body without thinking thoughts associated with sensual desire, and so on up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas without thinking thoughts associated with unwholesome dharmas, the noble disciple thus follows the Tathāgata's instructions.

"When the noble disciple follows the Tathāgata's instructions, the Tathāgata further trains the bhikṣu: 'You should, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining and dwelling in the fourth dhyāna.' When the noble disciple, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome dharmas, up to attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, the noble disciple thus follows the Tathāgata and stands without moving. Aggivessana, just as the wild elephant, following the elephant trainer's discipline, did not move: it did not raise its front legs, nor move its back legs; its thighs, flanks, tail, back, head, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk all did not stir, and thus the wild elephant, following the elephant trainer, stood without moving; so too, Aggivessana, when the noble disciple, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome dharmas, up to attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, the noble disciple thus follows the Tathāgata and stands without moving.

"When the noble disciple follows the Tathāgata and stands without moving, at that time he can endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, the oppression of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh speech and blows from sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point where life is about to end, he can bear all that is unpleasant. Aggivessana, just as the wild elephant, following the elephant trainer, stood without moving, and at that time it could endure swords, shields, spears, lances, halberds, axes, battle-axes, shouting and loud cries, whistling, blowing of conches, beating of drums, and striking of bells, and could endure them all; so too, Aggivessana, when the noble disciple follows the Tathāgata and stands without moving, at that time he can endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, the oppression of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh speech and blows from sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point where life is about to end, he can bear all that is unpleasant.

"Aggivessana, when the noble disciple, following the Tathāgata, can endure all this, at that time he is trained, well-trained, supremely trained, most supremely trained, supremely at peace, most supremely at peace, having removed all crookedness, evil, fear, foolishness, flattery, and deceit, purified and stilled of defilements, without stain and without blemish, worthy of being called, worthy of being invited, worthy of respect, worthy of veneration, truly worthy of offerings, a supreme field of merit for all gods and humans. Aggivessana, just as the wild elephant, when it could endure all these things, at that time it was trained, well-trained, supremely trained, most supremely trained, supremely swift, unsurpassably swift, fit to serve as the king's mount, to receive food from the king's stores, and to be called a royal elephant; so too, Aggivessana, when the noble disciple, following the Tathāgata, can endure all this, at that time he is trained, well-trained, supremely trained, most supremely trained, supremely at peace, most supremely at peace, having removed all crookedness, evil, fear, foolishness, flattery, and deceit, purified and stilled of defilements, without stain and without blemish, worthy of being called, worthy of being invited, worthy of respect, worthy of veneration, truly worthy of offerings, a supreme field of merit for all gods and humans.

"Aggivessana, when a young wild elephant dies untrained, it is said to have died untrained. When a middle-aged or old wild elephant dies untrained, it is said to have died untrained. Aggivessana, when a young noble disciple dies untrained and passes away, it is said that he passed away untrained. When a middle-aged or old noble disciple dies untrained and passes away, it is said that he passed away untrained. Aggivessana, when a young wild elephant dies well-trained, it is said to have died well-trained. When a middle-aged or old wild elephant dies well-trained, it is said to have died well-trained. Aggivessana, when a young noble disciple dies well-trained and passes away, it is said that he passed away well-trained. When a middle-aged or old noble disciple dies well-trained and passes away, it is said that he passed away well-trained."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The novice Aggivessana and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on the Stages of Training, Seventh.

---

End of Fascicle 52 of the Madhyamāgama.

## Middle Āgama Sūtras, Fascicle Fifty-Three

Translated during the Eastern Jin by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Sanghadeva

---

### (196) Sūtra on Zhouluo

*Second in the Series on Great Topics*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling among the Kurus, in a Kuru town called Zhouluo.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from sitting meditation, went to the World-Honored One, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew and sat to one side. He said to the World-Honored One: "It is wonderful, World-Honored One! It is marvelous! The meaning of dependent origination is so extremely profound, and its appearance is also extremely profound. Yet to me it appears as if it were very easy and shallow."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, do not speak in this way! Do not speak in this way! This dependent origination is extremely profound, and its appearance is also extremely profound. Ānanda, it is because of not understanding, not penetrating this dharma that sentient beings become like tangled thread, like a knotted ball of twine, like muñja grass and babaja grass, unable to escape from the lower realms of existence, the evil destinies, the cycle of birth and death. Ānanda, this is what makes dependent origination so extremely profound, and its appearance also extremely profound.

"Ānanda, if one asks whether aging and death have a condition, one should answer: 'They do.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for aging and death?' one should answer: 'Birth is the condition for aging and death.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether birth has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for birth?' one should answer: 'Existence is the condition for birth.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether existence has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for existence?' one should answer: 'Clinging is the condition for existence.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether clinging has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for clinging?' one should answer: 'Craving is the condition for clinging.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether craving has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for craving?' one should answer: 'Feeling is the condition for craving.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether feeling has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for feeling?' one should answer: 'Contact is the condition for feeling.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether contact has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for contact?' one should answer: 'The six sense bases are the condition for contact.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether the six sense bases have a condition, one should answer: 'They do.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for the six sense bases?' one should answer: 'Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether name-and-form has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for name-and-form?' one should answer: 'Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.'

"Ānanda, if one asks whether consciousness has a condition, one should answer: 'It does.' If one asks, 'What is the condition for consciousness?' one should answer: 'Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.'

"Ānanda, thus consciousness conditions name-and-form, name-and-form conditions consciousness, name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, the six sense bases condition contact, contact conditions feeling, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions clinging, clinging conditions existence, existence conditions birth, and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering. This is the arising of the entire world.

"Ānanda, with birth as condition there is aging and death. This statement that 'birth is the condition for aging and death,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no birth at all, of any kind whatsoever, anywhere at all: if there were no birth for devas in the deva realm, no birth for Brahmā beings, no birth for Māras, no birth for the deva realm, no birth for humans, no birth for animals, no birth for hungry ghosts, no birth for hell beings, no birth anywhere for any class of being; Ānanda, if there were utterly no birth of any kind, then with the complete cessation of birth, would there still be aging and death?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of aging and death, namely birth. Birth is the condition for aging and death.

"Ānanda, with existence as condition there is birth. This statement that 'existence is the condition for birth,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no existence at all, of any kind whatsoever: no existence in the desire realm, no existence in the form realm, no existence in the formless realm; Ānanda, if there were utterly no existence of any kind, then with the complete cessation of existence, would there still be birth?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of birth, namely existence. Existence is the condition for birth.

"Ānanda, with clinging as condition there is existence. This statement that 'clinging is the condition for existence,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no clinging at all, of any kind whatsoever: no clinging to desire, no clinging to views, no clinging to precepts and vows, no clinging to self-doctrine; Ānanda, if there were utterly no clinging of any kind, then with the complete cessation of clinging, would there still be existence?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of existence, namely clinging. Clinging is the condition for existence.

"Ānanda, with craving as condition there is clinging. This statement that 'craving is the condition for clinging,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no craving at all, of any kind whatsoever: no craving for forms, no craving for sounds, no craving for smells, no craving for tastes, no craving for tangibles, no craving for mental objects; Ānanda, if there were utterly no craving of any kind, then with the complete cessation of craving, would there still be clinging?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of clinging, namely craving. Craving is the condition for clinging.

"Ānanda, with feeling as condition there is craving. This statement that 'feeling is the condition for craving,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no feeling at all, of any kind whatsoever: no feeling born from eye-contact, no feeling born from ear-contact, no feeling born from nose-contact, no feeling born from tongue-contact, no feeling born from body-contact, no feeling born from mind-contact; Ānanda, if there were utterly no feeling of any kind, then with the complete cessation of feeling, would there still be craving?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of craving, namely feeling. Feeling is the condition for craving.

"Ānanda, furthermore, because of craving one engages in seeking; because of seeking one obtains gain; because of gain one makes decisions; because of decisions there arise desire and passion; because of desire and passion there is attachment; because of attachment there is possessiveness; because of possessiveness there is stinginess; because of stinginess there is guarding. Ānanda, because of guarding, in order to guard and protect, one takes up the sword and staff, engages in disputes and quarrels, there arise falsehood, deceit, and many other evil, unwholesome dharmas.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of guarding, in order to guard and protect, one takes up the sword and staff, engages in disputes and quarrels, there arise falsehood, deceit, and many other evil, unwholesome dharmas,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no guarding at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of guarding, would there still be, in order to guard and protect, the taking up of the sword and staff, disputes and quarrels, falsehood, deceit, and many other evil, unwholesome dharmas?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition, that because of guarding, in order to guard and protect, one takes up the sword and staff, engages in disputes and quarrels, and there arise falsehood, deceit, and many other evil, unwholesome dharmas. Guarding is the condition for these.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of stinginess there is guarding,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no stinginess at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of stinginess, would there still be guarding?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of guarding, namely stinginess. Stinginess is the condition for guarding.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of possessiveness there is stinginess,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no possessiveness at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of possessiveness, would there still be stinginess?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of stinginess, namely possessiveness. Possessiveness is the condition for stinginess.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of attachment there is possessiveness,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no attachment at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of attachment, would there still be possessiveness?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of possessiveness, namely attachment. Attachment is the condition for possessiveness.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of desire and passion there is attachment,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no desire and passion at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of desire and passion, would there still be attachment?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of attachment, namely desire and passion. Desire and passion are the condition for attachment.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of decisions there arise desire and passion,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no decisions at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of decisions, would there still be desire and passion?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of desire and passion, namely decisions. Decisions are the condition for desire and passion.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of gain there are decisions,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no gain at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of gain, would there still be decisions?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of decisions, namely gain. Gain is the condition for decisions.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of seeking there is gain,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no seeking at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of seeking, would there still be gain?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of gain, namely seeking. Seeking is the condition for gain.

"Ānanda, this statement that 'because of craving there is seeking,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no craving at all, of any kind, then with the complete cessation of craving, would there still be seeking?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of seeking, namely craving. Craving is the condition for seeking.

"Ānanda, thus these two dharmas, craving, merge into one through feeling. That is to say, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions seeking, seeking conditions gain, gain conditions decisions, decisions condition desire and passion, desire and passion condition attachment, attachment conditions possessiveness, possessiveness conditions stinginess, stinginess conditions guarding, and because of guarding, in order to guard and protect, one takes up the sword and staff, engages in disputes and quarrels, and there arise falsehood, deceit, and many other evil, unwholesome dharmas.

"Ānanda, with contact as condition there is feeling. This statement that 'contact is the condition for feeling,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no contact at all, of any kind whatsoever: no eye-contact, no ear-contact, no nose-contact, no tongue-contact, no body-contact, no mind-contact; Ānanda, if there were utterly no contact of any kind, then with the complete cessation of contact, would there still be feeling?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of feeling, namely contact. Contact is the condition for feeling.

"Ānanda, with name-and-form as condition there is contact. This statement that 'name-and-form is the condition for contact,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if there were no designations of name, no signs of name, no concepts of name, no designation dharmas of name; if there were absolutely no name, then with the complete absence of name, would there still be contact that is contact through designation?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Ānanda, if there were no forms of form, no signs of form, no resistance of form, no resistance dharmas of form; if there were absolutely no form, then with the complete absence of form, would there still be contact that is contact through resistance?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Ānanda, if there were no name and no form, then would there still be contact?"

Ānanda answered: "There would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of contact, namely name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for contact.

"Ānanda, with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form. This statement that 'consciousness is the condition for name-and-form,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if consciousness did not enter the mother's womb, would name-and-form develop in the mother's womb?"

Ānanda answered: "It would not."

"Ānanda, if consciousness entered the mother's womb but then departed, would name-and-form come to full development?"

Ānanda answered: "It would not."

"Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off and destroyed while still young, would name-and-form grow, develop, and become complete?"

Ānanda answered: "It would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of name-and-form, namely consciousness. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.
