"Ānanda, with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness. This statement that 'name-and-form is the condition for consciousness,' the meaning of this should be understood in the following way. Ānanda, if consciousness did not obtain a foundation in name-and-form, would consciousness have a foundation? Would consciousness then have birth, aging, sickness, death, and suffering?"

Ānanda answered: "It would not."

"Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition of consciousness, namely name-and-form. Name-and-form is the condition for consciousness.

"Ānanda, therefore name-and-form conditions consciousness and consciousness conditions name-and-form. Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, the six sense bases condition contact, contact conditions feeling, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions clinging, clinging conditions existence, existence conditions birth, and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering. This is the arising of the entire world.

"Ānanda, this is the meaning by which one should know: consciousness conditions name-and-form and name-and-form conditions consciousness. Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, the six sense bases condition contact, contact conditions feeling, feeling conditions craving, craving conditions clinging, clinging conditions existence, existence conditions birth, and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus arises this entire great mass of suffering. This is the arising of the entire world.

"Ānanda, regarding the statement about the self: in how many ways do those who make declarations about the self declare the self? Ānanda, either they declare the self as having form and being finite, declaring: 'My self has form and is finite.' Or they declare the self as having form and being infinite, declaring: 'My self has form and is infinite.' Or they declare the self as formless and finite, declaring: 'My self is formless and finite.' Or they declare the self as formless and infinite, declaring: 'My self is formless and infinite.'

"Ānanda, those who declare the self as having form and finite: they declare the self either with reference to the present as having form and finite, or they declare the self after death as having form and finite, or they think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to a declaration that 'form and finitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the view of a self having form and being finite.

"Ānanda, those who declare the self as having form and infinite: they declare the self either with reference to the present as having form and infinite, or they declare the self after death as having form and infinite, or they think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to a declaration that 'form and infinitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the view of a self having form and being infinite.

"Ānanda, those who declare the self as formless and finite: they declare the self either with reference to the present as formless and finite, or they declare the self after death as formless and finite, or they think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to a declaration that 'formlessness and finitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the view of a self being formless and finite.

"Ānanda, those who declare the self as formless and infinite: they declare the self either with reference to the present as formless and infinite, or they declare the self after death as formless and infinite, or they think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to a declaration that 'formlessness and infinitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the view of a self being formless and infinite.

"Ānanda, regarding the statement about the self: in how many ways do those who do not make declarations about the self not declare the self? Ānanda, either they do not declare the self as having form and being finite, not declaring: 'My self has form and is finite.' Or they do not declare the self as having form and being infinite, not declaring: 'My self has form and is infinite.' Or they do not declare the self as formless and finite, not declaring: 'My self is formless and finite.' Or they do not declare the self as formless and infinite, not declaring: 'My self is formless and infinite.'

"Ānanda, those who do not declare the self as having form and finite: they do not declare the self either with reference to the present as having form and finite, and they do not declare the self after death as having form and finite, and they do not think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to not declaring that 'form and finitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the non-declaration of a self having form and being finite.

"Ānanda, those who do not declare the self as having form and infinite: they do not declare the self either with reference to the present as having form and infinite, and they do not declare the self after death as having form and infinite, and they do not think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to not declaring that 'form and infinitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the non-declaration of a self having form and being infinite.

"Ānanda, those who do not declare the self as formless and finite: they do not declare the self either with reference to the present as formless and finite, and they do not declare the self after death as formless and finite, and they do not think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to not declaring that 'formlessness and finitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the non-declaration of a self being formless and finite.

"Ānanda, those who do not declare the self as formless and infinite: they do not declare the self either with reference to the present as formless and infinite, and they do not declare the self after death as formless and infinite, and they do not think thus: 'Even if I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.' Ānanda, this being the case, it amounts to not declaring that 'formlessness and infinitude constitute the self.' This is sufficient to explain the non-declaration of a self being formless and infinite.

"Ānanda, regarding the statement about seeing the self: in how many ways do those who see the self see the self? Ānanda, either they see feeling as the self, declaring: 'Feeling is my self.' Or they declare: 'Feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling.' Or they declare: 'Feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling; my self feels, for my self has the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, those who hold the view that 'feeling is my self' should be told: 'There are three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. Of these three feelings, which one do you regard as the self?' Ānanda, when one experiences pleasant feeling, at that time one does not experience painful feeling or neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling; one experiences only pleasant feeling. Ānanda, when one experiences painful feeling, at that time one does not experience pleasant feeling or neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling; one experiences only painful feeling. Ānanda, when one experiences neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, at that time one does not experience pleasant feeling or painful feeling; one experiences only neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling.

"Ānanda, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Ānanda, painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Ānanda, neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. If, when experiencing pleasant feeling, one thinks 'This is my self,' then when that pleasant feeling ceases, one should think 'My self has departed.' If, when experiencing painful feeling, one thinks 'This is my self,' then when that painful feeling ceases, one should think 'My self has departed.' If, when experiencing neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, one thinks 'This is my self,' then when that neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling ceases, one should think 'My self has departed.'

"That person views feeling as the self: in the present life, it is impermanent, mixed with pleasure and pain, subject to arising and cessation. Ānanda, therefore it is not appropriate to say: 'Feeling is my self.'

"Ānanda, those who hold the view that 'feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling': their self does not experience pleasant feeling, does not experience painful feeling, does not experience neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. If there is no feeling at all, saying 'This is my self,' is that appropriate?"

Ānanda answered: "It is not, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, therefore it is not appropriate to say: 'Feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling.'

"Ānanda, those who hold the view that 'feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling; my self feels, for my self has the dharma of feeling': such a person should be told: 'If feeling were to completely and entirely cease without remainder, with absolutely no feeling remaining, then with feeling already ceased, would one say "This is my self"?'"

Ānanda answered: "One would not, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, therefore it is not appropriate to say: 'Feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling; my self feels, for my self has the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu does not view feeling as the self, does not view the self as having no feeling, and does not view feeling as not the self yet the self as having the dharma of feeling, that person, not viewing in this way, has no clinging to anything in the world. Having no clinging, there is no fear. Having no fear, one individually attains nirvāṇa: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of existence.' I know it as it truly is.

"Ānanda, regarding the statement about the self: in how many ways do those who do not see the self not see the self? Ānanda, either they do not see feeling as the self, not declaring: 'Feeling is my self.' Or they do not declare: 'Feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling.' Or they do not declare: 'Feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling; my self feels, for my self has the dharma of feeling.'

"Ānanda, those who do not hold the view that 'feeling is my self' do not hold the view. Those who do not hold the view that 'feeling is not my self; my self has no feeling' do not hold the view. Those who do not hold the view that 'feeling is not my self, and my self is not without feeling; my self feels, for my self has the dharma of feeling' do not hold the view. That person, not viewing in this way, has no clinging to anything in the world. Having no clinging, there is no fear. Having no fear, one individually attains nirvāṇa: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of existence.' I know it as it truly is.

"Ānanda, in how many ways do those who refer to the self refer to the self? Some refer to form, saying: 'My self, whether small or large, has the extent of form.' Some do not refer to form, but refer to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of consciousness.'

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to form, saying 'My self has the extent of form': such a person either refers to form as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; or refers to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the adherence to a view of self regarding form.

"Ānanda, if one refers to feeling, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of feeling': such a person either refers to feeling as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; or refers to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the adherence to a view of self regarding feeling.

"Ānanda, if one refers to perception, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of perception': such a person either refers to perception as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; or refers to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the adherence to a view of self regarding perception.

"Ānanda, if one refers to formations, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of formations': such a person either refers to formations as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; or refers to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the adherence to a view of self regarding formations.

"Ānanda, if one refers to consciousness, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of consciousness': such a person either refers to consciousness as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; or refers to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the adherence to a view of self regarding consciousness.

"Ānanda, in how many ways do those who do not refer to the self not refer to the self? Some do not refer to form, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of form.' Some do not refer to feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, saying: 'My self, whether small or great, has the extent of consciousness.'

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to form, saying: 'My self has the extent of form': such a person does not refer to form as the self in the present life, saying: 'This is truly my self'; and does not refer to it as the self in the future, saying: 'Since I am not yet in this state, I shall bring about this transformation.'

"Ānanda, this being the case, it is sufficient to explain the non-adherence to a view of self regarding form.

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to feeling, saying: 'My self has the extent of feeling': such a person does not refer to feeling as the self in the present life, and does not refer to it as the self in the future. This is sufficient to explain the non-adherence to a view of self regarding feeling.

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to perception, saying: 'My self has the extent of perception': such a person does not refer to perception as the self in the present life, and does not refer to it as the self in the future. This is sufficient to explain the non-adherence to a view of self regarding perception.

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to formations, saying: 'My self has the extent of formations': such a person does not refer to formations as the self in the present life, and does not refer to it as the self in the future. This is sufficient to explain the non-adherence to a view of self regarding formations.

"Ānanda, if one does not refer to consciousness, saying: 'My self has the extent of consciousness': such a person does not refer to consciousness as the self in the present life, and does not refer to it as the self in the future. This is sufficient to explain the non-adherence to a view of self regarding consciousness.

"Ānanda, what do you think? Is form permanent, or is it impermanent?"

Ānanda answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, if it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

Ānanda answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, if it is impermanent and suffering, it is a dharma of change. Would a learned noble disciple see in this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

Ānanda answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Ānanda, what do you think? Is consciousness permanent, or is it impermanent?"

Ānanda answered: "Impermanent, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, if it is impermanent, is it suffering?"

Ānanda answered: "It is suffering, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, if it is impermanent and suffering, it is a dharma of change. Would a learned noble disciple see in this: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?"

Ānanda answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Ānanda, therefore, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether excellent or inferior, whether far or near: all form should be regarded with right wisdom as it truly is thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Likewise with feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, whether past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether excellent or inferior, whether far or near: all consciousness should be regarded with right wisdom as it truly is thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'

"Ānanda, a learned noble disciple who contemplates in this way becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Being liberated, the knowledge arises: 'I am liberated. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of existence.' I know it as it truly is.

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu's mind is thus liberated, that bhikṣu, if asked: 'Does the Tathāgata exist after death?' would say: 'This is not an appropriate question.' If asked: 'Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?' would say: 'This is not an appropriate question.' If asked: 'Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?' would say: 'This is not an appropriate question.' If asked: 'Does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death?' would say: 'This is not an appropriate question.' What is the reason? Ānanda, as far as what can be designated by words, as far as what can be designated by paths, as far as what can be designated by language, as far as what can be designated by explanation, as far as what can be designated by wisdom: within this range, the learned noble disciple, with wisdom, well knowing, well seeing, well penetrating, well realizing. Ānanda, if a learned noble disciple, through such knowing, such seeing, such penetrating, such realizing, were to say of the bhikṣu whose mind is liberated that he knows and sees, this would not be appropriate.

"Ānanda, there are seven stations of consciousness and two bases. What are the seven? Ānanda, some beings have different bodies and different perceptions, such as humans and some devas. This is the first station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have different bodies but the same perception, such as the Brahmā devas who are first born in the Brahmā heaven. This is the second station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have the same body but different perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara devas. This is the third station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have the same body and the same perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna devas. This is the fourth station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have completely transcended all perceptions of form, have eliminated perceptions of resistance, and do not attend to perceptions of diversity. They perceive 'space is infinite' and dwell in the base of infinite space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have completely transcended the base of infinite space. They perceive 'consciousness is infinite' and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness.

"Ānanda, some beings have completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness. They perceive 'there is nothing at all' and dwell in the base of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness.

"The two bases are: the base of beings without perception, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are the two bases.

"Ānanda, regarding the first station of consciousness, where beings have different bodies and different perceptions, such as humans and some devas: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the second station of consciousness, where beings have different bodies but the same perception, such as the Brahmā devas first born in the Brahmā heaven: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the third station of consciousness, where beings have the same body but different perceptions, such as the Ābhāsvara devas: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the fourth station of consciousness, where beings have the same body and the same perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna devas: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the fifth station of consciousness, where beings have completely transcended all perceptions of form, eliminated perceptions of resistance, do not attend to perceptions of diversity, perceive 'space is infinite,' and dwell in the base of infinite space: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the sixth station of consciousness, where beings have completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceive 'consciousness is infinite,' and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the seventh station of consciousness, where beings have completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, perceive 'there is nothing at all,' and dwell in the base of nothingness: if a bhikṣu knows this station, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this station?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the base of beings without perception: if a bhikṣu knows this base, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this base?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, regarding the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: if a bhikṣu knows this base, knows its arising, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its danger, and knows the escape from it, should that bhikṣu delight in this base?"

Ānanda answered: "He should not."

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, regarding these seven stations of consciousness and two bases, knows them as they truly are, knows their arising, knows their cessation, knows their gratification, knows their danger, and knows the escape from them, and through dispassion is liberated: Ānanda, this bhikṣu is called one liberated by wisdom.

"Ānanda, there are eight liberations. What are the eight? Having form, one perceives forms. This is the first liberation. Having no perception of internal form, one perceives external forms. This is the second liberation. Experiencing the beautiful liberation, one abides having personally realized it with the body. This is the third liberation. Having completely transcended all perceptions of form, having eliminated perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving 'space is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. This is the fourth liberation. Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, perceiving 'consciousness is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This is the fifth liberation. Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving 'there is nothing at all,' one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. This is the sixth liberation. Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the seventh liberation. Having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the eighth liberation.

"Ānanda, if a bhikṣu, regarding these eight liberations, can enter them in forward sequence, can enter them in reverse sequence, can enter them both forward and reverse, can enter whichever one he wishes, can dwell in it for as long as he wishes, and can emerge from it whenever he wishes; if he also attains the destruction of the outflows, realizes for himself with direct knowledge the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that is without outflows, and in the present life abides having personally realized and perfected it: Ānanda, this bhikṣu is called one liberated in both ways. Ānanda, there is no other way of liberation in both ways that is superior to or more excellent than this liberation in both ways."

The World-Honored One spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the other bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and practiced accordingly.

---

### (197) Sūtra on Āśvalāyana

*Third in the Series on Great Topics*

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's park.

At that time, many brāhmaṇa householders from Kosala and many brāhmaṇa householders from other regions gathered together in a certain lecture hall and jointly discussed the following: "The brāhmaṇas of Kāśī and Kosala, as well as brāhmaṇa householders from other regions: do they all believe that the ascetic Gautama teaches a dharma that says all four castes can become pure? We do not accept this."

At that time, among those brāhmaṇa householders there was a young man named Āśvalāyana. He was young in years, with a shaved head, being only sixteen years old, who was well versed in the three Vedas, able to recite and hold them, thoroughly understanding the words and texts with their commentaries, and who was fully accomplished in worldly knowledge, including the analysis of physiognomy. His teachers and those of previous generations all accepted him as a person of great learning. He was praised by all the brāhmaṇas.

The brāhmaṇas then said to the young man Āśvalāyana: "The ascetic Gautama teaches a dharma that says all four castes can become pure. You should go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him. If you can refute the ascetic Gautama, then for us brāhmaṇas from Kāśī and Kosala and from other regions, you will bring fame and glory."

At that time, the young man Āśvalāyana said to the brāhmaṇas: "The ascetic Gautama is a dharma speaker. Those who speak dharma are difficult to debate with and refute. I am unable to go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him."

A second time, the brāhmaṇas said to the young man Āśvalāyana: "The ascetic Gautama teaches a dharma that says all four castes can become pure. You should go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him. If you can refute the ascetic Gautama, then for us brāhmaṇas from Kāśī and Kosala and from other regions, you will bring fame and glory. Āśvalāyana, you are well versed in the three Vedas, able to recite and hold them, thoroughly understanding the words and texts with their commentaries, and fully accomplished in worldly knowledge, including the analysis of physiognomy. If you are unable to go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him, then who else would be able to do so?"

A second time, the young man Āśvalāyana said to the brāhmaṇas: "The ascetic Gautama is a dharma speaker. Those who speak dharma are difficult to debate with and refute. I am unable to go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him."

A third time, the brāhmaṇas said to the young man Āśvalāyana: "The ascetic Gautama teaches a dharma that says all four castes can become pure. You should go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him. If you can refute the ascetic Gautama, then for us brāhmaṇas from Kāśī and Kosala and from other regions, you will bring fame and glory. Āśvalāyana, you are well versed in the three Vedas, able to recite and hold them, thoroughly understanding the words and texts with their commentaries, and fully accomplished in worldly knowledge, including the analysis of physiognomy. If you are unable to go to the ascetic Gautama and debate with him and refute him, then who else would be able to do so? Āśvalāyana, do not retreat without trying!"

At that time, the young man Āśvalāyana was urged three times by the brāhmaṇas. Being unable to decline, he said: "Do not push me further. Since you insist, I will go."

Then the young man Āśvalāyana, together with the many brāhmaṇa householders from Kāśī, Kosala, and other regions, proceeded to the World-Honored One. After they had exchanged greetings, the young man Āśvalāyana sat to one side.

Then the young man Āśvalāyana said to the World-Honored One: "Gautama, the brāhmaṇas say thus: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā.' Gautama, what do you say about this?"

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, do the brāhmaṇas really say thus: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā'?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Indeed, Gautama."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Have you heard that in Yona and Kamboja and in other border regions, there are only two castes: masters and servants? Having been a master, one can become a servant; having been a servant, one can become a master. Have you heard this?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Indeed, I have heard this. In Yona and Kamboja and in other border regions, there are only two castes: masters and servants. Having been a master, one can become a servant; having been a servant, one can become a master."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā'?

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a kṣatriya kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death will that person go to a bad destination or not? Would this be fitting for him or not fitting? What would the brāhmaṇas say about this?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a kṣatriya kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death that person will go to a bad destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a brāhmaṇa kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death will that person go to a bad destination or not? Would this be fitting for him or not fitting?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a brāhmaṇa kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death that person will go to a bad destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a vaiśya kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death will that person go to a bad destination or not? Would this be fitting for him or not fitting?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a vaiśya kills living beings and so forth up to holding wrong views, after death that person will go to a bad destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a śūdra kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, uses divisive speech, uses harsh speech, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, bears ill will, and holds wrong views, after death will that person go to a bad destination or not? Would this be fitting for him or not fitting?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a śūdra kills living beings and so forth up to holding wrong views, after death that person will go to a bad destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā'? What is the reason? Because all four castes, if they kill living beings, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, use divisive speech, use harsh speech, engage in idle chatter, are covetous, bear ill will, and hold wrong views, after death they all go to a bad destination.

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a kṣatriya does not kill living beings, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not use divisive speech, does not use harsh speech, does not engage in idle chatter, is not covetous, does not bear ill will, and holds right views, after death will that person go to a good destination or not? Would this be fitting for him or not fitting? What would the brāhmaṇas say about this?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a kṣatriya does not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death that person will go to a good destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a brāhmaṇa does not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death will that person go to a good destination or not?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, if a brāhmaṇa does not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death that person will go to a good destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a vaiśya does not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death will that person go to a good destination or not?"

Āśvalāyana said: "That person will go to a good destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a śūdra does not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death will that person go to a good destination or not?"

Āśvalāyana said: "That person will go to a good destination. This is fitting, and the brāhmaṇas also say this."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior'? What is the reason? Because all four castes, if they do not kill living beings and so forth up to holding right views, after death they all go to a good destination.

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Is only the brāhmaṇa capable of practicing a mind of loving-kindness toward a certain direction, without enmity, without ill will, without anger, without dispute, being extremely vast, immeasurably expansive, pervading everything well? Are the kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra unable to do so?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. The kṣatriya is also capable of practicing a mind of loving-kindness toward a certain direction, without enmity, without ill will, without anger, without dispute, being extremely vast, immeasurably expansive, pervading everything well. Likewise the vaiśya and śūdra."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior'? What is the reason? Because all four castes are equally capable of practicing a mind of loving-kindness.

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Is only the brāhmaṇa capable of taking a bath-brush, going to the river, and washing away dust and dirt? Are the kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra unable to do so?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. The kṣatriya is also capable of taking a bath-brush, going to the river, and washing away dust and dirt. Likewise the vaiśya and śūdra."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure'? What is the reason? Because all four castes are equally capable of washing away dust and dirt.

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a kṣatriya king were to gather together a hundred types of wood: sāla wood, pine wood, sandalwood, and various other types of wood, and make a fire and produce flame, would that fire have flame, have heat, and be capable of functioning? Would the fire produced from a brāhmaṇa's fire-sticks made only from sāla wood also have flame, have heat, and be capable of functioning, while the fire from miscellaneous wood would have no flame, no heat, and be incapable of functioning?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. Whether fire is produced from sāla wood fire-sticks or from miscellaneous wood, all fire equally has flame, has heat, and is capable of functioning."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā'? What is the reason? Because all four castes equally can make fire and produce flame.

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a kṣatriya son were to marry a brāhmaṇa daughter, and the kṣatriya son and brāhmaṇa daughter gave birth to a child, would that child born from the kṣatriya son and brāhmaṇa daughter be similar to both the father and mother and be called both kṣatriya and brāhmaṇa?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, the child born from a kṣatriya son and brāhmaṇa daughter would be similar to both father and mother and could be called both kṣatriya and brāhmaṇa."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a brāhmaṇa son were to marry a kṣatriya daughter, and the brāhmaṇa son and kṣatriya daughter gave birth to a child, would that child born from the brāhmaṇa son and kṣatriya daughter be similar to both the father and mother and be called both brāhmaṇa and kṣatriya?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, the child born from a brāhmaṇa son and kṣatriya daughter would be similar to both father and mother and could be called both brāhmaṇa and kṣatriya."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior'?

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a brāhmaṇa son were to have his head shaved, put on kāṣāya robes, have right faith, leave the household to practice the Way, and be without home, while a kṣatriya also shaved his head, put on kāṣāya robes, had right faith, left the household to practice the Way, and was without home: is there any difference between these two?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. The brāhmaṇa can shave his head, put on kāṣāya robes, have right faith, leave the household to practice the Way, and be without home. The kṣatriya can likewise. Between the two there is no difference."

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? If a brāhmaṇa son were to have his head shaved, put on kāṣāya robes, have right faith, leave the household to practice the Way, and be without home, while a vaiśya or śūdra also did the same: is there any difference between these?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. The brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra can all shave their heads, put on kāṣāya robes, have right faith, leave the household to practice the Way, and be without home. Among these there is no difference."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā'?"

At that time, the young man Āśvalāyana said to the World-Honored One: "Although Gautama has explained thus, the brāhmaṇas still say: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior. Only brāhmaṇas are of fair complexion; other castes are of dark complexion. Only brāhmaṇas are pure; others are not pure. Only brāhmaṇas are the true sons of Brahmā, born from Brahmā's mouth, born of Brahmā, created by Brahmā, inheritors of Brahmā.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Do only brāhmaṇas own this land and not kṣatriyas?"

Āśvalāyana said: "No, Gautama. Kṣatriyas also own this land."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste'?

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Is it only among brāhmaṇas that, when a family's wealth increases, gold and silver, jewels, grain, slaves, servants, and various kinds of property and livestock multiply and increase? Or is it the same for kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras?"

Āśvalāyana said: "Gautama, among all four castes, when a family's wealth increases, gold and silver, jewels, grain, slaves, servants, and various kinds of property and livestock multiply and increase."

The World-Honored One said: "Āśvalāyana, this being the case, what strength, what basis do the brāhmaṇas have for saying: 'Only brāhmaṇas are the highest caste; other castes are inferior'?

"Āśvalāyana, what do you think? Among kṣatriyas, if there is one who kills living beings, steals, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 53

## Sūtra 199: The Sūtra on the Grounds of Foolishness and Wisdom, Eighth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now explain to you the dharma of foolishness and the dharma of wisdom. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it." The bhikṣus received the teaching and listened.

The Buddha said: "What is the dharma of foolishness? A foolish person has three characteristics of foolishness, three marks of foolishness, three signs of foolishness, by which a foolish person is described as foolish. What are the three? A foolish person thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil speech, and performs evil deeds. Therefore a foolish person is described as foolish. If a foolish person did not think evil thoughts, did not speak evil speech, and did not perform evil deeds, then a foolish person should not be described as foolish. Because a foolish person thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil speech, and performs evil deeds, therefore a foolish person is described as foolish. That foolish person, in the present life, experiences in body and mind three kinds of sorrow and suffering. How does a foolish person experience in body and mind three kinds of sorrow and suffering?

"A foolish person, wherever he goes, or when sitting in an assembly, or when in a lane, or when in a marketplace, or when at a crossroads, people discuss matters pertaining to foolish persons. A foolish person kills, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, and so on up to holding wrong views, and accomplishes countless other evil, unwholesome dharmas. If one who has accomplished countless evil, unwholesome dharmas is seen by others, they then speak of his evil. That foolish person, upon hearing this, then thinks: 'If one who accomplishes countless evil, unwholesome dharmas is seen by others who then speak of his evil, I too have these countless evil, unwholesome dharmas. If others know of them, they will also speak of my evil.' This is called the first sorrow and suffering that a foolish person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that foolish person also sees the king's men seize criminals and inflict various punishments upon them: cutting off hands, cutting off feet, cutting off both hands and feet, cutting off ears, cutting off noses, cutting off both ears and noses, or slicing the flesh piece by piece, pulling out the beard, pulling out the hair, or pulling out both beard and hair, or placing them in a cage and wrapping them in cloth to be burned, or covering them with sand and wrapping them with grass to be set ablaze, or placing them inside an iron donkey's belly, or placing them in an iron pig's mouth, or placing them in an iron tiger's mouth to be burned, or placing them in a copper cauldron, or placing them in an iron cauldron to be boiled, or cutting them to pieces, or piercing them with sharp prongs, or hooking them with hooks, or laying them on an iron bed and pouring boiling oil over them, or placing them in an iron mortar and pounding them with an iron pestle, or having them stung by venomous serpents, or whipping them with whips, or striking them with staffs, or beating them with clubs, or impaling them alive upon stakes, or beheading them. That foolish person, having seen this, then thinks: 'If one who accomplishes countless evil, unwholesome dharmas is known by the king and seized, such punishments are inflicted. I too have these countless evil, unwholesome dharmas. If the king knows, he will also inflict such punishments upon me.' Thus, this is called the second sorrow and suffering that a foolish person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that foolish person practices evil conduct of body, practices evil conduct of speech and mind. When at some time he falls ill and suffers, whether sitting or lying on a bed, whether sitting or lying on a couch, whether sitting or lying on the ground, his body experiences extreme suffering, very severe suffering, even to the point where his life is about to end. All those evil conducts of body, speech, and mind, at that time, loom overhead above him. Just as in the late afternoon when the sun descends behind a high mountain and its shadow looms down upon the ground, so too all those evil conducts of body, speech, and mind, at that time, loom overhead above him. He then thinks: 'These are my evil conducts of body, speech, and mind, looming overhead above me. In past times I did not create merit but created much evil. If there is a place for those who create evil, who are violent and act unreasonably, who do not create merit, do not create goodness, do not create a refuge from fear, a place of shelter and reliance, I shall go to that evil place.' From this arises regret, and having given rise to regret, he dies an unworthy death, comes to an unwholesome end of life. This is called the third sorrow and suffering that a foolish person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that foolish person practices evil conduct of body, practices evil conduct of speech and mind. Having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he certainly goes to an evil destination and is born in hell. Having been born there, he receives painful retribution, which is entirely unlovable, entirely unpleasant, and entirely disagreeable to the mind. If one were to say, 'Entirely unlovable, entirely unpleasant, and entirely disagreeable to the mind,' this describes hell. Why is that? Because hell is entirely unlovable, entirely unpleasant, and entirely disagreeable to the mind."

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! What is the suffering of hell like?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhikṣu! The suffering of hell cannot be fully described; it is simply called the suffering of hell. Bhikṣu! In hell there is only suffering."

The bhikṣu asked again: "World-Honored One! Can a simile be used to illustrate its meaning?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A simile can also be used to illustrate its meaning. Bhikṣu! It is like the king's men seizing a thief and bringing him before the anointed kṣatriya king. They say: 'Your Majesty! This thief is guilty. May Your Majesty punish him.' The anointed kṣatriya king orders: 'Take him away and punish this man's crime. In the morning, stab him with a hundred spears.' The king's men receive the order and take him away to punish him, stabbing him with a hundred spears in the morning, yet the man is still alive. The anointed kṣatriya king asks: 'How is that man?' The king's men answer: 'Your Majesty! The man is still alive.' The anointed kṣatriya king again orders: 'Go! At midday, stab him again with a hundred spears.' The king's men receive the order and at midday stab him again with a hundred spears, yet the man is still alive. The anointed kṣatriya king asks again: 'How is that man?' The king's men answer: 'Your Majesty! The man is still alive.' The anointed kṣatriya king again orders: 'Go! In the evening, stab him again with a hundred spears.' The king's men receive the order and in the evening stab him again with a hundred spears, yet the man is still alive. However, his entire body is pierced through, broken, shattered, and destroyed, with not a single spot intact, down to holes the size of coins. The anointed kṣatriya king asks again: 'How is that man?' The king's men answer: 'Your Majesty! The man is still alive, but his entire body is pierced through, broken, shattered, and destroyed, with not a single spot intact, down to holes the size of coins.' Bhikṣu! What do you think? If that man in one day is stabbed with three hundred spears, would that man's body and mind experience affliction and extreme sorrow and suffering?"

The bhikṣu answered: "World-Honored One! Being stabbed with even one spear, one would already experience extreme suffering. How much more so being stabbed with three hundred spears in one day! Would that man's body and mind not experience affliction and extreme sorrow and suffering?"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One picked up a stone in his hand, the size of a small bean, and said: "Bhikṣu! Do you see this stone I have picked up in my hand, the size of a small bean?"

The bhikṣu answered: "I see it, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One asked again: "Bhikṣu! What do you think? This stone I have picked up, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, which is larger?"

The bhikṣu answered: "The stone the World-Honored One has picked up in his hand, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, could never approach it. It is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison. The Snow Mountain King is simply extremely great, vastly great."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu! If this stone I have picked up, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, could never approach it, is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison, and the Snow Mountain King is simply extremely great, vastly great, in the same way, bhikṣu, if this man in one day is stabbed with three hundred spears, and because of this his body and mind experience affliction and extremely severe sorrow and suffering, compared to the suffering of hell, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, it could never approach it. It is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison. In hell the suffering is simply extreme, vastly extreme.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and with iron axes, blazing and glowing throughout, hew their bodies, making them eight-sided, or six-sided, or four-sided, or round, or high or low, or good or bad. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and with iron adzes, blazing and glowing throughout, hew their bodies, making them eight-sided, or six-sided, or four-sided, or round, or high or low, or good or bad. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and with iron spikes, blazing and glowing throughout, force them to sit upon them. Then with iron tongs they pry open their mouths, and with iron balls, blazing and glowing throughout, they place them in their mouths, burning the lips, burning the tongue, burning the gums, burning the throat, burning the heart, burning the stomach, and passing out through the bottom of the body. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and with iron stakes, blazing and glowing throughout, force them to sit upon them. Then with iron tongs they pry open their mouths, and with molten copper they pour it into their mouths, burning the lips, burning the tongue, burning the gums, burning the throat, burning the heart, burning the stomach, and passing out through the bottom of the body. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and on an iron ground, blazing and glowing throughout, make them lie face up. Spreading out their limbs, they bind and punish them, nailing both hands and both feet with iron nails, and driving a separate iron nail into their belly. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and on an iron ground, blazing and glowing throughout, make them lie face down. They pull the tongue out from the mouth and stretch it out with a hundred nails, without wrinkles, without folds, just as a cow's hide is stretched out with a hundred nails, without wrinkles, without folds. In the same way, beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands and on an iron ground, blazing and glowing throughout, make them lie face down, pull the tongue out from the mouth, and stretch it with a hundred nails, without wrinkles, without folds. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize their head-skin with their hands and flay it downward to the feet, then flay the skin from the feet upward to the head. They then take an iron chariot, blazing and glowing throughout, bind them to the chariot, and on an iron ground, blazing and glowing throughout, drag them back and forth. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens take fire, blazing and glowing throughout, and throw them up into the air and hurl them to the ground, then make them pick it up with their hands and pour it over their own bodies. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens make them climb up and down a mountain of fire, blazing and glowing throughout. When they step down, their skin, flesh, and blood are immediately burned away. When they lift their feet, their skin, flesh, and blood grow back as before. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? Beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands. Taking a great iron cauldron, blazing and glowing throughout, they lift them upside down, feet upward and head downward, and cast them into the cauldron. There within, they rise and sink, moving to the sides. Their own bodily foam comes out, and their bodies are boiled. Just as great beans, small beans, clustered beans, bitter beans, and mustard seeds are placed in a large water-filled cauldron with a fierce fire burning below, and those beans rise and sink within, moving to the sides, with their foam entangling as they boil, in the same way, beings born in hell, having been born there, the hell wardens seize them with their hands, and taking a great iron cauldron, blazing and glowing throughout, lift them upside down, feet upward and head downward, and cast them into the cauldron. There within, they rise and sink, moving to the sides. Their own bodily foam comes out, and their bodies are boiled. Being punished in this way, the suffering and anguish press upon them for a great many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, experiencing immeasurable suffering, extremely severe, vastly severe suffering. They never die until their evil, unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of hell? In those hells there is a hell called the Six Contacts. If beings are born there, having been born there, whatever forms the eye sees are unpleasant and disagreeable, not pleasant or agreeable; they are not delightful to the mind, not truly delightful; they are not joyous to the mind, not truly joyous. Whatever sounds the ear hears, whatever odors the nose smells, whatever flavors the tongue tastes, whatever tangibles the body feels, whatever dharmas the mind cognizes, they are unpleasant and disagreeable, not pleasant or agreeable; they are not delightful to the mind, not truly delightful; they are not joyous to the mind, not truly joyous. This is called the suffering of hell.

"Bhikṣu! I have in countless ways explained those hells and the affairs of hell. However, the suffering of hell cannot be fully described. In hell there is only suffering. Bhikṣu! If a foolish person sometimes emerges from hell and is born among animals, the animal realm is also extremely painful."

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of the animal realm? If beings are born among animals, there are those born in darkness, who grow in darkness and die in darkness. Who are they? They are earth-dwelling worms. A foolish person, because in past times he was attached to the flavors of food and practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he is born among animals, born in darkness, growing in darkness, and dying in darkness. This is called the suffering of the animal realm.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of the animal realm? If beings are born among animals, there are those born within bodies, who grow within bodies and die within bodies. Who are they? They are called wound-worms. A foolish person, because in past times he was attached to the flavors of food and practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he is born among animals, born within bodies, growing within bodies, and dying within bodies. This is called the suffering of the animal realm.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of the animal realm? If beings are born among animals, there are those born in water, who grow in water and die in water. Who are they? They are fish, makara fish, turtles, crocodiles, bāluṇī, timiṅgala, timiṅgilagala, and timitimiṅgilagala. A foolish person, because in past times he was attached to the flavors of food and practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he is born among animals, born in water, growing in water, and dying in water. This is called the suffering of the animal realm.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of the animal realm? If beings are born among animals, there are those who gnaw with their teeth and eat growing grass, trees, and plants. Who are they? They are elephants, horses, camels, cattle, donkeys, deer, water buffalo, and pigs. A foolish person, because in past times he was attached to the flavors of food and practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he is born among animals, gnawing with teeth on growing grass, trees, and plants for food. This is called the suffering of the animal realm.

"Bhikṣu! What is the suffering of the animal realm? If beings are born among animals, there are those who, smelling the odor of human urine and feces, run toward it, eating that as their food. Just as men and women, smelling the fragrance of food and drink, immediately go toward it, so it is said that those creatures eat that as their food. In the same way, bhikṣu, beings born among animals smell the odor of human urine and feces, run toward it, and eat that as their food. Who are they? They are chickens, pigs, dogs, jackals, crows, vultures, and kestrels. A foolish person, because in past times he was attached to the flavors of food and practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he is born among animals, eating feces and filth. This is called the suffering of the animal realm.

"Bhikṣu! I have in countless ways explained those animals and the affairs of animals. However, the suffering of the animal realm cannot be fully described. In the animal realm there is only suffering.

"Bhikṣu! If a foolish person emerges from the animal realm and is reborn as a human, this is extremely, vastly difficult. Why is that? Because among animals they do not practice benevolence and righteousness, do not practice propriety and law, do not practice sublime goodness. Those animals devour one another; the strong devour the weak, the large devour the small. Bhikṣu! It is like this entire earth filled with water, and there is a blind turtle whose lifespan is countless hundreds of thousands of years. On the surface of the water there is a small, light wooden plank with only one hole, blown about by the wind. Bhikṣu! What do you think? Could that blind turtle's head ever enter the single hole in that small, light wooden plank?"

The bhikṣu answered: "World-Honored One! It might possibly enter, but only after a very long time with great difficulty."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu! Perhaps after a hundred years the blind turtle comes from the east and once raises its head, but that small plank with one hole has been blown by the east wind to the south. Perhaps after a hundred years the blind turtle comes from the south and once raises its head, but that plank with one hole has been blown by the south wind to the west. Perhaps after a hundred years the blind turtle comes from the west and once raises its head, but that plank with one hole has been blown by the west wind to the north. Perhaps the blind turtle comes from the north and once raises its head, but that plank with one hole has been blown by the north wind to various other directions. Bhikṣu! What do you think? Could that blind turtle's head ever enter this plank with one hole?"

The bhikṣu answered: "World-Honored One! It might possibly enter, but only after a very long time with great difficulty."

"Bhikṣu! In the same way, that foolish person, emerging from the animal realm and being reborn as a human, is also vastly difficult. Why is that? Because among animals they do not practice benevolence and righteousness, do not practice propriety and law, do not practice sublime goodness. Those animals devour one another; the strong devour the weak, the large devour the small. Bhikṣu! If a foolish person sometimes emerges from the animal realm and is reborn as a human, if he has a family, it will be of a minor clan, low and base, wretched and poor, with little food and drink, where obtaining food is very difficult. Who are they? They are families of prison wardens, families of craftsmen, families of manual laborers, families of potters, and other such low and base families, wretched and poor, with little food and drink, where obtaining food is very difficult. Born into such a family, having been born there, he is either blind, or lame, or has shortened arms, or a hunched body, or is left-handed, of ugly complexion and sheep-faced, hideous and short-lived, used as a servant by others. He practices evil conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he returns to an evil destination and is born in hell.

"It is like two people gambling together. One of them, having taken such a course of play, first loses his male and female servants, then loses his wife and children, and then stakes his own body and is hung upside down in a smoke house. He thinks: 'Without eating or drinking, I took such a course of play and first lost my male and female servants, then lost my wife and children, and now staked my own body to be hung upside down in a smoke house.' Bhikṣu! This is a minor course of action, to lose male and female servants, lose wife and children, and stake one's own body to be hung upside down in a smoke house. Bhikṣu! The course of action that surpasses this is practicing evil conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, one returns to an evil destination and is born in hell. Bhikṣu! Of all courses of action, this is the most unlovable, truly the most unpleasant, and the most disagreeable to the mind. Bhikṣu! Have I not fully explained the dharma of foolishness?"

The bhikṣu answered: "Indeed, World-Honored One! You have fully explained the dharma of foolishness."

The World-Honored One said: "What is the dharma of wisdom? A wise person has three characteristics of wisdom, three marks of wisdom, three signs of wisdom, by which a wise person is described as wise. What are the three? A wise person thinks good thoughts, speaks good speech, and performs good deeds. Therefore a wise person is described as wise. If a wise person did not think good thoughts, did not speak good speech, and did not perform good deeds, then a wise person should not be described as wise. Because a wise person thinks good thoughts, speaks good speech, and performs good deeds, therefore a wise person is described as wise. A wise person, in the present life, experiences in body and mind three kinds of joy and happiness. How does a wise person experience in body and mind three kinds of joy and happiness in the present life?

"A wise person, wherever he goes, or when sitting in an assembly, or when in a lane, or when in a marketplace, or when at a crossroads, people discuss matters pertaining to wise persons. A wise person abstains from killing, abandons killing, abstains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, and so on up to abandoning wrong views and attaining right views, and accomplishes countless other wholesome dharmas. If one who has accomplished countless wholesome dharmas is seen by others, they then praise him. That wise person, upon hearing this, then thinks: 'If one who accomplishes countless wholesome dharmas is seen by others who then praise him, I too have these countless wholesome dharmas. If others know of them, they will also praise me.' This is called the first joy and happiness that a wise person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that wise person also sees the king's men inflicting various punishments upon thieves: cutting off hands, cutting off feet, cutting off both hands and feet, cutting off ears, cutting off noses, cutting off both ears and noses, or slicing the flesh piece by piece, pulling out the beard, pulling out the hair, or pulling out both beard and hair, or placing them in a cage and wrapping them in cloth to be burned, or covering them with sand and wrapping them with grass to be set ablaze, or placing them inside an iron donkey's belly, or placing them in an iron pig's mouth, or placing them in an iron tiger's mouth to be burned, or placing them in a copper cauldron, or placing them in an iron cauldron to be boiled, or cutting them to pieces, or piercing them with sharp prongs, or hooking them with hooks, or laying them on an iron bed and pouring boiling oil over them, or placing them in an iron mortar and pounding them with an iron pestle, or having them stung by venomous serpents, or whipping them with whips, or striking them with staffs, or beating them with clubs, or impaling them alive upon stakes, or beheading them. That wise person, having seen this, then thinks: 'If one who accomplishes countless evil, unwholesome dharmas is known by the king and seized, such punishments are inflicted. I do not have these countless evil, unwholesome dharmas. If the king knows, he will certainly never inflict such punishments upon me.' This is called the second joy and happiness that a wise person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that wise person practices wholesome conduct of body, practices wholesome conduct of speech and mind. When at some time he falls ill, whether sitting or lying on a bed, whether sitting or lying on a couch, whether sitting or lying on the ground, his body experiences extreme suffering, very severe suffering, even to the point where his life is about to end. All those wholesome conducts of body, speech, and mind, at that time, loom overhead above him. Just as in the late afternoon when the sun descends behind a high mountain and its shadow looms down upon the ground, so too all those wholesome conducts of body, speech, and mind, at that time, loom overhead above him. He then thinks: 'These are my wholesome conducts of body, speech, and mind, looming overhead above me. In past times I did not create evil but created much merit. If there is a place for those who do not create evil, who are not violent, who do not act unreasonably, who create merit, create goodness, create a refuge from fear, a place of shelter and reliance, I shall go to that good place.' He does not give rise to regret, and not having given rise to regret, he dies a worthy death and comes to a wholesome end of life. This is called the third joy and happiness that a wise person experiences in body and mind in the present life.

"Furthermore, that wise person practices wholesome conduct of body, practices wholesome conduct of speech and mind. Having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he certainly ascends to a good destination and is born above in heaven. Having been born there, he receives pleasant retribution, which is entirely lovable, entirely pleasant, and entirely agreeable to the mind. If one were to say, 'Entirely lovable, entirely pleasant, and entirely agreeable to the mind,' this describes a good destination. Why is that? Because a good destination is entirely lovable, entirely pleasant, and entirely agreeable to the mind."

At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! What is the happiness of a good destination like?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhikṣu! The happiness of a good destination cannot be fully described; it is simply called the happiness of a good destination. In a good destination there is only happiness."

The bhikṣu asked again: "World-Honored One! Can a simile be used to illustrate its meaning?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A simile can also be used to illustrate its meaning. It is like a wheel-turning king who has accomplished the seven treasures and the four kinds of wish-fulfilling powers. Bhikṣu! What do you think? That wheel-turning king, having accomplished the seven treasures and the four kinds of wish-fulfilling powers, would he on account of this experience in body and mind extreme joy and happiness?"

The bhikṣu answered: "World-Honored One! Having accomplished even one treasure and one wish-fulfilling power, one would already experience extreme joy and happiness. How much more so a wheel-turning king who has accomplished the seven treasures and the four kinds of wish-fulfilling powers! Would he not experience extreme joy and happiness?"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One picked up a stone in his hand, the size of a small bean, and said: "Bhikṣu! Do you see this stone I have picked up in my hand, the size of a small bean?"

The bhikṣu answered: "I see it, World-Honored One!"

The World-Honored One asked again: "Bhikṣu! What do you think? This stone I have picked up, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, which is larger?"

The bhikṣu answered: "The stone the World-Honored One has picked up in his hand, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, could never approach it. It is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison. The Snow Mountain King is simply extremely great, vastly great."

The World-Honored One said: "Bhikṣu!
