If this stone I have picked up, the size of a small bean, compared to the Snow Mountain King, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, could never approach it, is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison, and the Snow Mountain King is simply extremely great, vastly great, in the same way, bhikṣu, if a wheel-turning king has accomplished the seven treasures and the four kinds of wish-fulfilling powers, and that person's body and mind experience extreme joy and happiness, compared to the happiness of the heavens, a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand ten-thousand times, it could never approach it. It is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond simile, beyond comparison. The happiness of a good destination is simply the happiness of a good destination; in a good destination there is only happiness.

"Bhikṣu! What is the happiness of a good destination? In those good destinations there is a destination called the Six Contacts of Happiness. If beings are born there, having been born there, whatever forms the eye sees are pleasant and agreeable to the mind, they are truly pleasant and agreeable; they are delightful to the mind, they are truly delightful; they are joyous to the mind, they are truly joyous. Whatever sounds the ear hears, whatever odors the nose smells, whatever flavors the tongue tastes, whatever tangibles the body feels, whatever dharmas the mind cognizes are pleasant and agreeable to the mind, they are truly pleasant and agreeable; they are delightful to the mind, they are truly delightful; they are joyous to the mind, they are truly joyous. This is called the happiness of a good destination. Bhikṣu! I have in countless ways explained those good destinations and the affairs of good destinations. However, the happiness of good destinations cannot be fully described. In good destinations there is only happiness.

"Bhikṣu! If a wise person sometimes comes from a good destination and descends to be born in the human realm, if he has a family, it will be one of extreme wealth and comfort, with immeasurable money and treasure, many domestic animals, fiefdoms, food-producing estates, an abundance of rice and grain, and various kinds of livelihood provisions. Who are they? They are families of great kṣatriya elders, families of great brahmin elders, families of great householder elders, and other extremely wealthy and comfortable families, with immeasurable money and treasure, many domestic animals, fiefdoms, food-producing estates, an abundance of rice and grain, and various kinds of livelihood provisions. Born into such a family, he is handsome and lovable, respected and deferred to by the multitudes, of extreme renown, possessing great dignified virtue, loved by many, cherished by many. He practices wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, he returns to a good destination and is born in heaven.

"It is like two people gambling together. One of them, having taken such a course of play, wins much wealth. He thinks: 'Without tilling the fields, I took such a course of play and won much wealth.' Bhikṣu! This is a minor course of action, to win much wealth. Bhikṣu! The course of action that surpasses this is practicing wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this, on account of this, when the body perishes and life ends, one returns to a good destination and is born in heaven. Bhikṣu! Of all courses of action, this is the most lovable, the most pleasant, and the most agreeable to the mind. Bhikṣu! Have I not fully explained the dharma of a wise person?"

The bhikṣu said: "Indeed, World-Honored One! You have fully explained the dharma of a wise person."

The World-Honored One said: "These are the dharma of a foolish person and the dharma of a wise person. You should understand the dharma of a foolish person and the dharma of a wise person. Having understood the dharma of a foolish person and the dharma of a wise person, abandon the dharma of a foolish person and adopt the dharma of a wise person. You should train in this way."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received it and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sūtra on the Grounds of Foolishness and Wisdom, Eighth.

## (200) Sūtra on Ariṭṭha, Ninth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-trainer, gave rise to this evil view: "I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions.'" When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha and asked him: "Ariṭṭha, did you truly say this: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions'?"

At that time Ariṭṭha replied: "Venerables, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions.'"

The bhikṣus rebuked Ariṭṭha, saying: "Do not say such things! Do not falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One. To falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One is unwholesome, and the World-Honored One has never taught thus. Ariṭṭha, sensual pleasures have obstructions. The World-Honored One has taught in innumerable ways that sensual pleasures have obstructions. Ariṭṭha, you should quickly abandon this evil view."

After being rebuked by the bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha held firmly and forcefully to this evil view and declared unequivocally: "This is true; the rest is false." He did so three times.

The many bhikṣus, unable to make the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha abandon this evil view, rose from their seats and departed. They went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha has given rise to this evil view: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions.' World-Honored One, when we heard this, we went to the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha and asked: 'Ariṭṭha, did you truly say this: I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions?' The bhikṣu Ariṭṭha answered us: 'Venerables, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions.' World-Honored One, we rebuked him saying: 'Ariṭṭha, do not say such things! Do not falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One. To falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One is unwholesome, and the World-Honored One has never taught thus. Ariṭṭha, sensual pleasures have obstructions. The World-Honored One has taught in innumerable ways that sensual pleasures have obstructions. Ariṭṭha, you should quickly abandon this evil view.' After we rebuked him, he held firmly and forcefully to this evil view and declared unequivocally: 'This is true; the rest is false.' He did so three times. World-Honored One, since we were unable to make the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha abandon this evil view, we rose from our seats and departed."

When the World-Honored One heard this, he addressed a certain bhikṣu: "Go to where the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha is and say this: 'The World-Honored One summons you.'"

Thereupon, that bhikṣu received the World-Honored One's instruction, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times and departed. He went to where the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha was and said to him: "The World-Honored One summons you." The bhikṣu Ariṭṭha then went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Ariṭṭha, did you truly say: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions'?"

Ariṭṭha replied: "World-Honored One, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions.'"

The World-Honored One rebuked him: "Ariṭṭha, how do you understand me to have taught the Dharma thus? From whose mouth did you hear me teach the Dharma thus? You foolish person! Where I have not taught unequivocally, you speak unequivocally! You foolish person! When you heard the bhikṣus jointly rebuking you, you should have answered according to the Dharma: 'Let me now put the question to the bhikṣus.'"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Do you also understand me to have taught the Dharma thus: 'For one who practices sensual pleasures, there are no obstructions'?"

At that time the bhikṣus answered: "No."

The World-Honored One asked: "How do you understand my teaching of the Dharma?"

The bhikṣus answered: "We understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'Sensual pleasures have obstructions.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures have obstructions. 'Sensual pleasures are like a chain of bones.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a chain of bones. 'Sensual pleasures are like a lump of flesh.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a lump of flesh. 'Sensual pleasures are like a held torch.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a held torch. 'Sensual pleasures are like a pit of fire.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a pit of fire. 'Sensual pleasures are like a poisonous snake.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a poisonous snake. 'Sensual pleasures are like a dream.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like a dream. 'Sensual pleasures are like something borrowed.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like something borrowed. 'Sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree.' The World-Honored One has taught that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree. We understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Bhikṣus, you understand my teaching of the Dharma thus. Why is that? I also have taught thus: 'Sensual pleasures have obstructions.' I have taught that sensual pleasures have obstructions. 'Sensual pleasures are like a chain of bones.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a chain of bones. 'Sensual pleasures are like a lump of flesh.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a lump of flesh. 'Sensual pleasures are like a held torch.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a held torch. 'Sensual pleasures are like a pit of fire.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a pit of fire. 'Sensual pleasures are like a poisonous snake.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a poisonous snake. 'Sensual pleasures are like a dream.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like a dream. 'Sensual pleasures are like something borrowed.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like something borrowed. 'Sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree.' I have taught that sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! You understand my teaching of the Dharma thus. However, this foolish person Ariṭṭha has received and understood the meaning and the text in a distorted way. Because he has received and understood them in a distorted way, he falsely misrepresents me, thereby harming himself. He has committed an offense and a transgression, which is not pleasing to wise practitioners of the holy life, and he incurs great guilt. You foolish person, do you know that this is an evil and unwholesome state?"

Thereupon, the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha, having been rebuked to his face by the World-Honored One, was inwardly filled with sorrow and distress, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence and was without words, as if contemplating something.

After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha to his face, he addressed the bhikṣus: "If I have taught a Dharma and you have fully understood its meaning, you should receive and maintain it accordingly. If I have taught a Dharma and you have not fully understood its meaning, then you should ask me or the wise practitioners of the holy life. Why is that? There may be foolish people who receive and understand the meaning and the text in a distorted way. Because they have received and understood them in a distorted way, in whatever manner they understand the Dharma, be it the sūtras, hymns, expositions, verses, accounts of causes, compilations, accounts of origins, thus-said texts, birth stories, extensive explanations, unprecedented teachings, and explanations of meaning, they quarrel over knowing this meaning and do not accept liberation as the purpose of knowing this meaning. The purpose for which they seek to know this Dharma, they do not attain that purpose; they only endure extreme suffering and tire themselves in vain. Why is that? Because they have received and understood the Dharma in a distorted way.

"It is as if there were a person who wished to catch a snake and went out to seek one. While seeking the snake, wandering through wilderness and forests, he saw an extremely large snake and went forward and grasped it around the middle with his hand. The snake turned back its head and bit his hands, feet, and other limbs. The purpose for which that person sought to catch the snake, he did not attain that purpose; he only endured extreme suffering and tired himself in vain. Why is that? Because he did not skillfully understand the method of catching snakes. In the same way, there may be foolish people who receive and understand the meaning and the text in a distorted way. Because they have received and understood them in a distorted way, in whatever manner they understand the Dharma, be it the sūtras, hymns, expositions, verses, accounts of causes, compilations, accounts of origins, thus-said texts, birth stories, extensive explanations, unprecedented teachings, and explanations of meaning, they quarrel over knowing this meaning and do not accept liberation as the purpose of knowing this meaning. The purpose for which they seek to know this Dharma, they do not attain that purpose; they only endure extreme suffering and tire themselves in vain. Why is that? Because they have received and understood the Dharma in a distorted way.

"There may be sons of good families who receive and understand the meaning and the text correctly, without distortion. Because they have received and understood them correctly, without distortion, in whatever manner they understand the Dharma, be it the sūtras, hymns, expositions, verses, accounts of causes, compilations, accounts of origins, thus-said texts, birth stories, extensive explanations, unprecedented teachings, and explanations of meaning, they do not quarrel over knowing this meaning; they accept only liberation as the purpose of knowing this meaning. The purpose for which they seek to know this Dharma, they attain that purpose; they do not endure extreme suffering and are not wearied. Why is that? Because they have received and understood the Dharma without distortion.

"It is as if there were a person who wished to catch a snake and went out to seek one. While seeking the snake, holding an iron staff in hand, wandering through wilderness and forests, he saw an extremely large snake. He first pressed the snake's head down with the iron staff and then grasped it by the head with his hand. Although the snake coiled back its tail and wound around his hands, feet, and other limbs, it was unable to bite him. The purpose for which that person sought to catch the snake, he attained that purpose; he did not endure extreme suffering and was not wearied. Why is that? Because he skillfully understood the method of catching snakes. In the same way, there may be sons of good families who receive and understand the meaning and the text correctly, without distortion. Because they have received and understood them correctly, without distortion, in whatever manner they understand the Dharma, be it the sūtras, hymns, expositions, verses, accounts of causes, compilations, accounts of origins, thus-said texts, birth stories, extensive explanations, unprecedented teachings, and explanations of meaning, they do not quarrel over knowing this meaning; they accept only liberation as the purpose of knowing this meaning. The purpose for which they seek to know this Dharma, they attain that purpose; they do not endure extreme suffering and are not wearied. Why is that? Because they have received and understood the Dharma without distortion. I have for you throughout the long night taught the Dharma by the simile of the raft, wishing you to abandon it, not wishing you to cling to it.

"How have I for you throughout the long night taught the Dharma by the simile of the raft, wishing you to abandon it, not wishing you to cling to it? Suppose there were a mountain stream, very deep and extremely wide, with a long, swift, rapid current that has carried away many things. In it there is no boat, nor is there a bridge. Suppose someone came along who had business on the other shore and wished to cross. While seeking to cross, he thought thus: 'This mountain stream is very deep and extremely wide, with a long, swift, rapid current that has carried away many things. In it there is no boat, nor is there a bridge by which to cross. I have business on the other shore and wish to cross. By what means can I safely reach the other shore?' He thought further: 'Suppose I were to gather grass and wood here on this bank, bind them together to make a raft, and riding upon it, cross over.' He then gathered grass and wood on the bank, bound them together to make a raft, and riding upon it, crossed over safely to the other shore. He then thought: 'This raft of mine has been of great benefit. Riding this raft, I have safely come from that shore and crossed to this shore. Suppose I were to place it on my right shoulder or carry it on my head and go.' He then placed the raft on his right shoulder or carried it on his head and went. What do you think? Would that person, acting in this way, be doing what would benefit the raft?"

At that time the bhikṣus answered: "No."

The World-Honored One said: "How could that person act so as to benefit the raft? That person would think: 'This raft of mine has been of great benefit. Riding this raft, I have safely come from that shore and crossed to this shore. Suppose I were to put this raft back in the water or place it on the bank and leave it.' That person would then put the raft back in the water or place it on the bank and leave it behind. What do you think? Would that person, acting in this way, be doing what benefits the raft?"

At that time the bhikṣus answered: "Yes, it would."

The World-Honored One said: "In this way, I have for you throughout the long night taught the Dharma by the simile of the raft, wishing you to abandon it, not wishing you to cling to it. If you understand my teaching throughout the long night of the simile of the raft, then you should abandon even the Dharma, how much more so what is not the Dharma!

"Furthermore, there are six bases of views. What are the six? As for a bhikṣu, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether superior or inferior, whether near or far, all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever feelings, whatever perceptions, whatever view of 'this is not mine, I am not its,' and 'I shall not be, I shall not have being,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever view of 'what is seen, heard, cognized, and known, what is attained, what is examined, what the mind thinks upon, from this world to that world, from that world to this world,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever view of 'this is the self, this is the world, this is the "I," and I shall exist after death, permanent, unchanging, eternally indestructible,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is."

Thereupon a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined, faced the Buddha and said: "World-Honored One, can there be fear arising from internal causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "There can."

The bhikṣu further asked: "World-Honored One, how does fear arise from internal causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A bhikṣu who has such a view and speaks thus, 'Suppose I did not exist before; if I were to exist, I would not attain it.' He who has such a view and speaks thus becomes sorrowful and distressed, weeps and beats his breast and falls into madness. Bhikṣu, this is how fear arises from internal causes."

The bhikṣu praised the World-Honored One and further asked: "World-Honored One, can there be no fear arising from internal causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "There can."

The bhikṣu further asked: "World-Honored One, how is there no fear arising from internal causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A bhikṣu who does not have such a view and does not speak thus, 'Suppose I did not exist before; if I were to exist, I would not attain it.' He who does not have such a view and does not speak thus is not sorrowful, not distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness. Bhikṣu, this is how there is no fear arising from internal causes."

The bhikṣu praised the World-Honored One and further asked: "World-Honored One, can there be fear arising from external causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "There can."

The bhikṣu further asked: "World-Honored One, how does fear arise from external causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A bhikṣu who has such a view and speaks thus: 'This is the self, this is the world, this is the "I," and I shall exist after death.' He who has such a view and speaks thus may encounter a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is wise, intelligent, skillful in speech, and accomplished in wisdom. That Tathāgata or that disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all self-identity, teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints, all notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and for the sake of extinguishing the tendency of conceit. When that Tathāgata or that disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all self-identity, teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints, all notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and for the sake of extinguishing the tendency of conceit, that person becomes sorrowful and distressed, weeps and beats his breast and falls into madness, and speaks thus: 'I am annihilated, I am destroyed, I shall no longer exist.' Why is that? Because that bhikṣu, having long dwelt in what is unloved, unjoyful, and unpleasant in his thoughts, from much abiding therein becomes sorrowful and distressed, weeps and beats his breast and falls into madness. Bhikṣu, this is how fear arises from external causes."

The bhikṣu praised the World-Honored One and further asked: "World-Honored One, can there be no fear arising from external causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "There can."

The bhikṣu further asked: "World-Honored One, how is there no fear arising from external causes?"

The World-Honored One answered: "A bhikṣu who does not have such a view and does not speak thus: 'This is the self, this is the world, this is the "I," and I shall exist after death.' He who does not have such a view and does not speak thus may encounter a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is wise, intelligent, skillful in speech, and accomplished in wisdom. That Tathāgata or that disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all self-identity, teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints, all notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and for the sake of extinguishing the tendency of conceit. When that Tathāgata or that disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all self-identity, teaches the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints, all notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and for the sake of extinguishing the tendency of conceit, that person is not sorrowful, not distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness, and does not speak thus: 'I am annihilated, I am destroyed, I shall no longer exist.' Why is that? Because that bhikṣu, having long dwelt in what is loved, joyful, and pleasant in his thoughts, from much abiding therein is not sorrowful, not distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness. Bhikṣu, this is how there is no fear arising from external causes."

At that time, the bhikṣu praised the World-Honored One: "Excellent! Excellent!" Having praised him, he heard what the Buddha said, properly received, maintained, and recited it, and then fell silent.

Thereupon the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus: "Excellent! Excellent! Bhikṣus, having received what is to be received thus, upon receiving it, one does not become sorrowful, not distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness. Do you see anything received, that is to be received, from which one would become sorrowful, distressed, weep, beat one's breast, or fall into madness?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! You rely upon such a view that is to be relied upon, and having seen it, you do not become sorrowful, not distressed, do not weep, do not beat your breast, and do not fall into madness. Do you see any reliance upon such a view that is to be relied upon, having seen which, one would become sorrowful, distressed, weep, beat one's breast, or fall into madness?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Do you take up such a body that is permanent, unchanging, and indestructible? Do you see any body taken up that is permanent, unchanging, and indestructible?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! When one says, 'Because of a self, there is an "I"; without a view of self, there is no "I",' the self and what belongs to the self cannot be obtained or designated, and the view-basis in the mind, the bonds, and the latent tendencies also cannot be obtained or designated. Bhikṣus, is this not a complete explanation of views and what views are connected with, as in the case of the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha who was formerly a vulture-trainer?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Indeed so, World-Honored One. It is a complete explanation of views and what views are connected with, as in the case of the bhikṣu Ariṭṭha who was formerly a vulture-trainer."

"Furthermore, there are six bases of views. What are the six? As for a bhikṣu, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, whether internal or external, whether coarse or fine, whether superior or inferior, whether near or far, all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever formations of feeling, whatever perceptions, whatever view of 'this is not mine, I am not its,' and 'that shall not be, I shall not have being,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever view of 'what is seen, heard, cognized, and known, what is attained, what is examined, what the mind thinks upon, from this world to that world, from that world to this world,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is. Whatever view of 'this is the self, this is the world, this is the "I," and I shall exist after death, permanent, unchanging, eternally indestructible,' all of it is 'not mine, I am not its, and it is not my self.' Thus with wisdom one contemplates and knows it as it truly is.

"Whatever bhikṣu, regarding these six bases of views, does not see a self, and also does not see what belongs to a self, having thus not seen, does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, there is no fear. Because of having no fear, one attains parinirvāṇa. 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no further becoming,' one knows as it truly is. This is called a bhikṣu who has crossed the moat, passed over the moat, broken through the wall, is without a gate, and is a sage's mirror of wisdom. How does a bhikṣu cross the moat? The moat of ignorance has been ended and known, uprooted completely, crushed so as never to arise again. Thus a bhikṣu crosses the moat. How does a bhikṣu pass over the moat? The craving for existence has been ended and known, uprooted completely, crushed so as never to arise again. Thus a bhikṣu passes over the moat. How does a bhikṣu break through the wall? The endless cycle of birth and death has been ended and known, uprooted completely, crushed so as never to arise again. Thus a bhikṣu breaks through the wall. How is a bhikṣu without a gate? The five lower fetters have been ended and known, uprooted completely, crushed so as never to arise again. Thus a bhikṣu is without a gate. How is a bhikṣu a sage's mirror of wisdom? The conceit 'I am' has been ended and known, uprooted completely, crushed so as never to arise again. Thus a bhikṣu is a sage's mirror of wisdom. This is called a bhikṣu who has crossed the moat, passed over the moat, broken through the wall, is without a gate, and is a sage's mirror of wisdom.

"One thus rightly liberated, like the Tathāgata: though there be Indra and the gods, Īśāna, Brahmā and his retinue, they seek but cannot find what consciousness the Tathāgata depends upon. The Tathāgata is holy, the Tathāgata is cool, the Tathāgata is without affliction, the Tathāgata is not different. I speak thus: 'Certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas falsely misrepresent me with untrue and unreal words, saying the śramaṇa Gautama teaches nihilism, that he designates the annihilation and destruction of actually existing beings. But herein there is no "I" that I assert.' That Tathāgata, in the present life, teaches freedom from sorrow. If there are others who revile and abuse the Tathāgata, strike the Tathāgata, are angry and reproach the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata on that account does not become angry or resentful, and there is never any harmful intention. When others revile and abuse the Tathāgata, strike, are angry and reproach the Tathāgata, what is the Tathāgata's thought? The Tathāgata thinks thus: 'Whatever I formerly did, whatever I formerly created, on account of that, this comes to me.' Thus when reviled and abused, struck, and angrily reproached, the Tathāgata has this attitude. If there are others who are respectful toward the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying reverence, and honoring him, the Tathāgata on that account does not feel delight, does not feel joy, and the mind does not feel pleasure. When others are respectful toward the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying reverence, and honoring him, what is the Tathāgata's thought? The Tathāgata thinks thus: 'Whatever I now know and have cut off, on account of that, this comes to me.' When others are respectful toward the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying reverence, and honoring him, the Tathāgata has this attitude."

Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If there are others who revile and abuse you, strike, are angry and reproach you, or if there are those who are respectful, making offerings, paying reverence, and honoring you, you also on that account should not become angry or resentful, should not give rise to harmful intention, and also should not feel delight or joy, and your minds should not feel pleasure. Why is that? Because we are without a self and without what belongs to a self. It is like the dry grass and withered wood outside the gate of this Jeta Grove: if some other person were to take it away to burn with fire and use as they please, what do you think? Would that dry grass and withered wood have any such thought: 'That other person is taking me away to burn with fire and use as they please'?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"In the same way, if there are others who revile and abuse you, strike, are angry and reproach you, or if there are those who are respectful, making offerings, paying reverence, and honoring you, you also on that account should not become angry or resentful, should not give rise to harmful intention, and also should not feel delight or joy, and your minds should not feel pleasure. Why is that? Because we are without a self and without what belongs to a self. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Those who, through right wisdom, are liberated and pass away, they are not designated as having endless existence. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Those who have exhausted the five lower fetters and pass away are reborn in that realm and there attain parinirvāṇa, attaining the state of non-return, not returning to this world. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Those who have exhausted the three fetters, with lust, hatred, and delusion weakened, attain the state of once-returning between the heavens and the human realm; having once returned, they reach the end of suffering. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Those who have exhausted the three fetters attain the fruit of stream-entry, do not fall into evil destinies, are certain to proceed toward right awakening, and after at most seven returns between the heavens and the human realm, having completed seven returns, reach the end of suffering. My Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Thus my Dharma is well taught, disclosed and widely disseminated, without deficiency, spread and proclaimed, reaching even to devas and humans. Those who have faith and delight in me and pass away are all born in good destinations, as stated above, with further results."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Ariṭṭha Sūtra, Ninth.

---

## (201) The Sūtra on Sāti, Tenth of the Great Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Sāti, son of a fisherman, gave rise to this evil view: "I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.'" When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to where the bhikṣu Sāti was and asked him: "Sāti, did you truly say this: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising'?"

The bhikṣu Sāti answered: "Venerables, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.'"

At that time the bhikṣus rebuked the bhikṣu Sāti: "Do not say such things! Do not falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One. To falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One is unwholesome, and the World-Honored One has never taught thus. Bhikṣu Sāti, this consciousness arises due to conditions. The World-Honored One has taught in innumerable ways that consciousness arises due to conditions. When there are conditions, it arises; when there are no conditions, it ceases. Bhikṣu Sāti, you should quickly abandon this evil view."

After being rebuked by the bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Sāti held firmly and forcefully to this evil view and declared unequivocally: "This is true; the rest is false." He did so three times.

The many bhikṣus, unable to make the bhikṣu Sāti abandon this evil view, rose from their seats and departed. They went to where the Buddha was, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One, the bhikṣu Sāti has given rise to this evil view: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.' World-Honored One, when we heard this, we went to the bhikṣu Sāti and asked: 'Sāti, did you truly say this: I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.' The bhikṣu Sāti answered us: 'Venerables, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.' World-Honored One, we rebuked him saying: 'Bhikṣu Sāti, do not say such things! Do not falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One. To falsely misrepresent the World-Honored One is unwholesome, and the World-Honored One has never taught thus. Bhikṣu Sāti, this consciousness arises due to conditions. The World-Honored One has taught in innumerable ways that consciousness arises due to conditions. Consciousness, when there are conditions, arises; when there are no conditions, it ceases. Bhikṣu Sāti, you should quickly abandon this evil view.' After we rebuked him, he held firmly and forcefully to this evil view and declared unequivocally: 'This is true; the rest is false.' He did so three times. World-Honored One, since we were unable to make the bhikṣu Sāti abandon this evil view, we rose from our seats and departed."

When the World-Honored One heard this, he addressed a certain bhikṣu: "Go to where the bhikṣu Sāti is and say this: 'The World-Honored One summons you.'"

Thereupon, that bhikṣu received the World-Honored One's instruction, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times and departed. He went to where the bhikṣu Sāti was and said to him: "The World-Honored One summons you." The bhikṣu Sāti then went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Did you truly say: 'I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising'?"

The bhikṣu Sāti answered: "World-Honored One, I truly understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Which consciousness is this?"

The bhikṣu Sāti answered: "World-Honored One, it is this consciousness that speaks, perceives, acts, directs others to act, initiates, and sets in motion; it is that which, having done good or evil deeds, receives their retribution."

The World-Honored One rebuked him: "Sāti, how do you understand me to have taught the Dharma thus? From whose mouth did you hear me teach the Dharma thus? You foolish person! Where I have not taught unequivocally, you speak unequivocally! You foolish person! When you heard the bhikṣus jointly rebuking you, you should have answered according to the Dharma: 'Let me now put the question to the bhikṣus.'"

Thereupon the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Do you also understand me to have taught the Dharma thus: 'This same consciousness transmigrates and is reborn, without any other arising'?"

At that time the bhikṣus answered: "No."

The World-Honored One asked: "How do you understand my teaching of the Dharma?"

The bhikṣus answered: "We understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus: 'Consciousness arises due to conditions.' The World-Honored One has taught that consciousness arises due to conditions. 'Consciousness, when there are conditions, arises; when there are no conditions, it ceases.' We understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Bhikṣus, you understand my teaching of the Dharma thus. Why is that? I also have taught thus: 'Consciousness arises due to conditions.' I have taught that consciousness arises due to conditions. 'Consciousness, when there are conditions, arises; when there are no conditions, it ceases.' Consciousness is designated according to whatever condition it arises from, as that condition. When consciousness arises dependent on the eye and form, the consciousness that arises is called eye-consciousness. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body; when consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental objects, the consciousness that arises is called mind-consciousness. Just as with fire, which is designated according to whatever fuel it burns with: when fire is produced dependent on wood, it is called a wood fire; when fire is produced dependent on grass or dung, it is called a grass or dung fire. In the same way, consciousness is designated according to whatever condition it arises from. When consciousness arises dependent on the eye and form, the consciousness that arises is called eye-consciousness. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body; when consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental objects, the consciousness that arises is called mind-consciousness."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! You understand my teaching of the Dharma thus. However, this bhikṣu Sāti, a foolish person, has received and understood the meaning and the text in a distorted way. Because he has received and understood them in a distorted way, he falsely misrepresents me, thereby harming himself. He has committed an offense and a transgression, which is not pleasing to wise practitioners of the holy life, and he incurs great guilt. You foolish person, do you know that this is an evil and unwholesome state?"

Thereupon the bhikṣu Sāti, having been rebuked by the World-Honored One to his face, was inwardly filled with sorrow and distress, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence and was without words, as if contemplating something.

After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Sāti to his face, he addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall now teach you the Dharma that is ultimate, without vexation, without affliction, eternally unchanging, as contemplated by the wise. Listen well, listen well, and think upon it carefully." At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.

The Buddha said: "Do you see what is true?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Do you see what the Tathāgata truly teaches?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When the Tathāgata ceases, whatever is true, that also is subject to cessation. Do you see this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Do you see what has already been truly taught?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Do you see what the Tathāgata has already truly taught?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When the Tathāgata ceases, whatever is true, that also is subject to cessation. Have you already seen this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Is what has been truly taught free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Is what the Tathāgata has truly taught free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When the Tathāgata ceases, whatever is true, that also is subject to cessation. Is it free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When what is truly taught is thus seen with wisdom as it truly is, are all doubts and confusions extinguished?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When what the Tathāgata truly teaches is thus seen with wisdom as it truly is, are all doubts and confusions extinguished?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When the Tathāgata ceases, whatever is true, that also is subject to cessation. When this is seen with wisdom as it truly is, are all doubts and confusions extinguished?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Is what has been truly taught already free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Is what the Tathāgata has truly taught already free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "When the Tathāgata has ceased, whatever is true, that also is subject to cessation. Is it already free from doubt and confusion?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! If you know and see thus, would you say, 'This view of mine is thus pure,' and cling to it, cherish it, guard it, and not wish to let it go? Do you understand my teaching throughout the long night of the simile of the raft, knowing already that what was blocked should be opened?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! If you know and see thus, would you say, 'This view of mine is thus pure,' yet not cling to it, not cherish it, not guard it, and wish to let it go? Do you understand my teaching throughout the long night of the simile of the raft, knowing already that what was blocked should be opened?"

The bhikṣus answered: "Yes, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! If followers of other teachings were to come and ask you, 'Venerables, if you have such a pure view, what is its meaning, what is its purpose, what is its benefit?' How would you answer?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, if followers of other teachings were to come and ask us, 'Venerables, if you have such a pure view, what is its meaning, what is its purpose, what is its benefit?' we would answer thus: 'Venerables, it is for the purpose of disenchantment, for the purpose of dispassion, for the purpose of seeing and knowing as it truly is.' World-Honored One, if followers of other teachings were to come and ask us, we would answer thus."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! If followers of other teachings were to come and ask you, you should answer thus. Why is that? This teaching is to be contemplated thus: First, there is the food of physical nourishment, coarse and fine; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness. What is the cause, what is the condition of these four foods? From what do they arise? By what do they exist? Those four foods have craving as their cause, craving as their condition; they arise from craving; they exist by craving. What is the cause, what is the condition of craving? From what does it arise? By what does it exist? Craving has feeling as its cause, feeling as its condition; it arises from feeling; it exists by feeling. What is the cause, what is the condition of feeling? From what does it arise? By what does it exist? Feeling has contact as its cause, contact as its condition; it arises from contact; it exists by contact. What is the cause, what is the condition of contact? From what does it arise? By what does it exist? Contact has the six sense-bases as its cause, the six sense-bases as its condition; it arises from the six sense-bases; it exists by the six sense-bases. What is the cause, what is the condition of the six sense-bases? From what do they arise? By what do they exist? The six sense-bases have name-and-form as their cause, name-and-form as their condition; they arise from name-and-form; they exist by name-and-form. What is the cause, what is the condition of name-and-form? From what does it arise? By what does it exist? Name-and-form has consciousness as its cause, consciousness as its condition; it arises from consciousness; it exists by consciousness. What is the cause, what is the condition of consciousness? From what does it arise? By what does it exist? Consciousness has volitional formations as its cause, volitional formations as its condition; it arises from volitional formations; it exists by volitional formations. What is the cause, what is the condition of volitional formations? From what do they arise? By what do they exist? Volitional formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their condition; they arise from ignorance; they exist by ignorance.

"Thus, conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense-bases; conditioned by the six sense-bases there is contact; conditioned by contact there is feeling; conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is clinging; conditioned by clinging there is becoming; conditioned by becoming there is birth; conditioned by birth there is old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Thus this entire great mass of suffering arises. 'Conditioned by birth there is old age and death.' This is called 'conditioned by birth there is old age and death.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by birth there is old age and death. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by birth there is old age and death."

"'Conditioned by becoming there is birth.' This is called 'conditioned by becoming there is birth.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by becoming there is birth. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by becoming there is birth."

"'Conditioned by clinging there is becoming.' This is called 'conditioned by clinging there is becoming.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by clinging there is becoming. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by clinging there is becoming."

"'Conditioned by craving there is clinging.' This is called 'conditioned by craving there is clinging.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by craving there is clinging. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by craving there is clinging."

"'Conditioned by feeling there is craving.' This is called 'conditioned by feeling there is craving.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by feeling there is craving. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by feeling there is craving."

"'Conditioned by contact there is feeling.' This is called 'conditioned by contact there is feeling.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by contact there is feeling. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by contact there is feeling."

"'Conditioned by the six sense-bases there is contact.' This is called 'conditioned by the six sense-bases there is contact.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by the six sense-bases there is contact. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by the six sense-bases there is contact."

"'Conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense-bases.' This is called 'conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense-bases.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense-bases. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense-bases."

"'Conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form.' This is called 'conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form."

"'Conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness.' This is called 'conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness."

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations. This is what we think. Why is that? Because conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations. The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, with the cessation of birth, old age and death ceases. This is what we think. Why is that? Because with the cessation of birth, old age and death ceases."

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. This is what we think. Why is that? Because with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases."

"'With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases.' This is called 'with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases.' What do you think about this?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. This is what we think. Why is that? Because with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases."

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. This is what we think. Why is that? Because with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense-bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense-bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease, and sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair can cease. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Bhikṣus, you speak thus. Why is that? I also have taught thus: With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense-bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense-bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease, and sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair can cease. Thus this entire great mass of suffering ceases."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! If you know and see thus, would you think regarding the past: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? Through what cause did I exist in the past?'"

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 55
