## (202) The Pūrṇa Chapter of the Madhyamāgama: The Sūtra on Observing the Fast, First

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying at the Eastern Park in the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, Migāra's Mother Viśākhā bathed at dawn, put on clean white garments, and, surrounded by her sons, daughters-in-law, and other family members, went to where the Buddha was. She bowed her head in reverence, then stood to one side. The World-Honored One asked: "Householder's wife, have you bathed today?"

She answered: "World-Honored One, today I am observing the fast. Well-Gone One, today I am observing the fast."

The World-Honored One asked: "Householder's wife, what kind of fast are you observing today? There are three kinds of fasts. What are the three? The first is the cowherd boy's fast, the second is the Nirgrantha fast, and the third is the Noble Eightfold Fast. Householder's wife, what is meant by the cowherd boy's fast? It is like a cowherd boy who releases the cattle into the pasture in the morning and gathers them back to the village in the evening. When returning to the village, he thinks thus: 'Today I grazed the cattle in this place; tomorrow I shall graze them in that place. Today I watered the cattle in this place; tomorrow I shall water them in that place. Today the cattle lodged in this place; tomorrow they shall lodge in that place.' Householder's wife, in the same way, when a certain person observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'Today I ate such and such food; tomorrow I shall eat such and such food. Today I drank such and such drink; tomorrow I shall drink such and such drink. Today I savored such and such delicacies; tomorrow I shall savor such and such delicacies.' That person, throughout the day and night, is attached to and delights in desires. This is called the cowherd boy's fast. If one observes the fast in this way as a cowherd boy's fast, one does not obtain great benefit, does not obtain great fruit, has no great merit, and does not achieve widespread results.

"Householder's wife, what is meant by the Nirgrantha fast? There are those who go forth to train as Nirgranthas. They exhort people saying: 'You should, toward the east beyond a hundred yojanas, wherever there are sentient beings, for the sake of protecting them, abandon knife and staff. Likewise toward the south, west, and north beyond a hundred yojanas, wherever there are sentient beings, for the sake of protecting them, abandon knife and staff.' In this way they exhort people. They may have the notion of protecting some sentient beings, while having no notion of protecting other sentient beings. They say: 'On the fifteenth day, when you recite the Prātimokṣa, remove your clothing, stand naked, face the east, and speak thus: "I have no father or mother, nor do father and mother possess me. I have no wife or children, nor do wife and children possess me. I have no slaves or servants, nor was I born of slaves or servants."' Householder's wife, they wish to exhort people in truthful speech, but instead they exhort them in false and deceptive words. For that person, day after day seeing his father and mother, thinks: 'These are my father and mother.' His father and mother, day after day seeing their son, also think: 'This is our son.' He sees his wife and children and thinks: 'These are my wife and children.' His wife and children see him and also think: 'This is our lord.' He sees his slaves and servants and thinks: 'These are my slaves and servants.' His slaves and servants see him and also think: 'This is our master.' He uses these desires, using what was not given, not using what was given. This is called the Nirgrantha fast. If one observes the Nirgrantha fast in this way, one does not obtain great benefit, does not obtain great fruit, has no great merit, and does not achieve widespread results.

"Householder's wife, what is meant by the Noble Eightfold Fast? When a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons killing, abstains from killing, casts aside knife and staff, has shame and conscience, has a compassionate heart, benefits all beings even down to insects. He purifies his mind with regard to killing. I too, for the whole of my life, abandon killing, abstain from killing, cast aside knife and staff, have shame and conscience, have a compassionate heart, benefit all beings even down to insects. Today I purify my mind with regard to killing. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons taking what is not given, abstains from taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, delights in taking what is given, always enjoys giving, his mind delights in relinquishment, is joyful and without miserliness, does not hope for reward, does not conceal theft in his mind, and is able to restrain himself. He purifies his mind with regard to taking what is not given. I too, for the whole of my life, abandon taking what is not given, abstain from taking what is not given. I take only what is given, delight in taking what is given, always enjoy giving, my mind delights in relinquishment, I am joyful and without miserliness, do not hope for reward, do not conceal theft in my mind, and am able to restrain myself. I purify my mind with regard to taking what is not given. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons unchaste conduct, abstains from unchaste conduct, practices the holy life, with a sincere and pure mind, with conduct free from foulness, is separated from desire and abstains from sexual intercourse. He purifies his mind with regard to unchaste conduct. For this day and this night, I abandon unchaste conduct, abstain from unchaste conduct, practice the holy life, with a sincere and pure mind, with conduct free from foulness, separated from desire, abstaining from sexual intercourse. I purify my mind with regard to unchaste conduct. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons false speech, abstains from false speech. He speaks truth, delights in truth, abides in truth, is trusted by people, and does not deceive the world. He purifies his mind with regard to false speech. I too, for the whole of my life, abandon false speech, abstain from false speech. I speak truth, delight in truth, abide in truth, am trusted by people, and do not deceive the world. I purify my mind with regard to false speech. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness, abstains from intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness. He purifies his mind with regard to intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness. I too, for the whole of my life, abandon intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness, abstain from intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness. I purify my mind with regard to intoxicating liquor that causes heedlessness. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons high and broad beds, abstains from high and broad beds. He delights in low seats and beds, using either a low couch or a grass mat. He purifies his mind with regard to high and broad beds. For this day and this night, I abandon high and broad beds, abstain from high and broad beds. I delight in low seats and beds, using either a low couch or a grass mat. I purify my mind with regard to high and broad beds. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them; abstains from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them. He purifies his mind with regard to flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them. For this day and this night, I abandon flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them; I abstain from flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them. I purify my mind with regard to flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes, cosmetics, singing, dancing, music, and going to watch and listen to them. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he thinks thus: 'The Arahant, the True Person, for the whole of his life abandons eating at improper times, abstains from eating at improper times. He eats one meal, does not eat at night, and delights in eating at the proper time. He purifies his mind with regard to eating at improper times. For this day and this night, I abandon eating at improper times, abstain from eating at improper times. I eat one meal, do not eat at night, and delight in eating at the proper time. I purify my mind with regard to eating at improper times. By this factor I am equal to and no different from the Arahant.' Therefore the fast is observed.

"Having established oneself in this Noble Eightfold Fast, one should further cultivate five additional practices. What are the five? Householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Tathāgata: 'That World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' Having thus recollected the Tathāgata, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Tathāgata as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"It is like a person whose head is covered with grease and dirt; by means of oil, warm water, and human effort in washing and bathing, it becomes clean. In the same way, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Tathāgata: 'That World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Those to Be Tamed, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, called the Buddha, the World-Honored One.' Having thus recollected the Tathāgata, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Tathāgata as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. This is called the well-learned noble disciple observing the Brahmā fast, associating with Brahmā. Because of Brahmā, his mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Dharma: 'This Dharma is well expounded by the World-Honored One; it is ultimate, eternally unchanging, known by right wisdom, seen by right wisdom, realized by right wisdom.' Having thus recollected the Dharma, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Dharma as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"It is like a person whose body is covered with grease and impurities; by means of bran, washing-beans, warm water, and human effort in thoroughly washing and bathing, the body becomes clean. In the same way, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Dharma: 'This Dharma is well expounded by the World-Honored One; it is ultimate, eternally unchanging, known by right wisdom, seen by right wisdom, realized by right wisdom.' Having thus recollected the Dharma, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Dharma as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, this is called the well-learned noble disciple observing the Dharma fast, associating with the Dharma. Because of the Dharma, his mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Sangha: 'The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is well directed, upright, practices the essential path, and practices what leads to the goal. In the community of the Tathāgata there are truly those on the path of the Arahant, the True Person, those who have realized the fruit of Arahantship, those on the path of the Non-Returner, those who have realized the fruit of the Non-Returner, those on the path of the Once-Returner, those who have realized the fruit of the Once-Returner, those on the path of the Stream-Enterer, and those who have realized the fruit of Stream-Entry. These are the four pairs of persons, the eight types of noble individuals. This is the community of the World-Honored One's disciples, accomplished in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. They can be called upon, invited, given offerings, served, and revered; they are an excellent field of merit for devas and humans.' Having thus recollected the Sangha, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Sangha as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"It is like a person whose garments are covered with grease and impurities; by means of ash, soap-acacia, washing-beans, soapy water, and human effort in laundering, they become clean. In the same way, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the Sangha: 'The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is well directed, upright, practices the essential path, and practices what leads to the goal. In the community of the Tathāgata there are truly those on the path of the Arahant, the True Person, those who have realized the fruit of Arahantship, those on the path of the Non-Returner, those who have realized the fruit of the Non-Returner, those on the path of the Once-Returner, those who have realized the fruit of the Once-Returner, those on the path of the Stream-Enterer, and those who have realized the fruit of Stream-Entry. These are the four pairs of persons, the eight types of noble individuals. This is the community of the World-Honored One's disciples, accomplished in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. They can be called upon, invited, given offerings, served, and revered; they are an excellent field of merit for devas and humans.' Having thus recollected the Sangha, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the Sangha as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. This is called the well-learned noble disciple observing the Sangha fast, associating with the Sangha. Because of the Sangha, his mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects his own morality: 'Unbroken, without gaps, unstained, unpolluted, extremely broad, extremely great, without expectation of reward, praised by the wise, well endowed, well directed, well received, and well maintained.' Having thus recollected his own morality, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking morality as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"It is like a mirror that has become tarnished and unclear; by means of stone, polishing, and buffing, through human effort in treatment, it becomes bright and clean. In the same way, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects his own morality: 'Unbroken, without gaps, unstained, unpolluted, extremely broad, extremely great, without expectation of reward, praised by the wise, well endowed, well directed, well received, and well maintained.' Having thus recollected his own morality, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking morality as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. This is called the well-learned noble disciple observing the morality fast, associating with morality. Because of morality, his mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"Furthermore, householder's wife, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the devas: 'There truly are the Four Great Kings devas. If those devas were accomplished in faith, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such faith. If those devas were accomplished in morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such wisdom. There truly are the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas. If those devas were accomplished in faith, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such faith. If those devas were accomplished in morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such wisdom.' Having thus recollected, together with the devas' faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated. Householder's wife, by taking the devas as the object, the well-learned noble disciple's mind becomes calm and he obtains joy. If there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"It is like fine gold that has become tarnished and impure; by means of fire, bellows, drill, hammer, red earth, and human effort in polishing, buffing, and treating, it becomes bright and clean. In the same way, when a well-learned noble disciple observes the fast, he recollects the devas: 'There truly are the Four Great Kings devas. If those devas were accomplished in faith, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such faith. If those devas were accomplished in morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such wisdom. There truly are the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas. If those devas were accomplished in faith, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such faith. If those devas were accomplished in morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, having died here, they were reborn there; I too possess such wisdom.' Having thus recollected, together with the devas' faith, morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom, if there are any evil thoughts, they are thereby eliminated; whatever defiled, evil, and unwholesome states there are, they too are eliminated.

"Householder's wife, if one practices the Noble Eightfold Fast in this way: suppose there were the sixteen great countries, namely, first Aṅga, second Magadha, third Kāśī, fourth Kosala, fifth Kuru, sixth Pañcāla, seventh Aśmaka, eighth Avanti, ninth Cedi, tenth Vajjī, eleventh Vatsa, twelfth Malla, thirteenth Sūrasena, fourteenth Sūrāṣṭra, fifteenth Yona, and sixteenth Kamboja. Among all these countries, whatever wealth, treasures, gold, silver, maṇi gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, amber, crystal, agate, tortoiseshell, red stones, and rotating pearls there may be, and suppose a person were to be king over all of them, using them freely at will; yet all of that would not equal one-sixteenth of observing the Noble Eightfold Fast.

"Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If fifty human years equal one day and one night of the Four Great Kings devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Four Great Kings devas is five hundred such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Four Great Kings devas. Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If one hundred human years equal one day and one night of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa devas is one thousand such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa devas.

"Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If two hundred human years equal one day and one night of the Yāma devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Yāma devas is two thousand such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Yāma devas. Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If four hundred human years equal one day and one night of the Tuṣita devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Tuṣita devas is four thousand such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Tuṣita devas.

"Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If eight hundred human years equal one day and one night of the Nirmāṇarati devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati devas is eight thousand such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Nirmāṇarati devas. Householder's wife, for this reason I say that the pleasures of a human king do not compare to the pleasures of the devas. If one thousand six hundred human years equal one day and one night of the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, and in the same way thirty such days and nights make one month, twelve months make one year, and the lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas is sixteen thousand such years. Householder's wife, it is certainly possible that a son or daughter of good family who observes the Noble Eightfold Fast, when the body breaks up and life ends, may be reborn among the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas."

Thereupon, Migāra's Mother Viśākhā, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One! The Noble Eightfold Fast is truly wonderful, truly extraordinary! It has great benefit and great fruit, has great merit, and achieves widespread results. World-Honored One! From this day forward, for the whole of my life, I shall observe the Noble Eightfold Fast and, according to my ability, practice giving and cultivate merit."

Thereupon, Migāra's Mother, having heard what the Buddha taught, retained it well, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

The Buddha spoke thus. Migāra's Mother Viśākhā and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Observing the Fast, First.

---

## (203) The Pūrṇa Chapter of the Madhyamāgama: The Sūtra on Pūrṇa, Second

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Nālandā, staying in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.

At that time, the householder Pūrṇa, wearing clean white garments, with a white cloth wrapped around his head, leaning on a walking stick and holding a parasol, wearing worldly shoes, went from park to park, from pavilion to pavilion, from grove to grove, wandering about everywhere. Whenever he saw śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, he would say: "Venerable sirs, you should know that I have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs."

Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, with soft and gentle words, would say: "Indeed, worthy Pūrṇa, you have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs."

Then the householder Pūrṇa, wandering about everywhere, went to where the Buddha was. They exchanged greetings, and he stood before the Buddha leaning on his walking stick. The World-Honored One said: "Householder, there is a seat. If you wish to sit, please sit."

The householder Pūrṇa said: "Gautama, this is not right, this is not appropriate. Why is that? I have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs, yet the śramaṇa Gautama calls me 'householder'!"

The World-Honored One replied: "You have the marks and signs of a householder. Therefore I call you 'householder': there is a seat; if you wish to sit, please sit."

The World-Honored One repeated this up to three times: "Householder, there is a seat. If you wish to sit, please sit."

The householder Pūrṇa also repeated up to three times: "Gautama, this is not right, this is not appropriate. I have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs, yet the śramaṇa Gautama calls me 'householder'!"

The World-Honored One replied: "You have the marks and signs of a householder. Therefore I call you 'householder': there is a seat; if you wish to sit, please sit."

The World-Honored One asked: "How have you renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs?"

The householder Pūrṇa answered: "Gautama, all the wealth and possessions in my household I have completely given to my sons. I am without action and without seeking, just wandering about, merely going to obtain food to sustain my life. In this way I have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs."

The World-Honored One said: "Householder, in the Noble Dharma and Discipline, one does not sever worldly affairs in this way. Householder, in the Noble Dharma and Discipline there is an eightfold severance of worldly affairs."

Thereupon, the householder Pūrṇa set aside his walking stick, put down his parasol, and removed his worldly shoes. With palms joined toward the Buddha, he said: "Gautama, in the Noble Dharma and Discipline, what is this eightfold severance of worldly affairs?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Householder, a well-learned noble disciple relies on abandoning killing and severs killing; relies on abandoning taking what is not given and severs taking what is not given; relies on abandoning sexual misconduct and severs sexual misconduct; relies on abandoning false speech and severs false speech; relies on non-covetousness and severs covetousness; relies on non-harmfulness and non-anger and severs harmfulness and anger; relies on non-hatred, non-jealousy, and non-vexation and severs hatred, jealousy, and vexation; relies on non-arrogance and severs arrogance.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning killing and sever killing? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who kills will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I kill, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who kills receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on abandoning killing and sever killing?' He then relies on abandoning killing and severs killing. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning killing and sever killing.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning taking what is not given and sever taking what is not given? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who takes what is not given will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I take what is not given, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who takes what is not given receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on abandoning taking what is not given and sever taking what is not given?' He then relies on abandoning taking what is not given and severs taking what is not given. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning taking what is not given and sever taking what is not given.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning sexual misconduct and sever sexual misconduct? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who commits sexual misconduct will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I commit sexual misconduct, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who commits sexual misconduct receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on abandoning sexual misconduct and sever sexual misconduct?' He then relies on abandoning sexual misconduct and severs sexual misconduct. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning sexual misconduct and sever sexual misconduct.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning false speech and sever false speech? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who speaks falsely will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I speak falsely, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who speaks falsely receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on abandoning false speech and sever false speech?' He then relies on abandoning false speech and severs false speech. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on abandoning false speech and sever false speech.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-covetousness and sever covetousness? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who is covetous will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I am covetous, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who is covetous receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on non-covetousness and sever covetousness?' He then relies on non-covetousness and severs covetousness. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-covetousness and sever covetousness.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-harmfulness and non-anger and sever harmfulness and anger? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who is harmful and angry will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I am harmful and angry, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who is harmful and angry receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on non-harmfulness and non-anger and sever harmfulness and anger?' He then relies on non-harmfulness and non-anger and severs harmfulness and anger. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-harmfulness and non-anger and sever harmfulness and anger.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-hatred, non-jealousy, and non-vexation and sever hatred, jealousy, and vexation? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who has hatred, jealousy, and vexation will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I have hatred, jealousy, and vexation, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who has hatred, jealousy, and vexation receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on non-hatred, non-jealousy, and non-vexation and sever hatred, jealousy, and vexation?' He then relies on non-hatred, non-jealousy, and non-vexation and severs hatred, jealousy, and vexation. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-hatred, non-jealousy, and non-vexation and sever hatred, jealousy, and vexation.

"Householder, how does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-arrogance and sever arrogance? A well-learned noble disciple thinks thus: 'One who is arrogant will certainly receive evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I am arrogant, I will harm myself and also falsely accuse others. The devas and wise practitioners of the holy life will speak of my morality. In all directions my bad reputation will be heard. When the body breaks up and life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell. In this way, one who is arrogant receives this evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. Should I not rely on non-arrogance and sever arrogance?' He then relies on non-arrogance and severs arrogance. Thus does a well-learned noble disciple rely on non-arrogance and sever arrogance. This is what in the Noble Dharma and Discipline is called the eightfold severance of worldly affairs."

The householder asked: "Gautama, in the Noble Dharma and Discipline, is there only this severance of worldly affairs, or is there something further?"

The World-Honored One replied: "In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, there is not only this severance of worldly affairs; there is a further eightfold severance of worldly affairs by which one attains realization."

When the householder Pūrṇa heard this, he removed his white head-cloth, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, he said: "Gautama, in the Noble Dharma and Discipline, what is this further eightfold severance of worldly affairs by which one attains realization?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Householder, it is like a dog, hungry and emaciated, that goes to a butcher's place. The butcher or his apprentice strips the meat clean and throws a bone to the dog. The dog, having obtained the bone, gnaws at it here and there, splitting its lips, cracking its teeth, or injuring its throat, yet the dog cannot satisfy its hunger with this. Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a chain of bones. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a chain of bones: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like near a village, where a small piece of meat falls on open ground. A crow or a kite seizes that piece of meat and flies away, and the other crows and kites pursue it in competition. What do you think, householder? If that crow or kite does not quickly drop this small piece of meat, will the other crows and kites not pursue it in competition?"

The householder answered: "Indeed, Gautama."

"What do you think, householder? If that crow or kite quickly drops this small piece of meat, will the other crows and kites still pursue it in competition?"

The householder answered: "No, Gautama."

"Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a piece of meat. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a piece of meat: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like a person holding a burning torch, walking against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that person does not quickly drop it, will it not burn his hand and the rest of his limbs?"

The householder answered: "Indeed, Gautama."

"What do you think, householder? If that person quickly drops the torch, will it burn his hand and the rest of his limbs?"

The householder answered: "No, Gautama."

"Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a fire torch. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a fire torch: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like near a village, where there is a great pit of fire, filled with fire, with neither smoke nor flame visible. If a person comes along who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, who retains his normal mind, is self-possessed and autonomous, who prefers pleasure over pain and greatly abhors pain, who prefers life over death and greatly abhors death. What do you think, householder? Would this person enter the fire pit?"

The householder answered: "No, Gautama. Why is that? Seeing the fire pit, he would think: 'If I fall into the fire pit, I will certainly die; even if I do not die, I will surely suffer extreme pain.' Seeing the fire pit, he would think of keeping far away and would wish to escape from it."

"Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a fire pit. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a fire pit: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like near a village, where there is a great poisonous snake, extremely evil and painfully venomous, black and terrifying. If a person comes along who is not foolish, not deluded, not confused, who retains his normal mind, is self-possessed and autonomous, who prefers pleasure over pain and greatly abhors pain, who prefers life over death and greatly abhors death. What do you think, householder? Would this person extend his hand or other limbs and say: 'Bite me, bite me'?"

The householder answered: "No, Gautama. Why is that? Seeing the poisonous snake, he would think: 'If I extend my hand or other limbs for the snake to bite, I will certainly die; even if I do not die, I will surely suffer extreme pain.' Seeing the poisonous snake, he would think of keeping far away and would wish to escape from it."

"Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a poisonous snake. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a poisonous snake: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like a person who in a dream obtains the complete five sense pleasures and amuses himself. When he awakens, he sees none of them at all. Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like a dream. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like a dream: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like a person who borrows objects of enjoyment: palaces, towers, and pavilions, or parks, ponds, and bathing pools, or elephants, horses, and carriages, or silk and cotton blankets, or rings and bracelets, or fragrant necklaces and neck ornaments, or golden jeweled garlands, or fine and superior garments. Many people seeing this exclaim together: 'How excellent! How wonderful! If one has such possessions, one should enjoy oneself to the utmost in this way.' But the owner of those things reclaims them whenever he wishes, or has someone reclaim them, and immediately takes them back himself, or has someone take them back. Many people seeing this say together: 'That borrower was truly deceived; it was not a real loan.' Why is that? Because the owner reclaims them whenever he wishes, or has someone reclaim them, and immediately takes them back himself, or has someone take them back. Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like borrowed things. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like borrowed things: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that.

"Householder, it is like near a village, where there is a great fruit tree that always bears many fine, beautiful fruits. A person comes along, hungry and emaciated, wishing to eat the fruit. He thinks: 'This tree always bears many fine, beautiful fruits. I am hungry and emaciated and wish to eat the fruit. Yet beneath this tree there are no fallen fruits that I could eat my fill of and take away. I am able to climb the tree. Should I not climb this tree?' Having thought so, he climbs up. Then another person comes along, also hungry and emaciated, wishing to eat the fruit, carrying an extremely sharp axe. He thinks: 'This tree always bears many fine, beautiful fruits. Yet beneath this tree there are no fallen fruits that I could eat my fill of and take away. I am not able to climb the tree. Should I not chop this tree down?' He then proceeds to chop it down. What do you think, householder? If the person up in the tree does not quickly come down, when the tree falls to the ground, will it not break his arms and other limbs?"

The householder answered: "Indeed, Gautama."

"What do you think, householder? If the person up in the tree quickly comes down, when the tree falls to the ground, will it break his arms and other limbs?"

The householder answered: "No, Gautama."

"Householder, a well-learned noble disciple also thinks thus: 'Desires are like the fruits of a tree. The World-Honored One has said that desires are like the fruits of a tree: little pleasure and much suffering, with many calamities; one should distance oneself from them.' If there is this abandonment, separating from desires and separating from evil, unwholesome states, then all food and drink in this world will be completely and utterly exhausted; one should cultivate that. This is what in the Noble Dharma and Discipline is called the further eightfold severance of worldly affairs by which one attains realization.

"Householder, with initial thought and sustained thought stilled, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without initial thought and without sustained thought, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. Having separated from the desire for joy, dwelling with equanimity and without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, and experiencing happiness with the body, as the noble ones describe: 'One who has equanimity, mindfulness, and dwells happily,' he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. With the cessation of happiness and the cessation of suffering, with joy and sorrow having already ceased, neither suffering nor happy, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

"With his mind thus concentrated, pure, without defilement, without affliction, soft, well-established, and having attained an unshakable mind, he trains in and realizes the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. He knows this is suffering as it truly is; he knows this is the origin of suffering, he knows this is the cessation of suffering, he knows this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. He knows these are the taints as it truly is; he knows this is the origin of the taints, he knows this is the cessation of the taints, he knows this is the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of desire, liberated from the taint of existence, and liberated from the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' He knows it as it truly is."

When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Pūrṇa, being far removed from dust and defilement, the Dharma eye arose with regard to all phenomena. Thereupon, the householder Pūrṇa saw the Dharma, obtained the Dharma, realized the pure, white Dharma, cut through doubt, crossed beyond perplexity, had no other teacher, no longer depended on others, was without hesitation, had established himself in the fruit of realization, and in the Dharma of the World-Honored One attained fearlessness. He bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and said: "World-Honored One! Today I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the whole of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days.

"World-Honored One! Previously I wore clean white garments, wrapped my head with a white cloth, leaned on a walking stick and held a parasol, and wore worldly shoes. I went from park to park, from pavilion to pavilion, from grove to grove, wandering about everywhere. Whenever I saw śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, I would say: 'Venerable sirs, I have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs.' Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, with soft and gentle words, would say to me: 'Indeed, worthy Pūrṇa, you have renounced worldly life, severed worldly life, and abandoned all worldly affairs.'

"World-Honored One! At that time I was truly without wisdom yet placed myself in the position of the wise; I was truly without wisdom yet sacrificed as if wise; I was truly without wisdom yet ate as if wise; I was truly without wisdom yet served as if I were a wise person.

"World-Honored One! From this day forward, with regard to the community of bhikṣus and the World-Honored One's disciples, they truly have wisdom, are placed in the position of wisdom, truly have wisdom in their sacrifices, truly have wisdom in their food, truly have wisdom, and serve as wise persons.

"World-Honored One! Today I take refuge a second time in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the whole of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days.

"World-Honored One! Previously I had faith in and revered heterodox śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; from this day forward, I sever that.

"World-Honored One! Today I take refuge a third time in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay disciple. From this day forward, for the whole of my life, I take refuge until the end of my days."

The Buddha spoke thus. The householder Pūrṇa and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully received and practiced it.

End of the Sūtra on Pūrṇa, Second.
