## (204) Pulita Chapter: The Rāma Sūtra, Third

Thus have I heard.

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Eastern Park at the Hall of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the World-Honored One, during the afternoon, rose from his sitting meditation, came down from the hall, and told Venerable Ānanda: "I shall now go with you to bathe in the Aciravatī River."

Venerable Ānanda replied: "So be it."

Venerable Ānanda, carrying the door key, went around to all the rooms, wandering about. Seeing the bhikṣus, he spoke thus: "Venerables, let us all go together to the house of the brahmin Rāma." When the bhikṣus heard this, they went together to the house of the brahmin Rāma. The World-Honored One, taking Venerable Ānanda along, went to the Aciravatī River, left his robes on the bank, and entered the water to bathe. Having bathed, he came back out, dried his body, and put on his robes.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda stood behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and fanning the Buddha. Then Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, the house of the brahmin Rāma is extremely well arranged and most delightful. May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, go to the house of the brahmin Rāma." The World-Honored One silently accepted Venerable Ānanda's request. Thereupon the World-Honored One, taking Venerable Ānanda along, went to the house of the brahmin Rāma.

At that time, at the house of the brahmin Rāma, many bhikṣus had gathered and were sitting discussing the Dharma. The Buddha stood outside the door, waiting for the bhikṣus to finish their Dharma discussion. When the many bhikṣus had finished their discussion, they sat silently. The World-Honored One, knowing this, cleared his throat and knocked on the door. The bhikṣus heard and went to open the door. The World-Honored One then entered the house of the brahmin Rāma, had a seat spread before the assembly of bhikṣus, and sat down. He asked: "Bhikṣus, what were you just discussing? For what reason have you gathered here?"

The bhikṣus answered: "World-Honored One, we were just discussing the Dharma. It was for this Dharma matter that we gathered here."

The World-Honored One praised them: "Good! Good! When bhikṣus gather and sit together, they should engage in two activities: first, discussing the Dharma; second, noble silence. Why is that? I too shall teach you the Dharma. Listen carefully, listen carefully, and reflect well upon it."

The bhikṣus said: "So be it. We shall receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha said: "There are two kinds of seeking: first, the noble seeking; second, the ignoble seeking. What is the ignoble seeking? There is one who, being himself subject to illness, seeks what is subject to illness; being himself subject to old age, death, sorrow, grief, and distress, seeks what is subject to sorrow, grief, and distress; being himself subject to defilement, seeks what is subject to defilement. What does it mean to be subject to illness and to seek what is subject to illness? What are the things subject to illness? Sons, brothers are subject to illness. Elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, male and female servants, money, treasures, grain, and rice are things subject to illness and harm. Beings become attached to them through contact, stained by craving, proud and absorbed in them, not seeing the peril, not seeing the way of escape, and they take and use them. What are the things subject to old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement? Sons, brothers are subject to defilement. Elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, male and female servants, money, treasures, grain, and rice are things subject to defilement and harm. Beings become attached to them through contact, stained by craving, proud and absorbed in them, not seeing the peril, not seeing the way of escape, and they take and use them. That such a person, seeking the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, should attain the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa: this is impossible. That such a person, seeking the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, should attain the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement: this is impossible. This is called the ignoble seeking.

"What is the noble seeking? There is one who thinks thus: 'I myself am truly subject to illness, yet I pointlessly seek what is subject to illness. I myself am truly subject to old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, yet I pointlessly seek what is subject to defilement. Suppose I were now to seek the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, to seek the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement.' That person then seeks the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa. That he should attain the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa: this is certainly possible. That he seeks the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, and attains the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement: this is certainly possible.

"Before I had awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I too thought thus: 'I myself am truly subject to illness, yet I pointlessly seek what is subject to illness. I myself am truly subject to old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, yet I pointlessly seek what is subject to defilement. Suppose I were now to seek the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, to seek the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement?' At that time I was young, a youth with pure dark hair, in the prime of life, twenty-nine years old. At that time I was most abundantly engaged in pleasurable diversions, adorning myself and wandering about. At that time, though my father and mother wept and my relatives were unhappy, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the kāṣāya robes, and with faith left the household life for homelessness to study the path. I guarded the purity of my bodily actions and livelihood, and guarded the purity of my speech, mind, and livelihood. Having accomplished this body of moral precepts, wishing to seek the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, I went to Āḷāra Kālāma and asked him: 'Āḷāra, I wish to practice the holy life in your teaching. Would that be acceptable?' Āḷāra Kālāma answered me: 'Worthy one, I have no objection. If you wish to practice, then practice.' I further asked: 'Āḷāra, how is it that you have known, realized, and personally witnessed this teaching?' Āḷāra Kālāma answered me: 'Worthy one, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, I have attained and dwell in the sphere of nothingness. Therefore I have known, realized, and personally witnessed this teaching.'

"I then thought: 'It is not Āḷāra alone who has this faith; I too have this faith. It is not Āḷāra alone who has this energy; I too have this energy. It is not Āḷāra alone who has this wisdom; I too have this wisdom. Āḷāra has known, realized, and personally witnessed this teaching.' Wishing to realize this teaching, I dwelt alone in a secluded, empty, and quiet place, with a mind free from negligence, practicing diligently. Dwelling alone in a secluded, empty, and quiet place, with a mind free from negligence, practicing diligently, before long I realized that teaching. Having realized that teaching, I went again to Āḷāra Kālāma and asked: 'Āḷāra, is it this teaching that you have known, realized, and personally witnessed: namely, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, attaining and dwelling in the sphere of nothingness?' Āḷāra Kālāma answered me: 'Worthy one, it is this teaching that I have known, realized, and personally witnessed: namely, by transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, attaining and dwelling in the sphere of nothingness.' Āḷāra Kālāma further said to me: 'Worthy one, just as I have realized this teaching, so have you. Just as you have realized this teaching, so have I. Worthy one, come, let us together lead this community.' Thus, in the position of teacher, Āḷāra Kālāma placed me as his equal, honoring me with the highest respect, the highest offerings, and the highest joy.

"I then thought: 'This teaching does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to nirvāṇa. Suppose I were now to abandon this teaching and further seek the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement.' I then abandoned this teaching and sought the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement. Having done so, I went to Uddaka Rāmaputta and asked: 'Uddaka, I wish to study in your teaching. Would that be acceptable?' Uddaka Rāmaputta answered me: 'Worthy one, I have no objection. If you wish to study, then study.' I further asked: 'Uddaka, son of Rāma, what teaching have you known, realized, and personally witnessed?' Uddaka Rāmaputta answered me: 'Worthy one, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, I have attained and dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Worthy one, it is this teaching that my father Rāma knew, realized, and personally witnessed.'

"I then thought: 'It is not Rāma alone who has this faith; I too have this faith. It is not Rāma alone who has this energy; I too have this energy. It is not Rāma alone who has this wisdom; I too have this wisdom. Rāma knew, realized, and personally witnessed this teaching. Why should I not be able to know, realize, and personally witness this teaching?' Wishing to realize this teaching, I dwelt alone in a secluded, empty, and quiet place, with a mind free from negligence, practicing diligently. Dwelling alone in a secluded, empty, and quiet place, with a mind free from negligence, practicing diligently, before long I realized that teaching. Having realized that teaching, I went again to Uddaka Rāmaputta and asked: 'Uddaka, is it this teaching that your father Rāma knew, realized, and personally witnessed: namely, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, attaining and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?' Uddaka Rāmaputta answered me: 'Worthy one, it is this teaching that my father Rāma knew, realized, and personally witnessed: namely, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, attaining and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Uddaka further said to me: 'Just as my father Rāma realized this teaching, so have you. Just as you have realized this teaching, so did my father. Worthy one, come, let us together lead this community.' Uddaka Rāmaputta, in the position of his teacher, treated me as his teacher, honoring me with the highest respect, the highest offerings, and the highest joy.

"I then thought: 'This teaching does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to nirvāṇa. Suppose I were now to abandon this teaching and further seek the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement.' I then abandoned this teaching and sought the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement. Having done so, I went south of Elephant-Head Mountain to the brahmin village of Uruvela, called Senā. In that area, the ground was most delightful, the mountain forests were dense and lush, and the Nerañjarā River flowed clear with full banks. Having seen this, I thought: 'This land is most delightful, the mountain forests are dense and lush, and the Nerañjarā River flows clear with full banks. If a clansman wishes to study, he could study here. I too should study. I shall now study here.' I then took grass and went to the Bodhi Tree. Having arrived, I spread it down, laid out the sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged, making a vow: 'I shall not undo this sitting posture until I have attained the ending of all defilements.' I then did not undo my sitting posture until I attained the ending of all defilements. Seeking the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, I attained the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa. Seeking the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, I attained the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement. Knowledge and vision arose: the factors of the path became established. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. I knew this as it really is.

"Having first awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I further thought: 'Suppose I were now to teach the Dharma first to Āḷāra Kālāma?' At that time a deity, standing in the sky, spoke to me: 'Great sage, know that Āḷāra Kālāma has been dead for seven days now.' I also knew for myself that Āḷāra Kālāma had been dead for seven days. I further thought: 'Āḷāra Kālāma! That person has suffered a great loss, not having heard this Dharma. Had he heard this Dharma, he would have quickly understood the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma.'

"Having first awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I further thought: 'Suppose I were now to teach the Dharma first to Uddaka Rāmaputta?' A deity again stood in the sky and spoke to me: 'Great sage, know that Uddaka Rāmaputta has been dead for fourteen days now.' I also knew for myself that Uddaka Rāmaputta had been dead for fourteen days. I further thought: 'Uddaka Rāmaputta! That person has suffered a great loss, not having heard this Dharma. Had he heard this Dharma, he would have quickly understood the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma.'

"Having first awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I thought: 'To whom should I first teach the Dharma?' I further thought: 'In the past, the five bhikṣus served me with effort and were of much benefit to me. During my period of austerities, those five bhikṣus attended upon me. Suppose I were now to teach the Dharma first to those five bhikṣus?' I further thought: 'Where are those five bhikṣus now?' With my purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, I saw the five bhikṣus at the Deer Park in the Ṛṣipatana at Bārāṇasī. After dwelling at the Bodhi Tree, I gathered my robes, took up my bowl, and set out for the city of Kāśī at Bārāṇasī. At that time, the wanderer Upaka saw me coming from afar and said to me: 'Worthy Gautama, your faculties are pure, your form is supremely beautiful, and your face shines with radiance. Worthy Gautama, who is your teacher? From whom did you study the path? Whose teaching do you follow?' I then spoke to Upaka in verse:

'I am the supreme, the most excellent,
Unattached to all phenomena.
With all craving ended, liberated,
Self-awakened; whom would I call teacher?
Without equal, without superior,
Self-awakened to the unsurpassed awakening,
I am the Teacher of gods and humans, the Tathāgata,
Omniscient, accomplished in power.'

"Upaka asked me: 'Worthy Gautama, do you claim to be the victor?' I replied to him again in verse:

'Victors are those such as I,
Who have attained the ending of all defilements.
I have destroyed all unwholesome states;
Therefore, Upaka, I am the victor.'

"Upaka further asked me: 'Worthy Gautama, where do you intend to go?' I then replied to him in verse:

'I go to Bārāṇasī,
To beat the wondrous drum of the Deathless,
To turn the unsurpassed Dharma wheel,
Never before turned in the world.'

"Upaka said to me: 'Worthy Gautama, perhaps it may be so.' Having spoken thus, he turned onto a side path and departed. I went on by myself to the Ṛṣipatana Deer Park. At that time, the five bhikṣus saw me coming from afar, and they made an agreement among themselves, establishing a rule: 'Venerables, know that the ascetic Gautama is coming. He has many desires and many wants. He eats fine food and drink, good rice and grain, along with barley flour, ghee, and honey. He anoints his body with sesame oil. Now he comes again. You should all just remain seated. Be sure not to rise to greet him, nor bow to him. Set aside one seat, but do not invite him to sit. When he arrives, say to him: "Sir, if you wish to sit, sit wherever you like."' I then went to the five bhikṣus. At that time, the five bhikṣus could not withstand my supremely wondrous authority and power, and they immediately rose from their seats. Some took my robes and bowl, some spread a bed, some fetched water, wanting to wash my feet. I thought: 'These foolish people! How lacking in resolve they are! They established their own rule, yet now they violate their original agreement.' Having understood this, I sat upon the seat that the five bhikṣus had spread.

"At that time, the five bhikṣus addressed me by my clan name and called me 'sir.' I said to them: 'Five bhikṣus! I am the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly and Completely Awakened One. You should not address me by my clan name, nor should you call me "sir." Why is that? I sought the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa and attained the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa. I sought the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, and attained the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement. Knowledge and vision arose: the factors of the path became established. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. I knew this as it really is.' They said to me: 'Sir Gautama, previously, with such conduct, such practices, such austerities, you still could not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in noble knowledge and vision. How much less so now, when you have many desires and many wants, eating fine food and drink, good rice and grain, along with barley flour, ghee, and honey, anointing your body with sesame oil?' I further said: 'Five bhikṣus, have you ever before seen my faculties so pure, shining with radiance like this?' The five bhikṣus then answered me: 'We have never before seen your faculties so pure, shining with radiance. Worthy Gautama, your faculties are now pure, your form is supremely beautiful, and your face shines with radiance.'

"I then told them: 'Five bhikṣus, know that there are two extreme practices that those who pursue the path should not follow: first, the pursuit of sensual pleasures, a low and vulgar occupation, the way of ordinary people; second, self-torment and self-mortification, which is not the seeking of noble ones, the Dharma, and is not connected with any true purpose. Five bhikṣus, abandoning these two extremes, there is a middle way that produces clear vision and wisdom, that leads to concentration, and that brings about freedom, leading to wisdom, leading to awakening, leading to nirvāṇa. This is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to right concentration. These are the eight.' Intending to instruct and guide the five bhikṣus in accord with their readiness, I taught two of them while the other three went for alms. The three brought back food sufficient for all six. I taught three of them while the other two went for alms. The two brought back food sufficient for all six. Teaching them in this way, guiding them in this way, they sought the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa and attained the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa. They sought the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement, and attained the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement. Knowledge and vision arose: the factors of the path became established. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. They knew this as it really is.

"Thereupon the World-Honored One further told them: 'Five bhikṣus, there are five cords of sensual pleasure that are lovely, pleasing, agreeable, and memorable, connected with desire. What are the five? Forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, smells known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body. Five bhikṣus, foolish ordinary people who have not learned much, who have not met good friends, who do not know the noble Dharma, who do not train in the noble Dharma, become attached to these through contact, stained by craving, proud and absorbed in them, not seeing the peril, not seeing the way of escape, and they take and use them. Know that such persons follow Māra the Evil One, make themselves servants of Māra, fall into Māra's hands, are entangled in Māra's net, bound by Māra's snare, and cannot escape from Māra's snare. Five bhikṣus, just as a wild deer, caught in a snare, know that it follows the hunter, serves the hunter, falls into the hunter's hands, is entangled in the hunter's net. When the hunter comes, it cannot escape. So too, five bhikṣus, foolish ordinary people who have not learned much, who have not met good friends, who do not know the noble Dharma, who do not train in the noble Dharma, become attached to these five cords of sensual pleasure through contact, stained by craving, proud and absorbed in them, not seeing the peril, not seeing the way of escape, and they take and use them. Know that such persons follow Māra the Evil One, make themselves servants of Māra, fall into Māra's hands, are entangled in Māra's net, bound by Māra's snare, and cannot escape from Māra's snare.

"'Five bhikṣus, the well-learned noble disciple who has met good friends, who knows the noble Dharma, who trains in the noble Dharma, regarding these five cords of sensual pleasure, does not touch, does not become stained, does not crave, does not become attached, is not proud, does not become absorbed; he sees the peril, sees the way of escape, and so uses them. Know that such a person does not follow Māra the Evil One, does not make himself a servant of Māra, does not fall into Māra's hands, is not entangled in Māra's net, is not bound by Māra's snare, and is freed from Māra's snare. Five bhikṣus, just as a wild deer that has escaped from a snare, know that it does not follow the hunter, does not serve the hunter, does not fall into the hunter's hands, is not entangled in the hunter's net. When the hunter comes, it can escape. So too, five bhikṣus, the well-learned noble disciple who has met good friends, who knows the noble Dharma, who trains in the noble Dharma, regarding these five cords of sensual pleasure, does not touch, does not become stained, does not crave, does not become attached, is not proud, does not become absorbed; he sees the peril, sees the way of escape, and so uses them. Know that such a person does not follow Māra the Evil One, does not make himself a servant of Māra, does not fall into Māra's hands, is not entangled in Māra's net, is not bound by Māra's snare, and is freed from Māra's snare.

"'Five bhikṣus, whenever a Tathāgata arises in the world, a Worthy One, Perfectly and Completely Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Guide of Those to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, he has severed, up to the five hindrances that are impurities of the mind and weaknesses of wisdom. Secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, he attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna. With his mind thus concentrated, pure, unblemished, free from affliction, pliant, well-settled, and having attained imperturbability, he applies his mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the defilements and witnesses it directly. He knows this is suffering as it really is; he knows this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering, as it really is. He knows these are the defilements as it really is; he knows this is the origin of the defilements, this is the cessation of the defilements, this is the path leading to the cessation of the defilements, as it really is. Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the defilement of sensual desire, from the defilement of becoming, and from the defilement of ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. He knew this as it really is. At that time he walks freely, stands freely, sits freely, lies down freely. Why is that? Because he himself sees that immeasurable unwholesome states have been exhausted. Therefore he walks freely, stands freely, sits freely, lies down freely.

"'Five bhikṣus, just as in a remote, uninhabited place, there is a wild deer that walks freely, stands freely, crouches freely, lies down freely. Why is that? Because that wild deer is not within the hunter's territory. Therefore it walks freely, stands freely, crouches freely, lies down freely. So too, five bhikṣus, when a bhikṣu has ended the defilements and attained the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing for himself, realizing, and personally witnessing, he dwells having accomplished it. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. He knew this as it really is. At that time he walks freely, stands freely, sits freely, lies down freely. Why is that? Because he himself sees that immeasurable unwholesome states have been exhausted. Therefore he walks freely, stands freely, sits freely, lies down freely. Five bhikṣus, this is called the liberation without remainder; this is called the unailing, unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa; this is called the unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa free from old age, death, sorrow, grief, distress, and defilement.'"

Thus spoke the Buddha. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it with practice.

End of the Rāma Sūtra, Third.

---

## (205) Madhyamāgama, Pulita Chapter: The Sūtra on the Five Lower Fetters, Fourth

Thus have I heard.

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I have previously taught the five lower fetters. Have you all retained them?" The bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.

The World-Honored One asked again a second and a third time: "I have previously taught the five lower fetters. Have you all retained them?" The bhikṣus again remained silent and did not answer, all three times.

At that time, Venerable Māluṅkyāputta was in the assembly. Thereupon Venerable Māluṅkyāputta rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "The World-Honored One has previously taught the five lower fetters, and I have retained them."

The World-Honored One asked: "Māluṅkyāputta, I have previously taught the five lower fetters. Have you retained them?"

Venerable Māluṅkyāputta answered: "The World-Honored One has previously taught the first lower fetter, which I have retained: desire, hatred, self-identity view, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt. The World-Honored One has taught these as the five lower fetters, and I have retained them."

The World-Honored One rebuked him: "Māluṅkyāputta, how have you retained my teaching of the five lower fetters? Māluṅkyāputta, from whose mouth did you retain my teaching of the five lower fetters? Māluṅkyāputta, would not the many followers of other schools come and rebuke you with the simile of the infant child? Māluṅkyāputta, an infant child, small and tender, lying on its back, has no notion of desire; how much less could desire entangle and dwell in its mind? Yet because of its underlying tendency, one speaks of the tendency toward desire. Māluṅkyāputta, an infant child, small and tender, lying on its back, has no notion of beings; how much less could hatred entangle and dwell in its mind? Yet because of its underlying tendency, one speaks of the tendency toward hatred. Māluṅkyāputta, an infant child, small and tender, lying on its back, has no notion of self; how much less could self-identity view entangle and dwell in its mind? Yet because of its underlying tendency, one speaks of the tendency toward self-identity view. Māluṅkyāputta, an infant child, small and tender, lying on its back, has no notion of precepts; how much less could attachment to rules and rituals entangle and dwell in its mind? Yet because of its underlying tendency, one speaks of the tendency toward attachment to rules and rituals. Māluṅkyāputta, an infant child, small and tender, lying on its back, has no notion of dharmas; how much less could doubt entangle and dwell in its mind? Yet because of its underlying tendency, one speaks of the tendency toward doubt. Māluṅkyāputta, would not the many followers of other schools come and rebuke you with this simile of the infant child?" Thereupon Venerable Māluṅkyāputta, having been rebuked to his face by the World-Honored One, was inwardly distressed, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence, and was speechless, as though searching for something to say.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Māluṅkyāputta to his face, he sat in silence. Then Venerable Ānanda, who was standing behind the World-Honored One holding a fan and fanning the Buddha, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, now is the time! Well-Gone One, now is the time! If the World-Honored One would teach the bhikṣus the five lower fetters, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the World-Honored One, will well receive and well retain it."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, listen carefully and reflect well upon it."

Venerable Ānanda replied: "So be it. I shall receive the teaching and listen."

The Buddha said: "Ānanda, suppose someone is entangled by desire. When desire arises in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it really is. Not knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that desire grows ever more intense and cannot be controlled. This is a lower fetter. Ānanda, suppose someone is entangled by hatred. When hatred arises in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it really is. Not knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that hatred grows ever more intense and cannot be controlled. This is a lower fetter. Ānanda, suppose someone is entangled by self-identity view. When self-identity view arises in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it really is. Not knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that self-identity view grows ever more intense and cannot be controlled. This is a lower fetter. Ānanda, suppose someone is entangled by attachment to rules and rituals. When attachment to rules and rituals arises in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it really is. Not knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that attachment to rules and rituals grows ever more intense and cannot be controlled. This is a lower fetter. Ānanda, suppose someone is entangled by doubt. When doubt arises in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it really is. Not knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that doubt grows ever more intense and cannot be controlled. This is a lower fetter.

"Ānanda, if there is a path and a way to sever the five lower fetters, and one does not rely on this path and does not rely on this way, yet still severs the five lower fetters, this is impossible. Ānanda, just as a person who wants to obtain fruit, for the purpose of obtaining fruit, takes an axe and enters the forest. That person sees a tree endowed with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit. If that person does not cut the roots and trunk, yet obtains the fruit and returns home, this is impossible. So too, Ānanda, if there is a path and a way to sever the five lower fetters, and one does not rely on this path and does not rely on this way, yet still severs the five lower fetters, this is impossible. Ānanda, if there is a path and a way to sever the five lower fetters, and one relies on this path and relies on this way to sever the five lower fetters, this is certainly possible. Ānanda, just as a person who wants to obtain fruit, for the purpose of obtaining fruit, takes an axe and enters the forest. That person sees a tree endowed with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit. If that person cuts the roots and trunk and obtains the fruit and returns home, this is certainly possible. So too, Ānanda, if there is a path and a way to sever the five lower fetters, and one relies on this path and relies on this way to sever the five lower fetters, this is certainly possible.

"Ānanda, relying on what path and what way does one sever the five lower fetters? Ānanda, suppose someone is not entangled by desire. If desire-entanglement arises, he immediately knows how to abandon it as it really is. Knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that desire-entanglement ceases. Ānanda, suppose someone is not entangled by hatred. If hatred-entanglement arises, he immediately knows how to abandon it as it really is. Knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that hatred-entanglement ceases. Ānanda, suppose someone is not entangled by self-identity view. If self-identity view entanglement arises, he immediately knows how to abandon it as it really is. Knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that self-identity view entanglement ceases. Ānanda, suppose someone is not entangled by attachment to rules and rituals. If attachment to rules and rituals entanglement arises, he immediately knows how to abandon it as it really is. Knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that attachment to rules and rituals ceases. Ānanda, suppose someone is not entangled by doubt. If doubt-entanglement arises, he immediately knows how to abandon it as it really is. Knowing how to abandon it as it really is, that doubt-entanglement ceases. Ānanda, relying on this path and relying on this way, one severs the five lower fetters.

"Ānanda, just as the Ganges River, with its waters overflowing the banks. If a person comes who has business on the other bank and wishes to cross the river, he thinks: 'This Ganges River, with its waters overflowing the banks, I have business on the other bank and wish to cross, but my body has no strength to enable me to swim safely to the other bank.' Ānanda, know that this person has no strength. So too, Ānanda, if a person, regarding awakening, cessation, and nirvāṇa, whose mind does not incline toward it and is not pure, does not abide in liberation, Ānanda, know that this person is like that weak person without strength. Ānanda, just as the Ganges River, with its waters overflowing the banks. If a person comes who has business on the other bank and wishes to cross the river, he thinks: 'This Ganges River, with its waters overflowing the banks, I have business on the other bank and wish to cross, and my body now has strength to enable me to swim safely to the other bank.' Ānanda, know that this person has strength. So too, Ānanda, if a person, regarding awakening, cessation, and nirvāṇa, whose mind inclines toward it, is pure, and abides in liberation, Ānanda, know that this person is like that strong person.

"Ānanda, just as mountain floodwaters, very deep and extremely wide, flowing fast and swift, carrying much debris, with no boat and no bridge. Suppose a person comes who has business on the other bank and seeks to cross. As he seeks to cross, he thinks: 'These mountain floodwaters are very deep and extremely wide, flowing fast and swift, carrying much debris, with no boat and no bridge by which to cross. I have business on the other bank and wish to cross. By what means can I safely reach the other bank?' He further thinks: 'Suppose I now gather grass and wood from this bank, bind them into a raft, and riding upon it, cross over.' He then gathers grass and wood from the bank, binds them into a raft, and riding upon it, crosses over and reaches the other bank safely. So too, Ānanda, suppose a bhikṣu, relying upon disenchantment, depending on disenchantment, abiding in disenchantment, for the purpose of stilling bodily unwholesomeness, with his mind entering seclusion and concentration, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial application and sustained application, with joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first jhāna. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility.

"How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? When initial and sustained application have ceased, with inner tranquility and unification of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second jhāna. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility. How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? Dispassionate toward joy, desiring equanimity, dwelling without seeking, with right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and experiencing bodily happiness, as the noble ones describe: 'equanimous, mindful, and dwelling happily,' he attains and dwells in the third jhāna. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility. How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? With the cessation of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, he attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility.

"How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? Completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters the sphere of infinite space and dwells there. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility. How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? Completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells there. Depending on this state, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Depending on this state, having contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, abiding there, he will certainly attain the ending of defilements. If, abiding there, he does not attain the ending of defilements, he will certainly progress upward and attain a place of tranquility. How does he progress upward and attain a place of tranquility? Completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness and dwells there. Whatever feelings he has, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he contemplates those feelings as impermanent, contemplates their arising and passing away, contemplates dispassion, contemplates cessation, contemplates abandonment, contemplates relinquishment. Contemplating those feelings as impermanent in this way, contemplating their arising and passing away, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, contemplating abandonment, contemplating relinquishment, he does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, he is not afraid. Not being afraid, he attains complete nirvāṇa. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. He knew this as it really is.

"Just as not far from a village there is a great plantain tree. If a person takes an axe and splits the plantain tree, splitting it into pieces, splitting it into ten parts or into a hundred parts. Having split it into ten parts or into a hundred parts, he then peels apart leaf by leaf, and he cannot find any core, how much less any solid substance? Ānanda, so too, when a bhikṣu has whatever feelings, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he contemplates those feelings as impermanent, contemplates their arising and passing away, contemplates dispassion, contemplates cessation, contemplates abandonment, contemplates relinquishment. Contemplating those feelings as impermanent in this way, contemplating their arising and passing away, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, contemplating abandonment, contemplating relinquishment, he does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, he is not afraid. Not being afraid, he attains complete nirvāṇa. Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further becoming. He knew this as it really is."

Thereupon Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said: "World-Honored One, how wonderful! How remarkable! The World-Honored One has taught the bhikṣus, establishing support upon support, teaching the abandonment of defilements and the transcending of defilements. Yet the bhikṣus do not quickly attain the unsurpassed, the ultimate and final end."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Ānanda. So it is, Ānanda. How wonderful! How remarkable! I teach the bhikṣus, establishing support upon support, teaching the abandonment of defilements and the transcending of defilements. Yet the bhikṣus do not quickly attain the unsurpassed, the ultimate and final end. Why is that? Because there are differences of superior and inferior among people, and therefore in the practice of the path there are degrees of refinement and coarseness. Because there are degrees of refinement and coarseness in the practice of the path, therefore there are differences of superior and inferior among people. Ānanda, for this reason I say there are differences of superior and inferior among people."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it with practice.

End of the Sūtra on the Five Lower Fetters, Fourth.

---

## (206) Madhyamāgama, Pulita Chapter: The Sūtra on Impurities of the Mind, Fifth

Thus have I heard.

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī does not remove the five impurities from the mind and does not undo the five bonds of the mind, it is said that such a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī will surely decline. What does it mean to not remove the five impurities from the mind? Suppose someone doubts the World-Honored One, is hesitant, whose mind is not open, whose mind does not understand, whose mind is not at peace. If someone doubts the World-Honored One, is hesitant, whose mind is not open, whose mind does not understand, whose mind is not at peace, this is called not having removed the first impurity from the mind, namely regarding the World-Honored One. Likewise regarding the Dharma, the precepts, and the teaching. If there are fellow practitioners in the holy life whom the World-Honored One has praised, and one reproaches them, treats them lightly, irritates them, and harms them, with a mind that is not open, does not understand, and is not at peace, this is called the fifth impurity of the mind not removed, namely regarding fellow practitioners in the holy life.

"What does it mean to not undo the five bonds of the mind? Suppose someone is not free from staining of the body, not free from desire regarding the body, not free from love regarding the body, not free from craving regarding the body. If someone is not free from staining of the body, not free from desire, not free from love, not free from craving regarding the body, then that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation. If that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation, this is called the first bond of the mind not undone, namely regarding the body. Furthermore, regarding sensual pleasures, one is not free from staining, not free from desire, not free from love, not free from craving. If regarding sensual pleasures one is not free from staining, not free from desire, not free from love, not free from craving, then that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation. If that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation, this is called the second bond of the mind not undone, namely regarding sensual pleasures.

"Furthermore, suppose someone speaks of what accords with noble meaning, what is gentle and free from the hindrance of doubt, namely: speaking of precepts, speaking of concentration, speaking of wisdom, speaking of liberation, speaking of the knowledge and vision of liberation, speaking of diminishment, speaking of non-association, speaking of few desires, speaking of contentment, speaking of cutting off, speaking of dispassion, speaking of cessation, speaking of sitting in meditation, speaking of dependent origination. Such things as bhikṣus and renunciants speak of, yet that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation. If that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation, this is called the third bond of the mind not undone, namely regarding such teachings. Furthermore, one frequently mingles with laypeople, engaging in playfulness, pride, and failing to study. If one frequently mingles with laypeople, engaging in playfulness, pride, and failing to study, then that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation. If that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation, this is called the fourth bond of the mind not undone, namely regarding association with laypeople.

"Furthermore, having gained a small attainment, one stops midway and does not seek further progress. If, having gained a small attainment, one stops midway and does not seek further progress, then that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation. If that person's mind does not incline, is not at peace, does not settle, is not liberated, and he cuts off his own effort at sitting in meditation, this is called the fifth bond of the mind not undone, namely regarding further progress. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī does not remove these five impurities from the mind and does not undo these five bonds of the mind, it is said that such a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī will surely decline. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī well removes the five impurities from the mind and well undoes the five bonds of the mind, it is said that such a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has the Dharma of purification.

"What does it mean to well remove the five impurities from the mind? Suppose someone does not doubt the World-Honored One, is not hesitant, whose mind is open, whose mind understands, whose mind is at peace. If someone does not doubt the World-Honored One, is not hesitant, whose mind is open, whose mind understands, whose mind is at peace, this is called the first impurity well removed from the mind, namely regarding the World-Honored One. Likewise regarding the Dharma, the precepts, and the teaching. If there are fellow practitioners in the holy life whom the World-Honored One has praised, and one does not reproach them, does not treat them lightly, does not irritate them, does not harm them, with a mind that is open, understands, and is at peace, this is called the fifth impurity well removed from the mind, namely regarding fellow practitioners in the holy life.

"What does it mean to undo the five bonds of the mind? Suppose someone is free from staining of the body, free from desire, free from love, free from craving regarding the body. If someone is free from staining of the body, free from desire, free from love, free from craving regarding the body, then that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off. If that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off, this is called the first bond of the mind undone, namely regarding the body. Furthermore, regarding sensual pleasures, one is free from staining, free from desire, free from love, free from craving. If regarding sensual pleasures one is free from staining, free from desire, free from love, free from craving, then that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off. If that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off, this is called the second bond of the mind undone, namely regarding sensual pleasures.

"Furthermore, suppose someone speaks of what accords with noble meaning, what is gentle and free from the hindrance of doubt, namely: speaking of precepts, speaking of concentration, speaking of wisdom, speaking of liberation, speaking of the knowledge and vision of liberation, speaking of diminishment, speaking of non-association, speaking of few desires, speaking of contentment, speaking of cutting off, speaking of dispassion, speaking of cessation, speaking of sitting in meditation, speaking of dependent origination. Such things as bhikṣus and renunciants speak of, and that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off. If that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off, this is called the third bond of the mind undone, namely regarding such teachings. Furthermore, one does not frequently mingle with laypeople, does not engage in playfulness, is not proud, and pursues study. If one does not frequently mingle with laypeople, does not engage in playfulness, is not proud, and pursues study, then that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off. If that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off, this is called the fourth bond of the mind undone, namely regarding non-association with laypeople.

"Furthermore, having gained a small attainment, one does not stop midway but seeks further progress. If, having gained a small attainment, one does not stop midway but seeks further progress, then that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off. If that person's mind inclines, is at peace, settles, and is liberated, and his own effort at sitting in meditation is not cut off, this is called the fifth bond of the mind undone, namely regarding further progress. If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī well removes these five impurities from the mind and well undoes these five bonds of the mind, it is said that such a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has the Dharma of purification. Having established these ten factors, one further cultivates five dharmas.

"What are the five? One cultivates the basis of spiritual power consisting of concentration due to desire, accomplishing the power of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, relying on relinquishment, inclining toward the unconditioned. One cultivates the basis of spiritual power consisting of concentration due to energy, concentration due to mind, and concentration due to investigation, accomplishing the power of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, relying on relinquishment, inclining toward the unconditioned. Capability is the fifth. One who is accomplished in these fifteen factors of capability and self-exertion will certainly know, will certainly see, will certainly attain perfect and complete awakening, will reach the gate of the Deathless, will dwell near nirvāṇa. I say such a person will without fail reach nirvāṇa. Just as a hen that has laid ten eggs, or twelve, and at the proper times covers them, at the proper times warms them, at the proper times watches over them, even if the hen is sometimes negligent, among those chicks, some will use their feet and beaks to break through the eggshell and emerge safely. These will be the first. So too, when a bhikṣu is accomplished in these fifteen factors of capability and self-exertion, he will certainly know, will certainly see, will certainly attain perfect and complete awakening, will certainly reach the gate of the Deathless, will dwell near nirvāṇa. I say such a person will without fail attain nirvāṇa."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and received it with practice.

End of the Sūtra on Impurities of the Mind, Fifth.

# Madhyamāgama (Middle Length Āgamas)
## Fascicle 57
