### (205) Sūtra on the Five Supports

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are five supports. What are the five? First, killing living beings; second, taking what is not given; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, drinking alcohol."

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on killing living beings and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support. Just as a tree whose roots have been destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all wither. In the same way, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on killing living beings and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support."

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on taking what is not given and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support. Just as a tree whose roots have been destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all wither. In the same way, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on taking what is not given and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support."

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on sexual misconduct and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support. Just as a tree whose roots have been destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all wither. In the same way, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on sexual misconduct and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support."

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on false speech and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support. Just as a tree whose roots have been destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all wither. In the same way, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on false speech and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support."

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on drinking alcohol and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support. Just as a tree whose roots have been destroyed, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all wither. In the same way, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka or upāsikā, relies on drinking alcohol and does not abandon it, I say this person has fallen and lost their support."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (206) Sūtra on the Heart's Turmoil

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu's heart is in turmoil, unrestrained, unguarded, and unprotected in regard to the faculties, such a bhikṣu will certainly have deterioration in wholesome states, either by day or by night. It is like a city whose walls are destroyed and its moat is breached: the city lord will certainly suffer deterioration, either by day or by night. In the same way, if a bhikṣu's heart is in turmoil, unrestrained, unguarded, and unprotected in regard to the faculties, such a bhikṣu will certainly have deterioration in wholesome states, either by day or by night."

"If a bhikṣu's heart is not in turmoil, is restrained, guarded, and protected in regard to the faculties, such a bhikṣu will certainly not have deterioration in wholesome states, either by day or by night. It is like a city whose walls are intact and its moat is complete: the city lord will certainly not suffer deterioration, either by day or by night. In the same way, if a bhikṣu's heart is not in turmoil, is restrained, guarded, and protected in regard to the faculties, such a bhikṣu will certainly not have deterioration in wholesome states, either by day or by night."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (207) Sūtra on Arrows

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The uninstructed ordinary person experiences painful feeling, and at that time they grieve, weep, beat their breast, and cry out, falling into bewilderment. They experience two kinds of feeling: bodily feeling and mental feeling. It is like a person who is struck by one arrow, and then immediately struck by a second arrow. This person then experiences the feeling of two arrows. The uninstructed ordinary person is also like this: when they experience painful feeling, they grieve, weep, beat their breast, and cry out, falling into bewilderment. They experience two kinds of feeling: bodily feeling and mental feeling."

"When experiencing painful feeling, they give rise to aversion toward it. Having given rise to aversion toward painful feeling, the underlying tendency of aversion toward painful feeling lies latent in them. When experiencing painful feeling, they then seek delight in sensual pleasures. Why? Because the uninstructed ordinary person does not know any escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. When they seek delight in sensual pleasures, the underlying tendency of attachment to pleasant feeling lies latent in them. They do not know as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these feelings. Not knowing as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these feelings, the underlying tendency of ignorance toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling lies latent in them."

"If they experience pleasant feeling, they experience it as bound. If they experience painful feeling, they experience it as bound. If they experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they experience it as bound. This is called an uninstructed ordinary person who is bound by birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress. I say this person is bound by suffering."

"The well-instructed noble disciple, when experiencing painful feeling, does not grieve, does not weep, does not beat their breast, does not cry out, and does not fall into bewilderment. They experience only one kind of feeling: bodily feeling, not mental feeling. It is like a person who is struck by one arrow but is not struck by a second arrow. This person then experiences the feeling of only one arrow. The well-instructed noble disciple is also like this: when experiencing painful feeling, they do not grieve, do not weep, do not beat their breast, do not cry out, and do not fall into bewilderment. They experience only one kind of feeling: bodily feeling, not mental feeling."

"When experiencing painful feeling, they do not give rise to aversion toward it. Not giving rise to aversion toward painful feeling, the underlying tendency of aversion toward painful feeling does not lie latent in them. When experiencing painful feeling, they do not seek delight in sensual pleasures. Why? Because the well-instructed noble disciple knows an escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. Since they do not seek delight in sensual pleasures, the underlying tendency of attachment to pleasant feeling does not lie latent in them. They know as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these feelings. Knowing as it really is the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these feelings, the underlying tendency of ignorance toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling does not lie latent in them."

"If they experience pleasant feeling, they experience it as unbound. If they experience painful feeling, they experience it as unbound. If they experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they experience it as unbound. This is called a well-instructed noble disciple who is unbound from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and distress. I say this person is unbound from suffering."

"This is the distinction, this is the difference, this is what separates the well-instructed noble disciple from the uninstructed ordinary person."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (208) Sūtra on the Simile of the Raft

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you the Dharma by the simile of a raft. The Dharma should be abandoned, how much more what is not the Dharma. Listen well and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we are listening."

The Buddha said: "Suppose a person traveling on a road comes upon a great body of water. This side is dangerous and fearful, while the far shore is safe and without fear. There is no boat or bridge by which to cross to the far shore. That person thinks: 'This body of water is vast. This side is dangerous and fearful, while the far shore is safe and without fear. There is no boat or bridge by which to cross to the far shore. I should now gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves, and bind them into a raft. Riding on this raft, paddling with my hands and feet, I shall safely cross to the far shore.'"

"That person then gathers grass, wood, branches, and leaves, and binds them into a raft. Riding on this raft, paddling with hands and feet, they safely cross to the far shore. Having crossed to the far shore, that person thinks: 'This raft has been very useful to me. Riding on this raft, paddling with my hands and feet, I safely crossed from the dangerous shore to the safe shore. I should now carry this raft on my head or load it on my shoulders and go wherever I wish.' Bhikṣus, what do you think? If that person does this, would they be doing what should be done with the raft?"

The bhikṣus answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Bhikṣus, what should that person do to properly handle the raft? Having crossed to the far shore, that person should think: 'This raft has been very useful to me. Riding on this raft, paddling with my hands and feet, I safely crossed from the dangerous shore to the safe shore. I should now pull this raft up onto the bank, or push it back into the water, and go wherever I wish.' If that person does this, they would be doing what should be done with the raft. In the same way, I teach you the Dharma by the simile of a raft. The Dharma should be abandoned, how much more what is not the Dharma."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (209) Sūtra on [the Bhikṣu] Pūraṇa

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, early in the morning, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. The Venerable Ānanda thought: "It is still too early to enter Rājagṛha to beg for food. I should first go to the park of the followers of other paths."

Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the park of the followers of other paths. Upon arriving, he exchanged greetings with the followers of other paths, and after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side. At that time, the followers of other paths said to the Venerable Ānanda: "We wish to ask you a question. Will you permit it?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Ask as you wish. After hearing your question, I will consider it."

The followers of other paths said: "Friend Ānanda, what is the reason for practicing the holy life under the ascetic Gotama?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "It is for the sake of abandoning desire."

They asked again: "Friend Ānanda, is there a path, is there a practice for abandoning desire?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "There is a path, there is a practice for abandoning desire."

They asked: "Friend Ānanda, what is the path, what is the practice for abandoning desire?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is the path, this is the practice for abandoning desire."

The followers of other paths said: "Friend Ānanda, excellent is this path, excellent is this practice for abandoning desire. It is sufficient for the practice of non-distraction."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the followers of other paths said, neither delighted in it nor reproached it. Neither delighting nor reproaching, he rose from his seat and departed.

After begging for food in Rājagṛha, having finished his meal, the Venerable Ānanda went to the Buddha, bowed at his feet, and sat to one side. He then fully reported to the World-Honored One the entire conversation with the followers of other paths.

The World-Honored One said: "Excellent, excellent! Ānanda, you answered them correctly. Why? Because this Noble Eightfold Path is indeed for the sake of abandoning desire. Ānanda, this is the reason for practicing the holy life under me: it is for the sake of abandoning desire. The path for abandoning desire is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (210) Sūtra on Dharma and Meaning

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There are two things that a bhikṣu who has recently left the household life should train in. What are the two? First, the beauty of Dharma; second, the beauty of meaning. This is called the two things that a bhikṣu who has recently left the household life should train in."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (211) Sūtra on Great Emptiness

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying among the Śākyas, at Kapilavastu, at Nigrodha's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in the afternoon, rose from meditation, went to the lecture hall, and sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, I now dwell in inner emptiness."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One dwells in inner emptiness, the great emptiness."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, why do you say the World-Honored One dwells in the great emptiness?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "World-Honored One, I formerly heard the World-Honored One say, 'Ānanda, I now dwell in inner emptiness, the great emptiness.' This is what I formerly heard from the World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Ānanda, I said this, and it is correctly remembered, not forgotten, well retained, and exactly as it was heard. Ānanda, just as now in this Nigrodha's Park, there are no elephants, horses, cattle, or sheep, no wealth, no grain stores, no women or men, only this non-emptiness, namely, the assembly of bhikṣus; in the same way, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of a village, does not attend to the perception of people, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the forest. Their mind enters into the perception of the forest, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of a village are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of people are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the forest.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of a village. This field of perception is empty of the perception of people. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the forest.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of people, does not attend to the perception of the forest, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of earth. Their mind enters into the perception of earth, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it. Just as a bull's hide, when stretched with a hundred pegs, becomes free of wrinkles; in the same way, a bhikṣu does not attend to the high places, the low places, the rivers, the thorny undergrowth, the rocks, the uneven terrain on this earth, but attends to the oneness dependent on the perception of a flat earth."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of people are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the forest are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of people. This field of perception is empty of the perception of the forest. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the forest, does not attend to the perception of earth, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space. Their mind enters into the perception of the base of infinite space, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the forest are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of earth are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of the forest. This field of perception is empty of the perception of earth. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of earth, does not attend to the perception of the base of infinite space, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness. Their mind enters into the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of earth are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of earth. This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite space. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the base of infinite space, does not attend to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness. Their mind enters into the perception of the base of nothingness, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite space. This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, does not attend to the perception of the base of nothingness, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Their mind enters into the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness. This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of nothingness. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of the base of nothingness, does not attend to the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the signless concentration of mind. Their mind enters into the signless concentration of mind, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the six sense bases conditioned by this body and dependent on life.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of nothingness. This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the six sense bases conditioned by this body and dependent on life.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins of the past who entered into and dwelled in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness all entered into and dwelled in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Those ascetics and brahmins of the future who will enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness will all enter into and dwell in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Those ascetics and brahmins of the present who enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness all enter into and dwell in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should also train thus: I shall enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Ānanda, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and put it into practice.

### (212) Sūtra on Lesser Emptiness

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the Mansion of Migāra's Mother.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, in the afternoon, rose from meditation, went to the Buddha, bowed at his feet, and sat to one side. He then said to the World-Honored One: "At one time, the World-Honored One was staying among the Śākyas, at Kapilavastu, at Nigrodha's Park. At that time, I heard directly from the World-Honored One, received directly from the World-Honored One: 'Ānanda, I now often dwell in emptiness.' World-Honored One, did I correctly hear, correctly receive, correctly attend to, and correctly remember this?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda, you indeed correctly heard, correctly received, correctly attended to, and correctly remembered this. Ānanda, just as formerly, so now I also often dwell in emptiness. Ānanda, just as in this Mansion of Migāra's Mother, it is empty of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, wealth, grain stores, women, and men. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the assembly of bhikṣus."

"In the same way, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of a village, does not attend to the perception of people, but attends to the oneness dependent on the perception of the forest. Their mind enters into the perception of the forest, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it. They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of a village are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of people are not present here. "Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of people, does not attend to the perception of the forest, but attends to the oneness dependent on the perception of earth. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of earth.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

Their mind enters into the perception of the base of infinite space, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of earth are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space.' They know: 'This field of perception is empty of the perception of the forest. This field of perception is empty of the perception of earth. There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu does not attend to the perception of earth, does not attend to the perception of the base of infinite space, but attends only to the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness. Their mind enters into the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, and they find satisfaction, delight, stability, and resolution in it."

"They know thus: 'The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of earth are not present here. The troubles that would arise dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space are not present here. There is only this measure of trouble, namely, the oneness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.' There is only this non-emptiness, namely, the six sense bases conditioned by this body and dependent on life.' Thus, what is not there, they regard as empty of it. What remains there, they understand as truly present. Ānanda, this is also called dwelling in the real, unfalsified, pure descent into emptiness."

"Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins of the past who entered into and dwelled in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness all entered into and dwelled in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Those ascetics and brahmins of the future who will enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness will all enter into and dwell in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Those ascetics and brahmins of the present who enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness all enter into and dwell in this pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness."

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should also train thus: I shall enter into and dwell in the pure, unfalsified, supreme emptiness. Ānanda, you should train in this way."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha said, was delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (213) Sūtra on Dharma Assemblies

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach you about the Dharma assembly and what is not a Dharma assembly. Listen well and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we are listening."

The Buddha said: "What is not a Dharma assembly? If bhikṣus, when assembled together, engage in various kinds of worldly talk, namely: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of war, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of men, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of cities, talk of the seashore, and various other kinds of worldly talk, this is called not a Dharma assembly."

"What is a Dharma assembly? If bhikṣus, when assembled together, either teach the Dharma themselves, or request others to teach the Dharma, or else both remain in noble silence, this is called a Dharma assembly."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

### (214) Sūtra on Arrows (Second)

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "I shall teach about the short-lived and the long-lived. Listen well and pay close attention. I shall explain it for you."

The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, we are listening."

The Buddha said: "If a bhikṣu practices four things, they attain a short life. What are the four? First, they do not delight in going to see the Tathāgata. Second, they do not delight in hearing the correct Dharma. Third, they do not delight in making offerings to the Sangha. Fourth, they do not delight in observing the precepts. If a bhikṣu practices these four things, they attain a short life."

"If a bhikṣu practices four things, they attain a long life. What are the four? First, they delight in going to see the Tathāgata. Second, they delight in hearing the correct Dharma. Third, they delight in making offerings to the Sangha. Fourth, they delight in observing the precepts. If a bhikṣu practices these four things, they attain a long life."

The Buddha spoke thus. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, were delighted and put it into practice.

---

*End of Fascicle 57 of the Madhyamāgama*

# Fascicle 57 of the Madhyamāgama

---

## (207) Sūtra on Jianmao (Arrow-Hair), Sixth of the Pulita Section

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, one thousand two hundred and fifty people, receiving the summer retreat.

At that time, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed, at early dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. Having finished begging for food, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and went to the Peacock Grove, the garden of the heterodox practitioners.

At that time, in the Peacock Grove garden of the heterodox practitioners, there was a heterodox practitioner named Arrow-Hair (Jianmao), a man of renown and virtue, a patriarch of his school, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame, revered and honored by the assembly, who led a great following and was honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners. He was in a great assembly, clamorous and disorderly, uttering loud and great sounds, discussing all sorts of base and frivolous topics: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of young girls, talk of courtesans, talk of the world, talk of wilderness, talk of the sea, talk of people of the land. They were gathered together discussing such base and frivolous topics. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair saw the Buddha coming from afar and commanded his assembly, saying: "Be silent, all of you, and remain still. The ascetic Gautama is coming. His assembly is silent; he always delights in silence and praises silence. If he sees this assembly silent, perhaps he will come to visit us." Having commanded his assembly to be silent, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair himself remained silent.

The World-Honored One went to the place of the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Welcome, ascetic Gautama! It has been long since the ascetic Gautama has come here. Please be seated on this seat." The World-Honored One then sat on the seat that the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair had prepared. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair then exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin! What were you just discussing? For what reason have you gathered together here?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, let us set aside that discussion. That discussion was not refined. If the ascetic Gautama wishes to hear that discussion, it would not be difficult to hear it later."

The World-Honored One asked again, a second and third time: "Udāyin! What were you just discussing? For what reason have you gathered together here?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair also replied a second and third time: "Gautama, let us set aside that discussion. That discussion was not refined. If the ascetic Gautama wishes to hear that discussion, it would not be difficult to hear it later. Since the ascetic Gautama asks a second and third time, wishing to hear, I shall now tell it. Gautama, we were together with many brahmins of the country of Kosala, all gathered together in the Kosala assembly hall, and we discussed the following: 'The people of Aṅga-Magadha have great good fortune; the people of Aṅga-Magadha have obtained great good fortune. Such a great field of merit is in Rājagṛha together receiving the summer retreat, namely Pūraṇa Kassapa.' Why is that? Gautama, Pūraṇa Kassapa is a man of renown and virtue, a patriarch of his school, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame, revered and honored by the assembly, who leads a great following and is honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners. He is in this Rājagṛha together receiving the summer retreat. Likewise Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Kesakambalī.

"Gautama, Ajita Kesakambalī is a man of renown and virtue, a patriarch of his school, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame, revered and honored by the assembly, who leads a great following and is honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners, and is in this Rājagṛha together receiving the summer retreat. Earlier we also discussed the ascetic Gautama. This ascetic Gautama is a man of renown and virtue, a patriarch of his school, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame, revered and honored by the assembly, who leads a great assembly of bhikṣus, honored by one thousand two hundred and fifty people, and is also in this Rājagṛha together receiving the summer retreat. Gautama, we further had this thought: 'Among all these venerable ascetics and brahmins, who is revered, honored, served, and attended by their disciples? Who is not reviled by their disciples with rightful criticism, and who has no disciples who challenge their teacher, saying "This is simply unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave?' Gautama, we further had this thought: 'This Pūraṇa Kassapa is not revered, honored, served, or attended by his disciples. He is reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, and many disciples challenge their teacher, saying "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.'

"Gautama, in the past, Pūraṇa Kassapa would frequently raise his hands in the midst of his assembly of disciples and call out loudly: 'You all should stay! No one has come to ask you questions; people are asking me questions. You cannot resolve these matters; I can resolve these matters.' Yet his disciples, in the middle of his speech, would discuss other matters, not waiting for the teacher to finish speaking. Gautama, we further had this thought: 'Thus this Pūraṇa Kassapa is not revered, honored, served, or attended by his disciples. He is reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, and many disciples challenge their teacher: "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.' Likewise for Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Kesakambalī. Gautama, we had this thought: 'This Ajita Kesakambalī is not revered, honored, served, or attended by his disciples. He is reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, and many disciples challenge their teacher: "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.' Gautama, in the past, Ajita Kesakambalī would frequently raise his hands in the midst of his assembly of disciples and call out loudly: 'You all should stay! No one has come to ask you questions; people are asking me questions. You cannot resolve these matters; I can resolve these matters.' Yet his disciples, in the middle of his speech, would discuss other matters, not waiting for the teacher to finish speaking.

"Gautama, we further had this thought: 'Thus this Ajita Kesakambalī is not revered, honored, served, or attended by his disciples. He is reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, and many disciples challenge their teacher: "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.'

"Gautama, we further had this thought: 'This ascetic Gautama is revered, honored, served, and attended by his disciples. He is not reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, nor do any disciples challenge their teacher, saying "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.' Gautama, in the past, the ascetic Gautama would frequently be in great assemblies, surrounded by countless hundreds and thousands, teaching the Dharma. Among them, there was one person who snored in his sleep. Another person said to that person: 'Do not snore in your sleep! Do you not wish to hear the World-Honored One teach the subtle and wonderful Dharma, like sweet nectar?' That person then immediately became silent and made no sound. Gautama, we further had this thought: 'Thus this ascetic Gautama is revered, honored, served, and attended by his disciples. He is not reviled by his disciples with rightful criticism, nor do any disciples challenge their teacher, saying "This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not equitable," and then leave.'"

The World-Honored One, having heard this, asked the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair: "Udāyin, how many qualities do you see in me that cause my disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing from me?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, I see that Gautama has five qualities that cause his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing. What are the five? The ascetic Gautama is content with coarse clothing and praises contentment with coarse clothing. If the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse clothing and praises contentment with coarse clothing, this is what I see as the first quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing. Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse food and praises contentment with coarse food. If the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse food and praises contentment with coarse food, this is what I see as the second quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing.

"Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama eats little and praises eating little. If the ascetic Gautama eats little and praises eating little, this is what I see as the third quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing. Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse dwelling places and beds, and praises contentment with coarse dwelling places and beds. If the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse dwelling places and beds, and praises contentment with coarse dwelling places and beds, this is what I see as the fourth quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing. Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama practices secluded meditation and praises secluded meditation. If the ascetic Gautama practices secluded meditation and praises secluded meditation, this is what I see as the fifth quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing. These are what I see as the five qualities of the ascetic Gautama that cause his disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend him, always following and never departing."

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, it is not because of these five qualities that my disciples revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing. Udāyin, the robes I wear are cut according to holy practice, dyed in dull, unattractive colors; such are the holy robes dyed in dull, unattractive colors. Udāyin, some of my disciples wear, for their entire lifetime, only robes made from rags cast off on refuse heaps, yet they also say: 'My World-Honored One is content with coarse clothing and praises contentment with coarse clothing.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of contentment with coarse clothing, then on that account they would not revere, honor, serve, or attend me, nor would they follow me. Furthermore, Udāyin, I eat fine rice that is well-ripened, without husks, with countless varied flavors. Udāyin, some of my disciples, for their entire lifetime, eat only what they obtain through begging, discarded food, yet they also say: 'My World-Honored One is content with coarse food and praises contentment with coarse food.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of contentment with coarse food, then on that account they would not revere, honor, serve, or attend me, nor would they follow me.

"Furthermore, Udāyin, I eat as much as one vīra measure of food, or half a vīra. Udāyin, some of my disciples eat only as much as one kuṭha measure, or half a kuṭha, yet they also say: 'My World-Honored One eats little and praises eating little.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of eating little, then on that account they would not revere, honor, serve, or attend me, nor would they follow me. Furthermore, Udāyin, sometimes I stay in high pavilions or storied buildings. Udāyin, some of my disciples, after nine or ten months, sleep under cover for only one night, yet they also say: 'My World-Honored One is content with coarse dwelling places and beds, and praises contentment with coarse dwelling places and beds.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of contentment with coarse dwelling places and beds, then on that account they would not revere, honor, serve, or attend me, nor would they follow me.

"Furthermore, Udāyin, I constantly engage with the busy affairs of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Some of my disciples enter the assembly only once every half month, for the sake of purifying the Dharma, yet they also say: 'My World-Honored One practices secluded meditation and praises secluded meditation.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of secluded meditation, then on that account they would not revere, honor, serve, or attend me, nor would they follow me. Udāyin, it is not because of these five qualities that my disciples revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing.

"Udāyin, there are another five qualities that cause my disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing. What are the five? Udāyin, my disciples praise me on account of unsurpassed morality, saying: 'The World-Honored One practices the precepts, the great precepts. What he says accords with what he does; what he does accords with what he says.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of unsurpassed morality, then on that account they revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing. Furthermore, Udāyin, my disciples praise me on account of unsurpassed wisdom, saying: 'The World-Honored One practices wisdom, the highest wisdom. If any debater comes to contend with him, he can certainly defeat them. That is, concerning the true Dharma and Vinaya, nothing can be said against it; concerning what he himself teaches, no fault can be found.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of unsurpassed wisdom, then on that account they revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing.

"Furthermore, Udāyin, my disciples praise me on account of unsurpassed knowledge and vision, saying: 'The World-Honored One moves about with knowledge, not without knowledge; with vision, not without vision. He teaches the Dharma to his disciples with cause, not without cause; with conditions, not without conditions; in a way that can be answered, not in a way that cannot be answered; with liberation, not without liberation.' Udāyin, if my disciples praise me because of unsurpassed knowledge and vision, then on that account they revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing. Furthermore, Udāyin, my disciples, being weary of the arrow of craving, come to ask me: 'Is suffering thus suffering? Is the origin thus the origin? Is cessation thus cessation? Is the path thus the path?' I then answer them: 'Suffering is thus suffering; the origin is thus the origin; cessation is thus cessation; the path is thus the path.' Udāyin, if my disciples come to ask me, and I answer in a way that is pleasing and brings them joy, then on that account they revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing.

"Furthermore, Udāyin, for my disciples I teach and demonstrate the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, clearly realized, or I teach and demonstrate the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the defilements, clearly realized. Udāyin, if my disciples, within this true Dharma and Vinaya, attain acceptance and cross over, reaching the other shore, free from doubt and perplexity, without any hesitation regarding the good Dharma, then on that account they revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing. Udāyin, these are the other five qualities that cause my disciples to revere, honor, serve, and attend me, always following and never departing."

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Gautama, how marvelous! How extraordinary! You have well spoken of wonderful things, moistening my body like sweet nectar. Gautama, just as a great rain moistens all the high and low ground universally, so too the ascetic Gautama has well spoken of wonderful things for us, moistening my body like sweet nectar. World-Honored One, I understand. Well-Gone One, I comprehend. World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the assembly of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day forward, for my entire life, I take refuge, until the end of my life."

The Buddha spoke thus. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sixth Sūtra on Arrow-Hair

---

## (208) Sūtra on Arrow-Hair, Seventh of the Pulita Section of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove at the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the World-Honored One, after the night had passed, at early dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food. Having finished begging for food, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting cloth upon his shoulder, and went to the Peacock Grove, the garden of the heterodox practitioners.

At that time, in the Peacock Grove garden of the heterodox practitioners, there was a heterodox practitioner named Arrow-Hair, a man of renown and virtue, a patriarch of his school, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame, revered and honored by the assembly, who led a great following and was honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners. He was in a great assembly, clamorous and disorderly, uttering loud and great sounds, discussing all sorts of base and frivolous topics: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of young girls, talk of courtesans, talk of the world, talk of wilderness, talk of the sea, talk of people of the land. They were gathered together discussing such base and frivolous topics. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair saw the Buddha coming from afar and commanded his assembly, saying: "Be silent, all of you, and remain still. The ascetic Gautama is coming. His assembly is silent; he always delights in silence and praises silence. If he sees this assembly silent, perhaps he will come to visit us." Having commanded his assembly to be silent, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair himself remained silent.

The World-Honored One went to the place of the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his robe, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Welcome, ascetic Gautama! It has been long since the ascetic Gautama has come here. Please be seated on this seat." The World-Honored One then sat on the seat that the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair had prepared. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair then exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin! What were you just discussing? For what reason have you gathered together here?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, let us set aside that discussion. That discussion was not refined. If the ascetic Gautama wishes to hear that discussion, it would not be difficult to hear it later."

The World-Honored One asked again, a second and third time: "Udāyin! What were you just discussing? For what reason have you gathered together here?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair also replied a second and third time: "Gautama, let us set aside that discussion. That discussion was not refined. If the ascetic Gautama wishes to hear that discussion, it would not be difficult to hear it later. Since the ascetic Gautama asks a second and third time, wishing to hear, I shall now tell it. Gautama, I have deliberation, I have reflection; I abide in the ground of deliberation and the ground of reflection; I have wisdom and I have eloquence. There are those who claim to truly be omniscient, all-knowing and all-seeing, with nothing remaining unknown and nothing remaining unseen. I went to ask them about matters, yet they did not know. Gautama, I then thought: 'What sort of thing is this?'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, you who have deliberation and reflection, who abide in the ground of deliberation and the ground of reflection, who have wisdom and eloquence, who is it that claims to truly be omniscient, all-knowing and all-seeing, with nothing remaining unknown and nothing remaining unseen, whom you went to question, yet who did not know?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, it was Pūraṇa Kassapa. Why is that? Gautama, Pūraṇa Kassapa himself claims to truly be omniscient, all-knowing and all-seeing, with nothing remaining unknown and nothing remaining unseen. I have deliberation and reflection; I abide in the ground of deliberation and the ground of reflection; I have wisdom and eloquence. I went to ask him about matters, yet he did not know. Gautama, therefore I thought: 'What sort of thing is this?' Likewise for Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Kesakambalī. Gautama, Ajita Kesakambalī himself claims to truly be omniscient, all-knowing and all-seeing, with nothing remaining unknown and nothing remaining unseen. I have deliberation and reflection; I abide in the ground of deliberation and the ground of reflection; I have wisdom and eloquence. I went to ask him about matters, yet he did not know. Gautama, therefore I thought: 'What sort of thing is this?' Gautama, I further had this thought: 'If I were to go to the ascetic Gautama and ask about matters of the past, the ascetic Gautama would certainly be able to answer my questions about the past. If I were to go to the ascetic Gautama and ask about matters of the future, the ascetic Gautama would certainly be able to answer my questions about the future. Furthermore, whatever question I might ask the ascetic Gautama, the ascetic Gautama would certainly also be able to answer whatever I ask.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Enough, Udāyin, enough! Because through the long night you have had different views, different convictions, different delights, different desires, and different intentions, you cannot fully understand the meaning of what I say. Udāyin, I have disciples who, with cause and conditions, recollect innumerable past lives and previous births: one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, kalpas of formation, kalpas of dissolution, innumerable kalpas of formation and dissolution. A being was named thus; I was once born there, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of life, such an end of lifespan. Dying here, born there; dying there, born here. I was born in this place, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of life, such an end of lifespan. They come to ask me about matters of the past, and I answer their questions about the past. I also go and ask them about matters of the past, and they also answer my questions about the past. Whatever I ask them, they also answer whatever I ask.

"Furthermore, Udāyin, I have disciples with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, who see beings at the time of death and the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, of fine and not fine states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations, according to the deeds that these beings have performed, seeing them as they truly are. If a being has accomplished bodily bad conduct, has accomplished verbal and mental bad conduct, has slandered noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished deeds of wrong views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, that being will certainly fall to a bad destination and be born in hell. If a being has accomplished bodily good conduct, has accomplished verbal and mental good conduct, has not slandered noble ones, held right views, and accomplished deeds of right views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, that being will certainly ascend to a good destination and be born in heaven. They come to ask me about matters of the future, and I answer their questions about the future. I also go and ask them about matters of the future, and they also answer my questions about the future. Whatever I ask them, they also answer whatever I ask."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair said: "Gautama, if that is so, then I am even more confused, even more unseeing, falling into further delusion and sinking into ignorance, when the ascetic Gautama says thus: 'Udāyin, enough, enough! Because through the long night you have had different views, different convictions, different delights, different desires, and different intentions, you cannot fully understand the meaning of what I say. Udāyin, I have disciples who, with cause and conditions, recollect innumerable past lives and previous births: one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, kalpas of formation, kalpas of dissolution, innumerable kalpas of formation and dissolution. A being was named thus; I was once born there, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of life, such an end of lifespan. Dying here, born there; dying there, born here. I was born in this place, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of life, such an end of lifespan. They come to ask me about matters of the past, and I answer their questions about the past. I also go and ask them about matters of the past, and they also answer my questions about the past. Whatever I ask them, they also answer whatever I ask.

"'Furthermore, Udāyin, I have disciples with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, who see beings at the time of death and the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, of fine and not fine states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations, according to the deeds that these beings have performed, seeing them as they truly are. If a being has accomplished bodily bad conduct, has accomplished verbal and mental bad conduct, has slandered noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished deeds of wrong views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, that being will certainly fall to a bad destination and be born in hell. If a being has accomplished bodily good conduct, has accomplished verbal and mental good conduct, has not slandered noble ones, held right views, and accomplished deeds of right views, then because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, that being will certainly ascend to a good destination and be born in heaven. They come to ask me about matters of the future, and I answer their questions about the future. I also go and ask them about matters of the future, and they also answer my questions about the future. Whatever I ask them, they also answer whatever I ask.'

"Gautama, I cannot even recollect what I did and obtained in this present life. How could I possibly recollect, with cause and conditions, innumerable past lives and previous births? Gautama, I cannot even see a whirlwind ghost, let alone possess the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, seeing beings at the time of death and the time of birth, of good appearance and bad appearance, of fine and not fine states, going to good destinations and to bad destinations, according to the deeds that these beings have performed, and seeing them as they truly are. Gautama, I had this thought: 'If the ascetic Gautama were to ask me about the teachings I have learned from my teacher, perhaps I would be able to answer him in a way that is pleasing.'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what is the teaching you have learned from your teacher?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, he taught that there is a form that surpasses all forms; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what form is that?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, whatever form has no other form above it, that is the most supreme, the most excellent, and the most supreme of all. That form is the most supreme; that form is the highest."

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, it is like a person who says: 'The most beautiful woman in this country exists, and I desire to have her.' If someone were to ask him: 'Sir, do you know who this most beautiful woman in the country is? What is her clan, her name, her birth? Is she tall or short, stout or slender? Is she fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark? Is she a kṣatriya woman, or a brahmin, householder, or craftsman's woman? Is she from the east, south, west, or north?' That person would answer: 'I do not know.' Someone would then ask that person: 'Sir, if you do not know and have not seen the most beautiful woman in the country, her clan, her name, her birth, whether she is tall or short, stout or slender, fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark, whether she is a kṣatriya woman, brahmin, householder, or craftsman's woman, from the east, south, west, or north, then how can you say: "I desire to have that woman"?' Likewise, Udāyin, you say: 'He taught a form that surpasses all forms; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest.' When asked about that form, you do not know it."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair said: "Gautama, it is like burnished purple gold, the finest gold essence, well polished by a goldsmith, made bright and clean, placed upon white cloth and set in the sun. Its color is supremely fine, radiant and luminous. Likewise, Gautama, I say that form surpasses all forms; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest."

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Udāyin, what do you think? Take the burnished purple gold essence, placed upon white cloth and set in the sun, supremely fine in color, radiant and luminous; and the firefly in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the firefly is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the burnished purple gold essence."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what do you think? The firefly in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and an oil lamp burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the burning lamp is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the firefly."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what do you think? An oil lamp burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and a great bonfire of logs burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the great bonfire of logs is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the burning oil lamp."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what do you think? A great bonfire of logs burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and the morning star at dawn, cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the morning star is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the great bonfire of logs."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what do you think? The morning star at dawn, cloudless, radiant and luminous, and the radiance of the moon palace at midnight, cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the moon palace is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the morning star."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, what do you think? The radiance of the moon palace at midnight, cloudless, radiant and luminous, and the radiance of the sun palace in autumn, approaching midday, the sky clear and cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the sun palace is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the moon palace."

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, there are many devas. Although this sun and moon possess great supernatural powers, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great divine might, their radiance still does not equal the radiance of the devas. In the past, I once gathered together with the devas, discussed matters with them, and what I said was pleasing to those devas' minds. Yet I did not say: 'That form surpasses all forms; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest.' Udāyin, yet you, regarding the light and color of the firefly, the most inferior and most ugly, say that form surpasses all forms, that form is the most supreme, that form is the highest, and when questioned you do not know."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair said: "World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, with what intention do you say: 'World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement'?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, I said: 'That form surpasses all forms; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest.' The ascetic Gautama has now well examined me, well instructed me, well admonished me, and made my statement empty and without substance. Gautama, therefore I say: 'World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement.'" The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair then said: "Gautama, the next world is one of unalloyed pleasure. There is one path that unalloyed leads to the realization of this."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, how is the next world one of unalloyed pleasure? How is there one path that unalloyed leads to its realization?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, if someone abandons killing and refrains from killing, refrains from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, up to abandoning wrong views and attaining right views. Gautama, this is the next world of unalloyed pleasure, and this is the one path that unalloyed leads to its realization."

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Udāyin, what do you think? If someone abandons killing and refrains from killing, is that person's experience unalloyed pleasure, or is it mixed with suffering?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, it is mixed with suffering."

"If someone refrains from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, up to abandoning wrong views and attaining right views, is that person's experience unalloyed pleasure, or is it mixed with suffering?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, it is mixed with suffering."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, is it not the case that such a path mixed with suffering and pleasure leads to the realization?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, indeed such a path mixed with suffering and pleasure leads to the realization."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair said: "World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement."

The World-Honored One asked: "Udāyin, with what intention do you say: 'World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement'?"

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair replied: "Gautama, I previously said that the next world is one of unalloyed pleasure and that there is one path that unalloyed leads to its realization. The ascetic Gautama has now well examined me, well instructed me, well admonished me, and made my statement empty and without substance. Gautama, therefore I say: 'World-Honored One, I regret this statement. Well-Gone One, I regret this statement.'"

The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, there does exist a world of unalloyed pleasure, and there is one path that unalloyed leads to its realization."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair asked: "Gautama, how is there a world of unalloyed pleasure? How is there one path that unalloyed leads to its realization?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Udāyin, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, one who is unattached, perfectly and fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed, guide of those to be trained, teacher of devas and humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, he severs [the hindrances], up to the five hindrances, which are impurities of the mind and weaken wisdom. Secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He does not share the same morality, the same mind, or the same views as those devas. When initial and sustained thought have subsided, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He does not share the same morality, the same mind, or the same views as those devas. Separating from joy and desire, abiding in equanimity without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily pleasure, which the noble ones describe as dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He does not share the same morality, the same mind, or the same views as those devas. Udāyin, this is called the world of unalloyed pleasure."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair asked: "Gautama, is this the ultimate extent of unalloyed pleasure in the world?"

The World-Honored One replied: "The unalloyed pleasure in the world is not limited to just this. Udāyin, there is further one path that unalloyed leads to its realization."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair asked: "Gautama, how is there further one path that unalloyed leads to its realization?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Udāyin, a bhikṣu, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with initial thought and sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. He shares the same morality, the same mind, and the same views as those devas. When initial and sustained thought have subsided, with inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without initial thought or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna. He shares the same morality, the same mind, and the same views as those devas. Separating from joy and desire, abiding in equanimity without seeking, with right mindfulness and right knowledge, experiencing bodily pleasure, which the noble ones describe as dwelling happily with equanimity and mindfulness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna. He shares the same morality, the same mind, and the same views as those devas. Udāyin, this is called the one path that unalloyed leads to its realization."

The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair asked: "Gautama, is it for this unalloyed pleasure in the world, and for the sake of this one path that unalloyed leads to its realization, that the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Udāyin, my disciples do not practice the holy life under me for the sake of unalloyed pleasure in the world, nor for the sake of the one path that unalloyed leads to its realization. Udāyin, there is something yet more supreme, more excellent, and more superior, for the sake of realizing which my disciples practice the holy life under me."

Thereupon, that great assembly raised loud and great sounds: "That which is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most superior, for the sake of realizing it, the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama!"

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair commanded his assembly to be silent, and then said: "Gautama, what is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most superior, for the sake of realizing which the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Udāyin, when a bhikṣu, with pleasure having ceased and suffering having ceased, with joy and sorrow having previously ceased, in a state that is neither suffering nor pleasure, with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna. Udāyin, this is called the most supreme, the most excellent, the most superior, for the sake of realizing which my disciples practice the holy life under me."

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair rose from his seat, intending to bow at the Buddha's feet. At that point, the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair's own disciples, the fellow practitioners of the heterodox way, said to the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair: "Venerable one, it is now your time to be a teacher. Do you wish to become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama? It is not fitting that in your time of being a teacher you should become a disciple of the ascetic Gautama." Thus the disciples and fellow practitioners of the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair created an obstruction for the heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair, preventing him from practicing the holy life under the World-Honored One.

The Buddha spoke thus. The heterodox practitioner Arrow-Hair, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Seventh Sūtra on Arrow-Hair
