## (209) Sūtra on Vekhanassa, Eighth of the Pulita Section of the Madhyamāgama

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove at the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.

At that time, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa, in the afternoon, wandering about, went to the place of the Buddha. Having exchanged greetings, he asked: "Gautama, the supreme form! The supreme form! Gautama, the supreme form!"

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what form is that?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, whatever form has no other form above it, that is the most supreme, the most excellent, and the most superior. Gautama, that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest."

The World-Honored One said: "Kaccāna, it is like a person who says: 'The most beautiful woman in this country exists, and I desire to have her.' If someone were to ask him: 'Sir, do you know who this most beautiful woman in the country is? What is her clan, her name, her birth? Is she tall or short, stout or slender? Is she fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark? Is she a kṣatriya woman, or a brahmin, householder, or craftsman's woman? Is she from the east, south, west, or north?' That person would answer: 'I do not know.' Someone would then ask that person: 'Sir, if you do not know and have not seen the most beautiful woman in the country, her clan, her name, her birth, whether she is tall or short, stout or slender, fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark, whether she is a kṣatriya woman, brahmin, householder, or craftsman's woman, from the east, south, west, or north, then how can you say: "I desire to have that woman"?' Likewise, Kaccāna, you say: 'The supreme excellent form, the most excellent form; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest.' When asked about that form, you do not know it."

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa said: "Gautama, it is like burnished purple gold, the finest gold essence, well polished by a goldsmith, made bright and clean, placed upon white cloth and set in the sun. Its color is supremely fine, radiant and luminous. Likewise, Gautama, I say that supreme excellent form is the most excellent form; that form is the most supreme; that form is the highest."

The World-Honored One said: "Kaccāna, I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Kaccāna, what do you think? Take the burnished purple gold essence, placed upon white cloth and set in the sun, supremely fine in color, radiant and luminous; and the firefly in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the firefly is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the burnished purple gold essence."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what do you think? The firefly in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and an oil lamp burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the burning lamp is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the firefly."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what do you think? An oil lamp burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and a great bonfire of logs burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the great bonfire of logs is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the burning oil lamp."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what do you think? A great bonfire of logs burning in the darkness of night, radiant and luminous, and the morning star at dawn, cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the morning star is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the great bonfire of logs."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what do you think? The morning star at dawn, cloudless, radiant and luminous, and the radiance of the moon palace at midnight, cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the moon palace is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the morning star."

The World-Honored One asked: "Kaccāna, what do you think? The radiance of the moon palace at midnight, cloudless, radiant and luminous, and the radiance of the sun palace in autumn, approaching midday, the sky clear and cloudless, radiant and luminous. Of these two radiances, which is the most supreme and most excellent?"

The heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa replied: "Gautama, the radiance of the sun palace is more supreme and more excellent than the radiance of the moon palace."

The World-Honored One said: "Kaccāna, there are many devas. Although this sun and moon possess great supernatural powers, great majestic virtue, great blessings, and great divine might, their radiance still does not equal the radiance of the devas. In the past, I once gathered together with the devas, discussed matters with them, and what I said was pleasing to those devas' minds. Yet I did not say that the supreme excellent form is the most excellent form, that form is the most supreme, that form is the highest. Kaccāna, yet you, regarding the light and color of the firefly, the most inferior and most ugly, say that the supreme excellent form is the most excellent form, that form is the most supreme, that form is the highest, and when questioned you do not know."

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa, having been admonished face to face by the World-Honored One, internally harbored worry and distress, hung his head in silence, lost his eloquence and had no words, as if pondering something.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having admonished him face to face, further caused him to rejoice, saying: "Kaccāna, there are five qualities of sensual desire, agreeable, pleasing, delightful, associated with desire and pleasure: forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, scents known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body. Kaccāna, among forms, some are loved and some are not loved. If there is a person for whom a certain form is pleasing, satisfying, delightful, fulfilling, and wish-fulfilling, then even if another form is more supreme and more excellent, that person does not desire it, does not think about it, does not wish for it, does not seek it. For that person, this form is the most supreme and most excellent. Kaccāna, likewise for sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles. Kaccāna, among tangibles, some are loved and some are not loved. If there is a person for whom a certain tangible is pleasing, satisfying, delightful, fulfilling, and wish-fulfilling, then even if another tangible is more supreme and more excellent, that person does not desire it, does not think about it, does not wish for it, does not seek it. For that person, this tangible is the most supreme and most excellent."

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa, joining his palms toward the Buddha, said: "Gautama, how marvelous! How extraordinary! The ascetic Gautama has, through innumerable skillful means, explained for me the pleasures of desire, that desire's pleasure is foremost. Gautama, it is as though grass fire kindles a wood fire, and a wood fire kindles a grass fire. Just so, the ascetic Gautama has, through innumerable skillful means, explained for me the pleasures of desire, that desire's pleasure is foremost."

The World-Honored One said: "Enough, enough, Kaccāna! Because through the long night you have had different views, different convictions, different delights, different desires, and different intentions, you cannot fully understand the meaning of what I say. Kaccāna, my disciples, throughout the first and last parts of the night, constantly without sleeping, with right concentration and right intention, cultivate the factors of the path, until birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming, and they know it as it truly is. They fully understand what I say."

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa became angry toward the Buddha, giving rise to resentment and displeasure, wishing to slander the World-Honored One, wishing to diminish the World-Honored One. Slandering the World-Honored One thus, diminishing the World-Honored One thus, he said: "Gautama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past beginning of the world, do not know the future end of the world, do not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet they claim to have attained ultimate knowledge: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming,' and they know it as it truly is. Gautama, I think thus: 'How can these ascetics and brahmins, not knowing the past beginning of the world, not knowing the future end of the world, not knowing the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming," and know it as it truly is?'"

Thereupon, the World-Honored One had this thought: "This heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa is angry toward me, giving rise to resentment and displeasure, wishing to slander me, wishing to diminish me. Slandering me thus, diminishing me thus, he says to me: 'Gautama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past beginning of the world, do not know the future end of the world, do not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet they claim to have attained ultimate knowledge: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming," and they know it as it truly is.' Gautama says: 'I think thus: "How can these ascetics and brahmins, not knowing the past beginning of the world, not knowing the future end of the world, not knowing the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming,' and know it as it truly is?"'"

The World-Honored One, having understood this, said: "Kaccāna, if there are ascetics and brahmins who do not know the past beginning of the world, do not know the future end of the world, do not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there is no further becoming,' and they know it as it truly is, then they should speak thus: 'Set aside the past beginning of the world; set aside the future end of the world.' Kaccāna, I speak thus: 'Set aside the past beginning of the world; set aside the future end of the world.' Even if one cannot recollect a single past life, when my disciple bhikṣu comes, not deceitful, not fraudulent, sincere and straightforward, I instruct him. If he follows my instruction and practices accordingly, he will certainly come to know the true Dharma. Kaccāna, it is like an infant child, young and tender, lying on its back, whose hands and feet are bound by its parents. Later, when it has grown and its faculties are mature, the parents unbind its hands and feet. It only remembers the time of being unbound, not the time of being bound. Likewise, Kaccāna, I speak thus: 'Set aside the past beginning of the world; set aside the future end of the world.' Even if one cannot recollect a single past life, when my disciple bhikṣu comes, not deceitful, not fraudulent, sincere and straightforward, I instruct him. If he follows my instruction and practices accordingly, he will certainly come to know the true Dharma. Kaccāna, it is like a lamp that burns because of oil and a wick. If no one adds oil, nor replaces the wick, when the original oil is exhausted and no more is added, having nothing more to sustain it, it quickly goes out of itself. Likewise, Kaccāna, I speak thus: 'Set aside the past beginning of the world; set aside the future end of the world.' Even if one cannot recollect a single past life, when my disciple bhikṣu comes, not deceitful, not fraudulent, sincere and straightforward, I instruct him. If he follows my instruction and practices accordingly, he will certainly come to know the true Dharma. Kaccāna, it is like ten heaps of wood, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty heaps of wood, set ablaze and burning intensely; one can see the flames. But afterward, if no one adds more grass, wood, chaff, or refuse, when the original fuel is exhausted and no more is added, having nothing more to sustain it, it quickly goes out of itself. Likewise, Kaccāna, I speak thus: 'Set aside the past beginning of the world; set aside the future end of the world.' Even if one cannot recollect a single past life, when my disciple bhikṣu comes, not deceitful, not fraudulent, sincere and straightforward, I instruct him. If he follows my instruction and practices accordingly, he will certainly come to know the true Dharma."

When this Dharma was spoken, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa became free from dust, free from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all dharmas arose. Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Vekhanassa, having seen the Dharma, obtained the Dharma, realized the pure white Dharma, having no other refuge, no longer relying on others, having cut through doubt and crossed beyond perplexity, without any hesitation, having attained the fruit and realization, having attained fearlessness in the World-Honored One's Dharma, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet and said: "World-Honored One, I wish to go forth from the Buddha, to study the Way, to receive the full precepts, to become a bhikṣu, and to practice the holy life."

The World-Honored One said: "Excellent! Bhikṣu, practice the holy life."

The heterodox practitioner went forth from the Buddha, studied the Way, and immediately received the full precepts, becoming a bhikṣu, and practiced the holy life. The Venerable Vekhanassa, having gone forth and studied the Way, having received the full precepts, knew the Dharma and saw the Dharma, and ultimately attained the state of an arhat.

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Vekhanassa and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Eighth Sūtra on Vekhanassa

# Fascicle 58 of the Madhyamāgama

## (210) Sūtra on the Bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, the Ninth in the Pūlita Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Śrāvatī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the laywoman Viśākhā went to visit the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, bowed her head at her feet, sat to one side, and addressed the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, saying: "Noble One, I wish to ask some questions. Will you permit me to ask?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied: "Viśākhā, if you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider."

The laywoman Viśākhā then asked: "Noble One, 'self' is spoken of, and 'self' is said. What is this 'self'?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The World-Honored One has spoken of the five aggregates of clinging as the self. The form aggregate of clinging, and the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness aggregates of clinging: these are what the World-Honored One has spoken of as the five aggregates of clinging."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the view of self?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "An unlearned, ignorant ordinary person who does not see good teachers, who does not know the noble Dharma, who does not practice the noble Dharma, regards form as the self, regards the self as possessing form, regards form as being within the self, or regards the self as being within form. He regards feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the self, regards the self as possessing consciousness, regards consciousness as being within the self, or regards the self as being within consciousness. This is called the view of self."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the absence of the view of self?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "A well-learned noble disciple who sees good teachers, who knows the noble Dharma, who skillfully practices the noble Dharma, does not regard form as the self, does not regard the self as possessing form, does not regard form as being within the self, and does not regard the self as being within form. He does not regard feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as the self, does not regard the self as possessing consciousness, does not regard consciousness as being within the self, and does not regard the self as being within consciousness. This is called the absence of the view of self."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the cessation of the self?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When the form aggregate of clinging is cut off without remainder, abandoned, relinquished, exhausted, undefiled, extinguished, stilled, and disappeared; when the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness aggregates of clinging are cut off without remainder, abandoned, relinquished, exhausted, undefiled, extinguished, stilled, and disappeared: this is called the cessation of the self."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, 'aggregates' are spoken of, and 'aggregates of clinging' are spoken of. Are the aggregates identical to the aggregates of clinging, and the aggregates of clinging identical to the aggregates? Or are the aggregates one thing and the aggregates of clinging another?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "In some cases, the aggregates are the aggregates of clinging; in some cases, the aggregates are not the aggregates of clinging. How are the aggregates the aggregates of clinging? If form has outflows and is subject to clinging, and if feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have outflows and are subject to clinging, this is called the aggregates being the aggregates of clinging. How are the aggregates not the aggregates of clinging? If form is without outflows and not subject to clinging, and if feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without outflows and not subject to clinging, this is called the aggregates not being the aggregates of clinging."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the noble eightfold path?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The noble eightfold path is right view up to right concentration. These are called eight; this is called the noble eightfold path."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, is the noble eightfold path conditioned?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "Yes, the noble eightfold path is conditioned."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, how many categories are there?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "There are three categories: the category of morality, the category of concentration, and the category of wisdom."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, does the noble eightfold path subsume the three categories, or do the three categories subsume the noble eightfold path?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "It is not that the noble eightfold path subsumes the three categories; rather, the three categories subsume the noble eightfold path. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood: these three path factors are subsumed by the noble category of morality. Right mindfulness and right concentration: these two path factors are subsumed by the noble category of concentration. Right view, right intention, and right effort: these three path factors are subsumed by the noble category of wisdom. Thus it is not that the noble eightfold path subsumes the three categories; rather, the three categories subsume the noble eightfold path."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, does cessation have a counterpart?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "Cessation has no counterpart."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, how many factors does the first jhāna have?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The first jhāna has five factors: initial thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind. These are the five factors of the first jhāna."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is concentration? What is the sign of concentration? What is the power of concentration? What is the accomplishment of concentration? What is the cultivation of concentration?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When the wholesome mind attains one-pointedness, this is called concentration. The four foundations of mindfulness are called the sign of concentration. The four right efforts are called the power of concentration. The four bases of spiritual power are called the accomplishment of concentration. Repeatedly practicing and training in these wholesome dharmas, with constant, devoted, and diligent cultivation: this is called the cultivation of concentration."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, how many things are there such that, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "There are three things such that, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood. What are the three? First, life; second, warmth; third, consciousness. These are the three things such that, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the difference between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "For the dead, the life-span has expired, warmth has departed, and the sense faculties have decayed. For a bhikṣu who has entered the attainment of cessation, the life-span has not expired, warmth has not departed, and the sense faculties have not decayed. Between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the difference between entering the attainment of cessation and entering the attainment of non-perception?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "For a bhikṣu who has entered the attainment of cessation, perception and awareness cease. For one who has entered the attainment of non-perception, perception and awareness do not cease. Between entering the attainment of cessation and entering the attainment of non-perception, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the difference between emerging from the attainment of cessation and emerging from the attainment of non-perception?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, he does not have the thought: 'I am emerging from the attainment of cessation.' When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of non-perception, he has the thought: 'Did I have perception? Did I not have perception?' Between emerging from the attainment of cessation and emerging from the attainment of non-perception, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, when a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, does he have the thought: 'I am entering the attainment of cessation'?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, he does not have the thought: 'I am entering the attainment of cessation.' Rather, because he has previously cultivated his mind in this way, he therefore inclines toward it."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, when a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, does he have the thought: 'I am emerging from the attainment of cessation'?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, he does not have the thought: 'I am emerging from the attainment of cessation.' Rather, it is because of this body and the six sense bases conditioned by the life faculty that he emerges from the attainment."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, when a bhikṣu has emerged from the attainment of cessation, what does his mind delight in, what does it tend toward, what does it incline toward?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When a bhikṣu has emerged from the attainment of cessation, his mind delights in seclusion, tends toward seclusion, and inclines toward seclusion."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, how many kinds of feelings are there?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "There are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. What is the condition for their arising? They arise conditioned by contact."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is pleasant feeling? What is painful feeling? What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "When contact that is pleasant arises, giving rise to bodily and mental pleasant and wholesome feeling, that feeling is called pleasant feeling. When contact that is painful arises, giving rise to bodily and mental painful and unwholesome feeling, that feeling is called painful feeling. When contact that is neither painful nor pleasant arises, giving rise to bodily and mental feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, that feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, regarding pleasant feeling, what is its pleasure, what is its pain, what is its impermanence, what is its danger, and what is its underlying tendency? Regarding painful feeling, what is its pleasure, what is its pain, what is its impermanence, what is its danger, and what is its underlying tendency? Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, what is its pleasure, what is its pain, what is its impermanence, what is its danger, and what is its underlying tendency?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "Pleasant feeling: arising is pleasure, abiding is pleasure, but its alteration is pain. Its impermanence is itself its danger. Its underlying tendency is the tendency toward desire. Painful feeling: arising is pain, abiding is pain, but its alteration is pleasure. Its impermanence is itself its danger. Its underlying tendency is the tendency toward aversion. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling: not knowing pain and not knowing pleasure. Its impermanence is itself its alteration. Its underlying tendency is the tendency toward ignorance."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, does all pleasant feeling have the underlying tendency toward desire? Does all painful feeling have the underlying tendency toward aversion? Does all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling have the underlying tendency toward ignorance?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "Not all pleasant feeling has the underlying tendency toward desire. Not all painful feeling has the underlying tendency toward aversion. Not all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has the underlying tendency toward ignorance. How is there pleasant feeling without the underlying tendency toward desire? When a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, with initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first jhāna: this is called pleasant feeling without the underlying tendency toward desire. Why? Because this has abandoned desire. How is there painful feeling without the underlying tendency toward aversion? When one, seeking the higher liberation and bliss, yearning and longing, gives rise to sorrow and suffering: this is called painful feeling without the underlying tendency toward aversion. Why? Because this has abandoned aversion. How is there neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without the underlying tendency toward ignorance? When pleasure has ceased and pain has ceased, and when joy and sorrow have already been extinguished, with neither pain nor pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, one attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna: this is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling without the underlying tendency toward ignorance. Why? Because this has abandoned ignorance."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of pleasant feeling?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of pleasant feeling is painful feeling."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of painful feeling?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of painful feeling is pleasant feeling."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of pleasant feeling and painful feeling?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of pleasant feeling and painful feeling is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is ignorance."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of ignorance?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of ignorance is knowledge."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of knowledge?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā answered: "The counterpart of knowledge is nirvāṇa."

Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Noble One!" Having praised her, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully accepted the teaching.

She further asked: "Noble One, what is the counterpart of nirvāṇa?"

The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā said: "You wish to ask questions without end, yet your questioning cannot reach my limit. Nirvāṇa has no counterpart. Nirvāṇa has gone beyond the snare and is without snare; the snares have been utterly extinguished. It is for this purpose that one practices the holy life under the World-Honored One."

Thereupon, the laywoman Viśākhā, having heard what the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā said, well received it, well retained it, and well studied it. She then rose from her seat, bowed her head at the feet of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, circumambulated her three times, and departed.

Then the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, seeing that the laywoman Viśākhā had departed not long before, went to visit the Buddha, bowed her head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported to the Buddha the entirety of what she and the laywoman Viśākhā had discussed. With palms joined toward the Buddha, she said: "World-Honored One, in speaking thus and answering thus, have I misrepresented the World-Honored One? Did I speak what is true, speak what accords with the Dharma, speak in conformity with the Dharma? Within the Dharma, is there anything contradictory, contentious, or blameworthy?"

The World-Honored One answered: "Bhikṣuṇī, in speaking thus and answering thus, you have not misrepresented me. You have spoken what is true, spoken what accords with the Dharma, spoken in conformity with the Dharma. Within the Dharma, there is nothing contradictory, no contention, and no fault. Bhikṣuṇī, if the laywoman Viśākhā had come to me with these very phrases and these very words to ask me, I would have answered the laywoman Viśākhā with this very meaning, these very phrases, and these very words. Bhikṣuṇī, this meaning is as you have spoken it. You should uphold it thus. Why? Because this explanation is indeed the meaning."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, joyfully accepted and practiced it.

End of the ninth, the Sūtra on the Bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā.

---

## (211) The Sūtra on Mahākoṣṭhila, the Tenth in the Pūlita Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, in the afternoon, rose from his meditation and went to visit the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila. They exchanged greetings, and he sat to one side.

The Venerable Śāriputra said: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider."

The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, 'unwholesome' is spoken of as unwholesome, and 'unwholesome roots' are spoken of as unwholesome roots. What is unwholesome? What are the unwholesome roots?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct: these are unwholesome. Greed, aversion, and delusion: these are the unwholesome roots. These are what is called unwholesome, and these are what are called the unwholesome roots."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, 'wholesome' is spoken of as wholesome, and 'wholesome roots' are spoken of as wholesome roots. What is wholesome? What are the wholesome roots?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct: these are wholesome. Non-greed, non-aversion, and non-delusion: these are the wholesome roots. These are what is called wholesome, and these are what are called the wholesome roots."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, 'wisdom' is spoken of as wisdom. What is wisdom?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Because one knows, it is called wisdom. What does one know? One knows 'This is suffering' as it truly is; one knows 'This is the origin of suffering,' 'This is the cessation of suffering,' 'This is the path to the cessation of suffering' as it truly is. Because one knows in this way, it is called wisdom."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, 'consciousness' is spoken of as consciousness. What is consciousness?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Consciousness cognizes, therefore it is called consciousness. What does it cognize? It cognizes form; it cognizes sounds, odors, tastes, tactile objects, and mental objects. Consciousness cognizes, therefore it is called consciousness."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, wisdom and consciousness: are these two dharmas conjoined or separate? Can these two dharmas be separately designated?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "These two dharmas are conjoined and not separate; these two dharmas cannot be separately designated. Why? What wisdom knows is what consciousness cognizes. Therefore these two dharmas are conjoined and not separate, and these two dharmas cannot be separately designated."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, as for knowing, by what do you know?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "As for knowing, I know by means of wisdom."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what is the purpose of wisdom, what is its excellence, and what is its benefit?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Wisdom has the purpose of disenchantment, the purpose of dispassion, and the purpose of seeing as it truly is."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what is right view?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Knowing suffering as it truly is, knowing the origin, cessation, and path of suffering as it truly is: this is called right view."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions give rise to right view?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are two causes and two conditions that give rise to right view. What are the two? First, hearing from others; second, inner reflection. These are the two causes and two conditions that give rise to right view."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many factors support right view to attain the fruit of liberation of mind and the fruit of liberation by wisdom, to attain the benefit of liberation of mind and the benefit of liberation by wisdom?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are five factors that support right view to attain the fruit of liberation of mind and the fruit of liberation by wisdom, and to attain the benefit of liberation of mind and the benefit of liberation by wisdom. What are the five? First, being supported by truth; second, being supported by morality; third, being supported by learning; fourth, being supported by calm; fifth, being supported by insight. These are the five factors that support right view to attain the fruit of liberation of mind and the fruit of liberation by wisdom, and to attain the benefit of liberation of mind and the benefit of liberation by wisdom."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how does future existence come to be generated?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Ignorant ordinary people, without knowledge, without learning, covered by ignorance, bound by the fetter of craving, who do not see good teachers, who do not know the noble Dharma, who do not practice the noble Dharma: this is how future existence comes to be generated."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how does one not generate future existence?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "When ignorance has been exhausted and knowledge has arisen, one will certainly reach the end of suffering. This is how one does not generate future existence."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many kinds of feelings are there?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. What is the condition for their arising? They arise conditioned by contact."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, feeling, perception, and volition: are these three dharmas conjoined or separate? Can these three dharmas be separately designated?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Feeling, perception, and volition: these three dharmas are conjoined and not separate; these three dharmas cannot be separately designated. Why? What feeling feels is what perception perceives and what volition intends. Therefore these three dharmas are conjoined and not separate, and these three dharmas cannot be separately designated."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, does cessation have a counterpart?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Cessation has no counterpart."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, there are five faculties with different functions and different domains, each receiving its own domain: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty. These five faculties have different functions and different domains, each receiving its own domain. Who is it that receives all their domains, and who serves as their support?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "The five faculties have different functions and different domains, each receiving its own domain: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, and body faculty. These five faculties have different functions and different domains, each receiving its own domain. The mind receives all their domains, and the mind serves as their support."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what does the mind depend on and abide in?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "The mind depends on life; it depends on life and abides."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what does life depend on and abide in?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Life depends on warmth; it depends on warmth and abides."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, life and warmth: are these two dharmas conjoined or separate? Can these two dharmas be separately designated?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Life and warmth: these two dharmas are conjoined and not separate; these two dharmas cannot be separately designated. Why? Because of life there is warmth, and because of warmth there is life. Without life there is no warmth, and without warmth there is no life. Just as because of oil and a wick one can light a lamp, and within that lamp, because of the flame there is light, and because of light there is the flame; without the flame there is no light, and without light there is no flame. In the same way, because of life there is warmth, and because of warmth there is life; without life there is no warmth, and without warmth there is no life. Therefore these two dharmas are conjoined and not separate, and these two dharmas cannot be separately designated."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many things are there such that, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are three things such that, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood. What are the three? First, life; second, warmth; third, consciousness. These three things, when they leave the body, after death the body is cast aside in the charnel ground like a senseless piece of wood."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what is the difference between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "For the dead, the life-span has expired, warmth has departed, and the sense faculties have decayed. For a bhikṣu who has entered the attainment of cessation, the life-span has not expired, warmth has not departed, and the sense faculties have not decayed. Between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what is the difference between entering the attainment of cessation and entering the attainment of non-perception?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "For a bhikṣu who has entered the attainment of cessation, perception and awareness cease. For a bhikṣu who has entered the attainment of non-perception, perception and awareness do not cease. Between entering the attainment of cessation and entering the attainment of non-perception, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, what is the difference between emerging from the attainment of cessation and emerging from the attainment of non-perception?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, he does not have the thought: 'I am emerging from the attainment of cessation.' When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of non-perception, he has the thought: 'Did I have perception? Did I not have perception?' Between emerging from the attainment of cessation and emerging from the attainment of non-perception, this is the difference."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, when a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, which dharma ceases first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "When a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, the bodily formation ceases first, the verbal formation ceases next, and the mental formation ceases last."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, when a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, which dharma arises first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, the mental formation arises first, the verbal formation arises next, and the bodily formation arises last."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, when a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, how many contacts does he experience?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, he experiences three contacts. What are the three? First, the contact of imperturbability; second, the contact of nothingness; third, the contact of signlessness. When a bhikṣu emerges from the attainment of cessation, he experiences these three contacts."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness: do these three dharmas have different meanings and different terms, or one meaning with different terms?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness: these three dharmas have different meanings and different terms."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions give rise to the attainment of imperturbability?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are four causes and four conditions that give rise to the attainment of imperturbability. What are the four? When a bhikṣu, secluded from desires, secluded from unwholesome dharmas, up to attaining the fourth jhāna and dwelling therein: these are the four causes and four conditions that give rise to the attainment of imperturbability."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions give rise to the attainment of nothingness?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are three causes and three conditions that give rise to the attainment of nothingness. What are the three? When a bhikṣu, having completely transcended the perception of form, up to attaining the sphere of nothingness and dwelling therein: these are the three causes and three conditions that give rise to the attainment of nothingness."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions give rise to the attainment of signlessness?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are two causes and two conditions that give rise to the attainment of signlessness. What are the two? First, not attending to any signs; second, attending to the signless realm. These are the two causes and two conditions that give rise to the attainment of signlessness."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions are there for abiding in the attainment of signlessness?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are two causes and two conditions for abiding in the attainment of signlessness. What are the two? First, not attending to any signs; second, attending to the signless realm. These are the two causes and two conditions for abiding in the attainment of signlessness."

Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Venerable Koṣṭhila!" Having praised him, the Venerable Śāriputra joyfully accepted the teaching.

He further asked: "Venerable Koṣṭhila, how many causes and conditions are there for emerging from the attainment of signlessness?"

The Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila answered: "There are three causes and three conditions for emerging from the attainment of signlessness. What are the three? First, attending to all signs; second, not attending to the signless realm; third, because of this body, because of the six sense bases conditioned by the life faculty. These are the three causes and three conditions for emerging from the attainment of signlessness."

Thus, these two venerable ones praised each other, saying "Excellent! Excellent!" and joyfully accepted what each had said. They then rose from their seats and departed.

End of the tenth, the Sūtra on Mahākoṣṭhila.
