## (212) Sūtra on Omniscience, the First in the Chapter of Illustrations

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Udumbara, staying in the Universal Thorn Forest.

At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala heard that the ascetic Gotama was travelling in Udumbara, staying in the Universal Thorn Forest. Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala told a man: "Go to the ascetic Gotama's place and on my behalf inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual. Speak thus: 'King Pasenadi of Kosala inquires whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual.' Also say: 'King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come for an audience.'"

That man received the instruction, went to the Buddha's place, exchanged greetings, sat to one side, and said: "Gotama, King Pasenadi of Kosala inquires whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual. King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come for an audience."

The World-Honored One replied: "May King Pasenadi of Kosala now be safe and happy. May gods and humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings be safe and happy. If King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come, he may do so at his convenience." At that time, the messenger, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, rose from his seat, circumambulated three times, and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and attending the Buddha. After the messenger had left, the World-Honored One turned around and said: "Ānanda, come with me to the great east-facing hall. We shall open the windows and close the doors and stay in that private place. Today King Pasenadi of Kosala, with single-minded concentration, wishes to hear and receive the Dharma."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "So be it."

Thereupon the World-Honored One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to that great east-facing hall, opened the windows and closed the doors, arranged a seat in that private place, spread out the sitting cloth, and sat cross-legged.

At that time, the messenger returned to King Pasenadi of Kosala's place and reported: "Your Majesty, I have already conveyed the message to the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama now awaits Your Majesty. May Your Majesty decide when the time is right."

King Pasenadi of Kosala told his charioteer: "You may prepare the carriage. I now wish to go see the ascetic Gotama." The charioteer received the instruction and immediately prepared the carriage.

At that time, the sisters Somā and Sakulā were dining together with King Pasenadi of Kosala, and they heard that today King Pasenadi of Kosala would go to see the Buddha. They said: "Great King, if you are now going to see the World-Honored One, please on our behalf bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual. Speak thus: 'The sisters Somā and Sakulā bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual.'" King Pasenadi of Kosala silently accepted on behalf of the sisters Somā and Sakulā.

At that time, the charioteer, having finished preparing the carriage, reported: "Your Majesty, the carriage is prepared, at Your Majesty's pleasure."

When the King heard this, he mounted the carriage, departed from Udumbara, and went to the Universal Thorn Forest.

At that time, outside the gate of the Universal Thorn Forest, many bhikṣus were walking in meditation in the open. King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the bhikṣus and asked: "Venerables, where is the ascetic Gotama now? I wish to go see him."

The bhikṣus replied: "Great King, that great east-facing hall with windows open and doors closed: the World-Honored One is inside. If the Great King wishes to see him, you may go to that hall, stand outside, clear your throat and knock on the door. If the World-Honored One hears, he will surely open the door."

King Pasenadi of Kosala then dismounted from his carriage. Surrounded by his retinue, he walked to that great east-facing hall. Having arrived and standing outside, he cleared his throat and knocked on the door. The World-Honored One heard and opened the door. King Pasenadi of Kosala entered the hall, approached the Buddha, and said: "Gotama, the sisters Somā and Sakulā bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual."

The World-Honored One asked the King: "Did the sisters Somā and Sakulā have no other messenger?"

King Pasenadi of Kosala replied: "Gotama, you should know that today the sisters Somā and Sakulā were dining together with me. They heard that I was going to see the Buddha, and they said: 'Great King, if you go to see the Buddha, please on our behalf bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual.' Therefore I say to the World-Honored One: 'The sisters Somā and Sakulā bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual.' Gotama, Somā and Sakulā bow at the World-Honored One's feet and inquire whether the Holy One's body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, moving about with lightness and ease, with strength as usual."

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, may the sisters Somā and Sakulā now be safe and happy. May gods and humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings be safe and happy."

Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala exchanged greetings with the Buddha, sat to one side, and said: "Gotama, I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to speak?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala then asked: "Gotama, I have heard that the ascetic Gotama speaks thus: 'There has never been, there will never be, and there does not now exist any other ascetic or brahmin who is omniscient and all-seeing.' Gotama, do you recall saying this?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, I do not recall saying this: 'There has never been, there will never be, and there does not now exist any other ascetic or brahmin who is omniscient and all-seeing.'"

At that time, General Viḍūḍabha was standing behind King Pasenadi of Kosala, holding a fan and fanning the King. Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala turned around and asked General Viḍūḍabha: "The other day when the King was sitting with a great assembly, who first said that the ascetic Gotama speaks thus: 'There has never been, there will never be, and there does not now exist any other ascetic or brahmin who is omniscient and all-seeing'?"

General Viḍūḍabha replied: "Your Majesty, it was the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika who first said this."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala told a man: "Go to the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika's place and speak thus: 'King Pasenadi of Kosala summons you.'"

That man received the instruction and went to the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika's place, speaking thus: "Young man, King Pasenadi of Kosala summons you."

After that man had departed, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the World-Honored One: "Ascetic Gotama, was there perhaps a different statement differently received? Does the ascetic Gotama recall what he said?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, I recall having said thus: 'There has never been, there will never be, and there does not now exist any other ascetic or brahmin who can know everything at one time and see everything at one time.' Great King, I recall having said this."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What the ascetic Gotama says is as a teacher; what the ascetic Gotama says is as a good teacher. I wish to ask something further. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, there are these four classes: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans. Is there superiority and inferiority among them? Is there any distinction?"

The World-Honored One replied: "There are these four classes: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans. There is superiority and inferiority among them; there is distinction. The kṣatriya and brahmin classes are the most highly esteemed among human beings. The householder and artisan classes are of lower esteem among human beings. These four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, this is their superiority and inferiority, this is their distinction."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What the ascetic Gotama says is as a teacher; what the ascetic Gotama says is as a good teacher."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Gotama, I do not only ask about matters of this present life; I also wish to ask about matters of the next life. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, there are these four classes: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans. Is there superiority and inferiority among them, is there distinction regarding the next life?"

The World-Honored One replied: "There are these four classes: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans. There is superiority and inferiority among them; there is distinction regarding the next life. Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, if one accomplishes these five factors of severance, one will certainly gain the good teacher, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One. One will certainly attain what is agreeable, nothing disagreeable, and for a long time obtain benefit, safety, and happiness. What are the five?

"A well-learned noble disciple has faith rooted in the Tathāgata, established and firm, which none can take away, whether ascetics, brahmins, gods, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. This is called the first factor of severance.

"Furthermore, Great King, a well-learned noble disciple has few illnesses, possessing the way of balanced eating, neither too hot nor too cold, rightly happy and without conflict; that is, food and drink are properly digested, safely and peacefully. This is called the second factor of severance.

"Furthermore, Great King, a well-learned noble disciple is without deceit and without guile, straightforward, revealing himself as he truly is to the World-Honored One and to fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is called the third factor of severance.

"Furthermore, Great King, a well-learned noble disciple constantly practices diligence, abandoning what is evil and unwholesome, cultivating all wholesome dharmas, constantly arousing his mind, being concentrated and firm, establishing the roots of wholesomeness, not abandoning skillful means. This is called the fourth factor of severance.

"Furthermore, Great King, a well-learned noble disciple cultivates wisdom, contemplating the dharma of arising and ceasing, attaining such knowledge, noble wisdom, bright understanding, discriminating and fully comprehending, rightly putting an end to suffering. This is called the fifth factor of severance.

"Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, if one accomplishes these five factors of severance, one will certainly gain the good teacher, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One. One will certainly attain what is agreeable, nothing disagreeable, and for a long time obtain benefit, safety, and happiness. Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, this is their superiority and inferiority, this is their distinction regarding the next life."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What the ascetic Gotama says is as a teacher; what the ascetic Gotama says is as a good teacher. I wish to ask something further. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, is there superiority and inferiority, is there distinction regarding the practice of severance?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, there is superiority and inferiority, there is distinction regarding the practice of severance. Great King, what do you think? What is severed by one with faith, can one without faith sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one with few illnesses, can one with many illnesses sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one without deceit and guile, can one with deceit and guile sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one who is diligent, can one who is lazy sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one with wisdom, can one with bad wisdom sever that? That is impossible.

"It is like four drivers: an elephant driver, a horse driver, an ox driver, and a people driver. Among them, two are untrained and uncontrollable, and two are trained and controllable. Great King, what do you think? Those two who are untrained and uncontrollable, could they come to the ground of training and the ground of control and undertake the task of driving? That is impossible. Those two who are trained and controllable, could they come to the ground of training and the ground of control and undertake the task of driving? That is certainly possible.

"In the same way, Great King, what do you think? What is severed by one with faith, can one without faith sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one with few illnesses, can one with many illnesses sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one without deceit and guile, can one with deceit and guile sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one who is diligent, can one who is lazy sever that? That is impossible. What is severed by one with wisdom, can one with bad wisdom sever that? That is impossible. Thus, among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, this is their superiority and inferiority, this is their distinction regarding the practice of severance."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What the ascetic Gotama says is as a teacher; what the ascetic Gotama says is as a good teacher. I wish to ask something further. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, is there superiority and inferiority, is there distinction regarding severance itself?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, their severance is equal; there is no superiority or inferiority, no distinction regarding severance itself.

"Great King, suppose a kṣatriya youth comes from the east, takes dry sāla wood as a fire-stick, drills and produces fire. A brahmin youth comes from the south, takes dry sāla wood as a fire-stick, drills and produces fire. A householder youth comes from the west, takes dry sandalwood as a fire-stick, drills and produces fire. An artisan youth comes from the north, takes dry pālāśa wood as a fire-stick, drills and produces fire. Great King, what do you think? Those various persons taking various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drilling and producing fire, and among them someone adding dry grass and wood, producing smoke, producing flame, producing radiance. Great King, regarding their smoke and smoke, flame and flame, radiance and radiance, would you say there is any distinction?"

King Pasenadi of Kosala replied: "Gotama, those various persons taking various kinds of wood as fire-sticks, drilling and producing fire, and among them someone adding dry grass and wood, producing smoke, producing flame, producing radiance. Gotama, I would not say there is any distinction between their smoke and smoke, flame and flame, radiance and radiance."

"Just so, Great King. Among these four classes, kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans, all their severance is equal; there is no superiority or inferiority, no distinction regarding severance itself."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What the ascetic Gotama says is as a teacher; what the ascetic Gotama says is as a good teacher. I wish to ask something further. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, are there gods?"

The World-Honored One asked: "Great King, why do you ask whether there are gods?"

King Pasenadi of Kosala replied: "Gotama, if there are gods who have conflict and delight in conflict, they should come to this world. If there are gods who are without conflict and do not delight in conflict, they should not come to this world."

At that time, General Viḍūḍabha was standing behind King Pasenadi of Kosala, holding a fan and fanning the King. General Viḍūḍabha said: "Gotama, if there are gods without conflict who do not delight in conflict and who do not come to this world, let us set those gods aside. If there are gods with conflict who delight in conflict and who come to this world, the ascetic Gotama would certainly say that those gods are superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, and that the gods of this world could overpower and expel those gods."

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and attending the Buddha. Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda thought: "This General Viḍūḍabha is the son of King Pasenadi of Kosala, and I am the son of the World-Honored One. Now is the right time for son and son to discuss together."

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda said to General Viḍūḍabha: "I wish to ask you something; answer as you understand. General, what do you think? Within all the territories of King Pasenadi of Kosala, wherever his command reaches, because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, can he at will overpower and expel people?"

General Viḍūḍabha replied: "Ascetic, within all the territories of King Pasenadi of Kosala, wherever his command reaches, because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, he can at will overpower and expel people."

"General, what do you think? In territories that are not King Pasenadi of Kosala's, where his command does not reach, because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, can he at will overpower and expel those people?"

General Viḍūḍabha replied: "Ascetic, in territories that are not King Pasenadi of Kosala's, where his command does not reach, even though King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, he cannot at will overpower and expel those people."

The Venerable Ānanda further asked: "General, have you heard of the Thirty-three Gods?"

General Viḍūḍabha replied: "When I was at leisure with King Pasenadi of Kosala, I heard there are Thirty-three Gods."

"General, what do you think? Because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy conduct, can he at will overpower and expel those Thirty-three Gods?"

General Viḍūḍabha replied: "Ascetic, King Pasenadi of Kosala cannot even see the Thirty-three Gods, let alone overpower and expel them! To overpower and expel those Thirty-three Gods is impossible."

"Just so, General. If there are gods without conflict who do not delight in conflict and who do not come to this world, these gods are superior in merit and superior in holy conduct. If there are gods of this world with conflict who delight in conflict and come to this world, these gods of this world cannot even see those gods, let alone overpower and expel them. To overpower and expel those gods is impossible."

Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, what is this ascetic's name?"

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, this bhikṣu is named Ānanda; he is my attendant."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "What Ānanda says is as a teacher; what Ānanda says is as a good teacher. I wish to ask something further. Will you permit me to ask?"

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, if you wish to ask, ask whatever you please."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama, is there Brahmā?"

The World-Honored One asked: "Great King, why do you ask whether there is Brahmā? Great King, if I establish that there is Brahmā, that Brahmā is pure."

While the World-Honored One and King Pasenadi of Kosala were discussing this matter between them, the messenger brought the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika back and came to King Pasenadi of Kosala's place, saying: "Your Majesty, the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika has arrived and is here."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala asked the young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika: "The other day when the King was sitting with a great assembly, who first said that the ascetic Gotama speaks thus: 'There has never been, there will never be, and there does not now exist any other ascetic or brahmin who is omniscient and all-seeing'?"

The young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika replied: "Your Majesty, it was General Viḍūḍabha who first said it."

Having heard this, General Viḍūḍabha said: "Your Majesty, it was this young man Saṅkha Maṅgalika who first said it."

Thus those two argued back and forth about this matter. In the meanwhile, the charioteer then prepared the carriage and came to King Pasenadi of Kosala's place, saying: "Your Majesty, the carriage has arrived. May Your Majesty decide when the time is right."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the World-Honored One: "I asked Gotama about omniscience, and the ascetic Gotama answered me about omniscience. I asked the ascetic Gotama about the four classes and their purity, and the ascetic Gotama answered me about the four classes and their purity. I asked the ascetic Gotama about what is attained, and the ascetic Gotama answered me about what is attained. I asked the ascetic Gotama about Brahmā, and the ascetic Gotama answered me about Brahmā. If I were to ask about other matters, the ascetic Gotama would certainly answer me about other matters. Gotama, I now have many affairs and wish to return. I ask permission to depart."

The World-Honored One replied: "Great King, you may go when you deem it time."

King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard what the World-Honored One said, received and retained it well, rose from his seat, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, and departed.

The Buddha spoke thus. King Pasenadi of Kosala, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on Omniscience, the First.

---

## (213) Sūtra on the Dhamma-Ornament, the Second in the Chapter of Illustrations

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling among the Sakyans, in the Sakyan capital city named Medāḷumpa.

At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, together with the minister Dīgha Kārāyana, had gone out on some business to a town called Nagaraka. King Pasenadi of Kosala arrived at a park there and saw beneath the trees a place that was quiet and soundless, remote, free from evil, without people, suitable for secluded sitting. Seeing this, he was reminded of the World-Honored One. King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Dīgha Kārāyana, these trees here are quiet and soundless, remote, free from evil, without people, suitable for secluded sitting. It is in places like this that I have often gone to see the Buddha. Dīgha Kārāyana, where is the World-Honored One now? I wish to go see him."

Dīgha Kārāyana replied: "Your Majesty, I have heard that the World-Honored One is travelling among the Sakyans, in the Sakyan capital city named Medāḷumpa."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked further: "Dīgha Kārāyana, how far is the Sakyan capital city of Medāḷumpa from here?"

Dīgha Kārāyana replied: "Your Majesty, it is three krośas from here."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Dīgha Kārāyana, order the carriage to be prepared. I wish to go to the Buddha."

Dīgha Kārāyana received the instruction and ordered the carriage prepared, then reported: "Your Majesty, the carriage is ready, at Your Majesty's pleasure." King Pasenadi of Kosala then mounted the carriage, departed from the town, and went to the Sakyan capital city named Medāḷumpa.

At that time, outside the gate of Medāḷumpa, many bhikṣus were walking in meditation in the open. King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the bhikṣus and asked: "Venerables, where is the World-Honored One now passing the day?"

The many bhikṣus replied: "Great King, that great east-facing hall with windows open and doors closed: the World-Honored One is now passing the day inside. If the Great King wishes to see him, you may go to that hall, stand outside, clear your throat and knock on the door. If the World-Honored One hears, he will surely open the door."

King Pasenadi of Kosala then dismounted from his carriage. If there is a king, a kṣatriya anointed on the head, who has obtained the position of ruler over the great earth, he has five insignia: sword, parasol, flower garland, jeweled-handled fan, and ornamental sandals. He removed all of these and handed them to Dīgha Kārāyana. Dīgha Kārāyana thought: "His Majesty now certainly intends to enter alone. We should stay here and wait."

Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala, surrounded by his retinue, walked to that great east-facing hall. Having arrived and standing outside, he cleared his throat and knocked on the door. The World-Honored One heard and opened the door. King Pasenadi of Kosala entered the hall, approached the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, and three times announced his own name: "I am King Pasenadi of Kosala. I am King Pasenadi of Kosala."

The World-Honored One replied: "Indeed so, Great King. You are King Pasenadi of Kosala. You are King Pasenadi of Kosala." After King Pasenadi of Kosala had three times announced his own name, he bowed at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Great King, seeing what meaning do you thus humble yourself, bow at my feet, and attend to me with offerings and service?"

King Pasenadi of Kosala replied: "World-Honored One, I have a Dharma-confidence regarding the Buddha, and because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"World-Honored One, when I sit in the royal assembly, I see mothers quarreling with sons, sons quarreling with mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, relatives all quarreling with each other. When they quarrel, mothers speak ill of sons, sons speak ill of mothers, fathers and sons, brothers and sisters, relatives all speak ill of each other, how much more so with strangers! Yet I see the World-Honored One's disciples, the community of bhikṣus, practicing the holy life under the World-Honored One. Even if some bhikṣus have a small quarrel and give up the precepts and abandon the path, they do not speak ill of the Buddha, do not speak ill of the Dharma, do not speak ill of the Sangha, but only blame themselves: 'I have done wrong; I am without virtue. Why? Because I was unable to practice the holy life under the World-Honored One for the rest of my life.' This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who, for nine months or ten months, practice the holy life to a limited degree, then abandon it, return to their former clothes, and again become stained by desires, attached to desires, bound by desires. Arrogant and indulging, not seeing the danger, not seeing the way out, they delight in practicing sensual pleasures. Yet I see the World-Honored One's disciples, the community of bhikṣus, practicing the holy life for the rest of their lives, numbering in the hundreds of millions. Outside of this, I do not see such pure holy conduct as in the World-Honored One's community. This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who are emaciated and haggard, of extremely poor complexion, with white sores on their bodies, unpleasant to look at. I think: 'Why are these venerables emaciated and haggard, of extremely poor complexion, with white sores on their bodies, unpleasant to look at? These venerables must not enjoy practicing the holy life, or they have bodily illness, or they do evil things in secret. That is why these venerables are emaciated and haggard, of extremely poor complexion, with white sores on their bodies, unpleasant to look at.' I go and ask them: 'Venerables, why are you emaciated and haggard, of extremely poor complexion, with white sores on your bodies, unpleasant to look at? Do you not enjoy practicing the holy life? Do you have bodily illness? Do you do evil things in secret? Is that why you are emaciated and haggard, of extremely poor complexion, with white sores on your bodies, unpleasant to look at?' They answer me: 'Great King, it is a skin disease. Great King, it is a skin disease.'

"World-Honored One, I see the World-Honored One's disciples, the community of bhikṣus, joyful and dignified, with radiant faces, clean bodies, without striving and without seeking, eating the food of others' wives as carefully as deer, practicing the holy life for the rest of their lives. Seeing this, I think: 'Why are these venerables joyful and dignified, with radiant faces, clean bodies, without striving and without seeking, eating the food of others' wives as carefully as deer, practicing the holy life for the rest of their lives? These venerables must have attained freedom from desire, or attained the higher mind, dwelling happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty.' Therefore these venerables are joyful and dignified, with radiant faces, clean bodies, without striving and without seeking, eating the food of others' wives as carefully as deer, practicing the holy life for the rest of their lives. If one who practices sensual pleasures could be joyful and dignified, then I should be joyful and dignified. Why? Because I obtain the five strands of sensual pleasure easily and without difficulty. If these venerables have attained freedom from desire, have attained the higher mind, and dwell happily in the present life, easily and without difficulty, then therefore these venerables are joyful and dignified, with radiant faces, clean bodies, without striving and without seeking, eating the food of others' wives as carefully as deer, practicing the holy life for the rest of their lives. This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who are wise and intelligent, who declare themselves wise and intelligent, learned and resolute, well-versed in the scriptures, conquering strong opponents, clear in debate and discourse, whose fame and virtue are widely known, whose renown spreads throughout the world. Wherever they go, they demolish others' doctrines and immediately establish their own arguments, saying: 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him such and such questions. If he can answer, we will refute him; if he cannot answer, we will also refute him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is visiting a certain village or town. They go to the Buddha's place, and yet they dare not even ask the World-Honored One a question, let alone refute him! This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who are wise and intelligent, who declare themselves wise and intelligent, learned and resolute, well-versed in the scriptures, conquering strong opponents, clear in debate and discourse, whose fame and virtue are widely known, whose renown spreads throughout the world. Wherever they go, they demolish others' doctrines and immediately establish their own arguments, saying: 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him such and such questions. If he can answer, we will refute him; if he cannot answer, we will also refute him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is visiting a certain village or town. They go to the Buddha's place and ask the World-Honored One their questions. The World-Honored One answers them. Having heard the answer, they become delighted, bow at the Buddha's feet, circumambulate three times, and depart. This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who are wise and intelligent, who declare themselves wise and intelligent, learned and resolute, well-versed in the scriptures, conquering strong opponents, clear in debate and discourse, whose fame and virtue are widely known, whose renown spreads throughout the world. Wherever they go, they demolish others' doctrines and immediately establish their own arguments, saying: 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him such and such questions. If he can answer, we will refute him; if he cannot answer, we will also refute him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is visiting a certain village or town. They go to the Buddha's place and ask the World-Honored One their questions. The World-Honored One answers them. Having heard the answer, they become delighted, and they immediately take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. The World-Honored One accepts them as lay followers who take lifelong refuge until the end of their lives. This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I see some ascetics and brahmins who are wise and intelligent, who declare themselves wise and intelligent, learned and resolute, well-versed in the scriptures, conquering strong opponents, clear in debate and discourse, whose fame and virtue are widely known, whose renown spreads throughout the world. Wherever they go, they demolish others' doctrines and immediately establish their own arguments, saying: 'We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him such and such questions. If he can answer, we will refute him; if he cannot answer, we will also refute him and leave.' They hear that the World-Honored One is visiting a certain village or town. They go to the Buddha's place and ask the World-Honored One their questions. The World-Honored One answers them. Having heard the answer, they become delighted, and they immediately request from the World-Honored One the going forth and ordination, receiving full ordination and obtaining the status of bhikṣu. The Buddha then ordains them and confers full ordination, and they obtain the status of bhikṣu.

"After those venerables have gone forth, been ordained, and obtained the status of bhikṣu, they dwell alone in seclusion, with minds free from heedlessness, practicing diligently. Having dwelt alone in seclusion, with minds free from heedlessness, practicing diligently, they accomplish that for which sons of good family shave off their hair and beards, don the kāṣāya robes, and with faith leave the household life for homelessness to study the Way: the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life. In the present life they know for themselves, realize for themselves, and dwell having attained it: 'Birth is ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, there will be no further becoming; I know it as it truly is.' After those venerables have known the Dharma, they even attain arahatship. Having attained arahatship, they think: 'Venerables, how close I came to ruin, how close to loss! Why? Because before, when I was not an ascetic, I claimed to be an ascetic; when I was not practicing the holy life, I claimed to practice the holy life; when I was not an arahat, I claimed to be an arahat. Now I am truly an ascetic, truly practicing the holy life, truly an arahat.' This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, even though I am a king over my country, I have the innocent killed and the guilty killed. Yet when sitting in the royal assembly, I still cannot make people say: 'All of you stay put; no one is asking you about matters; they are asking me. You cannot decide this matter; I can decide it.' In the midst of this, they argue about other matters without waiting for the first matter to be concluded. Yet I have often seen the World-Honored One teaching the Dharma surrounded by a great assembly. Among them, one person falls asleep and snores. Someone tells him: 'Sir, do not sleep and snore! Do you not wish to hear the World-Honored One teach the Dharma, which is like ambrosia?' That person, hearing this, immediately becomes silent. I think: 'The Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One, supreme tamer of people, how wonderful! How remarkable! Why? Because without sword or staff, all are naturally in accord with the Dharma, in safety and happiness.' This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I give wealth and always praise my two ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, and their lives depend on me. Yet I cannot make those two ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, humble themselves and show me respect, reverence, offerings, and service, as they do for the World-Honored One, humbling themselves and showing respect, reverence, offerings, and service. This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, once when I went out with Isidatta and Purāṇa, we stayed together in a small hut. I wished to test the two ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, to see in which direction they would sleep with their heads: toward me, or toward the World-Honored One? Thereupon Isidatta and Purāṇa, during the first watch of the night, sat cross-legged in silent meditation. At midnight, hearing that the World-Honored One was in a certain direction, they turned their heads toward him and their feet toward me. Seeing this, I thought: 'These two ministers, Isidatta and Purāṇa, do not regard me as having superior virtue. Therefore they do not humble themselves and show me respect, reverence, offerings, and service, as they do for the World-Honored One, humbling themselves and showing respect, reverence, offerings, and service.' This is a Dharma-confidence I have regarding the Buddha. Because of this I think: 'The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One is well taught. The community of the World-Honored One's disciples is progressing well.'

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, I too am a king, and the World-Honored One too is a Dharma King. I too am a kṣatriya, and the World-Honored One too is a kṣatriya. I too am of Kosala, and the World-Honored One too is of Kosala. I am eighty years old, and the World-Honored One too is eighty. World-Honored One, because of these things, I am well able, for the rest of my life, to humble myself and show the World-Honored One respect, reverence, offerings, and service. World-Honored One, I now have many affairs and wish to return. I ask permission to depart."

The World-Honored One said: "Great King, you may go when you deem it time." Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and attending the Buddha. Thereupon the World-Honored One turned around and said: "Ānanda, if there are any bhikṣus dwelling in dependence on the Medāḷumpa grove, have them all assemble in the lecture hall."

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha's instruction, had all the bhikṣus dwelling in dependence on the Medāḷumpa grove assemble in the lecture hall. He returned to the Buddha's place and said: "World-Honored One, all the bhikṣus dwelling in dependence on the Medāḷumpa grove have assembled in the lecture hall. May the World-Honored One decide when the time is right."

Thereupon the World-Honored One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the lecture hall, and before the assembly of bhikṣus arranged his seat and sat down. He said: "Bhikṣus, just now King Pasenadi of Kosala spoke this Dhamma-Ornament Sūtra before me, then rose from his seat, bowed at my feet, circumambulated three times, and departed. Bhikṣus, you should receive and retain this Dhamma-Ornament Sūtra, recite it well and study it well. Why? Bhikṣus, this Dhamma-Ornament Sūtra is in accord with meaning, in accord with Dharma, and is the foundation of the holy life. It leads to wisdom, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa. If sons of good family with faith leave the household for homelessness to study the Way, they too should receive, retain, recite, and study this Dhamma-Ornament Sūtra."

The Buddha spoke thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on the Dhamma-Ornament, the Second.

---

## (214) Sūtra on Vehāpati, the Third in the Chapter of Illustrations

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying in Śrāvastī at the Eastern Park, in the Hall of Migāra's Mother, on account of a small matter. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, together with one bhikṣu, left Śrāvastī and went to the Eastern Park, the Hall of Migāra's Mother. Having finished his business, he took that bhikṣu and returned, going to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, mounted on a white elephant named Puṇḍarīka, together with the minister Sirivaḍḍha, had come out of Śrāvastī. The Venerable Ānanda, seeing King Pasenadi of Kosala coming from afar, asked his companion bhikṣu: "Is that King Pasenadi of Kosala?"

He answered: "It is."

The Venerable Ānanda then left the road and went aside to a tree.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, seeing the Venerable Ānanda from afar among the trees, asked: "Sirivaḍḍha, is that the ascetic Ānanda?"

Sirivaḍḍha replied: "It is."

King Pasenadi of Kosala told the minister Sirivaḍḍha: "Drive this elephant to the ascetic Ānanda's place." Having received the King's instruction, Sirivaḍḍha drove the elephant to the Venerable Ānanda's place.

Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, where have you come from and where are you going?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, I have come from the Eastern Park, the Hall of Migāra's Mother, and I am going to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Ānanda, if you have no urgent business at the Jeta Grove, could you come together with me to the Aciravatī River, out of compassion?" The Venerable Ānanda silently accepted on behalf of King Pasenadi of Kosala.

Thereupon King Pasenadi of Kosala had the Venerable Ānanda go in front, and they went together to the Aciravatī River. Having arrived, the King dismounted and took the elephant's blanket, folded it four times, spread it on the ground, and invited the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, please sit on this seat."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Enough, enough, Great King. Your heartfelt intention is sufficient. I have my own sitting cloth and will sit on that." Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda spread his sitting cloth, sat cross-legged.

King Pasenadi of Kosala exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda, sat to one side, and said: "Ānanda, I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, if you wish to ask, please ask. After you ask, I will consider."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, does the Tathāgata ever engage in bodily conduct that would be censured by ascetics and brahmins?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, the Tathāgata does not engage in bodily conduct that would be censured by ascetics, brahmins, the wise and intelligent, or by the rest of the world."

Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Ānanda! What I could not reach, that is, 'the wise and intelligent and the rest of the world,' Ānanda reaches it. Ānanda, if one who is not well acquainted criticizes or praises, we do not consider that truthful. Ānanda, if one who is well acquainted criticizes or praises, we consider that truthful. Ānanda, does the Tathāgata ever engage in bodily conduct that would be censured by ascetics, brahmins, the wise and intelligent, or by the rest of the world?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, the Tathāgata absolutely does not engage in bodily conduct that would be censured by ascetics, brahmins, the wise and intelligent, or by the rest of the world."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what kind of bodily conduct is this?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is unwholesome bodily conduct."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what is unwholesome bodily conduct?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that is blameworthy."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what is blameworthy bodily conduct?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that is censured by the wise."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, why is it censured by the wise?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that harms oneself, harms others, and harms both. It destroys wisdom, promotes unwholesome associations, does not attain nirvāṇa, does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to nirvāṇa. One who practices it does not know as it truly is what dharmas should be practiced, nor does one know as it truly is what dharmas should not be practiced. Not knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be practiced and what dharmas should not be practiced, one does not know as it truly is what dharmas should be accepted and what dharmas should not be accepted. Not knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be accepted and what dharmas should not be accepted, one does not know as it truly is what dharmas should be abandoned and what dharmas should not be abandoned. Not knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be abandoned and what dharmas should not be abandoned, one does not know as it truly is what dharmas should be accomplished and what dharmas should not be accomplished. Not knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be accomplished and what dharmas should not be accomplished, one does not practice what should be practiced, and practices what should not be practiced. Not practicing what should be practiced and practicing what should not be practiced, one does not accept what should be accepted, and accepts what should not be accepted. Not accepting what should be accepted and accepting what should not be accepted, one does not abandon what should be abandoned, and abandons what should not be abandoned. Not abandoning what should be abandoned and abandoning what should not be abandoned, one does not accomplish what should be accomplished, and accomplishes what should not be accomplished. Not accomplishing what should be accomplished and accomplishing what should not be accomplished, unwholesome dharmas increase and wholesome dharmas decrease. Therefore the Tathāgata absolutely does not practice such dharmas."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, why does the Tathāgata absolutely not practice such dharmas?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, because desire has been abandoned and desire is completely exhausted; anger has been abandoned and anger is completely exhausted; delusion has been abandoned and delusion is completely exhausted. The Tathāgata has severed all unwholesome dharmas and accomplished all wholesome dharmas. He is a teacher, a sublime teacher, a perfectly good teacher; a guide, a skillful guide; of good speech, sublime speech, perfectly good speech. Therefore the Tathāgata absolutely does not practice such dharmas."

King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Ānanda! The Tathāgata absolutely does not practice what should not be practiced. Why? Because the Tathāgata is the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One. Ānanda, you are the disciple of that teacher, studying the Way and seeking the unsurpassed, peaceful nirvāṇa. Even you do not practice such dharmas; how much less would the Tathāgata practice them?"

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, does the Tathāgata engage in bodily conduct that is not censured by ascetics, brahmins, the wise and intelligent, or by the rest of the world?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, the Tathāgata certainly engages in bodily conduct that is not censured by ascetics, brahmins, the wise and intelligent, or by the rest of the world."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what kind of bodily conduct is this?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is wholesome bodily conduct."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what is wholesome bodily conduct?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that is blameless."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, what is blameless bodily conduct?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that is not censured by the wise."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, why is it not censured by the wise?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, it is bodily conduct that does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. It develops wisdom, does not promote unwholesome associations, attains nirvāṇa, leads to wisdom, leads to awakening, leads to nirvāṇa. One who practices it knows as it truly is what dharmas should be practiced and what dharmas should not be practiced. Knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be practiced and what dharmas should not be practiced, one knows as it truly is what dharmas should be accepted and what dharmas should not be accepted. Knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be accepted and what dharmas should not be accepted, one knows as it truly is what dharmas should be abandoned and what dharmas should not be abandoned. Knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be abandoned and what dharmas should not be abandoned, one knows as it truly is what dharmas should be accomplished and what dharmas should not be accomplished. Knowing as it truly is what dharmas should be accomplished and what dharmas should not be accomplished, one practices what should be practiced and does not practice what should not be practiced. Practicing what should be practiced and not practicing what should not be practiced, one accepts what should be accepted and does not accept what should not be accepted. Accepting what should be accepted and not accepting what should not be accepted, one abandons what should be abandoned and does not abandon what should not be abandoned. Abandoning what should be abandoned and not abandoning what should not be abandoned, one accomplishes what should be accomplished and does not accomplish what should not be accomplished. Accomplishing what should be accomplished and not accomplishing what should not be accomplished, unwholesome dharmas decrease and wholesome dharmas increase. Therefore the Tathāgata certainly practices such dharmas."

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Ānanda, why does the Tathāgata certainly practice such dharmas?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Great King, because desire has been abandoned and desire is completely exhausted; anger has been abandoned and anger is completely exhausted; delusion has been abandoned and delusion is completely exhausted. The Tathāgata has accomplished all wholesome dharmas and severed all unwholesome dharmas. He is a teacher, a sublime teacher, a perfectly good teacher; a guide, a skillful guide; of good speech, sublime speech, perfectly good speech. Therefore the Tathāgata certainly practices such dharmas."

King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, Ānanda! The Tathāgata certainly practices what should be practiced. Why? Because the Tathāgata is the Worthy One Free from Attachment, the Perfectly Fully Enlightened One. Ānanda, you are the disciple of that teacher, studying the Way and seeking the unsurpassed, peaceful nirvāṇa. Even you practice such dharmas; how much more so must the Tathāgata practice them?

"Ānanda, you have spoken well, and I am delighted. Ānanda, you have spoken excellently, and I am greatly delighted. If village tax revenue is something Ānanda may properly accept, I would give village tax revenue as a Dharma offering. Ānanda, if elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep are things Ānanda may properly accept, I would give elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep as a Dharma offering. Ānanda, if women and maidens are what Ānanda may properly accept, I would give women and maidens as a Dharma offering. Ānanda, if gold and jewels are what Ānanda may properly accept, I would give gold and jewels as a Dharma offering. Ānanda, since all such things are not proper for Ānanda to accept, there is in the Kosalan royal house a garment called Vehāpati, the finest. A king once sent it as a gift, placed inside the handle of a parasol. Ānanda, among all the cotton garments of the Kosalan royal house, this Vehāpati garment is the foremost. Why? This Vehāpati garment is sixteen cubits long and eight cubits wide. I now wish to give this Vehāpati garment as a Dharma offering to Ānanda. Ānanda, you should make it into three robes and wear it, so that the Kosalan royal house may for a long time gain increase in merit."

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Enough, enough, Great King. Your heartfelt intention is sufficient. I already have three robes that I have accepted."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Ānanda, please allow me to give a simile. The wise, hearing a simile, understand the meaning. Just as when there is a great rain and the water of the Aciravatī River is full, overflowing both banks and flowing out. Ānanda, do you see this?"

The Venerable Ānanda replied: "I see it."

King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Just so, Ānanda, if you have three robes, give them to bhikṣus and bhikṣunīs, and gradually to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs. Ānanda, accept this Vehāpati garment and make three robes from it, so that the Kosalan royal house may for a long time gain increase in merit." The Venerable Ānanda silently accepted on behalf of King Pasenadi of Kosala.

Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala, knowing that the Venerable Ānanda had silently accepted, gave the Vehāpati garment as a Dharma offering to the Venerable Ānanda, then rose from his seat, circumambulated three times, and departed.

Not long after his departure, the Venerable Ānanda took the Vehāpati garment and went to the Buddha's place, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side, saying: "World-Honored One, this Vehāpati garment, which King Pasenadi of Kosala today gave me as a Dharma offering, I wish the World-Honored One would place both feet upon the Vehāpati garment, so that the Kosalan royal house may for a long time gain increase in merit."

Thereupon the World-Honored One placed both feet upon the Vehāpati garment and said: "Ānanda, whatever you discussed with King Pasenadi of Kosala, now relate it all to me in full."

Thereupon the Venerable Ānanda related in full to the Buddha everything he had discussed with King Pasenadi of Kosala, and with palms joined said: "Have I spoken thus without misrepresenting the World-Honored One? Have I spoken truly, in accord with the Dharma, spoken the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma, without any fault regarding what accords with the Dharma?"

The World-Honored One replied: "You have spoken thus without misrepresenting me. You have spoken truly, in accord with the Dharma, spoken the Dharma and what accords with the Dharma, without any fault regarding what accords with the Dharma. Ānanda, if King Pasenadi of Kosala had come to me with this meaning, these phrases, and these words to ask me, I too would have answered King Pasenadi of Kosala with this meaning, these phrases, and these words. Ānanda, this meaning is as you have spoken it. You should receive and retain it thus. Why? Because this explanation is precisely the meaning."

The Buddha spoke thus. The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of Sūtra on Vehāpati, the Third.

---

## (215) Sūtra on the First Attainment, the Fourth in the Chapter of Illustrations

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was travelling in Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Within all the territories of King Pasenadi of Kosala, wherever his command reaches, among them King Pasenadi of Kosala is the foremost. Yet King Pasenadi of Kosala is subject to change and alteration. A well-learned noble disciple, contemplating thus, becomes disenchanted with it. Being disenchanted with it, one does not even desire the foremost, how much less what is lower?

"The realm of the sun and moon, the area illuminated by their light, illuminating all directions, that is, the thousand-fold world. In this thousand-fold world, there are a thousand suns, a thousand moons, a thousand Aparagodānīyas, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Mount Sumerus, a thousand Four Great King heavens, a thousand sons of the Four Great Kings, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Śakra lords of gods, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Suyāma sons, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Tuṣita

# Madhyamāgama, Fascicle 59 (Continued)

*(Note: The text provided appears to be the concluding portion of a sūtra from Fascicle 59 of the Madhyamāgama.)*

---

"If there is one whose abandonment of pleasure is swift, because this abandonment of pleasure is swift, this abandonment is also called inferior. Among these, if there is one whose abandonment of suffering is slow, because this abandonment of suffering is slow, this abandonment is also called inferior. Among these, if there is one whose abandonment of suffering is swift, because this abandonment of suffering is swift, this abandonment is not widely spread and not broadly disseminated; even gods and humans do not praise it as widely spread. My abandonment is widely spread and broadly disseminated; even gods and humans praise it as widely spread. What is my abandonment that is widely spread and broadly disseminated, which even gods and humans praise as widely spread? It is the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration, these being eight. This is my abandonment that is widely spread and broadly disseminated, which even gods and humans praise as widely spread.

"Being as I am, those śramaṇas and brahmins who speak falsely and deceitfully, unskillfully and untruly, wrongly slander me. They indeed designate the annihilation and destruction of beings, yet they say, 'The śramaṇa Gautama makes no designations whatsoever.' They indeed designate the annihilation and destruction of beings. If there were no self, I would not speak thus. The Tathāgata, in this present life, cuts off and knows all things, attaining rest, cessation, extinction, and nirvāṇa."

Thus spoke the Buddha. The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
