# Fascicle Sixty of the Madhyamāgama

---

## (216) Sūtra on Love Giving Rise to Sorrow, Fifth of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin who had only one son, whom he loved and cherished with his whole heart, who was gentle and tender toward him, and whom he gazed upon without weariness. Suddenly the son died. After his death, the brahmin was filled with grief and sorrow, unable to eat or drink, not putting on clothes, nor applying fragrance. He only went to the cemetery to weep, remembering the place where his son used to lie. Thereupon, the brahmin wandered about everywhere and went to the Buddha's dwelling. They exchanged greetings with each other, and he sat down to one side.

The World-Honored One asked: "Brahmin, your faculties do not seem to be in their natural state of mind. Is that so?"

The brahmin answered: "How could my faculties be in their natural state of mind? Why is this? I had only one son, whom I loved and cherished with my whole heart, who was gentle and tender, and whom I gazed upon without weariness. He suddenly died. After his death, I have been filled with grief and sorrow, unable to eat or drink, not putting on clothes, nor applying fragrance. I only go to the cemetery to weep, remembering the place where my son used to lie."

The World-Honored One said: "So it is, brahmin! So it is, brahmin! When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

The brahmin said: "Gautama! How can you say that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish? Gautama, you should know that when love arises, joy and happiness of heart arise."

The World-Honored One repeated up to three times: "So it is, brahmin! So it is, brahmin! When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

The brahmin also repeated up to three times: "Gautama! How can you say that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish? Gautama, you should know that when love arises, joy and happiness of heart arise."

At that time, the brahmin, having heard what the Buddha said, did not say it was right but said it was wrong, and then rose from his seat, shook his head, and departed.

At that time, in front of the gate of the Jeta Grove, there were many city children playing at a gambling game together. The brahmin saw them from afar and then had this thought: "In the world, if there are any who are clever and wise, none surpass those who play at gambling. I should now go to them and tell them everything that I discussed with Gautama." Thereupon, the brahmin went to where the many city children were playing at their gambling game, and he told them everything that he and the World-Honored One had discussed together.

The many city gambling children, having heard this, said: "Brahmin! How can one say that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish? Brahmin, you should know that when love arises, joy and happiness of heart arise."

The brahmin, having heard this, then had this thought: "What the gambling children say is exactly the same as what I say." He nodded his head and departed.

Thereupon, this discussion spread far and wide, and eventually entered the royal palace. King Prasenajit of Kosala heard that the ascetic Gautama had said thus: "When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

He said to Queen Mallikā: "I have heard that Gautama said thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish.'"

Queen Mallikā, having heard this, said: "So it is, great king! So it is, great king! When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

King Prasenajit of Kosala said to Queen Mallikā: "When a teacher's tradition speaks, the disciple must agree. Because the ascetic Gautama is your teacher, you speak thus, and because you are his disciple, you speak thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish.'"

Queen Mallikā said: "Great king! If you do not believe it, you may go ask him yourself, or you may send a messenger."

Thereupon, King Prasenajit of Kosala instructed the brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha, saying: "Go to the ascetic Gautama's place and inquire on my behalf whether the ascetic Gautama's sacred body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, his movements light and convenient, and his strength as usual. Speak thus: 'King Prasenajit of Kosala inquires whether your sacred body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, your movements light and convenient, and your strength as usual.' Did the ascetic Gautama truly say thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish'? Nāḷijaṅgha! Whatever the ascetic Gautama may say, you should receive and retain it well. Why is this? Such a person would never speak falsely."

The brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha, having received the king's instructions, went to the Buddha's place. They exchanged greetings with each other, and he sat down to one side. He said: "Gautama! King Prasenajit of Kosala inquires whether your sacred body is well and strong, at ease and free from illness, your movements light and convenient, and your strength as usual. Did the ascetic Gautama truly say thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish'?"

The World-Honored One said: "Nāḷijaṅgha! I will now ask you; answer as you understand. Nāḷijaṅgha, what do you think? Suppose someone's mother were to die, and that person went mad, greatly confused in mind, stripped off his clothes and went naked, running about everywhere along the roads, saying thus: 'Good people! Have you seen my mother? Good people! Have you seen my mother?' Nāḷijaṅgha, by this matter one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish. Likewise with a father, brother, sister, or daughter-in-law dying: that person goes mad, greatly confused in mind, strips off his clothes and goes naked, running about everywhere along the roads, saying thus: 'Good people! Have you seen my daughter-in-law? Good people! Have you seen my daughter-in-law?' Nāḷijaṅgha, by this matter one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish. Nāḷijaṅgha, in the past there was a man whose wife went to visit her family home. Her relatives wished to take her away and remarry her to another. That woman, hearing of this, quickly hastened back to her husband's home and said to her husband: 'My lord! You should know that my relatives are trying to forcibly take your wife and marry her to another man. What do you intend to do?' Thereupon, that man seized his wife's arm, led her into the house, and said these words: 'Together to the next life! Together to the next life!' He then took a sharp knife and cut his wife to death, and also killed himself. Nāḷijaṅgha, by this matter one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

The brahmin Nāḷijaṅgha, having heard what the Buddha said, received and retained it well. He then rose from his seat, circumambulated three times, and departed. He returned to King Prasenajit of Kosala and said: "Your Majesty! The ascetic Gautama truly said thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish.'"

King Prasenajit of Kosala, having heard this, said to Queen Mallikā: "The ascetic Gautama truly said thus: 'When love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish.'"

Queen Mallikā said: "Great king! I ask the great king; please answer as you understand. What do you think? Does the king love General Viḍūḍabha?"

He answered: "I truly love him."

Mallikā further asked: "If General Viḍūḍabha were to change or become different, what would the king feel?"

He answered: "Mallikā! If General Viḍūḍabha were to change or become different, I would certainly be filled with grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

Mallikā said: "By this matter, one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

Mallikā further asked: "Does the king love the minister Śrī Aḍḍha, love the elephant Puṇḍarīka, love the maiden Vājīrī, love the royal parasol that blocks rain and sun, and love the kingdoms of Kāśī and Kosala?"

He answered: "I truly love them."

Mallikā further asked: "If Kāśī and Kosala were to change or become different, what would the king feel?"

He answered: "Mallikā! That by which I am endowed with the five pleasures of desire and enjoy myself comes from those two kingdoms. If Kāśī and Kosala were to change or become different, I would even lose my life, how much more would I not be filled with grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish!"

Mallikā said: "By this matter, one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

Mallikā asked the king: "What do you think? Do you love me?"

The king answered: "I truly love you."

Mallikā further asked: "If one day I were to change or become different, what would the king feel?"

He answered: "Mallikā! If one day you were to change or become different, I would certainly be filled with grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

Mallikā said: "By this matter, one can know that when love arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, vexation, and anguish."

King Prasenajit of Kosala said: "Mallikā! From this day forward, because of this matter, the ascetic Gautama is my teacher and I am his disciple. Mallikā, I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day onward, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

Thus spoke the Buddha. King Prasenajit of Kosala and Queen Mallikā, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Fifth Sūtra: Love Gives Rise to Sorrow

---

## (217) Sūtra of the Eight Cities, Sixth of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, not long after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, many senior and renowned monks were traveling in the city of Pāṭaliputra, staying in the Cock Park.

At that time, Daśama the householder of Aṭṭhaka was carrying many fine goods and had gone to the city of Pāṭaliputra to trade and sell. Thereupon, the householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka sold his many fine goods quickly and obtained great profit, and, rejoicing and elated, he left the city of Pāṭaliputra and went to visit the many senior and renowned monks at the Cock Park. He bowed his head at their feet and sat down to one side. At that time, the senior and renowned monks taught him the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him, bringing about his joy. Through countless skillful means they taught him the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him, bringing about his joy, and then remained silent.

At that time, after the senior and renowned monks had taught him the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him, bringing about his joy, the householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka said: "Venerable ones! Where is the Venerable Ānanda now staying? I wish to go see him."

The senior and renowned monks answered: "Householder! The Venerable Ānanda is now in Vaiśālī, at the Monkey Riverbank Lofty Pavilion. If you wish to see him, you may go there."

At that time, the householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the senior monks, circumambulated three times, and departed. He went to the Venerable Ānanda's place, bowed his head at his feet, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable Ānanda! I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Householder! If you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

The householder asked: "Venerable Ānanda! The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, endowed with the eye of wisdom, seeing the supreme meaning: did he ever teach a single dharma whereby a noble disciple, abiding therein, with the outflows completely exhausted and without remainder, attains liberation of mind?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "He did."

The householder asked: "Venerable Ānanda! The World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, endowed with the eye of wisdom, seeing the supreme meaning: how did he teach such a single dharma whereby a noble disciple, abiding therein, with the outflows completely exhausted and without remainder, attains liberation of mind?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "Householder! A well-learned noble disciple, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, attains up to the fourth dhyāna and abides therein. Depending on this state, he contemplates dharmas as dharmas. Depending on this state, contemplating dharmas as dharmas, that while abiding there he attains the exhaustion of outflows: this is possible. If, while abiding there, he does not attain the exhaustion of outflows, then by reason of this dharma, through desire for the dharma, love of the dharma, delight in the dharma, and serenity in the dharma, with loving delight and joy, he cuts off the five lower fetters completely. He is reborn by transformation there and attains parinirvāṇa there, attaining the dharma of non-return, never returning to this world.

"Furthermore, householder, a well-learned noble disciple, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervades one direction and abides therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely: with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all worlds, he abides therein. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all worlds, he abides therein. Depending on this state, he contemplates dharmas as dharmas. Depending on this state, contemplating dharmas as dharmas, that while abiding there he attains the exhaustion of outflows: this is possible. If, while abiding there, he does not attain the exhaustion of outflows, then by reason of this dharma, through desire for the dharma, love of the dharma, delight in the dharma, and serenity in the dharma, with loving delight and joy, he cuts off the five lower fetters completely. He is reborn by transformation there and attains parinirvāṇa there, attaining the dharma of non-return, never returning to this world. This is what the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, endowed with the eye of wisdom, seeing the supreme meaning, taught as that single dharma whereby a noble disciple, abiding therein, with the outflows completely exhausted and without remainder, attains liberation of mind.

"Furthermore, householder, a well-learned noble disciple transcends all perceptions of form, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and abides therein. In this state, he contemplates dharmas as dharmas. In this state, contemplating dharmas as dharmas, that while abiding there he attains the exhaustion of outflows: this is possible. If, while abiding there, he does not attain the exhaustion of outflows, then by reason of this dharma, through desire for the dharma, love of the dharma, delight in the dharma, and serenity in the dharma, with loving delight and joy, he cuts off the five lower fetters completely. He is reborn by transformation there and attains parinirvāṇa there, attaining the dharma of non-return, never returning to this world. This is what the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, endowed with the eye of wisdom, seeing the supreme meaning, taught as that single dharma whereby a noble disciple, abiding therein, with the outflows completely exhausted and without remainder, attains liberation of mind."

Thereupon, the householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka rose from his seat, bared one shoulder of his robe, joined his palms, and said: "Venerable Ānanda! How extraordinary! How remarkable! I asked the Venerable Ānanda about one gate of the deathless nectar, yet the Venerable Ānanda at once taught me twelve gates of the deathless Dharma. Now, through these twelve gates of the deathless nectar, one will certainly, depending on whichever one, attain a safe escape. Venerable Ānanda, it is like a house near a village, a great building with twelve doors. If a person enters that building for some purpose, and another person comes along who does not seek that person's benefit or welfare, who does not seek his safety, and sets fire to that building, Venerable Ānanda, that person can certainly escape safely through whichever of those twelve doors he depends upon. Likewise, I asked the Venerable Ānanda about one gate of the deathless nectar, yet the Venerable Ānanda at once taught me twelve gates of the deathless Dharma. Now, through these twelve gates of the deathless nectar, one will certainly, depending on whichever one, attain a safe escape. Venerable Ānanda, even in the Dharma and Vinaya of the brahmins, which teaches an unwholesome Dharma and Vinaya, they still make offerings to the teacher. How much more should I not make offerings to the great teacher, the Venerable Ānanda!"

Thereupon, during that very night, the householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka prepared extremely fine, pure, beautiful, and abundant food, both to eat and to swallow and digest. Having prepared the food, at dawn he laid out seats and invited the assembly of the Cock Park and the assembly of Vaiśālī, all gathering in one place. He himself brought the washing water, and then with the extremely fine, pure, beautiful, and abundant food, both to eat and to swallow and digest, he personally served and ladled it out, making sure they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels collected, and the washing water had been brought around, he took five hundred kinds of goods and purchased a dwelling, which he offered separately to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda, having accepted it, donated it to the Sangha of the universal community.

What the Venerable Ānanda taught was thus. The householder Daśama of Aṭṭhaka, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Sixth Sūtra: The Eight Cities

---

## (218) Sūtra on Anuruddha, Seventh of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣus, in the afternoon, rose from their meditation and went to the Venerable Anuruddha's place. They bowed their heads at his feet, sat down to one side, and said: "We wish to ask something. Will you permit us to speak?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! If you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

At that time, the bhikṣus asked: "How does a bhikṣu die well and have a good end of life?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! If a bhikṣu, separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, attains up to the fourth dhyāna and abides therein, this is called a bhikṣu who dies well and has a good end of life."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate good death and good end of life for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is not the ultimate good death and good end of life for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, worthy ones, if a bhikṣu attains the power of supernatural abilities, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of births and deaths, and the exhaustion of outflows, attaining the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, in this present life knowing for himself, realizing for himself, witnessing for himself, and abiding in the attainment: 'Birth is ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, I will not be subject to further existence,' knowing this as it truly is: this is called a bhikṣu who dies well and has a good end of life."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate good death and good end of life for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is the ultimate good death and good end of life for a bhikṣu."

Thereupon, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, received and retained it well. They then rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the Venerable Anuruddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

What the Venerable Anuruddha taught was thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Seventh Sūtra: Anuruddha

---

## (219) Sūtra on Anuruddha, Eighth of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the bhikṣus, in the afternoon, rose from their meditation and went to the Venerable Anuruddha's place. They bowed their heads at his feet, sat down to one side, and said: "We wish to ask something. Will you permit us to speak?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! If you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

At that time, the bhikṣus asked: "How does a bhikṣu die without distress and have an end of life without distress?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! If a bhikṣu has right view and attains the precepts beloved by noble ones, this is called a bhikṣu who dies without distress and has an end of life without distress."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is not the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, worthy ones, if a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, up to and including contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas, this is called a bhikṣu who dies without distress and has an end of life without distress."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is not the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, worthy ones, if a bhikṣu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervades one direction and abides therein. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below, universally and completely: with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all worlds, he abides therein. Likewise with compassion and sympathetic joy. With a mind imbued with equanimity, without bondage, without enmity, without anger, without contention, extremely vast and great, immeasurable, well cultivated, pervading all worlds, he abides therein. This is called a bhikṣu who dies without distress and has an end of life without distress."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is not the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, worthy ones, if a bhikṣu transcends all perceptions of form, up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and abides therein, this is called a bhikṣu who dies without distress and has an end of life without distress."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is not the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu. Furthermore, worthy ones, if a bhikṣu transcends the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and with the cessation of perception, attains the bodily realization of the cessation attainment and abides therein, and with wisdom-insight, all his outflows are completely exhausted, this is called a bhikṣu who dies without distress and has an end of life without distress."

At that time, the bhikṣus further asked: "Is that the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu?"

The Venerable Anuruddha answered: "Worthy ones! That is the ultimate death without distress and end of life without distress for a bhikṣu."

At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, received and retained it well. They then rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the Venerable Anuruddha's feet, circumambulated three times, and departed.

What the Venerable Anuruddha taught was thus. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Eighth Sūtra: Anuruddha

---

## (220) Sūtra on Views, Ninth of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, not long after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling in Rājagṛha, staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.

At that time, there was a certain non-Buddhist brahmin who had been a friend of the Venerable Ānanda before he left the household life. In the afternoon, he wandered about and went to the Venerable Ānanda's place. They exchanged greetings with each other, and he sat down to one side. He said to the Venerable Ānanda: "I wish to ask something. Will you permit me to ask?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "Brahmin! If you wish to ask, then ask. Having heard, I shall consider it."

The non-Buddhist brahmin then asked: "Those views that are set aside, excluded, and not fully explained: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': did the ascetic Gautama know these views as they should be known?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "Brahmin! Those views that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, set aside, excluded, and did not fully explain: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, knew these views as they should be known."

The non-Buddhist brahmin further asked: "Those views that the ascetic Gautama set aside, excluded, and did not fully explain: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': how did the ascetic Gautama know these views as they should be known?"

The Venerable Ānanda answered: "Brahmin! Those views that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, set aside, excluded, and did not fully explain: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': non-Buddhist brahmins, with such a basis, with such grasping, with such a destination, with such a birth, with such a reaching of the next life, such are the views that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, set aside, excluded, and did not fully explain: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.' In this way he knew these views; these views should be known in this way."

The non-Buddhist brahmin said: "I now take refuge in Ānanda."

The Venerable Ānanda said: "Brahmin! Do not take refuge in me. Just as I take refuge in the Buddha, you too should take refuge."

The non-Buddhist brahmin said: "Ānanda! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka. From this day onward, for the rest of my life I take refuge, until the end of my life."

What the Venerable Ānanda taught was thus. That non-Buddhist brahmin, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Ninth Sūtra: Views

---

## (221) The Simile of the Arrow Sūtra, Tenth of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta, alone in a quiet place, was sitting in meditation and contemplation. His mind formed this thought: "Those views that the World-Honored One has set aside, excluded, and not fully explained: 'The world is eternal,' 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': I do not desire this, I do not accept this, I do not approve of this. If the World-Honored One would definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I would practice the holy life under him. If the World-Honored One would not definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I would challenge him, abandon him, and leave. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': if the World-Honored One would definitively declare to me, 'This is the truth, all else is false,' I would practice the holy life under him. If the World-Honored One would not definitively declare to me, 'This is the truth, all else is false,' I would challenge him, abandon him, and leave."

Thereupon, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta, in the afternoon, rose from his meditation, went to the Buddha's place, bowed his head in salutation, sat down to one side, and said: "World-Honored One! Today, alone in a quiet place, I was sitting in meditation and contemplation. My mind formed this thought: 'Those views that the World-Honored One has set aside, excluded, and not fully explained: "The world is eternal," "The world is not eternal," "The world has an end," "The world has no end," "The life-force is identical with the body," "The life-force is different from the body," "The Tathāgata exists after death," "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death": I do not desire this, I do not accept this, I do not approve of this. If the World-Honored One definitively knows that the world is eternal, the World-Honored One should tell me. If the World-Honored One does not definitively know that the world is eternal, he should simply say, "I do not know." Likewise: "The world is not eternal," "The world has an end," "The world has no end," "The life-force is identical with the body," "The life-force is different from the body," "The Tathāgata exists after death," "The Tathāgata does not exist after death," "The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death": if the World-Honored One definitively knows, "This is the truth, all else is false," the World-Honored One should tell me. If the World-Honored One does not definitively know, "This is the truth, all else is false," he should simply say, "I do not know."'"

The World-Honored One asked: "Māluṅkyaputta! Did I ever say to you, 'The world is eternal; come and practice the holy life under me'?"

Māluṅkyaputta answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': did I ever say to you, 'This is the truth, all else is false; come and practice the holy life under me'?"

Māluṅkyaputta answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Māluṅkyaputta! Did you ever say to me, 'If the World-Honored One would definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I would practice the holy life under the World-Honored One'?"

Māluṅkyaputta answered: "No, World-Honored One."

"Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': Māluṅkyaputta, did you ever say to me, 'If the World-Honored One would definitively declare to me, "This is the truth, all else is false," I would practice the holy life under the World-Honored One'?"

Māluṅkyaputta answered: "No, World-Honored One."

The World-Honored One said: "Māluṅkyaputta! I originally made no such statement to you, and you originally made no such statement to me. You foolish man! Why do you falsely slander me?"

Thereupon, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta, having been rebuked and admonished to his face by the World-Honored One, harbored grief within, hung his head in silence, lost his ability to reply, and had nothing to say, as if searching for something.

Thereupon, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Māluṅkyaputta to his face, he addressed the bhikṣus: "If some foolish person were to think, 'If the World-Honored One does not definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I will not practice the holy life under the World-Honored One,' that foolish person would never come to know, and in the meantime he would die. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': if some foolish person were to think, 'If the World-Honored One does not definitively declare to me, "This is the truth, all else is false," I will not practice the holy life under the World-Honored One,' that foolish person would never come to know, and in the meantime he would die.

"It is like a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow. Because of the poisoned arrow, he suffers extreme pain. His relatives, out of concern and compassion, seek his benefit, welfare, and safety, and find a physician to remove the arrow. But that person then thinks: 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know what that person's clan name is, what his given name is, what his birth is, whether he is tall or short, stout or thin, whether he is dark, fair, or neither dark nor fair, whether he is of the kṣatriya class, the brahmin class, the merchant class, or the artisan class, whether he is from the east, the south, the west, or the north.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether that bow is made of thorny wood, mulberry wood, zelkova wood, or horn.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the bowstring binding is made of ox sinew, deer sinew, or silk.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the bow's color is black, white, red, or yellow.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the bowstring is made of sinew, silk, ramie, or hemp.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the arrow shaft is made of wood or bamboo.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the arrow binding is made of ox sinew, deer sinew, or silk.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the arrow feathers are from a vulture, an eagle, a crane, or a rooster.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know whether the arrowhead is a barb, a spear point, or a broad blade.' 'The arrow must not yet be pulled out. I should first know what the arrowhead maker's clan name is, what his given name is, what his birth is, whether he is tall or short, stout or thin, whether he is dark, fair, or neither dark nor fair, whether he is from the east, west, south, or north.' That person would never come to know these things, and in the meantime he would die.

"If some foolish person were to think, 'If the World-Honored One does not definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I will not practice the holy life under the World-Honored One,' that foolish person would never come to know, and in the meantime he would die. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': if some foolish person were to think, 'If the World-Honored One does not definitively declare to me, "This is the truth, all else is false," I will not practice the holy life under the World-Honored One,' that foolish person would never come to know, and in the meantime he would die.

"That one would practice the holy life under me because of the view that 'the world is eternal': this is not so. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': that one would practice the holy life under me because of such views: this is not so. That one would not practice the holy life under me because of having the view that 'the world is eternal': this is not so. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': that one would not practice the holy life under me because of having such views: this is not so.

"That one would practice the holy life under me because of not having the view that 'the world is eternal': this is not so. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': that one would practice the holy life under me because of not having such views: this is not so. That one would not practice the holy life under me because of not having the view that 'the world is eternal': this is not so. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': that one would not practice the holy life under me because of not having such views: this is not so.

"Whether one holds the view that 'the world is eternal,' there is birth, there is old age, there is sickness, there is death, grief, lamentation, sorrow, and anguish; thus does this entire great mass of suffering arise. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': there is birth, there is old age, there is sickness, there is death, grief, lamentation, sorrow, and anguish; thus does this entire great mass of suffering arise.

"That 'the world is eternal,' I do not definitively declare this. For what reason do I not definitively declare this? This is not connected with meaning, not connected with the Dharma, not the basis of the holy life; it does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to nirvāṇa. Therefore I do not definitively declare this. Likewise: 'The world is not eternal,' 'The world has an end,' 'The world has no end,' 'The life-force is identical with the body,' 'The life-force is different from the body,' 'The Tathāgata exists after death,' 'The Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death': I do not definitively declare these. For what reason do I not definitively declare these? They are not connected with meaning, not connected with the Dharma, not the basis of the holy life; they do not lead to wisdom, do not lead to awakening, do not lead to nirvāṇa. Therefore I do not definitively declare these. What dharma do I definitively declare? This meaning I definitively declare: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path to the cessation of suffering: these I definitively declare. For what reason do I definitively declare these? These are connected with meaning, connected with the Dharma, are the basis of the holy life; they lead to wisdom, lead to awakening, lead to nirvāṇa. Therefore I definitively declare these. Thus, what should not be spoken of, I do not speak of; what should be spoken of, I speak of. You should hold to this, you should train in this."

Thus spoke the Buddha. Those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

End of the Tenth Sūtra: The Simile of the Arrow

---

## (222) The Illustrative Sūtra, Eleventh of the Illustrative Chapter

Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling in the state of Śrāvastī, staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If one wishes to abandon ignorance, one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom, and contemplates the internal body as body, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom, and contemplates the internal body as body, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and dharmas as dharmas. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the four right efforts? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. For the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of not generating evil and unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of generating wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of maintaining, not forgetting, not regressing, increasing, expanding, fully cultivating and perfecting wholesome dharmas that have already arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the four right efforts? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. For the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of not generating evil and unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of generating wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. For the sake of maintaining, not forgetting, not regressing, increasing, expanding, fully cultivating and perfecting wholesome dharmas that have already arisen, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, strives vigorously, exerts his mind, and cuts them off. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four bases of supernatural power. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the four bases of supernatural power? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the base of supernatural power of concentration through desire, accomplishing the practice of abandoning, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. Likewise he cultivates the concentration through vigor and the concentration through mind. He cultivates the base of supernatural power of concentration through investigation, accomplishing the practice of abandoning, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four bases of supernatural power. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four bases of supernatural power. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the four bases of supernatural power? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the base of supernatural power of concentration through desire, accomplishing the practice of abandoning, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. Likewise he cultivates the concentration through vigor and the concentration through mind. He cultivates the base of supernatural power of concentration through investigation, accomplishing the practice of abandoning, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four bases of supernatural power.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the four dhyānas? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. Separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, he attains up to the fourth dhyāna and abides therein. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the four dhyānas? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. Separated from desires, separated from evil and unwholesome dharmas, he attains up to the fourth dhyāna and abides therein. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five faculties. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the five faculties? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five faculties. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the five faculties. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the five faculties? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the five faculties.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five powers. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the five powers? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five powers. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the five powers. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the five powers? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the five powers.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of awakening. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the seven factors of awakening? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. Likewise he cultivates the awakening factors of investigation of dharmas, vigor, joy, tranquility, and concentration. He cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of awakening. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of awakening. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the seven factors of awakening? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. Likewise he cultivates the awakening factors of investigation of dharmas, vigor, joy, tranquility, and concentration. He cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, tending toward the unconditioned. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of awakening.

"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the noble eightfold path. How should one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the noble eightfold path? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates right view, up to and including right concentration, making eight. This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the noble eightfold path. Likewise for the complete series of abandoning, liberating, transcending, uprooting, ceasing, comprehending, and directly knowing. One who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the noble eightfold path. How should one who wishes to directly know ignorance cultivate the noble eightfold path? When a Tathāgata appears in the world, Unattached, Perfectly and Fully Awakened, Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Trainer in the Way of the Dharma, Teacher of Gods and Humans, titled Buddha, World-Honored One, he abandons, up to and including the five hindrances which are defilements of mind and weakeners of wisdom. He cultivates right view, up to and including right concentration, making eight. This is called: one who wishes to directly know ignorance should cultivate the noble eightfold path.

# Postscript to the Later Edition of the Madhyamāgama

Long ago, the Dharma Master Shi [Daoan] brought forth in Chang'an the *Madhyamāgama*, the *Ekottarāgama*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Saṃgharakṣā*, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Vasumitra*, the *Tridharmakapravṛtti*, the *Dvayasaṃghāt Prātimokṣa*, and the *Prātimokṣanidāna*. These sūtras and vinaya texts altogether amounted to over a million words, yet they all deviated from the original and lost its meaning: the names did not match the substance, the language was vaguely arranged, and the phrasing and flavor were also off. This was truly because the translators were hasty and not yet skilled in the Jin language, which caused it to be so. Then Yan and Qin went to war with each other, and there was great chaos within the passes. Thereupon the skilled masters passed from the world, and so it was not possible to revise and correct these texts.

After several years had passed, when the area east of the passes had somewhat settled, the Ji Province monk Shi Fahe and the Kaśmīri śramaṇa Saṃghadeva gathered their disciples and together traveled to Luoyang. Over four or five years, through study and lecturing, they became thoroughly proficient, and Saṃghadeva gradually came to understand the Chinese language. Only then did they realize the errors of the earlier translations. Thereupon, Fahe, regretting the earlier mistakes, immediately had Saṃghadeva produce new editions of the *Abhidharma* and the *Vibhāṣā*. From that time onward, these sūtras and vinaya texts were gradually all revised and corrected. Only the *Madhyamāgama*, the *Saṃgharakṣā*, the *Vasumitra*, and the *Prātimokṣanidāna* had not yet been retranslated.

It happened that Saṃghadeva traveled onward to the capital, where he responded to the times and spread the Dharma, bestowing the gift of Dharma upon the Jiangzuo region. At that time, in the Jin state, the great elder, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, General of the Guard, Marquis of Dongting, the upāsaka Wang Yuanlin, constantly upheld and protected the True Dharma as his personal responsibility; he was the chief patron. For the purpose of producing the sūtra translations, he established a monastery and invited the virtuous monk Shi Huichi and over forty other śramaṇas devoted to doctrinal learning, providing them with everything they needed so that the four requisites were never lacking. He also specially invited the sūtra reciter Saṃgharakṣa, supporting him for several years. Then, in the first year of the Longan era of the Jin dynasty, the year dingyu [397 CE], on the tenth day of the eleventh month, within the boundaries of Jiankang County, Danyang Commandery, Yang Province, in that very monastery, they again produced this *Madhyamāgama*. They invited the Kaśmīri śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa to recite the Indic text, and invited Saṃghadeva to render the Indic into Jin Chinese. The Yu Province śramaṇa Daoci took down the text with his brush, and Li Bao of Wu and Kanghua together served as scribes. By the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month of the following year, the year wuxu [398 CE], the draft was completed. This *Madhyamāgama* contains altogether five recitation sections, a total of eighteen chapters, with two hundred and twenty-two sūtras, comprising a combined total of 514,825 characters, divided into sixty fascicles.

At that time, a great national crisis arose, and so the fair copy could not be made immediately. It was not until the fifth year [of the Longan era], the year xinchou [401 CE], that the final copy could be properly written, collated, and circulated. When comparing this translation with the earlier edition, there are great differences. Among these two hundred and twenty-two sūtras, if one were to weakly comply and conform to the old version, one would fear losing the sacred meaning. But if one followed the original text and established names, the categories would mostly differ from the old versions, going against established habits and not pleasing the sentiments of the assembly. For this reason, the translators could not act entirely on their own judgment, and at times altered the original to follow the old names.

Yet the five schools differ from one another; who can know which is correct? Daoci, in his foolish opinion, felt uneasy about this. Therefore, for all the revised names that deviated from the original, he excerpted them and noted them below, preserving both the new and old forms, compiling them separately into one fascicle appended to the table of contents, in order to show it to posterity. May future worthies thereby know the similarities and differences, and be able to make further inquiries. Should they perchance encounter an illumined one, a foreigner skilled in both Jin Chinese and the Indic languages, they may consult him on the gains and losses and amend the text to accord with correctness.
